Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 6):

We begin first with al-Fatiha. I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (1). Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds (2). The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Fatiha: 1–3], and so on to the end.

* First: Surah al-Fatiha was so named because the Noble Qur'an opens with it. It has been said that it is the first surah revealed in its entirety, and it has been said that the first surah revealed in its entirety was (Iqra' / "Read"), and that Allah completed it afterwards, and then the other surahs came. And Allah knows best.

The scholars said that this surah comprises the general meanings of the Qur'an: in tawhid (monotheism), in rulings (ahkam), in recompense, in the paths of the children of Adam, and other matters. For this reason it is called Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an). The umm (mother) is the reference point; whatever serves as the reference for a thing is called its umm. This surah has distinctive features that set it apart from others. Among them: it is a pillar (rukn) of the prayers, which are the best of the pillars of Islam after the two testimonies, so there is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book.

Among them also: it is a remedy (ruqyah). If it is recited over a sick person, he is healed by Allah's permission, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the one who recited it over a person stung by a scorpion (or snake): "And how did you know that it is a ruqyah?" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2276) and Muslim (2201/65), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]

Some people today have introduced an innovation (bid'ah) regarding this surah: they end their supplications with it and begin their sermons or occasions with it. This is an error. You find, for example, that a person supplicates, then supplicates, then supplicates, and then says, "Al-Fatiha!" What is "al-Fatiha"? From where did he get it? Or some people begin their sermons or occasions with it, and this too is an error, because acts of worship are founded on tawqif (divine stipulation, meaning they must be based on textual authority) and following (ittiba').

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. There is no need to discuss the basmalah in terms of its meaning or its grammatical analysis (i'rab), because it has been repeated before us many times. But the discussion is: is the basmalah a verse of al-Fatiha or not?

On this there is disagreement among the scholars.

Some of them say that it is a verse of al-Fatiha, and they recite it aloud in the audibly recited prayers, and they hold that the prayer is not valid except with the recitation of the basmalah, because it is part of al-Fatiha.

Others say that it is not part of al-Fatiha, and this is the correct view. The evidence for this is the textual report (nass) and the context (siyaq) of the surah.

As for the textual report: it has come in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted said: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves. When he says: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, He says: My servant has praised Me. When he says: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, He says: My servant has extolled Me. When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, He says: My servant has glorified Me. When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, He says: This is between Me and My servant in two halves. When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ – to the end – He says: This is for My servant, and for My servant is what he asks." [Narrated by Muslim (395) (38).] This is almost explicit that the basmalah is not part of al-Fatiha.

As for the context: al-Fatiha has seven verses by consensus. If you wish to distribute the seven verses over the subject matter of the surah, you will find that its midpoint is His saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, and this is the verse about which Allah said: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves." For ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ is one, ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is the second, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ is the third, and all of them belong to Allah. ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the fourth, meaning it is the middle now, and it has two parts: one part belongs to Allah and one part belongs to the servant. ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ belongs to the servant, ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ belongs to the servant, ﴿not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ belongs to the servant.

Then, in terms of the context of wording: if we said that the basmalah is a verse, it would follow that the seventh verse would be long, to the extent of how much? To the extent of two verses. It would have to be as long as two verses. Look: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ – how many lines is it for you? Two lines. ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is one line for me. ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ is less than one line, and ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ likewise, and ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ likewise. So how would there be proportion when some verses are less than a line and this one is two lines? Therefore the correct view, about which there is no doubt, is that the basmalah is not part of it, just as it (the basmalah) is not part of the rest of the surahs.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. (Al-hamd / praise) describes the one praised with perfection that is intrinsic (dhati), descriptive (wasfi), and active (fi'li). He is perfect in His essence, in His attributes, and in His actions. It is the description of the one praised with perfection together with love and exaltation. This qualification is necessary. The scholars said: mere description with perfection, without love or exaltation, is not called hamd; it is called madh (eulogy/flattery). For this reason it occurs from a person who does not love the one he praises but wants to gain something from him. You find some poets standing before the caliphs and bringing them great descriptions, not out of love for them but out of love for the wealth they give, or out of fear of them. But our praise of our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is with love and exaltation. Therefore the qualification is necessary in hamd: that it is the description of the one praised with perfection, together with love and exaltation.

And His saying ﴿Allah (lillah)﴾: Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This word is a proper name (alam) for our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and is not applied to anyone else. It is a proper name that other names follow, meaning that other names follow it. For this reason it always comes first, except in a few places, such as His saying: ﴿the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy (1), Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 1, 2]. Here this word follows what precedes it, but this is rare.

And His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾: the Lord (rabb) is the one in whom three attributes are combined: creation (khalq), sovereignty (mulk), and management (tadbir). He is the Creator, Mighty and Majestic; He is the Manager of all affairs; and He is the Owner of everything.

As for ﴿the worlds (al-'alamin)﴾: the scholars said that everything other than Allah is part of the 'alam (world), and they were described thus because they are a sign (alam) pointing to their Creator, glorified and exalted be He.

﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾: al-Rahman is an attribute of the divine name (lafz al-jalalah), and al-Rahim is another attribute. Al-Rahman is the one of vast mercy, and al-Rahim is the one whose mercy reaches (its objects). Al-Rahman describes Him, and al-Rahim describes His act. Had al-Rahim been mentioned alone and al-Rahman alone, both would include attribute and act. But when they are combined, al-Rahman is interpreted as referring to the attribute and al-Rahim as referring to the act: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. And mentioning ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ after mentioning lordship (rububiyyah) is evidence that His lordship, blessed and exalted be He, is founded upon mercy: mercy toward creation, vast mercy that reaches them.

﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatiha: 4]: "Master (malik)" is an attribute of "Lord." "The Day of Judgment (yawm al-din)" is the Day of Resurrection. Here "din" means what? Recompense (jaza'). It means recompense. That is, He, glorified and exalted be He, is the Owner of that day on which creatures will be recompensed, so there is no owner other than Him on that day.

If someone says: is He not the Owner of the Hereafter and of this world? The answer: yes, but the manifestation of His kingdom, His dominion, and His authority will occur on that day, because Allah, the Exalted, calls out: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. No one answers, so He says: ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. In this world, kings appear, and indeed there appear kings whose peoples believe that there is no owner except them. The communists, for example, do not believe that there is a lord of the heavens and the earth; they believe that life is wombs that push forth and earth that swallows, and that their lord is their president. Fine. So His dominion was specified with the Day of Judgment, because His kingdom and His dominion will be manifest on it.

In one of the seven canonical readings it is read ﴿Master (malik) of the Day of Judgment﴾ [the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamzah. See al-Taysir fi al-Qira'at al-Sab' (p. 27).] The malik (king) is more specific than the malik (owner): for the king is one with absolute authority, and no one is called king except one who has subjects beneath him. As for owner (malik with a short vowel, mālik), he does not have absolute authority, and he does not need to have subjects under him. For this reason you find a poor destitute man owns his cow, owns his sheep. But combining the two readings has great benefit: His sovereignty, glorified and exalted be He, is true sovereignty. For among creatures there is one who is a king but not an owner: he is called king in name only and has no share of management. And among people there is one who is an owner but not a king, like the common people. But the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is both Owner and King.

﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. "Na'budu" (we worship). If we asked for the grammatical analysis of ﴿iyyaka na'budu﴾, what would you answer?

* Student: It is a fronted direct object (maf'ul bihi muqaddam).

* The Shaykh: It is a fronted direct object. And why is it separated (iyyaka rather than attached as ka) when joining is possible? One could say "na'buduka" (we worship You). We say: if we joined it, an important matter would be lost, namely exclusivity (al-hasr). Here, since we fronted it for exclusivity, it had to be separated. If you said "ka na'budu," the sentence would not be correct and would not be Arabic. ﴿iyyaka﴾ means: not other than You. ﴿na'budu﴾ means: we humble ourselves to Him in the utmost humility. For this reason you find the believers – may Allah make me and you among them – placing the most noble parts of their bodies on the place where feet tread, out of humility before Allah, Mighty and Majestic. A person prostrates on the dust, his forehead fills with dirt, he prostrates on the place where feet tread – all of this in humility before Allah. And if a person said, "I will give you the whole world if you prostrate to me," the believer would never agree, because this humility is for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Worship includes carrying out everything Allah has commanded and abandoning everything Allah has forbidden, because whoever does not do so is not a worshipper. If he does not do what is commanded – meaning if he does not do what he was commanded – would he truly be a worshipper? Never. And if he does not abandon what is forbidden, he would not truly be a servant. The servant is one who agrees with the Worshipped One in His legislated intent. So worship entails that a person carry out everything he has been commanded to do and abandon everything he has been forbidden. But can this standing (of his) happen without Allah's help? No, it cannot. For this reason He said: ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾, meaning we ask for help only from You in worship. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, combines worship and seeking help, or reliance (tawakkul), in many places in the Noble Qur'an, because there is no standing in worship in its most perfect form except with Allah's help, entrusting oneself to Him, and relying upon Him.

﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6]. ﴿al-sirat / al-sirat﴾ has two readings: with sin [the reading of Qunbul from Ibn Kathir; the rest with pure sad. See al-Taysir (p. 27).] and with pure sad: ﴿al-sirat﴾ and ﴿al-sirat﴾. The intended meaning of "sirat" here is the path (tariq). The intended meaning of "guidance" (hidayah) here is guidance of direction (hidayat al-irshad) and guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq). So by your saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ you ask Allah for knowledge and action. For this reason it came transitive by itself to its object, not with the particle "ila" (to), which indicates the endpoint. Do you understand? So it includes guidance to the path, which is by knowledge, and guidance along the path, which is by action and success.

His saying ﴿the straight (al-mustaqim)﴾: the one without crookedness. This straight path that has no crookedness is clarified by Allah, the Exalted, in His saying in this verse: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7]. In this verse Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has specified the categories of people as three: those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour, those who have earned anger, and what? And those who are astray. Who are these? Those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour are those who knew the truth and acted upon it. Those who earned Allah's anger are those who knew the truth and did not act upon it. Those who are astray are those who acted without knowledge, ignorant, who want the truth and want worship, but are ignorant; they worshipped Allah without knowledge. Observe how He placed "those who earned anger" before "those who are astray," because their deviation from the path of those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour is more severe, since they deviated knowingly. One who deviates knowingly is more arrogant, more proud, and deserving of greater punishment than one who deviates without knowledge. Both groups are astray, because they are not upon guidance from Allah.

In His saying ﴿upon whom You have bestowed favour (an'amta 'alayhim)﴾ there are also two readings: ﴿'alayhim﴾ with a damma on the ha' and with a kasra. That is, ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned Your anger ('alayhum), nor of those who are astray﴾ is a seven-reading variant [recitation of Hamzah with a damma on the ha'; the rest with a kasra. See al-Taysir (p. 27).]. But I repeat what I said earlier: readings that are not in the mushaf should not be recited before the common people, for two reasons, indeed three reasons. The first reason: when common people see this magnificent Qur'an, which has filled their hearts with exaltation, if they see it one way and then another way, its standing will certainly fall in their eyes, because they are laypeople who do not distinguish. So the Qur'an should remain respected and not be altered in anything. Second: the reciter will be accused of not knowing. What does the layman know? If a person came and recited to him, for example, a reading other than that in his mushaf, he would pounce on him and perhaps strike him, perhaps expel him from the mosque. The Qur'an is extremely respected among the common people. It is with us, praise be to Allah, but if you bring what the layman does not know, woe to you from him. And this is a corruption: people will belittle you and say, "This one has no good in him; he does not know and does not recite." Yes. Now, if you recite before the layman, "﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour ('alayhum)﴾," he will say, "This one doesn't know; he is putting a damma on the (...) he says 'alayhum.' Why didn't he say 'alayhim' with a kasra?" The third corruption: when you recite before the laypeople, and the layman thinks well of you and says, "He only recited with knowledge," then he tries to imitate you another time and may err, and then he recites the Qur'an neither according to the mushaf nor according to the reciter who recited it to him. This is a corruption. For this reason 'Ali said: "Speak to people in what they know. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?" [al-Bukhari (127).]

And Ibn Mas'ud said: "You will not speak to a people a saying that their minds do not reach except that it will become a trial for some of them." [Muslim, in the Introduction (5).] What did 'Umar ibn al-Khattab do with Hisham ibn al-Hakam when he recited in Surat al-Furqan with a reading 'Umar had not heard? Yes, he seized him, threw him down, disputed with him, and denied his recitation, until they both came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and 'Umar said... He (the Prophet) said: "Recite." He recited, and he said: "It was revealed thus." He said to 'Umar: "Recite." He recited, and he said: "It was revealed thus." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2419) and Muslim (818/271), from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.] Because the Qur'an was first revealed in seven ahruf (modes/dialects). So if 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did what he did to a companion, what then about a layman who hears you reciting something other than your recitation? Yes? Woe to him from you, and praise be to Allah. Since the scholars agree that a person is not obliged to recite every reading, and that if he limits himself to one of the readings there is no harm, this calms the trial and its causes. The surah contains great benefits, and Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, explained it in Madarij al-Salikin with an explanation you will not find in any other book, a magnificent explanation. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾: the affirmation of Allah's complete praise, and the affirmation that He deserves it and is exclusively entitled to it. Completeness derives from the form of (al) in ﴿al-hamd﴾, and entitlement and exclusivity derive from the lam in ﴿lillah﴾.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the mention of Allah's attribute of divinity (uluhiyyah) before His attribute of lordship (rububiyyah). He did not say "to the Lord of the worlds," but said ﴿lillah rabb al-'alamin﴾. This is either because "Allah" is the specific proper name that all other names follow, or because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, placed divinity before the mention of His lordship, since the people to whom the messengers came denied divinity alone.

* Among its benefits is the comprehensiveness of Allah's lordship (rububiyyah) over all the worlds, as shown by His words ﴿the worlds﴾. We have already explained in the tafsir (exegesis) that by "the worlds" (al-'alam) is meant everything other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic: all creatures, both those that grow and those that do not, and both the rational and the non-rational.

﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. Among the benefits of this verse: affirming these two noble names, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, and affirming what they contain of mercy as an attribute (sifah) and mercy as an act (fi'l).

* Among its benefits: Allah's lordship, Mighty and Majestic, is founded upon mercy. When He said ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, it is as if a questioner asked: what kind of lordship is this? Is it a lordship of seizing and vengeance, or a lordship of mercy and bounty? So He said ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

* Among the benefits of the following verse, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ (or ﴿King﴾): affirming the sovereignty of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His dominion over the Day of Judgment. It was specified for that day because, as we mentioned in the tafsir, on that day all ownerships and all kings will vanish as well.

* Among its benefits: affirming the resurrection (al-ba'th), by His words ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾.

﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. Among its benefits: sincerity of worship to Allah, in His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾. The aspect of sincerity here is the fronting of the object (taqdim al-ma'mul).

* Among its benefits also: sincerity of seeking help from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by His words ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾, where the object is fronted.

If someone says: how can it be said that seeking help is to be sincerely directed to Allah, when Allah's words ﴿Cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2] affirm seeking assistance from other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic?

We say: seeking help is of two kinds. One is seeking help by entrusting (isti'anat tafwid), meaning that you rely upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and disown your own power and strength. This is exclusive to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The other is seeking help in the sense of partnership in what you want to accomplish. This is not worship, and for this reason Allah, Exalted, said ﴿Cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾.

If someone says: is seeking help from a created being permissible in all circumstances? We say: No. Seeking help from a created being is permissible only where the one sought for help is able to provide it. As for when he is not able, it is not permissible to seek his help. So if anyone seeks help from a grave, this is forbidden, rather it is shirk (association with Allah), because the occupant of the grave cannot even help himself, so how could he benefit you? And if someone seeks help from an absent person in a matter that he is not able to do, such as believing that a saint (wali) who is in the east of the world will assist him in his task in his own country, this is also shirk, major shirk, because he is not able to help you while he is there.

If someone says: is seeking help from a created being permissible? We say: the better course is not to do so. A person is commanded to help his brother, but it is not proper for him to ask for help from others, because seeking help from another is a form of blameworthy begging. But if you see your brother in need of assistance, you are commanded to help him. And if you do ask him for help, it is not forbidden; it is not forbidden for you. It is only leaving what is better, unless you know that your asking him is something that pleases him and gladdens his heart. In that case, if you ask him for help, you are doing him a kindness, and this does not count as blameworthy begging. As the Prophet ﷺ did when he entered his house and found the cooking pot on the fire with meat in it. When the food was brought to him, he said: "Did I not see the pot on the fire?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, but this is meat that was given as charity to Barirah." He said: "It is a charity for her, and it is a gift for us from it." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5279) and Muslim (1504/14), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.] Consider Barirah in that situation: would this matter be burdensome for her? Not at all; rather she would be pleased and rejoice in it. So, for example, if you ask your brother for help with some need while you know that he is pleased and rejoices in this, then your asking him is a kindness to him. But if you ask someone who sees your asking him as heavier upon him than Mount Uhud, would you ask him? No, because that puts him in an embarrassing position, and it also humiliates you.

Among the benefits of His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾: after seeking help for worship, a person turns to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, asking Him to guide him to the straight path. This is because worship necessarily requires sincerity, indicated by ﴿You alone we worship﴾; and seeking help to be strengthened in worship, by His words ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾; and following the Shari'ah, in His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. Thus these three verses comprise the whole religion: worship, which is the first; seeking help, which is the second; and following, which is the third. For the straight path is the Shari'ah that the messengers brought, and for us it is the Shari'ah that was brought by whom? Our Prophet Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family. This means that we must follow the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the eloquence of the Qur'an, in that the preposition has been omitted from ﴿Guide us﴾. That is, it did not say "guide us to" (ihdina ila), but said ﴿Guide us the path﴾. The benefit of this is that the request for guidance includes both the guidance of knowledge, which is indication, and the guidance of success (tawfiq). For guidance is divided into two kinds: the guidance of knowledge and instruction, and the guidance of success and action. The first contains nothing but mere indication, and Allah, glorified and exalted, has guided every person in this sense. The second contains success in being guided and in following the Shari'ah, and some people are deprived of this. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. ﴿We guided them﴾ means: We made the truth clear to them and pointed them to it, but they were not granted success in it. Therefore the preposition "ila" (to) was omitted, so that the request for guidance in this verse includes both the guidance of knowledge and instruction, and the guidance of success and following.

* Among its benefits: the path is divided into two kinds, straight and crooked. Whatever agrees with the truth is straight. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am 153]. And whatever opposes it is crooked.

Then He said: ﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾, and so on to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: mention of the detail after the general statement. ﴿Guide us to the straight path (6), the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾. This is because detail after generality has a benefit, for when speech comes to the soul in a general form, the soul waits eagerly for what? For detail and explanation. So He said ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾. Then there is also in it a second benefit, which is the clarification that those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor are upon the straight path.

* Among its benefits, as well as what follows it: the division of people into three categories. One category is those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor; another category is those with whom Allah is angry; and a third category is those who are astray. Those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor, as has already been mentioned, are those who knew the truth and followed it. As for those with whom Allah is angry, they are those who knew the truth and opposed it. As for those who are astray, they are those who were ignorant of the truth. The causes of going astray and deviating from the straight path are either ignorance or obstinacy. So who was it whose deviation was caused by obstinacy? They are those with whom Allah is angry, and foremost among them are the Jews. The others, whose deviation was caused by ignorance, are everyone who does not know the truth, and foremost among them are the Christians. This refers to their state before the mission (ba'thah), I mean the Christians. But after the mission, they knew the truth, and so they and the Jews became equal: all of them are those with whom Allah is angry, indeed they are worse, because they believe in naskh (abrogation), I mean the Christians. For this reason they believe that the Shari'ah of Jesus abrogates the Shari'ah of Moses. The Jews do not believe in that, so they are on a false path. But the Christians were inconsistent: they believed in the abrogation of Shari'ahs regarding Jesus in relation to the Shari'ah of Moses, and they did not believe in the abrogation of Shari'ahs regarding the Shari'ah of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, in relation to the Shari'ah of Jesus. Therefore they were contradictory, and their way was more corrupt than the way of the Jews.

In any case, this surah is great, and neither I nor anyone else can encompass its great meanings, but this is a drop from an ocean.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Alif, Lam, Mim (1). That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for those who are mindful of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 1–2].

This surah is called Surat al-Baqarah because the cow (al-baqarah) is mentioned in it. Know that naming is based on even the slightest connection. That is why you find some surahs that contain much discussion of a particular topic yet are not named after it, while others contain little and are named after that little. The naming of surahs is partly tawqifi (based on revelation or the Prophet's designation) and partly ijtihadi (based on scholarly reasoning). The Prophet ﷺ named Surat al-Baqarah and Surat Al 'Imran and many others, and in some of them the naming is tawqifi.

As for the basmalah, we have already discussed it, and we clarified that it is an independent verse that is recited at the beginning of every surah except Surat Bara'ah (at-Tawbah).

Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1). That is the Book.﴾ The word "Alif Lam Mim" is composed of three letters of the alphabet: alif, lam, and mim. So what is the meaning of these letters from which this word is composed? Many exegetes say: Allah knows best what He intended. This is without doubt a form of good manners toward Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and a restraint from what a person does not know. Some of them made them symbols for specific things, either from the names of Allah or from other events, but this has no basis in knowledge. Others said they are alphabetic letters with no meaning, and that we do not know any meaning for them according to the requirements of the Arabic language. The noble Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic language, and on this basis it is our right to say that they have no meaning, on the premise that the Qur'an is Arabic and that such combined letters have no meaning. This is the view of Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, the leading authority among the Successors in tafsir, and it is the view that the evidences support. But the question remains: why did Allah bring them if they have no meaning according to Arabic? We say: as an indication that this noble Qur'an, which has rendered you incapable, O Arabs, did not come with anything new from your speech. Rather, it came with what you arrange and build your speech from. Your speech consists of letters: alif, ba, ta, tha, and so on to the end. Did the Qur'an bring anything additional? No. Yet you were unable to compose the like of it. It rendered you incapable.

Allah, Exalted, has mentioned the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an in four ways: inimitability by the whole Qur'an, inimitability by ten surahs from it, inimitability by a single surah from it, and inimitability by its like. All of these are repeated in the Qur'an. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾. He, Exalted, also said: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented﴾ [Hud 13]. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce its like"﴾ [al-Isra' 88]. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Then let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful﴾ [at-Tur 34]. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has challenged creation to produce the like of this Qur'an, even a single verse, just as He challenged them to create the least of His creatures. He said: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ [al-Hajj 73].

So the preponderant view on this matter, namely the alphabetic letters with which some surahs begin, is that they have no meaning, but they have a purpose. That purpose is that this noble Qur'an did not come with anything new in the letters it uses. Rather, it came with the same letters from which you compose your speech, and yet it rendered you incapable. For this reason, you find that in surahs that begin with these alphabetic letters, mention of the Qur'an or something that can only come through revelation follows them. For example: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1). That is the Book﴾, where mention of the Qur'an follows. And ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1). The Romans have been defeated (2) in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome (3)﴾ [ar-Rum 1–3]. Here mention of the Qur'an does not appear, but what follows is something that could not be known except through revelation.

﴿That is the Book; there is no doubt in it﴾: "That" (dhalika) may be taken with "the Book" as its predicate, or we may take it as an adjective or as an appositive. If we take "the Book" as the predicate of "that," then His words "there is no doubt in it" become a new independent sentence. If we take it as an appositive or as an explanatory apposition, then "there is no doubt in it" becomes what? It becomes the predicate of the demonstrative. The Book indicated is the Qur'an. It is called a book because it is written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), and written in the scrolls held by the angels: ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder (11), so whoever wills may remember it (12), in honored scrolls (13), elevated and purified (14), in the hands of scribes (15)﴾ [‘Abasa 11–15]. And it is written in the copies of the Qur'an that are in our hands.

﴿There is no doubt in it﴾: "no doubt" (la rayb). What is the meaning of "rayb"? It means doubt. This is how most scholars explained it, that rayb is doubt. But Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him [see Majmu' al-Fatawa (20/423)], has an opinion regarding such synonymous words. He says: there is no word in the Arabic language that is exactly synonymous with another in every respect. There must be a difference between them. So rayb here is not identical to the doubt that stands opposite it in every respect, because rayb, he says, is doubt accompanied by anxiety and suspicion. It is therefore more specific than doubt. But there is no harm in explaining the word by what is close to it, especially when the addressee does not perceive the difference.

His words ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾: "la" here is the negation of the genus, so it includes even the least doubt, meaning that there is not even the slightest doubt in it.

His words ﴿guidance for those who are mindful of Allah﴾: "guidance" (huda) here means indication. The Qur'an itself does not grant guidance in the sense of success (tawfiq), but it guides in the sense of indication: ﴿guidance for those who are mindful of Allah﴾. In another verse: ﴿The month of Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was revealed as guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah 185]. What is the difference between this and that? We say: as for its being guidance for mankind, this is the basic principle, that the Qur'an can be a means of guidance for every person. As for attributing guidance to the mindful, this is because the mindful are the ones who benefited from it, so it became guidance for them. And who are the mindful? Those who carry out Allah's commands and abstain from Allah's prohibitions.

In this noble verse there is an explanation that the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, consists of letters, in contrast to those who say that His speech is the meaning subsisting in the soul. We will explain this. The principles of disagreement regarding this noble Qur'an, or regarding the speech of Allah in general, are these:

First: whoever says that Allah's speech is the meaning subsisting in His essence, and that what is transmitted of His speech or heard is merely an expression of it and not the speech of Allah itself, but is created.

Second: whoever says that Allah, Exalted, does not speak, and that His speech is created like all His other creatures.

And some say that Allah speaks with letters and sound, and that His speech is not merely the meaning, but both the wording and the meaning. The second position mentioned above is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah, while this last position is the doctrine of Ahl as-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, and their doctrine is the truth, because the evidences indicate it. Allah, Exalted, said concerning Moses: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mountain and brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam 52]. When he was far away, He said ﴿We called him﴾, because calling is for the distant. When he was near, meaning when Allah brought him close, He said ﴿and brought him near as a confidant﴾, that is, with a voice that was not a call. And in the authentic hadith: "Allah will call out on the Day of Resurrection, saying: 'O Adam!' He will say: 'At Your service and Your pleasure!' Then He will call out with a voice: 'Allah commands you to bring forth from your offspring a group for the Fire'" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3348) and Muslim (222/379), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. This is a matter that no one doubts. And if the disagreement had not arisen over it, we would not be discussing it, but it has arisen, so it is necessary to clarify the truth. The Mu'tazilah say: the Qur'an is a created thing among created things, sounds that Allah creates and letters that are written, so it is like all other creatures. Without doubt, if we say this, we nullify the command and the prohibition, because a command would then be a sound heard in this manner. Say: a sound heard in this manner, meaning as if it were an echo. Do you now see the sun, the moon, and the mountains as created in this manner? They say: this is a sound created in this manner, like the sound of thunder.

The Ash'aris say: speech is a meaning subsisting in the self, but God created sounds. So if we say that commands and prohibitions are created, then command and prohibition are nullified; because "qul" (say) is a word God created in the form of "qul," and it does not convey a command, and "wa la taqrabu al-zina" (Qur'an 17:32) — God created letters in this shape, and so they convey no prohibition. For this reason, whoever said that those who hold the Qur'an to be created, whether they make it an expression of the speech of God or hold it to be the speech of God, have nullified commands, prohibitions and all the sharia, spoke truly.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. "Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing. Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them. And who believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful." "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. Allah has sealed over their hearts and over their hearing, and over their eyes is a veil..." [Al-Baqarah 1-7]
* Shaykh: "And over their hearing," stop.
* Student: "Allah has sealed over their hearts and over their hearing, and over their eyes is a veil, and for them is a great punishment." [Al-Baqarah 7]
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, said: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. "Alif, Lam, Mim." The basmalah we have already discussed, so there is no need to repeat it. As for His saying "Alif, Lam, Mim," these are the letters of the alphabet, and we have already discussed them, so there is no need for debate or repetition.

"That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing." As for His saying "That is the Book; there is no doubt in it": if we make "al-Kitab" a description of "dhalika," then "la rayba fihi" is the predicate. If we make "al-Kitab" the predicate, then "dhalika al-Kitab" forms a resumptive sentence, whose place is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while it is free of doubt. As for His saying "la rayba fihi," that means "no doubt." Explaining "rayb" as "doubt" is only for approximation. The negation of doubt here is doubt concerning its authenticity, meaning there is no doubt that it is authentic and that it is from Allah.

Second: there is no doubt concerning what it contains of reports. Every report in the Noble Qur'an is, for every believer, free of doubt; rather, it is established truth. As for His saying "fihi," it has been said that it is the predicate of the negating "la," and it has been said that it is a fronted predicate for His saying "huda," but the better view is that it is the predicate of the negating "la." As for His saying "huda lil-muttaqin," it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the Book, meaning: while it is "guidance for the God-fearing." It is guidance for the God-fearing in two respects: the cognitive and the practical. As for the cognitive, it is guidance of indication, for the source of knowledge is this Noble Qur'an; it is what guides you to the truth and points you to it, and guides you to falsehood, clarifies it for you and warns you against it. As for the second, it is guidance of action, for the God-fearing are those who have been guided by it in action.

As for His saying "lil-muttaqin," it is an active participle, and its verb is "ittaqa." The meaning of "ittaqa" is: to take a shield against the punishment of Allah, and this is achieved only by performing the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. Accordingly, the most comprehensive definition of taqwa is that it is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by performing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions; it is performing commands and avoiding prohibitions.

Know that taqwa is sometimes paired with birr (righteousness), as in His saying: "Cooperate in righteousness and piety" [al-Ma'idah 2]; and sometimes it is paired with faith, as in this verse: "for the God-fearing. Who believe in the unseen." And sometimes it is mentioned alone; when mentioned alone it encompasses the whole religion, for the whole religion is a shield against the punishment of Allah. When it is paired with birr, birr becomes the performing of commands and taqwa becomes the abandoning of prohibitions. It is explained in every context according to that context.

Then He said: "Who believe in the unseen." This is one of the attributes of the God-fearing: that they believe in the unseen, meaning they affirm it and acknowledge it. What is meant by the unseen here is what is hidden from people of what Allah and His Messenger have informed about, whether it concerns the attributes of Allah, or what concerns the servants of Allah in the past, or what concerns the servants of Allah in the future. They believe in it: they believe in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His names and attributes, in His divinity and lordship. They also believe in what Allah has informed about the earlier nations, and in what Allah has informed about the future, from the knowledge of the Hereafter, for all of this falls under His saying "who believe in the unseen." "And establish prayer." Yes, does belief in the unseen include belief in the angels? Yes, for they are a world of the unseen.

"And establish prayer," meaning they bring it forth upright, without crookedness, and this is by fulfilling its obligations and avoiding what is prohibited in it. His saying "as-Salah" includes obligatory and voluntary prayer, for here it is a generic noun encompassing all prayer.

"And spend out of what We have provided for them." "Mimma razaqnahum" is a prepositional phrase attached to "yunfiqun." The meaning: they spend out of what We have given them. The first thing included in this is zakah: the spending of zakah, for they perform it. Accordingly, this verse is of the same kind as the other verses in which "yuqimuna al-salah wa yu'tuna al-zakah" appears [al-Ma'idah 55].

"Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful." "Those" refers to the God-fearing who have been guided by the Qur'an. "Upon guidance from their Lord": "upon guidance" means upon a straight path from Allah, Mighty and Majestic; Allah has guided them in knowledge and guided them in action.

"And those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain." This is also among their attributes.

"And those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain." This verse is conjoined to what preceded it by conjunction of attributes, not of persons. The original principle regarding conjoined items is that they be persons, but here the conjunction is of attributes, because those who believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you are the same as those who believe in the unseen and establish prayer. The conjunction of attributes with one another is nothing strange, neither in the Qur'an nor in the language of the Arabs. Allah the Exalted said: "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who decreed and guided, and who brought out the pasture, and made it dark brown stubble" [al-A'la 1-5]. This is a conjunction of attributes, some with others.

"And those who believe in what has been revealed to you," which is the Qur'an; and perhaps we may say it is more comprehensive than the Qur'an, based on His saying: "And Allah has sent down to you the Book and the wisdom" [al-Nisa 113]. So it is the Qur'an and the Sunnah. "And what was revealed before you": the earlier scriptures, such as the Torah and the Gospel.

"And of the Hereafter they are certain." "Bil-akhirah" is a prepositional phrase attached to "yuqinun." The word "hum" was used for emphasis; were it omitted and it said "wa bil-akhirah yuqinun," the sentence would be sound, but for emphasis the pronoun "hum" was brought. "Yuqinun" means they believe with a belief free of doubt, to which no possibility can reach, for certainty (yaqin) is definitive knowledge. This is among their attributes.

"Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful." "Those" refers to the God-fearing who believe in what has preceded. "Upon guidance from their Lord" means upon a path from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He said "from their Lord" to indicate that Allah's favor upon them in this is a special favor; it is a special lordship for them, not the general lordship.

"And those are the successful": He repeated "those" to draw attention to their merit and the loftiness of their rank. As for His saying "hum al-mufliḥun," the scholars say that "hum" here is a pronoun of separation (damir fasl), a pronoun that has no place in i'rab, for it was brought only for emphasis. They said its benefits are three: the first is emphasis; the second is restriction (hasr), which is specification; the third is indicating that what follows is a predicate and not an attribute. This is why it is called a pronoun of separation. That is, success is restricted to them. Success (falah) is attaining what is sought and being saved from what is feared.

Returning to these verses, we find that Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned in them what indicates several benefits. First: the demonstration that this Noble Qur'an is composed of the letters with which the Arabs speak; this is indicated by His saying "Alif, Lam, Mim," as we have made clear in the commentary.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the exalted rank of the Qur'an, indicated by His saying "dhalika al-Kitab." He pointed to it with the demonstrative for the distant although it is near, for it is before us, as an indication of its high rank. And by Allah, it is the highest of speech: "The best speech is the Book of Allah," as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to proclaim every Friday from the pulpit, saying: "Indeed the best speech is the Book of Allah" [Muslim (867/43), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah].

* Among the benefits of these verses: it is not permissible for anyone to doubt this Qur'an, and the Qur'an is not a place for doubt. The first meaning: it is not permissible for anyone to doubt this Qur'an, on the assumption that the negation here means a prohibition? 
* Student: The prohibition.
* Shaykh: The prohibition. The second: that this Qur'an is not a place for doubt, on the assumption that "la" is a negating particle. We have already explained to you in the commentary that His saying "la rayba fihi" has two views among the scholars. The first view: the negation here means prohibition, and the meaning is: do not doubt in it. The second view: the negation here is on its own basis, and the meaning is that the Qur'an has no doubt in it and no problem in it. Is it clear, O people? So among the benefits is the prohibition of doubting the Qur'an and the demonstration that it is not a place for doubt.

* Among the benefits of these verses: that the Qur'an is guidance for the God-fearing, clearly stated in the verse "guidance for the God-fearing." It follows from this benefit that when you see that Allah has bestowed upon you the understanding of His Book and acting upon it, know that you are of whom? Of whom, O people? Of the God-fearing, for Allah said: "guidance for the God-fearing." So if you see in yourself that Allah has bestowed upon you knowledge and action with His Book, rejoice, for you are among the God-fearing.

It also branches from this another benefit: if you see heedlessness and failure to benefit from the Qur'an, beware, for this indicates a deficiency in your taqwa; for if your taqwa were complete, this Qur'an would be guidance for you. It also follows from this: the encouragement toward taqwa, and that it is a means of being guided by the Qur'an, and that the more you fear Allah, the more you benefit from the Qur'an and are guided by it.

* Among the benefits of these verses: the excellence of belief in the unseen. If you wish, say: faith in its reality is belief in the unseen, by His saying "who believe in the unseen," for belief in the witnessed is not faith. Belief in what is seen and perceived is not faith, yes indeed. The evidence: Pharaoh denied the Lord of the worlds and said to Moses: "What is the Lord of the worlds?" And when drowning overtook him he said: "I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe" [Yunus 90]. There is in this all the humiliation there is. Previously he used to kill the Children of Israel if they did not agree with him; now he has become their follower. He did not say "I believe in Allah" or "in the Lord of the worlds"; he said "I believe in He in whom the Children of Israel believe." He used the relative pronoun, which indicates exaltation and glorification, then said "in whom the Children of Israel believe," to say: I am a follower of them, believing in what they believe; and this is the utmost of humiliation. Pay attention to this point.

Now, was the faith that Pharaoh expressed at that moment beneficial faith? No, and for this it was said to him: "Now?" It is of no benefit: "Now, and you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters" [Yunus 91]. And this is true.

Consider belief in a witnessed thing. Consider this matter: you say, "This is a door." Do I believe that this is a door? Yes? Is this faith?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: If you said, "I believe that there are men around me seeking knowledge," is this faith? Is it faith?
* Students: It is not faith.
* Shaykh: As for "there are men around me," true, it is not faith, because it is witnessed. As for "seeking knowledge," it is faith, because it is based on my assumption about what they intend by seeking knowledge, and whether they are eager or merely present in body without heart, or the like. In any case, make it, if Allah wills, faith; but do not make it faith in the unseen; make it faith in the perceptible.

Among the benefits of these noble verses: the excellence of prayer, and that it is the highest of physical acts. For this reason it always comes after faith, by His saying "and establish prayer."

* Among its benefits: the encouragement to establish prayer, and that a person performs it completely in the manner that pleases the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, who prescribed it for His servants. As for praying a prayer without spirit, or a prayer that is formally insufficient or the like, this is not establishing prayer. Have you understood? That is, a person may come and pray in the most perfect outward manner: he stands upright, with humility in the head, bows and is calm, prostrates and is calm, but his heart is in one valley and his body in another. Has he established it? No, he has not established it. It is husk, inflated husk with no kernel inside, because of the lack of khushu'. For this reason you will find many people who leave the prayer without sensing that they have hated evil or hated indecency, though Allah says: "Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing" [al-'Ankabut 45]. But they do not sense this, because it is a husk of prayer. We ask Allah to help us and you to have khushu' in prayer, for this is now the hardest thing we strive against: the matter of outward form, that a person performs prayer with outward calm, is easy; but speaking of the kernel, which is khushu', is difficult. Yet try again and again; whenever Satan pulls your heart, return it; be assured that from the moment you draw it to prayer and return it to prayer, it will return, you will find a tug-of-war, but persist, and in the end, if Allah wills, it will pass. Now, among establishing prayer is tranquility in it, which some people have lost, especially in the two pillars between bowing and prostration, and between the two prostrations. These two pillars are wronged by some people: you find him saying, "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah, Allahu akbar," and you ask, "What did you say? Did you become calm?" He did not become calm; for such a person there is no prayer, even if he prays until the Day of Judgment, because the Messenger said to the man: "Then raise [your head from bowing] until you stand upright" [Bukhari 757; Muslim 397/45, from Abu Hurayrah], and in another wording "until you are calm standing" [Ibn Majah 1060; Ahmad 18997]. Tranquility is necessary. In any case, there is no need to go through everything that some people neglect in prayer, for it is well known.

Among the benefits of these noble verses: the excellence of spending in the way of Allah, the excellence of spending wealth, by His saying "and spend out of what We have provided for them."

* Among its benefits: that the charity of a usurper is invalid. From where is it taken? "Out of what We have provided for them," for the usurper does not own the wealth he gives in charity, so his charity is not accepted.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 1–9 (part 4 of 6):**

* Among its benefits is the indication that stinginess is blameworthy, based on His words: ﴿from what We have provided them﴾. Did you acquire the wealth through your own earning? No. The One who gave you the wealth is Allah. ﴿From what We have provided them﴾: He did not say "from what they earned." Even what a person earns is by Allah's facilitation. How many people have knocked on every door of provision but were not granted success? So among the benefits of this noble verse is the virtue of spending. Here, however, He mentioned the source of the spending without specifying what it is spent on. We say: yes, but it has been specified in many other verses: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents...﴾ [Al-Baqarah 215]. The answer: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, meaning, what thing do they spend? ﴿Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents...﴾. It is as if He said: ask about what you spend on. Yes, ask on what you spend. ﴿Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents...﴾. ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, about what? Say it, you all. 
* The students: (...)
* The Shaykh: And what do they spend? What do they spend? So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents...﴾, thus specifying what it is spent on, because that is the important part. Many people may give away half of their wealth but in the way of the tyrant (ṭāghūt), whereas the beneficial thing is in the way of Allah, that is, in what pleases Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But it may be said that His words ﴿Whatever good you spend﴾ may indicate the source of the spending, which is that the spending should be good. In any case, here in this verse Allah left the spending unspecified: ﴿from what We have provided them they spend﴾, so it is general. It is said that this general statement is clarified in other texts of the Quran and the Sunnah.
