But when they confused people and said that Muhammad is an Arab sent to the Arabs, and cited the like of His saying ﴿It is He who has sent to the unlettered a messenger﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2], they created confusion and confused people.
He said: ﴿And conceal the truth while you know it﴾ [al-Baqarah 42]. Here, is the waw coordinating or the waw of accompaniment (wāw al-ma'iyyah)? It carries two meanings: the meaning may be, "Do not mix truth with falsehood, and do not conceal the truth while you know it," or it may be, "Do not mix truth with falsehood together with concealing the truth." But on this reading a difficulty remains: His saying ﴿do not mix truth with falsehood﴾ implies that they mention truth and falsehood. We say: yes, although they mention truth and falsehood, in reality they conceal the truth, because by mixing it with falsehood it remains hidden. So the waw may remain either coordinating or of accompaniment.
﴿And conceal the truth while you know it﴾: that is, you know that the truth lies in what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought, and that you are falsifiers in concealing it.
﴿And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah 43]. ﴿Establish prayer﴾ is general for all prayers, obligatory and voluntary. Giving zakah means giving it to those entitled to it, and it is the wealth that Allah the Exalted has made obligatory, indeed the portion or share that Allah the Exalted has made obligatory in zakatable wealth.
﴿And bow with those who bow﴾. Who are those who bow? They are this Ummah. That is, pray with them, along with their prayer, and adhere to their rulings and laws.
* In these verses there are benefits, among them: Allah the Exalted directs the address to the one addressed, either because he is more attentive than others, or because he is more deserving of complying. Here He directed it to them because they are more deserving of complying, since they have knowledge of the Prophet's ﷺ message and that it is true, which the Arabs do not have. The Arabs were ignorant and had no knowledge.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: reminding the servant of Allah's favours upon him, from His saying ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾.
Is this one of the means of calling to Allah, meaning that when we wish to call a person we remind him of the favours? The answer: yes, we remind him of the favours, because this is more conducive to his accepting the truth, and more conducive to his loving Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and love of Allah moves the servant to perform obedience to Him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah has the favour in His bestowing these things upon them, from His saying ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾. I mentioned to you a little while ago that He mentioned it with a verb because it is renewed and occurring, not something these people earned.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever fulfils his covenant with Allah, Allah fulfils His covenant to him, from His saying ﴿Fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant﴾. As you know, ﴿I will fulfil﴾ is the answer to the imperative in His saying ﴿Fulfil My covenant﴾, and for this reason it came in the jussive with the weak letter dropped.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever breaks the covenant of Allah is punished by being deprived of what Allah has ordained for the fulfilment of the covenant. This is because the explicit statement of the verse is that whoever fulfils to Allah, Allah fulfils to him, so the implicit meaning (mafhum) is that whoever does not fulfil will be punished and will not be given what he was promised.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to fulfil vows, because the one who vows has made a covenant with Allah, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and surely be among the righteous"﴾ [al-Tawbah 75]. So the one who vows has made a covenant with Allah the Exalted.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of making fear sincerely for Allah alone, from His saying ﴿iyyaya fa-irhabun﴾.
* Among its benefits: fear (ruhbah) is an act of worship, because Allah the Exalted commanded it and commanded that it be sincere.
If someone asks: is it permissible, or does it contradict monotheism, for a person to fear a beast or an enemy? No, this does not contradict monotheism. For this reason it occurred from the messengers: when the guests came to Ibrahim and did not eat, he "felt a fear of them" (awjasa minhum khīfah); and Musa, peace be upon him, when the sorcerers threw their ropes and staffs, he likewise "felt a fear within himself" (awjasa minhu khīfah). Likewise, natural fear, of what human nature requires, is not blameworthy. If we said to a person, "If you fear anyone other than Allah with a natural fear, you are a polytheist," this would be imposing what is beyond one's capacity, because a person's fear is a natural, instinctive fear; every person fears what he expects harm from.
If someone asks: if this fear prevents him from an obligation, is he forbidden from it or not? We say: yes, he is forbidden from it, because he is able to perform the obligation, unless the Sharia has excused him from it in this situation. If the Sharia has excused him in this situation, there is no blame on him for this fear. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is only Satan who frightens his allies, so do not fear them but fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Ali 'Imran 175]. However, if the Sharia gives you a dispensation to oppose what Allah commanded in this situation, there is no harm. For this reason, if a person wants to pray an obligatory prayer while near a short wall and fears that if he stands he will be exposed to the enemy, does he pray sitting? Yes, he prays sitting, because Allah the Exalted has excused him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun 16]. If the enemy is more than twice the number of the Muslims, are they obliged to endure them, or may they flee? They may flee. The main point is that natural fear does not make a person blameworthy unless it involves abandoning what Allah has obligated; if it does not involve that, he is not blamed for it.
* Among the benefits of the verse that follows: the Children of Israel are obliged to believe in the Qur'an that Muhammad, peace be upon him, brought, from His saying ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾.
* Among its benefits: the disbeliever is addressed with Islam, and this is agreed upon. But is he addressed with the branches of Islam? There is detail: if by being addressed you mean that he is commanded to perform them, then no, because he must first become Muslim and then perform them. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "Let the first thing you call them to be the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. If they respond to that, inform them that Allah has enjoined upon them five prayers in every day and night" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1395) and Muslim (19/31), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. Well, then, they are not addressed with the act itself, meaning it is not said to them "do it." So we do not say to a disbeliever, "Come and pray," but first we command him to do what? To Islam. If by being addressed you mean that they are addressed with the branches, meaning that they will be punished for them if they die in disbelief, then this is correct. For this reason it is said to the criminals: ﴿What has caused you to enter Saqar? They will say, "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor, and we used to engage in vain discourse with those who engage in it, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment until there came to us the certainty"﴾ [al-Muddaththir 42–47]. That is their habit until they died. The indication from the verse is that, were it not that they were addressed with the branches, their saying "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor" would be futile and pointless.
* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. How sound is the view of some scholars that Musa, peace be upon him, in the verse you mentioned, feared that the people would be tempted, and that he himself did not fear because he was upon the truth?
* The Shaykh: No, that is a mistake.
* The student: Is it false or not?
* The Shaykh: False. This view is false, and the verse refutes it: ﴿We said, "Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior"﴾ [Ta-Ha 68], and this indicates that he did fear.
* Student: Shaykh, ﴿iyyaya fa-irhabun﴾: if we supply an omitted verb, there is a difficulty in the verse.
* The Shaykh: And what is it?
* The student: The estimate: "And fear Me."
* The Shaykh: "And fear Me."
* The student: "Fear Me, so fear [Me]."
* The Shaykh: "So fear [Me]."
* The student: Where does the fā' fall here?
* The Shaykh: The fā', they said, is for the embellishment of the expression.
* The student: And ﴿irhabun﴾ is coordinated with "fear"?
* The Shaykh: If we supply "fear," then here we may say that it cannot be for the embellishment of the expression.
* The student: It is coordinating then?
* The Shaykh: It is coordinating. But if we say that the governing word may act on two objects, then it is for the embellishment of the expression.
* The student: Even if we say it is coordinating?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: "Fear Me, so fear [Me]."
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: Then the fā' here is..
* The Shaykh: Coordinating: that is, "if you fear Me, then fear [Me]." Yes.
* Student: If a disbeliever enters the mosque..
* The Shaykh: What? The mosque, yes.
* The student: (...) prayer?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. We say: pray. But we do not say "pray" in a way that obliges him. If we say "pray" and he says he is not a Muslim, we leave him alone. But we say: do not stay near the mosque, because that would embarrass the Muslims and challenge them. As for obliging him, saying "Enter, pray!" while he says "I am a disbeliever," we do not oblige him.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, what?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is something that is referred to the one in charge of this.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 40–43 (part 2 of 3):**

* Student: Shaykh, regarding the words of Allah, ﴿and conceal the truth while you know﴾, could the *waw* here be circumstantial?
* Shaykh: The words ﴿while you know﴾ are a circumstantial clause. The *waw* is circumstantial (*waw ḥāliyya*), and the whole clause is circumstantial.
* Student: The *waw* of accompaniment (*wāw al-maʿiyya*)?
* Shaykh: No. In the words ﴿and conceal﴾, the *waw* is the *waw* of accompaniment. Yes.
* Student: (...) Someone who fears the evil eye or the jinn (...)?
* Shaykh: Someone who fears the evil eye or the jinn should be told: use the beneficial litanies (*awrād*), such as the Verse of the Throne and the last two verses of Surat al-Baqarah, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾. I tell you: if you fear the jinn, they will harass you. This is why a person is most often afflicted by the jinn when he fears them. So beware, beware. Do not be afraid at all when you are in a dark place. Seek Allah's help and do not let it trouble you.
* Student: Ablution (*wuḍūʾ*) is prescribed for someone who wants to pray. If someone comes to the mosque for a different purpose, such as a errand or the like, should we say he needs to perform ablution?
* Shaykh: If you want to pray, then perform ablution. But if you come for an errand, there is no obligation on you.
* Student: What about sitting in the mosque?
* Shaykh: Yes, he may sit, because he is in a state without ablution. The Messenger's saying: «When one of you enters the mosque, he should not sit until he has prayed two rak'ahs»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1163) and Muslim (714/69), from the hadith of Abu Qatadah.]] is clearly addressed to one who is in a state of ablution.

* * *

* Student: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it. And do not exchange My signs for a small price, and fear Me alone. (41) And do not mix the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know. (42) And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow.﴾ [al-Baqarah 41–43].
* Shaykh: The saying of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted: ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾. What is the covenant of Allah and what is their covenant?
* Student: The covenant of Allah with them is that they establish prayer, give zakah, and support the messengers.
* Shaykh: Good. And their covenant?
* Student: The covenant of Allah, if they do that, is that He will admit them to Paradise and expiate their misdeeds.
* Shaykh: Well done. Where did you find that?
* Student: In Surat al-Ma'idah.
* Shaykh: What is the verse?
* Student: The saying of Allah, ﴿And you believe in My messengers and support them and lend Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Ma'idah 12].
* Shaykh: ﴿And Allah had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We appointed from among them twelve leaders﴾ [al-Ma'idah 12].
* Student: ﴿And Allah said, "Indeed, I am with you. If you establish prayer and give zakah and believe in My messengers and support them and lend Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever disbelieves after that among you has certainly strayed from the sound way."﴾ [al-Ma'idah 12].
* Shaykh: Well done. Now, the words ﴿and fear Me alone﴾. We mentioned its grammatical analysis (*iʿrāb*) earlier. Who knows the *iʿrāb*?
* Student: It is an object of a verb (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, according to the view of those who permit two objects for one governing word. Is there another view?
* Student: That ﴿Me﴾ is an object of an omitted verb.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: It is placed according to the context, so we say: "Fear Me," or "Be in awe of Me."
* Shaykh: This is another analysis, which says that ﴿Me﴾ is the object of an omitted verb that is to be supplied, meaning: "Me, fear," or "Me, beware," or something similar. Now, is there a difference between *rahbah* (awe) and *khawf* (fear)?
* Student: Yes. *Rahbah* is from something great (...).
* Shaykh: And *khawf*?
* Student: *Khawf* (...).
* Shaykh: *Khawf* is known. Yes.
* Student: *Rahbah* is fear, but it exceeds ordinary natural fear in that it has an effect on the one who is feared.
* Shaykh: On the one who is feared.
* Student: As for *khawf*, it is ordinary, well-known fear.
* Shaykh: Good. First, we must know that psychological states cannot ever be defined. Any person who tries to define psychological states cannot do so. If someone asks you, for example, "What is love (*maḥabba*)?" can you define it? If someone asks, "What is hatred (*karāha*)?" What? "What is fear?" Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, says in the book *Rawdat al-Muhibbin*: psychological states can never be defined by more than their wording. This is correct. Now, the saying: ﴿establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow﴾. If someone says: "Bowing is part of establishing prayer, so is there repetition in the verse?"
* Student: There is no repetition in it. Since He commanded them to perform the prayer, He commanded them to perform it in congregation with the believers of the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ.
* Shaykh: Excellent, may Allah bless you. So the second command is not the first command. Although, in reality, establishing the congregation is part of establishing prayer, it is mentioned explicitly because of its importance. Now, the saying of Allah: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth﴾. What is the *iʿrāb* of ﴿and conceal the truth﴾?
* Student: It is conjoined (*maʿṭūf*).
* Shaykh: Conjoined to what?
* Student: To what precedes it.
* Shaykh: What precedes it? Conjoined to what comes before it. What is before it?
* Student: ﴿Do not mix﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Do not mix﴾. Good. So concealing the truth is forbidden just as mixing the truth with falsehood is forbidden. So how many things are forbidden now? Two?
* Student: Mixing the truth with falsehood and concealing the truth.
* Shaykh: Mixing the truth with falsehood and concealing the truth. Is there another aspect?
* Student: There is a circumstantial clause.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: That the *waw* here is for accompaniment.
* Shaykh: That the *waw* is for accompaniment. On this view, is each one forbidden on its own, or what?
* Student: "Do not mix the truth, and do not conceal the truth..."
* Shaykh: So the prohibition is against combining them? Each one on its own is not forbidden? Now, which is preferable in meaning?
* Student: That the prohibition be against each one separately.
* Shaykh: That the prohibition be against each one separately. Why, when each is prohibited separately?
* Student: Because if both are prohibited, then they are combined.
* Shaykh: So combining them is more emphatic. Yes. May Allah bless you.

Now let us take the benefits. Where did we end what we wrote? At the saying: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾? Yes.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever exchanges the signs of Allah for a small price has a resemblance to the Jews. Those who study Islamic knowledge for the sake of worldly gain resemble the Jews, because the Jews are the ones who exchanged the signs of Allah for a small price. The Prophet ﷺ said in a hadith: «Whoever seeks knowledge by which the Face of Allah is sought, but seeks only to gain some worldly goods, will not smell the fragrance of Paradise»[[Abu Dawud (3664), Ibn Majah (252), and Ahmad (8457), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
At this point, many students are confused by those people who come in droves to the universities and schools seeking only the certificate. Are they among those who exchanged the signs of Allah for a small price? The answer: it depends on the intention. If a person wants nothing from it except to get a job and make a living, then he has exchanged the signs of Allah for a small price. The sign of this is that he cares only about reaching this position, even at the expense of knowledge and the Sharia. But if he does not want that, and wants only to reach the position that he attains through the certificate in order to occupy a place where he can benefit the Muslims, then he has not exchanged the signs of Allah for a small price. This is because concepts have changed now, and a person is weighed by the certificate he carries. Is that clear? So we say to those who go to the universities: there is no fault in you if you do not seek mere worldly gain, but seek to occupy a position through which you benefit the servants of Allah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: everything in this world is small. This is confirmed by the saying of Allah: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah, and you will not be wronged even the bit of a date-thread﴾ [an-Nisa' 77].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the laws of Allah are among His signs, as indicated by His saying: ﴿My signs for a small price﴾. The Jews sell religion for worldly gain. The reason the laws are among His signs is that they point to His wisdom, may He be exalted, and come in the most perfect manner, unlike what humans enact, which is deficient. First, because of the deficiency of human knowledge and their lack of comprehensive understanding. Second, because the interests are hidden from them, so they may think something is an interest when it is not, and they may think something that is not an interest is an interest. Third, even if we suppose that the man who enacted the system or law is the wisest and most knowledgeable of people about human conditions, his knowledge is still limited: limited in time and limited in place. As for time, that is obvious, because affairs change. What is in the interest of people in this era may be different in another era. As for place, a legislation enacted by humans may be suitable for the conditions of one nation in its place, but not for another nation. This is why, regrettably, many Muslims have gone astray by adopting Western laws and applying them to an Islamic society. There is a difference between the disbelieving European societies and Islamic societies, and we cannot apply what suits the situation of those people to what does not suit the situation of Muslims. This is supposing that it is suitable in its own place. How much more so if it is not suitable even in its own place? What is strange is that some people, may Allah grant us well-being, are found following laws enacted decades ago, whose own people who enacted them have since abandoned them. These people are like those who suck the marrow from bones after they have been thrown into the garbage. This is a clear matter: there are laws that were enacted for a disbelieving people, then their circumstances changed and they changed them. Then some Muslims came to these discarded laws, the empty husks, and began to chew on them. Does this fall under the saying: ﴿Do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾? Yes, it does fall under this. Yes.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of fearing Allah, may He be exalted, and singling Him out for fear. Yes, as indicated by His saying: ﴿and fear Me alone﴾. If someone says: "Does Allah not command us to guard against certain times and certain punishments at times? He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 281], and He says: ﴿And fear the Fire, which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Ali 'Imran 131], and He says: ﴿And fear a trial which will not afflict those who have wronged among you exclusively﴾ [al-Anfal 25]. How then can these be reconciled?"
We say: all these things that we are commanded to guard against, guarding against them is part of the fear of Allah, because they are created by Allah, may He be exalted, so guarding against them is part of the fear of Allah, may He be exalted.
* Among the benefits of the verse that follows, ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾: the obligation to clarify the truth and distinguish it from falsehood, so that one says: "This is the truth and this is falsehood," and does not obscure it for people, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾.
Among the mixing of truth with falsehood are those people who raise doubts either about the Qur'an or about its rulings and then do not resolve them. If they raised the doubt and resolved it, it would be less serious. However, raising doubts, even if they are resolved, when they are not widespread among people, is not in the interest of anyone. Pay attention to this point: raising a doubt, even if you resolve it, when it is not widespread among people, is a mistake. This is because once you open the doubt, you do not have certainty that you will remove it with the solutions you mention. Sometimes a doubt strikes the heart, and solutions are offered for it, but the person is not reassured by these solutions, so the doubt remains. If the person had been spared from it, that would have been better.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: there is only truth and falsehood, truth and falsehood. If you reflect on the Qur'an and the Sunnah, you will find that this is the case. Allah says: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 62].
And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba' 24]. And He the Exalted says: ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾ [Yunus 32]. And He the Exalted says: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf 29]. And the Prophet ﷺ said: «The Qur'an is a proof for you or against you»[[Narrated by Muslim (223/1), from the hadith of Abu Malik al-Ash'ari.]]. There is nothing that is neither truth nor falsehood; it is either truth or falsehood.
If someone says: "Is there not a level between the obligatory and the forbidden, and between the disliked and the recommended, namely the permissible?" We say: Yes, without doubt. But the permissible itself must be a means to something. If it is not a means to something, it becomes part of falsehood. As in the hadith: «Every amusement with which the son of Adam amuses himself is falsehood, except his play with his bow, with his family, and with his horse»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (1637) and Ibn Majah (2811), from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, with the wording: «And everything with which the Muslim man amuses himself is falsehood, except his shooting with his bow, his training of his horse, and his playing with his wife...».]].
These three things were excepted only because they serve a benefit; all of them return to a benefit.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of concealing the truth, as indicated by His saying: ﴿and conceal the truth﴾. But is it said that concealment only occurs after a request? The answer: Yes, concealment only occurs after a request. But a request is of two kinds: a request by the tongue of speech, and a request by the tongue of the situation. If someone comes to you and says, "What do you say about such-and-such?" this is a request by the tongue of speech. If you see people immersed in something forbidden, then requesting its clarification is by the tongue of the situation. Accordingly, a person must clarify the wrong and not wait until he is asked. If he is asked and conceals it because he does not know, there is no sin on him, as indicated by the saying of Allah: ﴿and conceal the truth while you know﴾. But if he does not know and says, "By Allah, I do not know," there is no harm. This is one point: if he does not know, then it is obligatory for him to remain silent and say, "I do not know."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 40–43 (part 3 of 3):

Second: If the scholar sees that it is in the public interest not to explain, there is no harm. There is no harm in concealing, as in the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Speak to the people in terms of what they know. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?"[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (127) with the wording: "Do you love that Allah and His Messenger be denied?"]] And Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "You will never speak to a people about a matter that their intellects cannot reach without it becoming a trial (fitnah) for some of them."[[Recorded by Muslim in the Introduction (5), with the same meaning.]] So if you see that it is in the public interest not to explain, then do not explain, and there is no blame on you.

Third: If the questioner's intention is to test you, or his intention is to seek out concessions (rukhas), and you know this, then you may refrain and say: "I will not tell you." A test is when someone comes to you and you know that the man knows the issue, but he asks you in order to test you: do you know it or not? Or he wants to take words from you in order to carry them to someone and report them to someone else. In that case you may refrain. Likewise, if you know that the man is seeking concessions, and he comes and asks you, saying: "I asked so-and-so and he said this is forbidden," while you know that the one he asked is a learned man and not ignorant, then you may refrain and say: "I will not answer you." But if the one he asked is a man you know to have no knowledge, whether one of the common people or one of the students of knowledge who have not matured, then if he says: "I am asking so-and-so for a ruling," you should give him a ruling, because that man's ruling carries no weight. But if a learned man you know to be your equal in knowledge, or greater than you, has given him a ruling, then you may say: "I will not give you a ruling," because this questioner in most cases seeks concessions. However, if he says to you: "By Allah, I asked so-and-so, but I was looking for you and did not find you, and out of necessity I asked so-and-so. But now that Allah has brought you, give me a ruling," then you should give him a ruling. Why? Because this man's situation is as if he were saying: "I am only at peace with your ruling." In that case it is binding on you to give him a ruling. Even if he has asked someone more knowledgeable than you, and you know that the man trusts only your words, you must give him a ruling.

So, when is concealing the truth realized?

* The students: After being asked.

* The Shaykh: After being asked, whether by the tongue of the situation or by the tongue of speech. We have mentioned cases in which it is permissible not to explain, but that is either for a public interest or to avert harm.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Some people ask, and their intention is not knowledge, nor anything of what we have mentioned in the lesson. Rather, their intention, O Shaykh, is to argue with some of their companions, not for the sake of reaching the truth, but for the sake of disputation. This happens in people's gatherings today. He says: "By Allah, so-and-so and I argued today, what do you think?"

* The Shaykh: This also, sometimes, is a dispute among people. A person comes to you asking, and his intention is not to reach sound knowledge so that he may act on it or not. Rather, his intention is to overpower, to defeat his companion. So it appears to me that this is closer to being obligatory, that this is closer to being obligatory, in order that the truth may spread, because if the matter remains a battleground among people, the truth is not made clear.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. Sometimes a person is asked while he is in an area where there are no scholars, and if the common people wanted to ask about every question that comes up, reaching the scholars would be difficult for them. So, for those students who have not reached the required level of knowledge, may they give rulings based on what they know?

* The Shaykh: Yes, they may give rulings based on what they know. It is obligatory upon him. "Convey from me, even if it is one verse,"[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3461) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]] For example, this student who has not reached a certain level in knowledge knows, for instance, from the words of such-and-such scholar, who is a scholar, and so he gives a ruling based on it.

* The student: He analogizes, or, I mean, he exercises some degree of independent reasoning (ijtihad). So this (...) is very necessary, because issues keep arising.

* The Shaykh: In any case, he says: "Ask someone else." He is in good health. As long as he is not certain, is it obligatory for him to give a ruling about what he does not know?!

* A student: If he fears that the questioner is asking as a test, may he answer contrary to the truth?

* The Shaykh: Contrary to the truth? No, glory be to Allah! I mean, if something is permissible, does he say it is forbidden?

* The student: No, any issue, I mean...

* The Shaykh: "Contrary to the truth" means this: the truth is that this is permissible, and he says it is forbidden. The truth is that this is not obligatory, and he says it is obligatory.

* * *

* A student: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Will you not then reason? (44) And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is a burden except upon the humble (khashi'un). (45) Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that they will return to Him. (46) O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds. (47) And fear a Day when no soul will avail another at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44–48]

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And establish prayer, and give zakat, and bow with those who bow.﴾ The address here is to the Children of Israel from the beginning of His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you.﴾ The Children of Israel are the Jews and the Christians, because Israel is the son of Isaac, son of Abraham, so his descendants are the Jews and the Christians.

He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat.﴾ "Establish" it means: bring it in its correct form. And just as Allah commanded the Children of Israel, He commanded this Ummah. The prayer here includes the obligatory and the voluntary.

﴿And give zakat﴾: pay the zakat. As those among you who know grammar know, the verb "ata" (to give) takes two objects when it means "to give." The first object here is "zakat," and the second object is omitted; the implied meaning is: its people, or those who deserve it. ﴿Give zakat.﴾ Zakat is worship, or it is the wealth given in obedience to Allah's command to its rightful recipients, from specific known types of wealth, namely: gold, silver, livestock, what comes out of the earth, and trade goods. There is a long disagreement among Muslim scholars about trade goods, but the correct view is that zakat on them is obligatory.

﴿Give zakat﴾: the spending of wealth is called zakat because it purifies the soul and cleanses it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity (sadaqah) by which you purify them and cause them to grow.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]

﴿And bow with those who bow﴾: that is, pray with those who pray. We say this because worship of Allah is not performed by bowing alone. That is, if a person wanted to worship Allah by merely bowing, we would say: this is an innovation (bid'ah). So the meaning is: pray with those who pray. Know that expressing worship by one of its parts indicates that this part is one of its pillars and essential components, and that worship cannot be valid without it. Expressing the whole by a part is well known in the Arabic language, and in the Noble Qur'an: ﴿the freeing of a neck (raqabah)﴾ [al-Nisa': 92], and what is meant is a slave, a complete slave. But as you have seen, the neck cannot be left without the body. So can we say: "freeing a finger"? No, because a finger may be lost while the body remains. Here we say: ﴿bow with those who bow﴾, that is, pray with those who pray. Bowing cannot be used to express prayer unless bowing is an inseparable part of it and essential to it.

* In this noble verse there is evidence that prayer was obligatory on the earlier nations, and that it included bowing, just as the prayer in our law includes bowing. This is also shown by Allah's saying to Mary: ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, and prostrate and bow with those who bow.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 43] So the earlier nations had a prayer that included bowing and prostration.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the earlier nations were also obligated to pay zakat, because there must be a test through zakat. Some people are miserly, for whom giving a single dirham is harder than many things. So servants are tested by paying zakat and giving some of their wealth, so that through this the reality of their faith is known. This is why zakat is called sadaqah. Why? Because it shows the truthfulness of its giver's faith.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of congregational prayer, based on His saying: ﴿bow with those who bow.﴾ Some scholars have used it as evidence in this way, but this inference may be disputed, since being together does not necessarily mean joining in the action. This is why it was said to Mary: ﴿be devoutly obedient to your Lord, and prostrate and bow with those who bow﴾, and women are not obligated to pray in congregation. Based on this, we say: using this verse as evidence for the obligation of congregational prayer requires some reconsideration. Then we add to this view that, in debate, one should not bring a proof that the opponent can easily refute, because that shows your weakness, and you may then be weakened by a strong proof you cannot repel, since you were weakened by this proof and your strength collapses. Consider Abraham's argument when the man said to him: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258]. Abraham did not argue with him by saying: "You give life and cause death? But you cannot bring the dead to life or cause the living to die; you only perform the causes." He turned away from that and said what? ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west,﴾ and the one who disbelieved was confounded. [al-Baqarah: 258]

So the point I am making to you is this: in the field of debate, do not bring a weak proof that your opponent can use against you. Perhaps you will argue with someone about the attributes of Allah in the field of creed, and you bring a weak proof, and your opponent uses it to overpower you. Do not bring any proof except one that the opponent cannot untie. So we do not accept that this verse proves the obligation of congregational prayer. But praise be to Allah, the obligation of congregational prayer is clear from other evidences.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 44:

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book?﴾ We have two actions: the first action is enjoining righteousness upon the people, and the second action is forgetting oneself. So, is the interrogative of denunciation directed at each one separately, or at both of them together?

* The students: At both of them together.

* The Shaykh: Yes, at both of them together. If you wish, you may say: the focus of the denunciation is His saying: ﴿while you forget yourselves﴾.

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people﴾. The interrogative here is for denunciation and astonishment: how do you enjoin the people while you forget yourselves?! ﴿Righteousness (al-birr)﴾ is goodness. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: one of them would command his relatives to follow the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and would say: "It is true." But his leadership and standing prevent him from believing in it. An example of this is that the Prophet ﷺ visited a Jewish boy who was sick. His time of death arrived while the Prophet ﷺ was with him, so the Prophet ﷺ invited him to right guidance. The boy looked at his father as if seeking his counsel, and his father said to him: "Obey Muhammad." His father was a Jew, yet he said: "Obey Muhammad." So the boy pronounced the testimony of truth. The Prophet ﷺ left while saying: "Praise be to Allah, who has saved him from the Fire through me."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1356) from the hadith of Anas.]] That is, through my call. So these Jews, among their rabbis, there were those who enjoined the people to righteousness, which is following the Messenger ﷺ, but they forgot themselves; they did not believe. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿while you recite the Book﴾. The waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning: and the situation is that you recite the Book. So you did not enjoin righteousness except with knowledge, yet despite that you forget yourselves. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ The interrogative here is for reproach, meaning: will you not have reason by which you perceive your error and your misguidance? And "reason" here is the reason of discernment (aql al-rushd), not the reason of legal accountability (aql al-taklif). This is because reason is of two types: a reason that is the basis of legal accountability, which is the perception and understanding of things; and a reason that is the basis of discernment, indeed it is discernment itself, which is that a person conducts himself well. The good conduct of a person is called "reason" because he restrains (ʿaqala) his conduct in what benefits him. Is that clear? Which of the two kinds of reason is intended here? The reason of discernment or the reason of legal accountability?

* The students: The reason of discernment.

* The Shaykh: The reason of discernment, otherwise they are all legally accountable. Fine. Now, this construction ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ has a difficulty: the fa is a conjunctive particle, the hamza is the interrogative particle, and it is well known that the interrogative hamza must come at the head of the sentence. Here the conjunctive fa would have been before the hamza. Therefore the grammarians of i'rab (grammatical analysis) differed regarding such a construction. Some of them said: the hamza enters upon an omitted element that is estimated according to the context. Others said: the fa has been displaced from its place, and the original is: "fa-a-la ta'qilun," but the hamza was moved forward because it has precedence, and the conjunctive particle was delayed, and it occurs after the fa. That is, the hamza occurs before it, as here, or before thumma, as in His saying: ﴿Is it then, when it has befallen you, that you believe in it?﴾ [Yunus 51], and before the waw, as in ﴿Have they not traveled in the earth?﴾ [al-Rum 9].

If you look at the grammatical rule, you would say: making the sentence depend on an omitted estimated element is closer to the rules. And if you look at the fact that sometimes the estimation is difficult for you, because the estimation must be an appropriate clause, you would say: then which of them should we adopt?

* A student: We adopt the second.

* The Shaykh: The second, because it is easier. In the second, you say: the fa is a conjunctive particle, and the clause after it is conjoined to what precedes it, and the original position of the fa is before the hamza, but it has been displaced, and the matter ends. You do not go searching and seeking what to estimate.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the reproach of those who enjoin righteousness and forget themselves, because that contradicts reason, and a severe warning has come concerning one who has this habit. The Prophet ﷺ informed that "a man will be brought and thrown into the Fire, and his intestines will spill out, and he will go round them as the donkey goes round its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, did you not used to order us to do what is right and forbid us from what is wrong?' He will say: 'I used to order you to do what is right but I would not do it, and I used to forbid you from what is wrong but I would do it.'"[[Narrated by Muslim (989/51) from the hadith of Usama ibn Zayd.]] He is among the people with the most severe punishment, and we seek refuge in Allah.

If someone says: based on the fact that this contradicts reason, and based on the severity of its punishment, shall we say to one who does not do what he is commanded and does not refrain from what he is forbidden: do not command and do not forbid?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: We say: No. Rather we say: command, and do what you command, because if he leaves the command while also leaving the doing, he commits two wrongs: the first is abandoning enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and the second is not fulfilling what he commands. Likewise, if he commits what he is forbidden and does not forbid it, he has committed what? Two corruptions: the first is abandoning the forbidding of wrong, and the second is his committing the wrong. Then we say: which of us has been spared from wrong?! If we said: no one should forbid wrong except one who has not committed wrong, no one would forbid wrong. And if we said: no one should command another to good except one who has himself done good, no one would command good. Which of us is free of fault?! Therefore we say: command what is right and strive against yourself to do it; forbid wrong and strive against yourself to leave it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the reproach of the scholar who acts contrary to his knowledge, and that when the scholar contradicts his knowledge, he is in a worse state than the ignorant person. From where is this derived?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. It is derived from His saying: ﴿while you recite the Book﴾. This is a matter upon which people have been created: when the scholar contradicts his knowledge, he becomes more deserving of blame than the ignorant person. Even the common people, when a scholar commits a wrong, you find them saying: how can you do this while you are a learned man?! Or if he leaves an obligation, they say: how can you leave this obligation while you are a scholar?! The noble verse is clear on this: ﴿while you recite the Book﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Book, when used in the singular, applies to all books, because these Jews recited the Book of Allah, the Qur'an, and they also recited the Torah. So they recited this and that.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the reproach of the Children of Israel, and that they are an ignorant, foolish people, deficient in judgment; as shown by His saying: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾

* Among its benefits: that whoever from this Ummah (nation) commands what is right but does not do it, or forbids what is wrong but does it, there is in him a resemblance to whom? To the Jews, because this is their habit, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* A student: May Allah be good to you. Is it by way of the fact that the Children of Israel includes the Jews and the Christians?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: When these texts appear in the Qur'an, we apply them to all of them.

* The Shaykh: To all of them, yes, indeed.

* The student: How (...)?

* The Shaykh: What?

* The student: It is known that...

* The Shaykh: It does not necessarily follow that when these people are addressed with a general description, the address is to all of them. This does not necessarily follow. Yes.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) responses to Nimrod's answer, moving to another proof that establishes his point: is this called hayda (evasion)? Or is hayda specific to the opponent himself?

* The Shaykh: No, no, this is not hayda. Rather, this is the establishment of the clearer proof.

* The student: Hayda only in the context of blame?

* The Shaykh: Hayda means a person deviates and moves to something else. But now the subject is one. 

* The student: He moved from one answer to another answer?

* The Shaykh: No, he moved from one proof to another proof, or the subject is one? ﴿He argued with Ibrahim concerning his Lord﴾, and Ibrahim wished to establish it.

* The student: So hayda, Shaykh, is used only in a style of...?

* The Shaykh: Hayda means, for example, that I speak with you on a subject and say, for example: "Buy me, for example, the book al-Mughni." Then you say: "By Allah, the book al-Muhadhdhab is fine and good, but what is this?" This is hayda: moving from one subject to another. But moving from a proof to a stronger one is not hayda.

* A student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, it has not become clear to me what the indication of the verse is that the earlier nations had the prayer and zakat as a legislated practice.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: That is, this verse ﴿Establish the prayer and give zakat and bow with those who bow﴾ means this Ummah.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ means their prayer, meaning their prayer and their zakat. There is no doubt that this carries a possibility, since the context of the verse may be said to indicate this. But the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat exist in the Torah. Read the verses of the Torah in which they appear, and you will find them.

* The student: Gathering this verse with others.

* The Shaykh: Yes, with others.

* A student: What troubled me is the statement of the Messenger ﷺ about the Jewish boy when he said: "Praise be to Allah, who has saved him from the Fire through me."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1356) from the hadith of Anas.]]

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: The difficulty is that the boy was not legally accountable.

* The Shaykh: No, no. "Ghulam" does not necessarily mean a small child. This boy was a ghulam who served the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Yes.

* A student: Someone sits in a gathering of condolence and reminds them, yes, that is (...). Is this an innovation (bid'ah)?

* The Shaykh: Without doubt, if a person came to a people gathered for condolence and said to them: "O my brothers, this is a matter that is written and unavoidable, and what Allah gave is His and what He took is His, and everything with Him has a specified term," and he advised them so that they would disperse, this is good.

* The student: In order to remind them.

* The Shaykh: But (...) he gave a sermon as if he were saying: remain upon what you are upon.

* The student: No, he did not approve of their sitting. He denounced their sitting; he only reminds them.

* The Shaykh: It does not contradict it. Ordinary sitting without a sermon.

* * *

* A student: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds. And fear a Day when no soul will avail another at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be aided. And when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive; and in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47–49]

Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. We have finished, I believe, with its exegesis and its benefits from what preceded? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer. And indeed, it is difficult except for the humble before Allah.﴾ Seek help in your affairs ﴿through patience﴾, meaning: upon it. ﴿And prayer﴾, which is the well-known act of worship. ﴿And indeed it﴾, i.e., the prayer or the seeking of help, ﴿is difficult﴾, i.e., burdensome, ﴿except for the humble﴾, i.e., those who submit humbly to the command of Allah.

Istiʿanah (seeking help) is asking for assistance. Seeking help through patience means that a person endures what is disliked, whether it is disliked by nature or by character, or for other reasons. The important thing is that he is patient, restrains himself, and makes himself bear the hardship until the desired goal is achieved. It is well established by experience that when a person is patient with something, he attains its aim, and when he becomes bored and lazy, he loses much good. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: «Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up»[[Narrated by Muslim (2664/34) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. Many people think that starting this work is beneficial to them, so they begin, but then they do not achieve their aim quickly, so they become weak, tired, and abandon it. So their earlier time has been wasted, has it not? Time has been wasted, perhaps a great deal of it, and he cannot be sure that if he turns away from the first and then begins a second, the same thing will not happen to him and he will abandon it too, and his life will pass without benefit. But if he is patient, while knowing that between him and his goal there is only the passing of days, and there is no reason to cut it off, then let him be patient. Let us suppose that a student of knowledge resolves to memorize Bulugh al-Maram, begins it, and continues, but then boredom overtakes him and he gives up. The time that passed is a loss for him, except for what remains in his mind or memory of what he memorized; otherwise it is gone. But if he persists and completes it, the aim is achieved. Apply this to other cases as well.

As for prayer: a person may say, how can it be a help to a person? Yes, we say it is a help, but it is not mere prayer; rather, true prayer is the one in which the prayer of the heart precedes the prayer of the limbs. As for our prayer today, it is mostly a prayer of the limbs and not of the heart. This is why you find that from the moment a person says Allahu Akbar, there open up to him, what? Heaps and wide, great doors of whisperings that have no benefit. Therefore, from the moment he gives the salam, they clear away from him and depart. But true prayer, in which a person feels that he is standing before Allah, and that it is a garden containing all the fruits of worship, he must forget, through this prayer, all of this world, he must, he must forget the whole world through this prayer; because he has connected with whom? With Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who is his beloved and the most beloved thing to him, so he forgets everything else. But the person who seeks help through prayer to find diversion in it while his heart is occupied with other things, the prayer does not benefit him in this respect, not at all. It is mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ «when a matter distressed him (i.e., weighed heavily upon him), he would turn to prayer»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1319) and Ahmad (23299) from Hudhayfah.]]. This is supported by his ﷺ occupation, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, in the tent on the day of Badr: with what? With prayer and earnest entreaty to his Lord for victory[[The intensity of the Prophet ﷺ's supplication and appeal to Allah the Exalted on the day of Badr is narrated by al-Bukhari (2915) from Ibn Abbas, and by Muslim (1763) from Ibn Abbas on the authority of Umar ibn al-Khattab. Prayer on that day is narrated by al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra (8574, 10367) from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]].

﴿Through patience and prayer﴾: the prayer here includes both obligatory and voluntary prayer. ﴿And indeed it﴾: it has been said that ﴿it﴾ refers to the prayer, and they gave as a reason that it is the nearest thing mentioned, and the rule in the Arabic language is that a pronoun refers to the nearest antecedent.

Second: prayer is an act of bringing into existence something that did not exist, because it is an action, while patience is restraint, and bringing into existence is superior to restraint. For this reason, the whole of Islam is an act of bringing into existence, meaning the creation of something, not the absence of something. Patience, as we said, is restraint, and bringing into existence is more noble and more expressive, so prayer deserved that the pronoun refer back to it.

Third: that His saying ﴿except for the humble﴾ cannot be taken to mean patience in an absolute sense, because among the disbelievers there are those who are more patient with their false gods than the believer is with his Lord, or with the law of his Lord, and with his deeds. ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: Walk on, and be steadfast for your gods﴾ [Sad 6], they urge them to be patient toward their gods. This view is closer to the truth and more correct.

It has also been said that His saying ﴿And indeed it﴾ refers to the seeking of help implied by His saying ﴿seek help﴾, because the verb (seek help) indicates a time and an event, that is, a time and a verbal noun, so the pronoun may refer to the verbal noun implied by the verb, are you with me? As in the Exalted saying ﴿Be just﴾, what? ﴿It﴾, i.e., the justice implied by His saying ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8]. But the first meaning is clearer. ﴿And indeed it﴾, i.e., the prayer, ﴿is difficult﴾, i.e., burdensome, ﴿except for the humble﴾, the people of humility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of submission to Him. This is why you find prayer heavy upon whom? Upon the hypocrites, because they have no faith; but it is light upon the believer. Indeed the Prophet ﷺ said: «Women and perfume have been made beloved to me of your world, and the coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer»[[Narrated by al-Nasa'i (3939) and Ahmad (12294, 14037) from Anas; the wording mentioned is that of al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (7/78), and Muhammad ibn Nasr in Ta'zim Qadr al-Salah (322).]], may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. So if Allah has made the coolness of your eye to be in prayer, then rejoice in good, for it is a sign of good, and a sign that you are among the humble.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, blessed and exalted, guides His servants to what? To seeking help through these two matters: patience and prayer.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of seeking help from other than Allah, but in matters where help is established as possible. The permissibility of seeking help from other than Allah in matters where help is established as possible. For example, if you seek a man to carry the goods with you to the house, is it permissible?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Good. If you seek help from someone who dictates the notes to you, saying: O so-and-so, help me with the dictation, it is permissible. The Prophet ﷺ said: «And your helping a man with his beast, by lifting him onto it or lifting his goods onto it, is charity»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2891) and Muslim (1009/56) from Abu Hurayrah.]].

As for seeking help in what offers no help, it is foolishness in intellect and misguidance in religion, and it may amount to shirk, such as seeking help from a dead person or an absent one who cannot help him because of his distance from him and his inability to reach him. This is foolishness and misguidance, and it may be shirk with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of patience, and that help is given through it in bearing the trials of affairs. This is a matter that is observed and does not need evidence to establish it, because it is obvious; all of us know this, do we not? Yes.

The scholars said: patience is of three types, and they derived this division from inductive observation:
First: patience in obeying Allah. Second: patience in refraining from disobeying Allah. Third: patience upon the decrees of Allah.

Patience in obedience is the most arduous and the most virtuous, because patience in obedience includes an action and a restraint, an action and a voluntary restraint: the action is performing the obedience, and the restraint is restraining the self from neglecting it and failing to establish it. Is that clear? So it is an active, positive bringing into being. Patience in refraining from disobedience contains only restraint, but it can sometimes be very severe, severe upon the self. This is why the Prophet ﷺ placed the young man whom a woman of rank and beauty invited, and he said: "I fear Allah," in the rank of the just ruler, in that Allah shades him in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (660) and Muslim (1031/91) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. Although the just ruler is more excellent, in rank, from this aspect, they are equal; because the strength of the motive in youth and the absence of an obstacle when he is alone with her make the likelihood of falling into the forbidden very strong. But he said, "I fear Allah." Perhaps this patience is harder for a person than praying twenty prayers. Patience in this situation may be harder for the person than twenty prayers. But we are not speaking of the accidental circumstances that befall some people; we are speaking of the matter in itself. So which is better? Patience in obedience, or patience in refraining from disobedience?

* A student: Patience in obedience.

* The Shaykh: Patience in obedience. Good. Patience upon the decrees of Allah is the lowest of them, but even so a person may find great hardship in it. However, we are not speaking of a particular patience in a particular person. Some people may lose their beloved, their son, or their wife, or the like, and this may be harder for them than a thousand prayers in terms of emotional reaction. Is it not so? But we are not talking about this. Patience upon the decrees of Allah is, in reality, not an action of yours, because what has befallen must befall, whether you are patient or not. If you grieve, regret, your sorrow intensifies, and your crying rises loudly, does that reverse what was decreed? No. So, as some of the predecessors said: either you are patient with the patience of the noble, or you forget like animals forget. Which of us has not been afflicted by a calamity ten years ago, for example, or less, or more? And have we forgotten it now? We have forgotten it as though it never came. Because, as the Salafi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: or you forget like animals forget. Yes.

So what are the types of patience? Three, in order: first, patience in obedience to Allah; second, refraining from disobedience to Allah; third, patience upon the decrees of Allah. Good. But take patience as a method and a path for yourself: be patient in matters and persevere through them, and do not despair, for when despair overcomes a person, he loses much good.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that prayer is among the things by which one seeks help in matters and affairs of life, in His saying: ﴿and prayer﴾, and we know with certainty that this is a true report with no doubt in it.

If someone says: I always pray and I find no help.

We say: you have not prayed. You have not prayed. You have performed the form of prayer but not its reality. This is why Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book, and establish prayer. Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut 45]. Many people enter into prayer and leave it without finding that their hearts have changed in terms of immorality and wrongdoing. They remain as they were; their hearts have not been softened by remembrance nor turned toward love of worship or anything else. We ask Allah to help us and you. The deficiency is great. This is why Allah's promise is true without doubt: prayer helps and forbids immorality and wrongdoing. But the prayer of most people today is the form of prayer, not its reality.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that if your sorrows are prolonged, then you must have patience and what? And prayer, patience and prayer. As for the saying of the common people: "If your worries grow great, take from the earth your length," do you know the meaning? That is, lie down: when a person lies down he takes from the earth his length. But if he is standing, how much does he take from the earth? The place of his feet, only the place of his feet. So this is not correct. Rather, we say: if your worries and sorrows multiply, then you must have patience and prayer, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer. And indeed it is difficult except for the humble﴾. Good. Shall we take the questions, or proceed? We take the questions.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Some people are patient with Allah's decrees but do not complain or speak about anything, yet it shows in their conduct. For example, one may be distressed but does not want to speak to anyone, or some small incident or situation happens and he acts in a hasty or similar way, even though he has not spoken about the calamity?

* The Shaykh: In any case, every person must be afflicted: "No affliction befalls except by the permission of Allah" [al-Taghabun 11]. But does this calamity make him do, say, or harbor something in his heart? The answer is no. He says: all of this is negated, if Allah wills. The believer does not do this. But he should restrain himself from being distressed. For example, a person may be afflicted by a calamity and not open himself to people as he usually does. This is natural. When the news of Ja'far's death reached the Prophet ﷺ, he sat in a place in the mosque where the signs of sorrow were visible, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, was overcome[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1299) and Muslim (935/30) from Aisha.]]. This is a natural thing. What is required by human nature is not held against a person, nor does it lower his rank, unless he indulges in it. Yes.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. Someone who sometimes finds in himself a lethargy toward seeking knowledge, whether in understanding or memorization, or who wants to attend to a worldly matter?

* The Shaykh: Understanding, memorization, or practice, and the last is the trial.

* The student: Or attending to a worldly matter. So do we derive from this verse the legitimacy of prayer when we need something of this kind?

* The Shaykh: If you help him, because by his prayer he will ask Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to ease his affair.

* The student: What is the meaning of "if he helps (...)"?

* The Shaykh: Allah helps him, because the soul of the one praying, as long as he is troubled and grieved about this matter, will direct all his supplication to this thing, and he is closest to his Lord when he is prostrating.

* The student: So, if he finds something of this kind, he goes and prays?

* The Shaykh: Did you hear the words? "When a matter distressed the Prophet ﷺ, he would turn to prayer"[[Previously cited.]].

* A student: May Allah be good to you. Does Allah's saying ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ include obligatory prayer and voluntary prayer?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed; (...) the obligatory is obligatory, it must (...).

* A student: May Allah be good to you. Yes, my question to your eminence, O Shaykh: two days ago, is it permissible to supplicate with "O Allah, make me among the patient"? You mentioned that the correct form is to say: "O Allah, help me to be patient." What is the difference between these two expressions?

* The Shaykh: Who said this?

* The student: No one, it was not in the lesson; it was on our way home.

* The Shaykh: I do not recall. It seems you may have misunderstood. Either you asked a question, I answered it, and you understood this... No, my brother: "O Allah, make me among the patient, the devout, those who enjoin good and forbid evil." "Be patient; indeed Allah is with the patient" [al-Baqarah 153].

* The student: So it is permissible that...

* The Shaykh: No, we will understand the answer after today.

* A student: What if, for example, a person was patient in obeying Allah but was not patient upon His decrees? Would he be called patient?

* The Shaykh: No, not in an absolute sense, just as one who repents from one sin but not others is not called "a penitent" in an absolute sense. Rather, one says: "penitent from such-and-such." This is a point a person should know. "Indeed Allah loves those who turn often in repentance and loves those who purify themselves" [al-Baqarah 222]. Would we say, for example, that a person who persists in a sin while repenting from it is included? No, because the absolute description applies only to absolute action. Yes.

* A student: In His saying ﴿And indeed it is difficult except for the humble﴾, we named "the difficult" as meaning "burdensome." Does it follow from this verse that the word "difficult" departs from its original meaning, its literal meaning?

* The Shaykh: You are one of the hadith scholars. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Indeed, they are both being punished, and they are not being punished for something great» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (216), Muslim (292/111) from Ibn Abbas], meaning: difficult for them.

Student: No, not in the lesson; it was on our way home.

* The Shaykh: I do not recall. It seems you may have misunderstood. Either you asked a question, I answered it, and you understood this... No, my brother: "O Allah, make me among the patient, the devout, those who enjoin good and forbid evil." "Be patient; indeed Allah is with the patient."

* The student: So it is permissible that...

* The Shaykh: No, we will understand the answer after today.

* Student: Suppose, for example, a person is patient in obeying Allah but is not patient with His decrees. Would he be called patient?
* Shaykh: No, not in an absolute sense. Just as one who repents from one sin but not from others is not called a penitent without qualification, but rather one says "penitent from such-and-such." This is a point a person should understand. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:222]. Do we say, for instance, that a person who persists in a sin while repenting from it is included in this? No, because an unqualified description applies only to unqualified action. Yes.

* Student: Regarding His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And indeed, it is burdensome except for the humble (khāshi'īn)﴾. We have interpreted "burdensome" (kabīrah) as meaning "difficult." Does this verse imply that the word (kabīrah) departs from its original meaning, its literal sense?

* Shaykh: You are one of the people of hadith. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, they are being punished, and they are not being punished for something great [kabīr]."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (216) and Muslim (292 / 111), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]] That is, difficult for them. In the narration of al-Bukhari: "Yes, indeed it is great [kabīr]."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (216) with the wording: "Then he said: Yes," and (6055) with the wording: "And indeed it is great."]] So it is great in sin, though not great in the act.

Student: "O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds (47). And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped (48). And [recall] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted upon you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord (49). And [recall] when We parted the sea for you and saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were watching (50). And [recall] when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers (51). Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful (52)."

Shaykh: We seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. All of these verses concern the Children of Israel, because this surah is Madani, and the Jews in Madina were numerous: three tribes when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madina. Therefore Allah related much of their news in this surah.

Among them, Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord, and that they will return to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 46]. ﴿Those who think﴾ means: those who are certain. The word "zann" (ẓann, think/assume) is used in the Arabic language with the meaning of certainty (yaqin), and it has many examples, among them the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Until, when the earth constricted for them despite its vastness, and their souls constricted for them, and they thought that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾ [at-Tawbah 118]. ﴿They thought﴾ means they were certain. So zann is used in the sense of yaqin, just as ʿilm (knowledge) is used in the sense of zann; they are interchangeable. ʿIlm is used in the sense of zann, as in the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, test them. Allah is most knowing of their faith. And if you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. ﴿If you know them﴾ means: if you think them to be. We say this because what is in the heart is known only by Allah, so it cannot be perceived except through indicators (qara'in), and indicators only yield zann. The point is that zann is used in the sense of yaqin, and ʿilm is used in the sense of zann. ﴿Who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ means: who are certain that they will meet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that is on the Day of Resurrection, as Allah the Exalted said concerning mankind in general: ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor and will meet it﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6]. So meeting Allah is inevitable. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you will be spoken to by his Lord, with no interpreter between them," every person will be spoken to by Allah with no interpreter between him and Him; "He will look to his right and see only what he sent forward, he will look to his left (meaning his left side) and see only what he sent forward, and he will look in front of his face and see only the Fire before his face. So protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (7512) and Muslim (1016/67) from the hadith of ʿAdi ibn Hatim.]] So every person will meet his Lord, but there is no doubt that the believer will receive glad tidings in this meeting, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him, and give good tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 223]. Therefore, praise be to Allah, we ask Allah to make us and you among the believers. That is, we will not fear this meeting, because Allah says: ﴿give good tidings to the believers﴾, meaning there is no fear upon them. For this reason Allah will privately converse with His believing servant and cover him with His screen (kanaf, meaning His concealment), and He will say: "Did you do such-and-such? Did you do such-and-such? Did you do such-and-such?" He will admit it, and Allah, the Exalted, will say: "Indeed I concealed it for you in the world, and today I forgive it for you."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52) from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar.]] ﴿They will meet their Lord, and that they will return to Him﴾. ﴿They will return to Him﴾ means on the Day of Resurrection, or does it mean they will return to Him in all their affairs? The answer: we say, if the verse admits a more general meaning, take the more general meaning, because the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is known to Him, and He knows what the word includes and what follows from it. Therefore, what necessarily follows from the speech of Allah is true, and what necessarily follows from the speech of the Prophet is true, while what necessarily follows from the speech of other than Allah and His Messenger may be true or false, and the speaker may or may not be bound by it. ﴿And that they will return to Him﴾ means: on the Day of Resurrection, or if you wish, say: they will return to Him in all their affairs.

* In this noble verse is the affirmation of meeting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah praised those who are certain of this affirmation. Among its implications, as many scholars have held, is the affirmation of seeing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because meeting (liqa') only occurs with facing one another, and this implies the establishment of vision. If the inference from this verse to the vision of Allah is sound, this is what is sought; and if the inference is not sound and becomes disputed, then we have many other proofs that establish the vision of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, on the Day of Resurrection.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these believers are certain that they will return to Allah in all their affairs, and this entails several things. First, fear of Allah; for as long as you know you will return to Allah, you will fear Him. Likewise, it entails watchfulness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: fear in the heart and watchfulness in the limbs, meaning that when they know they will return to Allah, they will fear Him in secret and in public. Likewise, it entails shame before Him: that He does not find you where He has commanded you, and that He does not find you where He has forbidden you.

Then, after mentioning these verses, God said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. And before this, in previous verses, God had reminded them of this. He said: ﴿Remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you﴾. Did God bestow blessings upon the Children of Israel? Yes, very many blessings, but they denied them. Whoever wants more knowledge on this matter should read the book *Ighathat al-Lahfan* by Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, for he clarified what God gave these people of blessings, exposed their secrets, and tore away their veils, may God have mercy on him.

As for His saying: ﴿Remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you﴾: ﴿My blessing﴾ is a singular noun but it is in the possessive form, so it conveys generality. The intended meaning of remembering it is not that a person says that God bestowed this or that upon him. Rather, the intended meaning is that he performs gratitude (*shukr*) for this blessing, and gratitude for a blessing is righteous action. The evidence that gratitude for a blessing is righteous action is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "God commanded the believers with what He commanded the Messengers, so He said: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you and give thanks to God, if it is Him you worship﴾, and He said regarding the Messengers: ﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾."[[Recorded by Muslim (1015/65) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] So He said ﴿do righteous deeds﴾ corresponding to God's saying to the believers, "give thanks for God's blessing."

As for His saying: ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾, it contains a display of God's favor upon them, since this blessing is one of the blessings of God, Mighty and Majestic, which He bestowed upon them. Also, ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ refers to elevation of rank and high standing. He singled it out for mention because it is the greatest of blessings, for rank is better than mere giving. Look at Surah Al-Bayyinah: God mentioned the disbelievers among the polytheists and the People of the Book, and mentioned their recompense before praising them with evil, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. They are the worst of creatures﴾ [Al-Bayyinah 6]. As for the believers, He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds are the best of creatures. Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [Al-Bayyinah 7-8], because high rank and standing are greater than every delight. Here He said: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾, so He mentioned this particular matter after the general one. His preferring them over the worlds is one of His blessings, but He singled it out for mention after the general statement to indicate its importance. God, Exalted is He, preferred them over the worlds. The word "the worlds" (*al-'alamin*) is used to mean all creation, as in God's saying: ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2]. What is meant by the verse here, ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾? Who is meant by "the worlds"?

* Student: All the worlds.

* Shaykh: All the worlds, correct. Now, here ﴿the worlds﴾ definitely does not mean the entire creation, because God said to this nation: ﴿You are the best nation produced for mankind﴾ [Ali 'Imran 110]. So the intended meaning of "the worlds" is those who came before them, or the worlds of their own time. There are possibilities here. As for the people of their own time, it is certain that God preferred them over the worlds of their time. As for this nation, we are certain that they were not preferred over the Children of Israel, and that this nation is superior to them. As for those who came before them, this is a matter of uncertainty, a matter of uncertainty. So we now have three possibilities. First: Were they preferred over this nation? Certainly not.
