Second: Were they preferred over the people of their own time, such as the people of Pharaoh and others? Certainly yes. Third: Were they preferred over those who came before them among the worlds? This, in my view, is uncertain. It may be that they were preferred over them, and it may be that they were not. In any case, even if we say they were preferred over the people of their own time, that is a great blessing upon them, for which they should thank God.

* In this noble verse, the direct address to the Children of Israel specifically indicates their dullness, and that they will not become sound except through direct address: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾.

* Among its benefits, also (among the benefits of this noble verse): it is obligatory upon the Children of Israel to remember God's blessing upon them and to be thankful for it, and among its thanks is that they follow whom? Muhammad ﷺ.

* Among its benefits: the verse shows that this blessing did not come through their own earning or effort, nor as an inheritance from their forefathers. Rather, it is from what? From God's blessing upon them: ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾. So it contains a display of God's favor.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Children of Israel were the most excellent people of the world in their time, because of His saying: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾.

* Among its benefits: when God favors someone with knowledge, wealth, or standing, that is a great blessing, because of His saying: ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. He singled it out for mention because of its importance.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the differing of people in rank, and that people are of different degrees. This is a known matter. Even among the Messengers, some are preferred over others, as God said: ﴿Those Messengers – We preferred some of them over others﴾ [Al-Baqarah 253], and God said: ﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [Al-Isra' 55]. So by what is preference earned? Preference is first and foremost a favor from God, Mighty and Majestic, and the intellects may not grasp why God preferred some over others. But the comprehensive principle is that whoever God grants knowledge, faith, and righteous deeds, this is a cause of his being preferred. God said: ﴿God will raise those among you who believe and those who were given knowledge by degrees﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 11].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾. ﴿Fear a Day﴾ means: take a shield against this Day. What is meant is the punishment of that Day, that is, fear the punishment that will occur on that Day, which is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿No soul will avail another soul in anything﴾ means that no soul will repel anything from another. The word "soul" (nafs) is indefinite in what context? In the context of negation. Because "soul" is the subject (fa'il) of "avail" (tajzi), it falls within the context of negation, and an indefinite noun in the context of negation conveys generality. Therefore no soul at all can avail another soul in anything, that is, repel anything from it. A father cannot (avail) his children, children cannot (avail) their fathers, a friend cannot (avail) his friend, and no one at all can (avail) anyone. Even the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, I can avail you nothing against God," which is agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), related by al-Bukhari (2753) and Muslim (206/351) from Abu Hurayrah, and he meant by this both this world and the Hereafter. His words ﴿in anything﴾ are also an indefinite noun in the context of negation, and when an indefinite noun is in the context of negation, it includes bringing benefit to someone or repelling harm from him. On the Day of Resurrection, no one can bring benefit to anyone or repel harm from him, whoever he may be. It may be objected that some people take from the good deeds of their oppressor and thereby benefit from them. We say: this oppressor is the one who has squandered his good deeds by wronging the servants of God.

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. In another reading: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ (with the feminine verb). On the reading ﴿tuqbal﴾ (feminine), the matter is clear, why? Because the subject is feminine, and a verb whose subject is feminine is feminine. On the reading with the yā' (masculine, yuqbal), we say: what permits it to be without the feminine marker are two things. The first is that the feminine is not real (ghayr haqiqi). The second is the separation between the verb and its subject, or its deputy subject (na'ib al-fa'il). For this reason Ibn Malik, may God have mercy on him, said:

"The feminine marking is only obligatory with a verb whose pronoun is attached, or one that denotes a female (dhat ḥirr)."

Then he mentioned that the masculine form is permitted with separation. When you say "qamat Hind" (Hind stood up), the feminine is required? "al-shams ṭala'at" (the sun rose), the feminine is required.
Ibn Malik, listen to what he says:

"The feminine marking is only obligatory with a verb whose pronoun is attached……………"
So the feminine is required. When you say "qalat li-qawmiha Hind" (Hind said to her people), is the masculine and feminine both permitted? Yes, both the masculine and feminine are permitted, because of the separation. When you say "sārat al-sayyārah" (the car moved), both the masculine and feminine are permitted, because the feminine is not real. The explanation has ended. Do you have questions, or shall we move on?

* Student: The question is about the previous lesson, the tafsir.

* Shaykh: The previous is past, unless this question occurred to you at that time.

* Student: Yes, it occurred to me at that time. We said that the dead are not reviled or cursed, because there is no benefit in it. Some people have instituted innovations (bid'ah) in religion, and some people adhere to them. So, for one who keeps company with those who refute these innovators, who speaks ill of this man and may curse him for his evil deeds, is there, I mean, any justification?

* Shaykh: This is a vague question about something vague. Yes, a man wrote and another man said, what? Give me something specific.

* Student: Some people instituted innovations, for example an innovation, and some people hold on to this innovation.

* Shaykh: And what is this innovation?

* Student: An innovation they call the Tijani prayer, they call it the Tijani prayer.

* Shaykh: The Fatihah.

* Student: Like (...) its adherents. A person is now compelled to curse them.

* Shaykh: He curses the one who founded this innovation.

* Student: Do you not say anything about this?

* Shaykh: I do not see it, it's the same thing we said. If he deserves the curse, God has cursed him, whether you curse him or not. But you may curse, for example, the principle: you say, "this principle is accursed," or the group in general. Cursing a group in general is not a problem. You say, for example, "this group is accursed," "the Jews are accursed," "the Christians are accursed," and the like.

* Student: God Most High said in the Qur'an: ﴿Surely the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 18], and His words ﴿So We shall lay the curse of God upon the liars﴾ [Ali 'Imran 61]. Is this to be taken absolutely, so that if a person lies and his lie is established, he is liable to be cursed, and likewise the wrongdoer, or is there detail in the matter?

* Shaykh: It is permissible in a general sense: you say, "the curse of God upon the wrongdoers." As for ﴿So We shall lay the curse of God upon the liars﴾, this is specific to the mubahalah (mutual imprecation).

* Student: If we forbid cursing a specific person, then let us also refrain from declaring a specific person a disbeliever (takfir) if his origin was Muslim, such as the extremist philosophers and the atheists, because if we judge their disbelief individually, we have judged them to the Fire.

* Shaykh: No. Once we judge their disbelief individually, it does not follow that we must curse them. Why? But as for calling them innovators and misguided, we must call them innovators and misguided, and we declare them disbelievers individually, yes indeed. However, on condition that the proof has been established against them. We do not know about these philosophers whether they were reasoned with, whether the truth was made clear to them, and now they have died.

* Student: Many of them, O Shaykh, are recorded in their biographies. For example, Ibn Kathir said in the biography of Ibn Sina that it was said (...) at the end of his life, and perhaps he repented. So this possibility, does it not prevent us from declaring them disbelievers, since disbelieving statements are established from them?

* Shaykh: In any case, as I said: we say, whoever says such-and-such is a disbeliever.

* Student: (...) ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾ [al-Ma'idah 13]. It is said that it is abrogated (mansukhah), and many (...) exegetes explained it in this sense by the verse of the sword. So what do we say about other than this..?

* Shaykh: We have not discussed this. We said that some exegetes said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword, and we made clear that this is an error, and we said: al-Ma'idah is among the last of what was revealed.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed. ﴿And remember when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with terrible torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a great trial from your Lord. (49) And when We divided the sea for you and delivered you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were watching. (50) And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers. (51) Then We pardoned you after that, that perhaps you would be grateful. (52) And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, that perhaps you would be guided. (53) And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves; that is better for you with your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [al-Baqarah 49–54].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed. God, blessed and exalted is He, said, reminding the Children of Israel of what God bestowed upon them. He said: ﴿And when We delivered you﴾, that is, remember when We delivered you, that is, remember this time in which your deliverance occurred. ﴿Delivered you﴾ means: We rescued you.

* Student: We stopped at the words of God Most High: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾.

* Shaykh: Are you sure?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. That is: intercession will not be accepted on behalf of a soul. Intercession is mediation for another to bring a benefit or repel a harm. This is intercession: mediation for another to bring a benefit or repel a harm. The intercession of the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, for the people of the Standing (on the Day of Resurrection), is that judgment be passed among them, by way of repelling harm, because they will suffer distress and grief beyond endurance. His intercession, peace be upon him, for the people of Paradise, that they enter it, is by way of bringing benefits. Intercession revolves around this. On the Day of Resurrection, no intercession will be accepted from any soul. ﴿Nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾, that is, nothing equal to it will be taken from it, meaning no ransom will be taken from it. It cannot be interceded for, nor can it offer a ransom. You know now that if a person is seized for a sin and then brings a ransom, it may be accepted from him, and if he asks a person of standing to intercede for him, it may be accepted. But on the Day of Resurrection there is neither intercession nor compensation. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾, that is, they will not be protected from God's punishment. In His words ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ there is a shift (iltifat) from address to third person, because He said ﴿And fear a Day﴾, and He did not say "nor will you be helped," but said ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, and made the pronoun plural, because ﴿soul﴾ ... ﴿soul﴾ is indefinite in the context of negation, so it is general.

In this verse: a warning about the Day of Resurrection, which occurs often in the Qur'an, such as His words ﴿And fear a Day on which you will be returned to God﴾ [al-Baqarah 281], and His words ﴿a Day that will make children grey-haired﴾ [al-Muzzammil 17].

* Among the benefits of this verse: no soul will avail another soul in anything, unlike this world, where one may avail another, but on the Day of Resurrection, no.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: intercession is not accepted for a guilty soul. This is like His words ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir 48]. But is this to be taken absolutely? We say: as for the people of innovation, they said it is absolute, and that the guilty person will not benefit from intercession. These are the Mu'tazilah. The second are the Khawarij. The correct view is that the one for whom intercession does not benefit is the disbeliever. The disbeliever will not benefit from intercession. As for non-disbelievers, the texts show that intercession may be accepted. On this basis, the generality in His words ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ is restricted by what the other texts indicate, namely that sinners may be interceded for. The hadiths on intercession are mutawatir (mass-transmitted), as has often been recited to you:

"Among what is mass-transmitted: the hadith 'whoever lies...', and whoever builds a mosque for God seeking reward; and the vision (of God), and intercession, and the Basin, and wiping over the two leather socks; and these are some of them."
The evidence is his word: intercession.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of intercession, and that some of it is accepted and some is not accepted.

If someone says: your affirmation of intercession may contradict the words of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿There is no trade in it, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾ [al-Baqarah 254], here He negates intercession, and it is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it is general. We say: Praise be to God, this is not the first text to which specification applies. The meaning is: no intercession without God's permission, and the many texts indicating that intercession is established by God's permission qualify that.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: on the Day of Resurrection there is no ransom. A person cannot offer a ransom by which he may be compensated, because of His words ﴿nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾.

* Among its benefits: no one will be helped on the Day of Resurrection if he is among the sinners. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another? (25) Rather, they are that day in submission﴾ [al-Saffat 25–26]. So no one will help anyone on the Day of Resurrection, neither the false gods, nor the masters, nor the wicked, nor others.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 49:**

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. Meaning: remember when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh. To whom is the address directed? To the Children of Israel, as evidenced by His words ﴿from the people of Pharaoh﴾. And ﴿We saved you﴾ means We delivered you from them and rescued you from their aggression and domination.

And His words ﴿from the people of Pharaoh﴾ mean his followers, his entourage and his henchmen, who carry out his orders by killing the sons of the Children of Israel and sparing their women. Is the intended meaning all of his followers, or only those followers who are close to him in treatment? The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it refers to all of his followers, and that Pharaoh's men do this, and likewise the "people of Pharaoh," his followers, transgress against the Children of Israel in Egypt. Then He said: ﴿who inflicted on you the terrible torment﴾, meaning: they inflicted it upon you. "Terrible torment" is an construction of a noun with its attribute, meaning the evil torment or the worst torment. Then He clarified this general statement with His words: ﴿slaughtering your sons and sparing your women﴾. In another verse: ﴿who inflicted on you the terrible torment and slaughtered your sons﴾ [Ibrahim 6], and in a third verse: ﴿who inflicted on you the terrible torment, killing your sons﴾ [al-A'raf 141]. Thus the punishments, or rather the aggression of the people of Pharaoh against the Children of Israel, take three forms:

The first form: killing by any means, by stoning, by strangling, by breaking the back, and the like.

The second: slaughtering, that they bring a person from the Children of Israel and slaughter him with a knife as a sheep is slaughtered.

The third: that they combine the terrible torment with slaughter, meaning, for example, that they beat them, squeeze their stomachs, cut their lips, and the like, and after that slaughter them. Thus they combine the two matters for them. Do not be surprised at this: there has occurred in this nation, I mean the nation of the call (to Islam), what is greater than that and worse than that. But the important point is that the torture and criminality that occurred from the people of Pharaoh against the Children of Israel are these three matters: slaughter, killing, and combining slaughter with terrible torment.

And His words: ﴿your sons and sparing your women﴾. Why were they empowered over the sons and yet the women were spared? ﴿sparing your women﴾ means they let them live; otherwise their lives already existed. Rather, they let them remain alive, while they killed the sons. Why? Some of the Israelites said: it was said to the people of Pharaoh that a boy would be born among the Children of Israel through whom your rule would end, so they began killing the sons out of fear that this boy would appear. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said by His decree that this boy would be raised in the lap of Pharaoh, because when his mother bore him, Allah revealed to her: "Nurse him." So she nursed him the colostrum that every newborn must have, and He said to her: ﴿If you fear for him, then cast him into the river﴾ [al-Qasas 7]. Her son. When she feared for him, she complied with Allah's command: she placed him in a chest and cast him into the river, that is, the sea, and this is from the perfection of her faith. But He said: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve. We will surely return him to you and make him among the messengers﴾ [al-Qasas 7]. So he fell into the hands of the people of Pharaoh: ﴿the people of Pharaoh picked him up so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. The lam here is for consequence (lam al-'aqibah), not for causation, because the people of Pharaoh did not pick him up for this purpose; they picked him up, and so he became an enemy and a grief for them. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the story, and we are not concerned with its context, because it is well known and is not before us tonight. The important point is that this is what some scholars said, based on reports transmitted from the Children of Israel. Why? What did they say?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Why do they slaughter their sons and spare the women?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Good. They said: they kill the sons so that this boy will not come out. But there is another view that may be even more striking, which is that they slaughter the sons and spare the women in order to have complete control, so that the community weakens and the women are compelled to serve the people of Pharaoh. This is the utmost humiliation: that one who was your enemy violates the honour of your women. This is the utmost humiliation. And if what was said about the Children of Israel is sound, we would say: it is possible that both are intended, indeed it is possible that both are meant.

﴿And in that there was a great trial from your Lord﴾. "Trial" means test. And His words ﴿in that﴾ use the plural "dhalikum," although the demonstrative noun is singular "dha." Why? We say: the demonstrative noun follows what it points to, and the kaf attached to it follows the addressee. Pay attention to the rule: the demonstrative follows what is indicated, and the kaf attached to it follows the one addressed. So if you point to two things while addressing one person, you say "dhanika." Allah said: ﴿These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Qasas 32]. And if you point to one thing while addressing two people, what do you say?

* Student: Dhalikuma.

* The Shaykh: You say "dhalikuma," as Yusuf said: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾ [Yusuf 37]. Here, in ﴿in that there was a trial﴾, what is pointed to?

* Student: One.

* The Shaykh: One, it refers to the torment. And the addressee?

* Students: Plural.

* The Shaykh: Plural, because He said: ﴿And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. So His words ﴿in that there was a trial﴾ mean a test and a tribulation from your Lord, who has dominion over the heavens and the earth and who disposes of you as He wills. For this reason He said: ﴿a trial from your Lord﴾, and did not say "from Allah." He said "from your Lord," indicating that since He is the Lord, He has the right to do with us whatever He wills. ﴿Great﴾ means greatly magnified and grand. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has spoken the truth: it is a great trial. We ask Allah to protect us from the evils of trials. It means that an enemy is empowered over you who slaughters you as lambs are slaughtered, and spares the women, violating their honour, humiliating them, and making them servants in his possession, whereas she was a queen in her own house before her guardian was slaughtered. This is a great trial. We ask Allah for safety.

* Student: May Allah reward you well. Now what is said about their killing according to the words of the Children of Israel, that (...)? Because of their faith, some people say that all the Children of Israel are believers.

* The Shaykh: This is not correct, because there is no war between them.

* Student: What is the meaning of inspiration of inspiration (wahy ilhami)?

* The Shaykh: Ilhami inspiration is that which is not a law, meaning for the benefit of the one to whom it is revealed, like His words: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ [al-Nahl 68]. He inspired it, because the root of ilham in the language is informing quickly and secretly; this is its root in the language. So when Allah inspires, for example, this bee, it does not mean that He sent Jibril to reveal to it, but rather He placed understanding in it and inspired it with its interests.

* Student: The intercession of the Prophet ﷺ for Abu Talib?

* The Shaykh: This is specific to the Messenger and also specific to Abu Talib. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not intercede for his father, but he interceded for his uncle, as we mentioned previously. We said: the intercession for his uncle was not because he was his uncle, but because of what he did of supporting Islam and defending it. And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is Most Appreciative and Forbearing; He permitted His Prophet to intercede for this man specifically.

* Student: May Allah reward you well. How is it, when Allah promised Musa's mother with His words: ﴿We will surely return him to you and make him among the messengers﴾, how is this inspiration? She explicitly has knowledge of the unseen.

* The Shaykh: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Musa: nurse him﴾, meaning Allah cast into her understanding and her mind that she should do this, and likewise He inspired into her heart this certainty that He would return him to her and make him among the messengers.

* Student: We said: the lam of the verb ﴿li-yakuna﴾, the lam here, they say: lam al-juhud.

* The Shaykh: What?

* The student: ﴿li-yakuna﴾, lam al-'aqibah.

* The Shaykh: Where?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, no, may Allah bless you: lam al-juhud is the one preceded by a negated kana.

* The student: This is called lam al-'aqibah.

* The Shaykh: This is lam al-'aqibah only. Clear?

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Is intelligence (dhaka') known or not known? Well, whoever does not know intelligence is not intelligent. Intelligence is known, isn't it? The word "zaka'" means purification of the soul, that is, they did not give their souls their purification through self-purification; they were given understanding but were not given knowledge, because they have no knowledge. For this reason you hardly find in the books of the theologians (ahl al-kalam) a verse of the Book of Allah that they cite as evidence, nor a hadith from the Messenger of Allah. ﴿They slaughtered your sons and spared your women﴾ [al-Baqarah 49]. This is the verse through which Allah reminds the Children of Israel, saying: ﴿when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh﴾.

He said: ﴿And in that there was a great trial from your Lord﴾, meaning: in what occurred there was a great trial from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, tests whom He wills, either with good or with evil, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned﴾ [al-Anbiya' 35]. The believer, praise be to Allah, may Allah make us and you among the believers, when he is tested with this or with that, attains the highest stations: if prosperity reaches him, he is thankful, and if adversity reaches him, he is patient, and it is good for him in both cases. But among people, when adversity tests one, he turns back on his heels, may Allah save us, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one who worships Allah on an edge﴾ [al-Hajj 11], meaning on the brink. ﴿If good befalls him, he is reassured by it; but if an trial befalls him, he turns back on his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. So Allah the Exalted tests the human being with this and with that, so hold fast to patience and await relief, for Allah the Exalted may test, and He, Glorified and Exalted, is Most Wise with His servants. And His words ﴿great﴾: Allah magnified it because it is truly great, that an enemy be empowered over them who slaughters their sons, spares their women, leaves the women widowed, and leaves the men who defend them destroyed, by slaughter at one time and by killing at another.

* Among the benefits of this verse: addressing the latter part of the nation with what was a blessing for its earlier part. This is because of His words ﴿And [remember] when We saved you﴾. It is known that those in the time of the Messenger ﷺ did not directly experience this deliverance, but it befell their fathers and ancestors. So the good that came to the earlier part of this nation is attained by the latter part of this nation. On this basis we may say: we were victorious at Badr, we were victorious at Hunayn, and we were victorious in the conquest (of Makkah), because the victory of our predecessors is a victory for us.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is obligatory upon the later generations of the nation to thank Allah for His blessing upon the earlier part of the nation, because Allah the Exalted reminds them of this so that they may thank Him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Exalted may empower some people over others, as He empowered Pharaoh over the Children of Israel, and this is the custom of Allah among the earlier and later generations. For this reason, when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Say: He is the One able to send upon you a punishment from above you﴾, the Prophet ﷺ said: "I seek refuge in Your Face," and when He said: ﴿or from beneath your feet﴾, he said: "I seek refuge in Your Face," and when He said: ﴿or to confuse you in factions and make you taste the violence of one another﴾, he said: "This is easier," or he said: "This is lesser." [This was narrated by al-Bukhari (4628) from the hadith of Jabir.] And there is no doubt that it is easier and lesser, because a person, in what he is afflicted with from the violence of others, may defend himself and be given victory, but when it comes from Allah from above or from beneath, he cannot. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "This is easier," or he said: "This is lesser."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the intensity of Pharaoh's rage against the Children of Israel, in that he used this punishment against them, which is: slaughtering the sons and sparing the women. There is no doubt that this is a tremendous infliction, neither upon the dead nor upon the living. We ask Allah for safety and well-being.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, blessed and exalted, tests the human being with what he dislikes, so that He, may He be exalted, may know who is patient and who is not patient: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those who strive among you and the patient, and We will test your reports﴾ [Muhammad 31].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the requirements of general lordship (rububiyyah 'ammah) is that Allah tests the human being with what he dislikes. In special lordship (rububiyyah khassah), Allah mentions what the person loves, whereas in general lordship it occurs both in what the servant dislikes and in what the servant loves, as shown by His words: ﴿And in that there was a great trial from your Lord﴾.

* Among its benefits: the greatness of this trial that befell the Children of Israel, and likewise if it befell others, it is a great trial. A mother witnesses her son being killed before her or slaughtered as a sheep is slaughtered, and likewise a daughter witnesses her father being treated in this way. There is no doubt that this is a great trial.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾. That is, remember another blessing, when He rescued you from the people of Pharaoh. Allah parted the sea for them. *Faraqa* means "to separate," and this happened when it split. He split the sea for them, meaning He divided and cleaved it so that they crossed through it and were saved. ﴿When We divided the sea for you﴾. And when did this happen? It happened when Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to travel by night with the believers who were with him, fearing the people of Pharaoh. When Pharaoh saw what the sorcerers had done, he gathered the people and said: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band, and indeed they have enraged us, and indeed we are a vigilant multitude﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 54–56]. He gathered the people and went out from Egypt. Allah revealed to Moses that he should travel by night with His believing servants toward the east. So he set out with them, and Pharaoh pursued them with his armies. When they reached the sea, ﴿the companions of Moses said, "Indeed, we are overtaken." He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me"﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 61–62]. Observe the difference between Moses' strength of trust in Allah and the weakness of the believers, although they were believers. But in hardships, firmness may be lost. ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ It is as if he were saying: Allah did not command me to set out except that He would guide me. So Allah commanded him to strike the sea with his staff, and he struck it, and in an instant the sea split. How many paths were there? There were twelve paths. And in an instant the sea dried up. Glory be to Allah, in an instant. Each divided part became like a towering mountain, that is, like a great mountain. Some of the scholars said that Allah, glorified and exalted, wanted the Children of Israel to be reassured, so He placed in each section of this water, which had become like mountains, a small opening, a gap, so that some of them could see one another and be reassured by one another. In any case, when Moses and his people had fully exited, Pharaoh entered, and Allah commanded that the sea close over them, and it closed.

For this reason He reminds them of this blessing once more: ﴿When We divided the sea for you﴾, that is, We split it for you until you crossed it. ﴿And We rescued you﴾, meaning We delivered you from drowning. ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾. Drowning is well known. The "people of Pharaoh" here includes first and foremost Pharaoh himself, but He expressed it with "the people of" in place of Pharaoh in order that no one would think that the drowning or the punishment was confined to Pharaoh alone. So He said "the people of Pharaoh." This is more concise than "Pharaoh and his household." The expression could be: "We drowned Pharaoh," or "We drowned the people of Pharaoh," or "We drowned Pharaoh and his household." As for "the people of Pharaoh," it is known that they were drowned only because Pharaoh followed them. Is it possible for the branch to be drowned without the root? It is not possible. For this reason Allah said of Pharaoh: ﴿He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and will lead them into the Fire, and wretched is the destination to which they are led﴾ [Hud 98]. Allah drowned the people of Pharaoh until they were all destroyed. When Pharaoh was overtaken by drowning, he said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit﴾ [Yunus 90]. It was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters. So today We will save you in your body that you may be a sign to those who come after you﴾ [Yunus 91–92]. That is, to those who remain after you. None remained except the Children of Israel, because all of the people of Pharaoh drowned. Allah, mighty and majestic, only rescued his body so that the Children of Israel would be assured of his drowning, because the Children of Israel had been terrified of him with great terror. Allah showed them his body so that they would be certain that he had drowned, for if they had not seen his body, every possibility would have come to them that he had escaped and would emerge. So Allah, exalted is He, showed them his body drowned, for their reassurance.

And His saying: ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on﴾. The clause here is circumstantial (*hali*), meaning: while the situation was that you were looking on. This is among the greatest blessings: that Allah destroys your enemy while you watch him. This is because your joy and happiness will increase when you see your enemy torn to every shred, while you have been delivered from this. For this reason Allah reminded them of this blessing, namely that their enemy was drowned while they were looking on.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: reminding the Children of Israel of what Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon them when He parted the sea for them. The reason the address is directed to those who were present in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) is that Allah's favor upon the earlier generation is also a favor upon its later generation. This is one aspect. There is another aspect I will mention now, which applies to what came before: those present here are the offspring of the earlier ones, and if the earlier ones had perished, the later ones would not have come into existence. Therefore the rescue of the first generation is in reality a rescue for them, though indirect. So the address to these people concerning the earlier blessings of rescue from drowning or from Pharaoh's killing of them has two aspects. The first aspect: what happened to the first of the community applies to its last. The second aspect: these people are the descendants of the earlier ones, and if the earlier ones had perished, these would not have survived; so in their survival is the survival of these later ones.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the demonstration of the power of Allah, mighty and majestic.

And you had escaped from this. For this reason Allah reminded them of this blessing, namely that their enemy was drowned while they were looking on.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: reminding the Children of Israel of what Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon them when He parted the sea for them.

The reason the address is directed to those who were present in the time of the Messenger is that Allah's favor upon the earlier generation is also a favor upon its later generation. This is one aspect. There is another aspect I will mention now, which applies to what came before: those present here are the offspring of the earlier ones, and if the earlier ones had perished, the later ones would not have existed. Therefore the rescue of the first generation is in reality a rescue for them, though indirect. So the address to these people concerning the earlier blessings of rescue from drowning or from the killing by Pharaoh has two aspects: the first aspect is that what happened to the first of the community is for its last. What?

* Student: A blessing for its last.

* Shaykh: So it is for its last.

The second aspect: these people are the descendants of the earlier ones, and if the earlier ones had perished, these would not have survived; so in their survival is the survival of these later ones.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the power of Allah, mighty and majestic. Its explanation: this flowing substance, which is water, was torn apart the moment Moses struck it with his staff. You know the Red Sea. How long is it? Its length is naturally long. But its width, for example from Africa to Asia, is long. I do not know exactly, but there is no doubt that ships sail on it. Yet in one instant, with one strike, the entire sea split and became a dry path. In this is evidence of the perfection of Allah's power, mighty and majestic.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the natural philosophers and their claim that things operate according to their natures, and that water is fluid and, if it freezes in cold, it freezes. We say to them: Allah, glorified and exalted, created natures for water, and He, glorified and exalted, is able to change these natures.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a thing which is known may be mentioned in an indefinite manner. This is due to His saying ﴿the sea﴾, because the *alif-lam* in "the sea" is for mental reference (*al-'ahd al-dhihni*), meaning a known referent in the mind. If we said that it is for generality, the mind would go in every direction: which sea is it? But because it is known, no specification is needed, being sufficient with what? With *alif-lam* that is for mental reference.

* A corollary of this benefit: if a person said, "By Allah, I will speak to the judge today about what happened in the town," then went to a man who is not one of the legal judges, meaning from the tribe known as the judge, and informed one of them of what occurred, would he be truthful in his oath or would he have broken it?

* Students: He would have broken it.

* Shaykh: He has broken it; he would be one who breaks his oath, because the apparent meaning of the expression is that *alif-lam* is for mental reference.

But know that an oath is restricted by intention. It is good here to digress on this subject. In oaths one refers first to the intention of the swearer if the wording allows it, then to the cause of the oath and what provoked it, the cause; then after that to specification; then to what the wording may bear. There are four levels. In oaths, one refers before anything else to intention. Then what?

* Students: The cause.

* Shaykh: Then specification, then what the wording may bear. I have mentioned intention first because Allah has stated it: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have intended in your oaths﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 89]. He made the reference what the person has resolved upon. In the second verse He said: ﴿but He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾ [Al-Baqarah 225].

If a man said, "By Allah, I will surely spend the night only on a stake, by Allah I will sleep tonight only on a stake," we would say: what is this talk? Only birds sleep on stakes. Do you know what a stake is?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: It is a...

* Student: A piece of firewood.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, a wooden peg driven into the wall, fixed in the wall so that clothes may be hung on it. So he said, "By Allah, I will not sleep tonight except on a stake." So, my boy, how can one sleep on a stake? Are you a bird? Then he went to a mountain around it and slept on it. Did he fulfill his oath or not?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: Why? Because this is what he intended, even though the apparent wording is otherwise. But this is what he intended. Is it clear?

And if he said, "By Allah, I will sleep tonight only on my bed," then went outside the town and slept on the ground, what of it, since he did not spread anything? He says: I intended that the earth is my bed, because Allah says: ﴿He made the earth a bed for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 22]. In any case, if the wording allows it, one refers to intention.

If he said, "By Allah, I will buy bread today," then went and bought a car, the day ended and he had not bought a single loaf. We say: now you owe expiation for breaking the oath. He says: I intended by bread a car. Is that acceptable?

* Students: It is not acceptable.

* Shaykh: Why?

* Students: The wording does not allow it.

* Shaykh: The wording does not allow it at all, so it is not accepted.

After that comes the cause. This is also important, and many people fall into it regarding divorce. For example, a man says to his wife: "If you speak to your brother, you are divorced," based on the fact that someone told him that your wife's brother is the one who is corrupting her against you. So he said, on the basis of this: "If you speak to your brother, you are divorced." Then it became clear that her brother is innocent of that, so she is not divorced. If she speaks to him, she is not divorced. Why? Because the cause turned out to be contrary to what the divorce was based upon.

Likewise, if he said, "By Allah, I will not enter this town," on the basis that the governor of the town is seeking him, looking for him. Yes. He said, "By Allah I will not enter it," then it became clear that the governor of the town is not seeking him. Does he enter the town or not?

* Students: He enters.

* Shaykh: The cause? Because it was based on what? On a cause that did not exist.

Specification. Specification is like having a small young animal, what is a *tali*?

* Students: A lamb.

* Shaykh: No, that is not a lamb; the young of sheep. He said, "By Allah, I will not eat the meat of this lamb," then the young animal grew and became a sheep, became a ram, and he ate it. Does he break the oath or not?

* Students: He does not break it.

* Shaykh: Specification, my brothers? If he specified, saying "this," then he breaks it, unless he intended: as long as it is in this state.

Another example: he said, "By Allah, I will not wear this shirt," and he specified it, then he altered it and made it trousers, and wore it. If he wore it, he owes expiation, because he specified, saying "this shirt," unless he intended that as long as it is a shirt, then no. Is it clear?

After this, we return to what?

* Student: What the wording may bear.

* Shaykh: To what the wording may bear. The word has a meaning in language, a meaning in the Shari'ah, and a meaning in custom. Sometimes all three coincide, and sometimes they differ. If all three coincide, the matter is clear: "heaven," "earth," "prayer." No, prayer differs between language and Shari'ah. If they coincide, the matter is clear. But if they differ in oaths, which do we give precedence? Do we give precedence to custom, or to language, or to the Shari'ah?

* Student: The Shari'ah.

* Shaykh: No, we give precedence to custom. So if he said, "By Allah, I will surely give a sheep to so-and-so," then he gave him a female goat, would he have fulfilled his oath or not?

* Students: (...)

* Shaykh: The custom among us is that he has not fulfilled it, because among us "sheep" means the female of the sheep, and this is a female goat, so he has not fulfilled it. Unless he says, "I intended by 'sheep' its linguistic meaning," then in that case he has fulfilled it, because he intended the linguistic meaning.

Likewise, if he said, "By Allah, I will not pray over so-and-so," then he went and prayed over him, does he break it or not?

* Student: He breaks it.

* Shaykh: He breaks it. But if the man says, "I meant supplication: I do not supplicate for him, and I also intended not to supplicate for him outside of the funeral prayer over him," we say: intention takes precedence over everything.

In any case, are the levels of oaths five?

* Students: Four.

* Shaykh: Four.

* Shaykh: The first?

* Students: Intention.

* Shaykh: Then?

* Students: The cause.

* Shaykh: The cause, the cause of the oath. Then?

* Students: Specification.

* Shaykh: Specification. Then?

* Students: What the wording may bear.

* Shaykh: What the wording may bear. Yes.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers. Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:51–52]. And ﴿And when We gave Moses the Scripture and the criterion that you might be guided.﴾ [2:53]. And ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator." And He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [2:54].

Shaykh: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights.﴾ Allah had originally set the appointment at thirty nights and completed it with ten, so the appointed time with his Lord was completed at forty nights. Allah set this period for his intimate communion (munajah) with Him. Moses appointed his brother Harun over his people, saying: ﴿Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters.﴾ [al-A'raf 7:142]. So Harun was Moses' successor over his people when he went to the appointment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Then the Children of Israel, out of their obstinacy and stubbornness, took a calf made of gold and worshipped it as a god. The originator of this idea was a man called al-Samiri. They fashioned from the jewelry, which it is said they had taken from the jewelry of the family of Pharaoh, a calf-shaped bull, and they made it hollow so that wind would enter from the back and exit from the mouth. When the wind entered, they heard from it a sound like the lowing of a bull. Al-Samiri said: "This is your god and the god of Moses. Moses went off seeking his god but forgot him and strayed." Then the thirty nights passed and became more, and he was still seeking this god, but he had forgotten and strayed. "This is your god and the god of Moses." Harun kept reminding them of this and saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command.﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:90]. He was a prophet, but they insisted out of arrogance and said: ﴿We will never cease being devoted to it until Moses returns to us.﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:91]. They persisted in worshipping the calf. Moses, peace be upon him, returned and found them in a state that was not pleasing, contrary to what he had left them upon, and he became angry. He threw down the tablets, which were the Torah that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had written with His own hand, throwing them out of intense anger. He seized his brother by the head and beard, dragging him toward himself forcefully, saying: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:92–93]. This was from intense anger; otherwise, in a state of contentment, he would surely have asked first, "How did they go astray?" before saying: ﴿What prevented you…﴾. But man is a human being, affected by what affects human states. ﴿[Harun] said, "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:94]. Note that he feared Moses, peace be upon him, would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel," because if he had spoken or increased his admonition, they would have split into two groups: one group with Harun and another with al-Samiri. So he, peace be upon him, refrained out of fear of this. Nevertheless, they were also insistent upon what they were doing; they took it as a god until they worshipped it. The story is set out in full in Surah Ta-Ha.

They took it as a god; therefore He said: ﴿Then you took the calf after him.﴾ ﴿The calf﴾ is the first object of ﴿you took﴾, and the second object is omitted; the implied meaning is: "Then you took the calf as a god." His words ﴿after him﴾ indicate that they did not take it immediately, but there was an interval: as I told you, when the period set by Moses, peace be upon him, had passed, and Allah had added to it, they said: "This is the god, but he has forgotten."

His words ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾: the waw here is for circumstance (hal), a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿you took﴾, meaning: "while the situation was that you were wrongdoers," with no excuse for you. And how could they have an excuse when their prophet Harun was saying: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command.﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:90].

After this ugly, monstrous act, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that.﴾ Look at His words ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾: were they wrongdoers to themselves, or to others? They were wrongdoers to themselves, for every disobedient person wrongs himself; if the harm of his disobedience extends to others, he has wronged both himself and others.

﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ means: We overlooked this act and lifted the punishment from you. ﴿that you might be grateful﴾ means: in order that you might give thanks. Here "la'alla" (perhaps/so that) indicates purpose (ta'lil). As we mentioned before, la'alla has several meanings, among them: purpose, which is very common in the Noble Quran; hope; wishing; apprehension and fear; and expectation. All of these are known from context.

His words ﴿that you might be grateful﴾: gratitude (shukr) is righteous action; this is how it appears in the Quran. The evidence is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying, 'O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds' [23:51], and He said regarding the believers: 'Eat of the good things We have provided you and give thanks to Allah' [2:172]."[[Reported by Muslim (1015/65).]] This indicates that gratitude is righteous action, and that is undoubtedly so.

Know that gratitude is only given in return for a favour, unlike praise (hamd). Praise is for the perfection of the one praised and for his bounty, so its cause is more general than gratitude; but gratitude is more general than praise in terms of its connection to the heart, the tongue, and the limbs, as the poet said:

"Blessings from me have benefited you in three ways: my hand, my tongue, and my heart concealed."

In these two verses there are several benefits. Among them: clarifying the faults of the Children of Israel, for they took the calf as a god when their prophet was absent.

Among its benefits: affirmation of the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as shown by His words ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾; an appointment is generally made between two parties by speech. Moreover, in that appointment Allah spoke to him, so much so that Moses, peace be upon him, out of his intense longing to see Allah, said: ﴿My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may look at You.﴾ [al-A'raf 7:143].

Among them: clarifying the foolishness of the wrathful nation, the Jews, when they took the calf as a god. What is astonishing is that they themselves fashioned the calf with their hands and then took it as a god. But do not be surprised: whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him. The pagan Arabs did something similar or worse. It is said that they would make a god from dates, and when they became hungry, they ate it. They did not claim it would bring them provision; they knew it could not possess that, yet they ate it. They also said that when they landed in a land, they would take four stones, choose the best of them to be a god, and place the other three as supports for the cooking pot on which they set it.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Children of Israel had no excuse for taking the calf as a god, because the proof had been established against them, as shown by His words ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾.

Does it follow from this verse that if they had taken the calf as a god without wrongdoing, they would not have been blamed? Or is it said that this is only a description of their state? Both are possible. It may be a description of their state, that they took it as a god without excuse; and it may be evidence that whoever is excused is not held accountable. The words of Allah support this: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sent to their mother [city] a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We would not destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Qasas 28:59].

Accordingly, the verse provides evidence that whoever commits a bad deed, whether shirk or less, while being excused, has no punishment. Then, if he claims to be Muslim, he is judged outwardly as a Muslim; and if he claims another religion and the religion of Islam has not reached him, he is treated in this world according to the religion he follows, and his affair in the Hereafter is with whom? With Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is the detailed ruling on the issue of excuse by ignorance.

If he calls himself a Muslim, bears witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishes prayer, gives zakat, performs Hajj and Umrah, and says he is a Muslim, but there is some shirk in him without knowledge, having lived in this land where this shirk is practised and not knowing it is shirk, then he is treated how? As a Muslim according to his outward state; and likewise, in the Hereafter Allah will not hold him accountable, because he is excused.

As for one who is excused but does not claim Islam and adheres to a specific religion, he is treated in this world as disbelievers, meaning the people of that religion; and in the Hereafter it is said: his affair is with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Among the benefits of the second verse: clarifying Allah's favour upon the Children of Israel, that after they committed this shirk founded on error in religion and foolishness in intellect, Allah pardoned them: ﴿Then We pardoned you.﴾

Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah pardons all sins without exception, but after repentance, as Allah said: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ [az-Zumar 39:53].

But if someone says: there is nothing in the noble verse indicating that they repented, it is answered: another verse shows that they turned in repentance to Allah and returned to Him, and that a cloud overshadowed them, and they were commanded to kill one another. When Allah knew from them the sincerity of their return to Him, and that they complied even to the point of killing, Allah pardoned them.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever is blessed by Allah with a religious blessing must give thanks for it, just as for a worldly blessing, as shown by His words ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful.﴾ Which is greater as a favour? The religious blessing is undoubtedly greater. So if Allah has favoured you with a religious blessing, consider it among the greatest blessings and give thanks for it; and thanks for religious blessings is of their kind. For example, whoever Allah has blessed with knowledge, thanks for that is to teach and spread his knowledge; likewise, whoever Allah has blessed with wealth, thanks for that wealth is to give charity from it, help the poor, keep the ties of kinship, and be dutiful to his parents.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming causes and wisdom in the acts of Allah. Where is this derived from? From His words ﴿that you might be grateful﴾. There is no doubt for us that all of Allah's acts and rulings are founded on causes and interests, though some of them are known and some are not. As for one who says that Allah's acts and rulings are not based on wisdom nor have any cause, he is undoubtedly astray in his religion and foolish in his intellect.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers. Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:51–52]. And ﴿And when We gave Moses the Scripture and the criterion that you might be guided.﴾ [2:53]. And ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator." And He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [2:54].

Then He, mighty and majestic, said, explaining another of the greatest blessings: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾. "Ātaynā Mūsā" means "We gave Moses." Ātaynā with the long alif takes two objects, unlike atynā, which takes only one object, because ātā with the long alif means "gave" (a'ṭā), while atā means "came" (jā'a). He says: ﴿We gave Moses the Book﴾, meaning We gave him it. The alif-lām in "al-Kitāb" is for a known reference (al-'ahd). Which known references? The mental (dhihnī) one, meaning the Book known to you, which is the Torah. It was called a "kitāb" (book) because it is written, for God wrote the Torah with His own hand, may He be exalted.

﴿And the Criterion﴾: the waw is a conjunction particle, and "al-Furqān" is conjoined to "al-Kitāb." Is it something other than it, or is it the same, being an instance of conjoining an attribute to the thing it describes? The answer is the second: al-Furqān is the very same as al-Kitāb, for the Torah is a furqān, by which God distinguished between truth and falsehood, between justice and injustice, between the friends of God and the enemies of God, and so on through everything by which distinction and differentiation occur. On this basis, its conjunction is of the type of conjoining an attribute to the thing described. Have you not seen the words of God, blessed and exalted: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who decreed and then guided﴾ [al-A'lā 1–3]? "Who decreed and then guided" is God, mighty and majestic, but this is an instance of conjoining an attribute to an attribute.

He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿So that you may be guided﴾. "La'alla" here expresses causation, as was mentioned before. "Tahtadūn" means you take the path of guidance. The guidance meant here, which God mentioned, is both guidance of direction (hidāyat al-irshād) and guidance of success (hidāyat al-tawfīq), because what Moses was given was knowledge, and whoever is guided by it has knowledge, and likewise knowledge yields action for whoever is granted success. So we interpret "guidance" here as what? As the guidance of knowledge and the guidance of success, the knowledge-based and the practical.

* In the noble verse there is evidence for several benefits:

* First: that Moses was a prophet, indeed a messenger, because God gave him the Book, and everyone to whom God gives the Book is a messenger, as He, exalted, said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 25].

* Among them: praise of the Torah, in that God named it a furqān.

* Among them: the wisdom in giving Moses the Book and the Criterion, which is guidance.

* Among them: that knowledge is a cause of guidance, as indicated by the causal "so that" in His words ﴿so that you may be guided﴾. But must the cause always be accompanied by its effect, or might an impediment exist? An impediment may exist, and so it cannot be objected that we find among scholars those who were not guided. We say: that is due to an impediment; otherwise the basic principle is that knowledge is the cause of guidance and that guidance occurs through knowledge, but there may be hindrances and diversions that cause a person not to benefit from the knowledge God has given him, as is well known.

As for "tahtadūn," is the guidance meant here the guidance of knowledge, or knowledge together with success? Knowledge in every case, and success for whomever God wills, (...) for guidance; but among people there are those who are guided and those who are not.

Then He mentioned another blessing, saying: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves"﴾ ﴿And when Moses said﴾ means: remember when Moses said to his people. The "qawm" (people) means the tribe, and the jurists say that "qawm" refers to the fourth grandfather and those below him; these are the people in the Arabic language.

He said: ﴿to his people, "O my people"﴾. He addressed them with the description of peoplehood, out of affection, kindness, and to show that he was sincerely advising them, because a person gives sincere advice to his own people. ﴿"O my people, indeed you have wronged yourselves"﴾: the sentence is emphasized to clarify the reality of their condition. ﴿Wronged﴾ here means: you diminished yourselves of their due, because "zulm" (wronging) originally means diminishing. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therein in anything﴾ [al-Kahf 33], meaning: did not diminish. This is the original meaning, but it may be intended to mean more than mere diminishing. Here, ﴿you have wronged yourselves﴾ means you diminished yourselves of their due, and that is by violating monotheism.

Then he said: ﴿by your taking the calf﴾. The "ba'" here is causal (sababiyyah), meaning: because of your taking the calf. "Ittikhadh" (taking) is a verbal noun whose verb is "ittakhadha," and it is annexed to its agent; the "ka" is the agent, and ﴿the calf﴾ is the first object. What is the second object?
* Student: A god.
* Shaykh: It is omitted. What is its implied form?
* Student: A god.
* Shaykh: A god. You wronged yourselves by taking the calf as a god that you worship besides Allah.

This calf, as was previously mentioned, was a golden calf in form, and the one who led people astray with it was a man called al-Samiri. They took it as a god, and we seek refuge with Allah. Then Moses (ﷺ) guided them to escape this great wrong, saying: ﴿So turn in repentance to your Creator﴾. "Tubu" (turn in repentance) is an imperative meaning "return," because tawbah and awb mean returning to Allah the Exalted. Repentance is by turning toward Allah, by performing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. If the wrong was by neglecting an obligation, then repentance is by performing it; and if the wrong was by committing a sin, then repentance is by abandoning it and ceasing from it.

﴿So turn in repentance to your Creator﴾: he did not say "to Allah," nor "to your Lord," in order to emphasize their blame and reproach, because al-Bari' means the Creator who takes care of His creation, a creator who cares for them. It is as if he is saying: how do you take the calf as a god and abandon your Creator who takes care of you? This is like Elias's saying to his people: ﴿Do you invoke Ba'l and leave the best of creators?﴾ [as-Saffat 125]. ﴿To your Creator﴾ means your creator. What else?
* Student: The one who cares for you.
* Shaykh: The one who cares for you.

﴿Then kill﴾: the "fa'" here is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), because His saying ﴿kill﴾ explains what was general in His saying ﴿turn in repentance﴾. Accordingly, the "fa'" is explanatory, meaning: so repent by this description.

﴿kill yourselves﴾ means: let some of you kill one another. It does not mean that each one kills himself, by consensus; no exegete has said that the meaning of His saying ﴿kill yourselves﴾ is that each one kills himself. Rather, the meaning is: some of you kill others. A person kills his son, his father, his brother. The point is that you prepare yourselves and take weapons—daggers, knives, and swords—and each of you attacks the other and kills him. Do you understand?

The exegetes differed as to whether this killing happened in darkness or happened openly without darkness. It was said: when they were commanded to do so, they said: "We cannot kill one another; a person would look at his son and kill him, at his father and kill him, at his brother, at his friend. This is impossible." So Allah cast darkness upon them, and they began to kill one another without knowing who killed.

It was also said: rather, they were killed openly without darkness, and this is more eloquent as evidence of the soundness of their repentance: a person kills whoever is in front of him. When Moses (ﷺ) saw that they would stop—because when some of them kill others, who remains?
* Student: One remains.
* Shaykh: One remains. When he saw that they would stop, he implored Allah the Exalted to lift the burden from them, and they were commanded to restrain themselves. It was also said: rather, their weapons fell from their hands. Allah knows best. The point is that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that nothing happened—meaning no darkness or anything of the kind—and that they were commanded to kill one another. This is more eloquent as evidence of the truthfulness of their repentance and their return to Allah the Exalted.

Some scholars went to the view that the meaning is: the innocent among you kill the guilty; that is, those who called to the worship of the calf and clung to it are killed, and those who disavowed it kill. Allah knows best. But the first view is apparent, because the innocent killing the guilty is not evidence of the sincerity of the repentance of the guilty, since a person may be killed while still persisting in sin, and that does not indicate his repentance. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿That is better for you with your Creator﴾.
* Student: The Prophet (ﷺ) said that in a hadith?
* Shaykh: Yes, Moses said it.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. ﴿That is better for you with your Creator﴾. ﴿That is better for you﴾: the referent of "that" is the killing. Here He said ﴿that﴾ and did not say "that" (in the singular)? Why?
* Student: A group.
* Student: Because they are a people.
* Student: Similar to a group.
* Shaykh: Because it is similar to a group, no.
* Student: The predicate of a group.
* Shaykh: Wrong, pay attention. He said ﴿dhalikum﴾, not "dhalika," and it does not point to a group.
* Student: It addresses a group and points to one.
* Shaykh: Correct: it addresses a group and points to one, which is the killing. The referent is singular, masculine, which is the killing, and the addressee?
* Student: A group.
* Shaykh: A group, who are his people.

﴿That is better for you with your Creator﴾: His saying ﴿better for you﴾ means better than not repenting, or better than not killing. This is a superlative with something that has no counterpart in the other side at all. Do you understand? This use of the superlative where the other party has nothing of it is attested in the Arabic language. But some say that the superlative is negated here, and it serves as evidence for the existence of good in this matter without assuming a comparand. For example, someone may say: if they had not killed themselves, would there be any good in that?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: There is no good in it. Then why did He say ﴿that is better for you﴾? We answer with two responses:

The first: this falls under the category of the superlative with something that has no part at all in the comparand, like His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their place of repose﴾ [al-Furqan 24]: "better in resting place" than the people of the Fire, although the people of the Fire have no good in their resting place.

Others say that here it is not a superlative of this kind; rather, it describes the matter as good only, and it is not a case of a comparison between a preferred and a less preferred thing at all: ﴿That is better for you with your Creator﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said—we do not say "the Prophet (ﷺ) said"; we say "Allah the Exalted said"—: ﴿Then He turned to you in forgiveness﴾. Is this the focal point of the mention of the blessing or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because the first part, ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾, mentions the sin and repentance from it. But the blessing is by what?
* Student: By the repentance.
* Shaykh: By Allah's turning to them in forgiveness; therefore He said: ﴿Then He turned to you﴾. And Allah's turning to His servant means that He is pleased with him after anger, and that He turns toward him after having turned away from him and averted from him. Yes: ﴿Then He turned to you﴾ is the words of Allah.
* Student: (...) a promise from him (ﷺ).
* Shaykh: No. Remember Allah's blessing when He said: ﴿Then He turned to you﴾; it is from the words of Allah.

As for His saying ﴿He turned to you﴾: what is the meaning of "taba"? It means He turned toward you after having been averse to you; or the meaning is: He turned, that is, He accepted the repentance, He accepted the repentance from you. Accepting their repentance necessarily entails that Allah turns toward them.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾. "Huwa" is a pronoun of separation (damir fasl), which some grammarians call a pronoun of support (damir 'imad), because the predicate relies on it, and a pronoun of separation because it separates the attribute from the predicate.

We have mentioned that it has three benefits. Who will mention them? The pronoun of separation has three benefits, which we mentioned earlier. What are they?
* Student: Separation.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Specifying the predicate for what follows it.
* Shaykh: Yes, meaning: separation, specifying it for what follows it as a predicate (...), that is fine. And the third?
* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: Emphasis, yes.

His saying ﴿at-Tawwab﴾ is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah), and He did not say "at-ta'ib" (the one who repents). That is because "ta'ib" indicates the bare act, whereas "tawwab" indicates its abundance, indicating its abundance. Allah the Exalted is abundant in repentance: abundant in His turning to His servant, and abundant in repentance because of the many people He turns to among mankind. He turns repeatedly toward His servant and turns toward many individuals whose repentance is frequent; therefore the form "at-Tawwab" came.

His saying ﴿ar-Rahim﴾ means: the one possessing mercy that reaches the one who is shown mercy, because here it is an attribute resembling the active participle but indicating the act: that is, He, the Exalted, is Merciful, meaning He is actually Merciful, showing mercy in act.

The repentance of Allah the Exalted, the description of Allah with repentance: it should be known that Allah's repentance toward the servant is of two kinds: a repentance preceding the servant's repentance, and a repentance following it. As for His repentance preceding the servant's repentance, it is His granting him success in repenting. As for His repentance following the servant's repentance, it is the acceptance of the repentance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Certainly Allah turned in mercy to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ [at-Tawbah 117], up to His saying: ﴿and to the three who were left behind﴾ [at-Tawbah 118]; before it: ﴿Then He turned to them that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [at-Tawbah 118]. ﴿He turned to them that they might repent; indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾.
* Student: Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: A question about the calf: did this calf have some kind of life?
* Shaykh: No. Allah made it clear: ﴿it had a lowing sound﴾ [al-A'raf 148], and there was no life in it, because Allah said: ﴿a calf, a body﴾ [al-A'raf 148], meaning it had no spirit.
* Student: The saying of al-Samiri: ﴿So I took a handful from the footprint of the messenger﴾ [Ta-Ha 96], its interpretation (...) is correct?
* Shaykh: Allah knows best. It is one of the Isra'iliyyat, which one neither confirms nor denies. But the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that there was nothing in it but merely a sound, a sound like the lowing of a calf. As for whether it had a spirit, no; because describing it as a body is evidence that it had no spirit, since if it had been said merely "a calf," one would suppose that it had a spirit. So the description "a body" removes this illusion.
* Student: And the handful?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: This handful?
* Shaykh: We do not know what effect it had on it: whether it had a good effect, such as making it hollow and shaped, for instance, or whether this handful had an effect on the sound of the calf. Many exegetes say that this sound is not the natural thing for such an object, and that the wind enters from its back and exits from its mouth, so that it produces a sound.
* Student: Shaykh, what is the difference between repentance regarding the servant and repentance regarding Allah (...)?
* Shaykh: There is no difference between them; it is all return. Unless we say that repentance from Allah means accepting the servant's repentance, yes; then its meaning would be other than return. But if we say that Allah turned to them, meaning He returned from His aversion toward them by turning toward them, then its meaning is one.

He said: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses"﴾: meaning, remember also, O Children of Israel. The address is to those who were in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), but His favor upon the nation's first is a favor upon its last. ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until﴾: "lan" (never) negates, but does it imply perpetuity or not?
* Student: It does not imply it.
* Shaykh: It does not imply perpetuity, unless it is restricted by something that indicates it. But it has three cases: sometimes it is restricted by something indicating a limit, like His saying here: ﴿we will never believe you until we see Allah﴾, and ﴿we will never cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us﴾ [Ta-Ha 91]. These are clear: when it is restricted by something indicating a limit, it does not indicate perpetuity and does not admit perpetuity. Right?

Sometimes it is restricted by something indicating perpetuity, like His saying: ﴿And they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Baqarah 95].

The third: it comes unrestricted: "Such-and-such will never stand." So if context indicates that it implies perpetuity, it is for perpetuity; and if context indicates that it does not imply it, it is open to both. For example: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do﴾ [al-Baqarah 24]—what is this (...)?
* Student: Perpetuity.
* Shaykh: Perpetuity; there is no "abadan" in it.
* Student: The context.
* Shaykh: But the context requires that. So this is the ruling of "lan." That is why Ibn Malik said in al-Kafiyah:

"Whoever sees negation with 'lan' as perpetual, / Then reject his saying, and support the other."

His saying "reject" (ardud): because the Mu'tazilah, and rather the Ash'arites, say that "lan" is for perpetuity; for this reason they cited Allah's saying to Moses: ﴿You will never see Me﴾ [al-A'raf 143], to argue that Allah will never be seen, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. But their view is undoubtedly rejected.

So ﴿we will never believe you﴾ means: we will never submit, never accept, and never acknowledge to you what you have brought. ﴿Until we see Allah openly﴾: "see" means "perceive with the eye," and for this reason it takes only one object, because it is a visual seeing. Its doer is?
* Student: We.
* Shaykh: Where? It is a concealed pronoun, permissibly concealed, its implied form being "we."

﴿Allah﴾ is the object. "Nara" is an imperfect verb whose doer is a pronoun concealed obligatorily, its implied form being "we." We told you: if the pronoun's implied form is "I," "we," or "you," it is obligatorily concealed; and if it is "he" or "she," it is permissibly concealed. But (...) these are self-evident matters, not difficult grammatical issues; perhaps those in primary school know them, and we will not be satisfied with less from you. Whenever the pronoun's implied form is "I," "we," or "you," it is obligatorily concealed; and when it is "he" or "she," it is permissibly concealed. Here the implied form is "we," so it is obligatorily concealed.

His saying ﴿jahratan﴾ is either a circumstantial accusative (hal) or an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: seeing openly. When did they say this? It was said: they said this when Moses (ﷺ) chose from among them seventy men...

Look at the verses with you now. Have you understood the two views or not? Have you understood the two views? The first view: they say that Moses (ﷺ) chose seventy men from his people for Allah's appointed time, and went with them; and when they were speaking with Allah and Allah was speaking to him, they said: ﴿we will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾. They say this statement occurred when Moses was going out to Allah's appointed time. Some scholars said: rather, when he brought the Torah, having returned from Allah's appointed time and the Torah had been sent down to him and he brought it, they said: "No, it is not from Allah. ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾."

* Student: The context supports the second.
* Shaykh: Which of them?
* Student: The last.
* Shaykh: The last one; because He said: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾, then He mentioned the story of the calf, which was after Moses brought the Torah; then after that He mentioned: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly"﴾. The apparent context indicates that this statement was when he brought the Torah and said: it is from Allah; so they said: ﴿we will never believe you﴾. But (...).

﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointment. So when the earthquake seized them, he said: "My Lord, had You willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? It is but Your trial; You send astray by it whom You will and guide whom You will.
