The concept of qaryah in the Arabic language differs from its concept in common usage, because in common usage a small town is called a qaryah and a large one is called a madinah (city). But in the Arabic language, which is the language of the Quran, there is no difference. Allah, exalted be He, named Makkah Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Towns), even though other places besides Makkah have very great cities, very great cities indeed. He called it Umm al-Qura. Likewise Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And how many a town was stronger in power than your town which drove you out﴾ [Muhammad 13]. And what is meant by "the town which drove you out"? Makkah. He says: ﴿how many a town was stronger in power﴾. Its meaning is that it was large and great, and yet Allah, exalted be He, called it a qaryah. This town: ﴿So eat from it wherever you wish, in plenty﴾. His saying: ﴿So eat from it﴾: "Enter and eat from it." The command here in His saying ﴿Enter﴾ we said is a cosmic command. ﴿So eat﴾: the command is for permission, meaning: We have permitted you to eat from it. ﴿Wherever you wish﴾: meaning, in whatever place you are in the town, in its center or its outskirts, you may eat what you wish.

His saying: ﴿in plenty (raghadan)﴾: meaning with tranquility and ease, without anyone opposing you in that or preventing you. And one should not say that this contradicts the Messenger ﷺ's saying: «Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me»[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (335), Muslim (521 / 3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. We say: because this is not booty; rather, they were permitted to eat from this land, whether by purchase, or by sharecropping, or the like (...).

﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾. ﴿Enter the gate﴾: which gate? The gate of the town, meaning the gate of the town, because towns have gates that protect them from inside and outside.

His saying: ﴿the gate﴾: this al- is for definiteness (al-'ahd). Which definiteness is it?
* Student: Mental (dhihni).
* Shaykh: Mental, because it has not been previously mentioned, and it is not present to the senses, because it is not present, so it is mental and understood from His saying ﴿the town﴾, because a town has a gate.

His saying: ﴿prostrating﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the waw in ﴿enter﴾.

What is meant by this prostration? It is said that it means humility (khudu'), as in His saying: ﴿Do you not see that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾ [Al-Hajj 18], and so on. So what is meant is humility.

It is also said that it means bowing (ruku'), as in His saying: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before Him in prostration﴾ [Yusuf 100]. And it is said that what is meant is literal prostration, because that is the apparent wording. On this view, it is not accepted that the meaning of the verse ﴿to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ is merely general humility; rather it is prostration, and every being has a prostration suited to it. Likewise, one does not accept that His saying ﴿and they fell down before Him in prostration﴾ means that they bowed; rather they literally prostrated, because His saying ﴿fell down﴾ indicates this. If we say that what is meant by His saying ﴿prostrating﴾ is literal prostration on the ground, there is a problem, because entering in this state is impossible: when a person is prostrating, he cannot enter; he remains fixed in his place, is he not? ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾: how can they enter the gate prostrating? The answer is simple: this state is not concurrent (muqarinah) with the action; rather it is a state in the future, because a state may sometimes be concurrent with the act and sometimes come after it. So the meaning is: when you enter the gate, then prostrate to Allah, exalted be He, in thanks for this blessing. For this reason, «When the Messenger ﷺ conquered Makkah, he prayed eight rak'ahs in the forenoon»[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (357), Muslim (336 / 71), from the hadith of Umm Hani.]]. Some scholars said that this is the prayer of the forenoon (sunnat al-duha), and some said it is the sunnah of the Conquest, meaning that the conquest has a sunnah: when a person enters, he prays. And this is closer to the truth, because if we say that prostration means its literal sense, we have not departed from the apparent wording. In interpreting the Quran and explaining the hadith, our obligation is to adhere to what? To the apparent wording, so long as no obstacle prevents it. If an obstacle prevents it, then it is permissible to depart from it; otherwise we must adhere to its apparent meaning. So: prostrating. ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, meaning: when you enter it, prostrate immediately without delay.

﴿And say: Hittah﴾. That is: say this word, hittah. Hittah is a noun of state from hatt, which means lowering or bringing down, as in your saying: "Hutta rahluhu" or "hatta rahlahu," meaning: he lowered his saddlebag. From it is what is related in the hadith of supplication during the prostration of recitation: «And remove from me a burden of sin through it»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (579), Ibn Majah (1053), and Ibn Khuzaymah (563).]]. So they were told hittah, which is a form from hatt, meaning bringing down. The meaning is: lower our sins from us. So it means: say "Our Lord, forgive us," meaning ask forgiveness from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, when you enter and prostrate. Do you understand? So the meaning of hittah is: lower our sins from us.

* Student: Shaykh, is there a prayer in the prostration of gratitude (sujud al-shukr)?
* Shaykh: No, it is independent.
* Student: One prostration or two?
* Shaykh: No, one prostration.

﴿Say hittah﴾: meaning, lower our sins from us, and it is an expression for seeking forgiveness. And what is the i'rab of hittah?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: Good. Should it not be in the accusative? They say it is the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: our request is hittah, or our matter is hittah, meaning our request that our sins be lowered. And the sentence of subject and predicate is in the position of accusative as the object of speech (maqul al-qawl).

﴿We will forgive you﴾. In another reading: ﴿You will be forgiven﴾. And in a third reading: ﴿He will be forgiven﴾. So there are three readings: ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾; ﴿Your sins will be forgiven you﴾; ﴿Your sins will be forgiven you﴾. All of them are sound readings; whichever you recite suffices.

His saying: ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾. Forgiveness (maghfirah) is the covering of the sin and passing over it. Covering the sin means that Allah covers your sin and overlooks it, so He does not punish you for it. This is forgiveness, because it is derived from maghfar. And what is the maghfar? The thing with which the head is protected in battle, is it not? Something like that?

**Student:** Is it called a helmet, O Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it is called a helmet. This is the *maghfar*, because it covers and protects. Whoever interprets *maghfirah* (forgiveness) as merely covering is mistaken, because when Allah, exalted is He, meets His believing servant on the Day of Resurrection, privately, and makes him acknowledge his sins, He says: "I concealed them for you in this world, and I forgive them for you today."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.]] That is, I overlook them and also conceal them.

As for His saying ﴿*khataya-kum*﴾ ("your wrongdoings"): it is the plural of *khati'ah*. *Khataya* is the plural of *khatiyyah*, like *mataya* is the plural of *matiyyah*. The *khatiyyah* is what a person commits of sins deliberately. This is *khati'ah*: what he commits of sins deliberately. What he commits unintentionally is called *ikhta'*. For this reason a distinction is made between *mukhti'* and *khati'*: the *khati'* is blameworthy, while the *mukhti'* is excused. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿*We will surely seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock*﴾ [al-'Alaq 15–16], and He says: ﴿*Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err*﴾ [al-Baqarah 286]. *Akhta'na* ("we erred") means he is *mukhti'*; *akhta'a* ("he erred") means he is *mukhti'*; and *khati'a* means he is *khati'*. So *al-khatiyyah* and *al-khati'ah* are what a person commits of violation deliberately. If it is out of ignorance, it is *ikhta'* and not *khati'ah*. Now look: if they do that, their wrongdoings will be forgiven for them. Beyond that: ﴿*And We will increase the good-doers*﴾, ﴿*We will increase the good-doers*﴾. This is above the forgiveness of wrongdoings; it is grace.

As for His saying ﴿*al-muhsinin*﴾ ("the good-doers"): they are those who practise *ihsan*. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained *ihsan*: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Whoever worships Allah in this manner is a *muhsin*. There is no doubt that if they had carried out what they were commanded, they would have been good-doers. But ﴿*those who did wrong substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾. Look: they did not say *hittah*, they replaced it. ﴿*Those who did wrong substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾. That is, His saying ﴿*substituted a statement*﴾. In reality there is a problem here: did they substitute a statement other than the one that was said to them, or did they substitute the statement that was said to them?

**Student:** They said something other than what was said to them.

**Shaykh:** Did they substitute the statement that was said to them, or did they substitute a statement other than what was said to them?

**Student:** A statement other than what was said to them. They said something other than what was said to them.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but the word (*baddala*), do you say: "I substituted the sheep with the lamb"?

**Student:** They substituted the statement that was said to them.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and here He says: ﴿*substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾.

**Student:** The same thing.

**Shaykh:** No, it is not the same. Here there is a difference: ﴿*substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾.

**Student:** So, the meaning is: they said something other than what was said to them?

**Shaykh:** The meaning of "they said" is well known, but we want to derive the meaning from the wording. Let us see now: is there an inversion (*qalb*) in the verse, or an implicit inclusion of meaning (*tadmin*)? If we take the apparent wording, it becomes: "They substituted a statement other than what was said to them," even though they substituted the statement that was said to them, replacing it with another statement. Therefore, scholars differed in explaining this verse. It was said that the meaning of *baddala* is *qalaa* (they said), so that ﴿*those who did wrong*﴾ said a statement other than what was said to them, as a substitution. That is, their intention was substitution and opposition, not that they erred, forgot, or the like. Here the substitution is at its most explicit, because it includes that they said a statement other than what was said to them, and said it with the intention of what? Substitution and opposition. With the intention of substitution and opposition. This is graver than if they had said it through forgetfulness or the like. They said it as a substitution. Here *baddala* has implicitly included the meaning of *qala* (said), but it expressed the statement through the word "substitution," in order to make clear that those who said something other than what was said to them had the purpose of substitution, that is, opposition.

Some of them said: the verse contains an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: ﴿*then those who did wrong substituted, by the statement that was said to them, a statement other than what was said to them*﴾. So there is an ellipsis in the verse, its implied sense being: "then those who did wrong substituted, by the statement that was said to them, a statement other than what was said to them." But as long as the verse can be explained without an ellipsis, that is preferable to explaining it through something that involves an ellipsis. Here *baddala* means *qala* (said), but He expressed the statement by the word "substitution," as a pointer to what?

**Student:** To opposition.

**Shaykh:** They said that for the sake of opposition, substitution, and alteration.

His saying ﴿*those who did wrong, a statement*﴾: He did not say "then they substituted" or "then you substituted." Rather, He used the apparent noun in place of the pronoun. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun has benefits. Do you understand? He did not say "then you substituted (...)," nor did He say "then they substituted." Rather, He said ﴿*then those who did wrong substituted*﴾: the apparent noun in place of the pronoun. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun has benefits. Who knows them? We have already covered them.

**Student:** Condemnation.

**Shaykh:** How is it condemnation?

**Student:** Severity, or the ugliness of this act.

**Shaykh:** That is, confirming that these people truly have this attribute. The meaning is that wherever the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun, it has benefits:

*The first benefit:* the confirmation or establishment that the referent of the pronoun possesses this attribute. That is, these people are wrongdoers. The meaning is a judgment against these people as wrongdoers; this is one benefit. So its benefit is the judgment upon the referent of the pronoun with this attribute that has been made apparent. Is it clear?

*Second:* this is also a standard for others. Everyone who substitutes a statement other than what was said to him is a wrongdoer. Thus the ruling is generalised through the general cause of the attribute. This is clear, and it is for two benefits. There may be other benefits that will come at the end of the verse.

**Student:** But substitution (...) in principle, we are commanded to follow Islam, or commanded to pray, and someone abandons prayer, so everything whose path is other than the path of Islam, is that substitution?

**Shaykh:** This is substitution. Did they not substitute the command Allah gave them to say *hittah*?

They said, as it is established in the hadith from the Messenger (ﷺ): "*Hintah fi shi'irah*" ("wheat in a barley grain"),[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (4479), Muslim (3015/1), and Ahmad (8110), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, whose wording is: "*fi sha'arah*" (in a hair).]] instead of asking Allah for forgiveness of sins. They said: No, we want food; we want to eat wheat in a barley grain. So there is a difference between this and that. Allah commanded them to seek forgiveness for the sins they had committed, but they sought a thing with which to fill their bellies. Entering the gate prostrating: Ibn 'Abbas and others said that they entered crawling on their buttocks.[[In the earlier hadith: they entered crawling on their buttocks.]] I seek refuge in Allah. This was mockery of Allah, the One who commanded them to enter prostrating, in gratitude to Allah for the blessing of victory. They said: No, we will not enter, nor will we walk; we will walk on our backsides. I seek refuge in Allah. That is, they crawled. Some of them mentioned that they also went backwards, not walking forward. As for the statement, they substituted it too. They substituted both the statement and the action; they substituted both the statement and the action.

This has also happened to some of this Ummah. The voice of the Arabs at the time of the Six-Day War, as the Jews say, was saying: "Tomorrow Umm Kulthum will sing in Tel Aviv." That is, thanks to Allah for this blessing: the singer will go and sing in the conquered lands. But in reality, the Jewish aircraft sang over the aircraft of this speaker. So the matter became the reverse, and in reality it is like an evil, because this resembles the statement of Abu Jahl: "We will not return until we reach Badr, drink wine, and pitch our tents."[[See Imta' al-Asma' (1/90–91), al-Durar fi Ikhtisar al-Maghazi wa al-Siyar (p. 113), al-Fusul fi Sirat al-Rasul (ﷺ) (p. 30), al-Iktifa' bima Tadammanahu min Maghazi Rasul Allah wa al-Thalatha al-Khulafa' (2/16).]] Look at the aims of the Arabs now in this war with the Jews: what are they? Merely a worldly matter, that they overcome and seize. But not for establishing the religion of Allah. No. For the one who establishes the religion of Allah, when he conquers the lands of Allah, does he allow singing girls to sing on the day of conquest? The Messenger (ﷺ) "entered in the year of the Conquest with his head bowed low, to the point that his chin-tuft almost touched the saddle from the intensity of his lowering his head, peace be upon him, while he recited the Qur'an: ﴿*Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory*﴾." There is a difference between this and that. Yes indeed. So I say: among this Ummah there are some who did what these Jews did; they did not enter humbly prostrating, nor saying: ﴿*Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, and make firm our feet*﴾ [Al 'Imran 147]. Rather they said: "We will enter and sing; singing girls will accompany us and sing over us." This is the fulfilment of the Messenger's (ﷺ) saying: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you, step by step, and span by span, to the point that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it too."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah with the wording: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, until if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would follow them."]]

﴿*And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you manna and quails. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.*﴾

* From His saying ﴿*And We shaded you with the clouds*﴾ is derived: the blessing of Allah, blessed and exalted, in what He prepared for His servants of shade. Shade from the heat is one of the blessings of Allah upon the servant, by His saying ﴿*And We shaded you with the clouds*﴾. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿*And He made for you shelters among the mountains*﴾ [al-Nahl 81], protecting you from the heat and also from the cold.

* In it also is evidence of the power of Allah, exalted and glorified is He, in that He made the clouds a shade for these people, and that He is the One who drives the clouds and manages them, blessed and exalted is He, as He wills.

* In it also is an explanation of the blessing of Allah upon the Children of Israel, by sending down manna and quails: food and drink that came to them without toil and without hardship. For this reason it is described as *manna*.

* In it also is evidence that the meat of birds is among the finest meats, because Allah prepared these birds for them, and did not prepare for them gazelles or rabbits, but birds. It is also the flesh of the people of Paradise: ﴿*and the meat of fowl of what they desire*﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 21].

* In it also is evidence that when Allah bestows a blessing upon a person, he should enjoy it and not deprive himself of it, by His saying ﴿*Eat of the good things with which We have provided you*﴾. A person should not abstain from lawful things out of self-restraint. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) said: whoever refrains from eating good things without a legitimate reason is blameworthy. This is correct, because he has abandoned what Allah permitted for him, and it is as if he is saying that he does not want Allah to have any favour over him. A person should not abstain from good things except for a legitimate reason. A legitimate reason may relate to his body, may relate to his religion, or may relate to others. A person may abstain from meat because his body does not accept it, so his abstaining from it is a matter of dietary regimen (*hamiyah*). A person may abstain from meat because he fears that his soul will become attached to it, until his concern becomes to consume his good things in the life of this world. A person may abstain from good provision out of consideration for others, as is related of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in the Year of Ashes (*'Am al-Ramadah*), the well-known year of drought:[[See al-Ahad wa al-Mathani (1/138) (113).]] he would not eat bread with meat; he would eat it only with date-wine, because he could not. He said: "I cannot be satisfied with meat while the Ummah is hungry." So this was for the sake of others. In sum: if he refrains from good things for a legitimate reason, he is not blameworthy; but if he refrains from them out of abstinence (*ta'affuf*), he is blameworthy.

* In it also is evidence that the Children of Israel were ungrateful for this blessing, by His saying ﴿*but they were wronging themselves*﴾.

* Among the benefits in it: the disobedient person does not wrong Allah, but wrongs himself. However, it is correct to say: this man has wronged himself with regard to the right of Allah, and with regard to the rights of people. We do not say that he wronged Allah; he wronged himself with regard to the right of Allah and with regard to the rights of people.

* Also among its benefits: everything we eat is from the provision of Allah, as in His saying ﴿*with which We have provided you*﴾.

* In it also: lawful provision is that which is good, by His saying ﴿*Eat of the good things*﴾; and that Allah, exalted is He, did not command eating what is foul; rather He forbade it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿*And when We said: Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating, and say: Hittah (relief), and We will forgive you your wrongdoings, and We will increase the good-doers*﴾.

* In it is affirmation that speech belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. And this speech is by the tongue of whom? Moses. So it affirms speech, and that Allah speaks. Is this true speech, or metaphorical? It is true, with a voice and with letters. But His voice, exalted and glorified is He, is not like the voice of any created being, and a person cannot imagine this voice, because it is magnificent.

* In it also is evidence that Allah, exalted is He, permitted the Children of Israel to enter Bayt al-Maqdis, by His saying ﴿*Enter this town*﴾.

* In it also is Allah's promise to them of entering it. From where is the promise derived? From the command to enter. The meaning is as if He says: "We have opened the gates for you, so enter."

* In it also is evidence for the permissibility of their eating, that is the Children of Israel, from this town they entered. But is it with compensation or without compensation?

**Students:** With compensation.

**Shaykh:** Yes. Spoils of war (*ghanimah*) are not permitted to them as they are permitted to us. But its meaning is that you may eat from it wherever you wish, in ease and contentment; He did not restrict you. However, it is not on the basis of spoils. It may be said that they may eat but not take ownership, and it becomes not a matter of spoils, just as, in the Islamic law, if I pass by an orchard I may eat from it, but I do not take possession of it. The particularity that was specific to this Ummah is the ownership of spoils. As for benefiting from the fruits of the lands they entered, that is permitted to them even in their law.

* In it also is evidence that whoever Allah has helped and granted conquest of lands must enter them in a manner of humility and submission, by His saying ﴿*And enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah*﴾. The Messenger (ﷺ), when he conquered Makkah, entered it with his head bowed. When Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Today is the day of slaughter; today the Ka'bah will be made lawful," and this reached the Prophet, peace be upon him, he said: "Sa'd has lied; rather today the Ka'bah will be magnified."[[al-Bukhari (4280), from the hadith of 'Urwah; see also Dala'il al-Nubuwwah by al-Bayhaqi (5/39).]] "Then he took the banner from him and gave it to his son Qays ibn Sa'd" as a rebuke to him for saying this word, although he had said it with good intention but without understanding. The Prophet, peace be upon him, made clear that this day is not one in which the Ka'bah is made lawful, but rather one in which the Ka'bah is magnified, because it was purified from idols and the lands were turned into Islamic lands after being lands of disbelief. Is there in this the making lawful of the Ka'bah? Never; rather in it is the magnification of the Ka'bah. But is there in it the making lawful of the tyrants who transgress against the Ka'bah? Yes indeed, that is correct.

* In this is evidence of the baseness of the Children of Israel and their opposition to Allah and His messengers, because they did not enter the gate prostrating; rather they entered crawling on their buttocks, going backwards, crawling, going backwards, out of arrogance and mockery. They said: instead of *hittah*, what? *Hintah* in a hair or in a barley grain. We only want something to fill our bellies; we do not want forgiveness of our sins. And we seek refuge in Allah.

And in it is evidence for the ugliness of ta'wil (interpretation that departs from the apparent meaning, here used pejoratively) and tahrif (distortion). These people distorted, and Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, likened the lam in "istawla" (he seized control), as held by the Jahmiyyah, to the nun that the Jews added in "hintah" (wheat). The Mu'tazilah, the Jahmiyyah, and also the Ash'ariyyah said: "istawa" means "istawla," so the lam in "istawa" according to them is the letter that was added, like the nun that was added in "hittah." They said "hintah," and this is correct. So they distorted the meaning in reality. The Children of Israel distorted both the wording and the meaning, while those distorted only the meaning, because they could not distort the wording. If they had distorted the wording of the Qur'an, the community would have risen against them and their misguidance would have become known. Therefore, in it is a clarification of the ugliness of distortion, distorting words from their places, whether verbal or conceptual.

And in it also: striving in jihad together with humility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and seeking forgiveness are a cause of forgiveness, due to His saying: ﴿We will forgive you your wrongdoings﴾, and for gaining more of His bounty, due to His saying: ﴿And We will increase the doers of good﴾.

And in it also is evidence that ihsan (excellence, doing good) is a cause of increase, whether it is ihsan in the worship of Allah or ihsan to the servants of Allah, for ihsan is a cause of increase. It has been established from the Messenger ﷺ that he said: "Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother,"[[Narrated by Muslim (2699) from Abu Hurayrah.]] and "Whoever is in the need of his brother, Allah is in his need."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2442) and Muslim (2580/58) from Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon those who did wrong a plague from the sky because they were defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah 59].

He said: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted﴾. In it is evidence for the prohibition of substitution in the words of Allah, which is distorting them. From where is this derived? From describing them with wrongdoing: ﴿those who did wrong substituted a word﴾.

And in it is evidence for mentioning part of a thing, where it is inferred from and the second part is dispensed with. That is, for example, here: did they oppose in speech, or in speech and action? The noble verse says ﴿substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾, by speech only, and it remained silent about action. But it has been established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that "they entered crawling on their backsides."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3403) and Muslim (3015/1).]] So they substituted both speech and action. Therefore it can be said: they substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, meaning they made the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in which there is the command to prostrate and the command to ask for forgiveness (hittah), into this entire word. So the intended meaning is not the same as the speech that is the counterpart of action. Rather, they substituted the word of Allah with another word, as if they had been told a word other than what they had been told. So the substitution is the substitution of speech only, or of action only, or of both speech and action?

* Students: Both action and speech.

* The Shaykh: No, no. In the Qur'an, what is meant is speech. We say: what is meant in the Qur'an is speech. If we say that the statement of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾ means: they substituted speech with speech, in the sense that they exchanged what they had been saying for another speech, then if we interpret the verse with this interpretation, it would have remained silent about the action which they made a substitute for what they were commanded. But if we say that the meaning of His statement ﴿those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾ is: they turned everything that had been said to them into another word, meaning as if they had been commanded to crawl on their backsides and to say "hintah fi sha'rah" (wheat in barley), then they substituted the original word that had been said with another word which they obeyed. On this basis, the verse includes the substitution of speech and action, includes the substitution of speech (...), and no problem remains in it. In reality, even if we assume we explained it by the first meaning, that they said other than what had been said to them, the hadith is sound and explicit in that, that they also substituted the action.

* The Student: Mentioning part of a thing dispenses with the other?

* The Shaykh: This is if we say that the speech they substituted is the speech that actually came from them. But if we say that they substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, meaning they made the command of Allah to them into a command for something else, which is what they did, meaning as if they distorted the command of Allah, that is, the word of Allah, then in that case it does not fall under the category of mentioning one of the two parts while dispensing with mentioning the other. And Allah knows best what He intended by His speech.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So We sent upon those who did wrong a plague from the sky.﴾ His statement ﴿So We sent﴾: the fa' is for causation. Did you understand? That is, because of what occurred from them of substitution, We sent down.

And His statement ﴿upon those who did wrong﴾ means: upon them. This is from the category of using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun. We mentioned in the previous lesson that it has three benefits. Did we?

* A student: I was not present.

* The Shaykh: Did we mention the benefit of using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun?

* A student: Using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun: alerting (...).

* A student: First, passing judgment on these people, or specifying these people with the judgment.

* The Shaykh: No, passing judgment on them with what this apparent noun indicates, which is that they did wrong. This is one.

* The Student: The second: that this description is general, the generality of the description with the generality of the ruling, the generality of the ruling with the generality of the description.

* The Shaykh: That is, its meaning is that so that it would be...

* The Student: General for them and for others.

* The Shaykh: So that it would be general for them and for others. Third, did we mention only these?

* The Student: Alerting.

* The Shaykh: No, alerting, we mentioned it, may Allah bless you, in the case where there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person), when a shift occurs from the third person to the second person or the reverse.

* The Student: And this (...) for emphasis?

* The Shaykh: It may happen that there is attentiveness in it, when a person's speech is structured so that a pronoun is expected, and then an apparent noun is used instead. This may be a means of drawing attention, so that the person becomes attentive, and it is said: why did the apparent noun come when the context of the speech requires a pronoun? It may be so.

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: But in any case, the matter intends generality, so that this ruling includes whoever resembles them.

* The Student: In the description.

* The Shaykh: And the second: passing judgment on them with what this apparent noun requires, namely that they did wrong.

And His statement, the Exalted: ﴿So We sent upon those who did wrong a plague﴾, meaning: a punishment, due to His statement, the Exalted: ﴿If you remove from us the plague﴾. Pharaoh said to Musa: ﴿If you remove from us the plague, we will surely believe in you and we will surely send with you the Children of Israel﴾ [al-A'raf 134]. That is, the punishment, and it is other than ar-rijs (filth), because ar-rijs is impurity and filth, while ar-rijz is punishment.

And His statement ﴿a plague from the sky﴾ means: a punishment from it. Like what? What punishment descends from the sky? Like stones, thunderbolts, hail, and others.

* A student: Winds.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

And His statement ﴿from the sky﴾: what is meant by "sky" here is height. It does not necessarily mean the preserved sky, because everything above you is called sky, unless there is a contextual indication, such as His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling, yet they, from its signs, are turning away﴾ [al-Anbiya' 32].

He said: ﴿because they were defiantly disobedient﴾. The ba' here is for causation, meaning "because of." The ma is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning "because of their having defiantly disobeyed." When it is verbal, it has already passed with us that the verbal particle transforms what follows it from a verb, indeed from the whole clause, into a verbal noun. His statement ﴿because they were defiantly disobedient﴾: kanu (were) refers to the past, or the intended meaning is (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 57–59 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, glorified and exalted be He, began to enumerate His blessings upon them in His saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ ﴿We shaded you with the clouds﴾. The noble verse says: "We shaded the clouds (al-ghamam)." Its apparent meaning is that the thing that shades is the clouds, as you say: "I shaded Zayd with a cloak." For this reason some grammarians of i'rab (grammatical analysis) held that the verse is to be read as: "And We shaded you with (bi) the clouds." Now, you say, "I shaded so-and-so." Is he the one who is shaded or the one by means of which shading is done? He is the one shaded. Here He said: ﴿We shaded you with the clouds﴾. But in my view it does not need any supplying of words, and what fully conveys the meaning is His saying: ﴿over you﴾. ﴿And We shaded you over﴾. Had He said only "We shaded the clouds," someone might have imagined that the clouds were the thing shaded. But He said: ﴿We shaded you over﴾, meaning, "We made it a shade over you." This happened in the wilderness (al-tih) when they wandered. And how long did they remain in the wilderness between Egypt and Syria? Forty years, wandering in the land. But Allah, blessed and exalted, showed them mercy. They had no water, no shelter, nothing. Yet Allah, glorified be He, showed them mercy and shaded them with the clouds. Al-ghamam is the thin white cloud. It is said that it refers to clouds in general, and it is said that it refers to cold clouds, which make the air cold because moisture forms from them and so the air cools. This last is the apparent meaning.

﴿And We sent down upon you al-manna and al-salwa﴾. ﴿We sent down upon you al-manna﴾. They say that al-manna is something resembling honey that descended upon them between the break of dawn and sunrise. When they rose, they ate from it. As for al-salwa, it is a bird, a soft and tender bird called al-sumana (quail), or something similar to it. Our teachers told us that it is al-safari. Al-safari is well known, a bird among the finest and most delicious of birds, and it is small (...).

* Shaykh: Was this death real, or was it sleep?
* Student: Real.
* Shaykh: Yes, real.
* Student: Because sleep is called wafat (death/taking).
* Shaykh: It is called wafat, yes. What are the stories, other than this one, in which the dead are brought back to life?
* Student: The story of the owner of the cow. Five stories. This is one. The story of Ibrahim with the birds: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [Al-Baqarah 260]. And the story of the one who passed by a town that lay in ruins upon its roofs.
* Shaykh: ﴿Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him﴾ [Al-Baqarah 259].
* Student: ﴿Those who went out from their homes, being thousands, fearing death; Allah said to them, "Die," then He gave them life﴾ [Al-Baqarah 243].
* Shaykh: Well done.
* Student: The story of the owner of the cow.
* Shaykh: Five stories in this surah in which Allah, exalted be He, gives life to the dead in this world.

The words of Allah, exalted be He: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾. What is its meaning?
* Student: Al-ghamam: it is said to be white cloud that shades them from the sun and cools the air.
* Shaykh: And what is the meaning of ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾?
* Student: This is a favor from Allah.
* Shaykh: Yes, and what does it mean?
* Student: That He made the clouds shade them.
* Shaykh: That He made the clouds shade them, exactly. Some people say that the verse should be read as "And We shaded you with the clouds," but the correct view is that it stays as it is: al-ghamam is the object of "We shaded," and the meaning is "We made it a shade over you." This is the meaning.

His saying: ﴿al-manna and al-salwa﴾. What is al-manna?
* Student: I do not know.
* Shaykh: You do not know them?
* Student: It is said that it is a drink resembling honey.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And al-salwa is a bird.
* Shaykh: Yes, one of the finest and most delicious birds, and among us it is called safari.
* Students: Sumani.
* Shaykh: Yes. Among us the sumani is called safari, because the bird is yellowish, and its meat is light and good.

As for al-manna, it is something that descends like honey. They say it descends upon the trees between dawn and sunrise, and they take from it, eat from it, and gather it. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Truffles are from al-manna»[[Agreed upon. Al-Bukhari (4478) and Muslim (2049 / 157–162), from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him.]], because it is obtained without toil. The apparent meaning of the hadith is that al-manna refers to everything that comes to them without toil, whether that particular thing is like honey or something else. On this basis, this explanation is more general than restricting it to that which resembles honey, because the Messenger ﷺ's saying «Truffles are from al-manna» uses min ("from") to indicate a part. This means that al-manna is more general and broader. Some scholars have said that it is everything obtained without toil, and on this basis the fuqa' (mushroom) enters into it, and the arajin also enters. Does it enter or not? It enters, because it is a food among the finest foods.

* Student: What are the arajin?
* Shaykh: The arajin, God willing, when they are abundant in the desert.
* Student: They are present now, this year they are present.
* Shaykh: Present, yes, this year they are present in abundance, and it is better that you show them to people, so that no one imagines they are mice or anything like that.
* Student: I have not known them, Shaykh.
* Another student: I also have not known them.
* Shaykh: The arajin is a white plant like fingers that comes out of (...). But this is white like cloth, and grows in the al-nafwal and al-jard. When it is cooked with food it is among the best things; sometimes you prefer it over meat. Sometimes people find it in a large place, meaning in great quantity. In these days someone gave me a large kind of it, and said that he found it in a place where they thought it was "ma'azim" (large), they thought it was bones because of how abundant it was.
* Student: But what about the 'arajun mentioned in the tafsir of the verse?
* Shaykh: No, the 'arajun in the Quran refers to what people call 'arajut, the bud of the date palm (hibb al-nakhl).
* Student: The date palm's bud (...).
* Shaykh: God willing, when it is abundant. It is now scarce in appearance, because it has dried out a little. When it becomes abundant, God willing, we will see, and you and I will go and look at it together.
* Student: Shaykh? A question in the form of an objection (...) regarding His saying: ﴿Kill yourselves﴾. They say: Is it wise for a community to be legislated to kill itself? And has this happened to humans since ancient times?
* Shaykh: Yes, we say: as for this religious community, no. For the religion of Islam, no, it is not prescribed. As for the earlier nations, they may have been punished with something of this kind, because Allah's command to them to kill themselves is like Allah's command to Ibrahim to slaughter his son. The purpose was testing. And if Allah, exalted be He, wished to destroy them by His act, through earthquakes or thunderbolts or otherwise, He might instead destroy them by their own actions, which would make the test more severe and greater.
* Student: Is it far from what reason can grasp or accept?
* Shaykh: No, reason fully accepts it. Even, for example, sometimes a master says to his slave, "Do such and such," wanting to test his sincerity in obedience. It is not far-fetched.
* Student: Some modern exegetes have denied it, saying it is unacceptable by the law and by reason that He would command them to kill themselves.
* Shaykh: These are among those about whom the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Let him take his seat in the Fire»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2950, 2951), who said: a hasan hadith.]], because they interpret the Quran according to their own opinions. They interpret the Quran according to their own opinions. They accept whatever agrees with their corrupt view and reject whatever they do not accept.

Then He said: ﴿Eat of the good things that We have provided for you﴾. ﴿Eat﴾: the command here is for permission (ibahah). The command is for permission, meaning: We have permitted you this that We sent down upon you, of al-manna and al-salwa.

His saying: ﴿of the good things﴾: this min is for specifying the kind, not for partiality, because they were permitted to eat all good things. Al-tayyib is the opposite of al-khabith (the bad). Something bad may be bad in itself, or it may be bad because of how it was acquired. What is bad in itself, such as carrion, pork, wine, and the like, is bad in itself, as Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination (rijs)﴾ [Al-An'am 145]. That is: impure and bad. This is forbidden in itself, forbidden to all people, to all people, to its owners and others. The second type is forbidden because of how it was acquired, such as what is taken by fraud, or by usury, or by lying, or the like. This is forbidden to the one who acquires it, and is not forbidden to others if they acquire it from him by a permissible means. What is forbidden because of its acquisition is forbidden to the one who acquired it, and is not forbidden to others if they acquire it from him by a permissible means. What proves this is that the Prophet ﷺ dealt with the Jews even though they used to eat unlawful gain (al-suht), which shows that it is not forbidden to someone other than the one who acquired it. What is forbidden because of its acquisition is not forbidden to someone other than the acquirer (...).

But it [the object] is an object of ﴿they wronged﴾, meaning they wronged themselves. He placed it first to indicate restriction, meaning: they wrong no one by this except themselves. As for Allah, blessed and exalted be He, they cannot wrong Him, because He, glorified and praised be He, is not harmed by their disobedience, just as He does not benefit from their obedience.

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿And when We said: Enter this town﴾. That is: Remember, O Children of Israel, when We said: Enter this town.

﴿Enter﴾: is this a cosmic command (kawni) or a legislative command (shar'i)? Both cosmic and legislative, because they were commanded to enter it prostrating, and they were commanded to enter the town in fighting, and it was also permitted to them. They did enter it in fact.

His saying: ﴿this town﴾. The exegetes differed about identifying this town. The correct view is that what is meant is Bayt al-Maqdis, because Musa said to them: ﴿Enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 21].

His saying: ﴿this town﴾. Qaryah (town) is derived from qary, which means gathering. A land is called qaryah because people gather in it. The concept of qaryah in the Arabic language differs from its concept in common usage, because in common usage a small town is called a qaryah and a large one is called a madinah (city). But in the Arabic language, which is the language of the Quran, there is no difference. Allah, exalted be He, named Makkah Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Towns), even though other places besides Makkah have very great cities, very great cities indeed. He called it Umm al-Qura. Likewise Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿And how many a town was stronger in power than your town which drove you out﴾ [Muhammad 13]. And what is meant by "the town which drove you out"? Makkah. He says: ﴿how many a town was stronger in power﴾. Its meaning is that it was large and great, and yet Allah, exalted be He, called it a qaryah. This town: ﴿So eat from it wherever you wish, in plenty﴾. His saying: ﴿So eat from it﴾: "Enter and eat from it." The command here in His saying ﴿Enter﴾ we said is a cosmic command. ﴿So eat﴾: the command is for permission, meaning: We have permitted you to eat from it. ﴿Wherever you wish﴾: meaning, in whatever place you are in the town, in its center or its outskirts, you may eat what you wish.

His saying: ﴿in plenty (raghadan)﴾: meaning with tranquility and ease, without anyone opposing you in that or preventing you. And one should not say that this contradicts the Messenger ﷺ's saying: «Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me»[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (335), Muslim (521 / 3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. We say: because this is not booty; rather, they were permitted to eat from this land, whether by purchase, or by sharecropping, or the like (...).

﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾. ﴿Enter the gate﴾: which gate? The gate of the town, meaning the gate of the town, because towns have gates that protect them from inside and outside.

His saying: ﴿the gate﴾: this al- is for definiteness (al-'ahd). Which definiteness is it?
* Student: Mental (dhihni).
* Shaykh: Mental, because it has not been previously mentioned, and it is not present to the senses, because it is not present, so it is mental and understood from His saying ﴿the town﴾, because a town has a gate.

His saying: ﴿prostrating﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the waw in ﴿enter﴾.

What is meant by this prostration? It is said that it means humility (khudu'), as in His saying: ﴿Do you not see that to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures﴾ [Al-Hajj 18], and so on. So what is meant is humility.

It is also said that it means bowing (ruku'), as in His saying: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down before Him in prostration﴾ [Yusuf 100]. And it is said that what is meant is literal prostration, because that is the apparent wording. On this view, it is not accepted that the meaning of the verse ﴿to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾ is merely general humility; rather it is prostration, and every being has a prostration suited to it. Likewise, one does not accept that His saying ﴿and they fell down before Him in prostration﴾ means that they bowed; rather they literally prostrated, because His saying ﴿fell down﴾ indicates this. If we say that what is meant by His saying ﴿prostrating﴾ is literal prostration on the ground, there is a problem, because entering in this state is impossible: when a person is prostrating, he cannot enter; he remains fixed in his place, is he not? ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾: how can they enter the gate prostrating? The answer is simple: this state is not concurrent (muqarinah) with the action; rather it is a state in the future, because a state may sometimes be concurrent with the act and sometimes come after it. So the meaning is: when you enter the gate, then prostrate to Allah, exalted be He, in thanks for this blessing. For this reason, «When the Messenger ﷺ conquered Makkah, he prayed eight rak'ahs in the forenoon»[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (357), Muslim (336 / 71), from the hadith of Umm Hani.]]. Some scholars said that this is the prayer of the forenoon (sunnat al-duha), and some said it is the sunnah of the Conquest, meaning that the conquest has a sunnah: when a person enters, he prays. And this is closer to the truth, because if we say that prostration means its literal sense, we have not departed from the apparent wording. In interpreting the Quran and explaining the hadith, our obligation is to adhere to what? To the apparent wording, so long as no obstacle prevents it. If an obstacle prevents it, then it is permissible to depart from it; otherwise we must adhere to its apparent meaning. So: prostrating. ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, meaning: when you enter it, prostrate immediately without delay.

﴿And say: Hittah﴾. That is: say this word, hittah. Hittah is a noun of state from hatt, which means lowering or bringing down, as in your saying: "Hutta rahluhu" or "hatta rahlahu," meaning: he lowered his saddlebag. From it is what is related in the hadith of supplication during the prostration of recitation: «And remove from me a burden of sin through it»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (579), Ibn Majah (1053), and Ibn Khuzaymah (563).]]. So they were told hittah, which is a form from hatt, meaning bringing down. The meaning is: lower our sins from us. So it means: say "Our Lord, forgive us," meaning ask forgiveness from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, when you enter and prostrate. Do you understand? So the meaning of hittah is: lower our sins from us.

* Student: Shaykh, is there a prayer in the prostration of gratitude (sujud al-shukr)?
* Shaykh: No, it is independent.
* Student: One prostration or two?
* Shaykh: No, one prostration.

﴿Say hittah﴾: meaning, lower our sins from us, and it is an expression for seeking forgiveness. And what is the i'rab of hittah?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: Good. Should it not be in the accusative? They say it is the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: our request is hittah, or our matter is hittah, meaning our request that our sins be lowered. And the sentence of subject and predicate is in the position of accusative as the object of speech (maqul al-qawl).

﴿We will forgive you﴾. In another reading: ﴿You will be forgiven﴾. And in a third reading: ﴿He will be forgiven﴾. So there are three readings: ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾; ﴿Your sins will be forgiven you﴾; ﴿Your sins will be forgiven you﴾. All of them are sound readings; whichever you recite suffices.

His saying: ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾. Forgiveness (maghfirah) is the covering of the sin and passing over it. Covering the sin means that Allah covers your sin and overlooks it, so He does not punish you for it. This is forgiveness, because it is derived from maghfar. And what is the maghfar? The thing with which the head is protected in battle, is it not? Something like that?

**Student:** Is it called a helmet, O Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it is called a helmet. This is the *maghfar*, because it covers and protects. Whoever interprets *maghfirah* (forgiveness) as merely covering is mistaken, because when Allah, exalted is He, meets His believing servant on the Day of Resurrection, privately, and makes him acknowledge his sins, He says: "I concealed them for you in this world, and I forgive them for you today."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.]] That is, I overlook them and also conceal them.

As for His saying ﴿*khataya-kum*﴾ ("your wrongdoings"): it is the plural of *khati'ah*. *Khataya* is the plural of *khatiyyah*, like *mataya* is the plural of *matiyyah*. The *khatiyyah* is what a person commits of sins deliberately. This is *khati'ah*: what he commits of sins deliberately. What he commits unintentionally is called *ikhta'*. For this reason a distinction is made between *mukhti'* and *khati'*: the *khati'* is blameworthy, while the *mukhti'* is excused. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿*We will surely seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock*﴾ [al-'Alaq 15–16], and He says: ﴿*Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err*﴾ [al-Baqarah 286]. *Akhta'na* ("we erred") means he is *mukhti'*; *akhta'a* ("he erred") means he is *mukhti'*; and *khati'a* means he is *khati'*. So *al-khatiyyah* and *al-khati'ah* are what a person commits of violation deliberately. If it is out of ignorance, it is *ikhta'* and not *khati'ah*. Now look: if they do that, their wrongdoings will be forgiven for them. Beyond that: ﴿*And We will increase the good-doers*﴾, ﴿*We will increase the good-doers*﴾. This is above the forgiveness of wrongdoings; it is grace.

As for His saying ﴿*al-muhsinin*﴾ ("the good-doers"): they are those who practise *ihsan*. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained *ihsan*: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Whoever worships Allah in this manner is a *muhsin*. There is no doubt that if they had carried out what they were commanded, they would have been good-doers. But ﴿*those who did wrong substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾. Look: they did not say *hittah*, they replaced it. ﴿*Those who did wrong substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾. That is, His saying ﴿*substituted a statement*﴾. In reality there is a problem here: did they substitute a statement other than the one that was said to them, or did they substitute the statement that was said to them?

**Student:** They said something other than what was said to them.

**Shaykh:** Did they substitute the statement that was said to them, or did they substitute a statement other than what was said to them?

**Student:** A statement other than what was said to them. They said something other than what was said to them.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but the word (*baddala*), do you say: "I substituted the sheep with the lamb"?

**Student:** They substituted the statement that was said to them.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and here He says: ﴿*substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾.

**Student:** The same thing.

**Shaykh:** No, it is not the same. Here there is a difference: ﴿*substituted a statement other than that which had been said to them*﴾.

**Student:** So, the meaning is: they said something other than what was said to them?

**Shaykh:** The meaning of "they said" is well known, but we want to derive the meaning from the wording. Let us see now: is there an inversion (*qalb*) in the verse, or an implicit inclusion of meaning (*tadmin*)? If we take the apparent wording, it becomes: "They substituted a statement other than what was said to them," even though they substituted the statement that was said to them, replacing it with another statement. Therefore, scholars differed in explaining this verse. It was said that the meaning of *baddala* is *qalaa* (they said), so that ﴿*those who did wrong*﴾ said a statement other than what was said to them, as a substitution. That is, their intention was substitution and opposition, not that they erred, forgot, or the like. Here the substitution is at its most explicit, because it includes that they said a statement other than what was said to them, and said it with the intention of what? Substitution and opposition. With the intention of substitution and opposition. This is graver than if they had said it through forgetfulness or the like. They said it as a substitution. Here *baddala* has implicitly included the meaning of *qala* (said), but it expressed the statement through the word "substitution," in order to make clear that those who said something other than what was said to them had the purpose of substitution, that is, opposition.

Some of them said: the verse contains an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: ﴿*then those who did wrong substituted, by the statement that was said to them, a statement other than what was said to them*﴾. So there is an ellipsis in the verse, its implied sense being: "then those who did wrong substituted, by the statement that was said to them, a statement other than what was said to them." But as long as the verse can be explained without an ellipsis, that is preferable to explaining it through something that involves an ellipsis. Here *baddala* means *qala* (said), but He expressed the statement by the word "substitution," as a pointer to what?

**Student:** To opposition.

**Shaykh:** They said that for the sake of opposition, substitution, and alteration.

His saying ﴿*those who did wrong, a statement*﴾: He did not say "then they substituted" or "then you substituted." Rather, He used the apparent noun in place of the pronoun. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun has benefits. Do you understand? He did not say "then you substituted (...)," nor did He say "then they substituted." Rather, He said ﴿*then those who did wrong substituted*﴾: the apparent noun in place of the pronoun. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun has benefits. Who knows them? We have already covered them.

**Student:** Condemnation.

**Shaykh:** How is it condemnation?

**Student:** Severity, or the ugliness of this act.

**Shaykh:** That is, confirming that these people truly have this attribute. The meaning is that wherever the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun, it has benefits:

*The first benefit:* the confirmation or establishment that the referent of the pronoun possesses this attribute. That is, these people are wrongdoers. The meaning is a judgment against these people as wrongdoers; this is one benefit. So its benefit is the judgment upon the referent of the pronoun with this attribute that has been made apparent. Is it clear?

*Second:* this is also a standard for others. Everyone who substitutes a statement other than what was said to him is a wrongdoer. Thus the ruling is generalised through the general cause of the attribute. This is clear, and it is for two benefits. There may be other benefits that will come at the end of the verse.

**Student:** But substitution (...) in principle, we are commanded to follow Islam, or commanded to pray, and someone abandons prayer, so everything whose path is other than the path of Islam, is that substitution?

**Shaykh:** This is substitution. Did they not substitute the command Allah gave them to say *hittah*?

They said, as it is established in the hadith from the Messenger (ﷺ): "*Hintah fi shi'irah*" ("wheat in a barley grain"),[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (4479), Muslim (3015/1), and Ahmad (8110), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, whose wording is: "*fi sha'arah*" (in a hair).]] instead of asking Allah for forgiveness of sins. They said: No, we want food; we want to eat wheat in a barley grain. So there is a difference between this and that. Allah commanded them to seek forgiveness for the sins they had committed, but they sought a thing with which to fill their bellies. Entering the gate prostrating: Ibn 'Abbas and others said that they entered crawling on their buttocks.[[In the earlier hadith: they entered crawling on their buttocks.]] I seek refuge in Allah. This was mockery of Allah, the One who commanded them to enter prostrating, in gratitude to Allah for the blessing of victory. They said: No, we will not enter, nor will we walk; we will walk on our backsides. I seek refuge in Allah. That is, they crawled. Some of them mentioned that they also went backwards, not walking forward. As for the statement, they substituted it too. They substituted both the statement and the action; they substituted both the statement and the action.

This has also happened to some of this Ummah. The voice of the Arabs at the time of the Six-Day War, as the Jews say, was saying: "Tomorrow Umm Kulthum will sing in Tel Aviv." That is, thanks to Allah for this blessing: the singer will go and sing in the conquered lands. But in reality, the Jewish aircraft sang over the aircraft of this speaker. So the matter became the reverse, and in reality it is like an evil, because this resembles the statement of Abu Jahl: "We will not return until we reach Badr, drink wine, and pitch our tents."[[See Imta' al-Asma' (1/90–91), al-Durar fi Ikhtisar al-Maghazi wa al-Siyar (p. 113), al-Fusul fi Sirat al-Rasul (ﷺ) (p. 30), al-Iktifa' bima Tadammanahu min Maghazi Rasul Allah wa al-Thalatha al-Khulafa' (2/16).]] Look at the aims of the Arabs now in this war with the Jews: what are they? Merely a worldly matter, that they overcome and seize. But not for establishing the religion of Allah. No. For the one who establishes the religion of Allah, when he conquers the lands of Allah, does he allow singing girls to sing on the day of conquest? The Messenger (ﷺ) "entered in the year of the Conquest with his head bowed low, to the point that his chin-tuft almost touched the saddle from the intensity of his lowering his head, peace be upon him, while he recited the Qur'an: ﴿*Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory*﴾." There is a difference between this and that. Yes indeed. So I say: among this Ummah there are some who did what these Jews did; they did not enter humbly prostrating, nor saying: ﴿*Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, and make firm our feet*﴾ [Al 'Imran 147]. Rather they said: "We will enter and sing; singing girls will accompany us and sing over us." This is the fulfilment of the Messenger's (ﷺ) saying: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you, step by step, and span by span, to the point that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it too."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah with the wording: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, until if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would follow them."]]

﴿*And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you manna and quails. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.*﴾

* From His saying ﴿*And We shaded you with the clouds*﴾ is derived: the blessing of Allah, blessed and exalted, in what He prepared for His servants of shade. Shade from the heat is one of the blessings of Allah upon the servant, by His saying ﴿*And We shaded you with the clouds*﴾. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿*And He made for you shelters among the mountains*﴾ [al-Nahl 81], protecting you from the heat and also from the cold.

* In it also is evidence of the power of Allah, exalted and glorified is He, in that He made the clouds a shade for these people, and that He is the One who drives the clouds and manages them, blessed and exalted is He, as He wills.

* In it also is an explanation of the blessing of Allah upon the Children of Israel, by sending down manna and quails: food and drink that came to them without toil and without hardship. For this reason it is described as *manna*.

* In it also is evidence that the meat of birds is among the finest meats, because Allah prepared these birds for them, and did not prepare for them gazelles or rabbits, but birds. It is also the flesh of the people of Paradise: ﴿*and the meat of fowl of what they desire*﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 21].

* In it also is evidence that when Allah bestows a blessing upon a person, he should enjoy it and not deprive himself of it, by His saying ﴿*Eat of the good things with which We have provided you*﴾. A person should not abstain from lawful things out of self-restraint. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) said: whoever refrains from eating good things without a legitimate reason is blameworthy. This is correct, because he has abandoned what Allah permitted for him, and it is as if he is saying that he does not want Allah to have any favour over him. A person should not abstain from good things except for a legitimate reason. A legitimate reason may relate to his body, may relate to his religion, or may relate to others. A person may abstain from meat because his body does not accept it, so his abstaining from it is a matter of dietary regimen (*hamiyah*). A person may abstain from meat because he fears that his soul will become attached to it, until his concern becomes to consume his good things in the life of this world. A person may abstain from good provision out of consideration for others, as is related of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in the Year of Ashes (*'Am al-Ramadah*), the well-known year of drought:[[See al-Ahad wa al-Mathani (1/138) (113).]] he would not eat bread with meat; he would eat it only with date-wine, because he could not. He said: "I cannot be satisfied with meat while the Ummah is hungry." So this was for the sake of others. In sum: if he refrains from good things for a legitimate reason, he is not blameworthy; but if he refrains from them out of abstinence (*ta'affuf*), he is blameworthy.

* In it also is evidence that the Children of Israel were ungrateful for this blessing, by His saying ﴿*but they were wronging themselves*﴾.

* Among the benefits in it: the disobedient person does not wrong Allah, but wrongs himself. However, it is correct to say: this man has wronged himself with regard to the right of Allah, and with regard to the rights of people. We do not say that he wronged Allah; he wronged himself with regard to the right of Allah and with regard to the rights of people.

* Also among its benefits: everything we eat is from the provision of Allah, as in His saying ﴿*with which We have provided you*﴾.

* In it also: lawful provision is that which is good, by His saying ﴿*Eat of the good things*﴾; and that Allah, exalted is He, did not command eating what is foul; rather He forbade it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿*And when We said: Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating, and say: Hittah (relief), and We will forgive you your wrongdoings, and We will increase the good-doers*﴾.

* In it is affirmation that speech belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. And this speech is by the tongue of whom? Moses. So it affirms speech, and that Allah speaks. Is this true speech, or metaphorical? It is true, with a voice and with letters. But His voice, exalted and glorified is He, is not like the voice of any created being, and a person cannot imagine this voice, because it is magnificent.

* In it also is evidence that Allah, exalted is He, permitted the Children of Israel to enter Bayt al-Maqdis, by His saying ﴿*Enter this town*﴾.

* In it also is Allah's promise to them of entering it. From where is the promise derived? From the command to enter. The meaning is as if He says: "We have opened the gates for you, so enter."

* In it also is evidence for the permissibility of their eating, that is the Children of Israel, from this town they entered. But is it with compensation or without compensation?

**Students:** With compensation.

**Shaykh:** Yes. Spoils of war (*ghanimah*) are not permitted to them as they are permitted to us. But its meaning is that you may eat from it wherever you wish, in ease and contentment; He did not restrict you. However, it is not on the basis of spoils. It may be said that they may eat but not take ownership, and it becomes not a matter of spoils, just as, in the Islamic law, if I pass by an orchard I may eat from it, but I do not take possession of it. The particularity that was specific to this Ummah is the ownership of spoils. As for benefiting from the fruits of the lands they entered, that is permitted to them even in their law.

* In it also is evidence that whoever Allah has helped and granted conquest of lands must enter them in a manner of humility and submission, by His saying ﴿*And enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah*﴾. The Messenger (ﷺ), when he conquered Makkah, entered it with his head bowed. When Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Today is the day of slaughter; today the Ka'bah will be made lawful," and this reached the Prophet, peace be upon him, he said: "Sa'd has lied; rather today the Ka'bah will be magnified."[[al-Bukhari (4280), from the hadith of 'Urwah; see also Dala'il al-Nubuwwah by al-Bayhaqi (5/39).]] "Then he took the banner from him and gave it to his son Qays ibn Sa'd" as a rebuke to him for saying this word, although he had said it with good intention but without understanding. The Prophet, peace be upon him, made clear that this day is not one in which the Ka'bah is made lawful, but rather one in which the Ka'bah is magnified, because it was purified from idols and the lands were turned into Islamic lands after being lands of disbelief. Is there in this the making lawful of the Ka'bah? Never; rather in it is the magnification of the Ka'bah. But is there in it the making lawful of the tyrants who transgress against the Ka'bah? Yes indeed, that is correct.

* In this is evidence of the baseness of the Children of Israel and their opposition to Allah and His messengers, because they did not enter the gate prostrating; rather they entered crawling on their buttocks, going backwards, crawling, going backwards, out of arrogance and mockery. They said: instead of *hittah*, what? *Hintah* in a hair or in a barley grain. We only want something to fill our bellies; we do not want forgiveness of our sins. And we seek refuge in Allah.

And in it is evidence for the ugliness of ta'wil (interpretation that departs from the apparent meaning, here used pejoratively) and tahrif (distortion). These people distorted, and Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, likened the lam in "istawla" (he seized control), as held by the Jahmiyyah, to the nun that the Jews added in "hintah" (wheat). The Mu'tazilah, the Jahmiyyah, and also the Ash'ariyyah said: "istawa" means "istawla," so the lam in "istawa" according to them is the letter that was added, like the nun that was added in "hittah." They said "hintah," and this is correct. So they distorted the meaning in reality. The Children of Israel distorted both the wording and the meaning, while those distorted only the meaning, because they could not distort the wording. If they had distorted the wording of the Qur'an, the community would have risen against them and their misguidance would have become known. Therefore, in it is a clarification of the ugliness of distortion, distorting words from their places, whether verbal or conceptual.

And in it also: striving in jihad together with humility before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and seeking forgiveness are a cause of forgiveness, due to His saying: ﴿We will forgive you your wrongdoings﴾, and for gaining more of His bounty, due to His saying: ﴿And We will increase the doers of good﴾.

And in it also is evidence that ihsan (excellence, doing good) is a cause of increase, whether it is ihsan in the worship of Allah or ihsan to the servants of Allah, for ihsan is a cause of increase. It has been established from the Messenger ﷺ that he said: "Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother,"[[Narrated by Muslim (2699) from Abu Hurayrah.]] and "Whoever is in the need of his brother, Allah is in his need."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2442) and Muslim (2580/58) from Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon those who did wrong a plague from the sky because they were defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah 59].

He said: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted﴾. In it is evidence for the prohibition of substitution in the words of Allah, which is distorting them. From where is this derived? From describing them with wrongdoing: ﴿those who did wrong substituted a word﴾.

And in it is evidence for mentioning part of a thing, where it is inferred from and the second part is dispensed with. That is, for example, here: did they oppose in speech, or in speech and action? The noble verse says ﴿substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾, by speech only, and it remained silent about action. But it has been established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that "they entered crawling on their backsides."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3403) and Muslim (3015/1).]] So they substituted both speech and action. Therefore it can be said: they substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, meaning they made the word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in which there is the command to prostrate and the command to ask for forgiveness (hittah), into this entire word. So the intended meaning is not the same as the speech that is the counterpart of action. Rather, they substituted the word of Allah with another word, as if they had been told a word other than what they had been told. So the substitution is the substitution of speech only, or of action only, or of both speech and action?

* Students: Both action and speech.

* The Shaykh: No, no. In the Qur'an, what is meant is speech. We say: what is meant in the Qur'an is speech. If we say that the statement of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾ means: they substituted speech with speech, in the sense that they exchanged what they had been saying for another speech, then if we interpret the verse with this interpretation, it would have remained silent about the action which they made a substitute for what they were commanded. But if we say that the meaning of His statement ﴿those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾ is: they turned everything that had been said to them into another word, meaning as if they had been commanded to crawl on their backsides and to say "hintah fi sha'rah" (wheat in barley), then they substituted the original word that had been said with another word which they obeyed. On this basis, the verse includes the substitution of speech and action, includes the substitution of speech (...), and no problem remains in it. In reality, even if we assume we explained it by the first meaning, that they said other than what had been said to them, the hadith is sound and explicit in that, that they also substituted the action.

* The Student: Mentioning part of a thing dispenses with the other?

* The Shaykh: This is if we say that the speech they substituted is the speech that actually came from them. But if we say that they substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, meaning they made the command of Allah to them into a command for something else, which is what they did, meaning as if they distorted the command of Allah, that is, the word of Allah, then in that case it does not fall under the category of mentioning one of the two parts while dispensing with mentioning the other. And Allah knows best what He intended by His speech.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So We sent upon those who did wrong a plague from the sky.﴾ His statement ﴿So We sent﴾: the fa' is for causation. Did you understand? That is, because of what occurred from them of substitution, We sent down.

And His statement ﴿upon those who did wrong﴾ means: upon them. This is from the category of using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun. We mentioned in the previous lesson that it has three benefits. Did we?

* A student: I was not present.

* The Shaykh: Did we mention the benefit of using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun?

* A student: Using an apparent noun in place of a pronoun: alerting (...).

* A student: First, passing judgment on these people, or specifying these people with the judgment.

* The Shaykh: No, passing judgment on them with what this apparent noun indicates, which is that they did wrong. This is one.

* The Student: The second: that this description is general, the generality of the description with the generality of the ruling, the generality of the ruling with the generality of the description.

* The Shaykh: That is, its meaning is that so that it would be...

* The Student: General for them and for others.

* The Shaykh: So that it would be general for them and for others. Third, did we mention only these?

* The Student: Alerting.

* The Shaykh: No, alerting, we mentioned it, may Allah bless you, in the case where there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person), when a shift occurs from the third person to the second person or the reverse.

* The Student: And this (...) for emphasis?

* The Shaykh: It may happen that there is attentiveness in it, when a person's speech is structured so that a pronoun is expected, and then an apparent noun is used instead. This may be a means of drawing attention, so that the person becomes attentive, and it is said: why did the apparent noun come when the context of the speech requires a pronoun? It may be so.

* The Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: But in any case, the matter intends generality, so that this ruling includes whoever resembles them.

* The Student: In the description.

* The Shaykh: And the second: passing judgment on them with what this apparent noun requires, namely that they did wrong.
