Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And [recall] when We shook the mountain over them as if it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with strength"﴾ [al-A'raf 171]. In that hour they rushed to prostrate and they prostrated, but they tilted in their prostration, looking at the mountain in fear of it. This is why it is said that the prostration of the Jews toward this community is a tilted prostration: you find him prostrating while raising one of his eyes. They said: this prostration, we prostrate to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in a manner of intimidation, so we continue to prostrate in this way. This was their prostration; this is the prostration of the Jews.
* Student: They consider it a means of closeness (qurbah)?
* Shaykh: Yes, they consider it a means of closeness. And in reality it has a counterpart in this community: the eclipse. For an eclipse is in reality a departure from the natural order: the moon comes between the earth and the sun, or the earth comes between the sun and the moon. This is why the Messenger (ﷺ) said: «Indeed Allah frightens His servants with them» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1059) and Muslim (912/24), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So Allah, glorified is He, made the sign of warning among the Children of Israel greater than [the sign given to] this community, because this community is closer to accepting the truth and to fear. The Children of Israel do not fear from this kind of eclipse; nothing frightens them except a mountain they know, raised above them as if it were a canopy.

Unfortunately, there are now among us those who have imitated the Jews in this matter. They no longer take warning from the eclipse; they only take warning when mountains are raised above their heads, may Allah protect us. Yet it is obligatory for a person to recognize what has taken this out of its natural course until it became in this state. Even if the whole world gathered to eclipse the sun or to make the moon eclipse, they could not. So what took it out of its course except Allah, glorified and exalted is He, for the purpose of warning and frightening? And according to those who say that the earth revolves, they say: the movement of the earth is what has been disturbed. We do not know; perhaps this movement, this disruption that has occurred within it, will lead to its destruction, and to greater eclipses and earthquakes. So we must fear. In any case, I say: this heavenly warning, as it occurred among the Children of Israel, has occurred in this community.

Allah, mighty and majestic is He, says: ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾. ﴿You turned away﴾ means you turned aside and withdrew from obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿after that﴾: referring to what? 
* Student: The raising of the mountain.
* Shaykh: The raising of the mountain. ﴿We raised above you the mountain﴾: after this repentance, at the time the mountain was raised, you turned away and did not mention it. You did not remember that the one who frightened you with this mountain might bring it upon you again.

﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾. ﴿So if not for the bounty﴾: "fadl" (bounty), what is its grammatical analysis (i'rab)? It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is obligatorily omitted, as Ibn Malik said:
"After 'lawla' the predicate is usually omitted; its omission is obligatory..."
meaning: "and if not for the bounty of Allah upon you (existed)". It was obligatory to omit it, being satisfied by the response of "lawla". ﴿you would have been﴾ is the response of "lawla": ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾.

His saying ﴿the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾: what kind of bounty and mercy is this? It is the sending of messengers and prophets to the Children of Israel after the mountain was raised. For Allah did not leave them; rather He sent messengers to them. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged for those who were Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]. So the bounty of Allah here is by what? By sending the messengers, which is the requirement of His mercy, because He, glorified and exalted is He, knows that creation cannot independently know how to worship Allah, glorified and exalted is He. For this reason He sent them messengers to guide them and make clear to them.

﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾: the lam here is attached to the response of "lawla", ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾, those who lost this world and the Hereafter, for the most losing of people are the disbelievers; they gained nothing from their worldly life nor from their Hereafter. So in this there is an affirmation, meaning that Allah showed favor to the Children of Israel and had mercy upon them (...)?
* Students: By sending the messengers.
* Shaykh: By sending the messengers, who remind them and admonish them so that they return to Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 62–74 (part 2 of 7):

﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ [al-Baqarah 65] His words: ﴿Certainly (laqad)﴾. The lam is a preface to an oath (al-lam al-muwatta'ah lil-qasam), and on this basis the sentence is—?
* A student: Emphatic.
* The Shaykh: Emphasized with three emphatics; what are they?
* The student: The implied oath, the lam, and qad.
* The Shaykh: The implied oath, the lam, and qad. That is, "wa-laqad" originally means: "By Allah, indeed..."
﴿And you certainly knew those who transgressed﴾: you knew with certainty of knowledge and recognized them with complete recognition. ﴿Those among you who transgressed﴾: to whom is the address? To the Children of Israel. And ﴿transgressed﴾ means they exceeded the limits and became tyrannical.

His words: ﴿in the matter of the Sabbath﴾, i.e., concerning the ruling of the day of Sabbath (al-Sabt), which is well known: the day after Friday. On this day Allah, blessed and exalted, had forbidden the Children of Israel to work and had forbidden them to hunt fish on that day, so that they might devote themselves to worship, because they were the ones who chose Saturday for themselves. So Saturday became theirs. This day which they had chosen for themselves, Allah forbade them work and fishing on it. Then Allah, glorified and exalted, tested them with what He had forbidden them, making it easy for them on that day to an extreme degree. So when Saturday came, the fish would come to the surface in great numbers (shurra'an). What is the meaning of shurra'an?
* A student: Visible.
* The Shaykh: Floating openly on the surface because of their abundance. But on other days than Saturday they would not see them. This is without doubt a trial and test from Allah, glorified and exalted, by which He tests His servants; He may make sins and the means of sin easier for them than the means of obedience and good, for the sake of testing and trial. These people did not endure this trial, may Allah protect us, so they devised a stratagem: they dug pits beside the sea and made between these pits and the sea a channel, meaning a small canal. When the fish came in great numbers, they would drive them with the water into this channel and into these pits. When the water receded, the fish could not return, because the channel was narrow and they could not move along it, and it might dry up completely. So when Saturday came, the fish would come and fall into these pits, and when it was night or the next day they would come and take them. Their jurists said to them: "How can you take them when it is forbidden to you?" They said: "We only hunted them on Sunday, we did not hunt them on Saturday." A stratagem, an obvious stratagem, is it not? It is true that they only hunted on Sunday, but they performed the cause by which they hunt on—when?
* The students: On Saturday.
* The Shaykh: On Saturday. So in reality they hunted on Saturday. And since this stratagem—may Allah protect us—appears sound, what is its reality?
* A student: Entanglement.
* The Shaykh: Entanglement in what is forbidden. That is, its outward appearance is correctness and permissibility, while its inward reality is corruption and prohibition. What were they punished with? They were punished by appearing like human beings outwardly, while inwardly they were beasts of prey. ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected"﴾ (we seek refuge in Allah). ﴿We said to them﴾: to the transgressors; ﴿We said to them﴾: to those who transgressed. ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected﴾: qiradah is the plural of qird, which is well known; khasi'in means banished, distant from the mercy of Allah (we seek refuge in Allah). So they were transformed into an animal most resembling a human being, just as their act most resembled a lawful, correct act while being forbidden inwardly. So the recompense was of the same kind as the deed.

In Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and with whom He was angry, and whom He made into apes and swine, and who worshipped the Taghut﴾ [al-Ma'idah 60]. Were these people of the town apes or swine? In Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And ask them about the town which was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them for what they used to defy. And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" they said, "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him." So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment for what they used to defy. So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected"﴾ [al-A'raf 163–166]. Is there a third verse? In al-Ma'idah: ﴿the apes and the swine﴾. I have not seen that these people of the town were apes and swine; they were only apes, just apes. Although some exegetes said that the people of this town became apes and swine, so their youth became apes and their elders swine, this needs to be established by a legal proof. Otherwise, the verses here and in al-A'raf mention only that they were apes, and the swine were another people who were transformed, may Allah protect us from that.

His words: ﴿So We said to them﴾: this saying ﴿Be﴾... ﴿We said﴾ ﴿Be﴾: is this command a cosmic command (kawni) or a legislative command (shar'i)?
* The students: Cosmic.
* The Shaykh: Cosmic. Can it be understood as a legislative command?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No, it cannot, is that not so? Because a person cannot change his own soul; can he change his soul?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: He cannot. So it is a cosmic command, like the words of Allah, exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam. He created him from dust; then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Ali 'Imran 59]. Is "Be" (kun) here a cosmic command or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: A cosmic command.

﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾

First: This story is elaborated in Surat al-A'raf. This town in which they transgressed was certainly by the sea, as His words indicate: ﴿which was by the sea﴾. It has been said it was Aylah, and it has been said it was other than that. What matters is not its name, but its location: that it was on the sea.

Second: Its people divided into three groups: a group that transgressed and devised stratagems against the prohibitions of Allah; a group that was upright and forbade the stratagems against the prohibitions of Allah; and a third group that remained silent, indeed discouraged others. They said to those who admonished: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?﴾ The others answered them that there must be in it one or two benefits: ﴿As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him.﴾ There is no doubt that those who forbade evil were saved. Is that not so?
* A student: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: And those who transgressed were transformed. We are left with those who remained silent, neither forbidding nor transgressing. What is their status?
* A student: They were transformed.
* The Shaykh: Do you decide this with such quick certainty?
* The student: Yes indeed, ﴿those who forbade evil were saved﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but ﴿when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden﴾.
* A student: The remaining category.
* The Shaykh: It does not contradict that. But the second group: did they not insolently persist in what they were forbidden?
* The student: These pronouns refer to the people of this town...
* The Shaykh: The silent ones did not deny, but did they forbid?
* The student: Yes, they insolently persisted in not forbidding.
* The Shaykh: Wait. ﴿And ask them about the town which was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾: ﴿when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾ refers to the transgressors. ﴿When their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them for what they used to defy. And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people..."﴾ Among whom?
* A student: Among those who transgressed.
* The Shaykh: Among those who transgressed? That is, some of their brothers, some of the transgressors, said to those who forbade: "Do not forbid," and they are among the transgressors?
* A student: No, they are among the silent ones, because Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿perhaps they will fear Him﴾; they say to them...
* The Shaykh: ﴿And ask them about the town which was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them, the people of the town, on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them for what they used to defy. And when a community among them﴾: among whom? Among the transgressors or among the people of the town?
* The students: Among the people of the town.
* The Shaykh: Among the people of the town? ﴿A community among them said﴾: the people of the town. ﴿Why do you admonish a people﴾: whom are they addressing?
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: No, they are addressing those who forbade. ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment? They said﴾: that is, the admonishers...
* A student: Does this statement they made place them in the first group?
* The Shaykh: Let us see. ﴿They said: As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him.﴾ They did not say this to justify those who said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah..."; they did not say it to justify the act of the transgressors. They said it out of despair regarding them, that is, they said: there is no benefit in this, it does not avert the punishment ﴿whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment﴾. They did not say, "Why do you admonish them, since they have done nothing?" For if they had said that, we would say they approved of their deed. But in reality they were like what exists now: some people despair, saying: "Why do you advise this man? There is no benefit, Allah does not guide him." This exists now. They said: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?﴾ meaning there is no benefit in advising them. Those others answered: we do not despair; we have a certain benefit, which is an excuse before Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿As an excuse to your Lord﴾, ﴿and perhaps they will fear Him﴾. This is a probable matter, for Allah guides a people from among the most astray and returns them to the truth. ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, ﴿forgot what they had been reminded of﴾: who?
* The students: The transgressors.
* The Shaykh: The transgressors. ﴿We saved those who forbade evil﴾: those who forbade evil; and He was silent about the rest.
﴿And We seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment for what they used to defy.﴾ Who are those who wronged?
* A student: All of them, those who were silent and those who acted.
* Another student: O Shaykh, did those who wronged not forbid them and despair, so they are included with those who forbade evil? They only despaired after they had taken the means.
* The Shaykh: We do not know. Let us examine the question, since Ibn 'Abbas and his mawla differed on it, so let us see. ﴿And We seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment for what they used to defy. So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden﴾ — this is certainly about the doers, not about those who said ﴿Why do you admonish﴾. ﴿So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ So those who became apes now: who are they?
* A student: The transgressors.
* The Shaykh: The transgressors, is that not so? ﴿And We seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment﴾: so now we are left with those who wronged. Did the silent ones wrong, so that they are included, or are those who wronged the ones who transgressed? I, from the context of the verse, am certain, and Allah knows best, that those who remained silent were not transformed into apes.
* A student: They were seized with punishment.
* The Shaykh: They were seized with a wretched punishment. But they were transformed into apes: those who were transformed into apes were only those who transgressed in the Sabbath. Those who transgressed in the Sabbath are without doubt those who were transformed. ﴿So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ Therefore some scholars say, as you said or as the brother said, that those who remained silent were punished. But on this view, one must not say that they were punished by being transformed into despised apes, because the verses are explicit that only those who transgressed were transformed into apes. But they were seized with what?
* A student: With punishment.
* The Shaykh: ﴿With a wretched punishment﴾, which Allah did not specify. ﴿With a wretched punishment﴾: if they are included in the phrase ﴿those who wronged﴾, then they were seized with a wretched punishment; if not, then they were not seized with a wretched punishment. Therefore, if someone said that the safe course is to remain silent about those who remained silent and to say: they are three categories: one category was certainly saved, one category was certainly punished, and one category whose state is not clear to us. Without doubt, by the principles of the Islamic legal rules, these who remained silent, if they approved of them, are like them; if they approved, the form of their transgression becomes their endorsement of the wrong. If they did not approve of them, which is the apparent case, but they despaired of them, then the punishment does not reach them. But they may be punished for the reason that it is obligatory upon them to enjoin good and forbid evil, whether the one commanded complies and the one forbidden desists or not. This is the obligation. Therefore these intelligent, shrewd people (plural of kayyis) said: ﴿As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him.﴾ And in truth, enjoining good and forbidding evil must occur even if the one commanded does not comply and the one forbidden does not desist, because it has two great benefits: the excuse before Allah, mighty and majestic, and second, the possibility that they fear Allah. I also say there is a third benefit: that it is recognized that this is an evil. Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because if we remained silent, we would say: "By Allah, we cannot act now; even if we commanded, they would not obey us." Meaning: if we remain silent, people will come after us, or in our time, and say: "These people do such things in front of the scholars and they said nothing." Many matters are now used as evidence against us and others: that the scholars used to do such and such, and so-and-so is alive and says nothing. Is this clear?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Until now. So there are in reality three benefits: the excuse before Allah, glorified and exalted; the clarification that this is an evil; and third, perhaps they will fear Allah.
* A student: What are the emphatics in ﴿And you certainly knew﴾?
* The Shaykh: There are: the lam and qad.
* A student: The reason?
* The Shaykh: That is, the reason it is emphasized? The reason is to establish the proof against them.
* The student: They were deniers of the proof?
* The Shaykh: No, no. Whether they acknowledged or denied, their action and their denial and rejection of the Messenger ﷺ is a reprehensible act. Therefore He said: ﴿And you certainly knew﴾. If they knew these people and that they were afflicted with this calamity for their transgression, then what is the matter with you that you transgress now and deny the Messenger, peace be upon him, while you know him as you know your sons?
* A student: Shaykh, what is the correct view?
* The Shaykh: I hold back on it, and Allah knows best. If I must judge, I judge that they were seized with a wretched punishment, not that they were transformed into apes.
* The student: Is it not said that the transgressors also received the wretched punishment? Their transformation into apes is a punishment for them?
* The Shaykh: Yes, yes. They were seized with a wretched punishment and were transformed into apes, because without doubt they are included among those who wronged; the transgressors are the first to enter the phrase ﴿those who wronged﴾.
* A student: Is the wretched punishment not itself the transformation into apes here?
* The Shaykh: No, that is part of it, part of the wretched punishment.
* A student: (...) the despairing ones were apes?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because they said: ﴿Allah is going to destroy them﴾, and rationally no one would approve of a person and be content with his act while knowing that among them...
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: (...) Not at all. Do you know that the act of this man is a cause of destruction and you are content with it? That is impossible.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 62–74 (part 3 of 7):

* Student: Shaykh, his saying: ﴿الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ ("those who did wrong") is correct (...), but his saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿أَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ﴾ ("We saved those who forbade evil"), is this not clear?
* The Shaykh: Just by implication (mafhum).
* The Student: Its implication is that those who did not forbid...
* The Shaykh: That those who did not forbid were not saved. And what is the implication of ﴿الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾?
* The Student: It is general (mujmal).
* The Shaykh: Its implication?
* The Student: Its implication is that those who did not do wrong were not seized with punishment.
* The Shaykh: That is one. And the implication of ﴿الَّذِينَ اعْتَدَوْا مِنْكُمْ فِي السَّبْتِ﴾ ("those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath"): that whoever did not transgress on the Sabbath was not turned into apes and swine? So we have: the turning into apes cannot apply to the silent ones, and the saving cannot apply to the silent ones either, right?
* The Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because "they" (the ones who were) saved were those who forbade evil. We remain with their being seized with the grievous punishment. Are they included among those who did wrong, because they did not carry out what was obligatory of denouncing the evil? Then they were seized with a grievous punishment that Allah did not specify. Or they did not do wrong and were not seized with the grievous punishment, and we remain silent about them and say: Allah knows best? In other words: we now are certain that they were not saved and were not seized to become apes, despised, they were not seized with this punishment; we remain in the matter of the grievous punishment. When does this grievous punishment befall them? When it is established that they are wrongdoers.
* The Student: But if we remain silent, have we not abandoned the implication of ﴿أَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ﴾?
* The Shaykh: No, because we have an explicit statement (manthuq), and it has an opposite implication.
* Student: The general texts.
* The Shaykh: In any case, praise be to Allah, this matter is not of such importance to us, in terms of what follows from it. Even the legal ruling in the Islamic Shari'ah is clear in the matter: the legal ruling in the Islamic Shari'ah is clear, and it is that denouncing evil is obligatory; a person must denounce evil when able. But he is not obliged to change the evil; because there is something we must also know, the difference between denouncing (inkar) and changing (taghyir). Changing means removing the evil. As for enjoining good and forbidding evil, this is obligatory in every case, because it is of the category of conveying (tabligh). We have three levels: conveying, commanding, and changing, and each is different from the next. Some people think the meaning is one and the matter is different, because changing is only through authority and command, meaning by the power of execution, like rulers who change, right?
* The Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The ruler can change: he strikes, or for example pours out the wine, clear?
* The Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Or he says... "If he is not able, then with his tongue." But he cannot change with his hand, he changes with his tongue, he commands others, and others... As for the matter of denouncing, it is obligatory on every person when able, as is known. And conveying is more comprehensive, because conveying is obligatory on you even if you have not seen the evil. You must say to people, for example: adultery is forbidden, theft is forbidden, drinking wine is forbidden, even if they were not drinking it. This is conveying. And enjoining good occurs when good is neglected. Conveying is obligatory: you say, prayer is obligatory, or not? Congregational prayer is obligatory, and ablution for such-and-such is obligatory, and so on through all the obligations: convey them. Commanding: when do you command them? When you see someone neglecting to perform them. Clear? The evil: you must inform the people that it is evil, but when do you forbid it?
* Student: (...) Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, mentioned that the fish do not come out on the surface of the water except (...) the fish in abundance. They wanted to trick Allah, may He be glorified and exalted; (...) they set up nets into which the fish enter and are caught, then they come on Sunday and take these fish. So they played a trick on Allah.
* The Shaykh: What is the trick?
* The Student: The trick is that they caught the fish on Saturday and took them on Sunday.
* The Shaykh: How, meaning?
* The Student: They place nets into which they enter; the catch happened on Saturday, and they took them on Sunday.
* The Shaykh: This is (...) a trick.
* Student: (...) that they opened the channels from outside the sea and made for them water-wheels, so the waves come and push the water laden with fish, and it enters inside these water-wheels and falls into the channels. Then on the next day the water recedes, and the fish cannot return, and they take them on Sunday.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, these are two descriptions. Some said: they set up nets into which the fish enter on Saturday and cannot leave. Others say: no, they open the water-wheels onto a body of water, then the fish enter it. By this act it is considered? What is the ruling, permissible or forbidden?
* Student: No, forbidden.
* The Shaykh: How forbidden? They only hunted on Sunday.
* The Student: They hunted on Saturday and played a trick by claiming they hunted on Sunday, but the hunting happened on Saturday.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, so this is a trick?
* The Student: This is a trick.
* The Shaykh: This is a trick, and tricks are forbidden?
* The Student: And tricks are forbidden.
* The Shaykh: Is the punishment of the same kind as the act?
* Student: The punishment (...).
* The Shaykh: How so?
* The Student: Because they were punished by being transformed into apes, so their forms became the forms of animals (...).
* The Shaykh: Or closest to a human?
* The Student: Yes, and it is closest.
* The Shaykh: Closest to a human in appearance, yes. And their act is closest to what is permissible, but in reality it is forbidden. Likewise, apes apparently resemble humans, because they understand. Indeed they say that sometimes sexual intercourse may occur between an ape and a woman, it desires her as a man desires her, but in reality, what is their reality? An animal, beasts.

Into how many parts did the people of this town divide?
* Student: Into three categories: people who transgressed, people who forbade evil, and people who remained silent.
* The Shaykh: Silent. Those who remained silent, did they have a role?
* Student: Those who remained silent said: Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy or punish?
* The Shaykh: ﴿مُهْلِكُهُمْ أَوْ مُعَذِّبُهُمْ﴾ ("whom Allah will destroy or punish").
* The Student: ﴿مُهْلِكُهُمْ﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿عَذَابًا شَدِيدًا﴾ ("with a severe punishment").
* The Student: ﴿عَذَابًا شَدِيدًا﴾.
* The Shaykh: The purpose of this statement: is it a prohibition from admonishing them, or what?
* The Student: Apparently it is a prohibition on the act (...) they despaired of Allah's mercy.
* The Shaykh: What is your view?
* Student: Apparently they despaired of being answered.
* The Shaykh: In other words, their intention was not prohibition, meaning, their intention was not that they were content with the evil?
* The Student: They were not content.
* The Shaykh: They were not content with the evil.
* The Student: But they despaired.
* The Shaykh: But they despaired, and said: How do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy or punish with a severe punishment? And the proof that they were not content with the evil is that they mentioned their punishment: ﴿اللَّهُ مُهْلِكُهُمْ أَوْ مُعَذِّبُهُمْ عَذَابًا شَدِيدًا﴾ [Al-A'raf 164].
* Student: Does this count as discouragement (tathbit)?
* The Shaykh: There is undoubtedly some kind of discouragement, there is some kind of discouragement. It may be that when they despaired, they thought that reminding is only obligatory if it benefits, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿فَذَكِّرْ إِنْ نَفَعَتِ الذِّكْرَى﴾ ("So remind, if reminding benefits") [Al-A'la 9].
* The Student: (...).
* Student: The third group has a difference of opinion (...) between the state of the group that transgressed and the state of the group that...
* The Shaykh: Forbade, ﴿أَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ وَأَخَذْنَا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا بِعَذَابٍ بَئِيسٍ بِمَا كَانُوا يَفْسُقُونَ﴾ ("We saved those who forbade evil, and seized those who did wrong with a grievous punishment for their defiance") [Al-A'raf 165].
* The Student: So the third group has a difference of opinion: is it included among those who did wrong, or did Allah, may He be exalted, remain silent about it, so we remain silent about it as He remained silent (...), that it is included with the wrongdoers (...).
* The Shaykh: That is: even if we say the third group was seized, they were seized with a grievous punishment, because those who were turned into apes were those who transgressed: ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمُ الَّذِينَ اعْتَدَوْا مِنْكُمْ فِي السَّبْتِ فَقُلْنَا لَهُمْ كُونُوا قِرَدَةً﴾ ("And you certainly know those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes") [Al-Baqarah 65], and He said: ﴿فَلَمَّا عَتَوْا عَنْ مَا نُهُوا عَنْهُ قُلْنَا لَهُمْ كُونُوا قِرَدَةً خَاسِئِينَ﴾ ("So when they became arrogant regarding what they had been forbidden, We said to them: Be apes, despised") [Al-A'raf 166].
Then the consideration remains: is the group that said ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا﴾ ("Why do you admonish a people") included in His saying ﴿أَخَذْنَا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا بِعَذَابٍ بَئِيسٍ﴾ ("We seized those who did wrong with a grievous punishment"), or not? We have said that there is a difference among the scholars regarding it, because Allah, the Exalted, mentioned two groups: ﴿أَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ وَأَخَذْنَا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾, so we have the saved, the seized, and the transformed. The transformed are certainly the third group, the transgressing group, and the saved are the saved group, which is clear. What remains: are those who did wrong included or not? One might say they are certainly not included, because they were not wrongdoers. But when He said: ﴿أَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ﴾, a speaker may say: the implication of "those who forbid" is His saying ﴿الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾, because Allah made them a counterpart to it: ﴿أَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ يَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ السُّوءِ وَأَخَذْنَا الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾, so He made them a counterpart. The counterpart of "those who forbid evil" includes both groups: the transgressing group, and the group that said ﴿لِمَ تَعِظُونَ قَوْمًا﴾. We say: praise be to Allah, this is not one of the matters we are obliged to prefer. We say: Allah knows best, when nothing is clear to us from the Qur'an apparently, then we say: Allah knows best.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا نَكَالًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَمَا خَلْفَهَا﴾ ("So We made it a deterrent for what was before it and what was after it") [Al-Baqarah 66]. ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا﴾: there is a difference regarding His saying ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا﴾, to whom does the pronoun in (ها, "it") refer? Does (جعلناها, "We made it") refer to the town, by His saying ﴿وَاسْأَلْهُمْ عَنِ الْقَرْيَةِ الَّتِي كَانَتْ حَاضِرَةَ الْبَحْرِ إِذْ يَعْدُونَ فِي السَّبْتِ﴾, and the referent is understood from the context? Or does it refer to the punishment? So We made the punishment, because Allah says: ﴿قُلْنَا لَهُمْ كُونُوا قِرَدَةً خَاسِئِينَ﴾, and ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا﴾ means: this punishment.

Let us follow the first: ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا﴾ means this town, ﴿نَكَالًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا﴾. What is the meaning of nakal (deterrent)? Tankil means that a person is dealt with in a way that he cannot return to what he was punished for. "Nakkaltuhu" means: I dealt with him by an act that he cannot return from what I punished him for. So His saying ﴿نَكَالًا﴾ means: We made it a punishment that deters what is before it and what is after it, that is, it prevents them from returning to this same act.

And His saying ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَمَا خَلْفَهَا﴾: if we say the pronoun (ها) refers to the town, what is the meaning of ﴿مَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا﴾? What is intended by it? What is before it of towns and what is behind it, meaning what was near it, because they knew of it, and they will desist.

It was said: the intended meaning is what is before it in time, not in place. But there is a problem with this: if we say what is before it is its future, how can what is behind it be deterred when it has passed? Have you not understood? We now have: what is before it in place, or what is before it in time? If we say in place, the matter is clear and there is no problem. If we say in time, there is a problem, because if you make ﴿مَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا﴾ its future and ﴿وَمَا خَلْفَهَا﴾ its past, it is not correct that it be a deterrent for its past. What is the reason? Because those who passed are not benefiting from it; they passed and ended. But they said: we answer this problem by making ﴿مَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا﴾ for those present in their era, and ﴿وَمَا خَلْفَهَا﴾ for what comes after, as in His saying: ﴿وَكَانَ وَرَاءَهُمْ مَلِكٌ يَأْخُذُ كُلَّ سَفِينَةٍ غَصْبًا﴾ ("And there was behind them a king who seized every ship by force") [Al-Kahf 79]. So khalf and wara' may refer to the front, the future, and according to this view there is no problem at all.

Which is more general: that it be made a deterrent for the towns around it, or a deterrent for those in its era and those after them?
* The Students: The second is more general.
* The Shaykh: The second is more general, yes, because everyone who comes after you is behind you, right? Whoever comes after you is behind you. So on this basis the second view is more preferable: that what is before it and behind it refers to time, not place, and this punishment is a deterrent for those in their era and those who came after them until the Day of Resurrection.

This is if we say the pronoun in (ها) refers to the town. You have understood the problem that arises for this view. What is the problem that arises for this view?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: The punishment.
* The Shaykh: That (ها) refers to the town, and there is a problem, and we answered it.
* Student: The problem regarding the town?
* The Shaykh: The problem regarding the town: that it has not been mentioned before. It has not been mentioned before. Say: it has not been mentioned before. But we answered it, what is it?
* Student: That it is understood.
* The Shaykh: From the context, it is understood from the context, by the proof of His saying in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿وَاسْأَلْهُمْ عَنِ الْقَرْيَةِ الَّتِي كَانَتْ حَاضِرَةَ الْبَحْرِ﴾.

If we say the pronoun (ها) refers to the punishment, so We made this punishment ﴿نَكَالًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَمَا خَلْفَهَا﴾, the meaning becomes: what is before it and after it of deeds, neither of time nor of place. That is: We made this punishment deter them from what is before it of sins and what is after it, meaning the sins they committed previously they do not commit again, and future sins they also do not commit, because whenever they remember this punishment, they fear it. Have you understood or not?

We have mentioned previously: if a Qur'anic verse can bear two meanings that do not contradict each other, it must be taken as both. If they contradict, one must weigh them and act on the stronger. If no preference is found, one must suspend judgment. Right? This rule has passed for us, and it is beneficial in tafsir and also in hadith, that if a verse can bear two meanings, what?
* Students: It must be taken, they do not contradict.
* The Shaykh: No, a necessary condition is: they do not contradict. It must be taken as both, because the speech of Allah is broader than our understanding. And if the two contradict, meaning like opposites and contradictories, for example, it is not possible to take it as two opposing meanings; it is taken as the stronger of them if a preference is found. If no preference is found, we must suspend judgment.
* Student: You mentioned that if the pronoun (ها) refers to the punishment ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا وَمَا خَلْفَهَا﴾, meaning, if they wanted to commit a sin, they would remember this punishment, because the punishment descended upon them and they became apes among animals. So how did they remember?
* The Shaykh: Yes, those apes did die, that is correct, this is a possibility. But these people are three categories: a category that remained silent, a category that forbade, and a category that transgressed and were turned into apes and died. The other categories who remained are those who may err and disobey Allah, right? They may err and disobey Allah, but they remember this matter and refrain from it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: In practice. But the last view is only valid if we take (ها) as referring to the punishment.
* Student: If it refers to the punishment, what would the meaning be?
* The Shaykh: The meaning would be: ﴿جَعَلْنَاهَا نَكَالًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا﴾ of deeds, meaning: it deters them from deeds. The intended sense is their kind, because the question the brother raised is valid, but the intended meaning is their kind, or those who were turned into apes and died are not left. So the meaning is that they remember if they intend a sin whose kind they had previously committed, they remember and are restrained, or if they intend a new sin whose kind they had not previously committed, they also remember and refrain,

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 62–74 (part 4 of 7):

And His saying: ﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾. We made it an admonition, meaning: a place of admonition. A place of admonition for whom? For the God-fearing who fear Allah. As for those whose hearts are hardened, who have no piety, they are not admonished by these signs. Allah, glorified and exalted, always restricts admonitions to the God-fearing, and to whoever has a heart or gives ear while being a witness, and the like, because the heart that is hard does not soften—we ask Allah for well-being. ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus 96, 97].

Of this type is what exists in our time: earthquakes, eclipses, floods, and violent winds. The God-fearing person is admonished by them and fears, and knows that Allah sent them as a punishment. The one who is not God-fearing does not have his heart softened, is not admonished, and says: these are natural matters, in which the punishment of Allah, glorified and exalted, has no effect at all. These are not truly God-fearing people. Otherwise, earthquakes are among the punishments: ﴿So they denied him, and the earthquake seized them﴾. And earthquakes are a tremor (rajfah), a tremor in the earth by which it is shaken. ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became, in their home, prostrate﴾ [al-'Ankabut 37].

For this reason some writers did not warn people about these earthquakes, did not warn them of sins, but instead began to speak and say: this is a chain of earthquakes that will extend to Jeddah and to such-and-such, and to such-and-such. Someone mentioned to me yesterday that they wrote in the newspapers that it would extend to Jeddah and go to such-and-such, and that the people of Jeddah were seized by such fear, both the absent and the present, and that they said: we will move to Makkah, because Makkah has not been struck by an earthquake. That is what they said. And someone from the people of Jeddah told me yesterday, here with us, that the Ministry of Information was compelled to deny this news and to have some of the newsmen speak on television about earthquakes and about Jeddah, that earthquakes will not come to it, and that most earthquakes occur in the seas—by the grace of Allah, most of them occur in the seas and not on dry land. Thus I heard it; or did you not follow this news? But the duty upon the Muslims, O people, the duty is not this. The duty is that they frighten people. Whatever we say, that these are natural causes: who has determined that the natural cause should be at this particular time, and upon this particular nation, except Allah? Their disobedience is written, and the affliction is written, and the time is fixed, and the place is fixed, from of old, in eternity. Suppose these have physical causes; but their determination at a time and upon the nation that dwelt on this part that shook? Is this not by the decree of Allah? By the decree of Allah, mighty and majestic. Then this is something written beforehand.

These were destined to disobey. But certainly it is known that the truth was made clear to them; had they been guided, the punishment would have been lifted from them, as it was lifted from the people of Yunus. The people of Yunus were seized by the punishment, but they believed, so Allah removed it from them: ﴿Why was there not a city that believed and its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus﴾ [Yunus 98]. ﴿Why was there not﴾ means: no city believed so that its faith benefited it after the might of Allah had descended upon it, except the people of Yunus.

What we intend is this: the legislated admonitions that come through revelation, and the cosmic admonitions that come through actual occurrence, by decree—none benefit from them except the God-fearing believers who know Allah. As for others, they do not benefit from them. ﴿And if they should see a piece of the sky falling﴾: a fragment of punishment descending upon them from the sky, ﴿they would say: a layered cloud﴾ [al-Tur 44]. Yes, we ask Allah for well-being.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when Musa said to his people: Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah 67]. This is among the trials of the Children of Israel. Listen to it: ﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾. The attribution of "people" to him (his people) is to show that peace be upon him could only say to them what contains good, because a person will advise his own people more than others, although the messengers, peace be upon them, advise their nations in general.

* Student: ﴿So We made it an exemplary punishment for what was before it and what was after it, and an admonition﴾. If this pronoun refers to the town, how can the town be the admonition?
* The Shaykh: We said: "admonition" means a place of admonition.
﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾ [al-Baqarah 67]: whose people? The Children of Israel. ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾: he said it in answer to something Allah mentioned in the course of the story: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it, and Allah brought forth what you were concealing﴾ [al-Baqarah 72].

A soul was killed among them. The exegetes have mentioned here many Israelite narrations concerning this matter, but we are not concerned to specify who this killer was and who this victim was: was he a cousin? Did he want his wealth? Did he want such-and-such? This does not concern us. Yes, a soul was killed, and they "disputed over it" (fa-dara'tum), meaning they quarrelled and pushed against one another until strife nearly erupted among them. There is no need for us to explain why it was killed or for what purpose; this is not among our concerns, because the Qur'an did not speak of it. The utmost we take from the Children of Israel is what contains no disparagement of the Qur'an or contradiction of it. They killed a soul and disputed over it, quarrelling, each claiming that the others had killed him, and strife nearly arose among them. They said: there is no need for us to fight and destroy one another; let us go to the Prophet of Allah Musa, and he will tell us who killed him. So they went to him, and he said to them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. He attributed the command to Allah; he did not say "I command you" or "slaughter," but said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, so that it would be more inviting to their acceptance and compliance, because if he had said "slaughter a cow," someone might suppose that this was from Musa's own opinion. But when he said ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾, the suspicion of personal reasoning is removed, is it not? And it became necessary that it be a serious statement, not a jest. Note ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾; and with this explicit wording ﴿to slaughter a cow﴾, they said: ﴿Do you take us for a joke?﴾ —we seek refuge in Allah— do you mock us? Although he attributed it to Allah. And this, we seek refuge in Allah from it, is from their rebelliousness: how is he their prophet, whom they know to be a prophet and believe in, and who attributes the command to Allah, and then they say: ﴿Do you take us for a joke?﴾ Is this possible? It is not possible. If the act had been attributed to him, we would say—though it is far-fetched—perhaps he meant... but this is far-fetched; meaning, given that he is a prophet and protected from mocking creation, it cannot occur. But we say to them, descending to their level of reasoning: if Musa, peace be upon him, had said it on his own, you would have said: perhaps this is his own opinion and not a command from Allah. Yet ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾, and then they say: ﴿Do you take us for a joke?﴾ The word "huzuwan" (jest) here is a verbal noun with the meaning of the passive participle: "do you take us as mocked-at?" It may also be "huzuan" in its original form, and the meaning becomes "do you take us as people of mockery?" so the genitive is removed and the annexed noun put in its place. In any case, it means: do you mock us? But it is stronger, because "taking" a thing means continuing in it: "I took the thing" means I made it something taken by me, as if it were a matter I accept and persist in. So it is greater than their saying "do you mock us?" As if you had taken us as a plaything, a toy for you: "to slaughter a cow?" What does a cow have to do with this victim? This is mockery. But what did he answer?
﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾. He did not say: "among the mockers." ﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾. The meaning of ignorance here is not committing an error unintentionally, but committing an error deliberately, because "ignorance" is applied to foolishness, as in His saying: ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon﴾ [al-Nisa' 17]. That is, I seek refuge in Allah from being among those of ignorance and foolishness, so as to take the servants of Allah in mockery—especially since I attributed the command to Allah. This is an impossible matter; therefore he sought refuge from it, because it is an unbefitting matter: first, it is not permissible to attribute to Allah a command that is not from Him; and second, it is not permissible for a person to take any of Allah's servants in mockery, especially in such a position.

In this is evidence that mocking creation is foolishness.
* Student: He did not say "among the mockers"; why?
* The Shaykh: In order to make clear that mocking people, or taking them in mockery, is ignorance and foolishness.
* Student: You said, O Shaykh, that "taking" means continuing in an action. Then the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And the people of Musa took, after him, from their ornaments, a calf, a body having a lowing sound﴾ [al-A'raf 148]: did they not continue in that?
* The Shaykh: No, no; until Musa came.
* The Student: That is, they did not continue in it throughout their lives.
* The Shaykh: Yes; it is not necessary, because continuation depends on the thing. It is not necessary that they continue throughout their lives. The meaning is that they were continuing in it; the verb indicates continuation. "I took this as a garment" means: wearing it constantly until it wears out. And these took it, and had Musa not come, they would have persisted in it.
* Student: "Huzuwan" with a dammah on the zay, or not?
* The Shaykh: "Huzuwan" with a dammah on the zay. Do you not have it with a dammah on the zay?
* The Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And there are also two other readings for it: ﴿huz'an﴾ and ﴿huzu'an﴾, three in total; there are two readings for it besides what is in the original.

Also in it, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾ has the reading with sukun: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾ ... ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ (...).
* Student: What is its basis?
* The Shaykh: The basis of this lightening; or does it have no basis?
(...)

His saying: ﴿They said: Do you take us for a joke?﴾ ﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah that I be among the ignorant﴾. ﴿I seek refuge﴾ means I hold fast to Allah, and seeking refuge is only in Allah, the Exalted, or in someone in what he is able to do, is it not? Yes: "Whoever seeks refuge from you, grant him refuge" [Abu Dawud 5109, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him].

﴿They said: Do you take us for a joke? He said: I seek refuge in Allah that I be among the ignorant﴾. So he disowned taking them in mockery—more than disowning it, he asked Allah to preserve him from it, and that this is a matter one should seek refuge from.

﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us, that He may show us what she is﴾. What is your view: had they gone and slaughtered a cow and complied with what they were commanded, the matter would have ended, because an unspecified "a cow" is easier; but an unspecified cow has no description at all. Yet they, we seek refuge in Allah, made it hard, so Allah made it hard for them. Likewise the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Religion will not be made hard upon itself by anyone except that it overcomes him" [al-Bukhari 39, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. Yes: everything in a person's affairs in which one seeks strictness is afflicted with greater strictness, even in matters of purification. Yes, some people, for example, may be afflicted with obsessive doubts, and then it opens up for them something even harsher, or he goes to wash his garment of something doubtful... (...) he is afflicted with a certain impurity, and the matter becomes harder for him. So the summary is: had they slaughtered a cow—any cow—the matter would have ended. But they, we seek refuge in Allah, said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us, that He may show us what she is﴾. Look at this ignorant manner: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾; they did not say "our Lord" or "call upon Allah," as if they were distant from Musa and from his Lord, the Exalted. ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾ placed him in the station of a servant sent to them. Yes, the one who calls upon his Lord is—we ask Allah for well-being—and this from their rebelliousness shows that the Children of Israel, we seek refuge in Allah, had rebelliousness, and that Allah, the Exalted, made Musa a prophet for them, and that they deserved to have someone like Musa, peace be upon him, in strength.

* Benefits from this verse:
* First: Allah, the Exalted, does not wrong anyone; whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, for him there is a reward.
* Second: The fruit of faith in Allah and the Last Day is the establishment of reward and the removal of fear and grief; fear of what lies ahead, and grief over what has passed.
* Third: In this there is no difference between one category and another. Those who are Jews, Christians, and Sabians are like the believers if they believe in Allah and the Last Day, although the believers of this nation are distinguished above others and have greater reward, yet they have their reward.
* Student: (...) the Sabians; what is the correct view about them?
* The Shaykh: The correct view is that they are those who do not ascribe to any religion originally; they do not ascribe to a religion. So if they believe in Allah and the Last Day, meaning, as messengers came to them whom they ascribe to.
* Fourth: Reward may differ according to nations, as indicated by His saying: ﴿then their reward is with their Lord﴾: "their reward," not simply "the reward." This nation has its reward multiplied, while earlier nations were not multiplied, is that not so? Then does ﴿their reward﴾ indicate this or not? It does, because He attributed the reward to the rewarded themselves, so they receive the reward that was decreed for them and written by Allah: if it is multiplied, it is multiplied; if it is not multiplied, it is not multiplied.
* Fifth: When praise is mentioned in the context of evil concerning a group, and among them are people of good, it is appropriate to mention those who are characterized by good, so that it does not (...); because after He said: ﴿That is because they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right﴾ [al-Baqarah 61], He made clear that among them were those who believed in Allah and the Last Day, and that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, for him is his reward, and no fear upon them, nor do they grieve.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No; because it is part of complete faith in Allah: faith in the messengers, faith in His angels and His books, and the decree, its good and its evil. All of this is included in faith in Allah, because Allah informed of it.

He said: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying]: Take what We have given you with determination and remember what is in it that you may fear Allah. Then you turned away after that﴾ [al-Baqarah 63, 64].

* In these two verses:
* First: Allah, blessed and exalted, reminds this nation—meaning the Children of Israel—of the covenant taken from them in His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount﴾. This reminder means obligation: so hold to the covenant, is that not so?
* Student: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: * Second: The rebelliousness of the Children of Israel, in that they did not believe except under the whip, as they say. Why? They did not believe except when the mount was raised above them, and it was said: either you take what We have given you with determination, or We will drop it upon you. Then they believed. This belief is in reality compelled, and every person believes at least out of fear of destruction.
* And also in it: evidence of the might of Allah, mighty and majestic, by His saying: ﴿and We raised above you the mount﴾. Allah, the Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿And when We uprooted the mountain above them as though it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf 171]. Who can carry Mount Sinai? No one can; no creature can carry it. But Allah, by His power, carried it and it became like a canopy. Great heavy stones, Allah held them by His power, just as He, majestic and exalted, holds the birds: ﴿in ranks, and folding their wings﴾ [al-Mulk 19]. When they fold them, you say: yes, they fold them when air enters and they lift themselves; but it is strange that they are "in ranks," their wings do not move, and yet they are propelled or sometimes stand still. Who holds them? None holds them but Allah. So in it also is evidence of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 62–74 (part 5 of 7):

* Also in it: evidence that the duty of the people of the religion is to hold to their Book with strength, not with weakness, softness, or compromise. No, it must be with strength, in practice and in calling others to it: practising it themselves and calling to it with strength, without slackness or laxity, because the matter is not accomplished except by this.

* Also in it: evidence that adhering to the revealed Book produces God-consciousness (taqwa). From where do we take this? From His saying: ﴿so that you may be mindful of God﴾. ﴿So that you may be mindful of God﴾ means: for the sake of your becoming among those who are mindful of God, Mighty and Majestic.

* The sixth benefit: the baseness of the Children of Israel. After the mountain returned to its place, what did they do? ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾. This is baseness, because the duty was for them to keep the first command in mind so that they would stand firm and persist in holding to it with strength. But they turned away after that, after they had seen the signs and turned away.

* The seventh benefit: the demonstration of God's favour, glorified and exalted, upon the Children of Israel, by His saying: ﴿Had it not been for God's favour upon you and His mercy, you would surely have been among the losers﴾. And this community, praise be to God, has a favour from God upon it greater than the favour upon the Children of Israel.

* Also in it: evidence that a person cannot be self-sufficient in achieving success (tawfiq). From where? And His saying: ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us"﴾ [2:68]. In it is a demonstration of the bad manners of the Children of Israel, for they did not say, "Call upon God for us," but said, ﴿"Call upon your Lord for us"﴾, as though they had placed themselves on one side and Moses and his Lord on the other.

And His saying: ﴿"Let Him make clear to us what it is"﴾. This request has no real basis, because the wording is clear: ﴿that you slaughter a cow﴾ [2:67]. The unqualified term is not general (mujmal, requiring explanation). What requires explanation is the general term; but a thing that is unqualified does not require explanation, because its meaning is clear. If you say, for example, "Honour a man," you do not need to ask, "What kind of man?" If you honour any man, the purpose is achieved. ﴿That you slaughter a cow﴾: if they slaughtered any cow at all, the purpose would be achieved. So the command is clear. But because of their obstinacy they said, ﴿"Let Him make clear to us what it is"﴾, and this request from them became obstinacy, not a genuine seeking of guidance, since the matter is clear: the word "cow," when unqualified, includes any cow whatsoever. For this reason, if they had slaughtered any cow that came their way, it would have sufficed.

﴿"Let Him make clear to us what it is." He said: "He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin"﴾. The phrase ﴿what it is﴾ is used to ask about the quiddity (mahiyya), i.e., "What is this? Is it of stone? Of clay? Of iron?" "What is it," meaning what is its essence? But Moses, peace be upon him, understood that they were not asking about the essence, because the essence of a cow is known, is it not?

* The students: Yes.

* The shaykh: Does anyone have doubts about the essence of a cow? Is it of wood, or iron, or chrysolite, or what?

* The students: No, it is clear.

* The shaykh: There is no confusion. The essence is clear. So we do not say that there is a diversion from what they asked, and that they were answered with something other than what they asked, since they asked about the essence and were answered with an explanation of the cow's age. We say: asking about the essence here is known to everyone to have not been the point. Why could it not be?

* The students: Because it is known.

* The shaykh: Because the essence of a cow is known.

﴿"Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is." He said: "He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin"﴾. The ﴿virgin﴾ (bikr) is well known: one that has not yet given birth and has not been mounted by the stallion. The ﴿old﴾ (fari") is known by its opposite. If the virgin is the young one that has not been mounted by the bull, then the old one is the aged, mature one. This kind of explanation, knowing a word through knowing its opposite, has a parallel in the Quran, such as His saying: ﴿so go forth in groups, or go forth all together﴾ [4:71]. If someone said to you, "What is the meaning of thubat?" would you go to the dictionary and look for its meaning?

* The students: No, it becomes clear.

* The shaykh: No, its meaning becomes clear from what is mentioned as its opposite, which is His saying: ﴿or go forth all together﴾. So what does (thubat) mean?

* The students: Scattered.

* The shaykh: Yes, scattered, individually.

﴿"Neither old nor virgin, but between that"﴾.

﴿Between that﴾ means middle-aged, the "middle" that is neither old nor young.

And His saying: ﴿between that﴾. (Dhaka) is a demonstrative (ism al-ishara, demonstrative pronoun), and the thing referred to is two: the old and the virgin. There is a difficulty with this, because we have previously discussed in the section on demonstratives that when the referent is two, the demonstrative must be in the dual form. Is that not so?

* The students: Indeed.

* The shaykh: And here the demonstrative is dual or singular?

* The students: Singular.

* The shaykh: Singular. So what is the answer to this? We say the answer is that ﴿between that﴾ means between that which was mentioned, the old and the virgin. Its meaning is that it is neither like this nor like that, but is middle-aged between what was mentioned. He said: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾. From whom is this command?

* The students: From Moses.

* The shaykh: From Moses, who says to the Children of Israel: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. By what was the command given? In His saying: ﴿God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. And if they had complied and hastened and slaughtered a middle-aged cow, the purpose would have been achieved. Here he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾, out of his eagerness that they hasten, so that they would not become strict again and be made more difficult for. And in His saying: ﴿what you are commanded﴾, who is the one commanding?

* The students: God.

* The shaykh: God, glorified and exalted. Here there is a difficulty in the section on relative pronouns, since it violates a rule we have studied.

* A student: A link (rabit).

* The shaykh: And what is the link?

* The student: "What you are commanded (ta'murunahu)."

* The shaykh: "What you are commanded (ta'murunahu)," or "what you are commanded with (ta'murun bihi)"?

* The student: "With (bihi)."

* The shaykh: Yes, "what you are commanded with." And what is the violation of the rule?

* The student: The omission.

* The shaykh: No, its omission is very common and conforms to the rule: ﴿He eats of what you eat, and drinks of what you drink﴾ [23:33]. This is very common.

* A student: We must benefit from mentioning it to avoid ambiguity.

* The shaykh: There is no ambiguity. Who knows? Read about the relative pronoun in the omission of the returning pronoun (al-ʿaʾid).

* A student: Because the relative clause is short, with the ...

* The shaykh: No, no. It is not short; it is a complete clause, "you are commanded."

* A student: Difference of the governing word.

* The shaykh: Did we not mention that if the returning pronoun is omitted when it is governed by a preposition, the preposition must match the preposition by which the relative pronoun is governed, in form, meaning, and what it relates to? Here the relative pronoun is in fact the object, governed in the accusative: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, meaning "do that which you are commanded with." We mentioned earlier that some scholars do not impose this condition, and say that if there is evidence for it, its omission is permitted even if the relative pronoun is not governed by the same preposition. Ibn Malik says:

Likewise is the one governed by the preposition by which the relative is governed, as in "He passed by the one I passed by," and it is correct.

So this serves as evidence for the second opinion on the question, namely that it is permissible to omit the governed returning pronoun even when the relative pronoun is not governed, and all the more so when it is governed by a preposition the relative pronoun was not governed by.

﴿So do what you are commanded﴾. They were obliged to do it even if their prophet had not commanded them, but they were a people of stubbornness and obstinacy. For this reason he gave them a second command. Yet despite this, ﴿they said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what its colour is"﴾. I seek refuge in God! What concern is its colour to you? But all of this is from obstinacy and strictness.

﴿What its colour is﴾ means: what is its colour? Black, white, grey-white? What is it?

﴿He said: "He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its yellow, delighting the beholders"﴾ [2:69]. They were made stricter. First, it was middle-aged, between the virgin and the old, with a range between them. So if they had brought one close to the virgin, or one close to the old, the purpose would have been achieved. But here they were made stricter: ﴿it is a yellow cow﴾. What does this exclude?

* A student: Other colours.

* The shaykh: Other colours besides yellow. This is one, and this is a small category, is it not?

* The students: Indeed.

* The shaykh: Second: ﴿bright in its yellow﴾. (Fāqi') means pure, meaning nothing is mixed with it to take it out of yellow. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿bright in its yellow﴾ is intensely yellow, that is, any colour that is pure is more evidently yellow.

Also, ﴿delighting the beholders﴾ means its yellow is not a yellow that causes grief or is disliked; rather it is a yellow that opens delight to the one who looks at it. This too is a tightening in several ways: ﴿yellow﴾, ﴿bright in its yellow﴾, and third, ﴿delighting the beholders﴾. This means that how many cows they walk among, this quality would not be found in them.

Some scholars mentioned that this is evidence that yellow colour is desirable, based on His saying ﴿delighting the beholders﴾, and they took this clause as an explanation of reality, saying that whoever wears yellow sandals remains in joy. But this is not correct.

When it is uncertain whether the clause is establishing a new meaning or explaining an existing fact, it is necessary to take it as establishing a new meaning. On this basis we say that ﴿delighting the beholders﴾ is a clause independent of what precedes it; that is, beyond being yellow and bright in its yellow, it also delights the beholders. Its yellow is not of a kind that causes a person grief, nor of a kind he dislikes, but rather it pleases him.

* A student: (...)?

* The shaykh: Between whether the clause is establishing a new meaning or explaining a reality. Is it not clear? It is establishing, meaning it is independent and conveys a meaning additional to the first.

* A student: Shaykh, is there a hadith forbidding the wearing of saffron-dyed clothing? [Reported by Muslim (2078/31) from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib.]

* The shaykh: Yes, indeed. Saffron-dyed (mu'asfar) means dyed with red safflower, a red colour.

* The student: With regard to this description God, glorified and exalted, has described, the yellow one... there is no blame in the yellow cow; its colour will indeed remain beautiful and it will be truly pure. When someone buys from the market any cow, our brokers look for the one that is yellow like this, and when you look you find it desirable, and in price it is more expensive than the other type.

* The shaykh: Well, that is its role, good. I think you...

* The student: So our Lord, indeed, wanted to make it stricter for them.

* The shaykh: Yes indeed. ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is"﴾. This is also a third request. ﴿"Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is; indeed the cows have become alike to us"﴾ [2:70]. The cow they were seeking has become confused for them. In reality, is there confusion in this?

* A student: There is not.

* The shaykh: He told them it is a cow, and its age was mentioned to them, and its colour was mentioned to them. Where, then, is the resemblance? But it is only one of the signs of God, glorified and exalted, so that God may make them stricter: ﴿We turn their hearts and their sights, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [6:110].

He says: ﴿indeed the cows have become alike to us﴾, meaning some of them resemble each other. The one that resembles others: we do not know which one is meant. This is from their obstinacy; otherwise the matter is clear. ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾. This last statement is a good one from them: ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾. They committed themselves to being guided, but they made it conditional on God's will. Some of the early scholars said: had they not said "if God wills," they would never have been guided to it. But the words "if God wills" are among the means of achieving the desired goal, as was said to Solomon, peace be upon him, when he said: "By God, I will surely go round tonight to ninety women, each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of God." The angel said to him: "Say: if God wills." But he did not say: "If God wills." The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "He went round to ninety women, and only one of them bore half a human being." Not a single one of them gave birth to a complete man. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Had he said: 'If God wills,' it would have attained his need, and they would have fought in the way of God." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2819) and Muslim (1654/24), in a similar wording, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]

So, their saying "if God wills" is one of the legitimate matters that bring a person to his goal.

And their saying: ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾ emphasised the guidance with two emphatic devices: "inna" and the "lam." A third emphasis is the nominal sentence, which is more forceful than the verbal sentence. They did not say, "We will be guided to it, if God wills," but rather said: ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾.

He answered them: ﴿He said: "He says it is a cow that is not broken to plough the earth nor to water the field, sound, with no blemish in it"﴾ [2:71]. This too is a tightening beyond what came before. ﴿It is a cow not broken﴾: the (dhalul) is of the pattern (fa'ul), meaning the one made docile, tamed for its owner. Its description as ﴿dhalul﴾ means ﴿that plough the earth﴾ and ﴿water the field﴾: made docile, ploughing the earth by tilling. I say: ﴿plough the earth﴾ means this tamed one, the one that ploughs the earth by tilling; one ploughs with it. I think you know how ploughing is done with cattle; you know it?

* The students: Yes indeed (...).

* The shaykh: Yes indeed, good. ﴿Nor water the field﴾ means it is not used for irrigation; it is neither a water-drawing animal nor a ploughing one. ﴿Sound﴾ means free from defects; it has no faults.

And His saying ﴿with no blemish in it﴾ means it has no colour contrary to its colour. It is derived from (washy), the embroidery of cloth, meaning decorating it with varied colours is called washy. So (shiyya) is derived from washy, as (ʿidda) is derived from waʿd. The meaning of ﴿with no blemish in it﴾ is that it has no second colour opposed to its colour. As already said, its colour is yellow; so it is yellow, with no black in it, no white in it, and no other colour. All of this is additional tightening upon them.

By this explanation we know that there is no need for what many exegetes mention here from the Israelite narratives (al-Isra'iliyyat), in which they say that this cow belonged to a man who was dutiful to his mother, and that they bought it from him for the filling of its hide with gold, meaning its skin filled with gold. These are all Israelite narratives that are neither to be believed nor disbelieved, but we should not attribute them to the Word of God. For the Word of God, the Mighty and Majestic, contains no indication of this. And if it were among the actual events, it would have been wise to mention it, why? Because of what it contains of encouragement to honour one's parents, so that we may take a lesson. So the correct approach is that in explaining the verse we say what God, the Mighty and Majestic, has said, and we do not touch on the other matters that the exegetes mention here as tales.

﴿They said: "Now you have brought the truth"﴾. Look, I seek refuge in God. ﴿Now you have brought the truth.﴾ Well, what about before?

* The students: According to the implication of their words.

* The shaykh: According to the implication of their words: that before this you had not brought falsehood. They had opened this story with their words: ﴿"Do you make a mockery of us?" He said: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant"﴾ [2:67]. Meaning: now we know you are not mocking, but that you are sincere. This is the evident meaning of the noble verse, and it is not strange, given their obstinacy, that they would say such a sentence. Some exegetes, to avoid this ugly meaning, said: what is meant by His saying ﴿with the truth﴾ is "with the complete explanation," meaning: now you have clarified to us its attributes. They thus made "truth" here mean "clarification." But the correct view is that "truth" here is the opposite of mockery and falsehood. This is shown by the fact that they opened this story with their words: ﴿"Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾. So after these discussions with Moses, the questions, and the requests made to God, the Mighty and Majestic, they said: ﴿"Now you have brought the truth"﴾, and we know that you are not mocking us, but that you are serious in what you say.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 2, verses 62–74 (part 6 of 7):**

﴿So they slaughtered it﴾: meaning, they searched for it. This sentence contains a brevity that is called in rhetoric (balaghah, the science of eloquence) "ellipsis by omission" (îjâz al-hadhf). In ellipsis by omission, sentences are left out that the context implies. There is also "concise brevity" (îjâz al-qasr), where a sentence contains many meanings while being brief. For example, ﴿And in retribution there is life for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 179]. What is this called?
* Students: Concise brevity.
* Shaykh: This is concise brevity, because this verse is a few words that indicate many meanings. But ﴿So he watered their flock for them, then turned back to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need." (24) Then one of the two women came to him walking shyly. She said, "Indeed, my father invites you so that he may reward you for what you watered for us"﴾ [Al-Qasas 24–25]. Does this contain ellipsis by omission or not?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, because the implied meaning of the verse is: "So he watered for them, then they went back to their father and told him the story, so he sent them for Musa. Then one of them came to him. He sent one of them to Musa, and one of them came to him walking shyly," and so on. Here, the verse ﴿So they slaughtered it﴾: if we took the verse at face value, the cow would already have been ready with them. But there had to be a search. They sought a cow that fit these descriptions in age, color, and work. Age?
* A student: Age. I did not understand the question.
* Shaykh: I am saying they found this cow with the descriptions. They found a cow that matched the descriptions in age, color, and work.
* The student: No, age, color.
* Shaykh: Age, what is it?
* The student: Age: a virgin.
* Shaykh: No, it is not a virgin.
* A student: A virgin, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: ﴿Neither old nor virgin﴾.
* A student: ﴿Middle-aged between that﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Middle-aged between that.﴾ And color?
* The student: Yellow, not resembling white or red, clearly bright.
* Shaykh: Good. What else? Complete it. Or are you still thinking?
* A student: ﴿Bright in color﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Bright in color.﴾ And as for His saying that it has no other color, who mentioned that?
* The student: ﴿Without any mark on it﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Without any mark on it.﴾ And also in work?
* The student: ﴿Not trained to plow﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Not trained to plow the earth or irrigate the field﴾. Yes. And with regard to soundness, it is also ﴿sound, without any mark﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it﴾. ﴿They slaughtered it﴾, as their prophet had commanded them. ﴿Though they had almost not done it﴾.

His saying ﴿though they had almost not done it﴾: there is a debate among the grammarians (nuhah) about whether (kâda, "to almost") behaves like other verbs or the opposite of other verbs. This is because kâda means "to come close to": ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ [Al-Baqarah 20], meaning it comes close to snatching their sight.

Some scholars say that the negation of kâda is an affirmation, and its affirmation is a negation. So if you say "He almost did such-and-such," it means he did not do it.
