If the act had been attributed to him, we would say—though it is far-fetched—perhaps he meant... but this is far-fetched; meaning, given that he is a prophet and protected from mocking creation, it cannot occur. But we say to them, descending to their level of reasoning: if Musa, peace be upon him, had said it on his own, you would have said: perhaps this is his own opinion and not a command from Allah. Yet ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾, and then they say: ﴿Do you take us for a joke?﴾ The word "huzuwan" (jest) here is a verbal noun with the meaning of the passive participle: "do you take us as mocked-at?" It may also be "huzuan" in its original form, and the meaning becomes "do you take us as people of mockery?" so the genitive is removed and the annexed noun put in its place. In any case, it means: do you mock us? But it is stronger, because "taking" a thing means continuing in it: "I took the thing" means I made it something taken by me, as if it were a matter I accept and persist in. So it is greater than their saying "do you mock us?" As if you had taken us as a plaything, a toy for you: "to slaughter a cow?" What does a cow have to do with this victim? This is mockery. But what did he answer?
﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾. He did not say: "among the mockers." ﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾. The meaning of ignorance here is not committing an error unintentionally, but committing an error deliberately, because "ignorance" is applied to foolishness, as in His saying: ﴿Repentance is only upon Allah for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon﴾ [al-Nisa' 17]. That is, I seek refuge in Allah from being among those of ignorance and foolishness, so as to take the servants of Allah in mockery—especially since I attributed the command to Allah. This is an impossible matter; therefore he sought refuge from it, because it is an unbefitting matter: first, it is not permissible to attribute to Allah a command that is not from Him; and second, it is not permissible for a person to take any of Allah's servants in mockery, especially in such a position.

In this is evidence that mocking creation is foolishness.
* Student: He did not say "among the mockers"; why?
* The Shaykh: In order to make clear that mocking people, or taking them in mockery, is ignorance and foolishness.
* Student: You said, O Shaykh, that "taking" means continuing in an action. Then the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And the people of Musa took, after him, from their ornaments, a calf, a body having a lowing sound﴾ [al-A'raf 148]: did they not continue in that?
* The Shaykh: No, no; until Musa came.
* The Student: That is, they did not continue in it throughout their lives.
* The Shaykh: Yes; it is not necessary, because continuation depends on the thing. It is not necessary that they continue throughout their lives. The meaning is that they were continuing in it; the verb indicates continuation. "I took this as a garment" means: wearing it constantly until it wears out. And these took it, and had Musa not come, they would have persisted in it.
* Student: "Huzuwan" with a dammah on the zay, or not?
* The Shaykh: "Huzuwan" with a dammah on the zay. Do you not have it with a dammah on the zay?
* The Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And there are also two other readings for it: ﴿huz'an﴾ and ﴿huzu'an﴾, three in total; there are two readings for it besides what is in the original.

Also in it, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾ has the reading with sukun: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you﴾ ... ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ (...).
* Student: What is its basis?
* The Shaykh: The basis of this lightening; or does it have no basis?
(...)

His saying: ﴿They said: Do you take us for a joke?﴾ ﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah that I be among the ignorant﴾. ﴿I seek refuge﴾ means I hold fast to Allah, and seeking refuge is only in Allah, the Exalted, or in someone in what he is able to do, is it not? Yes: "Whoever seeks refuge from you, grant him refuge" [Abu Dawud 5109, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him].

﴿They said: Do you take us for a joke? He said: I seek refuge in Allah that I be among the ignorant﴾. So he disowned taking them in mockery—more than disowning it, he asked Allah to preserve him from it, and that this is a matter one should seek refuge from.

﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us, that He may show us what she is﴾. What is your view: had they gone and slaughtered a cow and complied with what they were commanded, the matter would have ended, because an unspecified "a cow" is easier; but an unspecified cow has no description at all. Yet they, we seek refuge in Allah, made it hard, so Allah made it hard for them. Likewise the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Religion will not be made hard upon itself by anyone except that it overcomes him" [al-Bukhari 39, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. Yes: everything in a person's affairs in which one seeks strictness is afflicted with greater strictness, even in matters of purification. Yes, some people, for example, may be afflicted with obsessive doubts, and then it opens up for them something even harsher, or he goes to wash his garment of something doubtful... (...) he is afflicted with a certain impurity, and the matter becomes harder for him. So the summary is: had they slaughtered a cow—any cow—the matter would have ended. But they, we seek refuge in Allah, said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us, that He may show us what she is﴾. Look at this ignorant manner: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾; they did not say "our Lord" or "call upon Allah," as if they were distant from Musa and from his Lord, the Exalted. ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾ placed him in the station of a servant sent to them. Yes, the one who calls upon his Lord is—we ask Allah for well-being—and this from their rebelliousness shows that the Children of Israel, we seek refuge in Allah, had rebelliousness, and that Allah, the Exalted, made Musa a prophet for them, and that they deserved to have someone like Musa, peace be upon him, in strength.

* Benefits from this verse:
* First: Allah, the Exalted, does not wrong anyone; whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, for him there is a reward.
* Second: The fruit of faith in Allah and the Last Day is the establishment of reward and the removal of fear and grief; fear of what lies ahead, and grief over what has passed.
* Third: In this there is no difference between one category and another. Those who are Jews, Christians, and Sabians are like the believers if they believe in Allah and the Last Day, although the believers of this nation are distinguished above others and have greater reward, yet they have their reward.
* Student: (...) the Sabians; what is the correct view about them?
* The Shaykh: The correct view is that they are those who do not ascribe to any religion originally; they do not ascribe to a religion. So if they believe in Allah and the Last Day, meaning, as messengers came to them whom they ascribe to.
* Fourth: Reward may differ according to nations, as indicated by His saying: ﴿then their reward is with their Lord﴾: "their reward," not simply "the reward." This nation has its reward multiplied, while earlier nations were not multiplied, is that not so? Then does ﴿their reward﴾ indicate this or not? It does, because He attributed the reward to the rewarded themselves, so they receive the reward that was decreed for them and written by Allah: if it is multiplied, it is multiplied; if it is not multiplied, it is not multiplied.
* Fifth: When praise is mentioned in the context of evil concerning a group, and among them are people of good, it is appropriate to mention those who are characterized by good, so that it does not (...); because after He said: ﴿That is because they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right﴾ [al-Baqarah 61], He made clear that among them were those who believed in Allah and the Last Day, and that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, for him is his reward, and no fear upon them, nor do they grieve.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No; because it is part of complete faith in Allah: faith in the messengers, faith in His angels and His books, and the decree, its good and its evil. All of this is included in faith in Allah, because Allah informed of it.

He said: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying]: Take what We have given you with determination and remember what is in it that you may fear Allah. Then you turned away after that﴾ [al-Baqarah 63, 64].

* In these two verses:
* First: Allah, blessed and exalted, reminds this nation—meaning the Children of Israel—of the covenant taken from them in His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount﴾. This reminder means obligation: so hold to the covenant, is that not so?
* Student: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: * Second: The rebelliousness of the Children of Israel, in that they did not believe except under the whip, as they say. Why? They did not believe except when the mount was raised above them, and it was said: either you take what We have given you with determination, or We will drop it upon you. Then they believed. This belief is in reality compelled, and every person believes at least out of fear of destruction.
* And also in it: evidence of the might of Allah, mighty and majestic, by His saying: ﴿and We raised above you the mount﴾. Allah, the Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿And when We uprooted the mountain above them as though it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf 171]. Who can carry Mount Sinai? No one can; no creature can carry it. But Allah, by His power, carried it and it became like a canopy. Great heavy stones, Allah held them by His power, just as He, majestic and exalted, holds the birds: ﴿in ranks, and folding their wings﴾ [al-Mulk 19]. When they fold them, you say: yes, they fold them when air enters and they lift themselves; but it is strange that they are "in ranks," their wings do not move, and yet they are propelled or sometimes stand still. Who holds them? None holds them but Allah. So in it also is evidence of the power of Allah, glorified and exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 62–74 (part 5 of 7):

* Also in it: evidence that the duty of the people of the religion is to hold to their Book with strength, not with weakness, softness, or compromise. No, it must be with strength, in practice and in calling others to it: practising it themselves and calling to it with strength, without slackness or laxity, because the matter is not accomplished except by this.

* Also in it: evidence that adhering to the revealed Book produces God-consciousness (taqwa). From where do we take this? From His saying: ﴿so that you may be mindful of God﴾. ﴿So that you may be mindful of God﴾ means: for the sake of your becoming among those who are mindful of God, Mighty and Majestic.

* The sixth benefit: the baseness of the Children of Israel. After the mountain returned to its place, what did they do? ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾. This is baseness, because the duty was for them to keep the first command in mind so that they would stand firm and persist in holding to it with strength. But they turned away after that, after they had seen the signs and turned away.

* The seventh benefit: the demonstration of God's favour, glorified and exalted, upon the Children of Israel, by His saying: ﴿Had it not been for God's favour upon you and His mercy, you would surely have been among the losers﴾. And this community, praise be to God, has a favour from God upon it greater than the favour upon the Children of Israel.

* Also in it: evidence that a person cannot be self-sufficient in achieving success (tawfiq). From where? And His saying: ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us"﴾ [2:68]. In it is a demonstration of the bad manners of the Children of Israel, for they did not say, "Call upon God for us," but said, ﴿"Call upon your Lord for us"﴾, as though they had placed themselves on one side and Moses and his Lord on the other.

And His saying: ﴿"Let Him make clear to us what it is"﴾. This request has no real basis, because the wording is clear: ﴿that you slaughter a cow﴾ [2:67]. The unqualified term is not general (mujmal, requiring explanation). What requires explanation is the general term; but a thing that is unqualified does not require explanation, because its meaning is clear. If you say, for example, "Honour a man," you do not need to ask, "What kind of man?" If you honour any man, the purpose is achieved. ﴿That you slaughter a cow﴾: if they slaughtered any cow at all, the purpose would be achieved. So the command is clear. But because of their obstinacy they said, ﴿"Let Him make clear to us what it is"﴾, and this request from them became obstinacy, not a genuine seeking of guidance, since the matter is clear: the word "cow," when unqualified, includes any cow whatsoever. For this reason, if they had slaughtered any cow that came their way, it would have sufficed.

﴿"Let Him make clear to us what it is." He said: "He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin"﴾. The phrase ﴿what it is﴾ is used to ask about the quiddity (mahiyya), i.e., "What is this? Is it of stone? Of clay? Of iron?" "What is it," meaning what is its essence? But Moses, peace be upon him, understood that they were not asking about the essence, because the essence of a cow is known, is it not?

* The students: Yes.

* The shaykh: Does anyone have doubts about the essence of a cow? Is it of wood, or iron, or chrysolite, or what?

* The students: No, it is clear.

* The shaykh: There is no confusion. The essence is clear. So we do not say that there is a diversion from what they asked, and that they were answered with something other than what they asked, since they asked about the essence and were answered with an explanation of the cow's age. We say: asking about the essence here is known to everyone to have not been the point. Why could it not be?

* The students: Because it is known.

* The shaykh: Because the essence of a cow is known.

﴿"Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is." He said: "He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin"﴾. The ﴿virgin﴾ (bikr) is well known: one that has not yet given birth and has not been mounted by the stallion. The ﴿old﴾ (fari") is known by its opposite. If the virgin is the young one that has not been mounted by the bull, then the old one is the aged, mature one. This kind of explanation, knowing a word through knowing its opposite, has a parallel in the Quran, such as His saying: ﴿so go forth in groups, or go forth all together﴾ [4:71]. If someone said to you, "What is the meaning of thubat?" would you go to the dictionary and look for its meaning?

* The students: No, it becomes clear.

* The shaykh: No, its meaning becomes clear from what is mentioned as its opposite, which is His saying: ﴿or go forth all together﴾. So what does (thubat) mean?

* The students: Scattered.

* The shaykh: Yes, scattered, individually.

﴿"Neither old nor virgin, but between that"﴾.

﴿Between that﴾ means middle-aged, the "middle" that is neither old nor young.

And His saying: ﴿between that﴾. (Dhaka) is a demonstrative (ism al-ishara, demonstrative pronoun), and the thing referred to is two: the old and the virgin. There is a difficulty with this, because we have previously discussed in the section on demonstratives that when the referent is two, the demonstrative must be in the dual form. Is that not so?

* The students: Indeed.

* The shaykh: And here the demonstrative is dual or singular?

* The students: Singular.

* The shaykh: Singular. So what is the answer to this? We say the answer is that ﴿between that﴾ means between that which was mentioned, the old and the virgin. Its meaning is that it is neither like this nor like that, but is middle-aged between what was mentioned. He said: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾. From whom is this command?

* The students: From Moses.

* The shaykh: From Moses, who says to the Children of Israel: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾. By what was the command given? In His saying: ﴿God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. And if they had complied and hastened and slaughtered a middle-aged cow, the purpose would have been achieved. Here he said: ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾, out of his eagerness that they hasten, so that they would not become strict again and be made more difficult for. And in His saying: ﴿what you are commanded﴾, who is the one commanding?

* The students: God.

* The shaykh: God, glorified and exalted. Here there is a difficulty in the section on relative pronouns, since it violates a rule we have studied.

* A student: A link (rabit).

* The shaykh: And what is the link?

* The student: "What you are commanded (ta'murunahu)."

* The shaykh: "What you are commanded (ta'murunahu)," or "what you are commanded with (ta'murun bihi)"?

* The student: "With (bihi)."

* The shaykh: Yes, "what you are commanded with." And what is the violation of the rule?

* The student: The omission.

* The shaykh: No, its omission is very common and conforms to the rule: ﴿He eats of what you eat, and drinks of what you drink﴾ [23:33]. This is very common.

* A student: We must benefit from mentioning it to avoid ambiguity.

* The shaykh: There is no ambiguity. Who knows? Read about the relative pronoun in the omission of the returning pronoun (al-ʿaʾid).

* A student: Because the relative clause is short, with the ...

* The shaykh: No, no. It is not short; it is a complete clause, "you are commanded."

* A student: Difference of the governing word.

* The shaykh: Did we not mention that if the returning pronoun is omitted when it is governed by a preposition, the preposition must match the preposition by which the relative pronoun is governed, in form, meaning, and what it relates to? Here the relative pronoun is in fact the object, governed in the accusative: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, meaning "do that which you are commanded with." We mentioned earlier that some scholars do not impose this condition, and say that if there is evidence for it, its omission is permitted even if the relative pronoun is not governed by the same preposition. Ibn Malik says:

Likewise is the one governed by the preposition by which the relative is governed, as in "He passed by the one I passed by," and it is correct.

So this serves as evidence for the second opinion on the question, namely that it is permissible to omit the governed returning pronoun even when the relative pronoun is not governed, and all the more so when it is governed by a preposition the relative pronoun was not governed by.

﴿So do what you are commanded﴾. They were obliged to do it even if their prophet had not commanded them, but they were a people of stubbornness and obstinacy. For this reason he gave them a second command. Yet despite this, ﴿they said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what its colour is"﴾. I seek refuge in God! What concern is its colour to you? But all of this is from obstinacy and strictness.

﴿What its colour is﴾ means: what is its colour? Black, white, grey-white? What is it?

﴿He said: "He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its yellow, delighting the beholders"﴾ [2:69]. They were made stricter. First, it was middle-aged, between the virgin and the old, with a range between them. So if they had brought one close to the virgin, or one close to the old, the purpose would have been achieved. But here they were made stricter: ﴿it is a yellow cow﴾. What does this exclude?

* A student: Other colours.

* The shaykh: Other colours besides yellow. This is one, and this is a small category, is it not?

* The students: Indeed.

* The shaykh: Second: ﴿bright in its yellow﴾. (Fāqi') means pure, meaning nothing is mixed with it to take it out of yellow. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿bright in its yellow﴾ is intensely yellow, that is, any colour that is pure is more evidently yellow.

Also, ﴿delighting the beholders﴾ means its yellow is not a yellow that causes grief or is disliked; rather it is a yellow that opens delight to the one who looks at it. This too is a tightening in several ways: ﴿yellow﴾, ﴿bright in its yellow﴾, and third, ﴿delighting the beholders﴾. This means that how many cows they walk among, this quality would not be found in them.

Some scholars mentioned that this is evidence that yellow colour is desirable, based on His saying ﴿delighting the beholders﴾, and they took this clause as an explanation of reality, saying that whoever wears yellow sandals remains in joy. But this is not correct.

When it is uncertain whether the clause is establishing a new meaning or explaining an existing fact, it is necessary to take it as establishing a new meaning. On this basis we say that ﴿delighting the beholders﴾ is a clause independent of what precedes it; that is, beyond being yellow and bright in its yellow, it also delights the beholders. Its yellow is not of a kind that causes a person grief, nor of a kind he dislikes, but rather it pleases him.

* A student: (...)?

* The shaykh: Between whether the clause is establishing a new meaning or explaining a reality. Is it not clear? It is establishing, meaning it is independent and conveys a meaning additional to the first.

* A student: Shaykh, is there a hadith forbidding the wearing of saffron-dyed clothing? [Reported by Muslim (2078/31) from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib.]

* The shaykh: Yes, indeed. Saffron-dyed (mu'asfar) means dyed with red safflower, a red colour.

* The student: With regard to this description God, glorified and exalted, has described, the yellow one... there is no blame in the yellow cow; its colour will indeed remain beautiful and it will be truly pure. When someone buys from the market any cow, our brokers look for the one that is yellow like this, and when you look you find it desirable, and in price it is more expensive than the other type.

* The shaykh: Well, that is its role, good. I think you...

* The student: So our Lord, indeed, wanted to make it stricter for them.

* The shaykh: Yes indeed. ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is"﴾. This is also a third request. ﴿"Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is; indeed the cows have become alike to us"﴾ [2:70]. The cow they were seeking has become confused for them. In reality, is there confusion in this?

* A student: There is not.

* The shaykh: He told them it is a cow, and its age was mentioned to them, and its colour was mentioned to them. Where, then, is the resemblance? But it is only one of the signs of God, glorified and exalted, so that God may make them stricter: ﴿We turn their hearts and their sights, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [6:110].

He says: ﴿indeed the cows have become alike to us﴾, meaning some of them resemble each other. The one that resembles others: we do not know which one is meant. This is from their obstinacy; otherwise the matter is clear. ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾. This last statement is a good one from them: ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾. They committed themselves to being guided, but they made it conditional on God's will. Some of the early scholars said: had they not said "if God wills," they would never have been guided to it. But the words "if God wills" are among the means of achieving the desired goal, as was said to Solomon, peace be upon him, when he said: "By God, I will surely go round tonight to ninety women, each of whom will bear a boy who will fight in the way of God." The angel said to him: "Say: if God wills." But he did not say: "If God wills." The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "He went round to ninety women, and only one of them bore half a human being." Not a single one of them gave birth to a complete man. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Had he said: 'If God wills,' it would have attained his need, and they would have fought in the way of God." [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2819) and Muslim (1654/24), in a similar wording, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.]

So, their saying "if God wills" is one of the legitimate matters that bring a person to his goal.

And their saying: ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾ emphasised the guidance with two emphatic devices: "inna" and the "lam." A third emphasis is the nominal sentence, which is more forceful than the verbal sentence. They did not say, "We will be guided to it, if God wills," but rather said: ﴿And we, if God wills, shall surely be guided﴾.

He answered them: ﴿He said: "He says it is a cow that is not broken to plough the earth nor to water the field, sound, with no blemish in it"﴾ [2:71]. This too is a tightening beyond what came before. ﴿It is a cow not broken﴾: the (dhalul) is of the pattern (fa'ul), meaning the one made docile, tamed for its owner. Its description as ﴿dhalul﴾ means ﴿that plough the earth﴾ and ﴿water the field﴾: made docile, ploughing the earth by tilling. I say: ﴿plough the earth﴾ means this tamed one, the one that ploughs the earth by tilling; one ploughs with it. I think you know how ploughing is done with cattle; you know it?

* The students: Yes indeed (...).

* The shaykh: Yes indeed, good. ﴿Nor water the field﴾ means it is not used for irrigation; it is neither a water-drawing animal nor a ploughing one. ﴿Sound﴾ means free from defects; it has no faults.

And His saying ﴿with no blemish in it﴾ means it has no colour contrary to its colour. It is derived from (washy), the embroidery of cloth, meaning decorating it with varied colours is called washy. So (shiyya) is derived from washy, as (ʿidda) is derived from waʿd. The meaning of ﴿with no blemish in it﴾ is that it has no second colour opposed to its colour. As already said, its colour is yellow; so it is yellow, with no black in it, no white in it, and no other colour. All of this is additional tightening upon them.

By this explanation we know that there is no need for what many exegetes mention here from the Israelite narratives (al-Isra'iliyyat), in which they say that this cow belonged to a man who was dutiful to his mother, and that they bought it from him for the filling of its hide with gold, meaning its skin filled with gold. These are all Israelite narratives that are neither to be believed nor disbelieved, but we should not attribute them to the Word of God. For the Word of God, the Mighty and Majestic, contains no indication of this. And if it were among the actual events, it would have been wise to mention it, why? Because of what it contains of encouragement to honour one's parents, so that we may take a lesson. So the correct approach is that in explaining the verse we say what God, the Mighty and Majestic, has said, and we do not touch on the other matters that the exegetes mention here as tales.

﴿They said: "Now you have brought the truth"﴾. Look, I seek refuge in God. ﴿Now you have brought the truth.﴾ Well, what about before?

* The students: According to the implication of their words.

* The shaykh: According to the implication of their words: that before this you had not brought falsehood. They had opened this story with their words: ﴿"Do you make a mockery of us?" He said: "I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant"﴾ [2:67]. Meaning: now we know you are not mocking, but that you are sincere. This is the evident meaning of the noble verse, and it is not strange, given their obstinacy, that they would say such a sentence. Some exegetes, to avoid this ugly meaning, said: what is meant by His saying ﴿with the truth﴾ is "with the complete explanation," meaning: now you have clarified to us its attributes. They thus made "truth" here mean "clarification." But the correct view is that "truth" here is the opposite of mockery and falsehood. This is shown by the fact that they opened this story with their words: ﴿"Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾. So after these discussions with Moses, the questions, and the requests made to God, the Mighty and Majestic, they said: ﴿"Now you have brought the truth"﴾, and we know that you are not mocking us, but that you are serious in what you say.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 2, verses 62–74 (part 6 of 7):**

﴿So they slaughtered it﴾: meaning, they searched for it. This sentence contains a brevity that is called in rhetoric (balaghah, the science of eloquence) "ellipsis by omission" (îjâz al-hadhf). In ellipsis by omission, sentences are left out that the context implies. There is also "concise brevity" (îjâz al-qasr), where a sentence contains many meanings while being brief. For example, ﴿And in retribution there is life for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 179]. What is this called?
* Students: Concise brevity.
* Shaykh: This is concise brevity, because this verse is a few words that indicate many meanings. But ﴿So he watered their flock for them, then turned back to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need." (24) Then one of the two women came to him walking shyly. She said, "Indeed, my father invites you so that he may reward you for what you watered for us"﴾ [Al-Qasas 24–25]. Does this contain ellipsis by omission or not?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, because the implied meaning of the verse is: "So he watered for them, then they went back to their father and told him the story, so he sent them for Musa. Then one of them came to him. He sent one of them to Musa, and one of them came to him walking shyly," and so on. Here, the verse ﴿So they slaughtered it﴾: if we took the verse at face value, the cow would already have been ready with them. But there had to be a search. They sought a cow that fit these descriptions in age, color, and work. Age?
* A student: Age. I did not understand the question.
* Shaykh: I am saying they found this cow with the descriptions. They found a cow that matched the descriptions in age, color, and work.
* The student: No, age, color.
* Shaykh: Age, what is it?
* The student: Age: a virgin.
* Shaykh: No, it is not a virgin.
* A student: A virgin, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: ﴿Neither old nor virgin﴾.
* A student: ﴿Middle-aged between that﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Middle-aged between that.﴾ And color?
* The student: Yellow, not resembling white or red, clearly bright.
* Shaykh: Good. What else? Complete it. Or are you still thinking?
* A student: ﴿Bright in color﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Bright in color.﴾ And as for His saying that it has no other color, who mentioned that?
* The student: ﴿Without any mark on it﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Without any mark on it.﴾ And also in work?
* The student: ﴿Not trained to plow﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Not trained to plow the earth or irrigate the field﴾. Yes. And with regard to soundness, it is also ﴿sound, without any mark﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it﴾. ﴿They slaughtered it﴾, as their prophet had commanded them. ﴿Though they had almost not done it﴾.

His saying ﴿though they had almost not done it﴾: there is a debate among the grammarians (nuhah) about whether (kâda, "to almost") behaves like other verbs or the opposite of other verbs. This is because kâda means "to come close to": ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ [Al-Baqarah 20], meaning it comes close to snatching their sight.

Some scholars say that the negation of kâda is an affirmation, and its affirmation is a negation. So if you say "He almost did such-and-such," it means he did not do it. And if you say "He did not almost do such-and-such," it means he did it. They base this on the verse, since ﴿though they had almost not done it﴾ means they did it. Look: they did it, did they not?
* Students: They did it.
* Shaykh: They did it. But the correct view, without doubt, is that it is like other verbs: its negation is a negation and its affirmation is an affirmation. So if you say "He almost did not do it," it means he did not do it and did not come close to doing it. In that case, did these people not come close to doing it? If it were not for His saying ﴿So they slaughtered it﴾, we would say they did not slaughter it and did not come close to slaughtering it.

If someone says: this leads to contradiction, because when you say ﴿So they slaughtered it﴾ and also that they did not come close to doing it, that is a contradiction?

It is said: there is no contradiction, because the time differs. They had not come close to doing it before the slaughter. That is, all their earlier questions were stubborn attempts, perhaps to get out of it. Then ﴿they slaughtered it﴾ reluctantly. So the negation of coming close differs from the action in what? In time. In that case there is no contradiction. The contradiction would be if we said they slaughtered it at a time when they had not come close to slaughtering it, because the one who slaughters is not described as "he almost did not do it," since the slaughterer did it.

So kâda is like other verbs, and its meaning is "came close." When a negative particle comes before it, it negates the approach, and when the approach is negated, the action is negated. Is that right?
* Students: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: If you say, "I did not come close to doing it," it is known that you did not do it, is that not so?
* Students: Of course.
* Shaykh: As for its affirmation being an affirmation: if you say, "I almost did it," it means you came close to doing it, but you did not do it. You came close to the action, but I did not do it. Is this clear, everyone?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Once we have established this, what remains in the noble verse ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it﴾? How do you say that "they had almost not done it" means "they did not come close to doing it," while Allah says ﴿So they slaughtered it﴾? Is this not a contradiction? So what do we answer?

We say: there is no contradiction, because the time differs. At first they had not come close to doing it, because of their stubbornness. At the end they did it. So there is no contradiction. A person often feels within himself that he will never do such a deed, then before he knows it, he is doing it.

What do you say about the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by a wave, above which is a wave, above which is a cloud, darkness upon darkness; if he extends his hand, he can hardly see it﴾ [Al-Nur 40]? Does this contradict what we said?
* Students: No.
* A student: He did not see it.
* Shaykh: He did not see it, meaning?
* Students: He did not see it... that is evidence for us.
* Shaykh: Yes, evidence for us. Some people think that ﴿he can hardly see it﴾ means he sees it with difficulty. This idea comes to some people's minds. But ﴿he can hardly see it﴾ means he does not see it, and does not come close to seeing it. So this is evidence for what we have established.

If you say, "I almost flew with joy at my success," did I actually fly?
* Students: I came close.
* Shaykh: You came close, but I did not fly. So this is just a matter of the surface. The saying of some grammarians, may Allah have mercy on them, that the negation of kâda is an affirmation and its affirmation is a negation is not correct. Ibn Hisham refuted this in his book al-Mughni.
* A student: What did they rely on?
* Shaykh: They relied on the fact that if he says, "I almost did not do it," it indicates that I...?
* The student: I was not doing it.
* Shaykh: That I did not do this thing, that I almost did not do it. But I did it. They relied on the verse. In reality, this does not hold. The saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "I was almost unable to pray the 'Asr until the sun was about to set" [Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (596) and Muslim (631/209), from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah]. Did the Messenger pray before sunset or not?
* Students: He prayed before sunset.
* Shaykh: Before sunset?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Look, "I almost did not pray the 'Asr until the sun almost set." Did he not come close to praying?
* Students: He did not come close.
* Shaykh: Did he pray before sunset or not?
* Students: He prayed before sunset.
* Shaykh: No, brother, because when 'Umar [Ibn al-Khattab] said what he said, the Messenger said: "By Allah, I did not pray it." Then they got up to Batħān, performed ablution, and prayed after the sun had set.
* A student: No, it seems they prayed after sunset.
* Shaykh: Yes, they prayed after sunset. Because here he said, "I almost did not pray." That is, the prayer did not come close. He did not say: "I did not pray until the sun almost set." He said: "I did not come close to praying." That is, because of the intensity of the fighting, it was not possible for me to be near the prayer. Near the prayer is not the same as performing the prayer. He was near it until the sun was about to set. When the sun came close to setting, he came close to the prayer.
* A student: He prayed.
* Shaykh: No, he did not pray. He came close to praying. When the sun came close to setting, he came close to praying. When it set, he prayed.
* The student: Shaykh, was the one who said it not 'Umar?
* Shaykh: It was 'Umar who said it, and the Messenger said: "By Allah, I did not pray it."
* The student: He said: "I was not awakened until (...)."
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. The one who said it was 'Umar, as we said at the end. The one 'Umar said, and the Messenger said, "By Allah, I did not pray it." Then they got up and prayed. So here the hadith does not show that 'Umar prayed before sunset, because he did not come close to praying until the sun came close to setting. When the sun came close to setting, he came close to praying. Then did he pray or not?

The hadith shows that he did not pray. He and the Messenger got up after sunset, performed ablution from Batħān, and prayed.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it, while Allah was to bring out what you were concealing﴾ [Al-Baqarah 72]. Allah established the story before He reminded them of the cause. He established the story for the Children of Israel before He explained the cause. What was the cause of Musa's saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾?

The cause was that they killed a soul and disputed over it, each pushing the blame away. Each one claimed that the other was the killer. Without doubt this leads to great strife, and the victim had died, and no one could tell who had killed him after his death. So Allah, blessed and exalted, showed them, or rather commanded them, to slaughter this cow so that it would be a sign and the killer of this victim would be known. After they killed this soul and disputed over it, He attributed the killing to them as a group, even though some of them certainly did not approve of it. Those who demand the killer's execution did not approve of the killing. But, as we have explained before, when a deed is done by some of the community and the rest remain silent, it is considered the deed of all.

And His saying ﴿disputed (ad-dâra'tum)﴾: what does "disputed" mean?
* A student: Pushing back.
* Shaykh: It means disagreement and pushing away. Each one defends himself against the accusation. From it comes the hadith "Avert the hudud (prescribed punishments) by doubts" [Ibn Kathir said in Tuhfat al-Talib (p. 226): I have not seen this hadith in this wording. The closest thing to it is what al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Avert the hudud from the Muslims as much as you can. If there is a way out for him, let him go, for the imam's error in pardoning is better than his error in punishing." He said it was also narrated as a statement of 'A'ishah's, and that is more authentic. See Nasb al-Rayah (3/333) and al-Maqasid al-Hasanah (p. 74).] meaning, repel them. ﴿And when you disputed over it﴾. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is to bring out what you were concealing﴾. This is evidence that they concealed it. For if the killers had confessed to the killing, would there have been any dispute?
* Students: No, there would have been no dispute.
* Shaykh: There would be no dispute and nothing would happen. But they concealed it, so Allah, blessed and exalted, brought out what they had concealed through this great verse.
* A student: Were their questions aimed at escaping?
* Shaykh: It seems, and Allah knows best, that they were stubborn in order to escape it. His saying ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 71] indicates this, just as if someone commands you to do something and you dislike complying, you find yourself being stubborn: "What does it want? What color is it? What?"
* A student: Does this not indicate their eagerness to carry it out?
* Shaykh: No, not at all. This is why Allah mentions it to them as a rebuke. If this were eagerness to carry it out, they would be praised for this matter. Allah would not say ﴿So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it﴾, because this contains the utmost condemnation of them, and we seek refuge in Allah.
* A student: Shaykh, were these questions asked in one session or in several sessions?
* Shaykh: Allah knows best. I do not know whether it was in one session, or whether they asked for this cow in several sessions, returned to him, disagreed about it, and returned to him again. Allah knows. We do not know.

He said: ﴿And disputed over it, while Allah was to bring out what you were concealing﴾. Everything you conceal of matters, Allah the Exalted will bring out. Is this specific to them, or is it also for this community?
* A student: (...)
* Shaykh: No, this is on the Day of Resurrection. The Day of Resurrection is well known (...). The conjunction requires a difference, so it is not valid to interpret mercy as favor, but favor is one of the effects of mercy.
* Also in it: the affirmation of causes and their connection to their effects, based on His saying: ﴿Were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾ [Al-Baqarah 64].

This is an explicit statement affirming causes. No one denies causes except the Ash'ariyyah, who have come up with something that sensible people laugh at, let alone wise ones. What did they say? They said: causes are not effective, and their effects occur with them, not by them. If a piece of paper enters the fire and burns, they say: "The fire did not burn it, but it burned in its presence, not by it." If you eat food and become full, they say: "You were not satisfied by the food, but in its presence." Yet if the food were piled in front of you and you did not eat it, you would not be satisfied. Likewise, if the papers and sticks were left near the fire, they would not burn.

They also say: if you strike a glass bottle with a stone and it breaks, the breaking did not happen by the stone, but in its presence. Yet if you place this stone's weight on the glass four times without throwing it, the glass does not break, even though it is on the glass's surface, not merely beside it. In short, this is something that foolish people laugh at, let alone wise people. All of this comes from an attempt to declare that something not connected to Allah's will exists in the dominion of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. We say: Allah made causes necessitate their effects and made effects dependent on causes, and this is part of His wisdom.
* A student: The obligation to convey what Allah has revealed, due to His saying ﴿and remember what is in it﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿remember what is in it﴾. If it is for others, then this indicates the obligation to convey. If the meaning is "remember it in your souls for the sake of admonition," then there is no evidence in it.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you have certainly known those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and humiliated"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 65].
* In it is a rebuke of those present in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) for not believing in him. What is the reason for this?
* A student: Knowledge.
* Shaykh: Because they knew what had befallen their predecessors of punishment due to disobedience. So it was incumbent on them that this be an admonition to them, by which they would refrain from disobeying Allah.
* Also in it is evidence for the prohibition of legal tricks (hiyal), and that one who uses a trick does not escape transgression, based on His saying ﴿those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾ first. Tricks are more eloquent than doing a thing openly, first because they combine the corruption of the prohibited act with the corruption of deceiving Allah, the Mighty and Exalted. The one who uses a trick to obtain usury falls into usury and, beyond that, deceives Allah, the Mighty and Exalted. If you reflect on the tricks of the Jews regarding the Sabbath, and their tricks in selling the fat of dead animals, which was forbidden to them, when they melted it, sold it, and ate its price, you find that it is easier than the tricks many people today use for usury. It is easier, yet Allah still sent down His vengeance upon them. The Messenger (ﷺ) also warned us, as in the Musnad with a chain that is acceptable, that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Do not commit what the Jews committed, lest you make the prohibitions of Allah lawful by the smallest tricks" [I did not find this hadith in the Musnad. It was narrated by Ibn Battah in Ibtal al-Hiyal (pp. 46–47) from Abu Hurayrah. Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir (1/293 and 3/493): "This is a good chain." Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said in al-Fatawa al-Kubra (3/123): "This is a good chain, the kind al-Tirmidhi and others sometimes authenticate and sometimes consider good."].
* The second benefit: one who uses a trick to do what is forbidden falls into it, and the trick does not help him.
* The third benefit: showing Allah's wisdom in matching punishments to sins. Is that right?
* A student: Yes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 62–74 (part 7 of 7):

* The Shaykh: Because the punishment was that they were transformed into apes, "khasi'in" (despised, humiliated). First, the sin they committed was an act whose outward form resembled what is permissible, but whose reality was not permissible. The ape's form resembles the human, but it is not human. So the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. This is also indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So We seized each one for his sin; among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles...﴾ [al-'Ankabut 40], and so on to the end of the verse.
* In it is also a proof of the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿Be apes, despised.﴾ In an instant, they were transformed, they and their offspring, into apes. In a single moment they became apes, may Allah protect us.
* The fifth benefit: the affirmation that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, speaks, by His saying: ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes, despised."﴾
* The sixth benefit: those from this town who were transformed into apes are those who transgressed regarding the Sabbath. As for those who forbade evil, they were saved. As for those who said: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?﴾ [al-A'raf 164], these were passed over in silence, or we say: they were seized with a severe punishment, but were not transformed into apes.
* The seventh benefit, in His saying: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it and what lay behind it﴾: that punishments include a deterrent for those who did not commit the act. Is that correct or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because of His saying: ﴿for what lay before it and what lay behind it,﴾ whether in time or in place. We said: ﴿what lay before it﴾ with respect to time means those present in their era, and ﴿what lay behind it﴾ means those who come after them. As for if it is place, the matter is clear: what lies before it, in front of it, and what lies behind it, around it, i.e. what is before it and behind it and around it.
* A student: The benefit?
* The Shaykh: The benefit is that punishments are a deterrent to those who did not commit the act.
* The eighth benefit: From this we may derive the benefit of the legal penalties (hudud) established in this world, the legal penalties and their punishments: the punishment for fornication, the punishment for theft, and so on. What are their benefits?
* The students: That they are a deterrent.
* The Shaykh: That they are a deterrent for those other than the perpetrator, and for the perpetrator himself, so that he does not return to this sin again.
* The ninth benefit: that those who benefit from such admonitions are the God-fearing (al-muttaqun).
* The tenth benefit: admonitions are of two kinds: cosmic (kawniyyah) and legislative (shar'iyyah). The cosmic is the decreed (qadariyyah), cosmic and legislative. Here, is it cosmic or legislative? The admonition?
* The students: Cosmic.
* The Shaykh: Cosmic and decreed, because Allah sent upon them the punishment that became a deterrent for what lay before it and what lay behind it. ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you an admonition from your Lord and a cure for what is in the breasts﴾ [Yunus 57]. This is a legislative admonition. Which is stronger: the legislative admonitions or the cosmic ones?
* The students: The cosmic... only.
* The Shaykh: For donkeys, the cosmic is greater; for believers, the legislative is greater, because the believer's benefit from the laws is greater than his benefit from the decree of what is decreed. But the dullness of the donkey: ﴿The example of those who were charged with the Torah then did not carry it is like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 5]. This one is admonished more by cosmic matters. And yet, if hardness comes to the heart..
As His saying: ﴿what you used to conceal﴾, and whatever a person conceals, Allah, the Exalted, knows it: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 235].
And in it, the *sixth benefit*: a clarification of Allah's blessing upon the Children of Israel in making clear the actual matter, for it is among the blessings of Allah that He makes the actual matter clear to them, so that they may be upon insight regarding their affair. Is that correct or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is it not also derived from this that clarifying hidden matters over which difference and dispute arise is among the blessings of Allah? Indeed yes. For example, if we differ on matters and the affair nearly escalates to the point of strife, then Allah makes clear what elucidates it; this is one of the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, upon us, because by it He removes this disagreement and this dispute.
* A student: Is nothing derived from mentioning the cause after relating the matter?
* The Shaykh: After relating the story?
* The student: Yes, its delay.
* The Shaykh: The benefit of delaying the mention of the cause before the story is hastening to mention the blessing before explaining its cause.
﴿So We said: "Strike him with part of it."﴾ "Said" (qulna) is on the tongue of Musa. Is that so or not?
* It is derived from it: that the speech of a messenger is the speech of the one who sent him, of course if it is by his command. The speech of a messenger that is by Allah's command is speech of Allah.
* The second benefit: the part with which the slain man was struck from the cow is not known. What is the proof?
* The students: ﴿with part of it.﴾
* The Shaykh: Because of His saying ﴿with part of it﴾: Allah left it indefinite, and some exegetes' attempt to specify it is an attempt with no need, because the intent is the verse.
* The third benefit: the seeker of knowledge should attend to the meaning, the meaning of the story and its purpose, rather than the identity of the person it concerned. For this reason we see that it is an excess that some people do when a hadith says: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, such and such," and you find some people exerting themselves and burdening themselves in identifying this man. This is not necessary. What matters is: what is it? The meaning of the story and its subject. As for knowing what this man was, what this Bedouin was, what this she-camel was, or what this donkey was, this is not necessary, since the intent in matters is their meanings and what they lead to. So the indefiniteness in His saying ﴿with part of it﴾ does no harm, and Allah has specified it for them without doubt, or Allah left it indefinite for us alone, saying ﴿with part of it﴾ and did not clarify it for us, because this is not an important matter.
* And we derive from it a benefit: if they were commanded to strike him with only part of it and no specific part was designated for them, we derive from it that the indefinite among multiple options is easier for the one under obligation than the specific: that is, if you are told: do some of these things, that is easier than if you are told: do this particular thing. Is that correct or not? Thus there is ease for the servants when they are given choice among multiple matters (...).
He described them with hardness of heart, by His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that.﴾
* And in it also: a proof of the baseness of the Children of Israel, to whom these blessings came, yet they did not soften toward the truth, rather their hearts hardened despite the manifestation of these blessings among them.
And in it also, the *third benefit*: ﴿Then they are like stones﴾ is a comparison of the intelligible to the perceptible, because stones are a perceptible thing, while the hardness of the heart is an intelligible matter. The meaning is not that the heart, which is the lump of flesh, becomes hard; the heart is the same heart, but what is meant is that it hardens through its turning away from the truth and its arrogance toward it. It is a non-physical matter likened to a physical one, and this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an: comparing the intelligible to the perceptible so that it becomes clear.
* And in it: that stones are the hardest thing used as a metaphor, and He did not say "like iron," because iron softens by fire.
* And in it also: a proof that stones are distinguished from their hearts, because in them there is good, namely: ﴿For indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split and water comes out of them, and indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾, whereas these people, may Allah protect us, are the opposite.
* And in it also: a proof of the vastness of the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ or ﴿of what they do.﴾ Is this attribute among Allah's negative attributes or affirmative attributes?
* A student: Negative.
* The Shaykh: Is it negative or affirmative? Did Allah negate it of Himself ﴿And Allah is not unaware﴾ or did He affirm it?
* The students: He negated it.
* The Shaykh: Did He say: Allah is heedless? Or ﴿And Allah is not unaware﴾?
* The students: ﴿And Allah is not unaware.﴾
* The Shaykh: ﴿And Allah is not unaware﴾; so it is a negative attribute. It has already passed with us that the negative attributes which Allah negates of Himself include two things: the negation of this attribute, and the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite. So here we say that in His saying ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is the negation of heedlessness of Allah, the Exalted, regarding their deeds: ﴿And Allah is not unaware.﴾
* And in it: the affirmation of the perfection of its opposite, which is knowledge and watchfulness: that Allah, the Exalted, is watchful over their deeds and knows them: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾
* And among the benefits of this verse: that inanimate things know Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿And indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾. This is a proof that they know Allah, and this is a matter established from other verses, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 1], and ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing except that it glorifies [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra' 44].
* And also among its benefits: the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿out of fear of Allah﴾; because fear (khashyah) is fear combined with knowledge, by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. So whoever knows the greatness of Allah, the Exalted, must fear Him: ﴿And indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah.﴾
* And in the verse also: a proof of the perfect power of Allah, the Exalted, in that He made these solid stones from which rivers gush forth. Is that correct or not? And Musa ﷺ would strike the stone with his staff, and it would burst forth and gush out springs by the power of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted.

When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the punishments He inflicted on the Children of Israel, the humiliation, the poverty, and the wrath, He then made clear that He does not wrong anyone, and that all the believers, whether from the Children of Israel or from others, have their reward with Allah. This is the connection between this verse and what precedes it. When He said ﴿and they earned wrath from Allah, that was because they﴾ [al-Baqarah 61], He showed that whoever among them believed and did righteous deeds, Allah would not waste their reward. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah 62].

His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, and then His saying ﴿whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾: is the second "belief" the same as the first, so that the first was general and was then specified by His saying ﴿in Allah and the Last Day﴾? Or is the first meant as a restricted belief, meaning that ﴿those who believed﴾ is general with respect to everything that must be believed in, and His saying ﴿whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾ is a qualification of His saying ﴿and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians﴾? On this reading there is no repetition.

There is a difference of opinion among the commentators (mufassirun). Some said that His saying ﴿whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾ is the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾. But the correct view is that Allah mentioned five categories: those who believed, those who were Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians, which makes four groups [in the sentence, after the first].

﴿whoever believed﴾ refers back to His saying ﴿those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians﴾. The intended meaning of "those who believed" is the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Those who were Jews" means the Jews, the followers of Musa (Moses), and "the Christians" means the followers of Isa (Jesus).

As for the Sabians, opinions about them differ in several ways. Some say that the Sabians are a sect of the Christians. Some say they are a sect of the Jews. Some say they are a sect of the Majus (Magians). Some say they are a distinct nation that follows its own particular religion. And some say they are those who have no religion, who remained upon the natural disposition (fitrah) and did not follow any religion, but when they believe in Allah and the Last Day, this matter applies to them. This last view is the closest to the truth. This is why the Quraysh called the Prophet (ﷺ) "the Sabian", because he had departed from the religion of his people. So the Sabians are not a sect of the Jews and the Christians; rather they are a distinct nation. This is because the basic principle in coordination (ʿatf) is difference, both in kind and in type.

Then we say: in the Arabic language, the word "Sabi" means one who departs from a religion. These are people who follow no religion and remain upon their natural disposition. If messengers are sent to them and they believe in Allah and the Last Day, they will be rewarded. Or do they have no reward because they were Sabians? They will be rewarded. For this reason we say: the Jews are not blamed merely because they are Jews, and the Christians are not blamed merely because they are Christians; but if they believe, they will have their reward. ﴿whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾. So Allah tells you: there are four categories: the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians. Whoever among them believed in Allah and the Last Day, meaning the three categories other than the believers, Allah will not waste their reward.

﴿so they will have their reward with their Lord﴾. ﴿Their reward﴾ means their recompense. Allah, exalted is He, called the recompense "ajr" (reward, wage) because He has obligated Himself to repay it, just as the one who hires a worker is obligated to pay the wage to whom?

* Students: To the worker.
* Shaykh: To the worker.
* Student: When we said ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ refers to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and if we take it that way, how do we say, when Allah, mighty and majestic is He, concluded with ﴿whoever believed in Allah﴾?
* Shaykh: Yes, but ﴿whoever believed﴾ is specific to ﴿those who were Jews﴾.
* Student: So it means: the three categories, not the four?
* Shaykh: No, not the four; only the three categories.
* Student: The Sabians, it has been said that they are the Majus?
* Shaykh: No, a sect of them.
* Student: A sect of the Majus.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. They are not the Majus. This is why Allah mentioned them in Surat al-Hajj together with the Majus.
And here we will complete the verse and return to comparing it with Surat al-Hajj, as I said regarding al-Hajj, God willing.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, (...). We mentioned that some say: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾ refers to all of them. For the three categories it is clear that a qualification is necessary: ﴿whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾. Is that clear? But regarding the first two, they say: regarding the first two, if we make it refer to all four, then His saying ﴿those who believed﴾ becomes general (mujmal), and ﴿whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾ becomes detailed or clarifying (mubayyan), detailed and clarifying. So ﴿whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day﴾ refers back to His saying ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, but in the manner of clarification and specification. As for if we say that ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ is a separate category, and ﴿whoever believed﴾ is a substitute for those who were Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians, then there is no problem. We have said that the more preferred basic reading is that His saying ﴿whoever believed﴾ refers to the three categories, because the basic principle in speech is establishing (ta'sis) a new meaning, and belief, when stated without qualification, means belief in what must be believed in: belief in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and other things.

His saying ﴿so they will have their reward with their Lord﴾ is a guarantee (kafalah) from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, a pledge and a binding commitment to this reward. It is a reward that is not lost; it is not unknown. It is known to whom? With whom?
* Student: Their Lord.
* Shaykh: With Allah, glorified and exalted is He, who does not break His promise. ﴿Allah does not fail His promise﴾ [ar-Rum 6].

﴿with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾. Fear (khawf) is concern about what lies ahead. Grief (huzn) is sorrow over what has passed. This is the difference between them. This is why it is said of one who is struck by a calamity: did he grieve or did he fear?
* Student: He grieved.
* Shaykh: He grieved. And it is said of one who faces a frightening or terrifying matter, what is it said?
* Student: He feared.
* Shaykh: He feared. So fear is concern about what is to come, and grief is sorrow over what has passed. A person is grieved by what he has lost of what he loves, or by some hardship that has befallen him.
* Student: Is grief not said to be about the present?
* Shaykh: No, grief is about the future. Concern (hamm) is what occurs in the present and the future: "I was concerned about the matter, and I directed my resolve toward it." As for grief (ghamm), it is something that presses upon the heart, so a person is saddened by it...
* Student: About what has occurred.
* Shaykh: About what has passed. Grief is about what has passed, and concern is about what is to come.
His saying ﴿no fear will be upon them﴾: from what? From everything that is feared in the future, such as the punishment of the grave, the punishment of the Fire, and other things.
﴿nor will they grieve﴾: over what has passed of the worldly life. For the disbeliever grieves over what has passed of the worldly life and laments it: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, after which you will not be helped. And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive. Lest a soul say, "Oh, my regret over what I neglected in regard to Allah"﴾ [az-Zumar 54–56]. Grief and lament. As for the believers, they do not grieve over what has passed, because they have made the most of it through obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and they do not fear a future matter, as in His saying: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with injustice, for them is security, and they are the guided﴾ [al-An'am 82], ﴿so no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾.

Then Allah reminded them, He reminded the Children of Israel, of a covenant He had taken from them. He said: ﴿And [recall] when We took your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah 63]. Meaning: remember when We took your covenant. The mithaq (covenant) is a heavy, emphasized pledge, and it is named after the wathaq, which is the rope with which a captive is bound. The rope with which a captive is bound is called wathaq. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike the necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, then secure the bonds (wathaq)﴾ [Muhammad 4]. So the mithaq is the heavy pledge taken from a person. From where is it derived? From the wathaq, which is the rope with which the prisoner is tied and fastened.

﴿We took your covenant and raised above you the mountain﴾. ﴿Raised above you﴾ means above your heads, but not directly; above.

The Tur is the well-known mountain. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, raised it over the Children of Israel when they neglected obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, as a warning to them. He said to them: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾. "Take it" means accept it and act upon it. ﴿with strength﴾: what is meant by strength here? Resolve and implementation. The meaning of ﴿with strength﴾ is with resolve, implementation, and application. What is its opposite? Its opposite is that a person takes it weakly and lax-ly. So the meaning is: take it with strength. Therefore we take the particle "bi" in His saying ﴿with strength﴾ to mean accompaniment, and strength means resolve and energy, while its opposite is laziness and slackness. ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾.

His saying ﴿what We have given you﴾ means what We have granted you, from where? From the Torah, from the Book. Those to whom We gave the Book: take this Book, the Torah that Musa (ﷺ) brought, with strength.

﴿and remember what is in it﴾: meaning do not neglect anything of it. His saying ﴿what is in it﴾: "ma" is a relative pronoun, and it conveys what? Generality. So: remember everything that is in it and act upon it.

﴿that you may become righteous﴾ ("la'alla" here expresses purpose): that is, so that you may fear Allah, mighty and majestic is He. So taking hold of what Allah gave them with strength, and remembering what is in it and implementing it, leads to taqwa (piety). For acts of obedience pull one another along: ﴿O you who believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 183]. Acts of obedience pull one another along, because when a person tastes obedience, he becomes energetic and seeks another act of obedience, and his heart is nourished; the more it is nourished by this obedience, the more it desires another. Conversely with sins: sins bring about estrangement between the servant and Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and aversion, may Allah protect us, and sins pull one another along. This is why Allah has already told us: ﴿That is because they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah 61].

So the reason that taking hold of the Book of Allah is a cause of piety is this: acts of obedience pull one another along, because when a person tastes them and they reach his heart, he craves them and seeks them and advances. Like the student of knowledge: when he attains knowledge and gains some of it, you find him insatiable. This is why some scholars said: there are two insatiable seekers, the seeker of this world and the seeker of knowledge. And likewise, in reality, the seeker of worship, for he is always enamored with worship.

﴿Then you turned away after that﴾ [al-Baqarah 64]: after this warning and the mountain being above them, at that time they humbled themselves and became submissive. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And [recall] when We shook the mountain over them as if it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with strength"﴾ [al-A'raf 171]. In that hour they rushed to prostrate and they prostrated, but they tilted in their prostration, looking at the mountain in fear of it. This is why it is said that the prostration of the Jews toward this community is a tilted prostration: you find him prostrating while raising one of his eyes. They said: this prostration, we prostrate to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in a manner of intimidation, so we continue to prostrate in this way. This was their prostration; this is the prostration of the Jews.
* Student: They consider it a means of closeness (qurbah)?
* Shaykh: Yes, they consider it a means of closeness. And in reality it has a counterpart in this community: the eclipse. For an eclipse is in reality a departure from the natural order: the moon comes between the earth and the sun, or the earth comes between the sun and the moon. This is why the Messenger (ﷺ) said: «Indeed Allah frightens His servants with them» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1059) and Muslim (912/24), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So Allah, glorified is He, made the sign of warning among the Children of Israel greater than [the sign given to] this community, because this community is closer to accepting the truth and to fear. The Children of Israel do not fear from this kind of eclipse; nothing frightens them except a mountain they know, raised above them as if it were a canopy.

Unfortunately, there are now among us those who have imitated the Jews in this matter. They no longer take warning from the eclipse; they only take warning when mountains are raised above their heads, may Allah protect us. Yet it is obligatory for a person to recognize what has taken this out of its natural course until it became in this state. Even if the whole world gathered to eclipse the sun or to make the moon eclipse, they could not. So what took it out of its course except Allah, glorified and exalted is He, for the purpose of warning and frightening? And according to those who say that the earth revolves, they say: the movement of the earth is what has been disturbed. We do not know; perhaps this movement, this disruption that has occurred within it, will lead to its destruction, and to greater eclipses and earthquakes. So we must fear. In any case, I say: this heavenly warning, as it occurred among the Children of Israel, has occurred in this community.

Allah, mighty and majestic is He, says: ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾. ﴿You turned away﴾ means you turned aside and withdrew from obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿after that﴾: referring to what? 
* Student: The raising of the mountain.
* Shaykh: The raising of the mountain. ﴿We raised above you the mountain﴾: after this repentance, at the time the mountain was raised, you turned away and did not mention it. You did not remember that the one who frightened you with this mountain might bring it upon you again.

﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾. ﴿So if not for the bounty﴾: "fadl" (bounty), what is its grammatical analysis (i'rab)? It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is obligatorily omitted, as Ibn Malik said:
"After 'lawla' the predicate is usually omitted; its omission is obligatory..."
meaning: "and if not for the bounty of Allah upon you (existed)". It was obligatory to omit it, being satisfied by the response of "lawla". ﴿you would have been﴾ is the response of "lawla": ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾.

His saying ﴿the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾: what kind of bounty and mercy is this? It is the sending of messengers and prophets to the Children of Israel after the mountain was raised. For Allah did not leave them; rather He sent messengers to them. Allah said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged for those who were Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]. So the bounty of Allah here is by what? By sending the messengers, which is the requirement of His mercy, because He, glorified and exalted is He, knows that creation cannot independently know how to worship Allah, glorified and exalted is He. For this reason He sent them messengers to guide them and make clear to them.

﴿And if not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾: the lam here is attached to the response of "lawla", ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾, those who lost this world and the Hereafter, for the most losing of people are the disbelievers; they gained nothing from their worldly life nor from their Hereafter. So in this there is an affirmation, meaning that Allah showed favor to the Children of Israel and had mercy upon them (...)?
* Students: By sending the messengers.
* Shaykh: By sending the messengers, who remind them and admonish them so that they return to Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 62–74 (part 2 of 7):

﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected."﴾ [al-Baqarah 65] His words: ﴿Certainly (laqad)﴾. The lam is a preface to an oath (al-lam al-muwatta'ah lil-qasam), and on this basis the sentence is—?
* A student: Emphatic.
* The Shaykh: Emphasized with three emphatics; what are they?
* The student: The implied oath, the lam, and qad.
* The Shaykh: The implied oath, the lam, and qad. That is, "wa-laqad" originally means: "By Allah, indeed..."
﴿And you certainly knew those who transgressed﴾: you knew with certainty of knowledge and recognized them with complete recognition. ﴿Those among you who transgressed﴾: to whom is the address? To the Children of Israel. And ﴿transgressed﴾ means they exceeded the limits and became tyrannical.

His words: ﴿in the matter of the Sabbath﴾, i.e., concerning the ruling of the day of Sabbath (al-Sabt), which is well known: the day after Friday. On this day Allah, blessed and exalted, had forbidden the Children of Israel to work and had forbidden them to hunt fish on that day, so that they might devote themselves to worship, because they were the ones who chose Saturday for themselves. So Saturday became theirs. This day which they had chosen for themselves, Allah forbade them work and fishing on it. Then Allah, glorified and exalted, tested them with what He had forbidden them, making it easy for them on that day to an extreme degree. So when Saturday came, the fish would come to the surface in great numbers (shurra'an). What is the meaning of shurra'an?
* A student: Visible.
* The Shaykh: Floating openly on the surface because of their abundance. But on other days than Saturday they would not see them. This is without doubt a trial and test from Allah, glorified and exalted, by which He tests His servants; He may make sins and the means of sin easier for them than the means of obedience and good, for the sake of testing and trial. These people did not endure this trial, may Allah protect us, so they devised a stratagem: they dug pits beside the sea and made between these pits and the sea a channel, meaning a small canal. When the fish came in great numbers, they would drive them with the water into this channel and into these pits. When the water receded, the fish could not return, because the channel was narrow and they could not move along it, and it might dry up completely. So when Saturday came, the fish would come and fall into these pits, and when it was night or the next day they would come and take them. Their jurists said to them: "How can you take them when it is forbidden to you?" They said: "We only hunted them on Sunday, we did not hunt them on Saturday." A stratagem, an obvious stratagem, is it not? It is true that they only hunted on Sunday, but they performed the cause by which they hunt on—when?
* The students: On Saturday.
* The Shaykh: On Saturday. So in reality they hunted on Saturday. And since this stratagem—may Allah protect us—appears sound, what is its reality?
* A student: Entanglement.
* The Shaykh: Entanglement in what is forbidden. That is, its outward appearance is correctness and permissibility, while its inward reality is corruption and prohibition. What were they punished with? They were punished by appearing like human beings outwardly, while inwardly they were beasts of prey. ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised and rejected"﴾ (we seek refuge in Allah). ﴿We said to them﴾: to the transgressors; ﴿We said to them﴾: to those who transgressed. ﴿Be apes, despised and rejected﴾: qiradah is the plural of qird, which is well known; khasi'in means banished, distant from the mercy of Allah (we seek refuge in Allah). So they were transformed into an animal most resembling a human being, just as their act most resembled a lawful, correct act while being forbidden inwardly. So the recompense was of the same kind as the deed.

In Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and with whom He was angry, and whom He made into apes and swine, and who worshipped the Taghut﴾ [al-Ma'idah 60]. Were these people of the town apes or swine? In Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And ask them about the town which was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them for what they used to defy.
