He said: al-Tha'labi mentioned it.]], may Allah be pleased with him, that he explained the words of the Exalted, ﴿abiding therein for ages⟩ [an-Naba' 23], as meaning countable years. Is that correct?
* Shaykh: I do not know whether it is correct or not, but it does not indicate restriction. ﴿Abiding therein for ages⟩: years, great and long years, we ask Allah for safety. Some of them say that ﴿abiding therein for ages⟩ is restricted by His words: ﴿They will taste therein neither coolness nor drink⟩ [an-Naba' 24], and that after these ages in which they ﴿taste therein neither coolness nor drink (24) except boiling water and purulent discharge⟩ [an-Naba' 24-25], other kinds of punishment will be brought to them. In any case, all of these are among the ambiguous verses (mutashabih), and we have clear verses (muhkam), and it is obligatory upon the believer to refer the ambiguous to the clear.

﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel⟩: that is, the pact of the Children of Israel. Al-mithaq means the covenant ('ahd), and the covenant is called mithaq because the one who makes the agreement is bound by it, like a rope with which hands and feet are bound, meaning it obliges.

As for His words, ﴿Children of Israel⟩: who is Israel? Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. So the Children of Israel are cousins of the Arabs, because the Arabs are the sons of Isma'il, and these are from the Children of Israel, and their common grandfather is Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel⟩: what is this covenant? ﴿Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents, and to relatives, orphans and the needy, and speak good to people, and establish prayer and give zakat; then you turned away⟩. The covenant included eight articles:

The first article: ﴿Worship none but Allah.﴾ Did they fulfil it or not? They worshipped other than Allah. They worshipped the Messiah, son of Maryam, did they not? And 'Uzayr, they said: "the son of Allah." So they did not fulfil it. As for His words, ﴿worship⟩: what is the meaning of 'ibadah? It is humility and submission, derived from "a paved path" (tariq mu'abbad), meaning one made smooth. That is the first.

The second article: ﴿And be good to parents⟩, that is: show kindness to parents, show kindness to parents with kindness, or act toward parents with kindness. His words, ﴿to parents⟩, refer to the father and the mother. Is it the nearest only, or even the more distant? The nearest. But the more distant also have a right, though not like the right of the father and mother, the closest; for this reason their inheritance differs, and what is due to them in the remaining rights differs.

He said: ﴿And be good to parents⟩, ﴿good⟩ in what? In speech and action, in wealth and standing, and in all the ways of kindness; because Allah stated it absolutely, everything called kindness is included in His words ﴿and be good to parents⟩. This is obligatory because the favour of parents upon their child is the one that follows the favour of Allah upon them; for this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, said about Luqman: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents⟩ [Luqman 14].

They are the cause of your existence, the cause of your sustenance and your upbringing; and although existence is from Allah and sustenance is from Allah, by what means did you come? By way of the parents. Had it not been for the two parents, you would have been nothing.

* Student: Do the paternal uncle and maternal uncle count as parents?
* Shaykh: They are not parents, but their ties are part of goodness to parents.
* Student: So, for example, one cuts off ties with the paternal uncle or maternal uncle?
* Shaykh: He has not completed goodness to his parents.
* Student: Shaykh, the prepositional phrase is placed first, ﴿and be good to parents⟩; does it indicate restriction?
* Shaykh: It is not connected with "goodness." If it were connected with "goodness," it would indicate restriction and its being placed first would be for emphasis. But it is not connected; for this reason we gave you an estimate: we said the estimate is "act," or "be good to them," so it is a verbal noun for a deleted verb.

﴿And to relatives⟩: (dhi) means "possessor of," (...) dhu, dhu al-qurba?
* Student: It is conjoined to ﴿and to parents⟩.
* Shaykh: So "dhu al-qurba" is conjoined to His words ﴿and to parents⟩? That is: and goodness to the possessor of kinship. Dhi means "possessor," and al-qurba means kinship, and it includes kinship through the mother and kinship through the father, because "al-qurba" came after "parents," meaning the kinship of the mother and the kinship of the father.

The word al-qurba, I think, is it a description or not? It means kinship. So whoever is closer has a greater right to this. For example, you owe more in maintaining ties with a paternal uncle than you owe in maintaining ties with the sons of a paternal uncle; you owe more in maintaining ties with a maternal uncle than with the sons of a maternal uncle, because these are more specifically related than those after them.

* Student: Shaykh, does this not contradict the Arabic language?
* Shaykh: Contradict what?
* Student: "Qaraba" being the relatives of a man on his father's side?
* Shaykh: No, not even in the language. Who told you that "qaraba" means a man's relatives through his father? That is a customary usage, and not even a customary one. Even some people call their maternal uncles "family." I want to go... (...) until now, is it not so? When you used to spend the morning at your maternal uncles', did you not say: "I will spend the morning with my family today"?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, I used to say it when I was young: "I want to spend the morning with my family, the Al-so-and-so."
* Student: The common people say: the maternal uncle is a parent?
* Shaykh: No, this maternal uncle (...).
* Student: He says: the maternal uncle is closer than the paternal uncle for a reason. That is, when a man is about to make a bequest concerning his children, for example, a man has died and his children are small, and he entrusts them to their maternal uncle.
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: Closer than their paternal uncle, because their paternal uncle devours them.
* Shaykh: No, I mean more merciful?
* Student: More merciful.
* Shaykh: He comes through the mother, and she is more merciful than the father.
* Student: More merciful indeed, this is a real fact.
* Shaykh: In any case: kinship through the mother is kinship beyond doubt, even by custom, yes indeed.

﴿And the orphans⟩: al-yatama is the plural of yatim, the one whose father died before reaching maturity, male or female. It does not apply to one whose mother died while the father is present, since the father is alive, and he provides for them, raises them and educates them. But when the father dies, he was the earner for his children, so the young children who have not reached maturity become orphans. He enjoined concern for orphans because they have no one to raise or support them, since their father has died; so they are objects of compassion, mercy and care.

﴿And the needy⟩: al-masakin is the plural of miskin, the one whom poverty has made still (askanahu al-faqr). When "masakin" is used alone it includes the poor (fuqara'), and when "fuqara'" is used alone it includes the needy (masakin). When they are mentioned together, "fuqara'" has its own meaning and "masakin" has its own meaning.

﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents, and to relatives, orphans and the needy.﴾

Here His words: ﴿the needy⟩ are included among the poor or not? ﴿and to relatives, orphans and the needy⟩? The needy here are the poor, and they were called needy because poverty stilled them, because when a person becomes rich he becomes overbearing, increases, rises and exalts himself, and when he is poor it is the opposite. Here the poor are included with the needy, because "fuqara'" and "masakin" are among the terms that, when mentioned together, differ, and when they differ, they combine. In words that when combined separate, and when separated combine, and what is the name for this? Words that when combined separate and when separated combine: "fuqara'," when alone, has the meaning of both poor and needy, and "masakin," when alone, has the meaning of both poor and needy; but when said together, as in the verse of zakat, ﴿Zakat is only for the poor and the needy﴾ [at-Tawba 60], "fuqara'" has its own meaning and "masakin" has its own meaning. Now that they are combined they differ: the faqir is one who has none of the sufficiency or has less than half of it, and the miskin is one who has half of the sufficiency but less than full sufficiency. Have you understood the difference between them? Similarly, "al-birr" and "al-taqwa": when "al-birr" is said alone it includes "taqwa," and when "taqwa" is said alone it includes "birr"; but when "al-birr wa al-taqwa" is said together, "birr" is doing obedience and "taqwa" is avoiding sin. Likewise "iman" and "islam."

The point is: words in the Arabic language, especially the legal realities (haqa'iq shar'iyyah), when combined separate, and when separated combine.

And His Exalted words: ﴿and speak good to people⟩, and in one reading: ﴿hasanan⟩, ﴿and speak good to people⟩, ﴿and speak good to people⟩, ﴿hasanan⟩. This too is part of the covenant Allah took from the Children of Israel: that they should speak good to people. Good speech includes goodness in its form and in its meaning. In its form, it should be with gentleness, softness and absence of harshness and severity; this is its form. In its meaning, it should be beneficial, because every good speech is beneficial and every beneficial speech is good. So it is good in form and in meaning: its form is gentleness and softness, and its meaning is that it be beneficial. Enjoining good is good, is it not? Good. Forbidding evil? Good. Teaching beneficial knowledge? Good. Greeting people with peace, and asking how they have risen and how they have spent the evening, and the like, this is good.

The opposite of good speech is two things: evil speech, and speech that is neither evil nor good. As for evil speech, it is forbidden; and as for speech that is neither evil nor good, it is not commanded. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ said: «Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6018), and Muslim (47/74) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Have you understood now? So ﴿speak good to people⟩, or ﴿hasanan⟩, its opposite is: two matters: evil speech, which is forbidden, or what is not described as good nor evil, which is not commanded.

﴿And establish prayer⟩: ﴿establish the prayer⟩ means: say "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, hayya 'ala al-salah, hayya 'ala al-falah"; has the prayer been established?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No, indeed. This is called the iqamah for the prayer. But ﴿establish the prayer⟩ means: bring it standing, that is, upright, without deficiency, and that is by having its pillars, conditions and obligations, and its complements as well. The performance of complements is part of establishing it. One who prays without tranquillity has not established it; one who prays after the time without an excuse has not established it; one who prays before the time has not established it; one who prays without purification has not established it. The point is: one must bring it with these conditions, its pillars and obligations, and complete it with its complements. ﴿Establish the prayer⟩: this prayer includes establishing the obligatory and the voluntary. For this reason, before you enter into a voluntary prayer, it is not obligatory upon you; but once you enter it, it becomes obligatory to bring its conditions, pillars and obligations. Do you not say: "I pray as I wish (...)"? You stand before Him and say: ﴿You alone we worship⟩ [al-Fatiha 5].

Likewise here, ﴿then you turned away⟩. Had He said "then they turned away," it would apply only to the earlier Children of Israel. But when He says ﴿then you turned away⟩, and it was revealed in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, what does it include? It includes even those present in the time of the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿then you turned away⟩, meaning: you, O Children of Israel, turned away from now until what came before. The benefit here is the shift of address from their predecessors to their successors. There is also a second point: did all their predecessors turn away?
* Student: Except a few.
* Shaykh: Except a few of them. Even in the time of the Messenger, not all of them turned away; among them a few believed in the Messenger, peace be upon him, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, for he believed in the Messenger ﷺ. Many also, several people; when you hear "so-and-so al-Qurazi," he is from the Banu Qurayza, from the Jews, who embraced Islam.

﴿Then you turned away, except a few of you﴾: ﴿turned away⟩ means you turned away from fulfilling this covenant. ﴿Except a few of you⟩ means: except a small group of you. And ﴿qalilan⟩ here is in the accusative by what? By exception (istithna'), because when you say "the people stood except Zayd," you must put "Zayd" in the accusative. If someone says: why did you put it in the accusative? We say: look at the exception; if someone reads "qama al-qawmu illa Zaydun," we say this is an error, not valid in the Arabic language, because in an exception after a complete affirmative sentence it must be in the accusative.

﴿Except a few of you, while you are turning away (mu'ridun)﴾: the clause here is circumstantial: "you turned away in aversion," because one who turns away may not have aversion; he may turn away while his heart is attached to what is beyond, but when he turns away with aversion, there is no hope that he will later accept. This is more severe: the one who turns away in aversion is worse than the one who turns away without aversion. Have you understood? ﴿Except a few of you, while you are turning away﴾: this clause, ﴿while you are turning away⟩, is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the "ta'" in ﴿then you turned away⟩.

* Student: Does "tawalla" not mean "turning away (i'rad)"?
* Shaykh: No. "Tawalla" means leaving a thing behind the back, but when it is accompanied by i'rad it must be explained, because i'rad is with the heart and tawalla is with the body; the meaning of tawalla is that one cannot hope for a return.

﴿And when We took your covenant﴾: that is, remember when We took your covenant. Allah reminds them of the covenants He took from them. What is this covenant? We have already seen that mithaq means covenant, but what is the covenant that took place, and the document?

First: ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾. Safk and safh have the same meaning, and shedding blood is spilling it, and shedding blood here means killing, as the Messenger ﷺ said about Makkah: «It is not lawful for a man who believes in Allah and the Last Day to shed blood therein»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (104), and Muslim (1354/446) from Abu Shurayh, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. What is the meaning of «to shed blood therein»? To kill a sacred soul. His words ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾ mean: do not spill it by killing. And His words ﴿your blood⟩: how is it "your blood"? Does a person spill his own blood? "Your blood" means the blood of some of you, but the one community is like one body; for this reason the Messenger ﷺ said: «The protection of the Muslims is one; the lowest of them may grant it, and the furthest of them protects by it»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (7300), and Muslim (1370/467) from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, up to "the lowest of them"; the rest of the hadith from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with him, in Abu Dawud (2751).]]. So the one community is as if it were one body; is this understood?

﴿And do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾: the same word, ﴿yourselves⟩. A person does not expel himself from his home, but he expels some of them, that is, he expels his people. His words ﴿you expel yourselves from your homes⟩ mean: this is exile. So there is no transgression by killing, and no transgression by expulsion from the homeland.

There is no doubt that exile from the homeland, we seek refuge in Allah, is like killing, and perhaps worse, because a person lives humiliated when he is expelled from his land; he lives humiliated in two respects: in one respect, he has been overpowered in his land, and this is humiliation; in another respect, he has become a stranger in the second land, not living among them as one of them. For this reason the expulsion of souls from homes has been equated with killing: ﴿And do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾.

Then, after this covenant, you persisted in it, acknowledged it, and bore witness to it. The acknowledgment was not absent from you or forgotten by you; rather it remains and continues. And after this covenant, its acknowledgment, and bearing witness to it, after all this: ﴿Then you are these who kill yourselves﴾. ﴿Then you are these﴾ — what is the meaning of "these" (hā'ulā')? It means: O you (yā hā'ulā'), and it is not the predicate of the subject. A beginner student of grammar may say: "﴿Then you are these﴾: 'you' (antum) is the subject and 'these' (hā'ulā') is its predicate." We say: No. "You" (antum) is the subject, and "these" (hā'ulā') is a vocative (munādā) from which the vocative particle has been omitted; meaning: then you, O these. The address is to those who were in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, since fighting took place among them. ﴿You kill﴾ (taqtulūna) is the predicate of the subject. ﴿You kill yourselves (anfusakum)﴾ — is its predicate here a clause or a single word? What does Ibn Mālik say in the Alfiyya?

* Student: "And a predicate comes as a single word and comes as a clause."

* The Shaykh:
"And as a single word it comes, and as a clause it comes..." ∗∗∗ .....................

The predicate ﴿taqtulūna﴾ is a clause. ﴿You kill yourselves﴾ means: some of you kill others of you. ﴿And you expel a group of you from their homes﴾ — you drive them out from the homes. This occurred among the Jewish factions near the time of the Prophet's ﷺ mission: some of them killed others, and some of them expelled others from their homes.

Then He said: ﴿You support one another against them in sin and aggression﴾. In my view there is a reading ﴿tazzāharūna﴾ with the ẓā' doubled, which originates from tatazāharūna (you support one another). And tazāharūna means: you exalt yourselves, because ẓuhūr (supremacy) means elevation. God Most High said: ﴿He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawba 33], meaning: to make it high. Elevation was called ẓuhūr from ẓahr (back), because the highest part of an animal is its back. So His saying ﴿tazāharūna﴾ means: you exalt yourselves over them.

﴿In sin and aggression﴾ — sin and aggression: what is the difference between them? Sin (ithm) is disobedience, and aggression (ʿudwān) is transgression against others. Every aggression is a sin, but not every sin is an aggression, except against oneself. So a man who, for example, smokes tobacco is sinful and transgressing.

* Student: Against himself.

* The Shaykh: Against himself. Leave aside "against himself"; but against others, no.

A man who kills a protected person? He is sinful and transgressing. One who expels him from his land? Sinful and transgressing. Therefore He said: ﴿You support one another against them in sin and aggression﴾. Sin: disobedience; aggression: transgressing against another without right and oppressing him. They — may God protect us — after the covenant had been taken from them with acknowledgment and witness, did not fulfill it: they expelled themselves from their homes and supported one another against them in sin and aggression.

Has anyone of this nation done the same? Yes, it has occurred, confirming the Messenger's ﷺ saying: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you" [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2180) and Aḥmad (21897), the wording is his, from the hadith of Abū Wāqid al-Laythī (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu); and it was narrated by al-Bukhārī (7320) and Muslim (2669), from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) with the wording: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you..."]. Among the Muslims there have occurred those who expelled themselves from their homes, and those who killed themselves, some killing others and some expelling others from their homes.

* The student: Shaykh, is the "min" in ﴿min diyārihim﴾ partitive or not?

* The Shaykh: No, this one is for the starting point (ibtidāʾ).

﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾. In another reading: ﴿tafdūhum﴾. Look at the contradiction: ﴿if they come to you as captives﴾ — "yatūkum" or "yu'tūkum"? ﴿yatūkum﴾ means they come to you. ﴿Captives (usārā)﴾ — it is also said "usrā", but that is not a reading; usārā is the plural of asīr, and the asīr is one whom his enemy has gained control over. It is not necessary that he be bound with rope; that is not required, but generally he is taken captive. God says to the Jews: you now kill yourselves, you expel a group of you from their homes, you exalt yourselves over them in sin and aggression, and then you contradict yourselves: if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, meaning you free them from captivity by ransom; because this is obligatory upon them — it is obligatory that they ransom one another and remove harm from one another. Is this faith or not? It is faith in part and disbelief in part; therefore He said: ﴿And it is forbidden to you to expel them﴾ — meaning, you ransom the captives, while their expulsion is forbidden to you: expel them from where? From their homes. So you, may God protect us, have not established faith in the whole Book; therefore He said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ The interrogative here is for denunciation and reproach, and the fāʾ in His saying ﴿afa-tu'minūna﴾ is a conjunctive particle. What is the element it is conjoined to? Where is the element conjoined to? Who knows the element conjoined to?

* Student: It is omitted.

* The Shaykh: And what is the estimate?

* Student: It is estimated according to the context, so here (...).

* The Shaykh: "Are you contradicting," for example?

* Student: Are you contradicting.

* The Shaykh: Are you contradicting? So you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part. There is another view among the grammarians: there is no need to estimate a conjoined element; we say the hamza is interrogative, the fāʾ is a conjunctive particle, and there is inversion, the original being: "a-fa-tu'minūna." These examples have passed us many times, and we have told you that this is better, because it is easier; for estimation sometimes eludes a person, and sometimes he does not know the appropriate word. But when you say: the fāʾ is a conjunctive particle, and this is what we mentioned: every hamza that is followed by a conjunctive particle, its way is to make the hamza interrogative and the fāʾ or wāw or thumma a conjunction, according to what comes in the speech; and the conjoined element is either estimated according to the context, or it is what preceded; and there is inversion in the speech between the conjunctive particle and the interrogative hamza. Yes, indeed.

That is: its meaning is "then do you believe..." in this way, or "are you contradicting," or "you contradict, so you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part"; whatever suits you, you carry out, and what does not suit you, you leave and do not carry out. This is one who worships God in this manner; in reality he has not worshipped God, but has worshipped his own desire. When a legal ruling suits him, he says, "Welcome and gladly, upon the eye and head; we judge by the Book and the Sunna and submit to God and His Messenger." And when the truth goes against him or what he dislikes: "By God, this needs interpretation, or perhaps we did not understand the meaning, or perhaps it applies to some circumstances," or he disobeys God directly, plainly, without interpretation and without anything else. Is there now among the nation one who does this? There is, very many. Even some people think in themselves: "By God, this is the easy opinion of Abū Ḥanīfa on this issue, so he takes it." In another place, the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfa is stricter than that of the Ḥanbalīs, so he takes the opinion of the Ḥanbalīs. In a third place the opinion of al-Shāfiʿī is easier than all of them, so he takes the opinion of al-Shāfiʿī. Then he comes to the opinion of Imam Mālik and says: "Mālik is the imam of the abode of migration; we take the opinion, because it is the easiest of the opinions." Someone who loves his belly and loves eating; and Mālik is known for being lenient about foods, saying all animals are lawful except a few simple things; he says: "The opinion of Mālik is the correct opinion," and begins eating whatever comes along, yet in other matters he does not agree with this. What do you think of him?

Is this a believer in truth? No, because one who follows the Sharia of God does not go about seeking concessions and taking the sayings of the scholars only if they agree with his desire, and otherwise leaving them. He knows that this scholar is closer to the correct than that scholar, and takes his saying, whether it agrees with his desire or opposes it. Is it clear? This is the obligation upon the Muslim. But (...) for every issue he follows the opinion of a scholar whenever it agrees with his desire; he may even act on two opinions in two situations: in this year he takes the opinion of so-and-so, which suits him, and in another year the opinion of someone else.

* Student: In Ḥajj.

* The Shaykh: In Ḥajj and outside Ḥajj. A person, for example, ate camel meat and touched a woman with desire, so he said: "I will take the Shāfiʿī opinion that my ablution is not nullified by eating camel meat, and I will take the opinion of the one who holds that touching a woman with desire does not nullify ablution, or the Ḥanbalī opinion that touching a woman in any case does not nullify ablution; because al-Shāfiʿī holds that touching a woman in any case nullifies ablution; if his hand touches her he must perform ablution." This man shook a woman's hand and said: "How are you? How is your condition?" and said: "I will take the Ḥanbalī opinion of not nullifying ablution, and I will take the Shāfiʿī opinion of not nullifying ablution by camel meat, and I will pray." We say to him: your prayer now is not valid; is it valid according to both opinions or not? For the Ḥanbalīs say: your prayer is not valid, because you ate camel meat; and al-Shāfiʿī says: it is not valid, because you touched a woman. But he is not concerned; "It is nothing to you; I am free in what I have erred in." We say to him: this is not correct, because this is trifling with the religion of God. Therefore some scholars said: whoever follows concessions becomes a heretic (tazandaqa). The well-known ruling is that he becomes a sinner (fāsiq), but some of them say he becomes a heretic, because the reality is that he did not intend God Most High by this worship. These are people about whom God says: ﴿They believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part﴾: whatever agrees with them they believe in, and whatever does not agree with them they disbelieve and reject. This is not the practice of one who worships God Most High.

God Most High says: ﴿Then what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world﴾ — I seek refuge in God. Where is the hijāziyya? We have not applied it. We all know, as we read in Ibn Mālik's Alfiyya, that the hijāziyya operates; the Qur'an is in the dialect of the Hijaz. The negation was annulled: ﴿fa-mā jazāʾu﴾ ﴿illā﴾; therefore its operation is nullified. Ibn Mālik, may God have mercy on him, says in the Alfiyya, read the verse:

* Student:
إِعْمَالَ لَيْسَ أُعْمِلَتْ مَا دُوْنَ إِنْ ∗∗∗ مَعَ بَقَا الْنَّفْي وَتَــــــرْتِيبٍ زُكِنْ

* The Shaykh:
إِعْمَالَ لَيْسَ أُعْمِلَتْ مَا دُوْنَ إِنْ ∗∗∗ مَعَ بَقَا الْنَّفْي وَتَــــــرْتِيبٍ زُكِنْ

Here the negation has not remained; therefore its operation was cancelled: ﴿fa-mā jazāʾuhu﴾. Recompense, requital, and punishment have the same or similar meaning. Recompense is rewarding the doer for his deed; meaning: your reward for this deed is nothing but disgrace in the life of this world. What is the meaning of disgrace (khizy)? Disgrace is humiliation — may God protect us — humiliation.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the severest punishment. And God is not unaware of what you do﴾. ﴿ʿammā yaʿmalūna﴾ — and in another reading, I think the well-known reading is ﴿taʿmalūna﴾, which is in the mushaf, and there is a reading ﴿ʿammā yaʿmalūna﴾, and God knows best.

His saying: ﴿bi-ghāfilin ʿammā yaʿmalūna﴾ — is this a negative attribute or an affirmative one? ﴿wa-mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūna﴾ — negative or affirmative? Did we not say that the attributes of God are of two kinds, negative and affirmative? The affirmative are those He affirmed for Himself, and the negative are those He negated. Here ﴿wa-mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin﴾ — is it negation or affirmation?

* Student: Negation.

* The Shaykh: His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ — to whom does the pronoun refer?

* Student: To the Children of Israel.

* The Shaykh: Yes. What is the meaning of covenant (mīthāq)?

* Student: The covenant is the pledge.

* The Shaykh: What is the aspect of its resemblance to the covenant?

* Student: The pledge binds a person and restrains him from leaving the pledge.

* The Shaykh: Meaning, as a person is bound by a tie or the like?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: His saying: ﴿Do not shed your blood﴾ — what is meant by it?

* Student: Do not kill a protected soul.

* The Shaykh: Is the meaning of shedding blood the killing of a soul? His saying ﴿tasfikūna dimāʾakum﴾ — can one shed his own blood?

* Student: (...) does not kill (...) himself, but it falls upon the Children of Israel.

* The Shaykh: Why? For what reason?

* Student: Because whoever kills a Muslim...

* Another student: That is, do not kill one another.

* The Shaykh: But why did He say "kill yourselves"?

* Student: As an indication that the individual of the nation, that the nation is like the individual.

* The Shaykh: That the nation is like the individual, like one body; so the killing of one of them is as if he had killed himself.

His saying: ﴿Then you are these﴾ — what is the parsing of ﴿these﴾?

* Student: "Then you, O these."

* The Shaykh: And what is its parsing, what is it?

* Student: A vocative.

* The Shaykh: A vocative from which the vocative particle was removed. Is it not valid that it be the predicate of the subject?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: Where is the predicate of the subject?

* Student: It is not suitable to be.

* The Shaykh: Where is its predicate?

* Student: Its predicate?

* The Shaykh: Yes, "you" (antum), where is its predicate?

* Student: ﴿anfusakum﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Then you﴾ ﴿anfusakum﴾ — that is not suitable.

* Student: The clause ﴿taqtulūna anfusakum﴾.

* The Shaykh: The clause ﴿taqtulūna anfusakum﴾.

His saying: ﴿tazāharūna ʿalayhim﴾ — what is its meaning?

* Student: You exalt yourselves.

* The Shaykh: You exalt yourselves. ﴿tazāharūna ʿalayhim﴾ — how is the meaning "you exalt yourselves"?

* Student: (...) by aggression.

* The Shaykh: It is also said: you assist, ﴿tazāharūna﴾ apparently means: he helped, you support one another against them.

His saying: ﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾ — what is its meaning?

* Student: That is, as captives.

* The Shaykh: And what is the meaning of ﴿tufādūhum﴾?

* Student: They offer some money (...).

* The Shaykh: These allies, who are the Aws and the Khazraj, were idol-worshippers before Islam, and there would be wars and fighting between them. The Jews would come and assist their allies against their people. For example, the Banū al-Naḍīr assisted the Khazraj against whom? Against the Aws. Then the Banū Qurayẓa stood with their allies the Aws, so the Jews killed one another, although it was forbidden to them in the Torah. Then, if one of them was taken captive, they would come to ransom him, meaning they would take him back by ransom: for example, if the Aws captured one of the Banū al-Naḍīr, they would offer a ransom to take him. Thus they became contradictory; for look at the covenant that was taken from them: ﴿Do not shed your blood and do not expel yourselves from your homes; then you acknowledged and you were witnesses (84). Then you are these who kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes﴾ — they broke the covenant (...), did they not? ﴿Then you are these who kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes﴾ — they broke the covenant in both matters, did they not?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾ — this is part of the covenant; meaning, the covenant was also taken from you that if they are taken captive, it is obligatory upon you to ransom them. Do you understand?

Then He said: ﴿And it is forbidden to you to expel them﴾ — this sentence refers back to what preceded: you expel yourselves from your homes and support one another against them in sin and aggression, while their expulsion is forbidden to you. So they now believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part. How do they believe? In the matter of ransom they believe in it and ransom; the matter of killing souls and expulsion they do not believe in. So they believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part. The covenant taken from them now consists of three obligations: that they not kill themselves, not expel themselves from their homes, and ransom them. They fulfilled one and abandoned two.

It is said that His saying ﴿tazāharūna ʿalayhim bi-l-ithmi wa-l-ʿudwān﴾ is also part of the covenant; meaning, that you do not support one another against them, you do not assist anyone against them. So on this view the covenant comprises four clauses, and they broke how many? Three of them, and believed in one; therefore God rebuked them by saying: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾

The commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 79–86 (part 5 of 5):

His saying: ﴿فَمَا جَزَاءُ مَنْ يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ مِنْكُمْ﴾ What is meant by "jaza'" (recompense)? The punishment. What is its punishment? ﴿إِلَّا خِزْيٌ فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَيَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ يُرَدُّونَ إِلَى أَشَدِّ الْعَذَابِ﴾ "There is nothing for those who do that among you except disgrace in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be consigned to the most severe punishment."

The disgrace that befell them in this world is very clear. The Banu Qurayzah were killed, their fighting men, and their women and children were taken captive. The Banu al-Nadir were expelled by the Prophet (ﷺ) from their homes, as Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Hashr: ﴿يُخْرِبُونَ بُيُوتَهُمْ بِأَيْدِيهِمْ وَأَيْدِي الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ "They destroy their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers" [al-Hashr 2].

This is the disgrace in this world, and we seek refuge with Allah. As for the Hereafter, for them is the punishment: ﴿وَيَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ يُرَدُّونَ إِلَى أَشَدِّ الْعَذَابِ وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ "And on the Day of Resurrection they will be consigned to the most severe punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do." With this, the meaning of the verse becomes fully clear. To whom is it addressed? To the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir, for a covenant was taken from them concerning these matters, but they fulfilled some of it and abandoned some of it.

﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا بِالْآخِرَةِ﴾ "Those are the ones who have bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter." ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to these Jews who broke the covenant. They bought the world with the Hereafter. Here "ishtira'" (buying) means choosing: they took the world and gave up the Hereafter. So the Hereafter, in their eyes, is something disdained and sold, while the world is something desired and bought. How many Muslims today resemble the Jews! How many buy the world with the Hereafter despite the abundance of knowledge at present! But "the reciters have multiplied and the jurists have become few." Reciters are many, knowledge is abundant, and the proof is established, yet most people disobey Allah the Exalted, we seek refuge with Allah, knowingly and with insight, buying the life of this world with the Hereafter. It is said, for example: lying in buying and selling is forbidden, yet they lie; it is said: deception is forbidden, yet they deceive; it is said: betraying those in authority is forbidden, yet they betray; it is said: concerning guardianship over your women, you must act in what is best for them, yet they act in what is best for themselves. And judge the rest by this. So among the nation of Muslims today there are people who resemble these Jews in having bought the life of this world with the Hereafter. They have renounced the Hereafter as if it were nothing, yet they cling to the world with their molars. We ask Allah for safety, and that He guide us and them.

His saying: ﴿الدُّنْيَا﴾ in ﴿الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ describes this life as "the lower" (dunya), and "dunya" is an elative form (ism tafdil).

*Student: No.

*Shaykh: No? It is an elative form (ism tafdil); its masculine is adna, as one says "rajul adna" and "imra'ah dunya," from "dunuw" (nearness), whether this nearness is of rank or of time. The world, in reality, is characterized by two kinds of nearness: nearness of time, because it precedes the Hereafter, or not? Which is first? The world, so it is nearer; and nearness of rank and station, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا (١٦) وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَى﴾ "Rather, you prefer the life of this world, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring" [al-A'la 16–17].

As for our saying that it is an elative form, what is the meaning? That in it there is excess... no. It is an elative form in terms of morphological pattern (wazn sarfi), because the morphological scale has a pattern they call ism al-tafdil.

*Student: (...)?

*Shaykh: The lowly world. You understood a meaning other than what I intended.

His saying: ﴿بِالْآخِرَةِ﴾ The letter "ba'" here is for exchange. Does it always enter on the price or on the thing priced?

*Student: On the thing priced.

*Shaykh: No, my brother, it enters on the price. The "ba'" enters on the price: "I bought the garment for a dinar." So the price for them is the Hereafter, given up, and the thing bought is the world.

His saying: ﴿بِالْآخِرَةِ﴾ is the life of the Hereafter. The life of the Hereafter, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said, is: ﴿الْحَيَوَانُ﴾ [al-Ankabut 64]. The world is a life, and the Hereafter is "hayawan." The meaning of "hayawan" is complete life; for this reason it came in this pattern with the alif and nun, to indicate completeness: the most complete life is the life of the Hereafter.

He said: ﴿فَلَا يُخَفَّفُ عَنْهُمُ الْعَذَابُ وَلَا هُمْ يُنْصَرُونَ﴾ "So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped." (We seek refuge with Allah.) ﴿لَا يُخَفَّفُ﴾ means it will not be eased, neither in duration nor in intensity and severity. And can anyone repel it from them? ﴿وَلَا هُمْ يُنْصَرُونَ﴾ "nor will they be helped," i.e., they will not be protected from the punishment of Allah.

﴿وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ فِي النَّارِ لِخَزَنَةِ جَهَنَّمَ ادْعُوا رَبَّكُمْ يُخَفِّفْ عَنَّا يَوْمًا مِنَ الْعَذَابِ﴾ [Ghafir 49] "Those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell: Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment." (We seek refuge with Allah.) They are despairing. They did not say: "let Him bring us out of the Fire," nor did they say: "let Him lighten it for us always," but: ﴿يُخَفِّفْ عَنَّا يَوْمًا مِنَ الْعَذَابِ﴾. (We seek refuge with Allah.) They wish that the punishment be lightened for them for a single day, out of what? Out of what has no end: eternity, we seek refuge with Allah. They wish to taste even one day of lightening out of everlasting, unending duration. But that will not happen for them, so it is said to them: ﴿أَوَلَمْ تَكُ تَأْتِيكُمْ رُسُلُكُمْ بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ قَالُوا بَلَى قَالُوا فَادْعُوا﴾ [Ghafir 50] "Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs? They said: Yes. They said: Then call upon..." Will it benefit them or not? ﴿وَمَا دُعَاءُ الْكَافِرِينَ إِلَّا فِي ضَلَالٍ﴾ "And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error." It will not benefit them, we seek refuge with Allah.

So here He says: ﴿فَلَا يُخَفَّفُ عَنْهُمُ الْعَذَابُ﴾ "the punishment will never be lightened for them," not even at some times? Never. ﴿وَلَا هُمْ يُنْصَرُونَ﴾. How great the matter would be if hearts were attentive, but most hearts are heedless. We ask Allah to awaken our hearts and yours.

*Student: ﴿وَوَيْلٌ لَهُمْ مِمَّا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾, ﴿وَقَالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنَا النَّارُ﴾

*Shaykh: This is the beginning of the benefits.

* Benefit derived from this verse: ﴿وَقَالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنَا النَّارُ﴾ that the Jews affirm the Hereafter and that there is a Fire, as shown by their saying: ﴿وَقَالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنَا النَّارُ إِلَّا أَيَّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾.

* The second benefit: that they spoke about Allah without knowledge, either falsely or ignorantly, and the closer view is that it is falsehood, and that these are baseless claims: ﴿لَنْ تَمَسَّنَا النَّارُ إِلَّا أَيَّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾.

* The third benefit: the excellence of the Qur'an's argumentation, for it restricted this claim to one of two options, both of which are negated: ﴿أَتَّخَذْتُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَهْدًا﴾ ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ عَلَى اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. And this, of course, is according to the view that "am" here is connective (muttasilah) or disjunctive (munqati'ah)?

*Student: Connective.

*Shaykh: According to the view that it is connective. As for the view that it is disjunctive, there is only one binding argument, namely: ﴿أَتَّخَذْتُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَهْدًا فَلَنْ يُخْلِفَ اللَّهُ عَهْدَهُ﴾. In any case, there is in it the excellence of the Qur'an's argumentation.

* The fourth benefit: that Allah the Exalted and Majestic will never break His promise. Do you understand? That He does not break His promise includes two great attributes: truthfulness and power, for one who breaks a promise does so either out of lying or out of inability. So the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿لَا يُخْلِفُ الْمِيعَادَ﴾ "does not break the promise," is evidence of His perfect truthfulness and perfect power.

His saying: ﴿وَعْدَهُ﴾ But does He break His threat?

*Student: He may forgive it.

*Shaykh: Yes, He may forgive it; but this is perfection and praise. The poet said:

وَإِنِّي وَإِنْ أَوْعَدْتُهُ أَوْ وَعَدْتُهُ ∗∗∗ لَمُخْلِفُ إِيعَادِي وَمُنْجِزُ مَوْعِدِي

"Indeed I, if I threaten him or promise him, am one who breaks my threat and fulfills my promise."

"Awadtuhu" (I threatened him) refers to evil, and "wa'attuhu" (I promised him) refers to good; for this reason he said: "lamukhlifun i'adi wa munjizun mau'idi" (one who breaks my threat and fulfills my promise).

So Allah, blessed and exalted, may pardon: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ وَيَغْفِرُ مَا دُونَ ذَلِكَ لِمَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ "Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with; but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" [al-Nisa' 48].

Is this a promise or a threat here? A promise. That is, if the Jews were not touched by the Fire except for a number of days, then... from it. This is a promise.

* The fifth benefit: that it is among the habits of the Jews to speak about Allah without knowledge, as shown by His saying: ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ عَلَى اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾.

Speaking about Allah, as previously explained in the tafsir, includes speaking about Him regarding His rulings, His essence, and His attributes. Do you understand? Whoever speaks about Him without knowledge, meaning he makes lawful or unlawful, has spoken about Allah without knowledge; and whoever says anything about His names and attributes has spoken about Allah without knowledge. Whoever says: "The intended meaning of the hand is power," has spoken about Allah what he does not know. Who told you that? The word "yad" (hand) may denote power, and may denote a literal hand, and may denote blessing. So whoever tells you that Allah intended by it power or strength, that person has spoken about Allah without knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 79–86 (part 1 of 5):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah 79]. ﴿Fawaylun (woe)﴾ is a word of threat, by which Allah the Exalted threatens those who are characterized by this attribute. It is the subject (mubtada'), and the subject was permitted to begin with it although it is indefinite (nakirah).

* Student: (...) The predicate is a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur).
* Shaykh: That is not enough. If you said "a man in the house," would it be correct? Do you have anything other than this?
* Student: An indefinite that has been made specific (nakirah mukhassasah).
* Shaykh: What is it in this case?
* Student: ﴿Li-alladhina (for those who)﴾.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿li-alladhina﴾ is the predicate of the subject. ﴿Li-alladhina﴾ is the predicate of a subject; it is not a qualifier of it.
* Student: ﴿Li-alladhina﴾ is the predicate?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. And what do you say? Because it conveys meaning (afadat). What does Ibn Malik say?
* Student: He says: the indefinite...
* Shaykh: "As long as it conveys meaning." So the criterion for permissibility is conveying meaning. It is enough for us to say: it conveyed meaning. "Woe to so-and-so," for example, conveys meaning. As for the specific meaning of it, they say: because it is a threat, and it conveys the meaning of a threat. And they say in the case of ﴿salamun 'alaykum (peace be upon you)﴾ [al-An'am 54]: because it is a supplication. So as for our saying, what permitted beginning with it is that it is a threat, and a threat conveys meaning. Yes indeed.

﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah"﴾. ﴿Li-alladhina yaktubuna al-kitaba bi-aydihim (for those who write the Scripture with their own hands)﴾. His saying ﴿al-kitab (the Scripture)﴾ means "the written thing" (al-maktub), and fi'al in the sense of maf'ul (passive participle) occurs often in the Arabic language, with examples including firash (in the sense of maf'ruash, "spread out"), ghiras (in the sense of maghrus, "planted"), and bina' (in the sense of ?).

* Student: Mabni (built).
* Shaykh: (Mabni), and sirat (in the sense of mashrut, "laid down").

His saying ﴿yaktubuna al-kitaba bi-aydihim (they write the Scripture with their own hands)﴾: this phrase is an emphatic object of the verb, since writing is not done except by the hand. That is, they write it with their own hands; they do not order others. They personally carry out this great crime.

﴿Thumma yaqulun (then they say)﴾ after they wrote it with their own hands and knew that it was made by their hands, ﴿yaqulna hadha min 'indi Allah (they say, "This is from Allah")﴾. ﴿Hadha min 'indi Allah (This is from Allah)﴾ -I seek refuge in Allah- came down from Allah. Their saying ﴿min 'indi Allah (from Allah)﴾ means: the Book of Allah, because a book that comes from Him is the Book of Allah. Why? The reason is: ﴿li-yashtaru bihi thamanan (to exchange it for a small price)﴾.

His saying ﴿hadha min 'indi Allah (this is from Allah)﴾: is it a subject and predicate?

* Students: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: It is a subject built on sukun. ﴿Hadha (this)﴾: ha is for alerting, and dha is a demonstrative noun built on sukun in a nominative position as subject, and ﴿min 'indi Allah (from Allah)﴾ is a prepositional phrase attached to an omitted predicate of the subject.

His saying ﴿li-yashtaru bihi (that they may exchange it)﴾: the lam is for causation (ta'lil), or not?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: ﴿Li-yashtaru bihi (that they may exchange it)﴾. The lam attached to the verb can be for causation, as in ﴿li-yashtaru bihi﴾; it can be for consequence (al-'aqibah), as in His saying ﴿fa-iltaqatahu al Fir'awn li-yakuna lahum 'aduwwan wa hazanan (so the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief)﴾ [al-Qasas 8]; it can be extra (za'idah), as in ﴿yuridun li-yutfi'u nur Allah (they want to extinguish the light of Allah)﴾ [al-Saff 8], meaning: they want to extinguish, because the verb (yurid) takes its object directly without a preposition; it can be for command, as in ﴿li-yunfiq dhu si'atin min si'atih (let the wealthy spend from his wealth)﴾ [al-Talaq 7]; and it can be for emphasizing negation, called lam al-juhud (the lam of denial), as in ﴿wa ma kana Allah li-yu'adhdhibahum (and Allah would not punish them)﴾ [al-Anfal 33], and ﴿lam yakuni Allah li-yaghfira lahum (Allah would not forgive them)﴾ [al-Nisa 137].

So the lam attached to the present-tense verb has five aspects. Do you want this, or shall we leave it? But I see that you are eager for grammar. They say: grammar in speech is like salt in food. So we say: the lam that enters on the present-tense verb has five aspects. The lam here, ﴿li-yashtaru bihi﴾, is the lam of causation. They write it and say, "This is from Allah," deceiving for this purpose.

* Student: The last lam?
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: ﴿Li-yashtaru﴾.
* Shaykh: This lam is for causation, ﴿li-yashtaru bihi﴾.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: The lam of denial.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the correct view is that it is for threat.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: There is no evidence for it. Yes indeed.

He says: ﴿li-yashtaru bihi thamanan (that they may exchange it for a small price)﴾. ﴿Li-yashtaru bihi (that they may exchange it)﴾: the original form of yashtaru was yashtaruna, but the nun was dropped because the verb is governed by "an (that)." The estimate is: li-an yashtaru. His saying ﴿yashtaru (they exchange)﴾ means: they sell, or they take?

* Students: They take.
* Shaykh: And shara?
* Students: Sold.
* Shaykh: Sold. Common people now use shara to mean "bought" (ashtara), took. In reality shara means "gave" (a'ta), in the sense of "sold," and baa'a means "gave," and ibtaa'a means "took." Yabtai'u means: he takes, the form ifta'ala from shara. The form ifta'ala from baa'a in the sense of taking, is it so? And fa'ala from shara, and from baa'a in the sense of "gave." Yes indeed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And among people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 207]. ﴿Yashri (sells)﴾ means "sells."

﴿Li-yashtaru bihi thamanan qalilan (that they may exchange it for a small price)﴾. The thaman (price) is the compensation; the compensation for a thing is called a thaman. That is: that they may take with it a price, ﴿qalilan (small)﴾, meaning the opposite of much. And it is known that "much" refers to quantity or to quality?

* Student: To quantity.
* Shaykh: To quantity. What is this small price? It is leadership, status, and the like. They write and say, "This is from Allah," in order to deceive the servants of Allah with it: to permit what is forbidden, to drop an obligation, to curry favor with a leader, or similar things, so that people will be subdued by them. But all of this that occurs is a small price. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: the enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [al-Nisa 77]. Whatever happens in this world of leadership, status, wealth, and children is little. The Prophet ﷺ said in the authentic hadith narrated by Ahmad, from the hadith of al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad: «The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than this world and everything in it»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2892), and Ahmad in his Musnad (15563), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd ibn Malik; the wording is Ahmad's.]]. From the world: which world? All of it, from its beginning to its end, with its leaderships, wealth, sons, palaces, and everything in it. The place of a whip: how far does a whip reach? About a meter. The place of a whip is better than the world and everything in it. So the world is little. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life (16). While the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la 16-17]. If you rise by your knowledge one degree, it is better for you than being above the heads of the peaks in worldly fashion, is it not so?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because all of that will vanish, but what is with Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, remains and does not vanish. Yes indeed. ﴿Li-yashtaru bihi thamanan qalilan﴾.

Then He emphasized, saying: ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾. The punishment is according to the deed. Earlier it was stated absolutely, meaning there is no repetition in the verse. ﴿So woe to those who write﴾ is absolute: we do not know what the measure of this woe is. He said: ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾, saying: this woe is according to what? According to what they wrote. ﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾, and woe to them for what they earn by this writing. This small enjoyment or small price that they earned, will they be punished with it or not?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: They will be punished with it. Then they will be punished for what results from misguiding creation until the Day of Resurrection. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection»[[Narrated by Muslim (1017/69), and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (8946), from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, with nearly this wording.]]. But among us in the Islamic nation, they wrote with their own hands and said: "This is better than what is with Allah" -I seek refuge in Allah. They wrote books which they call "The Green Book," and said: "This is better than the Qur'an." They brought a prayer called "The Prayer of the Opener," and said: "This is better than reciting the Qur'an six hundred times" -I seek refuge in Allah. Would that they had said, "This is from Allah." Rather, their speech implies that what they wrote is better than what came from Allah -and we seek refuge in Allah. Yes indeed. They have become -and we seek refuge in Allah- more wicked than these Jews; they have become more wicked than the Jews.

﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾. The benefits, God willing, will come in the next lesson, because this verse contains great benefits related to this Ummah, especially to its scholars, and they are among the things included in their lies. Yes, brother, your question?

* Student: (...) Does it not include the material (mali)?
* Shaykh: We said: it includes everything in this world of wealth, status, and leadership.
* Student: The little (...)?
* Shaykh: It is well known that "little" refers to quantity, while "weak" refers to quality. This is well known. But nothing prevents it from being little in both respects, and it being used in both meanings.
* Student: Now, O Shaykh, when you advise many people to keep away from luxury in worldly life in particular, they cite against you the hadith of the Messenger ﷺ (...): «Indeed Allah loves, for example, that the effect of His blessing be seen upon His servant»[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2819), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]].
* Shaykh: He loves that the effect of His blessing be seen upon His servant, that is correct. But the effect of blessing is shown by gratitude, not by arrogance, because among the most important effects of blessing is thankfulness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason the Messenger (...) Allah had blessed him, forgiving him what preceded of his sins and what followed. And what did he do?

* Student: He stood in prayer at night.
* Shaykh: He stood until his feet cracked, and said: «Shall I not love to be a grateful servant?»[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (4837) from the hadith of 'A'isha, and the wording is his, and by Muslim (2819/79) from the hadith of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.]]. As for one to whom Allah gives wealth and says: "I will show off, and show off," this is not the correct effect of blessing.

* Student: They cite from the Book, O Shaykh, saying: ﴿And do not forget your share of the world﴾ [al-Qasas 77]?
* Shaykh: Excellent. Your share of it is that you do not forget your share. If Allah gives you wealth, you should enjoy it in a permissible way. As for one who says, "I have wealth, but I want to make my book ugly, my vehicle ugly, my bed ugly, and my house ugly, and we want to marry only an old woman," no, this is not correct. Do not forget your share of the world; Allah did not say: abandon the whole world, remember Him, and sit down. We do not oppose them; we respond to them. I tell you this so that you may respond to them with it.

* Student: This verse. Some people write verses, meaning they want the sunnah of treatment and medicine (...)?
* Shaykh: God willing, this will come in the benefits.

﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. Among the things they said and lied about, the Jews say: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days, and after these numbered days we will come out of it, and you will be left in it, meaning the Messenger ﷺ and his companions. This is false speech and vain wishes. How can these people be touched by the Fire only for numbered days! For this reason Allah denounced them.

﴿And they said: "It will not touch us"﴾. ﴿Tamassana (touch us)﴾: it will afflict us (...).

That it is the actual situation. This does not mean that if someone said something and claimed it was from himself while it was not from himself, he is excluded from this threat.

* The second benefit: that those who write the Book, write it with their own hands (...) to realize this matter, meaning: they do not, for example, order or hint, but they personally do it with their own hands, out of arrogance and obstinacy, without concern.

* The third point here: is the threat only upon those who write the Book with their own hands? Or also upon those who then say: "This is from Allah"? They then say: "This is from Allah."

* The third benefit: that they do this for the sake of leadership, wealth, and status; as shown by His saying: ﴿to exchange it for a small price﴾.

* The fourth benefit: that the world in its entirety, however great it becomes, is little, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: the enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [al-Nisa 77], is it not so?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: However great it becomes, it is little. We have already passed the authentic hadith: «The place of a whip of one of us in Paradise is better than this world and everything in it»[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (22797).]].

* The fifth benefit: that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed; as shown by His saying: ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾.

* The sixth benefit: the establishment of causes and effects; as shown by His saying: ﴿for what their hands have written﴾, for this is an explanation of the cause of the threat ﴿So woe to them﴾, and the reason is that they wrote with their hands. This is different from the first benefit, because the first benefit is that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, so He recompensed them according to what they wrote.

* The seventh benefit: that the punishment for saying something about Allah without knowledge includes the act itself and what results from it of forbidden earnings; as shown by His saying: ﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾. This is evidence that whatever results from a forbidden act of earning, a person is sinful for it. That is, a person sins by committing the forbidden act and by what he earns from it. Do you understand? For example, a person does a forbidden deed, such as cheating, so he is sinful for the cheating, and the gain he took from it is also sinful for him. So the forbidden act and what results from it are all sin; as shown by His saying: ﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾. Can this verse be used to derive the prohibition of taking a wage for writing the Qur'an?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿They write the Scripture with their own hands﴾.
* Student: ﴿Then they say, "This is from Allah"﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Then they say, "This is from Allah"﴾, and it is not from Allah, and it is not from Him. Therefore it cannot be used as evidence for the prohibition of taking a wage for writing the Qur'an, or not?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Because here they were not punished for writing the Torah, for example. If they had written the Torah as it was revealed, they would not have been punished for it. But they were punished for writing and saying: "This is from Allah," when it was not from Him. Yes indeed.

Among their lies against Allah is their saying: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. ﴿They said (qalu)﴾: the pronoun refers to the Jews. ﴿Lan tamassana (will not touch us)﴾ means: will not afflict us. ﴿The Fire (al-nar)﴾ means the Fire of the Hereafter. ﴿Illa ayyaman (except for days)﴾: ﴿ayyaman (days)﴾ is indefinite for paucity, and ﴿ma'dudah (numbered)﴾ also emphasizes paucity, meaning: except for a few numbered days. So what are these numbered days? The well-known view, which is the most apparent, and Allah knows best, is that they are the days of their worship of the calf. How many?

* Student: Forty.
* Shaykh: Forty days; these are the numbered days. They said: the Fire will not touch us except these days only, and after that we will come out of it, and you will remain in it, meaning the Messenger ﷺ and his community. They say: you are the ones for the Fire, but we will be touched only for a few numbered days. We say: your acknowledgment against yourselves is accepted, and your claim that you will come out of the Fire is a claim with no proof.

For this reason Allah, challenging them, said: ﴿Have you taken a covenant with Allah?﴾ ﴿Qul (Say)﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿Have you taken a covenant with Allah?﴾ ﴿Attakhadhtum (have you taken)﴾ means "akhadhtum (you took)," meaning: you have a covenant. The covenant is a pledge and commitment. That is: do you have a commitment from Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, to that effect? If you have it, ﴿then Allah will not break His covenant﴾, because Allah does not break His promise. The meaning of yukhlifu (break) is: to make a replacement, which is the failure to fulfill. Here there is a distinction between khalafahu yakhlufuhu and akhlafahu yukhlifuhu. The difference: akhlafahu means he made a successor for him; yakhlufuhu means he makes a successor for him: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba' 39]. As for khalafa yakhlufu, its meaning is that the thing became a successor to what preceded it. You say: "the heat succeeded the cold," meaning it came after it, so it became its successor. Therefore: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction, and give me in return something better than it"[[Narrated by Muslim (918/3), from the hadith of Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her.]].

* Student: He made a successor for him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 79–86 (part 2 of 5):

* The Shaykh: "wa-akhlif lī"? "Wa-akhlif lī khayran minhā"?
* Student: "Wa-akhlif."
* The Shaykh: "Wa-akhlif lī khayran minhā" means: make for me something better. Like ﴿Whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [34:39], it gives a replacement. Here ﴿So Allah will not break His covenant﴾: meaning He will not make a replacement for His covenant, which would be non-fulfilment of it. Rather, He, glorified and exalted, will fulfil it: ﴿So Allah will not break His covenant﴾.
* Student: The past tense?
* The Shaykh: "Akhlafa."
He said: ﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ Regarding ﴿am﴾ here, it has been said that it is connective (muttasilah), and it has been said that it is disconnected (munqati'ah). We have already gone over the difference between the connective and the disconnected, have we not? What is the difference between them?
* Student: The interrogative.
* The Shaykh: No, the connective am and the disjunctive am?
* Student: The disconnected one has the meaning of (bal), and the connective one does not have the meaning of (bal).
* The Shaykh: With the meaning of what?
* Student: With the meaning of the interrogative.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: With the meaning of (hal).
* The Shaykh: No. The disconnected (am) has the meaning of (aw), as in ﴿It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [2:6], meaning: or you did not warn them. That is one difference. What is the second difference?
* Student: The disconnected one is not accompanied by its counterpart.
* The Shaykh: It is not accompanied by an equivalent ('adil), which is the counterpart. The connective one occurs between two equivalents. That is one difference. ﴿It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾: two equivalents, "you warned them or you did not warn them." Here, is it connective or disconnected? It has been said it is disconnected, and on this view the meaning is: "Rather, you say about Allah what you do not know." And it has been said it is connective, meaning: "Have you taken a covenant with Allah, so that you claim it? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?" On both assessments, neither this nor that. Reflect.
* Student: They say...
* The Shaykh: They say about Allah what they do not know. On both assessments, they say about Allah what they do not know. That is, whether it means "Rather, you say about Allah what you do not know," i.e., you did not take a covenant with Allah, or the meaning is "Have you taken with Allah, or do you say," the answer is: since the first has been negated, which is taking a covenant, the second is established, which is saying what they do not know. So on this assessment the judgment rests with the human being. On the first assessment, where am means bal, from where is the judgment? From Allah. The judgment is from Allah. That is, on the first assessment that it is connective, the meaning becomes: "Have you taken a covenant with Allah, or have you said about Allah what you do not know?" Then we investigate and see whether they have a covenant from Allah. The answer is no. So when the first is negated, the second is established. That is, we know that we establish the second by investigation: we searched and found no covenant, so it is determined that they said about Allah what they do not know.
On the second assessment, where am means bal, we need not investigate. Allah, glorified and exalted, Himself judges them that they say about Allah what they do not know, because He said: ﴿Have you taken a covenant with Allah?﴾ and this interrogative is for denial. That is, you did not take a covenant; rather, you say about Allah what you do not know. Do you understand now?
So the verse on both assessments indicates that they said about Allah what they do not know. But on the assessment that am is connective, the judgment that they say about Allah what they do not know returns to the person who investigates and finds they have no covenant. On the view that it means (bal), the judgment is from Allah: Allah nullified their taking a covenant with Him, then He judged that they say about Allah what they do not know. So then, if they have no covenant with Allah and they have said about Allah what they do not know, is their claim true?
* The students: False.
* The Shaykh: False, yes. Their claim is false, because since they have no covenant and do not say what they know, their claim is false.
Allah, the Exalted, said, explaining who will be touched by the Fire and who will not, so He said: ﴿Yes﴾. The commentators said that (bala) here means (bal), and it is for transition (idrab intiqali): ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin surrounds him﴾. There is also a reading: ﴿khaṭī'ātuh﴾ in the plural.
The phrase ﴿man kasaba﴾: is (man) conditional or relative?
* Student: Conditional.
* The Shaykh: If we say it is conditional, then what supports it is His saying: ﴿then those are the companions of the Fire﴾, since the response is joined with the fā'. This supports that it is conditional. If we say it is relative, then what supports it is His saying in the second verse: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, where "those who" is a relative pronoun, so ﴿man kasaba﴾ means "the one who earned." The answer regarding the fā' in His saying ﴿fa-ulā'ika﴾ is that since the relative resembles the conditional in indicating generality, it is permissible for its predicate to be joined with the fā'.
The phrase ﴿man kasaba sayyi'a﴾: observe ﴿kasaba﴾ and not "did" (‘amila), though in some places it is said "‘amila," as in ﴿and those who did evil deeds﴾ [7:153], which is well known. Kasb means the acquisition of a thing as a result of an action.
﴿kasaba sayyi'a﴾. As for ﴿sayyi'a﴾: the sayyi'ah is what causes harm (yasū'); its root is sayw'ah, since it derives from sā'a yasū'u, with a waw. Its original form is sayw'ah on the pattern fay'ilah. An irregularity (i'lal) occurred in it. What was the irregularity? The waw was changed to yā'. What was its cause? The waw and the yā' came together in one word, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw had to become yā'. Then the yā' was assimilated into the yā', and it became (sayyi'ah).
﴿wa-aḥāṭat bihi khaṭī'atuh﴾: iḥāṭah linguistically means encompassing. ﴿aḥāṭat﴾ means it became like a wall around him and like a rampart; that is, it surrounded him from every side. As for ﴿khaṭī'atuh﴾: when we see that "encompassed" is in the feminine form, the plural form is more fitting, meaning many, and encompassing from every side requires multiplicity, does it not? It requires multiplicity. Therefore the second reading may be more fitting. Nevertheless, it does not contradict the reading in the Mushaf, which is ﴿khaṭī'atuh﴾, because khaṭī'ah is a singular noun in construct, and a singular noun in construct conveys generality. For this reason, if a man says "my slave is free" and he has four slaves, all of them are freed, even though he said only "my slave." This is shown by His saying: ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you cannot number it﴾ [14:34]. Observe ﴿taʿuddū niʿmat Allāh﴾: here "favour" is singular, and the construct conveys generality, not unity. If it conveyed unity, we could count it.
* Student: Shaykh, is this not evidence of its greatness?
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: The reading ﴿wa-aḥāṭat bihi khaṭī'atuh﴾?
* The Shaykh: Yes. But if we say that encompassing is of the kind of the wall and rampart surrounding a thing, it requires a quantity, which is the meaning of the second reading.
As for ﴿khaṭī'atuh﴾ and ﴿sayyi'ah﴾: what is the meaning of ﴿sayyi'ah﴾ and ﴿wa-aḥāṭat bihi khaṭī'atuh﴾? Are they one meaning, that this evil deed extended until it encompassed him? Or is the sayyi'ah one thing and the khaṭī'ah another? This is the well-known view among the commentators: they say the sayyi'ah here is the evil of disbelief, and his khaṭī'ah is what is other than disbelief, because it, may Allah protect us, encompasses the person. If we adopt this view, then khaṭī'ah corresponds to sayyi'ah in the sense that it is one; that is, this evil encompassed him until, may Allah protect us, it prevented him from success.
﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾. We want to parse this now. ﴿Fa-ulā'ika﴾: what is its grammatical analysis?
* Student: The fā' is connective to the response.
* The Shaykh: To the response, if (man) is conditional, or connective of the predicate to the subject, if it is relative.
* Student: ulā': a demonstrative noun, and the kāf.
* The Shaykh: And what is its place in the i'rab?
* Student: In the place of nominative, as subject.
* The Shaykh: And what is it built upon?
* Student: ulā': a demonstrative built on the presumed ḍamm; ulā' is kasra-ended, but built on...
* The Shaykh: Built on what? Built on kasra?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Remarkable. What does Ibn Mālik say? "And among them is dhū fatḥ..."
* Student: "...and dhū kasr."
* The Shaykh: But (...) and kasr.
* Student: So a subject in the nominative, not nominative.
* The Shaykh: That will not do.
* Student: Subject in the nominative.
* The Shaykh: No, you do not say "nominative"; every indeclinable word cannot be described as nominative, accusative or genitive. You say: built on kasra in the place of nominative, built on kasra in the place of nominative as subject.
* The Shaykh: And the kāf?
* Student: The kāf is an attached pronoun.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Detached.
* The Shaykh: No, what do you say? The kāf.
* Student: The kāf is an attached pronoun in a place.
* The Shaykh: The kāf is what?
* Student: For address.
* The Shaykh: And is it a noun or a verb?
* Student: The predicate of the subject.
* The Shaykh: The kāf is the predicate of the subject? Ulā' is the subject, so the kāf is?
* Student: Its predicate.
* The Shaykh: Its predicate. That is incorrect. What do you say? (Ulā'ika), the kāf, and what is its i'rab?
* Student: Object.
* The Shaykh: Object? And what governs it in the accusative? What do you say about the kāf? Have we not studied grammar until now, that you are heedless of this point?
* Student: The attached pronoun of address, built on fatḥa, in the place of genitive by annexation.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: But that is wrong: it is a particle indicating address, with no place in the i'rab.
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct. The kāf is a particle of address with no place in i'rab. We told you: Ibn Mālik says about the kāf:
...................... *** ....... wa-bihi al-kāfa ṣilā fi al-buʿdi aw bi-thamma fuh aw hannā *** ..................... a particle that is (...). "Wa-bihi al-kāfa ṣilā fi al-buʿdi."
* Student: What is al-buʿd?
* The Shaykh: That is: when the indicated thing is distant, the kāf is brought.
﴿Ulā'ika aṣḥābu al-nār﴾: (aṣḥāb) is the predicate of the subject, nominative by the subject, its sign of nominative is an apparent ḍamma at its end. (aṣḥāb) is construct and (al-nār) is its genitive annexed noun, its sign of genitive is an apparent kasra at its end. (hum) is a detached pronoun.
* Student: Separating pronoun (faṣl).
* The Shaykh: Is it not a separating pronoun? Your Malik is evidently not fully... (hum) is a detached pronoun built on sukūn in the place of nominative as subject. (fī) is a preposition and (hā) is a genitive noun built on sukūn in the place of genitive. (khālidūn) is the predicate of the subject. Which subject? (hum). (khālidūn) is nominative by the subject, its sign of nominative is the wāw standing in for the ḍamma, because it is a broken plural.
* Student: Sound masculine plural.
* The Shaykh: Sound masculine plural or broken plural?
* Student: Sound masculine.
* The Shaykh: Sound, yes. Because the sign of the sound masculine plural is when the singular is unchanged, it is sound. (khālid) is singular; add wāw and nūn: (khālidūn). But rijāl, what is its singular?
* The students: Rajul.
* The Shaykh: Changed?
* The students: Changed.
* The Shaykh: What changed? The letters changed and the form changed too.
* Student: If we reverse it, Shaykh, ﴿khālidūn﴾ is the subject and ﴿hum﴾ is the predicate?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not permitted: ﴿hum fīhā khālidūn﴾.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Ulā'ika aṣḥāb al-nār﴾. ﴿Aṣḥāb﴾ is the plural of ṣāḥib, meaning the people of the Fire, and they are called its companions because of their constant presence in it, may Allah protect us.

His saying ﴿khālidūn﴾ means remaining, staying; khulūd means staying and permanence, and from it is His saying: ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Abiding﴾ [50:34].

Then Allah, the Exalted, said, in contrast to the disbelievers, and this is generally the Qur'an's method: when it mentions one thing, it mentions its opposite. He said: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾. ﴿Āmanū﴾ means: they affirmed what must be believed, with acceptance and submission. This is faith; it is not possible for faith to be mere assent without acceptance of the thing and acknowledgment of it, then submission and surrender to the Sharia brought by the one in whom one believes. Is that correct?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And what is the meaning of ﴿āmanū﴾?
* Student: ﴿Āmanū﴾ means they affirmed.
* The Shaykh: With what?
* Student: With the Sharia; ﴿āmanū﴾, they affirmed.
* The Shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Observe ﴿āmanū﴾: whenever ﴿āmanū﴾ occurs in the Qur'an, it means: they affirmed what must be believed, with acceptance and submission, meaning they accept it, acknowledge it, and submit to it.

His saying ﴿ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt﴾ means they did righteous deeds. Action includes speech and act, and action is not opposed to speech; rather what is opposed to speech is act. Otherwise speech and act are both action: speech is the action of the tongue and act is the action of the limbs. So ﴿ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt﴾: if someone said, "Did he not say 'they said the righteous things'?" we say: it is included in action, because action includes speech and act. But when it is said "act," it is opposed to speech.

His saying ﴿ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt﴾ means they said them with their tongues and did them with their limbs, and ﴿al-ṣāliḥāt﴾ means the righteous deeds. So what is the righteous? The people of knowledge said: a deed that combines two conditions: sincerity, and following the Messenger ﷺ. Sincerity is for whom? For Allah. Following is for the Messenger ﷺ. The evidence that this is the righteous deed is His saying in the ḥadīth qudsī: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I leave him and his partnership." (Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.)

So what is lacking in this? Sincerity. And His Messenger ﷺ said: "Whoever does a deed on which there is not our command, it is rejected." (Muslim, from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her; in another narration: "Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected," al-Bukhārī and Muslim.) What is lacking in this? Following. And the Messenger ﷺ also said: "Every condition not in the Book of Allah is void, even if it is a hundred conditions." (al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Ibn Mājah, from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.)

So the point is: the righteous deed is that which combines what? That which combines sincerity and following.

Those who combined these two matters, faith and righteous deeds, ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾. Here ﴿alladhīna āmanū﴾: we want to parse it now. ﴿Alladhīna āmanū﴾ is the subject, ﴿wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt﴾ is conjoined to ﴿āmanū﴾, and (ulā') is what in i'rab?
* Student: Predicate.
* The Shaykh: No, wrong. It is a second subject, and we have already gone over that the predicate

*"And a singular comes, and a sentence comes, containing the meaning for which it was brought."*

Correct? So we say (ulā') is the second subject, and ﴿aṣḥāb al-janna﴾ is the predicate of the second subject, and the clause of the second subject and its predicate is in the place of nominative as predicate of the first subject.
