Otherwise it could be parsed as a relative pronoun, but since the subject of the censure is present, it is preferable to parse it as an indefinite noun so that it serves as a specifier.
* Student: Could it be a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya) particle?
* Shaykh: No, it cannot be maṣdariyya. As for His words ﴿ishtarawā﴾, most of the commentators explained it as meaning "sold" (bā'ū). In the Arabic language, however, it does not mean "sold" but "bought," "took," "exchanged" (i'taḍū). Accordingly we say: ﴿ishtarawā bihi anfusahum﴾ means they ransomed them, they ransomed their souls and exchanged them. This is the preferred reading, and some exegetes held it: (ishtarā) retains its literal sense, because they, may Allah protect us, believe that by this path, which is disbelief, they have chosen for themselves the most upright path. Or is it not the most upright path?
* The students: The most upright path.
* Shaykh: The most upright path. So it is as though they bought their souls and exchanged them for a path that would destroy them. When the Qur'anic expression can bear a meaning, it is preferable to keep it as it stands, on its apparent sense. Otherwise, explaining it as "sold" is clearer and closer: "Wretched is the thing for which they sold themselves, their disbelief," meaning that they took disbelief and sold their souls. But keeping it on its apparent sense, so that the meaning becomes that they bought their souls, according to their belief, with a matter by which they would perish if they took it, is preferable and better. It is as though, on this reading, which is the apparent sense of the Qur'an, they saw disbelief as a gain and a good to be purchased, by which they could save themselves from destruction.
His exalted words ﴿anfusahum﴾ mean their essences, and "nafs" is applied to the self. ﴿an yakfurū﴾ means their disbelief. ﴿an yakfurū﴾: here (an) is maṣdariyya, and the verb after it is interpreted as a verbal noun, and it is the subject of the censure. What is the grammatical status of the subject of praise or censure? It is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). ﴿an yakfurū bimā anzala Allāh﴾: ﴿bimā﴾ is a relative pronoun meaning (alladhī), and what is meant by ﴿bimā anzala Allāh﴾ is the Qur'an, because He said earlier: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming what was with them﴾. These Jews disbelieved in what Allah sent down, which is the Qur'an. ﴿an yakfurū bimā anzala Allāh baghyan﴾: ﴿baghyan﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlih), its governing verb being ﴿yakfurū﴾. Many of them explained (baghy) as envy, but the apparent meaning is that it is more specific than envy, and that it includes the sense of aggression, because the one who transgresses (bāghī) is the aggressor, as it is said: "Upon the transgressor the cycles turn," and it is said:
............................ ∗∗∗ and transgression is the pasture of its seeker, and it is poisonous.
So baghy is not merely envy. Envy may indeed be among its causes, and those who explained it as envy explained it by its cause. But in reality we must explain it by its apparent sense: it is aggression which envy drove them to. His words ﴿an yakfurū bimā anzala Allāh baghyan an yunazzila Allāh min fadlihi ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾ mean: transgressing in their envy, that Allah should send down of His bounty. What is meant by bounty here is revelation, the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ [Yunus: 58]. His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ min ʿibādih﴾: fadl in the language means an increase of giving; this is the lexical meaning, but what is meant here is the Qur'an or the revelation. It has already passed with us in the principles of exegesis that the meaning is not the same as what is intended: the meaning is what the wording requires by lexical usage, and what is intended is what the context requires. His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ min ʿibādih﴾: ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun. Whom does it refer to? In reality the Qur'an was sent down upon the Prophet, peace be upon him, sent down to mankind: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1]. Accordingly we say: ﴿min fadlihi ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾ is best explained as meaning the Messenger, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾: what is the meaning of will (mashī'a)?
* The students: Will (irāda).
* Shaykh: The universal will (irāda kawniyya), not the legislative will (irāda shar'iyya). Here His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾: every verse in which will is mentioned, brothers, is restricted by wisdom; it is not bare will. For this reason we say ﴿man yashāʾ﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), who is worthy of this sending down, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. As for His words ﴿min ʿibādih﴾, is the meaning of "servants" here the legislative servanthood or the general servanthood?
* Students: The legislative.
* Students: The general.
* Shaykh: If it were replaced, let us see: "upon whom He wills of the believers," "upon whom He wills of His creation." What is meant?
* The students: Creation.
* Shaykh: It differs. But is the verse here "upon whom He wills of creation," so that the will is general over all created beings? When it is joined with wisdom, it means He sends down only upon one who is worthy of messengerhood and faith. Here the object of the will is broader. If we say "of His believing servants," the object of the will becomes more specific. But this removes the objection that some people suppose, that it could apply to a disbeliever being a messenger. When we know that will is restricted by wisdom, that possibility is excluded, and ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ min ʿibādih﴾ means those upon whom wisdom requires that Allah send down of His bounty.

He said: ﴿So they returned with wrath upon wrath﴾, I seek refuge in Allah. ﴿bā'ū﴾ means they returned. ﴿bighaḍab﴾: the (bā') here indicates accompaniment, meaning they returned accompanied by wrath. Wrath from where? From Allah, the Exalted. It is indefinite for magnification. For this reason some said the wrath meant is the wrath of Allah and others besides Him; even the believing servants of His are angered by the deeds and conduct of these people. His words ﴿ʿalā ghaḍab﴾ are like His words ﴿darkness, some above others﴾ [al-Nur: 40], meaning wrath added upon another wrath that preceded it.
So what is the wrath with which they returned? And what was the wrath that came before it? We say: the wrath with which they returned is that they, may Allah protect us, disbelieved in what they recognised: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾. That is one wrath. The earlier wrath is that they killed the prophets: ﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group they denied and a group they killed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 70]. And a third wrath as well, because the meaning of His words ﴿they returned with wrath upon wrath﴾ may be like His words: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], meaning repeated again and again. It may be wrath upon wrath, meaning many wraths.
Among them also transgression, aggression and envy. Indeed Allah the Exalted sends down upon whomever He wills of His servants. Perhaps it is even more than this: they committed deeds that call for wrath, so layers of wrath were heaped upon them, may Allah protect us. ﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾ He did not say "for them." Such a usage the rhetoricians call "stating the apparent in place of the pronoun," and it has benefits:
The first benefit: intending generality, so that the punishment includes them and others. That is one benefit. The second benefit: alerting the addressee. The third benefit: stating the cause. The fourth benefit: passing judgment on them by this attribute, because if Allah had said "and for them is a humiliating punishment," would they be disbelievers or not? The verse would not have judged them to be disbelievers. But when He said ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, they became deserving of this attribute.
So the benefits are four: alerting the addressee, intending generality, stating the cause, and passing judgment on them according to the implication of this attribute, namely that they are disbelievers.
His words ﴿ʿadhāb﴾ mean punishment. His words ﴿muhīn﴾ mean possessing humiliation and abasement. This is the correspondence of the punishment to its cause: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40]. Since what drove them to this disbelief was arrogance: ﴿You waxed arrogant, so a group you denied﴾, with what were they punished? With humiliation, with this punishment, may Allah protect us. ﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾: He humiliates them and abases them. And even if there were no humiliation for them, may Allah protect us, except the Exalted's words to them: ﴿Be silent therein and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108].

﴿And they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth, confirming what is with them. Say: "Why did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91].

Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down"﴾. Here the speaker is left unspecified, because it is not fixed to one particular person. The speaker may be the Messenger, peace be upon him, or it may be one of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them; for this reason He said ﴿and when it is said to them﴾, omitting the agent so that it is more comprehensive and general.
﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾: faith is intended as affirmation together with acceptance and submission, and not everyone who affirms is a believer until he accepts and submits. The proof of this is that Abu Talib affirmed but was not a believer, because he did not accept and did not submit. So ﴿believe in what Allah has sent down﴾ means affirm it together with accepting it and submitting to it.
His words ﴿bimā anzala Allāh﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is a relative pronoun, and what is meant is the Great Qur'an. ﴿anzala﴾ means from Him, and this is evidence of two important matters. The first matter: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. The reason is that the Qur'an is speech, and speech is not a self-subsisting entity but an attribute in something else. If it is an attribute in something else and it comes from Allah, it must be the speech of Allah.
Also in it is evidence for the second important matter: the highness of Allah, glorified and exalted. His highness is one of the necessary attributes of His essence; for this reason highness is an essential attribute, one of the essential attributes from which Allah is never separated, from eternity to eternity. This differs from settling upon the Throne, which is one of the active attributes connected with His will. For this reason He said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth﴾, ﴿then settled upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. (Thumma) indicates what?
* Student: Sequence of events (ta'qib).
* Shaykh: Ordering (tartib). This shows that when He created the heavens and the earth He was not yet settled on the Throne. As for highness, it is one of the necessary attributes of His essence, glorified and exalted. It has been shown, as we passed in the creed, by the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, reason, and innate nature: five proofs all indicating the highness of Allah, glorified and exalted, in His essence, just as He knows by His attributes. So it establishes the highness of Allah, glorified and exalted, because if His speech, while descending, indicates that the speaker of it is high, then...
It has passed with us that His highness does not contradict His being with us, nor His descent to the lowest heaven. He descends to the lowest heaven while being high above His creation, and we cannot suppose that these are contradictory. For a human, it would be contradictory not to be high while descending; but for the Creator, glorified be He, He remains high, and He descends as He wills. We do not liken Him to His creation, nor imagine His attributes, nor ask about their modality. Asking about it, as Imam Malik said, is an innovation: "The istiwa' is known, the modality is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (867) and al-I'tiqad (54), with the wording: "The istiwa' is not unknown, the modality is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."]]
﴿They said﴾: this is the answer to ﴿when﴾. ﴿When it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down"﴾, ﴿bimā anzala Allāh﴾: He did not add "in the Qur'an" either, so that the argument against them would be stronger, because it was sent down from where? From Allah, and what is sent down from Allah must be believed in. But the answer is ﴿They said: "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾. This answer and this affirmation imply the negation of the statement addressed to them, as though they were saying: we do not believe in it, but we believe in what was sent down to us. Have you understood, brothers?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: So this statement of theirs contains the denial of a truth and the claim of a truth. As for the denial of truth, they denied that they believe in what Allah sent down, because their words "We believe in what was sent down to us" mean, in effect, "and we do not believe in what Allah sent down." As for the claim of truth, they say "We believe in what was sent down to us," and this is a claim, for if they truly believed in what was sent down to them, they would have believed in this that Allah sent down, because their own books that were sent down confirm this Book that was sent down. So had they truly believed in them, they would have believed in this Qur'an. Thus they became deniers of the truth and claimants of the truth, and they were liars in their claim and wrongdoers in their denial, is that not so?
* The students: Indeed.
* Shaykh: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will establish the proof against them at the end of the verse, with an evidence they themselves acknowledge.
﴿They said: "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾: for example, the Christians say "We believe in what was sent down to us," meaning the Gospel, and the Jews mean the Torah, and both groups are liars; they did not believe in what was sent down to them.
Then He said: ﴿And they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth﴾. ﴿They disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾: that is, in what is other than it. "Waraʾ" comes in the sense of "other than." Among its uses is this verse: ﴿they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾, that is, beyond what was sent down to them.
And what is meant by "what is beyond it"? The Qur'an. The Qur'an with respect to both groups, and the Qur'an and the Gospel with respect to the Jews, because the Jews also did not believe in the Gospel; the Jews claim that they killed the one who brought the Gospel, who is Jesus son of Mary.
His words ﴿they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth, confirming﴾: the clause ﴿while it is the truth﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from ﴿mā﴾ in His words ﴿bimā warāʾahu﴾, meaning: while what is beyond it, which they disbelieve in, is the truth. Truth means what is established, and its opposite is falsehood, which is what is lost in vain and gives no benefit. Truth is what is established, beneficial and useful, and without doubt this description applies to the Qur'an.
His words ﴿confirming﴾ are also a circumstantial clause from whom? From (huwa), that is, the pronoun: meaning, while it is confirming what is with them. ﴿confirming what is with them﴾: we mentioned that in its explanation there are two views.
The first view: that it informed of them, so it came as a confirmation of what they had reported. Is that not confirming?
Second: that it confirms them and declares them to be true. For this reason it is part of the method of this Qur'an: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers; each believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], and the Last Day. So it confirms what came before on two counts. The first count: it came confirming them, because they had informed of it, so it confirmed them. What would you think if it had not come? That would have been a denial, meaning that the previous books would have been denied, and far be it from them. But it came confirming them. Second: it says of them that they are true, and it affirms the revelation of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the scrolls of Abraham, and it also makes belief in them obligatory.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 90–91 (part 2 of 3):

And His saying: ﴿for what is with them﴾. And what is "what is with them"? The Torah and the Gospel. The Christians believe in the Gospel and the Torah, while the Jews believe in the Torah and disbelieve in the Gospel; and for this reason they were worse than the Christians.

Now He says, establishing the proof against them: ﴿Say: "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah"﴾. The address in His saying ﴿Say﴾ is either to the Messenger ﷺ or to everyone who can be addressed. If it is to the Messenger ﷺ, then His saying ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ has an unspecified subject. Who is it? The Messenger ﷺ. He left it unspecified so that it would be known that what he said is the saying of those who believe in it, and this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an. Look at ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatihah 7]: the favour He attributed to Allah alone, while the anger came unspecified; because when Allah is angry with a people, He is angry with everyone who is a friend of Allah. Therefore He said: ﴿those who have earned anger﴾.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Believe in what Allah has sent down"﴾. If we say that the address in His saying ﴿Say﴾ is to the Messenger ﷺ, and he is the one who says ﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾, then the unspecified subject here serves a purpose: that this saying of the Messenger ﷺ is also said by every believer in him. Yes indeed.

As for if we say that the address in His saying ﴿Say: "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah"﴾ is to everyone who can be addressed, then the unspecified subject in the first part does not refer to the Messenger ﷺ alone.

﴿Say: "Why then do you kill"﴾, ﴿Why do you kill the prophets of Allah before?﴾ The lām is a preposition (ḥarf jarr), or not? The lām, my brothers, the lām?

* A student: The fāʾ is a preposition.
* The Shaykh: The fāʾ is a conjunction (ḥarf ʿaṭf), and the lām is a preposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And why is the lām also a preposition? Where are you? (...) (لِمَ) — لِمَ تفعل كذا: I say to you now: "Why did you do that?" What is the lām? The lām is a preposition. "Mimma taghḍab?" The mīm is a preposition. ﴿عَمَّ يَتَسَاءَلُونَ﴾ [al-Naba' 1]: (ʿan) is a preposition. ﴿لِمَ تَقُولُونَ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ﴾ [al-Saff 2]: the lām is a preposition. ﴿لِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ﴾: the lām is a preposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Its origin is the interrogative (ma) (مَا الاستفهامية). When a preposition enters upon it, its alif must be deleted. The interrogative ma, when a preposition enters upon it, its alif must be deleted. You say: (لِمَ), and (فِيمَ), "They said: 'Then what is the deed for, O Messenger of Allah?'"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4696) and al-Tirmidhi (3075), from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him).]] And (عَمَّ), and (عَلَامَ), and (مِمَّ), and (حَتَّامَ), and (إلَامَ). Is it clear now? The lām is a preposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) The lām is a preposition. So the lām is a preposition, and mā is an interrogative noun from which the alif has been dropped for lightness. How do we write (حتى) in this case? We write it with an alif, not with yā', so (حتى ما) becomes like حَتَّامَ? How do we write (إلى) in (إلام)? We write the lām and alif, not with yā', as is customary; the lām-alif of (إلام). (عَلَامَ)? We write ʿalā with an alif, not with yā', as is customary; it becomes like عَلَّامَ, and the mīm without an alif.

﴿Why do you kill﴾: this lām is in reality for challenge and obligation. That is: if you are truthful in your saying, "We believe in what was sent down to us," then why do you kill the prophets of Allah? Is this one who kills a prophet a believer? Does one who kills a prophet believe in him, O people? No, never. How do you kill the prophets of Allah while you believe in him?

﴿Why then do you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ has two readings: ﴿أَنْبِئَاءَ اللَّهِ﴾ with a hamzah, and ﴿أَنْبِيَاءَ اللَّهِ﴾ with a yā', like النبي and النبيء; the plural of النبيء is أنبئاء, and the plural of النبي is أنبياء.

Just as His saying ﴿وَهُوَ الْحَقُّ﴾ — because this follows the general rule and is not specific to this; that is, ﴿وَهْوَ الْحَقُّ﴾ has a reading with sukūn.

* A student: أنبئاءُ?
* The Shaykh: ﴿أَنْبِئَاءَ﴾ with a fatḥah.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).

﴿the prophets of Allah before﴾: that is, before this Qur'an. And regarding His saying ﴿مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾, we want to ask: from this, what is the preposition?

* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: مِن is a preposition. مِن?
* The student: If it were a preposition, it would govern what follows it.
* The Shaykh: (...).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Could it be a preposition that does not govern? You know the crane now; the crane does not carry, even if it is something big (...). What do you say?
* A student: A preposition.
* The Shaykh: A preposition. So there remains a difficulty: why was ﴿مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ not in the genitive?
* A student: Because the mudāf ilayhi was deleted and it was built on ḍamm, intending the meaning intended.
* The Shaykh: The mudāf ilayhi was deleted and its meaning intended. So it is built on ḍamm, is that right? And we told you that qabl and baʿd: either the mudāf ilayhi is mentioned, or it is deleted and its meaning is intended, or it is deleted and its wording is intended, or it is deleted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended. If it is deleted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended, then it is tanwīn-ed according to the governing factors. If it is deleted and its wording is intended, then it is not tanwīn-ed according to the governing factors. If it is deleted and its meaning is intended, then it is built on ḍamm. If it is annexed, then it follows the governing factors and is not tanwīn-ed. Is it clear?
* A student: What is the estimate (taqdīr) of its meaning? What is the estimate?
* The Shaykh: The estimate: "from before that."

﴿from before, if you are believers﴾: (in) here is conditional, and (mu'minīn) means: in your claim of faith. You say: "We believe in what was sent down to us," so why do you kill the prophets of Allah if you are believers? This sentence is to refute them.

And His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾: (in) here is conditional, so where is the response of the condition? This occurs often in the Qur'an. Some people say that the response of the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "if you are believers, then why do you kill." Others say that in such a case it does not need a response, because the response is only needed to clarify a meaning, and the meaning here is clear without it. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, leans toward this and says that such a case does not need a response, because the response is only needed to clarify meaning, and here the meaning is clear without it. Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned that this applies even to the response of an oath; that is, an oath may not need a response when the meaning is understood. He discussed this in his book al-Tibyān fī Aqsām al-Qur'ān.

* A student: According to the Shaykh's saying (...).
* The Shaykh: The response of the oath: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَنْ زَكَّاهَا﴾. So this verse...
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is the preferred view.
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: Perhaps. In any case (...) if the response is understood (...).

Now let us take the benefits:

* First: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their souls, that they should disbelieve﴾.
* From this verse is derived: that disbelief is a blameworthy trait, even if a person climbs by it to his worldly aims; due to His saying ﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their souls, that they should disbelieve﴾. Is that right?
* The second benefit: that the disbelief of the Children of Israel was nothing but envy and rebellion; due to His saying ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾.
* The third benefit: that whoever rejects the truth from this Ummah does so because "so-and-so," whom he sees as lesser than himself, is the one who brought it, and so he resembles the Jews. Did you understand, O people? There are some people who, when someone advises them and guides them to the truth, despise that person and regard him as nothing (...), then reject it, why? Because it came from him; had it come from so-and-so or someone else, he would have accepted it. We say: someone in this state has a resemblance to whom? To the Jews.
* The fourth benefit: that a person must know the truth by the truth, not by men. So long as what is said is true, follow it, from whatever source it comes. Do not say: "By Allah, this was brought by someone less knowledgeable than me," or "I fear that if I accept from this man, he will gain for himself, for example, pride and self-importance, and the like." Accept the truth for the sake of the truth, not because so-and-so brought it.
* The fifth benefit: that knowledge is among the greatest of the favours of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; due to His saying ﴿that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills﴾. There is no doubt that knowledge is better than wealth. If you want to know the difference between the excellence of knowledge and the excellence of wealth, look at the scholars in the time of the earlier caliphs: the caliphs' remembrance has faded, while the scholars of their time have remained remembered, are they not? Their remembrance has remained. They teach people while they are in their graves, whereas those caliphs have been forgotten, except for a caliph who has lasting monuments, whom those who know those monuments remember as belonging to so-and-so. This shows that the excellence of knowledge is greater than the excellence of wealth; due to His saying ﴿of His bounty﴾.
* The benefit that follows: the affirmation of Allah's will; due to His saying ﴿upon whom He wills﴾. Will (mashī'ah) is the same as volition (irādah), is it not? No, will is not the same as volition; will is a part, a division, of volition: it is the universal volition (al-irādah al-kawniyyah). As for the legislative volition (al-irādah al-shar'iyyah), it is not part of will.
* The benefit that follows: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants. What I want to say is that this favour which Allah sends down does not make the one favoured a lord to be worshipped; rather, he remains a servant even if he is distinguished in favour; due to His saying ﴿of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾.
* This benefit has branches, which we clarify: whoever Allah has given favour does not, by it, leave the state of being a servant. Therefore he does not rise to the rank of what? Lordship (rubūbiyyah). So the Messenger ﷺ is a servant among the servants of Allah, is he not? A servant among the servants of Allah. We do not say that when revelation came to him he was elevated until he became a lord who possesses benefit and harm and knows the unseen. No.
* Also branching from it: whoever Allah has given of His favour, especially in matters of knowledge, should be more devoted to Allah than others. Why? Because Allah, Exalted, has given him of His favour, so his obligation to Allah is greater than his obligation to others, is it not so? The greater the blessing from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, the more it demands gratitude. Is it clear? The greater the blessing, the more it demands gratitude. If Allah bestows two blessings upon you, how much gratitude is due from you? Two gratitudes. Three blessings? Three gratitudes, and so on. So if Allah has blessed you with the knowledge you have inherited from your Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, you must be all the more humble toward Allah, toward the truth, and toward creation. Is it clear?
* Branching from this, a third branch: those deluded ones, may Allah keep us safe, whom their own selves have deluded through the knowledge they have been given, have in reality been deprived of the favour, deprived of the excellence of knowledge, is that not so? (...) and by Allah's refuge, when Allah favoured them with knowledge, they exalted themselves and became arrogant, to the point that they may not accept the truth; they may resemble the Children of Israel in the second benefit.
* The benefit that follows: that punishments accumulate according to sins. From where do we take this?
* The students: ﴿So they earned anger upon anger﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿So they earned anger upon anger﴾. So punishments, may Allah keep us safe, accumulate just as sins accumulate, a fitting recompense.
* The benefit that follows: that those who sold their souls for disbelief in what Allah has sent down are disbelievers; due to His saying ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾.
* The benefit that follows also: that the arrogant one is punished with the opposite of his condition; due to His saying ﴿humiliating﴾, He humiliates them after they had exalted themselves, so they were punished, may Allah keep us safe, with what befits their sins. Upon this has the custom of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in His creation proceeded. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut 40], and He, Exalted, says: ﴿as a recompense, adequate﴾ [al-Naba' 26].

The benefit that follows: the eloquence of the Qur'an. Because this phrase ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾, instead of "and for them," gives us a benefit greater than if the pronoun "and for them" had come. What benefit do we gain? That these are disbelievers. Had it said "and for them," we would not know what their rank is in the religion of Allah. But when He said ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾, we learned that they are disbelievers.

* The second benefit: the generality that such an act makes a person a disbeliever, they and others.
* The third benefit also: clarifying the cause of the ruling, which is the humiliating punishment. What is its cause? What is the cause of the humiliating punishment? Its cause is disbelief: ﴿and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾, that is, because of their disbelief. We have already noted that when a ruling is attached to a description, it indicates that the description is the cause of that ruling, and that the ruling strengthens according to the strength of that description. Is that right?

If you say, for example: "Cut off the thief's hand," that is, because he stole; that is, because he is a thief. The causation here is clear.

If you say: "Honour the God-fearing one," that is, because of his piety; and the more his piety increases, the more his honour increases. Yes indeed.

* A student: His saying ﴿and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, because this, while being a punishment, humiliates them.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No (...). In any case, not every punishment is painful, and not every punishment is humiliating.
* A student: The punishment of the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: Even the punishment of the Hereafter. But when it is said "humiliating," it means it reaches the utmost degree of humiliation; it is more emphatic than mere punishment.
* A student: And is "humiliating" a descriptive adjective that establishes meaning (ṣifah ta'sīsiyyah)?
* The Shaykh: A descriptive adjective that establishes meaning, yes.
* A student: (...) ﴿out of envy﴾ (...) envy, the prohibition of envy?
* The Shaykh: We said: yes, the prohibition of envy and aggression.
* The student: (...) the anger of Allah, and that it is obligatory for the servant to be angry for the sake of Allah's anger. How is this, ﴿So they earned anger upon anger﴾?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. From it is derived: the affirmation of anger for Allah. Although it is not entirely clear, ﴿they earned anger﴾ means that the apparent meaning is that the anger is from Allah. So it is derived from it the affirmation of Allah's anger, Glorified and Exalted. And Allah's anger is one of His attributes of what kind? Actions (fi'liyyah), because it is connected to His will, Glorified and Exalted, and every attribute connected to will is an attribute of action.
* A student: The anger is from Allah, Glorified and Exalted. We say: how is it that anger is placed upon anger, when here the anger is one?
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: The anger is one?
* The Shaykh: No (...). Anger multiplies according to the multiplicity of its causes. That is: Allah was angry with them for doing such-and-such, then angry a second time for doing such-and-such, and so on; it multiplies according to the multiplicity of its causes. Are there benefits after the second?
* A student: The vastness of Allah's favour; due to His saying ﴿of His bounty﴾ (...).
* The Shaykh: If we make (min) partitive, it is evidence of the vastness of Allah's favour. If we make it explanatory of the kind, there is no evidence in it. But making it partitive is preferable, because it indicates a meaning beyond mere explanation of kind.

And is it derived from ﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their own souls﴾ that the soul is a trust (amānah) with the servant?

* A student: Because Allah blamed selling it (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, or ﴿ishtaraw﴾ means "chose." This is evidence that the soul is a trust with the servant: he may not burden it with what is hard for it, nor deprive it of Allah's favour. Therefore the Messenger ﷺ said to ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, when he said to him: "Indeed your soul has a right over you."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1153) and Muslim (1159/186, 188), from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

Then in the Qur'an, how often we pass by ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 57]: wronging themselves. So the soul in reality has a right over you, that you look after it as it should be looked after. Therefore a person must defend himself outside of strife; why? To protect it, because this is its right. He must eat when he is hungry, drink when he is thirsty, and clothe himself when he fears the cold, and so on, is that complete?

* A student: Shaykh, His saying ﴿and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾: the prepositional phrase indicates restriction (ḥaṣr); the prepositional phrase is fronted. Is the humiliating punishment for them alone?
* The Shaykh: "For the disbelievers," that is, to the exclusion of the defiantly sinful, for example?
* The student: Or for others.
* The Shaykh: Perhaps it is derived from it that non-disbelievers also have a punishment, but it does not reach the degree of humiliation, because they have not reached the extent of arrogance toward what Allah has sent down. And it may be said: it is for the sake of observing the rhyme endings (fawāṣil), though it is valid, and the humiliating punishment is not exclusive to the disbelievers.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say: "We believe in what was sent down to us."﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 90–91 (part 3 of 3):

* One benefit derived from this verse is the exposure of the deception of these Jews, for they said: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ while they were lying. Their intention was only to reject the truth, not to hold fast to it. Pay attention, brothers, is it clear?
* The students: It is clear.
* The Shaykh: Because they said: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ while they were lying in this claim. Had they been truthful, they would have believed in the noble Qur'an.
* The second benefit: belief in what Allah has sent down is incumbent upon every person of sound natural disposition (fitrah), who is called to it, based on the view that (qīla) is used in an indefinite form, so it includes everyone.
* The third benefit: whoever from this Ummah is called to the truth and says, "My school is such-and-such, meaning I will not turn away from it," resembles whom? The Jews. This is because, when you are called to the truth, you must look into (...) the truth; if it is the truth, it becomes obligatory for you to follow it. As for saying, "By Allah, no, my school is Shafi'i, I do not follow the Hanbali," or "I am Hanbali and I do not follow the Shafi'i," there is no permission for this, and it bears a resemblance to the Jews.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 90–91 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their souls: that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down, out of envy that Allah should send down His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90] (bi'sa) is a past-tense verb used to express censure, and its counterpart is (ni'ma), a past-tense verb used to express praise. Are (bi'sa) and (ni'ma) rigid (jamid) or inflected (mutasarrif)?
* Student: Rigid.
* Shaykh: Rigid. They accept the feminine ta' (ta' al-ta'nith) without any problem. They do not form a present-tense verb, an imperative, or a verbal noun; likewise (bi'sa). So both are rigid, used to express praise or censure.
As for His words ﴿bi'samā ishtarawā﴾ (mā) is a relative pronoun meaning (alladhī): "Wretched is that which they sold themselves for." Or it may be an indefinite noun with a descriptive clause, because (mā) can be an indefinite noun described by a following clause, and it can be an indefinite noun serving as a qualifier. You say: "I passed by what pleases you," meaning "by something that pleases you." Here they said: we make it an indefinite noun described by a clause, so that it is a specifier (tamyīz), in the accusative: "Wretched is a thing for which they sold themselves." The subject of the praise or censure is His words ﴿an yakfurū bimā anzala Allāh﴾, meaning their disbelief in what Allah has sent down. Otherwise it could be parsed as a relative pronoun, but since the subject of the censure is present, it is preferable to parse it as an indefinite noun so that it serves as a specifier.
* Student: Could it be a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya) particle?
* Shaykh: No, it cannot be maṣdariyya. As for His words ﴿ishtarawā﴾, most of the commentators explained it as meaning "sold" (bā'ū). In the Arabic language, however, it does not mean "sold" but "bought," "took," "exchanged" (i'taḍū). Accordingly we say: ﴿ishtarawā bihi anfusahum﴾ means they ransomed them, they ransomed their souls and exchanged them. This is the preferred reading, and some exegetes held it: (ishtarā) retains its literal sense, because they, may Allah protect us, believe that by this path, which is disbelief, they have chosen for themselves the most upright path. Or is it not the most upright path?
* The students: The most upright path.
* Shaykh: The most upright path. So it is as though they bought their souls and exchanged them for a path that would destroy them. When the Qur'anic expression can bear a meaning, it is preferable to keep it as it stands, on its apparent sense. Otherwise, explaining it as "sold" is clearer and closer: "Wretched is the thing for which they sold themselves, their disbelief," meaning that they took disbelief and sold their souls. But keeping it on its apparent sense, so that the meaning becomes that they bought their souls, according to their belief, with a matter by which they would perish if they took it, is preferable and better. It is as though, on this reading, which is the apparent sense of the Qur'an, they saw disbelief as a gain and a good to be purchased, by which they could save themselves from destruction.
His exalted words ﴿anfusahum﴾ mean their essences, and "nafs" is applied to the self. ﴿an yakfurū﴾ means their disbelief. ﴿an yakfurū﴾: here (an) is maṣdariyya, and the verb after it is interpreted as a verbal noun, and it is the subject of the censure. What is the grammatical status of the subject of praise or censure? It is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). ﴿an yakfurū bimā anzala Allāh﴾: ﴿bimā﴾ is a relative pronoun meaning (alladhī), and what is meant by ﴿bimā anzala Allāh﴾ is the Qur'an, because He said earlier: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming what was with them﴾. These Jews disbelieved in what Allah sent down, which is the Qur'an. ﴿an yakfurū bimā anzala Allāh baghyan﴾: ﴿baghyan﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlih), its governing verb being ﴿yakfurū﴾. Many of them explained (baghy) as envy, but the apparent meaning is that it is more specific than envy, and that it includes the sense of aggression, because the one who transgresses (bāghī) is the aggressor, as it is said: "Upon the transgressor the cycles turn," and it is said:
............................ ∗∗∗ and transgression is the pasture of its seeker, and it is poisonous.
So baghy is not merely envy. Envy may indeed be among its causes, and those who explained it as envy explained it by its cause. But in reality we must explain it by its apparent sense: it is aggression which envy drove them to. His words ﴿an yakfurū bimā anzala Allāh baghyan an yunazzila Allāh min fadlihi ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾ mean: transgressing in their envy, that Allah should send down of His bounty. What is meant by bounty here is revelation, the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ [Yunus: 58]. His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ min ʿibādih﴾: fadl in the language means an increase of giving; this is the lexical meaning, but what is meant here is the Qur'an or the revelation. It has already passed with us in the principles of exegesis that the meaning is not the same as what is intended: the meaning is what the wording requires by lexical usage, and what is intended is what the context requires. His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ min ʿibādih﴾: ﴿man﴾ is a relative pronoun. Whom does it refer to? In reality the Qur'an was sent down upon the Prophet, peace be upon him, sent down to mankind: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1]. Accordingly we say: ﴿min fadlihi ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾ is best explained as meaning the Messenger, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾: what is the meaning of will (mashī'a)?
* The students: Will (irāda).
* Shaykh: The universal will (irāda kawniyya), not the legislative will (irāda shar'iyya). Here His words ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾: every verse in which will is mentioned, brothers, is restricted by wisdom; it is not bare will. For this reason we say ﴿man yashāʾ﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), who is worthy of this sending down, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. As for His words ﴿min ʿibādih﴾, is the meaning of "servants" here the legislative servanthood or the general servanthood?
* Students: The legislative.
* Students: The general.
* Shaykh: If it were replaced, let us see: "upon whom He wills of the believers," "upon whom He wills of His creation." What is meant?
* The students: Creation.
* Shaykh: It differs. But is the verse here "upon whom He wills of creation," so that the will is general over all created beings? When it is joined with wisdom, it means He sends down only upon one who is worthy of messengerhood and faith. Here the object of the will is broader. If we say "of His believing servants," the object of the will becomes more specific. But this removes the objection that some people suppose, that it could apply to a disbeliever being a messenger. When we know that will is restricted by wisdom, that possibility is excluded, and ﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ min ʿibādih﴾ means those upon whom wisdom requires that Allah send down of His bounty.

He said: ﴿So they returned with wrath upon wrath﴾, I seek refuge in Allah. ﴿bā'ū﴾ means they returned. ﴿bighaḍab﴾: the (bā') here indicates accompaniment, meaning they returned accompanied by wrath. Wrath from where? From Allah, the Exalted. It is indefinite for magnification. For this reason some said the wrath meant is the wrath of Allah and others besides Him; even the believing servants of His are angered by the deeds and conduct of these people. His words ﴿ʿalā ghaḍab﴾ are like His words ﴿darkness, some above others﴾ [al-Nur: 40], meaning wrath added upon another wrath that preceded it.
So what is the wrath with which they returned? And what was the wrath that came before it? We say: the wrath with which they returned is that they, may Allah protect us, disbelieved in what they recognised: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾. That is one wrath. The earlier wrath is that they killed the prophets: ﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a group they denied and a group they killed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 70]. And a third wrath as well, because the meaning of His words ﴿they returned with wrath upon wrath﴾ may be like His words: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], meaning repeated again and again. It may be wrath upon wrath, meaning many wraths.
Among them also transgression, aggression and envy. Indeed Allah the Exalted sends down upon whomever He wills of His servants. Perhaps it is even more than this: they committed deeds that call for wrath, so layers of wrath were heaped upon them, may Allah protect us. ﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾ He did not say "for them." Such a usage the rhetoricians call "stating the apparent in place of the pronoun," and it has benefits:
The first benefit: intending generality, so that the punishment includes them and others. That is one benefit. The second benefit: alerting the addressee. The third benefit: stating the cause. The fourth benefit: passing judgment on them by this attribute, because if Allah had said "and for them is a humiliating punishment," would they be disbelievers or not? The verse would not have judged them to be disbelievers. But when He said ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, they became deserving of this attribute.
So the benefits are four: alerting the addressee, intending generality, stating the cause, and passing judgment on them according to the implication of this attribute, namely that they are disbelievers.
His words ﴿ʿadhāb﴾ mean punishment. His words ﴿muhīn﴾ mean possessing humiliation and abasement. This is the correspondence of the punishment to its cause: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40]. Since what drove them to this disbelief was arrogance: ﴿You waxed arrogant, so a group you denied﴾, with what were they punished? With humiliation, with this punishment, may Allah protect us. ﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾: He humiliates them and abases them. And even if there were no humiliation for them, may Allah protect us, except the Exalted's words to them: ﴿Be silent therein and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108].

﴿And they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth, confirming what is with them. Say: "Why did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91].

Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down"﴾. Here the speaker is left unspecified, because it is not fixed to one particular person. The speaker may be the Messenger, peace be upon him, or it may be one of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them; for this reason He said ﴿and when it is said to them﴾, omitting the agent so that it is more comprehensive and general.
﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾: faith is intended as affirmation together with acceptance and submission, and not everyone who affirms is a believer until he accepts and submits. The proof of this is that Abu Talib affirmed but was not a believer, because he did not accept and did not submit. So ﴿believe in what Allah has sent down﴾ means affirm it together with accepting it and submitting to it.
His words ﴿bimā anzala Allāh﴾: ﴿mā﴾ is a relative pronoun, and what is meant is the Great Qur'an. ﴿anzala﴾ means from Him, and this is evidence of two important matters. The first matter: the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. The reason is that the Qur'an is speech, and speech is not a self-subsisting entity but an attribute in something else. If it is an attribute in something else and it comes from Allah, it must be the speech of Allah.
Also in it is evidence for the second important matter: the highness of Allah, glorified and exalted. His highness is one of the necessary attributes of His essence; for this reason highness is an essential attribute, one of the essential attributes from which Allah is never separated, from eternity to eternity. This differs from settling upon the Throne, which is one of the active attributes connected with His will. For this reason He said: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth﴾, ﴿then settled upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. (Thumma) indicates what?
* Student: Sequence of events (ta'qib).
* Shaykh: Ordering (tartib). This shows that when He created the heavens and the earth He was not yet settled on the Throne. As for highness, it is one of the necessary attributes of His essence, glorified and exalted. It has been shown, as we passed in the creed, by the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, reason, and innate nature: five proofs all indicating the highness of Allah, glorified and exalted, in His essence, just as He knows by His attributes. So it establishes the highness of Allah, glorified and exalted, because if His speech, while descending, indicates that the speaker of it is high, then...
It has passed with us that His highness does not contradict His being with us, nor His descent to the lowest heaven. He descends to the lowest heaven while being high above His creation, and we cannot suppose that these are contradictory. For a human, it would be contradictory not to be high while descending; but for the Creator, glorified be He, He remains high, and He descends as He wills. We do not liken Him to His creation, nor imagine His attributes, nor ask about their modality. Asking about it, as Imam Malik said, is an innovation: "The istiwa' is known, the modality is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (867) and al-I'tiqad (54), with the wording: "The istiwa' is not unknown, the modality is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."]]
﴿They said﴾: this is the answer to ﴿when﴾. ﴿When it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down"﴾, ﴿bimā anzala Allāh﴾: He did not add "in the Qur'an" either, so that the argument against them would be stronger, because it was sent down from where? From Allah, and what is sent down from Allah must be believed in. But the answer is ﴿They said: "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾. This answer and this affirmation imply the negation of the statement addressed to them, as though they were saying: we do not believe in it, but we believe in what was sent down to us. Have you understood, brothers?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: So this statement of theirs contains the denial of a truth and the claim of a truth. As for the denial of truth, they denied that they believe in what Allah sent down, because their words "We believe in what was sent down to us" mean, in effect, "and we do not believe in what Allah sent down." As for the claim of truth, they say "We believe in what was sent down to us," and this is a claim, for if they truly believed in what was sent down to them, they would have believed in this that Allah sent down, because their own books that were sent down confirm this Book that was sent down. So had they truly believed in them, they would have believed in this Qur'an. Thus they became deniers of the truth and claimants of the truth, and they were liars in their claim and wrongdoers in their denial, is that not so?
* The students: Indeed.
* Shaykh: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will establish the proof against them at the end of the verse, with an evidence they themselves acknowledge.
﴿They said: "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾: for example, the Christians say "We believe in what was sent down to us," meaning the Gospel, and the Jews mean the Torah, and both groups are liars; they did not believe in what was sent down to them.
Then He said: ﴿And they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth﴾. ﴿They disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾: that is, in what is other than it. "Waraʾ" comes in the sense of "other than." Among its uses is this verse: ﴿they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾, that is, beyond what was sent down to them.
And what is meant by "what is beyond it"? The Qur'an. The Qur'an with respect to both groups, and the Qur'an and the Gospel with respect to the Jews, because the Jews also did not believe in the Gospel; the Jews claim that they killed the one who brought the Gospel, who is Jesus son of Mary.
His words ﴿they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth, confirming﴾: the clause ﴿while it is the truth﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from ﴿mā﴾ in His words ﴿bimā warāʾahu﴾, meaning: while what is beyond it, which they disbelieve in, is the truth. Truth means what is established, and its opposite is falsehood, which is what is lost in vain and gives no benefit. Truth is what is established, beneficial and useful, and without doubt this description applies to the Qur'an.
His words ﴿confirming﴾ are also a circumstantial clause from whom? From (huwa), that is, the pronoun: meaning, while it is confirming what is with them. ﴿confirming what is with them﴾: we mentioned that in its explanation there are two views.
The first view: that it informed of them, so it came as a confirmation of what they had reported. Is that not confirming?
Second: that it confirms them and declares them to be true. For this reason it is part of the method of this Qur'an: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers; each believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], and the Last Day. So it confirms what came before on two counts. The first count: it came confirming them, because they had informed of it, so it confirmed them. What would you think if it had not come? That would have been a denial, meaning that the previous books would have been denied, and far be it from them. But it came confirming them. Second: it says of them that they are true, and it affirms the revelation of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the scrolls of Abraham, and it also makes belief in them obligatory.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 90–91 (part 2 of 3):

And His saying: ﴿for what is with them﴾. And what is "what is with them"? The Torah and the Gospel. The Christians believe in the Gospel and the Torah, while the Jews believe in the Torah and disbelieve in the Gospel; and for this reason they were worse than the Christians.

Now He says, establishing the proof against them: ﴿Say: "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah"﴾. The address in His saying ﴿Say﴾ is either to the Messenger ﷺ or to everyone who can be addressed. If it is to the Messenger ﷺ, then His saying ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ has an unspecified subject. Who is it? The Messenger ﷺ. He left it unspecified so that it would be known that what he said is the saying of those who believe in it, and this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an. Look at ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatihah 7]: the favour He attributed to Allah alone, while the anger came unspecified; because when Allah is angry with a people, He is angry with everyone who is a friend of Allah. Therefore He said: ﴿those who have earned anger﴾.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Believe in what Allah has sent down"﴾. If we say that the address in His saying ﴿Say﴾ is to the Messenger ﷺ, and he is the one who says ﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾, then the unspecified subject here serves a purpose: that this saying of the Messenger ﷺ is also said by every believer in him. Yes indeed.

As for if we say that the address in His saying ﴿Say: "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah"﴾ is to everyone who can be addressed, then the unspecified subject in the first part does not refer to the Messenger ﷺ alone.

﴿Say: "Why then do you kill"﴾, ﴿Why do you kill the prophets of Allah before?﴾ The lām is a preposition (ḥarf jarr), or not? The lām, my brothers, the lām?

* A student: The fāʾ is a preposition.
* The Shaykh: The fāʾ is a conjunction (ḥarf ʿaṭf), and the lām is a preposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And why is the lām also a preposition? Where are you? (...) (لِمَ) — لِمَ تفعل كذا: I say to you now: "Why did you do that?" What is the lām? The lām is a preposition. "Mimma taghḍab?" The mīm is a preposition. ﴿عَمَّ يَتَسَاءَلُونَ﴾ [al-Naba' 1]: (ʿan) is a preposition. ﴿لِمَ تَقُولُونَ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ﴾ [al-Saff 2]: the lām is a preposition. ﴿لِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ﴾: the lām is a preposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Its origin is the interrogative (ma) (مَا الاستفهامية). When a preposition enters upon it, its alif must be deleted. The interrogative ma, when a preposition enters upon it, its alif must be deleted. You say: (لِمَ), and (فِيمَ), "They said: 'Then what is the deed for, O Messenger of Allah?'"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4696) and al-Tirmidhi (3075), from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him).]] And (عَمَّ), and (عَلَامَ), and (مِمَّ), and (حَتَّامَ), and (إلَامَ). Is it clear now? The lām is a preposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) The lām is a preposition. So the lām is a preposition, and mā is an interrogative noun from which the alif has been dropped for lightness. How do we write (حتى) in this case? We write it with an alif, not with yā', so (حتى ما) becomes like حَتَّامَ? How do we write (إلى) in (إلام)? We write the lām and alif, not with yā', as is customary; the lām-alif of (إلام). (عَلَامَ)? We write ʿalā with an alif, not with yā', as is customary; it becomes like عَلَّامَ, and the mīm without an alif.

﴿Why do you kill﴾: this lām is in reality for challenge and obligation. That is: if you are truthful in your saying, "We believe in what was sent down to us," then why do you kill the prophets of Allah? Is this one who kills a prophet a believer? Does one who kills a prophet believe in him, O people? No, never. How do you kill the prophets of Allah while you believe in him?

﴿Why then do you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ has two readings: ﴿أَنْبِئَاءَ اللَّهِ﴾ with a hamzah, and ﴿أَنْبِيَاءَ اللَّهِ﴾ with a yā', like النبي and النبيء; the plural of النبيء is أنبئاء, and the plural of النبي is أنبياء.

Just as His saying ﴿وَهُوَ الْحَقُّ﴾ — because this follows the general rule and is not specific to this; that is, ﴿وَهْوَ الْحَقُّ﴾ has a reading with sukūn.

* A student: أنبئاءُ?
* The Shaykh: ﴿أَنْبِئَاءَ﴾ with a fatḥah.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).

﴿the prophets of Allah before﴾: that is, before this Qur'an. And regarding His saying ﴿مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾, we want to ask: from this, what is the preposition?

* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: مِن is a preposition. مِن?
* The student: If it were a preposition, it would govern what follows it.
* The Shaykh: (...).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Could it be a preposition that does not govern? You know the crane now; the crane does not carry, even if it is something big (...). What do you say?
* A student: A preposition.
* The Shaykh: A preposition. So there remains a difficulty: why was ﴿مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ not in the genitive?
* A student: Because the mudāf ilayhi was deleted and it was built on ḍamm, intending the meaning intended.
* The Shaykh: The mudāf ilayhi was deleted and its meaning intended. So it is built on ḍamm, is that right? And we told you that qabl and baʿd: either the mudāf ilayhi is mentioned, or it is deleted and its meaning is intended, or it is deleted and its wording is intended, or it is deleted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended. If it is deleted and neither its wording nor its meaning is intended, then it is tanwīn-ed according to the governing factors. If it is deleted and its wording is intended, then it is not tanwīn-ed according to the governing factors. If it is deleted and its meaning is intended, then it is built on ḍamm. If it is annexed, then it follows the governing factors and is not tanwīn-ed. Is it clear?
* A student: What is the estimate (taqdīr) of its meaning? What is the estimate?
* The Shaykh: The estimate: "from before that."

﴿from before, if you are believers﴾: (in) here is conditional, and (mu'minīn) means: in your claim of faith. You say: "We believe in what was sent down to us," so why do you kill the prophets of Allah if you are believers? This sentence is to refute them.

And His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾: (in) here is conditional, so where is the response of the condition? This occurs often in the Qur'an. Some people say that the response of the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "if you are believers, then why do you kill." Others say that in such a case it does not need a response, because the response is only needed to clarify a meaning, and the meaning here is clear without it. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, leans toward this and says that such a case does not need a response, because the response is only needed to clarify meaning, and here the meaning is clear without it. Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned that this applies even to the response of an oath; that is, an oath may not need a response when the meaning is understood. He discussed this in his book al-Tibyān fī Aqsām al-Qur'ān.

* A student: According to the Shaykh's saying (...).
* The Shaykh: The response of the oath: ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَنْ زَكَّاهَا﴾. So this verse...
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is the preferred view.
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: Perhaps. In any case (...) if the response is understood (...).

Now let us take the benefits:

* First: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their souls, that they should disbelieve﴾.
* From this verse is derived: that disbelief is a blameworthy trait, even if a person climbs by it to his worldly aims; due to His saying ﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their souls, that they should disbelieve﴾. Is that right?
* The second benefit: that the disbelief of the Children of Israel was nothing but envy and rebellion; due to His saying ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾.
* The third benefit: that whoever rejects the truth from this Ummah does so because "so-and-so," whom he sees as lesser than himself, is the one who brought it, and so he resembles the Jews. Did you understand, O people? There are some people who, when someone advises them and guides them to the truth, despise that person and regard him as nothing (...), then reject it, why? Because it came from him; had it come from so-and-so or someone else, he would have accepted it. We say: someone in this state has a resemblance to whom? To the Jews.
* The fourth benefit: that a person must know the truth by the truth, not by men. So long as what is said is true, follow it, from whatever source it comes. Do not say: "By Allah, this was brought by someone less knowledgeable than me," or "I fear that if I accept from this man, he will gain for himself, for example, pride and self-importance, and the like." Accept the truth for the sake of the truth, not because so-and-so brought it.
* The fifth benefit: that knowledge is among the greatest of the favours of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; due to His saying ﴿that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills﴾. There is no doubt that knowledge is better than wealth. If you want to know the difference between the excellence of knowledge and the excellence of wealth, look at the scholars in the time of the earlier caliphs: the caliphs' remembrance has faded, while the scholars of their time have remained remembered, are they not? Their remembrance has remained. They teach people while they are in their graves, whereas those caliphs have been forgotten, except for a caliph who has lasting monuments, whom those who know those monuments remember as belonging to so-and-so. This shows that the excellence of knowledge is greater than the excellence of wealth; due to His saying ﴿of His bounty﴾.
* The benefit that follows: the affirmation of Allah's will; due to His saying ﴿upon whom He wills﴾. Will (mashī'ah) is the same as volition (irādah), is it not? No, will is not the same as volition; will is a part, a division, of volition: it is the universal volition (al-irādah al-kawniyyah). As for the legislative volition (al-irādah al-shar'iyyah), it is not part of will.
* The benefit that follows: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants. What I want to say is that this favour which Allah sends down does not make the one favoured a lord to be worshipped; rather, he remains a servant even if he is distinguished in favour; due to His saying ﴿of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾.
* This benefit has branches, which we clarify: whoever Allah has given favour does not, by it, leave the state of being a servant. Therefore he does not rise to the rank of what? Lordship (rubūbiyyah). So the Messenger ﷺ is a servant among the servants of Allah, is he not? A servant among the servants of Allah. We do not say that when revelation came to him he was elevated until he became a lord who possesses benefit and harm and knows the unseen. No.
* Also branching from it: whoever Allah has given of His favour, especially in matters of knowledge, should be more devoted to Allah than others. Why? Because Allah, Exalted, has given him of His favour, so his obligation to Allah is greater than his obligation to others, is it not so? The greater the blessing from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, the more it demands gratitude. Is it clear? The greater the blessing, the more it demands gratitude. If Allah bestows two blessings upon you, how much gratitude is due from you? Two gratitudes. Three blessings? Three gratitudes, and so on. So if Allah has blessed you with the knowledge you have inherited from your Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, you must be all the more humble toward Allah, toward the truth, and toward creation. Is it clear?
* Branching from this, a third branch: those deluded ones, may Allah keep us safe, whom their own selves have deluded through the knowledge they have been given, have in reality been deprived of the favour, deprived of the excellence of knowledge, is that not so? (...) and by Allah's refuge, when Allah favoured them with knowledge, they exalted themselves and became arrogant, to the point that they may not accept the truth; they may resemble the Children of Israel in the second benefit.
* The benefit that follows: that punishments accumulate according to sins. From where do we take this?
* The students: ﴿So they earned anger upon anger﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿So they earned anger upon anger﴾. So punishments, may Allah keep us safe, accumulate just as sins accumulate, a fitting recompense.
* The benefit that follows: that those who sold their souls for disbelief in what Allah has sent down are disbelievers; due to His saying ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾.
* The benefit that follows also: that the arrogant one is punished with the opposite of his condition; due to His saying ﴿humiliating﴾, He humiliates them after they had exalted themselves, so they were punished, may Allah keep us safe, with what befits their sins. Upon this has the custom of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in His creation proceeded. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut 40], and He, Exalted, says: ﴿as a recompense, adequate﴾ [al-Naba' 26].

The benefit that follows: the eloquence of the Qur'an. Because this phrase ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾, instead of "and for them," gives us a benefit greater than if the pronoun "and for them" had come. What benefit do we gain? That these are disbelievers. Had it said "and for them," we would not know what their rank is in the religion of Allah. But when He said ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾, we learned that they are disbelievers.

* The second benefit: the generality that such an act makes a person a disbeliever, they and others.
* The third benefit also: clarifying the cause of the ruling, which is the humiliating punishment. What is its cause? What is the cause of the humiliating punishment? Its cause is disbelief: ﴿and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾, that is, because of their disbelief. We have already noted that when a ruling is attached to a description, it indicates that the description is the cause of that ruling, and that the ruling strengthens according to the strength of that description. Is that right?

If you say, for example: "Cut off the thief's hand," that is, because he stole; that is, because he is a thief. The causation here is clear.

If you say: "Honour the God-fearing one," that is, because of his piety; and the more his piety increases, the more his honour increases. Yes indeed.

* A student: His saying ﴿and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, because this, while being a punishment, humiliates them.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No (...). In any case, not every punishment is painful, and not every punishment is humiliating.
* A student: The punishment of the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: Even the punishment of the Hereafter. But when it is said "humiliating," it means it reaches the utmost degree of humiliation; it is more emphatic than mere punishment.
* A student: And is "humiliating" a descriptive adjective that establishes meaning (ṣifah ta'sīsiyyah)?
* The Shaykh: A descriptive adjective that establishes meaning, yes.
* A student: (...) ﴿out of envy﴾ (...) envy, the prohibition of envy?
* The Shaykh: We said: yes, the prohibition of envy and aggression.
* The student: (...) the anger of Allah, and that it is obligatory for the servant to be angry for the sake of Allah's anger. How is this, ﴿So they earned anger upon anger﴾?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. From it is derived: the affirmation of anger for Allah. Although it is not entirely clear, ﴿they earned anger﴾ means that the apparent meaning is that the anger is from Allah. So it is derived from it the affirmation of Allah's anger, Glorified and Exalted. And Allah's anger is one of His attributes of what kind? Actions (fi'liyyah), because it is connected to His will, Glorified and Exalted, and every attribute connected to will is an attribute of action.
* A student: The anger is from Allah, Glorified and Exalted. We say: how is it that anger is placed upon anger, when here the anger is one?
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: The anger is one?
* The Shaykh: No (...). Anger multiplies according to the multiplicity of its causes. That is: Allah was angry with them for doing such-and-such, then angry a second time for doing such-and-such, and so on; it multiplies according to the multiplicity of its causes. Are there benefits after the second?
* A student: The vastness of Allah's favour; due to His saying ﴿of His bounty﴾ (...).
* The Shaykh: If we make (min) partitive, it is evidence of the vastness of Allah's favour. If we make it explanatory of the kind, there is no evidence in it. But making it partitive is preferable, because it indicates a meaning beyond mere explanation of kind.

And is it derived from ﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their own souls﴾ that the soul is a trust (amānah) with the servant?

* A student: Because Allah blamed selling it (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, or ﴿ishtaraw﴾ means "chose." This is evidence that the soul is a trust with the servant: he may not burden it with what is hard for it, nor deprive it of Allah's favour. Therefore the Messenger ﷺ said to ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, when he said to him: "Indeed your soul has a right over you."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1153) and Muslim (1159/186, 188), from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

Then in the Qur'an, how often we pass by ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 57]: wronging themselves. So the soul in reality has a right over you, that you look after it as it should be looked after. Therefore a person must defend himself outside of strife; why? To protect it, because this is its right. He must eat when he is hungry, drink when he is thirsty, and clothe himself when he fears the cold, and so on, is that complete?

* A student: Shaykh, His saying ﴿and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾: the prepositional phrase indicates restriction (ḥaṣr); the prepositional phrase is fronted. Is the humiliating punishment for them alone?
* The Shaykh: "For the disbelievers," that is, to the exclusion of the defiantly sinful, for example?
* The student: Or for others.
* The Shaykh: Perhaps it is derived from it that non-disbelievers also have a punishment, but it does not reach the degree of humiliation, because they have not reached the extent of arrogance toward what Allah has sent down. And it may be said: it is for the sake of observing the rhyme endings (fawāṣil), though it is valid, and the humiliating punishment is not exclusive to the disbelievers.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say: "We believe in what was sent down to us."﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 90–91 (part 3 of 3):

* One benefit derived from this verse is the exposure of the deception of these Jews, for they said: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ while they were lying. Their intention was only to reject the truth, not to hold fast to it. Pay attention, brothers, is it clear?
* The students: It is clear.
* The Shaykh: Because they said: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ while they were lying in this claim. Had they been truthful, they would have believed in the noble Qur'an.
* The second benefit: belief in what Allah has sent down is incumbent upon every person of sound natural disposition (fitrah), who is called to it, based on the view that (qīla) is used in an indefinite form, so it includes everyone.
* The third benefit: whoever from this Ummah is called to the truth and says, "My school is such-and-such, meaning I will not turn away from it," resembles whom? The Jews. This is because, when you are called to the truth, you must look into (...) the truth; if it is the truth, it becomes obligatory for you to follow it. As for saying, "By Allah, no, my school is Shafi'i, I do not follow the Hanbali," or "I am Hanbali and I do not follow the Shafi'i," there is no permission for this, and it bears a resemblance to the Jews.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 92–95 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:92]

His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ﴾ (*wa-la-qad jaakum*, "and indeed he came to you"). The *lam* here is the *lam* of preparation for an oath (*al-lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam*), and *qad* is for confirmation (*lil-tahqiq*). We have already noted that when *qad* precedes a past-tense verb it is for confirmation, and when it precedes a present-tense verb it is for diminution (*lil-taqlil*). However, it may also be for confirmation, as in His saying: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ مَا أَنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ﴾ [an-Nur 24:64] ("Indeed He knows what you are upon"), and His saying: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الْمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنْكُمْ﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:18] ("Indeed Allah knows those among you who hinder"). In these, *qad* is undoubtedly for confirmation and not for diminution. If we say that the *lam* is for emphasis, *qad* is for confirmation, and the *lam* is the preparation for an oath, then the sentence is emphasized by three emphatics.

﴿وَلَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ﴾: The address is to the Jews. The evidence that it is to the Jews is His saying ﴿مُوسَى﴾ (Moses), because Moses was their prophet. Here He addressed them by the category of the people, not by the individuals, since Moses did not come to those who were present in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ); rather, he came to the Children of Israel, of whom they are a part.

His saying ﴿بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾ (*bil-bayyinat*, "with the clear proofs"): The *ba'* here is for accompaniment (*lil-musahabah*) or for transitivity (*lil-ta'diyah*). That is, "he came to you accompanied by the clear proofs," or "the clear proofs are what he brought," in which case it is for transitivity. The meaning of *al-bayyinat* is an adjective for an omitted noun, i.e., "with the clear signs" (*bil-ayat al-bayyinat*), meaning the signs indicating his prophethood. Among them: the hand, the staff, the stone, the splitting of the sea, the locusts sent upon the family of Pharaoh, the years of drought, and many other things: the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

His saying ﴿بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾: *al-bayyin* means "the manifest," i.e., they are signs manifest as evidence of his prophethood. Despite this, He says ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ ("then you took the calf"). *Thumma* ("then") indicates a delay, i.e., sequence with an interval. That is, after a period of time had passed in which you were able to contemplate these signs and recognize them, what actually happened is that you did not raise your heads to them: ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ ("you took the calf after him"). ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ﴾ (*ittakhadhtum*, "you took"): we passed over this recently. What is it among its uses? It is *al-tasyir* (making something into something). Among its uses is *al-tasyir*, as in ﴿اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ خَلِيلًا﴾ [an-Nisa 4:125] ("Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend"), meaning He made him. So this verb takes two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate. The first object is *al-'ijl* (the calf) in ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾. Where is the second object?

*Student:* "A god" (*ilahan*).

*Shaykh:* It is omitted, its estimated form being "a god." Omitting what is known is permissible.

His saying ﴿الْعِجْلَ﴾ (*al-'ijl*, "the calf"): it is the young of the cow, and it was not a calf of a living animal; rather, it was a calf made of jewelry. They fashioned a calf from jewelry, and the Samiri misled them and led them astray. This calf had a lowing (*khuwar*). It is said that this was a real lowing, and it is said that it was the sound of the wind entering from its back and exiting from its mouth. But, may Allah protect us, he (the Samiri) said to them: ﴿هَذَا إِلَهُكُمْ وَإِلَهُ مُوسَى فَنَسِيَ﴾ [Taha 20:88] ("This is your god and the god of Moses, but he forgot"). This is because Moses had left them to his Lord's appointment, which was thirty days, and Allah increased it by ten, so it became forty days.
