* Shaykh: The second is the first? ﴿truthful﴾. For the truthful is the one whose truthfulness comes first in their claim, then establishing that the Hereafter is theirs, then wishing for death. Thus whenever one condition enters into another condition, the second is the first. Like the poet's saying:
"If you call upon us for help, if you are terrified, you will find from us strongholds of honour adorned by generosity."
Where are the condition and the condition? "If you call upon us for help, if you are terrified." Certainly, the terror comes before the seeking of help, does it not? So the meaning becomes: that if you are terrified and then seek our help, you will find strongholds of honour adorned by generosity.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the second condition, according to the correct view, does not need a response in this type of construction.

* * *

I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what God has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they reject what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of God before, if you were believers?"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91].
* From this noble verse is derived: the arrogance and obstinacy of the Jews, because they say: "We will not believe except in what was sent down to us."
* The second benefit: whoever opposes the truth for the sake of a leader among the imitators (muqallidun) shares a resemblance with the Jews who ﴿said, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and reject what is beyond it﴾. So if it is said to a person, for example: "This is the judgment of God," and he says: "My school is such-and-such," we say to him: he resembles whom? The Jews. Whether his school is Hanafi, Hanbali, Shafi'i, Maliki, or Zahiri, everyone to whom the truth is made clear and who says "I will not follow it" bears a resemblance to them.
* The third benefit: the condemnation of one who does not believe in the truth.
* And the fourth benefit: the obligation to accept the truth from whoever brings it.
* And the fifth benefit: silencing the opponent by establishing the proof against him from his own deed. How so? God established the proof against these Jews from their own actions, because they said: "We believe in what was sent down to us," yet they had killed the prophets of God who came to them with the Book. Is their claim "we believe in what was sent down to us" true or not? It is not true, because if they were truly believers they would not have killed them. For this reason He said: ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of God before, if you were believers?﴾.
* Among the benefits also: the Messenger is called a Prophet, because His saying ﴿the prophets of God﴾ means His messengers, since they killed those to whom the message had been conveyed.
* And in it also is evidence that faith requires accepting the truth from whoever brings it, by His saying ﴿if you were believers﴾, for it is obligatory upon you not to kill them but to accept from them.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs; then you took the calf [as deity] after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:92].
* In this verse also: establishing the proof against the obstinacy of the Jews. How so?
* Student: (...) they took the calf.
* Shaykh: Moses had come to them with clear proofs.
* Student: After Moses had come to them with clear proofs.
* Shaykh: They took the calf as a deity.
* The second benefit: the foolishness of these Jews. Why?
* Student: (...) Because they saw the truth and then turned away from it.
* Shaykh: This is evidence of their obstinacy, but what about their foolishness, and that they have no sound judgment?
* Student: Their taking the calf as a deity.
* Shaykh: Correct. Their taking the calf as a deity. There is no doubt that this is foolishness: a calf that you take as a god.
* The third benefit: these Jews worshipped the calf out of wrongdoing, not out of ignorance, but they were wrongdoers.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And what is its place in i'rab? The sentence?
* Student: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).
* Shaykh: A circumstantial clause, from the subject of ﴿you took﴾.
* The fourth benefit: these Jews seized the opportunity of Moses' absence, which indicates their awe of him, since they seized the opportunity of his absence because they feared him? 
* Student: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs; then you took the calf﴾, meaning: during his absence..
* Shaykh: From where did you derive it in the verse?
* Student: I derived it from another verse.
* Shaykh: A verse other than this one.
* Student: ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾ (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ (after him), in accordance with His saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾, meaning: after Musa (Moses).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and listen." They said, "We hear and we disobey." And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief. Say: "Wretched is what your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ [al-Baqarah 92].

* From this verse it is derived that Allah took the covenant from the Children of Israel to have faith. From where is this derived?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The second benefit: that the Children of Israel did not believe except unwillingly and against their noses (i.e., forced)?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* The third benefit: a demonstration of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Above them.
* The fourth benefit: a proof that the affair of the whole universe is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, glorified and exalted, is able to break customary norms?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾, because this is a breaking of the customary norm, which shows that the whole affair of the universe is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation to receive the Sharia of Allah with strength, without laziness or slackness. From where do we take it?
* Student: ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾. The obligation is that a person receives the Sharia of Allah with strength and resolve, not with slackness and laziness.
* Student: Shaykh, did Allah give them the strength, or did they take it with strength?
* Shaykh: No. ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾ means: accept the Sharia of Allah with strength and vigor.
* Among the benefits of this verse: a demonstration of the rebelliousness (ʿutuww) of the Children of Israel. You will not find a verse without this benefit in it. From where do we take the rebelliousness of the Children of Israel?
* Student: ﴿with strength﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿with strength﴾? No, my brother.
* Student: ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾. This is the most eloquent expression of rebelliousness, and we seek refuge with Allah. Had they not heard, it would have been said they were excused by their ignorance. But ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: hearing is of two kinds: hearing of acceptance (istijabah) and hearing of perception (idrak). From where do we take that hearing is of two kinds: hearing of acceptance and hearing of perception?
* Student: His saying: ﴿And listen. They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾.
* Shaykh: Which of them is it: the hearing of perception or the hearing of acceptance?
* Student: From their saying ﴿We hear﴾, it is the hearing of perception.
* Shaykh: Yes. And where is the hearing of acceptance?
Also among the benefits of the verse: the true believer is not commanded by his faith to commit sins.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿if you are believers﴾ means: if you were truly believers, you would not have taken the calf as a god.
* Also among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, Exalted, does not attribute evil to Himself, but mentions it in the passive form. From where do we take it?
* Student: ﴿commands you﴾.
* Shaykh: No. Do you understand the question? The benefit of the verse is that evil, or what is similar to it, is not attributed by Allah to Himself; He attributes it in the passive voice. From His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink into their hearts﴾. Allah did not say, "Allah cast into their hearts the love of the calf," but He said ﴿they were made to drink into their hearts﴾. Is there a parallel to it in the Qur'an? And what is it?
* Student: ﴿And that we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10].
* Shaykh: ﴿And that we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾.
* Student: What is the benefit, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: The benefit is that evil and what derives from it is not attributed by Allah to Himself in the active voice, but in the passive voice. Because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Evil is not attributed to You" [Muslim (771/201), from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib]. Is it understood, everyone?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: This was covered for us in the chapter on divine decree (qadar) in creed (ʿaqidah), and we mentioned that evil is in the object, not in the act. Allah's decree: everything is by the decree and predestination of Allah, even as the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Even incapacity and shrewdness" [Muslim (2655/18), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar], and good and evil. But evil, in relation to Allah's act of it, is good, not evil. It is good, because Allah only created it for a profound wisdom and a praiseworthy end, even if it is evil. I think we mentioned about eight benefits for the creation of disliked things and evils. Perhaps, God willing, some of them are in your memory, or (...)?
* Student: Some of them...
* Shaykh: In any case, this benefit must be known: that the act of Allah is never evil, whatever it is; all of it is good, because Allah is Wise. But evil is in what? In the objects and the creatures. As for the act itself, it is not evil. We gave the example of a man who cauterizes his son with fire. Fire is painful and burning, but he wants him to be healed. So this object that results from the agent is painful and burning evil, but the cauterizing itself, for its praiseworthy end, is what?
* Student: It is good.
* Shaykh: It is good.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "If the Last Abode with Allah is exclusively yours, apart from the people, then wish for death, if you are truthful."﴾ In this verse there is a refutation of the Jews who said: "For us is the Hereafter and for you is the world," ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. What is its refutation? What is its refutation?
* Student: ﴿Say: "If the Last Abode is yours"﴾.
* Shaykh: No. What is the refutation of the Jews in this?
* Student: ﴿then wish for death﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿then wish for death﴾, and Allah said: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth﴾.
* The second benefit, which is based on a difference over the interpretation of the verse: the permissibility of mubahalah (mutual invocation of curse) to establish the truth. However, it is based on a difference over the interpretation of the verse. From where do we take it?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿then wish for death﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, from His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾. And what is this opinion we pointed to, which we said is based on it being a case of mubahalah?
* Student: That their interpretation, that His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾ is on (...), if you claim that the Hereafter is exclusively yours.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is one view. The second view is that the verse is meant in its apparent sense and is not a case of mubahalah. We mentioned that Ibn Kathir weakened it and said: if the matter were so, they would also have obligated us with it. We explained that what Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned is not binding, since if they had referred the matter to the Prophet, peace be upon him, they would have wished for death. But they did not refer it, because they were the claimants, so the obligation fell on them.
* There is also in it a proof, which comes with this proof, of the lie of the Jews in what they claim, and we have mentioned this. And in it also is a proof: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, that the disbeliever dislikes death because of what he knows of the bad outcome?
* Student: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾? His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: No. We said: because of what he dislikes of the bad outcome?
* Student: ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾.
* Another student: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth﴾.
* Shaykh: The proof is taken from ﴿because of what their hands have put forth﴾, meaning that they know they will be punished for their sins, so they cannot wish for death, lest they reach the punishment. In the verse there is also a proof for establishing causation (sababiyyah). From where do we take it?
* Student: From the letter bāʾ.
* Shaykh: From the bāʾ in His saying ﴿because of what their hands have put forth﴾. Who among the people of innovation (ahl al-bidʿah) denies causes?
* Student: The Qadariyyah.
* Shaykh: The Qadariyyah, no.
* Student: The Ash'arites.
* Shaykh: And who else? The Jahmiyyah. The Ash'arites and the Jahmiyyah. The Mu'tazilah, on the contrary, make it obligatory that there be a cause in origin, and they make the cause necessitating, and for this reason they hold that it is obligatory for Allah, as has passed, to do what is good or best, with differences among them.
In it is also the establishment of knowledge for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From where do we take it?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: And what is the indication of the meaning from His saying ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Then what is the evidence that this indicates Allah's knowledge? And what is the indication of its implying Allah's knowledge?
* Student: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: Apparently it is an arrow without an archer. ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, you say in it the establishment of Allah's knowledge. What is its basis?
* Student: The establishment of Allah's knowledge is in it. The question would be ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, His saying: ﴿Knowing﴾.
* Shaykh: No, it is correct: in ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ the establishment of knowledge is present. But is the establishment of knowledge also present in ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾?
* The students: That is, ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾ means that Allah is Knowing... His knowledge that they will never wish for it.
* Shaykh: Because they did not wish for it. Allah said: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, and in fact they did not wish for it. So the matter occurred as He reported, which shows that what is known is in accordance with His knowledge, or not?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: If they had wished for it, far be it from that, the matter would not indicate this. But they will never wish for it, and in fact they did not wish for death. Had they wished for it, they would have died.
* And in it also is the establishment of knowledge in another part of the verse, in His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾.
* And in it also is a proof for the permissibility of specifying a general statement for the purpose of threat, or for a better and more comprehensive purpose: specifying a general statement for a purpose.
* Student: In His saying ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, Allah is Knowing of everyone (...).
* Shaykh: Of the wrongdoers and others. But He specified them here for the purpose of threat. Do you understand now? We are not saying only knowledge; can all general statements be restricted to some of their instances for a purpose?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 92–95 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:92]

His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ﴾ (*wa-la-qad jaakum*, "and indeed he came to you"). The *lam* here is the *lam* of preparation for an oath (*al-lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam*), and *qad* is for confirmation (*lil-tahqiq*). We have already noted that when *qad* precedes a past-tense verb it is for confirmation, and when it precedes a present-tense verb it is for diminution (*lil-taqlil*). However, it may also be for confirmation, as in His saying: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ مَا أَنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ﴾ [an-Nur 24:64] ("Indeed He knows what you are upon"), and His saying: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الْمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنْكُمْ﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:18] ("Indeed Allah knows those among you who hinder"). In these, *qad* is undoubtedly for confirmation and not for diminution. If we say that the *lam* is for emphasis, *qad* is for confirmation, and the *lam* is the preparation for an oath, then the sentence is emphasized by three emphatics.

﴿وَلَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ﴾: The address is to the Jews. The evidence that it is to the Jews is His saying ﴿مُوسَى﴾ (Moses), because Moses was their prophet. Here He addressed them by the category of the people, not by the individuals, since Moses did not come to those who were present in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ); rather, he came to the Children of Israel, of whom they are a part.

His saying ﴿بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾ (*bil-bayyinat*, "with the clear proofs"): The *ba'* here is for accompaniment (*lil-musahabah*) or for transitivity (*lil-ta'diyah*). That is, "he came to you accompanied by the clear proofs," or "the clear proofs are what he brought," in which case it is for transitivity. The meaning of *al-bayyinat* is an adjective for an omitted noun, i.e., "with the clear signs" (*bil-ayat al-bayyinat*), meaning the signs indicating his prophethood. Among them: the hand, the staff, the stone, the splitting of the sea, the locusts sent upon the family of Pharaoh, the years of drought, and many other things: the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

His saying ﴿بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾: *al-bayyin* means "the manifest," i.e., they are signs manifest as evidence of his prophethood. Despite this, He says ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ ("then you took the calf"). *Thumma* ("then") indicates a delay, i.e., sequence with an interval. That is, after a period of time had passed in which you were able to contemplate these signs and recognize them, what actually happened is that you did not raise your heads to them: ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ ("you took the calf after him"). ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ﴾ (*ittakhadhtum*, "you took"): we passed over this recently. What is it among its uses? It is *al-tasyir* (making something into something). Among its uses is *al-tasyir*, as in ﴿اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ خَلِيلًا﴾ [an-Nisa 4:125] ("Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend"), meaning He made him. So this verb takes two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate. The first object is *al-'ijl* (the calf) in ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾. Where is the second object?

*Student:* "A god" (*ilahan*).

*Shaykh:* It is omitted, its estimated form being "a god." Omitting what is known is permissible.

His saying ﴿الْعِجْلَ﴾ (*al-'ijl*, "the calf"): it is the young of the cow, and it was not a calf of a living animal; rather, it was a calf made of jewelry. They fashioned a calf from jewelry, and the Samiri misled them and led them astray. This calf had a lowing (*khuwar*). It is said that this was a real lowing, and it is said that it was the sound of the wind entering from its back and exiting from its mouth. But, may Allah protect us, he (the Samiri) said to them: ﴿هَذَا إِلَهُكُمْ وَإِلَهُ مُوسَى فَنَسِيَ﴾ [Taha 20:88] ("This is your god and the god of Moses, but he forgot"). This is because Moses had left them to his Lord's appointment, which was thirty days, and Allah increased it by ten, so it became forty days. He said to them: Moses has gone astray from his god, and this is why he is late and has not returned. He has gone astray and has not been guided to his god. So this is your god and the god of Moses, may Allah protect us. So they took it as a god. This indicates the foolishness of the Children of Israel, because they were the ones who made this jewelry with their own hands, so how could it be a god? Nevertheless, they took it as a god after Moses had gone.

His saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ (*min ba'dihi*, "after him"): Does it mean after his death, or after his departure for his Lord's appointment?

*Students:* After his departure.

*Shaykh:* After his departure for his Lord's appointment. This is the only possibility, because Moses returned to them and said to the Samiri regarding his god: ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ ثُمَّ لَنَنْسِفَنَّهُ فِي الْيَمِّ نَسْفًا﴾ [Taha 20:97] ("We will surely burn it, then we will surely scatter it into the sea, scattering"), and this was carried out. Moses, peace be upon him, burned it and scattered it into the sea, into the ocean.

﴿وَأَنْتُمْ ظَالِمُونَ﴾ (*wa-antum zalimun*, "while you were wrongdoers"): *zalimun* means transgressors (*mu'tadun*). The root meaning of *zulm* is deficiency, and aggression is called *zulm* because it is a deficiency in the right of the one who is wronged. I say: the root meaning of *zulm* is deficiency, based on His saying: ﴿كِلْتَا الْجَنَّتَيْنِ آتَتْ أُكُلَهَا وَلَمْ تَظْلِمْ مِنْهُ شَيْئًا﴾ [al-Kahf 18:33] ("Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short of it in anything"), i.e., did not diminish. The clause ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ ظَالِمُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) in the accusative position. It is a circumstantial clause from what? From the subject of ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ﴾, meaning "while the reality is that you are wrongdoers." Which is more severe in ugliness: that a person takes an ugly deed while he is a wrongdoer who knows he is wrongdoing, or that he takes it while he is ignorant? The first is more severe. Yes indeed.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* No, more than this, because His saying ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى تِسْعَ آيَاتٍ بَيِّنَاتٍ﴾ [al-Isra 17:101] ("We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs") does not imply restriction. He did not say, for example, "the signs are the nine." And even if He had said it, it would have been (...).

*Student:* What is the distinction of these nine?

*Shaykh:* The distinction of these nine is that they became a proof against the Children of Israel, because of the destruction of their enemy and its manifestation through them. So they are stronger than others and greater.

He said: ﴿وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَكُمْ﴾ (*wa-idh akhadhna mithaqakum*, "and when We took your covenant"). ﴿إِذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when"): what is its *i'rab* (grammatical analysis)? This appears often in the Qur'an, and the scholars parse it as an object of an omitted verb, whose estimated form is "remember" (*udhkur*). If the address is to more than one person, it is estimated as "remember" in the plural (*udhkuru*): "remember when We took your covenant." *Mithaq* means covenant, and the covenant was named *mithaq* because it is secured (*yatawaththaq*) by it (...).

from taking the Torah, and they began to witness it. When they saw the mount above them as if it were a canopy, they prostrated, prostrating out of fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They began looking at the mountain while they pleaded to Allah, glorified and exalted, that He remove it from them. For this reason, some people of knowledge mentioned that they considered the best prostration with which they could prostrate to Allah to be prostrating with their eyes toward the sky, saying: "This prostration is one by which Allah saved us, so it is the most noble prostration for us." Thus, when one prostrates, his head is raised in such a way.

﴿وَرَفَعْنَا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ﴾ ("and We raised the mount above you") as a threat to them. ﴿خُذُوا﴾ (*khudhu*, "take"): an imperative verb, and it is in the accusative position as a quoted speech of an omitted saying, i.e., "We said: take what We have given you." ﴿بِقُوَّةٍ﴾ (*biquwwatin*, "with strength"): meaning with diligence and vigor. Diligence is firm resolve, and vigor is the strength in carrying it out. What is meant by "what We have given you"? What is its meaning?

*Students:* The Torah.

*Shaykh:* The Torah.

﴿وَاسْمَعُوا﴾ (*wasma'u*, "and listen"): a command to listen, and it is not listening with the ear, but listening in submission and response. They were commanded to take the Torah with strength and to listen, i.e., to respond and submit. The answer was: ﴿قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾ ("They said: We heard and we disobeyed"), may Allah protect us, "we heard with our ears and disobeyed with our deeds." They did not listen with the listening that was demanded of them; rather, they were arrogant toward it.

His saying: ﴿قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾: The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that they said this verbally: ﴿سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾. Some said: "They said 'we heard' with their tongues, but they disobeyed with their deeds," so the expression of disobedience refers to their actions, and they did not say with their tongues, "We disobeyed." But we say, in rebuttal to this view: what prevents them from saying ﴿سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾, when they are the ones who said to Moses: ﴿لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّى نَرَى اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:55] ("We will not believe you until we see Allah openly")? What is the obstacle? Those who were bold enough to say "we will not believe you until we see Allah openly" would be bold enough to say "we heard and we disobeyed." It seems that those who said that the meaning of disobedience here is the act of disobedience, and not that they said with their tongues "we disobeyed," were saying that they committed themselves to this while the mountain was over their heads. Whoever is in this condition cannot possibly say this matter; one who has a mountain above him cannot say "we heard and we disobeyed." But we say: there is no obstacle to the firm intention they displayed, after the threat was lifted from them, being the reality of the matter.

What is disobedience? Disobedience is opposing a command. If you wish, say: it is leaving obedience. This disobedience is departing from obedience, whether that is in opposing what is commanded or in committing what is forbidden. Do you understand? Disobedience occurs in abandoning what is commanded and in committing what is prohibited. So whoever abandons congregational prayer, which is obligatory for him, is a disobedient person, and it is appropriate to say: "This one disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." And whoever commits adultery, steals, or drinks wine is also disobedient to Allah and His Messenger.

﴿قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا وَأُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ ("They said: We heard and we disobeyed, and the calf was made to sink into their hearts"), may Allah protect us. ﴿أُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ﴾ (*ushribu fi qulubihim*, "were made to imbibe into their hearts"): some said that it is with an omitted modifier, i.e., "the love of the calf was made to sink into their hearts," because the calf itself cannot be absorbed into the heart. The meaning of *ushribu* is that this love was made as if it were water given to drink to the heart. So it mixed with the heart, did it not? It mixed with it, just as water mixes with clay (*al-madar*) when it is soaked into it. Do you know *al-madar*? Who knows it?

*Student:* Sugar and lemon.

*Shaykh:* No. *Al-madar* is dried clay. People here call it (*al-jumh*); I do not know whether it is Arabic or colloquial. Dried clay is called *madar*.

*Student:* O Shaykh, *al-madar* is red clay?

*Shaykh:* No, it is not required to be red. Do you mean pottery?

*Student:* No, here we call red clay *madar*, not this clay.

*Shaykh:* No, every dried clay is called *madar*. The point is that this heart, may Allah protect us, had the calf made to sink into it. But He expressed it with the calf to indicate their love for it, because it is more forceful, as if the calf itself had entered their hearts. This is more emphatic, may Allah protect us.

His saying ﴿أُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ﴾: Who made this sink into their hearts? Allah, glorified and exalted. But it is part of the eloquence of the Qur'an that what Allah dislikes is often expressed in the passive voice, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «وَالشَّرُّ لَيْسَ إِلَيْكَ» ("and evil is not attributed to You")[[Recorded by Muslim (771/201) from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Allah, the Exalted, said about the jinn: ﴿وَأَنَّا لَا نَدْرِي أَشَرٌّ أُرِيدَ بِمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ أَمْ أَرَادَ بِهِمْ رَبُّهُمْ رَشَدًا﴾ [al-Jinn 72:10] ("And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance"). They said: "evil was intended" (*shar ureed*, passive), and they did not attribute it to Allah, but they attributed guidance to Allah. The point is that these people, may Allah protect us, had the calf made to sink into their hearts, and this is a trial: that something Allah does not approve of should sink into a person's heart, may Allah protect us. This is among the greatest trials, whether it is the love of a worshipped thing or the love of a sought-after thing. The love of wealth may sink into a person's heart until he forgets the interests of his religion and his worldly life. The love of marriage may sink into a person's heart until it sometimes leads him into what is forbidden, may Allah protect us. Measure everything else by this.

Allah, glorified and exalted, may test a servant with affliction because he is worthy of being tested in that way. For this reason He said: ﴿أُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْعِجْلَ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾ ("the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of their disbelief"). The *ba'* here is causal (*lil-sababiyyah*), i.e., because of their disbelief in Allah that preceded the worship of the calf. This is because they, may Allah protect us, had intended sin before they fell into it, and so they became disbelievers in Him. Then the calf was made to sink into their hearts until they could no longer turn away from it. Aaron, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿يَا قَوْمِ إِنَّمَا فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ وَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ فَاتَّبِعُونِي وَأَطِيعُوا أَمْرِي﴾ [Taha 20:90] ("O my people, you are only being tested by it. Indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command"), even though Aaron was the deputy and successor of Moses. But what was their answer to Aaron? ﴿لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عَاكِفِينَ حَتَّى يَرْجِعَ إِلَيْنَا مُوسَى﴾ [Taha 20:91] ("We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us"). They persisted, may Allah protect us, because the calf had been made to sink into their hearts by their disbelief.

﴿قُلْ بِئْسَمَا يَأْمُرُكُمْ بِهِ إِيمَانُكُمْ﴾ ("Say: Wretched is what your faith commands you to do"). *Qul* (say): whom does Allah address? Moses?

*Student:* The Prophet (ﷺ).

*Shaykh:* He addresses the Prophet (ﷺ), or He addresses anyone to whom the address can be directed, i.e., "Say, O addressee," or "Say, O Prophet."

﴿بِئْسَمَا يَأْمُرُكُمْ بِهِ إِيمَانُكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Wretched is what your faith commands you to do, if you are believers"). ﴿بِئْسَ﴾ (*bi'sa*, "wretched"): here is it a past-tense verb that is fixed (*jamid*) or one that is inflected (*mutasarrif*)?

*Students:* Fixed.

*Shaykh:* Fixed. Do you know the fixed verb from the non-fixed?

*Student:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* And what is the fixed verb?

*Student:* The fixed verb is one that is not inflected.

*Shaykh:* Such as?

*Student:* *Bi'sa* (...).

*Shaykh:* *'Asa*?

*Student:* *'Asa* is fixed.

*Shaykh:* Some say that it may be *ya'su* or *ya'si*, but the more correct view is that it is fixed.

*Shaykh:* And *laysa*?

*Student:* Fixed.

*Shaykh:* Fixed.

A fixed past-tense verb used to express dispraise.

His saying ﴿بِئْسَمَا﴾: What is the *i'rab* of *ma*? It is an indefinite noun in the accusative position, built on sukun, in the accusative position as a specifier (*tamyiz*), i.e., "wretched is a thing your faith commands you to do." *Bi'sa*, *ni'ma*, and similar words require a specified item (*mukhassas*). Where is the specified item? It is omitted, indicated by the context, i.e., "wretched is a thing your faith commands you to do: the worship of the calf." That is, if the worship of the calf is what your faith requires, then does your faith command you with a sound matter or with an ugly matter? With an ugly matter. That is, where is your faith when the calf has been made to sink into your hearts? This faith you claim, which made the worship of the calf beloved to you, and you worshipped it.

Is the attribution of the command to faith real or not? Yes, it is real. This is because it has already been noted that there is no metaphorical expression in the Qur'an, based on the view that words have no inherent meanings, and that their meanings are understood from context and circumstantial indicators. So the "command" of faith to them means what faith requires. For example, you love a thing; what does your love for it require? Inclination toward it and eagerness to obtain it. You hate a thing; what does your hatred of it require? Aversion from it and distance from it, and not reaching it by any means. So their faith, which they claim, commanded them with a matter that faith does not require, namely the worship of the calf.

His saying ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("if you are believers"): this is a conditional clause for the category, and its purpose is challenge, i.e., "if you are truly believers, how can your faith command you with this ugly deed?" Allah, glorified and exalted, said ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ because He had earlier mentioned about them: ﴿وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ آمِنُوا بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ قَالُوا نُؤْمِنُ بِمَا أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْنَا﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91] ("When it is said to them, 'Believe in what Allah has revealed,' they say, 'We believe in what was revealed to us'"). Was it revealed to them that they should worship the calf? No, that was not revealed to them. So if you are truly believers, why does your faith command you with this ugly act, which is the worship of the calf?

*Student:* O Shaykh, the *i'rab* of *ma*?

*Shaykh:* Regarding the *i'rab* of *ma*, we say: it is an indefinite noun, built on sukun, in the accusative position as a specifier.

*Student:* A specifier (...)?

*Shaykh:* A specifier of the omitted subject.

*Student:* The subject of *bi'sa*?

*Shaykh:* The omitted subject of *bi'sa*.

*Student:* (...).

*Shaykh:* It is not far-fetched. For this reason, we preferred that this view is the reality, and that what is meant is not abandoning action. Those who went to the view that it is an expression for abandoning action said: "They could not say ﴿سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾ while the mountain was over their heads, so this must be what is meant." But we say: this is not an obstacle, because they say that when the threat was lifted from them. Such words do not concern them; they do not mention what happened to them before.

*Student:* O Shaykh, is the estimate of *ma* "wretched is the thing that your faith commands you to do"?

*Shaykh:* No, "wretched is a thing" (*bi'sa shay'an*), because the specifier must be indefinite and cannot come definite.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿قُلْ إِنْ كَانَتْ لَكُمُ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ خَالِصَةً مِنْ دُونِ النَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُا الْمَوْتَ﴾ ("Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is exclusively yours, apart from the people, then wish for death").

﴿قُلْ إِنْ كَانَتْ لَكُمُ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ خَالِصَةً﴾: Is *kana* here complete or incomplete?

*Students:* Incomplete. Complete.

*Shaykh:* Complete?

*Student:* Incomplete.

*Shaykh:* Incomplete. Where is its predicate? It is permissible for its predicate to be the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿لَكُمُ الدَّارُ﴾ ("for you is the abode"), with ﴿خَالِصَةً﴾ ("exclusively") being a circumstantial modifier of ﴿الدَّارُ﴾, meaning "in the state of being exclusively ﴿خَالِصَةً مِنْ دُونِ النَّاسِ﴾ (apart from the people)." It is also permissible that the predicate is ﴿خَالِصَةً﴾: "Say: If the Last Abode is exclusively yours, apart from the people." The meaning is the same either way.

God says: ﴿Say, "If the Last Abode with God is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of other people"﴾. By "the Last Abode" is meant Paradise. He said this, or was commanded to say it, because they had said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:80], and then (they claimed) you would be left in the Fire while we would be in Paradise. This is the speech of the Jews. What does the one who says this claim? He claims that the Last Abode belongs to him exclusively, to the exclusion of people. For this reason the Jews claim that they are "the chosen people of God" and say, "God has preferred us over the worlds," and they claim that the Hereafter belongs to them alone, and that whoever among them deserves the Fire enters it for a few days and then leaves for Paradise. So God says: ﴿Say, "If the Last Abode with God is yours exclusively"﴾. The exegetes explained "exclusive" as meaning "specifically yours," because the meaning of ﴿exclusively﴾ is "specific." It is also possible that the intended meaning of "exclusive" is that which nothing mixes with, meaning that no one shares it with you. Both meanings lead to the same result.

And His saying: ﴿then wish for death﴾. The fā' (then)? What is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the fā'?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The answer to what?
* Student: The condition (shart).
* Shaykh: And what is it?
* Student: "Say."
* Shaykh: "If it is" is the linking element (rābiṭah). The response had to be linked to it with the fā' because the verb after it is an imperative, and they have said that it is obligatory to link the response with the fā' in seven places.
* Student: Six.
* Shaykh: Six places?
* Shaykh (reciting the verse): Nominal (ismiyyah), imperative (ṭalabiyyah), and the one with a non-derived noun, and with mā, qad, lan, and with the future particle (tanfīs).
Seven places, in which it is obligatory that the fā' be joined.

And His saying: ﴿wish for death﴾, meaning: seek its occurrence. Wishing (tamannī) is also seeking the occurrence of something beloved, is it not? How is that? Because if ﴿the Last Abode with God is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of other people﴾, then the Last Abode is better than this world, and what does a person wish for? That he moves to what is better. If you were in an old, dilapidated house, and you feared it would fall on you, would you say, "I wish I lived in a new house"?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: You would say that. These people say: "The Hereafter is ours." And if the Hereafter is theirs, then the Hereafter is without doubt better than this world. So if you see that the Hereafter is yours, it becomes necessary for you to wish for death in order to reach what is better. Do you understand? This is a challenge to them. For this reason God the Exalted says here: ﴿but they will never wish for it, ever﴾, and likewise in Surat al-Jumu'ah He says: ﴿and they will never wish for it, ever﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:7]. This is because God knows that they will not wish for it, so He challenged them with it, since it is not possible for them to wish for it, as they love this world more than the Hereafter, as will come later. The apparent meaning of the noble verse, as we have explained now, is that God commanded His Prophet to challenge them: if the Last Abode is yours, as you claim, then wish for death so that you may reach it. This is without doubt the apparent meaning of the noble verse, and it is what Ibn Jarir and many exegetes preferred.

Some scholars held that the intended meaning of ﴿then wish for death﴾ is: then engage us in mutual imprecation (mubāhalah), and wish death upon whichever of us is lying. This is like His saying in Surat Ali 'Imran: ﴿Whoever disputes with you concerning him after knowledge has come to you, say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us invoke earnestly and invoke the curse of God upon the liars"﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:61]. And what would be the meaning of wishing for death? By way of what? By way of mubāhalah. Ibn Kathir preferred this, and he weakened the first view on the basis that if the intended meaning were that they wish for the occurrence of death, they would argue against us too and say: "You also, if you say the Last Abode is yours, then wish for death," because the challenge being directed at us with this is no more appropriate than our challenge to you with it. They could then say: "We do not wish for death, because you too say the Last Abode is yours, and that the Jews after the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ) are in the Fire. So will you wish for death too?" This is not valid, because we do not wish for death, and it is not legislated for us to wish for death. The best of people is one whose life is long and whose deeds are good. A person wishes that God extend his life so that he may increase righteous deeds from which he benefits, and does not wish for death. Even if he is among the most pious of people, he does not wish for death.

This meaning which Ibn Kathir inclined to is really very strong, though it contradicts the apparent context. But it is strong, very strong. Those who adopted the apparent context said: "We take by it, because the setting is one of challenge, and God knew that they would not do it, and they were not wishing for death, nor would they respond to us by saying: 'You wish for it.' They are the claimants, and God knew that they would never wish for it, nor would they say: 'Wish for it yourselves.'" As we said, this is a specific matter about which God spoke, and He informed us of what the outcome would be without the event occurring. God says: ﴿but they will never wish for it﴾. But the second is: ﴿and they will never wish for it, ever﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:7]. So which do we take? We take what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires, and we say: this is a particular matter about which God informed us that it will not occur. Or we take what the general meaning that Ibn Kathir adopted supports.
* Student: (...) Does the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) clarify the meaning?
* Shaykh: They did not mention an occasion of revelation. Ibn 'Abbas's apparent statement is that it concerns mubāhalah. It is well known that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) is referred to in tafsir, because he was a Companion who devoted himself to tafsir, and the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated for him that Allah teach him ta'wil [[Reported by al-Bukhari (75), and Ahmad (2397), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him).]].
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, it can be mubāhalah in another manner, because the mubāhalah with the Christians mentioned in Surat Ali 'Imran was a mubāhalah with the Christians who said what they said about 'Isa. They were asked to engage in mubāhalah, but they refused, submitted, and agreed to pay the jizyah. As for these, it is mubāhalah with the Jews.
* Student: Is wishing for death not permissible?
* Shaykh: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: «None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him. If he must, let him say: O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is good for me, and cause me to die when death is good for me» [[Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (6351), and Muslim (2680/10), from the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him).]].
* Student: And if he fears trial (fitnah)?
* Shaykh: As for if he fears trial, he says: «O Allah, if You intend a trial for Your servants, then take me to You without being tried» [[Reported by al-Tirmidhi (3233), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. He does not say, "Cause me to die," because he does not know; perhaps his remaining in the trial is good for him and for others. Perhaps God will save people through his hands, people who would not have been saved had he not been among them. He says: «take me to You without being tried».
* Student: So if he knows his weakness, for example?
* Shaykh: He says these words: «take me to You without being tried», thereby restricting the request for death to being untried, whether now or after some time.
* Student: Mubāhalah (...)?
* Shaykh: Mubāhalah is as God said: ﴿we call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:61]. The two groups gather and invoke God, the Exalted and Most High, that the curse of God be upon the liar, or that the liar dies, or that such and such happens to the liar. In reality, mubāhalah exposes one to affliction; therefore a person should not engage in mubāhalah except when it is in the interest of Islam. When it is in the interest of Islam, there is no harm. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) rejected the issue of al-'awl (increase of shares in inheritance) and said: "Whoever wishes, I will engage him in mubāhalah" [[Reported by Sa'id ibn Mansur (37), and its wording: "Let them gather, and let us place our hands on the corner (of the Ka'bah), then we will invoke and place the curse of God upon the liars, (if they do not affirm) what God has judged by what they said."]]. This is if what is reported from him is correct.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: We have said: the context of the verse and what follows indicates that the intended meaning is that they wish for death without mubāhalah. That is the apparent wording without doubt. But the meaning mentioned by Ibn Kathir is that they might argue against us and say: "You also say the Last Abode is ours, so wish for it."
* Student: In His saying: ﴿if it is﴾ and ﴿then wish﴾, there is a condition and a response to the condition. Ibn Kathir estimated something between the verb and the response, meaning: "then let us engage in mubāhalah, then he wishes"?
* Shaykh: Yes, then wish for death by way of mubāhalah.
* Student: So the wish comes after the mubāhalah?
* Shaykh: The wish is part of the form of mubāhalah. The wish is part of the form of mubāhalah. You say, for example: "O Allah, whoever among us is a liar, cause him to die," or "let him die." This is part of mubāhalah. So His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾ means: "then engage us in mubāhalah by wishing for death."
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: In any case, we now have the apparent wording and the meaning. So shall we take the apparent wording and say that the objection Ibn Kathir mentioned is refuted, because God informed us that they will never wish for it, and they will never say: "Wish for it yourselves." He did not say: "They will say to you: wish for it." They will not say that, and they will not be inspired to it, because they know, note this, the Jews. If the Jews knew that if they said to the Muslims, "Wish for death in this situation," would they wish for it or not?
* Student: They would wish for it.
* Shaykh: They would wish for it and would not mind. Therefore they will not say to the Muslims, "Wish for death," and they will not wish for it themselves. So remaining with the apparent wording is more appropriate, and God knows best.
* Student: (...) wishing and mubāhalah, meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «If the Jews had wished, they would have died (...) and if those who engage in mubāhalah had come out, they would have returned»[[Reported by Ahmad, no. (2225), and al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra (10995), from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own (mawquf).]]..
* Shaykh: "And they would not have found their families." I do not know whether this is a hadith or not. I do not know. If it is authentic, it indicates that the apparent wording is intended, that is, "then wish for death" in reality, without mubāhalah. Yes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is unseen (ghayb), for martyrdom is unseen. Wishing for martyrdom means that a person dies in a particular state; it does not mean hastening death.
* Student: If we know that the apparent wording (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but for example we know (...). Wishing for martyrdom does not necessitate wishing for death; the meaning of wishing for martyrdom is that you die in a specific state. Yes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: In the way of God. This is of the same kind as completing martyrdom.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. In any case, we prefer the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and we say: their objection against us will not occur, because they know that if they raised that objection against us, we would wish for it, since the purpose is to establish the proof. But they will not do it, because they know the reality of the matter: for whom is the Hereafter?
* Student: For the believers.
* Shaykh: For the Muslims. They know that the Hereafter belongs to the Muslims, because they recognize the Prophet (ﷺ) just as they recognize their sons, and that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and that he brought the truth. They know this, and they know that they themselves are also upon falsehood. But out of envy, as God the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿out of envy that God should send down of His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:90].

God the Exalted said: ﴿Then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾. This is a condition within a condition: ﴿if it is﴾, then wish ﴿if you are﴾. This is a condition within a condition. Which of them comes first? The first or the second?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: The second is the first? ﴿truthful﴾. For the truthful is the one whose truthfulness comes first in their claim, then establishing that the Hereafter is theirs, then wishing for death. Thus whenever one condition enters into another condition, the second is the first. Like the poet's saying:
"If you call upon us for help, if you are terrified, you will find from us strongholds of honour adorned by generosity."
Where are the condition and the condition? "If you call upon us for help, if you are terrified." Certainly, the terror comes before the seeking of help, does it not? So the meaning becomes: that if you are terrified and then seek our help, you will find strongholds of honour adorned by generosity.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the second condition, according to the correct view, does not need a response in this type of construction.

* * *

I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what God has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they reject what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of God before, if you were believers?"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91].
* From this noble verse is derived: the arrogance and obstinacy of the Jews, because they say: "We will not believe except in what was sent down to us."
* The second benefit: whoever opposes the truth for the sake of a leader among the imitators (muqallidun) shares a resemblance with the Jews who ﴿said, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and reject what is beyond it﴾. So if it is said to a person, for example: "This is the judgment of God," and he says: "My school is such-and-such," we say to him: he resembles whom? The Jews. Whether his school is Hanafi, Hanbali, Shafi'i, Maliki, or Zahiri, everyone to whom the truth is made clear and who says "I will not follow it" bears a resemblance to them.
* The third benefit: the condemnation of one who does not believe in the truth.
* And the fourth benefit: the obligation to accept the truth from whoever brings it.
* And the fifth benefit: silencing the opponent by establishing the proof against him from his own deed. How so? God established the proof against these Jews from their own actions, because they said: "We believe in what was sent down to us," yet they had killed the prophets of God who came to them with the Book. Is their claim "we believe in what was sent down to us" true or not? It is not true, because if they were truly believers they would not have killed them. For this reason He said: ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of God before, if you were believers?﴾.
* Among the benefits also: the Messenger is called a Prophet, because His saying ﴿the prophets of God﴾ means His messengers, since they killed those to whom the message had been conveyed.
* And in it also is evidence that faith requires accepting the truth from whoever brings it, by His saying ﴿if you were believers﴾, for it is obligatory upon you not to kill them but to accept from them.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs; then you took the calf [as deity] after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:92].
* In this verse also: establishing the proof against the obstinacy of the Jews. How so?
* Student: (...) they took the calf.
* Shaykh: Moses had come to them with clear proofs.
* Student: After Moses had come to them with clear proofs.
* Shaykh: They took the calf as a deity.
* The second benefit: the foolishness of these Jews. Why?
* Student: (...) Because they saw the truth and then turned away from it.
* Shaykh: This is evidence of their obstinacy, but what about their foolishness, and that they have no sound judgment?
* Student: Their taking the calf as a deity.
* Shaykh: Correct. Their taking the calf as a deity. There is no doubt that this is foolishness: a calf that you take as a god.
* The third benefit: these Jews worshipped the calf out of wrongdoing, not out of ignorance, but they were wrongdoers.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And what is its place in i'rab? The sentence?
* Student: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).
* Shaykh: A circumstantial clause, from the subject of ﴿you took﴾.
* The fourth benefit: these Jews seized the opportunity of Moses' absence, which indicates their awe of him, since they seized the opportunity of his absence because they feared him? 
* Student: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs; then you took the calf﴾, meaning: during his absence..
* Shaykh: From where did you derive it in the verse?
* Student: I derived it from another verse.
* Shaykh: A verse other than this one.
* Student: ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾ (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ (after him), in accordance with His saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾, meaning: after Musa (Moses).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and listen." They said, "We hear and we disobey." And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief. Say: "Wretched is what your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ [al-Baqarah 92].

* From this verse it is derived that Allah took the covenant from the Children of Israel to have faith. From where is this derived?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The second benefit: that the Children of Israel did not believe except unwillingly and against their noses (i.e., forced)?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* The third benefit: a demonstration of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Above them.
* The fourth benefit: a proof that the affair of the whole universe is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, glorified and exalted, is able to break customary norms?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾, because this is a breaking of the customary norm, which shows that the whole affair of the universe is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation to receive the Sharia of Allah with strength, without laziness or slackness. From where do we take it?
* Student: ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾. The obligation is that a person receives the Sharia of Allah with strength and resolve, not with slackness and laziness.
* Student: Shaykh, did Allah give them the strength, or did they take it with strength?
* Shaykh: No. ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾ means: accept the Sharia of Allah with strength and vigor.
* Among the benefits of this verse: a demonstration of the rebelliousness (ʿutuww) of the Children of Israel. You will not find a verse without this benefit in it. From where do we take the rebelliousness of the Children of Israel?
* Student: ﴿with strength﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿with strength﴾? No, my brother.
* Student: ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾. This is the most eloquent expression of rebelliousness, and we seek refuge with Allah. Had they not heard, it would have been said they were excused by their ignorance. But ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: hearing is of two kinds: hearing of acceptance (istijabah) and hearing of perception (idrak). From where do we take that hearing is of two kinds: hearing of acceptance and hearing of perception?
* Student: His saying: ﴿And listen. They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾.
* Shaykh: Which of them is it: the hearing of perception or the hearing of acceptance?
* Student: From their saying ﴿We hear﴾, it is the hearing of perception.
* Shaykh: Yes. And where is the hearing of acceptance?
Also among the benefits of the verse: the true believer is not commanded by his faith to commit sins.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿if you are believers﴾ means: if you were truly believers, you would not have taken the calf as a god.
* Also among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, Exalted, does not attribute evil to Himself, but mentions it in the passive form. From where do we take it?
* Student: ﴿commands you﴾.
* Shaykh: No. Do you understand the question? The benefit of the verse is that evil, or what is similar to it, is not attributed by Allah to Himself; He attributes it in the passive voice. From His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink into their hearts﴾. Allah did not say, "Allah cast into their hearts the love of the calf," but He said ﴿they were made to drink into their hearts﴾. Is there a parallel to it in the Qur'an? And what is it?
* Student: ﴿And that we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10].
* Shaykh: ﴿And that we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾.
* Student: What is the benefit, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: The benefit is that evil and what derives from it is not attributed by Allah to Himself in the active voice, but in the passive voice. Because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Evil is not attributed to You" [Muslim (771/201), from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib]. Is it understood, everyone?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: This was covered for us in the chapter on divine decree (qadar) in creed (ʿaqidah), and we mentioned that evil is in the object, not in the act. Allah's decree: everything is by the decree and predestination of Allah, even as the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Even incapacity and shrewdness" [Muslim (2655/18), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar], and good and evil. But evil, in relation to Allah's act of it, is good, not evil. It is good, because Allah only created it for a profound wisdom and a praiseworthy end, even if it is evil. I think we mentioned about eight benefits for the creation of disliked things and evils. Perhaps, God willing, some of them are in your memory, or (...)?
* Student: Some of them...
* Shaykh: In any case, this benefit must be known: that the act of Allah is never evil, whatever it is; all of it is good, because Allah is Wise. But evil is in what? In the objects and the creatures. As for the act itself, it is not evil. We gave the example of a man who cauterizes his son with fire. Fire is painful and burning, but he wants him to be healed. So this object that results from the agent is painful and burning evil, but the cauterizing itself, for its praiseworthy end, is what?
* Student: It is good.
* Shaykh: It is good.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "If the Last Abode with Allah is exclusively yours, apart from the people, then wish for death, if you are truthful."﴾ In this verse there is a refutation of the Jews who said: "For us is the Hereafter and for you is the world," ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. What is its refutation? What is its refutation?
* Student: ﴿Say: "If the Last Abode is yours"﴾.
* Shaykh: No. What is the refutation of the Jews in this?
* Student: ﴿then wish for death﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿then wish for death﴾, and Allah said: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth﴾.
* The second benefit, which is based on a difference over the interpretation of the verse: the permissibility of mubahalah (mutual invocation of curse) to establish the truth. However, it is based on a difference over the interpretation of the verse. From where do we take it?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿then wish for death﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, from His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾. And what is this opinion we pointed to, which we said is based on it being a case of mubahalah?
* Student: That their interpretation, that His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾ is on (...), if you claim that the Hereafter is exclusively yours.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is one view. The second view is that the verse is meant in its apparent sense and is not a case of mubahalah. We mentioned that Ibn Kathir weakened it and said: if the matter were so, they would also have obligated us with it. We explained that what Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned is not binding, since if they had referred the matter to the Prophet, peace be upon him, they would have wished for death. But they did not refer it, because they were the claimants, so the obligation fell on them.
* There is also in it a proof, which comes with this proof, of the lie of the Jews in what they claim, and we have mentioned this. And in it also is a proof: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, that the disbeliever dislikes death because of what he knows of the bad outcome?
* Student: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾? His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: No. We said: because of what he dislikes of the bad outcome?
* Student: ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾.
* Another student: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth﴾.
* Shaykh: The proof is taken from ﴿because of what their hands have put forth﴾, meaning that they know they will be punished for their sins, so they cannot wish for death, lest they reach the punishment. In the verse there is also a proof for establishing causation (sababiyyah). From where do we take it?
* Student: From the letter bāʾ.
* Shaykh: From the bāʾ in His saying ﴿because of what their hands have put forth﴾. Who among the people of innovation (ahl al-bidʿah) denies causes?
* Student: The Qadariyyah.
* Shaykh: The Qadariyyah, no.
* Student: The Ash'arites.
* Shaykh: And who else? The Jahmiyyah. The Ash'arites and the Jahmiyyah. The Mu'tazilah, on the contrary, make it obligatory that there be a cause in origin, and they make the cause necessitating, and for this reason they hold that it is obligatory for Allah, as has passed, to do what is good or best, with differences among them.
In it is also the establishment of knowledge for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From where do we take it?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: And what is the indication of the meaning from His saying ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Then what is the evidence that this indicates Allah's knowledge? And what is the indication of its implying Allah's knowledge?
* Student: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: Apparently it is an arrow without an archer. ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, you say in it the establishment of Allah's knowledge. What is its basis?
* Student: The establishment of Allah's knowledge is in it. The question would be ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, His saying: ﴿Knowing﴾.
* Shaykh: No, it is correct: in ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ the establishment of knowledge is present. But is the establishment of knowledge also present in ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾?
* The students: That is, ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾ means that Allah is Knowing... His knowledge that they will never wish for it.
* Shaykh: Because they did not wish for it. Allah said: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, and in fact they did not wish for it. So the matter occurred as He reported, which shows that what is known is in accordance with His knowledge, or not?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: If they had wished for it, far be it from that, the matter would not indicate this. But they will never wish for it, and in fact they did not wish for death. Had they wished for it, they would have died.
* And in it also is the establishment of knowledge in another part of the verse, in His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾.
* And in it also is a proof for the permissibility of specifying a general statement for the purpose of threat, or for a better and more comprehensive purpose: specifying a general statement for a purpose.
* Student: In His saying ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, Allah is Knowing of everyone (...).
* Shaykh: Of the wrongdoers and others. But He specified them here for the purpose of threat. Do you understand now? We are not saying only knowledge; can all general statements be restricted to some of their instances for a purpose?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 92–95 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf [for worship] after him while you were wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:92]

His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ﴾ (*wa-la-qad jaakum*, "and indeed he came to you"). The *lam* here is the *lam* of preparation for an oath (*al-lam al-muwatti'ah lil-qasam*), and *qad* is for confirmation (*lil-tahqiq*). We have already noted that when *qad* precedes a past-tense verb it is for confirmation, and when it precedes a present-tense verb it is for diminution (*lil-taqlil*). However, it may also be for confirmation, as in His saying: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ مَا أَنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ﴾ [an-Nur 24:64] ("Indeed He knows what you are upon"), and His saying: ﴿قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الْمُعَوِّقِينَ مِنْكُمْ﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:18] ("Indeed Allah knows those among you who hinder"). In these, *qad* is undoubtedly for confirmation and not for diminution. If we say that the *lam* is for emphasis, *qad* is for confirmation, and the *lam* is the preparation for an oath, then the sentence is emphasized by three emphatics.

﴿وَلَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ﴾: The address is to the Jews. The evidence that it is to the Jews is His saying ﴿مُوسَى﴾ (Moses), because Moses was their prophet. Here He addressed them by the category of the people, not by the individuals, since Moses did not come to those who were present in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ); rather, he came to the Children of Israel, of whom they are a part.

His saying ﴿بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾ (*bil-bayyinat*, "with the clear proofs"): The *ba'* here is for accompaniment (*lil-musahabah*) or for transitivity (*lil-ta'diyah*). That is, "he came to you accompanied by the clear proofs," or "the clear proofs are what he brought," in which case it is for transitivity. The meaning of *al-bayyinat* is an adjective for an omitted noun, i.e., "with the clear signs" (*bil-ayat al-bayyinat*), meaning the signs indicating his prophethood. Among them: the hand, the staff, the stone, the splitting of the sea, the locusts sent upon the family of Pharaoh, the years of drought, and many other things: the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood.

His saying ﴿بِالْبَيِّنَاتِ﴾: *al-bayyin* means "the manifest," i.e., they are signs manifest as evidence of his prophethood. Despite this, He says ﴿ثُمَّ اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ ("then you took the calf"). *Thumma* ("then") indicates a delay, i.e., sequence with an interval. That is, after a period of time had passed in which you were able to contemplate these signs and recognize them, what actually happened is that you did not raise your heads to them: ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ ("you took the calf after him"). ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ﴾ (*ittakhadhtum*, "you took"): we passed over this recently. What is it among its uses? It is *al-tasyir* (making something into something). Among its uses is *al-tasyir*, as in ﴿اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ خَلِيلًا﴾ [an-Nisa 4:125] ("Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend"), meaning He made him. So this verb takes two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate. The first object is *al-'ijl* (the calf) in ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾. Where is the second object?

*Student:* "A god" (*ilahan*).

*Shaykh:* It is omitted, its estimated form being "a god." Omitting what is known is permissible.

His saying ﴿الْعِجْلَ﴾ (*al-'ijl*, "the calf"): it is the young of the cow, and it was not a calf of a living animal; rather, it was a calf made of jewelry. They fashioned a calf from jewelry, and the Samiri misled them and led them astray. This calf had a lowing (*khuwar*). It is said that this was a real lowing, and it is said that it was the sound of the wind entering from its back and exiting from its mouth. But, may Allah protect us, he (the Samiri) said to them: ﴿هَذَا إِلَهُكُمْ وَإِلَهُ مُوسَى فَنَسِيَ﴾ [Taha 20:88] ("This is your god and the god of Moses, but he forgot"). This is because Moses had left them to his Lord's appointment, which was thirty days, and Allah increased it by ten, so it became forty days. He said to them: Moses has gone astray from his god, and this is why he is late and has not returned. He has gone astray and has not been guided to his god. So this is your god and the god of Moses, may Allah protect us. So they took it as a god. This indicates the foolishness of the Children of Israel, because they were the ones who made this jewelry with their own hands, so how could it be a god? Nevertheless, they took it as a god after Moses had gone.

His saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ (*min ba'dihi*, "after him"): Does it mean after his death, or after his departure for his Lord's appointment?

*Students:* After his departure.

*Shaykh:* After his departure for his Lord's appointment. This is the only possibility, because Moses returned to them and said to the Samiri regarding his god: ﴿لَنُحَرِّقَنَّهُ ثُمَّ لَنَنْسِفَنَّهُ فِي الْيَمِّ نَسْفًا﴾ [Taha 20:97] ("We will surely burn it, then we will surely scatter it into the sea, scattering"), and this was carried out. Moses, peace be upon him, burned it and scattered it into the sea, into the ocean.

﴿وَأَنْتُمْ ظَالِمُونَ﴾ (*wa-antum zalimun*, "while you were wrongdoers"): *zalimun* means transgressors (*mu'tadun*). The root meaning of *zulm* is deficiency, and aggression is called *zulm* because it is a deficiency in the right of the one who is wronged. I say: the root meaning of *zulm* is deficiency, based on His saying: ﴿كِلْتَا الْجَنَّتَيْنِ آتَتْ أُكُلَهَا وَلَمْ تَظْلِمْ مِنْهُ شَيْئًا﴾ [al-Kahf 18:33] ("Both gardens yielded their produce and did not fall short of it in anything"), i.e., did not diminish. The clause ﴿وَأَنْتُمْ ظَالِمُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) in the accusative position. It is a circumstantial clause from what? From the subject of ﴿اتَّخَذْتُمُ﴾, meaning "while the reality is that you are wrongdoers." Which is more severe in ugliness: that a person takes an ugly deed while he is a wrongdoer who knows he is wrongdoing, or that he takes it while he is ignorant? The first is more severe. Yes indeed.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* No, more than this, because His saying ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا مُوسَى تِسْعَ آيَاتٍ بَيِّنَاتٍ﴾ [al-Isra 17:101] ("We had certainly given Moses nine clear signs") does not imply restriction. He did not say, for example, "the signs are the nine." And even if He had said it, it would have been (...).

*Student:* What is the distinction of these nine?

*Shaykh:* The distinction of these nine is that they became a proof against the Children of Israel, because of the destruction of their enemy and its manifestation through them. So they are stronger than others and greater.

He said: ﴿وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَكُمْ﴾ (*wa-idh akhadhna mithaqakum*, "and when We took your covenant"). ﴿إِذْ﴾ (*idh*, "when"): what is its *i'rab* (grammatical analysis)? This appears often in the Qur'an, and the scholars parse it as an object of an omitted verb, whose estimated form is "remember" (*udhkur*). If the address is to more than one person, it is estimated as "remember" in the plural (*udhkuru*): "remember when We took your covenant." *Mithaq* means covenant, and the covenant was named *mithaq* because it is secured (*yatawaththaq*) by it (...).

from taking the Torah, and they began to witness it. When they saw the mount above them as if it were a canopy, they prostrated, prostrating out of fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They began looking at the mountain while they pleaded to Allah, glorified and exalted, that He remove it from them. For this reason, some people of knowledge mentioned that they considered the best prostration with which they could prostrate to Allah to be prostrating with their eyes toward the sky, saying: "This prostration is one by which Allah saved us, so it is the most noble prostration for us." Thus, when one prostrates, his head is raised in such a way.

﴿وَرَفَعْنَا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ﴾ ("and We raised the mount above you") as a threat to them. ﴿خُذُوا﴾ (*khudhu*, "take"): an imperative verb, and it is in the accusative position as a quoted speech of an omitted saying, i.e., "We said: take what We have given you." ﴿بِقُوَّةٍ﴾ (*biquwwatin*, "with strength"): meaning with diligence and vigor. Diligence is firm resolve, and vigor is the strength in carrying it out. What is meant by "what We have given you"? What is its meaning?

*Students:* The Torah.

*Shaykh:* The Torah.

﴿وَاسْمَعُوا﴾ (*wasma'u*, "and listen"): a command to listen, and it is not listening with the ear, but listening in submission and response. They were commanded to take the Torah with strength and to listen, i.e., to respond and submit. The answer was: ﴿قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾ ("They said: We heard and we disobeyed"), may Allah protect us, "we heard with our ears and disobeyed with our deeds." They did not listen with the listening that was demanded of them; rather, they were arrogant toward it.

His saying: ﴿قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾: The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that they said this verbally: ﴿سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾. Some said: "They said 'we heard' with their tongues, but they disobeyed with their deeds," so the expression of disobedience refers to their actions, and they did not say with their tongues, "We disobeyed." But we say, in rebuttal to this view: what prevents them from saying ﴿سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾, when they are the ones who said to Moses: ﴿لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّى نَرَى اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:55] ("We will not believe you until we see Allah openly")? What is the obstacle? Those who were bold enough to say "we will not believe you until we see Allah openly" would be bold enough to say "we heard and we disobeyed." It seems that those who said that the meaning of disobedience here is the act of disobedience, and not that they said with their tongues "we disobeyed," were saying that they committed themselves to this while the mountain was over their heads. Whoever is in this condition cannot possibly say this matter; one who has a mountain above him cannot say "we heard and we disobeyed." But we say: there is no obstacle to the firm intention they displayed, after the threat was lifted from them, being the reality of the matter.

What is disobedience? Disobedience is opposing a command. If you wish, say: it is leaving obedience. This disobedience is departing from obedience, whether that is in opposing what is commanded or in committing what is forbidden. Do you understand? Disobedience occurs in abandoning what is commanded and in committing what is prohibited. So whoever abandons congregational prayer, which is obligatory for him, is a disobedient person, and it is appropriate to say: "This one disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." And whoever commits adultery, steals, or drinks wine is also disobedient to Allah and His Messenger.

﴿قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا وَأُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْعِجْلَ﴾ ("They said: We heard and we disobeyed, and the calf was made to sink into their hearts"), may Allah protect us. ﴿أُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ﴾ (*ushribu fi qulubihim*, "were made to imbibe into their hearts"): some said that it is with an omitted modifier, i.e., "the love of the calf was made to sink into their hearts," because the calf itself cannot be absorbed into the heart. The meaning of *ushribu* is that this love was made as if it were water given to drink to the heart. So it mixed with the heart, did it not? It mixed with it, just as water mixes with clay (*al-madar*) when it is soaked into it. Do you know *al-madar*? Who knows it?

*Student:* Sugar and lemon.

*Shaykh:* No. *Al-madar* is dried clay. People here call it (*al-jumh*); I do not know whether it is Arabic or colloquial. Dried clay is called *madar*.

*Student:* O Shaykh, *al-madar* is red clay?

*Shaykh:* No, it is not required to be red. Do you mean pottery?

*Student:* No, here we call red clay *madar*, not this clay.

*Shaykh:* No, every dried clay is called *madar*. The point is that this heart, may Allah protect us, had the calf made to sink into it. But He expressed it with the calf to indicate their love for it, because it is more forceful, as if the calf itself had entered their hearts. This is more emphatic, may Allah protect us.

His saying ﴿أُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ﴾: Who made this sink into their hearts? Allah, glorified and exalted. But it is part of the eloquence of the Qur'an that what Allah dislikes is often expressed in the passive voice, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «وَالشَّرُّ لَيْسَ إِلَيْكَ» ("and evil is not attributed to You")[[Recorded by Muslim (771/201) from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Allah, the Exalted, said about the jinn: ﴿وَأَنَّا لَا نَدْرِي أَشَرٌّ أُرِيدَ بِمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ أَمْ أَرَادَ بِهِمْ رَبُّهُمْ رَشَدًا﴾ [al-Jinn 72:10] ("And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance"). They said: "evil was intended" (*shar ureed*, passive), and they did not attribute it to Allah, but they attributed guidance to Allah. The point is that these people, may Allah protect us, had the calf made to sink into their hearts, and this is a trial: that something Allah does not approve of should sink into a person's heart, may Allah protect us.
