This is among the greatest trials, whether it is the love of a worshipped thing or the love of a sought-after thing. The love of wealth may sink into a person's heart until he forgets the interests of his religion and his worldly life. The love of marriage may sink into a person's heart until it sometimes leads him into what is forbidden, may Allah protect us. Measure everything else by this.

Allah, glorified and exalted, may test a servant with affliction because he is worthy of being tested in that way. For this reason He said: ﴿أُشْرِبُوا فِي قُلُوبِهِمُ الْعِجْلَ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾ ("the calf was made to sink into their hearts because of their disbelief"). The *ba'* here is causal (*lil-sababiyyah*), i.e., because of their disbelief in Allah that preceded the worship of the calf. This is because they, may Allah protect us, had intended sin before they fell into it, and so they became disbelievers in Him. Then the calf was made to sink into their hearts until they could no longer turn away from it. Aaron, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿يَا قَوْمِ إِنَّمَا فُتِنْتُمْ بِهِ وَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمُ الرَّحْمَنُ فَاتَّبِعُونِي وَأَطِيعُوا أَمْرِي﴾ [Taha 20:90] ("O my people, you are only being tested by it. Indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command"), even though Aaron was the deputy and successor of Moses. But what was their answer to Aaron? ﴿لَنْ نَبْرَحَ عَلَيْهِ عَاكِفِينَ حَتَّى يَرْجِعَ إِلَيْنَا مُوسَى﴾ [Taha 20:91] ("We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us"). They persisted, may Allah protect us, because the calf had been made to sink into their hearts by their disbelief.

﴿قُلْ بِئْسَمَا يَأْمُرُكُمْ بِهِ إِيمَانُكُمْ﴾ ("Say: Wretched is what your faith commands you to do"). *Qul* (say): whom does Allah address? Moses?

*Student:* The Prophet (ﷺ).

*Shaykh:* He addresses the Prophet (ﷺ), or He addresses anyone to whom the address can be directed, i.e., "Say, O addressee," or "Say, O Prophet."

﴿بِئْسَمَا يَأْمُرُكُمْ بِهِ إِيمَانُكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Wretched is what your faith commands you to do, if you are believers"). ﴿بِئْسَ﴾ (*bi'sa*, "wretched"): here is it a past-tense verb that is fixed (*jamid*) or one that is inflected (*mutasarrif*)?

*Students:* Fixed.

*Shaykh:* Fixed. Do you know the fixed verb from the non-fixed?

*Student:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* And what is the fixed verb?

*Student:* The fixed verb is one that is not inflected.

*Shaykh:* Such as?

*Student:* *Bi'sa* (...).

*Shaykh:* *'Asa*?

*Student:* *'Asa* is fixed.

*Shaykh:* Some say that it may be *ya'su* or *ya'si*, but the more correct view is that it is fixed.

*Shaykh:* And *laysa*?

*Student:* Fixed.

*Shaykh:* Fixed.

A fixed past-tense verb used to express dispraise.

His saying ﴿بِئْسَمَا﴾: What is the *i'rab* of *ma*? It is an indefinite noun in the accusative position, built on sukun, in the accusative position as a specifier (*tamyiz*), i.e., "wretched is a thing your faith commands you to do." *Bi'sa*, *ni'ma*, and similar words require a specified item (*mukhassas*). Where is the specified item? It is omitted, indicated by the context, i.e., "wretched is a thing your faith commands you to do: the worship of the calf." That is, if the worship of the calf is what your faith requires, then does your faith command you with a sound matter or with an ugly matter? With an ugly matter. That is, where is your faith when the calf has been made to sink into your hearts? This faith you claim, which made the worship of the calf beloved to you, and you worshipped it.

Is the attribution of the command to faith real or not? Yes, it is real. This is because it has already been noted that there is no metaphorical expression in the Qur'an, based on the view that words have no inherent meanings, and that their meanings are understood from context and circumstantial indicators. So the "command" of faith to them means what faith requires. For example, you love a thing; what does your love for it require? Inclination toward it and eagerness to obtain it. You hate a thing; what does your hatred of it require? Aversion from it and distance from it, and not reaching it by any means. So their faith, which they claim, commanded them with a matter that faith does not require, namely the worship of the calf.

His saying ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("if you are believers"): this is a conditional clause for the category, and its purpose is challenge, i.e., "if you are truly believers, how can your faith command you with this ugly deed?" Allah, glorified and exalted, said ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ because He had earlier mentioned about them: ﴿وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ آمِنُوا بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ قَالُوا نُؤْمِنُ بِمَا أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْنَا﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91] ("When it is said to them, 'Believe in what Allah has revealed,' they say, 'We believe in what was revealed to us'"). Was it revealed to them that they should worship the calf? No, that was not revealed to them. So if you are truly believers, why does your faith command you with this ugly act, which is the worship of the calf?

*Student:* O Shaykh, the *i'rab* of *ma*?

*Shaykh:* Regarding the *i'rab* of *ma*, we say: it is an indefinite noun, built on sukun, in the accusative position as a specifier.

*Student:* A specifier (...)?

*Shaykh:* A specifier of the omitted subject.

*Student:* The subject of *bi'sa*?

*Shaykh:* The omitted subject of *bi'sa*.

*Student:* (...).

*Shaykh:* It is not far-fetched. For this reason, we preferred that this view is the reality, and that what is meant is not abandoning action. Those who went to the view that it is an expression for abandoning action said: "They could not say ﴿سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا﴾ while the mountain was over their heads, so this must be what is meant." But we say: this is not an obstacle, because they say that when the threat was lifted from them. Such words do not concern them; they do not mention what happened to them before.

*Student:* O Shaykh, is the estimate of *ma* "wretched is the thing that your faith commands you to do"?

*Shaykh:* No, "wretched is a thing" (*bi'sa shay'an*), because the specifier must be indefinite and cannot come definite.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿قُلْ إِنْ كَانَتْ لَكُمُ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ خَالِصَةً مِنْ دُونِ النَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُا الْمَوْتَ﴾ ("Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is exclusively yours, apart from the people, then wish for death").

﴿قُلْ إِنْ كَانَتْ لَكُمُ الدَّارُ الْآخِرَةُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ خَالِصَةً﴾: Is *kana* here complete or incomplete?

*Students:* Incomplete. Complete.

*Shaykh:* Complete?

*Student:* Incomplete.

*Shaykh:* Incomplete. Where is its predicate? It is permissible for its predicate to be the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿لَكُمُ الدَّارُ﴾ ("for you is the abode"), with ﴿خَالِصَةً﴾ ("exclusively") being a circumstantial modifier of ﴿الدَّارُ﴾, meaning "in the state of being exclusively ﴿خَالِصَةً مِنْ دُونِ النَّاسِ﴾ (apart from the people)." It is also permissible that the predicate is ﴿خَالِصَةً﴾: "Say: If the Last Abode is exclusively yours, apart from the people." The meaning is the same either way.

God says: ﴿Say, "If the Last Abode with God is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of other people"﴾. By "the Last Abode" is meant Paradise. He said this, or was commanded to say it, because they had said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:80], and then (they claimed) you would be left in the Fire while we would be in Paradise. This is the speech of the Jews. What does the one who says this claim? He claims that the Last Abode belongs to him exclusively, to the exclusion of people. For this reason the Jews claim that they are "the chosen people of God" and say, "God has preferred us over the worlds," and they claim that the Hereafter belongs to them alone, and that whoever among them deserves the Fire enters it for a few days and then leaves for Paradise. So God says: ﴿Say, "If the Last Abode with God is yours exclusively"﴾. The exegetes explained "exclusive" as meaning "specifically yours," because the meaning of ﴿exclusively﴾ is "specific." It is also possible that the intended meaning of "exclusive" is that which nothing mixes with, meaning that no one shares it with you. Both meanings lead to the same result.

And His saying: ﴿then wish for death﴾. The fā' (then)? What is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the fā'?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The answer to what?
* Student: The condition (shart).
* Shaykh: And what is it?
* Student: "Say."
* Shaykh: "If it is" is the linking element (rābiṭah). The response had to be linked to it with the fā' because the verb after it is an imperative, and they have said that it is obligatory to link the response with the fā' in seven places.
* Student: Six.
* Shaykh: Six places?
* Shaykh (reciting the verse): Nominal (ismiyyah), imperative (ṭalabiyyah), and the one with a non-derived noun, and with mā, qad, lan, and with the future particle (tanfīs).
Seven places, in which it is obligatory that the fā' be joined.

And His saying: ﴿wish for death﴾, meaning: seek its occurrence. Wishing (tamannī) is also seeking the occurrence of something beloved, is it not? How is that? Because if ﴿the Last Abode with God is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of other people﴾, then the Last Abode is better than this world, and what does a person wish for? That he moves to what is better. If you were in an old, dilapidated house, and you feared it would fall on you, would you say, "I wish I lived in a new house"?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: You would say that. These people say: "The Hereafter is ours." And if the Hereafter is theirs, then the Hereafter is without doubt better than this world. So if you see that the Hereafter is yours, it becomes necessary for you to wish for death in order to reach what is better. Do you understand? This is a challenge to them. For this reason God the Exalted says here: ﴿but they will never wish for it, ever﴾, and likewise in Surat al-Jumu'ah He says: ﴿and they will never wish for it, ever﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:7]. This is because God knows that they will not wish for it, so He challenged them with it, since it is not possible for them to wish for it, as they love this world more than the Hereafter, as will come later. The apparent meaning of the noble verse, as we have explained now, is that God commanded His Prophet to challenge them: if the Last Abode is yours, as you claim, then wish for death so that you may reach it. This is without doubt the apparent meaning of the noble verse, and it is what Ibn Jarir and many exegetes preferred.

Some scholars held that the intended meaning of ﴿then wish for death﴾ is: then engage us in mutual imprecation (mubāhalah), and wish death upon whichever of us is lying. This is like His saying in Surat Ali 'Imran: ﴿Whoever disputes with you concerning him after knowledge has come to you, say: "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves; then let us invoke earnestly and invoke the curse of God upon the liars"﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:61]. And what would be the meaning of wishing for death? By way of what? By way of mubāhalah. Ibn Kathir preferred this, and he weakened the first view on the basis that if the intended meaning were that they wish for the occurrence of death, they would argue against us too and say: "You also, if you say the Last Abode is yours, then wish for death," because the challenge being directed at us with this is no more appropriate than our challenge to you with it. They could then say: "We do not wish for death, because you too say the Last Abode is yours, and that the Jews after the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ) are in the Fire. So will you wish for death too?" This is not valid, because we do not wish for death, and it is not legislated for us to wish for death. The best of people is one whose life is long and whose deeds are good. A person wishes that God extend his life so that he may increase righteous deeds from which he benefits, and does not wish for death. Even if he is among the most pious of people, he does not wish for death.

This meaning which Ibn Kathir inclined to is really very strong, though it contradicts the apparent context. But it is strong, very strong. Those who adopted the apparent context said: "We take by it, because the setting is one of challenge, and God knew that they would not do it, and they were not wishing for death, nor would they respond to us by saying: 'You wish for it.' They are the claimants, and God knew that they would never wish for it, nor would they say: 'Wish for it yourselves.'" As we said, this is a specific matter about which God spoke, and He informed us of what the outcome would be without the event occurring. God says: ﴿but they will never wish for it﴾. But the second is: ﴿and they will never wish for it, ever﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:7]. So which do we take? We take what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires, and we say: this is a particular matter about which God informed us that it will not occur. Or we take what the general meaning that Ibn Kathir adopted supports.
* Student: (...) Does the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) clarify the meaning?
* Shaykh: They did not mention an occasion of revelation. Ibn 'Abbas's apparent statement is that it concerns mubāhalah. It is well known that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) is referred to in tafsir, because he was a Companion who devoted himself to tafsir, and the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicated for him that Allah teach him ta'wil [[Reported by al-Bukhari (75), and Ahmad (2397), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him).]].
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, it can be mubāhalah in another manner, because the mubāhalah with the Christians mentioned in Surat Ali 'Imran was a mubāhalah with the Christians who said what they said about 'Isa. They were asked to engage in mubāhalah, but they refused, submitted, and agreed to pay the jizyah. As for these, it is mubāhalah with the Jews.
* Student: Is wishing for death not permissible?
* Shaykh: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: «None of you should wish for death because of a harm that has befallen him. If he must, let him say: O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is good for me, and cause me to die when death is good for me» [[Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (6351), and Muslim (2680/10), from the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him).]].
* Student: And if he fears trial (fitnah)?
* Shaykh: As for if he fears trial, he says: «O Allah, if You intend a trial for Your servants, then take me to You without being tried» [[Reported by al-Tirmidhi (3233), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. He does not say, "Cause me to die," because he does not know; perhaps his remaining in the trial is good for him and for others. Perhaps God will save people through his hands, people who would not have been saved had he not been among them. He says: «take me to You without being tried».
* Student: So if he knows his weakness, for example?
* Shaykh: He says these words: «take me to You without being tried», thereby restricting the request for death to being untried, whether now or after some time.
* Student: Mubāhalah (...)?
* Shaykh: Mubāhalah is as God said: ﴿we call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:61]. The two groups gather and invoke God, the Exalted and Most High, that the curse of God be upon the liar, or that the liar dies, or that such and such happens to the liar. In reality, mubāhalah exposes one to affliction; therefore a person should not engage in mubāhalah except when it is in the interest of Islam. When it is in the interest of Islam, there is no harm. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) rejected the issue of al-'awl (increase of shares in inheritance) and said: "Whoever wishes, I will engage him in mubāhalah" [[Reported by Sa'id ibn Mansur (37), and its wording: "Let them gather, and let us place our hands on the corner (of the Ka'bah), then we will invoke and place the curse of God upon the liars, (if they do not affirm) what God has judged by what they said."]]. This is if what is reported from him is correct.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: We have said: the context of the verse and what follows indicates that the intended meaning is that they wish for death without mubāhalah. That is the apparent wording without doubt. But the meaning mentioned by Ibn Kathir is that they might argue against us and say: "You also say the Last Abode is ours, so wish for it."
* Student: In His saying: ﴿if it is﴾ and ﴿then wish﴾, there is a condition and a response to the condition. Ibn Kathir estimated something between the verb and the response, meaning: "then let us engage in mubāhalah, then he wishes"?
* Shaykh: Yes, then wish for death by way of mubāhalah.
* Student: So the wish comes after the mubāhalah?
* Shaykh: The wish is part of the form of mubāhalah. The wish is part of the form of mubāhalah. You say, for example: "O Allah, whoever among us is a liar, cause him to die," or "let him die." This is part of mubāhalah. So His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾ means: "then engage us in mubāhalah by wishing for death."
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: In any case, we now have the apparent wording and the meaning. So shall we take the apparent wording and say that the objection Ibn Kathir mentioned is refuted, because God informed us that they will never wish for it, and they will never say: "Wish for it yourselves." He did not say: "They will say to you: wish for it." They will not say that, and they will not be inspired to it, because they know, note this, the Jews. If the Jews knew that if they said to the Muslims, "Wish for death in this situation," would they wish for it or not?
* Student: They would wish for it.
* Shaykh: They would wish for it and would not mind. Therefore they will not say to the Muslims, "Wish for death," and they will not wish for it themselves. So remaining with the apparent wording is more appropriate, and God knows best.
* Student: (...) wishing and mubāhalah, meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «If the Jews had wished, they would have died (...) and if those who engage in mubāhalah had come out, they would have returned»[[Reported by Ahmad, no. (2225), and al-Nasa'i in al-Sunan al-Kubra (10995), from Ibn 'Abbas as a statement of his own (mawquf).]]..
* Shaykh: "And they would not have found their families." I do not know whether this is a hadith or not. I do not know. If it is authentic, it indicates that the apparent wording is intended, that is, "then wish for death" in reality, without mubāhalah. Yes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is unseen (ghayb), for martyrdom is unseen. Wishing for martyrdom means that a person dies in a particular state; it does not mean hastening death.
* Student: If we know that the apparent wording (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but for example we know (...). Wishing for martyrdom does not necessitate wishing for death; the meaning of wishing for martyrdom is that you die in a specific state. Yes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: In the way of God. This is of the same kind as completing martyrdom.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. In any case, we prefer the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and we say: their objection against us will not occur, because they know that if they raised that objection against us, we would wish for it, since the purpose is to establish the proof. But they will not do it, because they know the reality of the matter: for whom is the Hereafter?
* Student: For the believers.
* Shaykh: For the Muslims. They know that the Hereafter belongs to the Muslims, because they recognize the Prophet (ﷺ) just as they recognize their sons, and that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and that he brought the truth. They know this, and they know that they themselves are also upon falsehood. But out of envy, as God the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿out of envy that God should send down of His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:90].

God the Exalted said: ﴿Then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾. This is a condition within a condition: ﴿if it is﴾, then wish ﴿if you are﴾. This is a condition within a condition. Which of them comes first? The first or the second?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: The second is the first? ﴿truthful﴾. For the truthful is the one whose truthfulness comes first in their claim, then establishing that the Hereafter is theirs, then wishing for death. Thus whenever one condition enters into another condition, the second is the first. Like the poet's saying:
"If you call upon us for help, if you are terrified, you will find from us strongholds of honour adorned by generosity."
Where are the condition and the condition? "If you call upon us for help, if you are terrified." Certainly, the terror comes before the seeking of help, does it not? So the meaning becomes: that if you are terrified and then seek our help, you will find strongholds of honour adorned by generosity.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the second condition, according to the correct view, does not need a response in this type of construction.

* * *

I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what God has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they reject what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of God before, if you were believers?"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91].
* From this noble verse is derived: the arrogance and obstinacy of the Jews, because they say: "We will not believe except in what was sent down to us."
* The second benefit: whoever opposes the truth for the sake of a leader among the imitators (muqallidun) shares a resemblance with the Jews who ﴿said, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and reject what is beyond it﴾. So if it is said to a person, for example: "This is the judgment of God," and he says: "My school is such-and-such," we say to him: he resembles whom? The Jews. Whether his school is Hanafi, Hanbali, Shafi'i, Maliki, or Zahiri, everyone to whom the truth is made clear and who says "I will not follow it" bears a resemblance to them.
* The third benefit: the condemnation of one who does not believe in the truth.
* And the fourth benefit: the obligation to accept the truth from whoever brings it.
* And the fifth benefit: silencing the opponent by establishing the proof against him from his own deed. How so? God established the proof against these Jews from their own actions, because they said: "We believe in what was sent down to us," yet they had killed the prophets of God who came to them with the Book. Is their claim "we believe in what was sent down to us" true or not? It is not true, because if they were truly believers they would not have killed them. For this reason He said: ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of God before, if you were believers?﴾.
* Among the benefits also: the Messenger is called a Prophet, because His saying ﴿the prophets of God﴾ means His messengers, since they killed those to whom the message had been conveyed.
* And in it also is evidence that faith requires accepting the truth from whoever brings it, by His saying ﴿if you were believers﴾, for it is obligatory upon you not to kill them but to accept from them.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs; then you took the calf [as deity] after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:92].
* In this verse also: establishing the proof against the obstinacy of the Jews. How so?
* Student: (...) they took the calf.
* Shaykh: Moses had come to them with clear proofs.
* Student: After Moses had come to them with clear proofs.
* Shaykh: They took the calf as a deity.
* The second benefit: the foolishness of these Jews. Why?
* Student: (...) Because they saw the truth and then turned away from it.
* Shaykh: This is evidence of their obstinacy, but what about their foolishness, and that they have no sound judgment?
* Student: Their taking the calf as a deity.
* Shaykh: Correct. Their taking the calf as a deity. There is no doubt that this is foolishness: a calf that you take as a god.
* The third benefit: these Jews worshipped the calf out of wrongdoing, not out of ignorance, but they were wrongdoers.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And what is its place in i'rab? The sentence?
* Student: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).
* Shaykh: A circumstantial clause, from the subject of ﴿you took﴾.
* The fourth benefit: these Jews seized the opportunity of Moses' absence, which indicates their awe of him, since they seized the opportunity of his absence because they feared him? 
* Student: ﴿And Moses had certainly come to you with clear proofs; then you took the calf﴾, meaning: during his absence..
* Shaykh: From where did you derive it in the verse?
* Student: I derived it from another verse.
* Shaykh: A verse other than this one.
* Student: ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾ (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾ (after him), in accordance with His saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِهِ﴾, meaning: after Musa (Moses).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and listen." They said, "We hear and we disobey." And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief. Say: "Wretched is what your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ [al-Baqarah 92].

* From this verse it is derived that Allah took the covenant from the Children of Israel to have faith. From where is this derived?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The second benefit: that the Children of Israel did not believe except unwillingly and against their noses (i.e., forced)?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* The third benefit: a demonstration of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Above them.
* The fourth benefit: a proof that the affair of the whole universe is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, glorified and exalted, is able to break customary norms?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾, because this is a breaking of the customary norm, which shows that the whole affair of the universe is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation to receive the Sharia of Allah with strength, without laziness or slackness. From where do we take it?
* Student: ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾. The obligation is that a person receives the Sharia of Allah with strength and resolve, not with slackness and laziness.
* Student: Shaykh, did Allah give them the strength, or did they take it with strength?
* Shaykh: No. ﴿Hold firmly to what We have given you﴾ means: accept the Sharia of Allah with strength and vigor.
* Among the benefits of this verse: a demonstration of the rebelliousness (ʿutuww) of the Children of Israel. You will not find a verse without this benefit in it. From where do we take the rebelliousness of the Children of Israel?
* Student: ﴿with strength﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿with strength﴾? No, my brother.
* Student: ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾. This is the most eloquent expression of rebelliousness, and we seek refuge with Allah. Had they not heard, it would have been said they were excused by their ignorance. But ﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: hearing is of two kinds: hearing of acceptance (istijabah) and hearing of perception (idrak). From where do we take that hearing is of two kinds: hearing of acceptance and hearing of perception?
* Student: His saying: ﴿And listen. They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾.
* Shaykh: Which of them is it: the hearing of perception or the hearing of acceptance?
* Student: From their saying ﴿We hear﴾, it is the hearing of perception.
* Shaykh: Yes. And where is the hearing of acceptance?
Also among the benefits of the verse: the true believer is not commanded by his faith to commit sins.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿if you are believers﴾ means: if you were truly believers, you would not have taken the calf as a god.
* Also among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, Exalted, does not attribute evil to Himself, but mentions it in the passive form. From where do we take it?
* Student: ﴿commands you﴾.
* Shaykh: No. Do you understand the question? The benefit of the verse is that evil, or what is similar to it, is not attributed by Allah to Himself; He attributes it in the passive voice. From His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink into their hearts﴾. Allah did not say, "Allah cast into their hearts the love of the calf," but He said ﴿they were made to drink into their hearts﴾. Is there a parallel to it in the Qur'an? And what is it?
* Student: ﴿And that we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn 10].
* Shaykh: ﴿And that we know not whether evil is intended for those upon the earth or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾.
* Student: What is the benefit, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: The benefit is that evil and what derives from it is not attributed by Allah to Himself in the active voice, but in the passive voice. Because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Evil is not attributed to You" [Muslim (771/201), from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib]. Is it understood, everyone?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: This was covered for us in the chapter on divine decree (qadar) in creed (ʿaqidah), and we mentioned that evil is in the object, not in the act. Allah's decree: everything is by the decree and predestination of Allah, even as the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Even incapacity and shrewdness" [Muslim (2655/18), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar], and good and evil. But evil, in relation to Allah's act of it, is good, not evil. It is good, because Allah only created it for a profound wisdom and a praiseworthy end, even if it is evil. I think we mentioned about eight benefits for the creation of disliked things and evils. Perhaps, God willing, some of them are in your memory, or (...)?
* Student: Some of them...
* Shaykh: In any case, this benefit must be known: that the act of Allah is never evil, whatever it is; all of it is good, because Allah is Wise. But evil is in what? In the objects and the creatures. As for the act itself, it is not evil. We gave the example of a man who cauterizes his son with fire. Fire is painful and burning, but he wants him to be healed. So this object that results from the agent is painful and burning evil, but the cauterizing itself, for its praiseworthy end, is what?
* Student: It is good.
* Shaykh: It is good.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "If the Last Abode with Allah is exclusively yours, apart from the people, then wish for death, if you are truthful."﴾ In this verse there is a refutation of the Jews who said: "For us is the Hereafter and for you is the world," ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾. What is its refutation? What is its refutation?
* Student: ﴿Say: "If the Last Abode is yours"﴾.
* Shaykh: No. What is the refutation of the Jews in this?
* Student: ﴿then wish for death﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿then wish for death﴾, and Allah said: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth﴾.
* The second benefit, which is based on a difference over the interpretation of the verse: the permissibility of mubahalah (mutual invocation of curse) to establish the truth. However, it is based on a difference over the interpretation of the verse. From where do we take it?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿then wish for death﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, from His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾. And what is this opinion we pointed to, which we said is based on it being a case of mubahalah?
* Student: That their interpretation, that His saying ﴿then wish for death﴾ is on (...), if you claim that the Hereafter is exclusively yours.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is one view. The second view is that the verse is meant in its apparent sense and is not a case of mubahalah. We mentioned that Ibn Kathir weakened it and said: if the matter were so, they would also have obligated us with it. We explained that what Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned is not binding, since if they had referred the matter to the Prophet, peace be upon him, they would have wished for death. But they did not refer it, because they were the claimants, so the obligation fell on them.
* There is also in it a proof, which comes with this proof, of the lie of the Jews in what they claim, and we have mentioned this. And in it also is a proof: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, that the disbeliever dislikes death because of what he knows of the bad outcome?
* Student: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾? His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: No. We said: because of what he dislikes of the bad outcome?
* Student: ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾.
* Another student: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth﴾.
* Shaykh: The proof is taken from ﴿because of what their hands have put forth﴾, meaning that they know they will be punished for their sins, so they cannot wish for death, lest they reach the punishment. In the verse there is also a proof for establishing causation (sababiyyah). From where do we take it?
* Student: From the letter bāʾ.
* Shaykh: From the bāʾ in His saying ﴿because of what their hands have put forth﴾. Who among the people of innovation (ahl al-bidʿah) denies causes?
* Student: The Qadariyyah.
* Shaykh: The Qadariyyah, no.
* Student: The Ash'arites.
* Shaykh: And who else? The Jahmiyyah. The Ash'arites and the Jahmiyyah. The Mu'tazilah, on the contrary, make it obligatory that there be a cause in origin, and they make the cause necessitating, and for this reason they hold that it is obligatory for Allah, as has passed, to do what is good or best, with differences among them.
In it is also the establishment of knowledge for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From where do we take it?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: And what is the indication of the meaning from His saying ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Then what is the evidence that this indicates Allah's knowledge? And what is the indication of its implying Allah's knowledge?
* Student: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾.
* Shaykh: Apparently it is an arrow without an archer. ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, you say in it the establishment of Allah's knowledge. What is its basis?
* Student: The establishment of Allah's knowledge is in it. The question would be ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, His saying: ﴿Knowing﴾.
* Shaykh: No, it is correct: in ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ the establishment of knowledge is present. But is the establishment of knowledge also present in ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾?
* The students: That is, ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾ means that Allah is Knowing... His knowledge that they will never wish for it.
* Shaykh: Because they did not wish for it. Allah said: ﴿But they will never wish for it﴾, and in fact they did not wish for it. So the matter occurred as He reported, which shows that what is known is in accordance with His knowledge, or not?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: If they had wished for it, far be it from that, the matter would not indicate this. But they will never wish for it, and in fact they did not wish for death. Had they wished for it, they would have died.
* And in it also is the establishment of knowledge in another part of the verse, in His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾.
* And in it also is a proof for the permissibility of specifying a general statement for the purpose of threat, or for a better and more comprehensive purpose: specifying a general statement for a purpose.
* Student: In His saying ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, Allah is Knowing of everyone (...).
* Shaykh: Of the wrongdoers and others. But He specified them here for the purpose of threat. Do you understand now? We are not saying only knowledge; can all general statements be restricted to some of their instances for a purpose?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 96–105 (part 1 of 10):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life﴾. This (...).

* Student: What is the ruling on mubahalah (mutual invocation of divine curse)?
* Shaykh: The ruling on mubahalah is that it is permissible in important matters aimed at establishing the truth and refuting falsehood. It has been narrated that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, denied 'awl (the proportional reduction of heirs' shares when the total of the fixed shares exceeds the estate, a rule of inheritance known as al-faraid) and said: "Whoever wishes, I will invoke a curse upon him concerning this. Indeed, the One who counted the grains of sand of 'Alij cannot allow it to be applied to the estate." [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (6/253).]] He then mentioned the shares that necessitate 'awl.
So it is not objectionable for a person to invoke a curse regarding important matters in order to establish the truth, but on the condition that he has knowledge of the matter, lest the matter turn out to be otherwise and he be mistaken.
* Student: Shaykh, did the Messenger ﷺ invite them (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, he invited them, but they did not respond. He invited the delegation of Najran. As for the story of the Jews, it is not reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invited them to mubahalah. However, Ibn Kathir used to favor this view and say: "There is no evidence for this matter."
* Student: How is mubahalah performed? How is mubahalah?
* Shaykh: Mubahalah originates from ibtihal (earnest supplication) to Allah through prayer. For example, I say such-and-such and you say such-and-such. You say: "Come, let us gather and say: 'The curse of Allah be upon the liars,' or 'whichever of us is lying will be afflicted with such-and-such,'" or something similar.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life, and [more covetous] than those who associated others with Allah﴾. The lam here is a preface to an oath, and the sentence is emphasized by the lam and by the heavy nun of emphasis in His words ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ (la-tajidannahum, "you will surely find them"), and by the implied oath, which is: "By Allah, you will surely find them." Here, the dal in ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ is fatha, and it is a present-tense verb with no particle governing it to put it in the accusative. So why is the dal vowelled with fatha?
Because it is attached to the nun of emphasis, and a present-tense verb attached to the nun of emphasis is built on fatha. And His words ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ is a verb that we have studied recently, which governs two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate. The first object is the ha' in ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾, and the second object is ﴿أَحْرَصَ النَّاسِ﴾.
The address in ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ is either addressed to the Messenger ﷺ, since he is the first one addressed by the Quran, and an address to the leader or imam is an address to his followers. So every address in the Quran to the Messenger ﷺ is an address to his community, except what the evidence shows is specific to him, such as His words ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast? And We removed from you your burden﴾ [al-Sharh 1–2], and what is similar to it, which is specific to him. The address is to the Messenger, or it is addressed to anyone who can be addressed; that is, "you will surely find them, O you who are addressed by this noble Quran." To whom is the noble Quran addressed?
* Students: All people.
* Shaykh: All people, it is addressed to all people. He said: ﴿you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life﴾. ﴿أَحْرَصَ﴾ is a comparative form (ism tafdil), ﴿أَحْرَصَ النَّاسِ﴾ is a comparative form. And what is ḥirs (covetousness)? Ḥirs is: that a person is greedy for a thing and anxious about losing it. Greed for a thing together with anxiety about losing it is called ḥirs, and ḥirs necessitates exerting effort. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ said: "Be eager for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up." [[Narrated by Muslim (2664/34) from Abu Hurayrah, with the wording: "... and do not be incapable."]]
* Student: Shaykh, the waw?
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: The waw of ḥayawa?
* Shaykh: Ḥayawa?
* Student: It is written with a waw, I am saying: the waw, what?
* Shaykh: On (ḥayawa). May Allah keep you safe. This is the old orthography, the old script of the Mushaf in this form. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, saw that it is better to retain the old 'Uthmanic orthography as it was. Otherwise it would be (ḥayat) with an alif.
* Student: Some people make mistakes, the ones who cannot...?
* Shaykh: Yes, the ones who cannot be read, we do not understand. For this reason the scholars differed on this issue, and I think we have mentioned their opinions to you. We said: the scholars differed regarding the writing of the noble Quran: must it remain in the 'Uthmanic script (rasm 'Uthmani), or is it permissible to transfer it to the conventional script (al-rasm al-istilahi), or is there a distinction between the scholar and the ignorant?
We mentioned three opinions in this regard, and that the correct view is that it is permissible. Because if the convention at the time of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, when he wrote the Mushaf, had been other than this convention, he would have written it according to it. And was the Quran revealed as something recited or as something written?
* Students: Recited.
* Shaykh: Recited. Nevertheless, what has been mentioned (...) is feared, meaning that some of those who spell out the Quran letter by letter, and who have not received it orally from the mouths of shaykhs, say: al-ṣalāh is also written (al-ṣalawh), and al-zakāh likewise, and al-ribā with a waw, and so on. For this reason, it is most important that a person recites the Book of Allah under the guidance of a reciter who teaches him until he knows it perfectly.

﴿the most covetous of people for life﴾ ﴿you will surely find them﴾, meaning the Jews. ﴿the most covetous of people for life﴾: here ﴿حَيَاة﴾ is indefinite and he did not say "the life." So it means that they are covetous of life, even if it is little, even if they are given only a single moment; they are the most covetous of people for it. It is not the complete, long life; rather, it is any life for which they are covetous.

He said: ﴿and [more covetous] than those who associated others with Allah﴾. The exegetes differed regarding His words ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا﴾ (and of those who associated others with Allah): is it the beginning of a new statement, separate from what precedes it, with the implied meaning: "And of those who associated others with Allah is one who wishes that he would live a thousand years"? Although this is possible in wording, it is very far in meaning. Therefore, the correct view is the second opinion: that it is conjoined to His words ﴿النَّاسِ﴾ (people). That means: "you will surely find them the most covetous of people, and more covetous than those who associated others with Allah." That is, the Jews are more covetous than the polytheists, despite the fact that the Jews are People of the Book who believe in resurrection, Paradise and Hellfire, while the polytheists do not believe in that. Whoever does not believe in resurrection becomes the most covetous of people for life, because he thinks that when he dies, that is the end; he will not return. So you find him greedy for this life, which he regards as his capital, and he sees no other life. So these Jews are the most covetous of people, even more than those who associated others with Allah. This is the correct view, and it is an instance of specifying something after a general category. Why? Because the polytheists are from where?
* Students: From the people.
* Shaykh: From the people. The polytheists are from the people. So the most covetous of people and [more covetous than] those who associated others with Allah, even though the polytheists are among the people. So he is more covetous than this category of people who do not believe in resurrection.

His words ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا﴾ mean: "with Allah." The details of shirk are not what is discussed here. Its place is, God willing, in the Book of Tawhid, where it is said that tawhid is divided into three categories, and each category of tawhid has a corresponding category of shirk. These three categories each divide into minor and major, and also into hidden and manifest.
* Student: The first opinion.
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا﴾, the first opinion.
* Shaykh: The first opinion says that this is separate from what precedes it, and that the meaning of the verse is: "And of those who associated others with Allah is one who wishes that he would live a thousand years." His words: ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا يَوَدُّ أَحَدُهُمْ لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ﴾ (And of those who associated others with Allah is one who wishes that he would be granted a life of a thousand years). ﴿يَوَدُّ﴾: what is the meaning of al-mawadda?
* Student: Wishing.
* Another student: Loving.
* Shaykh: Loving and wishing. And His words ﴿أَحَدُهُمْ﴾ (one of them): to whom does the pronoun refer? The Jews or the polytheists?
* Student: To the Jews, if we take the second opinion, it refers to the Jews.
* Shaykh: As for the first opinion, it is clear that it refers only to the polytheists. The second opinion allows that the pronoun refers to the Jews, in which case the sentence ends at His words ﴿أَشْرَكُوا﴾. It also allows that it refers to the polytheists: ﴿one of them wishes that he would be granted a life of a thousand years﴾. Which of these do you consider more likely?
* Student: The second is more eloquent.
* Shaykh: The second is more eloquent? That it refers to the polytheists? What is its reasoning?
* Student: It refers to the Jews, since the polytheists, one of them wishes to live a thousand years, and the Jews are eager for life, so the Jews are greater in this.
* Another student: Shaykh, can we say that the Jews are included among the polytheists, meaning they have shirk?
* Shaykh: No, no, that is not correct, it is not right.
* Student: It refers to the Jews because the address...
* Shaykh: Is it preferred by the context? Preference by context? And there is also preference by meaning. If ﴿يَوَدُّ أَحَدُهُمْ﴾ refers to the polytheists, Mahmud [al-Zamakhshari] held that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, which is more likely. Mahmud gave two reasons: first, that the pronoun originally refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun, and the polytheists are nearest here. Second, if the polytheist wishes to live a thousand years, and the Jew is more covetous of life than him, then the Jew must wish to live more than a thousand years. Is that not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: If we say the pronoun refers to the Jews, the context supports it, but it indicates that the one who wishes for a thousand years is who?
* Students: The Jews.
* Shaykh: The Jews. So it becomes clear that the first is more eloquent, because if they are more covetous than the polytheist who wishes to live a thousand years, that is greater proof that they—that is, the Jews—love life.

His words ﴿أَحَدُهُمْ لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ أَلْفَ سَنَة﴾ (one of them wishes he would be granted a life of a thousand years): ﴿لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ﴾. What is the meaning of al-ta'mir? It is an increase in lifespan, and lifespan is life.
His words ﴿لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ﴾: is this (law) conditional?
* Student: No, it is not conditional.
* Shaykh: It is not conditional, but it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya). Whenever it comes after (wadda), it is masdariyya: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam 9]: ﴿وَدُّوا لَوْ تُدْهِنُ﴾, so (law) here is masdariyya. ﴿They would wish that they were out among the desert Bedouins﴾ [al-Ahzab 20]: ﴿يَوَدُّوا لَوْ أَنَّهُمْ بَادُونَ فِي الْأَعْرَابِ﴾. So this (law) is masdariyya; whenever (law) comes after (wadda), it is masdariyya. And what is the meaning of masdariyya? It means that (law) and what follows it are interpreted as a verbal noun, so it is said: "one of them wishes his longevity" (yawaddu ahadahum ta'mirahu). ﴿ألف سنة﴾ a thousand years, known. And the sanah (year): it is the lunar year. What is meant by sanah here? The solar (Gregorian) year or the lunar year?
* Student: The Gregorian.
* Shaykh: The Gregorian?
* Student: Because they follow the Gregorian calendar, their reckoning is by the Gregorian calendar. This is clear (...).
* Shaykh: The Gregorian calendar is a recent development, and the Jews do not recognize the Messiah as a prophet. Words, when used without qualification, are interpreted according to their legal meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them four are sacred﴾ [al-Tawbah 36]. So the measure of time that Allah set for His servants is by lunar months: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say, "They are measures of time for the people and for Hajj"﴾ [al-Baqarah 189]. For whom? For the Arabs and for Hajj? ﴿for the people and for Hajj﴾, all people. Therefore, this latter calendar is not based on any principle of religion; it is not a religious calendar. All calendars, as far as we know, until this one came about, were based on the lunar calendar, because it is a visible, sensory sign. But are these European months a visible sensory sign?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: Not at all. They are purely conventional. Some of them reach thirty-one days, and others return to twenty-eight, without any reason or cause. So they are not based on any principle. Some calculators have tried to convert these months into a fixed number, making the year thirteen months instead of twelve, and some have tried to make them a fixed number without adding months, but the clergy rose against this.
(...) ﴿And glad tidings for the believers. Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il—indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah 97–98].
* Shaykh: His words ﴿مَنْ كَانَ عَدُوًّا﴾ (whoever is an enemy): to whom does it refer?
* Student: Those who say that Jibril is an evil spirit that descends for wars.
* Shaykh: He is our enemy? Who said that?
* Student: The Jews.
* Shaykh: The Jews. His words ﴿لِجِبْرِيلَ﴾ (to Jibril): are there variant readings?
* Student: ﴿جَبْرِيل﴾, ﴿جَبْرَئِل﴾ and ﴿جَبْرَائِيل﴾.
* Shaykh: Well done. Is Jibril an angel or a prophet?
* Student: An angel.
* Shaykh: An angel entrusted with a task?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: With what?
* Student: With bringing the Quran down to the Messenger ﷺ.
* Shaykh: With revelation. He is entrusted with revelation.
His words ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾ (indeed, he has brought it down): is this the response of the conditional or does it indicate it?
* Student: It indicates it.
* Shaykh: Where is the response of the conditional?
* Student: The clause.
* Shaykh: Where is the clause?
* Student: ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, so it is the response of the conditional. Are you disagreeing with Mustafa, who said it indicates it? Do you disagree with him?
* Student: I disagree.
* Shaykh: Good. Disagreement toward good is good.
* Student: It has been said that the response of the conditional is ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾, this is the response of the conditional. It has also been said that it is not the response of the conditional, but rather a reason for the response, and the response of the conditional is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "then let him die of rage."
* Shaykh: What do you say about this answer?
* Students: Correct.
* Shaykh: Correct. Which of them is closer?
* Student: The closer one is that it is omitted.
* Shaykh: The closer one is that it is omitted?
* Student: The one I preferred.
* Shaykh: The one you preferred, or the one I preferred?
* Student: I preferred it.
* Shaykh: Me? What do you say?
* Student: No, the more likely view is that it is the response of the conditional.
* Shaykh: That it is the response of the conditional? Because the basic principle is?
* Student: Because the basic principle is the presence of the response of the conditional.
* Shaykh: Non-omission. The basic principle is non-omission. Then His words, "then let him die of rage," in this style, mean an estimate that is not appropriate. Although He says: ﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾ [Al 'Imran 119], yet in this context it is not appropriate. The correct view is that His words ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾ are the response of the conditional. But what is its connection? What is the connection between His words ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾ and His words ﴿مَنْ كَانَ عَدُوًّا لِجِبْرِيلَ﴾?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, not grammatically, but semantically. Grammatically, it is the response of the conditional. Semantically?
* Student: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, indeed he has brought it down upon your heart﴾, indeed he brought the Quran down upon the heart of a human being.
* Shaykh: But what is the semantic connection between the response of the conditional and the protasis?
* Student: That is, those who say Jibril is their enemy: the enemy always brings evil things, while Jibril, peace be upon him, brings things sent down from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so he brings good things.
* Shaykh: It is as if it were a reason for the ruling. The meaning is: ﴿whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾, indeed, there is nothing in him that merits enmity except that he has brought it down upon your heart, and this should not be a cause for enmity. In rhetoric they say: emphasizing a dispraise by means resembling praise, and emphasizing praise by means resembling dispraise. This resembles that. A poet says:

"And there is no fault in them, save that their swords
bear notches from the clashing of the battalions."

They have no fault except this. Is this a fault or a praise?
* Students: Praise.
* Shaykh: Praise. But it is emphasizing a dispraise by means resembling praise. So the correct view is that this is the response of the conditional.
His words ﴿عَلَى قَلْبِكَ﴾ (upon your heart): why was the heart chosen? ﴿نَزَّلَهُ عَلَى قَلْبِكَ﴾, why did He not say "upon you"? Why did He specify the heart?
* Student: Because it is the seat of knowledge, the place of...
* Shaykh: Of comprehension, the place of understanding and comprehension. His words ﴿بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ (by the permission of Allah): what is meant by "the permission of Allah" here?
* Student: By the command of Allah.
* Shaykh: By the command of Allah? Correct.
* Student: Is it not valid to say by His will?
* Shaykh: It is valid (...), the meaning is the command.
Permission is divided into two types: permission that is cosmic (kawni) and permission that is legislative (shar'i). Whatever relates to legal rulings is legislative permission; the permission of Allah is of two kinds: legislative and decreed (qadari). Whatever relates to legal rulings is legislative, and whatever relates to cosmic matters, such as creation, provision, governance and the like, is decreed permission. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent [lies] against Allah?﴾ [Yunus 59]. What is this? Is it legislative or decreed?

**Students:** Legislative (sharʿi).

**Shaykh:** Legislative, because by divine decree (qadar) He has permitted them to do it. They made lawful what they willed and prohibited what they willed. ﴿Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 42:21]

**Student:** Legislative.

**Shaykh:** Legislative. What is the evidence that it is legislative?

**Student:** His saying: ﴿prescribed﴾.

**Shaykh:** His saying: ﴿prescribed for them in religion﴾. Also, it is permitted by decree (qadar). What they prescribed in religion is permitted by decree. Had He not permitted it, it would not have happened. Had He not permitted it by decree, it would not have occurred. So they prescribed in religion what Allah did not permit by legislation (shar'an), but He permitted it by decree (qadaran).

﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255] Is this permission legislative or decreed (kawni qadari)?

**Students:** Both decreed and legislative.

**Shaykh:** ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ This is decreed (kawni), because it relates to governance and action. ﴿Intercede﴾ is a verb connected with Allah's permission and decree. So the permission meant here is the decreed, universal permission.

The difference between them in meaning and in effect: In meaning, whatever relates to legal rulings is legislative permission (idhn shar'i), and whatever relates to cosmic matters is decreed permission (idhn kawni). In effect: with legislative permission, the permitted act may or may not occur. With decreed permission, it must occur.

A second difference, also from (...): legislative permission concerns what Allah is pleased with and loves: ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:3]. Decreed permission may concern what Allah is pleased with, or what He is not pleased with. Is this understood, everyone?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Here in the verse: ﴿He has brought it down upon your heart by permission of Allah﴾. Which of the two kinds is this?

**Students:** Decreed.

**Shaykh:** Decreed. ﴿Confirming what was before it﴾: ﴿confirming﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). A circumstantial clause of whom? Of the pronoun in ﴿He has brought it down﴾. That is: He sent it down while it confirms what is before it. ﴿What was before it﴾ means what came before it, since "what is before it" has already preceded you. What is meant by "what is before it" is the Torah, the Gospel, and other books that foretold the revelation of the Qur'an. The Qur'an's confirmation of them has two aspects.

The first aspect: Did it bear witness to their truthfulness or not?

The second aspect: It came in agreement with what they had foretold. Thus it confirmed them in fact, because they themselves foretold this Qur'an, and it came confirming them.

﴿And guidance﴾ is conjoined to ﴿confirming﴾. Guidance (hudan) means indication (dalalah), and it may also mean success (tawfiq). The Qur'an is likewise guidance in the sense of indication and in the sense of success. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿By it Allah guides those who pursue His approval to the ways of peace﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:16]. This is undoubtedly the guidance of success, because the guidance of indication is for everyone, whether they follow Allah's approval or not. But the guidance of success is only for those who follow Allah's approval.

﴿A guidance and good tidings﴾: ﴿good tidings﴾ means glad tidings (bishara). Glad tidings is information about what gladdens, though it may also come in information about what harms, as in His saying: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21].

﴿For the believers﴾: Here faith (iman) means legislative faith, not the linguistic faith that is familiar among people, which is merely assent (tasdiq). In reality, faith is not identical to assent, and so it differs from assent in what it relates to. One says "he believed in it (amana bihi)" but does not say "he assented to it (saddaqa bihi)", or does one say it?

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** One says "saddaqa bihi," but it is not like... it does not follow the pattern of "amana bihi." It has another meaning. Furthermore, faith indicates security and stability. For this reason some scholars said that it applies to unseen matters and not to perceptible matters. This may be open to question, because when Allah said to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ he said: ﴿Yes, but to be assured in my heart﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:260]. Here his heart was strengthened by a perceptible matter. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:3]. This shows that faith may be in what is witnessed, otherwise His saying ﴿in the unseen﴾ would serve no purpose.

In any case, faith here is in reality: assent that includes what?

**Student:** Acceptance and submission.

**Shaykh:** It must include acceptance and submission: acceptance regarding reports and submission regarding rulings. If there is neither acceptance nor submission, it is not faith, even if... We have mentioned many proofs of this, that mere assent is not faith.

Here Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾. Does ﴿for the believers﴾ relate to ﴿guidance and good tidings﴾, or only to the second?

**Student:** Only to the second.

**Shaykh:** If we say it relates only to the second, there is no difficulty. If we say it relates to the first, there is a difficulty, because the Qur'an is guidance for mankind, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿The month of Ramadan is that in which the Qur'an was revealed as guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185]. In that case, if we say the phrase relates to both guidance and good tidings together, it requires an explanation of how to reconcile it with His saying: ﴿guidance for the people﴾. The reconciliation is to say: the guidance meant here is the guidance of benefit, meaning what benefits and is followed as guidance is only for the believers. Allah the Blessed and Exalted says about man in the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, be he grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan 76:3]. That is, whether he is grateful or ungrateful, Allah has guided him to the way, meaning He made it clear to him, manifest and explained. But among people there are those who are grateful and among them those who are ungrateful.

**Student:** Often it comes (...).

**Shaykh:** It does come, but qualified. It only comes qualified.

**Student:** What is the difference between the two?

**Shaykh:** There is a difference between them, like the difference between motion and rest. If we say ﴿confirming what was before it﴾ means that it bears witness to their truthfulness, does this mean that it says these books are true and from Allah, which requires us to believe in them? That is if we say "confirming them" means bearing witness to their truthfulness. And if we say it agrees with what they foretold, its meaning is that they foretold that the Qur'an would descend, and it descended. There is a difference between them.

**Student:** In rulings, meaning (...)?

**Shaykh:** It is well known that our faith in the previous books is not the faith of witnesses. Rather, it is faith of assent and following, in what our Sharia requires us to follow them in. As for what our Sharia contradicts, ﴿For each of you We prescribed a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48].

**Student:** Shaykh, His saying about Ramadan: ﴿guidance for the people﴾, do we not restrict "the people" to the believers?

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** Then what is the meaning of guiding others?

**Shaykh:** The guidance of indication, like the verse we recited to you: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, be he grateful or ungrateful﴾.

**Student:** There is no difficulty with that one, but Ramadan presents a difficulty. What is the meaning of guiding non-believers?

**Shaykh:** Yes, He guides them by indication. ﴿Guidance for the people﴾ means indication for them.

**Student:** Does the Qur'an refer back to it?

**Shaykh:** The Qur'an is indication, yes, indication throughout the whole Qur'an.

**Student:** So it does not refer back to the month?

**Shaykh:** No, it does not refer back to the month. It refers to the Qur'an. He said: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and messengers and Jibril and Mikal - then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. ﴿Whoever﴾ (man): is it a conditional noun or not, or is it a conditional particle?

**Student:** Conditional.

**Shaykh:** Conditional. The evidence for that is its response: ﴿then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. So it is conditional.

His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah﴾, following His saying ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾, is evidence that whoever is an enemy to Jibril is an enemy to Allah. This is supported by the authentic hadith: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him." [Reported by al-Bukhari (6502) from Abu Hurayrah.] ("I have declared war against him") means: I have declared war upon him. So the connection with what precedes it is that whoever is an enemy to Jibril is an enemy to Allah.

His saying ﴿and His angels﴾ means and an enemy to His angels. "Angels" is the plural of "malak" (angel). They said that "malak" is derived from "al-alukah," which is message, because Allah says: ﴿who makes the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir 35:1]. So "malaika" means messengers, that is, messengers. His saying ﴿and His angels﴾ indicates that enmity toward Jibril is enmity toward all the angels, because the reality is that such enmity is enmity toward a person represented in a genus. An enemy of one member of this class is an enemy of all.

His saying ﴿and His messengers﴾: There is no mention of the messengers in the noble verse, but it is known that whoever is an enemy to the angels is an enemy to the messengers (peace be upon them), because the angels, especially Jibril, descend upon the messengers with revelation, victory, and support: ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed"﴾ [al-Anfal 8:12]. So whoever is an enemy to the angels is an enemy to the messengers, and an enemy to others too, namely their followers.

His saying ﴿and Jibril and Mikal﴾: Jibril is well known, and there are the previously mentioned readings. I have ﴿Jabra'il﴾ and ﴿Jabra'il﴾, the previously mentioned readings.

His saying ﴿Mikal﴾: there are two other readings, namely ﴿Mika'il﴾ and ﴿Mika'il﴾, like Jibril. Whoever is an enemy to Jibril is also an enemy to Mika'il. It has already been mentioned that the Jews used to say: "Who is our friend among the angels? Mika'il. As for Jibril, he is our enemy." But Allah the Exalted clarified in this noble verse that whoever is an enemy to Jibril is an enemy to Mika'il as well, because Mika'il and Jibril are both messengers who carry out what they were commanded. Just as Mika'il is charged with rain and plants, Jibril is charged with what?

**Student:** With revelation.

**Shaykh:** With revelation. Both are obedient and submissive. How can you be an enemy to one and not the other, when they are equal in worshipping Allah, the Exalted, and in hearing and obeying Him?

His saying ﴿then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾ is the response of the condition. ﴿Then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾: whoever is an enemy to Allah, Allah is an enemy to him. This is the meaning: whoever is an enemy to Jibril, Allah is an enemy to him; whoever is an enemy to the angels, Allah is an enemy to him; whoever is an enemy to Mika'il, Allah is an enemy to him. Here He said ﴿then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾, and there is a rhetorical point in it. What is it?

**Student:** The shift from the third person (ghayba).

**Shaykh:** It is the explicit noun in place of the pronoun. He did not say "Allah is an enemy to him," for two benefits: one is verbal, and the other is semantic. The verbal benefit is the harmony of verse endings (ra'us al-ayi). Is that right?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Because if He had said "Allah is an enemy to him," the verse would not harmonize with what comes before and after it. So for the harmony of verse endings it came as: ﴿then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾.

If someone says: What is your evidence that Allah the Exalted observes or takes into account the harmony of verse endings? We say: We have evidence in Surah Ta-Ha, where the magicians said: ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:70]. We know of no benefit for this except observing the harmony of verse endings. Otherwise, Musa is always mentioned before Harun, and he deserves precedence because he is superior to him. But in this verse He put Harun before Musa, which shows that among the eloquence of the Qur'an is that its verse endings harmonize, so that there is no dissonance between them. Sometimes they do not harmonize, but there is a reason for it that is understood from the context.

The second benefit is semantic, and it includes two matters:

First: a ruling that whoever is an enemy to Allah and what is joined to Him, the Exalted, is a disbeliever. That is, a ruling that these people are disbelievers.

Second: that every disbeliever, whether the cause of his disbelief is hostility to Allah or not, is an enemy to Allah. Every disbeliever is an enemy to Allah: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:1]. Those meant are the disbelievers of Quraysh. Yet they were not enemies to Jibril; we do not know that they were enemies to Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil.

So the benefit of His saying ﴿then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾ has two benefits. What is the first benefit?

**Student:** Observing the harmony of verse endings.

**Shaykh:** Yes, and that is a verbal benefit. But let us see the second. What is the second?

**Student:** The second: the ruling on whoever is an enemy to Allah.

**Shaykh:** It concerns the meaning, and under it are two matters.

**Student:** The ruling on whoever is an enemy to Allah is disbelief (...)

**Shaykh:** And the second: enmity is not restricted to those who oppose Allah. Allah's enmity toward the disbeliever is not restricted to those who oppose Allah; rather, every disbeliever is an enemy to Allah, the Exalted. So whoever opposes Allah and hates Him, may we be protected, or hates His Sharia, or regards Him as unjust in what He decrees for him, is he a disbeliever or not?

He is a disbeliever, because Allah says: ﴿an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. Whoever is an enemy to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is a disbeliever in Him. Even if he prays, fasts, pays zakat, and performs Hajj, as long as he feels that Allah is his enemy, may we be protected, he is a disbeliever.

From this we understand that the Jews, by this enmity toward Jibril, were disbelievers. Nevertheless, they had the rulings of Jews: taking the jizya from them, allowing them to remain upon their religion, the permissibility of their slaughtered animals, and the permissibility of marrying their women, even though Allah has stated that He is their enemy. But Surah al-Ma'idah is among the last to be revealed, and for this reason the scholars said that all the rulings mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah are firm (muhkam); none of them is abrogated (mansukh). Everything in it is non-abrogated. Then Allah the Exalted said.

**Student:** His saying ﴿and Jibril and Mikal﴾ is the specific following the general (min 'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm)?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it is the specific following the general.

**Student:** The idafa of the angels to the messengers, of what type of idafa is it?

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** ﴿and His angels and His messengers﴾?

**Shaykh:** Because, as you said, whoever is an enemy to one member of a genus is considered an enemy to the whole genus.

**Student:** No, I mean the idafa of Allah to the angels, to Himself?

**Shaykh:** Because they are His messengers.

**Student:** An idafa of worship?

**Shaykh:** An idafa of honor and dignity, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:26-27]. And He said: ﴿then indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you verses that are clear﴾. ﴿Certainly﴾ (la-qad) recurs for us often in the Noble Qur'an, and we have explained that it is?

**Student:** Introductory (mu'attifa).

**Shaykh:** That the lam is introductory to the oath, that qad is for confirmation, and that accordingly the sentence is emphasized with three emphases.

﴿We have sent down to you﴾: sending down (inzal) happens only from above to below. This is because the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and Allah the Exalted is above His servants, having risen over His Throne in a manner befitting Him, the Exalted. Highness is among His essential attributes that are necessarily His, from eternity to eternity, and denying that He is high in His essence is disbelief, because it is among the necessary essential attributes. As for His rising over the Throne, it is among the attributes of action, because it relates to His will. For this reason, reason perceives that Allah the Exalted is on high, but it does not perceive that He has risen over the Throne unless the revelation establishing it were present. We have already mentioned the story of Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni. He, may Allah have mercy on him, had a chair on Friday on which he sat to explain to the people. Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni was one of the Ash'arites among the theologians (mutakallimun), and he used to deny that Allah is on high. He said in the course of his speech: "Allah was, and there was no place; and He is now as He was." What did he mean? The denial that He is above. So someone said to him: who?

**Students:** Abu al-'Ala al-Hamadhani.

The Sheikh: Abu al-'Ala al-Hamadani. Someone said to him: "O Sheikh, set aside the talk of exaltedness. What do you say about what every person finds in himself, who says: 'O Lord,' finding within himself a necessity to seek elevation?" He slapped his head and said: "Al-Hamadani has bewildered me, al-Hamadani has bewildered me," because he had found no answer to it. Matters of innate nature (fitrah) cannot be answered, correct or not?

The students: Correct.

The Sheikh: Now you find the old woman who has not studied and does not understand the Qur'an or anything. When she supplicates, where does she direct her hands? She turns them upward, even though she has not studied and does not understand the Qur'an. This is something necessary and innate. Therefore, the exaltedness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is among the necessary attributes of His essence, among His essential attributes, from which He is never separated, eternally.

His saying: ﴿to you, signs﴾. ﴿Signs﴾ is the plural of (āyah). In language, āyah means a sign, but in reality it is more precise than a sign. A sign is explained by it for clarification, otherwise it is more precise, because it is a sign with evidence. That is, it includes the sign and the proof. The difference between a sign and a proof is that a sign is merely a sign only, whereas a proof is convincing to the soul and necessitates that it submit. This is the difference between a bare sign and a proof. In reality, the āyah is a sign with proof. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, always explain a thing by what is close to it, even if there is a difference between them, as they say: ﴿This is the Book; there is no doubt in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2]. What is the meaning of ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾?

A student: No doubt.

The Sheikh: No doubt. Although rayb is different from shakk (doubt), there is a subtle meaning between them, since rayb is doubt accompanied by anxiety, whereas shakk is absolute doubt, where a person has nothing that necessitates his being anxious because of this doubt. But the commentators explain things by what is close to them, approximately. So the āyāt mean signs, but they are signs, proofs necessitating the soul's affirmation, necessitating affirmation. Are these āyāt that Allah sent down to His Messenger ﷺ cosmic (kawniyyah) or legislative (shar'iyyah)?

The students: Legislative.

The Sheikh: Legislative. The āyāt of Allah are divided into two categories: cosmic and legislative. The night, the day, the sun and the moon are cosmic signs: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ [Fussilat 37]. These are cosmic signs. As for the legislative signs, they are what Allah sent down to His Messenger, and the most noble and greatest of them is this magnificent Qur'an.

His saying: ﴿clear signs﴾. Al-bayyin means the clear, that is, what is clear in its indication and sign. The Qur'an is clear, but observe that it is clear in itself, and it does not necessarily follow that it is explanatory for everyone. Among people, signs increase them in blindness, as Allah the Exalted said in Surah Fussilat: ﴿And it is for them a blindness. Those are called from a distant place﴾ [Fussilat 44], although He says: ﴿This is an explanation for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran 138]. There is no doubt that the Qur'an is an explanation that explains, but it is for the one whom Allah has not blinded in insight. As for the one whom Allah has blinded in insight, may Allah protect us, he does not benefit from the Qur'an: ﴿When Our signs are recited to him, he says: "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 13], because it does not reach his heart and mind, due to the rust that has settled on his heart from what he earned. ﴿No! Rather, what they used to earn has rusted upon their hearts﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 14]. So they are clear in themselves, but does it become an explanation for everyone?

We say: whoever turns away from them and is arrogant, they will not be an explanation for him: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is disease, it adds to their filth, upon their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [At-Tawbah 125]. As for the one who is attentive to them, eager for them, who takes them as a lamp for himself, takes them as a method he follows, then without doubt they are clear signs for him from which he benefits to the utmost.

Therefore He said: ﴿And none disbelieves in them﴾, that is, in these clear signs, ﴿except the defiantly disobedient (al-fāsiqūn)﴾. And ﴿None disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al-Baqarah 99]. Here, kufr means concealment in an approximate sense, but it is implicitly including the meaning of denial (juhūd). For this reason, it takes the preposition bi, so it is said: kafara bihi (he disbelieved in it). As for concealment, it takes a direct object, as in sataraha and satarat-hā (he concealed it, she concealed it). But kufr here takes bi because it includes the meaning of denial, and every denial is undoubtedly a concealment. His saying: ﴿al-fāsiqūn﴾, the fāsiq is one who goes out of obedience, because fisq means going out of obedience. However, fisq is divided into two types: fisq that is meant as the fisq of kufr, and fisq that is meant as what is less than that. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you faith and has made it beautiful in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief, defiance and disobedience﴾ [Al-Hujurat 7]. Here, is fisq different from kufr? It is different from kufr, and the proof for that is that it is conjoined to it, and the basic principle in conjunction is difference.
