Their saying: ﴿bidarrina bihi min ahad﴾ means: neither a husband with his wife nor any person. ﴿Except by the permission of God﴾: the permission of decree, and by it is meant the will; the permission of decree is the will, meaning: except if God wills. If God permits it, they harm; otherwise not, because magic is a cause of harm, and a cause is not an agent in itself, but acts by the powerful influence God placed in it. And He who placed in it this influential power is able to strip it from it, so it does not harm; because causes are not independent in action. For this reason He said: ﴿they could not harm anyone with it except by the permission of God﴾.
He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and they learned what harms them and does not benefit them﴾, and this is the worst kind of learning, ﴿they learned what harms them and does not benefit them﴾; because the sciences a person learns are divided into three kinds: harmful, beneficial, and harmful in one respect and beneficial in another. Harmful and beneficial absolutely, harmful in one respect and beneficial in another; and one may bring a fourth kind: neither harmful nor beneficial, and in reality this is harmful, because it contains the harm of wasting time and occupying oneself with what is more important. So God says here: ﴿what harms them and does not benefit them﴾; thus it is knowledge with no good in it, and a person cannot learn a knowledge that has no benefit but rather harm, unless he is a fool and ignorant.
He said: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾. The lam is a preface to the oath, and "qad" is for confirmation, and on this basis the sentence is emphasized with three emphases: the implied oath, the lam, and "qad". The pronoun in His saying ﴿And they certainly knew﴾ refers to the Jews who followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman, and what was sent down to the two angels of learning magic. These people knew ﴿that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾. This lam is the lam of initiation, and it is suspended from acting, the acting of "knew" ('alima). And from where did they know that? They knew it from the saying of the two angels: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾, and the disbeliever has no share in the Hereafter. These people knew this, but they, God forbid, insisted on practicing this work. His saying ﴿liman ishtarahu﴾: I say the lam is for initiation, suspending "'alima" from acting; "man" is an initiating subject, a relative pronoun, and the clause ﴿ma lahu fi al-akhirati﴾ is the predicate of "man", and it is also the clause ﴿ma lahu fi al-akhirati min khalaq﴾, a clause composed of a subject and predicate, and it is in the position of a nominative predicate of the relative clause ﴿liman ishtarahu﴾. The meaning of "ishtarahu" is: learned it, because these people, in learning it, were as though they were purchasers of a thing, and the purchaser takes the thing out of desire, since the purchaser pays money only for what he loves more than it; so God likened this learning to purchasing, because of the intensity of their attachment to it. His saying ﴿ma lahu﴾ means: what belongs to whoever purchased it. ﴿Fi al-akhirah﴾: the Hereafter is what follows this world, the abode of permanence, since the world is a abode of passage, but the Hereafter is the abode of permanence. ﴿Min khalaq﴾ means: a share. They knew that whoever purchased it has no share in the Hereafter because every disbeliever has no share in the Hereafter; for their share of the Hereafter is what? The Fire, and the Fire is not a share; they wish to be rid of it, saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 107], and they say: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us.' He will say: 'Indeed, you will remain.'﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 77]. Does one who wishes to be freed from what he is in have a share of it? Never, except punishment, and we seek refuge in God: ﴿no share for him in the Hereafter﴾.
God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾. ﴿Wa-labi'sa﴾: what do we say about the parsing of the lam? If we say it is for initiation, it is not suitable, because it entered upon a verbal sentence. But we say: it is a preface to the oath; "by God, wretched is what they sold their souls for." "Bi'sa" is a past-tense verb used to express censure, and it is rigid (non-inflecting). Shall we say it is in the heat?
* Student: It is rigid; it does not inflect.

The Shaykh: It does not inflect; it remains fixed even in the days of summer heat. Likewise (ni'ma, "what an excellent"), ( 'asa, "perhaps"), (laysa, "is not"), and many other verbs that they call the rigid verbs (al-af'al al-jamidah), because they do not change from their place. They do not inflect into the present tense or the imperative. As for His saying ﴿Wretched is what they have sold themselves for﴾: (ma) here is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) serving as the subject of (bi'sa, "wretched is"), and the object of the dispraise is omitted. As for His saying ﴿what they have sold themselves for﴾: (shara) here means (baa), "sold," because (ash-shira') is a sale, while (al-ishtira') is taking, taking the goods. The buyer seeks and the seller brings. Is that right or not? In our colloquial dialect we say: "So-and-so bought (sharaa) such-and-such from so-and-so," meaning he purchased it. But in the Arabic language, no. (Sharaa) means (baa), "sold." ﴿And among the people is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 207]: that is, who sells it. Here, ﴿Wretched is what they have sold themselves for﴾ means: they sold themselves for it. How did they sell themselves for it? Yes: because when they acquired magic, what was the price they paid for this magic? Themselves. In reality they lost themselves. Now in this world they have no gain whatsoever, and in the Hereafter they have no gain either. Therefore He said: ﴿Wretched is what they have sold themselves for, if only they knew.﴾ Here (law, "if only") should be begun with, and one should pause at His saying ﴿Wretched is what they have sold themselves for﴾. Because if you connected it, the dispraise would apply in the state of their knowing; but if they did not know, it would not be dispraised. That is, if you said: ﴿Wretched is what they have sold themselves for, if only they knew,﴾ the dispraise would apply when? When they know. That is, when they do not know it is not dispraise. But the matter is the reverse. In other words, I say: it is indeed wretched what they sold themselves for, whether they knew or not. So (law) is the beginning of a new statement. The better pause is at His saying ﴿and wretched is what they have sold themselves for﴾, and then you begin: ﴿if only they knew.﴾ That is, if they had been people of knowledge who benefit from their knowledge, they would not have sold themselves for this magic, and they would have avoided it. But their action shows that they are among those of ignorance. Their action shows that they are among those of ignorance. The ignorance meant here is not the lack of knowledge but the foolishness (as-safah), because it has already passed us that ignorance may be meant as foolishness and may be meant as lack of knowledge. ﴿If only they knew.﴾

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, a reward from Allah would have been better.﴾

Student: Is (law) here conditional?

The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿if only they knew﴾ is conditional. That is: if they knew, they would not have sold themselves, as we have explained.

﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah﴾: they believe with their hearts and fear Allah with their limbs. Faith is in the heart and piety is in the limbs. This is when the two are mentioned together. If they are not mentioned together, faith includes piety and piety includes faith, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Taqwa is here," and he pointed to his chest.[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi in as-Sunan (1927) and Ahmad in al-Musnad (7727), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]] His saying ﴿if they had believed and feared Allah﴾: faith is repeated often in the Qur'an, and piety is repeated often. We have mentioned that faith, according to Ahl as-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, is affirmation together with acceptance and submission; otherwise it is not faith. Taqwa is taking a shield from the punishment of Allah, and that is by doing the commands of Allah and avoiding His prohibitions, because it is from (wiqayah, "protection"). The root of taqwa is (waqwa), but a morphological alteration occurred, so it became (taqwa). So this taqwa is taking a protection from the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is the most comprehensive of what has been said about its meaning. Others have said: taqwa is that you act in obedience to Allah upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and that you leave disobedience to Allah upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah. And some have said:

Leave sins, small and great, that is taqwa.
Walk as one walking over a field of thorns, wary of what he sees.
Do not belittle any small thing, for mountains are made of pebbles.

But what we have said is the most comprehensive in meaning overall.

His saying ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, a reward﴾: (al-mathubah) and (ath-thawab) mean the recompense, and it is named so because it derives from (thaba, yathubu), meaning he returned, since the recompense is as if the person's deed returns to him and its benefit and fruit come back to him. His saying ﴿a reward from Allah﴾ is certainly, as in ﴿Indeed Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [ar-Ra'd 31].

The second benefit of attributing it to Allah is that it will be greater than what the servant imagines, because the gift of the Mighty is mighty. Is that right or not? The gift is according to the giver. The gift of a miser is small, and the gift of a generous person is large. If a miser gives a person one qirsh, he says: "By Allah, today I have lost, I gave one qirsh!" But the generous person, if he gives him a thousand riyals, does not care and does not boast, because he is generous. So Allah the Exalted attributed the reward to Himself: ﴿from Allah﴾, for both reasons: the first is the servant's assurance of obtaining it, and the second is to show the greatness of this reward, because the reward of the Mighty must be great.

His saying ﴿better﴾: better than what? The preferable view is that we say it is absolute goodness, better than everything, not merely better than the benefit they obtained through magic, but better than everything. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The place of the whip of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and what is in it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2892) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Indeed he said: "The two rak'ahs of Fajr are better than the world and what is in it."[[Narrated by Muslim (725/96) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.]] That is, the two rak'ahs of the Fajr Sunnah are better than the world and what is in it. Therefore ﴿better﴾: the preferable view is that we take it as unrestricted, absolute goodness, better than everything, not only than the benefit they obtained by learning magic or from anything else.

Grammatical analysis of the verse (i'rab): ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah﴾: (anna) here has an open hamzah, meaning it is interpreted as a verbal noun together with what follows, because (anna) with an open hamzah is one of the particles of the verbal noun. (Inna) and (an) are both verbal particles, so they and what follows are interpreted as a verbal noun. The grammarians differed on the case of this verbal noun. Some said it is the subject of an omitted verb, and the estimate is: "And if their faith and their taqwa had been established." Others said rather that it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, and the sense is: "And if their faith and their piety were established."

His saying ﴿a reward from Allah is better﴾: the lam falls in the answer to (law). (Mathubah) is the subject (mubtada'), and it is indefinite, and the beginning with an indefinite noun is permitted because it is qualified by His saying ﴿from Allah﴾. The predicate of the subject is His saying ﴿better﴾, and the sentence is the answer to (law), not the predicate of the subject, because the predicate of the subject is omitted.

﴿Indeed a reward from Allah is better﴾: this is like the previous one; one pauses at His saying ﴿a reward from Allah is better﴾.

His saying ﴿if only they knew﴾: that is, if they had known, they would have believed and feared Allah. So this (law) is conditional, and its answer is omitted, its estimate being: they would have believed and feared Allah.

﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen.﴾ Introducing the ruling with a call indicates concern for it, because the call causes the addressee to pay attention. If I say to you: "Do such-and-such," or I say: "O so-and-so, do such-and-such," which is more effective in attracting attention? "O so-and-so" is more effective. So introducing the ruling with the call indicates concern for it. Then the call with the description of faith indicates that carrying out this ruling is a requirement of faith, and that missing it is a deficiency in faith. For one cannot address anyone saying "O believer, do such-and-such" except because his faith requires that he do such-and-such, and one cannot say "O believer, do such-and-such" except because if he does not do it, his faith is deficient. On this basis we say: introducing the ruling with the call using the description of faith shows that adhering to it is a requirement of faith, and that opposing it or missing it is a deficiency of faith.

Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When you hear Allah say: ﴿O you who have believed,﴾ then give it your ear." That is, listen to it, because it is a call from Allah to you: ﴿O you who have believed,﴾ a call from Allah to you, so give it your ear, that is, listen to it. "For it is either good, in which case you are commanded to it, or evil, in which case you are forbidden from it."[[Narrated by Ibn al-Mubarak in az-Zuhd (36) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]] What we have here is the prohibition: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina"﴾, that is, do not say, when calling the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Ra'ina, Ra'ina." It comes from (al-mura'ah), which is attention to a thing and preserving it. The Companions used to say "Ra'ina" when they wished to speak to the Messenger ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah, Ra'ina." But the Jews used to say: "O Muhammad, Ra'ina," meaning by it an evil sense. They meant ra'inan, the active participle from (ar-ru'unah), which means that a person lacks dignity. So the Jews intended by this word an evil meaning, while the Muslims undoubtedly did not intend an evil meaning, but meant (al-mura'ah). But since the word was the same and could bear this and that, they (the believers) were forbidden to say it, out of courtesy and to stay away from suspicion. Also because some people feign faith, like the hypocrites, who might say "Ra'ina" while intending what the Jews intended. Therefore the believers were forbidden from this: ﴿do not say Ra'ina﴾.

Student: What is the meaning of ﴿Ra'ina﴾?

The Shaykh: We told you: it is from al-mura'ah. "Ra'ina" is an imperative verb.

Student: The intended meaning?

The Shaykh: The intended meaning is "listen to us."

﴿But say "Unzurna"﴾: that is, for example, if you want the Messenger to wait for you, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna," from (an-nazar) in the sense of waiting. That is, do not say "Ra'ina," because the Jews say this word intending an evil meaning.

﴿Say "Unzurna"﴾ is an imperative verb from where? From (an-nazar) in the sense of waiting. (An-nazar) comes in the sense of waiting, as in His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds?﴾ [al-Baqarah 210]. So if you want the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to wait for you, whether standing or sitting, or in any state, do not say "Ra'ina," but say "Unzurna." When He forbade something, He mentioned its replacement, so that a person would not be confused when forbidden from something as to what he should say instead. So Allah clarified the replacement, which has no ambiguity.

﴿Say "Unzurna" and listen﴾: (isma'u), listen, is it hearing as perception or as acceptance? It is perception and acceptance. But perception may be a known matter. ﴿Listen﴾ means listening with understanding and acceptance: ﴿Do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal 21]. That is, listen to what you are commanded and what you are forbidden. What you are commanded, do it; what you are forbidden, leave it.

Then He threatened: ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ (Alim) means painful, and (al-'adhab) means punishment. The disbelievers here are the Jews, and likewise whoever among the Muslims opposes the command, for him is a painful punishment. For opposing the command of Allah, if it is done absolutely, is apostasy, and Allah forbid, and its doer deserves the painful punishment. ﴿And listen. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ As for the believers, they have lasting bliss.

Student: Like the saying "Ra'ina" (...), is there anything in it?

The Shaykh: No, there is nothing in it. After the Messenger there is nothing in it; this is specific to addressing the Messenger ﷺ.

Student: I heard that some people forbid it, saying it is not permissible...?

The Shaykh: No, no.

Student: (...) say "Unzurna"?

The Shaykh: They do not know, they do not know. (...) you say "Ra'in" (...) the shop, there is no harm in it.

Student: (...).

The Shaykh: There is no harm.

Student: Shaykh, is not the language of the Jews Hebrew?

The Shaykh: Yes, but Hebrew is very close to Arabic; it is among the languages closest to Arabic. Also the Jews in Madinah learned from the Arabs; they learned the Arabic language and began to read and converse in Arabic.

He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture, nor the polytheists, would not wish﴾: is (ma) conditional?

Student: No, it is negative.

The Shaykh: Negative? Yes. (Yawaddu) means "love," and (al-wadd) is the highest kind of love; it is the one next to (al-khullah, "intimate friendship"), which is the highest type, and (al-wadd) is what approaches it. ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture would not wish﴾, that is, they do not love, ﴿among the People of the Scripture nor the polytheists﴾. His saying ﴿those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture﴾: is (min) partitive or explanatory? 

Student: Explanatory.

The Shaykh: What is the difference between this and that?

Student: If we say...

The Shaykh: The meaning becomes that all the People of the Scripture are disbelievers, and the meaning becomes: those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists would not wish. Also ﴿nor the polytheists﴾ becomes conjoined to His saying ﴿among the People of the Scripture﴾, meaning: those who disbelieved from these and from those would not wish. For this reason He said ﴿nor the polytheists﴾ and did not say "nor the polytheists" in the nominative, because if it were conjoined to ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ it would have been phrased "nor the polytheists" (in the nominative). So on this basis (min) is for specifying the category: those who disbelieved from this category, which are the People of the Scripture, and likewise from the polytheists. The sense of the verse: those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture nor among the polytheists would not wish. What do they not wish? They do not wish what? ﴿That there be sent down upon you any good from your Lord﴾. ﴿That there be sent down upon you﴾ is the object of (yawaddu), meaning: they do not wish the sending down of good.

﴿That there be sent down upon you any good﴾: (min) is grammatically superfluous, and (khayr) is the deputy subject, meaning that good is sent down upon you. Good here includes the good of this world and the Hereafter. If the disbelievers among the People of the Scripture, the Jews and Christians, and the polytheists were able to prevent rain from falling upon the Muslims, they would do so, because they do not wish any good to descend upon us. If they were able to prevent beneficial knowledge from reaching us, they would do so. Is this specific to the People of the Scripture in the time of the Messenger ﷺ?

Student: General.

The Shaykh: General. For this reason it came in the present tense, ﴿would not wish﴾, which indicates continuity. They do not wish that any good from our Lord be sent down upon us. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But Allah selects for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾

His saying ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ means they do not love. His saying ﴿among the People of the Scripture﴾ is an explanation of (those), and His saying ﴿nor the polytheists﴾ is conjoined to ﴿among the People of the Scripture﴾, so ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ includes the People of the Scripture and the polytheists. These do not wish that it be sent down upon you. In one canonical recitation: ﴿that it be sent down upon you (anzala)﴾, a recitation of the seven. The difference between (yunazzala, with the doubled zay) and (yunzala) is that tanzil is sending down a thing piece by piece, while (inzal) is sending it down all at once. So they do not wish either this or that: they do not wish good to be sent down all at once, nor to be sent down piece by piece.

Student: With the doubling, piece by piece?

The Shaykh: Yes, with the doubling, piece by piece.

Many scholars have said that when two recitations exist and one of them contains an extra letter, it is better to recite that one, because of the increased reward, since each letter carries ten good deeds. However, the correct view on this question is that a person should recite sometimes with this recitation and sometimes with that one, just as we say regarding the practical Sunnah (the Prophet's ﷺ actions): when its forms differ, it is better to do this once and that once. This applies to the reciter who recites for himself or recites to students of knowledge. As for one who recites to the general public, he should not depart from the familiar recitation, because when the Qur'an is recited to ordinary people in a way other than what they are used to, their hearts reject it, and then they become disrespectful toward the Qur'an and belittle it. For this reason, a person should take this matter into account. Some people recite the various recitation variants (qira'at) before the general public. Allah knows their intention, whether they want to teach or want to be said to be a scholar of the qira'at. Allah knows their intention; we have not opened their hearts. But this is not a wise method of teaching, for the general public has a different standing from students of knowledge.

And His saying: ﴿that there should be sent down upon you any good from your Lord﴾. It is possible to say that "min" (from) is extra (ziyadah), and the meaning is: that there should be sent down upon you good from your Lord. Or we can take "min" as included within the negation, so that it refers to generality, meaning: any good, whether little or much. This is the better view.

And His saying: ﴿any good from your Lord﴾. What is meant by "good" here? Is it the good of the Hereafter, that is, revelation? Or the good of this world and the Hereafter, which includes this and what is sent down of rain or other things? The second is the better view, that it is inclusive. For those who disbelieve, among the People of the Book and the polytheists, never wish that any good should be sent down to the Muslims, neither religious good nor worldly good. But Allah, exalted is He, refuted this against them by His saying: ﴿But Allah selects for His mercy whom He wills﴾. The verb (yakhtassu, "selects") is used both intransitively and transitively. If it is intransitive, then "man" (whom) is the subject of "yakhtassu," and the meaning of "yakhtassu" is: he singles out for His mercy whom He wills, just as you say: "I specified him with this thing," meaning: I singled him out with it. In this case, "man" is the subject. The verb is also used transitively, meaning "yakhussu" (specifies), so: He specifies for His mercy whom He wills. In this case, "man" is the direct object of "yakhtassu." The meaning in both cases is one: Allah, exalted is He, specifies for His mercy whom He wills, so whomever Allah specifies receives this mercy.

And His saying: ﴿for His mercy whom He wills﴾ includes the mercy that results in the mercy of religion and of this world, and that which results in the mercy of religion or of this world, because Allah, exalted is He, selects whom He wills for this. And His saying: ﴿for His mercy﴾, because this revelation that was sent down upon the Messenger ﷺ is from Allah's mercy upon him and upon them.

And His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾. As we have stated many times, this is connected with what? With wisdom. That is, His selection of whom He wills for mercy is based on His wisdom, blessed and exalted is He. So whoever His wisdom requires that He show mercy to, He shows mercy to, and whoever His wisdom does not require that He select for mercy, He does not show mercy to.

﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾. ﴿Allah﴾ is the subject (mubtada', topic), and ﴿Possessor﴾ (dhu) is its predicate (khabar). "Dhu" means "possessor" (sahib). ﴿bounty﴾ (fadl) means giving beyond what necessity requires. And His saying: ﴿great﴾ means: vast, abundant, large. So greatness here refers to both quantity and quality. Among His bounty, blessed and exalted is He, is that He has singled out this Ummah with great distinctions that He has given to no one else. Among them, for example, is what is in the hadith of Jabir in the two Sahihs: «I have been given five things that none before me has been given: I was helped by terror (ru'b) across a distance of a month's journey…» to the end of the hadith. This is among what Allah has singled out for whomever He wills.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whatever a verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring forth one better than it or similar to it﴾. First, the grammar (i'rab) and the recitations:
﴿Whatever (ma) We abrogate﴾: "ma" is conditional (shartiyyah), a conditional noun that jazms (apocopates) two verbs: the first is the verb of the condition (fi'l al-shart), and the second is its response and consequence.

* A student: O Shaykh, have we not taken the benefits of the previous verse?
* The Shaykh: Yes, we did not take them, let us move on.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: So can we stop here?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Then, God willing, we will stop here and take the benefits.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching the people magic﴾.
* From this verse it is derived that the Jews took magic from the devils, as shown by His saying: ﴿they followed what the devils recited﴾. What confirms this is that one of them bewitched the Prophet ﷺ. This is "Labid ibn al-A'sam bewitched the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him," as is well known.
* Among its benefits: magic is among the works of devils, as shown by His saying: ﴿what the devils recited﴾, meaning what they followed over the kingdom of Solomon.
* Among its benefits: devils used to engage in magic even in the time of Solomon, despite his great authority over them, as shown by His saying: ﴿over the kingdom of Solomon﴾.
* One of the benefits of the verse: Solomon did not approve of that, as shown by His saying: ﴿Solomon did not disbelieve﴾, meaning he did not sanction them in this matter. For this reason, disbelief is negated from him, since if he had sanctioned them, and far be it from him to sanction them, he would have been sanctioning disbelief.
* Among its benefits: Allah, exalted is He, may decree the means of disobedience as a trial for people, such as sending down the two angels who teach people magic. This is the facilitation of this matter as a test and examination. There are other examples of this: the trial through making the means of disobedience easy. Among them?
* A student: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ [al-A'raf 163].
* The Shaykh: Among them is the story of the People of the Sabbath, to whom the fish were made easily available on what day? On Saturday, the day when fishing was forbidden for them.
* Among them: what Allah tested this Ummah with regarding game: ﴿Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and spears can reach, that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah 94].
* Among them: what the Prophet ﷺ pointed to in his saying: «A man whom a woman of rank and beauty invited, and he said: Indeed I fear Allah.»
* Also among them: the story of Joseph, when the wife of the ruler (al-Aziz) locked the doors and was alone with him: ﴿And she said: Come, you!﴾ [Yusuf 23]. This is a trial from Allah, mighty and majestic, in this great matter. The point is that Allah, exalted is He, tests a person by making the means of disobedience easy for him. So beware, beware: when the means of disobedience become available to you, do not do it. Be cautious. See this as like a sparrow to which poison is offered in bait, so be on guard.
* From the noble verse it is derived that a person is obligated to advise people, even if that causes them to turn away from him. They said: ﴿And they did not teach anyone until they said: We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾. So if you have a commodity that is not good, and someone wants to buy it from you, do you stay silent and let him buy it and go?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: You must warn him. You say: Look, it is not good. If he buys it, it is his affair; otherwise, let him decide. There was a well-known man among us for his truthfulness who, when he had a commodity and was asked about it, would tell the truth, to the point that among what he said was: "People praise it, but I (...) to this extent." But where is this in our present time? The point is that this shows that among sincere advice is that a person informs others of the matter as it is, even if that leads people to turn away from him.
* Among its benefits: learning magic is disbelief, as shown by His saying: ﴿we are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾.
* Among them also: teaching magic is disbelief as well: ﴿but the devils disbelieved, teaching the people magic﴾. The phrase ﴿teaching﴾ is a cause (ta'lil) for the disbelief. So learning magic and teaching magic are both disbelief.

Is the repentance of a sorcerer accepted? There is a difference of opinion. Some scholars said: his repentance is not accepted. Others said: his repentance is accepted, and this is the correct view, because of the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar 53]. As for if we say that magic is not disbelief, and that killing the sorcerer is a prescribed penalty (hadd), then if he repents before he is captured, the penalty falls from him; but if he repents after he is captured, it does not fall, because the prescribed penalties do not fall when a person repents after being captured.

* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: They have no evidence except that they say: this is because of the enormity of his disbelief, since it is great disbelief, so his repentance is not accepted. It is said: it is not greater than insulting Allah, exalted is He.
* A student: Is the correct view that he is killed as a prescribed penalty or as a disbeliever?
* The Shaykh: The correct view is that he is killed as a disbeliever. The verse indicates this, because he disbelieves.
* A student: His ruling is the ruling of a disbeliever regarding execution?
* The Shaykh: His ruling is the ruling of a disbeliever regarding execution, except that if he repents, his repentance is accepted and the execution is lifted from him.
* A student: Does repentance make prescribed penalties fall?
* The Shaykh: Prescribed penalties fall if repentance occurs before capture, before he is captured, because Allah said regarding highway robbers: ﴿except those who repent before you have power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 34].
* A student: What about the rights of people?
* The Shaykh: No, the rights of people do not fall by repentance. For example, if this sorcerer destroyed people's wealth, it is not dropped by repentance. He must compensate for these funds. Or, for example, if he afflicted a person with paralysis by sorcery, or something similar, compensation is taken from him.
* A student: (...) they do not like the beard (...).
* The Shaykh: They bewitch a person?
* The student: The beard (...) they do not like the beard.
* The Shaykh: Yes, they do not like it.
* The student: (...) how is the beard (...)?
* The Shaykh: We are researching magic.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: So this is by way of analogy (qiyas). If they say this, then read the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone because they say: We believe, and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 2], and read His saying: ﴿And among people is one who says: We believe in Allah, but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut 10]. Say: I will not shave. Do not shave your beard. If they seize you and force you and shave it, then the sin is upon them.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Among the benefits of the verse: among the greatest kinds of magic is one whose effect is separating a man from his wife. This is among the greatest types of magic, as shown by His saying: ﴿so they learn from the two what they use to cause separation between a man and his wife﴾. This is because among the matters most beloved to the devils is separating a man from his wife. It has been established in a sound hadith: "Indeed, Satan places his throne upon the water and sends his troops into the earth to cause corruption. One of them comes and says: I did such-and-such. Another says: I did such-and-such. Then a third says: I did such-and-such. Then one of them comes and says: I did not stop with him until I separated him from his wife." Then what does he do? «He embraces him and says: You are the one (who did it).» This is evidence that among the most important and significant aspects of magic is separating a man from his wife. There is also a counterpart to this, which is binding a man to his wife, so that he, may Allah protect us, is afflicted with infatuation and cannot live even for a moment without his wife in front of him. For this reason, this matter overwhelms some people. We ask Allah for well-being.
* Also among them: causes have no effect except by the permission of Allah: ﴿and they could not harm anyone with it except by permission of Allah﴾.
* Among them: the power of Allah, mighty and majestic, is above causes, and whatever causes exist, if Allah has not permitted them, they will not benefit. Does this ruling we have derived from the verse oblige us not to take means?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: Why? If we say that the cause does not act except by Allah's permission (...), we do nothing?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. We say: the principle is that causes are effective by Allah's permission, so you take the cause. Marry so that children may be born to you, do good deeds so that you may enter Paradise. We say the same about the rest of the causes. Take medicine so that you are healed, stay away from the leper so that you are protected from him, and similar things. Is that clear? The point is that these causes do not mean they are effective by themselves; they cannot be prevented from their effect. Rather, they are effective by Allah's permission.
* Among them: an indication that one should always turn to Allah, as shown by His saying: ﴿except by permission of Allah﴾. So when you know that everything is by Allah's permission, to whom do you turn? To Him, glorified and exalted, both to bring benefits and to repel harms.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: learning magic is pure harm with no good in it, as shown by His saying: ﴿and they learn what harms them and does not benefit them﴾. ﴿What harms them﴾ affirms its harm, and ﴿does not benefit them﴾ negates its benefit.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the disbelief of the sorcerer is disbelief that takes one out of the religion (millah). From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾. ﴿Khalaq﴾ means share or portion. And no one here has no share in the Hereafter except the disbeliever. As for the believer, however much he is punished, he has a share in the Hereafter.
* A student: Is there any detail regarding the disbelief of the sorcerer?
* The Shaykh: No, there is no detail. The correct view is that there is no detail.
* Among the benefits of the verse also: affirmation of recompense, as shown by His saying: ﴿he has no share in the Hereafter﴾.
* Also among its benefits: these Jews committed the learning of magic knowingly, as shown by His saying: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾. By this they deserved the description of anger, and they became those who earned anger (maghdub 'alayhim), because everyone who knows the truth and opposes it has earned anger. For this reason, Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "Whoever among our scholars becomes corrupt has in him a resemblance to the Jews, and whoever among our worshippers becomes corrupt has in him a resemblance to the Christians." This is because scholars sin knowingly, so they are like the Jews, and worshippers sin out of misguidance, so they are like the Christians.
Also among them: the blame of these Jews for what they chose for themselves: ﴿And wretched is that for which they sold themselves﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the one with knowledge who benefits from his knowledge is the one who guards against such matters, as shown by His saying: ﴿if they had known﴾, meaning: if they had been people of beneficial knowledge, they would not have purchased this thing that harms them and does not benefit them, and which they knew that whoever purchases it has no share in the Hereafter.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, a reward from Allah would have been better, if they had known.﴾
In this is evidence of the vastness of Allah's forbearance, since He presents to them faith and piety: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah﴾, meaning in the past and in the future. This is among His customs, exalted is He, that He presents repentance to sinners. Consider His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who put to trial the believing men and believing women and then do not repent will have the punishment of Hell﴾ [al-Buruj 10]. See, they burn His allies, and then He presents repentance to them. The implication of "Indeed, those who put to trial the believing men and believing women and then do not repent will have the punishment of Hell" is that if they repent, nothing is upon them, and they do not have the punishment of Hell.
* Among the benefits of the verse: through faith and piety, one attains the reward of Allah: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, a reward from Allah would have been [better]﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 2, verses 96–105 (part 10 of 10)**

* Among its benefits: Allah's reward is better for those who believe and fear Him than the whole of this world. This is from His saying: ﴿Better﴾ ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, a reward from Allah would have been better﴾. From where? From everything. Whatever a person gains in this world, the reward with Allah for faith and God-consciousness (taqwa) is better.
* We also take it from, and from the saying of the people of Qarun to him, and from the saying of the sincere advisers among the Children of Israel. They said to those who wished they had what Qarun had: ﴿Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Qasas 80]. Here, compare ﴿believed and feared Allah﴾. It becomes clear to you that taqwa is righteous action. We have already explained that taqwa is taking a protection from the punishment of Allah by doing what He commanded and avoiding what He forbade.
* Also among them: the action of these Jews, and their choice of what contains disbelief, namely teaching magic, is the action of one who is ignorant. This is from His saying: ﴿If only they knew﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina," but say, "Unthurna," and listen. And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾.

* From this verse it is derived that one should use good manners in speech. This is from His saying: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina," but say, "Unthurna."﴾ The root of ﴿Ra'ina﴾: from where? Its origin is from al-mura'ah (consideration, attentiveness). One says ra'aahu, yura'eehi (he considered him, he considers him). ﴿Ra'ina﴾ is an imperative verb from ra'a, yura'i (to consider). But the Jews would say it intending that it be from al-ru'una (foolishness, rudeness), meaning abuse and insult, and it means stupidity. The Companions would say to the Messenger (ﷺ), when they asked him for a delay in something, "Ra'ina" (meaning "have consideration for us"). The Jews rejoiced at this, because the Companions of Muhammad would be insulting him. So Allah forbade them from this. From this is derived the use of good manners in speech, and in the sense of avoiding words that give the impression of what? Abuse and insult. Even if it is not abuse and insult in the language of that people, but it gives the impression of abuse and insult, then it is part of good manners for a person to avoid them.
* Also among them: faith requires all noble characteristics, because observing good manners in speech is one of the noble characteristics. And to whom is this command addressed? To the believers. So this is evidence that faith requires this. Faith, therefore, requires all noble characteristics.
* From this follows the third benefit: observing noble characteristics is part of faith, that they are part of faith. Just as noble characteristics are also an expansion of the chest and breadth (of heart). A person who has noble characteristics is loved by people and honored among them, and this too is part of the faith that benefits him with whom? With Allah.
* Among the benefits of the verse: one who forbids something should give people something in its place, and not forbid them and leave them in confusion (...). ﴿And listen﴾. Here, does the word "listen" mean the listening of response or the listening of comprehension?
* The students: The listening of response.
* The shaykh: Or this and that, this and that. But if you say the listening of response, the listening of response cannot happen except after the listening of comprehension. It does not mean that you listen and disobey, that you listen and obey: ﴿and listen﴾.

Among them: a warning against opposing the command of Allah, and that it is from the deeds of the disbelievers. This is from His saying: ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture, nor the polytheists, wish that there should be sent down to you any good from your Lord. But Allah selects for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾.

* From this verse is derived: the clarification of the enmity of non-Muslims toward Muslims. He mentioned two categories that encompass all the categories of those given the Scripture, namely the Jews and the Christians, and the polytheists, who are all the people of idols. From the noble verse it is derived that all of them are enemies of the Muslims. From where do we take that they are enemies? That they do not wish good for the Muslims.
* Among the benefits of the verse: it is obligatory upon us to beware of every action that proceeds from the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists, and to know that all their conduct is an attempt to prevent good from reaching the Muslims.
* Among them: we derive from the noble verse that the enemies of the Muslims, among the Jews, Christians and polytheists, also try (because whoever wishes for something seeks to obtain it) to destroy the economy of the Muslims, or not? Because the soundness of the economy and social solidarity are from good.
* Also among them, we derive: that these disbelievers also wish to prevent the Muslims from military advancement, because it is good.
* Also among them: we know that these disbelievers strive against the Muslims with everything that turns them away from their religion. Why? Because the turning of believers toward religion is good and a cause of good. ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf 96]. These disbelievers, everything that turns people away from their religion, such as amusements and games and obstruction of anything whatsoever, they wish for this. And if you want to know, look at their terrifying, frightening plans which they present to the Muslims, as if they are wearing two garments of falsehood, claiming that they are the good ones, presented to people, but in reality they are a lie, a lie.
* Among them: it is forbidden for Muslims to put these disbelievers in any leadership. Since we know that they do not wish good for us, they will never lead us to good whatever the matter. Can one who does not wish you good lead you to good? Or guide you to good? It is impossible. For this reason it is forbidden to give them authority over the Muslims, whether in planning, in systems, or in anything else. They must be under the command of the Muslims and under the management of the Muslims. If we seek their help, we seek it only for what we know of our interests, while they remain under our authority. But to give them authority over the Muslims, we know with certainty from the words of our Lord, who knows what is in the hearts, that they want for us nothing but evil. Since they do not wish good for us, good will not come to us from them. They do not wish that good should come to us from anyone other than them. They do not wish ﴿that there should be sent down to you any good from your Lord﴾. They are not from them. How can they bring us good? Therefore it is obligatory upon us, the youth of the Muslims, to be alert to this matter, from the shaykhs of the Muslims. All Muslims must be alert to this matter, and that their enemies among the People of the Book and the polytheists want nothing for them but evil, and that if they were able to prevent rain and the springs of the earth, they would do so. So on this basis it is obligatory upon us to beware of their plans and to always hold a bad opinion of them, because thinking well of one who is not deserving of it is nothing but humiliation, humiliation and weakness. One who is deserving of good opinion, let good opinion be held of him, because you cannot walk with anyone except that you hold a good opinion of him. But for one who is not deserving of that, thinking well of him is weakness, cowardice, feebleness and humiliation. For this reason we must beware of them, of their leaders, and of their plans, because they do not wish that any good from our Lord should be sent down to us. This is why He said: ﴿of good﴾, meaning any good, whether religious or worldly. For this reason the Jews envied the Muslims when the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) came to them, and they believed in him, and this Book was sent down. That is, they disliked this Book, and they do not wish this.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the good of Allah is not turned back by the desire of one who desires or the aversion of one who dislikes. From where do we take it? ﴿But Allah selects for His mercy whom He wills﴾. So it is impossible for these Jews, Christians and polytheists to prevent the bounty of Allah. On this basis came the authentic hadith: "Know that if the nation were to gather together to benefit you with something, they would not benefit you except with something that Allah has already written for you; and if they were to gather together to harm you with something, they would not harm you except with something that Allah has already written against you."[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (2425) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]
* Also among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the will of Allah, from His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾; and the affirmation of mercy, from His saying: ﴿for His mercy﴾; and the affirmation of volition, from His saying: ﴿selects﴾, for selection indicates volition; and the affirmation of bounty, from His saying: ﴿possessor of great bounty﴾; and the affirmation that His bounty is not like the bounty of others. The bounty of others is limited bounty, while the bounty of Allah is great bounty with no limit. Allah the Exalted multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.

What contradicts this verse is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of the people in animosity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah; and you will find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks and because they are not arrogant﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82]?

* Student: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflow with tears﴾ [al-Ma'idah 83], to the end of the verse. The completion of the verse indicates that these Christians, who are the most affectionate of people toward the believers (...)?
* The shaykh: That is, they are Christians of a specific kind. They are not all the Christians. For Allah says: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah 51]. Some Jews and Christians are allies of one another, and this is a observable matter. Whoever follows history finds that the Christians are always with the Jews, and the Jews always with the Christians, because they have a common enemy, which is the Muslims. Whoever has a common enemy, even if they are enemies among themselves, they love to destroy this enemy, so they unite against it.
* Student: Did this specific kind of Christians exist in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), or do they still remain?
* The shaykh: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks and because they are not arrogant (82). And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82–83]. So whenever this kind of Christian is found, whether during the life of the Messenger or after his death.
* Student: Could even Jews become Muslim?
* The shaykh: That is not what is meant by support. But among them are priests and monks, and they are not arrogant. But the Christians now are arrogant. It does not mean that if even one of them becomes Muslim we apply this ruling to the whole group. Their heads, their elders and their rabbis are the opposite of that.
* Student: O shaykh, does the verse not point out that they believed?
* The shaykh: Who?
* Student: These Christians (...).
* The shaykh: No. ﴿Because among them﴾, not all of them.
* Student: Yes, but does it not answer this doubt, that the verse (...)?
* The shaykh: No. The verse does not indicate that they all believed, because his saying: ﴿That is because among them are priests﴾... unless it is said: "and because they, when they hear." And do not make ﴿And when they hear﴾ refer back to the priests and monks. It is possible to say: among the Christians there were those who believed during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). The Christians who believed during the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, yes indeed (...).
* Student: (...)?
* The shaykh: (...).
* Student: O shaykh, is it not derived from the verse that everyone who does not wish good for the Muslims (...)?
* The shaykh: Yes, it is derived: that whoever does not wish good for the Muslims has some resemblance to the Jews and Christians. This is a beautiful benefit: the person who does not wish good for the Muslims has in him some resemblance to the Jews and Christians, because in reality whoever does not concern himself with the affairs of the Muslims is not of them, and whoever wishes them evil, or does not wish them good, has not wished good for them, then he has in him some resemblance to the Jews and Christians. Those who do not wish that the Ummah be upright upon the methodology of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih)? These do not wish that any good from our Lord be sent down to us, because continuing upon the methodology of the pious predecessors is what contains the good.

So those who want us, for example, to walk the path that these Jews and Christians have walked, of openness to this world and abandoning the Hereafter behind the back, saying: "Let us concern ourselves with physical entertainment rather than the life of the hearts," these have in them a resemblance to the Jews and Christians. For the reality of the matter is that the sincere believer, sincere to the faith and to the believers, is one who wants the believers to remain upright upon the religion of Allah by any means, and does not want to make them affluent so as to destroy them. Affluence that entails people turning away from the religion of Allah is in reality not affluence but destruction. It is the cause of entering the Fire: ﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent (45), and they used to persist in the great violation (46), and they used to say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected? (47) Or our forefathers, the former ones?"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 45–48]. All these descriptions have now been found among many Muslims because of what the world has been opened to them. We ask Allah for safety.

* Student: O shaykh, the Christians (...) from the Arabs. We are not Christians; rather, we are Masihiyyun (Christians in the sense of "Messianic"). Someone agrees with them and says: "You are Masihiyyun," because they (...). The Qur'an calls them Nasara (Christians). They are close to the Muslims (...) the verse (...). If this is their expression, then we say: whoever calls them Nasara (...)?
* The shaykh: Even after calling them Masihiyyin is an error, because the Masihi means one affiliated with the Messiah, and this Messiah is innocent of them. This is more problematic than Nasara.
* Student: (...)?
* The shaykh: No, because they say "Masihiyyun" in order to justify that they are on a religion. This is the reason they changed. For this reason they did not turn away from "Nasara" except in later eras, the eras of colonialism. Otherwise, they were called Nasara in the books of the jurists, even the later ones. But when colonialism took over and its power grew in some lands, and writers in the colonized lands began to speak of "al-Masihiyyin," then as soon as you hear "Masihi" you feel that he is upon a correct religion, because the Messiah 'Isa ibn Maryam is the Messenger of Allah, so his religion is correct. But "Nasara," you do not understand from it this understanding.
* Student: (...)?
* The shaykh: Not at all.
* Student: (...).
* The shaykh: I think he said: "Nasara." We call them Nasara as Allah named them, and the meaning of Nasara became not from al-nusrah (help), Nasara being a relation to a place.
* Student: (...).
* The shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...)?
* The shaykh: Yes, it is known. We say: whoever believes in what the Messenger brought has a double reward.
* Student: Are they called Nasara?
* The shaykh: No. We now say: Muslims. If they believe, they become Muslims.
* Student: To which lands are they related?
* The shaykh: To a place called, it is said, al-Nasirah, and it is said that in a place (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 96–105 (part 1 of 10):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life﴾. This (...).

* Student: What is the ruling on mubahalah (mutual invocation of divine curse)?
* Shaykh: The ruling on mubahalah is that it is permissible in important matters aimed at establishing the truth and refuting falsehood. It has been narrated that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, denied 'awl (the proportional reduction of heirs' shares when the total of the fixed shares exceeds the estate, a rule of inheritance known as al-faraid) and said: "Whoever wishes, I will invoke a curse upon him concerning this. Indeed, the One who counted the grains of sand of 'Alij cannot allow it to be applied to the estate." [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (6/253).]] He then mentioned the shares that necessitate 'awl.
So it is not objectionable for a person to invoke a curse regarding important matters in order to establish the truth, but on the condition that he has knowledge of the matter, lest the matter turn out to be otherwise and he be mistaken.
* Student: Shaykh, did the Messenger ﷺ invite them (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, he invited them, but they did not respond. He invited the delegation of Najran. As for the story of the Jews, it is not reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invited them to mubahalah. However, Ibn Kathir used to favor this view and say: "There is no evidence for this matter."
* Student: How is mubahalah performed? How is mubahalah?
* Shaykh: Mubahalah originates from ibtihal (earnest supplication) to Allah through prayer. For example, I say such-and-such and you say such-and-such. You say: "Come, let us gather and say: 'The curse of Allah be upon the liars,' or 'whichever of us is lying will be afflicted with such-and-such,'" or something similar.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life, and [more covetous] than those who associated others with Allah﴾. The lam here is a preface to an oath, and the sentence is emphasized by the lam and by the heavy nun of emphasis in His words ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ (la-tajidannahum, "you will surely find them"), and by the implied oath, which is: "By Allah, you will surely find them." Here, the dal in ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ is fatha, and it is a present-tense verb with no particle governing it to put it in the accusative. So why is the dal vowelled with fatha?
Because it is attached to the nun of emphasis, and a present-tense verb attached to the nun of emphasis is built on fatha. And His words ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ is a verb that we have studied recently, which governs two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate. The first object is the ha' in ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾, and the second object is ﴿أَحْرَصَ النَّاسِ﴾.
The address in ﴿لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ﴾ is either addressed to the Messenger ﷺ, since he is the first one addressed by the Quran, and an address to the leader or imam is an address to his followers. So every address in the Quran to the Messenger ﷺ is an address to his community, except what the evidence shows is specific to him, such as His words ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast? And We removed from you your burden﴾ [al-Sharh 1–2], and what is similar to it, which is specific to him. The address is to the Messenger, or it is addressed to anyone who can be addressed; that is, "you will surely find them, O you who are addressed by this noble Quran." To whom is the noble Quran addressed?
* Students: All people.
* Shaykh: All people, it is addressed to all people. He said: ﴿you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life﴾. ﴿أَحْرَصَ﴾ is a comparative form (ism tafdil), ﴿أَحْرَصَ النَّاسِ﴾ is a comparative form. And what is ḥirs (covetousness)? Ḥirs is: that a person is greedy for a thing and anxious about losing it. Greed for a thing together with anxiety about losing it is called ḥirs, and ḥirs necessitates exerting effort. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ said: "Be eager for what benefits you, seek help from Allah, and do not give up." [[Narrated by Muslim (2664/34) from Abu Hurayrah, with the wording: "... and do not be incapable."]]
* Student: Shaykh, the waw?
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: The waw of ḥayawa?
* Shaykh: Ḥayawa?
* Student: It is written with a waw, I am saying: the waw, what?
* Shaykh: On (ḥayawa). May Allah keep you safe. This is the old orthography, the old script of the Mushaf in this form. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, saw that it is better to retain the old 'Uthmanic orthography as it was. Otherwise it would be (ḥayat) with an alif.
* Student: Some people make mistakes, the ones who cannot...?
* Shaykh: Yes, the ones who cannot be read, we do not understand. For this reason the scholars differed on this issue, and I think we have mentioned their opinions to you. We said: the scholars differed regarding the writing of the noble Quran: must it remain in the 'Uthmanic script (rasm 'Uthmani), or is it permissible to transfer it to the conventional script (al-rasm al-istilahi), or is there a distinction between the scholar and the ignorant?
We mentioned three opinions in this regard, and that the correct view is that it is permissible. Because if the convention at the time of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, when he wrote the Mushaf, had been other than this convention, he would have written it according to it. And was the Quran revealed as something recited or as something written?
* Students: Recited.
* Shaykh: Recited. Nevertheless, what has been mentioned (...) is feared, meaning that some of those who spell out the Quran letter by letter, and who have not received it orally from the mouths of shaykhs, say: al-ṣalāh is also written (al-ṣalawh), and al-zakāh likewise, and al-ribā with a waw, and so on. For this reason, it is most important that a person recites the Book of Allah under the guidance of a reciter who teaches him until he knows it perfectly.

﴿the most covetous of people for life﴾ ﴿you will surely find them﴾, meaning the Jews. ﴿the most covetous of people for life﴾: here ﴿حَيَاة﴾ is indefinite and he did not say "the life." So it means that they are covetous of life, even if it is little, even if they are given only a single moment; they are the most covetous of people for it. It is not the complete, long life; rather, it is any life for which they are covetous.

He said: ﴿and [more covetous] than those who associated others with Allah﴾. The exegetes differed regarding His words ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا﴾ (and of those who associated others with Allah): is it the beginning of a new statement, separate from what precedes it, with the implied meaning: "And of those who associated others with Allah is one who wishes that he would live a thousand years"? Although this is possible in wording, it is very far in meaning. Therefore, the correct view is the second opinion: that it is conjoined to His words ﴿النَّاسِ﴾ (people). That means: "you will surely find them the most covetous of people, and more covetous than those who associated others with Allah." That is, the Jews are more covetous than the polytheists, despite the fact that the Jews are People of the Book who believe in resurrection, Paradise and Hellfire, while the polytheists do not believe in that. Whoever does not believe in resurrection becomes the most covetous of people for life, because he thinks that when he dies, that is the end; he will not return. So you find him greedy for this life, which he regards as his capital, and he sees no other life. So these Jews are the most covetous of people, even more than those who associated others with Allah. This is the correct view, and it is an instance of specifying something after a general category. Why? Because the polytheists are from where?
* Students: From the people.
* Shaykh: From the people. The polytheists are from the people. So the most covetous of people and [more covetous than] those who associated others with Allah, even though the polytheists are among the people. So he is more covetous than this category of people who do not believe in resurrection.

His words ﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا﴾ mean: "with Allah." The details of shirk are not what is discussed here. Its place is, God willing, in the Book of Tawhid, where it is said that tawhid is divided into three categories, and each category of tawhid has a corresponding category of shirk. These three categories each divide into minor and major, and also into hidden and manifest.
* Student: The first opinion.
* Shaykh: What is it?
* Student: ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا﴾, the first opinion.
* Shaykh: The first opinion says that this is separate from what precedes it, and that the meaning of the verse is: "And of those who associated others with Allah is one who wishes that he would live a thousand years." His words: ﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوا يَوَدُّ أَحَدُهُمْ لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ﴾ (And of those who associated others with Allah is one who wishes that he would be granted a life of a thousand years). ﴿يَوَدُّ﴾: what is the meaning of al-mawadda?
* Student: Wishing.
* Another student: Loving.
* Shaykh: Loving and wishing. And His words ﴿أَحَدُهُمْ﴾ (one of them): to whom does the pronoun refer? The Jews or the polytheists?
* Student: To the Jews, if we take the second opinion, it refers to the Jews.
* Shaykh: As for the first opinion, it is clear that it refers only to the polytheists. The second opinion allows that the pronoun refers to the Jews, in which case the sentence ends at His words ﴿أَشْرَكُوا﴾. It also allows that it refers to the polytheists: ﴿one of them wishes that he would be granted a life of a thousand years﴾. Which of these do you consider more likely?
* Student: The second is more eloquent.
* Shaykh: The second is more eloquent? That it refers to the polytheists? What is its reasoning?
* Student: It refers to the Jews, since the polytheists, one of them wishes to live a thousand years, and the Jews are eager for life, so the Jews are greater in this.
* Another student: Shaykh, can we say that the Jews are included among the polytheists, meaning they have shirk?
* Shaykh: No, no, that is not correct, it is not right.
* Student: It refers to the Jews because the address...
* Shaykh: Is it preferred by the context? Preference by context? And there is also preference by meaning. If ﴿يَوَدُّ أَحَدُهُمْ﴾ refers to the polytheists, Mahmud [al-Zamakhshari] held that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, which is more likely. Mahmud gave two reasons: first, that the pronoun originally refers to the nearest previously mentioned noun, and the polytheists are nearest here. Second, if the polytheist wishes to live a thousand years, and the Jew is more covetous of life than him, then the Jew must wish to live more than a thousand years. Is that not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: If we say the pronoun refers to the Jews, the context supports it, but it indicates that the one who wishes for a thousand years is who?
* Students: The Jews.
* Shaykh: The Jews. So it becomes clear that the first is more eloquent, because if they are more covetous than the polytheist who wishes to live a thousand years, that is greater proof that they—that is, the Jews—love life.

His words ﴿أَحَدُهُمْ لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ أَلْفَ سَنَة﴾ (one of them wishes he would be granted a life of a thousand years): ﴿لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ﴾. What is the meaning of al-ta'mir? It is an increase in lifespan, and lifespan is life.
His words ﴿لَوْ يُعَمَّرُ﴾: is this (law) conditional?
* Student: No, it is not conditional.
* Shaykh: It is not conditional, but it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya). Whenever it comes after (wadda), it is masdariyya: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam 9]: ﴿وَدُّوا لَوْ تُدْهِنُ﴾, so (law) here is masdariyya. ﴿They would wish that they were out among the desert Bedouins﴾ [al-Ahzab 20]: ﴿يَوَدُّوا لَوْ أَنَّهُمْ بَادُونَ فِي الْأَعْرَابِ﴾. So this (law) is masdariyya; whenever (law) comes after (wadda), it is masdariyya. And what is the meaning of masdariyya? It means that (law) and what follows it are interpreted as a verbal noun, so it is said: "one of them wishes his longevity" (yawaddu ahadahum ta'mirahu). ﴿ألف سنة﴾ a thousand years, known. And the sanah (year): it is the lunar year. What is meant by sanah here? The solar (Gregorian) year or the lunar year?
* Student: The Gregorian.
* Shaykh: The Gregorian?
* Student: Because they follow the Gregorian calendar, their reckoning is by the Gregorian calendar. This is clear (...).
* Shaykh: The Gregorian calendar is a recent development, and the Jews do not recognize the Messiah as a prophet. Words, when used without qualification, are interpreted according to their legal meaning. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them four are sacred﴾ [al-Tawbah 36]. So the measure of time that Allah set for His servants is by lunar months: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say, "They are measures of time for the people and for Hajj"﴾ [al-Baqarah 189]. For whom? For the Arabs and for Hajj? ﴿for the people and for Hajj﴾, all people. Therefore, this latter calendar is not based on any principle of religion; it is not a religious calendar. All calendars, as far as we know, until this one came about, were based on the lunar calendar, because it is a visible, sensory sign. But are these European months a visible sensory sign?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: Not at all. They are purely conventional. Some of them reach thirty-one days, and others return to twenty-eight, without any reason or cause. So they are not based on any principle. Some calculators have tried to convert these months into a fixed number, making the year thirteen months instead of twelve, and some have tried to make them a fixed number without adding months, but the clergy rose against this.
(...) ﴿And glad tidings for the believers. Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il—indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah 97–98].
* Shaykh: His words ﴿مَنْ كَانَ عَدُوًّا﴾ (whoever is an enemy): to whom does it refer?
* Student: Those who say that Jibril is an evil spirit that descends for wars.
* Shaykh: He is our enemy? Who said that?
* Student: The Jews.
* Shaykh: The Jews. His words ﴿لِجِبْرِيلَ﴾ (to Jibril): are there variant readings?
* Student: ﴿جَبْرِيل﴾, ﴿جَبْرَئِل﴾ and ﴿جَبْرَائِيل﴾.
* Shaykh: Well done. Is Jibril an angel or a prophet?
* Student: An angel.
* Shaykh: An angel entrusted with a task?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: With what?
* Student: With bringing the Quran down to the Messenger ﷺ.
* Shaykh: With revelation. He is entrusted with revelation.
His words ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾ (indeed, he has brought it down): is this the response of the conditional or does it indicate it?
* Student: It indicates it.
* Shaykh: Where is the response of the conditional?
* Student: The clause.
* Shaykh: Where is the clause?
* Student: ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, so it is the response of the conditional. Are you disagreeing with Mustafa, who said it indicates it? Do you disagree with him?
* Student: I disagree.
* Shaykh: Good. Disagreement toward good is good.
* Student: It has been said that the response of the conditional is ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾, this is the response of the conditional. It has also been said that it is not the response of the conditional, but rather a reason for the response, and the response of the conditional is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "then let him die of rage."
* Shaykh: What do you say about this answer?
* Students: Correct.
* Shaykh: Correct. Which of them is closer?
* Student: The closer one is that it is omitted.
* Shaykh: The closer one is that it is omitted?
* Student: The one I preferred.
* Shaykh: The one you preferred, or the one I preferred?
* Student: I preferred it.
* Shaykh: Me? What do you say?
* Student: No, the more likely view is that it is the response of the conditional.
* Shaykh: That it is the response of the conditional? Because the basic principle is?
* Student: Because the basic principle is the presence of the response of the conditional.
* Shaykh: Non-omission. The basic principle is non-omission. Then His words, "then let him die of rage," in this style, mean an estimate that is not appropriate. Although He says: ﴿Say: Die in your rage﴾ [Al 'Imran 119], yet in this context it is not appropriate. The correct view is that His words ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾ are the response of the conditional. But what is its connection? What is the connection between His words ﴿فَإِنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ﴾ and His words ﴿مَنْ كَانَ عَدُوًّا لِجِبْرِيلَ﴾?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, not grammatically, but semantically. Grammatically, it is the response of the conditional. Semantically?
* Student: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, indeed he has brought it down upon your heart﴾, indeed he brought the Quran down upon the heart of a human being.
* Shaykh: But what is the semantic connection between the response of the conditional and the protasis?
* Student: That is, those who say Jibril is their enemy: the enemy always brings evil things, while Jibril, peace be upon him, brings things sent down from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so he brings good things.
* Shaykh: It is as if it were a reason for the ruling. The meaning is: ﴿whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾, indeed, there is nothing in him that merits enmity except that he has brought it down upon your heart, and this should not be a cause for enmity. In rhetoric they say: emphasizing a dispraise by means resembling praise, and emphasizing praise by means resembling dispraise. This resembles that. A poet says:

"And there is no fault in them, save that their swords
bear notches from the clashing of the battalions."

They have no fault except this. Is this a fault or a praise?
* Students: Praise.
* Shaykh: Praise. But it is emphasizing a dispraise by means resembling praise. So the correct view is that this is the response of the conditional.
His words ﴿عَلَى قَلْبِكَ﴾ (upon your heart): why was the heart chosen? ﴿نَزَّلَهُ عَلَى قَلْبِكَ﴾, why did He not say "upon you"? Why did He specify the heart?
* Student: Because it is the seat of knowledge, the place of...
* Shaykh: Of comprehension, the place of understanding and comprehension. His words ﴿بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ (by the permission of Allah): what is meant by "the permission of Allah" here?
* Student: By the command of Allah.
* Shaykh: By the command of Allah? Correct.
* Student: Is it not valid to say by His will?
* Shaykh: It is valid (...), the meaning is the command.
Permission is divided into two types: permission that is cosmic (kawni) and permission that is legislative (shar'i). Whatever relates to legal rulings is legislative permission; the permission of Allah is of two kinds: legislative and decreed (qadari). Whatever relates to legal rulings is legislative, and whatever relates to cosmic matters, such as creation, provision, governance and the like, is decreed permission. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent [lies] against Allah?﴾ [Yunus 59]. What is this? Is it legislative or decreed?

**Students:** Legislative (sharʿi).

**Shaykh:** Legislative, because by divine decree (qadar) He has permitted them to do it. They made lawful what they willed and prohibited what they willed. ﴿Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 42:21]

**Student:** Legislative.

**Shaykh:** Legislative. What is the evidence that it is legislative?

**Student:** His saying: ﴿prescribed﴾.

**Shaykh:** His saying: ﴿prescribed for them in religion﴾. Also, it is permitted by decree (qadar). What they prescribed in religion is permitted by decree. Had He not permitted it, it would not have happened. Had He not permitted it by decree, it would not have occurred. So they prescribed in religion what Allah did not permit by legislation (shar'an), but He permitted it by decree (qadaran).

﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255] Is this permission legislative or decreed (kawni qadari)?

**Students:** Both decreed and legislative.

**Shaykh:** ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ This is decreed (kawni), because it relates to governance and action. ﴿Intercede﴾ is a verb connected with Allah's permission and decree. So the permission meant here is the decreed, universal permission.

The difference between them in meaning and in effect: In meaning, whatever relates to legal rulings is legislative permission (idhn shar'i), and whatever relates to cosmic matters is decreed permission (idhn kawni). In effect: with legislative permission, the permitted act may or may not occur. With decreed permission, it must occur.

A second difference, also from (...): legislative permission concerns what Allah is pleased with and loves: ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:3]. Decreed permission may concern what Allah is pleased with, or what He is not pleased with. Is this understood, everyone?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Here in the verse: ﴿He has brought it down upon your heart by permission of Allah﴾. Which of the two kinds is this?

**Students:** Decreed.

**Shaykh:** Decreed. ﴿Confirming what was before it﴾: ﴿confirming﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). A circumstantial clause of whom? Of the pronoun in ﴿He has brought it down﴾. That is: He sent it down while it confirms what is before it. ﴿What was before it﴾ means what came before it, since "what is before it" has already preceded you. What is meant by "what is before it" is the Torah, the Gospel, and other books that foretold the revelation of the Qur'an. The Qur'an's confirmation of them has two aspects.

The first aspect: Did it bear witness to their truthfulness or not?

The second aspect: It came in agreement with what they had foretold. Thus it confirmed them in fact, because they themselves foretold this Qur'an, and it came confirming them.

﴿And guidance﴾ is conjoined to ﴿confirming﴾. Guidance (hudan) means indication (dalalah), and it may also mean success (tawfiq). The Qur'an is likewise guidance in the sense of indication and in the sense of success. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿By it Allah guides those who pursue His approval to the ways of peace﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:16]. This is undoubtedly the guidance of success, because the guidance of indication is for everyone, whether they follow Allah's approval or not. But the guidance of success is only for those who follow Allah's approval.

﴿A guidance and good tidings﴾: ﴿good tidings﴾ means glad tidings (bishara). Glad tidings is information about what gladdens, though it may also come in information about what harms, as in His saying: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21].

﴿For the believers﴾: Here faith (iman) means legislative faith, not the linguistic faith that is familiar among people, which is merely assent (tasdiq).
