His words: ﴿Those, it was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾ [al-Baqara 114]. What is its meaning? ﴿Those, it was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾: what is its meaning?
* Student: The hypocrites, it was not right for them to enter these mosques, because their hearts are not sincere with God (...).
* Shaykh: And who else understands?
* Student: The meaning is that those who prevent people, it is not right for them to enter the mosques except while fearful.
* Shaykh: Yes, correct. That is, it was the proper course that these should not enter it except in fear, because they are disbelievers in God, mighty and majestic, so they have no right to enter the mosques except in fear. So how can they prevent the servants of God? Or the meaning has another aspect: that this is a report carrying the meaning of a prohibition; that is, do not let them enter it when you have prevailed over them, except in fear. Or it is good news from God, mighty and majestic, that those who prevented the mosques, among them the polytheists who prevented the Prophet ﷺ from the Sacred Mosque, will be overcome, and they will not enter it except with their hearts trembling. So there are three possibilities now.

From this noble verse, several benefits can now be derived:

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 109–114 (part 6 of 7):

Either it is a prohibition, meaning: do not let them enter them except in fear; or it describes the state of these people, that it was not proper for them to enter the mosques, let alone to prevent the servants of Allah from them; or it is a glad tiding from Allah that the Muslims will prevail over them and dominance will be theirs, such that these people will not enter the mosques except in a state of fear.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, it falls under this; it points to (...) its complete meaning, it points to that.

Among the benefits of the verses now: ﴿And they say: None will enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian.﴾ [al-Baqarah 111]

From this noble verse is derived: the explanation of the self-admiration that the Jews and Christians had.

And also derived from it: that what they claimed is a lie, because of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿These are their wishful thoughts.﴾

* And among the benefits of the verse: that whoever is deceived by wishful thinking and covets high ranks without working for them, there is also in him a resemblance to the Jews and Christians.

And among them: the justice of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in addressing His servants; where He said: ﴿Say: Bring your proof.﴾ Why? Because this is from the category of what? Taking the opponent into consideration. From the category of taking the opponent into consideration: that if you have evidence, then bring it. And this is undoubtedly among the most eloquent forms of justice; otherwise, judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great.

And among them: that these people have no proof for what they claimed, as evidenced by the fact that they did not bring it.

And also among them: that they are liars, because of His saying: ﴿If you are truthful.﴾ And if they had even the slightest means of justifying and confirming their claim, they would have brought it. Therefore they are liars.

Then the Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good—he will have his reward with his Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [al-Baqarah 112]

From this noble verse is derived: that the people of Paradise are those who combine two attributes: sincerity to Allah, by His saying: ﴿Whoever submits his face to Allah﴾; and the second: following His legislation, by His saying: ﴿while being a doer of good﴾.

* And among the benefits of the verse: that good intention alone is not sufficient to justify worship, or to justify devotion to Allah. Good intention alone is not sufficient to justify devotion to Allah. From where do we take this? Because He said: ﴿while being a doer of good﴾.

It follows from this benefit that the people of innovation have no reward for their innovations, even with good intention. Why? Because of the lack of ihsan, which is following (the Sunnah). So the person of innovation, if he says: "I only intended good," we say: "But you did not do good." The reward is conditional on two things: submitting one's face to Allah, and the second, ihsan.

And among them: the affirmation of reward in the Hereafter: ﴿then he will have his reward with his Lord﴾, and that deeds will not be lost.

And among them: the affirmation of recompense, or does the previous one suffice?
So among them: that recompense is of the same kind as the deed.

And among them: the magnitude of this honour, by its attribution to Allah in His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾.

And among them: the absence of fear and grief for whoever worships Allah, the Exalted, with these two attributes, which are? Sincerity and following. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing—those will have security﴾ [al-An'am 82]. So whoever worships Allah, the Exalted, with these two attributes, there is no fear for him and no grief.

And among them: the good end of the believers, since fear and grief are removed from them, whereas those who do not believe have their hearts filled with terror and also grief. Yes, and grief. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the means of connection will be cut off from them﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 167], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret﴾ [Maryam 39], and other verses indicating the regret of those who were not guided to the path of the Praiseworthy.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And the Jews said﴾

* Student: We said: the innovator has no reward. But if he is a follower (muqallid), who imitates while having good intention, but he does not know, will he have a reward?

* The Shaykh: He has no reward (...).

* Student: Only, meaning he is excused by the second part of the conditions of action, and he came with the first part..?

* The Shaykh: But this action, he is not rewarded for it because it is an innovation, even if he is ignorant; because if he were knowing, what would result for him? Sin, he would incur sin. So if he is ignorant, we say: you are excused by ignorance, but this does not benefit him; because every action has two conditions: sincerity and following. So if following is absent, it is not accepted, and if it is not accepted, it does not benefit him.

* Student: And if there is a difference of opinion, such as wiping the face, some see it as an innovation and some see it as recommended?

* The Shaykh: If there is a difference of opinion, then according to what his ijtihad leads him to. If his ijtihad leads him to the view that this is prescribed, both he and others, then he is rewarded, because he is working for Allah while seeing himself as a follower. As for the person of innovation, the ignorant person of innovation may be rewarded for the general intention of good purpose; the general intention is not the intention of this innovation in particular. He is rewarded for his good purpose in a general sense. But being rewarded for his intention in this innovated act is not possible.

﴿And the Jews said: The Christians are not upon anything; and the Christians said: The Jews are not upon anything; while they recite the Book. Thus said those who do not know the like of their words…﴾ to the end [al-Baqarah 113]

This also contains evidence that the disbelieving nations declare one another to be disbelievers. The Jews say: the Christians are not upon anything, and the Christians say: the Jews are not upon anything. And the correct position is with whom? After the mission of the Messenger, all of them are in error; but before the mission of the Messenger, the correct position was with the Christians, since the Jews were not upon anything.

* And among the benefits of the verse: the condemnation of speech when it is made with knowledge; the condemnation of speech that opposes the truth when it is made with knowledge; by His saying: ﴿while they recite the Book﴾, for this clause adds to the ugliness of what they said, since they said that while reciting the Book and knowing the truth.

* And among the benefits of the verse: that this saying which the Jews and Christians said has been inherited from those before them, and inherited by those after them; by His saying: ﴿Thus said those who do not know the like of their words﴾.

* And among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the Day of Resurrection; by His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

And among them: the affirmation of judgment for Allah: ﴿So Allah will judge between them﴾.

And also among the benefits of the verse: that these people who differed regarding truth and falsehood, the judgment between them will take place on the Day of Resurrection before Allah. He will say to the one who has the truth: you are upon truth; and to the one who has falsehood: you are upon falsehood. Which of them will be the one who is refuted?

* The students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ [an-Nisa' 141].

For this reason, there is no ruling that clearly declares to one opponent that the truth is his and not his opponent's, except in this case. That is: the judge does not say, for example, to the two opponents: there will be no way for your companion over you; he does not say that until it becomes clear, each presenting his proof. But here Allah has made clear that the disbelievers have no way over the believers, why? Because the proof is established and clear to all.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein and strives toward their ruin? Those would not have entered them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾

In this is evidence that sins differ; by His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾, and "more unjust" is a comparative form, and the comparative form requires one who is preferred and one over whom he is preferred. Just as sins differ, so acts of obedience differ; some are better than others. And when deeds differ, the doer differs accordingly; some people are stronger in faith than others. By this we know that the correct position is the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, that faith increases and decreases, varying greatly, not only in the inward acquisition nor in the outward acquisition; it varies. People differ in certainty, and they differ in outward deeds, whether in speech or action. Their difference in certainty is, I think, known. Even a person himself varies in his statements from time to time: at times his mind and heart become clear, as if he were witnessing the Hereafter with his own eyes; and at other times heedlessness overcomes him. For this reason Allah said to Ibrahim: ﴿Did you not believe? He said: Yes, but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. And people's differing in knowledge is a known matter. Now, if a man comes to me and says: so-and-so has arrived, and that man is trustworthy to me, I have knowledge of it; then if another comes and says: so-and-so has arrived, my knowledge increases; if a third comes, my knowledge increases; and when I see him myself, it increases. Thus matters of knowledge vary in how hearts perceive them. Likewise people differ in statements: one who glorifies Allah ten times is more than one who glorifies Him five times, is he not? This increase is an increase in quantity of faith. Likewise it varies through deeds: one who prays six units is more than one who prays two units. Thus the preponderant position, without doubt, is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, that faith increases and decreases. Who opposed them in this? Two groups opposed them: the Murji'ah, the Kharijites and the Mu'tazilah. The Murji'ah said: faith does not increase nor decrease, because faith is the affirmation of the heart, and people do not differ in it; the most wicked and the most just are equal in faith, to the point that they made the faith of Jibril like the faith of Shaytan—we seek refuge in Allah. They said: because each of them affirms Allah, and faith is a person's affirmation of Allah, and it does not vary. Ibn al-Qayyim says:

"People in faith are one thing, like the comb when its teeth are equal."

Then he said: Chapter.

"Ask the accursed father of the jinn, do you know the Merciful, or have you become one who denies?
Ask Thamud and 'Ad, nay, ask before them the enemies of Nuh, the nation of the Flood."

And so on to the end of what he said. So according to them people are equal: a man who commits adultery, steals, drinks wine and kills an inviolable soul, but he believes in Allah; and a righteous man who is farthest from sins and strongest in obedience to Allah; faith in this and in that is equal. Is this reasonable? It is not reasonable. The Kharijites and the Mu'tazilah opposed them in this, saying: faith does not increase nor decrease; but if a single particle of it is lost, all of it is lost. The adulterer, if he prays, fasts, pays zakah, performs Hajj, and testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, is a disbeliever, not a believer. And the extremist Murji'ah, what do they say? A believer of complete faith—look—strange innovations, we seek refuge in Allah. Whereas the People of the Sunnah and the Community say: faith increases and decreases in quantity and in quality, in the affirmation of the heart, in the statements of the tongue, and in the deeds of the limbs. And the verse before us indicates this. What is the mode of indication from the verse? That sins differ, and it follows from this that doers differ, because whoever commits a greater sin becomes greater in guilt and sin.

And among the benefits of the verse: the prohibition of preventing the mosques from having His name mentioned therein, whether by prayer, reciting the Qur'an, teaching knowledge, or otherwise. It is not permissible to prevent the mosques of Allah from His name being mentioned in them.

And among the benefits of the verse: the permissibility of closing mosques for the interest of the mosques, such as closing them out of fear of their being corrupted or stolen or the like; because what is forbidden is: that His name be mentioned therein; that is the prohibited act and the injustice. Some scholars used this verse as evidence for the prohibition of taḥajjur. Do you know taḥajjur? That a person reserves a place for himself in the row by claiming it. He said: because this prevents this place from having the name of Allah mentioned in it, since this place is most rightly held by the one who arrived first. So you now placed your sandals; do these sandals mention and glorify (Allah)?

* Student: Only, other than glorification which...

* The Shaykh: Other than glorification for which the mosque was built; otherwise the mosque would be filled with sandals and people walking. But they do not glorify with the glorification for which the mosque was built. Now you have prevented this place from a man who comes to it and mentions the name of Allah in it, or not? This is the mode of inference. And there is no doubt that taḥajjur is forbidden: that a person places his shoe and goes off to sell and buy, or goes, for example, to his house to enjoy his children and family; this is not permissible. As for yes, if the person is in the same mosque and needs to take this place and remain in it, and goes to benefit in another part of the mosque, then there is no doubt that he is first to the mosque; but he saw that this place is now unsuitable for him. Yet even in this matter, if for example he is in the second row and people have reached him and filled the row up to him, it is obligatory for him to go to his place in the first row; because if he remains there he has prevented this place from having the name of Allah mentioned in it.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the honour of mosques, by their attribution to Allah: ﴿the mosques of Allah﴾.

And among them: that it is not permissible to place in them anything that would be a cause of shirk; because the mosques of Allah means the place of prostration to Him. If we place in them what would be a cause of shirk, we have taken them out of their purpose, such as what?

* Student: Graves.

* The Shaykh: Yes, that we bury the dead in them; this is forbidden, because it is a means to shirk, so we would have taken the mosques out of their purpose.

And among them: the obligation of purifying the mosques. From where do we take this? From their attribution to Allah, which requires their honour and magnification. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate and those who stand and bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj 26].

Can we say: and among them that people are equal in them?

* Student: Yes (...).

* The Shaykh: No, from the fact that Allah attributed them to Himself, and people are the servants of Allah, equal in relation to Allah. We do not say: this man is noble, generous, wealthy, an amir, a minister, a king, and he must be the one put forward in these mosques. People are equal in them, because they are the mosques of Allah; so everyone who comes to these mosques to worship Allah, there is no difference between him and others.

Now, can it be derived from this noble verse that it is permissible for a scholar to reserve a place for teaching in these mosques? Then it is permissible; it is permissible to take a place and make it for remembrance (dhikr); but when the prayer is established, he does not prevent people, saying: do not pray in my place; he and others are equal. But if he takes a place for sitting and teaching people or giving admonition to people, then he has the right.

And among them (among the benefits of the verse): that the remembrance of Allah must be by His name. So you say: lā ilāha illā Allāh, Subḥān Allāh, Subḥāna Rabbika Rabbi al-'Izzati 'ammā yaṣifūn, Subḥāna Rabbī al-'Aẓīm; you mention Him by His name, because of His saying: ﴿that His name be mentioned therein﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]. The mention of Him, the Exalted, by the singular pronoun is an innovation, and it is not remembrance, like the method of the Sufis who say: the best remembrance is that you say: Huwa, huwa, huwa, huwa, huwa. Why? Because you do not witness anything but Allah—we seek refuge in Allah. They consider the perfect state of a person to be annihilation (fana'), that he be annihilated from witnessing anything other than Allah, so that in their view nothing is witnessed but the Creator. So do not say: lā ilāha illā Huwa, thereby affirming two, one negated and one affirmed; rather say: Huwa, huwa, huwa, according to the swaying of their heads. This is without doubt an innovation, and it is not a remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; rather it is among the abominations.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of destroying mosques; by His saying: ﴿and strives toward their ruin﴾. Destruction, as we said in the commentary, is both material and immaterial. Among the material is that one breaks the lamps, strips off the plaster, for example, cuts the wires, tears the carpets, and the like.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No, no, this is good; this is repair (ta'mir), not destruction. And among the immaterial (ma'nawi) forms of it is doing something that disturbs those who pray and those who recite. For if he disturbs them, they cannot properly remember Allah. And there is no doubt that preventing people from properly remembering Allah is destruction, isn't it? It is destruction and corruption in the immaterial sense, destruction and corruption in the immaterial sense. For this reason the scholars said: it is forbidden to raise one's voice in reciting the Qur'an while in the mosque if it disturbs those who are praying, even though one is raising one's voice in the remembrance of Allah.

Among the benefits of the noble verse, in His saying: ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear.﴾: good news for the believers that the final outcome is theirs. Those who prevented them will not enter them except while fearful. This is according to one of the possibilities we mentioned.

And among them: the punishment of one who prevents Allah's mosques from having His name mentioned in them and strives to ruin them is disgrace and shame in this world, and a great torment in the Hereafter.

* And among the benefits of the verse: when a sin involves transgression against the servants, Allah may combine two punishments for its doer: the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. As for when it is against Allah, Allah the Most High does not combine two punishments for it: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much.﴾ [ash-Shura 30].

The scholars said: meaning, He does not combine two punishments for a person. And this applies when the sin relates to whom? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic; for He does not exact His right from His servant twice. But if the sin relates to a created being, Allah may combine two punishments for this doer: the punishment of this world, why? Just as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, He heals the heart of the wronged, the heart of the one who was transgressed against, isn't that so? And there is no doubt that a person, for example, if someone transgresses against you and then you see Allah's punishment upon him, you rejoice that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has taken retribution for you from him. So the summary, my brothers: if someone says: how can they have disgrace in this world and a great torment in the Hereafter, when Allah the Most High does not combine two punishments? We say: because this punishment relates to the right of a created being, so Allah punished its doer in this world and the Hereafter, so that the wronged person may witness that Allah has taken retribution for him.

And among them: the affirmation of the Day of Resurrection, by His saying: ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great torment.﴾

And among them: that the torment of the Hereafter is greater than the torment of this world, just as the bliss of the Hereafter is greater than the bliss of this world. But Allah, Glorified and Exalted, shows His servants a sample of both this and that, because the understanding of the threat and the understanding of the promise are not sound except by what? Except by witnessing a sample of that. If Allah had, for example, threatened with the Fire, we would not know what the Fire is: would we fear it? We would fear only a general, overall fear. Likewise, if He had promised bliss in Paradise, and we do not know what this bliss is, we would not have desire for it, as when we are shown it and find its counterpart in name in this world.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 115].

﴿To Allah belong the east and the west.﴾ The lam here indicates ownership and exclusivity. That is, Allah the Exalted is the Owner of the east and the west, and the entire world is nothing but east and west. Thus Allah the Exalted owns everything. Is al-mashriq (the east) a place of sunrise or a time of sunrise? It is a place, and al-maghrib (the west) is likewise a place. The words al-mashriq and al-maghrib occur in the Qur'an in three forms: singular, dual and plural. Here He says: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾; in another verse He says: ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 28]; in a second verse He says: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman 17]; and in a third: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij 40].

How can these three forms be reconciled? We say: as for al-mashriq (singular), it does not contradict al-mashariq (plural) or al-mashriqayn (dual), why? Because it is a singular noun with the definite article al-, so it denotes the whole category, whether one or many. As for ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ and ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests﴾, the combination of them may be explained in one of two ways: either the plural al-mashariq and al-magharib are used in consideration of the risers and setters (of the sun)—for who rises and sets other than the sun? The moon and the stars, and who can count the stars?—and the dual is used in consideration of the sunrise of winter and the sunrise of summer. In winter the sun rises at the farthest south, and in summer at the farthest north, and between them are vast distances known only to Allah. Consider the distance between its sunrise in winter and its sunrise in the days of summer: it is an enormous distance, perhaps thousands upon thousands [of miles], given the size of the earth. Thus the dual is used in this respect. Furthermore, you will notice that most of Surat al-Rahman is in the dual form, or not? Therefore it was verbally appropriate that al-mashriq and al-maghrib be mentioned in the dual. As for the context of majesty, ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests, indeed We are able [40] to replace them with better than them﴾ [al-Ma'arij 40–41]. Which form came? The plural form, because the plural indicates majesty more than the dual, since the dual is explicit in indicating restriction (to two). So ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ means: the east of every riser and the west of every setter.

﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.﴾ Let us look at (ayna): what is its grammatical analysis? I think we know it?
* Student: It is a adverb of place (ẓarf).
* Shaykh: No, it is an adverb, but more specifically it is conditional. Ayna is conditional, mā is redundant (zā'idah), and tuwallū is the verb of the condition. Is tuwallū a present tense verb, a past tense verb, or an imperative?
* Student: Present tense.
* Shaykh: What is the evidence that it is present tense?
* Student: That it is jussive; its position is in the jussive position.
* Shaykh: Do you say tuwallūn? Yes, in the Qur'an: ﴿On the Day you turn back in retreat﴾ [Ghafir 33]. So tuwallū is a present-tense verb in the jussive, governed by the conditional particle, and the sign of its jussive is the deletion of the nūn—and the wāw is the subject?
* Student: The deletion of the nūn?
* Shaykh: Yes, the deletion of the nūn, and the wāw is the subject.

Now, His saying ﴿then there is the Face of Allah﴾: the fa' is the linking particle for the answer of the condition; thamma is a demonstrative, an adverb, but it is a demonstrative used for the distant; it is related to an omitted predicate that is a preposed predicate (khabar muqaddam); wajh is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and the sentence consisting of the subject and its predicate is in the jussive position as the answer of the condition. We have now finished the grammar.

What is the meaning of tuwallū? Tuwallū means you face (tatajjahū). His saying fa-thamma means: there, and it points to the direction toward which you turned.

As for His saying ﴿the Face of Allah﴾, the exegetes from the early and later generations differed about it. Some of them said: what is meant is the real Face of Allah. Some scholars said: what is meant is the direction; wajh here means jihah (direction), i.e., in the place to which you have turned is the direction of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah encompasses everything, encompasses everything. So there are two opinions among the scholars, but the preponderant view is that what is meant is the real Face, because that is the basic meaning and nothing prevents it. The Prophet ﷺ informed that Allah the Exalted is in front of the face of the one praying[[From the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), raised to the Prophet: "When one of you prays, let him not spit in front of his face, for Allah is in front of his face when he prays." Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (406) and Muslim (547/50).]]. And where do those who pray face? One faces east, another west, another north, another south, according to his location: the people of Yemen face north, the people of Shām face south, the people of Najd face west, and the people of Egypt face east—is it clear? Each one faces a direction, but this direction that unites them is the qiblah, and each one faces the Face of Allah. Accordingly, Allah the Mighty and Majestic's meaning of the verse is: wherever you turn in your prayer, you are turning toward Allah, whether to the east, or to the west, or to the south, or to the north. Have you understood? A similar meaning is found in: ﴿Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east and the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 177].

The Shaykh: But what is its meaning? Badi' means?
* Student: Fā'il, meaning fa'il.
* Shaykh: Fa'il means?
* Student: Means maf'ul; that is, badi' means (mab'ud).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Means mubdi'.
* Shaykh: Means mubdi' (fa'il in the sense of muf'il). Good, it has a counterpart in the Arabic language.
* Student: It has a counterpart, fa'il.
* Shaykh: Like?
* Student: Like the poet's saying: "mā anā bi-ḥāfiẓihi" (I am not its keeper).
* Another student: Qatil.
* Shaykh: No, because qatil means maqtul.
* Student: Raḥīm.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Alīm means mu'lim.
* Shaykh: Alīm means mu'lim.
* Student: Samī'.
* Shaykh: Samī' means musmi', correct.
* Student: Samī' means sāmi'?
* Shaykh: No, it means musmi', and on this is the poet's saying: samī' means musmi'.
* Student:
"Amin Rayḥānata al-dā'ī al-samī' ∗∗∗ yu'arriquni wa-aṣḥābī hujū'"
* Shaykh: "Amin Rayḥāna al-dā'ī al-samī'," meaning: the one who makes [it] heard.
"yu'arriqunī wa-aṣḥābī hujū'." Samī' means al-musmi'. And ﴿Badī' al-samawāti wal-arḍ﴾ means its originator of them without precedent, the one who brought them into being without a prior pattern.

What is the purpose of this sentence, and what is the purpose of His saying ﴿Badī' al-samawāti wal-arḍ﴾? Who knows?

The response to those who said: Allah has taken a son. That is, the One who is able to originate the heavens and the earth is able to create a son without a father; because the Christians said: the Messiah is the son of Allah—and where is his father? He came from a mother, so where is his father? They said: his father is Allah. The angels, from where did they come? They said: they are daughters of Allah. So Allah said: ﴿Badī' al-samawāti wal-arḍ﴾, meaning: the One who is able to originate the heavens and the earth is able to create a human being without a father.

His saying: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ali 'Imran 47]. And what is the meaning of "when He decrees"?
* Student: When He intends to decree it.
* Shaykh: When He intends to decree it. Does the verb come to mean its intention?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Like?
* Student: "When he stands up for prayer."
* Shaykh: From the Qur'an?
* Student: His saying: ﴿When you stand up﴾.
* Shaykh: Then wash? Yes, and His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 98], i.e., when you intend to recite it.

What is the evidence for interpreting qaḍā as meaning arāda (intended)? What is the evidence that qaḍā means arāda, that it intends to decree?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By evidence from the Qur'an, because the Qur'an explains part of itself by part; find for us a verse from the Qur'an as evidence.
* Student: You mean other than this verse?
* Shaykh: Other than this verse?
* Student: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23]?
* Shaykh: No, the bane of knowledge is forgetfulness. Allahu akbar! ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82].

However, I told you: it is permissible to take qaḍā not to mean arāda, but to mean "did something"; so when He does it, He says to it "Be," and it is—that is, when He decrees something, that is not a difficult matter for Him; for its decree requires only that He say "Be," and it is.

In His saying ﴿fa-yakūnu﴾ there are two readings. Are there two readings of fa-yakūnu?
* Student: What we mentioned.
* Shaykh: What we mentioned?
* Student: There is the naṣb (accusative), fa-yakūna as an answer to the command, or on the assumption of an omitted conditional verb?
* Shaykh: Then he is.
* Student: And the second, fa-yakūnu in the rafʿ (nominative).
* Shaykh: That is, on the assumption of resumption (istiʾnāf), i.e., so he is.

There are two readings: the naṣb ﴿fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu kun fa-yakūna﴾, and the second reading: ﴿fa-yakūnu﴾. On the reading with naṣb it is an answer to the command: "Be," so by that it comes to be; the fa' indicates causation. On the reading with rafʿ it is resumptive: i.e., so He is; when He says to it "Be," it comes to be. Is this kun complete or incomplete?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Complete. And what is the reason? Or because completeness is better than incompleteness?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Amazing, correct?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Then let us complete the verse.

﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ Here, is the decree (al-qaḍāʾ) universal (kawnī) or legislative (shar'ī)? We say: it is universal; the decree is universal, and qaḍā may mean arāda an yaqḍiya, as is shown by His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]. ﴿When He intends a thing﴾—He did not say "when He decrees a thing," He said "when He intends," and the verb is used for its concurrent intention, like His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ and ﴿When you stand up for prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6]. The Prophet ﷺ, when he entered the lavatory, would say: "I seek refuge in Allah from the male and female evil spirits"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (142) and Muslim (375/122), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]; i.e., when he intended to enter. As for His saying ﴿amran﴾ (a matter): is amr the singular of awāmir (commands) or the singular of umūr (matters)?
* Student: The singular of umūr.
* Shaykh: The singular of umūr; that is, affairs. I.e., when He decrees an affair of His affairs, glorified and exalted is He, that is not difficult for Him: ﴿fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu kun fa-yakūn﴾—one word, "Be," without repetition; so it comes to be, it comes to be as Allah the Exalted wills.

His saying ﴿fa-innamā yaqūlu﴾: (innamā) is a particle of restriction, i.e., He says to it only "Be." Here kun is complete, i.e., "come into existence" (ḥadatha yaḥdutha uḥdith), so it is complete. ﴿Fa-yakūnu﴾ is also complete, i.e., so it comes to be, i.e., so it comes into existence as Allah the Exalted commanded. The purpose of this sentence is also to establish that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) is not a son of Allah; for by what was he [created]? By a pairing between Maryam and Allah the Exalted? No, but by the word "Be." Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Ali 'Imran 59]. Adam was created without a father or a mother; ﴿He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾, i.e., "Be a human," and he was. So the One who is able to create Adam without a father or mother is more able to create a human without a father, from a mother without a father.

As for His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu kun fa-yakūn﴾—look: if you want an example of this, recite the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿It is only one shout (zajrah), and at once they are on the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at 13–14]. One shout with which He drives all creatures—all creatures that were annihilated and perished since He created them until the Day of Resurrection—He drives them with one shout so that they stand up alive, and they stand up. Look: ﴿and at once they are on the surface of the earth﴾: "idhā" here is the sudden-occurrence particle (fujā'iyyah), as you know, and the sudden particle indicates immediacy and immediate sequence. ﴿Then at once they are on the surface of the earth﴾: who counts these creatures?
* Student: None counts them but their Creator.
* Shaykh: None counts them except the One who created them with their different kinds, forms, greatness and smallness, with one word. Glory be to Allah the Great! So at once they are on the surface of the earth; this is evidence of His perfect power, majesty and might, and that when He intends a thing nothing can thwart Him; He says to it, "Be," and it is. So how do you say, "From where will ʿĪsā come? From where will the angels come?" With this, the verse contains evidence refuting this view in several respects:
First: ﴿Glorified is He﴾.
Second: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾.
Third: ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 116]. Fourth: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. And what comes after?
Fifth: ﴿And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. Five aspects, all of which indicate the falsity of the claim of those who say that Allah has taken a son, on the argument that this is a matter that cannot happen except by being a son of Allah. ﴿fa-innamā yaqūlu lahu kun fa-yakūn﴾.
* Student: There are things, like the creatures, that He did not create by "Be"—such as the heavens and the earth and things He did not create by "Be"; is it only [some things] and the rest He says to the thing "Be"?
* Shaykh: Who said they were not created by "Be"?
* Student: But in six days?
* Shaykh: Good. The six days are a gradual coming-into-being, finished in six days; everything that comes into being must have been told "Be."
* Student: (...) like Adam?
* Shaykh: Everything. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was. The verse ﴿His command, when He intends a thing﴾, and the whole cosmos is His intention.
* Student: But He created him with His hand?
* Shaykh: (...) with His hand, and He said to him, "Be," and he was.
* Student: "I created with My hands"—made creation with My hands, or with My two hands (...)?
* Shaykh: Correct, but along with being created by the hand, it is also by the word; then He said to him, "Be," and he was.
* Student: The sequence "fa-yakūnu" indicates its existence (...) now?
* Shaykh: Yes; the origin of creation now, the formation of Adam by the hand of Allah the Mighty and Majestic—there is no doubt that Allah intended it. Indeed, the saying "Be" may not be said except after He has completed its creation with His hand; He did not say "Be" except after He had completed its creation with His hand, so creation and formation by the hand occur without anything being said to it. Its becoming a human being, a person, is by the word "Be."
* Student: Then is there nothing (...)?
* Shaykh: I do not know of anything.
* Student: Allah the Exalted wrote the Torah and the Psalms with His hand, then said "Be"?
* Shaykh: Legislative matters are not said to be "Be"; even the whole Qur'an did not say "Be"; the Qur'an was spoken and Jibril brought it down; its words are not said to be themselves words.
* Student: Also writing.
* Shaykh: Writing is among His words? That is why the Torah is considered one of the words of Allah.
* Student: Shaykh, there is a difference between "yatakawwan" and "yakūn": it comes into being gradually, but does Allah after the sequence with fa' mean it does become actual?
* Shaykh: When He intends, for everything He intends He says "Be." For example, this embryo: Allah the Exalted intended that it become a drop, and it was; He said "Be a drop," and it was; then a clot, and so on until the end. Then afterwards: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation﴾. Everything is what Allah intends, whether it develops gradually or occurs suddenly; and I do not know of anything occurring suddenly like this except through development, because it is part of Allah the Exalted's way that development occurs in the law and in destiny; everything must have a gradation until it is complete and finished. And we now have the generality of ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾ [Ali 'Imran 47], and every matter is decreed for Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 115–119 (part 2 of 4):

﴿فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُ كُنْ فَيَكُونُ﴾ This is what can be excluded from this generality, except for something we know with certainty was excluded from it. It is correct that Adam's creation by Allah, by His hand, is something we cannot say means that whenever Allah wants to create something from him He says to him: "Be," and we cannot assert this. Allah, glorified and exalted, may by His will have brought him into being with His hand as He willed, and then said to him: "Be," meaning: be a complete human being. As for the hadith: «أَجْعَلُ مَنْ خَلَقْتُهُ بِيَدَيَّ كَمَنْ خَلَقْتُهُ بِكَلِمَتِي» [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (147) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]] this must be examined, and I do not know whether it is authentic; God willing, verify it for us.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
﴿وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ لَوْلَا يُكَلِّمُنَا اللَّهُ أَوْ تَأْتِينَا آيَةٌ﴾ [al-Baqarah 118] These are the ones who denied the messengers, and what is meant by them are those of the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿كَذَلِكَ قَالَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ "Likewise said those before them." Those who do not know are those of the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. They said: ﴿لَوْلَا يُكَلِّمُنَا اللَّهُ أَوْ تَأْتِينَا آيَةٌ﴾ "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign come to us?" So they proposed to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, things, while the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had come with greater than them, and yet they did not believe in those either. This shows that their proposal was nothing but obstinacy and stubbornness, and not intended to reach the truth, because the Messenger ﷺ came with greater than what they proposed. ﴿قَالَ الَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ لَوْلَا يُكَلِّمُنَا اللَّهُ﴾. Does the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, necessarily fail because the sign they asked for, which is Allah speaking to them, is absent?
* Students: No, it does not necessarily follow.
* Shaykh: It does not necessarily follow, because what is established is not restricted to a single proof; that is, things may have multiple proofs. The establishment of the Messenger's prophethood, peace and blessings be upon him, does not depend on these signs they proposed, since he has brought signs stronger than them. For this reason, it is an established principle that the absence of a specific proof does not entail the absence of what it proves, why? Because what is proven has multiple proofs. If we assume it was not established by this proof, it has been established by another proof. When Abraham debated the one who said: "I give life and cause death," he brought another proof: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْتِي بِالشَّمْسِ مِنَ الْمَشْرِقِ فَأْتِ بِهَا مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. The point is that to those who said: "Why does Allah not speak to us?" we say: Allah's speaking to you does not necessarily entail the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, nor does its absence entail his untruthfulness, because there are signs and proofs stronger than what you claim. So your saying: "It must come to us, this specific sign" is not accepted, since signs indicating his truthfulness exist. Your demand for this specific sign is stubbornness, like if you asked a person for a need and he fulfilled it for you, and you said: "No, I will only accept it from so-and-so, and it is the same need." What does this mean?
* Student: Stubbornness.
* Shaykh: The meaning of this is stubbornness. Your request has been fulfilled. As for your being stubborn about such and such without any cause, and these people without cause; for Allah speaking to them is not something they want as an honor from Allah to them through speech. They do not want this. If they wanted this, we would say: it is a reasonable request. But what do they want by it?
* Student: Incapacitating (the Messenger).
* Shaykh: They want by it to establish the prophethood of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. They say: "If you are truthful, let Allah speak to us." Do you understand or not? I am now saying: if they had asked that Allah speak to them as an honor for them, their request would have been reasonable, but they asked that Allah speak to them so that the Messenger's ﷺ prophethood would be established by that.
We say: this claim of yours is stubbornness, since the Messenger ﷺ came with something greater than this. Likewise they said: ﴿أَوْ تَأْتِينَا آيَةٌ﴾. Subhan Allah! ﴿أَوْ تَأْتِينَا آيَةٌ﴾? As if no sign had come to them proving the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and this is denial. So the first is stubbornness, and the second is denial. The first: stubbornness in their insisting on a specific thing, saying: "Will you bring it or we will not believe?" The second: denial and rejection, or "let a sign come to us"; for there is no doubt that great signs came to them. The greatest sign that came to them is this Qur'an. Allah, exalted is He, said to them: ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ فِي رَيْبٍ مِمَّا نَزَّلْنَا عَلَى عَبْدِنَا فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِنْ مِثْلِهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah 23]. Bring a surah like it. Could you?
* Students: No, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Then, is the Qur'an from Muhammad ﷺ? No; if it were from Muhammad, they would have been able to bring its like, since they are like him, although he was the most eloquent of them because of the revelation sent down to him. So: ﴿أَوْ تَأْتِينَا آيَةٌ﴾ we say: this last proposal is undoubtedly denial and rejection. Why?
* Student: Because a sign has already come to them.
* Shaykh: Because a sign has already come to them, indeed signs. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿كَذَلِكَ قَالَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah 118]. "Likewise" means: like this statement, said those before them. On this basis, ﴿مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ﴾ "like their statement" is an emphasis of His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾, meaning: a statement like this was said and proposed by those before them. The people of Musa said: ﴿لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّى نَرَى اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. "We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly," and "Show us Allah openly, or we will not believe you." This is the way of those who deny the messengers: they deny and they propose, and they were given signs greater than what they proposed. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿كَذَلِكَ قَالَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ﴾. The purpose of His saying: ﴿كَذَلِكَ قَالَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ﴾ is to console the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. Right?
* Students: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: Because a person who is afflicted, when he sees that others have been afflicted, is consoled by that, and this is well known. Right? Suppose, for example, thieves raided houses and stole a hundred riyals from one person. Of course he grieves, but when another says: "Two hundred were stolen from me," what happens?
* Student: ... it becomes easy.
* Shaykh: It becomes easy for him, very easy. When al-Khansa's brother Sakhr died, she said:
"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself. / They do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him with consolation."
Allah, exalted, consoles His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, that this statement said to you has been said to those before you: ﴿كَذَلِكَ قَالَ الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ﴾. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿تَشَابَهَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾ Look: the earlier and later ones, their hearts are alike in rejecting and nullifying the truth, in obstinacy, stubbornness and denial, from the time the messengers were sent until their seal, Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and even until the Day of Resurrection. The hearts of the people of disbelief, may Allah protect us, and obstinacy are alike; only the style differs, the subject is one, but the style differs. These may propose one thing and those another, but the discussion concerns the type of proposal and non-acceptance: ﴿تَشَابَهَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾. For this reason He said: ﴿تَشَابَهَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ﴾. Notice: about the statement He says ﴿مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ﴾, and about the hearts He says ﴿تَشَابَهَتْ﴾. So does this mean that similarity (mushabahah) is the same as equivalence (mumathalah) or not? What we established earlier is that similarity is not like equivalence, because mushabahah means approximation, and mumathalah means equality, right?
* Students: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: There is no doubt that hearts resemble one another even when statements are identical, since among these people there may be what is not among those, of intense disbelief and obstinacy, but the statements are identical.
Allah, exalted, said: ﴿قَدْ بَيَّنَّا الْآيَاتِ لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾ "bayyanna" means "we made clear," since (bâna) means "became apparent," and (bayyana) means "made apparent." And His saying ﴿الْآيَاتِ﴾ is the plural of āyah, which is the sign that specifies what it indicates; every sign that specifies what it indicates is called āyah. So the signs that specify the one to whom they are signs are called āyāt, and Allah's signs are the indications pointing to Him, that is, specifying Him, glorified and exalted. The scholars mentioned that they are divided into two types: legislative signs and cosmic signs. The legislative signs are what the messengers brought of revelation, and they are signs because there is no parallel to them in truthfulness of reports, goodness of narratives, and justice of rulings. The legislative signs of Allah have no parallel in human speech in these three matters: truthfulness of reports; goodness of narratives, that is, all the stories in the Qur'an (...) are all beneficial stories and great lessons; and the third, justice of rulings, for which there is no parallel at all. However much you find of systems, laws, and sayings, both well-known and not, you cannot find the like of this Qur'an. Therefore it is a sign from the signs of Allah.
Likewise the cosmic signs, whose manifestness is greater and clearer, because you can argue with them rationally against the one who denies Allah or not, like...?
* Student: The night and the day, the sun and the moon.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, like the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon, the night and the day, and everything.
"And in everything there is a sign that indicates that He is One."
These are signs, O brothers. Allah says that He has made them clear, but to whom? ﴿لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾ The one with certainty, the signs become clear to him and he knows them, while the doubter is not made clear. The doubter does not get clarity, may Allah protect us, and matters may be obscured to him, and he may move from doubt to the stage of denial, because doubt, as you know, is a stage between two stages: between affirmation and denial. So it may be that with doubt, may Allah protect us, he reaches the point of denial. Doubt is not sufficient for faith. In this verse, ﴿قَدْ بَيَّنَّا الْآيَاتِ﴾ is evidence that Allah has established the proof, and that the signs do not benefit everyone; they benefit only the one who is certain. As for the doubter, the signs do not benefit him: ﴿وَمَا تُغْنِي الْآيَاتُ وَالنُّذُرُ عَنْ قَوْمٍ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ [Yunus 101].
* Student: Shaykh, is this statement the statement of the Jews of Medina, that the surah is Medinan?
* Shaykh: Which of them?
* Student: Those who said the surah is Medinan.
* Shaykh: No, it is general. That is, ﴿وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is general, and (qala) is a past-tense verb that includes what existed at the time the verse was revealed and what preceded it.
* Student: (...) it is the splitting of the moon, the splitting of the moon (...) so does...?
* Shaykh: No, the scholars said: they asked for an unspecified sign.
* Student: Were they answered?
* Shaykh: Yes, they were answered with this sign, and those who are destroyed when they propose are answered; if they ask for a specific sign and are answered with it, they will be destroyed.
Allah, exalted, said: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ بَشِيرًا وَنَذِيرًا﴾ [al-Baqarah 119]. That is, the meaning is that those who say: ﴿لَوْلَا يُكَلِّمُنَا اللَّهُ﴾ are answered with this verse: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ﴾. And "inna" is for emphasis. Where is its subject?
* Student: (...).
* Another student: Its subject is the pronoun.
* Shaykh: And where is the pronoun?
* Student: "We" (nahnu).
* Shaykh: And where is "we"?
* Student: "(na)", Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Its subject is (na), but the nun was deleted only to avoid the succession of similar sounds, although sometimes (innana) is not deleted, ﴿وَإِنَّنَا لَفِي شَكٍّ﴾ [Hud 62]. But do not say its subject is the alif, lest one of you say its subject is the alif, since the alif is not a pronoun except when attached to a verb, like qala, qama, and what is similar.
﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ To whom were you sent? The recipients are omitted to indicate generality, since the Prophet ﷺ is sent to all creation, while other messengers were sent to whom?
* Students: To their own people specifically.
* Shaykh: To their own people specifically. As for the Messenger: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ﴾.
And His saying: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ The "bi" here is for accompaniment and association, meaning: We sent you accompanied by the truth; or the meaning is: carrying the truth with this message. That is, the verse may bear two meanings: one, that your sending is true; the second, that what you were sent with is true. Have you understood the difference between the two meanings?
Both meanings are established: the Messenger's prophethood, peace and blessings be upon him, is true, and accordingly the "bi" is for association; and what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent with is true, and accordingly the "bi" is for accompaniment, meaning your message is accompanied by truth, since what you brought is true. We said that truth is the opposite of falsehood, and it is what is firm and stable. If it is attributed to reports, it means truthfulness; if it is attributed to rulings, it means justice. What the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought is true in its reports and in its rulings: ﴿وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ صِدْقًا وَعَدْلًا﴾ [al-An'am 115]. It is apparently not hidden from everyone that truth is accepted and desired by every soul, is it not so?
* Students: Indeed.
* Shaykh: If so, whoever seeks the truth finds it, and whoever turns away from it to falsehood is punished by being deprived of it. Have you understood?
﴿بِالْحَقِّ بَشِيرًا وَنَذِيرًا﴾ May Allah bless and grant him peace. ﴿بَشِيرًا﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of whom?
* Student: Of the kaf in ﴿أَرْسَلْنَاكَ﴾.
* Shaykh: Of the kaf in ﴿أَرْسَلْنَاكَ﴾, which is the object. And ﴿وَنَذِيرًا﴾: another circumstantial state by means of the conjunction. Thus Allah combined in him being a bringer of good news and a warner, because what he brought includes commands and prohibitions; what fits commands is good news, and what fits prohibitions is warning. Accordingly, the prophethood of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, combines glad tidings and warning. Who is given glad tidings by it, and who is warned by it?
Allah explained this in several verses: in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿لِيُنْذِرَ بَأْسًا شَدِيدًا مِنْ لَدُنْهُ وَيُبَشِّرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الَّذِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ الصَّالِحَاتِ أَنَّ لَهُمْ أَجْرًا حَسَنًا﴾ [al-Kahf 2]. Likewise He said: ﴿فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَاهُ بِلِسَانِكَ لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ الْمُتَّقِينَ وَتُنْذِرَ بِهِ قَوْمًا لُدًّا﴾ [Maryam 97].
So the Messenger ﷺ is a bringer of good news to the God-fearing who do righteous deeds, and a warner to the lud, the plural of alladd, meaning the obstinate adversary. He warns them of worldly punishment, or otherworldly punishment, or both?
* Students: Both.
* Shaykh: Both, yes, both or one of them. Punishment must come to them; and if we say that punishment includes depriving a person of obedience and faith, then he must be punished with both: worldly and religious punishment. ﴿بَشِيرًا وَنَذِيرًا وَلَا تُسْأَلُ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ الْجَحِيمِ﴾. In His saying ﴿وَلَا تُسْأَلُ﴾ there are two readings. One: ﴿وَلَا تُسْأَلُ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ الْجَحِيمِ﴾ with the negative particle "la" and the verb in the passive voice, meaning: you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire; that is, Allah will not ask you about them, because you have delivered the message, and the reckoning is upon whom? Upon Allah. The second reading: ﴿وَلَا تَسْأَلْ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ الْجَحِيمِ﴾, where "la" is a prohibitive particle and "tas'al" is an imperfect verb in the active voice: do not you ask, or: do not ask, O addressee.
According to the first reading, ﴿وَلَا تُسْأَلُ﴾ means you will not be asked about them, and how they did not believe; your duty is only to deliver, and ours is the reckoning.
According to the second reading, ﴿وَلَا تَسْأَلْ﴾ ﴿وَلَا تَسْأَلْ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ الْجَحِيمِ﴾ is meant as warning and threat; that is, do not ask about their conditions, for they are in a state that needs no asking, may Allah protect us, because they are the companions of the Blazing Fire. The Blazing Fire is the Fire; we ask Allah for well-being. "Ashab" (companions): a companion is one who is constantly with something; that is, does anyone ask about the condition of the companions of the Fire, whether they are in bliss or in affliction?
* Student: From the context this is known.
* Shaykh: Do not ask about their condition, for they are, may Allah protect us, in a state that a person cannot imagine, and this is the utmost of warning to these deniers, opponents, who are the companions of the Blazing Fire.
* Student: Bashir, from where is it derived?

Sheikh: Bashir (بشير) comes from al-bushra (البشرى, "good news"), a verbal noun of bashsha (بَشَّر, "to give good news"). The tabshir, as we said, I think has passed us before, but I can remind you of it again: al-bushra and al-bashara are the giving of news that gladdens, and it is not used for anything other than what gladdens, except occasionally. The reason it is called "bushra" is the visible effect it has on the skin (al-bashara), for when a person is pleased, the lines of his face brighten. "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased, his face would light up until it was like a piece of the moon" (ﷺ). [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3556) and Muslim (2769/53), from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik, with the wording: "When he was pleased, his face would light up until it was like a piece of the moon."] This is something evident: you can tell that a person is sad by his face, and you can tell that he is happy when his face shines. The term al-bushara may also be used in mockery, or to emphasise how severely the news will strike them with something painful: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾. As for al-indhar (الإنذار), it is informing of what is feared, i.e., of that which one fears. The Messenger (ﷺ) is undoubtedly a bringer of good news of what gladdens, which is Paradise, and a warner of what is feared, which is the Fire.

Student: That which harms the ill-omened person is that his facial features change, so its linguistic derivation is confirmed. What is this?

Sheikh: Yes, but by custom and usage, these two terms are only used for what gladdens, because a person's face changing due to what pleases him is something desirable, in which a person finds rest. For him to be given good news of something that affects him adversely, even though his face changes, the matter is disliked. Custom has established that bushra is only used for loved things. It may be used either as mockery, as some scholars said regarding His words: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾, or literally, on the basis that the body or the skin is affected by that.

Student: So each is according to what it is attached to and according to the meaning?

Sheikh: But the origin of bushra is only in what gladdens.

Student: The evidence?

Sheikh: Because a change in the skin due to this is something desirable that a person loves, so it is said only of what gladdens. Even if a person is affected by what pains him or what he fears, one does not say "bashsharahu" (he gave him good news) except as mockery or rarely. It does not follow that because the derivation has this meaning, it must extend to other meanings, as we said, for example, in the case of "jam'" (جمع): Muzdalifah is called Jam' because people gather in it, but 'Arafah is not called Jam' even though people gather in it. This is not a necessary implication.

He said: ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. ﴿Al-Jahim﴾ is the great Fire. It has many names, among them: al-Nar (the Fire), al-Jahim, al-Sa'ir, and Jahannam. All of these are for the differences in its attributes, though it is one.

Student: Is al-Hawiyah among its names?

Sheikh: No, it is not one of its names. But in reality it has a bottom, into which a thing plunges, yet it is not called al-Hawiyah.

Then he said: ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾. It seems the Prophet (ﷺ) loved to win over the Jews and Christians, and whoever loves to win them over loves that they be pleased with him. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made clear that these Jews and Christians are a people of obstinacy; they will never be pleased with you, however much you win them over, and however much you incline towards them through conciliation rather than affection, for they will never be pleased. For this reason, when the Messenger (ﷺ) first arrived in Madinah, he loved to agree with the People of the Book in matters that were not forbidden, but later he abandoned them and opposed them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾, i.e., their religion. (...) That is, even though they do not believe until he speaks to them.

His words: ﴿Or a sign comes to us﴾. What is meant by it?

Student: ﴿Or a sign comes to us﴾, i.e., a miracle.

Sheikh: A sign of what?

Student: A sign of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Sheikh: Yes.

His words: ﴿Those before them said the same as what they say﴾. Who is meant by "those before them"?

Student: The Jews and the Christians.

Sheikh: Yes. Do you remember anything of what they said?

Student: Their saying, the saying of the Jews: ﴿Show us Allah plainly﴾.

Sheikh: To Musa: ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. Yes. His words: ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾. What is the meaning of similarity?

Student: Similarity is close to (...).

Sheikh: The closeness of one thing to another.

His words: ﴿We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾. What is its place in relation to what precedes it? Its position in meaning relative to what precedes it?

Student: Causal explanation (ta'lil).

Sheikh: Causal explanation of what?

Student: A causal explanation of the refutation of their claim, and that it is of no benefit, and that the Qur'an is complete, and that their saying is merely obstinacy, since the signs have been made clear to them.

Sheikh: That is, a refutation of their saying: ﴿Or a sign comes to us﴾. Allah then said: ﴿We have made the signs clear﴾, meaning the signs have come clear too, there is no ambiguity.

Student: Is it a circumstantial clause (hali), Sheikh?

Sheikh: No, it is an independent resumptive clause (isti'nafiyyah) to refute them, an independent clause to refute their saying: ﴿Or a sign comes to us﴾. It is not a circumstantial clause, because it is not a restriction on what precedes it; the circumstantial clause is a restriction on what precedes it. This clause is an independent one refuting their saying: ﴿Or a sign comes to us﴾, meaning that the signs have already come clear.

His exalted words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾. What is the ba' (ب) here?

Student: Accompaniment (mulabasah).

Sheikh: Yes, and companionship (musahabah). What is the meaning of ﴿We sent you with the truth﴾?

Student: We sent you with the true word.

Sheikh: And what does "with the true word" mean?

Student: We sent you; i.e., affirming with the truth.

Sheikh: And what else?

Another student: It means that the truth accompanies you, and likewise you act upon the truth, meaning it is constant with you.

Sheikh: Accompaniment and companionship. The meaning of accompaniment is that your message is true; the message is true. The meaning of companionship is that what you brought is true, so the message is true, and what was brought with it, which was sent with it, is also true. What is the truth in terms of rulings?

Student: That which is established and firm.

Sheikh: That which is established and firm, well done. And when it is attributed to rulings, what is meant by it?

Student: Justice.

Sheikh: And when it is attributed to reports?

Student: Truthfulness.

Sheikh: What is meant by it is truthfulness.

His words: ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. There are two readings. What are they?

Student: The reading ﴿And you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ (with the jussive, tasal), and the reading ﴿And you will not be questioned﴾ (tus'alu, passive).

Sheikh: And what is the difference between them?

Student: "You will not be asked (tus'alu)": we will not be asked about their condition.

Sheikh: And their reckoning is with Allah, and "you will not ask"?

Student: That is: you will not ask about their conditions.

Sheikh: They are in a state to be pitied. We said previously that the two readings give two meanings, so it is as if He says: do not ask about them and do not be charged with them, and also they are in a state that does not require asking about them, because they are, may Allah protect us, in a punishment with no equal. We ask Allah for well-being.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 115].

* Benefits drawn from this noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion, because the east and the west encompass everything, so there is in it the generality of Allah's dominion.

Also: the all-encompassing nature of Allah the Exalted over everything, by His words: ﴿wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾.

Another benefit of the verse: because Allah's dominion over the east and the west is general, both in creation and in determination, He possesses the east and the west in terms of direction. We have told you that His words: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ [al-Baqarah 106], all of it up to the abrogation of the qibla, is a preparation for changing the qibla. It is as if Allah says: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ [al-Baqarah 142]; so if He wills, He makes the direction to the right, and if He wills, He makes it to the left, ﴿so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾.

Another benefit of the verse: the permissibility of praying facing whichever direction you are in, in case of excuse, as many scholars have explained it that way: the permissibility of praying in case of excuse facing wherever your face is.

* Among its benefits: the permissibility of praying facing the direction of one's travel during a journey when the prayer is voluntary. The verse has been interpreted this way too, but the verse is broader than this.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the Face for Allah, Glorified and Exalted, by His words: ﴿the Face of Allah﴾.

* Among its benefits: that Allah the Exalted has a place, by His words: ﴿there﴾ (fathamma), because thamma indicates a place. But where is He?

Student: Above the heavens.

Sheikh: Yes, in the height. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the slave girl: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the sky." [Narrated by Muslim (537/33) from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami.] In it is a refutation of two misguided innovations. The first: the innovation of the Hululiyyah, who claim that Allah is in every place in His essence; their saying is false, refuted by revelation, reason, and innate nature as well. The second: the saying of the negators (nufat) and the mu'attilah, who say that Allah is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither above the world nor below it, neither to the right of the world nor to its left, neither connected to the world nor separated from it. Some scholars said about this saying: if we were asked to describe non-existence, we would find no description more comprehensive for non-existence than this statement, because that is what is non-existent in reality.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the affirmation of two of Allah's names: Wasi' (All-Encompassing) and 'Alim (All-Knowing). ﴿Wasi' 'Alim﴾: Wasi', in what respect? All His attributes are vast without limit; His knowledge has no end, His power has no end, His hearing has no end; everything of His attributes is at the highest degree of vastness and encompassing. Knowledge too encompasses everything: ﴿so that you may know that Allah is over all things competent, and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq 12].

* Also from it we derive the affirmation of hearing and knowledge; we derive a second attribute from combining hearing and knowledge, to indicate that Allah's knowledge is vast, vast in the sense that nothing of every knowable thing escapes it, neither on earth nor in heaven.

* Among its benefits: the exclusivity of Allah's dominion. From where is this taken?

Student: From the fronting of the predicate (taqdim al-khabar).

Sheikh: The fronting of the predicate in His words: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west﴾.

﴿And they say: Allah has taken a son. Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 116].

* Benefits drawn from this verse: the demonstration of human arrogance and transgression, in that they insulted Allah, Glorified and Exalted, with this great insult, saying that Allah has taken a son. In the authentic hadith: "The son of Adam insults Me, and he has no right to do so; and the son of Adam denies Me, and he has no right to do so. As for his insulting Me, it is his saying: Allah has taken a son. As for his denying Me, it is his saying: He will not restore me as He originated me." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (4974) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]

This is among the greatest transgressions, may Allah protect us. In it is evidence of the transgression of the human being as such and his arrogance, by His words: ﴿Allah has taken a son﴾. As mentioned in the tafsir, it refers to three groups: who are they?

* Students: The Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists.

Sheikh: The Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists.

Among the benefits of the verse: that Allah refuted this false claim in several ways:

First: in His words, Glorified be He, for His exaltation above deficiency requires that He be exalted above taking a son, because taking a son is intended for: 

* Student: Assistance.

Sheikh: Yes, assistance, and meeting a need, or preserving the lineage. Allah the Exalted is exempt from all that. He is also exempt from resemblance; if He had a son, he would be a likeness of Allah.

Second: Allah refuted this claim by His words: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. A possession cannot be a son of its owner; indeed, if a person owns his son, what happens according to the Sharia? He is freed upon him. So the owned cannot be a son of the owner. Allah is the Creator, and all else is created. How can the created be a son of the Creator?

The third refutation of this claim: all the servants, every servant in the heavens and the earth, are humbly submissive to Him, and a son does not have the humility of a slave. If all are slaves to Him, how can any of them be a son to Him? Does a slave humble himself before his father as he humbles himself before his master? No.

The fourth: He, Glorified and Exalted, is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, i.e., their Creator. The One who is able to create the heavens and the earth is able to create a human without a father. They claim that He has no father, but His father is Allah, so He says: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. The One capable of originating them is capable of having a son, capable of creating a human without a father, as He said: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir 57].

The fifth: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. Whoever has this power, is it impossible for Him to produce a son without a father?

* Students: It is not impossible.

Sheikh: It is not impossible. Thus their doubt by which they argued that Jesus is the son of Allah is refuted.

* Student: Sheikh, "all are devoutly obedient to Him" includes rational and non-rational beings; and "devoutly obedient" (qanitun) applies to rational beings?

Sheikh: By way of predominance (taghlib). Now we have finished the evidences by which Allah refuted this false claim, and we return to the benefits of this verse. First: the impossibility of Allah having a son. What is the evidence?

Student: The five aspects.

Sheikh: The five aspects, these five aspects.

Second: the generality of Allah's dominion, Glorified and Exalted, by His words: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾.

* Among the benefits: that Allah has no partner in His dominion. From where is this taken?

Student: From the fronting of the predicate.

Sheikh: From the fronting of the predicate: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾.

* Also: qunut (devout obedience) is used with two meanings: a general meaning and a specific meaning. The specific meaning is the qunut of worship and obedience, as in His words: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾ [al-Zumar 9]. This is the qunut of what?

* Students: Worship.

Sheikh: Obedience and lawful worship. And as in His words: ﴿She believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Tahrim 12], and as in His words: ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, and prostrate, and bow with those who bow﴾ [Al 'Imran 43].

The second meaning is the general qunut of humble submission, which includes everyone in the heavens and the earth, as in this verse: ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾. Even the disbelievers are devoutly obedient to Allah?

* Students: Yes.

Sheikh: Even the disbelievers, in this sense, are devoutly obedient to Allah, Glorified and Exalted.

* Also: the greatness of Allah's power, Glorified and Exalted, and what is it? In His originating the heavens and the earth, for they are great creations.

* Also: the wisdom of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, because these heavens and earth are in a marvelous, wondrous order. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance﴾ [al-Mulk 3].

This vast, great, magnificent system does not fail or change over the passing of years and ages, and what indicates this?

* Students: The power of Allah.

Sheikh: A power that is supreme and dazzling, and a great, supreme wisdom as well. Everything is arranged in a wondrous, harmonious way; nothing collides with another to corrupt it, and nothing changes another, but each proceeds according to what it was commanded. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat 12].

So, ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: benefits drawn from it: power, might, and wisdom.

* Student: (...) the heaven (...).

Sheikh: Yes.

* Also: the heavens are plural in number, for the plural indicates number. How many are they?

* Students: Seven.

The Shaykh: Seven, and they are, as Allah the Exalted says: stacked (*tibaq*), ﴿Do you not see how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nuh 15]. One above another. The Qur'an, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims all establish that the heaven is a perceptible body. It is not as the people of atheism say, that what is above us is a height with no end. This is disbelief: whoever believes it becomes a disbeliever, because he rejects the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims.

* Another benefit: Allah, glory be to Him, is not incapable of anything, and nothing can resist His command, because He says: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [Ali 'Imran 47].

* Another: the establishment that *al-qada'* (divine decree/judgment) is of two kinds: *qada' qadari* (decree of divine predestination) and *qada' shar'i* (legislative decree). The *qadari* decree is like this verse: ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾, meaning: He determines it as a cosmic, created reality, ﴿He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ The *shar'i* decree is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23]. Did He decree this as a *shar'i* or a *qadari* decree?

* The students: *Shar'i*.

* The Shaykh: *Shar'i*. For if He had decreed it as a *qadari* decree, no one would have associated partners with Allah, and all of mankind would have been worshippers of Allah. So it is a *shar'i* decree. The difference between them is that the *shar'i* decree may or may not take effect; that is, the one subject to it may or may not do it. The cosmic decree must take effect, and must occur in the one decreed upon. Just as I have now mentioned the difference between general *qunut* and specific *qunut*: specific *qunut* is praiseworthy for the one who is obedient, while general *qunut* is not praiseworthy, because it is submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in a cosmic and predestined sense.

* One of the benefits of the verse: the affirmation that Allah speaks, as in His saying: ﴿then He only says to it﴾.

* Another: that His speech is by letters.

* A student: ﴿Qul﴾ ("Say").

* The Shaykh: No, *qul* is not there; it is *kun* ("Be").

* The student: No, *kun*.

* The Shaykh: *Kun*. *Kun* consists of letters.

* Another: that the speech of Allah is heard. In ﴿then He only says to it, "Be"﴾, the particle *lahu* ("to it") explicitly directs the speech to the one addressed. Had He not been speaking so that it hears, there would be no point in directing it. For this reason, the one to whom the command is directed hears it and complies.

* Another: that inanimate matter is subject to Allah, glory be to Him, even inanimate matter. What is the basis for this? Because His saying ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ includes matters relating to living beings and matters relating to inanimate things. So when Allah says to inanimate matter, "Be," it is.

Another benefit of the verse, [the Shaykh continues]: that between Allah's command to bring something into being and its coming into being there is no delay. There is no delay at all; it occurs immediately. From where is this derived?

* A student: From the use of the particle *fa-* ("then").
