Where is the oath? The oath is what the lām indicates in His saying ﴿And if you follow﴾, since the implied meaning is: "By Allah, if you follow..." And where is the condition?
* Student: (in).
* Shaykh: (in). The answer: ﴿you would have from Allah no ally or helper﴾. ﴿You would have﴾ (mā laka) is the answer to the oath. If it were the answer to the condition, the (fa') would have to accompany it, since it is a negation. But it is the answer to the oath, so the (fa') does not accompany it. Where is the answer to the condition? It was said that it is omitted, indicated by the answer to the oath. It was also said that it is not needed, since the sentence is complete without it. This second view is the preferred one: it is not needed for the sentence to be complete without it. The evidence for this is that it has not come in any style of the Arabic language. If it has not come in any style of the Arabic language, this shows that the sentence is independent of it and that there is no need for it.

He says: ﴿And if you follow their desires﴾. Notice: He said ﴿their religion﴾, then He said ﴿their desires﴾, because this religion they are upon is not a religion of guidance, but a religion of desire. Therefore He said: ﴿And if you follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge﴾, because they are upon desire and not upon guidance. For if they were upon guidance, the Jews would have been obligated to believe in the Messiah ʿIsa ibn Maryam, and all of them would have been obligated to believe in Muhammad ﷺ. But their religion is desire, not guidance. Likewise, every person who follows other than what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, brought, and is fanatical about it, we say: your religion is desire, not guidance.

His saying ﴿after what has come to you of knowledge﴾ refers to the revelation that came to the Prophet ﷺ, whether it was the Quran or the Sunnah.

His saying ﴿what has come to you of knowledge﴾: is it the knowledge that came to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him? Yes, knowledge. Allah says to him: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write one with your right hand﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut 29:48]. The Messenger was not a scholar; he was an unlettered prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who did not know, did not read, and did not write. But Allah sent down to him this knowledge, so that by it he became a prophet who brought beneficial knowledge and righteous action.

﴿you would have from Allah no ally or helper﴾. What is the i'rab of (mā laka)? What is the i'rab of (mā)?
* Student: Negation.
* Shaykh: Negation, yes, ﴿mā laka﴾.

His saying ﴿from an ally﴾: what is its i'rab?
* Student: A preposition.
* Shaykh: A preposition. And ﴿waliyy﴾?
* Student: Genitive.
* Shaykh: Genitive?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is its position in i'rab, ﴿waliyy﴾? 
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It has no position in i'rab? That is, is it a direct object, for example, governed by something? What is its position in i'rab?
* Student: Genitive in form, nominative in position.
* Shaykh: What does that mean in terms of i'rab?
* Student: That it is the subject (mubtada').
* Shaykh: That it is the subject, correct.

﴿waliyy﴾ is a subject, nominative, marked by a presumed ḍammah on its final letter, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the position by the vowel of the preposition. ﴿min waliyy﴾. Its original form: "you have from Allah an ally," and ﴿laka﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as the fronted predicate. The clause ﴿mā laka min Allāh﴾ has no position in i'rab, because it is...?
* The students: The answer to the oath.
* Shaykh: Because it is the answer to the oath.

﴿mā laka min Allāh min waliyy﴾. As for the name of Allah, exalted is He, its explanation, meaning and derivation has already been discussed.

His saying ﴿min waliyy﴾: the waliyy is the one who takes charge of another by protecting and safeguarding him. So the meaning is: no one takes charge of your protection except Allah, mighty and majestic. And no one takes charge of your support, and there is no helper who repels (harm) from you. Then the punishment of Allah would befall you, even if you had many soldiers, many police, or great power. If you follow other than the law of Allah, no one will protect you from Allah, and no one will support you apart from Him. For support and guardianship come through guidance, by following the guidance of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with injustice, for them is security﴾ [al-An'am 6:82]. Security is only through faith and the absence of injustice. ﴿You would have from Allah no ally or helper﴾.

* Student: Shaykh, is ﴿waliyy﴾ a verbal noun (maṣdar) (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not a verbal noun. (walī) here is on the pattern (faʿīl) from wilāyah.
* Student: Shaykh, the restriction here, ﴿after what has come to you of knowledge﴾, does it have an implied meaning (mafhūm)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it has an implied meaning, because before the Messenger ﷺ was forbidden from following them, he used to love agreeing with the People of the Book. When he was commanded to oppose them, he was no longer able to oppose them.
* Student: In terms of the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl), is the one who follows (...) excused?
* Shaykh: Yes, the one who follows other than Islam without knowledge is excused. But if he is negligent, this will come to us in the benefits (of the verse), in the benefits of the verse, God willing.

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with its true recitation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:121]. ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾ is said to be the predicate of the subject. In that case the second clause, ﴿they believe in it﴾, is a resumptive (istiʾnāfiyyah) clause. 

It was also said that His saying ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah), and that ﴿they believe in it﴾ is the predicate of the subject. Let us see by meaning which of them is more preferable.

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾: We gave them the Book. Is the giving here legislative or cosmic?
* The students: Legislative.
* Shaykh: Or all of it? It is cosmic and legislative: cosmic, because Allah decreed that He would give them the Book, and He gave it to them; and it is also legislative, because it contains the laws and the explanation. Those to whom He gave the Book are either this nation alone or it and others. The more preferable view is that it includes everyone to whom Allah gave the Book. The word "Book" is generic, so it includes the Quran, the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and other books of Allah, mighty and majestic.

His saying ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾: ﴿they recite it﴾. Recitation (tilāwah) is applied to the recitation of the wording, which is reading; to the recitation of the meaning, which is interpretation (tafsīr); and to the recitation of the ruling, meaning following it, which is adherence. So recitation applies to the recitation of the wording; recitation of the meaning means that a person follows the meaning and does not distort it; and recitation of the ruling is following what the Quran rules. These three meanings of recitation are included in His saying ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾. Verbal recitation means reciting the Quran with the wording it must have, with its i'rab as it came, without changing it. So one does not say, for example, "al-ḥamda lillāhi rabba al-ʿālamīn" with changes. Rather, one says ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ without alteration, because it was revealed that way, so it must be recited that way. Recitation of the meaning means that one explains it according to what Allah and His Messenger intended. For example, one says: "The meaning of this verse is such-and-such, according to what Allah intended." And how do we know what Allah intends by it? Did Allah say: "I intended by My speech such-and-such"? The answer is no, He did not say that. But He said: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shuʿaraʾ 26:195].

So we know what Allah, exalted is He, intends by this Quran, because it came in the Arabic language. And this meaning in the Arabic language is what this wording or this context requires. So we will have known the meaning of the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic. This is the recitation of the meaning. 

Recitation of the ruling: carrying out the commands, avoiding the prohibitions, and affirming the reports. This is the recitation of the ruling: that you follow what this Quran has ruled, and acknowledge what it has reported. You act, act how? And you abandon the prohibitions and believe the reports. Then you are reciting it with its true recitation. But if you are arrogant or deny it, then you have not recited it with its true recitation.

In His saying ﴿with its true recitation﴾, this is from the construction of a quality attributed to its qualified noun: that is, "the true recitation," meaning the recitation of earnestness, steadfastness, and not deviating to the right or left. As for i'rab, it is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), because it is annexed to the verbal noun, like His saying in the Alfiyyah:

"...like 'jiddan kulla al-jidd' (in earnest, wholly in earnest)..." Here: "recite it with its true recitation."

﴿They recite it with its true recitation; those believe in it﴾. ﴿Those﴾ refers back to "those who were given the Book," who were given the Book and who recite it with its true recitation. That is: those who possess this attribute, who recite the Book with its true recitation, believe in it. As for those who do not recite it with its true recitation, they are not believers in it. Rather, they have a deficiency of faith in proportion to their opposition. Faith increases and decreases; therefore He said: ﴿those believe in it﴾. Referring to them with the far demonstrative is evidence of their elevated rank, like His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:5]. This is evidence of their high station and rank.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 120–123 (part 2 of 4):

He said: ﴿They are the ones who believe in it﴾. Iman (faith) linguistically means affirmation (tasdiq), but in the Shari'ah (sacred law) it is affirmation qualified by acceptance (qabul) and submission (idhan). Affirmation alone is not sufficient; acceptance and submission are also required. The evidence for this is that Abu Talib is not called a believer, even though he affirmed and acknowledged (the Prophet's message), but he lacked acceptance and submission. So a person who affirms what is said is not thereby called a believer. Some people rejoiced at Gagarin, Gagarin, I think you remember him, the Russian man who was the first to go up to the moon, I think, and he said: "I now acknowledge that this creation has a Creator who governs it." People rejoiced greatly and said, "He has believed!" Has he believed? Not at all, he did not believe, because this is merely a rational deduction that every intelligent person knows. Every intelligent person knows that this vast, orderly, wondrous universe has a Creator who governs and arranges it, just as we know that this mosque has a builder, and that this light has a source that lit it, and so on. The upshot is that this is not faith. Merely acknowledging Allah, glorified and exalted be He, does not count as faith, nor does merely acknowledging the Messenger (ﷺ). The hypocrites say: ﴿We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun 1]. But even so, if they were sincere in their testimony, Allah would not have called them liars. He said: "They say, 'We bear witness,' but they are liars," because they have no submission or acceptance. Rather, their hearts reject it, and we seek refuge in Allah. Therefore, ﴿They are the ones who believe in it﴾ because they ﴿recite it with its true recitation﴾. Whoever does not recite the Qur'an with its true recitation, in the three senses we mentioned, is deficient in faith, and may lose it entirely.

He said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾.

* Student: So what is the predicate (khabar), O Shaykh?

* Shaykh: We mentioned that scholars have two opinions regarding the predicate. One opinion is ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾, and the other opinion is ﴿they are the ones who believe in it﴾. According to this latter opinion, ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), meaning: those to whom We gave the Book, while they recite it with its true recitation, they are the ones who believe in it. The judgment that they believe in it is then conditional on their being described as reciting it with its true recitation. The sentence's grammatical analysis (i'rab) on this reading is a single sentence, but the subject is qualified. On the second opinion, the statement consists of two clauses: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recite it with its true recitation﴾ and ﴿They are the ones who believe in it﴾. However, the first grammatical analysis is closer to the correct reading, because the discussion here concerns belief in what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought. Only one who recites the Book with its true recitation believes in it, whether it is the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. None believes in it with true belief except one who recites it with true recitation. Accordingly, the qualifier "those to whom We gave the Book" with "they recite it with its true recitation" is better, meaning: whoever is given the Book and, being described thus, recites it with its true recitation, is the one who believes in it.

* Student: Should the statement of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾ be taken as a predicate? It creates a problem, because the one who does not recite it with its true recitation has been placed first (...)?

* Shaykh: No, no, it is not a predicate (...). It is a pure predicate. This also strengthens that the clause ﴿they recite it﴾ is a circumstantial clause.

And His statement: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾.

* Student: O Shaykh, can ﴿those﴾ be a second predicate?

* Shaykh: No, no. Whether it is a second predicate or a resumptive new clause depends on what we said about ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾ being the predicate.

* Student: If it is the predicate?

* Shaykh: The stronger view is that it is a circumstantial clause.

* Student: It cannot be the predicate.

* Shaykh: I say: the stronger view is that it is a circumstantial clause, and that it being the predicate is the weaker view.

His statement: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾. Is ﴿whoever﴾ here a conditional particle that jussifies the verb? ﴿disbelieves﴾ is jussive, ﴿in it﴾ means in the Book, ﴿those are the losers﴾. The clause ﴿those are the losers﴾ is the answer of the condition, and it is joined by the particle fa' (then), because it is a nominal sentence. A nominal sentence that is the answer of a condition must be joined by fa', like its counterparts mentioned in the verse:

A nominal sentence, an imperative, a verb of praise (jamid), and with ma, qad, la (in), and with the future particles (tanfis), these seven, when they come as the answer of a condition, are joined with fa'.

And His statement: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾. He did not say, "whoever disbelieves in it has lost," but rather used a nominal sentence, which conveys what? Permanence and continuity. He used the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) in ﴿they﴾ to convey restriction (hasr) and emphasis. The meaning is: those who disbelieved in it are the losers and no others. Accordingly, everyone who is not a believer is a loser. This man has millions of dirhams, cars, real estate, sons, wives, family, and a kingdom, but he is a disbeliever. What do we say? He is a loser. In reality, he has not profited from this wealth, nor from his children. ﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Zumar 15]. This wealth does not benefit him; rather it will be a source of regret for him, because he will lose it. He will lose it, or it will be lost to him. Either he dies leaving it behind, or it escapes him.

And His statement: ﴿Those are the losers﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿the losers﴾? The root of khusran (loss) is deficiency. For this reason it is said "he profited" (rabih), and its opposite is "he lost" (khasir). These are the ones upon whom deficiency has befallen, and no others, because however much of this world they are given, it is transient and perishing, so it does not benefit them.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah 122].

﴿O Children of Israel﴾. Israel is Ya'qub (Jacob) the son of Ishaq (Isaac), the son of Ibrahim (Abraham). The intended meaning of "his descendants" here is anyone who is descended from him, male or female, because it has already passed in our lessons that the word "banu" (sons of) is specific to males unless it refers to a tribe, in which case it includes male and female.

And His statement: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour﴾. The reminder here of the favour is not merely so that a person recalls that Allah previously bestowed a favour upon him. Rather, the intent is that one should take this favour, or this remembrance of it, as a path to thanking Allah, by complying with His command and avoiding His prohibition. That is, do not forget what He bestowed upon you and thereby disbelieve in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but believe in him and follow him as a repayment for this favour.

And His statement: ﴿My favour﴾ is a singular noun in construct, so it encompasses all the blessings that Allah bestowed upon them, and Allah the Exalted bestowed many blessings upon them.

And His statement: ﴿And that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. This is also a case of mentioning the specific after the general (atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm). Otherwise, preference over the worlds is undoubtedly a blessing, but since it is a high rank, Allah the Exalted singled it out for mention, preferring them over people.

And His statement: ﴿And that I preferred you﴾ over them, i.e., I made you better than them. Musa (ﷺ) alluded to this in his saying: ﴿O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given to anyone among the worlds﴾ [al-Ma'idah 20]. This is part of His preference over the worlds.

And His statement: ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed﴾ is it past or present?

* Students: Past.

* Shaykh: Then ﴿And that I preferred you﴾ is also past. Allah preferred them over the worlds when He bestowed His favours upon them, and that was before this nation existed. As for after the existence of this nation, this nation is more excellent, more excellent than the Children of Israel, as the texts of the Book and the Sunnah indicate.

And His statement: ﴿over the worlds﴾. Who is intended by "the worlds"? The intended meaning is all that is other than Allah, and it may also refer only to the children of Adam. So here, if "the worlds" means everything other than Allah, that is evidence that the Children of Israel were preferred even over the angels. If we say the intended meaning of "the worlds" is the world of the children of Adam, who are of their kind, then it does not include the angels or the jinn. This is because "world" (alam) may refer to all that is other than Allah, and it may refer to something specific, namely the children of Adam, when the context indicates it. As you say: the world of animals, the world of humans, the world of jinn, and more specifically: the world of beasts, the world of insects, the world of such-and-such.

It is called a "world" (alam) because it is a sign (alam) pointing to its Creator, glorified and exalted be He. All these creatures contain evidence and great signs of the existence of Allah, praised and glorified be He. So they are signs of the existence of Allah, and of what these creatures contain of manifestation of mercy, wisdom, and blessing.

* Student: Which of the two meanings is more correct, "the worlds"?

* Shaykh: The closer one, and Allah knows best, is the last: the specific world that is of their kind.

﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾ [al-Baqarah 123].

﴿Fear a Day﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿fear﴾? Take a protection (wiqaya) from the punishment that befalls you. Taqwa (piety, God-consciousness) linguistically, according to morphological derivation, originally was (wqwy), then the waw was changed to a ta', becoming (taqwa), and it derives from wiqaya (protection). The one who complies with the commands of Allah, the Exalted, has undoubtedly taken protection from the punishment of Allah.

﴿Fear a Day﴾ does not undoubtedly mean "fear a day lest it occur," because this day must occur. Rather, fear what happens on it: from punishment and retribution for the one who opposed. And He said: ﴿no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾. So your fathers' preference over the worlds will not avail you anything. Do not say: "We have fathers who were preferred over the worlds, and we will be saved from the Fire or from the punishment of this Day through them." No. ﴿No soul will avail another soul in anything﴾, except that a parent may avail his child? 

* Students: It does not avail.

* Shaykh: It does not avail? Nor a child?

* Students: Nor a child.

* Shaykh: ﴿On that Day a man will flee from his brother, and from his mother and his father, and from his wife and his children. For every man among them on that Day will have a matter that will occupy him﴾ [Abasa 34–37].

The evidence for generality is that His statement ﴿soul﴾ is an indefinite noun in what context?

* Student: Negation.

* Shaykh: Negation. So it is?

* Student: General.

* Shaykh: It is general. An indefinite noun in the context of negation, prohibition, condition, or rhetorical interrogation is general. Here the indefinite noun is in the context of negation, so it is general: no soul avails another soul in anything. The Prophet (ﷺ) would not avail his father in anything. He said to a man: "My father and your father are in the Fire" [Muslim], and he would not avail his mother in anything. He asked Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for permission to seek forgiveness for his mother, and was forbidden [Muslim]. And whoever is below the Messenger (ﷺ) is even more so.

So ﴿no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾.

And His statement ﴿in anything﴾ is also an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it generalizes: any thing whatsoever. This does not conflict with legitimate intercession (shafa'a shar'iyya), which is established by the Sunnah, because this verse is specified by it.

And He said: ﴿Nor will ransom be accepted from it﴾. "Nor will ransom be accepted from it," i.e., from a soul, and who accepts or rejects? Allah, glorified and exalted be He. And "'adl" (ransom, equivalent) means what equals it. That is, even if they bring the equivalent, it will not be accepted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, even if they had all that is on earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah 36], and Allah will not accept that from them.

* Student: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is on earth and the like of it with it﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it from the evil of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Zumar 47].

In any case, if these people brought all that is on earth and the like of it, to ransom themselves from the punishment, it would not benefit them. This is the meaning of His statement: ﴿Nor will ransom be accepted from it﴾. So "'adl" means the equivalent, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿or an equivalent of that in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah 95], and ﴿or expiation is feeding the needy or an equivalent of that in fasting﴾, i.e., what equals it in fasting. Therefore "'adl" means equivalence.

﴿Nor will ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾. Intercession (shafa'a) in the Arabic language derives from shif' or shafʿ (with fatha), which is what is called a pair: two are a shaf' (pair), because each one is a shaf' to the other. So intercession linguistically derives from shaf', meaning a pair. But in terminology it means mediating for another to bring about a benefit or to repel a harm. That is intercession: that you mediate for someone else to bring about a benefit or repel a harm. The intercession for the people of the Fire that they may leave it is repelling harm, and the intercession for the people of Paradise that they enter Paradise is bringing about benefit. On this Day ﴿no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾. And ﴿intercession﴾ is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it generalizes to any intercession, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir 48]. This noble verse is general, but it is specified by what the Sunnah has established regarding the affirmation of general and specific intercession. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) intercedes among the people of the place of standing that judgment be passed among them [Bukhari and Muslim], and it is also established from him that he intercedes for the people of grave sins that they not enter the Fire, and for those who have entered the Fire that they be brought out of it [Bukhari and Muslim]. Accordingly, the generality in His statement ﴿nor will intercession benefit it﴾ is specified by what the Sunnah has established regarding what? Intercession.

And His statement: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. How can "they" be helped when the context refers to a singular noun? Observe: ﴿soul﴾ ﴿no soul avails another soul﴾, ﴿nor will ransom be accepted from it﴾, i.e., the soul, ﴿nor will it benefit it﴾, i.e., the soul, ﴿nor will they be helped﴾? The context would require: "nor will it be helped, nor will it, i.e., the soul, be helped." But He said: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾. We say: He returned the pronoun to it in terms of meaning, because since ﴿soul﴾ is general, ﴿no soul avails another soul﴾, generality indicates plurality and multitude, so the pronoun returned to the soul in terms of what?

* Students: Meaning.

* Shaykh: In terms of meaning, not in terms of wording. If it were in terms of wording, He would have said "nor will it be helped." In terms of meaning, because ﴿soul﴾ is general.

Then there is another verbal observation, which is observing the verse endings (fawasil). Observing the endings is a matter the Qur'an has been revealed with, to the extent that for the sake of it the less excellent is placed before the more excellent. Do you recall this?

* Students: Yes: ﴿We believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha 70].

* Shaykh: ﴿the Lord of Harun and Musa﴾, because the whole of Surah Ta-Ha ends on the letter alif, except for a few verses. So observing the verse endings is part of the eloquence of the Qur'an. Here we say: He used the plural with regard to meaning, and observing the endings with regard to wording.

* Student: A question, O Shaykh, regarding ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [Abasa 34–35]. Here He placed "brother" before "his mother and his father"?

* Shaykh: No, that is not from this, because the endings do not differ. If He had said "from his father, his mother, and his brother," it would not have differed. But it is the ordering.

* Student: The brother before the mother and father, and after them his companion and his children?

* Shaykh: Yes, in order. Because a person's affection for his brother is less than his affection for his mother and father.

* Student: (...) his companion and his children..?

* Shaykh: Yes, his companion and his children are closer to him than his mother and father, is that not so?

* Student: (...) removing a legal evidence by evidence..?

* Shaykh: We said: removing the ruling of a legal evidence or its wording by a legal evidence. Removing or lifting the ruling of a legal evidence, or its wording, by a legal evidence. We told you this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 120–123 (part 3 of 4):

* Student: Five sucklings make marriage prohibited[[Recorded by Muslim (1452 / 24) from the hadith of 'Aishah, and its wording is: "Among what was revealed of the Qur'an was ten known sucklings that make marriage prohibited, then they were abrogated by five known sucklings, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died while they were among what is recited of the Qur'an."]].
* Shaykh: Make sure.
* Student: (...) its wording and its ruling entirely.
* Shaykh: Yes, the five.
* Student: The five.
* Shaykh: It appears the group does not agree with you, (...)?
* Students: The ten.
* Shaykh: The ten. The ruling of the five remains.
* Student: The ten from the beginning.
* Student: Yes, from the beginning.
* Shaykh: Is abrogation (naskh) (the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) rationally possible and actually occurring in the Shariah, or not?
* Student: It occurs.
* Shaykh: It occurs in the Shariah. What is the evidence?
* Student: The evidence is ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾.
* Shaykh: The evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or similar to it﴾ [al-Baqarah 106].
Is it rationally possible?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is its basis?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Do you understand now? Some scholars say it is not rationally possible, and this is an error, because what has occurred in the Shariah is undoubtedly rationally possible; the Shariah does not bring the impossible. But we say: it is rationally possible, indeed rationally necessary. What is its basis? Abrogation takes into account the development of the one addressed by the ruling and the extent of his receptiveness to it, and that this ruling at this particular time is a benefit, while at the earlier time it was not a benefit. And it does not necessitate, as has been said, that God's knowledge changes. That is impossible. Rather, the ruling changed because the benefit differed, either by the change of time, or by the change of the condition of the one addressed, or by the change of place as well.
* Student: Why do we not say it is transmitted (samʿi) and not rational?
* Shaykh: No, we say it is rational too.
* Student: O Shaykh, they answer this by saying, for example: the circumstance that necessitated the first ruling may recur, may happen a second time.
* Shaykh: Yes, if it occurs, it is established.
* Student: So, for example, temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah), which was permitted in a time of hardship, could a harder situation than it come upon this community?
* Shaykh: Yes, a harder situation could come. Had the Messenger not said: "Until the Day of Resurrection"[[Recorded by Muslim (1406 / 28) from the hadith of Sabrah ibn Ma'bad with the wording: "Indeed it is forbidden from this day of yours until the Day of Resurrection."]], we would have said it (is permissible). For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, held the opinion that it is permissible in cases of necessity.
* Student: If we say (...) they did not enter upon us from this door.
* Shaykh: No, they do enter upon us. He says: because the benefit now required, it has become clear that it is prohibited and forbidden until the Day of Resurrection, and there can absolutely be no benefit in it in the future.
* Student: There was a benefit in the past?
* Shaykh: Yes, there was a benefit.
* Student: This is a mistake.
* Shaykh: But God knows that the benefit after this time can never occur, can never occur, because if we did not say so, it would follow that the rulings of Allah, glorified and exalted, do not follow benefits.
* Student: No, not all rulings are acts of worship (ta'abbudi).
* Shaykh: Wow! You find that all the abrogated rulings are in accordance with wisdom. If we find, for example, the abrogation of wine, we find it was gradual. The obligation of prayer, we find it was gradual. The obligation of fasting, we find it was gradual, and so on.
* Student: O Shaykh, regarding wine: if we speak of benefit, we say: if a person embraces Islam and continues to drink wine, should we proceed gradually with him?
* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps we would say this. Suppose we forbade him from wine immediately, and he would recoil from Islam and return to his religion; it is possible we say: we deal with him by the more important first, then the more important. We see this, we see the gradualness in da'wah even in the present time.
The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah 119]. What is the meaning of the "ba'" here?
* Student: For accompaniment.
* Shaykh: Accompaniment. And how is his being sent with the truth? Does the meaning mean that his message is true, or that what he was sent with is true?
* Student: Both meanings.
* Shaykh: Both meanings? That is, do we take one, or both together?
* Student: Both together.
* Shaykh: Good, excellent. What is the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of ﴿as a bearer of good news and a warner﴾?
* Student: A circumstantial clause (hal).
* Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of what?
* Student: A circumstantial clause of ﴿We have sent you﴾.
* Shaykh: Of all of this world?
* Student: No, of ﴿We have sent you﴾.
* Shaykh: Of ﴿We have sent you﴾ entirely: verb, subject and object?
* Student: No, of (we have sent).
* Shaykh: Of the verb?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: No, that is not suitable.
* Student: Of the kaf (the pronoun "you").
* Shaykh: Of the kaf? Correct.
The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]. What is the meaning of the interrogative here?
* Student: No one is more unjust.
* Shaykh: No one is more unjust. That means what? "No" (la). What is its grammatical analysis?
* Student: It is a negation.
* Shaykh: A negation. So the interrogative is in the sense of negation. What is the rhetorical eloquence in the interrogative coming to mean negation?
* Student: Here it emphasizes the greatness of this matter.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: That it is tinged with challenge.
* Shaykh: Tinged in the sense of challenge. That is, as if, because of the strength of the negation, it were said: Who is more unjust? Tell me. If there is anyone more unjust, bring him. So it is tinged with the sense of challenge.
The phrase ﴿who is more unjust﴾ occurs many times in the Qur'an: ﴿who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 114], ﴿and who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ [al-An'am 21], and similar. How do we reconcile them?
* Student: This is for emphasis.
* Shaykh: Yes, but here, ﴿who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾ means there is no one more unjust than him. ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ means there is no one more unjust than him, what is (...)?
* Student: All of them are wrongdoers.
* Shaykh: All of them are wrongdoers, meaning.
* Student: Whoever conceals testimony is a wrongdoer.
* Shaykh: All of them are wrongdoers, but here (more unjust) means: greater in injustice. And who is greater in injustice than one who prevents the mosques of Allah? No one is greater in injustice than him. No one is greater in injustice than one who fabricates a lie against Allah.
* Student: It is included in it...
* Shaykh: Does anyone know?
* Student: (min), the estimate of (min).
* Shaykh: What is the estimate of (min)?
* Student: That is: "Then who is greater," no one is greater, meaning there is no one greater.
* Shaykh: Whatever can be estimated with (min) other than it will do.
* Student: Or (min) is partitive.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: No one is greater than him in this respect.
* Shaykh: In the fabrication of lies against others, there is no one more unjust than one who fabricates against Allah. So the one who fabricates against other than Allah is lighter than him. This is its basis: every verse is interpreted according to its specific meaning. Whoever prevents someone from entering a house, the greatest of those who prevent entry into houses are those who prevent the mosques of Allah. The greatest of those who lie against others is the one who lies against Allah. So the aspect here is distinct. Another answer?
* Student: That they are on one level.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: That is, since this has no negation except that someone equal to the injustice...
* Shaykh: Yes, that is, the negation: there is no one more unjust than him.
* Student: No one more unjust than him.
* Shaykh: And it does not carry the negation of equality. The meaning would be that they all share in being most unjust.
* Student: On an equal level.
* Shaykh: On an equal level. But the first meaning is more precise, because the one who fabricates a lie against Allah is not equal to the one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them. Rather, every matter has its own aspect.
The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿the Originator of the heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah 117]. What is the meaning of ﴿the Originator of the heavens﴾?
* Student: He created them without a previous pattern.
* Shaykh: So (badi') means?
* Student: Innovator (mubdi').
* Shaykh: Innovator. Does (fa'il) come in the sense of (muf'il)? Because it is known that (fa'il) means (fa'il, the active agent)?
* Student: It does come.
* Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: ʿAlim in the sense of muʿlim, samiʿ in the sense of musmiʿ.
* Shaykh: Do you bring these from yourself? Then qadir in the sense of muqdir, jamil in the sense of mujmil, and hakim in the sense of muhkim. It is clear, from the speech of the Arabs.
* Student: Samiʿ in the sense of musmiʿ?
* Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: Shahid (witness)? From the speech of the Arabs?
* Shaykh: From the speech of the Arabs or from the Qur'an.
* Student: Like the saying of the poet:
"Is it from Raihanah, the caller who listens (al-sami')? It keeps me awake, and my companions are hungry."
* Shaykh: Yes, this is evidence. The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah 10] mean what?
* Students: Painful (mu'lim).
* Shaykh: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ means: painful (mu'lim, in the sense of causing pain). So badi' here means mubdi', and it has evidence in the Arabic language and in the Qur'an.
The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿when He decrees﴾?
* Student: That is: when He wills to decree it.
* Shaykh: When He wills to decree it. Is the action expressed by the verb as an expression of His will? Has the expression of the action been used in terms of His will?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6].
* Shaykh: What?
* Student: That is: when you wish to pray.
* Shaykh: And elsewhere? Is there no evidence?
* Student: The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾ [al-Nahl 98].
* Shaykh: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ means what?
* Student: When you wish to recite.
* Shaykh: The Prophet ﷺ, when he entered the toilet, would say: "I seek refuge in Allah from the male and female evil spirits"[[Agreed upon; recorded by al-Bukhari (142) and Muslim (375 / 122) from the hadith of Anas, and the wording is Muslim's.]]. That is: when he wished to enter.
Some scholars have cited the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿until you follow their religion﴾, as evidence that disbelief is one religion, and that a Jew inherits from a Christian and vice versa. What is your opinion of this inference?
* Student: We did not take the benefits.
* Shaykh: You did not take its benefits? Strange. From ﴿and you will never be pleased﴾?
* Student: Yes.
The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat. And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 110].
Why did He not say: "you will find it"?
* Student: The answer to the conditional "ma".
* Shaykh: The answer to the conditional "ma". And the answer of the conditional is?
* Student: Jussive (majzum).
* Shaykh: Jussive. Yes (...).
﴿Until you follow their religion. Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance﴾.
* From this noble verse is derived: the obstinacy of the Jews and Christians, since they are not pleased with anyone unless he follows their religion.
* Also derived from it: that whoever is not pleased except with that will try to bring others than Jews and Christians into Judaism and Christianity.
* Among its benefits: caution against the Jews and Christians, since they do not wish for anyone that he be other than a Jew or a Christian.
* And among them: that disbelief is one religion, based on His saying: ﴿their religion﴾. In terms of its opposition to Islam, it is one religion. As for its types, they are many religions: Judaism is a religion, Christianity is a religion, Buddhism is a religion, and so on for the rest of the religions. But all of these, in terms of their opposition to Islam, are considered one religion, because the name of disbelief applies to them. So it is a genus, and the religions are its species.
* And among them: refutation of the people of disbelief with this phrase: ﴿the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance﴾. The meaning: if the guidance of Allah is with you, then you are guided; otherwise, you are astray.
* And among them: that innovations are misguidance, based on His saying: ﴿the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance﴾. Here (huwa) is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), as we passed earlier, and it conveys restriction of guidance to what? To the guidance of Allah. Therefore innovations are not guidance. ﴿What is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus 32]. Accordingly, from this noble verse is derived: that all innovations are misguidance, as is established by the hadith from the Messenger ﷺ[[Recorded by Muslim (867 / 43) from the hadith of Jabir.]].
* And among them: the prohibition of following the desires of Jews and Christians, based on His saying: ﴿And if you followed their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against Allah no protector or helper﴾.
* And among them: that what the Jews and Christians hold is not a religion, but a desire, based on His saying: ﴿their desires﴾. He did not say "their religion" as He said in the first verse. In the first, He said: ﴿you will never be pleased﴾, ﴿until you follow their religion﴾, because they themselves believe they are upon a religion and a faith. But ﴿if you followed their desires﴾ shows that Allah clarified that this is not a religion nor a creed, but a desire, and not guidance.
* And among them: that whoever follows desire after knowledge is more astray and more severely misguided, based on His saying: ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against Allah no protector or helper﴾.
* And also among the benefits of the verse: that whoever Allah intends harm for, there is no repelling of it, based on His saying: ﴿you would have against Allah no protector or helper﴾.
* And among them: that it is obligatory to attach the heart to Allah, in fear and hope, because when you know that you have no protector and no helper, where does your heart attach? To Allah or to other than Him? To Allah. So do not attach your heart, O Muslim, except to your Lord.
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with its true recitation. Those believe in it﴾.
* From this noble verse is derived: the favour of Allah, glorified and exalted, upon one to whom Allah has given the Book and who recites it with its true recitation.
* And among its benefits: that merely being given the Book is not a virtue for a person; rather, the virtue lies in reciting it.
* And among them: that belief in a thing has a sign, belief has a sign, and its sign is action, based on His saying, when He said: ﴿they recite it with its true recitation﴾, He said: ﴿those believe in it﴾.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that whoever opposes the Qur'an in some matter, that is evidence of a deficiency in his faith. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿they recite it with its true recitation, those believe in it﴾. The meaning of that is: if they do not recite it with its true recitation, they did not believe in it, and their faith is diminished by the amount that their recitation is diminished.
* And among them: that the recitation of the Qur'an is of two kinds: a true recitation, and a deficient recitation that is not the reality. The true recitation is that a person recites its words and its meaning, acts by its rulings, and believes in its reports. All four of these that passed before us are its true recitation.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that the disbeliever in the Qur'an, however much he attains of worldly things, is a loser, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾. And how can he be a loser when he has acquired wealth, children, and magnificent vehicles and lofty palaces? Because all of these will go and vanish, or he will be removed from them and they will not benefit him. So it is established that they are the losers, as in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not let your wealth or your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun 9]. And since the one who is distracted by these from the remembrance of Allah thinks he is profiting, He said: ﴿And whoever does that, those are the losers﴾, meaning: even if they profit.
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾.
* From the benefits of this verse: a reminder to the Children of Israel of the favour of Allah upon them, based on His saying: ﴿remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾.
* And among them: that remembering a favour does not mean that a person merely recalls it in his heart; rather, it means that he gives thanks for it. Merely mentioning that Allah has bestowed a favour upon him is not sufficient; he must give thanks. This is what Allah commanded the Children of Israel.
* And among them: that favour comes from Allah alone, based on His saying: ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾. Had anyone possessed a favour, Allah would have said so, because the requirement of justice is that Allah say: "and the favour of so-and-so son of so-and-so," as He said to His Prophet: ﴿And when you said to him who was blessed by Allah and you blessed﴾ [al-Ahzab 37].

* Among its lessons: the excellence of people before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying: ﴿And that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. What Allah favored them with has already been mentioned: He placed prophets among them, made them kings, and gave them what He had not given anyone else in the worlds.

* Among its lessons: this preference is not general until the Day of Resurrection, because this Ummah is better than them, based on the saying of the Most High: ﴿You are the best nation ever raised up for mankind﴾ [Aal 'Imran 110]. So "the worlds" is a general term intended in a particular sense. What is it intended to mean, brothers?
* The students: Their own era.
* The Shaykh: The scholars of their time.

﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾

* From this verse is derived: the affirmation of the Day of Resurrection.
* It is also derived: that this Day is severe, and one must guard against it and beware of it.
* Among its benefits: that on that Day no soul will benefit another soul in anything: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38].
Nothing will benefit you except your own deeds, not your son, nor your father, nor your sister, nor your brother.
* Among its lessons: whoever deserves punishment on that Day, no compensation will be accepted from him, i.e., nothing that could ransom him from the punishment.
Among its lessons: the affirmation of intercession on that Day. From where do we derive it?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: But this is a negation?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: So it is said: intercession will not benefit it. He did not say: there is no intercession in it. Therefore the principle of intercession exists in it, so intercession on that Day is affirmed, but it is restricted by two conditions: the permission of Allah to the intercessor, and His approval of the one for whom intercession is made, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], and the Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 28].
* Among its lessons: that the disbelievers will not benefit from intercession, based on the Most High's saying in another verse: ﴿So the intercession of the intercessors will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir 48].
* Among its lessons: that no one can help another against the punishment of Allah, based on His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾.
* A student: The connection of Allah's saying before: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will ransom be taken from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 48], but here: ﴿nor will compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾.
* The Shaykh: It is a matter of advancing and delaying. The connection, and Allah knows best, is the variety of styles only; nothing else appears to me.

**Ibn 'Uthaymin's Commentary (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah al-Baqarah, Verses 124–126 (Part 1 of 5)**

Then He said: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 124]. Who is the one doing the testing? God. Is Abraham the one directly after the verb? Ibn Malik says:

*"The original order is that the subject comes first, and the original order for the object is that it comes separated [after]."*

But he also said:

*"It may come contrary to the original order..."*

*"...."*

This is one of the cases that come contrary to the original order. So ﴿Ibrahim﴾ is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and ﴿Rabbuhu﴾ is a delayed subject (fa'il mu'akhkhar). Is this arrangement, in this form and this manner, obligatory or permissible?

*Students:* Obligatory.

*Shaykh:* Obligatory. Because if you put the subject first, the pronoun would refer back to something later, both in wording and in rank, and this is prohibited. For this reason he said:

*"...... And rare is [a structure] like: 'Zan nuruhu al-shajar' [the tree adorned its light]."*

This is rare and is not to be used as a model. As for the parallel to the verse, he said:

*"And common is [a structure] like: 'Khaafa Rabbahu 'Umar' [Umar feared his Lord]."*

*"......"*

﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested by his Lord﴾: there is a qira'ah (recitation variant) in ﴿Ibrahim﴾: ﴿Ibraham﴾, ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested by his Lord﴾ with Ibraham. It is an Arabic dialect and is recited in Arabic (Ibraham).

*Student:* Ibraham?

*Shaykh:* With a mim. The point is that the ya' is replaced by an alif: instead of Ibrahim, it is Ibraham.

*Student:* Is it a Sab'i (canonical seven-reading) variant?

*Shaykh:* Yes, it is Sab'i.

*Student:* Did the letters change?

*Shaykh:* No, they did not change.

*Student:* So the ya'?

*Shaykh:* Yes, but in the 'Uthmani script the alif is written in place of the ya'.

And His saying: ﴿Ibrahim Rabbuhu﴾, ﴿Rabbuhu﴾ is the subject (fa'il). Here He attributes lordship (rububiyyah) to Abraham, and this is a special lordship, because we have already said that rububiyyah corresponds to 'ubudiyyah (servitude). Just as servitude is of two kinds, special and general, lordship is also of two kinds, special and general. Both appear together in the words of the magicians: ﴿They said: We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-A'raf 121], this is general; ﴿The Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ [Al-A'raf 122], this is special. So here it is special lordship. There is no doubt that God's lordship over the messengers, especially those of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm), who are they?

*Student:* Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad ﷺ.

*Shaykh:* Yes, it is the most special of the lordships.

And His saying: ﴿with words﴾: this is what he was tested with. Ibtila' (testing) is examination and trial. What are these words? Are they cosmic (kawniyyah), legislative (shar'iyyah), or of the cosmic and legislative kinds? God has left them unspecified, so they are cosmic and legislative words, or they combine both. So what are these words? The commentators differ about them, and the most correct opinion is that they are everything God commanded Abraham with, whether cosmic or legislative: everything He commanded him, or decreed for him, is a "word." For example, he was tested by the command to sacrifice his son. Did he sacrifice him or not?

*Students:* He sacrificed him.

*Shaykh:* He sacrificed him?

*Student:* He did not sacrifice him.

*Shaykh:* Yes, that is right. God said to him: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [As-Saffat 105]. So he effectively sacrificed him, even though he did not actually do it. He complied with God's command. Was this a test or not? It was a test, one of the greatest tests. Likewise God tested him by having a fire kindled for him and throwing him into it. This is among the cosmic words. Was he patient or not? He was patient, patient and seeking reward. Every matter God decreed for him that requires patience and perseverance, or that He commanded him, is likewise included in His saying ﴿with words﴾. This is the correct view. Some said the words with which he was tested were: ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾. But this is not really a test; rather, it is the result of the test. When he was tested, ﴿and he fulfilled them﴾, he completed these cosmic or legislative words. Who can complete all the cosmic and legislative words of God, may He be exalted? Not everyone can endure that, except those whom God grants success. For this reason God described Abraham as one who fulfilled, saying: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [An-Najm 37]. That is, he completed what God commanded him and what he was tested with.

When he fulfilled them, God, may He be glorified and exalted, honored His servant and granted him this imamah (leadership). Is it not true that through patience and certainty one attains leadership in religion? Through patience and certainty one attains leadership in religion: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾ [As-Sajdah 24]. This is one point. ﴿And they were certain of Our signs﴾ is the second. Abraham was one of these people. ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾.

﴿Ja'iluka﴾ means "one who makes you" (musayyiruka). It takes two objects because it derives from ja'ala (to make), which here means sayyara (to make into). The first object is the kaf (the "you" pronoun), which is in the genitive position through being attached to the noun, and the second object is ﴿Imaman﴾.

An imam is one who is followed, whether in good or in evil. But there is no doubt that what is meant here is leadership in good.

If someone asks: show us evidence that leadership in evil is also called imamah?

We say: God's saying, ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [Al-Qasas 41]. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever establishes a bad practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." [Reported by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah.] This is because he became an imam, one who is followed.

﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾. Is ﴿lil-nas﴾ (for the people) general or not? It is general to those who come after him, not to those who came before him. But to those who came after him he became an imam, up to the Seal of the Messengers, Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [An-Nahl 123]. So he is an imam.

﴿He said: And of my offspring﴾: meaning, "And make from my offspring imams." Here, is the min (of) in ﴿min dhurriyyati﴾ partitive (lil-tab'id) or explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins)? It may be explanatory of the kind, and on that basis ﴿dhurriyyati﴾ can apply to all his descendants, meaning: "make all my offspring imams." It may also be partitive, in which case the meaning is: "make some of my offspring imams." Which is closer?

*Students:* It is explanatory of the kind.

*Shaykh:* That is, he asked God that all his offspring be imams? This could be either. But whichever it is, whether it is explanatory of the kind or partitive, God granted him this in a restricted form, saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

*Student:* (...)

*Shaykh:* No, not even some of them. Not every part of them is an imam. In any case, whether we say it is explanatory of the kind or partitive, God answered him with a restricted answer, saying: ﴿does not reach﴾, meaning does not attain, ﴿my covenant﴾, meaning My pledge to you concerning this, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, the wrongdoers among your offspring, whether the wrongdoing is general or specific, greater or lesser. The wrongdoer cannot be an imam. For this reason He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. ﴿My covenant﴾ is the subject (fa'il), and ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ is the object? That is, "I will make from your offspring an imam, but the wrongdoer is not included in that." For this reason God did not appoint a wrongdoer by way of the covenant. But it may be objected that some of Abraham's descendants were wrongdoers, though not with a major wrong, is that not so? Who, for example?

*Student:* Al-Hajjaj.

*Shaykh:* Yes, but they were not imams. For example, among the caliphs of the Umayyad dynasty there were wrongdoers, and among the caliphs of the 'Abbasid dynasty there were wrongdoers. But we have not heard that any of them committed a wrong so great that it took him out of Islam. This question will be addressed, God willing, later.

His saying: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested﴾. What is the meaning of ibtila' (testing)?

*Student:* Examination.

*Shaykh:* Examination. And what put ﴿Ibrahim﴾ in the accusative?

*Student:* It is an object.

*Shaykh:* An object of what?

*Student:* An object of ﴿ibtala﴾ (tested).

*Shaykh:* Where is the subject?

*Student:* ﴿Rabbuhu﴾.

*Shaykh:* ﴿Rabbuhu﴾.

Are there two readings of ﴿Ibrahim﴾?

*Students:* There is ﴿Ibrahim﴾, and there is ﴿Ibraham﴾.

*Shaykh:* Ibraham. In every place in Al-Baqarah, wherever it occurs in Al-Baqarah, there are two readings: Ibraham and Ibrahim. Outside Al-Baqarah there is disagreement.

What are the words with which God tested Abraham? What are these words? Are they cosmic or legislative?

*Students:* Cosmic and legislative.

*Shaykh:* Cosmic and legislative?

*Student:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* Prove it. Yes, good. The cosmic, such as?

*Student:* The cosmic, such as: (...) into the fire.

*Shaykh:* His being thrown into the fire, good. And the legislative?

*Student:* The legislative, such as when he left his wife and son, and when he killed his son.

*Shaykh:* He was commanded to sacrifice his son.

*Student:* He was commanded to sacrifice his son.

*Shaykh:* And likewise, the breaking of the idols and other things. So is the correct view that these words are specific or not specific?

*Students:* Not specific.

*Shaykh:* Not specific. But they are great words containing trial and testing.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿Imaman﴾?

*Student:* That is, the imam is the model who is followed.

*Shaykh:* In good or in evil?

*Student:* In good, and it may be in evil.

*Shaykh:* And it may be in evil. Such as?

*Student:* ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [Al-Qasas 41].

*Shaykh:* Yes, ﴿leaders calling to the Fire﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Imaman﴾. What governs it in the accusative?

*Student:* ﴿Imaman﴾?

*Shaykh:* Yes.

*Student:* It is in the accusative because of ("maker," ja'il).

*Shaykh:* ("maker") as what?

*Student:* An object.

*Shaykh:* The first, or the second, or the third?

*Student:* The second.

*Shaykh:* The second?

*Student:* The first is the kaf, and ﴿Imaman﴾ is the second.

*Shaykh:* And ﴿Imaman﴾ is the second.

*Student:* And imaman is the second.

*Shaykh:* The second, because ﴿ja'il﴾ comes from ja'ala, and it governs the accusative.

*Student:* Two objects.

*Shaykh:* Two objects.

His saying: ﴿And of my offspring﴾. What is the meaning of His saying ﴿And of my offspring﴾?

*Student:* That is, "and make from my offspring."

*Shaykh:* Imams.

*Shaykh:* Did God answer this supplication?

*Student:* He answered it with a restricted answer.

*Shaykh:* Restricted? In what He said?

*Student:* In His saying: ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

*Shaykh:* In His saying: ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

What is meant here by "covenant"?

*Student:* Leadership.

*Shaykh:* "My covenant does not reach"? Who knows? That is, what I pledge to you does not reach the wrongdoers. It is as if He is saying: I pledge this to you and give you a covenant concerning it, except that it does not reach the wrongdoers.

He said: ﴿And [mention] when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾ [Al-Baqarah 125]. ﴿Idh﴾ here is temporal, and it is connected to an omitted element. Its estimated form is?

*Student:* "Remember."

*Shaykh:* "Remember." That is, "Remember, O Muhammad, to the people this matter which We have made [a matter] for the people."

﴿Ja'alna﴾ means "We made" (sayyarna).

﴿Al-Bayt﴾ (the House): the definite article here is for mental familiarity (al-'ahd al-dhihni), and what is meant is the Ka'bah, because it is the House of God, may He be exalted. It is mentioned, and then with the article for magnification and exaltation. That is, "the familiar House that is not unknown and not forgotten. We made it a mathabah."

Mathabah means a place of return. That is, people return to it and go back to it from all the regions of the world, whether they return to it with their bodies or with their hearts. Those who come to it as pilgrims or as those performing 'umrah return to it with their bodies, and those who turn toward it every day in their prayers return to it with their hearts. They never cease to remember this House every day and night. Indeed, facing it is one of the conditions for the validity of their prayers.

His saying: ﴿and a sanctuary (amnan)﴾: that is, "and We made it a sanctuary for the people."

"It was not made lawful for anyone after me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of the day." [Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (1349) and Muslim (1353/445) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. The wording of al-Bukhari is: "It was not made lawful for anyone before me or after me; it was made lawful for me for an hour of the day."] This was only out of necessity, because this House could not be cleansed of this polytheism except by this permission. God made it lawful for him for an hour of the day out of necessity, and that was the hour of the Conquest. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "Its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday." [Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (104) and Muslim (1354/446) from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi.] So it is sacred even for the Messenger ﷺ. This is the meaning of its being a sanctuary. The Prophet ﷺ answered a question that may be posed: "If anyone takes license to fight the Messenger of God ﷺ, say: God permitted His Messenger, but He did not permit you."

The judgment belongs to God, the Most High, the Great. He permitted His Messenger ﷺ in that hour, but He did not permit anyone else. This is the meaning of its being a sanctuary: that people are safe. It was a sanctuary because it is a place of worship, rites, and sacred sites (mash'ar). Had it been a place of fear, people would not have performed their worship in the most perfect manner. For this reason carrying weapons in the Sanctuary (haram) is forbidden, so that every person may be safe. By this we know the enormity of the crime of those who spread fear among Muslims during the seasons of Hajj, and that they are, God forbid, among the greatest of people in crime. For God made this city safe at all times. So how much more so at the time of performing the rites of Hajj, for which it was made safe in the first place. This, God forbid, is a great violation of God's sanctities. For this reason this city must be safe.

When 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, was stabbed while he was on his mount at Mina, one of the Kharijites stabbed him with a dagger he had, until his leg stuck to the stirrup, may God be pleased with him. Al-Hajjaj came to visit him.

*Student:* Ibn 'Umar was?

*Shaykh:* Yes, Ibn 'Umar. Al-Hajjaj came to visit him and said to him: "You are the one who did this to us? I used to forbid anyone from carrying a weapon in the Sanctuary." [Reported by al-Bukhari (966).] This is evidence that this House is absolutely safe. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 67]. This safety is general, even for the disbelievers. Yet God says: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there; but if they fight you, then kill them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 191]. Is that in defense or in aggression?

*Students:* In defense.

*Shaykh:* In defense. There is a difference between killing in defense and killing in aggression.

*Student:* Is the making (ja'l) here cosmic or legislative?

*Shaykh:* No, this is legislative.

*Student:* Shaykh, if (...) in the religion of the disbelievers, is it not to be established?

*Shaykh:* That is, it is impossible for the disbelievers ever to take control of it, because the Messenger ﷺ said: "There is no hijrah after the Conquest." [Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (2783) and Muslim (1353/445) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] And it is not possible to migrate from it except if it is a land of disbelief.

﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah 125]. "Take" means "make."

*Student:* (...) Shaykh, is there not an objection to this?

*Shaykh:* No, there is no objection to this, because this is directed at him and does not remain in it.

His saying: ﴿And take﴾ means "make" or "appoint." There are two readings: the first is ﴿ittakhidhu﴾ in the imperative form, and the second is ﴿ittakhadhu﴾ in the past tense. That is: "and the people took," as a mathabah for the people, and "they took from the station of Abraham." Or: "and you took from the station of Abraham a place of prayer."

His saying: ﴿take from the station of Abraham﴾. The maqam is the place of standing. It has two usages: a general usage, which is the place where he stood in worship, and a specific usage, which is his station for building the Ka'bah. According to the first, general usage, all the stations and sacred sites of Hajj are from the station of Abraham. Do you understand?

According to the first, general usage, the meaning of maqam as his station for worship includes all the sacred sites of Hajj: 'Arafat, Muzdalifah, the Jamarat, al-Safa and al-Marwah, and so on. According to the second, specific usage, the term refers to the particular stone on which Abraham, peace be upon him, stood to raise the foundations of the House. This is the famous station, known to everyone.

His saying: ﴿musalla﴾ (a place of prayer). Does it mean a place of linguistic prayer, which is supplication? Or a place of legal (sharʿi) prayer?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 124–126 (part 2 of 5):

* The students (al-Talaba): the legal (shar'iyyah) sense.
* The Shaykh: According to the first (meaning), it is a place of supplication, and according to the second, it is a place of the well-known legal prayer. When the Messenger ﷺ came to it after circumambulating, he recited: ﴿And take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾. This shows that the Messenger (ﷺ) explained it in its specific sense, the particular station. However, many exegetes explained it in both senses, and they said: this is a mention of one of the individual instances of the general term, because it is included in it. The specific is included in the general, and not the reverse.

As for His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Take from the Station of Abraham﴾, the specific station is the stone on which the building of the Ka'bah was raised. The historians differ over whether it was adjoining the Ka'bah or was separated from it in its present place.

Most historians hold that it was attached to the Ka'bah, and that the one who moved it back to this place was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Based on that, the caliph has the right to consider moving it from its place if he sees benefit in that. But if we say that this was its place during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), then it apparently is not permissible to change it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it, and when the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it, we have no right to move it back from it. One of the students of knowledge wrote a treatise on this subject, and some scholars endorsed it, and among those who endorsed it was Shaykh 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Baz. He held that it is permissible to move it from its place for the sake of benefit and expansion, based on what is well known among the historians, that it was adjoining the Ka'bah and then was moved back. There is no doubt that if it were moved back from its place, that would avert a harm, namely the harm of those people who gather around it in the seasons (of Hajj and 'Umrah), and there is in it a kind of harm or a kind of mischief, namely that it distances it from those circumambulating at times other than the seasons. Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: At times other than the seasons, the tawaf area is almost empty, it is not crowded. We could place it, for example, at the colonnade (al-riwaq), meaning it would be far from the people... (...). In other words, the benefits here conflict. Is it better that it remain in its place, or better that it be moved back from its place? If the benefits are equal, then it is better that what is as it was remain as it was, and also out of caution against confusion and disagreement over this matter. As for the matter of congestion, the crowding of worshippers upon those circumambulating, this can be removed by awareness-raising if it is effective, or by prohibition and enforcement if it is not. In truth, in my opinion, it has decreased somewhat in recent years; this year I see that it is little, because people have become aware.
* A student: O Shaykh, if it were delayed it would become a plaything (...). Anyone would move it; every caliph would have his own opinion.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, perhaps. Each one would have his own opinion.
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. The two rak'ahs of the Station: if during Hajj the mosque is crowded, is it permissible to pray them outside the mosque?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is permissible, because these two rak'ahs are legislated, and they have a place that is better than others, which is behind the Station. If the place is not available, the legislated prayer remains.
* The student: Even if outside the mosque?
* The Shaykh: Even if outside. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, prayed them at Dhu Tuwa, in a distant place.
* A student: The verse: ﴿And take from the Station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾, does it mean that it is a sunnah for one to... after the tawaf?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is a sunnah. And His saying: ﴿And take from the Station of Abraham﴾ has two readings: ﴿Ibrahaam﴾ and ﴿Ibraheem﴾. And His saying: ﴿a place of prayer (musalla)﴾, is it the second object of (ittakhadhu, "take"), or the first object?
* The students: The first object.
* The Shaykh: The first object? And the second?
* The students: The prepositional phrase.
* The Shaykh: The implied prepositional phrase. And His saying ﴿musalla﴾: is it in the accusative with a visible fatha or with an implied fatha?
* A student: The latter; it is in the accusative with an implied fatha.
* The Shaykh: With an implied fatha. That is why it is written with a yā'. It is a defective noun ending in alif: musalla, so it is in the accusative with an implied fatha on its last letter, preventing its appearance is the difficulty of pronunciation (al-ta'adhdhur). And the tanwin in it?
* A student: It is a lightening.
* The Shaykh: It is a compensation (ʿiwad), a compensation for the omitted alif. ﴿And We charged Abraham﴾ or ﴿Ibraahaam﴾ ﴿and Isma'il, that purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Baqarah 125]. ﴿'Ahid-na (We charged)﴾: al-'ahd (covenant, charge) is a command concerning something important. It is not mere instruction; it is only a covenant when the matter is important. For example: Abu Bakr entrusted (ʿahida) the caliphate to 'Umar, that is, he bequeathed it to him. And it is well known that the most important of the affairs of the Muslims is the caliphate.

As for His saying: ﴿And Isma'il﴾, he is the son of Ibrahim, the father of the Arabs, and he is the one who was to be sacrificed according to the correct opinion. That is, he is the one whom Allah commanded Ibrahim to slaughter, and he is the one who said to his father: ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast﴾ [as-Saffat 102].

As for the view of the one who says it was Isaac, it is far-fetched. Some scholars have said that this is transmitted from the Children of Israel, because the Children of Israel wish that the one to be sacrificed was Isaac, since he was their father, rather than Isma'il, who was their uncle, the father of the Arabs. But whoever reflects on the verses of as-Saffat, or the verses of as-Saffat, will know with a knowledge that nearly approaches certainty that the one to be sacrificed was Isma'il. Because Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in the midst of these verses, He said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [as-Saffat 112], after He had mentioned the story in full, He said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous. And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the doer of good and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾ [as-Saffat 112–113]. How then could he speak first of his resolve to slaughter him and the dialogue that took place between them, and then say: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾?

Good news is only given after (the event). So if Isaac were the one to be sacrificed, it would not be correct to say: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾.

And His saying: ﴿that purify﴾. ﴿We charged Abraham﴾ ﴿that purify﴾: is this (anna) a lightened form of the heavy (anna)?
* A student: Verbal (maṣdariyyah).
* The Shaykh: It is not verbal.
* A student: Explanatory (mufassirah).
* The Shaykh: The explanatory (anna) is followed by a command, as in ﴿We revealed to him: make the ark﴾ [al-Mu'minun 27]. Apparently it is verbal.
* A student: ﴿Purify﴾, is it not a command?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it has a reason. Correct, purify, yes. Indeed, then it can be explanatory, because 'ahidna contains the meaning of saying without its letters. So it is explanatory, meaning that the covenant is His saying: ﴿Purify My House﴾. Purify: is a command verb. And His saying ﴿My House﴾: what is intended by it is the Ka'bah, and Allah, exalted is He, attributed it to Himself as an attribution of honour, and not an attribution of a part or of a quality. So it is an attribution of honour. By this we know that what is attributed to Allah is divided into two parts, or three?
* A student: Three.
* The Shaykh: The first: that it is a self-subsisting entity (ʿayn qā'imah bi-nafsihā).
The second: that it is an attribute of that entity or in that entity.
The third: that it is an attribute of Allah.
If it is a self-subsisting entity, then its attribution is an attribution of honour, like: the she-camel of Allah, the House of Allah. If it is an attribute connected to an entity, like the spirit, if we say it is an attribute, or that it is a body connected to another created body, then it is also created, and its attribution is an attribution of honour, and it is created, like: ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit, so fall down prostrating to him﴾ [al-Hijr 29]. And if it is an attribute, then it is an attribute of Allah, meaning that if the attributed thing is a meaning that does not subsist apart from Allah, then it is an attribute of Allah, like: ﴿until he hears the words of Allah﴾ [at-Tawbah 6], and like: the might of Allah, the power of Allah, and what is similar to that. Here it is from the first category: ﴿My House﴾. The House is a self-subsisting entity, so its attribution to Him is by way of an attribution of honour.

And His saying: ﴿My House for those who circle it﴾, meaning those who circumambulate it. The second: ﴿those who stay in devotion﴾, those who remain in it for worship. The third: ﴿those who bow and prostrate﴾, those who pray in it. And prayer is expressed by bowing and prostration because they are two of its pillars. It was mentioned earlier in passing that when a part of an act of worship is used to refer to it, this is evidence that this part is a pillar of it, without which it is not valid. Here He began with those who circumambulate, because they are specific to that House, then He followed with those who stay in devotion, because it is a wider circle than those who circumambulate, but it is restricted to the mosques. Then He said: ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾, and this is not restricted to mosques. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (335), and Muslim (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.] So Allah, glorified and exalted be He, began with the most specific and then the more specific: what is most specific to the Sacred House is tawaf, then i'tikaf. As for prayer, it is not restricted to a place. For this reason some scholars say: a king vowed to Allah a vow that he would worship Allah with an act of worship that no one would share with him. He consulted some scholars, and they said: what shall we do? If he fasts, it is possible that there will be people fasting. If he prays, it is possible that there will be people praying. If he gives charity, it is possible that there will be people giving charity. So they went to a scholar, who said to them: clear the tawaf area for him, meaning let him circumambulate alone. Then can anyone share it with him or not?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No one can share it with him, because in reality no one circumambulates except around this House.
