* A student: Does this contradict the text: "Do not prevent anyone who circumambulates this House" [Abu Dawud (1894), and al-Tirmidhi (868), from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im]?
* The Shaykh: No. The point is that this resolves the matter. As for whether it is permissible or not, they forbid it for other than this reason. But there is no way to fulfil this vow except by this.
* A student: It is not possible, O Shaykh (...).
* The Shaykh: Where?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is possible without preventing the people. It is possible if he comes in the last part of the night, meaning at times other than the seasons you will sometimes find it empty, or he comes, for example, after sunrise, always, except in the days of 'Umrah when there are crowds.
* The student: Or in Ramadan at midday sometimes.
* The Shaykh: The point is, in any case, it is possible for him to find it. And His saying: ﴿for those who circle it﴾, purify for those who circumambulate: the lam here is for causation, meaning for their sake. And His saying: ﴿those who bow and prostrate﴾: ruka' is known to be the plural of (rāki'), and sujud is the plural of (sājid), and it may be a verbal noun, (sajada, yasjudu, sujudan). But sujud and quʿud are a verbal noun and at the same time a plural. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Pray sitting, all of you" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (378), and Muslim (411/77), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik]. ﴿That purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate﴾.
* A student: O Shaykh, "those who bow and prostrate" is different from (...).
* The Shaykh: And what then?
* The student: Different from "those who bow and prostrate" (...).
* The Shaykh: And bowing and prostration are singled out because they are the most excellent postures. Bowing is more excellent than standing, and prostration is more excellent than it. For this reason we say: standing is superior to bowing and prostration by mention of it. If standing is mentioned, what is it?
* The students: The Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: The speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, is better than everything. And the mention (of Allah) is glorification (tasbih), and the mention of bowing and prostration is glorification, and glorification is less sacred than the Qur'an. Although glorification is undoubtedly an exaltation of Allah, it is not like the Qur'an. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, the Wise, gave each pillar of the prayer what is specific to it: this one is singled out by the excellence of its mention, and this one is singled out by the excellence of its posture.
* A student: O Shaykh, do we not say that bowing and prostration are the most specific attributes of prayer? That is, one is not bowing or prostrating to Allah while (...)?
* The Shaykh: What do you mean?
* The student: That is, the most specific attributes of prayer?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not correct, because the prostration of recitation is a prostration without prayer.
* The student: According to this opinion.
* The Shaykh: It is not valid.
* A student: O Shaykh, ﴿Take from the Station﴾: how is (min) here, is it partitive or explanatory? Also, if we took the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer, could we pray on top of the stone?
* The Shaykh: His saying: "take from," this (min) is for clarification of the kind (bayaniyyah), meaning take from this station. It is also permissible that it is taken to contain the meaning of (fi, "in"), meaning take in this station a place for prayer.
* A student: But since the Station is the stone, it cannot be that they take it as a place of prayer?
* The Shaykh: Yes, take from it. Its meaning is not upon it. Take from it a place. The Messenger explained it as meaning that one prays beside it.
* The student: Does this not favour that the rites of Hajj in general (...) the Station of Abraham in general is (...) Hajj?
* The Shaykh: In reality, each has its preponderance. As for the Prophet's explanation (ﷺ), there is no doubt that it is clear that he meant this station. And if we intend the general sense, the usage of prayer in the language would refute it.

He says: ﴿That purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate (125). And when Abraham said: My Lord, make this a secure city﴾.
* A student: His saying "purify." I said: Abraham is the one who built the House, O Shaykh. Why did He say "purify"?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but Isma'il was helping him: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il﴾ [al-Baqarah 127].
* The student: No, no, I mean, how does one purify something that is already pure, when he is the one who built the House?
* The Shaykh: Yes, even if he built it, what then? It may be that this House will be exposed to impurity, to filth, so they purify it.
* A student: His saying "purify" is a command given during the building?
* The Shaykh: It is permissible that it was a command during the building, because something may befall it during the building or after it. It is not impossible.
* A student: Does purification include physical and spiritual purity?
* The Shaykh: By Allah, there is room for consideration. As for spiritual purity, unless it is by way of analogy: if physical purification is obligatory, then spiritual purification is more fitting.
* The student: (...) this?
* The Shaykh: That is not the apparent meaning, because He said: ﴿for those who circle it﴾, He did not say "purify it" and leave it general. And the purification is ﴿for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate﴾, and only physical purity suits it.
* The student: (...) the circumambulators and those who stay in devotion (...) idols were found, so they could not...?
* The Shaykh: No, they could. There were three hundred and sixty idols, and the people were circumambulating around them.

﴿And when Abraham said﴾, meaning: and remember when Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾. And we say concerning it what we said before, the reading ﴿Ibraahaam﴾. ﴿And when Abraham said: My Lord, make this a secure city﴾. ﴿Make (ij'al)﴾ means appoint (sayyir). ﴿This﴾, the one indicated, is Makkah. And His saying: ﴿a city (baladan)﴾. The word "balad" is the name for every inhabited place, whether it is a large city or a small city; all of it is called a balad. Allah, exalted is He, has called Makkah a balad, as in His saying: ﴿And this secure land﴾ [at-Tin 3], and He called it a qaryah (town), as in His saying: ﴿And how many a town, stronger than your town which expelled you, have We destroyed﴾ [Muhammad 13].

And His saying: ﴿secure (aminan)﴾. Some exegetes said: meaning secure for whoever is in it, because the city itself is not described as secure or fearful. The city is land and buildings, so it is not described as secure or fearful. What is secure is its people. But what should be taken in its apparent sense is that the city itself should be secure. When the city is secure, those in it are secure, and this is more eloquent, because if someone came and destroyed the building, the building would not be secure; it would become exposed to someone who would destroy it. So its being secure is more comprehensive than explaining it as "secure for its people," because it includes the city and those in it. For this reason He said: ﴿and provide its people (ahlahu)﴾, He distinguished and did not say "provide it," because it cannot be provided for. ﴿Provide its people with fruits, those among them who believe﴾. ﴿Provide (urzuq)﴾: is it a command verb or a verb of supplication?
* The students: Supplication.
* The Shaykh: Supplication. ﴿Its people (ahlahu)﴾ is the first object, and ﴿of the fruits (min al-thamarat)﴾ is the second object.

Please tell me which would be most useful.

The Shaykh: Ibrahim asked that imamate be given to his descendants in general. Allah answered him, except that He, glory be to Him, excluded the wrongdoer, for he does not deserve to be an imam. He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. Its meaning is: I do commit this to you, but My covenant does not include the wrongdoers.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return (mathabah) for the people and a sanctuary, and [said], "Take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer"﴾ [al-Baqarah 125].

From this verse the excellence of the Sacred House is derived in two respects: that it is a place of return (mathabah), and that it is a sanctuary (amn).

* Among the benefits of the verse: the manifestation of the mercy of Allah, mighty and majestic. When He made this House a place of return, and people must return to it, He showed them mercy by making it a sanctuary, He showed them mercy by making it a sanctuary.

* Among the benefits of the verse: every place that is a place of return for the people must be a sanctuary. For this reason the scholars disliked carrying weapons in the mosques. They said: because mosques are places of security. But if need calls for it, there is no harm in it. The point is that everything that is, by the Law, a place of return to which people return by the Law, must be secure, so that people may be safe in performing their acts of worship.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation to take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer, based on His saying: ﴿and take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾. What is the indication of obligation here?

* The students: The imperative.

* The Shaykh: The imperative. The basis of it is obligation. If we say that by "the station" is meant all the rites of Hajj, then there is no difficulty. Or not?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Because in it is the obligation of standing at 'Arafah, Muzdalifah and Mina. If we say that what is meant is the two rak'ahs after the tawaf, then there is a difficulty, for the majority of scholars hold that they are sunnah, while Imam Malik went to the view that they are obligatory. What a person should do is not abandon them, because the Messenger, peace be upon him, explained the verse by them: he came forward to the station of Abraham and recited: ﴿and take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, exalted is He, honours His servant. Observe Ibrahim: when he fulfilled the words, and what benefits came to him from this? As a result, Allah made him an imam for the people, and commanded the people to take his station as a place of prayer, commanded the people to take his station as a place of prayer. This is part of his imamate. It may also be said: the House that Ibrahim built, its glorification is in reality considered a virtue (manqabah) of Ibrahim, because Ibrahim is the one who built it.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to purify the House from physical and spiritual impurities. Is that so? Say: yes or no?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: From where do we take it? ﴿We covenanted﴾ ﴿that purify﴾. We have already mentioned that covenant means a command entrusted by inspiration. This is supported by His saying, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only unclean, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawbah 28]. For this reason it is not permitted for polytheists or others among the people of disbelief to enter the boundaries (amyal) of the Haram, because if they enter them they draw near to it, they draw near to the Sacred Mosque, and Allah says: ﴿let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾.

And among them: the requirement that the place of tawaf be pure, based on His saying: ﴿for those who circumambulate﴾.

From it is derived, with greater reason, the requirement that the clothing of those who circumambulate be pure, and that it is not permitted to circumambulate in a najis garment, because a person's contact with garments is closer than his contact with a place. Is that clear?

Is the obligation of purity from minor impurity (hadath) derived from it or not? It may be derived from it and it may not be derived from it. That is because purity from minor impurity is not a physical najasah. The one in a state of hadath is not najis, otherwise, if he touched you while you were wet, he would make you najis. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said to Abu Hurayrah when he was in a state of janabah: «Indeed the believer does not become najis.» [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (285) and Muslim (371) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]

And among the benefits of the verse: that tawaf is only around the Ka'bah, based on His saying: "purify it for them." For this reason the scholars said: it is a condition for the validity of tawaf that it be in the mosque, in the Sacred Mosque, the mosque of the Ka'bah, and that if one circumambulates outside the mosque it does not suffice him. So if a person wanted, for example, to go around the Sacred Mosque from its outer side, it would not suffice him. As for those who circumambulate within the same mosque, whether above or below, these it suffices.

* A student: The main thing is (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the main thing is that it be in the mosque. Did he not say: beyond the pillars is not permitted?

* The student: (...) those who circumambulate added.

* The Shaykh: You mean even if they went out of the mosque?

* The student: Even if they went out of the mosque.

* The Shaykh: He waits, because they finish; they are not sitting (...).

* The student: Perhaps in the future it did not make them (...).

* The Shaykh: Even in the future he waits until he exits. It is necessary that they be in the mosque.

* The student: Within the bounds of the mosque.

* The Shaykh: Within the bounds of the mosque. On this basis one must beware of circumambulating above the Sa'i area, because some people may circumambulate with the Sa'i area: when the Sa'i area goes around, he enters with it, because the Sa'i area above has doors and below has doors, so he might circumambulate with the Sa'i area. One must therefore beware, because the Sa'i area is not part of the mosque. As you see, the Sa'i area is separated from the mosque, and this separation is necessary; for if it were part of the mosque, a woman who menstruates after tawaf would not perform Sa'i, because she would then be obliged to remain in the mosque.

And also among them: the excellence of these four acts of worship: tawaf, i'tikaf, ruku' and sujud, since He commanded that the House be purified for them. Does the difference between the first, which is in the sound masculine plural form, and the second, which is a broken plural, have a legal benefit, or only a verbal benefit? That is, He said: "for those who circumambulate, and those who abide, and those who bow and prostrate," but He said: ﴿and the bowers, the prostrators﴾?

It may be said: "those who circumambulate, and those who abide, and the bowers" — the form ruka' (fu'al-type plural) indicates abundance, because prayer has two bowings at least, and in it there are at least four prostrations; this is the duality. As for the witr, it has one bowing and two prostrations.

It may also be said that this is a matter of variation of expression, because it is part of eloquence that words come in different forms, since that is more lively. And Allah knows best.

* A student: Shaykh, could there be ten prostrations?

* The Shaykh: In one prayer?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: In one obligatory prayer, you mean? Six prostrations?

* The student: The Maghrib prayer (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, ten or six? Six tashahhuds, tashahhuds (...) six tashahhuds.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Tashahhuds? We do not know; in any case, this is rare, six tashahhuds are rare.

* The student: Does prayer in the Sa'i area suffice a person if he is in the mosque?

* The Shaykh: No, except if the rows are connected, when the sanctuary and the mosque are full and the rows are joined (...).

* The student: Shaykh, did the Prophet's prayer at the station of Abraham and his recitation of the verse not occur?

* The Shaykh: Which of them?

* The student: The Prophet's recitation.

* The Shaykh: It is possible that he said it by way of example.

* The student: Yesterday we mentioned in its explanation that we said: is it not permitted to deviate from it?

* The Shaykh: No, we said: this strengthens that view, but it does not prevent other views. We said: this is preponderant, but it does not prohibit.

* The student: Why did he not recite the verse when he stood at 'Arafah and when he stood at Muzdalifah, did he not recite it?

* The Shaykh: Perhaps because when the Prophet, peace be upon him, began the tawaf and prayed, he had not yet exited from his ihram, as you know. And it is not necessary to cite a verse as evidence for every act. Rather, there is no doubt that what preceded indicates that the intended meaning is the two rak'ahs only.

He says: ﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits"﴾ [al-Baqarah 126], and so on to the end.

In this verse there is an indication of the excellence of Abraham, because His saying: ﴿when he said﴾ was previously explained as meaning: "and remember when he said." And had this not been a matter deserving of mention and announcement, it would not have been commanded. Therefore in this is evidence of the excellence of Abraham, peace be upon him, since this statement of his was made the subject of mention.

* Among the benefits of the verse: a person is never free from needing to call upon Allah, whatever his rank. No one is ever independent of supplication, based on His saying: ﴿My Lord, make﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: supplication has an effect in attaining the desired end, whether it is averting a disliked thing or bringing about a loved thing. Do you understand?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Because if supplication had no effect, supplication would be pointless. As for the saying of one who says: "There is no need for supplication: if Allah has written this for me, it will happen whether I supplicate or not, and if it has not been written for you, it will not happen whether you supplicate or not," our answer to this is: "Yes, it may be written, and what follows from that?"

* The students: Upon supplication.

* The Shaykh: Upon your supplication. It is written, but on condition that you supplicate. So call upon Allah. Just as if someone said: "By Allah, I will not eat food. If Allah wants me to live, I will live without eating, and if He wants me to die, I will die even if I fill my stomach up to the throat." What do we say? Rather, eating is a cause of life. So denying that supplication is a cause is denying self-evident matters, because we know with certainty, from what we have been told, from what we have witnessed, and from what has happened to us, that Allah, glory be to Him, answers supplication. Is that so or not?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Allah, exalted is He, has related to us in the Qur'an many stories in which there is an answer to supplication. We have also heard from others, of matters not related in the Qur'an, many cases in which supplication was answered. Likewise it happens to a person himself: things happen for which he calls upon Allah, and he sees with his own eyes that they came as a result of his supplication. So the Law and reality both refute the one who denies the effect of supplication.

* A student: Shaykh, the claim that when Abraham was thrown into the fire he said: "As for from You, no, O Jibril; and from Allah, yes; His seeing my state suffices instead of my asking," is it correct?

* The Shaykh: No, no, that is a lie. His knowledge of his state suffices instead of my asking, or replaces my asking: this is a lie.

And among them, among the benefits of the verse: we have mentioned the excellence of Abraham (...) by this supplication.

And also among them: his compassion, peace be upon him, toward those who come to this House, because making the House secure includes kindness toward those among the people who visit it.

And also among the benefits of the verse: the compassion of Abraham, also in that he asked Allah to provide his people with fruits, based on His saying: ﴿and provide its people with fruits﴾.

And among its benefits: the good manners of Abraham, peace be upon him, in that he did not generalize in this supplication, but said: ﴿provide with fruits whoever among its people believes﴾, out of fear of Allah that He might say to him: "Whoever believes, I will provide him." But the matter turned to the opposite of the first case: in the first, Allah specified his supplication, and here it is the opposite; he generalized.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the provision of Allah is inclusive of the believer and the disbeliever, based on His saying: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾. So provision is general, inclusive of the believer and the disbeliever, indeed of humans and animals: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision, and He knows its place of dwelling and its place of storage﴾ [Hud 6].

You see some small creatures on the earth with nothing around them, yet Allah makes provision easy for them, bringing it to them from where they do not perceive or expect. Strange stories are told about these matters. Some small, deaf, blind animals are seen, for whom Allah brings provision, and they eat whatever they need. And Allah is capable of all things.

And among the benefits of the noble verse also: that the provision of non-believers does not continue, based on His saying: ﴿Then I will give him enjoyment for a little, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 126].

It is derived from the implication of the noble verse that the provision of believers continues, because Allah, exalted is He, restricted the brief enjoyment to whom? To the disbelievers. So the meaning is that Allah's provision for the believers is continuous. And I say: Allah's provision for the believers is a paradise in this world and in the Hereafter. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will not taste death therein except the first death, and He will protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾ [al-Dukhan 56].

This exception, according to most scholars, is an exception; and of what type? Disjunctive (munqati'). But in reality, even if we say it is disjunctive, and that the meaning is "but the first death, they have already tasted it, so they will not die a second time," as Abu Bakr said: "By Allah, Allah will not gather for you two deaths." [Related by al-Bukhari (1242) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.] Yet it points to the fact that the people of Paradise are in bliss in this world and in the Hereafter. This is the reality, for there is no one more content of heart or more joyful than the people of knowledge and faith, based on His saying: ﴿so We will surely give him a good life﴾ [al-Nahl 97].

And one of the early generation (salaf) said: "If the kings and the sons of kings knew what we are in, they would fight us over it with swords." A person finds great ease in obedience when he is in purity of heart, sincerity and faith. He finds a pleasure that cannot be weighed against the whole world. For this reason the Messenger called this "sweetness": the sweetness of faith. So there is a taste that a person perceives. It may even reach the point that he finds the scent of Paradise while he is still in this world, as Anas ibn al-Nadr is thought to have said: "Indeed I find the scent of Paradise beyond Uhud." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (4048) and Muslim (1903/148), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.] He said this while in battle, and Allah made him perceive the scent of Paradise while he was in this world. This is one of Allah's honours to a person, so that when he breathes in this fragrance (...) he would not exchange it for the whole world. Rather, this matter that he perceived with his senses requires that he had already perceived it with his heart, through what Allah has informed of in His Book and upon the tongue of His Messenger, may blessings and peace be upon him.

And among them: the affirmation of the punishment of the Fire.

* A student: (...) from the words of Ibn Taymiyyah.

* Another student: But is the permissibility of istithna' (exception) derived from it, Shaykh (...)?

* The Shaykh: What is the istithna', and what type is it?

* The student: His exception, glory be to Him: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾.

* The Shaykh: The istithna', what is the istithna'? Where is the istithna'?

* The student: The istithna' is in ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾.

* The Shaykh: That is generalization. The exception is in Abraham's words: ﴿whoever believes﴾, ﴿and provide its people﴾, ﴿whoever believes﴾. For this is a substitution (badal) which implies excluding some individuals, the individuals of his people. This is where there is an exception. I mean the exception in meaning, not in technical terminology. If you mean the kind of exception like: "O Allah, forgive me if You will," then there is no evidence for it in the verse.

* A student: No, I mean: one makes an exception, "O Allah, forgive (...)?"

* The Shaykh: Yes, perhaps it is permissible to derive from the verse the specification of what is not an exception; that is, specifying a person's supplication with a particular attribute, such as: "O Allah, if he is a wrongdoer, then repay him for his wrong," or "avenge me against him," or something similar.

In the noble verse: is there an affirmation of the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, based on His saying: ﴿He said﴾? Or not? And that it is with letters and sound. What is the evidence that it is with letters?

* The students: ﴿He said﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿He said﴾ is a report of His saying.

* A student: It is composed of letters.

* The Shaykh: Because ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾, for example, is composed of letters; these are letters, so it is letters. But what is the evidence that it is with sound?

* A student: His answer to Abraham.

* Students: In the answer (...).

* The Shaykh: The dialogue with Abraham. Had Abraham not heard, this dialogue would not have been valid.

And among them: the affirmation of Allah's hearing, because He hears Abraham while he speaks to Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

And also among them: the affirmation of the Last Day.

This is coordinated with ﴿whoever believes﴾ and ﴿and provide its people﴾ and ﴿whoever believes﴾. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾, meaning: "then I will provide for him." We have said previously that Abraham, peace be upon him, only said ﴿whoever believes﴾ in obedience to the discipline of Allah, mighty and majestic, when He said at the beginning: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾; he then said ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾. Disbelief (kufr) linguistically means concealment, and from it comes the name of the palm's sheath (kafur al-nakhlah), because it covers the spathe. But in the Law it is departure from Islam; that is, whoever is not a Muslim is a disbeliever. We have also previously mentioned that disbelief revolves around two matters: the first is arrogance (istikbar), and the second is denial (juhud). Then: are disbelief and polytheism the same, or is there a general and specific relation between them, or are they mutually exclusive like two separate things?

Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin said: We say that there is a general and specific relationship between them. Every polytheist (mushrik) is a disbeliever (kafir), but not every disbeliever is a polytheist. One who denies and rejects this is not a polytheist, but he is a disbeliever. One who calls upon another god besides Allah is a polytheist, and at the same time he is a disbeliever. So the relationship between them is one of general and specific. Unless the speaker means by shirk the following of one's desires, for following desires is shirk in the broader sense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you seen the one who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah 23]. Allah, glorified and exalted, made the following of desires a form of taking something as a god. On this basis we say: if by shirk is meant its broader sense, then every disbeliever is a polytheist in this sense. But in terms of the technical (iṣṭilāḥī) meaning that defines its concept, the relationship between shirk and kufr is what?

* Student: General and specific.

* Shaykh: General and specific. And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then I will let him enjoy [it] briefly﴾. In another reading it is ﴿fa-umti'uhu﴾, from al-imtā' or from al-tamtī'. Tamtī' or imtā' means that a person is given his provision (balgha) from this world, that he is given just enough provision from the world to enjoy for as long as Allah wills. But He said: ﴿briefly﴾. What is this period that Allah described as brief?

It is the worldly life. The brevity here applies both to the time and to the enjoyment itself: the time, and the enjoyment itself. The time is short, however long a person's life may extend, it is short. However long a person's life extends, it is little. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As if they had not remained but an hour of a day, a proclamation﴾ [al-Ahqaf 35].

Likewise, the enjoyment itself is little. Even what a person attains in this world of pleasure and enjoyment is in reality little, because it is mixed with disturbance, both within the enjoyment itself and in what surrounds it, before it or after it, as the poet said:

One day is against us and one day is for us,
and one day we are afflicted and one day we are gladdened.

Another poet said:

There is no sweetness to life while its pleasures are troubled
by the remembrance of death and old age.

So the brevity in this world is on two counts. The first count is the time: however long the time is for a person, it is little. The second is the enjoyment itself: it is little, because it is not perfect. It is deficient, preceded by disturbance and followed by disturbance, and in itself it is also not complete.

﴿Then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Aḍṭarruhu﴾ means: I will force him to the punishment of the Fire. Allah made this a compulsion because every person flees from the punishment of the Fire, but, Allah forbid, he has no escape from it, because it is he who did the deeds that necessitate it. As long as he did them, that is, did the deeds that necessitate the Fire, he and his own self are responsible, and for this reason He said: ﴿I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire.﴾ And if you want to see that this matter is compelled, consider what Allah the Exalted mentioned about the state of the wrongdoers at the time of death: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are extending their hands, [saying], "Release your souls"﴾ [al-An'am 93].

It is as if they are straining against their own souls and resisting them, and it is said to them: "Release your souls." This is in contrast to the believer, we ask Allah to make me and you among them. At the time of death his soul rejoices in departing and leaving the body becomes easy for him, because it is given the glad tidings of "rest, bounty, and a Lord who is not angry" (cf. Qur'an 56:89–93). So it knows from now that it wishes to move from this world to this bliss. This is in contrast to those to whom it is said, Allah forbid: ﴿Release your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs﴾ [al-An'am 93].

As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿to the punishment of the Fire﴾. Punishment (al-'adhāb) means the penalty through which a person is pained. And ﴿the Fire﴾ (al-nār) is a well-known name. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rāb) may be difficult for you, because we have not covered this section before. ﴿Wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Biʾsa﴾ is a past-tense verb that is rigid (jāmid) and performative (inshā'ī), meant for blame. So it is a rigid verb for blame. Is it performative or declarative (khabarī)?

* Students: Performative.

* Shaykh: Performative. And ﴿al-maṣīr﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of ﴿biʾsa﴾. They say that (biʾsa), (niʿma) and similar words necessarily require a subject and a specified object (makhṣūṣ). The subject is "al-maṣīr," and the specified object is omitted, its estimated form being: "and wretched is the destination, it (hiya)." For if you do not estimate this, the sentence does not refer back to what preceded it. So we say: the specified object is omitted, its estimated form being "hiya," and "wretched is the destination, it." Al-maṣīr means the place of becoming (makān al-ṣayrūrah), that is, the final return to which a person arrives. This is Allah's speech, exalted is His remembrance, about the Fire, praising it with this blame, saying that it is a wretched destination. Every person who hears this from the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will recoil from this Fire and will not do the deeds of its people.

* Student: Shaykh, is al-maṣīr a place or the outcome itself?

* Shaykh: It is a place of becoming. This "maṣīr," as they call it in colloquial speech, or as we use it here, can be a noun of place, a noun of time, or a verbal noun. All of them begin with the letter mīm. So depending on the context, it is a mīmī verbal noun, or an adverb of place or an adverb of time.

* Student: (...) in the Qur'an (...)?

* Shaykh: How so?

* Student: An example of a noun of place, and then there was a becoming.

* Shaykh: No. In this position, in this kind of construction, there was no becoming. It occurs whenever one wills.

* Student: So it occurs often in the Qur'an: ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾ and ﴿and to Him is the destination﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. This is about the same thing; there was no becoming.

* Student: "Wretched is the destination, their destination," or what?

* Shaykh: No. "Wretched is the destination, it," because He said: ﴿the punishment of the Fire﴾. "And wretched is the destination, it," meaning the Fire. It refers back to the Fire.

**Ibn 'Uthaymin's Commentary (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah al-Baqarah, Verses 124–126 (Part 1 of 5)**

Then He said: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 124]. Who is the one doing the testing? God. Is Abraham the one directly after the verb? Ibn Malik says:

*"The original order is that the subject comes first, and the original order for the object is that it comes separated [after]."*

But he also said:

*"It may come contrary to the original order..."*

*"...."*

This is one of the cases that come contrary to the original order. So ﴿Ibrahim﴾ is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and ﴿Rabbuhu﴾ is a delayed subject (fa'il mu'akhkhar). Is this arrangement, in this form and this manner, obligatory or permissible?

*Students:* Obligatory.

*Shaykh:* Obligatory. Because if you put the subject first, the pronoun would refer back to something later, both in wording and in rank, and this is prohibited. For this reason he said:

*"...... And rare is [a structure] like: 'Zan nuruhu al-shajar' [the tree adorned its light]."*

This is rare and is not to be used as a model. As for the parallel to the verse, he said:

*"And common is [a structure] like: 'Khaafa Rabbahu 'Umar' [Umar feared his Lord]."*

*"......"*

﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested by his Lord﴾: there is a qira'ah (recitation variant) in ﴿Ibrahim﴾: ﴿Ibraham﴾, ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested by his Lord﴾ with Ibraham. It is an Arabic dialect and is recited in Arabic (Ibraham).

*Student:* Ibraham?

*Shaykh:* With a mim. The point is that the ya' is replaced by an alif: instead of Ibrahim, it is Ibraham.

*Student:* Is it a Sab'i (canonical seven-reading) variant?

*Shaykh:* Yes, it is Sab'i.

*Student:* Did the letters change?

*Shaykh:* No, they did not change.

*Student:* So the ya'?

*Shaykh:* Yes, but in the 'Uthmani script the alif is written in place of the ya'.

And His saying: ﴿Ibrahim Rabbuhu﴾, ﴿Rabbuhu﴾ is the subject (fa'il). Here He attributes lordship (rububiyyah) to Abraham, and this is a special lordship, because we have already said that rububiyyah corresponds to 'ubudiyyah (servitude). Just as servitude is of two kinds, special and general, lordship is also of two kinds, special and general. Both appear together in the words of the magicians: ﴿They said: We believe in the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Al-A'raf 121], this is general; ﴿The Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ [Al-A'raf 122], this is special. So here it is special lordship. There is no doubt that God's lordship over the messengers, especially those of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm), who are they?

*Student:* Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad ﷺ.

*Shaykh:* Yes, it is the most special of the lordships.

And His saying: ﴿with words﴾: this is what he was tested with. Ibtila' (testing) is examination and trial. What are these words? Are they cosmic (kawniyyah), legislative (shar'iyyah), or of the cosmic and legislative kinds? God has left them unspecified, so they are cosmic and legislative words, or they combine both. So what are these words? The commentators differ about them, and the most correct opinion is that they are everything God commanded Abraham with, whether cosmic or legislative: everything He commanded him, or decreed for him, is a "word." For example, he was tested by the command to sacrifice his son. Did he sacrifice him or not?

*Students:* He sacrificed him.

*Shaykh:* He sacrificed him?

*Student:* He did not sacrifice him.

*Shaykh:* Yes, that is right. God said to him: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [As-Saffat 105]. So he effectively sacrificed him, even though he did not actually do it. He complied with God's command. Was this a test or not? It was a test, one of the greatest tests. Likewise God tested him by having a fire kindled for him and throwing him into it. This is among the cosmic words. Was he patient or not? He was patient, patient and seeking reward. Every matter God decreed for him that requires patience and perseverance, or that He commanded him, is likewise included in His saying ﴿with words﴾. This is the correct view. Some said the words with which he was tested were: ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾. But this is not really a test; rather, it is the result of the test. When he was tested, ﴿and he fulfilled them﴾, he completed these cosmic or legislative words. Who can complete all the cosmic and legislative words of God, may He be exalted? Not everyone can endure that, except those whom God grants success. For this reason God described Abraham as one who fulfilled, saying: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [An-Najm 37]. That is, he completed what God commanded him and what he was tested with.

When he fulfilled them, God, may He be glorified and exalted, honored His servant and granted him this imamah (leadership). Is it not true that through patience and certainty one attains leadership in religion? Through patience and certainty one attains leadership in religion: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾ [As-Sajdah 24]. This is one point. ﴿And they were certain of Our signs﴾ is the second. Abraham was one of these people. ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾.

﴿Ja'iluka﴾ means "one who makes you" (musayyiruka). It takes two objects because it derives from ja'ala (to make), which here means sayyara (to make into). The first object is the kaf (the "you" pronoun), which is in the genitive position through being attached to the noun, and the second object is ﴿Imaman﴾.

An imam is one who is followed, whether in good or in evil. But there is no doubt that what is meant here is leadership in good.

If someone asks: show us evidence that leadership in evil is also called imamah?

We say: God's saying, ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [Al-Qasas 41]. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever establishes a bad practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." [Reported by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah.] This is because he became an imam, one who is followed.

﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾. Is ﴿lil-nas﴾ (for the people) general or not? It is general to those who come after him, not to those who came before him. But to those who came after him he became an imam, up to the Seal of the Messengers, Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [An-Nahl 123]. So he is an imam.

﴿He said: And of my offspring﴾: meaning, "And make from my offspring imams." Here, is the min (of) in ﴿min dhurriyyati﴾ partitive (lil-tab'id) or explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins)? It may be explanatory of the kind, and on that basis ﴿dhurriyyati﴾ can apply to all his descendants, meaning: "make all my offspring imams." It may also be partitive, in which case the meaning is: "make some of my offspring imams." Which is closer?

*Students:* It is explanatory of the kind.

*Shaykh:* That is, he asked God that all his offspring be imams? This could be either. But whichever it is, whether it is explanatory of the kind or partitive, God granted him this in a restricted form, saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

*Student:* (...)

*Shaykh:* No, not even some of them. Not every part of them is an imam. In any case, whether we say it is explanatory of the kind or partitive, God answered him with a restricted answer, saying: ﴿does not reach﴾, meaning does not attain, ﴿my covenant﴾, meaning My pledge to you concerning this, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, the wrongdoers among your offspring, whether the wrongdoing is general or specific, greater or lesser. The wrongdoer cannot be an imam. For this reason He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. ﴿My covenant﴾ is the subject (fa'il), and ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ is the object? That is, "I will make from your offspring an imam, but the wrongdoer is not included in that." For this reason God did not appoint a wrongdoer by way of the covenant. But it may be objected that some of Abraham's descendants were wrongdoers, though not with a major wrong, is that not so? Who, for example?

*Student:* Al-Hajjaj.

*Shaykh:* Yes, but they were not imams. For example, among the caliphs of the Umayyad dynasty there were wrongdoers, and among the caliphs of the 'Abbasid dynasty there were wrongdoers. But we have not heard that any of them committed a wrong so great that it took him out of Islam. This question will be addressed, God willing, later.

His saying: ﴿And [mention] when Abraham was tested﴾. What is the meaning of ibtila' (testing)?

*Student:* Examination.

*Shaykh:* Examination. And what put ﴿Ibrahim﴾ in the accusative?

*Student:* It is an object.

*Shaykh:* An object of what?

*Student:* An object of ﴿ibtala﴾ (tested).

*Shaykh:* Where is the subject?

*Student:* ﴿Rabbuhu﴾.

*Shaykh:* ﴿Rabbuhu﴾.

Are there two readings of ﴿Ibrahim﴾?

*Students:* There is ﴿Ibrahim﴾, and there is ﴿Ibraham﴾.

*Shaykh:* Ibraham. In every place in Al-Baqarah, wherever it occurs in Al-Baqarah, there are two readings: Ibraham and Ibrahim. Outside Al-Baqarah there is disagreement.

What are the words with which God tested Abraham? What are these words? Are they cosmic or legislative?

*Students:* Cosmic and legislative.

*Shaykh:* Cosmic and legislative?

*Student:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* Prove it. Yes, good. The cosmic, such as?

*Student:* The cosmic, such as: (...) into the fire.

*Shaykh:* His being thrown into the fire, good. And the legislative?

*Student:* The legislative, such as when he left his wife and son, and when he killed his son.

*Shaykh:* He was commanded to sacrifice his son.

*Student:* He was commanded to sacrifice his son.

*Shaykh:* And likewise, the breaking of the idols and other things. So is the correct view that these words are specific or not specific?

*Students:* Not specific.

*Shaykh:* Not specific. But they are great words containing trial and testing.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿Imaman﴾?

*Student:* That is, the imam is the model who is followed.

*Shaykh:* In good or in evil?

*Student:* In good, and it may be in evil.

*Shaykh:* And it may be in evil. Such as?

*Student:* ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [Al-Qasas 41].

*Shaykh:* Yes, ﴿leaders calling to the Fire﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Imaman﴾. What governs it in the accusative?

*Student:* ﴿Imaman﴾?

*Shaykh:* Yes.

*Student:* It is in the accusative because of ("maker," ja'il).

*Shaykh:* ("maker") as what?

*Student:* An object.

*Shaykh:* The first, or the second, or the third?

*Student:* The second.

*Shaykh:* The second?

*Student:* The first is the kaf, and ﴿Imaman﴾ is the second.

*Shaykh:* And ﴿Imaman﴾ is the second.

*Student:* And imaman is the second.

*Shaykh:* The second, because ﴿ja'il﴾ comes from ja'ala, and it governs the accusative.

*Student:* Two objects.

*Shaykh:* Two objects.

His saying: ﴿And of my offspring﴾. What is the meaning of His saying ﴿And of my offspring﴾?

*Student:* That is, "and make from my offspring."

*Shaykh:* Imams.

*Shaykh:* Did God answer this supplication?

*Student:* He answered it with a restricted answer.

*Shaykh:* Restricted? In what He said?

*Student:* In His saying: ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

*Shaykh:* In His saying: ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

What is meant here by "covenant"?

*Student:* Leadership.

*Shaykh:* "My covenant does not reach"? Who knows? That is, what I pledge to you does not reach the wrongdoers. It is as if He is saying: I pledge this to you and give you a covenant concerning it, except that it does not reach the wrongdoers.

He said: ﴿And [mention] when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary﴾ [Al-Baqarah 125]. ﴿Idh﴾ here is temporal, and it is connected to an omitted element. Its estimated form is?

*Student:* "Remember."

*Shaykh:* "Remember." That is, "Remember, O Muhammad, to the people this matter which We have made [a matter] for the people."

﴿Ja'alna﴾ means "We made" (sayyarna).

﴿Al-Bayt﴾ (the House): the definite article here is for mental familiarity (al-'ahd al-dhihni), and what is meant is the Ka'bah, because it is the House of God, may He be exalted. It is mentioned, and then with the article for magnification and exaltation. That is, "the familiar House that is not unknown and not forgotten. We made it a mathabah."

Mathabah means a place of return. That is, people return to it and go back to it from all the regions of the world, whether they return to it with their bodies or with their hearts. Those who come to it as pilgrims or as those performing 'umrah return to it with their bodies, and those who turn toward it every day in their prayers return to it with their hearts. They never cease to remember this House every day and night. Indeed, facing it is one of the conditions for the validity of their prayers.

His saying: ﴿and a sanctuary (amnan)﴾: that is, "and We made it a sanctuary for the people."

"It was not made lawful for anyone after me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of the day." [Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (1349) and Muslim (1353/445) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. The wording of al-Bukhari is: "It was not made lawful for anyone before me or after me; it was made lawful for me for an hour of the day."] This was only out of necessity, because this House could not be cleansed of this polytheism except by this permission. God made it lawful for him for an hour of the day out of necessity, and that was the hour of the Conquest. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "Its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday." [Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (104) and Muslim (1354/446) from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi.] So it is sacred even for the Messenger ﷺ. This is the meaning of its being a sanctuary. The Prophet ﷺ answered a question that may be posed: "If anyone takes license to fight the Messenger of God ﷺ, say: God permitted His Messenger, but He did not permit you."

The judgment belongs to God, the Most High, the Great. He permitted His Messenger ﷺ in that hour, but He did not permit anyone else. This is the meaning of its being a sanctuary: that people are safe. It was a sanctuary because it is a place of worship, rites, and sacred sites (mash'ar). Had it been a place of fear, people would not have performed their worship in the most perfect manner. For this reason carrying weapons in the Sanctuary (haram) is forbidden, so that every person may be safe. By this we know the enormity of the crime of those who spread fear among Muslims during the seasons of Hajj, and that they are, God forbid, among the greatest of people in crime. For God made this city safe at all times. So how much more so at the time of performing the rites of Hajj, for which it was made safe in the first place. This, God forbid, is a great violation of God's sanctities. For this reason this city must be safe.

When 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, was stabbed while he was on his mount at Mina, one of the Kharijites stabbed him with a dagger he had, until his leg stuck to the stirrup, may God be pleased with him. Al-Hajjaj came to visit him.

*Student:* Ibn 'Umar was?

*Shaykh:* Yes, Ibn 'Umar. Al-Hajjaj came to visit him and said to him: "You are the one who did this to us? I used to forbid anyone from carrying a weapon in the Sanctuary." [Reported by al-Bukhari (966).] This is evidence that this House is absolutely safe. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 67]. This safety is general, even for the disbelievers. Yet God says: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there; but if they fight you, then kill them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 191]. Is that in defense or in aggression?

*Students:* In defense.

*Shaykh:* In defense. There is a difference between killing in defense and killing in aggression.

*Student:* Is the making (ja'l) here cosmic or legislative?

*Shaykh:* No, this is legislative.

*Student:* Shaykh, if (...) in the religion of the disbelievers, is it not to be established?

*Shaykh:* That is, it is impossible for the disbelievers ever to take control of it, because the Messenger ﷺ said: "There is no hijrah after the Conquest." [Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (2783) and Muslim (1353/445) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.] And it is not possible to migrate from it except if it is a land of disbelief.

﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah 125]. "Take" means "make."

*Student:* (...) Shaykh, is there not an objection to this?

*Shaykh:* No, there is no objection to this, because this is directed at him and does not remain in it.

His saying: ﴿And take﴾ means "make" or "appoint." There are two readings: the first is ﴿ittakhidhu﴾ in the imperative form, and the second is ﴿ittakhadhu﴾ in the past tense. That is: "and the people took," as a mathabah for the people, and "they took from the station of Abraham." Or: "and you took from the station of Abraham a place of prayer."

His saying: ﴿take from the station of Abraham﴾. The maqam is the place of standing. It has two usages: a general usage, which is the place where he stood in worship, and a specific usage, which is his station for building the Ka'bah. According to the first, general usage, all the stations and sacred sites of Hajj are from the station of Abraham. Do you understand?

According to the first, general usage, the meaning of maqam as his station for worship includes all the sacred sites of Hajj: 'Arafat, Muzdalifah, the Jamarat, al-Safa and al-Marwah, and so on. According to the second, specific usage, the term refers to the particular stone on which Abraham, peace be upon him, stood to raise the foundations of the House. This is the famous station, known to everyone.

His saying: ﴿musalla﴾ (a place of prayer). Does it mean a place of linguistic prayer, which is supplication? Or a place of legal (sharʿi) prayer?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 124–126 (part 2 of 5):

* The students (al-Talaba): the legal (shar'iyyah) sense.
* The Shaykh: According to the first (meaning), it is a place of supplication, and according to the second, it is a place of the well-known legal prayer. When the Messenger ﷺ came to it after circumambulating, he recited: ﴿And take the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾. This shows that the Messenger (ﷺ) explained it in its specific sense, the particular station. However, many exegetes explained it in both senses, and they said: this is a mention of one of the individual instances of the general term, because it is included in it. The specific is included in the general, and not the reverse.

As for His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Take from the Station of Abraham﴾, the specific station is the stone on which the building of the Ka'bah was raised. The historians differ over whether it was adjoining the Ka'bah or was separated from it in its present place.

Most historians hold that it was attached to the Ka'bah, and that the one who moved it back to this place was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Based on that, the caliph has the right to consider moving it from its place if he sees benefit in that. But if we say that this was its place during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), then it apparently is not permissible to change it, because the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it, and when the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it, we have no right to move it back from it. One of the students of knowledge wrote a treatise on this subject, and some scholars endorsed it, and among those who endorsed it was Shaykh 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Baz. He held that it is permissible to move it from its place for the sake of benefit and expansion, based on what is well known among the historians, that it was adjoining the Ka'bah and then was moved back. There is no doubt that if it were moved back from its place, that would avert a harm, namely the harm of those people who gather around it in the seasons (of Hajj and 'Umrah), and there is in it a kind of harm or a kind of mischief, namely that it distances it from those circumambulating at times other than the seasons. Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: At times other than the seasons, the tawaf area is almost empty, it is not crowded. We could place it, for example, at the colonnade (al-riwaq), meaning it would be far from the people... (...). In other words, the benefits here conflict. Is it better that it remain in its place, or better that it be moved back from its place? If the benefits are equal, then it is better that what is as it was remain as it was, and also out of caution against confusion and disagreement over this matter. As for the matter of congestion, the crowding of worshippers upon those circumambulating, this can be removed by awareness-raising if it is effective, or by prohibition and enforcement if it is not. In truth, in my opinion, it has decreased somewhat in recent years; this year I see that it is little, because people have become aware.
* A student: O Shaykh, if it were delayed it would become a plaything (...). Anyone would move it; every caliph would have his own opinion.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, perhaps. Each one would have his own opinion.
* A student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. The two rak'ahs of the Station: if during Hajj the mosque is crowded, is it permissible to pray them outside the mosque?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is permissible, because these two rak'ahs are legislated, and they have a place that is better than others, which is behind the Station. If the place is not available, the legislated prayer remains.
* The student: Even if outside the mosque?
* The Shaykh: Even if outside. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, prayed them at Dhu Tuwa, in a distant place.
* A student: The verse: ﴿And take from the Station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾, does it mean that it is a sunnah for one to... after the tawaf?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is a sunnah. And His saying: ﴿And take from the Station of Abraham﴾ has two readings: ﴿Ibrahaam﴾ and ﴿Ibraheem﴾. And His saying: ﴿a place of prayer (musalla)﴾, is it the second object of (ittakhadhu, "take"), or the first object?
* The students: The first object.
* The Shaykh: The first object? And the second?
* The students: The prepositional phrase.
* The Shaykh: The implied prepositional phrase. And His saying ﴿musalla﴾: is it in the accusative with a visible fatha or with an implied fatha?
* A student: The latter; it is in the accusative with an implied fatha.
* The Shaykh: With an implied fatha. That is why it is written with a yā'. It is a defective noun ending in alif: musalla, so it is in the accusative with an implied fatha on its last letter, preventing its appearance is the difficulty of pronunciation (al-ta'adhdhur). And the tanwin in it?
* A student: It is a lightening.
* The Shaykh: It is a compensation (ʿiwad), a compensation for the omitted alif. ﴿And We charged Abraham﴾ or ﴿Ibraahaam﴾ ﴿and Isma'il, that purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate﴾ [al-Baqarah 125]. ﴿'Ahid-na (We charged)﴾: al-'ahd (covenant, charge) is a command concerning something important. It is not mere instruction; it is only a covenant when the matter is important. For example: Abu Bakr entrusted (ʿahida) the caliphate to 'Umar, that is, he bequeathed it to him. And it is well known that the most important of the affairs of the Muslims is the caliphate.

As for His saying: ﴿And Isma'il﴾, he is the son of Ibrahim, the father of the Arabs, and he is the one who was to be sacrificed according to the correct opinion. That is, he is the one whom Allah commanded Ibrahim to slaughter, and he is the one who said to his father: ﴿O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast﴾ [as-Saffat 102].

As for the view of the one who says it was Isaac, it is far-fetched. Some scholars have said that this is transmitted from the Children of Israel, because the Children of Israel wish that the one to be sacrificed was Isaac, since he was their father, rather than Isma'il, who was their uncle, the father of the Arabs. But whoever reflects on the verses of as-Saffat, or the verses of as-Saffat, will know with a knowledge that nearly approaches certainty that the one to be sacrificed was Isma'il. Because Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in the midst of these verses, He said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [as-Saffat 112], after He had mentioned the story in full, He said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous. And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are the doer of good and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾ [as-Saffat 112–113]. How then could he speak first of his resolve to slaughter him and the dialogue that took place between them, and then say: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾?

Good news is only given after (the event). So if Isaac were the one to be sacrificed, it would not be correct to say: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾.

And His saying: ﴿that purify﴾. ﴿We charged Abraham﴾ ﴿that purify﴾: is this (anna) a lightened form of the heavy (anna)?
* A student: Verbal (maṣdariyyah).
* The Shaykh: It is not verbal.
* A student: Explanatory (mufassirah).
* The Shaykh: The explanatory (anna) is followed by a command, as in ﴿We revealed to him: make the ark﴾ [al-Mu'minun 27]. Apparently it is verbal.
* A student: ﴿Purify﴾, is it not a command?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it has a reason. Correct, purify, yes. Indeed, then it can be explanatory, because 'ahidna contains the meaning of saying without its letters. So it is explanatory, meaning that the covenant is His saying: ﴿Purify My House﴾. Purify: is a command verb. And His saying ﴿My House﴾: what is intended by it is the Ka'bah, and Allah, exalted is He, attributed it to Himself as an attribution of honour, and not an attribution of a part or of a quality. So it is an attribution of honour. By this we know that what is attributed to Allah is divided into two parts, or three?
* A student: Three.
* The Shaykh: The first: that it is a self-subsisting entity (ʿayn qā'imah bi-nafsihā).
The second: that it is an attribute of that entity or in that entity.
The third: that it is an attribute of Allah.
If it is a self-subsisting entity, then its attribution is an attribution of honour, like: the she-camel of Allah, the House of Allah. If it is an attribute connected to an entity, like the spirit, if we say it is an attribute, or that it is a body connected to another created body, then it is also created, and its attribution is an attribution of honour, and it is created, like: ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit, so fall down prostrating to him﴾ [al-Hijr 29]. And if it is an attribute, then it is an attribute of Allah, meaning that if the attributed thing is a meaning that does not subsist apart from Allah, then it is an attribute of Allah, like: ﴿until he hears the words of Allah﴾ [at-Tawbah 6], and like: the might of Allah, the power of Allah, and what is similar to that. Here it is from the first category: ﴿My House﴾. The House is a self-subsisting entity, so its attribution to Him is by way of an attribution of honour.

And His saying: ﴿My House for those who circle it﴾, meaning those who circumambulate it. The second: ﴿those who stay in devotion﴾, those who remain in it for worship. The third: ﴿those who bow and prostrate﴾, those who pray in it. And prayer is expressed by bowing and prostration because they are two of its pillars. It was mentioned earlier in passing that when a part of an act of worship is used to refer to it, this is evidence that this part is a pillar of it, without which it is not valid. Here He began with those who circumambulate, because they are specific to that House, then He followed with those who stay in devotion, because it is a wider circle than those who circumambulate, but it is restricted to the mosques. Then He said: ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾, and this is not restricted to mosques. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (335), and Muslim (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.] So Allah, glorified and exalted be He, began with the most specific and then the more specific: what is most specific to the Sacred House is tawaf, then i'tikaf. As for prayer, it is not restricted to a place. For this reason some scholars say: a king vowed to Allah a vow that he would worship Allah with an act of worship that no one would share with him. He consulted some scholars, and they said: what shall we do? If he fasts, it is possible that there will be people fasting. If he prays, it is possible that there will be people praying. If he gives charity, it is possible that there will be people giving charity. So they went to a scholar, who said to them: clear the tawaf area for him, meaning let him circumambulate alone. Then can anyone share it with him or not?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No one can share it with him, because in reality no one circumambulates except around this House.
* A student: Does this contradict the text: "Do not prevent anyone who circumambulates this House" [Abu Dawud (1894), and al-Tirmidhi (868), from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im]?
* The Shaykh: No. The point is that this resolves the matter. As for whether it is permissible or not, they forbid it for other than this reason. But there is no way to fulfil this vow except by this.
* A student: It is not possible, O Shaykh (...).
* The Shaykh: Where?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is possible without preventing the people. It is possible if he comes in the last part of the night, meaning at times other than the seasons you will sometimes find it empty, or he comes, for example, after sunrise, always, except in the days of 'Umrah when there are crowds.
* The student: Or in Ramadan at midday sometimes.
* The Shaykh: The point is, in any case, it is possible for him to find it. And His saying: ﴿for those who circle it﴾, purify for those who circumambulate: the lam here is for causation, meaning for their sake. And His saying: ﴿those who bow and prostrate﴾: ruka' is known to be the plural of (rāki'), and sujud is the plural of (sājid), and it may be a verbal noun, (sajada, yasjudu, sujudan). But sujud and quʿud are a verbal noun and at the same time a plural. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Pray sitting, all of you" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (378), and Muslim (411/77), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik]. ﴿That purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate﴾.
* A student: O Shaykh, "those who bow and prostrate" is different from (...).
* The Shaykh: And what then?
* The student: Different from "those who bow and prostrate" (...).
* The Shaykh: And bowing and prostration are singled out because they are the most excellent postures. Bowing is more excellent than standing, and prostration is more excellent than it. For this reason we say: standing is superior to bowing and prostration by mention of it. If standing is mentioned, what is it?
* The students: The Qur'an.
* The Shaykh: The speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, is better than everything. And the mention (of Allah) is glorification (tasbih), and the mention of bowing and prostration is glorification, and glorification is less sacred than the Qur'an. Although glorification is undoubtedly an exaltation of Allah, it is not like the Qur'an. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, the Wise, gave each pillar of the prayer what is specific to it: this one is singled out by the excellence of its mention, and this one is singled out by the excellence of its posture.
* A student: O Shaykh, do we not say that bowing and prostration are the most specific attributes of prayer? That is, one is not bowing or prostrating to Allah while (...)?
* The Shaykh: What do you mean?
* The student: That is, the most specific attributes of prayer?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not correct, because the prostration of recitation is a prostration without prayer.
* The student: According to this opinion.
* The Shaykh: It is not valid.
* A student: O Shaykh, ﴿Take from the Station﴾: how is (min) here, is it partitive or explanatory? Also, if we took the Station of Abraham as a place of prayer, could we pray on top of the stone?
* The Shaykh: His saying: "take from," this (min) is for clarification of the kind (bayaniyyah), meaning take from this station. It is also permissible that it is taken to contain the meaning of (fi, "in"), meaning take in this station a place for prayer.
* A student: But since the Station is the stone, it cannot be that they take it as a place of prayer?
* The Shaykh: Yes, take from it. Its meaning is not upon it. Take from it a place. The Messenger explained it as meaning that one prays beside it.
* The student: Does this not favour that the rites of Hajj in general (...) the Station of Abraham in general is (...) Hajj?
* The Shaykh: In reality, each has its preponderance. As for the Prophet's explanation (ﷺ), there is no doubt that it is clear that he meant this station. And if we intend the general sense, the usage of prayer in the language would refute it.

He says: ﴿That purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate (125). And when Abraham said: My Lord, make this a secure city﴾.
* A student: His saying "purify." I said: Abraham is the one who built the House, O Shaykh. Why did He say "purify"?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but Isma'il was helping him: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il﴾ [al-Baqarah 127].
* The student: No, no, I mean, how does one purify something that is already pure, when he is the one who built the House?
* The Shaykh: Yes, even if he built it, what then? It may be that this House will be exposed to impurity, to filth, so they purify it.
* A student: His saying "purify" is a command given during the building?
* The Shaykh: It is permissible that it was a command during the building, because something may befall it during the building or after it. It is not impossible.
* A student: Does purification include physical and spiritual purity?
* The Shaykh: By Allah, there is room for consideration. As for spiritual purity, unless it is by way of analogy: if physical purification is obligatory, then spiritual purification is more fitting.
* The student: (...) this?
* The Shaykh: That is not the apparent meaning, because He said: ﴿for those who circle it﴾, He did not say "purify it" and leave it general. And the purification is ﴿for those who circle it, and those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate﴾, and only physical purity suits it.
* The student: (...) the circumambulators and those who stay in devotion (...) idols were found, so they could not...?
* The Shaykh: No, they could. There were three hundred and sixty idols, and the people were circumambulating around them.

﴿And when Abraham said﴾, meaning: and remember when Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾. And we say concerning it what we said before, the reading ﴿Ibraahaam﴾. ﴿And when Abraham said: My Lord, make this a secure city﴾. ﴿Make (ij'al)﴾ means appoint (sayyir). ﴿This﴾, the one indicated, is Makkah. And His saying: ﴿a city (baladan)﴾. The word "balad" is the name for every inhabited place, whether it is a large city or a small city; all of it is called a balad. Allah, exalted is He, has called Makkah a balad, as in His saying: ﴿And this secure land﴾ [at-Tin 3], and He called it a qaryah (town), as in His saying: ﴿And how many a town, stronger than your town which expelled you, have We destroyed﴾ [Muhammad 13].

And His saying: ﴿secure (aminan)﴾. Some exegetes said: meaning secure for whoever is in it, because the city itself is not described as secure or fearful. The city is land and buildings, so it is not described as secure or fearful. What is secure is its people. But what should be taken in its apparent sense is that the city itself should be secure. When the city is secure, those in it are secure, and this is more eloquent, because if someone came and destroyed the building, the building would not be secure; it would become exposed to someone who would destroy it. So its being secure is more comprehensive than explaining it as "secure for its people," because it includes the city and those in it. For this reason He said: ﴿and provide its people (ahlahu)﴾, He distinguished and did not say "provide it," because it cannot be provided for. ﴿Provide its people with fruits, those among them who believe﴾. ﴿Provide (urzuq)﴾: is it a command verb or a verb of supplication?
* The students: Supplication.
* The Shaykh: Supplication. ﴿Its people (ahlahu)﴾ is the first object, and ﴿of the fruits (min al-thamarat)﴾ is the second object.
