It may even reach the point that he finds the scent of Paradise while he is still in this world, as Anas ibn al-Nadr is thought to have said: "Indeed I find the scent of Paradise beyond Uhud." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (4048) and Muslim (1903/148), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.] He said this while in battle, and Allah made him perceive the scent of Paradise while he was in this world. This is one of Allah's honours to a person, so that when he breathes in this fragrance (...) he would not exchange it for the whole world. Rather, this matter that he perceived with his senses requires that he had already perceived it with his heart, through what Allah has informed of in His Book and upon the tongue of His Messenger, may blessings and peace be upon him.

And among them: the affirmation of the punishment of the Fire.

* A student: (...) from the words of Ibn Taymiyyah.

* Another student: But is the permissibility of istithna' (exception) derived from it, Shaykh (...)?

* The Shaykh: What is the istithna', and what type is it?

* The student: His exception, glory be to Him: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾.

* The Shaykh: The istithna', what is the istithna'? Where is the istithna'?

* The student: The istithna' is in ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾.

* The Shaykh: That is generalization. The exception is in Abraham's words: ﴿whoever believes﴾, ﴿and provide its people﴾, ﴿whoever believes﴾. For this is a substitution (badal) which implies excluding some individuals, the individuals of his people. This is where there is an exception. I mean the exception in meaning, not in technical terminology. If you mean the kind of exception like: "O Allah, forgive me if You will," then there is no evidence for it in the verse.

* A student: No, I mean: one makes an exception, "O Allah, forgive (...)?"

* The Shaykh: Yes, perhaps it is permissible to derive from the verse the specification of what is not an exception; that is, specifying a person's supplication with a particular attribute, such as: "O Allah, if he is a wrongdoer, then repay him for his wrong," or "avenge me against him," or something similar.

In the noble verse: is there an affirmation of the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, based on His saying: ﴿He said﴾? Or not? And that it is with letters and sound. What is the evidence that it is with letters?

* The students: ﴿He said﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿He said﴾ is a report of His saying.

* A student: It is composed of letters.

* The Shaykh: Because ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾, for example, is composed of letters; these are letters, so it is letters. But what is the evidence that it is with sound?

* A student: His answer to Abraham.

* Students: In the answer (...).

* The Shaykh: The dialogue with Abraham. Had Abraham not heard, this dialogue would not have been valid.

And among them: the affirmation of Allah's hearing, because He hears Abraham while he speaks to Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

And also among them: the affirmation of the Last Day.

This is coordinated with ﴿whoever believes﴾ and ﴿and provide its people﴾ and ﴿whoever believes﴾. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾, meaning: "then I will provide for him." We have said previously that Abraham, peace be upon him, only said ﴿whoever believes﴾ in obedience to the discipline of Allah, mighty and majestic, when He said at the beginning: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾; he then said ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾. Disbelief (kufr) linguistically means concealment, and from it comes the name of the palm's sheath (kafur al-nakhlah), because it covers the spathe. But in the Law it is departure from Islam; that is, whoever is not a Muslim is a disbeliever. We have also previously mentioned that disbelief revolves around two matters: the first is arrogance (istikbar), and the second is denial (juhud). Then: are disbelief and polytheism the same, or is there a general and specific relation between them, or are they mutually exclusive like two separate things?

Shaykh Ibn 'Uthaymin said: We say that there is a general and specific relationship between them. Every polytheist (mushrik) is a disbeliever (kafir), but not every disbeliever is a polytheist. One who denies and rejects this is not a polytheist, but he is a disbeliever. One who calls upon another god besides Allah is a polytheist, and at the same time he is a disbeliever. So the relationship between them is one of general and specific. Unless the speaker means by shirk the following of one's desires, for following desires is shirk in the broader sense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you seen the one who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah 23]. Allah, glorified and exalted, made the following of desires a form of taking something as a god. On this basis we say: if by shirk is meant its broader sense, then every disbeliever is a polytheist in this sense. But in terms of the technical (iṣṭilāḥī) meaning that defines its concept, the relationship between shirk and kufr is what?

* Student: General and specific.

* Shaykh: General and specific. And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿then I will let him enjoy [it] briefly﴾. In another reading it is ﴿fa-umti'uhu﴾, from al-imtā' or from al-tamtī'. Tamtī' or imtā' means that a person is given his provision (balgha) from this world, that he is given just enough provision from the world to enjoy for as long as Allah wills. But He said: ﴿briefly﴾. What is this period that Allah described as brief?

It is the worldly life. The brevity here applies both to the time and to the enjoyment itself: the time, and the enjoyment itself. The time is short, however long a person's life may extend, it is short. However long a person's life extends, it is little. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿As if they had not remained but an hour of a day, a proclamation﴾ [al-Ahqaf 35].

Likewise, the enjoyment itself is little. Even what a person attains in this world of pleasure and enjoyment is in reality little, because it is mixed with disturbance, both within the enjoyment itself and in what surrounds it, before it or after it, as the poet said:

One day is against us and one day is for us,
and one day we are afflicted and one day we are gladdened.

Another poet said:

There is no sweetness to life while its pleasures are troubled
by the remembrance of death and old age.

So the brevity in this world is on two counts. The first count is the time: however long the time is for a person, it is little. The second is the enjoyment itself: it is little, because it is not perfect. It is deficient, preceded by disturbance and followed by disturbance, and in itself it is also not complete.

﴿Then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Aḍṭarruhu﴾ means: I will force him to the punishment of the Fire. Allah made this a compulsion because every person flees from the punishment of the Fire, but, Allah forbid, he has no escape from it, because it is he who did the deeds that necessitate it. As long as he did them, that is, did the deeds that necessitate the Fire, he and his own self are responsible, and for this reason He said: ﴿I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire.﴾ And if you want to see that this matter is compelled, consider what Allah the Exalted mentioned about the state of the wrongdoers at the time of death: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are extending their hands, [saying], "Release your souls"﴾ [al-An'am 93].

It is as if they are straining against their own souls and resisting them, and it is said to them: "Release your souls." This is in contrast to the believer, we ask Allah to make me and you among them. At the time of death his soul rejoices in departing and leaving the body becomes easy for him, because it is given the glad tidings of "rest, bounty, and a Lord who is not angry" (cf. Qur'an 56:89–93). So it knows from now that it wishes to move from this world to this bliss. This is in contrast to those to whom it is said, Allah forbid: ﴿Release your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth, and for being arrogant toward His signs﴾ [al-An'am 93].

As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿to the punishment of the Fire﴾. Punishment (al-'adhāb) means the penalty through which a person is pained. And ﴿the Fire﴾ (al-nār) is a well-known name. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rāb) may be difficult for you, because we have not covered this section before. ﴿Wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿Biʾsa﴾ is a past-tense verb that is rigid (jāmid) and performative (inshā'ī), meant for blame. So it is a rigid verb for blame. Is it performative or declarative (khabarī)?

* Students: Performative.

* Shaykh: Performative. And ﴿al-maṣīr﴾ is the subject (fā'il) of ﴿biʾsa﴾. They say that (biʾsa), (niʿma) and similar words necessarily require a subject and a specified object (makhṣūṣ). The subject is "al-maṣīr," and the specified object is omitted, its estimated form being: "and wretched is the destination, it (hiya)." For if you do not estimate this, the sentence does not refer back to what preceded it. So we say: the specified object is omitted, its estimated form being "hiya," and "wretched is the destination, it." Al-maṣīr means the place of becoming (makān al-ṣayrūrah), that is, the final return to which a person arrives. This is Allah's speech, exalted is His remembrance, about the Fire, praising it with this blame, saying that it is a wretched destination. Every person who hears this from the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will recoil from this Fire and will not do the deeds of its people.

* Student: Shaykh, is al-maṣīr a place or the outcome itself?

* Shaykh: It is a place of becoming. This "maṣīr," as they call it in colloquial speech, or as we use it here, can be a noun of place, a noun of time, or a verbal noun. All of them begin with the letter mīm. So depending on the context, it is a mīmī verbal noun, or an adverb of place or an adverb of time.

* Student: (...) in the Qur'an (...)?

* Shaykh: How so?

* Student: An example of a noun of place, and then there was a becoming.

* Shaykh: No. In this position, in this kind of construction, there was no becoming. It occurs whenever one wills.

* Student: So it occurs often in the Qur'an: ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾ and ﴿and to Him is the destination﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. This is about the same thing; there was no becoming.

* Student: "Wretched is the destination, their destination," or what?

* Shaykh: No. "Wretched is the destination, it," because He said: ﴿the punishment of the Fire﴾. "And wretched is the destination, it," meaning the Fire. It refers back to the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 127–128 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il [with him]﴾ [al-Baqarah 127]. When Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned that He made this House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, He explained how this House came into being, saying: ﴿And when [Ibrahim] raised﴾. ﴿And when (idh)﴾ here is an adverbial clause whose governing verb is omitted. What is the estimated (taqdir) wording?

* Student: "Remember."

* The Shaykh: "Remember when he raised." Regarding his saying ﴿idh yarfa'u﴾ ("when he raised"): you say ﴿yarfa'u﴾ is a present-tense verb, and the present tense refers to the present or the future, whereas the raising of the House is in the past. However, the present tense is used for the past here as "narration of the state" (hikayat al-hal), as if Ibrahim were raising it right now. That is, they are reminded of this situation as though it were being witnessed before them now. So here the present tense is used for narration of the state.

As for his saying ﴿Ibrahim﴾, it has two readings. What are they? ﴿Ibrahim﴾ and ﴿Ibrahim﴾ (with variant vowelling). ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is the object of ﴿yarfa'u﴾: he raises the foundations from the House. ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is the plural of ﴿qa'ida﴾, and the qa'ida of a thing is its foundation. From this comes the term "qawa'id" in jurisprudence and grammar: grammar is called qawa'id because it is the foundation upon which the pronunciation of eloquent Arabic speech is built, and the qawa'id of jurisprudence are the general principles to which individual issues are referred. So what are the qawa'id? The foundations. His saying ﴿min al-bayt﴾ ("from the House") is an explanation of the foundations, and it functions as a circumstantial element (hal): i.e., these foundations being from the House. By "the House" is meant the Ka'bah, so the (al-) here is the (al-) of mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni). His saying ﴿wa-Isma'il﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Ibrahim﴾. Thus he shared with his father in raising the foundations. If someone asks: why was Isma'il not mentioned alongside Ibrahim, i.e., although they were both partners, why did it not say "when Ibrahim and Isma'il raised the foundations of the House," because each of them was a raiser? What is the answer?

Answer: Because the principal is Ibrahim, and Isma'il was an assistant. The one who laid the foundations was Ibrahim, peace be upon him; as for Isma'il, he was a helper and aide.

Then He said: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾ [al-Baqarah 127]. ﴿Rabb﴾ is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been omitted; the original is "ya Rabbana" ("O our Lord"). The particle of calling was omitted to begin with the one being called upon, the one addressed, who is Allah. His saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾ and so on: this clause has an omitted governing verb. What is its estimated wording? What is the estimated wording of ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il [with him]: Our Lord, accept from us﴾?

* Student: "(...)."

* The Shaykh: "No."

* Student: "The particle of calling, 'O our Lord'."

* The Shaykh: "No, no, leave the particle of calling omitted."

* Student: "They both say: O our Lord, accept from us."

* The Shaykh: "Yes. They say: 'Our Lord,' they say; and the clause (yaqulani, 'they both say') is in the accusative position."

Because the one calling wants something to happen, and the occurrence of things belongs to the category of decree (taqdir), and decree is more closely connected with lordship (rububiyyah) than with divinity (uluhiyyah). Is the point clear? ﴿Rabbana﴾: you said, "Lord, give me." Does giving relate to lordship or to divinity?

* The students: "To lordship."

* The Shaykh: "To lordship, because it is an act, and everything related to Allah's acts belongs to lordship. So when it is an act, it is appropriate to call upon Allah the Exalted by the attribute that is more closely connected to that act than another attribute. ﴿Rabbana﴾, because lordship is that by which the act is done; Allah, blessed and exalted, does by it whatever He wills."

As for his saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾: did both of them say this with their tongues? That is, does each one say, "Our Lord, accept from us," or does one speak while the other says Amen? It allows both meanings, but the apparent wording indicates that both of them say it, either that Ibrahim says "Our Lord, accept from us" and Isma'il follows him, or that this one says it at one time and that one says it at another. It should not be said that one of them speaks while the other says Amen, like the story of Musa and Harun, for we do not say so, because Musa and Harun: Allah mentioned that the speaker was Musa: ﴿And Musa said: Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿He said: Your supplication has been answered [, so remain upright]﴾ [Yunus 88–89]. Was Harun a supplicant? No. But the scholars said: he was saying Amen while Musa was supplicating, and Musa is the one who supplicates explicitly in the verse. As for this verse, the apparent meaning is that each of them says: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾.

As for his saying ﴿taqabbal minna﴾: what is the meaning of acceptance? Acceptance is taking a thing and being pleased with it, and from it is what the jurists mention in their saying: a sale is concluded by offer (ijab) and acceptance (qabul). Allah's acceptance of a deed is that He receives it with pleasure, so He is pleased with its doer; and when Allah is pleased with its doer, He necessarily grants him the reward He promised him.

His saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾: this is in reality the crux; the crux is acceptance, not the deed. How many a person does many deeds and they are not accepted from him, so they do not benefit him; and how many a person does few deeds and they are accepted from him, so Allah benefits him by them. So the crux is acceptance.

His saying ﴿taqabbal minna innaka anta al-Sami' al-'Alim﴾: this clause is a justification (ta'lil). What kind of justification is it? It is a justification for seeking acceptance, not for acceptance itself: i.e., we ask You to accept, and You, our Lord, are All-Hearing, All-Knowing. His saying ﴿innaka anta al-Sami' al-'Alim﴾: I told you that this clause is a justification for what came before, and it is emphasized by two emphasizers. One of them is what? The clause is emphasized by two emphasizers, one of which is what? ﴿innaka anta al-Sami' al-'Alim﴾: this clause alone is emphasized by two emphasizers. What are they?

* Student: "The first is 'inna', the nun."

* The Shaykh: "Inna."

* Student: "And the second: 'anta'."

* The Shaykh: "'Anta'; because 'anta' is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl). We have already covered this in rhetoric, and in our discussions we always say: the pronoun of separation gives emphasis. In ﴿innaka anta﴾, we say ﴿anta﴾ is a pronoun of separation which has no grammatical position (la mahal lahu min al-i'rab)."

﴿al-Sami'﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. Al-Sami' is one of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it has two meanings: one is "the one who responds" (al-mustajib), and the other is "the one who hears sounds" (al-sami' lil-aswat). So it means perceiving what is heard and responding to supplication. As for the first, which is perceiving what is heard, its examples are many, such as His saying: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80]; and His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband﴾ [al-Mujadila 1]; and His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said: Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Al 'Imran 181]. As for the second, which means responding, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39], the meaning of "sami'" is "responding." Likewise is the saying of the worshipper: "Allah hears the one who praises Him," meaning: He responds to the one who praises Him. Here we ask: is hearing, in both its meanings, one of Allah's essential attributes (sifat dhatiyyah) or one of His attributes of action (sifat fi'liyyah)?

* Student: "Both essential and of action."

* The Shaykh: "How? All of them are essential and of action?"

* Student: "The hearing which is the hearing of sounds is essential, and the response is of action."

* The Shaykh: "What do you say? Correct, because response is linked to His will: if He wills, He responds, and if He wills, He does not respond. As for perceiving what is heard, it is inseparable from His attributes; He has never ceased and never ceases to be All-Hearing, since the opposite of hearing is deafness, and deafness is a defect, and Allah is exalted above every defect."

What fits supplication when you say: "My Lord, respond to my supplication, indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing"? Which of the two meanings?

* Student: "The response."

* The Shaykh: "All of them; because if He did not hear, for example, if you said that He does not hear your supplication, He would not respond; and if He heard the voice but delayed the response, your request would not have been fulfilled. So it includes both matters. When you say, 'Indeed You are the All-Hearing,' you mean: O Lord, indeed You hear me and respond to me."

As for his saying ﴿al-'Alim﴾: what is al-'Alim? Al-'Alim means "the one possessing knowledge." The knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, encompasses every existent, every non-existent, every possible, every impossible, and every necessary thing; that is, it relates to everything. Allah's knowledge relates to everything: He knows what has been, what will be, and what would have been had it not been, how it would have been, glory be to Him and exalted. What is the proof that it relates to impossibilities?

* Student: "His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ahqaf 33]."

* The Shaykh: "No."

* Student: "Relating to His knowledge?"

* The Shaykh: "Yes, His knowledge."

* Student: "To impossibilities?"

* The Shaykh: "Yes."

* Student: "﴿Indeed, He is, of all things, Knowing﴾ [al-Shura 12]."

* The Shaykh: "No, that is for generality. Can you bring a clear text about impossible matters?"

* Student: "﴿And that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq 12]."

* Another student: "﴿If Allah had wished to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾ [al-Zumar 4]."

* The Shaykh: "Yes, and this?"

* Student: "Impossible."

* The Shaykh: "﴿Had there been within them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya' 22]. He knows that the heavens and the earth would be ruined if there were gods in them other than Allah, and this is an impossible matter. Its relation to the necessary: an example?"

* Student: "His saying: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it﴾ [Saba' 2]."

* The Shaykh: "Is this necessary? The very existence of the earth is among the permissible matters; if Allah had willed, the earth would not have existed."

* Student: "﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of the unseen﴾ [Fatir 38]."

* The Shaykh: "We do not want generality; we want something specific. This was covered before in tawhid. The necessary?"

* Student: "﴿He knows the secret and that which is more hidden﴾ [Ta-Ha 7]."

* The Shaykh: "No."

* Student: "﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him knowledge of the Hour﴾, necessary and required."

* The Shaykh: "What sort? Is the Hour necessary to exist? But is its necessity rational or revealed?"

* Student: "Both, because it is absolute."

* The Shaykh: "We may say so. ﴿Allah testifies that there is no deity except Him, and [so do] the angels﴾ [Al 'Imran 18]. His singling out for divinity is a necessary matter, and He has testified to it; He testified to it for Himself, and testimony necessarily includes knowledge without doubt. As for its relation to possibilities, it is abundant: everything Allah has told us He knows of the affairs of creation relates to possible matters."

Know that whoever denies Allah's knowledge is a disbeliever; everyone who denies Allah's knowledge is a disbeliever, whether he denies it regarding His actions or regarding His creation. So if someone says that Allah, exalted, does not know what the servant does, he is a disbeliever, just as one who says that Allah does not know what He does Himself. For this reason, Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah declared the extreme Qadariyyah disbelievers, those who said that Allah does not know the actions of servants. This was also covered earlier in tawhid: we said that the extreme Qadariyyah deny Allah's knowledge of the actions of servants, and say that Allah does not know what is in the hand of a person. Whoever denies Allah's knowledge of the servants' actions is without doubt a disbeliever, because Allah says: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf 16], and He, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿Did they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private conversations?﴾ [al-Tawbah 78].

So the one who says that Allah does not know the servant's actions: is he a believer in these verses, or a disbeliever in them? He is a disbeliever in them. For this reason the scholars, al-Shafi'i and others, said about the Qadariyyah, not those who deny knowledge, but the Qadariyyah who deny that Allah created the actions of servants and decreed them: "Debate them with knowledge; if they acknowledge it, they are refuted, and if they deny it, they have disbelieved."

It is now clear that the knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted, encompasses everything: in the necessary and in the impossible, and in the possible, in what He does Himself and in what the servants do. Your belief in this obliges you to be mindful of Him, to fear Him, to comply with His command, and to avoid His prohibition; for as soon as you know that He knows you, you will fear Him, feel shame before Him when you disobey, and desire what is with Him when you obey.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, said, relating what Ibrahim and Isma'il said: ﴿Our Lord, and make us both Muslims [in submission] to You﴾. ﴿Muslimayn﴾ (both Muslims): why did He say "muslimayn"? Because they are two. ﴿Rabbana wa-aj'alna muslimayn laka﴾: his saying ﴿wa-aj'alna﴾ comes with a waw because it is conjoined to his saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾; that is: "Our Lord, and [accept from us, and] make us, along with Your acceptance, Muslims to You."

His saying ﴿aj'alna muslimayn laka﴾ means: make us Muslims. There is a difficulty here: there is no doubt that Ibrahim and Isma'il were Muslims, and from their Islam was the raising of the foundations of the House; so how do they ask Allah to make them Muslims when they were already Muslims? The answer: what is meant is steadfastness (al-thabat), or the realization of that; because a person, setting aside Ibrahim and Isma'il, may not have Islam realized within himself, since the Muslim is one who has submitted his heart to Allah and his limbs. Submission of the limbs is easy, and everyone can achieve it, even the hypocrites; but the difficult thing is submission of the heart. The Messenger, peace be upon him, swore that no one submits until his heart submits: [Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3672) and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (4/165), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.] So what is meant by Islam here is increase in it and steadfastness upon it: ﴿muslimayn laka﴾.

Know that Islam in its narrower sense means only what Muhammad ﷺ brought, and in its broader sense it includes everything the messengers brought. Everything the messengers brought is Islam; but in the narrower sense, which applies after the mission of the Messenger, peace be upon him, it means only what Muhammad ﷺ brought. Otherwise, as you have seen, Ibrahim and Isma'il say: ﴿make us Muslims to You﴾, and the Queen of Sheba said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Naml 44], and Ya'qub said to his sons: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah 132], and the disciples said: ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran 52], and so on. So Islam in the general sense includes everything the messengers brought; therefore, if someone asks: are the Jews and Christians Muslims? We say: in the general sense they are Muslims; but in the narrower sense, which is the Islam brought by the Messenger, peace be upon him, no, they are not Muslims as long as they remain upon Judaism and Christianity. When they enter Islam, they become Muslims.

* Student: "So it is said to them 'Muslims' (...) at the present time?"

* The Shaykh: "No, no; now they are not called 'Muslims'; they are Muslims in the general sense only, and they are not among those present in this age. Everyone who lived after the mission of the Messenger: the Muslim is one who follows what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought."

﴿And from our descendants a Muslim nation [submitting] to You﴾. Notice the qualification: i.e., "and make from our descendants," make from them; he did not say "make our descendants a Muslim nation," but said ﴿from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. ﴿Dhurriyyatina﴾: who is meant? Those who branched from them: the descendants of a person are those who branch from him.

﴿Ummatan muslimatan laka﴾: who is this nation? It is the nation of Muhammad ﷺ; because no one can be truly described as a descendant of Ibrahim and Isma'il except the nation of Muhammad ﷺ, since the Jews and Christians were Muslims while their laws were in force, but they are not descendants of Ibrahim and Isma'il: they are descendants of Ibrahim only, and not of Isma'il. So on this basis, the Muslim nation meant is the nation of Muhammad ﷺ (...).

﴿Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.

From this verse is derived: the virtue of building the Ka'bah, since Allah commanded His Prophet to mention this situation: ﴿And [remember] when [Ibrahim] raised﴾.

And from it: the virtue of Ibrahim and Isma'il, in that they undertook raising these foundations.

Among its benefits: the builder should lay foundations before building, based on His words: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾. If one builds without a foundation, the structure collapses.

Another benefit: the原 primary role in this construction belonged to Abraham, because He mentioned him first: ﴿Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾, then joined Ishmael with him by saying ﴿and Ishmael﴾. This shows that Abraham, peace be upon him, was the principal one.

Another: the importance of acceptance (qabul), and that what counts is not the deed itself. Many a worker gets nothing from his work but fatigue. This is taken from His words, after their work: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾.

Another: affirmation of two of Allah's names, the All-Hearing (al-Samee') and the All-Knowing (al-Aleem). We have already explained that each of Allah's names indicates an attribute of His, and sometimes two or more attributes, according to the logical connection between one meaning and another. Also, each of Allah's names indicates an effect when that name is transitive (muta'addi).

Another: seeking a means (tawassul) to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, through His names and attributes. From where is this taken? ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. This is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of His words ﴿accept from us﴾. That is, "Because You are All-Hearing and All-Knowing, we ask You to accept from us."

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims [in submission] to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You. And show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

From this is derived: the intense need of a person for his Lord, since he repeated the phrase ﴿Our Lord﴾, and that he is in need of Allah's particular lordship (rububiyyah), which calls for special care.

Another: a person needs Allah's firmness, otherwise he would perish. This is from His words ﴿and make us Muslims [in submission]﴾. Though both of them were certainly Muslims, being prophets, does this submission persist except by Allah's grace? No. Allah, Exalted, said to His Messenger, peace be upon him: ﴿And if We had not strengthened you, you would have almost inclined to them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [the punishment] of life and double [the punishment] of death﴾ [al-Isra' 74–75].

Another: the importance of sincerity (ikhlas). From His words ﴿Muslims [in submission] to You﴾, this indicates sincerity, the sincere submission of Islam to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He said in another verse: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good will have his reward with his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 112].

Another: a person should include his descendants in his supplication, because righteous offspring are among the fruits of a righteous person. From His words ﴿and from our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You﴾. Abraham also said in another verse: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim 35]. The righteousness of one's descendants is of great importance to a person.

Another: that the original state of a human being is ignorance. From His words ﴿and show us our rites﴾, meaning: "Inform us of them."

Another: that worship is based on revealed prescription (tawqifiyyah). That is, a person does not worship according to his own temperament, but until Allah shows him the act of worship. From where is this taken? ﴿and show us our rites﴾. Therefore, worship is tawqifiyyah.

Another: the prohibition of worshipping Allah by means He has not prescribed, because they asked Allah to show them their rites. Had worship not depended on this, they would have worshipped without this request.

Another: that every person needs Allah's repentance-accepting mercy, from His words ﴿and accept our repentance﴾, since no person is free from shortcoming.

Another: affirmation that the Accepting of repentance (al-Tawwab) and the Merciful (al-Raheem) are two of Allah's names, Glorified and Exalted, and their explanations have already been given.

Another: the legitimacy of seeking a means to Allah through His names and attributes, because His words ﴿Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ are a causal explanation of the earlier request. Thus it is a means by which the supplicant reaches the attainment of his request.

Another: that seeking a means should be through a name that suits the one being asked or the need. That is, seeking a means through a name that suits the need. From where do we take this?

* A student: ﴿And accept our repentance; indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾.
* A student: If a person now asks Allah to provide him with a specific sustenance, but he mentions with it a name of Allah that does not suit it?
* The Shaykh: No. We have now understood that seeking a means should be through a name that suits the need, based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf 180].

So among its benefits: one should not conclude supplication with a name that does not suit the need. If someone says, "O Allah, forgive me, for You are severe in punishment," does it suit? It does not suit. This is not appropriate. You ask for forgiveness and seek a means to Allah through the severity of His punishment! For this reason it is said that a Bedouin heard a reciter reading: ﴿And as for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned as a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty and Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 38], but he said: "And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" (...). Cutting off and forgiving? This is not possible. So he said to him: "Repeat the verse?" He repeated it in this way: ﴿cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned as a deterrent from Allah﴾, "and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" (...). He repeated it a third time in the correct form: ﴿as a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty and Wise.﴾ He said: "Now [it is correct], for Allah, Mighty and Wise, cut off [the hand]. Had He forgiven and been merciful, He would not have cut it off." For this reason Allah, Exalted, said concerning those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger: ﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth [to cause] corruption is that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be exiled from the land. That is for them a disgrace in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment, except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 33–34]. What is the meaning of this? And what is the meaning of concluding it with "Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾?

* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of its conclusion, brothers? It means that the punishment is lifted from them. ﴿except for those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. He did not say, "So leave them." He said: ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: the punishment is lifted from them. Is this understood?

* A student: What is the difference between your saying, "It is recommended that seeking a means be through a name that suits the need," and your saying, "It is not appropriate to conclude supplication with something that does not suit the need" (...)?

* The Shaykh: No. "It is recommended" (yanbaghi) refers to what is required. The other, "it is not appropriate" (la yanbaghi), refers to what is not praiseworthy.

* The student: All of them are "it is not appropriate."

* The Shaykh: One is "it is recommended," and one is "it is not appropriate." What is recommended is that it be a name that suits the need, and what is not appropriate is...?

* The student: A name that does not suit.

* The Shaykh: That is, if someone said: "If I conclude with a name that does not suit the need, is there sin in it?" From where do we rule that there is sin in it, except from the twelfth benefit?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 127–128 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il [with him]﴾ [al-Baqarah 127]. When Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned that He made this House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, He explained how this House came into being, saying: ﴿And when [Ibrahim] raised﴾. ﴿And when (idh)﴾ here is an adverbial clause whose governing verb is omitted. What is the estimated (taqdir) wording?

* Student: "Remember."

* The Shaykh: "Remember when he raised." Regarding his saying ﴿idh yarfa'u﴾ ("when he raised"): you say ﴿yarfa'u﴾ is a present-tense verb, and the present tense refers to the present or the future, whereas the raising of the House is in the past. However, the present tense is used for the past here as "narration of the state" (hikayat al-hal), as if Ibrahim were raising it right now. That is, they are reminded of this situation as though it were being witnessed before them now. So here the present tense is used for narration of the state.

As for his saying ﴿Ibrahim﴾, it has two readings. What are they? ﴿Ibrahim﴾ and ﴿Ibrahim﴾ (with variant vowelling). ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is the object of ﴿yarfa'u﴾: he raises the foundations from the House. ﴿al-qawa'id﴾ is the plural of ﴿qa'ida﴾, and the qa'ida of a thing is its foundation. From this comes the term "qawa'id" in jurisprudence and grammar: grammar is called qawa'id because it is the foundation upon which the pronunciation of eloquent Arabic speech is built, and the qawa'id of jurisprudence are the general principles to which individual issues are referred. So what are the qawa'id? The foundations. His saying ﴿min al-bayt﴾ ("from the House") is an explanation of the foundations, and it functions as a circumstantial element (hal): i.e., these foundations being from the House. By "the House" is meant the Ka'bah, so the (al-) here is the (al-) of mental reference (al-'ahd al-dhihni). His saying ﴿wa-Isma'il﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Ibrahim﴾. Thus he shared with his father in raising the foundations. If someone asks: why was Isma'il not mentioned alongside Ibrahim, i.e., although they were both partners, why did it not say "when Ibrahim and Isma'il raised the foundations of the House," because each of them was a raiser? What is the answer?

Answer: Because the principal is Ibrahim, and Isma'il was an assistant. The one who laid the foundations was Ibrahim, peace be upon him; as for Isma'il, he was a helper and aide.

Then He said: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾ [al-Baqarah 127]. ﴿Rabb﴾ is a vocative from which the particle of calling has been omitted; the original is "ya Rabbana" ("O our Lord"). The particle of calling was omitted to begin with the one being called upon, the one addressed, who is Allah. His saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾ and so on: this clause has an omitted governing verb. What is its estimated wording? What is the estimated wording of ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il [with him]: Our Lord, accept from us﴾?

* Student: "(...)."

* The Shaykh: "No."

* Student: "The particle of calling, 'O our Lord'."

* The Shaykh: "No, no, leave the particle of calling omitted."

* Student: "They both say: O our Lord, accept from us."

* The Shaykh: "Yes. They say: 'Our Lord,' they say; and the clause (yaqulani, 'they both say') is in the accusative position."

Because the one calling wants something to happen, and the occurrence of things belongs to the category of decree (taqdir), and decree is more closely connected with lordship (rububiyyah) than with divinity (uluhiyyah). Is the point clear? ﴿Rabbana﴾: you said, "Lord, give me." Does giving relate to lordship or to divinity?

* The students: "To lordship."

* The Shaykh: "To lordship, because it is an act, and everything related to Allah's acts belongs to lordship. So when it is an act, it is appropriate to call upon Allah the Exalted by the attribute that is more closely connected to that act than another attribute. ﴿Rabbana﴾, because lordship is that by which the act is done; Allah, blessed and exalted, does by it whatever He wills."

As for his saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾: did both of them say this with their tongues? That is, does each one say, "Our Lord, accept from us," or does one speak while the other says Amen? It allows both meanings, but the apparent wording indicates that both of them say it, either that Ibrahim says "Our Lord, accept from us" and Isma'il follows him, or that this one says it at one time and that one says it at another. It should not be said that one of them speaks while the other says Amen, like the story of Musa and Harun, for we do not say so, because Musa and Harun: Allah mentioned that the speaker was Musa: ﴿And Musa said: Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world, our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.﴾ ﴿He said: Your supplication has been answered [, so remain upright]﴾ [Yunus 88–89]. Was Harun a supplicant? No. But the scholars said: he was saying Amen while Musa was supplicating, and Musa is the one who supplicates explicitly in the verse. As for this verse, the apparent meaning is that each of them says: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾.

As for his saying ﴿taqabbal minna﴾: what is the meaning of acceptance? Acceptance is taking a thing and being pleased with it, and from it is what the jurists mention in their saying: a sale is concluded by offer (ijab) and acceptance (qabul). Allah's acceptance of a deed is that He receives it with pleasure, so He is pleased with its doer; and when Allah is pleased with its doer, He necessarily grants him the reward He promised him.

His saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾: this is in reality the crux; the crux is acceptance, not the deed. How many a person does many deeds and they are not accepted from him, so they do not benefit him; and how many a person does few deeds and they are accepted from him, so Allah benefits him by them. So the crux is acceptance.

His saying ﴿taqabbal minna innaka anta al-Sami' al-'Alim﴾: this clause is a justification (ta'lil). What kind of justification is it? It is a justification for seeking acceptance, not for acceptance itself: i.e., we ask You to accept, and You, our Lord, are All-Hearing, All-Knowing. His saying ﴿innaka anta al-Sami' al-'Alim﴾: I told you that this clause is a justification for what came before, and it is emphasized by two emphasizers. One of them is what? The clause is emphasized by two emphasizers, one of which is what? ﴿innaka anta al-Sami' al-'Alim﴾: this clause alone is emphasized by two emphasizers. What are they?

* Student: "The first is 'inna', the nun."

* The Shaykh: "Inna."

* Student: "And the second: 'anta'."

* The Shaykh: "'Anta'; because 'anta' is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl). We have already covered this in rhetoric, and in our discussions we always say: the pronoun of separation gives emphasis. In ﴿innaka anta﴾, we say ﴿anta﴾ is a pronoun of separation which has no grammatical position (la mahal lahu min al-i'rab)."

﴿al-Sami'﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. Al-Sami' is one of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it has two meanings: one is "the one who responds" (al-mustajib), and the other is "the one who hears sounds" (al-sami' lil-aswat). So it means perceiving what is heard and responding to supplication. As for the first, which is perceiving what is heard, its examples are many, such as His saying: ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80]; and His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband﴾ [al-Mujadila 1]; and His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said: Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Al 'Imran 181]. As for the second, which means responding, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39], the meaning of "sami'" is "responding." Likewise is the saying of the worshipper: "Allah hears the one who praises Him," meaning: He responds to the one who praises Him. Here we ask: is hearing, in both its meanings, one of Allah's essential attributes (sifat dhatiyyah) or one of His attributes of action (sifat fi'liyyah)?

* Student: "Both essential and of action."

* The Shaykh: "How? All of them are essential and of action?"

* Student: "The hearing which is the hearing of sounds is essential, and the response is of action."

* The Shaykh: "What do you say? Correct, because response is linked to His will: if He wills, He responds, and if He wills, He does not respond. As for perceiving what is heard, it is inseparable from His attributes; He has never ceased and never ceases to be All-Hearing, since the opposite of hearing is deafness, and deafness is a defect, and Allah is exalted above every defect."

What fits supplication when you say: "My Lord, respond to my supplication, indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing"? Which of the two meanings?

* Student: "The response."

* The Shaykh: "All of them; because if He did not hear, for example, if you said that He does not hear your supplication, He would not respond; and if He heard the voice but delayed the response, your request would not have been fulfilled. So it includes both matters. When you say, 'Indeed You are the All-Hearing,' you mean: O Lord, indeed You hear me and respond to me."

As for his saying ﴿al-'Alim﴾: what is al-'Alim? Al-'Alim means "the one possessing knowledge." The knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, encompasses every existent, every non-existent, every possible, every impossible, and every necessary thing; that is, it relates to everything. Allah's knowledge relates to everything: He knows what has been, what will be, and what would have been had it not been, how it would have been, glory be to Him and exalted. What is the proof that it relates to impossibilities?

* Student: "His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ahqaf 33]."

* The Shaykh: "No."

* Student: "Relating to His knowledge?"

* The Shaykh: "Yes, His knowledge."

* Student: "To impossibilities?"

* The Shaykh: "Yes."

* Student: "﴿Indeed, He is, of all things, Knowing﴾ [al-Shura 12]."

* The Shaykh: "No, that is for generality. Can you bring a clear text about impossible matters?"

* Student: "﴿And that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq 12]."

* Another student: "﴿If Allah had wished to take a son, He would have chosen from what He creates whatever He wills﴾ [al-Zumar 4]."

* The Shaykh: "Yes, and this?"

* Student: "Impossible."

* The Shaykh: "﴿Had there been within them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya' 22]. He knows that the heavens and the earth would be ruined if there were gods in them other than Allah, and this is an impossible matter. Its relation to the necessary: an example?"

* Student: "His saying: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it﴾ [Saba' 2]."

* The Shaykh: "Is this necessary? The very existence of the earth is among the permissible matters; if Allah had willed, the earth would not have existed."

* Student: "﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of the unseen﴾ [Fatir 38]."

* The Shaykh: "We do not want generality; we want something specific. This was covered before in tawhid. The necessary?"

* Student: "﴿He knows the secret and that which is more hidden﴾ [Ta-Ha 7]."

* The Shaykh: "No."

* Student: "﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him knowledge of the Hour﴾, necessary and required."

* The Shaykh: "What sort? Is the Hour necessary to exist? But is its necessity rational or revealed?"

* Student: "Both, because it is absolute."

* The Shaykh: "We may say so. ﴿Allah testifies that there is no deity except Him, and [so do] the angels﴾ [Al 'Imran 18]. His singling out for divinity is a necessary matter, and He has testified to it; He testified to it for Himself, and testimony necessarily includes knowledge without doubt. As for its relation to possibilities, it is abundant: everything Allah has told us He knows of the affairs of creation relates to possible matters."

Know that whoever denies Allah's knowledge is a disbeliever; everyone who denies Allah's knowledge is a disbeliever, whether he denies it regarding His actions or regarding His creation. So if someone says that Allah, exalted, does not know what the servant does, he is a disbeliever, just as one who says that Allah does not know what He does Himself. For this reason, Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah declared the extreme Qadariyyah disbelievers, those who said that Allah does not know the actions of servants. This was also covered earlier in tawhid: we said that the extreme Qadariyyah deny Allah's knowledge of the actions of servants, and say that Allah does not know what is in the hand of a person. Whoever denies Allah's knowledge of the servants' actions is without doubt a disbeliever, because Allah says: ﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf 16], and He, glory be to Him and exalted, says: ﴿Did they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private conversations?﴾ [al-Tawbah 78].

So the one who says that Allah does not know the servant's actions: is he a believer in these verses, or a disbeliever in them? He is a disbeliever in them. For this reason the scholars, al-Shafi'i and others, said about the Qadariyyah, not those who deny knowledge, but the Qadariyyah who deny that Allah created the actions of servants and decreed them: "Debate them with knowledge; if they acknowledge it, they are refuted, and if they deny it, they have disbelieved."

It is now clear that the knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted, encompasses everything: in the necessary and in the impossible, and in the possible, in what He does Himself and in what the servants do. Your belief in this obliges you to be mindful of Him, to fear Him, to comply with His command, and to avoid His prohibition; for as soon as you know that He knows you, you will fear Him, feel shame before Him when you disobey, and desire what is with Him when you obey.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, said, relating what Ibrahim and Isma'il said: ﴿Our Lord, and make us both Muslims [in submission] to You﴾. ﴿Muslimayn﴾ (both Muslims): why did He say "muslimayn"? Because they are two. ﴿Rabbana wa-aj'alna muslimayn laka﴾: his saying ﴿wa-aj'alna﴾ comes with a waw because it is conjoined to his saying ﴿Rabbana taqabbal minna﴾; that is: "Our Lord, and [accept from us, and] make us, along with Your acceptance, Muslims to You."

His saying ﴿aj'alna muslimayn laka﴾ means: make us Muslims. There is a difficulty here: there is no doubt that Ibrahim and Isma'il were Muslims, and from their Islam was the raising of the foundations of the House; so how do they ask Allah to make them Muslims when they were already Muslims? The answer: what is meant is steadfastness (al-thabat), or the realization of that; because a person, setting aside Ibrahim and Isma'il, may not have Islam realized within himself, since the Muslim is one who has submitted his heart to Allah and his limbs. Submission of the limbs is easy, and everyone can achieve it, even the hypocrites; but the difficult thing is submission of the heart. The Messenger, peace be upon him, swore that no one submits until his heart submits: [Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3672) and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (4/165), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.] So what is meant by Islam here is increase in it and steadfastness upon it: ﴿muslimayn laka﴾.

Know that Islam in its narrower sense means only what Muhammad ﷺ brought, and in its broader sense it includes everything the messengers brought. Everything the messengers brought is Islam; but in the narrower sense, which applies after the mission of the Messenger, peace be upon him, it means only what Muhammad ﷺ brought. Otherwise, as you have seen, Ibrahim and Isma'il say: ﴿make us Muslims to You﴾, and the Queen of Sheba said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Naml 44], and Ya'qub said to his sons: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah 132], and the disciples said: ﴿And bear witness that we are Muslims﴾ [Al 'Imran 52], and so on. So Islam in the general sense includes everything the messengers brought; therefore, if someone asks: are the Jews and Christians Muslims? We say: in the general sense they are Muslims; but in the narrower sense, which is the Islam brought by the Messenger, peace be upon him, no, they are not Muslims as long as they remain upon Judaism and Christianity. When they enter Islam, they become Muslims.

* Student: "So it is said to them 'Muslims' (...) at the present time?"

* The Shaykh: "No, no; now they are not called 'Muslims'; they are Muslims in the general sense only, and they are not among those present in this age. Everyone who lived after the mission of the Messenger: the Muslim is one who follows what the Messenger, peace be upon him, brought."

﴿And from our descendants a Muslim nation [submitting] to You﴾. Notice the qualification: i.e., "and make from our descendants," make from them; he did not say "make our descendants a Muslim nation," but said ﴿from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. ﴿Dhurriyyatina﴾: who is meant? Those who branched from them: the descendants of a person are those who branch from him.

﴿Ummatan muslimatan laka﴾: who is this nation? It is the nation of Muhammad ﷺ; because no one can be truly described as a descendant of Ibrahim and Isma'il except the nation of Muhammad ﷺ, since the Jews and Christians were Muslims while their laws were in force, but they are not descendants of Ibrahim and Isma'il: they are descendants of Ibrahim only, and not of Isma'il. So on this basis, the Muslim nation meant is the nation of Muhammad ﷺ (...).

﴿Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.

From this verse is derived: the virtue of building the Ka'bah, since Allah commanded His Prophet to mention this situation: ﴿And [remember] when [Ibrahim] raised﴾.

And from it: the virtue of Ibrahim and Isma'il, in that they undertook raising these foundations.

Among its benefits: the builder should lay foundations before building, based on His words: ﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾. If one builds without a foundation, the structure collapses.

Another benefit: the原 primary role in this construction belonged to Abraham, because He mentioned him first: ﴿Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾, then joined Ishmael with him by saying ﴿and Ishmael﴾. This shows that Abraham, peace be upon him, was the principal one.

Another: the importance of acceptance (qabul), and that what counts is not the deed itself. Many a worker gets nothing from his work but fatigue. This is taken from His words, after their work: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾.

Another: affirmation of two of Allah's names, the All-Hearing (al-Samee') and the All-Knowing (al-Aleem). We have already explained that each of Allah's names indicates an attribute of His, and sometimes two or more attributes, according to the logical connection between one meaning and another. Also, each of Allah's names indicates an effect when that name is transitive (muta'addi).

Another: seeking a means (tawassul) to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, through His names and attributes. From where is this taken? ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. This is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of His words ﴿accept from us﴾. That is, "Because You are All-Hearing and All-Knowing, we ask You to accept from us."

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, and make us Muslims [in submission] to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You. And show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

From this is derived: the intense need of a person for his Lord, since he repeated the phrase ﴿Our Lord﴾, and that he is in need of Allah's particular lordship (rububiyyah), which calls for special care.

Another: a person needs Allah's firmness, otherwise he would perish. This is from His words ﴿and make us Muslims [in submission]﴾. Though both of them were certainly Muslims, being prophets, does this submission persist except by Allah's grace? No. Allah, Exalted, said to His Messenger, peace be upon him: ﴿And if We had not strengthened you, you would have almost inclined to them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [the punishment] of life and double [the punishment] of death﴾ [al-Isra' 74–75].

Another: the importance of sincerity (ikhlas). From His words ﴿Muslims [in submission] to You﴾, this indicates sincerity, the sincere submission of Islam to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He said in another verse: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good will have his reward with his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 112].

Another: a person should include his descendants in his supplication, because righteous offspring are among the fruits of a righteous person. From His words ﴿and from our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You﴾. Abraham also said in another verse: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim 35]. The righteousness of one's descendants is of great importance to a person.

Another: that the original state of a human being is ignorance. From His words ﴿and show us our rites﴾, meaning: "Inform us of them."

Another: that worship is based on revealed prescription (tawqifiyyah). That is, a person does not worship according to his own temperament, but until Allah shows him the act of worship. From where is this taken? ﴿and show us our rites﴾. Therefore, worship is tawqifiyyah.

Another: the prohibition of worshipping Allah by means He has not prescribed, because they asked Allah to show them their rites. Had worship not depended on this, they would have worshipped without this request.

Another: that every person needs Allah's repentance-accepting mercy, from His words ﴿and accept our repentance﴾, since no person is free from shortcoming.

Another: affirmation that the Accepting of repentance (al-Tawwab) and the Merciful (al-Raheem) are two of Allah's names, Glorified and Exalted, and their explanations have already been given.

Another: the legitimacy of seeking a means to Allah through His names and attributes, because His words ﴿Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ are a causal explanation of the earlier request. Thus it is a means by which the supplicant reaches the attainment of his request.

Another: that seeking a means should be through a name that suits the one being asked or the need. That is, seeking a means through a name that suits the need. From where do we take this?

* A student: ﴿And accept our repentance; indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾.
* A student: If a person now asks Allah to provide him with a specific sustenance, but he mentions with it a name of Allah that does not suit it?
* The Shaykh: No. We have now understood that seeking a means should be through a name that suits the need, based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf 180].

So among its benefits: one should not conclude supplication with a name that does not suit the need. If someone says, "O Allah, forgive me, for You are severe in punishment," does it suit? It does not suit. This is not appropriate. You ask for forgiveness and seek a means to Allah through the severity of His punishment! For this reason it is said that a Bedouin heard a reciter reading: ﴿And as for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned as a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty and Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 38], but he said: "And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" (...). Cutting off and forgiving? This is not possible. So he said to him: "Repeat the verse?" He repeated it in this way: ﴿cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned as a deterrent from Allah﴾, "and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" (...). He repeated it a third time in the correct form: ﴿as a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty and Wise.﴾ He said: "Now [it is correct], for Allah, Mighty and Wise, cut off [the hand]. Had He forgiven and been merciful, He would not have cut it off." For this reason Allah, Exalted, said concerning those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger: ﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon earth [to cause] corruption is that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be exiled from the land. That is for them a disgrace in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment, except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 33–34]. What is the meaning of this? And what is the meaning of concluding it with "Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾?

* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the meaning of its conclusion, brothers? It means that the punishment is lifted from them. ﴿except for those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. He did not say, "So leave them." He said: ﴿So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: the punishment is lifted from them. Is this understood?

* A student: What is the difference between your saying, "It is recommended that seeking a means be through a name that suits the need," and your saying, "It is not appropriate to conclude supplication with something that does not suit the need" (...)?

* The Shaykh: No. "It is recommended" (yanbaghi) refers to what is required. The other, "it is not appropriate" (la yanbaghi), refers to what is not praiseworthy.

* The student: All of them are "it is not appropriate."

* The Shaykh: One is "it is recommended," and one is "it is not appropriate." What is recommended is that it be a name that suits the need, and what is not appropriate is...?

* The student: A name that does not suit.

* The Shaykh: That is, if someone said: "If I conclude with a name that does not suit the need, is there sin in it?" From where do we rule that there is sin in it, except from the twelfth benefit?

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them﴾. "Purify them" means developing their character. Tazkiyah means development and purification: he develops their characters and purifies them from every vice. This is how the Messenger's law (peace and blessings be upon him) was: developing virtuous character and purifying from every vice. He commands righteousness, commands what is good, commands excellence, commands maintaining ties of kinship, commands truthfulness, and commands every good, everything in which there is good for a person in his religion and his worldly life, for Islam commands it, and this is tazkiyah. And he forbids the opposite of that: he forbids sin, severing ties of kinship, transgression, disobedience to parents, lying, deceit, and other blameworthy traits. This is tazkiyah.

Do you know what the state of people was before Islam? As for their worship, do not ask: shirk and disbelief. As for their social conditions, do not ask about them either: the strong devoured the weak, the rich devoured the poor, they consumed usury multiplied many times over, they raided one another, they taunted one another about lineages, and they called to the causes of jahiliyyah, and so on. Islam came and demolished all of this. Whoever reflects on history before and after the sending of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), before his mission and after it, will know the great difference between the state of people before the mission and their state after it, and the meaning of His saying ﴿and purify them﴾ will become clear to him.

﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾. We say about it here what we said about the i'rab of ﴿Indeed You, You are the Oft-Returning, the Merciful﴾, and we take ﴿You﴾ as a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl). What is its place in i'rab?

* Student: It has no place in i'rab.
* Shaykh: It has no place in i'rab. A separating pronoun has no place in i'rab. And ﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾ is the predicate of (inna), and ﴿al-Ḥakīm﴾ is a second predicate.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: The kāf is the subject of (inna), ﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿al-Ḥakīm﴾ is another predicate. ﴿al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm﴾ has already been discussed, I think? ﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾ means the one possessing ʿizzah, and ʿizzah means strength and dominance. He, glorified and exalted, possesses strength and dominance; nothing overpowers Him and nothing can frustrate Him. And ﴿al-Ḥakīm﴾: it was mentioned that it is derived from what?
* Student: From ḥikmah.
* Shaykh: From ḥukm and ḥikmah, from both together. We said that ḥukm is of two kinds: kawnī (universal/decreed) and sharʿī (legislative). And ḥikmah is also of two kinds: ḥāliyyah (inherent/structural) and ghāʾiyyah (purposive). Ḥukm is of two kinds: sharʿī and kawnī. What is an example of the sharʿī?
* Student: The sharʿī?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 23].
* Shaykh: No, there is no ḥukm in it; qaḍā. Who knows?
* Student: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Māʾidah 38].
* Shaykh: The root ḥ-k-m indicates al-Ḥakīm. As for the legal rulings (aḥkām sharʿiyyah), we say: obligatory, recommended, disliked, prohibited, and permissible.
* Student: His saying in the verse of al-Mumtaḥanah: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 10].
* Shaykh: Correct: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾. Likewise His saying: ﴿Do they seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah? And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Māʾidah 50]. This is the sharʿī ḥukm we mentioned. What is an example of the kawnī ḥukm?
* Student: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 16].
* Shaykh: No, that is the kawnī command. Do you want the kawnī ḥukm? His saying: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me﴾ [Yūsuf 80]. What comes after? ﴿Or Allah judges for me﴾, a kawnī ḥukm, because the sharʿī ḥukm did not prevent him from returning to the land. ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾. Do you understand?

The difference between the kawnī and sharʿī ḥukm: the kawnī ḥukm must, of necessity, take place; the sharʿī ḥukm may or may not be carried out, a person may comply and fulfill the ruling or may not comply. Also, the sharʿī ḥukm is established by the Law, and its affirmation is by what Allah loves, while the kawnī is by what He loves and what He does not love. This is regarding al-Ḥakīm as derived from what?

* Student: From ḥukm.
* Shaykh: And as derived from ḥikmah? We said that ḥikmah is ḥāliyyah and ghāʾiyyah. The ḥāliyyah is the existence of a thing in a particular form: this is ḥikmah. A person being of upright stature, his head in this form, his hands, likewise his legs, and what Allah created in him: this is ḥikmah ḥāliyyah. And the prayer being in this manner, standing, bowing, prostration, sitting and the like, and zakah being at these measures and at these times: this too is ḥikmah of what kind? Ḥāliyyah. And that these matters exist for a praiseworthy end is ḥikmah ghāʾiyyah, for Allah, exalted, did not bring things into existence, whether universally or legislatively, except for a praiseworthy purpose. ﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah 129].

The connection of ʿizzah and ḥikmah here to the sending of the Messenger is very evident, because everything the Messenger brings is wisdom, and in it is ʿizzah: ﴿And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8]. Look: ﴿and to the believers﴾, not "and to the Arabs"? To the believers, whether Arab or non-Arab. Whoever is a believer in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, standing by the command of Allah, has ʿizzah. Whoever is not like that, Allah has not guaranteed him ʿizzah. ʿIzzah belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers. Therefore it is obligatory upon us that the bond between us be the bond of faith alone, for there cannot be ʿizzah and unity upon good except by this bond alone.

* Student: Shaykh, is there not ḥikmah in (...)?
* Shaykh: We said there is ḥikmah in (...), but it is connected with the purposive wisdom, because for such-and-such a reason such-and-such was legislated or such-and-such occurred.

He said: ﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Ibrahim except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. (Man) is an interrogative noun.
* Student: No (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿Wa man yarghab﴾, ﴿man yarghab﴾.
* Student: Relative (khabariyyah).
* Shaykh: Relative! ﴿man yarghab﴾: (man) here, we have the first and second ... ﴿man yarghab﴾ (man) is an interrogative noun.
* Student: No (...).
* Shaykh: It is an interrogative noun used to mean negation, as shown by His saying ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. So (man) here is an interrogative noun and it is the subject, and the clause ﴿yarghab﴾ is its predicate. The clause ﴿yarghab﴾, that is, a present-tense verb as its predicate. We do not say here that (man) is conditional. Yes, if the verse were "and whoever turns away from the creed of Ibrahim, he has made a fool of himself," it would be conditional, but this is more eloquent: ﴿man yarghab﴾ means no one turns away from the creed of Ibrahim.

And His saying ﴿yarghab ʿan millah﴾: it is said raghiba fī kadhā and raghiba ʿan. What is the difference?
* Student: He turned away from it.
* Shaykh: Raghiba fīhi means he sought it. And raghiba ʿanhu?
* Student: It means he abandoned it.
* Shaykh: He abandoned it and shunned it. Here ﴿man yarghab ʿan millat Ibrahim﴾ means: he abandons it, or seeks it?
* The students: He abandons it.
* Shaykh: He abandons it.

And His saying ﴿millat Ibrahim﴾: millah means religion, that is, the religion of Ibrahim. The religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is that he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim submitting to Allah, and was not among the polytheists. Ibrahim is al-Khalīl (peace be upon him), the father of the prophets and the most honourable of them after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah made him an imam: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah﴾ [al-Naḥl 120]. He made his creed the upright ḥanīf creed. If that is so, does anyone turn away from the upright ḥanīf creed? Yes, one who makes a fool of himself does; therefore He said: ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. ﴿Safiha nafsahu﴾ has been said to mean: he was ignorant of himself, that is, he was ignorant of what is due to it and wasted it. And it has been said: safiha means he caused it to fall into safah (foolishness). ﴿Safiha nafsahu﴾: he caused it to fall into foolishness. The opposite of safah is rushd. The first meaning: the opposite of safah is?
* The students: Knowledge.
* Shaykh: Its opposite is knowledge.

We may say: in the expression using a word that admits two meanings there is a great subtlety, namely that ﴿safiha﴾ is apt for both: ignorance, and causing it to fall into foolishness. He is in reality ignorant if he did not intentionally oppose, and a fool if he intentionally opposed. So the person who turns away from the creed of Ibrahim has caused himself to fall into foolishness and did not act with rushd; then if he does so knowingly, he is a fool.

﴿And We had indeed chosen him in this world﴾: the sentence here is emphasised by three emphasisers: the implied oath, the lam, and qad; because the lam here is a preface to the oath, and the sense is: "By Allah, indeed." ﴿Iṣṭafaynāhu﴾ is an iftiʿāl form from ṣafwah, meaning it is derived from this; the root is (ṣafā yaṣfū). So the meaning of iṣṭafaynāhu is: We chose him until he became the elite of creation. Allah chose him in this world above all the prophets except Muhammad (ﷺ). And His saying ﴿iṣṭafaynāhu fī al-dunyā﴾ means: We made him a chosen one among creation, and Allah took him as a khalīl.

﴿And indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾: (inna-hu) here is inna and its noun, and ﴿fī al-ākhirah﴾?
* Student: A predicate.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿min al-ṣāliḥīn﴾ is the predicate, but ﴿fī al-ākhirah﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative): and indeed he, in the state of being in the Hereafter, is among the righteous. In this world Allah chose and selected him; in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous who fulfilled what Allah obligated upon them toward Him and toward His creation. This sentence is emphasised by two emphasisers: inna and the lam alone. Here Allah mentioned choosing in this world and righteousness in the Hereafter. Is there a subtlety in the difference between the two states or not? It seems to me, and Allah knows best, that there is a subtlety there, though we do not know it; is there a subtlety we know or not? Without doubt the two expressions differ, but why? Let us reflect: this world is a house of desires and trial, so none is patient with these desires or with this trial except one above another, is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: When a person sincerely devotes himself to Allah, he becomes an elite among the servants of Allah, is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: The Hereafter is not like that; even the disbelievers come to believe there. But the difference is between one who is among the righteous and one who is not, for when they are exposed to the Fire: ﴿Is this not the truth? They will say: Yes, by our Lord﴾ [al-Anʿām 30], ﴿Did there not come to you messengers with clear proofs? They say: Yes﴾ [Ghāfir 50], ﴿They say: Woe to us, who has raised us from our sleeping place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truly﴾ [Yāsīn 52]. Thus it shows that they believe, but they are not among the righteous.

﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit﴾: this too follows as praise of Ibrahim. Notice how, when He glorified the House of Allah, Allah, glorified and exalted, is Shakūr and Ḥalīm, praised him with this great praise, made him an imam, explained his choosing in this world, and that in the Hereafter he is among the righteous; this state too is part of the praise of him. ﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit﴾ may be connected to His saying ﴿We had indeed chosen him﴾: We had indeed chosen him when his Lord said to him, and it may be connected to an omitted element, meaning: remember when his Lord said to him, so that it is a command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to make mention of this state in which Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was.

﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit﴾. He said: hearing and obeying?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. He did not delay nor refuse: ﴿He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾. A submission that includes tawḥīd of worship, ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾ includes tawḥīd of lordship, names and attributes: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾. So he submitted completely without hesitation. How many were told by their Lord, "Submit," and did not submit! Of the children of Adam, nine hundred and ninety-nine are said to be told "submit" and did not, for they are all among the people of the Fire; nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand of the children of Adam are all in the Fire, and one of them is in Paradise. But this one, his Lord said to him "Submit," and he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." This is a very praiseworthy quality, deserving that he be mentioned for it.

It is general to the root of Islam and to the branches of Islam. Even in the branches he submitted: he saw in a dream that he would slaughter his son, and he carried it out?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: He carried it out. Allah said to him: ﴿And We called to him: O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 104–105]. He carried it out even though this was his only son, he had no other; he was given him in old age, and he reached the age of striving with him, meaning he reached the age of walking with him. This is the time when a person is most attached to his son, for a small child may not capture the soul, and a grown son has become independent and the desire for him has departed; but one at this stage is the utmost of the heart's attachment. He saw in his sleep that he was slaughtering him, and he carried it out, except that he wished to test his son, when he said: ﴿I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think. He said: O my father, do what you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 102]. And Allah mentioned the story.

* Student: His saying ﴿We had indeed chosen him in this world﴾, did He not mention the Messenger or the prophets before him?
* Shaykh: Yes, because the context is about Ibrahim. He mentioned ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent﴾ [Ṣād 47] and ﴿O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 42], but here the context is praise of Ibrahim.

* Student: ﴿He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: Because the Lord must be complete. The Lord whose lordship is general to all the worlds must be complete; otherwise it would not be correct for Him to be Lord of the worlds.
