Allah, Exalted is He, said in the rest of the supplication of Abraham and Ishmael: ﴿رَبَّنَا وَابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِنْهُمْ يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ﴾ ("Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses").

From the benefits of the verse: the necessity of people for the sending of messengers. That is why Abraham and Ishmael supplicated; they asked Allah, Exalted is He, to send a messenger among them.

Also from its benefits: that a messenger being from among them is closer to acceptance of his call, because they know him, as Allah said: ﴿مَا ضَلَّ صَاحِبُكُمْ وَمَا غَوَى﴾ ("Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred") [An-Najm 53:2]. Reflect on His saying: ﴿صَاحِبُكُمْ﴾ ("your companion"), where He attributed him to them: your companion whom you know, and you know the soundness of his mind, and you know his trustworthiness; he did not stray and did not err. From where is this benefit taken? From His saying: ﴿مِنْهُمْ﴾.

* And from the benefits of the verse: the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, had Allah, Exalted is He, place in him the good that he recites the verses, teaches the Book, and teaches wisdom: ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ﴾ ("He recites to them Your verses, and teaches them the Book and wisdom, and purifies them").

And from it: the mission of the Prophet ﷺ includes mention of Allah's signs in creation and in the law, and includes teaching the Book, in recitation and meaning, and it also includes wisdom, which is knowledge of the secrets of the Sharia, and it includes the purification of people, because of His saying: ﴿وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ﴾.

From its benefits, then: this Sharia is complete, because the Prophet's ﷺ mission includes these sublime meanings, which indicates the perfection of his Sharia.

And from it: affirmation of might and wisdom for Allah in His saying: ﴿إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ﴾ ("Indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise").

And from it: affirmation of these two names for Allah, al-ʿAzīz and al-Ḥakīm, and we have already explained the meaning of ʿizzah (might) and ḥikmah (wisdom) in the commentary.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَمَنْ يَرْغَبُ عَنْ مِلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ إِلَّا مَنْ سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾ ("And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous").

From this noble verse it is derived: that rectitude lies in following the religion of Abraham, because of His saying: ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾.

And from its benefits also: that opposing this religion is foolishness; however wise a person may be among his people, he is considered foolish if he does not adhere to the Sharia of Allah.

And from it: the virtue of Abraham, in that Allah chose him and selected him over the worlds, because of His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا﴾.

And from it: affirmation of the Hereafter, because of His saying: ﴿فِي الْآخِرَةِ﴾.

And from it: that righteousness is a description of the prophets and those below them. Thus the Prophet may be described as righteous, and the followers of the Messenger may be described as righteous. That is why the prophets, peace be upon them, greeted the Messenger ﷺ on the night of the Ascension (Mi'raj) by saying: "Welcome, the righteous brother and the righteous prophet" [[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (349) and Muslim (163/263), from the hadith of Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So they described him with righteousness.

**Student:** Does the conjunction imply difference (...)?

**Shaykh:** It does not require difference. Differing attributes may be combined in one person; difference in attributes is not difference in persons.

And also from the benefits of the verse: that the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, is the best of religions, and it is monotheism (tawhid), the upright ḥanīfiyyah, the easy religion, because he said: ﴿وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِ إِنَّنِي بَرَاءٌ مِمَّا تَعْبُدُونَ (٢٦) إِلَّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾ ("And when Abraham said to his father and his people: Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me") [Az-Zukhruf 43:26–27].

And from it: that those who oppose the messengers are foolish, as Allah described them by His saying: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهُمْ لَا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ("Deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not reason") [Al-Baqarah 2:171]. They, although they may be clever and have knowledge of crafts and politics, are in reality foolish, because the intelligent person is the one who follows only what the messengers brought. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾.

**Student:** Shaykh, why is the following of Abraham specified, even though there were prophets before him with the same call?

**Shaykh:** Yes. He is specified because he, peace be upon him, is the father of the prophets with respect to the Children of Israel and the Arabs, since all the prophets after him were from his offspring, from the descendants of Abraham. Therefore he was singled out for this. That is why it is said that people have three fathers: Adam, Noah, and Abraham, except that Abraham was a father to the Arabs and the Israelites only.

**Student:** Shaykh, is it permissible to praise the Prophet ﷺ to his face?

**Shaykh:** To his face?

**Student:** To his face, meaning in his presence. Would this not fall outside the general scope of the hadith?

**Shaykh:** Which hadith?

**Student:** The hadith: "Beware of excessive praise, for it is slaughter," and the prohibition of excessive praise?

**Shaykh:** That is a question not related to this lesson.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** In any case, the Prophet only forbade praise when it was feared to cause harm. That is why he said: "Woe to you, you have cut off the neck of your companion" [[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2662) and Muslim (3000/65), with this wording from Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]], and he said: "When you see those who praise excessively, throw dust in their faces" [[Related by Muslim (3002/69), from the hadith of al-Miqdad, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. But if harm is not feared, there is no problem. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr praised the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, greatly in the poem "Bānat Suʿād" [[Related by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (3/579) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (10/243), from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him.]], while the Messenger was listening. Likewise Hassan ibn Thabit and other poets praised the Prophet ﷺ, because he deserved it and because no harm was feared from him.

**Student:** And if someone claims, "I am not someone who would be harmed"?

**Shaykh:** If he claims that, we say: then harm is feared for you now. As long as you have praised yourself, then trial is upon you.

**Student:** Shaykh, is there a difference between teaching and reciting in His saying: ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ﴾?

**Shaykh:** Yes. The difference is that teaching includes teaching the wording and the meaning, while recitation may occur without teaching them.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** By meaning, or by instructing them through study. Teaching is more specific. When I recite the Qur'an to you, I am reciting it, and this is not teaching; but when I spell it out to you letter by letter and word by word, this is teaching.

**Student:** (...) ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ﴾?

**Shaykh:** The Book refers to the Qur'an.

**Student:** And the verses?

**Shaykh:** The first verses are not restricted to the verses that indicate Allah.

He said: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾. From this verse is derived: the virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, in that he neither delayed nor was arrogant. He was not arrogant, because he said: ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ﴾ ("I have submitted"). He did not delay, because he said ﴿إِذْ قَالَ﴾ ("when he said") then ﴿قَالَ﴾ ("he said"), so this was an immediate response to his saying: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ﴾. ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾.

And from it: the affirmation of Allah's general lordship over every individual, because of His saying: ﴿لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("the Lord of the worlds").

And from it: an indication that creation is among the signs of Allah, because they are called "worlds" (ʿālamīn), as they are a sign of their Creator, Glorified and Exalted is He.

And from it: the connection between His saying ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ﴾ ("I have submitted") and ﴿رَبّ﴾ ("Lord"), as if the lordship is the reason for ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ﴾. The Lord is the one who deserves to be submitted to; the Lord is the Creator. That is why Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, denounced the worship of idols and explained the reason for that: they do not create. ﴿وَالَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ لَا يَخْلُقُونَ شَيْئًا وَهُمْ يُخْلَقُونَ (٢٠) أَمْوَاتٌ غَيْرُ أَحْيَاءٍ وَمَا يَشْعُرُونَ أَيَّانَ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ ("Those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are created. [They are] dead, not alive, and they do not know when they will be resurrected") [An-Nahl 16:20–21]. Thus the connection of mentioning Islam together with lordship is made clear.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ وَيَعْقُوبُ يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ("And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and so did Jacob: 'O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims'").

From this verse it is derived:

First: the importance of this enjoinment, because by whom was it given special care?

**Student:** Abraham.

**Shaykh:** Abraham and Jacob. Abraham is the father of the Arabs and the Israelites, and Jacob is the father of?

**Student:** The Israelites.

**Shaykh:** The Israelites. These two noble messengers cared for it, by making it something to be enjoined.

And from it: that this enjoinment should be cared for, following the example of whom?

**Student:** Abraham.

**Shaykh:** Following Abraham and Jacob.

And from it: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, chose for His servants from the religion that which is most upright for their interests, because of His saying: ﴿اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ﴾ ("He chose for you"), i.e., He selected it. Had it not been most upright in sustaining the interests of the servants, Allah would not have chosen it for His servants.

And from it: that address should be gentle. From where do we take this?

**Student:** ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾, for calling them by sonship implies acceptance of what is conveyed to them.

And also from it: that a person must always renew his covenant with himself so that death does not come upon him while he is heedless, because of His saying: ﴿فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾.

And from it: that deeds are judged by their endings, because of His saying: ﴿فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾. It is not enough that a person submits at the beginning of his life or in its middle; he must continue until he dies, until he meets Allah, Exalted is He, while upon Islam.

**Student:** Is the saying ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾ the statement of Jacob or not?

**Shaykh:** They all say it; the enjoinment is from both of them.

**Student:** He said: ﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ﴾?

**Shaykh:** Abraham said to his sons: ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾, and Jacob likewise said it.

**Student:** The pronoun in ﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا﴾ refers to what?

**Shaykh:** It is said: it refers to the religion. And it is said: it refers to His saying: ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾.

**Student:** That is, he enjoined them to say, "We have submitted"?

**Shaykh:** Yes, they say it with their tongues and their hearts.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them﴾. "Purify them" means developing their character. Tazkiyah means development and purification: he develops their characters and purifies them from every vice. This is how the Messenger's law (peace and blessings be upon him) was: developing virtuous character and purifying from every vice. He commands righteousness, commands what is good, commands excellence, commands maintaining ties of kinship, commands truthfulness, and commands every good, everything in which there is good for a person in his religion and his worldly life, for Islam commands it, and this is tazkiyah. And he forbids the opposite of that: he forbids sin, severing ties of kinship, transgression, disobedience to parents, lying, deceit, and other blameworthy traits. This is tazkiyah.

Do you know what the state of people was before Islam? As for their worship, do not ask: shirk and disbelief. As for their social conditions, do not ask about them either: the strong devoured the weak, the rich devoured the poor, they consumed usury multiplied many times over, they raided one another, they taunted one another about lineages, and they called to the causes of jahiliyyah, and so on. Islam came and demolished all of this. Whoever reflects on history before and after the sending of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), before his mission and after it, will know the great difference between the state of people before the mission and their state after it, and the meaning of His saying ﴿and purify them﴾ will become clear to him.

﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾. We say about it here what we said about the i'rab of ﴿Indeed You, You are the Oft-Returning, the Merciful﴾, and we take ﴿You﴾ as a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl). What is its place in i'rab?

* Student: It has no place in i'rab.
* Shaykh: It has no place in i'rab. A separating pronoun has no place in i'rab. And ﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾ is the predicate of (inna), and ﴿al-Ḥakīm﴾ is a second predicate.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: The kāf is the subject of (inna), ﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿al-Ḥakīm﴾ is another predicate. ﴿al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm﴾ has already been discussed, I think? ﴿al-ʿAzīz﴾ means the one possessing ʿizzah, and ʿizzah means strength and dominance. He, glorified and exalted, possesses strength and dominance; nothing overpowers Him and nothing can frustrate Him. And ﴿al-Ḥakīm﴾: it was mentioned that it is derived from what?
* Student: From ḥikmah.
* Shaykh: From ḥukm and ḥikmah, from both together. We said that ḥukm is of two kinds: kawnī (universal/decreed) and sharʿī (legislative). And ḥikmah is also of two kinds: ḥāliyyah (inherent/structural) and ghāʾiyyah (purposive). Ḥukm is of two kinds: sharʿī and kawnī. What is an example of the sharʿī?
* Student: The sharʿī?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 23].
* Shaykh: No, there is no ḥukm in it; qaḍā. Who knows?
* Student: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Māʾidah 38].
* Shaykh: The root ḥ-k-m indicates al-Ḥakīm. As for the legal rulings (aḥkām sharʿiyyah), we say: obligatory, recommended, disliked, prohibited, and permissible.
* Student: His saying in the verse of al-Mumtaḥanah: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 10].
* Shaykh: Correct: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾. Likewise His saying: ﴿Do they seek the judgment of the Jahiliyyah? And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Māʾidah 50]. This is the sharʿī ḥukm we mentioned. What is an example of the kawnī ḥukm?
* Student: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 16].
* Shaykh: No, that is the kawnī command. Do you want the kawnī ḥukm? His saying: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me﴾ [Yūsuf 80]. What comes after? ﴿Or Allah judges for me﴾, a kawnī ḥukm, because the sharʿī ḥukm did not prevent him from returning to the land. ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah judges for me﴾. Do you understand?

The difference between the kawnī and sharʿī ḥukm: the kawnī ḥukm must, of necessity, take place; the sharʿī ḥukm may or may not be carried out, a person may comply and fulfill the ruling or may not comply. Also, the sharʿī ḥukm is established by the Law, and its affirmation is by what Allah loves, while the kawnī is by what He loves and what He does not love. This is regarding al-Ḥakīm as derived from what?

* Student: From ḥukm.
* Shaykh: And as derived from ḥikmah? We said that ḥikmah is ḥāliyyah and ghāʾiyyah. The ḥāliyyah is the existence of a thing in a particular form: this is ḥikmah. A person being of upright stature, his head in this form, his hands, likewise his legs, and what Allah created in him: this is ḥikmah ḥāliyyah. And the prayer being in this manner, standing, bowing, prostration, sitting and the like, and zakah being at these measures and at these times: this too is ḥikmah of what kind? Ḥāliyyah. And that these matters exist for a praiseworthy end is ḥikmah ghāʾiyyah, for Allah, exalted, did not bring things into existence, whether universally or legislatively, except for a praiseworthy purpose. ﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah 129].

The connection of ʿizzah and ḥikmah here to the sending of the Messenger is very evident, because everything the Messenger brings is wisdom, and in it is ʿizzah: ﴿And to Allah belongs honour, and to His Messenger and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 8]. Look: ﴿and to the believers﴾, not "and to the Arabs"? To the believers, whether Arab or non-Arab. Whoever is a believer in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, standing by the command of Allah, has ʿizzah. Whoever is not like that, Allah has not guaranteed him ʿizzah. ʿIzzah belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers. Therefore it is obligatory upon us that the bond between us be the bond of faith alone, for there cannot be ʿizzah and unity upon good except by this bond alone.

* Student: Shaykh, is there not ḥikmah in (...)?
* Shaykh: We said there is ḥikmah in (...), but it is connected with the purposive wisdom, because for such-and-such a reason such-and-such was legislated or such-and-such occurred.

He said: ﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Ibrahim except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. (Man) is an interrogative noun.
* Student: No (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿Wa man yarghab﴾, ﴿man yarghab﴾.
* Student: Relative (khabariyyah).
* Shaykh: Relative! ﴿man yarghab﴾: (man) here, we have the first and second ... ﴿man yarghab﴾ (man) is an interrogative noun.
* Student: No (...).
* Shaykh: It is an interrogative noun used to mean negation, as shown by His saying ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. So (man) here is an interrogative noun and it is the subject, and the clause ﴿yarghab﴾ is its predicate. The clause ﴿yarghab﴾, that is, a present-tense verb as its predicate. We do not say here that (man) is conditional. Yes, if the verse were "and whoever turns away from the creed of Ibrahim, he has made a fool of himself," it would be conditional, but this is more eloquent: ﴿man yarghab﴾ means no one turns away from the creed of Ibrahim.

And His saying ﴿yarghab ʿan millah﴾: it is said raghiba fī kadhā and raghiba ʿan. What is the difference?
* Student: He turned away from it.
* Shaykh: Raghiba fīhi means he sought it. And raghiba ʿanhu?
* Student: It means he abandoned it.
* Shaykh: He abandoned it and shunned it. Here ﴿man yarghab ʿan millat Ibrahim﴾ means: he abandons it, or seeks it?
* The students: He abandons it.
* Shaykh: He abandons it.

And His saying ﴿millat Ibrahim﴾: millah means religion, that is, the religion of Ibrahim. The religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is that he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim submitting to Allah, and was not among the polytheists. Ibrahim is al-Khalīl (peace be upon him), the father of the prophets and the most honourable of them after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah made him an imam: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah﴾ [al-Naḥl 120]. He made his creed the upright ḥanīf creed. If that is so, does anyone turn away from the upright ḥanīf creed? Yes, one who makes a fool of himself does; therefore He said: ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. ﴿Safiha nafsahu﴾ has been said to mean: he was ignorant of himself, that is, he was ignorant of what is due to it and wasted it. And it has been said: safiha means he caused it to fall into safah (foolishness). ﴿Safiha nafsahu﴾: he caused it to fall into foolishness. The opposite of safah is rushd. The first meaning: the opposite of safah is?
* The students: Knowledge.
* Shaykh: Its opposite is knowledge.

We may say: in the expression using a word that admits two meanings there is a great subtlety, namely that ﴿safiha﴾ is apt for both: ignorance, and causing it to fall into foolishness. He is in reality ignorant if he did not intentionally oppose, and a fool if he intentionally opposed. So the person who turns away from the creed of Ibrahim has caused himself to fall into foolishness and did not act with rushd; then if he does so knowingly, he is a fool.

﴿And We had indeed chosen him in this world﴾: the sentence here is emphasised by three emphasisers: the implied oath, the lam, and qad; because the lam here is a preface to the oath, and the sense is: "By Allah, indeed." ﴿Iṣṭafaynāhu﴾ is an iftiʿāl form from ṣafwah, meaning it is derived from this; the root is (ṣafā yaṣfū). So the meaning of iṣṭafaynāhu is: We chose him until he became the elite of creation. Allah chose him in this world above all the prophets except Muhammad (ﷺ). And His saying ﴿iṣṭafaynāhu fī al-dunyā﴾ means: We made him a chosen one among creation, and Allah took him as a khalīl.

﴿And indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾: (inna-hu) here is inna and its noun, and ﴿fī al-ākhirah﴾?
* Student: A predicate.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿min al-ṣāliḥīn﴾ is the predicate, but ﴿fī al-ākhirah﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative): and indeed he, in the state of being in the Hereafter, is among the righteous. In this world Allah chose and selected him; in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous who fulfilled what Allah obligated upon them toward Him and toward His creation. This sentence is emphasised by two emphasisers: inna and the lam alone. Here Allah mentioned choosing in this world and righteousness in the Hereafter. Is there a subtlety in the difference between the two states or not? It seems to me, and Allah knows best, that there is a subtlety there, though we do not know it; is there a subtlety we know or not? Without doubt the two expressions differ, but why? Let us reflect: this world is a house of desires and trial, so none is patient with these desires or with this trial except one above another, is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: When a person sincerely devotes himself to Allah, he becomes an elite among the servants of Allah, is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: The Hereafter is not like that; even the disbelievers come to believe there. But the difference is between one who is among the righteous and one who is not, for when they are exposed to the Fire: ﴿Is this not the truth? They will say: Yes, by our Lord﴾ [al-Anʿām 30], ﴿Did there not come to you messengers with clear proofs? They say: Yes﴾ [Ghāfir 50], ﴿They say: Woe to us, who has raised us from our sleeping place? This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truly﴾ [Yāsīn 52]. Thus it shows that they believe, but they are not among the righteous.

﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit﴾: this too follows as praise of Ibrahim. Notice how, when He glorified the House of Allah, Allah, glorified and exalted, is Shakūr and Ḥalīm, praised him with this great praise, made him an imam, explained his choosing in this world, and that in the Hereafter he is among the righteous; this state too is part of the praise of him. ﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit﴾ may be connected to His saying ﴿We had indeed chosen him﴾: We had indeed chosen him when his Lord said to him, and it may be connected to an omitted element, meaning: remember when his Lord said to him, so that it is a command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to make mention of this state in which Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was.

﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit﴾. He said: hearing and obeying?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. He did not delay nor refuse: ﴿He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾. A submission that includes tawḥīd of worship, ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾ includes tawḥīd of lordship, names and attributes: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾. So he submitted completely without hesitation. How many were told by their Lord, "Submit," and did not submit! Of the children of Adam, nine hundred and ninety-nine are said to be told "submit" and did not, for they are all among the people of the Fire; nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand of the children of Adam are all in the Fire, and one of them is in Paradise. But this one, his Lord said to him "Submit," and he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." This is a very praiseworthy quality, deserving that he be mentioned for it.

It is general to the root of Islam and to the branches of Islam. Even in the branches he submitted: he saw in a dream that he would slaughter his son, and he carried it out?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: He carried it out. Allah said to him: ﴿And We called to him: O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 104–105]. He carried it out even though this was his only son, he had no other; he was given him in old age, and he reached the age of striving with him, meaning he reached the age of walking with him. This is the time when a person is most attached to his son, for a small child may not capture the soul, and a grown son has become independent and the desire for him has departed; but one at this stage is the utmost of the heart's attachment. He saw in his sleep that he was slaughtering him, and he carried it out, except that he wished to test his son, when he said: ﴿I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think. He said: O my father, do what you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 102]. And Allah mentioned the story.

* Student: His saying ﴿We had indeed chosen him in this world﴾, did He not mention the Messenger or the prophets before him?
* Shaykh: Yes, because the context is about Ibrahim. He mentioned ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen and the excellent﴾ [Ṣād 47] and ﴿O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 42], but here the context is praise of Ibrahim.

* Student: ﴿He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: Because the Lord must be complete. The Lord whose lordship is general to all the worlds must be complete; otherwise it would not be correct for Him to be Lord of the worlds.

* Student: Shaykh, what is the meaning that Allah, exalted, revealed to the Messenger ﴿to follow the creed of Ibrahim﴾ [al-Naḥl 123], and in the hadith: "Indeed the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad (ﷺ)"?
* Shaykh: Yes, well said. The guidance of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) includes the guidance of Ibrahim and more, because the guidance of Ibrahim is sincerity and tawḥīd in general, but the branches of Islam differ, for Allah says: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Māʾidah 48]. Originally, tawḥīd and sincerity are the creed of Ibrahim, the creed to be followed, but the branches of Islam were perfected by the Law which the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) followed; therefore the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons, and Yaʿqūb﴾. In one reading: ﴿wa-awṣā bihā﴾. As for "Ibrahim" in the first and second occurrence, there is the reading we mentioned to you before, which is ﴿Ibrāhām﴾, ﴿wa-waṣṣā bihā Ibrāhām﴾, and you say ﴿Ibrāhīm﴾..
* Student: In the whole Qur'an?
* Shaykh: No, not in the whole Qur'an; in this surah, in most of the Qur'an, in a few places there is no (Ibrāhām).
* Student: Shaykh, did he add a letter?
* Shaykh: And what is it?
* Student: The alif.
* Shaykh: And a letter was lost: he added a letter and lost a letter. Where is the loss?
* Student: Gemination (taḍʿīf).
* Shaykh: Gemination, yes. ﴿wa-waṣṣā bihā﴾ and ﴿wa-awṣā bihā Ibrāhīm﴾. In reality this does not meet the three conditions for a reading. And what are the three conditions for a reading? Did we dictate them to you in two verses? The conditions of the readings?
* Student: His saying:

**Shaykh:** Now, ﴿وَصَّى بِهَا﴾ and ﴿أَوْصَى بِهَا﴾ (both forms mean "enjoined it"). The verse, "yahwī" (contains)?

**Student:** "Mā yahwī" (what it contains).

**Shaykh:** "Mā yahwī"? So the pillars mentioned are based on what is most common. We have already encountered the omission of a conjunction particle, a particle that has a meaning, of this kind. This particle has no meaning: the interrogative hamza and the doubling (tadh'īf) have no meaning. But earlier we encountered the omission of a particle that carries meaning. What is it?

**Student:** ﴿قَالُوا﴾ and ﴿وَقَالُوا﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿قَالُوا﴾ and ﴿وَقَالُوا﴾. Where is it?

**Student:** ﴿وَقَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ وَلَدًا﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:116] ("And they said: Allah has taken a son").

**Shaykh:** Correct. And the reading?

**Student:** ﴿قَالُوا﴾ ("they said," without the conjunction).

**Shaykh:** And the reading without the conjunction is: ﴿قَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ﴾. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ وَاسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ قَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing. They said: Allah has taken...") ﴿وَاسِعٌ عَلِيمٌ (١١٥) وَقَالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("...All-Knowing (115). And they said: Allah has taken...").

﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا﴾: the pronoun "hā" (it) refers to this great word, which is: ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"). It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the religion (millah): he enjoined this religion. The meaning is the same, i.e., the religion of Abraham is: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("When his Lord said to him, 'Submit,' he said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds'").

﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ﴾ ("And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons"). Tawsiyah (enjoinment) is a firm covenant concerning an important matter, is it not? What is tawsiyah?

**Student:** Tawsiyah is a covenant concerning an important matter.

**Shaykh:** A firm covenant concerning an important matter.

And his saying: ﴿إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ﴾, ﴿بَنِيهِ﴾: what is its grammatical position?

**Student:** Object.

**Shaykh:** It is the object of ﴿وَصَّى﴾. That is why it is in the accusative with the ya' (بَنِيهِ), because it is...?

**Students:** Attached to the sound masculine plural.

**Shaykh:** Attached to the sound masculine plural.

He says: ﴿وَيَعْقُوبُ﴾. ﴿وَيَعْقُوبُ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿إِبْرَاهِيمُ﴾, meaning: likewise Jacob enjoined it upon his sons.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Isaac is not mentioned, because Isaac is the one enjoined. Who enjoined him? Abraham. Then Jacob came, who is the grandson of Abraham through his son, and he enjoined it upon his sons. That is, likewise Jacob enjoined it. Jacob was named so because he was "ʿaqab" (the heel/follower) of Isaac. This holds if we say that it is a derived noun. But if we say it is a non-derived proper noun, then there is no need to give this explanation; we say: Ya'qub is a non-derived proper noun.

And his saying: ﴿يَعْقُوبُ﴾. Who is the most famous of Jacob's sons? Joseph. Jacob said: ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾ or (يَا بُنَيَّ)?

**Students:** ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾. What is the difference between (يَا بَنِي) and (يَا بُنَيَّ)?

**Students:** (بَنِي) is plural.

**Shaykh:** (بَنِي) is plural. (بُنَيَّ) is a singular diminutive. In (يَا بَنِي), where is the nūn that substitutes for the tanwīn in the singular noun?

**Student:** It is gone.

**Shaykh:** Where?

**Student:** Because it is in the vocative.

**Shaykh:** If it were in the vocative, would you say: يَا بَنُونَ? Call out...would you say: "Yā banūn"?

**Student:** The vocative noun is in construct (مضاف), the nūn was dropped for the construct.

**Shaykh:** The nūn is dropped for the construct. You say: هؤلاء مسلمو مكة ("These are the Muslims of Makkah"), and the Prophet ﷺ fought the polytheists of Makkah (مشركي مكة). Do you understand? So the nūn is dropped for the construct, just as the tanwīn is dropped for the construct. You say: اشتريت كتابًا ("I bought a book"), and you say: اشتريت كتاب النحو ("I bought a grammar book"), with (كتاب) without tanwīn.

**Student:** Construct to the first person pronoun ya'?

**Shaykh:** To the first person pronoun ya', yes.

﴿يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ﴾ ("O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion"). Notice: he said ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾ for softening and for acceptance, for the acceptance of the call. This is from the aspect of tenderness, so that they will accept the call. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ﴾: "iṣṭafā" means chose, and ﴿لَكُمُ﴾ means for your sake, ﴿اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ﴾ for your sake. ﴿الدِّينَ﴾: what is the religion? Religion is worship and action, and it is also applied to recompense. In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾ ("Master of the Day of Judgment") [Al-Fatiha 1:4], what is meant by "dīn"?

**Student:** Recompense.

**Shaykh:** Recompense. And in His saying: ﴿وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ الْإِسْلَامَ دِينًا﴾ ("And I have approved for you Islam as a religion") [Al-Ma'idah 5:3]? Worship. So dīn is applied to this and to that: to action and to the recompense for it. From this is their saying: "Kamā tadīn tudān" (as you act, so you will be repaid), meaning as you work, so you will be recompensed.

**Student:** The grammatical analysis of ﴿لَكُمُ﴾?

**Shaykh:** A prepositional phrase (jār wa majrūr) related to ﴿اصْطَفَى﴾.

**Student:** In a position of accusative as a purpose object (maf'ūl li-ajlihi)?

**Shaykh:** No, the lām is simply for causation.

**Student:** It is not called a maf'ūl li-ajlihi?

**Shaykh:** No, it is not called a maf'ūl li-ajlihi.

﴿لَكُمُ الدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ﴾: the fā' is for consequence (tafrī'), meaning: on the basis of this choice, hold fast to this religion. And ﴿لَا تَمُوتُنَّ﴾: the lā here is a prohibitive particle, and it is well known that the prohibitive lā apocopates the verb. Here ﴿تَمُوتُنَّ﴾: what is the final letter of the verb? The tā'. Why is it not apocopated?

**Student:** It is apocopated by the deletion of the nūn.

**Shaykh:** This is one of the five verbs, so it is apocopated by deletion of the nūn. ﴿فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ﴾, and the nūn here is for emphasis. Its original form is: tamūtūnanna. The nūn was deleted for apocopation, becoming: fa-lā tamūtūn. Then the wāw was deleted because two consonants met: the wāw, which is the pronoun, was deleted because two consonants met, since the doubled nūn at its beginning is sukūn and the wāw is also sukūn, so the wāw is deleted. Ibn Mālik said:

"If two consonants meet, vowel the first one with a kasra,
and if the second is a soft letter, its deletion is deserved."

Allah, Exalted is He, said in the rest of the supplication of Abraham and Ishmael: ﴿رَبَّنَا وَابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِنْهُمْ يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ﴾ ("Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses").

From the benefits of the verse: the necessity of people for the sending of messengers. That is why Abraham and Ishmael supplicated; they asked Allah, Exalted is He, to send a messenger among them.

Also from its benefits: that a messenger being from among them is closer to acceptance of his call, because they know him, as Allah said: ﴿مَا ضَلَّ صَاحِبُكُمْ وَمَا غَوَى﴾ ("Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred") [An-Najm 53:2]. Reflect on His saying: ﴿صَاحِبُكُمْ﴾ ("your companion"), where He attributed him to them: your companion whom you know, and you know the soundness of his mind, and you know his trustworthiness; he did not stray and did not err. From where is this benefit taken? From His saying: ﴿مِنْهُمْ﴾.

* And from the benefits of the verse: the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, had Allah, Exalted is He, place in him the good that he recites the verses, teaches the Book, and teaches wisdom: ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ﴾ ("He recites to them Your verses, and teaches them the Book and wisdom, and purifies them").

And from it: the mission of the Prophet ﷺ includes mention of Allah's signs in creation and in the law, and includes teaching the Book, in recitation and meaning, and it also includes wisdom, which is knowledge of the secrets of the Sharia, and it includes the purification of people, because of His saying: ﴿وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ﴾.

From its benefits, then: this Sharia is complete, because the Prophet's ﷺ mission includes these sublime meanings, which indicates the perfection of his Sharia.

And from it: affirmation of might and wisdom for Allah in His saying: ﴿إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ﴾ ("Indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise").

And from it: affirmation of these two names for Allah, al-ʿAzīz and al-Ḥakīm, and we have already explained the meaning of ʿizzah (might) and ḥikmah (wisdom) in the commentary.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَمَنْ يَرْغَبُ عَنْ مِلَّةِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ إِلَّا مَنْ سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾ ("And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous").

From this noble verse it is derived: that rectitude lies in following the religion of Abraham, because of His saying: ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾.

And from its benefits also: that opposing this religion is foolishness; however wise a person may be among his people, he is considered foolish if he does not adhere to the Sharia of Allah.

And from it: the virtue of Abraham, in that Allah chose him and selected him over the worlds, because of His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْنَاهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا﴾.

And from it: affirmation of the Hereafter, because of His saying: ﴿فِي الْآخِرَةِ﴾.

And from it: that righteousness is a description of the prophets and those below them. Thus the Prophet may be described as righteous, and the followers of the Messenger may be described as righteous. That is why the prophets, peace be upon them, greeted the Messenger ﷺ on the night of the Ascension (Mi'raj) by saying: "Welcome, the righteous brother and the righteous prophet" [[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (349) and Muslim (163/263), from the hadith of Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So they described him with righteousness.

**Student:** Does the conjunction imply difference (...)?

**Shaykh:** It does not require difference. Differing attributes may be combined in one person; difference in attributes is not difference in persons.

And also from the benefits of the verse: that the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, is the best of religions, and it is monotheism (tawhid), the upright ḥanīfiyyah, the easy religion, because he said: ﴿وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِ إِنَّنِي بَرَاءٌ مِمَّا تَعْبُدُونَ (٢٦) إِلَّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾ ("And when Abraham said to his father and his people: Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me") [Az-Zukhruf 43:26–27].

And from it: that those who oppose the messengers are foolish, as Allah described them by His saying: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهُمْ لَا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ("Deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not reason") [Al-Baqarah 2:171]. They, although they may be clever and have knowledge of crafts and politics, are in reality foolish, because the intelligent person is the one who follows only what the messengers brought. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾.

**Student:** Shaykh, why is the following of Abraham specified, even though there were prophets before him with the same call?

**Shaykh:** Yes. He is specified because he, peace be upon him, is the father of the prophets with respect to the Children of Israel and the Arabs, since all the prophets after him were from his offspring, from the descendants of Abraham. Therefore he was singled out for this. That is why it is said that people have three fathers: Adam, Noah, and Abraham, except that Abraham was a father to the Arabs and the Israelites only.

**Student:** Shaykh, is it permissible to praise the Prophet ﷺ to his face?

**Shaykh:** To his face?

**Student:** To his face, meaning in his presence. Would this not fall outside the general scope of the hadith?

**Shaykh:** Which hadith?

**Student:** The hadith: "Beware of excessive praise, for it is slaughter," and the prohibition of excessive praise?

**Shaykh:** That is a question not related to this lesson.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** In any case, the Prophet only forbade praise when it was feared to cause harm. That is why he said: "Woe to you, you have cut off the neck of your companion" [[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2662) and Muslim (3000/65), with this wording from Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]], and he said: "When you see those who praise excessively, throw dust in their faces" [[Related by Muslim (3002/69), from the hadith of al-Miqdad, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. But if harm is not feared, there is no problem. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr praised the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, greatly in the poem "Bānat Suʿād" [[Related by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (3/579) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (10/243), from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him.]], while the Messenger was listening. Likewise Hassan ibn Thabit and other poets praised the Prophet ﷺ, because he deserved it and because no harm was feared from him.

**Student:** And if someone claims, "I am not someone who would be harmed"?

**Shaykh:** If he claims that, we say: then harm is feared for you now. As long as you have praised yourself, then trial is upon you.

**Student:** Shaykh, is there a difference between teaching and reciting in His saying: ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ﴾?

**Shaykh:** Yes. The difference is that teaching includes teaching the wording and the meaning, while recitation may occur without teaching them.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** By meaning, or by instructing them through study. Teaching is more specific. When I recite the Qur'an to you, I am reciting it, and this is not teaching; but when I spell it out to you letter by letter and word by word, this is teaching.

**Student:** (...) ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِكَ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ﴾?

**Shaykh:** The Book refers to the Qur'an.

**Student:** And the verses?

**Shaykh:** The first verses are not restricted to the verses that indicate Allah.

He said: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾. From this verse is derived: the virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, in that he neither delayed nor was arrogant. He was not arrogant, because he said: ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ﴾ ("I have submitted"). He did not delay, because he said ﴿إِذْ قَالَ﴾ ("when he said") then ﴿قَالَ﴾ ("he said"), so this was an immediate response to his saying: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ﴾. ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ أَسْلِمْ قَالَ أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾.

And from it: the affirmation of Allah's general lordship over every individual, because of His saying: ﴿لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("the Lord of the worlds").

And from it: an indication that creation is among the signs of Allah, because they are called "worlds" (ʿālamīn), as they are a sign of their Creator, Glorified and Exalted is He.

And from it: the connection between His saying ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ﴾ ("I have submitted") and ﴿رَبّ﴾ ("Lord"), as if the lordship is the reason for ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ﴾. The Lord is the one who deserves to be submitted to; the Lord is the Creator. That is why Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, denounced the worship of idols and explained the reason for that: they do not create. ﴿وَالَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ لَا يَخْلُقُونَ شَيْئًا وَهُمْ يُخْلَقُونَ (٢٠) أَمْوَاتٌ غَيْرُ أَحْيَاءٍ وَمَا يَشْعُرُونَ أَيَّانَ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ ("Those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, and they are created. [They are] dead, not alive, and they do not know when they will be resurrected") [An-Nahl 16:20–21]. Thus the connection of mentioning Islam together with lordship is made clear.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ وَيَعْقُوبُ يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ("And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and so did Jacob: 'O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims'").

From this verse it is derived:

First: the importance of this enjoinment, because by whom was it given special care?

**Student:** Abraham.

**Shaykh:** Abraham and Jacob. Abraham is the father of the Arabs and the Israelites, and Jacob is the father of?

**Student:** The Israelites.

**Shaykh:** The Israelites. These two noble messengers cared for it, by making it something to be enjoined.

And from it: that this enjoinment should be cared for, following the example of whom?

**Student:** Abraham.

**Shaykh:** Following Abraham and Jacob.

And from it: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, chose for His servants from the religion that which is most upright for their interests, because of His saying: ﴿اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ﴾ ("He chose for you"), i.e., He selected it. Had it not been most upright in sustaining the interests of the servants, Allah would not have chosen it for His servants.

And from it: that address should be gentle. From where do we take this?

**Student:** ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾, for calling them by sonship implies acceptance of what is conveyed to them.

And also from it: that a person must always renew his covenant with himself so that death does not come upon him while he is heedless, because of His saying: ﴿فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾.

And from it: that deeds are judged by their endings, because of His saying: ﴿فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾. It is not enough that a person submits at the beginning of his life or in its middle; he must continue until he dies, until he meets Allah, Exalted is He, while upon Islam.

**Student:** Is the saying ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ﴾ the statement of Jacob or not?

**Shaykh:** They all say it; the enjoinment is from both of them.

**Student:** He said: ﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ﴾?

**Shaykh:** Abraham said to his sons: ﴿يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَى لَكُمُ الدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾, and Jacob likewise said it.

**Student:** The pronoun in ﴿وَوَصَّى بِهَا﴾ refers to what?

**Shaykh:** It is said: it refers to the religion. And it is said: it refers to His saying: ﴿أَسْلَمْتُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾.

**Student:** That is, he enjoined them to say, "We have submitted"?

**Shaykh:** Yes, they say it with their tongues and their hearts.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 2, verses 133–135 (part 1 of 2)**

He said: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ Is the (am) here connected (muttasilah) or disconnected (munqati'ah)?

* Student: Disconnected.
* Another student: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected? The connected (muttasilah) "am" is the one that comes between two equal things, as we studied in rhetoric (balaghah). Here it does not come between two equal things, so it is disconnected. The grammarians say that the disconnected "am" has the meaning of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah. So, "bal" and the interrogative hamzah, meaning the interrogative hamzah. The meaning of ﴿Or were you﴾ is: "Rather, were you witnesses?"

As for His saying ﴿you were﴾, the pronoun refers to the Jews, the Jews who claimed that they were upon the truth and that this was the bequest of their father Ya'qub, and who adhered to what they were upon. It may also refer to all those addressed, and the intended meaning would then be to inform them of what happened from Ya'qub when death approached him. This possibility is preferable, because there is no evidence here that it refers to the Jews. Rather, the verses are all general, and they are also disconnected from many earlier verses about the Jews. So the meaning is an affirmation of what Ya'qub bequeathed when he died.

As for His saying ﴿witnesses﴾, it is the plural of shahid or shahid, meaning present.

As for His saying ﴿when﴾ (idh) ﴿approached﴾, this idh is a noun of time built on sukun in a position of nasb, meaning: at the time when Ya'qub's death approached. As for His saying ﴿approached Ya'qub, death﴾, why is it in the accusative (nasb) even though it comes after the verb? Do you say "approached Ya'qubu" or "approached Ya'quba"?

* Student: "Approached Ya'quba."
* Shaykh: Which means it is in the accusative after the verb? If you say, for example, "approached 'Abdullah"?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: An object? Where is the subject?
* Student: The subject is ﴿the death﴾.
* Shaykh: Excellent, may God bless you. Yes indeed. ﴿Ya'qub﴾ is in the accusative because it is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and ﴿the death﴾ is a delayed subject (fa'il mu'akhkhar). Do you understand? Because what approaches is death, and what is approached is Ya'qub. So it is a fronted direct object.

﴿When death approached Ya'qub, when he said﴾: this ﴿when﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿when﴾. That is, "when death approached, when he said." That is, "Or were you witnesses also when he said."

﴿to his sons: What will you worship after me?﴾ Who are the sons of Ya'qub? Isma'il? Yusuf and his brothers, eleven men. Death approached him, so his sons were present, or he had them brought, and he said to them: ﴿What will you worship after me?﴾

As for His saying ﴿after me﴾, it means after my time, not after my essence, because they were not worshipping him. They worship God. So the meaning of ﴿after me﴾ is after my death, that is, after the time in which I am present with you. Now you worship God, so what will you worship after me? Do you understand? The meaning is not "What will you worship after me," as if I were your object of worship now, so whom will you worship after me? That is definitely not the intended meaning.

﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. ﴿We will worship your God﴾: they began with it because they were addressing him. ﴿And the God of your fathers﴾: "fathers" is the plural of "father." So who are they? Ibrahim, who in relation to him is a grandfather, or not?

* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And Isma'il, who in relation to him is an uncle, and Ishaq, who in relation to him is a direct father. As for applying the title of fatherhood to Ibrahim and to Ishaq, the matter is clear, is it not?

* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because Ishaq is his father, and Ibrahim is his grandfather, and a grandfather is a father. Indeed, God said to this nation, between which and Ibrahim there are ages: ﴿the religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ [al-Hajj 78]. But the difficulty lies in Isma'il being a father to him while being his uncle. It is said, as the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Umar: "Did you not realize that the paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father?" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (1468) and Muslim (983/11), with his wording, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] The "sinw" (twin) is a branch or two branches that share one root. So he is mentioned along with the fathers, because he is the twin of the father, since the uncle is the twin of the father. And as the Messenger ﷺ said: "The maternal aunt is in the position of the mother" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2699) and Muslim (1783/91), from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him; the wording is al-Bukhari's]. Likewise we say: the uncle is in the position of the father. Is this understood, everyone?

It is also said that this is a case of taghlib (predominance of one term over another), and that the word "father" is not applied to an uncle in its literal sense except when it is paired with the real father. Based on this, if we say, for example, there is no difficulty at all, because taghlib is permissible in the Arabic language. It is said: "al-Qamarān" (the two moons), and what is meant by them?

* The students: The sun and the moon.
* Shaykh: The sun and the moon. It is also said: "al-'Umarān" (the two 'Umars), and who are they?

* Student: Abu Bakr and 'Umar.
* Shaykh: Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

As for His saying ﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾, what is the grammatical case (i'rab) of ﴿Ibrahim﴾?

* Student: It is an apposition (badal).
* Shaykh: An apposition from ﴿your fathers﴾. And there is a reading ﴿Ibrahama﴾.

﴿One God﴾: ﴿God﴾ (ilahan) here is a circumstantial accusative (hal). They call it a preparatory circumstantial (hal muwatta'ah), but that is based on the view that "ilah" is not a derived noun. The correct view is that it is derived, and that it means "mallah" (one who is worshipped). On this basis it is a genuine circumstantial (hal mu'assasah), not a preparatory one, because the preparatory circumstantial is one that paves the way for a derived noun, such as ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 2]. Here "Qur'anan" is not derived, whereas the circumstantial, as we have explained earlier, is derived. Some scholars said it is like that, and this is based on the view that "Allah" and "ilah" are not derived. The correct view is that they are derived. On this basis, ﴿ilahan﴾ is in the accusative as a...?

* Student: The circumstantial.
* Shaykh: The circumstantial. ﴿Wahidan﴾ (one) is another circumstantial, repeated. ﴿God, one God﴾: we worship Him as one God. This is evidence that worship (ibadah) and divinity (uluhiyyah) have one meaning, but worship is considered in relation to the worshipper, and divinity in relation to the God. For this reason, the scholars call the doctrine of Tawhid "Tawhid al-'Ibadah," and some say "Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah."

* Student: And if it is a preparatory circumstantial, what is the grammatical case of ﴿wahidan﴾?
* Shaykh: A circumstantial, in any case.
* Student: Would it not become an apposition, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, it would not be an apposition.
* Student: An apposition from ﴿ilahan﴾.
* Shaykh: No, it would not be an apposition, because an apposition means that if you delete the substituted noun, the sentence still stands, and here the sentence would not stand.
* Student: And what is the benefit of saying it is a circumstantial, since "one" is understood from your saying "God" (ilah)?
* Shaykh: No, "ilahan" is indefinite, and the indefinite conveys generality but does not preclude sharing. If I said to you, for example, "Honor a man," does that mean: "and do not honor anyone else"?

* Student: No.
* Shaykh: No, it does not convey that.
* Student: Would it not be an emphasis, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, it would not. If they had said, "We worship none but a God," perhaps, but it does not indicate unity unless they say "wahidan" (one).

﴿One God, and we are to Him Muslims﴾. ﴿We﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿Muslims﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and ﴿to Him﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) attached to ﴿Muslims﴾. It was placed before it to convey exclusivity (hasr) in meaning, and to observe the rhyme of the verses (fawasil al-ayat) in form. ﴿And we are to Him﴾: that is, to this One God, glorified and exalted, we are Muslims. Islam means submission and sincerity. ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Al 'Imran 20], meaning I made it purely for God. It is applied to submission, which is outward and inward Islam.

Yes. Continuity and permanence, unlike a verbal sentence, which conveys renewal and continuity.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾. The pronoun ﴿that﴾ refers to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and those who preceded them. The Jews used to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ about these figures, so God explained that these are a nation (ummah). Here "ummah" means a group, and in the Qur'an it has several meanings. The first meaning: a group, as here. What is the second meaning?

* Student: The second meaning: that which follows one religion.
* Shaykh: No, that is a subset of the group. A group upon one religion is an ummah.
* Student: A period of time.
* Shaykh: A period of time. Such as?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And he who was saved of the two and remembered after a time (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45].
* Shaykh: ﴿And he who was saved of the two said, and remembered after a time (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45], meaning after a period of time. The third?

* Student: A leader (imam).
* Shaykh: A leader. Such as?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation (ummah)﴾ [al-Nahl 120].
* Shaykh: Because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾. Yes. After that?

* Student: (...) meaning?
* Shaykh: Yes, meaning a leader? ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾?
* Student: A model.
* Shaykh: We already mentioned it.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22].
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: A way.
* Shaykh: Yes, a way and a creed. ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾ means upon a way and a creed that we follow. So "ummah" in the Noble Qur'an has four meanings.

﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾: it has gone by. ﴿It will have what it earned, and you will have what you earned﴾ [al-Baqarah 134]. You will not be asked about what they did, and they will not be asked about what you did. How excellent is this verse to recite in every situation resembling this. For example, if some people say: "Some of the Companions did such-and-such"? You may say: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away; it will have what it earned, and you will have what you earned﴾. Like what is related of "the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, who was asked about what happened among the Companions, and he said to them: 'That is blood that Allah cleansed our swords from, so we will cleanse our tongues from it'" [Related by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah (9/114) with the wording: "That is blood that Allah cleansed my hands from, so I do not wish to dye my tongue with it"], may Allah have mercy on him. This is a great statement. Based on this, dispute about those who came before has no place. Finished. ﴿They have what they earned, and you have what you earned﴾. But the dispute is about the present matter, and that is what truth must be made clear in and falsehood refuted in. ﴿They have what they earned, and you have what you earned, and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾. You are not responsible. You will be asked about what...?

* The students: About what you do.
* Shaykh: About what you used to do. As for about what they used to do, no, you will not be asked, because their reckoning is with God, the Mighty and Majestic, and you will not be asked about them. This is why it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not revile the dead, for they have gone to what they put forward" [Related by al-Bukhari (6516) from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her]. In another wording: "lest you harm the living" [Related by al-Tirmidhi (1982) and Ahmad in his Musnad (18209) from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, may Allah be pleased with him]. And they said...

* Student: Is there not a reading "and they will not be asked (...)"?
* Shaykh: What I have is "and you will not be asked," there is no variant reading.
* Student: If there is one, would the meaning not hold?
* Shaykh: It would not be sound: "(and they will not be asked about what they used to do)." How would "they will not be asked" make sense? Who would ask them?
* Student: It does not work?
* Shaykh: It does not work.

﴿They say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided﴾. ("Hud") is the plural of ("ha'id"), as we studied in al-Bukhari, like "'awdh," the plural of "'a'idh." ﴿Hudan﴾ means from the Jews. Who says ﴿Be Jews﴾?

* The students: The Jews.
* Shaykh: The Jews. ﴿Or Christians﴾ is said by the Christians. ﴿And you will be guided﴾: he did not say "you are guided," even though it is a present-tense verb that is raised by the presence of the nun. Why was the nun dropped? Because it is the answer to the imperative. We have previously discussed, I think yesterday or before, whether the answer to the imperative is jussive by itself, or jussive by an implied condition. There are two views among the grammarians, and the correct view is that it is jussive by itself, because it does not need an estimated condition. Those who say this are the Jews and the Christians, addressing whom? They address the Muslims. They say: If you want guidance, then be Jews or Christians. Like the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) within this nation. That is, the followers of other religions in relation to the nation in general say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." The people of innovation, in relation to the People of the Sunnah and the Community, say: "Be such-and-such, and you will be guided." The Ash'aris say: "Be Ash'aris, and you will be guided." The Mu'tazilites say: "Be Mu'tazilites, and you will be guided." The Qadianis say: "Be Qadianis, and you will be guided." The Tijanis say: "Be Tijanis, and you will be guided." The Sufis say: "Be Sufis, and you will be guided." And on this basis, make your analogies.

*(The poet says):*
"Each claims union with Layla, but Layla does not acknowledge them in that."
Each one says: the truth is with me. But ﴿If you dispute about anything, refer it back to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59]. For this reason God said: ﴿Say﴾ in response to those who call you to Judaism from the Jews, or to Christianity from the Christians: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion (millah)...﴾. Is "bal" here for abrupt rejection (idrab ibtali) or for transition (idrab intiqali)?

* The students: For rejection (ibtali).
* Shaykh: For rejection, because it cancels what preceded it. That is: "rather, we do not follow him, and we will not be Jews or Christians." ﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim﴾. By this explanation that I mentioned to you, it becomes clear to us in what way ﴿millah﴾ is in the accusative?

* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: It is an object of an implied verb, whose estimate is: "Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim." "Millah" means religion, as previously mentioned, and the religion of Ibrahim is Tawhid, meaning we follow the Tawhid of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and submission to Him, because Ibrahim ﴿his Lord said to him: Submit. He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah 131]. This is the religion (millah).

﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf﴾. ﴿Ḥanīfan﴾ is grammatically a circumstantial (ḥal) from ﴿Ibrahim﴾. It is one of the curiosities that a circumstantial be from the genitive-attached noun (mudaf ilayh). Is there anything in Ibn Malik's words that points to this?

* Student: Yes, it is his saying: "And do not permit..."
* Shaykh: "A time-noun..."
* Student: "And does not come..." I do not know.
* Student: His saying:
"Or it was a part of what is attributed to it, or like its part, so do not err."
* Shaykh: What is "Or it was a part of what is attributed to it"?
* Student:
"And do not permit a circumstantial from the attributed noun to it, unless the attributed noun requires its action."

* Shaykh: "Or it was a part of what is attributed to it, or like its part, so do not err." This falls under his saying: "...... or like its part, so do not err." He said: ﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf﴾ is a circumstantial from ﴿Ibrahim﴾. Is this circumstantial a fixed (lazimah) circumstantial or a changing (mutanaqqilah) circumstantial?

* Student: Fixed.
* Shaykh: Fixed. Then it has no implication. It does not mean that Ibrahim was sometimes a ḥanīf and sometimes inclined away, not a ḥanīf. Rather, he was ḥanīf, a fixed attribute of his, peace be upon him. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾. This is an emphasis of His saying ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, because the ḥanīf is one who inclines away from everything other than Tawhid, derived from "ḥanaf al-rijl," meaning the inclination of the foot. So he inclines away from everything other than Tawhid. Therefore ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ is an emphasis of this circumstantial, a semantic emphasis (tawkid ma'nawi), not a grammatical one. It is not a grammatical emphasis, because grammatical emphasis is well known, and it is not of this form. But it is a semantic emphasis, meaning that he, peace be upon him, was not of the polytheists. Was he not of the polytheists in what has passed, or in what is to come?

* Student: In what has passed.
* Shaykh: We said: "kāna" (was), when it does not indicate an event, indicates that its subject is characterized by its predicate, like ﴿And God was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa' 96]. Does that mean that God was that in the past and not now? Or is He characterized by forgiveness and mercy? He is characterized by it. So His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ does not mean that he was not so during the past part of his life and then became so. Rather, it means that this attribute is negated from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 133–135 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿from among the polytheists﴾ — does it encompass the negation of both minor and major shirk, or not? Shirk, as is well known among us, is minor and major. This is the path we follow; the Messenger ﷺ followed it, and we follow it, God willing, and we hope that Allah will let us die upon it. This is the true Hanifite creed (al-millah al-Hanifiyyah) that brings the servant to his Lord. ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153].

Then Allah, the Exalted, said, commanding this Ummah to declare this great creed: ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 136] — we believe in Allah. Faith (iman) is the affirmation of the heart that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. This is the view of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah. As for the Murji'ah, among whom are the Ash'arites, faith is merely affirmation by the heart, and according to them it neither increases nor decreases. Ibn al-Qayyim and others among the people of the Sunnah said: If you say that faith is merely affirmation by the heart, then Iblis is a believer, because he acknowledges Allah, saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad 82]; so, according to this, he would be a believer.

* Student: "Affirmation by the heart that necessarily entails...?"

* Shaykh: "That necessarily entails acceptance and submission. According to your view, Abu Talib would also be a believer, because he affirmed [the truth]. This is one of the most false opinions — one of the most false opinions. So we say: faith is affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission."

* Student: "And how did they respond, O Shaykh? How did they answer this very strong objection?"

* Shaykh: "That is, how do they respond to this?"

* Student: "Does your remark not include Iblis and others?"

* Shaykh: "Yes indeed. They distort [the texts] just as they distorted the verses and hadiths about the Divine Attributes. They say: his arrogance in refusing to prostrate is evidence that he is not a believer. We say to them: how can it be evidence that he is not a believer when he affirms [Allah]? Is a person held accountable for what he does not affirm? Is a speaker held accountable for something contrary to his utterance? — we do not say 'a person,' because Satan is not a human being."

* Student: "No. And at the last moment he says, 'O Lord,' even at the last minute?"

* Shaykh: "Who?"

* Student: "Iblis affirms at the last minute."

* Shaykh: "Yes, yes."

* Student: "And as he was descending from Paradise, he still says:"

* Shaykh: "Yes indeed."

* Student: ﴿My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Hijr 36].

* Shaykh: "Yes, yes. The point is, in any case, the people of falsehood distort words from their places. This is the method of all the people of falsehood regarding evidences: when they are unable to refute the chain of narration and its authenticity, they manage to do so. Even if a hadith is in the Two Sahihs, they say: this is a solitary report (khabar ahad) and does not establish creedal matters. This is their method — and we seek refuge in Allah. Thus, all the narrators of the Two Sahihs, if the hadith is not mutawatir, they have criticized it and said that their reports cannot be used as evidence for any creedal matter at all. They have demolished half the Shari'ah or more. Is not the majority of the Shari'ah solitary reports?"

* The students: "Solitary reports."

* Shaykh: "Solitary reports. The majority of the Shari'ah consists of solitary reports. In truth, this view is false even in practical matters. When a person performs an action that is not a matter of creed, is it possible for him to act without believing that it is from the command of Allah?"

* Student: "He must believe it."

* Shaykh: "He must believe it. So then, physical acts are based on what?"

* The students: "On creed."

* Shaykh: "On creed. So according to their view, we would conclude: then we do not establish practical rulings either, since one cannot act upon a ruling without believing that the one who ruled it is Allah. The point is that we say: these false foundations regarding faith — that it is mere affirmation, and that it neither increases nor decreases — are the general doctrine of the Murji'ah. Who are the Murji'ah? The Ash'arites and the Jahmiyyah. The Jahmiyyah are also Murji'ah, and for this reason the Ash'arites agree with the Jahmiyyah on the question of irja' (deferral); they agree with them. The Mu'tazilah agree with the Jahmiyyah on the question of the Attributes and deny them."

* Student: "(...)."

* Shaykh: "The Attributes, the Attributes of Allah."

* Student: "(...)?"

* Shaykh: "The Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah agree on the Attributes, but they differ on the question of faith. The Mu'tazilah say: faith is speech, creed, and action, a unified whole; if part of it is lost, all of it is lost. For this reason they regard the perpetrator of a major sin as having left faith. Note that the people of falsehood declare one another misguided in some matters — I mean, they mislead one another, although they may not rule them to be disbelievers, but they say: these are astray. So then, what is faith in the language?"

* The students: "Affirmation."

* Shaykh: "Affirmation. And in the Shari'ah: (...). And this is a claim (...)."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons: What will you worship after me?﴾ [al-Baqarah 133], to the end.

* From this noble verse is derived: that tawhid is the testament of the prophets, by His saying: ﴿What will you worship after me? They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾.

* Among its benefits: that death is a reality even for the prophets. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾ [Al 'Imran 144].

* Among them: the permissibility of making a bequest at the approach of one's end, by His saying: ﴿And Ibrahim instructed his sons with it﴾ before this, and ﴿when he said to his sons: What will you worship after me? They said: We will worship your God﴾ — and this is like a testament to them. However, it is required that the one making the bequest be conscious of what he says; if he is not conscious of what he says, his bequest is not valid.

* And it is derived from this: the preference of the correct view that the grandfather is a father. From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿The God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾ — for Ibrahim was his grandfather, not his father."

* Among the benefits of the verse: that it is permissible to apply the term "father" to an uncle, by way of precedence (taghlib). From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿and Isma'il﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿And Isma'il﴾ — for Isma'il was an uncle, not a father."

* Among them: that the sons of Ya'qub were upon tawhid, since they said: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾, and there is no doubt that this is tawhid on their part.

* Also among them, among the benefits of the verse: following the fathers. Human souls are naturally inclined to follow their fathers; but if it is upon truth, it is truth, and if it is upon falsehood, it is falsehood, by their saying: ﴿and the God of your fathers﴾. For this reason, those who attended the death of Abu Talib said to him: "Will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (1360) and Muslim (24/39) from the hadith of al-Musayyib ibn Hazn.]

* Among the benefits of the verse: the sincerity of Islam to Allah, where He said: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾. The ﴿Him﴾ — the aspect of sincerity lies in fronting the object: in ﴿lahu﴾, because ﴿lahu﴾ is connected to ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, so it is an object fronted, and it is known that fronting the object conveys restriction (hasr).

* Among them: the affirmation of Allah's oneness, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿one God﴾.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* From this verse is derived: that one should not occupy oneself with what the fathers used to do, by His saying: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾, meaning: they have now passed on and submitted to Allah. As for you, O Jews of the Prophet's time (peace be upon him), you must consider what you have earned for yourselves. Occupying oneself with what the fathers were upon is a waste of time and may be harmful.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it indicates that we should remain silent about what occurred among the Companions, or not?

* Student: "Yes indeed."

* Shaykh: "Because we say as Allah said to those people: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn.﴾ So we are now concerned with ourselves. As for what happened between Mu'awiyah and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, or between 'Ali and 'A'ishah, and the like, this is a matter that does not concern us now. Our duty is to say: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any resentment toward those who believe. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Hashr 10]."

* Student: "Does this include other than the Companions?"

* Shaykh: "Others besides the Companions are also included, and a person should not occupy himself with such matters, but should look to what benefits him in his religion and his worldly life."

* Among them: that a person is [responsible for] his own deeds, by His saying: ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn﴾. No one is given credit for another's deeds, nor is anything taken from him for them: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38].

* Among them: that the later generation is not asked about the deeds of the earlier one, or not?

* The students: "Yes."

* Shaykh: "The reverse? Is the earlier asked about the deeds of the later?"

* Student: "Perhaps."

* Shaykh: "Perhaps. The earlier may be asked about the deeds of the later, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas 41]. The earlier one may be a person of innovation who is followed in his innovation, so he becomes one who points to misguidance; upon him is its burden and the burden of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection. Do you understand? But the later one is not asked about the deeds of the earlier one."

If it is said: Does the end of the verse nullify its beginning? ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn, and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾ — the answer is: No; for if they called to misguidance or to truth and we later followed them, then this is from their earnings, so for them is what they earned.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the justice of Allah, the Exalted, and that He does not hold anyone accountable for what he did not do, by His saying: ﴿and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* Among them: the affirmation of questioning, and that a person will be questioned. From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾. The explicit wording of the verse is clear: the negation of being asked about the deeds of others; its implicit meaning is the affirmation of being asked about one's own deeds, and that you are accountable for your deeds, and this is so."

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided. Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a Hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾. In this verse there is a call and a claim. Where is the call?

* The students: ﴿Be﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ — and the claim is ﴿you will be guided﴾."

* From it is derived: that the people of falsehood call to their misguidance and claim good in it. ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ is a call to misguidance; ﴿you will be guided﴾ is the claim that this is good. Likewise, these Jews inherited this from those who went astray in this Ummah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you."* [Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (21897), and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (6702), from the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi (may Allah be pleased with him).]

Are there people of innovation in the Ummah or not? They call to misguidance and claim that it is the truth. For example, the Mu'tazilah call to i'tizal and say: the good is with us, we are those who declare Allah free of deficiencies; and you, O affirmers of the Attributes, you are anthropomorphists (mujassimah), you are literalist anthropomorphists — is that so or not? And transcendence (tanzih) is with us. These called to misguidance and claimed it to be truth and good. Then the Ash'arites said: we are "the stump that the camel rubs against" (judhaylaha al-muhakkak), we are the people of the matter. You Mu'tazilah are in error, and the Salaf are anthropomorphists or delegationists (mufawwidah). If they are delegationists, they are at peace with them, because the delegationist according to the Ash'arites is one who does not go beyond reciting the Qur'an and the hadith. This is the delegationist: delegation of meaning and modality. For this reason you will find the Ash'arites saying: the方法 of the Salaf is delegation, and the method of the later scholars is affirmation of meanings.
