So our method is more knowledgeable and wiser than yours, O Salaf; and this is correct. If the method of the Salaf were, as they claim, merely recitation — as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who know not the Scripture except wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah 78] — merely reading, then, we would testify before Allah that the method of the later scholars is better, because it affirms that the Qur'an has a reality and a meaning, revealed so that we may worship Allah by this meaning.

But we say: you have lied about the method of the Salaf. What is the true method of the Salaf? Delegation regarding what they cannot know: the reality of these Attributes and their modality. No one can speak about this modality at all. But the meaning — do they delegate it or not? They affirm the meaning fitting to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So they are more knowledgeable, wiser, and safer. Do you understand? The Ash'arites say: we are the ones with the truth; follow us only. The truth is with us. You affirm for Allah only seven Attributes and seven states, with a difference between us and them regarding the modality of affirming these Attributes. For example: speech is affirmed by us and also by them, but what is speech according to them?

* Student: "The meaning subsisting in the self."

* Shaykh: "Speech is the meaning subsisting in the soul, one meaning whether it comes in the form of a question, a report, a command, or a prohibition, and whether it is the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. But it is expressed through these different expressions so that it may be a report, a command, a prohibition, a question, the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. This is not affirmation in reality. So the point, my brothers, is this: every caller to misguidance has in him a resemblance to the Jews and Christians. The callers to unveiling today say: let the woman be liberated, let her enjoy life, do not cover her, do not blind her eyes with the veil; let her walk with people — this is freedom, is it not? ﴿Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾ — the same thing: loosen the reins for her for the sake of freedom, because this is good. Is it just that you go out to stroll and sightsee and stand at this shop and that shop while she is confined in the house? Likewise, every caller to misguidance will surely adorn this misguidance with what deceives the stranger. So he resembles whom? The Jews and Christians."

* From the benefits of the verse: confronting falsehood with truth: ﴿Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a Hanif﴾. A person must follow a path, but is it truth or falsehood? Allah affirmed falsehood in His saying: ﴿Rather﴾; and we have mentioned in the commentary that ﴿bal﴾ here is for the retractive turning away (al-idrab al-ibtali).

* From the benefits of the verse: praise of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in that we are followers of him in his religion; this is one. Another aspect: describing him as a Hanif. A third aspect: describing him as not having been of the polytheists. Thus in this there is praise of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from three aspects. First, his imamate. What is the aspect of his being an imam?

* The students: (...).

* Shaykh: "In that we are commanded to follow him, and the one followed is the imam. Second, that he is a Hanif, inclining away from every religion other than Islam. Third: he had no shirk in his deeds, ﷺ."

* From the benefits of the verse: that shirk is impossible for the prophets, by His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾.

* Among them: that Judaism and Christianity are a type of shirk, because His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾, in contrast to their call to Judaism and Christianity, indicates that they are a type of shirk. Everyone who disbelieves in Allah has in him some type of shirk; but if he takes a god, it is shirk in reality and actuality, and otherwise it is shirk in the sense of following desire.

* Student: "In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾, some grammarians say that ﴿Isma'il﴾ is conjoined to ﴿God﴾, meaning: the God of Isma'il and Ishaq?"

* Shaykh: "No, this is far-fetched; I say this is far-fetched, because it scatters the structure of the verse."

* Student: "It can be resolved as a matter of attribution..."

* Shaykh: "No, this is well known in the Arabic language. The Messenger said, peace be upon him: 'The paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father'* [Related by Muslim (983/11) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. There is no omission here."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 2, verses 133–135 (part 1 of 2)**

He said: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ Is the (am) here connected (muttasilah) or disconnected (munqati'ah)?

* Student: Disconnected.
* Another student: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected? The connected (muttasilah) "am" is the one that comes between two equal things, as we studied in rhetoric (balaghah). Here it does not come between two equal things, so it is disconnected. The grammarians say that the disconnected "am" has the meaning of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah. So, "bal" and the interrogative hamzah, meaning the interrogative hamzah. The meaning of ﴿Or were you﴾ is: "Rather, were you witnesses?"

As for His saying ﴿you were﴾, the pronoun refers to the Jews, the Jews who claimed that they were upon the truth and that this was the bequest of their father Ya'qub, and who adhered to what they were upon. It may also refer to all those addressed, and the intended meaning would then be to inform them of what happened from Ya'qub when death approached him. This possibility is preferable, because there is no evidence here that it refers to the Jews. Rather, the verses are all general, and they are also disconnected from many earlier verses about the Jews. So the meaning is an affirmation of what Ya'qub bequeathed when he died.

As for His saying ﴿witnesses﴾, it is the plural of shahid or shahid, meaning present.

As for His saying ﴿when﴾ (idh) ﴿approached﴾, this idh is a noun of time built on sukun in a position of nasb, meaning: at the time when Ya'qub's death approached. As for His saying ﴿approached Ya'qub, death﴾, why is it in the accusative (nasb) even though it comes after the verb? Do you say "approached Ya'qubu" or "approached Ya'quba"?

* Student: "Approached Ya'quba."
* Shaykh: Which means it is in the accusative after the verb? If you say, for example, "approached 'Abdullah"?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: An object? Where is the subject?
* Student: The subject is ﴿the death﴾.
* Shaykh: Excellent, may God bless you. Yes indeed. ﴿Ya'qub﴾ is in the accusative because it is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and ﴿the death﴾ is a delayed subject (fa'il mu'akhkhar). Do you understand? Because what approaches is death, and what is approached is Ya'qub. So it is a fronted direct object.

﴿When death approached Ya'qub, when he said﴾: this ﴿when﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿when﴾. That is, "when death approached, when he said." That is, "Or were you witnesses also when he said."

﴿to his sons: What will you worship after me?﴾ Who are the sons of Ya'qub? Isma'il? Yusuf and his brothers, eleven men. Death approached him, so his sons were present, or he had them brought, and he said to them: ﴿What will you worship after me?﴾

As for His saying ﴿after me﴾, it means after my time, not after my essence, because they were not worshipping him. They worship God. So the meaning of ﴿after me﴾ is after my death, that is, after the time in which I am present with you. Now you worship God, so what will you worship after me? Do you understand? The meaning is not "What will you worship after me," as if I were your object of worship now, so whom will you worship after me? That is definitely not the intended meaning.

﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. ﴿We will worship your God﴾: they began with it because they were addressing him. ﴿And the God of your fathers﴾: "fathers" is the plural of "father." So who are they? Ibrahim, who in relation to him is a grandfather, or not?

* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And Isma'il, who in relation to him is an uncle, and Ishaq, who in relation to him is a direct father. As for applying the title of fatherhood to Ibrahim and to Ishaq, the matter is clear, is it not?

* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because Ishaq is his father, and Ibrahim is his grandfather, and a grandfather is a father. Indeed, God said to this nation, between which and Ibrahim there are ages: ﴿the religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ [al-Hajj 78]. But the difficulty lies in Isma'il being a father to him while being his uncle. It is said, as the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Umar: "Did you not realize that the paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father?" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (1468) and Muslim (983/11), with his wording, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] The "sinw" (twin) is a branch or two branches that share one root. So he is mentioned along with the fathers, because he is the twin of the father, since the uncle is the twin of the father. And as the Messenger ﷺ said: "The maternal aunt is in the position of the mother" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2699) and Muslim (1783/91), from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him; the wording is al-Bukhari's]. Likewise we say: the uncle is in the position of the father. Is this understood, everyone?

It is also said that this is a case of taghlib (predominance of one term over another), and that the word "father" is not applied to an uncle in its literal sense except when it is paired with the real father. Based on this, if we say, for example, there is no difficulty at all, because taghlib is permissible in the Arabic language. It is said: "al-Qamarān" (the two moons), and what is meant by them?

* The students: The sun and the moon.
* Shaykh: The sun and the moon. It is also said: "al-'Umarān" (the two 'Umars), and who are they?

* Student: Abu Bakr and 'Umar.
* Shaykh: Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

As for His saying ﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾, what is the grammatical case (i'rab) of ﴿Ibrahim﴾?

* Student: It is an apposition (badal).
* Shaykh: An apposition from ﴿your fathers﴾. And there is a reading ﴿Ibrahama﴾.

﴿One God﴾: ﴿God﴾ (ilahan) here is a circumstantial accusative (hal). They call it a preparatory circumstantial (hal muwatta'ah), but that is based on the view that "ilah" is not a derived noun. The correct view is that it is derived, and that it means "mallah" (one who is worshipped). On this basis it is a genuine circumstantial (hal mu'assasah), not a preparatory one, because the preparatory circumstantial is one that paves the way for a derived noun, such as ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 2]. Here "Qur'anan" is not derived, whereas the circumstantial, as we have explained earlier, is derived. Some scholars said it is like that, and this is based on the view that "Allah" and "ilah" are not derived. The correct view is that they are derived. On this basis, ﴿ilahan﴾ is in the accusative as a...?

* Student: The circumstantial.
* Shaykh: The circumstantial. ﴿Wahidan﴾ (one) is another circumstantial, repeated. ﴿God, one God﴾: we worship Him as one God. This is evidence that worship (ibadah) and divinity (uluhiyyah) have one meaning, but worship is considered in relation to the worshipper, and divinity in relation to the God. For this reason, the scholars call the doctrine of Tawhid "Tawhid al-'Ibadah," and some say "Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah."

* Student: And if it is a preparatory circumstantial, what is the grammatical case of ﴿wahidan﴾?
* Shaykh: A circumstantial, in any case.
* Student: Would it not become an apposition, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, it would not be an apposition.
* Student: An apposition from ﴿ilahan﴾.
* Shaykh: No, it would not be an apposition, because an apposition means that if you delete the substituted noun, the sentence still stands, and here the sentence would not stand.
* Student: And what is the benefit of saying it is a circumstantial, since "one" is understood from your saying "God" (ilah)?
* Shaykh: No, "ilahan" is indefinite, and the indefinite conveys generality but does not preclude sharing. If I said to you, for example, "Honor a man," does that mean: "and do not honor anyone else"?

* Student: No.
* Shaykh: No, it does not convey that.
* Student: Would it not be an emphasis, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, it would not. If they had said, "We worship none but a God," perhaps, but it does not indicate unity unless they say "wahidan" (one).

﴿One God, and we are to Him Muslims﴾. ﴿We﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿Muslims﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and ﴿to Him﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) attached to ﴿Muslims﴾. It was placed before it to convey exclusivity (hasr) in meaning, and to observe the rhyme of the verses (fawasil al-ayat) in form. ﴿And we are to Him﴾: that is, to this One God, glorified and exalted, we are Muslims. Islam means submission and sincerity. ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Al 'Imran 20], meaning I made it purely for God. It is applied to submission, which is outward and inward Islam.

Yes. Continuity and permanence, unlike a verbal sentence, which conveys renewal and continuity.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾. The pronoun ﴿that﴾ refers to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and those who preceded them. The Jews used to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ about these figures, so God explained that these are a nation (ummah). Here "ummah" means a group, and in the Qur'an it has several meanings. The first meaning: a group, as here. What is the second meaning?

* Student: The second meaning: that which follows one religion.
* Shaykh: No, that is a subset of the group. A group upon one religion is an ummah.
* Student: A period of time.
* Shaykh: A period of time. Such as?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And he who was saved of the two and remembered after a time (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45].
* Shaykh: ﴿And he who was saved of the two said, and remembered after a time (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45], meaning after a period of time. The third?

* Student: A leader (imam).
* Shaykh: A leader. Such as?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation (ummah)﴾ [al-Nahl 120].
* Shaykh: Because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾. Yes. After that?

* Student: (...) meaning?
* Shaykh: Yes, meaning a leader? ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾?
* Student: A model.
* Shaykh: We already mentioned it.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22].
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: A way.
* Shaykh: Yes, a way and a creed. ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾ means upon a way and a creed that we follow. So "ummah" in the Noble Qur'an has four meanings.

﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾: it has gone by. ﴿It will have what it earned, and you will have what you earned﴾ [al-Baqarah 134]. You will not be asked about what they did, and they will not be asked about what you did. How excellent is this verse to recite in every situation resembling this. For example, if some people say: "Some of the Companions did such-and-such"? You may say: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away; it will have what it earned, and you will have what you earned﴾. Like what is related of "the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, who was asked about what happened among the Companions, and he said to them: 'That is blood that Allah cleansed our swords from, so we will cleanse our tongues from it'" [Related by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah (9/114) with the wording: "That is blood that Allah cleansed my hands from, so I do not wish to dye my tongue with it"], may Allah have mercy on him. This is a great statement. Based on this, dispute about those who came before has no place. Finished. ﴿They have what they earned, and you have what you earned﴾. But the dispute is about the present matter, and that is what truth must be made clear in and falsehood refuted in. ﴿They have what they earned, and you have what you earned, and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾. You are not responsible. You will be asked about what...?

* The students: About what you do.
* Shaykh: About what you used to do. As for about what they used to do, no, you will not be asked, because their reckoning is with God, the Mighty and Majestic, and you will not be asked about them. This is why it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not revile the dead, for they have gone to what they put forward" [Related by al-Bukhari (6516) from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her]. In another wording: "lest you harm the living" [Related by al-Tirmidhi (1982) and Ahmad in his Musnad (18209) from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, may Allah be pleased with him]. And they said...

* Student: Is there not a reading "and they will not be asked (...)"?
* Shaykh: What I have is "and you will not be asked," there is no variant reading.
* Student: If there is one, would the meaning not hold?
* Shaykh: It would not be sound: "(and they will not be asked about what they used to do)." How would "they will not be asked" make sense? Who would ask them?
* Student: It does not work?
* Shaykh: It does not work.

﴿They say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided﴾. ("Hud") is the plural of ("ha'id"), as we studied in al-Bukhari, like "'awdh," the plural of "'a'idh." ﴿Hudan﴾ means from the Jews. Who says ﴿Be Jews﴾?

* The students: The Jews.
* Shaykh: The Jews. ﴿Or Christians﴾ is said by the Christians. ﴿And you will be guided﴾: he did not say "you are guided," even though it is a present-tense verb that is raised by the presence of the nun. Why was the nun dropped? Because it is the answer to the imperative. We have previously discussed, I think yesterday or before, whether the answer to the imperative is jussive by itself, or jussive by an implied condition. There are two views among the grammarians, and the correct view is that it is jussive by itself, because it does not need an estimated condition. Those who say this are the Jews and the Christians, addressing whom? They address the Muslims. They say: If you want guidance, then be Jews or Christians. Like the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) within this nation. That is, the followers of other religions in relation to the nation in general say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." The people of innovation, in relation to the People of the Sunnah and the Community, say: "Be such-and-such, and you will be guided." The Ash'aris say: "Be Ash'aris, and you will be guided." The Mu'tazilites say: "Be Mu'tazilites, and you will be guided." The Qadianis say: "Be Qadianis, and you will be guided." The Tijanis say: "Be Tijanis, and you will be guided." The Sufis say: "Be Sufis, and you will be guided." And on this basis, make your analogies.

*(The poet says):*
"Each claims union with Layla, but Layla does not acknowledge them in that."
Each one says: the truth is with me. But ﴿If you dispute about anything, refer it back to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59]. For this reason God said: ﴿Say﴾ in response to those who call you to Judaism from the Jews, or to Christianity from the Christians: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion (millah)...﴾. Is "bal" here for abrupt rejection (idrab ibtali) or for transition (idrab intiqali)?

* The students: For rejection (ibtali).
* Shaykh: For rejection, because it cancels what preceded it. That is: "rather, we do not follow him, and we will not be Jews or Christians." ﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim﴾. By this explanation that I mentioned to you, it becomes clear to us in what way ﴿millah﴾ is in the accusative?

* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: It is an object of an implied verb, whose estimate is: "Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim." "Millah" means religion, as previously mentioned, and the religion of Ibrahim is Tawhid, meaning we follow the Tawhid of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and submission to Him, because Ibrahim ﴿his Lord said to him: Submit. He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah 131]. This is the religion (millah).

﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf﴾. ﴿Ḥanīfan﴾ is grammatically a circumstantial (ḥal) from ﴿Ibrahim﴾. It is one of the curiosities that a circumstantial be from the genitive-attached noun (mudaf ilayh). Is there anything in Ibn Malik's words that points to this?

* Student: Yes, it is his saying: "And do not permit..."
* Shaykh: "A time-noun..."
* Student: "And does not come..." I do not know.
* Student: His saying:
"Or it was a part of what is attributed to it, or like its part, so do not err."
* Shaykh: What is "Or it was a part of what is attributed to it"?
* Student:
"And do not permit a circumstantial from the attributed noun to it, unless the attributed noun requires its action."

* Shaykh: "Or it was a part of what is attributed to it, or like its part, so do not err." This falls under his saying: "...... or like its part, so do not err." He said: ﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf﴾ is a circumstantial from ﴿Ibrahim﴾. Is this circumstantial a fixed (lazimah) circumstantial or a changing (mutanaqqilah) circumstantial?

* Student: Fixed.
* Shaykh: Fixed. Then it has no implication. It does not mean that Ibrahim was sometimes a ḥanīf and sometimes inclined away, not a ḥanīf. Rather, he was ḥanīf, a fixed attribute of his, peace be upon him. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾. This is an emphasis of His saying ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, because the ḥanīf is one who inclines away from everything other than Tawhid, derived from "ḥanaf al-rijl," meaning the inclination of the foot. So he inclines away from everything other than Tawhid. Therefore ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ is an emphasis of this circumstantial, a semantic emphasis (tawkid ma'nawi), not a grammatical one. It is not a grammatical emphasis, because grammatical emphasis is well known, and it is not of this form. But it is a semantic emphasis, meaning that he, peace be upon him, was not of the polytheists. Was he not of the polytheists in what has passed, or in what is to come?

* Student: In what has passed.
* Shaykh: We said: "kāna" (was), when it does not indicate an event, indicates that its subject is characterized by its predicate, like ﴿And God was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa' 96]. Does that mean that God was that in the past and not now? Or is He characterized by forgiveness and mercy? He is characterized by it. So His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ does not mean that he was not so during the past part of his life and then became so. Rather, it means that this attribute is negated from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 133–135 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿from among the polytheists﴾ — does it encompass the negation of both minor and major shirk, or not? Shirk, as is well known among us, is minor and major. This is the path we follow; the Messenger ﷺ followed it, and we follow it, God willing, and we hope that Allah will let us die upon it. This is the true Hanifite creed (al-millah al-Hanifiyyah) that brings the servant to his Lord. ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153].

Then Allah, the Exalted, said, commanding this Ummah to declare this great creed: ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 136] — we believe in Allah. Faith (iman) is the affirmation of the heart that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. This is the view of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah. As for the Murji'ah, among whom are the Ash'arites, faith is merely affirmation by the heart, and according to them it neither increases nor decreases. Ibn al-Qayyim and others among the people of the Sunnah said: If you say that faith is merely affirmation by the heart, then Iblis is a believer, because he acknowledges Allah, saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad 82]; so, according to this, he would be a believer.

* Student: "Affirmation by the heart that necessarily entails...?"

* Shaykh: "That necessarily entails acceptance and submission. According to your view, Abu Talib would also be a believer, because he affirmed [the truth]. This is one of the most false opinions — one of the most false opinions. So we say: faith is affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission."

* Student: "And how did they respond, O Shaykh? How did they answer this very strong objection?"

* Shaykh: "That is, how do they respond to this?"

* Student: "Does your remark not include Iblis and others?"

* Shaykh: "Yes indeed. They distort [the texts] just as they distorted the verses and hadiths about the Divine Attributes. They say: his arrogance in refusing to prostrate is evidence that he is not a believer. We say to them: how can it be evidence that he is not a believer when he affirms [Allah]? Is a person held accountable for what he does not affirm? Is a speaker held accountable for something contrary to his utterance? — we do not say 'a person,' because Satan is not a human being."

* Student: "No. And at the last moment he says, 'O Lord,' even at the last minute?"

* Shaykh: "Who?"

* Student: "Iblis affirms at the last minute."

* Shaykh: "Yes, yes."

* Student: "And as he was descending from Paradise, he still says:"

* Shaykh: "Yes indeed."

* Student: ﴿My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Hijr 36].

* Shaykh: "Yes, yes. The point is, in any case, the people of falsehood distort words from their places. This is the method of all the people of falsehood regarding evidences: when they are unable to refute the chain of narration and its authenticity, they manage to do so. Even if a hadith is in the Two Sahihs, they say: this is a solitary report (khabar ahad) and does not establish creedal matters. This is their method — and we seek refuge in Allah. Thus, all the narrators of the Two Sahihs, if the hadith is not mutawatir, they have criticized it and said that their reports cannot be used as evidence for any creedal matter at all. They have demolished half the Shari'ah or more. Is not the majority of the Shari'ah solitary reports?"

* The students: "Solitary reports."

* Shaykh: "Solitary reports. The majority of the Shari'ah consists of solitary reports. In truth, this view is false even in practical matters. When a person performs an action that is not a matter of creed, is it possible for him to act without believing that it is from the command of Allah?"

* Student: "He must believe it."

* Shaykh: "He must believe it. So then, physical acts are based on what?"

* The students: "On creed."

* Shaykh: "On creed. So according to their view, we would conclude: then we do not establish practical rulings either, since one cannot act upon a ruling without believing that the one who ruled it is Allah. The point is that we say: these false foundations regarding faith — that it is mere affirmation, and that it neither increases nor decreases — are the general doctrine of the Murji'ah. Who are the Murji'ah? The Ash'arites and the Jahmiyyah. The Jahmiyyah are also Murji'ah, and for this reason the Ash'arites agree with the Jahmiyyah on the question of irja' (deferral); they agree with them. The Mu'tazilah agree with the Jahmiyyah on the question of the Attributes and deny them."

* Student: "(...)."

* Shaykh: "The Attributes, the Attributes of Allah."

* Student: "(...)?"

* Shaykh: "The Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah agree on the Attributes, but they differ on the question of faith. The Mu'tazilah say: faith is speech, creed, and action, a unified whole; if part of it is lost, all of it is lost. For this reason they regard the perpetrator of a major sin as having left faith. Note that the people of falsehood declare one another misguided in some matters — I mean, they mislead one another, although they may not rule them to be disbelievers, but they say: these are astray. So then, what is faith in the language?"

* The students: "Affirmation."

* Shaykh: "Affirmation. And in the Shari'ah: (...). And this is a claim (...)."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons: What will you worship after me?﴾ [al-Baqarah 133], to the end.

* From this noble verse is derived: that tawhid is the testament of the prophets, by His saying: ﴿What will you worship after me? They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾.

* Among its benefits: that death is a reality even for the prophets. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾ [Al 'Imran 144].

* Among them: the permissibility of making a bequest at the approach of one's end, by His saying: ﴿And Ibrahim instructed his sons with it﴾ before this, and ﴿when he said to his sons: What will you worship after me? They said: We will worship your God﴾ — and this is like a testament to them. However, it is required that the one making the bequest be conscious of what he says; if he is not conscious of what he says, his bequest is not valid.

* And it is derived from this: the preference of the correct view that the grandfather is a father. From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿The God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾ — for Ibrahim was his grandfather, not his father."

* Among the benefits of the verse: that it is permissible to apply the term "father" to an uncle, by way of precedence (taghlib). From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿and Isma'il﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿And Isma'il﴾ — for Isma'il was an uncle, not a father."

* Among them: that the sons of Ya'qub were upon tawhid, since they said: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾, and there is no doubt that this is tawhid on their part.

* Also among them, among the benefits of the verse: following the fathers. Human souls are naturally inclined to follow their fathers; but if it is upon truth, it is truth, and if it is upon falsehood, it is falsehood, by their saying: ﴿and the God of your fathers﴾. For this reason, those who attended the death of Abu Talib said to him: "Will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (1360) and Muslim (24/39) from the hadith of al-Musayyib ibn Hazn.]

* Among the benefits of the verse: the sincerity of Islam to Allah, where He said: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾. The ﴿Him﴾ — the aspect of sincerity lies in fronting the object: in ﴿lahu﴾, because ﴿lahu﴾ is connected to ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, so it is an object fronted, and it is known that fronting the object conveys restriction (hasr).

* Among them: the affirmation of Allah's oneness, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿one God﴾.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* From this verse is derived: that one should not occupy oneself with what the fathers used to do, by His saying: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾, meaning: they have now passed on and submitted to Allah. As for you, O Jews of the Prophet's time (peace be upon him), you must consider what you have earned for yourselves. Occupying oneself with what the fathers were upon is a waste of time and may be harmful.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it indicates that we should remain silent about what occurred among the Companions, or not?

* Student: "Yes indeed."

* Shaykh: "Because we say as Allah said to those people: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn.﴾ So we are now concerned with ourselves. As for what happened between Mu'awiyah and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, or between 'Ali and 'A'ishah, and the like, this is a matter that does not concern us now. Our duty is to say: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any resentment toward those who believe. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Hashr 10]."

* Student: "Does this include other than the Companions?"

* Shaykh: "Others besides the Companions are also included, and a person should not occupy himself with such matters, but should look to what benefits him in his religion and his worldly life."

* Among them: that a person is [responsible for] his own deeds, by His saying: ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn﴾. No one is given credit for another's deeds, nor is anything taken from him for them: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38].

* Among them: that the later generation is not asked about the deeds of the earlier one, or not?

* The students: "Yes."

* Shaykh: "The reverse? Is the earlier asked about the deeds of the later?"

* Student: "Perhaps."

* Shaykh: "Perhaps. The earlier may be asked about the deeds of the later, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas 41]. The earlier one may be a person of innovation who is followed in his innovation, so he becomes one who points to misguidance; upon him is its burden and the burden of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection. Do you understand? But the later one is not asked about the deeds of the earlier one."

If it is said: Does the end of the verse nullify its beginning? ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn, and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾ — the answer is: No; for if they called to misguidance or to truth and we later followed them, then this is from their earnings, so for them is what they earned.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the justice of Allah, the Exalted, and that He does not hold anyone accountable for what he did not do, by His saying: ﴿and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* Among them: the affirmation of questioning, and that a person will be questioned. From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾. The explicit wording of the verse is clear: the negation of being asked about the deeds of others; its implicit meaning is the affirmation of being asked about one's own deeds, and that you are accountable for your deeds, and this is so."

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided. Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a Hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾. In this verse there is a call and a claim. Where is the call?

* The students: ﴿Be﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ — and the claim is ﴿you will be guided﴾."

* From it is derived: that the people of falsehood call to their misguidance and claim good in it. ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ is a call to misguidance; ﴿you will be guided﴾ is the claim that this is good. Likewise, these Jews inherited this from those who went astray in this Ummah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you."* [Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (21897), and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (6702), from the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi (may Allah be pleased with him).]

Are there people of innovation in the Ummah or not? They call to misguidance and claim that it is the truth. For example, the Mu'tazilah call to i'tizal and say: the good is with us, we are those who declare Allah free of deficiencies; and you, O affirmers of the Attributes, you are anthropomorphists (mujassimah), you are literalist anthropomorphists — is that so or not? And transcendence (tanzih) is with us. These called to misguidance and claimed it to be truth and good. Then the Ash'arites said: we are "the stump that the camel rubs against" (judhaylaha al-muhakkak), we are the people of the matter. You Mu'tazilah are in error, and the Salaf are anthropomorphists or delegationists (mufawwidah). If they are delegationists, they are at peace with them, because the delegationist according to the Ash'arites is one who does not go beyond reciting the Qur'an and the hadith. This is the delegationist: delegation of meaning and modality. For this reason you will find the Ash'arites saying: the方法 of the Salaf is delegation, and the method of the later scholars is affirmation of meanings. So our method is more knowledgeable and wiser than yours, O Salaf; and this is correct. If the method of the Salaf were, as they claim, merely recitation — as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who know not the Scripture except wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah 78] — merely reading, then, we would testify before Allah that the method of the later scholars is better, because it affirms that the Qur'an has a reality and a meaning, revealed so that we may worship Allah by this meaning.

But we say: you have lied about the method of the Salaf. What is the true method of the Salaf? Delegation regarding what they cannot know: the reality of these Attributes and their modality. No one can speak about this modality at all. But the meaning — do they delegate it or not? They affirm the meaning fitting to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So they are more knowledgeable, wiser, and safer. Do you understand? The Ash'arites say: we are the ones with the truth; follow us only. The truth is with us. You affirm for Allah only seven Attributes and seven states, with a difference between us and them regarding the modality of affirming these Attributes. For example: speech is affirmed by us and also by them, but what is speech according to them?

* Student: "The meaning subsisting in the self."

* Shaykh: "Speech is the meaning subsisting in the soul, one meaning whether it comes in the form of a question, a report, a command, or a prohibition, and whether it is the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. But it is expressed through these different expressions so that it may be a report, a command, a prohibition, a question, the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. This is not affirmation in reality. So the point, my brothers, is this: every caller to misguidance has in him a resemblance to the Jews and Christians. The callers to unveiling today say: let the woman be liberated, let her enjoy life, do not cover her, do not blind her eyes with the veil; let her walk with people — this is freedom, is it not? ﴿Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾ — the same thing: loosen the reins for her for the sake of freedom, because this is good. Is it just that you go out to stroll and sightsee and stand at this shop and that shop while she is confined in the house? Likewise, every caller to misguidance will surely adorn this misguidance with what deceives the stranger. So he resembles whom? The Jews and Christians."

* From the benefits of the verse: confronting falsehood with truth: ﴿Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a Hanif﴾. A person must follow a path, but is it truth or falsehood? Allah affirmed falsehood in His saying: ﴿Rather﴾; and we have mentioned in the commentary that ﴿bal﴾ here is for the retractive turning away (al-idrab al-ibtali).

* From the benefits of the verse: praise of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in that we are followers of him in his religion; this is one. Another aspect: describing him as a Hanif. A third aspect: describing him as not having been of the polytheists. Thus in this there is praise of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from three aspects. First, his imamate. What is the aspect of his being an imam?

* The students: (...).

* Shaykh: "In that we are commanded to follow him, and the one followed is the imam. Second, that he is a Hanif, inclining away from every religion other than Islam. Third: he had no shirk in his deeds, ﷺ."

* From the benefits of the verse: that shirk is impossible for the prophets, by His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾.

* Among them: that Judaism and Christianity are a type of shirk, because His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾, in contrast to their call to Judaism and Christianity, indicates that they are a type of shirk. Everyone who disbelieves in Allah has in him some type of shirk; but if he takes a god, it is shirk in reality and actuality, and otherwise it is shirk in the sense of following desire.

* Student: "In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾, some grammarians say that ﴿Isma'il﴾ is conjoined to ﴿God﴾, meaning: the God of Isma'il and Ishaq?"

* Shaykh: "No, this is far-fetched; I say this is far-fetched, because it scatters the structure of the verse."

* Student: "It can be resolved as a matter of attribution..."

* Shaykh: "No, this is well known in the Arabic language. The Messenger said, peace be upon him: 'The paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father'* [Related by Muslim (983/11) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. There is no omission here."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 2, verses 133–135 (part 1 of 2)**

He said: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ Is the (am) here connected (muttasilah) or disconnected (munqati'ah)?

* Student: Disconnected.
* Another student: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected? The connected (muttasilah) "am" is the one that comes between two equal things, as we studied in rhetoric (balaghah). Here it does not come between two equal things, so it is disconnected. The grammarians say that the disconnected "am" has the meaning of "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah. So, "bal" and the interrogative hamzah, meaning the interrogative hamzah. The meaning of ﴿Or were you﴾ is: "Rather, were you witnesses?"

As for His saying ﴿you were﴾, the pronoun refers to the Jews, the Jews who claimed that they were upon the truth and that this was the bequest of their father Ya'qub, and who adhered to what they were upon. It may also refer to all those addressed, and the intended meaning would then be to inform them of what happened from Ya'qub when death approached him. This possibility is preferable, because there is no evidence here that it refers to the Jews. Rather, the verses are all general, and they are also disconnected from many earlier verses about the Jews. So the meaning is an affirmation of what Ya'qub bequeathed when he died.

As for His saying ﴿witnesses﴾, it is the plural of shahid or shahid, meaning present.

As for His saying ﴿when﴾ (idh) ﴿approached﴾, this idh is a noun of time built on sukun in a position of nasb, meaning: at the time when Ya'qub's death approached. As for His saying ﴿approached Ya'qub, death﴾, why is it in the accusative (nasb) even though it comes after the verb? Do you say "approached Ya'qubu" or "approached Ya'quba"?

* Student: "Approached Ya'quba."
* Shaykh: Which means it is in the accusative after the verb? If you say, for example, "approached 'Abdullah"?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: An object? Where is the subject?
* Student: The subject is ﴿the death﴾.
* Shaykh: Excellent, may God bless you. Yes indeed. ﴿Ya'qub﴾ is in the accusative because it is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam), and ﴿the death﴾ is a delayed subject (fa'il mu'akhkhar). Do you understand? Because what approaches is death, and what is approached is Ya'qub. So it is a fronted direct object.

﴿When death approached Ya'qub, when he said﴾: this ﴿when﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿when﴾. That is, "when death approached, when he said." That is, "Or were you witnesses also when he said."

﴿to his sons: What will you worship after me?﴾ Who are the sons of Ya'qub? Isma'il? Yusuf and his brothers, eleven men. Death approached him, so his sons were present, or he had them brought, and he said to them: ﴿What will you worship after me?﴾

As for His saying ﴿after me﴾, it means after my time, not after my essence, because they were not worshipping him. They worship God. So the meaning of ﴿after me﴾ is after my death, that is, after the time in which I am present with you. Now you worship God, so what will you worship after me? Do you understand? The meaning is not "What will you worship after me," as if I were your object of worship now, so whom will you worship after me? That is definitely not the intended meaning.

﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. ﴿We will worship your God﴾: they began with it because they were addressing him. ﴿And the God of your fathers﴾: "fathers" is the plural of "father." So who are they? Ibrahim, who in relation to him is a grandfather, or not?

* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And Isma'il, who in relation to him is an uncle, and Ishaq, who in relation to him is a direct father. As for applying the title of fatherhood to Ibrahim and to Ishaq, the matter is clear, is it not?

* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because Ishaq is his father, and Ibrahim is his grandfather, and a grandfather is a father. Indeed, God said to this nation, between which and Ibrahim there are ages: ﴿the religion of your father Ibrahim﴾ [al-Hajj 78]. But the difficulty lies in Isma'il being a father to him while being his uncle. It is said, as the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Umar: "Did you not realize that the paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father?" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (1468) and Muslim (983/11), with his wording, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] The "sinw" (twin) is a branch or two branches that share one root. So he is mentioned along with the fathers, because he is the twin of the father, since the uncle is the twin of the father. And as the Messenger ﷺ said: "The maternal aunt is in the position of the mother" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2699) and Muslim (1783/91), from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him; the wording is al-Bukhari's]. Likewise we say: the uncle is in the position of the father. Is this understood, everyone?

It is also said that this is a case of taghlib (predominance of one term over another), and that the word "father" is not applied to an uncle in its literal sense except when it is paired with the real father. Based on this, if we say, for example, there is no difficulty at all, because taghlib is permissible in the Arabic language. It is said: "al-Qamarān" (the two moons), and what is meant by them?

* The students: The sun and the moon.
* Shaykh: The sun and the moon. It is also said: "al-'Umarān" (the two 'Umars), and who are they?

* Student: Abu Bakr and 'Umar.
* Shaykh: Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

As for His saying ﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾, what is the grammatical case (i'rab) of ﴿Ibrahim﴾?

* Student: It is an apposition (badal).
* Shaykh: An apposition from ﴿your fathers﴾. And there is a reading ﴿Ibrahama﴾.

﴿One God﴾: ﴿God﴾ (ilahan) here is a circumstantial accusative (hal). They call it a preparatory circumstantial (hal muwatta'ah), but that is based on the view that "ilah" is not a derived noun. The correct view is that it is derived, and that it means "mallah" (one who is worshipped). On this basis it is a genuine circumstantial (hal mu'assasah), not a preparatory one, because the preparatory circumstantial is one that paves the way for a derived noun, such as ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 2]. Here "Qur'anan" is not derived, whereas the circumstantial, as we have explained earlier, is derived. Some scholars said it is like that, and this is based on the view that "Allah" and "ilah" are not derived. The correct view is that they are derived. On this basis, ﴿ilahan﴾ is in the accusative as a...?

* Student: The circumstantial.
* Shaykh: The circumstantial. ﴿Wahidan﴾ (one) is another circumstantial, repeated. ﴿God, one God﴾: we worship Him as one God. This is evidence that worship (ibadah) and divinity (uluhiyyah) have one meaning, but worship is considered in relation to the worshipper, and divinity in relation to the God. For this reason, the scholars call the doctrine of Tawhid "Tawhid al-'Ibadah," and some say "Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah."

* Student: And if it is a preparatory circumstantial, what is the grammatical case of ﴿wahidan﴾?
* Shaykh: A circumstantial, in any case.
* Student: Would it not become an apposition, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, it would not be an apposition.
* Student: An apposition from ﴿ilahan﴾.
* Shaykh: No, it would not be an apposition, because an apposition means that if you delete the substituted noun, the sentence still stands, and here the sentence would not stand.
* Student: And what is the benefit of saying it is a circumstantial, since "one" is understood from your saying "God" (ilah)?
* Shaykh: No, "ilahan" is indefinite, and the indefinite conveys generality but does not preclude sharing. If I said to you, for example, "Honor a man," does that mean: "and do not honor anyone else"?

* Student: No.
* Shaykh: No, it does not convey that.
* Student: Would it not be an emphasis, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, it would not. If they had said, "We worship none but a God," perhaps, but it does not indicate unity unless they say "wahidan" (one).

﴿One God, and we are to Him Muslims﴾. ﴿We﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿Muslims﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and ﴿to Him﴾ is a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) attached to ﴿Muslims﴾. It was placed before it to convey exclusivity (hasr) in meaning, and to observe the rhyme of the verses (fawasil al-ayat) in form. ﴿And we are to Him﴾: that is, to this One God, glorified and exalted, we are Muslims. Islam means submission and sincerity. ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Al 'Imran 20], meaning I made it purely for God. It is applied to submission, which is outward and inward Islam.

Yes. Continuity and permanence, unlike a verbal sentence, which conveys renewal and continuity.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾. The pronoun ﴿that﴾ refers to Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, and those who preceded them. The Jews used to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ about these figures, so God explained that these are a nation (ummah). Here "ummah" means a group, and in the Qur'an it has several meanings. The first meaning: a group, as here. What is the second meaning?

* Student: The second meaning: that which follows one religion.
* Shaykh: No, that is a subset of the group. A group upon one religion is an ummah.
* Student: A period of time.
* Shaykh: A period of time. Such as?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿And he who was saved of the two and remembered after a time (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45].
* Shaykh: ﴿And he who was saved of the two said, and remembered after a time (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45], meaning after a period of time. The third?

* Student: A leader (imam).
* Shaykh: A leader. Such as?
* Student: His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation (ummah)﴾ [al-Nahl 120].
* Shaykh: Because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾. Yes. After that?

* Student: (...) meaning?
* Shaykh: Yes, meaning a leader? ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation﴾?
* Student: A model.
* Shaykh: We already mentioned it.
* Student: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22].
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: A way.
* Shaykh: Yes, a way and a creed. ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community (ummah)﴾ means upon a way and a creed that we follow. So "ummah" in the Noble Qur'an has four meanings.

﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾: it has gone by. ﴿It will have what it earned, and you will have what you earned﴾ [al-Baqarah 134]. You will not be asked about what they did, and they will not be asked about what you did. How excellent is this verse to recite in every situation resembling this. For example, if some people say: "Some of the Companions did such-and-such"? You may say: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away; it will have what it earned, and you will have what you earned﴾. Like what is related of "the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, who was asked about what happened among the Companions, and he said to them: 'That is blood that Allah cleansed our swords from, so we will cleanse our tongues from it'" [Related by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah (9/114) with the wording: "That is blood that Allah cleansed my hands from, so I do not wish to dye my tongue with it"], may Allah have mercy on him. This is a great statement. Based on this, dispute about those who came before has no place. Finished. ﴿They have what they earned, and you have what you earned﴾. But the dispute is about the present matter, and that is what truth must be made clear in and falsehood refuted in. ﴿They have what they earned, and you have what you earned, and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾. You are not responsible. You will be asked about what...?

* The students: About what you do.
* Shaykh: About what you used to do. As for about what they used to do, no, you will not be asked, because their reckoning is with God, the Mighty and Majestic, and you will not be asked about them. This is why it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not revile the dead, for they have gone to what they put forward" [Related by al-Bukhari (6516) from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her]. In another wording: "lest you harm the living" [Related by al-Tirmidhi (1982) and Ahmad in his Musnad (18209) from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, may Allah be pleased with him]. And they said...

* Student: Is there not a reading "and they will not be asked (...)"?
* Shaykh: What I have is "and you will not be asked," there is no variant reading.
* Student: If there is one, would the meaning not hold?
* Shaykh: It would not be sound: "(and they will not be asked about what they used to do)." How would "they will not be asked" make sense? Who would ask them?
* Student: It does not work?
* Shaykh: It does not work.

﴿They say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided﴾. ("Hud") is the plural of ("ha'id"), as we studied in al-Bukhari, like "'awdh," the plural of "'a'idh." ﴿Hudan﴾ means from the Jews. Who says ﴿Be Jews﴾?

* The students: The Jews.
* Shaykh: The Jews. ﴿Or Christians﴾ is said by the Christians. ﴿And you will be guided﴾: he did not say "you are guided," even though it is a present-tense verb that is raised by the presence of the nun. Why was the nun dropped? Because it is the answer to the imperative. We have previously discussed, I think yesterday or before, whether the answer to the imperative is jussive by itself, or jussive by an implied condition. There are two views among the grammarians, and the correct view is that it is jussive by itself, because it does not need an estimated condition. Those who say this are the Jews and the Christians, addressing whom? They address the Muslims. They say: If you want guidance, then be Jews or Christians. Like the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) within this nation. That is, the followers of other religions in relation to the nation in general say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." The people of innovation, in relation to the People of the Sunnah and the Community, say: "Be such-and-such, and you will be guided." The Ash'aris say: "Be Ash'aris, and you will be guided." The Mu'tazilites say: "Be Mu'tazilites, and you will be guided." The Qadianis say: "Be Qadianis, and you will be guided." The Tijanis say: "Be Tijanis, and you will be guided." The Sufis say: "Be Sufis, and you will be guided." And on this basis, make your analogies.

*(The poet says):*
"Each claims union with Layla, but Layla does not acknowledge them in that."
Each one says: the truth is with me. But ﴿If you dispute about anything, refer it back to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59]. For this reason God said: ﴿Say﴾ in response to those who call you to Judaism from the Jews, or to Christianity from the Christians: ﴿Say: Rather, the religion (millah)...﴾. Is "bal" here for abrupt rejection (idrab ibtali) or for transition (idrab intiqali)?

* The students: For rejection (ibtali).
* Shaykh: For rejection, because it cancels what preceded it. That is: "rather, we do not follow him, and we will not be Jews or Christians." ﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim﴾. By this explanation that I mentioned to you, it becomes clear to us in what way ﴿millah﴾ is in the accusative?

* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: It is an object of an implied verb, whose estimate is: "Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim." "Millah" means religion, as previously mentioned, and the religion of Ibrahim is Tawhid, meaning we follow the Tawhid of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and submission to Him, because Ibrahim ﴿his Lord said to him: Submit. He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah 131]. This is the religion (millah).

﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf﴾. ﴿Ḥanīfan﴾ is grammatically a circumstantial (ḥal) from ﴿Ibrahim﴾. It is one of the curiosities that a circumstantial be from the genitive-attached noun (mudaf ilayh). Is there anything in Ibn Malik's words that points to this?

* Student: Yes, it is his saying: "And do not permit..."
* Shaykh: "A time-noun..."
* Student: "And does not come..." I do not know.
* Student: His saying:
"Or it was a part of what is attributed to it, or like its part, so do not err."
* Shaykh: What is "Or it was a part of what is attributed to it"?
* Student:
"And do not permit a circumstantial from the attributed noun to it, unless the attributed noun requires its action."

* Shaykh: "Or it was a part of what is attributed to it, or like its part, so do not err." This falls under his saying: "...... or like its part, so do not err." He said: ﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf﴾ is a circumstantial from ﴿Ibrahim﴾. Is this circumstantial a fixed (lazimah) circumstantial or a changing (mutanaqqilah) circumstantial?

* Student: Fixed.
* Shaykh: Fixed. Then it has no implication. It does not mean that Ibrahim was sometimes a ḥanīf and sometimes inclined away, not a ḥanīf. Rather, he was ḥanīf, a fixed attribute of his, peace be upon him. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾. This is an emphasis of His saying ﴿ḥanīfan﴾, because the ḥanīf is one who inclines away from everything other than Tawhid, derived from "ḥanaf al-rijl," meaning the inclination of the foot. So he inclines away from everything other than Tawhid. Therefore ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ is an emphasis of this circumstantial, a semantic emphasis (tawkid ma'nawi), not a grammatical one. It is not a grammatical emphasis, because grammatical emphasis is well known, and it is not of this form. But it is a semantic emphasis, meaning that he, peace be upon him, was not of the polytheists. Was he not of the polytheists in what has passed, or in what is to come?

* Student: In what has passed.
* Shaykh: We said: "kāna" (was), when it does not indicate an event, indicates that its subject is characterized by its predicate, like ﴿And God was Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa' 96]. Does that mean that God was that in the past and not now? Or is He characterized by forgiveness and mercy? He is characterized by it. So His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ does not mean that he was not so during the past part of his life and then became so. Rather, it means that this attribute is negated from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 133–135 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿from among the polytheists﴾ — does it encompass the negation of both minor and major shirk, or not? Shirk, as is well known among us, is minor and major. This is the path we follow; the Messenger ﷺ followed it, and we follow it, God willing, and we hope that Allah will let us die upon it. This is the true Hanifite creed (al-millah al-Hanifiyyah) that brings the servant to his Lord. ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 153].

Then Allah, the Exalted, said, commanding this Ummah to declare this great creed: ﴿Say: We believe in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 136] — we believe in Allah. Faith (iman) is the affirmation of the heart that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. This is the view of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah. As for the Murji'ah, among whom are the Ash'arites, faith is merely affirmation by the heart, and according to them it neither increases nor decreases. Ibn al-Qayyim and others among the people of the Sunnah said: If you say that faith is merely affirmation by the heart, then Iblis is a believer, because he acknowledges Allah, saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad 82]; so, according to this, he would be a believer.

* Student: "Affirmation by the heart that necessarily entails...?"

* Shaykh: "That necessarily entails acceptance and submission. According to your view, Abu Talib would also be a believer, because he affirmed [the truth]. This is one of the most false opinions — one of the most false opinions. So we say: faith is affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission."

* Student: "And how did they respond, O Shaykh? How did they answer this very strong objection?"

* Shaykh: "That is, how do they respond to this?"

* Student: "Does your remark not include Iblis and others?"

* Shaykh: "Yes indeed. They distort [the texts] just as they distorted the verses and hadiths about the Divine Attributes. They say: his arrogance in refusing to prostrate is evidence that he is not a believer. We say to them: how can it be evidence that he is not a believer when he affirms [Allah]? Is a person held accountable for what he does not affirm? Is a speaker held accountable for something contrary to his utterance? — we do not say 'a person,' because Satan is not a human being."

* Student: "No. And at the last moment he says, 'O Lord,' even at the last minute?"

* Shaykh: "Who?"

* Student: "Iblis affirms at the last minute."

* Shaykh: "Yes, yes."

* Student: "And as he was descending from Paradise, he still says:"

* Shaykh: "Yes indeed."

* Student: ﴿My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Hijr 36].

* Shaykh: "Yes, yes. The point is, in any case, the people of falsehood distort words from their places. This is the method of all the people of falsehood regarding evidences: when they are unable to refute the chain of narration and its authenticity, they manage to do so. Even if a hadith is in the Two Sahihs, they say: this is a solitary report (khabar ahad) and does not establish creedal matters. This is their method — and we seek refuge in Allah. Thus, all the narrators of the Two Sahihs, if the hadith is not mutawatir, they have criticized it and said that their reports cannot be used as evidence for any creedal matter at all. They have demolished half the Shari'ah or more. Is not the majority of the Shari'ah solitary reports?"

* The students: "Solitary reports."

* Shaykh: "Solitary reports. The majority of the Shari'ah consists of solitary reports. In truth, this view is false even in practical matters. When a person performs an action that is not a matter of creed, is it possible for him to act without believing that it is from the command of Allah?"

* Student: "He must believe it."

* Shaykh: "He must believe it. So then, physical acts are based on what?"

* The students: "On creed."

* Shaykh: "On creed. So according to their view, we would conclude: then we do not establish practical rulings either, since one cannot act upon a ruling without believing that the one who ruled it is Allah. The point is that we say: these false foundations regarding faith — that it is mere affirmation, and that it neither increases nor decreases — are the general doctrine of the Murji'ah. Who are the Murji'ah? The Ash'arites and the Jahmiyyah. The Jahmiyyah are also Murji'ah, and for this reason the Ash'arites agree with the Jahmiyyah on the question of irja' (deferral); they agree with them. The Mu'tazilah agree with the Jahmiyyah on the question of the Attributes and deny them."

* Student: "(...)."

* Shaykh: "The Attributes, the Attributes of Allah."

* Student: "(...)?"

* Shaykh: "The Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah agree on the Attributes, but they differ on the question of faith. The Mu'tazilah say: faith is speech, creed, and action, a unified whole; if part of it is lost, all of it is lost. For this reason they regard the perpetrator of a major sin as having left faith. Note that the people of falsehood declare one another misguided in some matters — I mean, they mislead one another, although they may not rule them to be disbelievers, but they say: these are astray. So then, what is faith in the language?"

* The students: "Affirmation."

* Shaykh: "Affirmation. And in the Shari'ah: (...). And this is a claim (...)."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons: What will you worship after me?﴾ [al-Baqarah 133], to the end.

* From this noble verse is derived: that tawhid is the testament of the prophets, by His saying: ﴿What will you worship after me? They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾.

* Among its benefits: that death is a reality even for the prophets. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾ [Al 'Imran 144].

* Among them: the permissibility of making a bequest at the approach of one's end, by His saying: ﴿And Ibrahim instructed his sons with it﴾ before this, and ﴿when he said to his sons: What will you worship after me? They said: We will worship your God﴾ — and this is like a testament to them. However, it is required that the one making the bequest be conscious of what he says; if he is not conscious of what he says, his bequest is not valid.

* And it is derived from this: the preference of the correct view that the grandfather is a father. From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿The God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾ — for Ibrahim was his grandfather, not his father."

* Among the benefits of the verse: that it is permissible to apply the term "father" to an uncle, by way of precedence (taghlib). From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿and Isma'il﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿And Isma'il﴾ — for Isma'il was an uncle, not a father."

* Among them: that the sons of Ya'qub were upon tawhid, since they said: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾, and there is no doubt that this is tawhid on their part.

* Also among them, among the benefits of the verse: following the fathers. Human souls are naturally inclined to follow their fathers; but if it is upon truth, it is truth, and if it is upon falsehood, it is falsehood, by their saying: ﴿and the God of your fathers﴾. For this reason, those who attended the death of Abu Talib said to him: "Will you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (1360) and Muslim (24/39) from the hadith of al-Musayyib ibn Hazn.]

* Among the benefits of the verse: the sincerity of Islam to Allah, where He said: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾. The ﴿Him﴾ — the aspect of sincerity lies in fronting the object: in ﴿lahu﴾, because ﴿lahu﴾ is connected to ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, so it is an object fronted, and it is known that fronting the object conveys restriction (hasr).

* Among them: the affirmation of Allah's oneness, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿one God﴾.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* From this verse is derived: that one should not occupy oneself with what the fathers used to do, by His saying: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away﴾, meaning: they have now passed on and submitted to Allah. As for you, O Jews of the Prophet's time (peace be upon him), you must consider what you have earned for yourselves. Occupying oneself with what the fathers were upon is a waste of time and may be harmful.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it indicates that we should remain silent about what occurred among the Companions, or not?

* Student: "Yes indeed."

* Shaykh: "Because we say as Allah said to those people: ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn.﴾ So we are now concerned with ourselves. As for what happened between Mu'awiyah and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, or between 'Ali and 'A'ishah, and the like, this is a matter that does not concern us now. Our duty is to say: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any resentment toward those who believe. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Hashr 10]."

* Student: "Does this include other than the Companions?"

* Shaykh: "Others besides the Companions are also included, and a person should not occupy himself with such matters, but should look to what benefits him in his religion and his worldly life."

* Among them: that a person is [responsible for] his own deeds, by His saying: ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn﴾. No one is given credit for another's deeds, nor is anything taken from him for them: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir 38].

* Among them: that the later generation is not asked about the deeds of the earlier one, or not?

* The students: "Yes."

* Shaykh: "The reverse? Is the earlier asked about the deeds of the later?"

* Student: "Perhaps."

* Shaykh: "Perhaps. The earlier may be asked about the deeds of the later, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾ [al-Qasas 41]. The earlier one may be a person of innovation who is followed in his innovation, so he becomes one who points to misguidance; upon him is its burden and the burden of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection. Do you understand? But the later one is not asked about the deeds of the earlier one."

If it is said: Does the end of the verse nullify its beginning? ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn, and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾ — the answer is: No; for if they called to misguidance or to truth and we later followed them, then this is from their earnings, so for them is what they earned.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the justice of Allah, the Exalted, and that He does not hold anyone accountable for what he did not do, by His saying: ﴿and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* Among them: the affirmation of questioning, and that a person will be questioned. From where is this taken?

* The students: ﴿and you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾. The explicit wording of the verse is clear: the negation of being asked about the deeds of others; its implicit meaning is the affirmation of being asked about one's own deeds, and that you are accountable for your deeds, and this is so."

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided. Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a Hanif, and he was not of the polytheists﴾. In this verse there is a call and a claim. Where is the call?

* The students: ﴿Be﴾.

* Shaykh: "﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ — and the claim is ﴿you will be guided﴾."

* From it is derived: that the people of falsehood call to their misguidance and claim good in it. ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ is a call to misguidance; ﴿you will be guided﴾ is the claim that this is good. Likewise, these Jews inherited this from those who went astray in this Ummah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you."* [Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (21897), and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (6702), from the hadith of Abu Waqid al-Laythi (may Allah be pleased with him).]

Are there people of innovation in the Ummah or not? They call to misguidance and claim that it is the truth. For example, the Mu'tazilah call to i'tizal and say: the good is with us, we are those who declare Allah free of deficiencies; and you, O affirmers of the Attributes, you are anthropomorphists (mujassimah), you are literalist anthropomorphists — is that so or not? And transcendence (tanzih) is with us. These called to misguidance and claimed it to be truth and good. Then the Ash'arites said: we are "the stump that the camel rubs against" (judhaylaha al-muhakkak), we are the people of the matter. You Mu'tazilah are in error, and the Salaf are anthropomorphists or delegationists (mufawwidah). If they are delegationists, they are at peace with them, because the delegationist according to the Ash'arites is one who does not go beyond reciting the Qur'an and the hadith. This is the delegationist: delegation of meaning and modality. For this reason you will find the Ash'arites saying: the方法 of the Salaf is delegation, and the method of the later scholars is affirmation of meanings. So our method is more knowledgeable and wiser than yours, O Salaf; and this is correct. If the method of the Salaf were, as they claim, merely recitation — as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who know not the Scripture except wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah 78] — merely reading, then, we would testify before Allah that the method of the later scholars is better, because it affirms that the Qur'an has a reality and a meaning, revealed so that we may worship Allah by this meaning.

But we say: you have lied about the method of the Salaf. What is the true method of the Salaf? Delegation regarding what they cannot know: the reality of these Attributes and their modality. No one can speak about this modality at all. But the meaning — do they delegate it or not? They affirm the meaning fitting to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So they are more knowledgeable, wiser, and safer. Do you understand? The Ash'arites say: we are the ones with the truth; follow us only. The truth is with us. You affirm for Allah only seven Attributes and seven states, with a difference between us and them regarding the modality of affirming these Attributes. For example: speech is affirmed by us and also by them, but what is speech according to them?

* Student: "The meaning subsisting in the self."

* Shaykh: "Speech is the meaning subsisting in the soul, one meaning whether it comes in the form of a question, a report, a command, or a prohibition, and whether it is the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. But it is expressed through these different expressions so that it may be a report, a command, a prohibition, a question, the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. This is not affirmation in reality. So the point, my brothers, is this: every caller to misguidance has in him a resemblance to the Jews and Christians. The callers to unveiling today say: let the woman be liberated, let her enjoy life, do not cover her, do not blind her eyes with the veil; let her walk with people — this is freedom, is it not? ﴿Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾ — the same thing: loosen the reins for her for the sake of freedom, because this is good. Is it just that you go out to stroll and sightsee and stand at this shop and that shop while she is confined in the house? Likewise, every caller to misguidance will surely adorn this misguidance with what deceives the stranger. So he resembles whom? The Jews and Christians."

* From the benefits of the verse: confronting falsehood with truth: ﴿Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a Hanif﴾. A person must follow a path, but is it truth or falsehood? Allah affirmed falsehood in His saying: ﴿Rather﴾; and we have mentioned in the commentary that ﴿bal﴾ here is for the retractive turning away (al-idrab al-ibtali).

* From the benefits of the verse: praise of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in that we are followers of him in his religion; this is one. Another aspect: describing him as a Hanif. A third aspect: describing him as not having been of the polytheists. Thus in this there is praise of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from three aspects. First, his imamate. What is the aspect of his being an imam?

* The students: (...).

* Shaykh: "In that we are commanded to follow him, and the one followed is the imam. Second, that he is a Hanif, inclining away from every religion other than Islam. Third: he had no shirk in his deeds, ﷺ."

* From the benefits of the verse: that shirk is impossible for the prophets, by His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾.

* Among them: that Judaism and Christianity are a type of shirk, because His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾, in contrast to their call to Judaism and Christianity, indicates that they are a type of shirk. Everyone who disbelieves in Allah has in him some type of shirk; but if he takes a god, it is shirk in reality and actuality, and otherwise it is shirk in the sense of following desire.

* Student: "In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾, some grammarians say that ﴿Isma'il﴾ is conjoined to ﴿God﴾, meaning: the God of Isma'il and Ishaq?"

* Shaykh: "No, this is far-fetched; I say this is far-fetched, because it scatters the structure of the verse."

* Student: "It can be resolved as a matter of attribution..."

* Shaykh: "No, this is well known in the Arabic language. The Messenger said, peace be upon him: 'The paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father'* [Related by Muslim (983/11) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. There is no omission here."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 136–141 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say, "We believe in Allah"﴾. "Say" (qooloo): to whom is the address? To the Messenger (ﷺ) and his entire community together. The meaning of "saying" here is saying with the tongue and with the heart. Saying with the tongue is uttering it, and saying with the heart is believing in it. The heart has speech and action, and the body has speech and action: the body's speech is with the tongue and its action is with the limbs; the heart's speech is its affirmation and acknowledgment of a thing, and its action is its movement, such as its love, its hope, its fear, its awe, and the like. These are movements of the heart. "Say with your tongues." And what comes next?

* The students: "And with your hearts."
* The Shaykh: "And with your hearts." ﴿We believe in Allah﴾. Faith (iman) has been discussed earlier many times: in the linguistic sense it is affirmation (tasdeeq), and in the legal sense it is affirmation that entails or necessitates acceptance and submission. ﴿We believe in Allah﴾: belief in Allah includes four matters: belief in His existence, belief in His lordship (rububiyyah), belief in His divinity (uluhiyyah), and belief in His names and attributes. Belief in Allah includes these four matters. Now let us consider: the communists who deny the existence of Allah, do they believe in Allah?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: Which of the four is missing from them? All four, all four. As long as they do not believe in existence, they are not believers in lordship, nor in divinity, nor in the names and attributes. Is that not so?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Those who believe in Allah but associate others with Him, and say, for example, that the qutb (the axis) or the ghawth (the helper) manages affairs, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) manages affairs, and the like: these believe in Allah in terms of existence, but they do not believe in lordship or divinity, nor in the names and attributes either.
