* And among its benefits: that the religion of Allah, exalted is He, is the best, most complete and most comprehensive of religions, and the most upright in serving the interests of the servants, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً﴾.
* And among its benefits: the obligation of sincerity, sincerity of worship to Him, as shown by His words: ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾, where the object is placed first to indicate exclusivity (*ḥaṣr*).
* And among them: that reason requires adherence to religion, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً﴾, for reason guides to the obligation, or that which is of reason, namely adhering to the best. Every person with sound reason, his reason commands him to adhere to the best.

Then He said: ﴿قُلْ أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ وَهُوَ رَبُّنَا وَرَبُّكُمْ وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُخْلِصُونَ﴾ (*Say: Do you dispute with us about Allah while He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him*).
* From this verse is derived: the rebuke of the Jews and Christians who dispute with the Muslims about Allah while acknowledging that He is their Lord, as shown by His words: ﴿قُلْ أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ وَهُوَ رَبُّنَا وَرَبُّكُمْ﴾.
* And among its benefits: the censure of one who disputes about a matter he acknowledges. They dispute about Allah while acknowledging that He is their Lord; He is our Lord and your Lord.
* And among them: the obligation of disassociation from the deeds of the disbelievers, as shown by His words: ﴿وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ﴾, for what is meant is disassociation from what they are upon.
* And among them: that a person should take pride in the truth he is upon, because He said: ﴿وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا﴾. We take pride in them and are free of your deeds.
* And among them: that it is not permissible to imitate the enemies of Allah, for imitation is conformity in action. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever imitates a people is one of them" [narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4031), from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both]. And here He says: ﴿وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ﴾, so we are distinct from you, and you are distinct from us.
* And among them: the obligation of sincerity to Allah, as shown by the placing of the object first in His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُخْلِصُونَ﴾.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ إِنَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطَ كَانُوا هُودًا أَوْ نَصَارَى﴾ (*Or do you say that Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the tribes were Jews or Christians?*). There are two readings: ﴿أَمْ يقُولُونَ﴾ (*am yaqūlūna*, "or do they say") and ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ﴾ (*am taqūlūna*, "or do you say"). On the second reading, ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ﴾ is part of what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded to say, because He said: ﴿قُلْ أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ﴾, meaning: "And say: Do you say that Ibrahim...?" As for the reading with the *yāʾ*, ﴿أَمْ يقُولُونَ﴾, this sentence is from the speech of Allah, as has passed.
* So among the benefits of this verse: the refutation of the claim of these Jews and Christians that Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the tribes were Jews or Christians. This claim is false. So what describes these people? Muslims. Islam describes them. Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the tribes were not Jews or Christians; rather they were Muslims submitting to Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
* And among them: referring the knowledge of these matters to Allah: ﴿قُلْ أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾ (*Say: Are you more knowing or is Allah?*).
* And among them: the refutation of the people of distortion (*taḥrīf*) concerning the names and attributes of Allah, who say: "What is permissible for Allah by reason we affirm, and what is impossible for Him by reason we deny, is it not so?"
* **Students:** Yes.
* **The Shaykh:** There are people who say this, such as the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'arites and others. We say to all of them in reply: ﴿أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾. Are you more knowledgeable about what is permissible for Allah, what is impossible for Him, and what is obligatory for Him, or is Allah more knowledgeable about what is impossible for Him, what is permissible for Him, and what is obligatory for Him? Allah is more knowing. This is in truth a binding, overwhelming and silencing argument against those who regulate the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, by their intellects, saying: "It is obligatory for Allah to have such-and-such, and impossible for Him to have such-and-such." ﴿أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾.
* And among the benefits of this verse: the gravity of concealing knowledge, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ كَتَمَ شَهَادَةً عِنْدَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (*And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah?*). The scholar of the Sharīʿah of Allah is a witness to Allah concerning this Sharīʿah, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿شَهِدَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ وَأُولُو الْعِلْمِ﴾ (*Allah witnesses that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge*) [Āl ʿImrān 18]. So every person who conceals knowledge has concealed a testimony he has from Allah. Moreover, in this is the gravity of its sin. From where is this derived?
* **Students:** ﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** ﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ كَتَمَ شَهَادَةً عِنْدَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾. For this reason it was said concerning His words, exalted is He: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ النَّبِيِّينَ وَالصِّدِّيقِينَ وَالشُّهَدَاءِ﴾ (*Those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets, the steadfast in truth, the martyrs*) [an-Nisāʾ 69]: it was said that what is meant by the martyrs (*shuhadāʾ*) are the people of knowledge.
* And among them: the perfection of Allah's knowledge and His watchfulness over His servants, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (*And Allah is not unaware of what you do*).
* And among them: the affirmation of negative attributes, which are what Allah negated from Himself. From where?
* **Students:** ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ﴾. This is a negative attribute, not a positive one. Negative attributes, as has passed with us, include the affirmation of the perfection of their opposite, because of the perfection of His watchfulness and His knowledge, glorified and exalted is He; He is not unaware of what we do.
* And among them: warning a person and cautioning him against disobedience. From where is it derived? Warning a person against disobedience, from where?
* **A student:** ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** How so? What is the aspect of this warning?
* **The student:** The affirmation that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is not unaware of...
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, but what is the aspect of the warning?
* **The student:** It means it warns the person: "Know, O person, that Allah is watching you in all your deeds."
* **The Shaykh:** So beware of disobedience. For example, when you threaten a person with something you say: "I am not unaware of you." ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾.
* And among them: the attribution of the deed to the doer, and in it is a refutation of the Jabriyyah, as shown by His words: ﴿عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾. Do you know its aspect? In it is the refutation of the Jabriyyah, who say that man does not act, but is compelled. Is it clear?
* **Students:** Yes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 136–141 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say, "We believe in Allah"﴾. "Say" (qooloo): to whom is the address? To the Messenger (ﷺ) and his entire community together. The meaning of "saying" here is saying with the tongue and with the heart. Saying with the tongue is uttering it, and saying with the heart is believing in it. The heart has speech and action, and the body has speech and action: the body's speech is with the tongue and its action is with the limbs; the heart's speech is its affirmation and acknowledgment of a thing, and its action is its movement, such as its love, its hope, its fear, its awe, and the like. These are movements of the heart. "Say with your tongues." And what comes next?

* The students: "And with your hearts."
* The Shaykh: "And with your hearts." ﴿We believe in Allah﴾. Faith (iman) has been discussed earlier many times: in the linguistic sense it is affirmation (tasdeeq), and in the legal sense it is affirmation that entails or necessitates acceptance and submission. ﴿We believe in Allah﴾: belief in Allah includes four matters: belief in His existence, belief in His lordship (rububiyyah), belief in His divinity (uluhiyyah), and belief in His names and attributes. Belief in Allah includes these four matters. Now let us consider: the communists who deny the existence of Allah, do they believe in Allah?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: Which of the four is missing from them? All four, all four. As long as they do not believe in existence, they are not believers in lordship, nor in divinity, nor in the names and attributes. Is that not so?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Those who believe in Allah but associate others with Him, and say, for example, that the qutb (the axis) or the ghawth (the helper) manages affairs, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) manages affairs, and the like: these believe in Allah in terms of existence, but they do not believe in lordship or divinity, nor in the names and attributes either.

Those who believe in Allah and in His lordship, and that He is the Lord who acts and creates, whom none shares in this, but they worship others alongside Him, saying: ﴿They only bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [az-Zumar 3]. In what did they believe? In existence and lordship, but not in divinity.

Those who believe in all of this but do not believe in the names and attributes: either they deny the names and attributes, or they deny the names but not the attributes, or they deny some of the attributes. These have not believed in Allah with respect to the names and attributes; they have not attained true faith, so their faith is deficient. Thus belief in Allah includes four matters: belief in His existence, in His lordship, in His divinity, and in His names and attributes.

﴿And what was revealed to us﴾: meaning, "and we believe in what was revealed to us." Here "mā" is a relative pronoun, built on sukun, in the position of a genitive, conjoined to the preceding word "Allah" (it is coordinated with "Allah"). And "what was revealed to us" includes the Qur'an, which is revealed, and it also includes the Sunnah, by His saying: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and the wisdom﴾ [an-Nisa 113]. The wisdom is the Sunnah. So "what was revealed to us" is the Qur'an and the Sunnah. ﴿And what was revealed to Ibrahim﴾: was something revealed to Ibrahim? Yes, it was revealed to him, because he was a prophet and messenger, so it was revealed to him. What was revealed to him? We know the scrolls that Allah mentioned in two places in the Qur'an. Where?

* A student: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Ibrahim﴾ [al-A'la 18-19].

* The Shaykh: ﴿The scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa﴾. And what else?

* A student: ﴿Has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Musa, and of Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾ [an-Najm 36-37].

* The Shaykh: Yes, in Surah an-Najm. And what was revealed to Isma'il: Isma'il was a prophet to whom something was revealed. We do not know what was revealed to him; we know nothing of it, but it was certainly revealed to him. Know that everyone mentioned in the Qur'an among the prophets is a prophet and messenger. Some people raise doubts, saying: is everyone mentioned in the Qur'an a messenger? Some of them Allah did not describe as messengers, but we say that he is a messenger. What is the evidence? ﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you; among them are those We have related to you, and among them are those We have not related to you. And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾ [Ghafir 78].

And He said in Surah an-Nisa: ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you﴾ [an-Nisa 164]. Every prophet mentioned in the Qur'an is a messenger, without exception. ﴿And what was revealed﴾.

* A student: I say: Adam?

* The Shaykh: No. Adam is not mentioned as having a people, and it is not mentioned that he was a prophet in the Qur'an. His story is mentioned.

* A student: Harun?

* The Shaykh: A prophet, a prophet and messenger.

* A student: Harun?

* The Shaykh: Yes, a messenger: ﴿So say: indeed, we are both messengers of your Lord﴾.

* A student: Qarun?

* The Shaykh: Qarun? No, he says Harun.

* The student: Harun?

* The Shaykh: ﴿Isma'il and Ishaq and Ya'qub and the tribes﴾. Ishaq and Ya'qub also had something revealed to them, but we do not know it; it is not mentioned what was revealed to them. The "asbat" is the plural of "sibt"; it is said they are the sons of Ya'qub, among whom is Yusuf. It is also said that what was revealed to the asbat means the prophets of the Children of Israel in general; all the prophets of the Children of Israel who were not named, since the Children of Israel descended from the sons of Ya'qub. So the meaning of the asbat is not the twelve sons of Ya'qub only, but all the prophets of the Children of Israel.

And His saying: ﴿And what was given to Musa and Isa, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord﴾. "What was given to Musa and Isa": what was bestowed. "Utiya" means "u'tiya" (was given), and "ataa" (came) means "ja'a" (came); that is, the triliteral "ataa" means "came," and the quadriliteral "aataa" means "gave." ﴿And We gave them a great kingdom﴾ [an-Nisa 54]: "ataynahum" means? 

* The students: We gave them.

* The Shaykh: We gave them. ﴿And We have brought you the truth﴾?

* A student: We brought you.

* The Shaykh: We brought you; it does not mean "We gave you." ﴿What was given to Musa﴾: what was bestowed. From where were they given, and what were they given?

* A student: Signs.

* The Shaykh: What they were given of signs, and also what they were given of revelation. Allah the Exalted gave them revelation and signs. Was Musa given signs?

* A student: The Torah.

* The Shaykh: No, the Torah is revelation. Of the signs there were nine: the hand, the staff, and what else?

* A student: (...) Subhanahu wa Ta'ala.

* The Shaykh: The nine signs that Allah mentioned: the hand, which he puts into his garment and it comes out white without harm; and the staff, in which there are three great signs: when he throws it, it turns into a serpent; when he strikes the rock with it, it gushes forth springs; and when he struck the sea with it, it split, and each part was like a great mountain. These are among the great signs of Allah, glory be to Him.

As for Isa, he was given great signs too, among them: that he would create from clay the form of a bird, a figure shaped like a bird, then breathe into it and it becomes a bird. In another reading, ﴿a bird﴾ (tair) becomes "ta'iran" (a flying bird). If we combine the two, since we have said that the two readings are two meanings, it becomes a bird and flies by the same act, a flying bird. Is it permissible for a person to make a statue in the shape of a bird?

* A student: No, it is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: If Allah permits it, it is permissible: ﴿And when you shape from clay like the form of a bird by My permission﴾ [al-Ma'idah 110]. If Allah permits it, it is permissible. When Allah permitted the angels to prostrate to Adam, indeed He commanded them to prostrate to Adam, their prostration to Adam became obedience, and their refusal became disbelief. When Iblis was arrogant, he disbelieved. Whereas no one prostrates to a human being now.

(...) He gives life to the dead by Allah's permission, and brings the dead out of their graves by Allah's permission; he revives them before burial and brings them out of their graves after burial: ﴿And when you bring forth the dead by My permission﴾ [al-Ma'idah 110]. This was among the signs of Allah given to Isa. The scholars said: the sign of Musa was the staff because in his time sorcery had reached its peak, and the sign of Isa was in bringing the dead to life and in healing the blind and the leper, because medicine had reached its peak in his time. Yes, and Allah the Exalted challenges every people with what suits their era, and this Qur'an is a sign for all time, because it is for all creation until the Day of Resurrection.

(...) Here someone may ask: why did He phrase it as ﴿What was revealed to us, and what was revealed to Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾ etc., and for Musa and Isa He said ﴿What was given to Musa and Isa﴾ and did not say "what was revealed to Musa and Isa"? Is there wisdom in the difference of expression or not?

We say: according to what appears to us, and Allah knows best, there is a verbal wisdom and a semantic wisdom. The verbal wisdom: so that the same meanings are not repeated with one word. If he had said "what was revealed and what was revealed," how many times would it be repeated? Four times: "what was revealed to us," "what was revealed to Ibrahim," "what was revealed to Musa," and "what was revealed to the prophets." It is well known that among the methods of eloquence is brevity in repeating words to a certain extent.

As for the semantic benefit: Musa's and Isa's religions remained until the time of revelation, their religions remained until the time of revelation, and their followers boasted of the signs they were given. The Christians say: Isa son of Maryam revived the dead, and did such and such; and these [the Jews] say that Allah split the sea for Musa, saved him and drowned his enemy, and the like. So Allah the Exalted made clear in this that this community believes in these signs and what was given of revelation and signs.

As for His saying: ﴿and what was given to the prophets from their Lord﴾, this, and Allah knows best, uses "what was given to the prophets" in a general sense, because the prophets mentioned in this verse are few relative to their number. Therefore He expressed it with "giving" to include all the signs they were given. Allah said: ﴿And We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Baqarah 163]. His saying: ﴿what was given to the prophets from their Lord﴾: "min" here indicates the starting point, because this giving is from Allah. In His saying "from their Lord" there is an attribution of lordship to them in a particular way, though Allah is the Lord of all; but this is a special lordship. In His saying "from their Lord," the meaning is that they themselves cannot bring these signs or this revelation; they receive it from Allah and are not independent in these signs. Even the Messenger (ﷺ), when asked for signs, could he bring them? No, he could not. Therefore when they proposed several signs, he said: ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord; am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ [al-Isra 93]. I do not possess the ability to bring signs: ﴿The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner﴾ [al-'Ankabut 50].

﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾: this sentence is included within the content of the statement. That is, say: "We believe" in this manner: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾. To whom does the pronoun refer? To the prophets.

His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ means: in belief, not in following; because in following we are commanded to follow whom? Muhammad (ﷺ), by His saying: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48]. So in the law we distinguish between them, and we follow only the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), which abrogated all previous religions. As for belief, and that they are messengers, that they are from Allah, and that they are truthful in what they brought, they are on equal footing with us: all of them are truthful in what they brought, and all of them are messengers from Allah. Does His saying "We make no distinction between any of them" also include ranks?

* A student: It does not include it.

* The Shaykh: Why? Because they differ in merit: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Baqarah 253]; ﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ [al-Isra 55]. So we have distinction in rank, distinction in law, and distinction in belief in them. Which of the three matters is it that we do not distinguish between any of them? Belief in them, and the conviction that they are truthful, and that they are messengers of Allah, mighty and majestic.

﴿And to Him we are Muslims﴾. He said "naḥnu" (we), and here He used the plural pronoun from His saying "Say, we believe in Allah" up to "and we," so that the believer feels that he and his brother are like one soul, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The believer to the believer is like a building, one part of it strengthening the other." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (481) and Muslim (2585/65) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with him).] That is, "and we" means all believers.

His saying: ﴿lahu﴾ (to Him): the pronoun refers to whom? To Allah, glory be to Him. That is, "and we are to Allah." This is the pronoun returning to the nearer antecedent, although the rule is that the pronoun refers to the nearest mention; here the pronoun refers to the earlier one, because it is ﴿We believe in Allah﴾, and ﴿and we are to Him﴾, meaning to Allah we are Muslims, even though several things came after it, yet it returns to Allah. If it is asked: what is the evidence that the pronoun returns to Allah the Mighty and Majestic? We say: the evidence for that is, first, the pronoun is singular, and second, sincerity is for whom? For Allah.

His saying: ﴿lahu muslimun﴾: he placed the object first for two purposes or two wisdoms: semantic and verbal. The semantic is to convey exclusivity, which we sometimes express as restriction. The verbal benefit is observing the endings (fawasil), the endings of the verses. If someone says: what is your proof that observing the endings is valid? We say: the proof is what Allah mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa"﴾ [Ta-Ha 70], although in another verse it is ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ [al-A'raf 122]. Here Harun was placed before Musa in observance of the verse endings. We know of nothing beyond this; there is no doubt that Musa is better than Harun. Accordingly, we say that in His saying ﴿nahnu lahu muslimun﴾, the fronting of the object is for two benefits: semantic and verbal.

His saying: ﴿muslimun﴾: "Islam" of one thing to another means its being exclusive to it. So the meaning of Islam here is complete submission to Allah the Mighty and Majestic with sincerity. Allah said: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good﴾ [al-Baqarah 112]. Here it is submission of intention: ﴿submits his face to Allah﴾. As for action, He said: ﴿while being a doer of good﴾. The sum is that Islam here includes sincere submission, complete sincere submission to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* A student: Shaykh, why is "al-asbat" in the genitive when it is coordinated with something in the accusative?

* The Shaykh: Where are the grammarians? A problem. He says: how is "al-asbat" in the genitive when it is coordinated with what?

* The student: With the accusative?

* The Shaykh: With the accusative.

* The students: With the genitive.

* The Shaykh: We say: it is coordinated with a genitive. Did you not read the noun that does not take tanwin because of foreignness (ajamah)?

* The student: Meaning all of them are subject to foreignness?

* The Shaykh: Yes, yes.

* The student: Ibrahim.

* The Shaykh: Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. Do you understand? The evidence for this, look at ﴿And what was revealed to Ibrahim﴾. Is "ila" not a preposition?

* The student: Yes indeed.

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. It is in the genitive by a fatha substituting for a kasra, because it is a noun that does not take tanwin, since these names are pre-Arabic.

﴿And to Him we are Muslims (136). And if they believe in the like of what you believe in﴾ [al-Baqarah 136-137].

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The predicate of "nahnu."

* The student: "Lahu" is a pronoun of separation (damir fasl).

* The Shaykh: "Lahu," no. It is a prepositional phrase governed by "muslimun."

* The student: "Nahnu."

* The Shaykh: A subject. "Nahnu muslimun lahu": we are submitters to Him.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...) The pronoun of separation does not contain the preposition lam (...). Furthermore, the pronoun of separation, you know, takes the form of the nominative, or not? In the nominative form, a separate pronoun in the nominative. This is an attached pronoun.

* Student: (...) Shaykh (...) subject?

* The Shaykh: No, "nahnu," what is its grammatical position?

* The student: Subject (...) predicate.

* The Shaykh: No, no. "Nahnu muslimun lahu" — this is the meaning; that is why we said the object was fronted. If it were a subject with the predicate fronted, we would not have said "the object was fronted," we would have said "the predicate was fronted."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 136–141 (part 2 of 3):**

* Student: In His words, ﴿And what was given to Musa and 'Isa﴾, sometimes 'Isa is followed by "son of Maryam" (...) sometimes he says (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed, it does no harm.
* Student: Is there no benefit in it?
* Shaykh: No, there is none.
* Student: Shaykh, does the law of 'Isa (peace be upon him) differ from that of Musa (peace be upon him) (...)? Does it differ from Musa's, or is it because the Injil was revealed to this one, and what (...)?
* Shaykh: It differs?
* Student: I mean, is its law in agreement (with Musa's), or how?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is in agreement.
* Student: With the Children of Israel. And we said their religions are all (...)?
* Shaykh: All in agreement. The Injil agrees with the Torah, except that it contains some relaxations for the Children of Israel (...). And the Torah, ﴿by which the prophets who submitted judge for those who were Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44], up to 'Isa. However, the Injil contains some matters that were lightened. Yes, indeed.
* Student: Shaykh, is the mention of "the prophets" after Musa and 'Isa (...)?
* Shaykh: This does not indicate that, but it does convey the mention of the general after the specific ('atf al-'amm 'ala al-khass).

﴿And if they believe in the like of what you believed, then they have been guided﴾. Who are "they"?

* Students: The Jews and the Christians.
* Shaykh: The Jews and the Christians, because these verses all follow one another: ﴿And they say, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided." Say, "Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a hanif"﴾ [al-Baqarah 135]; ﴿Say, "We believe in Allah"﴾; ﴿And if they believe in the like of what you believed﴾; ﴿If they believe﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians, ﴿in the like of what you believed, then they have been guided﴾. Regarding ﴿the like﴾, the grammarians (al-mu'rabun, those who analyse grammatical case) differed concerning the particle "ba'" and the word "mithl", which of them is the superfluous (za'id) element. It was said that "mithl" is the superfluous element, and the intended meaning is: "If they believe in what you believed," and that "mithl" is superfluous in meaning, meaning it conveys an added meaning, namely that if they believe, it is not just any belief but a belief that matches your belief. Accordingly, the superfluity is in the word "mithl", and the original is "if they believe in what you believed", but "mithl" is used to clarify that their belief does not suffice as mere belief in what you believed, absolutely; it must match and be equivalent to what you believed.

It was also said that the superfluous element is the "ba'", the prepositional particle, and the intended meaning is: "If they believe the like of what you believed, the like of what you believed", meaning "the like of that which you believed", and the second "ba'" is also superfluous, meaning "the like of what you believed in", that is, the like of your belief.

So now we have two opinions: some hold that the superfluous element is "mithl", and others hold that it is the "ba'". All agree that the intended superfluity is grammatical (i'rabi), not semantic, for it has a meaning. It is well known that nouns are not made superfluous, and that superfluity is common in particles. Superfluity in particles is common, is it not? As we went over in the Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik. But superfluity in nouns is rare, why? Because a noun is a word that comes with a meaning in itself, while a particle is a word that comes with a meaning in something else. It is known that if we weighed with the straight scale, what comes with meaning in something else would be more deserving of superfluity than what comes with meaning in itself. For this reason some grammarians denied the superfluity of nouns and said: "Nouns cannot be made superfluous; a noun is a word that has meaning in its own essence, so it cannot be superfluous, unlike the particle." Accordingly, the superfluity is in the "ba'", meaning: "If they believe the like of what you believed," that is, "the like of your belief." On either of the two possibilities, from the standpoint of grammar, the meaning is one: if they believe with a belief that matches your belief and is equivalent to it in every respect, then they have been guided. The "fa'" here is a connective marking the answer to the condition, the answer to the conditional clause, which is His words ﴿if they believe﴾.

His words ﴿they have been guided﴾ mean they took the path of guidance, and the guidance here is the guidance of knowledge and of success (tawfiq), because they believed on knowledge, so they were granted success and were guided.

As for His words ﴿then they have been guided﴾: is the guidance here absolute or not? It is so, absolute guidance, just as the Muslims who believed in the described manner are guided with absolute guidance. Incidentally, they say that some Christians in Egypt argued against the Muslims and said: "Why do you consider our women lawful while you do not allow us to have your women?" It is a sound argument. Why? That a Muslim is permitted to take a Christian woman, but a Christian man is not permitted to take a Muslim woman? They said: "Because we believe in your Prophet, and you do not believe in our prophet." Is that correct? It is correct, because we believe in your Prophet and you do not believe in our prophet. "Believe in our prophet and we will give you our daughters."

﴿then they have been guided, but if they turn away﴾. ﴿Turn away﴾ is turning away in the sense of aversion; "tawalla" means "a'rada" (turned away). And turned away from what? From belief in the like of what you believed. If they turn away and avert, ﴿then they are only in opposition﴾. Look, this is a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah), to indicate continuance and permanence, and it came with ﴿innama﴾, which indicates restriction. That is: their condition is nothing but opposition. ﴿Then they are only in opposition.﴾ Look at the predicate now: it is an adverbial phrase (zarf), as shown by "fi" which indicates place, as if opposition encompasses them from every side: they are immersed in opposition. And "shiqaq" means disagreement, and in all its meanings it revolves around this, even in His words, ﴿And indeed the wrongdoers are in extreme opposition﴾ [al-Hajj 53]. Some said that "shiqaq" here means misguidance, but the correct view is that its meaning is disagreement; wherever it occurs in the Quran it means disagreement. Although some say it comes for disagreement, and comes for misguidance, and comes for enmity, the correct view is that wherever it occurs it means disagreement; even the enemy is opposed to his enemy, and the misguided is opposed to the guided. This is supported by the fact that the original meaning of "shiqaq" is that each of the two parties is on one side and the other is on another side, and thus each opposes the other. The meaning is: they are in disagreement with you, and this disagreement will inevitably lead to enmity. For this reason, there is no doubt that between the believers and the Jews and Christians there is enmity, is that not so?

* Students: Certainly.
* Shaykh: ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate others with Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82]. There is also enmity from the Christians, and their enmity is evident. But His words, ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward the believers those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82], are for a reason, namely ﴿that is because among them are priests and monks﴾ [al-Ma'idah 82], to the end. As for the Christians who transgressed and oppressed the Muslims, they do not enter into this verse. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah 51].

So the Jews and the Christians, since they did not believe, became in opposition and disagreement with us, and this disagreement must lead to enmity and hatred and, consequently, to fighting. And the matter has occurred: the Muslims fought the Jews, is that not so?

* Students: Certainly.
* Shaykh: And they fought the Christians, the Byzantines, all of them Christians. After that they fought the Christians in the Crusades, and they will fight them again until Islam enters their capital, Rome, and this must happen in the future. So these Jews and Christians, we are in opposition with them. For this reason He said, ﴿then they are only in opposition﴾. It is as if a person, when he hears ﴿then they are only in opposition﴾, may be intimidated and fearful, so Allah reassured the believers with His words: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾. Here, ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾: this sentence contains a subject, a verb, and two objects, or not? The subject?

* Student: Allah.
* Shaykh: Allah, Allah. And the first object?
* Student: The "ka" (you).
* Shaykh: The "ka". And the second object?
* Student: The "ha" (them).
* Shaykh: The "ha". The two pronouns are attached. Is attachment obligatory here, or permissible? If it were in other than the Quran... the Quran is known; it must be followed.
* Student: The first is obligatory and the second is permissible.
* Shaykh: The first is obligatory and the second permissible? Give us evidence from the words of Ibn Malik.
* Student: ........................ *** "It resembled him in its inflection, the difference is connected" (...)
* Shaykh: Like that?
* Student: "Like that, khiltaniyhi" (...).
* Shaykh: Which of these three? Ibn Malik mentioned *salniyhi*, *kunTuhu*, and *khiltaniyhi*. Which of these three?
* Student: *Khiltaniyhi*.
* Shaykh: *Khiltaniyhi*. Do you agree with this?
* Student: Yes, indeed, *khilt* has two objects.
* Shaykh: Because *khilt* has two objects, correct. And this one has two objects, but it is an error, as becomes clear. This one falls under his words: *salniyhi*.

"Connect, or separate, the pronoun ha' in *salniyhi*..." *** ...... Why? Because *khiltaniyhi* governs two objects whose origin is subject and predicate. Is it not one of the sisters of *zanna* (to think)? Is it not "khal" (to think), one of the sisters of "zanna"?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: So it governs two objects whose origin is subject and predicate, while *salniyhi* governs two objects whose origin is not subject and predicate, so it belongs to the sisters of *kasa* (to clothe). *Sa-yakfikahum* now governs two objects; do their origins consist of subject and predicate?

* Students: No.
* Shaykh: Because it is not correct to say, "You are them." Can the *ka* be the subject and the *ha* the predicate? It is not correct. Is it clear? Then it falls under his words *salniyhi* and what resembles it; this is among "and what resembles it".

﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾. The scholars say the *sin* here is for futurity (*tanfis*), and it has two benefits, which we mentioned before, and which of Hamid or Adam clarifies them? The *sin* here is for futurity, and it conveys two things, the first of which Adam gives me? (...)

The second is the nearness of the occurrence, its certainty and proximity, unlike *sawfa*, which indicates certainty but with a delay, a delay. His words, ﴿So He will suffice you﴾: thus Allah, glorified and exalted, guaranteed His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that if they do not believe in the like of what the believers believed, and turn away, then Allah, the Exalted, will suffice you against them soon. ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them.﴾ And praise be to Allah that this occurred soon. The Messenger ﷺ did not pass away until he expelled the Jews from Madinah, and he conquered their fortresses at Khaybar, and left them there as workers. In the caliphate of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, he expelled them even from Khaybar. So Allah sufficed the believers against their evil, and praise be to Allah.

﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. *Al-Samee'* (the All-Hearing) is one of the names of Allah, and *al-'Aleem* (the All-Knowing) is also one of His names, may He be blessed and exalted. It has already been mentioned that *al-Samee'* has two meanings: one is the one who responds, and from it is His words, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39], and from it the words of the worshipper, "Allah hears whoever praises Him" (*sami'a Allahu liman hamidah*), meaning He responded, or answered, to whoever praised Him. The other meaning is perception of what is heard: hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard. We mentioned previously, in the section on creed, that this hearing, along with perception, conveys either a threat, or an affirmation, or support. It conveys a threat as in His words... Hearing for threat? 

* Student: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of the one who argues with you﴾ [al-Mujadilah 1].
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Those who say that Allah is the third of three.
* Shaykh: Yes, but that is not it. He says, ﴿They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Allah is the third of three"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 73]. Who?
* Student: The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor, and we are rich"﴾ [Ali 'Imran 181].
* Shaykh: Correct?
* Student: No.
* Student: Correct.
* Shaykh: Correct. This is a threat. And in His words, ﴿Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes [We do]﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80], this is for threat. And for affirmation, like: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of the one who argues with you concerning her husband﴾ [al-Mujadilah 1]. And for support? ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha 46]. So based on this we say: *al-Samee'* conveys two things: first, affirming it as one of the names of Allah; second, affirming hearing to Him. Hearing is divided into two kinds: the hearing of response and the hearing of perception. The hearing of perception is also divided into three kinds, or the hearing of perception may imply a threat, or may imply affirmation, or may imply support, according to context.

As for His words, ﴿al-'Aleem﴾, *al-'Aleem* is also one of the names of Allah. The knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, encompasses everything, in total and in detail. As for the total, it is His words, ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ [al-Baqarah 282]: "everything", a general term. As for the detail, like His words, ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. And not a leaf falls but that He knows it﴾ [al-An'am 59]. And what grows? That is a fortiori. ﴿And not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry but that it is in a clear register﴾: that is, He knows it and it is written as well. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision, and He knows its place of residence and its place of storage﴾ [Hud 6]. Not a creature... who counts the creatures? None counts them except Allah, their species, let alone their individuals and types. So the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, encompasses everything in total and in detail, and relates to the past, the present, and the future, does it not? In the past: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]. ﴿What is behind them﴾: what has passed; ﴿what is before them﴾: the present and the future.

His words here: ﴿and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. Someone may say: it seems more appropriate to say, "and He is the Strong, the Mighty," since He said, ﴿So Allah will suffice you﴾. So what is the answer regarding ending it with hearing and knowledge?

* Student: (...) Medina, they are whispering, an inner whispering.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
* Student: Strength, might, and wisdom all begin from the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted; they all enter into the wisdom and knowledge of Allah, so He takes whatever He wills.
* Shaykh: Yes. In any case, everything belongs to Him, and everything is conjoined with knowledge and wisdom. But the more appropriate, as it seems to us, and the apparent to me, and Allah knows best, is that since the scheming of these opponents against the Messenger ﷺ may be by words and may be by deeds, and scheming is a hidden matter, not an open war such that we would say it must be met with strength and might, He said, ﴿and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, even regarding matters you are unaware of, which they do not disclose or openly display, such as hostility to the Messenger ﷺ. Indeed Allah, the Exalted, is All-Hearing and All-Knowing. This is what appeared to me, and Allah knows best. ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

﴿The baptism of Allah﴾.

* Student: (...) the wisdom (...) ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ (...).
* Shaykh: What do you mean? Do you mean it is difficult to pronounce?
* Student: (...) in meaning.
* Shaykh: Do you mean this contradicts eloquence?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: As for its length, it is because it contains meanings: the *sin* must be present, and also the addressee: "so He will suffice you against them" must be addressed to him in that way, and the third-person pronoun, I do not see anything in it.
* Student: And the *fa'* is the answer to the condition.
* Shaykh: And the *fa'* is the answer to the condition.

﴿The baptism of Allah﴾. *Sibgha* (baptism, dye): *al-Sibgh* means color, as you know. What is meant by "the baptism of Allah"? They said: the intended meaning is the religion of Allah. The baptism of Allah is the religion of Allah. Religion was called *sibgha* because its effect appears on the one who acts by it, for the religious person shows the effect of religion on him: it appears on the features of his face, appears in his conduct, appears in his humility, his bearing, and his entire state. He is like dye for cloth, whose effect appears on it. It was also said that it is called *sibgha* because it clings to a person as dye clings to cloth. Does it prevent us from saying that it was named so for both reasons together?

* Students: It does not prevent it.

* **The Shaykh:** It is not prevented. It is a *ṣibghah* (dye) because it adheres to a person, and it is also a *ṣibghah* because its effect is visible on the one who acts by it. What is the reason for the accusative in His words ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ (*ṣibghata Llāh*, "the dye of Allah"), with *ṣibghatan* rather than *ṣibghatu*? It has been said that it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar maʿnawī*) corresponding to His words ﴿آمَنَّا﴾ (*āmannā*, "we believed"), in ﴿قُولُوا آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ﴾ (*qūlū āmannā bil-Lāh*, "Say: We believed in Allah"), since *āmannā* means religion. The implied sense would be: "We adopted the religion of Allah." There is no doubt that this is far-fetched, because ﴿آمَنَّا﴾ is in a different verse before it. Or not? Say "no" or "yes."
* **Students:** Yes.
* **The Shaykh:** It is in the preceding verse, in another verse before it, and it is unlikely that this is connected to it. Also, there are many intervening phrases between them. Therefore it is in the accusative as an incitement (*ʾighrāʾ*), meaning: "Hold fast to the dye of Allah! Hold fast to the dye of Allah! Let these people not turn you away from your religion; hold fast to it." As for His words ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ﴾, it is attributed to Him because it comes from Him. The Sharīʿah came from Allah, and no one legislates for creation except their Creator, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾ (*And who is better than Allah in dye? And we are worshippers of Him*) [al-Baqarah 138] (...).
* **A student:** One of the conditions of leadership (*imāmah*) is that a person does what he is commanded. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, fulfilled what Allah, glorified and exalted is He, had commanded him, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, informed him that He would make him (...). Therefore, for a person to attain leadership, he must carry out (...).
* **The Shaykh:** (...).
* **The student:** Is it that when Allah commanded him with what He commanded, and he complied, Allah made him an imam for the people?
* **The Shaykh:** So it is derived from this that whoever carries out the commands of Allah, Allah makes him an imam, correct? Allah makes him an imam, and this is true. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿وَجَعَلْنَا مِنْهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا لَمَّا صَبَرُوا وَكَانُوا بِآيَاتِنَا يُوقِنُونَ﴾ (*And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and were certain of Our signs*) [as-Sajdah 24]. Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "By patience and certainty, leadership in religion is attained." This is understood from His words, exalted is He: ﴿لَمَّا صَبَرُوا وَكَانُوا بِآيَاتِنَا يُوقِنُونَ﴾.
* **A student:** (...) ﴿وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ﴾ (*And [mention] when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il*) [al-Baqarah 127]. Some of the exegetes say that this (...) Isma'il (...).
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, indeed, because the original is Ibrahim.
Here Allah, mighty and majestic is He, says: ﴿وَقَالُوا كُونُوا هُودًا أَوْ نَصَارَى تَهْتَدُوا﴾ (*And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided"*) [al-Baqarah 135]. We mentioned that this claim exists among the people of innovation (*ahl al-bidʿah*) of this Ummah. Is that correct?
* **A student:** Each sect calls to what it is upon. For example, the Ash'ariyyah say: "Be Ash'arites, you will be guided," and the Jahmiyyah say: "Be Jahmites, you will be guided." Each one claims it.
* **The Shaykh:** Correct. So it means that whoever opposes the truth and calls to it, meaning to his way, and thinks that he is upon guidance, is similar to whom?
* **Students:** To the Jews and Christians.
* **The Shaykh:** To the Jews and Christians. With what did Allah answer those who said: "You will be guided"?
* **A student:** ﴿قُلْ بَلْ مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ (*Say: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim*).
* **The Shaykh:** And what is the *iʿrāb* (grammatical analysis) of *millata* (*the religion*)?
* **A student:** Object (*mafʿūl bihi*).
* **The Shaykh:** Object of what?
* **The student:** Of the verb *nattabiʿu* (*we follow*). *Nattabiʿu millata*.
* **The Shaykh:** Of a deleted verb. Its estimation: "Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim." What do you say about this?
* **Students:** (...)?
* **The Shaykh:** Correct. So the religion of Ibrahim is that in which there is guidance, not Judaism or Christianity.
What is the benefit of His words: ﴿أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ وَهُوَ رَبُّنَا وَرَبُّكُمْ وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ﴾ (*Do you dispute with us about Allah while He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds*) [al-Baqarah 139]?
* **A student:** (...) the benefit.
* **The Shaykh:** From His words: ﴿وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ﴾? Everyone knows that for us are our deeds and for you are yours. So what is the benefit of it? Is it a statement of the obvious, like the saying of one who says: "The sky is above us and the earth is below us"? What is its benefit?
* **A student:** (...) For us are our deeds and for you are yours, meaning that (...) with Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and He is our Lord and your Lord. It will not benefit you (...) with Allah, it will not benefit you, for each has his own deed and relies upon (...).

His words, exalted is He: ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾ (*The dye of Allah. And who is better than Allah in dye? And we are worshippers of Him*).
* From the benefits of this noble verse: ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ shows the obligation of adherence to the religion of Allah, because the meaning is: "Hold fast to the dye of Allah."
* And among its benefits: that this religion is true, because Allah attributed it to Himself, and everything attributed to Allah is true.
* And among its benefits: that the religion of Allah, exalted is He, is the best, most complete and most comprehensive of religions, and the most upright in serving the interests of the servants, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً﴾.
* And among its benefits: the obligation of sincerity, sincerity of worship to Him, as shown by His words: ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾, where the object is placed first to indicate exclusivity (*ḥaṣr*).
* And among them: that reason requires adherence to religion, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللَّهِ صِبْغَةً﴾, for reason guides to the obligation, or that which is of reason, namely adhering to the best. Every person with sound reason, his reason commands him to adhere to the best.

Then He said: ﴿قُلْ أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ وَهُوَ رَبُّنَا وَرَبُّكُمْ وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُخْلِصُونَ﴾ (*Say: Do you dispute with us about Allah while He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him*).
* From this verse is derived: the rebuke of the Jews and Christians who dispute with the Muslims about Allah while acknowledging that He is their Lord, as shown by His words: ﴿قُلْ أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ وَهُوَ رَبُّنَا وَرَبُّكُمْ﴾.
* And among its benefits: the censure of one who disputes about a matter he acknowledges. They dispute about Allah while acknowledging that He is their Lord; He is our Lord and your Lord.
* And among them: the obligation of disassociation from the deeds of the disbelievers, as shown by His words: ﴿وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ﴾, for what is meant is disassociation from what they are upon.
* And among them: that a person should take pride in the truth he is upon, because He said: ﴿وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا﴾. We take pride in them and are free of your deeds.
* And among them: that it is not permissible to imitate the enemies of Allah, for imitation is conformity in action. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever imitates a people is one of them" [narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4031), from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both]. And here He says: ﴿وَلَنَا أَعْمَالُنَا وَلَكُمْ أَعْمَالُكُمْ﴾, so we are distinct from you, and you are distinct from us.
* And among them: the obligation of sincerity to Allah, as shown by the placing of the object first in His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُخْلِصُونَ﴾.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ إِنَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطَ كَانُوا هُودًا أَوْ نَصَارَى﴾ (*Or do you say that Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the tribes were Jews or Christians?*). There are two readings: ﴿أَمْ يقُولُونَ﴾ (*am yaqūlūna*, "or do they say") and ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ﴾ (*am taqūlūna*, "or do you say"). On the second reading, ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ﴾ is part of what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded to say, because He said: ﴿قُلْ أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ﴾, meaning: "And say: Do you say that Ibrahim...?" As for the reading with the *yāʾ*, ﴿أَمْ يقُولُونَ﴾, this sentence is from the speech of Allah, as has passed.
* So among the benefits of this verse: the refutation of the claim of these Jews and Christians that Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the tribes were Jews or Christians. This claim is false. So what describes these people? Muslims. Islam describes them. Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and the tribes were not Jews or Christians; rather they were Muslims submitting to Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
* And among them: referring the knowledge of these matters to Allah: ﴿قُلْ أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾ (*Say: Are you more knowing or is Allah?*).
* And among them: the refutation of the people of distortion (*taḥrīf*) concerning the names and attributes of Allah, who say: "What is permissible for Allah by reason we affirm, and what is impossible for Him by reason we deny, is it not so?"
* **Students:** Yes.
* **The Shaykh:** There are people who say this, such as the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'arites and others. We say to all of them in reply: ﴿أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾. Are you more knowledgeable about what is permissible for Allah, what is impossible for Him, and what is obligatory for Him, or is Allah more knowledgeable about what is impossible for Him, what is permissible for Him, and what is obligatory for Him? Allah is more knowing. This is in truth a binding, overwhelming and silencing argument against those who regulate the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, by their intellects, saying: "It is obligatory for Allah to have such-and-such, and impossible for Him to have such-and-such." ﴿أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾.
* And among the benefits of this verse: the gravity of concealing knowledge, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ كَتَمَ شَهَادَةً عِنْدَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (*And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah?*). The scholar of the Sharīʿah of Allah is a witness to Allah concerning this Sharīʿah, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿شَهِدَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ وَأُولُو الْعِلْمِ﴾ (*Allah witnesses that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge*) [Āl ʿImrān 18]. So every person who conceals knowledge has concealed a testimony he has from Allah. Moreover, in this is the gravity of its sin. From where is this derived?
* **Students:** ﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** ﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ كَتَمَ شَهَادَةً عِنْدَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾. For this reason it was said concerning His words, exalted is He: ﴿فَأُولَئِكَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنَ النَّبِيِّينَ وَالصِّدِّيقِينَ وَالشُّهَدَاءِ﴾ (*Those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets, the steadfast in truth, the martyrs*) [an-Nisāʾ 69]: it was said that what is meant by the martyrs (*shuhadāʾ*) are the people of knowledge.
* And among them: the perfection of Allah's knowledge and His watchfulness over His servants, as shown by His words: ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (*And Allah is not unaware of what you do*).
* And among them: the affirmation of negative attributes, which are what Allah negated from Himself. From where?
* **Students:** ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ﴾. This is a negative attribute, not a positive one. Negative attributes, as has passed with us, include the affirmation of the perfection of their opposite, because of the perfection of His watchfulness and His knowledge, glorified and exalted is He; He is not unaware of what we do.
* And among them: warning a person and cautioning him against disobedience. From where is it derived? Warning a person against disobedience, from where?
* **A student:** ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾.
* **The Shaykh:** How so? What is the aspect of this warning?
* **The student:** The affirmation that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is not unaware of...
* **The Shaykh:** Yes, but what is the aspect of the warning?
* **The student:** It means it warns the person: "Know, O person, that Allah is watching you in all your deeds."
* **The Shaykh:** So beware of disobedience. For example, when you threaten a person with something you say: "I am not unaware of you." ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾.
* And among them: the attribution of the deed to the doer, and in it is a refutation of the Jabriyyah, as shown by His words: ﴿عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾. Do you know its aspect? In it is the refutation of the Jabriyyah, who say that man does not act, but is compelled. Is it clear?
* **Students:** Yes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 142–143 (part 1 of 6):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That was a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ The discussion of its benefits has already been given, so let one refer back to what preceded.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah which they had been facing?"﴾ His saying: ﴿will say﴾: the sin (sīn) is for futurity (tanfīs), and when it enters upon the present-tense verb it makes it specific to the future. When lam enters upon the present-tense verb, it makes it specific to the past; when sin enters upon it, it makes it specific to the future; and when it is bare, it is suitable for both the present and the future. So here He says: ﴿will say﴾, referring to the future. And His saying ﴿will say﴾ also indicates, along with futurity, the certainty that this thing will occur, or not? It has already passed us that it indicates certainty, and it also indicates the nearness of this thing, unlike sawfa, which indicates a distant future.

And His saying: ﴿the foolish (sufahā’)﴾ is the plural of safīh, and the safīh is one who does not handle his own affairs well. Everyone who opposes wisdom in his conduct is a safīh. Just as the safīh is not entrusted with wealth, by His saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ [al-Nisa’ 5], so too he is not entrusted with religion. These foolish ones are foolish in their religion, not in their wealth; they may be capable in wealth but foolish in religion. And what is foolishness in religion? Allah explained it in His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah 130]. So everyone who turns away from the religion of Ibrahim, which is submission to Allah, exalted is He, with perfect tawhid, is a fool.

And His saying: ﴿from the people﴾ explains the foolish, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: in the state of being from the people.

The content of the saying (maqūl al-qawl): ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they had been facing?﴾ This is the content of the saying in His words ﴿will say﴾, so the clause ﴿What has turned them﴾ is in the accusative position as the content of the saying. And His saying ﴿What has turned them﴾: what is its i'rab? What is the i'rab of ﴿What has turned them﴾?

* Student: Interrogative mā.

* Shaykh: Yes, (mā) is an interrogative noun, meaning: what thing has turned them?

And ﴿has turned them away from their qiblah﴾ means: has diverted them, ﴿what has turned them away from their qiblah﴾ means: has diverted them from their qiblah.

And His saying ﴿from their qiblah﴾ means: that which they face. The qiblah of a person is what he faces, and what is meant by it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), because when the Messenger ﷺ first arrived in Madinah he was facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, that is, either a year and four months or a year and five months.

If he was facing Bayt al-Maqdis, where would the Ka'bah be in relation to him? On his right, or on his left, or behind him?

* Student: Behind him.

* Shaykh: It would be behind him.

* Student: On his left.

* Shaykh: It would be on his left?

* Student: Yes.

* Students: It would be behind him.

* Shaykh: It would be directly behind him, it would be behind him. For this reason Ibn 'Umar said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ relieving himself facing Syria, with his back to the Ka'bah" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (148) and Muslim (266/62) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and its wording is: "facing the qiblah with his back to it"]. So on this basis the Prophet ﷺ was facing Bayt al-Maqdis. Was he facing it by a command or by ijtihad? The scholars differed on this. Some of them said: it was by ijtihad, and the Prophet ﷺ loved to agree with the People of the Book in matters in which he had not been commanded otherwise, until the Arabs entered Islam, and then he opposed the People of the Book. Some scholars said: it was by a command from Allah, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am 90]. ﴿Their guidance﴾ is general in everything they do, and ﴿follow﴾ means: follow, and the hā’ is for pausing. And this verse ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided﴾ is in which surah?

* Students: al-An'am.

* Shaykh: It is in Surat al-An'am, which is Makkan. They said that the Messenger ﷺ, while in Makkah, was also facing Bayt al-Maqdis, but he would place the Ka'bah between himself and it, so he would pray from the direction between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone. Thus they said.

* Student: It raises a difficulty, since Ibrahim's qiblah was the Ka'bah.

* Shaykh: Yes, he combines them.

* Student: And when he migrated to Madinah, Ibrahim's qiblah was the Ka'bah, and some of the prophets (...)?

* Shaykh: They say that he, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when it was said: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ and was commanded to follow them, he began to combine the two matters, praying between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone, and then he would be facing both the Ka'bah and Bayt al-Maqdis. Allah knows best about this, because this matter is not established historically. Otherwise it has been said, and it has been said that in Makkah he faced the Ka'bah, and in Madinah, by his own ijtihad, he faced Bayt al-Maqdis.

In any case, it was by the command of Allah, whether it was by an ijtihad which Allah approved for him, or by a command from Allah. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, remained on this for sixteen or seventeen months, and the Jews rejoiced at this when he agreed with them on their qiblah. But when he turned away from this qiblah, the Jews began to speak, and the polytheists spoke, and it was said: and the hypocrites spoke. What is the reason? Why did he turn away? Every day he has a qiblah, meaning every day he has a religion. So this man is not firmly established, and so they began, may Allah protect us, to find fault. Reflect on His saying: ﴿from their qiblah﴾, and He did not say: from the qiblah they were upon. This idafah (attribution) indicates that they themselves were the ones who chose this qiblah, so how do they deny it today? He did not say "from the qiblah" but ﴿from their qiblah﴾, attributing it to them, as if they were the ones who had chosen it, so how do they turn away from it today?

And His saying: ﴿which they had been facing﴾ is it past or future?

* Students: Past.

* Shaykh: Past, considering their saying, it is past. But considering the noble verse, it is not past, rather the Qur'an speaks of what will be said. ﴿Which they had been facing﴾: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, informed His Prophet ﷺ of what would happen and informed him of the answer to it.

From here the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, derived this principle: that one should know in advance what will happen to a person. He said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Verily you are going to a people of the Book" [related by Muslim (19/29), from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him], so that he would be prepared. Here Allah informed him that these foolish ones would say this statement, and then He informed him of how to respond to them.

﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾. ﴿To Allah﴾ is the predicate placed first, and ﴿the east﴾ is the delayed subject. Placing the predicate before its proper place of postponement indicates restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning: to Allah alone belong the east and the west. He is the One who directs whom He wills to the east, and whom He wills to the west, and whom He wills to the north, and whom He wills to the south. He specified the east and the west because the sun rises and sets between them, and you always find that directions are referred to as east and west, because they are the origin, they are the origin.

And His saying: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾: al-mashriq is the place of sunrise. Sunrise of what?

* Student: The sun and the moon.

* Shaykh: Only the sun and the moon?

* Student: And the stars.

* Shaykh: And the stars. The east and the west are mentioned in the Qur'an in three forms: in the singular, in the dual, and in the plural. The singular is like this verse. The dual?

* Student: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes. And the plural?

* Student: ﴿Lord of the two easts﴾.

* Shaykh: No, this is dual. Yes, in the Qur'an the east and the west have also been put in the plural?

* Student: ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij 40]?

* Shaykh: What is "Lord of the easts and the wests"? Recite the verse.

* Student: ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests, indeed We are able﴾.

* Shaykh: Recite the verse. Recite the beginning of the verse.

* Student: ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests﴾.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾. The reconciliation between them is that the singular is considered in terms of direction, namely the direction of east and west; the dual is considered in terms of the two risings of winter and summer, for between them is a great distance; and the plural is considered in terms of the risings of the stars, the moon and the sun, or in terms of the rising and setting of each day, because for the sun each day has a rising and a setting, and for the moon likewise a rising and a setting.

﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, so He is the Owner, glorified and exalted is He, of the directions. He turns His servants toward them as He wills, and we have nothing but hearing and obeying. He said to us: face toward such-and-such, hearing and obeying; He said: face toward such-and-such, hearing and obeying; He said: prostrate to Allah, we said: hearing and obeying; He said: prostrate to Adam, and the angels prostrated. The essential matter is that you be obedient to Allah, that is the essential matter, not that you face this or that. Have you understood, O brothers? Prostration to other than Allah is shirk, and for Adam, when Allah commanded the angels to do it, it was obedience and worship. Killing a soul without right, especially killing a child, is among the greatest major sins, and when it was obedience to Allah in the command to Ibrahim to slaughter his son, it was an act of nearness. So the criterion is obedience to Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. ﴿Guides﴾ means directs and grants success. His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾ is the object of ﴿guides﴾, and it is general, but it has already been explained to us that everything tied to the will of Allah is accompanied by wisdom. ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ means those who are worthy of guidance. ﴿To a straight path﴾. The will (mashī'ah) is the universal will (irādah kawniyyah), and it is not divided as the (general) will is divided. As for irādah, it has already been explained to us that it is divided into universal will (irādah kawniyyah) and legislative will (irādah shar'iyyah). As for mashī'ah, it is one category only, and it is universal.

And His saying: ﴿to a path﴾: ṣirāṭ is on the pattern fi'āl, and it has the meaning of maf'ūl, that is, something passed through (maṣrūṭ). The ṣarṭ is passing through quickly, and from it the people's saying: ẓaraṭtu kadhā, ẓaraṭtu al-laḥmah. What does it mean?

* Student: I swallowed it quickly.

* Shaykh: I swallowed it quickly. For this reason it is said: ẓirāṭ, and ṣirāṭ, and ṣirāṭ with three letters.

* Student: Sab'iyyah (in the seven readings)?

* Shaykh: No, in the Arabic language. As for the recitation, it is al-ṣirāṭ and al-sirāṭ with sīn and ṣād. So ṣirāṭ means maṣrūṭ, that is, passed through quickly. The scholars said: passing over the ṣirāṭ quickly occurs only when it combines three attributes: width (si'ah), straightness (istiqāmah), and evenness (istiwā'). If it is wide, straight and level, it is a ṣirāṭ; otherwise it is a shuwayri' or something similar. This ṣirāṭ, for example, if it becomes narrow, is not a ṣirāṭ, because it is not possible to pass over it quickly. If it is winding to the right and left, likewise. If it is raised and lowered, likewise. So a ṣirāṭ is what combines three attributes; the road that combines three attributes is called a ṣirāṭ: width, straightness, and evenness.

﴿to a straight path﴾: this is emphasis, meaning a straight path in passing over it and crossing it; it does not obstruct, but is clear and evident.

* Student: Shaykh, how is the ṣirāṭ? Is the ṣirāṭ of the Hereafter different?

* Shaykh: Yes, it is different. It is reported in a hadith. Restrict this by what the text restricts it.

﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. Among His guidance to the straight path is that He guided this nation to the qiblah with which the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is pleased.

﴿And thus﴾: we have (kāf) and we have (dhā), a demonstrative noun, so we need to know what is pointed to, and what the prepositional phrase relates to. The kāf here is a noun meaning (like), and it is in the accusative position as an absolute object: like that We made you. What is "that"? The referent is what preceded, namely the making of the qiblah toward the Ka'bah, that is, like this making which We made for you, your facing the qiblah: ﴿We made you a community of the middle way﴾. So we, praise be to Allah, were guided to the straight path by this qiblah, and We made us a middle community. For this reason Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad [related by Ahmad in his Musnad (25029), from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her] that among the things the Jews envy us for is facing the Ka'bah; the Ka'bah was made our qiblah, and they envy us for this quality, and likewise for saying amin behind the imam, and likewise for straightening the rows. In sum, this, facing the qiblah, is among what they envied us for. Why? Because the Ka'bah is the first house established for the people and the greatest house on earth, and there is no house toward which one of the pillars of Islam is directed except the Ka'bah; no house is visited by the pillar of Hajj except the Ka'bah. So it is the best house established for the people and the first house. Therefore we are envied when we face it. For this reason the Jews raised a great uproar over the turning from the qiblah to the Ka'bah, and they, may Allah protect us, together with the hypocrites and those who support them among the polytheists, raised a great affair, to the extent that some Muslims, may Allah protect us, apostatized from Islam upon hearing the ornate speech of these Jews and others.

﴿And thus We made you a community﴾: ﴿We made you﴾ here, is it the meaning of belief or the meaning of transformation?

* Students: Transformation.

* Shaykh: Transformation, meaning: We made you. The kāf is the first object, and ﴿a community﴾ is the second object. ﴿We made you a community﴾: ummah here means group. It has already been explained to us that in the Qur'an it is used in four meanings?

* Student: In the sense of group.

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: In the sense of faith.

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: Time.

* Shaykh: Yes, and the fourth?

* Student: Religion.

* Shaykh: Religion and creed, correct. Its example in the sense of group is this verse. Its example in the sense of religion?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, a religion (millah), is "ummah" that?

* Student: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed this, your community, is one community﴾ [al-Mu'minun 52].

* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿And indeed this, your community, is one community﴾. And in the sense of leader (imamah)?

* Student: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Ibrahim was a community﴾ [al-Nahl 120].

* Shaykh: Yes. In the sense of time?

* Student: The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And he remembered after a time (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45].

* Shaykh: In the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the one of the two who was saved and remembered after a time (ummah)﴾.

﴿Thus We made you a community of the middle way﴾: ﴿wasaṭan﴾ means just (ʿadl), chosen and excellent. So the wasaṭ means the just, the best. From it is the middle prayer (al-ṣalāh al-wusṭā) because of its excellence, that is, the most excellent. So wasaṭ means just and best, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. Know that it is said wasaṭ (with fatḥah) and wasṭ (with sukūn). When is it with sukūn?

* Student: It is with sukūn when it is the middle of a group, when it is among several things; and it is with fatḥah when it is the middle of one thing.

* Shaykh: Yes. When it is the middle of one thing it is with fatḥah on the sīn, and when it is among a group it is with sukūn on the sīn. For this reason they say: their imam, that is, the imam of the naked, stands wasṭahum (in their midst), and it is said: it is sunnah to stand at the head of a man in funeral prayer and at the wasaṭ of a woman.

﴿A community of the middle way﴾, that is, just and excellent. ﴿That you may be witnesses over the people﴾: the lām in His saying ﴿that you may be﴾ is the lām of causation (ta'līl), and it is not the lām of consequence (ʿāqibah). We have already been shown the difference between the lām of consequence and the lām of causation: the lām of consequence enters upon a matter not intended, but the outcome turned out to be that; the lām of causation enters upon a matter that is intended. Allah made us a middle community for this wisdom: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 142–143 (part 2 of 6):**

﴿شُهَدَاءَ﴾ (shuhada', "witnesses") is the plural of shahid. ﴿عَلَى النَّاسِ﴾ ("over the people") is general, covering this world and the Hereafter. But in the Hereafter it is stronger, greater, clearer and more manifest. So we are now witnesses over the people, testifying that the earlier peoples before us were visited by messengers, and that they divided into two groups: those who affirmed and those who denied. Among the people were those who denied their prophet and no one believed him, and among them were those who followed him, one man or two men, and among them were those who followed him in a group, and among them were those who followed him in great numbers. And the most numerous followers of messengers that we know of, after our Prophet ﷺ, were those of Musa (Moses) ﷺ. We are witnesses now. By what did we come to know this testimony? Through...

* Student: Revelation.
* Shaykh: Yes, through the most pure and trustworthy of people, who is the Messenger ﷺ. For this reason He said: ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾.

Likewise, we will be witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection, when the people are gathered. The messengers will be asked, "Did you deliver the message?" They will say, "Yes." Then the nations will be asked, "Did you receive the message?" They will say, "No bringer of good news or warner came to us; no one came to us." It will be said, "Who will testify for you?" (to the messengers). They will say, "Muhammad and his community." So they will be called as witnesses on the Day of Resurrection, and they will testify, and thus they will be witnesses over the people. So ﴿witnesses over the people﴾ in what? In this world and the Hereafter. We bear witness, but our testimony in this world has no visible effect except establishing the proof against those among them who were obstinate and whom we encountered. As for the Hereafter, it is the testimony that has the great effect.

﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾: The Prophet ﷺ bears witness over his community that he conveyed the clear message. It is established from him ﷺ that he said on the Day of 'Arafah, at the greatest gathering he had with the Companions: "Have I not conveyed (the message)?" They said, "Yes." He said, "O Allah, bear witness. Have I not conveyed (the message)?" They said, "Yes." He said, "O Allah, bear witness. Have I not conveyed (the message)?" They said, "Yes." He said, "O Allah, bear witness."[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); recorded by al-Bukhari (4403) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and the wording is his; and by Muslim (1679/31) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] So the Prophet ﷺ called his Lord to witness the acknowledgment of his community that he had conveyed the message. He ﷺ conveyed the clear message, and he left his community on the clear path. He did not die until Allah perfected the religion through him. Nothing that people need in their religion, in its fundamentals and its details, remains except that he ﷺ explained it with clear explanation. Praise be to Allah. So the Messenger is a witness over this Ummah. Allah the Exalted said in Surat an-Nisa': ﴿So how (will it be) when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these?﴾ [an-Nisa' 41]. That is, how will the situation be on that great Day? For this reason, when "Ibn Mas'ud recited to the Prophet ﷺ and reached this verse, the Prophet ﷺ said to him: 'That is enough for you'" (...) He said: "I turned and his eyes were shedding tears."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (5050) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]] ﷺ, because this is a great matter. So we are witnesses over the people, and the Prophet ﷺ is a witness over us. He bears witness over us that we were given the message and the proof was established against us, and we have no excuse in any way. For this reason, no one has an excuse, after guidance has become clear to him, for opposing Allah and His Messenger: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers - We will give him what he has taken and drive him into Hell, and evil it is as a destination﴾ [an-Nisa' 115].

* Student: Is it recommended for the one who is reciting the Quran to be read to, to say "Enough"?
