* Shaykh: When he reaches the place where he should stop, he says, "Enough," or he says, "Stop." There is nothing wrong with that.
* Student: Do I mean that the Prophet's saying "Enough for you" is taken as a Sunnah?
* Shaykh: No. What is derived from it is the permissibility of a person saying to the reciter: "Stop." That is what is derived from it. We do not say: let him recite and tire himself while you are obligated to listen.
* Student: So I say "Enough" meaning...?
* Shaykh: No, it is not necessary. "Enough for you" is a phrase intended to mean stopping. "Enough for you," or "Stop," according to the language he understands.
* Student: Does he not say "Allah the Mighty has spoken the truth"?
* Shaykh: No, that is not the place for it. In another place, if he sees something that the noble verse supports, he says, "Allah the Mighty has spoken the truth." But when he has stopped at the Quran, no. "Allah the Mighty has spoken the truth" was introduced by the later reciters from their own minds. Yes.
* Student: Does ﴿a median (wasatan)﴾ not include the meaning that this Ummah was guided to the path of moderation between extremism?
* Shaykh: Yes, yes. It includes that it is moderate in its religion. This will come, God willing, in the mention of the benefits.

And His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels﴾. Notice the trial and the test. ﴿We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾, which was facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), ﴿except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels﴾. ﴿That We might know﴾: Does the meaning of the verse mean renewed knowledge for Allah, that Allah does not know until a thing occurs?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: No, and no one holds this view. But we said in answering this: the intended meaning is knowledge of manifestation, or knowledge that has consequences for reward, because the knowledge of Allah which exists from eternity does not have consequences for reward until the servant is tested and observed. Or it is knowledge of manifestation, meaning knowledge that the thing has occurred, so that He knows it has occurred. The first knowledge is knowledge that it will occur. There is a difference between knowing that a thing will occur and knowing that it has occurred. Some scholars of rhetoric (ahl al-ma'ani) said: ﴿na'lam﴾ here has the meaning of the past, meaning: "Except that We had known." That is, "We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We had known who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels." But although this has a possible basis in the wording, it has no basis in meaning, because it does not fit that Allah did not make this qiblah except because He knows who will remain and who will not. This has no basis. Rather, "We did not make it except for the test, so that He would know who submits and who does not submit": ﴿who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels﴾. So the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, followed the Messenger in this, or not?
* Student: With the greatest following.
* Shaykh: With the greatest following. A man came to them while they were praying Fajr in Quba' and said: "The Prophet ﷺ has had a Quran revealed to him, commanding that he face the Ka'bah." They were bowing, so they turned while bowing before (...) facing the Ka'bah. This is great following. Likewise in Banu Salamah, in the Masjid of the Two Qiblahs, they were also informed, and they turned.
(...) Why did ﴿And the Messenger will be﴾ come in the accusative case?
* Student: As a predicate (khabar).
* Shaykh: A predicate. What is the predicate? It conveys the meaning: "that you would be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger would testify to your truthfulness and your uprightness."

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger﴾.

His saying: ﴿And We did not make﴾: (ma) is a negation particle, and (ja'alna, "We made") here may carry the sense of "We made into" (tasyir), meaning "We rendered," or the sense of "We legislated" (shar'). On the first meaning, (ja'ala) requires two objects: "And We did not render the qiblah which you used to face..." It requires two objects if ja'alna is taken in the sense of tasyir. On the second meaning it does not require two objects: "And We did not legislate the qiblah which you used to face except for such-and-such." Have you understood, everyone?

As for the second meaning, that (ja'ala) means "legislated," in the Noble Quran ja'ala comes with the meaning of shara', as in His saying: ﴿Allah did not prescribe any bahirah or sa'ibah or wasilah or ham﴾ [al-Ma'idah 103]. What is the meaning of ﴿did not prescribe (ma ja'ala)﴾?
* Students: "Did not legislate."
* Shaykh: That is, "did not legislate." Otherwise it exists by decree. On this meaning there is no difficulty left in the verse. That is: "We did not legislate the qiblah which you used to face, which is your direction toward Bayt al-Maqdis, except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger when We turned you away from it, from who would turn back on his heels." As for the reading of tasyir ("We rendered"), it requires two objects. Where are the two objects?
* Student: The first is the second kaf.
* Shaykh: The second kaf of what?
* Student: ﴿ja'alnakum﴾. The subject is in ja'alnakum.
* Shaykh: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾.
* Student: Omitted, certainly omitted.
* Student: The Masjid al-Haram.
* Shaykh: "And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face a qiblah except that We might know." It was also said: the first object is ﴿the qiblah﴾ and the second is ﴿which you used to face﴾, meaning: "And We did not make the qiblah, it is that which you used to face, except that We might know who would follow the Messenger." And it was said the opposite: "And We did not make that which you used to face the qiblah," so that ﴿which you used to face﴾ is the first object and ﴿the qiblah﴾ is the second object.

In my view, the first of the three opinions is the closest to correct: that the second object is omitted, and ﴿which you used to face﴾ is a description of the qiblah: "We did not make the qiblah which you used to face a qiblah except that We might know who would follow the Messenger." Omitting the second object of verbs of making into (af'al al-tasyir) is common, and Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned it. Have you?
* Student:
"And omitting a non-essential element is permitted, if it does not cause harm..."
* Shaykh: No, that is about the non-essential element (fadlah).
* Student:
"...and sometimes its omission is obligatory."
* Student: In the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah)?
* Shaykh: No, in verbs of thinking and their sisters (zanna wa akhawatuha). He mentioned a general rule in reality, in the chapter on the subject, which is:
"And omitting what is known is permissible..."
This is general. As for the chapter on zanna, he said:
"And do not permit here, without evidence, the omission of two objects or of one object."
Its implication is: with evidence it is permitted. And here there is no doubt that the evidence is clear: ﴿We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾. What was the qiblah he used to face?
* Student: Bayt al-Maqdis.
* Shaykh: It was his facing toward Bayt al-Maqdis.
﴿except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels﴾. (ma) is a negation particle and (illa) is a restrictive particle. This exception is from the most general states (istithna' min a'amm al-ahwal). When the exception is of this type, they say it is an exception from the most general states. That is, "We did not make this qiblah in any state except this one only: that We might know who follows."

In His saying ﴿ja'alna﴾ and in His saying ﴿na'lam﴾ there is some difficulty, because (na) and (na'lam) are pronouns that indicate plurality, and it is known that Allah is one God, glorified and exalted. So what is the answer?
* Student: That it is the form of self-magnification.
* Shaykh: That (na) here is for glorification, not for plurality. This is common in the Quran, such as: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr 9]. There is no doubt that it is One who sent down the Reminder, and the one who guards it is One. So this falls under what category?
* Students: Glorification.
* Shaykh: Glorification.

As for His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾, the lam is for purpose: "that We might know," meaning "in order that We might know."

﴿who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back﴾. Some grammarians mentioned that (na'lam, "We know") here is implicitly given the meaning of "distinguish" (numayyiz), with proof from His saying: ﴿that Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [al-Anfal 37]. They said that this kind of construction shows that the verb is for distinguishing: "to distinguish who follows from who turns back on his heels." And this is not far-fetched, that this verb carries the meaning of distinguishing together with indicating knowledge, since there is no distinguishing except after knowledge. We have mentioned earlier that when a verb is given the meaning of another verb, it indicates its original meaning and the meaning it has been given.

In His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾ there is also some difficulty, which was mentioned shortly before: its apparent meaning is that Allah does not know except after this test occurs. It is known that Allah, glorified and exalted, knew what would happen until the Day of Resurrection and beyond it. Is that not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: How does He say "We did not do this except that We might know," when He is knowing? The answer has been given in two ways. The first: that what is meant is knowledge that has consequences for reward, and knowledge that has consequences for reward only occurs after the test and the compliance or non-compliance. Is that not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Allah the Exalted cannot punish anyone according to His knowledge before testing him: ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 15]. So what is meant by knowledge here? Knowledge that has consequences for reward. The second answer: what is meant is knowledge of manifestation, because His knowledge, glorified and exalted, of what will be is knowledge that it will be. And His knowledge of what was is knowledge that it was, and it became manifest and clear. There is a difference between the two kinds of knowledge: the first is knowledge of what will be, and the second is knowledge of what has been. Have you understood?

Some grammarians said: (na'lam) is an imperfect verb with the meaning of the past: "na'lam" is an imperfect verb with the meaning of the past, meaning: "except that We had already known who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels." This, although it has a basis, namely that the imperfect is sometimes used to express the past, is far-fetched, because there is no wisdom in it. For the meaning of the verse would be: "We did not make this except because We had already known who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels." Then it would be said: so what is the benefit? The correct view is the first two, and the best of them is that the meaning of knowledge here is the knowledge that has consequences for reward, because it is clear and there is no artificiality in it.

And His saying: ﴿except that We might know who would follow the Messenger﴾: Who is meant by "the Messenger" here? Muhammad ﷺ. So is the (al) here for mental definiteness (al-'ahd al-dhihni) or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Or the one of mention (al-'ahd al-dhikri)?
* Student: The mental kind, where it is mentioned.
* Shaykh: The mental kind. That is, even if he had not been mentioned before, it is known in minds that what is meant is Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.

And His saying: ﴿who follows (man yattabi')﴾. The basic meaning of ittiba' is walking behind a person. It varies according to context: if it relates to physical matters, its meaning is that you walk behind him in the street, on the road, and similar things. If it relates to non-physical matters, the meaning is emulation of his actions and sayings. Here, is it linked to physical or non-physical matters?
* Students: Non-physical.
* Shaykh: Non-physical, so the meaning is emulation in his sayings and actions.

﴿except that We might know who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels﴾. Notice the great difference: this one follows, walking behind him, and the other turns back on his heels, returning. It is not enough that he simply stands still; no, he returns. And this is the worst form of opposing Allah and His Messenger, that a person walks on a line opposite to the Prophet ﷺ, and so he becomes one who opposes Allah and His Messenger. And indeed this happened: some of those who had embraced Islam apostatized when the qiblah was changed, and they said: "Muhammad has no certainty about his affair. Today he has one qiblah, and tomorrow another." They did not know that this confirms his prophethood. In reality this confirms his prophethood, because the lying person is eager not to contradict himself and not to retreat, since contradiction and retreat are a stain upon him. But the truthful person does not care about saying what has been revealed to him, whether it agrees with what he had before or differs. So what happened is in reality evidence of his truthfulness, even though the Jews criticized him, saying that Muhammad has no stability in his affair, and those weak in Islam who followed them agreed. ﴿except that We might know who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels﴾. And where are the two heels?
* Students: The back part of the foot.
* Shaykh: The back part of the foot. Now let us see questions. Your question?
* Student: Does the knowledge of Allah mean that there will be among you those who are sick...?
* Shaykh: ﴿He knew that there would be﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 142–143 (part 3 of 6):**

* **Student:** ﴿He knows that there will be among you﴾ [al-Muzzammil 20]. Here, Allah the Exalted knew that there would be among you sick people, though they did not yet exist but would exist. Then He also knew about the qiblah, those who would turn back on their heels... because Allah, glory be to Him, knows (...). So would this be closer to the word, meaning (...) in the past?
* **Shaykh:** Yes, Allah knows without doubt that it will happen. But what is the benefit of legislating this when He already knew? The important point is that the benefit of the legislation that took place, the change of the qiblah, is the great benefit that Allah, exalted is He, knows so that He may punish or reward. As we said, the meaning of knowledge being tied to reward and punishment is better than our saying "that we may know" meaning "that We knew." Otherwise there is no benefit.
* **Student:** (...) Allah knows?
* **Shaykh:** No. If we say His knowledge is tied to reward, there is no contradiction at all.
* **Student:** The first is the knowledge of the recompense that is tied to punishment, and the second is the knowledge of manifestation to Allah, exalted is He. What is the difference between them?
* **Shaykh:** The difference between them is that the first, "that We may know," means our definite knowledge, which is tied to reward and punishment. As for the second, they say: the first knowledge is knowledge that something will happen, and the second is knowledge that it has happened. There is a difference. For example, if you know now that tomorrow such-and-such will happen, this is knowledge of what will be. Of course, my knowledge may fail, but Allah's knowledge does not fail. When it happens, it becomes another knowledge, that it has occurred. So the difference between the earlier knowledge, which is knowledge that it will be (because it is not knowledge that it was), and the later knowledge, which is knowledge that it was, means that the intended knowledge in His saying ﴿except that We may know﴾ is the knowledge that comes about at the time of the thing's occurrence, not the knowledge of the thing before it happens, which is knowledge that it will happen.
* **Student:** A group apostatized; were they mentioned in the biographies (al-siyar)?
* **Shaykh:** No, they were not named. Even the exegetes did not specify them. They said only: a group of Muslims apostatized.
* **Student:** Perhaps they were from the Jews, about whom it is said: ﴿Believe at the beginning of the day and reject at its end﴾ [Ali 'Imran 72].
* **Shaykh:** Perhaps. But the apparent meaning of the Noble Qur'an, ﴿except that We may know who follows the Messenger﴾, is that they were Muslims who turned back on their heels, because the Jews were already turned back on their heels from the outset.
* **Student:** We said the Messenger is (al) for the mental (dhihni) reference; the description of the Messenger came earlier with the definite article.
* **Shaykh:** Where?
* **Student:** With the "al," ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾. The second "Messenger," is the "al" here for mental reference?
* **Shaykh:** No, it is for verbal (dhikri) reference. The first is for mental reference.
* **Student:** O Shaykh, ﴿turns back on his heels﴾ means he walks backward?
* **Shaykh:** Yes, he walks backward.

﴿And indeed, it was [a matter] greatly difficult, except for those whom Allah guided﴾. ﴿And indeed, it was﴾: the pronoun refers to the event, meaning: indeed, this event, which is the changing of the qiblah, was greatly difficult. Do you say that "in" here is negating? That is, "it was not greatly difficult"?
* **Students:** No.
* **Shaykh:** This is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and its noun is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). The implied meaning is: "Indeed, it was greatly difficult."
* **Student:** A witness for it.
* **Shaykh:** What is it?
* **Student:**
"And inna is lightened, so its action becomes rare, and the lam must accompany it when it is left inoperative.
And it does not come before the one with the lam..........
* **Shaykh:** No.
"And the verb, if it is not [an abrogating verb]..........
* **Student:**
"And the verb, if it is not an abrogating [verb], you will not find it with inna, which is linked..."
* **Shaykh:** Usually.
* **Student:**
".......................... ........ with inna, which is linked..."
* **Shaykh:** This abrogating verb now is "kana" (was).

﴿And indeed, it was﴾: where is the predicate of "inna"? The clause of "kana," with its subject and predicate: ﴿And indeed, it was greatly difficult﴾. The "lam" here is for emphasis. It is also permissible to say it separates the negating "in" from the lightened "in." That is why Ibn Malik said:
"..........................  And the lam must accompany it when it is left inoperative."
﴿And indeed, it was greatly difficult﴾, meaning: great, burdensome. The word "kibar" (greatness) is used for something burdensome and great. From it is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying about the two people in the graves: «Indeed they are being punished, and they are not being punished for something major» (Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (216) and Muslim (292/111) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him). "Kabir" here means: something burdensome for them, even if it is among the major sins. But it means burdensome. That is, this matter is burdensome, except for those whom Allah guided. On whom is this matter burdensome? On those who want religion to follow their desires, those who say, when the Shari'ah comes contrary to what they want, that it is a burdensome matter and they dislike it. On those who, when they are told "this is forbidden" while they want it, find it hard. This is common. Many people now find certain legislated matters very difficult, whether they are commands to do something or prohibitions. But whomever Allah has guided, the legislated matters are easy for him, whether they agree with his desire or oppose it. ﴿The only statement of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾ [al-Nur 51]. This is the statement of the believers. So we say: ﴿And indeed, it was greatly difficult﴾, meaning: burdensome.

﴿except for those whom Allah guided﴾: "alladhina" is a relative pronoun and needs a relative clause (silah).
* **Student:** And a connective (rabt).
* **Shaykh:** And a connective. Is it a connective or a returning pronoun ('a'id)?
* **Student:** A returning pronoun.
* **Shaykh:** A returning pronoun. No, it is not all one thing. The connective is in the predicate of the subject. As for the relative clause, it is the returning pronoun; it needs a returning pronoun.

﴿except for those whom Allah guided﴾: the returning element is a pronoun, and here we do not have a pronoun. The implied meaning is: "Allah guided them." So the returning element is then an implied object pronoun. ﴿except for those whom Allah guided﴾, meaning: Allah guided them. The guidance intended here is the guidance of knowledge and the guidance of success. Take note, the guidance of knowledge and of success. As for it being the guidance of knowledge, it is because those who fear Allah are the scholars: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. The scholars of whom?
* **Students:** Of Allah.
* **Shaykh:** The scholars of Him. This is contrary to those who say the intended "scholars" are the scholars of the age who know how to make the atom and how to dig the earth and similar things. On their claim, the people of factories in America, Russia, England, and France would be more fearful of Allah than Muslims today, because they have more knowledge than we do. But they are lying in that. What is intended is: "Only those of His servants who have knowledge of Him fear Allah," the scholars of Allah, of His names and attributes, of His rulings, and of His decree and destiny. These are the ones who fear Him. The meaning also requires this, because one fears only someone whom he knows deserves to be feared. Therefore it is necessary that the intended "scholars" be the scholars of Allah.

We also said: ﴿except for those whom Allah guided﴾ this is the guidance of knowledge, because when they know, they fear Allah, exalted is He, and they do not dislike His law, and it is not burdensome or difficult for them. Likewise the guidance of success: take note, O people, this is important. The guidance of success means that when a servant is granted success to submit to Allah, exalted is He, his religion becomes easy for him. It becomes easier for him than anything else. From this we know that those who follow the hadith are the most rightly guided of people.

The guidance of success also means: when a servant is granted success to accept what the Shari'ah has brought, the matter becomes easy for him and is not difficult. I said that the People of Hadith (ahl al-hadith) are the people most specifically described by this, because it is not difficult for them, when a ruling from the Messenger (ﷺ) comes, to follow it. But the people of partisanship among the adherents of the schools (madhahib) find it difficult. You find them, when their school is opposed by the clear text of a statement from the Messenger (ﷺ), facing one of two situations: either they become stubborn, pay no heed, abandon the hadith, and follow what they are upon of schools, and this is dangerous; or they follow what they are upon of schools while being anxious about opposing the text, but they cannot abandon their partisanship, and they are in anxiety about opposing the text. As for the People of Hadith, they do not care. None of them, if he knows a hadith, minds if he has one opinion today and another tomorrow. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, is sometimes reported to have several opinions on a single issue, because whenever a proof appeared to him, he adopted it.
* **Student:** He adopted it.
* **Shaykh:** He adopted it and abandoned the first. Sometimes he himself stated that he had retracted something; the matter became clear to him and he returned to it. This never harms a person. Rather, it makes people trust him more, when they know that he follows the evidence wherever it leads.
* **Student:** You mentioned that some people dislike what Allah has sent down to them and want religion to follow their desires. But they do not disbelieve, O Shaykh. How, given that they dislike what Allah sent down?
* **Shaykh:** Allah mentioned in the Qur'an that they disbelieve: ﴿So how will it be when the angels take them, striking their faces and their backs?﴾ [Muhammad 27].
* **Student:** ﴿But those who disbelieve, for them is destruction, and He will waste their deeds. That is because they disliked what Allah revealed, so He has nullified their deeds﴾ [Muhammad 8–9].
* **Shaykh:** ﴿they disliked what Allah revealed, so He has nullified their deeds﴾ [Muhammad 9]. This dislike may be directed at the entire Shari'ah, since "ma" here is a relative pronoun that covers all of it. It may also be directed at part of it. As for dislike of all of the Shari'ah, there is no doubt of their disbelief. As for dislike of part of it, this requires detail, because one may disbelieve by it and one may not, depending on what that disliked matter is.
* **Student:** Is there a difference between disliking something and finding it burdensome?
* **Shaykh:** Yes, because what is burdensome for him...
* **Student:** And it means it is hard, but it is burdensome for him to do this...
* **Shaykh:** It is burdensome for him to do, but dislike...
* **Student:** Is this a Muslim or not a Muslim?
* **Shaykh:** Yes, this is a Muslim. But the first one hates it, hates what has happened.
* **Student:** (...) The context of the verse here is on (...) the disbelievers in the first place.
* **Shaykh:** Which of them?
* **Student:** In the verse that our brother mentioned.
* **Shaykh:** ﴿they disliked what Allah revealed﴾.
* **Student:** On...
* **Shaykh:** In general, on those who disbelieve, in general.
* **Student:** O Shaykh, you find one who hates the beard (...).
* **Shaykh:** Meaning: he forces himself to do it, and it is heavy on him. It is heavy on him, but he forces himself to do it. This, in any case, is deficiency in faith, because it is obligatory on him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, and then find within themselves no discomfort from what you have judged and submit in full submission﴾ [al-Nisa' 65]. Submission alone is not enough; the absence of discomfort is required, meaning: constriction in the chest...
* **Student:** (...)
* **Shaykh:** (...) But he is deficient in faith. Therefore he now tries to struggle against himself, to struggle against himself in order to do it. It is hoped for him in the future that Allah will bless him with accepting the truth and being content with it.
* **Student:** O Shaykh, Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab mentioned that whoever does not accept Islam...
* **Shaykh:** Who?
* **Student:** Whoever hates something that the Messenger brought, even if he acts upon it.
* **Shaykh:** By Allah, it does not appear to me to be absolute, if he hates anything at all. Only if he hates it in order to disbelieve in it. This may happen, but I do not think a Muslim hates this thing in order to disbelieve in it. He may hate it because, for example, it prevents him from an action he wants, such as if he disliked prayer in the mosque or congregational prayer or similar things. He did not hate them because he disbelieves in them, but because he has customers now at the shop, and their return would cause him to lose them. This may occur. In reality, the matter is not on its absolute terms, and I do not think the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, intended the absolute. Unless he intended hatred of it as disbelief: he hates Allah and says, "What is this Shari'ah?" for example. Like some people, may Allah protect us, who hate it, mock it, and belittle it. In that case, yes. These matters are in reality very subtle, among the most subtle there are. Scholars sometimes use expressions in them concerning prohibition and warning, but in reality they need detailed explanation.
* **Student:** (...)
* **Shaykh:** Yes, precision is necessary in this.
* **Student:** As for the ignorant who dislike this thing because they think it has not been reported?
* **Shaykh:** No, this is not considered. It is obligatory for him to learn, because he is not like one who knows and dislikes. He says: "Until now it has not been established for me that it is from what Allah sent down." We say: such people must learn so that they may know.
* **Student:** O Shaykh, in jihad, did Allah mention that it was disliked? How does this matter work?
* **Shaykh:** Yes. ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah 216]. That is, a person dislikes fighting out of fear for his own life, from fear of being killed. He does not dislike it because it is the law of Allah, nor does he hate it. But people differ. Among the believers are those who love jihad and fighting. But human nature, by its natural disposition, dislikes fighting out of fear of being killed.
* **Student:** O Shaykh, in Surat al-Nisa' this is explained: ﴿Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You would delay us to a near term﴾ [al-Nisa' 77]. So they disliked its legislation, but not the Companions...
* **Shaykh:** Yes, the Companions...

He said: ﴿And indeed, it was greatly difficult, except for those whom Allah guided﴾.

And His saying: ﴿except for those whom Allah guided﴾ attributed the act to Himself, because everything is by Allah's decree and destiny.

﴿And Allah would never make your faith ineffective. Indeed, Allah is to the people Kind and Merciful﴾. There is grammatical analysis (i'rab) and meaning in this verse. ﴿And Allah would never make...﴾ the "lam" in His saying ﴿li-yudi'a (to make ineffective)﴾: what do they call it?
* **Student:** The lam of denial (lam al-juhud).
* **Shaykh:** The lam of denial. Is there denial in the Qur'an? Denial, meaning negation: the lam of negation. Therefore this lam has a rule: it occurs after a negated "kana" (was/be). The lam that comes after a negated "kana" is called the lam of denial.
﴿And Allah would never make...﴾: where is the negated "kana"?
* **Student:** "Ma kana" (would never).
* **Shaykh:** "Ma kana."
﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾ [al-Nisa' 137]: the negated "kana"?
* **Student:** "Lam yakun" (did not be).
* **Shaykh:** "Lam yakun Allah" (Allah did not be), ﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾.
I am not going to punish you?
* **Student:** This is not (...).
* **Shaykh:** Other than "ma", it means negation: "not being," meaning: I am not going to punish you. This is from the standpoint of grammatical analysis.
From the standpoint of meaning: whenever "ma kana Allah li-kadha" (it would not be for Allah to do such-and-such) occurs in the Qur'an, it indicates a matter that is impossible in the extreme, like "la yanbaghi" (it is not fitting) and "ma yanbaghi" (it is not appropriate). When "la yanbaghi" or "ma yanbaghi" occurs in the Qur'an, it refers to an impossible matter, not something whose abandonment is merely preferable. When we say "la yanbaghi an taf'al kadha" (you should not do such-and-such), the meaning is that it is preferable to abandon it. But when you find "la yanbaghi" or "ma yanbaghi," the meaning is that it is impossible and impermissible: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ [Ya-Sin 40]. Is that possible?
* **Students:** No.
* **Shaykh:** It is not possible. ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam 92]. What does that mean? Impossible and impermissible. "Indeed Allah does not sleep, and it is not befitting for Him to sleep" (Related by Muslim (179/293) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him). The meaning is that it is impossible. Here, when one says "ma kana" or "lam yakun," the meaning is that it is not possible, impossible.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 142–143 (part 4 of 6):

﴿And Allah would never let your faith (īmānakum) go to waste.﴾ That is: the negation of this is absolute, and its impossibility is absolute. ﴿To let your faith go to waste⦆ — (yuḍī'a) means: to leave it unrewarded, without any recompense for it. And the word ﴿your faith﴾ is meant here as your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This is how the scholars explained it: that by īmān here is meant their prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis. The prayer was called īmān either because actions are part of faith, as is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah and it is the correct view, and they used this verse as evidence, saying: faith here is the prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis, so actions are faith. And it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Faith has seventy-some branches; the highest of them is the saying 'there is no god but Allah,' and the lowest is removing harm from the road, and modesty is a branch of faith."[[Narrated by Muslim (35/58), and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (9004), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah radiya Allahu 'anhu; the wording is al-Tabarani's.]] So the saying "there is no god but Allah" is among the actions, among the actions of the tongue; and "removing harm from the road" is among the actions of the limbs; and "modesty is a branch of faith"..
* Student: Among the actions of the hearts.
* Shaykh: Among the actions of the hearts. And faith is also applied to belief (i'tiqad), as in his saying: "Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (4777), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah radiya Allahu 'anhu, and Muslim (8/1), from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab radiya Allahu 'anhu.]] "that you believe in Allah" — this is the belief of the heart. Faith according to Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah includes: belief of the heart, saying of the tongue, action of the heart, and action of the limbs, all four.
﴿Your faith﴾, that is: your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis will not be lost with Allah. Even those who died during the interval (al-fatrah), their prayers are not lost. Some exegetes mentioned that the occasion of revelation of this verse was that the Jews kept saying to the Muslims: those among you who prayed toward the qiblah — the qiblah before the change — their prayers have been lost, and they have no reward for them. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And Allah would never let your faith go to waste.﴾ So faith in reality is complying with the command of Allah and His Messenger. Although facing Bayt al-Maqdis before people were commanded to turn toward it, and after they were commanded to turn away from it, is not part of the Shari'ah, and this is common: by the Shari'ah is meant what conforms to the command, even though at times it may contradict the Shari'ah. We have mentioned great and momentous examples of this, such as prostration to other than Allah (...).
* Student: To Adam, it is obedience.
* Shaykh: And to Adam, abandoning it is disbelief; abandoning prostration to Adam is disbelief, is it not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And killing a son is among the greatest of major sins, and it was in regard to Ibrahim?
* Student: Among the greatest acts of drawing near (to Allah).
* Shaykh: Among the greatest acts of drawing near. We say: therefore, in reality, there is no consideration of the type of act; the consideration is the command to do the act or the prohibition of it, because the human being is a servant.
And his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is toward the people Most Kind, Most Merciful.﴾ Ra'uf has two readings: ﴿la-Ra'uf⦆ without a waw, and ﴿la-Ra'uf⦆ with a waw, and both are canonical (sab'iyyah) readings.
﴿Indeed, Allah is toward the people la-Ra'uf﴾ — I think this sentence is emphasized by two emphatics: one is (inna), and the second is the lam. ﴿Indeed, Allah toward the people...﴾ And (al-nas), its origin is al-unas, as was mentioned before, or not?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: But because of frequent use it was lightened by dropping the hamzah, like Allah, whose origin is al-Ilah, and because of its frequent use it was lightened by dropping the hamzah.
And his saying: ﴿Ra'uf⦆ The scholars said: ra'fah is the most intense mercy, its most intense form; it is a special mercy with some gentleness in it. And al-Rahim is the one characterized by mercy. They said: ra'uf was placed before Rahim even though ra'uf is more emphatic, for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil); Rahim, for the sake of the rhyme, is more emphatic than Ra'uf.
And his saying: ﴿la-Ra'uf Rahim⦆ and He did not say: la-Ra'uf Rahman; because this relates to His act, that is, His mercy. We have mentioned in the explanation of the basmalah that al-Rahman refers to the attribute and al-Rahim refers to the act: He is Rahman, of vast mercy, and Rahim, who shows mercy by this mercy. This is close to the meaning of some people's saying: al-Rahman is general mercy, and al-Rahim is particular mercy.
Then the Exalted said: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky.﴾
﴿Qad⦆ here is for confirmation, and ﴿nara⦆ is a present-tense verb with the meaning of the past, is it so? Because the meaning is: We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky. It was also said: it is a present-tense verb not with the meaning of the past, and what is meant is continuity and perpetuity, and it is a metonymy for the frequent turning of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, of his face toward the sky; because "we have seen the turning" may indicate only one occurrence, but "We see" indicates continuity.
And his saying: ﴿the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ — how did he turn it toward the sky? Yes; because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to raise his gaze to the sky awaiting the descent of Jibril for the change of the qiblah, because he loved that the qiblah be toward the Ka'bah, since it is the first house placed for mankind. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that the Ka'bah was the qiblah of all the prophets, and that the orientation of the Jews toward Bayt al-Maqdis and the Christians toward the east was among their distortions by which they distorted their religion. This is how he mentioned it; I think it passed before me in the book of Iman or in the book of Nubuwwat, I forget, but he mentioned this.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: No, a separate book; I saw it before (...).
And his saying ﴿in the sky﴾: ﴿the turning of your face in the sky⦆ — (fi) is for location, and it is known that the face of the Messenger is in his body; but the meaning is that he looks in the sky, that is, in the height.
* Student: (fi) in the sense of (ila)?
* Shaykh: No, in the direction of the sky; he turns it in the direction of the sky, looking.
﴿So We will surely turn you⦆ — this fa' is for derivation (tafri'), because what follows it is derived from what precedes it; and "nuwalliyannaka" means: We will direct you (nuwajjihannaka); ﴿to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face⦆ — this placement ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾ indicates that Allah, glorified and exalted, gave him what he wanted before explaining His ruling to him. Then He said: ﴿So turn your face⦆ (...).
Among the people who have no wisdom and no knowledge of the secrets of Allah's Shari'ah, who object to the Prophet ﷺ's change from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah — Allah the Exalted answered them, and indeed commanded His Prophet to answer them by saying: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾
I think we mentioned in ﴿their qiblah﴾ three readings.
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: And no reading?
* Students: And no reading.
* Shaykh: Except, a reading in which (...).
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: The well-known reading is ﴿qiblatihim⦆, meaning with a kasrah on the ha' and a dammah on the mim. The second reading: with a dammah on the ha' and the mim: ﴿qiblatuhumu alladhi⦆.
* Student: And a dammah on the ta'?
* Shaykh: No, only the dammah of the pronoun; the pronoun's building is on the dammah.
Shaykh: What did we say?
* Student: We said: permissibility of giving reasons for rulings by lordship.
* Shaykh: No, giving reasons for rulings by what lordship requires: the Shari'ah rulings by what Lordship requires, in order to silence people so that no dispute arises. If it is said: why is this? You say: because Allah is Lord and does what He wills; why did He make lawful this and prohibit that? You say: because He is Lord. Why do people turn from the east to the west, from the west to the east, from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah? Because that is by the requirement of Allah's lordship: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾ [al-Baqarah 142].
* And among the benefits of the verse: that the enemy argues against his enemy with what stirs his pride; the enemy argues against the enemy with what stirs his zeal and binds him; by His saying: ﴿from their qiblah﴾, they did not say: from the qiblah, as if they were saying: you used to face that, so what turned you away from it? This may stir a person's feelings so that he remains upon what he is upon. And he said: yesterday you chose it and today you deny it and reject it? So the opponent always provokes his opponent with what stirs his pride, in order to establish the proof against him: ﴿from their qiblah which they were upon⦆.
* And among the benefits of the verse: the generality of Allah's dominion, the Mighty and Majestic; by His saying: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾.
* And among its benefits: affirmation of Allah's will: ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾. It has passed with us often that every verse containing affirmation of will is accompanied by wisdom, because Allah's will is not mere will; rather, He, the Exalted, does nothing and legislates nothing except for wisdom.
* And among them: affirmation that guidance is in Allah's hand: ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾.
* And among them: the validity of the Jabriyyah's argument for the doctrine of compulsion (jabr).
* Students: It is not valid.
* Shaykh: Alright, the verse is before us: ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path⦆.
* Student: (...) this verse specifically (...).
* Shaykh: We say: the Jabriyyah, even if they argue with a verse like this, have no proof; because arguing with some of the Qur'an and not others is disbelief in it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [al-Baqarah 85]. The Qur'an is from one speaker, is it not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: So its absolute in one place is restricted in another place, and its general in one place is explained in another place. Indeed the Messenger ﷺ restricts the Qur'an, explains it, and specifies it. Clear? So there is no evidence in it except for one who looks with a one-eyed view; the one-eyed looks from the side of the sound eye but does not see from the side of the blind eye; and what is obligatory is that a person looks at the texts with two piercing eyes, not one eye. Alright, so this benefit is false; arguing with the verse for the correctness of the Jabriyyah's doctrine is invalid. Complete? Alright.
* And among the benefits of the verse: praise of this Ummah, because it is the one upon the straight path; for the first to enter under His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path⦆ are this Ummah who turned from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah.
* Student: Shaykh, do you see, you say: the path is that it is the straight one (...) His saying: ﴿straight⦆?
* Shaykh: Yes, this is mentioned in the tafsir.
Alright, then among its benefits: the virtue of this Ummah in being guided to a straight path.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that opposing the Shari'ah is misguidance, and as it is foolishness, it is also misguidance; because the Shari'ah is the straight path, so it is guidance, and whatever is other than it is misguidance and crookedness. Yes, and the discussion of this verse is concluded.
He said: ﴿And thus We made you a median nation that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you, and We did not make the qiblah...﴾ to the end.
* Among the benefits of this verse: that what Allah chose for this Ummah of facing His House is because of its being a median nation; because of its being a median nation, Allah chose for it to face — what? — the Sacred Mosque; by His saying: ﴿And thus⦆, that is, like that choice for you, We chose you and made you a median nation.
* And among it: the virtue of this Ummah over all other nations; by His saying..
* Student: ﴿that you may be witnesses﴾.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿median﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Median﴾, that is: just and excellent.
* And among it: the justice (adalah) of this Ummah; by His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾, and the witness's word is accepted. The Ummah here means the Ummah of response (ummat al-ijabah). From here we know the acumen of the jurists, who said: the just person is one who is upright upon the religion of Allah; because this Ummah is a median Ummah when it is upon the religion of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; so it is a witness, and its testimony is accepted when it is upright upon this religion and is a true Ummah. Therefore from this the definition of justice is derived: that the just one is the one who is upright upon the religion of Allah.
* And among the benefits of this verse: that this Ummah bears witness over the nations on the Day of Resurrection; by His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. If someone says: how does it bear witness when it did not see?
* Student: We say: but it heard.
* Shaykh: Yes, we say: but it heard; it heard from one whose report is more truthful than direct observation, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him.
And among the benefits of the verse also: that our Prophet ﷺ will be a witness over us on the Day of Resurrection, a witness over us by his trustworthiness; and it was said, as has passed: a witness over us that he conveyed. Whichever it is, it is among the virtues of this Ummah.
* And among them: the affirmation of the Prophet ﷺ's messengership; by His saying: ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾.
* And among them: that there is no messenger after him. From where is this taken? Because the (al) here is for previous reference (al-'ahd), and He is addressing this Ummah, so the known Messenger in it is one: who? The Messenger ﷺ; and it follows from this that there will be no messenger after him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 142–143 (part 5 of 6):

* Among the benefits of the verse: Allah the Exalted may test His servants with the legal rulings (al-ahkam al-shar'iyyah), whether an obligation, a prohibition, or an abrogation (naskh, the lifting of a previous ruling by a later one). From where do we take this? ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels﴾. Pay attention, pay attention to this. Indeed Allah may try you with wealth. He gives you wealth in order to test you: will you fulfil its due or not? This is a trial, because most of those who are tested with wealth become defiant and miserly: defiant in one respect, miserly in another. Then they transgress in acquiring wealth, and they go astray in its disposal and its management. Is this understood, O brothers? Good. Beware that Allah may bless you with knowledge, and knowledge carries a duty, and the first of it is the fear of Allah and awe of Him: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. So if you do not fear Allah through your knowledge, know that it is a proof against you. It is a test from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and it is no small matter. Likewise there is another test for the people of knowledge: that they do not conceal it (we ask Allah for safety and that He help us to dispense it and teach it), that they do not conceal it in any place where the need calls for its explanation, from the questioner, whether by the tongue of speech or by the tongue of circumstance. The questioner by the tongue of speech comes (...), someone asks you. And the questioner by the tongue of circumstance is when people are in need of an explanation of Allah's ruling in this matter; even though he does not ask with the tongue of speech and come saying, "Teach me," nevertheless the state of the people requires that the truth in this matter be made clear to them. Is this understood? This too is a duty that you must be attentive to: fear of Allah through your knowledge. Second: the clarification of ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Al 'Imran 187]. If Allah blesses you with well-being, this too is a trial. The point is that Allah tests a person with the legal rulings and with the decree of creation, with the legal decree and with the cosmic decree. Examples of testing have already passed us, by making the causes of disobedience easy for a person: we mentioned an example in this Ummah and an example among the Children of Israel. Among the Children of Israel, in the matter of the Sabbath, when they were forbidden fish on the Sabbath, they were given fish that came to them ﴿openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they did not keep Sabbath, they did not come﴾ [al-A'raf 163]. And in this Ummah, Allah tested them while they were in a state of ihram (pilgrim's sanctity) with hunting, in great abundance, reachable by their hands and their spears, not needing arrows. A man would catch the game with his hand or with his spear (...) upon it and take it. But ﴿that Allah may make evident who fears Him in the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah 94]. So did they fear Him in the unseen or not? Yes, may Allah be pleased with them, they feared Him in the unseen; they did not come to it, because it was forbidden. So Allah the Exalted may test a person with the obligation of worship, and the greatest test, as far as I know, is what befell Ibrahim the Friend (al-Khalil), upon him be peace, in the slaughter of his only son and the fruit of his heart, he having no other, and when the son reached the age of striving with him, in the fullest attachment of the heart to him, neither young so that he might be abandoned nor old so that he might be dispensed with. ﴿When he reached with him the age of striving﴾ [al-Saffat 102], that is, in companionship, walking with him and going with him. He was commanded to slaughter him, and did they agree? They agreed, the son and the father, and they submitted to the Lord of the worlds, and he laid him down upon his forehead, so that he would not see his face, or so that the son would not see the knife and be frightened. The Messenger, if the hadith is authentic, commanded that the blades be hidden from the animals in their sharpening (akhrajahu Ibn Majah (3172) and Ahmad (5864) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar). This was a great trial, and yet he carried it out. The point, my brothers, is that Allah the Exalted may test a person with matters, cosmic or legal, in order that He may know, the Exalted; for as it has been said: "At the time of testing a man is honoured or humiliated," and gold is not known for its quality except by placing it upon the fire, and aloes-wood does not reveal its fragrance except by touching the fire. So there must be something. For this reason He said: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger﴾, from the one who turns about and does not go right or left, ﴿from who would turn back on his heels﴾ [al-Baqarah 143], so he returns, and we seek refuge in Allah.
* A student: O Shaykh, leaving it (...) like killing..
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: Leaving it for his son and for his wife is a trial.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is a trial, but (...)?
* The student: (...) if one leaves (...) the prayer?
* The Shaykh: No, this is far lighter.
* A student: Shaykh, is it permissible with your distance from (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, no, is it not stronger than this? Because this is patience in obedience to Allah. Ibrahim's case is patience in obedience, and this is patience in refraining from disobedience.
* A student: Is there one greater than (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, and it is greater than (...) as well, even greater than (...), in kind and in reality; because a person restraining the soul from its desire is easier than his slaughtering his son with his own hand.
* A student: However high a person's faith reaches to this degree.
* The Shaykh: Indeed, it is very difficult; we ask Allah for well-being, and praise be to Allah in every state.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation to follow the Messenger ﷺ, as in His saying: ﴿that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger﴾. Allah tested the servants so that He would know whether they follow the Messenger. Therefore following the Messenger is obligatory; otherwise there would be no need to test the people by it.
* And among them: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, from His saying: ﴿that We might make evident﴾. Allah's knowledge is all-encompassing. Allah's knowledge encompasses what? Everything: ﴿that you may know that Allah is over all things competent, and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. An objection to this verse and its answer has already been mentioned earlier.
* And among them: that apostasy from Islam is a reversal (inqilab), from His saying: ﴿from who would turn back on his heels﴾, for it is a reversal backwards.
* And among them: that progress is in reality in Islam, and as for the reactionaries, in reality they are those who oppose Islam, is it not so? Yes indeed. We do not say this from ourselves or in defence of ourselves; we say it from the words of Allah: ﴿from who would turn back on his heels﴾. Whoever says to the people who hold fast to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, "These are reactionaries," we say: "Rather, you are the reactionary, because Allah called opposition to the Messenger ﷺ a reversal on the heels, and there is no more eloquent description of such a return." A person who returns on his heels returns blindly, and we seek refuge in Allah, not knowing what lies behind him.
* And among the benefits of the verse: that changing the qiblah is difficult, difficult except for a particular group of people: ﴿and indeed it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾. As has passed in the tafsir, this often happens to a person: some legal commands are hard for him, and avoiding some legal prohibitions is hard for him. But with complete faith this hardship disappears and it becomes easy. The scholars differed as to which is better: a man who performs worship with hardship and abandons sin with hardship, and another who performs worship with ease and abandons sin with ease. Some scholars said: the first is better, because he is a mujahid who struggles against his soul, he is weary. Others said: rather the second is better, because worship has mixed into his blood and flesh until it has become his nature, so that he is at ease only with it. What do you think?
* A student: One distinguishes between obedience and disobedience. In obedience you are able to do it, but in disobedience, leaving it with hardship earns reward, so the second is better.
* A student: The first has the reward of the hardship.
* The Shaykh: The correct position is to say: as for the one who does it with ease, facility and submission, this is without doubt more complete in state; his state is more complete than the first's, is it not so? Because he is at peace and rejoices. The second's state is lower, but he is rewarded for striving against his soul in obedience and in abstaining from disobedience; he is rewarded. But the first, the best state of the first is far more complete, because he acts with light, with light, faith, certainty and steadfastness. As for this second, whom we said is less excellent and has the reward of hardship, perhaps Allah the Mighty and Majestic will bestow His favour upon him, and He is the Most Generous of the generous, so that worship becomes easy in his soul, and he performs it with comfort. This is the meaning of the saying of some scholars: "We sought knowledge for other than Allah, but it refused to be anything but for Allah" (see Jami' Ma'mar (20475) and al-Madkhal of al-Bayhaqi (519), from Ma'mar who said: it used to be said, "A man seeks knowledge for other than Allah, and knowledge refuses him until it is for Allah"). So a person may at first perform worship with hardship and feel a kind of weariness in carrying it out; but when Allah knows from his intention that his purpose and seeking are sincere, He makes obedience easy for him until it becomes his nature.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, this shows that this is the more complete state for you to be in.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the manifestation of favour, the manifestation of Allah the Mighty and Majestic's favour upon the one whom Allah has guided. From where do we take this?
* A student: The attribution of guidance to Him.
* The Shaykh: The attribution of guidance to Him: ﴿and indeed it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾. He used the explicit relative pronoun "those who" (alladhina) rather than "whoever" (man): ﴿those whom Allah guided﴾. Yes, and He has favour over us, praise be to Allah. We ask Allah for steadfastness, through guidance. A person sees that the greatest favour Allah has bestowed upon him is that He guided him to Islam. There is no doubt that it is greater, by Allah, than food, drink, marriage, dwelling and everything else, for it is the life of this world and the Hereafter, whereas the delights of this world are only the life of this world and pass away. So the greatest favour Allah bestows upon a person is that Allah guides him. A person must feel this, and must not claim favour over his Lord through his religion; rather he must believe that the favour belongs to Allah upon him, that He guided him, so that he may increase in love for Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Whenever he performs an act of worship he loves Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because He brought him closer to Him through it, and because He is the One who guided him to it. How many people have gone astray, is it not so? ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ [al-An'am 116]. Most of those on earth are all astray. So it is incumbent upon a person to feel this feeling, O brothers: you should feel that since Allah guided you to faith, this is the greatest favour He has bestowed upon you: ﴿and indeed it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾. For this reason Allah said to the Messenger ﷺ concerning the Bedouins: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam﴾ [al-Hujurat 17]. The answer is: ﴿Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me. Rather, Allah has conferred favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Hujurat 17], in your claim that you are believers. So recognise the reality: ﴿Rather, Allah has conferred favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful﴾. And look at the grace and generosity: He is the One who conferred favour upon us with guidance, and then He says in Surat al-Rahman: ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman 60]. It is as though we were the ones who did good, and He repaid us for it with good. Great blessings! Although the good is His first and last: He did good to us first and He does good to us last. But this is from His favour, glory be to Him, and from His gratitude for His servant's striving: ﴿Indeed this has been for you a reward, and your striving has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insan 22]. Glory be to Allah! You are the One who bestows favour upon us and enables us to it, and then You say: ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾. This is truly a great favour, praise be to Allah. So: ﴿and indeed it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that Allah the Exalted does not waste the reward of a doer who acts on the basis of faith, from His saying: ﴿And Allah would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾. Every deed you do proceeding from faith will not be lost; you will find it recorded, whether a word, an action, or an intention in the heart. "Whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, a full good deed is recorded for him" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6491) and Muslim (131/207), from Abu Hurayrah). ﴿And Allah would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-Ra'uf and al-Rahim, and the attribute they include: ra'fah (tenderness) and rahmah (mercy). These are two names of Allah included in this verse, and the attribute.
It is also said: and the effect? Yes, and the effect. It has already passed for us that the Most Beautiful Names, when transitive, include three matters: the name, the attribute, and the effect, which is the act. When they are intransitive, they include only two: the name and the attribute. Al-Hayy includes the name and the attribute; al-Rahim includes the name, the attribute, and the effect, which is the act. He has a mercy with which He shows mercy, and He has a mercy with which He shows mercy and sends it to whom He wills.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation that mercy is general to all people, from His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is, toward the people, Ra'uf and Rahim﴾. This is general, but if the people are believers, His mercy is continuous and specific, continuous in this world and the Hereafter. Otherwise, the disbelievers are encompassed by Allah's mercy in this world and by His justice in the Hereafter: in the Hereafter they are recompensed with justice and equity, and in this world with bounty and kindness, and perhaps Allah the Exalted punishes them with justice: ﴿Indeed Allah is, toward the people, Ra'uf and Rahim﴾.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾.
* A student: Among the benefits is that action is part of faith.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, among the benefits of the verse, it is correct: that action is part of faith. Among the benefits of the verse is that action is part of faith, from His saying: ﴿your faith﴾, for it was interpreted as the prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, that action enters into faith. The basis for this is found in the legal texts, that action is part of faith: "Faith has seventy-some branches, the highest of which is the saying 'There is no god but Allah,' and the lowest of which is removing harmful things from the road, and modesty is a branch of faith" (agreed upon; al-Bukhari (9) and Muslim (35/58), the wording being his, from Abu Hurayrah). This is the words of the Messenger ﷺ. Action is undoubtedly part of faith, but its meaning is that it proceeds from faith, proceeds from faith; faith is what brings it into being. For this reason the action of the hypocrite is not counted as part of faith. Why? The hypocrite's prayer, his remembrance of Allah, and his expenditures are not counted as faith, because they are stripped of faith; they do not proceed from faith. Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah affirm that action is part of faith. The Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij agree with them on that, saying: action is part of faith. The Murji'ah disagree with them, saying: action is not part of faith. Have you understood? Good. But Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah differ from the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij in that the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij say: action is part of faith, but if it is absent, faith is absent. So the perpetrator of a major sin is outside faith in their view. However, the Mu'tazilah say he is in an intermediate position between the two positions, and the Khawarij say he is a disbeliever. Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah say: we do not concede this to you. We say: the believer who disobeys is a believer by his faith and a sinner by his major sin; or we say he is a believer with deficient faith; or we say he is a believer with deficient faith. Yes.
* A student: O Shaykh, is it derived from the verse the acceptance of the testimony of the blind, from His saying: ﴿witnesses﴾?
* The Shaykh: Yes, and the deaf and the mute.
* The student: Not only the blind?
* The Shaykh: No, it must be all who lack the senses. We say: yes, the testimony of the blind, the deaf, and the mute is accepted in what they are able to perceive. In what they are able to perceive it is accepted. But if a blind man comes and says, "I testified that I saw the crescent," do we accept it?
* A student: No.

Shaykh: It is not accepted. A deaf man who cannot hear even a cannon fired next to his ear comes and says, "I heard the whispering of so-and-so and so-and-so, and they were beside me." That is not accepted. But if the deaf man comes and says, "I saw so-and-so doing such-and-such, and his eyes were sound," it is accepted. The point is that testimony rests on uprightness ('adalah) and on the possibility of what is testified to, such as perception: it is necessary that it be possible for the witness to have perceived what he testifies to. This goes back to the two foundations in every matter. You see strength and trustworthiness, which Allah indicated in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas 26], and ﴿A powerful one from among the jinn said﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for it﴾ [an-Naml 39]. If you reflect on strength and trustworthiness, you will find them in all deeds, that they are two pillars of every work. Strength is the ability to carry out the work, and trustworthiness is reliability. Trustworthiness returns to religion, and strength returns to the ability to carry out the work that one claims to practise.

Student: It indicates that whoever does a deed based on what he has heard of Allah's law and what he has known of Allah's law is a mujtahid (...) a mujtahid who has a reward for this.

Shaykh: From where?

Student: ﴿Allah would never let your faith go to waste﴾, [referring to] the Companions who died.

Shaykh: No, because their ruling at the time of their action was that they acted upon the truth, which had not been abrogated.

Student: The saying ﴿to which you were [formerly] accustomed﴾: does the wording or the context indicate that they were not on a qiblah?

Shaykh: Yes, because there is in it an sense of superiority (istil'a)?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: No. Acting upon a thing is considered a superiority over it, a moral superiority, as you say: "You are in the state in which I inform him."

Student: Shaykh, regarding the question ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾, you mentioned that objecting to the Shari'ah is foolishness and that opposing the law is misguidance, although misguidance is included within foolishness?

Shaykh: No. Foolishness (safah) is more specific than misguidance (dalal), because the one who is astray may be so out of ignorance of it, out of ignorance rather than foolishness. There is, for example, misguidance and there is foolishness. The foolish person opposes, meaning that foolishness is the departure from right guidance (rushd), and he opposes while knowing. As for misguidance, it is from ignorance.

Student: (...) regarding establishing wisdom from the lam in His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you were [formerly] facing except that We might make evident who follows the Messenger﴾?

Shaykh: Yes, in this verse also, in His saying ﴿And We did not make the qiblah﴾, there is an establishment of wisdom for Allah. The establishment of wisdom is derived from His saying ﴿except that We might make evident﴾, because the lam here is for causation (ta'lil), and this is the correct view. We have already encountered that some grammarians say that the lam here is not for causation but for consequence (al-'aqibah), meaning: "except that, because We had known."

Student: Shaykh, regarding the disobedient ones (fasiqin) from this Ummah who are not upright (ghayr 'udul), can they be witnesses over the people?

Shaykh: Outwardly, no. The apparent ruling is that their testimony is not accepted unless they die in uprightness, in which case it is accepted, or unless Allah forgives them.

Student: A hadith has been narrated: "Indeed, those who curse much will not be witnesses before Allah."

Shaykh: Yes: "Indeed, those who curse much will not be witnesses or intercessors on the Day of Resurrection." [Narrated by Muslim (2598/86) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda'.]

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: We mentioned two opinions in the tafsir of it, and now we have mentioned two opinions: (...) a witness over you by your compliance, so that it is for you; and we mentioned "a witness over you" by your delivery, that he delivered to you, so he is a witness for himself against others.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: No, no, the first, meaning "for you"; the first meaning is "for you."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 142–143 (part 1 of 6):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That was a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ The discussion of its benefits has already been given, so let one refer back to what preceded.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah which they had been facing?"﴾ His saying: ﴿will say﴾: the sin (sīn) is for futurity (tanfīs), and when it enters upon the present-tense verb it makes it specific to the future. When lam enters upon the present-tense verb, it makes it specific to the past; when sin enters upon it, it makes it specific to the future; and when it is bare, it is suitable for both the present and the future. So here He says: ﴿will say﴾, referring to the future. And His saying ﴿will say﴾ also indicates, along with futurity, the certainty that this thing will occur, or not? It has already passed us that it indicates certainty, and it also indicates the nearness of this thing, unlike sawfa, which indicates a distant future.

And His saying: ﴿the foolish (sufahā’)﴾ is the plural of safīh, and the safīh is one who does not handle his own affairs well. Everyone who opposes wisdom in his conduct is a safīh. Just as the safīh is not entrusted with wealth, by His saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property﴾ [al-Nisa’ 5], so too he is not entrusted with religion. These foolish ones are foolish in their religion, not in their wealth; they may be capable in wealth but foolish in religion. And what is foolishness in religion? Allah explained it in His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim except one who makes a fool of himself﴾ [al-Baqarah 130]. So everyone who turns away from the religion of Ibrahim, which is submission to Allah, exalted is He, with perfect tawhid, is a fool.

And His saying: ﴿from the people﴾ explains the foolish, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: in the state of being from the people.

The content of the saying (maqūl al-qawl): ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they had been facing?﴾ This is the content of the saying in His words ﴿will say﴾, so the clause ﴿What has turned them﴾ is in the accusative position as the content of the saying. And His saying ﴿What has turned them﴾: what is its i'rab? What is the i'rab of ﴿What has turned them﴾?

* Student: Interrogative mā.

* Shaykh: Yes, (mā) is an interrogative noun, meaning: what thing has turned them?

And ﴿has turned them away from their qiblah﴾ means: has diverted them, ﴿what has turned them away from their qiblah﴾ means: has diverted them from their qiblah.

And His saying ﴿from their qiblah﴾ means: that which they face. The qiblah of a person is what he faces, and what is meant by it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), because when the Messenger ﷺ first arrived in Madinah he was facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, that is, either a year and four months or a year and five months.

If he was facing Bayt al-Maqdis, where would the Ka'bah be in relation to him? On his right, or on his left, or behind him?

* Student: Behind him.

* Shaykh: It would be behind him.

* Student: On his left.

* Shaykh: It would be on his left?

* Student: Yes.

* Students: It would be behind him.

* Shaykh: It would be directly behind him, it would be behind him. For this reason Ibn 'Umar said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ relieving himself facing Syria, with his back to the Ka'bah" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (148) and Muslim (266/62) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and its wording is: "facing the qiblah with his back to it"]. So on this basis the Prophet ﷺ was facing Bayt al-Maqdis. Was he facing it by a command or by ijtihad? The scholars differed on this. Some of them said: it was by ijtihad, and the Prophet ﷺ loved to agree with the People of the Book in matters in which he had not been commanded otherwise, until the Arabs entered Islam, and then he opposed the People of the Book. Some scholars said: it was by a command from Allah, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am 90]. ﴿Their guidance﴾ is general in everything they do, and ﴿follow﴾ means: follow, and the hā’ is for pausing. And this verse ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided﴾ is in which surah?

* Students: al-An'am.

* Shaykh: It is in Surat al-An'am, which is Makkan. They said that the Messenger ﷺ, while in Makkah, was also facing Bayt al-Maqdis, but he would place the Ka'bah between himself and it, so he would pray from the direction between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone. Thus they said.

* Student: It raises a difficulty, since Ibrahim's qiblah was the Ka'bah.

* Shaykh: Yes, he combines them.

* Student: And when he migrated to Madinah, Ibrahim's qiblah was the Ka'bah, and some of the prophets (...)?

* Shaykh: They say that he, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, when it was said: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ and was commanded to follow them, he began to combine the two matters, praying between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone, and then he would be facing both the Ka'bah and Bayt al-Maqdis. Allah knows best about this, because this matter is not established historically. Otherwise it has been said, and it has been said that in Makkah he faced the Ka'bah, and in Madinah, by his own ijtihad, he faced Bayt al-Maqdis.

In any case, it was by the command of Allah, whether it was by an ijtihad which Allah approved for him, or by a command from Allah. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, remained on this for sixteen or seventeen months, and the Jews rejoiced at this when he agreed with them on their qiblah. But when he turned away from this qiblah, the Jews began to speak, and the polytheists spoke, and it was said: and the hypocrites spoke. What is the reason? Why did he turn away? Every day he has a qiblah, meaning every day he has a religion. So this man is not firmly established, and so they began, may Allah protect us, to find fault. Reflect on His saying: ﴿from their qiblah﴾, and He did not say: from the qiblah they were upon. This idafah (attribution) indicates that they themselves were the ones who chose this qiblah, so how do they deny it today? He did not say "from the qiblah" but ﴿from their qiblah﴾, attributing it to them, as if they were the ones who had chosen it, so how do they turn away from it today?

And His saying: ﴿which they had been facing﴾ is it past or future?

* Students: Past.

* Shaykh: Past, considering their saying, it is past. But considering the noble verse, it is not past, rather the Qur'an speaks of what will be said. ﴿Which they had been facing﴾: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, informed His Prophet ﷺ of what would happen and informed him of the answer to it.

From here the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, derived this principle: that one should know in advance what will happen to a person. He said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Verily you are going to a people of the Book" [related by Muslim (19/29), from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him], so that he would be prepared. Here Allah informed him that these foolish ones would say this statement, and then He informed him of how to respond to them.

﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾. ﴿To Allah﴾ is the predicate placed first, and ﴿the east﴾ is the delayed subject. Placing the predicate before its proper place of postponement indicates restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning: to Allah alone belong the east and the west. He is the One who directs whom He wills to the east, and whom He wills to the west, and whom He wills to the north, and whom He wills to the south. He specified the east and the west because the sun rises and sets between them, and you always find that directions are referred to as east and west, because they are the origin, they are the origin.

And His saying: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾: al-mashriq is the place of sunrise. Sunrise of what?

* Student: The sun and the moon.

* Shaykh: Only the sun and the moon?

* Student: And the stars.

* Shaykh: And the stars. The east and the west are mentioned in the Qur'an in three forms: in the singular, in the dual, and in the plural. The singular is like this verse. The dual?

* Student: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾.

* Shaykh: Yes. And the plural?

* Student: ﴿Lord of the two easts﴾.

* Shaykh: No, this is dual. Yes, in the Qur'an the east and the west have also been put in the plural?

* Student: ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij 40]?

* Shaykh: What is "Lord of the easts and the wests"? Recite the verse.

* Student: ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests, indeed We are able﴾.

* Shaykh: Recite the verse. Recite the beginning of the verse.

* Student: ﴿Lord of the easts and the wests﴾.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾. The reconciliation between them is that the singular is considered in terms of direction, namely the direction of east and west; the dual is considered in terms of the two risings of winter and summer, for between them is a great distance; and the plural is considered in terms of the risings of the stars, the moon and the sun, or in terms of the rising and setting of each day, because for the sun each day has a rising and a setting, and for the moon likewise a rising and a setting.

﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, so He is the Owner, glorified and exalted is He, of the directions. He turns His servants toward them as He wills, and we have nothing but hearing and obeying.
