Shaykh: No. Acting upon a thing is considered a superiority over it, a moral superiority, as you say: "You are in the state in which I inform him."

Student: Shaykh, regarding the question ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾, you mentioned that objecting to the Shari'ah is foolishness and that opposing the law is misguidance, although misguidance is included within foolishness?

Shaykh: No. Foolishness (safah) is more specific than misguidance (dalal), because the one who is astray may be so out of ignorance of it, out of ignorance rather than foolishness. There is, for example, misguidance and there is foolishness. The foolish person opposes, meaning that foolishness is the departure from right guidance (rushd), and he opposes while knowing. As for misguidance, it is from ignorance.

Student: (...) regarding establishing wisdom from the lam in His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you were [formerly] facing except that We might make evident who follows the Messenger﴾?

Shaykh: Yes, in this verse also, in His saying ﴿And We did not make the qiblah﴾, there is an establishment of wisdom for Allah. The establishment of wisdom is derived from His saying ﴿except that We might make evident﴾, because the lam here is for causation (ta'lil), and this is the correct view. We have already encountered that some grammarians say that the lam here is not for causation but for consequence (al-'aqibah), meaning: "except that, because We had known."

Student: Shaykh, regarding the disobedient ones (fasiqin) from this Ummah who are not upright (ghayr 'udul), can they be witnesses over the people?

Shaykh: Outwardly, no. The apparent ruling is that their testimony is not accepted unless they die in uprightness, in which case it is accepted, or unless Allah forgives them.

Student: A hadith has been narrated: "Indeed, those who curse much will not be witnesses before Allah."

Shaykh: Yes: "Indeed, those who curse much will not be witnesses or intercessors on the Day of Resurrection." [Narrated by Muslim (2598/86) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda'.]

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: We mentioned two opinions in the tafsir of it, and now we have mentioned two opinions: (...) a witness over you by your compliance, so that it is for you; and we mentioned "a witness over you" by your delivery, that he delivered to you, so he is a witness for himself against others.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: No, no, the first, meaning "for you"; the first meaning is "for you."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 144–146 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Indeed We see the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We shall surely turn you to a qibla (direction of prayer) that will please you.﴾ The fa' (فَ) — we have mentioned that it is for tafriʿ (consequence, deduction). The lam in His words ﴿لَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾ (lanuwalliyannaka) is the lam of preface to an oath (lam al-muwatti'a lil-qasam). So the sentence is emphasised by three things, three emphatics: the implied oath, the lam, and the nun: ﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾. It was expressed in the form of magnification ﴿لَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾, because He, glorified and exalted is He, is Great, so the nun here is for majesty. His words ﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾ mean: "so We shall surely cause you to turn to a qibla, so We shall surely cause you to turn to a qibla." Accordingly, the kaf is the first object and "qiblatan" is the second object. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾ is "so We shall surely turn you (ḥawwalna)," and on this meaning, His words ﴿قِبْلَةً﴾ are in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, i.e., "so We shall surely turn you to a qibla that will please you." Is this understood? And His words ﴿قِبْلَةً﴾: the meaning of qibla is the thing that one faces and turns his face toward. His words ﴿قِبْلَةً﴾ are indefinite for magnification (qiblatan). His words ﴿تَرْضَاهَا﴾ mean: you are content with it, you love it and accept it. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, accepted this and that, but he loved that he be turned toward the Ka'bah.

After Allah, may He be exalted, had preceded this introduction, He said: ﴿Indeed We see the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We shall surely turn you to a qibla that will please you. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.﴾ ﴿فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾. "Walli" means: face it, turn your face toward it. In His words ﴿وَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ﴾, "wajh" (face) is the first object and "shatr" is the second object. The meaning of shatr here is the direction, i.e., the direction of the Sacred Mosque. In His words ﴿فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾, it is also meant to include the whole body, because the body, by its form and nature, when the face faces a direction, the whole body becomes facing it. In His words ﴿شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ﴾: the masjid originally means the place of prostration. It has been said that the masjad (with fatḥa) is the place of prostration, and the masjid (with kasra) is the place prepared for prostration, so there is a difference between them: the built place prepared for prostration is called masjid (with kasra), while the place where one has actually prostrated is called masjad (with fatḥa). In His words ﴿الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾, "al-Ḥarām" is an adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah) from ḥurm, which means prohibition. It was called ḥarām because certain things are prohibited in it that are not prohibited elsewhere, and because it is respected and revered. What is meant by it? What is meant by the Sacred Mosque here is the Ka'bah and what surrounds it of the well-known structure.

In His words ﴿شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ﴾ ("toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it"), He shifted from addressing the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to addressing his community, saying: ﴿وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ﴾, because the address to the Prophet ﷺ is an address to him and to the community, since he is the imam, and an address directed to the imam is an address to him and to his community. A parallel to this is that a minister, for example, says to a commander: "Head to such-and-such," meaning: head, and whoever follows you of the soldiers. Likewise the address directed to the Messenger ﷺ is for him and for the community. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ﴾ [At-Talaq 1] — He addressed the Prophet ﷺ first, then said: ﴿إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ﴾, because the ruling is for him and for his community. Moreover, if this verse came after the revelation of His saying: ﴿لَا يَحِلُّ لَكَ النِّسَاءُ مِنْ بَعْدُ﴾ [Al-Ahzab 52], then the address was directed to the community, because it is impossible for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to divorce. He said: ﴿وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ﴾. This "ḥaythu" is an adverb of place, but it is conditional, to which "mā" has been added in pronunciation only, for emphasis, without meaning. It is permissible outside the Qur'an to say "ḥaythu kunta," but in the Qur'an it is not changed. His words ﴿كُنْتُمْ﴾ is the conditional verb. Where is the answer of the condition?

[Here the lesson includes the exchange below, rendered as recorded.]

Wherever you were in Makkah, and whoever was (...) and whoever was far from it. This is why the expression came with His words ﴿شَطْرَهُ﴾, meaning "toward it." Does it include the one who is inside the Ka'bah or not? Yes, it includes him, because of the generality of His words ﴿حَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ﴾. So if he is inside the Ka'bah, he faces in front of his face from whichever direction he is in, isn't that so? From whichever direction, except that some scholars say: he does not face the door if it is open unless it has a threshold, because there must be an object (shakhis) in front of him, so that it can properly be said that he turned his face toward it. Good. If we are outside the house but in the mosque, do we circle around it or not? We circle around it, because if we stood in a straight line, we would not have turned our faces toward it, i.e., toward its direction; whoever moves out of its alignment would have turned his face toward something else, because it is now confined. If we move away, some scholars say: if you are in Makkah, face the Mosque, and if you are outside Makkah, face Makkah. But this is approximate. The correct view in this matter is that whoever is able to see the very Ka'bah must face the very building and not leave its alignment; whoever cannot see it, because of distance or something intervening, is satisfied with the direction, by His saying: ﴿لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا﴾ [Al-Baqarah 286].

* Student: And if a pillar stands between them, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, a pillar can be faced around. Do you mean in the mosque?
* Student: A pillar or an object placed (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, this can still hit its very building even if intervening.
* Student: The intended looking is not the aim; the aim is the direction.
* Shaykh: Yes, the aim is that you be facing it.
* Student: On this view, is it not permissible to pray on the roof of the Ka'bah?
* Shaykh: Yes, on the view that a shakhis is necessary, we do not pray on its roof; but its roof has a wall, the roof has a wall that reaches up above the knee, yes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is nothing at all; that is why I told you: the threshold of the door suffices according to those who say a shakhis is necessary; they say the threshold of the door suffices.
* Student: (...) does he pray or not?
* Shaykh: No, but they say the important thing is that there be a shakhis in front of him, meaning something raised standing in front of him.

And His words ﴿حَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ﴾ — does it include the one who is in an airplane? Yes, or on a ship, or a train, or a car: he must face the qibla. But when we mention the benefits, we will mention, God willing, what is excepted from this.

And His words ﴿وَإِنَّ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ لَيَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("Indeed those who were given the Scripture certainly know that it is the truth from their Lord"). ﴿الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ﴾: "al-kitab" here is generic, and it is the Torah and the Gospel, and those who were given it are the Jews and the Christians. His words ﴿لَيَعْلَمُونَ﴾: the lam here is for emphasis, so the sentence is emphasised by "inna" and the lam. ﴿أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: "anna-hu" means your facing the Sacred Mosque; ﴿الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ — but they, may Allah protect us, distort it. Otherwise, they know that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, would face the Ka'bah. From where did they know that? From what came in their books describing the Messenger ﷺ, for they know that this unlettered Prophet would turn toward the Ka'bah. His words ﴿لَيَعْلَمُونَ﴾: knowledge is the perception of a thing with certainty, and what else? Corresponding to reality. His words ﴿أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: we have mentioned that al-haqq means the established thing; if it is attributed to a report, it is truthfulness (sidq), and if it is attributed to a ruling, it is justice ('adl). Allah says: ﴿وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ صِدْقًا وَعَدْلًا﴾ [Al-An'am 115]. His words ﴿أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: "al-Rabb" we have stated repeatedly is the Creator, the Owner, the Perfect in authority. He attributed lordship here to them, ﴿مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾, to establish the proof against them, since they acknowledge His lordship, and whoever acknowledges His lordship must acknowledge His rulings and His disposition, because the Lord has absolute dominion, disposing as He wills; otherwise He is Lord of all. But this is the benefit of attributing it to them.

﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("And Allah is not unaware of what they do"). Is "mā" here Hijazi or Tamimi?

* Student: Hijazi.
* Shaykh: And what is the evidence?
* Student: Because it has an effect (it governs the predicate).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And even the Tamimi usage applies.
* Student: I say: the Qur'an is in the Hijazi reading.
* Shaykh: That is correct, because the Qur'an is in the language of Quraysh, and the evidence for this is His saying in Surah Yusuf: ﴿مَا هَذَا بَشَرًا﴾ [Yusuf 31], and He did not say "basharun," and ﴿إِنْ هَذَا إِلَّا مَلَكٌ كَرِيمٌ﴾ [Yusuf 31]. So the Qur'an is in the language of Quraysh, and Quraysh are Hijazis, not Tamimis. His words ﴿بِغَافِلٍ﴾: the "ba'" is grammatically extra but meaningfully useful. What is its benefit?

* Students: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: Emphasis. So in His words ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ﴾, the "ba'" is grammatically a superfluous preposition, and "ghafil" is the predicate of "mā," in the accusative by it, its sign of accusative being an implied fatḥah on its end, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the kasra of the superfluous preposition. His words ﴿بِغَافِلٍ﴾: ghaflah is heedlessness and forgetfulness regarding a thing. His words ﴿عَمَّا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun conveying generality, meaning regarding whatever deed they do, whether it is an inner act or an outward act, i.e., whether it relates to the limbs or to the hearts; so it includes belief, speech and action. His words ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ convey a warning to these people, because the purpose of this sentence is to warn them against their opposition, since they denied what they know to be the truth from their Lord. Is this attribute ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ one of Allah's positive attributes or negative ones? A negative one, negated. We have mentioned previously that negative attributes are not meant as mere negation, but along with that they are meant to establish the perfection of the opposite. For example, ﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ entails perfect knowledge and perfect watchfulness over their deeds, free of any heedlessness. We have mentioned previously that bare negation does not entail perfection, since it may entail deficiency, and may indicate neither praise nor deficiency. Do you remember the example of a negation that entails deficiency?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this does not entail perfection. It is impossible that negating something of Allah entails deficiency at all. That is, negating heedlessness does not entail deficiency; because of His perfection, He is not heedless. Who knows?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is a negation of something blameworthy, and it does not entail perfection; rather it is deficiency.
* Student: Your saying: "The weak does not oppress."
* Shaykh: Possible.
* Student: He does not oppress because of his weakness, since he is incapable of oppression.
* Student: From outside the Qur'an or from the Qur'an?
* Shaykh: No, from outside the Qur'an.
* Student:
*A tribe that does not betray a covenant,*
*and does not wrong people even by a mustard seed.*
* Shaykh: Correct.
*A tribe that does not betray a covenant,*
*and does not wrong people even by a mustard seed.*
When I hear this speech I say: these people are faithful and not aggressors, faithful, they do not betray a covenant, not aggressors, they do not wrong people. In reality he described them with deficiency, described them with deficiency, do you understand? Likewise the poet's saying:

*But my people, though they are of noble lineage,*
*are not at all of evil, though they are wronged.*
*They repay the wrong of wrongdoers with forgiveness,*
*and for the evil of the evil, they repay with kindness.*

Does this praise them or blame them?

* Student: Apparently it praises them.
* Shaykh: The apparent meaning of the speech is that it praises them, but the reality is that he intends?
* Students: Blame.
* Shaykh: Yes. As for what entails neither deficiency nor praise, like if you say: "Our wall does not wrong anyone," the wall does not wrong anyone, because it is not capable of wronging. Negating wronging of it is not praise. But regarding Allah, the matter is the reverse: every attribute negated of Him entails the perfection of its opposite in praise.

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ بِكُلِّ آَيَةٍ مَا تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾ ("Even if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qibla"). In ﴿لَئِنْ﴾ there are two conflicting elements: an oath and a condition. The oath is indicated by the lam, because the lam falls in the answer of the implied oath, meaning: "by Allah, if..." The second, which contends with the oath, is the conditional "in." Each of the oath and the condition requires an answer. Where is the answer in His words ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ﴾? His words ﴿مَا تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾. Is this answer to the condition or to the oath?

* Student: To the condition.
* Shaykh: The answer to the condition?
* Student: To the oath, before the condition.
* Shaykh: No, this is the answer to the oath. Ibn Malik says:

*Omit, when a condition and an oath gather, the answer of whichever is placed later, and it is obligatory.*

The one placed later now is the condition, and accordingly His words ﴿مَا تَبِعُوا﴾ are the answer of the oath, having no grammatical place, because a clause that is the answer of an oath has no grammatical place. The omitted answer of the condition is indicated by the answer of the oath. His words ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ﴾: "in" and what?

* Students: Conditional.
* Shaykh: Conditional. "Atayta" means "ji'ta" (you came). ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ﴾ means: the Jews and the Christians. ﴿بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ﴾: the "ba'" is for accompaniment, meaning accompanied by every sign. ﴿آيَةٍ﴾ means a sign of the truth of what you brought to them: even if you brought them every sign indicating the truth of what you came with, ﴿مَا تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾: what is "qiblatak"? The Ka'bah. That is, they would not follow this qibla nor turn toward it, even if you brought them every sign, because they do not want the truth; rather they are obstinate. For one who knows the truth and does not follow it is obstinate; there is no benefit: you bring him every sign and he does not understand, does not accept. His words ﴿بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ مَا تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾: one may say that just as they do not follow his qibla, they do not follow his religion either. Yes, they do not follow his religion, because it is necessarily part of following the religion to follow the qibla. His words ﴿مَا تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾: someone may say that this qibla is specific to this community, since He attributed it to them, saying ﴿قِبْلَتَكَ﴾. But the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the Sacred Mosque is the qibla of all the Prophets, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إِنَّ أَوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ لَلَّذِي بِبَكَّةَ مُبَارَكًا﴾ [Al 'Imran 96].

Thus the Shaykh al-Islam said: the Sacred Mosque is the qibla of all the Prophets, but their followers among the Jews and the Christians are the ones who altered this qibla.

He said: ﴿وَمَا أَنْتَ بِتَابِعٍ قِبْلَتَهُمْ﴾ ("And you are not one who follows their qibla"). Is the "wa" here a conjunctive "wa" or an initiating "wa"?

* Student: Conjunctive.
* Shaykh: Is this "wa" conjunctive or initiating?
* Student: Initiating.
* Shaykh: This is initiating, because if we made it conjunctive upon His words ﴿مَا تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾, the meaning would become: "and you are not a follower of their qibla while you bring the signs that show the truth of what you came with." And it is known that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, could never follow them absolutely. This is, Allah knows best, the reason for the nominal sentence in His words ﴿وَمَا أَنْتَ بِتَابِعٍ﴾ and "hum," and the verbal sentence in His words ﴿مَا تَبِعُوا قِبْلَتَكَ﴾: they do not follow the Messenger's qibla, and it is impossible for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to be a follower of their qibla, because their qibla is a denounced innovation that the Sharia did not bring. Moreover, even if it were supposed that the religions they follow had brought this qibla, it was abrogated by the qibla of Islam. His words ﴿مَا أَنْتَ بِتَابِعٍ قِبْلَتَهُمْ﴾: what governs "qiblatahum" in the accusative?

* Student: The active participle.
* Shaykh: Yes, it is in the accusative by the active participle. Now, outside the Qur'an, if one said "bitabi'i qiblatihim" (in the genitive), it would be correct, and the construction would be verbal-nominal-in-form only.

Tafsir of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Karim) on Surah 2, verses 144–146 (part 2 of 4):

﴿And you are not one to follow their qibla, nor are some of them followers of the qibla of others.﴾ ﴿Some of them﴾, meaning those who were given the Book, ﴿are not followers of the qibla of others﴾. So the Jews do not follow the qibla of the Christians, and the Christians do not follow the qibla of the Jews. For the Christians say that the Jews are disbelievers, and the Jews say that the Christians are disbelievers who are not upon the truth. This is why they deny 'Isa (ﷺ), and say that he was, may Allah protect us, the son of fornication. They indeed tried to kill him, but it was made to appear to them (that they had done so), and they killed his lookalike, and they began to say: "We killed the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam," boasting of this. May Allah destroy them. These people are enemies of one another, yet with respect to the Muslims they are allies of one another. ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies; they are allies of one another, and whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:51]. Some of them support others against the Muslims, but as for affirming each other's religion, they do not accept it: these do not accept the Jews, and those do not accept the Christians. This is why we have already mentioned that the Jews said: ﴿The Christians are not upon anything﴾, and the Christians said: ﴿The Jews are not upon anything﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:113].

﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.﴾

* Student: Regarding ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾, do both the Jews and the Christians have a qibla or not?
* Shaykh: Yes, this needs clarifying. ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others.﴾ The qibla of the Jews is toward Bayt al-Maqdis, the Rock, and the qibla of the Christians is toward the east, facing the sun. The Jews say to the Christians: "You are misguided," and the Christians say to the Jews: "You are misguided," and neither follows the other in the qibla. ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers.﴾ Regarding the words ﴿And if you were to follow﴾, we say about them what we said about ﴿And if you were to bring﴾: there is an oath and a condition in it. Is the response for the oath or for the condition? For the oath, which is His saying: ﴿indeed you would be﴾. This is why it was not joined with the fa' (فاء), for if it were the response of the condition it would have been required to be joined with the fa', since it is a nominal clause. ﴿And if you were to follow﴾: to whom is the address? To the Prophet (ﷺ). And (إن) the conditional particle does not necessitate or entail the existence of its condition; (إن) the conditional does not entail the existence of the condition. We only say this lest someone say: Is it possible that the Messenger (ﷺ) would follow their desires after the knowledge that came to him? No, it is not possible. How can He say: ﴿If you were to associate partners (with Allah)﴾? We say: this does not entail its response, the response of the occurrence of the condition; it does not entail it. Did not Allah the Exalted say: ﴿If you were to associate, your deeds would surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar 39:65]?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And is this possible? No. Did not Allah say: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:81], and is this possible or not? It is not possible. Therefore a condition attached with (إن) does not entail occurrence. Note the difference: we are not saying it cannot occur; we are saying it does not entail occurrence, meaning it may occur in some things and may not occur in others. Is the language understood? I say: there is a difference between "does not entail occurrence" and "does not require occurrence." If we say "does not require occurrence," that is not correct, for what is attached with (إن) may occur. When we say "does not entail," the meaning is that it is not necessarily occurring. It is not necessary. Something may be attached with (إن) while being impossible. As for His saying ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, (هوى) is plural of (هوى) (desires). The origin of (الهوى) is inclination, and from it one says of a star "hawa" when it inclines and falls. Al-hawa is generally used for inclination away from the truth, and its opposite is al-huda (guidance). So one says: following desire after guidance. Do you understand? Can al-hawa be used for guidance? If the hadith is authentic, which is the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): «None of you truly believes until his desire is in line with what I have brought»[[Narrated by Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunnah (15), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Madkhal (209), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]], then it is evidence that al-hawa can be in good as it can be in evil; however, generally al-hawa is in evil. ﴿After the knowledge that has come to you﴾ is connected to (you followed).
* Student: This hadith is not authentic.
* Shaykh: I say: if it is authentic. If it is not authentic, it is no longer evidence that al-hawa comes in the sense of al-huda.
* Student: Is the consideration of the hadith a linguistic matter, regardless of its authenticity?
* Shaykh: No, but if it is not authentic, it is not valid to say that al-hawa is used for something praiseworthy, because everything in the Qur'an and Sunnah that mentions al-hawa is about blameworthy matters.
* Student: Although some have criticized its chain and some have graded it sound, its supporting evidence from the Qur'an is ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:65].
* Shaykh: Yes, its meaning is correct, there is no doubt about the meaning, but as for the wording... Fine. His saying ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ is connected to (you followed), meaning if this following occurs after knowledge, then it is wrongdoing. His saying ﴿after what has come to you﴾ occurs in the Qur'an in three forms: this is one; the second is ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:37]; and the third is ﴿after what has come to you of knowledge﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:120]. Is that right? As for ﴿من بعد ما جاءك من العلم﴾ and ﴿بعد الذي جاءك من العلم﴾ there is no difference between them, except that (ما) is used in the sense of (الذي). As for ﴿مِن بعد ما جاءك﴾, it is more emphatic than ﴿بعد الذي جاءك﴾, stronger, because (مِن) indicates that knowledge came to him and then a interval passed, and this matter occurred after the arrival of knowledge. Similarly, the use of (من) is more emphatic: His saying: ﴿And between us and you is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat 41:5] is stronger than "and between us and you is a barrier," because (من) indicates a distance before the barrier and then a barrier; unlike "and between us and you is a barrier," which does not indicate this. And His saying ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾: what is meant by knowledge? The knowledge of the Shari'ah and the revelation that the Messenger (ﷺ) brought. ﴿Indeed you﴾ is the response of the oath. ﴿Indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾ (إذن) — is it (إذ) that we encountered earlier, with the addition, or something else?
* Student: No, this is an adverb of time.
* Shaykh: It is an adverb of time, there is no doubt. But when we said that they are (إذ, وإذن, وإذا), and that these three particles differ in tense: (إذ) for the past, (إذا) for the future, and (إذن) for the present, meaning ﴿indeed you then﴾, in the state of following their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, in this state ﴿you would be among the wrongdoers﴾. Allah emphasized it with (إن), (إذن) and the lam in His saying ﴿لَمِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic has spoken truly. Whoever follows the desires of those who are astray and those who earned anger after correct, legislated knowledge has come to him is, without doubt, among the wrongdoers. Consider the gentleness in addressing the Messenger (ﷺ): He did not say "you would then be a wrongdoer" but said ﴿among the wrongdoers﴾, which is undoubtedly a gentleness in style. For if I were to say to you: "You are a wrongdoing man," which is stronger in effect: that, or saying "you are among the wrongdoers"? The first is stronger in effect on the soul. So we say that His saying ﴿Indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾ is a gentleness of style toward the Messenger (ﷺ). Its parallel: look at His saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away, that the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would have purified himself﴾ [‘Abasa 80:1–3]. When you read ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, you think the one who frowned and turned away is someone other than the Messenger (ﷺ), another man. But the intended one is the Prophet (ﷺ). Thus Allah the Mighty and Majestic showed gentleness in style regarding His saying ﴿among the wrongdoers﴾, because the pronoun in "the wrongdoers" refers to whom? To someone other than the Messenger, to the wrongdoer. But if He had said "you are a wrongdoer," the pronoun would refer to himself. ﴿Indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾
* Student: Is it specific to the Messenger or...?
* Shaykh: What is specific?
* Student: ﴿Indeed you would then be among...﴾?
* Shaykh: No, it applies to the Messenger and others. His saying: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾.
* Student: Shaykh, (...)?
* Shaykh: No. The intended are the wrongdoers who did not act justly in their conduct, because injustice in origin is deficiency, which is the absence of justice. It may reach the level of disbelief or may not, depending on what one follows: if he follows them in a matter that does not take one out of the religion, he is not outside the religion; if he follows them in a matter that does take one out, then he becomes outside it.

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons.﴾ ﴿Those﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), so where is the predicate (khabar)?
* Student: ﴿They recognize him﴾.
* Shaykh: The clause ﴿they recognize him﴾. And His saying ﴿We gave them﴾: We gave them. Is the giving here legislative or cosmic?
* Students: Both cosmic and legislative.
* Shaykh: Yes, it combines both: cosmic and legislative, because the Book is legislative, and the giving here is cosmic: Allah decreed that the Book be sent down to them, and it was sent down. His saying ﴿We gave them the Book﴾: the verb here takes two objects; the first is the pronoun (ha'), and the second is the Book. Are their original forms subject and predicate or not?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: They are not originally subject and predicate? 
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: Yes, so they belong to the sisters of (kasa), concerning which Ibn Malik said:
"And the second of the two is like the second of the two in kasa..."
The pronoun in His saying ﴿they recognize him﴾ refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾: the kaf is for comparison, and (ma) is verbal (masdariyyah). Meaning?
* Student: Meaning they know...
* Shaykh: No, no, I mean ﴿as they recognize﴾ — the kaf?
* Student: For comparison.
* Shaykh: For comparison, and it is a preposition; and (ma)?
* Student: Verbal.
* Shaykh: Verbal, meaning?
* Student: They know.
* Shaykh: No, interpret it as a noun: i.e., like the recognition of their sons. Here the verb used is ﴿they recognize him﴾ rather than "they know him," because generally knowledge is expressed about intelligible matters grasped by inner sense, while recognition is used or expressed about sensible matters perceived by the outer senses. I say to you: Do you recognize so-and-so? Or I say: Do you know so-and-so? What do you say?
* Students: "Do you recognize (عرفت)."
* Shaykh: You recognize so-and-so; you do not say "I know"; but I say "Do you recognize so-and-so, so you know what he did." Here we placed knowledge with the action and recognition with the person. So ﴿they recognize him﴾ here is not in the sense of ﴿they know him﴾, because knowledge pertains to intelligibles or attributes, while recognition is used for persons. His saying ﴿they recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾: ﴿their sons﴾ is the plural of (ibn), and He specified it over daughters because a person's attachment to a male is stronger than his attachment to a female, so he knows him better. Isn't that so?
* Student: Doesn't it include daughters?
* Shaykh: No, "ibn" does not include daughters; "awlad" is what includes both daughter and son.
* Student: As a generalization?
* Shaykh: No, it is not a generalization. ﴿Their sons⁠﴾, because a person's attachment to a son is more than his attachment to a daughter, so his knowledge of him is more than of a daughter. Clear? This is the reason He expressed "sons" rather than "daughters."
* Student: And "banun" is also only male children?
* Shaykh: "Banun" is only males. He expressed "abna'" rather than "awlad" or "banat," because a person's attachment to a male child is greater than to a female, so he knows him better. Allah mentioned about man that when he is given the good news of a female, ﴿his face becomes dark, and he suppresses grief﴾ [al-Nahl 16:58], and ﴿when one of them is given good news of what he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes dark and he suppresses grief﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:17]. This is why, in washing the urine of a male, sprinkling (nadh) suffices, but for the urine of a small female who does not eat food, washing is required; a small male who does not eat food—sprinkling suffices for him. Washing is required for the female, because a son is generally treated more gently than a daughter. There are other reasons, and a third reason we studied in jurisprudence: the second reason is that the urine of a male spreads, because it exits forcefully and projecting, soiling more clothing, making its avoidance difficult. They also said that the male is naturally stronger than the female, and that he refines waste more than the female does. It was said: because the female was created from blood and the male from clay, but this is not correct. The first considerations are closer. Some said it is devotional (ta'abbudi) and we do not know the wisdom. In any case, this is not a matter for our present study; we only say that He expressed "sons" for this reason.
﴿And indeed a group of them conceal the truth while they know﴾. Allah is greater! The justice in Qur'anic expression: ﴿And indeed a group of them conceal the truth﴾, meaning a portion of them conceal the truth, and it is known from this that another portion does not conceal the truth, and this is the reality: among the Christians, like the Negus, some believed, and among the Jews, like 'Abdullah ibn Salam, some believed and did not conceal the truth. But a group of them conceal the truth, meaning they hide it and do not make it clear, may Allah protect us. This is why Allah mentioned in Surah Al 'Imran that some of them say to others: "How can you convey guidance from Muhammad and his companions? If you make it clear, they will argue with you about it before your Lord. Will you not use reason?" So they counsel one another to concealment, may Allah protect us.
His saying ﴿while they know﴾: the clause is in the place of an accusative of circumstance (hal) from the subject of ﴿conceal﴾. Where is the subject of ﴿conceal﴾?
* Students: The waw.
* Shaykh: The waw. Meaning: they conceal while they know it is true. This is stronger in censure: that they conceal the truth while knowing it, so they conceal it knowingly, and are deliberate wrongdoers. ﴿They conceal the truth while they know﴾, meaning: they know it.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾

* * *

﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky.﴾ I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will like. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.﴾

From here begins the ruling on changing the qibla. From this noble verse is derived: the affirmation of the seeing of Allah the Mighty, from His saying ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face﴾.
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of looking toward the sky, ﴿the turning of your face toward the sky﴾, and that there is no bad manners toward Allah except in the state of prayer; during prayer it is not permissible for a person to raise his gaze to the sky.
* Among them: the affirmation of Allah's highness, because the Messenger (ﷺ) turned his face toward the sky, because revelation came to him from the sky.
That he turn toward the Ka'bah, but did he do so?
* Students: He did not do so.
* Shaykh: He did not do so except after Allah commanded him.
* Among them: the affirmation of Allah's greatness, the Glorified and Exalted, by His saying ﴿So We will surely turn you﴾, for the plural pronoun here is for magnification.
* Among them: that the Prophet (ﷺ) loved to turn toward the Ka'bah, by His saying ﴿that you will like﴾ together with His saying ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 144–146 (part 3 of 4):

* Among the benefits: the obligation to face the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), based on His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾.
* Among them: the face is the most honored of the limbs, since it is used to refer to the whole body: ﴿your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾.
* Among them: what the Malikis have cited as evidence that the one praying should look at the place directly in front of his face, based on His saying: ﴿your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾. When a person turns his face, he looks in the direction of his face. This question has been disputed among the scholars. The well-known position of the Malikis is that the one praying looks in the direction of his face. According to Imam Ahmad, he looks at the place of his prostration (sujud), and this is the position of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah. They cite as evidence a mursal report from Muhammad ibn Sirin: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to lower his head and look at the place of his prostration."[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musannaf (6561) from the hadith of Ibn Sirin.]] Some scholars said: the imam and the one praying alone look at the place of prostration, but the follower (ma'mum) looks at his imam. They cite hadiths in al-Bukhari, namely: "When the Messenger (ﷺ) prayed the eclipse prayer, he informed his companions that Paradise and the Fire had been shown to him. He said to them: 'That was when you saw me advance and retreat.'"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1212) from the hadith of Aishah.]] This is evidence that they could see him.
* Among them: when a pulpit (minbar) was made for him, he stood on it to pray. He would stand, bow and rise, and when he wanted to prostrate he would descend and say: "I did this so that you would follow me and learn my prayer."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (917) and Muslim (544/44) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi.]] This is evidence that they could see him.
* Also among them: when they were informed that the Messenger (ﷺ) "used to recite in the silent prayer," they were asked: "How do you know that?" They said: "By the movement of his beard."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (746) from the hadith of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt.]] All of these are in the Sahih, and this is evidence that the follower looks at his imam. Also, it is more effective in following him, because the imam may stand or sit, perhaps by forgetfulness, so if the follower looks at the imam, that is more effective in following him. As for the imam and the one praying alone, they look at the place of prostration. This view is acceptable, especially if the follower needs to do so, such as when he cannot hear and wants to look at the imam in order to follow him, or the like.
* A student: If he is far away, does he observe him (by looking)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he observes him if he needs to turn. Or does he do it without turning? Some scholars who say that one looks at the place of prostration have made an exception for when one is in the tashahhud. Then one looks at his index finger, based on the saying of Ibn al-Zubayr, or al-Zubayr (I forget): "He did not let his gaze go beyond his pointing (finger)."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (990) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr.]] So during the tashahhud, when pointing, one looks at the finger.
Among what some of them make an exception to this is when you are in the Sacred Mosque and you are looking at the Ka'bah: then you look at the Ka'bah.
Among them: when you are in fear and the enemy is around you, then you look toward the enemy. So these three matters that are excepted, we say: as for the exception of the tashahhud, or raising the finger during the tashahhud, this has been reported in a hadith, so it is excepted. As for when the Ka'bah is in front of you, there is no basis for it. There is no reason for you to look at the Ka'bah, especially since when a person looks at the Ka'bah and people are circling it, he may become distracted. As for when there is fear, this falls under His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and take your precaution﴾ [an-Nisa' 102]. It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he sent a scout, and he would look toward the mountain pass to see whether the scout had come or not.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (2501) and Ibn Khuzaymah (486) from the hadith of Sahl ibn al-Hanzaliyyah.]] This is evidence that in a state of fear he looks at what protects him from that fear, and there is no blame on him.
* A student: In the prayer of fear, some people (...)?
* The Shaykh: (...) this is clear.
And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the greatness of this mosque, as it is described as "sacred" (haram), meaning one that has sanctity. For this reason, whoever enters it is safe, and whoever enters it is legislated to perform a rite of pilgrimage (nusuk), either obligatorily or as a recommendation, unlike other places. For this reason, everything in it is safe. Everything that has life in it is safe, even inanimate things, or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: No, even inanimate things. Trees are safe; it is not permissible to cut them within the Sacred Mosque.
* The student: Is it a plant?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is alive. It is alive, so if the tree dries out, it is permissible to break it, and it has no sanctity.
Among them: the obligation to face the qiblah wherever a person is, whether on land, sea, or in the air, based on His saying: ﴿Wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾. The obligation to face the qiblah is dropped in some situations, as we have gone over. The obligation to face the qiblah is dropped in which situations?
* A student: In voluntary prayer while traveling, except where...
* The Shaykh: Wherever he is facing. That is one. And the second?
* A student: In extreme fear.
* The Shaykh: In extreme fear, if it is not possible to face the qiblah. And the third?
* A student: If he does not know where the qiblah is.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: If he is on a mount while performing a voluntary prayer.
* The Shaykh: The brother has mentioned it.
* A student: If he is sick.
* The Shaykh: That is, in the case of inability: inability to face the qiblah due to illness or a broken back. If his back is bent away from the qiblah, or the like. And the fourth situation: can we include this among these situations, if the qiblah is uncertain to him, or is that not possible?
* The students: It is not possible.
* The Shaykh: It is not possible, because he is commanded to make an effort (ijtihad), he is commanded to make an effort. But if he errs, he is excused. Otherwise, at the time of prayer he must believe that the direction he has faced is correct. So uncertainty is not an exception, because the reality is that one may not pray unless he believes he is facing the qiblah. This differs from what we mentioned a little while ago: the one who is unable knows that the qiblah is behind him, and he prays facing other than the qiblah while knowing this. Likewise in extreme fear, and likewise the one performing a voluntary prayer while traveling.
* A student: What about fighting, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: In extreme fear.
* A student: Does extreme fear not fall under inability?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not fall under inability, because he is able. He can face it, but he is afraid, so he can turn and stand, but he fears for himself. The one who is unable cannot move or turn. So there are three matters that are excepted.
* Among the benefits of the verses: the Shari'ah takes into account the unity of Muslims in their physical orientation, just as it takes into account their unity in their inner, intellectual orientation. He says: ﴿Wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾. Now Muslims in all parts of the world are facing one qiblah. Is this tawhid or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: It is tawhid, especially since they face this direction and unite in this unity in the greatest practical symbol, or the greatest practical obligation, which is prayer. This shows that the Shari'ah takes complete care of the unity of Muslims in their religion: their unity in physical orientation and likewise in inner, intellectual orientation. I have avoided the word "spiritual" (ruhi), because I do not consider it valid. It is not right to say "spiritual and physical," since the spirit and the body are one thing, and purifying the spirit is purifying the body. This word "spirit" seems to have come from the Christians. For this reason, you will only find it in the expressions of later scholars who were influenced by Western culture. You will generally find that the earlier scholars always said "body and heart," as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah 10], attaching the matter to the heart.
* A student: ﴿They ask you about the spirit﴾ [al-Isra' 85]?
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is not what they mean. By "spirit" they mean what relates to acts of worship. What relates to acts of worship is the spirit, as they tell you, "the spirit." In reality, acts of worship benefit both the body and the spirit together, and the spirit is part of the body and the body is part of it.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the stubbornness of the Jews and Christians. It shows their stubbornness in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. Yet despite that, may God protect us, they reviled the Prophet (ﷺ) with a great reviling.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that what comes from God is truth, based on His saying: ﴿that it is the truth﴾, attributed to whom?
* The students: To God, exalted is He.
* The Shaykh: To God: ﴿from their Lord﴾.
* Among them: these obstinate People of the Book are stubborn while having complete knowledge and while acknowledging the lordship of God. Once they had acknowledged God's lordship over them and knew the truth, they were obligated to submit to it and to be the most deserving of people to follow it, because they have knowledge of that.
* Among them: the absence of heedlessness on the part of God, exalted is He, regarding their deeds, which implies His perfect knowledge and comprehensive encompassment of them. It is not enough to say only "the absence of heedlessness." We say: which implies perfect knowledge and encompassment, based on His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾.
* Among them: the validity of dividing the attributes into affirmative (thubutiyyah) and negative (salbiyyah). What we have here is negative. Attributes negated by any negating particle, whether (ma), (laysa), (la), (ghayr), or the like, are negative attributes. We have gone over that God does not negate of Himself except what is a deficiency, and that every negation implies the perfection of its opposite, because it is negated due to the perfection of its opposite. So, due to the completeness of His knowledge and encompassment, heedlessness is negated of Him.
* Among them: a warning to these obstinate People of the Book who were given the Scripture and knew the truth, because His saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ contains a clear warning.
Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And even if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah, nor are you a follower of their qiblah, nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others﴾ [al-Baqarah 145].
* A student: (...) In the previous verse, the turning of his face toward Bayt al-Maqdis was (...) from God?
* The Shaykh: Yes, that verse has passed us.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, from His saying: ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾.
* The student: ﴿from their Lord﴾: is it not inferred that the Qur'an (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not inferred. But what is inferred is the affirmation of the earlier scriptures, which were part of the message.
He said: ﴿And even if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Messenger (ﷺ) was eager for the guidance of creation, because His saying: "even if you brought them every sign" shows that he, peace and blessings be upon him, presented the signs and clarified the realities, but they did not benefit.
* Among them: the intensity of the stubbornness of these People of the Book, and that however many signs they were given, they did not submit to them and would never follow them.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation to submit to the truth when its signs become apparent, because this verse was revealed in the context of blame. This shows the obligation to follow the truth when its signs become clear.
* Among them: the blaming of some fanatics in their adherence to taqlid (blind imitation). How so? Because among the sectarian fanatics are those who, even if you bring them every sign, will not follow it, but if you bring them a statement from the words of their shaykhs, they say: "We hear and obey." For this reason, Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, in al-Fatwa al-Hamawiyyah, cited mostly the statements of scholars, including Ash'aris and others, and said: "Not everyone whose statement we cite do we agree with. But because some groups have attached themselves to an imam or a school, if you bring them every sign, they will not follow it until you bring them something from the words of their own (group)." This is among the methods of wisdom in calling people: a person convinces the opponent with something he cannot deny or oppose, if it is brought to him from the words of his own follower. Those fanatics for the schools, if we say to them: "This is Imam al-Shafi'i, Imam Malik, Imam Ahmad, Imam Abu Hanifah, all of whom reject being followed in opposition to the Book and the Sunnah, and they say: 'Throw our statements against the wall,'" and they have many expressions to this effect. If they themselves say this, are those who are fanatical for them while opposing the evidence truly imitators of them?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No, they did not truly imitate them. If they had truly imitated them, then when the evidence became clear to them, they would have acted upon it. But they did not truly imitate them; rather, they were fanatical in a way that is not praiseworthy, as long as the evidence is established. As for when the evidence is not established for a person, whether he is one who seeks evidence and is able to know the ruling from the evidences, or not, in any case he is excused if he imitates someone he thinks is closer to the truth. But when the evidence is clear and explained, imitation is forbidden. For this reason, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, said: "Imitation is like eating carrion." When is it permitted?
* The students: In necessity.
* The Shaykh: In necessity, it is permitted in necessity. But when slaughtered meat is available, you do not eat carrion. When the evidence from the Book and the Sunnah is present and made clear to a person, it is not permissible for him to imitate. For this reason, God did not command asking the people of knowledge except when one lacks knowledge, saying: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know, with clear proofs and scriptures﴾ [an-Nahl 43-44]. But if we know by the clear proofs and scriptures, then we do not ask them. We speak by the clear proofs and the scriptures.
* Among them, among the benefits of the verse: the impossibility of a Muslim following any Jew or Christian: ﴿nor are you a follower of their qiblah﴾. The impossibility is shown by the fact that the sentence here is a nominal sentence: "nor are you a follower of their qiblah." A true believer cannot follow the enemies of God, or adopt their opinions, ideas, and orientations. The Prophet (ﷺ) protected this to the utmost degree when he said: "Whoever imitates a people is one of them."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4031) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.]] So we must be careful and keep away from imitating the enemies of God and following them, whether in matters of worship or in matters of custom. Imitating them is forbidden and may lead to disbelief and polytheism, may God protect us. The main point is that His saying: ﴿nor are you a follower of their qiblah﴾ teaches that a believer cannot follow these people in their religion.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that the Jews and Christians do not follow one another. Rather, some of them misguide others. The Jews consider the Christians not to be Muslims, and the Christians consider the Jews not to be Muslims either. Each of them considers the other misguided. But against Islam they are one hand, ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and Christians as allies; they are allies of one another﴾ [al-Ma'idah 51]. They are one hand against Islam, because they are all enemies of Islam, yet among themselves some of them misguide others. Each one considers the other to not be upon a correct creed.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that following the Jews and Christians is following desire, not guidance: ﴿And if you followed their desires﴾.
* Also among them: they are not upon guidance, the Jews and Christians, since God, exalted is He, made what they are upon a desire and not guidance.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a person is not held accountable for following opposition except after the proof has been established against him, based on His saying: ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. A person may follow others out of ignorance and is not held accountable for it, although he is called astray, but he is not called a wrongdoer. Wrongdoing is only established for one who knew the truth and opposed it. As for one who is ignorant of the truth and was not granted success to it, it is said that he is astray, but it is not said that he is a wrongdoer, because he did not intentionally oppose it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 144–146 (part 4 of 4)**

* Among the benefits of the verse: it shows that knowledge in its true sense is the knowledge of the Sharia (divine law). ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. The verse uses the definite article (*al*), which conveys completeness: ﴿the knowledge﴾. There is no doubt that complete knowledge, which deserves praise and commendation, is knowledge of what?
* Students: Of the Sharia.
* Shaykh: Of the Sharia. For this reason we say that the era of prophethood is the era of knowledge. Our present age is not an age of knowledge; in truth, our age is an age of ignorance, ignorance of Allah and His Sharia. As for knowledge of this world, it is not (true) knowledge, because this kind of knowledge, does it remain?
* Students: No, it vanishes.
* Shaykh: It vanishes with the vanishing of this world; it does not remain. But knowledge of the Sharia remains, because it is the path and the means to reaching Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the abode of His honour. It is therefore the real, lasting knowledge. For this reason He said: ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. We often hear someone panting and saying: "This is the age of knowledge, the age of progress," and some of them say: "the age of light," exaggerating. This is an error. Yes, we say "the age of knowledge," but it must be qualified; it must be qualified, there is no harm in that. People today have worldly sciences that those before them did not have. But to say that the knowledge which deserves praise, knowledge in its unqualified sense, is the Sharia knowledge: ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾.
* Also, among the benefits of the verse: that wrongdoing, justice and other matters are attached to actions, not to persons. In other words, there is no relationship between Allah, Exalted, and any of His creatures such that He shows them favour or special consideration. Whoever opposes Him is a wrongdoer. We do not say, for example: "This man is close to the Messenger (ﷺ), so his sins will be expiated because of his closeness to the Messenger (ﷺ)," or say: "This person is a Qurashi, of the lineage of the nobles, of the lineage of Banu Hashim, so his sins will be expiated." If the Messenger (ﷺ), to whom Allah says: ﴿If you were to follow their desires﴾ ﴿then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾, then what about those below the Messenger (ﷺ)? Is that not so?
* Students: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: That is to say, no one here is shown favour by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because of his lineage, his ancestry, or his standing among people. No: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat 13].
* Among the benefits of the verse: it is permissible to make something conditional on a matter that will not occur. ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you﴾: this is a conditional statement, but it is hypothetical and cannot happen. It cannot happen because of Allah's words: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [an-Najm 3]. Allah says of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾, so one who does not speak from desire cannot be asked to follow desire. If his speech is not from desire, then his action is likewise; so the Messenger (ﷺ) cannot possibly follow their desires.
* Among the benefits of the verse: a warning to the Ummah against following the desires of those who do not believe. The reasoning is this: if this description would apply to the Messenger (ﷺ), were he to follow their desires, then those below him are all the more so. Thus the verse contains a warning that we must be extremely cautious about following the desires of the enemies of Allah. Would that we could awaken the Ummah from what it has fallen into now, following the desires of the enemies of Allah, and explain to them that this is wrongdoing, and that wrongdoing is darkness on the Day of Resurrection, and that the pasture of the one who seeks wrongdoing is grievous, so that people follow what?
* Students: Guidance.
* Shaykh: The guidance brought by Muhammad (ﷺ), as Allah says: ﴿Certainly guidance has come to them from their Lord﴾ [an-Najm 23].
* Student: I say: based on the principle that a person is not held accountable until the proof has been established against him, may we say of the grave-worshippers that they are misguided but not polytheists, and that their act is shirk, but they are not held accountable unless the proof has been established against them?
* Shaykh: Only once you have established the proof, yes. But we treat them as polytheists in matters such as not performing the funeral prayer over them, or not burying them in the graveyards of the Muslims, and similar things, because their outward condition now is the outward condition of committing shirk. But before Allah we do not affirm with certainty that they are in the Fire; the proof may not have been established against them. Furthermore, this, in reality, regarding the nearby Islamic lands, is in my view an impossible hypothetical; it is a matter of supposition. That is to say, there are people there who say that this is shirk. They hear someone say: "This is shirk." The earth is never without a scholar who makes the truth clear. For example, let us suppose that in these Arab lands, where graves are now worshipped besides Allah, do you think there are no scholars among them who guide them to the truth?
* Students: Of course there are.
* Shaykh: There are. There are scholars among them who explain to them that this is wrong, that it is forbidden, that it is shirk and kufr. But they persist, because they have followers who imitate them and consider them to be upon the truth.
* Student: Does it happen that (...) directed (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not possible. The address is explicit: ﴿It has been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds would surely become worthless, and you would surely be among the losers﴾ [az-Zumar 65]. ﴿It has been revealed to you and to those before you﴾ is explicit. And we said during the course of the tafsir that a conditional statement is not meant to imply that the condition occurs: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [az-Zukhruf 81]. This is not possible.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but with respect to Allah, this does not benefit them before Him.
* Student: What does it imply? What is its implication?
* Shaykh: Its implication is that they are the noblest of people by lineage. That is to say, the human race: people are like ores (of metal), so the lineage of Banu Hashim is noble, then the lineage of Quraysh, then the Arabs are more excellent than others in respect of lineage.
* Student: Does this not mean the reward is greater for the deed?
* Shaykh: No. The reward may be greater, or it may be less, according to the faith in a person's heart. For this reason, if some people of Banu Hashim came, we would say, from among some of the Companions: "The mudd of one of them does not reach (in merit) the mudd of one of them." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of them spent gold equal to Uhud, he would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it," even if he were of Banu Hashim.[[al-Bukhari (3673) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, with the wording being his; and Muslim (2540/221) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
* Student: So they do not benefit from this closeness?
* Shaykh: They do benefit. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "The best of you in Islam are the best of you in the Jahiliyyah."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3374) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] They benefit in that, if they are equal to others in piety, they are given precedence in the rulings. As for their ranks with Allah, the apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that they have a certain honour in that. But an unbeliever does not benefit from his closeness to the Messenger (ﷺ).
* Student: You mentioned in a book (...), you mentioned it in a summarised book, that he says that (...) imitation of (...) of knowledge of a thing (...).
* Shaykh: Ah, yes, that is correct. Whoever is unable to benefit by reaching knowledge of a matter should imitate (another).
* Student: The question: is he obliged to ask (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes. He asks the one he imitates. Even today, a person among the students of knowledge who is able to know the truth by its evidence sometimes encounters questions to which he cannot arrive at the evidence. He cannot, so it is not his obligation (to do so). Questions arise that require haste and not deliberation; that is, they require an immediate ruling, and you do not have the evidence now, and searching for that evidence may be difficult, such that the matter passes before a ruling is decided upon. So what do we do then?
* Student: We imitate.
* Shaykh: We have no recourse but imitation. We look for the person who, in our estimation, is closest to correctness, and we imitate him.
* Student: Shaykh, how did the Messenger (ﷺ) (...) how did He emphasise (...), the answer: ﴿then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. This was emphasised in order to warn, to intensify the warning. For this reason it was emphasised, not merely with *inna* and the *lam*; in reality it was emphasised by an oath: ﴿And if you were to follow﴾. So the whole sentence is emphasised by an oath, and then the answer to the oath is emphasised with *inna* and the *lam*.
* Student: Is the soul not itself the heart?
* Shaykh: The heart? No. By "soul" (*ruh*) is meant the self by which the body has life. Everything by which there is life is a *ruh*. For this reason Allah, Exalted, says in the Qur'an: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ [ash-Shura 52]. So Allah named the Qur'an a *ruh* because by it there is life.
* Student: Honourable Shaykh, how can the heart be the source of life?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. The heart has life in it, and the neck also has life in it; if a person's neck is cut, he has no life left.
* Student: What if, so that everything is formed from the heart, so to speak?
* Shaykh: No, it is not called that. I do not know that it is called a *ruh*. Rather, as the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "In the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107), from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]]
* Student: Shaykh, what is in the hadith: "Souls are armies mustered; those that recognise one another become attuned"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3336) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, and Muslim (2638/159) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, this is correct. Because your own soul, which is in your body, recognises the soul of another person as soon as you meet him; you feel affection for him the moment you encounter him, and you feel aversion the moment you see him. The souls of the wicked, when they see a wicked person, feel affection for him, and when they see the people of goodness, they reject them. Likewise the people of goodness with the people of wickedness. This is the meaning of his saying: "armies mustered."
﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise him as they recognise their own sons. And indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah 146]. This returns to (or explains) the condition of the Jews and the Christians. Was their obstinacy due to ignorance of the Messenger (ﷺ)? No. It serves to establish the strength of the denunciation against them, because they were persisting in obstinacy with knowledge.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the prophethood of the Messenger (ﷺ) is established in the earlier revelations, because of His words: ﴿they recognise him as they recognise their own sons﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: it shows that a person's attachment to a son is stronger than his attachment to a daughter, because of His words: ﴿as they recognise their own sons﴾. He knows more about his son than he knows about his daughter.
Allah was gentle in addressing the Messenger (ﷺ) when He said, as we explained in the tafsir: ﴿then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾, and He did not say "you are a wrongdoer," because this phrase, ﴿then you would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾, is gentler than saying "you are a wrongdoer." We mentioned a clear example of this gentleness in the address from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the Prophet (ﷺ). What is it?
* Student: ﴿May Allah pardon you﴾ [at-Tawbah 43].
* Shaykh: Any other?
* Student: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [Abasa].
* Shaykh: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know?﴾ [Abasa 1–3], and He did not say "you frowned and turned away."
The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise him as they recognise their own sons﴾. What is the meaning of His words: ﴿We gave them﴾? What is the meaning of ﴿We gave them﴾?
* Student: It means "We gave them."
* Shaykh: How many objects does it govern? Where is the first object?
* Student: The first is the pronoun, and the second is "the Book."
* Shaykh: Where is the predicate of the subject? ﴿Those to whom We gave them﴾, because *alladhina* (those who) is the subject, so where is its predicate?
* Student: ﴿They recognise him﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿They recognise him﴾, well done. The pronoun in His words ﴿they recognise him﴾ refers to whom?
* Student: It refers to ﴿those who were given the Book﴾.
* Shaykh: The pronoun in ﴿they recognise him﴾ is the *ha'* (the "him"). In ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book, they recognise him﴾, the *ha'* refers to whom?
* Student: To Muhammad (ﷺ).
* Shaykh: To the Prophet (ﷺ), yes. Is there a difficulty here, since he has not been mentioned before?
* Student: What is the difficulty?
* Shaykh: What is the difficulty, that the Messenger (ﷺ) has not been mentioned before?
* Student: But he is known by mental reference (*al-'ahd al-dhihni*).
* Shaykh: That is not what this pronoun is about.
* Student: It is mentioned in the books of (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, we have been speaking about the wording that we have now. In the context of the Qur'an, the Messenger (ﷺ) has not been mentioned before, so that we could say the pronoun refers to him.
* Student: Because the Qur'an is in the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ)...
* Another student: (...) because it is known.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is known from the context, and we may say that he was mentioned before: ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah 143], ﴿And We did not make the direction which you used to face except that We might make evident who would follow the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah 143], ﴿And you are not one to follow their qiblah﴾.
* Student: If we say the pronoun refers to the nearest mentioned noun, is the nearest mentioned noun "the Book"?
* Shaykh: They recognise the Book. What is the benefit of recognising their Book?
* Student: They recognise that it is the truth.
* Shaykh: They recognise that their Book is true?
* Student: The Book is the Qur'an.
* Shaykh: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ means the Jews and the Christians, the Children of Israel. They recognise Muhammad as they recognise their own sons.
Why did He single out the sons? Why did He single out the sons, rather than the daughters, in ﴿as they recognise their own sons﴾?
* Student: I do not know.
* Shaship: We mentioned it in the tafsir.
* Student: That is to say (...).
* Shaykh: That is to say, his recognition of them is stronger than his recognition of his daughters, because of his great care for them. That is one opinion. What is the second opinion? What do you say?
* Student: It is by way of *taghlib* (predominance of the masculine).
* Shaykh: No, there is nothing in it but this. But perhaps he wants to be like Ibn Jinni, who has two opinions for every question. There is nothing in it but this: He singled out the sons for mention because the soul is more attached to them than to daughters, so a person's recognition of them is greater than his recognition of daughters.
His words: ﴿and they know﴾. What is the grammatical position of this clause?
* Student: It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*).
* Shaykh: As a circumstantial clause. From where?
* Student: They know (...) ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise him﴾.
* Shaykh: A circumstantial clause of "the Book"? The Book has no connection (to it)?
* Student: It is not the Book.
* Shaykh: Where is it? Give me the element that the circumstantial clause refers to, and specify it.
* Student: "Those," or the *waw* (the "and they").
* Another student: It is a circumstantial clause of the subject of ﴿they conceal﴾.
* Shaykh: Of the subject of ﴿they conceal﴾. Why did He restrict their concealment to knowledge? Why did He restrict it by knowing, saying: ﴿they conceal the truth while they know﴾?
(...) And from the Christians?
* Student: An-Najashi.
* Shaykh: An-Najashi, yes.
* Student: Waraqah.
* Shaykh: Waraqah? No, he was an Arab, but he became a Christian.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 144–146 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Indeed We see the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We shall surely turn you to a qibla (direction of prayer) that will please you.﴾ The fa' (فَ) — we have mentioned that it is for tafriʿ (consequence, deduction). The lam in His words ﴿لَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾ (lanuwalliyannaka) is the lam of preface to an oath (lam al-muwatti'a lil-qasam). So the sentence is emphasised by three things, three emphatics: the implied oath, the lam, and the nun: ﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾. It was expressed in the form of magnification ﴿لَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾, because He, glorified and exalted is He, is Great, so the nun here is for majesty. His words ﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾ mean: "so We shall surely cause you to turn to a qibla, so We shall surely cause you to turn to a qibla." Accordingly, the kaf is the first object and "qiblatan" is the second object. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾ is "so We shall surely turn you (ḥawwalna)," and on this meaning, His words ﴿قِبْلَةً﴾ are in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, i.e., "so We shall surely turn you to a qibla that will please you." Is this understood? And His words ﴿قِبْلَةً﴾: the meaning of qibla is the thing that one faces and turns his face toward. His words ﴿قِبْلَةً﴾ are indefinite for magnification (qiblatan). His words ﴿تَرْضَاهَا﴾ mean: you are content with it, you love it and accept it. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, accepted this and that, but he loved that he be turned toward the Ka'bah.

After Allah, may He be exalted, had preceded this introduction, He said: ﴿Indeed We see the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We shall surely turn you to a qibla that will please you. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.﴾ ﴿فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾. "Walli" means: face it, turn your face toward it. In His words ﴿وَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ﴾, "wajh" (face) is the first object and "shatr" is the second object. The meaning of shatr here is the direction, i.e., the direction of the Sacred Mosque. In His words ﴿فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾, it is also meant to include the whole body, because the body, by its form and nature, when the face faces a direction, the whole body becomes facing it. In His words ﴿شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ﴾: the masjid originally means the place of prostration. It has been said that the masjad (with fatḥa) is the place of prostration, and the masjid (with kasra) is the place prepared for prostration, so there is a difference between them: the built place prepared for prostration is called masjid (with kasra), while the place where one has actually prostrated is called masjad (with fatḥa). In His words ﴿الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ﴾, "al-Ḥarām" is an adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah) from ḥurm, which means prohibition. It was called ḥarām because certain things are prohibited in it that are not prohibited elsewhere, and because it is respected and revered. What is meant by it? What is meant by the Sacred Mosque here is the Ka'bah and what surrounds it of the well-known structure.

In His words ﴿شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ﴾ ("toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it"), He shifted from addressing the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to addressing his community, saying: ﴿وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ﴾, because the address to the Prophet ﷺ is an address to him and to the community, since he is the imam, and an address directed to the imam is an address to him and to his community. A parallel to this is that a minister, for example, says to a commander: "Head to such-and-such," meaning: head, and whoever follows you of the soldiers. Likewise the address directed to the Messenger ﷺ is for him and for the community. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ﴾ [At-Talaq 1] — He addressed the Prophet ﷺ first, then said: ﴿إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ﴾, because the ruling is for him and for his community. Moreover, if this verse came after the revelation of His saying: ﴿لَا يَحِلُّ لَكَ النِّسَاءُ مِنْ بَعْدُ﴾ [Al-Ahzab 52], then the address was directed to the community, because it is impossible for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to divorce. He said: ﴿وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ﴾. This "ḥaythu" is an adverb of place, but it is conditional, to which "mā" has been added in pronunciation only, for emphasis, without meaning. It is permissible outside the Qur'an to say "ḥaythu kunta," but in the Qur'an it is not changed. His words ﴿كُنْتُمْ﴾ is the conditional verb. Where is the answer of the condition?

[Here the lesson includes the exchange below, rendered as recorded.]

Wherever you were in Makkah, and whoever was (...) and whoever was far from it. This is why the expression came with His words ﴿شَطْرَهُ﴾, meaning "toward it." Does it include the one who is inside the Ka'bah or not? Yes, it includes him, because of the generality of His words ﴿حَيْثُ مَا كُنْتُمْ﴾. So if he is inside the Ka'bah, he faces in front of his face from whichever direction he is in, isn't that so? From whichever direction, except that some scholars say: he does not face the door if it is open unless it has a threshold, because there must be an object (shakhis) in front of him, so that it can properly be said that he turned his face toward it. Good. If we are outside the house but in the mosque, do we circle around it or not? We circle around it, because if we stood in a straight line, we would not have turned our faces toward it, i.e., toward its direction; whoever moves out of its alignment would have turned his face toward something else, because it is now confined. If we move away, some scholars say: if you are in Makkah, face the Mosque, and if you are outside Makkah, face Makkah. But this is approximate. The correct view in this matter is that whoever is able to see the very Ka'bah must face the very building and not leave its alignment; whoever cannot see it, because of distance or something intervening, is satisfied with the direction, by His saying: ﴿لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا﴾ [Al-Baqarah 286].

* Student: And if a pillar stands between them, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, a pillar can be faced around. Do you mean in the mosque?
* Student: A pillar or an object placed (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, this can still hit its very building even if intervening.
* Student: The intended looking is not the aim; the aim is the direction.
* Shaykh: Yes, the aim is that you be facing it.
* Student: On this view, is it not permissible to pray on the roof of the Ka'bah?
