The command is entirely His; we belong to Allah. Yet, with their affirmation that they are owned by Allah, they hope for His reward. For this reason they say: ﴿and indeed to Him we will return﴾. So we hope that He who afflicted us with this calamity will, upon our return to Him, recompense us with something better than it. They combined here the affirmation of lordship in their saying ﴿indeed we belong to Allah﴾, with the affirmation and faith in recompense, a recompense that requires righteous deeds, for they say: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾. So we hope for His reward, though He has done to us what is His possession and in His hand. Here they combined the work of the heart and the utterance of the tongue: the work of the heart is patience, and the utterance of the tongue is their saying: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾.
The Sunnah has come with an addition to this as well, that a person says: "O Allah, reward me in my calamity"[[Related by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salama.]] And is it "akhlif" or "wa-akhlif"?
* Student: "Wa-akhlif."
* Shaykh: "Akhlif" [from the quadriliteral], "Akhlif li khayran minhā" [give me in return something better than it]. From the triliteral, it means one thing replaces another, as the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "and be a successor to him in his family"[[Related by Muslim (920/7) from the hadith of Umm Salama.]], meaning be a successor (khalifa) to him. But "akhlif," meaning make for him a successor from it. And here we say: "Akhlif li," meaning make for me a successor from it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾ [Saba 39]?
* Students: "Yukhlifuhu," "yakhlafuhu."
* Shaykh: Do not make mistakes! ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾. Yes, ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾. May Allah guide you. Do you not have courage? Do you not have courage at all? How can you be defeated before me when you are right?
* Student: So it is "yukhlifuhu."
* Shaykh: ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾, meaning He makes for it a successor. It is not that He himself replaces it and becomes a successor... it means He makes for it a successor. So if it is from the quadriliteral, "akhlafa 'alayhi" means He made for him a successor in place of it. But if it is from the triliteral, "khalafahu" means he himself became a successor. Do you understand?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 154–157 (part 2 of 2):

Now, [the Prophet (ﷺ) said]: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in its place"[[Recorded by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]]. That is, make for me a successor better than it. So we say what Allah has guided us to say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return. O Allah, reward us in our affliction and give us something better in its place." If a person says this as a believer seeking reward, Allah the Mighty and Majestic will reward him for his affliction and give him something better in its place.

The evidence for this is the story of Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her. She loved her cousin Abu Salamah very intensely. When he died, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had told her this hadith, she said: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in its place"[[Recorded by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]]. She kept thinking to herself: "Who will be a successor to Abu Salamah?" She believed that there would be a successor better than him, but who would it be? It did not occur to her that the Messenger (ﷺ) would be that successor. Glory be to Allah, who became her successor?

* A student: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

* The Shaykh: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Allah gave her something better than him. The Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication for Abu Salamah when he died, may Allah be pleased with him, was: "O Allah, forgive Abu Salamah, raise his rank among the guided, widen his grave for him, and illuminate it for him." And "give him a successor in his posterity." Not "and let me replace him," no mistake: "and give him a successor in his posterity"[[Recorded by Muslim (920/7) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]].

* A student: Shaykh, "wa-akhlif-hu"?

* The Shaykh: No, "wa-ukhluf-hu fi 'aqibihi," yes, meaning let him have a successor. What happened? His successor in his posterity was the best successor. Who? The Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the supplications, we hope they were answered, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic is generous and bountiful.

* A student: Shaykh, in this verse, ﴿الَّذِينَ إِذَا أَصَابَتْهُمْ مُصِيبَةٌ﴾ ("those who, when a disaster strikes them"), do we say that this is obligatory patience or contentment?

* The Shaykh: No, this is obligatory patience.

Now, His saying ﴿إِنَّا لِلَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed we belong to Allah"). Where is the predicate of inna?

* A student: It is omitted.

* The Shaykh: What is the estimated term?

* The student: "Sa'irun" (we will go).

* The Shaykh: "Inna sa'iruna lillah"?

* The student: I don't think it is "raji'un."

* The Shaykh: And "wa-inna ilayhi raji'un," which comes after it?

* The student: "Raji'un" is the predicate.

* The Shaykh: The predicate is "raji'un"?

* A student: Yes.

* Another student: We could say the prepositional phrase "lillah" is the predicate, and the sentence... this is the predicate.

* The Shaykh: Where is the predicate?

* The student: "Fa-inna nahnu" (then indeed we).

* Another student: This sentence is a sentence, this sentence is a sentence...

* The Shaykh: The prepositional phrase is the predicate. ﴿إِنَّا لِلَّهِ﴾ is the predicate. But is it the predicate itself, or is it attached to an omitted term whose estimate is "kā'inan" (being)?

* The students: Attached.

* The Shaykh: There is a disagreement on this, between two opinions. As for ﴿وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ﴾, the predicate of inna is His saying ﴿رَاجِعُونَ﴾. "Ilayhi" is attached to "raji'un," and it was placed before "raji'un" to convey restriction (exclusivity), in terms of meaning, and to match the verses' endings, in terms of wording.

* A student: Does it not need an estimate?

* The Shaykh: Which one? In the last one?

* The student: In "inna ilayhi raji'un."

* The Shaykh: No, there is no need for it.

And His saying: ﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("Those upon them are blessings from their Lord") [al-Baqarah 157].

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("those"): the demonstrative here is for the distant, because of the elevated rank of these people, may Allah be pleased with them and make us among them. ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ means: those who are characterized by these attributes.

﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject. Correct?

* A student: "Ulaika" is the subject.

* The Shaykh: And "'alayhim salawat": "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject.

* The student: No, "salawat" is a second subject.

* The Shaykh: And what about "'alayhim"?

* The student: "'Alayhim" is a preposed predicate.

* The Shaykh: Preposed, yes. So "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject, but it is a second subject. The sentence made of the second subject and its predicate is in the nominative position as the predicate of the first subject.

﴿عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾. The scholars differed over the meaning of "salawat." But the most correct of the opinions is that what is meant is praise of them in the highest assembly. So the meaning is that Allah praises these people in the highest assembly, to raise their mention and elevate their status.

His saying ﴿وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾ ("and mercy"): coordinating it with "salawat" indicates that they are different, and this refutes the view of those who say that Allah's salat means mercy.

His saying ﴿وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾ means that what is desired is attained for them through it, because mercy is either the attainment of what is desired or the removal of what is disliked. Here, mercy includes both: removal of what is disliked and attainment of what is loved.

His saying ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("and those are the guided"): this is a nominal sentence presented in a restrictive manner. What is the means of restriction here?

* A student: The demonstrative.

* The Shaykh: No, the demonstrative is not a means of restriction.

* A student: The separating pronoun "hum."

* The Shaykh: The separating pronoun is in ﴿هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾. "Ulaika" means: the patient ones who say what has been mentioned, they are the guided, who were guided to the path of truth and placed it in its right place. This statement they say, together with patience, is guidance. This is the opposite of those who do not endure calamities, neither with their hearts, nor with their tongues, nor with their limbs. Are they guided or astray?

* The students: Astray.

* The Shaykh: Astray. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) considered that from the deeds of disbelief, when he said: "Two things among people are disbelief in them: slandering lineage, and wailing over the dead"[[Recorded by Muslim (67/121) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. Wailing is a sign of impatience. This shows that guidance lies in patience, in submitting the matter to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, awaiting His reward, and seeking it. And His saying: ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾.

Then He said: ﴿إِنَّ الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةَ مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah") [al-Baqarah 158].

Among the benefits of this noble verse is His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَقُولُوا لِمَنْ يُقْتَلُ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أَمْوَاتٌ بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ وَلَكِنْ لَا تَشْعُرُونَ﴾ ("And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, 'They are dead.' Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive") [al-Baqarah 154].

First: the prohibition of applying the word "dead" to martyrs, based on His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَقُولُوا لِمَنْ يُقْتَلُ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أَمْوَاتٌ﴾. It is understood from our saying "absolutely" (without qualification) that if what is meant by this death is the separation of the soul from the body, then it is correct. For this reason, they always say "died as a martyr," so they qualify this death and do not use it absolutely.

* A student: Shaykh, is it correct to say, "This is a martyr," meaning they do not know the intention of the one who died? Is it correct for them to say, "He died as a martyr"? I mean, now every person who dies...

* The Shaykh: As for the Companions, we say, "He died as a martyr."

* The student: For non-Companions?

* The Shaykh: No. With regard to this, for the Companions, we do not affirm it definitively for a specific individual. We do not definitively affirm it for a particular person. But we say: whoever is killed unjustly, whoever is killed defending the truth, is a martyr. So the testimony for them is a general testimony.

* A student: Is it permissible to say, "This one is a martyr," on the basis that he is a martyr?

* The Shaykh: Yes. First, with regard to the rulings of this world, we treat him as a martyr: we do not wash him, we do not shroud him, we pray over him, and we bury him in his clothes.

* A student: What if he was killed inside the land, I mean, not in jihad?

* The Shaykh: In jihad, may Allah bless you. The one who is killed in the way of Allah.

* The student: I mean, his enemies killed him with bullets, for example?

* The Shaykh: No, no, that is not it. There is a disagreement among the scholars about this. What matters is the one who is killed in the way of Allah. But as for testifying that he is a martyr in the Hereafter, we do not affirm this definitively. Rather we say: whoever dies in this kind of death is a martyr. This is a general testimony, just as we say, "Every believer is in Paradise." But do you testify that a specific person is in Paradise?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: No, you do not testify. For this reason, it is not appropriate to say, "So-and-so is a martyr," except for those whose martyrdom is established by a text, such as the martyrs of Uhud and others like them.

* A student: What if many people agree on that?

* The Shaykh: On what?

* The student: That he is a martyr, and that Allah chose him?

* The Shaykh: If they agree on praising him, scholars have differed on this. Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) holds that it is permissible to testify for him that he is in Paradise, and also to testify that he is a martyr. Some scholars say: no, we stop at what the text has stated. Praise be to Allah: if he is, in Allah's sight, among the people of Paradise and among the martyrs, then our refraining from testifying for him does not prevent that with Allah. Is it clear?

And if he is not one of the martyrs, or not one of the believers, then we have exposed ourselves to danger.

* A student: Is it permissible to apply to any Companion who died that he died as a martyr? I mean, may a person apply it?

* The Shaykh: Those who were killed in the way of Allah.

* The student: From among the Companions.

* The Shaykh: Yes, because the term "martyrs of Uhud" was established in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah approved it.

* A student: I think there was a Companion who used to say, "So-and-so is a martyr," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "No, ..."

* The Shaykh: No, they said: "in Paradise."

* A student: They said: "So-and-so is a martyr (...)."

* The Shaykh: Yes, a martyr, or in Paradise?

* The student: Yes, they said: "Congratulations to him on martyrdom."

* The Shaykh: Yes, but this one said "martyr" or "in Paradise"?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: In any case, this would be covered by the text. What the Messenger stated, we do not speak about, whether affirming or denying it.

His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ﴾ ("rather, they are alive") contains an affirmation of the martyrs' life, according to His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ﴾. An objection to this statement, or to this benefit, is: is this life like the life of this world?

If someone says: What is the evidence that the prophets are alive? Because they are superior to the martyrs. Without doubt they are superior to the martyrs. If they are superior, and Allah has granted the martyrs this life, this shows that they are alive. This is the well-known view among the scholars. Allah made the martyr alive only because he caused his own death in the way of Allah. He is the one who brought about death in the way of Allah, so Allah rewarded him for this death by making him alive in His presence.

* It is derived from this that Allah's favor upon the doer is more complete than the doer's own deed. This is because the doer, who is the martyr, caused his own death, and so deprived himself of the continuation of life for two years, three years, ten years, or a hundred years. Is that not so? But his life through this martyrdom has no end? Never. It lasts until the Resurrection, and then comes eternal life. This is evidence that Allah's generosity in giving and reward exceeds the deed of the doer. This is a matter well known to all of you: "A good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples"[[An agreed-upon hadith. Al-Bukhari (6491) and Muslim (131/207), from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Indeed Allah wrote the good deeds and the bad deeds."]].

* And among them: the virtue of jihad in the way of Allah, because the text states ﴿فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("in the way of Allah"). This is an important matter, because many people intend that this is jihad and go out for it, since it is jihad and fighting against the enemies of Allah. But the sense that this is "in the way of Allah," that is, on the path that leads to Allah, is more eloquent. An analogy: now, all of us, when the caller to prayer calls, perform ablution, come to the mosque, pray, and strive for the prayer to be complete. Is that so or not? This is a reality. But when we perform ablution, do we feel that we are carrying out Allah's command in His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصَّلَاةِ فَاغْسِلُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾ ("O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces") [al-Ma'idah 6], or do we not feel this sense?

* A student: We feel it.

* The Shaykh: Whenever you perform ablution?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt. But do you feel that you are doing what Allah commanded you in general? But do you feel that now you are fulfilling Allah's command when performing ablution? Or do you feel you are performing ablution just for prayer, and that is all?

* A student: I perform ablution just for prayer, and that is all.

* The Shaykh: You perform ablution just for prayer, and that is all. This is the most common case. It is rare for a person to remember and say: "Hearing and obeying, O Lord." So now I wash my face, wash my hands, wipe my head, and wash my feet. Do you understand? The predominance in us is the intention of the deed, not the intention of the One for whom the deed is done. This is what predominates in us. Likewise, when you come to establish the prayer, you strive for its completeness and its humility. It is rare that you feel you are obeying the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿وَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾ ("and establish prayer") [al-Baqarah 43]. I am not saying this does not exist. It exists, but it is little. Most people say: "Because I pray, I complete my prayer, since it is better, because it is better than an incomplete prayer." But our feeling that this is obedience to our Lord's command is rare. The important thing is that the phrase ﴿فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ is significant and must be noticed.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the life of the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection), based on His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ﴾. It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "when a person is buried, two angels come to him, and Allah returns his soul to him, and two angels come to him and ask him about his Lord, his religion, and his prophet"[[Recorded by Ahmad in al-Musnad (14722), and Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunnah (892), with this wording, from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

* And among them: the affirmation of the bliss of the grave, based on His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("rather, they are alive with their Lord").

* And among them: that they enjoy bliss in Paradise, based on His saying ﴿يُرْزَقُونَ﴾ ("they are provided for").

* And among them: the affirmation of Allah's exaltedness. ﴿إِنَّ الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةَ مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah"). Al-Safa and al-Marwah are two well-known hills. Al-Safa is said to be the hill of Abu Qubays, and the second is Qu'aiqi'an. They are to the east of the Ka'bah. Umm Isma'il, may Allah be pleased with her, used to climb them to see whether anyone was nearby, after her dates and water ran out, her milk dried up, and her son became hungry.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 154–157 (part 1 of 2):

(لا) This is negating, ﴿وَلَا تَقُولُوا﴾ is prohibitive, and for this reason the verb is in the jussive. What is the evidence for its jussive form?
* Student: The deletion of the nun.
* Shaykh: The deletion of the nun. ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 154]. ﴿Of those who are killed﴾ means "concerning those who." The prohibition here on saying applies both to saying with the tongue and to saying in the heart. Saying with the tongue is to say, "They have died," and saying in the heart is to believe that they have died. Have you understood?
And His words, ﴿those who are killed﴾, mean those who are killed in the way of Allah. The one killed in the way of Allah is the one who is killed because he fights so that the word of Allah is supreme. People differ in fighting, that is, in the motive that drives them to it. Among them is one whose motive is zealous loyalty to his people, like the fighting of the Arabs, for the Arabs fight out of tribal zeal; they declare it, saying, "We fight for Arabism." By this they nullify the martyrdom they might otherwise gain, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the way of Allah."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (123) and Muslim (1904/150) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] And if they had said, instead of "we fight for Arabism," "we fight for Islam and the protection of the lands of Islam," they would have been fighting in the way of Allah.
A man may fight out of bravery. What is the meaning of bravery? That is, he is a brave person who loves fighting, so he fights for that reason. Is he then in the way of Allah?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No. He fights so that his position is seen and he is known as a brave champion. This also is not in the way of Allah. None is in the way of Allah except one who fights so that the word of Allah is supreme. So the one who is killed in the way of Allah, that is, on His path, which is His religion, that is, for the sake of this religion and its elevation, this is the one about whom you say, "Do not say they are dead."
And His words, ﴿dead﴾, are the predicate of an omitted subject. Its estimated form is?
* Student: "They."
* Shaykh: "They are dead."
Here the prohibition might seem problematic to a person: how can we not say they are dead when they have died? So we say: the intended meaning here is, do not say they are dead with absolute death, which is the separation of the soul from the body. That exists, and if their souls had not separated from their bodies we would not have buried them, and they would still be remaining, eating and drinking. But absolute death, no. The evidence is the corrective negation in His words: ﴿Rather, they are alive﴾, meaning, rather they are alive. So "alive" is the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿Rather, they are alive﴾ is the plural of "living." ﴿With their Lord﴾ ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran 169], with Allah, because if their souls were placed in the crops of green birds..
* Student: ﴿But you do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah 154].
* Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾: but you, O living ones in this world, do not perceive this life in the Hereafter. Yes, we do not perceive it, and had Allah not informed us of it we would not have known of it, because it belongs to the unseen world, and the unseen world is not encompassed by the perception of the living. For this reason it is obligatory, regarding the unseen world, to stop at what revelation has brought, neither advancing nor delaying, neither in this matter nor in others, even regarding the names and attributes of Allah, and even regarding what Allah has informed us about Paradise, Hellfire and the like. We must stop, neither transgressing nor falling short.
If someone said: How are they punished in the Fire forever, and remain, while we see that the Fire burns? What is the answer?
We say: Yes, they are burned, but their bodies are replaced. ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [an-Nisa 56], and their intestines are cut to pieces: ﴿and they will be given boiling water to drink, which will cut up their bowels﴾ [Muhammad 15]. But the world of the Hereafter is not like the world of this life.
﴿But you do not perceive﴾. ﴿Rather, they are alive, but﴾: "but" here, does it govern or not?
* Student: It does not govern.
* Shaykh: It does not govern?
* Student: Because it is lightened.
* Shaykh: Because it is lightened, and when "but" (lakin) is lightened it does not govern. Is there evidence for this from the words of Ibn Malik?
* Student: Yes.
"And when inna is lightened, its governing is rare..." ....................
* Shaykh: Yes, inna.
* Student: This is from its sisters.
* Student: Yes, but this is "but" (lakin).
* Student: "And when lakin is lightened, it is intended..."
"And ka'anna too is lightened..." ....................
* Student: Shaykh, is there a difference between (...)?
* Shaykh: There is no difference between the attacker and the defender.
* Student: But, I mean, the one in the way of Allah goes to visit the enemy?
* Shaykh: How does he visit the enemy? What do you mean by visiting the enemy? (...).
﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah 155].
These are several things, four calamities:
First: He said, ﴿And We will surely test you﴾, and the clause here is emphasized by three emphases: the oath, the lam, and the nun, the nun of emphasis. The verb here with the nun of emphasis is built on the fathah, is it not?
* Student: Yes, it is built on the fathah.
* Shaykh: Where is the end of the verb?
* Student: The waw.
* Shaykh: The waw. Its original form is "nabluu," and when the nun of emphasis was attached to it, it took a fathah, a fathah was put on it.
﴿And We will surely test you﴾: this is an emphatic oath from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and "nabluu" means "We test."
And His words, ﴿We will test you with something of fear﴾: fear is dread, and it includes general fear and specific fear. General fear is like when the land is threatened by an enemy, and specific fear is like when a person is tried in himself by someone who frightens and terrifies him. This occurs, and this also occurs.
And His words, ﴿of fear and hunger﴾: hunger is the opposite of satiety. Hunger has two causes. The first cause: scarcity of food. The second cause: scarcity of the wealth by which food is obtained. Have you understood?
There is also a third cause: illness, which makes satiety impossible. A person may have much wealth and much food, but he eats and is not satisfied. This too is a trial, this too is a trial.
Hunger's effect is not grasped except by one who has experienced it, indeed all calamities are not grasped except by one who has experienced them; as for one who has not experienced them, he does not know. It has a great and serious matter. If you want to know it, then during fasting on long days you find yourself, when hungry, in pain, strained and empty, though you hope that you will break your fast, that is, you hope, or know with certainty, that this hunger will pass. How is this hunger a trial?
﴿and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾. ﴿A loss of wealth﴾: the wealth meant for trade, such as earnings.
﴿And lives﴾: does this include livestock and the like, or do we say that livestock are lives but are included under wealth?
* Student: They are included under wealth.
* Shaykh: They are included under wealth, so "lives" here means the lives of human beings. ﴿And fruits﴾: the fruits are the fruits of the palm trees, the grapes and others. This also occurs. Calamities come, we ask Allah for safety and well-being, sweeping away people, livestock, crops and wealth, and storms come likewise. But for many people they are natural phenomena that do not stir their conscience or alarm their feelings, and we seek refuge in Allah. They do not see them as anything; they say, "These are natural disasters," and this is a matter that has become customary. This is a great error. We must make these things part of the trial by which Allah tests His servants. This trial, for the one who is struck by it, is very evident, and for the one who was not struck but heard of it, it is also evident, because it tests the one who was not struck: will he take warning and be instructed or not? Is that not so? For the one afflicted by such a thing there is no doubt that he is tried, but the one spared from it is also tried, because it makes it an admonition and a lesson. Allah the Exalted said about the town that became apes, despised: ﴿So We made it an example for what was before it and what came after it﴾ [al-Baqarah 66].
And He, glorified and exalted, said when mentioning the stories of those who denied the messengers, in the story of Yusuf, I think: ﴿Indeed, in their stories is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].
Then He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 155].
He, may His remembrance be exalted, knew that people divide, regarding these calamities with which they are tested, into two kinds: the patient and the discontent. Does the discontent one's discontent turn back the decree?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: It does not turn it back, but it becomes a regret for him, as Allah the Glorified and Exalted said in Surah Al 'Imran: ﴿Those who said of their brothers while they sat [at home], "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed"﴾ [Al 'Imran 168].
Before it: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed, so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ [Al 'Imran 156].
It does not remove the event that has occurred, but it becomes a regret in the heart. If he does not endure and is discontent, it becomes a regret in his heart that avails him nothing. For this reason some of the early scholars said: "Either you bear it with the patience of the noble, or you forget it with the forgetting of animals," because a person, however the world may be, its events follow one another and some of them make others forgotten, so he forgets. Now consider in yourself: have we not been struck by calamities? We have been struck by calamities in our bodies, in our families, and in our wealth, but with the passage of time they are forgotten. So if we do not endure, we do not earn a reward; but if we endure, we earn a reward, and what Allah has decreed will happen regardless.
﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 155]. Who are the patient? They are those who restrain themselves from discontent with Allah's decree. These are the ones who endure in this matter, who restrain themselves from discontent with Allah's decree. We have already covered that a person's stations at the time of calamity are four: four stations.
* Student: Discontent with everything, then patience, then contentment, then gratitude.
* Shaykh: Yes, four stations: discontent, then patience, then contentment, then gratitude. Discontent is forbidden, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) disavowed one who is discontent. He said: "He is not of us who strikes the cheeks, tears the collars, and calls with the call of the Jahiliyyah."[[Related by Muslim (103/165) from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]
Patience is obligatory, because Allah the Exalted commanded it in many verses, and the default in a command is what?
* Students: Obligation.
* Shaykh: Obligation. And because there is no meaning to not being discontent except patience. As for contentment, the scholars have two views on whether it is obligatory, and the correct view is that it is recommended (sunnah) and not obligatory. As for gratitude, it is recommended by consensus, and it is higher than contentment.
We now need the difference between contentment and patience. What is the difference between them?
* Student: Contentment is for what one loves and dislikes... (...).
* Shaykh: Originally, what one loves is not a calamity. Everything one loves is a calamity. Let us say: Allah gives us what (...).
* Student: Contentment is more general than discontent.
* Shaykh: Well done! We mentioned that the other day.
* Student: Patience is that one restrains himself and struggles against himself along with the pain.
* Shaykh: Yes, along with the pain and the aversion at what has happened. And contentment?
* Student: And contentment is that one is pleased with what Allah has decreed for him.
* Shaykh: The opposite of aversion; that is, it means that there is no difference in his mind between what has happened and what has not happened; it is all one. He is like a dead body before the washer, meaning that it does not concern him; he goes along with Allah's decree and destiny. If good befalls him, he is grateful; if harm befalls him, he is patient and content, and there is not even the slightest aversion in his soul. This is a great state, and it is rarely attained by a person. For this reason those who said it is not obligatory and said it is recommended said: it is difficult for souls. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286].
As for gratitude, how is one grateful for being afflicted? Now, if one of you were seized and I struck him, if I could strike him we would strike him in return; and if I could not?
* Student: He would cry out.
* Shaykh: He would cry out!! And he dislikes it, and perhaps he says, "This is our tutor, we must be patient with him." But how is he grateful? We say: a person may be afflicted with calamities from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and he may thank Allah for them in two respects. First, he thanks Allah: he knows that Allah has done this only for a wisdom, a wisdom that may be for the person's good, for if he continued in blessings he might perhaps transgress, increase and exalt himself, because he is human: ﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq 6-7].
When he sees himself as self-sufficient, needing no one and nothing, he may immediately transgress and increase, and we seek refuge in Allah. So he thanks Allah for this blessing, because it may be a training for him. Do you understand? Like a father who strikes his son to discipline him.
Second: he thanks Allah because these calamities are beneficial in every case, beyond the benefit of training a person and knowing himself and returning to Allah. They are beneficial because if you are patient, the reward of the patient is confirmed for you; and if you are not content or not grateful, you are expiated of your sins by them, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed.[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (5640) and Muslim (2572/49) from the hadith of 'A'isha, with the wording of al-Bukhari: "No calamity afflicts a Muslim except that Allah expiates by it some of his sins, even the thorn that pricks him," and the wording of Muslim: "No calamity afflicts a Muslim..."]] He is expiated of sins through them. So is Allah thanked for this matter?
* Students: Yes, indeed.
* Shaykh: Yes, Allah is thanked for this matter. This is the aspect by which a person gives thanks for calamities.
﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return"﴾ [al-Baqarah 156].
When a calamity afflicts them and its occurrence in them is confirmed, ﴿they say: "Indeed we belong to Allah"﴾. The lam indicates what?
* Student: Ownership.
* Shaykh: Belonging: we are the possession of Allah. The owned thing is acted upon by its owner as he wills. So if we are Allah's possession, He, glorified and exalted, is our Lord and does with us as He wills: He brought us into being, sustained us and restores us, and if He wills He withholds from us. The command is entirely His; we belong to Allah. Yet, with their affirmation that they are owned by Allah, they hope for His reward. For this reason they say: ﴿and indeed to Him we will return﴾. So we hope that He who afflicted us with this calamity will, upon our return to Him, recompense us with something better than it. They combined here the affirmation of lordship in their saying ﴿indeed we belong to Allah﴾, with the affirmation and faith in recompense, a recompense that requires righteous deeds, for they say: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾. So we hope for His reward, though He has done to us what is His possession and in His hand. Here they combined the work of the heart and the utterance of the tongue: the work of the heart is patience, and the utterance of the tongue is their saying: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾.
The Sunnah has come with an addition to this as well, that a person says: "O Allah, reward me in my calamity"[[Related by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salama.]] And is it "akhlif" or "wa-akhlif"?
* Student: "Wa-akhlif."
* Shaykh: "Akhlif" [from the quadriliteral], "Akhlif li khayran minhā" [give me in return something better than it]. From the triliteral, it means one thing replaces another, as the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "and be a successor to him in his family"[[Related by Muslim (920/7) from the hadith of Umm Salama.]], meaning be a successor (khalifa) to him. But "akhlif," meaning make for him a successor from it. And here we say: "Akhlif li," meaning make for me a successor from it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾ [Saba 39]?
* Students: "Yukhlifuhu," "yakhlafuhu."
* Shaykh: Do not make mistakes! ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾. Yes, ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾. May Allah guide you. Do you not have courage? Do you not have courage at all? How can you be defeated before me when you are right?
* Student: So it is "yukhlifuhu."
* Shaykh: ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾, meaning He makes for it a successor. It is not that He himself replaces it and becomes a successor... it means He makes for it a successor. So if it is from the quadriliteral, "akhlafa 'alayhi" means He made for him a successor in place of it. But if it is from the triliteral, "khalafahu" means he himself became a successor. Do you understand?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 154–157 (part 2 of 2):

Now, [the Prophet (ﷺ) said]: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in its place"[[Recorded by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]]. That is, make for me a successor better than it. So we say what Allah has guided us to say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return. O Allah, reward us in our affliction and give us something better in its place." If a person says this as a believer seeking reward, Allah the Mighty and Majestic will reward him for his affliction and give him something better in its place.

The evidence for this is the story of Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her. She loved her cousin Abu Salamah very intensely. When he died, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had told her this hadith, she said: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in its place"[[Recorded by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]]. She kept thinking to herself: "Who will be a successor to Abu Salamah?" She believed that there would be a successor better than him, but who would it be? It did not occur to her that the Messenger (ﷺ) would be that successor. Glory be to Allah, who became her successor?

* A student: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

* The Shaykh: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Allah gave her something better than him. The Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication for Abu Salamah when he died, may Allah be pleased with him, was: "O Allah, forgive Abu Salamah, raise his rank among the guided, widen his grave for him, and illuminate it for him." And "give him a successor in his posterity." Not "and let me replace him," no mistake: "and give him a successor in his posterity"[[Recorded by Muslim (920/7) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]].

* A student: Shaykh, "wa-akhlif-hu"?

* The Shaykh: No, "wa-ukhluf-hu fi 'aqibihi," yes, meaning let him have a successor. What happened? His successor in his posterity was the best successor. Who? The Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the supplications, we hope they were answered, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic is generous and bountiful.

* A student: Shaykh, in this verse, ﴿الَّذِينَ إِذَا أَصَابَتْهُمْ مُصِيبَةٌ﴾ ("those who, when a disaster strikes them"), do we say that this is obligatory patience or contentment?

* The Shaykh: No, this is obligatory patience.

Now, His saying ﴿إِنَّا لِلَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed we belong to Allah"). Where is the predicate of inna?

* A student: It is omitted.

* The Shaykh: What is the estimated term?

* The student: "Sa'irun" (we will go).

* The Shaykh: "Inna sa'iruna lillah"?

* The student: I don't think it is "raji'un."

* The Shaykh: And "wa-inna ilayhi raji'un," which comes after it?

* The student: "Raji'un" is the predicate.

* The Shaykh: The predicate is "raji'un"?

* A student: Yes.

* Another student: We could say the prepositional phrase "lillah" is the predicate, and the sentence... this is the predicate.

* The Shaykh: Where is the predicate?

* The student: "Fa-inna nahnu" (then indeed we).

* Another student: This sentence is a sentence, this sentence is a sentence...

* The Shaykh: The prepositional phrase is the predicate. ﴿إِنَّا لِلَّهِ﴾ is the predicate. But is it the predicate itself, or is it attached to an omitted term whose estimate is "kā'inan" (being)?

* The students: Attached.

* The Shaykh: There is a disagreement on this, between two opinions. As for ﴿وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ﴾, the predicate of inna is His saying ﴿رَاجِعُونَ﴾. "Ilayhi" is attached to "raji'un," and it was placed before "raji'un" to convey restriction (exclusivity), in terms of meaning, and to match the verses' endings, in terms of wording.

* A student: Does it not need an estimate?

* The Shaykh: Which one? In the last one?

* The student: In "inna ilayhi raji'un."

* The Shaykh: No, there is no need for it.

And His saying: ﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("Those upon them are blessings from their Lord") [al-Baqarah 157].

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("those"): the demonstrative here is for the distant, because of the elevated rank of these people, may Allah be pleased with them and make us among them. ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ means: those who are characterized by these attributes.

﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject. Correct?

* A student: "Ulaika" is the subject.

* The Shaykh: And "'alayhim salawat": "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject.

* The student: No, "salawat" is a second subject.

* The Shaykh: And what about "'alayhim"?

* The student: "'Alayhim" is a preposed predicate.

* The Shaykh: Preposed, yes. So "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject, but it is a second subject. The sentence made of the second subject and its predicate is in the nominative position as the predicate of the first subject.

﴿عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾. The scholars differed over the meaning of "salawat." But the most correct of the opinions is that what is meant is praise of them in the highest assembly. So the meaning is that Allah praises these people in the highest assembly, to raise their mention and elevate their status.

His saying ﴿وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾ ("and mercy"): coordinating it with "salawat" indicates that they are different, and this refutes the view of those who say that Allah's salat means mercy.

His saying ﴿وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾ means that what is desired is attained for them through it, because mercy is either the attainment of what is desired or the removal of what is disliked. Here, mercy includes both: removal of what is disliked and attainment of what is loved.

His saying ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("and those are the guided"): this is a nominal sentence presented in a restrictive manner. What is the means of restriction here?

* A student: The demonstrative.

* The Shaykh: No, the demonstrative is not a means of restriction.

* A student: The separating pronoun "hum."

* The Shaykh: The separating pronoun is in ﴿هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾. "Ulaika" means: the patient ones who say what has been mentioned, they are the guided, who were guided to the path of truth and placed it in its right place. This statement they say, together with patience, is guidance. This is the opposite of those who do not endure calamities, neither with their hearts, nor with their tongues, nor with their limbs. Are they guided or astray?

* The students: Astray.

* The Shaykh: Astray. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) considered that from the deeds of disbelief, when he said: "Two things among people are disbelief in them: slandering lineage, and wailing over the dead"[[Recorded by Muslim (67/121) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. Wailing is a sign of impatience. This shows that guidance lies in patience, in submitting the matter to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, awaiting His reward, and seeking it. And His saying: ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾.

Then He said: ﴿إِنَّ الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةَ مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah") [al-Baqarah 158].

Among the benefits of this noble verse is His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَقُولُوا لِمَنْ يُقْتَلُ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أَمْوَاتٌ بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ وَلَكِنْ لَا تَشْعُرُونَ﴾ ("And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, 'They are dead.' Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive") [al-Baqarah 154].

First: the prohibition of applying the word "dead" to martyrs, based on His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَقُولُوا لِمَنْ يُقْتَلُ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أَمْوَاتٌ﴾. It is understood from our saying "absolutely" (without qualification) that if what is meant by this death is the separation of the soul from the body, then it is correct. For this reason, they always say "died as a martyr," so they qualify this death and do not use it absolutely.

* A student: Shaykh, is it correct to say, "This is a martyr," meaning they do not know the intention of the one who died? Is it correct for them to say, "He died as a martyr"? I mean, now every person who dies...

* The Shaykh: As for the Companions, we say, "He died as a martyr."

* The student: For non-Companions?

* The Shaykh: No. With regard to this, for the Companions, we do not affirm it definitively for a specific individual. We do not definitively affirm it for a particular person. But we say: whoever is killed unjustly, whoever is killed defending the truth, is a martyr. So the testimony for them is a general testimony.

* A student: Is it permissible to say, "This one is a martyr," on the basis that he is a martyr?

* The Shaykh: Yes. First, with regard to the rulings of this world, we treat him as a martyr: we do not wash him, we do not shroud him, we pray over him, and we bury him in his clothes.

* A student: What if he was killed inside the land, I mean, not in jihad?

* The Shaykh: In jihad, may Allah bless you. The one who is killed in the way of Allah.

* The student: I mean, his enemies killed him with bullets, for example?

* The Shaykh: No, no, that is not it. There is a disagreement among the scholars about this. What matters is the one who is killed in the way of Allah. But as for testifying that he is a martyr in the Hereafter, we do not affirm this definitively. Rather we say: whoever dies in this kind of death is a martyr. This is a general testimony, just as we say, "Every believer is in Paradise." But do you testify that a specific person is in Paradise?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: No, you do not testify. For this reason, it is not appropriate to say, "So-and-so is a martyr," except for those whose martyrdom is established by a text, such as the martyrs of Uhud and others like them.

* A student: What if many people agree on that?

* The Shaykh: On what?

* The student: That he is a martyr, and that Allah chose him?

* The Shaykh: If they agree on praising him, scholars have differed on this. Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) holds that it is permissible to testify for him that he is in Paradise, and also to testify that he is a martyr. Some scholars say: no, we stop at what the text has stated. Praise be to Allah: if he is, in Allah's sight, among the people of Paradise and among the martyrs, then our refraining from testifying for him does not prevent that with Allah. Is it clear?

And if he is not one of the martyrs, or not one of the believers, then we have exposed ourselves to danger.

* A student: Is it permissible to apply to any Companion who died that he died as a martyr? I mean, may a person apply it?

* The Shaykh: Those who were killed in the way of Allah.

* The student: From among the Companions.

* The Shaykh: Yes, because the term "martyrs of Uhud" was established in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah approved it.

* A student: I think there was a Companion who used to say, "So-and-so is a martyr," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "No, ..."

* The Shaykh: No, they said: "in Paradise."

* A student: They said: "So-and-so is a martyr (...)."

* The Shaykh: Yes, a martyr, or in Paradise?

* The student: Yes, they said: "Congratulations to him on martyrdom."

* The Shaykh: Yes, but this one said "martyr" or "in Paradise"?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: In any case, this would be covered by the text. What the Messenger stated, we do not speak about, whether affirming or denying it.

His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ﴾ ("rather, they are alive") contains an affirmation of the martyrs' life, according to His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ﴾. An objection to this statement, or to this benefit, is: is this life like the life of this world?

If someone says: What is the evidence that the prophets are alive? Because they are superior to the martyrs. Without doubt they are superior to the martyrs. If they are superior, and Allah has granted the martyrs this life, this shows that they are alive. This is the well-known view among the scholars. Allah made the martyr alive only because he caused his own death in the way of Allah. He is the one who brought about death in the way of Allah, so Allah rewarded him for this death by making him alive in His presence.

* It is derived from this that Allah's favor upon the doer is more complete than the doer's own deed. This is because the doer, who is the martyr, caused his own death, and so deprived himself of the continuation of life for two years, three years, ten years, or a hundred years. Is that not so? But his life through this martyrdom has no end? Never. It lasts until the Resurrection, and then comes eternal life. This is evidence that Allah's generosity in giving and reward exceeds the deed of the doer. This is a matter well known to all of you: "A good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples"[[An agreed-upon hadith. Al-Bukhari (6491) and Muslim (131/207), from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Indeed Allah wrote the good deeds and the bad deeds."]].

* And among them: the virtue of jihad in the way of Allah, because the text states ﴿فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("in the way of Allah"). This is an important matter, because many people intend that this is jihad and go out for it, since it is jihad and fighting against the enemies of Allah. But the sense that this is "in the way of Allah," that is, on the path that leads to Allah, is more eloquent. An analogy: now, all of us, when the caller to prayer calls, perform ablution, come to the mosque, pray, and strive for the prayer to be complete. Is that so or not? This is a reality. But when we perform ablution, do we feel that we are carrying out Allah's command in His saying: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصَّلَاةِ فَاغْسِلُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ﴾ ("O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces") [al-Ma'idah 6], or do we not feel this sense?

* A student: We feel it.

* The Shaykh: Whenever you perform ablution?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt. But do you feel that you are doing what Allah commanded you in general? But do you feel that now you are fulfilling Allah's command when performing ablution? Or do you feel you are performing ablution just for prayer, and that is all?

* A student: I perform ablution just for prayer, and that is all.

* The Shaykh: You perform ablution just for prayer, and that is all. This is the most common case. It is rare for a person to remember and say: "Hearing and obeying, O Lord." So now I wash my face, wash my hands, wipe my head, and wash my feet. Do you understand? The predominance in us is the intention of the deed, not the intention of the One for whom the deed is done. This is what predominates in us. Likewise, when you come to establish the prayer, you strive for its completeness and its humility. It is rare that you feel you are obeying the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿وَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾ ("and establish prayer") [al-Baqarah 43]. I am not saying this does not exist. It exists, but it is little. Most people say: "Because I pray, I complete my prayer, since it is better, because it is better than an incomplete prayer." But our feeling that this is obedience to our Lord's command is rare. The important thing is that the phrase ﴿فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ is significant and must be noticed.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of the life of the barzakh (the intermediate state between death and resurrection), based on His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ﴾. It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "when a person is buried, two angels come to him, and Allah returns his soul to him, and two angels come to him and ask him about his Lord, his religion, and his prophet"[[Recorded by Ahmad in al-Musnad (14722), and Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunnah (892), with this wording, from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

* And among them: the affirmation of the bliss of the grave, based on His saying ﴿بَلْ أَحْيَاءٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("rather, they are alive with their Lord").

* And among them: that they enjoy bliss in Paradise, based on His saying ﴿يُرْزَقُونَ﴾ ("they are provided for").

* And among them: the affirmation of Allah's exaltedness. ﴿إِنَّ الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةَ مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah"). Al-Safa and al-Marwah are two well-known hills. Al-Safa is said to be the hill of Abu Qubays, and the second is Qu'aiqi'an. They are to the east of the Ka'bah. Umm Isma'il, may Allah be pleased with her, used to climb them to see whether anyone was nearby, after her dates and water ran out, her milk dried up, and her son became hungry.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 154–157 (part 1 of 2):

(لا) This is negating, ﴿وَلَا تَقُولُوا﴾ is prohibitive, and for this reason the verb is in the jussive. What is the evidence for its jussive form?
* Student: The deletion of the nun.
* Shaykh: The deletion of the nun. ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 154]. ﴿Of those who are killed﴾ means "concerning those who." The prohibition here on saying applies both to saying with the tongue and to saying in the heart. Saying with the tongue is to say, "They have died," and saying in the heart is to believe that they have died. Have you understood?
And His words, ﴿those who are killed﴾, mean those who are killed in the way of Allah. The one killed in the way of Allah is the one who is killed because he fights so that the word of Allah is supreme. People differ in fighting, that is, in the motive that drives them to it. Among them is one whose motive is zealous loyalty to his people, like the fighting of the Arabs, for the Arabs fight out of tribal zeal; they declare it, saying, "We fight for Arabism." By this they nullify the martyrdom they might otherwise gain, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the way of Allah."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (123) and Muslim (1904/150) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]] And if they had said, instead of "we fight for Arabism," "we fight for Islam and the protection of the lands of Islam," they would have been fighting in the way of Allah.
A man may fight out of bravery. What is the meaning of bravery? That is, he is a brave person who loves fighting, so he fights for that reason. Is he then in the way of Allah?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No. He fights so that his position is seen and he is known as a brave champion. This also is not in the way of Allah. None is in the way of Allah except one who fights so that the word of Allah is supreme. So the one who is killed in the way of Allah, that is, on His path, which is His religion, that is, for the sake of this religion and its elevation, this is the one about whom you say, "Do not say they are dead."
And His words, ﴿dead﴾, are the predicate of an omitted subject. Its estimated form is?
* Student: "They."
* Shaykh: "They are dead."
Here the prohibition might seem problematic to a person: how can we not say they are dead when they have died? So we say: the intended meaning here is, do not say they are dead with absolute death, which is the separation of the soul from the body. That exists, and if their souls had not separated from their bodies we would not have buried them, and they would still be remaining, eating and drinking. But absolute death, no. The evidence is the corrective negation in His words: ﴿Rather, they are alive﴾, meaning, rather they are alive. So "alive" is the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿Rather, they are alive﴾ is the plural of "living." ﴿With their Lord﴾ ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran 169], with Allah, because if their souls were placed in the crops of green birds..
* Student: ﴿But you do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah 154].
* Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾: but you, O living ones in this world, do not perceive this life in the Hereafter. Yes, we do not perceive it, and had Allah not informed us of it we would not have known of it, because it belongs to the unseen world, and the unseen world is not encompassed by the perception of the living. For this reason it is obligatory, regarding the unseen world, to stop at what revelation has brought, neither advancing nor delaying, neither in this matter nor in others, even regarding the names and attributes of Allah, and even regarding what Allah has informed us about Paradise, Hellfire and the like. We must stop, neither transgressing nor falling short.
If someone said: How are they punished in the Fire forever, and remain, while we see that the Fire burns? What is the answer?
We say: Yes, they are burned, but their bodies are replaced. ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [an-Nisa 56], and their intestines are cut to pieces: ﴿and they will be given boiling water to drink, which will cut up their bowels﴾ [Muhammad 15]. But the world of the Hereafter is not like the world of this life.
﴿But you do not perceive﴾. ﴿Rather, they are alive, but﴾: "but" here, does it govern or not?
* Student: It does not govern.
* Shaykh: It does not govern?
* Student: Because it is lightened.
* Shaykh: Because it is lightened, and when "but" (lakin) is lightened it does not govern. Is there evidence for this from the words of Ibn Malik?
* Student: Yes.
"And when inna is lightened, its governing is rare..." ....................
* Shaykh: Yes, inna.
* Student: This is from its sisters.
* Student: Yes, but this is "but" (lakin).
* Student: "And when lakin is lightened, it is intended..."
"And ka'anna too is lightened..." ....................
* Student: Shaykh, is there a difference between (...)?
* Shaykh: There is no difference between the attacker and the defender.
* Student: But, I mean, the one in the way of Allah goes to visit the enemy?
* Shaykh: How does he visit the enemy? What do you mean by visiting the enemy? (...).
﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾ [al-Baqarah 155].
These are several things, four calamities:
First: He said, ﴿And We will surely test you﴾, and the clause here is emphasized by three emphases: the oath, the lam, and the nun, the nun of emphasis. The verb here with the nun of emphasis is built on the fathah, is it not?
* Student: Yes, it is built on the fathah.
* Shaykh: Where is the end of the verb?
* Student: The waw.
* Shaykh: The waw. Its original form is "nabluu," and when the nun of emphasis was attached to it, it took a fathah, a fathah was put on it.
﴿And We will surely test you﴾: this is an emphatic oath from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and "nabluu" means "We test."
And His words, ﴿We will test you with something of fear﴾: fear is dread, and it includes general fear and specific fear. General fear is like when the land is threatened by an enemy, and specific fear is like when a person is tried in himself by someone who frightens and terrifies him. This occurs, and this also occurs.
And His words, ﴿of fear and hunger﴾: hunger is the opposite of satiety. Hunger has two causes. The first cause: scarcity of food. The second cause: scarcity of the wealth by which food is obtained. Have you understood?
There is also a third cause: illness, which makes satiety impossible. A person may have much wealth and much food, but he eats and is not satisfied. This too is a trial, this too is a trial.
Hunger's effect is not grasped except by one who has experienced it, indeed all calamities are not grasped except by one who has experienced them; as for one who has not experienced them, he does not know. It has a great and serious matter. If you want to know it, then during fasting on long days you find yourself, when hungry, in pain, strained and empty, though you hope that you will break your fast, that is, you hope, or know with certainty, that this hunger will pass. How is this hunger a trial?
﴿and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits﴾. ﴿A loss of wealth﴾: the wealth meant for trade, such as earnings.
﴿And lives﴾: does this include livestock and the like, or do we say that livestock are lives but are included under wealth?
* Student: They are included under wealth.
* Shaykh: They are included under wealth, so "lives" here means the lives of human beings. ﴿And fruits﴾: the fruits are the fruits of the palm trees, the grapes and others. This also occurs. Calamities come, we ask Allah for safety and well-being, sweeping away people, livestock, crops and wealth, and storms come likewise. But for many people they are natural phenomena that do not stir their conscience or alarm their feelings, and we seek refuge in Allah. They do not see them as anything; they say, "These are natural disasters," and this is a matter that has become customary. This is a great error. We must make these things part of the trial by which Allah tests His servants. This trial, for the one who is struck by it, is very evident, and for the one who was not struck but heard of it, it is also evident, because it tests the one who was not struck: will he take warning and be instructed or not? Is that not so? For the one afflicted by such a thing there is no doubt that he is tried, but the one spared from it is also tried, because it makes it an admonition and a lesson. Allah the Exalted said about the town that became apes, despised: ﴿So We made it an example for what was before it and what came after it﴾ [al-Baqarah 66].
And He, glorified and exalted, said when mentioning the stories of those who denied the messengers, in the story of Yusuf, I think: ﴿Indeed, in their stories is a lesson for those of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].
Then He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 155].
He, may His remembrance be exalted, knew that people divide, regarding these calamities with which they are tested, into two kinds: the patient and the discontent. Does the discontent one's discontent turn back the decree?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: It does not turn it back, but it becomes a regret for him, as Allah the Glorified and Exalted said in Surah Al 'Imran: ﴿Those who said of their brothers while they sat [at home], "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed"﴾ [Al 'Imran 168].
Before it: ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed, so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts﴾ [Al 'Imran 156].
It does not remove the event that has occurred, but it becomes a regret in the heart. If he does not endure and is discontent, it becomes a regret in his heart that avails him nothing. For this reason some of the early scholars said: "Either you bear it with the patience of the noble, or you forget it with the forgetting of animals," because a person, however the world may be, its events follow one another and some of them make others forgotten, so he forgets. Now consider in yourself: have we not been struck by calamities? We have been struck by calamities in our bodies, in our families, and in our wealth, but with the passage of time they are forgotten. So if we do not endure, we do not earn a reward; but if we endure, we earn a reward, and what Allah has decreed will happen regardless.
﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah 155]. Who are the patient? They are those who restrain themselves from discontent with Allah's decree. These are the ones who endure in this matter, who restrain themselves from discontent with Allah's decree. We have already covered that a person's stations at the time of calamity are four: four stations.
* Student: Discontent with everything, then patience, then contentment, then gratitude.
* Shaykh: Yes, four stations: discontent, then patience, then contentment, then gratitude. Discontent is forbidden, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) disavowed one who is discontent. He said: "He is not of us who strikes the cheeks, tears the collars, and calls with the call of the Jahiliyyah."[[Related by Muslim (103/165) from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]]
Patience is obligatory, because Allah the Exalted commanded it in many verses, and the default in a command is what?
* Students: Obligation.
* Shaykh: Obligation. And because there is no meaning to not being discontent except patience. As for contentment, the scholars have two views on whether it is obligatory, and the correct view is that it is recommended (sunnah) and not obligatory. As for gratitude, it is recommended by consensus, and it is higher than contentment.
We now need the difference between contentment and patience. What is the difference between them?
* Student: Contentment is for what one loves and dislikes... (...).
* Shaykh: Originally, what one loves is not a calamity. Everything one loves is a calamity. Let us say: Allah gives us what (...).
* Student: Contentment is more general than discontent.
* Shaykh: Well done! We mentioned that the other day.
* Student: Patience is that one restrains himself and struggles against himself along with the pain.
* Shaykh: Yes, along with the pain and the aversion at what has happened. And contentment?
* Student: And contentment is that one is pleased with what Allah has decreed for him.
* Shaykh: The opposite of aversion; that is, it means that there is no difference in his mind between what has happened and what has not happened; it is all one. He is like a dead body before the washer, meaning that it does not concern him; he goes along with Allah's decree and destiny. If good befalls him, he is grateful; if harm befalls him, he is patient and content, and there is not even the slightest aversion in his soul. This is a great state, and it is rarely attained by a person. For this reason those who said it is not obligatory and said it is recommended said: it is difficult for souls. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 286].
As for gratitude, how is one grateful for being afflicted? Now, if one of you were seized and I struck him, if I could strike him we would strike him in return; and if I could not?
* Student: He would cry out.
* Shaykh: He would cry out!! And he dislikes it, and perhaps he says, "This is our tutor, we must be patient with him." But how is he grateful? We say: a person may be afflicted with calamities from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and he may thank Allah for them in two respects. First, he thanks Allah: he knows that Allah has done this only for a wisdom, a wisdom that may be for the person's good, for if he continued in blessings he might perhaps transgress, increase and exalt himself, because he is human: ﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq 6-7].
When he sees himself as self-sufficient, needing no one and nothing, he may immediately transgress and increase, and we seek refuge in Allah. So he thanks Allah for this blessing, because it may be a training for him. Do you understand? Like a father who strikes his son to discipline him.
Second: he thanks Allah because these calamities are beneficial in every case, beyond the benefit of training a person and knowing himself and returning to Allah. They are beneficial because if you are patient, the reward of the patient is confirmed for you; and if you are not content or not grateful, you are expiated of your sins by them, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed.[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (5640) and Muslim (2572/49) from the hadith of 'A'isha, with the wording of al-Bukhari: "No calamity afflicts a Muslim except that Allah expiates by it some of his sins, even the thorn that pricks him," and the wording of Muslim: "No calamity afflicts a Muslim..."]] He is expiated of sins through them. So is Allah thanked for this matter?
* Students: Yes, indeed.
* Shaykh: Yes, Allah is thanked for this matter. This is the aspect by which a person gives thanks for calamities.
﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return"﴾ [al-Baqarah 156].
When a calamity afflicts them and its occurrence in them is confirmed, ﴿they say: "Indeed we belong to Allah"﴾. The lam indicates what?
* Student: Ownership.
* Shaykh: Belonging: we are the possession of Allah. The owned thing is acted upon by its owner as he wills. So if we are Allah's possession, He, glorified and exalted, is our Lord and does with us as He wills: He brought us into being, sustained us and restores us, and if He wills He withholds from us. The command is entirely His; we belong to Allah. Yet, with their affirmation that they are owned by Allah, they hope for His reward. For this reason they say: ﴿and indeed to Him we will return﴾. So we hope that He who afflicted us with this calamity will, upon our return to Him, recompense us with something better than it. They combined here the affirmation of lordship in their saying ﴿indeed we belong to Allah﴾, with the affirmation and faith in recompense, a recompense that requires righteous deeds, for they say: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾. So we hope for His reward, though He has done to us what is His possession and in His hand. Here they combined the work of the heart and the utterance of the tongue: the work of the heart is patience, and the utterance of the tongue is their saying: ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return﴾.
The Sunnah has come with an addition to this as well, that a person says: "O Allah, reward me in my calamity"[[Related by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salama.]] And is it "akhlif" or "wa-akhlif"?
* Student: "Wa-akhlif."
* Shaykh: "Akhlif" [from the quadriliteral], "Akhlif li khayran minhā" [give me in return something better than it]. From the triliteral, it means one thing replaces another, as the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "and be a successor to him in his family"[[Related by Muslim (920/7) from the hadith of Umm Salama.]], meaning be a successor (khalifa) to him. But "akhlif," meaning make for him a successor from it. And here we say: "Akhlif li," meaning make for me a successor from it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾ [Saba 39]?
* Students: "Yukhlifuhu," "yakhlafuhu."
* Shaykh: Do not make mistakes! ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾. Yes, ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾. May Allah guide you. Do you not have courage? Do you not have courage at all? How can you be defeated before me when you are right?
* Student: So it is "yukhlifuhu."
* Shaykh: ﴿And whatever you spend, He replaces it﴾, meaning He makes for it a successor. It is not that He himself replaces it and becomes a successor... it means He makes for it a successor. So if it is from the quadriliteral, "akhlafa 'alayhi" means He made for him a successor in place of it. But if it is from the triliteral, "khalafahu" means he himself became a successor. Do you understand?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 154–157 (part 2 of 2):

Now, [the Prophet (ﷺ) said]: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in its place"[[Recorded by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]]. That is, make for me a successor better than it. So we say what Allah has guided us to say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return. O Allah, reward us in our affliction and give us something better in its place." If a person says this as a believer seeking reward, Allah the Mighty and Majestic will reward him for his affliction and give him something better in its place.

The evidence for this is the story of Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her. She loved her cousin Abu Salamah very intensely. When he died, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had told her this hadith, she said: "O Allah, reward me in my affliction and give me something better in its place"[[Recorded by Muslim (918/3) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]]. She kept thinking to herself: "Who will be a successor to Abu Salamah?" She believed that there would be a successor better than him, but who would it be? It did not occur to her that the Messenger (ﷺ) would be that successor. Glory be to Allah, who became her successor?

* A student: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

* The Shaykh: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Allah gave her something better than him. The Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication for Abu Salamah when he died, may Allah be pleased with him, was: "O Allah, forgive Abu Salamah, raise his rank among the guided, widen his grave for him, and illuminate it for him." And "give him a successor in his posterity." Not "and let me replace him," no mistake: "and give him a successor in his posterity"[[Recorded by Muslim (920/7) from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]].

* A student: Shaykh, "wa-akhlif-hu"?

* The Shaykh: No, "wa-ukhluf-hu fi 'aqibihi," yes, meaning let him have a successor. What happened? His successor in his posterity was the best successor. Who? The Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the supplications, we hope they were answered, because Allah the Mighty and Majestic is generous and bountiful.

* A student: Shaykh, in this verse, ﴿الَّذِينَ إِذَا أَصَابَتْهُمْ مُصِيبَةٌ﴾ ("those who, when a disaster strikes them"), do we say that this is obligatory patience or contentment?

* The Shaykh: No, this is obligatory patience.

Now, His saying ﴿إِنَّا لِلَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed we belong to Allah"). Where is the predicate of inna?

* A student: It is omitted.

* The Shaykh: What is the estimated term?

* The student: "Sa'irun" (we will go).

* The Shaykh: "Inna sa'iruna lillah"?

* The student: I don't think it is "raji'un."

* The Shaykh: And "wa-inna ilayhi raji'un," which comes after it?

* The student: "Raji'un" is the predicate.

* The Shaykh: The predicate is "raji'un"?

* A student: Yes.

* Another student: We could say the prepositional phrase "lillah" is the predicate, and the sentence... this is the predicate.

* The Shaykh: Where is the predicate?

* The student: "Fa-inna nahnu" (then indeed we).

* Another student: This sentence is a sentence, this sentence is a sentence...

* The Shaykh: The prepositional phrase is the predicate. ﴿إِنَّا لِلَّهِ﴾ is the predicate. But is it the predicate itself, or is it attached to an omitted term whose estimate is "kā'inan" (being)?

* The students: Attached.

* The Shaykh: There is a disagreement on this, between two opinions. As for ﴿وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ﴾, the predicate of inna is His saying ﴿رَاجِعُونَ﴾. "Ilayhi" is attached to "raji'un," and it was placed before "raji'un" to convey restriction (exclusivity), in terms of meaning, and to match the verses' endings, in terms of wording.

* A student: Does it not need an estimate?

* The Shaykh: Which one? In the last one?

* The student: In "inna ilayhi raji'un."

* The Shaykh: No, there is no need for it.

And His saying: ﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("Those upon them are blessings from their Lord") [al-Baqarah 157].

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("those"): the demonstrative here is for the distant, because of the elevated rank of these people, may Allah be pleased with them and make us among them. ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ means: those who are characterized by these attributes.

﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ﴾: "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject. Correct?

* A student: "Ulaika" is the subject.

* The Shaykh: And "'alayhim salawat": "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject.

* The student: No, "salawat" is a second subject.

* The Shaykh: And what about "'alayhim"?

* The student: "'Alayhim" is a preposed predicate.

* The Shaykh: Preposed, yes. So "'alayhim" is a preposed predicate, and "salawat" is a postponed subject, but it is a second subject. The sentence made of the second subject and its predicate is in the nominative position as the predicate of the first subject.

﴿عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾. The scholars differed over the meaning of "salawat." But the most correct of the opinions is that what is meant is praise of them in the highest assembly. So the meaning is that Allah praises these people in the highest assembly, to raise their mention and elevate their status.

His saying ﴿وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾ ("and mercy"): coordinating it with "salawat" indicates that they are different, and this refutes the view of those who say that Allah's salat means mercy.

His saying ﴿وَرَحْمَةٌ﴾ means that what is desired is attained for them through it, because mercy is either the attainment of what is desired or the removal of what is disliked. Here, mercy includes both: removal of what is disliked and attainment of what is loved.

His saying ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("and those are the guided"): this is a nominal sentence presented in a restrictive manner. What is the means of restriction here?

* A student: The demonstrative.

* The Shaykh: No, the demonstrative is not a means of restriction.

* A student: The separating pronoun "hum."

* The Shaykh: The separating pronoun is in ﴿هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾. "Ulaika" means: the patient ones who say what has been mentioned, they are the guided, who were guided to the path of truth and placed it in its right place. This statement they say, together with patience, is guidance. This is the opposite of those who do not endure calamities, neither with their hearts, nor with their tongues, nor with their limbs. Are they guided or astray?

* The students: Astray.

* The Shaykh: Astray. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) considered that from the deeds of disbelief, when he said: "Two things among people are disbelief in them: slandering lineage, and wailing over the dead"[[Recorded by Muslim (67/121) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. Wailing is a sign of impatience. This shows that guidance lies in patience, in submitting the matter to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, awaiting His reward, and seeking it. And His saying: ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْمُهْتَدُونَ﴾.

Then He said: ﴿إِنَّ الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةَ مِنْ شَعَائِرِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah") [al-Baqarah 158].
