This view has strong grounds, because the verse is in the context of His words: ﴿And among the people are those who take rivals besides Allah, whom they love as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 165]. They hope from this love to attain their aims, but it will not benefit them. ﴿And their bonds are cut off from them﴾. The same applies to everyone who clings to a means that Allah has not made a means of salvation: it will betray him when he needs it most. So those who hold to the supplication of saints, the supplication of prophets, the supplication of messengers, and, all the more so, the supplication of trees and stones and the like, these will betray them when they most need them. For example, their supplication to the Messenger that he save them from the Fire will not benefit them, and likewise their supplication to anyone other than the messengers will not benefit them.

﴿And those who followed will say: If only we had another chance, we would disown them as they have disowned us﴾ [al-Baqarah 167]. ﴿Those who followed﴾, the followers, say: ﴿If only we had another chance﴾. *Law* here is not conditional; it is for wishing, meaning: "If only we had a return." The evidence that it is for wishing is that the verb after it is in the subjunctive: ﴿we would disown them﴾, *fa-nataba'arra'*, which is in the subjunctive by the hidden *an* after the *fa'* of causation.

We have already noted that *law* occurs in Arabic in how many ways? In three ways: it is conditional, it is for wishing, and it is verbal (*masdariyyah*, introducing a noun clause). The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 2] are the verbal kind. His words: ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another﴾ [al-Baqarah 253] are conditional. His words here: ﴿If only we had another chance, we would disown them﴾ [al-Baqarah 167] are for wishing. Similar is ﴿If only we had another chance, we would be among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 102], and in another verse: ﴿If only I had another chance, I would be among the good-doers﴾ [al-Zumar 58].

His words: ﴿If only we had another chance﴾. *Al-karrah* is a return to something. What is meant here by the return? To what? To the world. ﴿We would disown them there, in the world, if we returned, as they disowned us here, in the Hereafter, and we would repay them with what they repaid us with.** But as the common people say, "Wishing is the capital of the bankrupt." Does this wish benefit them or not? No. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them, and they will never come out of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 167]. *-A'udhu billah.* ﴿Thus﴾: what is the grammatical analysis of ﴿thus﴾? Who among you will do it?

* A student: The *kaf* is a particle of comparison, a preposition, and *dha* is a demonstrative noun built on sukun in the genitive position, and the *lam* (...) and the *kaf* (...).

* The Shaykh: Good. And the prepositional phrase, what is its position in the grammatical structure?

* The student: It is an object.

* The Shaykh: You agree with what?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: You do not agree with what? And what do you have, and what do you disagree with in it?

* The student: (...) its grammatical analysis?

* The Shaykh: Yes, we want its grammatical analysis.

* The student: The *kaf* is connected to (...).

* The Shaykh: The followed, yes. ﴿Allah will show them their deeds﴾. This occurs frequently in the Qur'an, like ﴿And thus they do﴾ and ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah 143]. There are very many in the Qur'an. They say: the *kaf* here is a noun meaning "like," and it is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) whose governing verb is the verb that follows it.

As for His words: ﴿Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them﴾ [al-Baqarah 167], do you want to analyze this too? ﴿Allah will show them their deeds as regrets for them﴾?

* A student: ﴿will show them﴾ is a present-tense verb.

* The Shaykh: Excellent.

* A student: No, *yurri* is a present-tense verb that takes two objects, and the *ha'* in ﴿will show them﴾ is the first object (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: And the word of majesty (Allah) is the subject in the nominative, and its sign of nominative case is the visible *damma*.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: And ﴿their deeds﴾ is the second object, and the *ha'* is a possessive pronoun.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: And ﴿regrets﴾ is the third object.

* The Shaykh: You said it takes two objects.

* The student: No, it takes three.

* The Shaykh: It takes three?

* The student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And what made it take three objects?

* The student: Because it is from *ara* (to show).

* The Shaykh: From *ara*, *yuri*? So the addition of the *hamza* is what made it take three objects. Fine. Is there evidence for this from the words of Ibn Malik?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, have we given it?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It makes them see their deeds as regrets upon them: ﴿Allah will show them their deeds﴾.

﴿Regrets﴾ is the plural of *hasrah*, which is remorse together with contraction and grief. *-Wal-'iyadhu billah* (and we seek refuge in Allah). These people will be shown their deeds on the Day of Resurrection in this way, and they will be filled with regret. Now consider: what will be the feelings of these followers at that time? Their feeling of remorse, disappointment and loss is unimaginable. The deeds they did for these leaders will become a loss for them and a source of remorse. Through them they lose their worldly life and their Hereafter, *-wal-'iyadhu billah*. This is the greatest kind of regret, the greatest regret is like this: that a person loses his worldly life and his Hereafter for the sake of following these masters, nobles and dignitaries. Later, if Allah wills, in the mention of the benefits, there will be what branches out from this great matter.

He says: ﴿And they will never come out of the Fire﴾. *Ma* here is negative, but it works like *laysa* (is not). *Hum* is its subject, and *bikharijina* is its predicate, emphasized with the *ba'*.

﴿And they will never come out of the Fire﴾: so then they are what? They are abiding in it. Allah, glorified and exalted, has mentioned that abiding in the Fire is eternal. In how many places in the Qur'an? In three places: in Surah al-Nisa', in Surah al-Ahzab, and in Surah al-Jinn. Allah mentioned eternity in these three places. Through this we recognize the weakness of the view of some of the early and later scholars that the Fire and whoever is in it will perish and cease. The weakness of this view is that we say: the eternity of the abiding one's abiding requires what? The eternity of the place in which he abides. Otherwise it would not be correct to call it eternal. If the Fire were to perish, there would be no eternity for the one who abides in it, because it would come to an end. The correct view, held by the majority of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, is that the Fire and the Garden will not perish. As for the Garden, this is agreed upon. As for the Fire, there is disagreement from some early and later scholars, but the correct view is that it will not perish.

* A student: Shaykh, they attribute eternity to the murderer and to all? We do not say this?

* The Shaykh: There is no eternity. The murderer does not have eternity, no, there is no eternity [for him].

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O mankind, eat from whatever is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ [al-Baqarah 168].

﴿O mankind﴾: this verse came in Surah al-Baqarah, and Surah al-Baqarah is Medinan. It has already been mentioned that a similar address came: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. Many authors on the principles of tafsir (*usul al-tafsir*, the foundations of Qur'anic interpretation) have stated that in Medinan surahs the address generally uses ﴿O you who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 104], because when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, migrated to Medina, Medina became a land of Islam, and it was the first Islamic city in this message. So the direction was addressed to it with ﴿O you who believe﴾. But this is not a rule. Rather, it is a weak principle, because many verses in Medinan surahs contain ﴿O mankind﴾. Surah al-Nisa' is Medinan or Meccan? Medinan, and it contains several verses with ﴿O mankind﴾. Here it says ﴿O mankind﴾. It has already been mentioned that *al-nas* originally was *al-unas*, and the *hamza* was dropped for ease. The intended meaning of *al-nas* is the children of Adam.

﴿O mankind, eat from whatever is on the earth﴾. ﴿Eat﴾ is an imperative verb. As for His words, ﴿from whatever is on the earth﴾, *min* may be explanatory of the kind, or it may be partitive. But the explanatory sense is preferable, and the words of Allah, the Exalted, support it: ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾ [al-Baqarah 29]. All that is on the earth, not just part of it. So the stronger of the two possibilities is that *min* is explanatory of the kind, meaning: eat from this whatever you wish.

His words: ﴿eat from whatever is on the earth﴾ include everything on the earth: trees, crops, herbs, and others, everything on the earth, and also animals, and animals too, because they are on the earth.

His words: ﴿lawful and good﴾. Is ﴿lawful﴾ here in the accusative as a state (*hal*) of *ma* (whatever), or as an object of ﴿eat﴾?

* The students: A state.

* The Shaykh: Apparently it is a state, meaning: eat it while it is lawful, that is, made lawful (*muhallalan*), so it has the sense of a passive participle, made lawful.

His words: ﴿good﴾ is another state, meaning while it is good. The good includes what is good in itself and what is good in its acquisition. Good in itself is what is not forbidden, because everything forbidden is corrupt. The evidence is: ﴿and He makes unlawful for them the corrupt things﴾ [al-A'raf 157]. Another proof: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it except that it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure﴾ [al-An'am 145].

Based on this we say: the good includes what is good in its essence and what is good in its acquisition. The good in its essence, we said, is what is not corrupt. The good in its acquisition is what has been acquired in a lawful way. So what is acquired through usury, is it good or not good? It is not good. The payment of a soothsayer?

* Students: It is not good.

* The Shaykh: It is not good, it is corrupt. The earnings of a prostitute, meaning the wages of a fornicatress?

* A student: It is not good.

* The Shaykh: It is not good, it is corrupt. The price of a dog? Good. The price of tobacco?

* Students: Corrupt.

* The Shaykh: Corrupt? Yes. So we say: the good is what is good in its substance and in its acquisition.

﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. ﴿Do not follow﴾: *la* is a prohibitive particle. Following (*ittiba'*) means that a person takes up what another has done, like the one who tracks a trail, following the track of a camel or a beast or the like.

His words: ﴿footsteps of Satan﴾: the plural of *khatwah*. *Khutwah* with a *damma* is different from *khatwah* with a *fatha*. *Khatwah* with a *fatha* is one step, from *khuta* (steps). *Khutwah* is the act of a person moving his foot from one place to another to walk.

His words: ﴿footsteps of Satan﴾ means his deeds, which he does and steps toward. It includes association with Allah and everything less than that. We know that Satan, as Allah, mighty and majestic, has taught us, commands what kind of thing? He commands indecency: ﴿He only commands you to evil and indecency, and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah 169]. So everything Allah has forbidden is among the footsteps of Satan, whether it is out of arrogance, denial, mockery, or otherwise. Everything Allah has forbidden is among the footsteps of Satan, because he commands it, proclaims it and calls to it, so it is among his steps. Among these is eating with the left hand, because Satan eats with his left hand and drinks with his left hand. Whoever eats with his left hand or drinks with his left hand has followed the footsteps of Satan. For this reason, the preponderant view on this question is that this is forbidden, and that a person may not eat with his left hand or drink with his left hand. But if someone says: "If you are eating and want to drink, what do you do? Do you drink with your right hand?"

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: They say: drink with the left hand, so that you do not soil the cup. We say this is not correct, because the cup does not get soiled. Even if you drink with your right hand, you can hold it by its bottom between your thumb and forefinger and drink. If it is assumed that it gets soiled, it gets soiled slightly at its base, not at its rim from which people drink, so that we could say you have made it dirty for them. But because people have become lax about this matter, or because they believe what many scholars have held, that drinking with the left hand is disliked, the matter has become trivial to them. Otherwise, whoever knows that it is forbidden, as is known to everyone, is not permitted to make it lawful except in cases of necessity.

* A student: Shaykh, is it permissible to put the cup down like this?

**Shaykh:** Yes. If he makes it like this, he is between permissibility and prohibition, just as he is between the right and the left. ﴿Indeed, Allah has set a measure for everything﴾ [At-Talaq 3]. So just as you now are not purely using the right hand nor purely the left, you have neither fallen into what is forbidden nor fully complied with what is commanded. You have not complied with the command, and you have not fallen into the prohibition. We do not say that you did something forbidden, because the left hand was not used exclusively. But there is no doubt that the more perfect practice is to use the right hand exclusively.

**Student:** What if he drinks with both hands?

**Shaykh:** It is the same matter, except that it becomes heavy. If he cannot manage with the right hand, then there is no harm, since this is a need.

**Student:** And eating?

**Shaykh:** Eating. I do not think it is a cause (for concern).

**Student:** He eats with two hands?

**Shaykh:** He eats with two hands? Yes, this would be similar.

**Student:** A bone, or something?

**Shaykh:** A bone or a melon?

**Students:** Bread.

**Shaykh:** No. With bread, he holds it with the left hand and cuts with the right; there is nothing wrong with that. Likewise with a bone. Even with a bone, it is not necessary (...). In any case, with need there is no harm, because we said that this is not purely left-handed, so he has not fallen into the prohibition.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, and it is crunchy, the nerve that..

**Student:** Shaykh, what is confusing, Shaykh, is the straw. If there is a straw (...) and he holds it with the left hand, like holding a cup with the left hand?

**Shaykh:** (...)?

**Student:** No, I mean even if, I mean, if the thing happens, no (...).

**Shaykh:** We say this is drinking with the left hand.

**Student:** It is not drinking with the left hand.

**Shaykh:** How?

**Student:** He drank through the straw?

**Shaykh:** But in its origin, in its origin, even if the cup is with him, he did not drink with the same hand. He is drinking by means of the cup. The cup is a means. That is, instead of drinking from the rim of the cup, he drank from this pipe.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Yes. He holds this cup with the right hand, or this one you sucked through, and he sucked.

**Student:** (...) without intention?

**Shaykh:** What, without intention?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** If the person is heedless at that time and unaware, then he is of the same category as one who did something forbidden while unaware. He has no sin. But a person must pay attention to these things.

**Student:** So it is forbidden, Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it is forbidden.

**Student:** ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾.

Alright. ﴿The steps of Satan﴾. Is "Shayṭān" from (sh-ṭ-n), so that the nūn is original, or from (sh-y-ṭ), so that the nūn is added? We say it is from (sh-ṭ-n), because it is declined (ṣarf) in the Qur'an: ﴿And he is not the word of an accursed Satan﴾ [At-Takwir 25]. If it were from (sh-y-ṭ), the nūn and the alif would be additional, and it would be diptote (not declined). However, it may be said that it is not diptote, because its feminine is (shayṭāna). What makes a word diptote is when its feminine is of the form fa'lā, like sakrān and sakrā (...).

It is (named so) when he is far from the mercy of Allah, because of his distance from the mercy of Allah, the Exalted.

He said: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾. "Enemy" is the opposite of "friend." The jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, defined it by saying: "Whoever is displeased by another's misfortune, or whose joy distresses him, is an enemy." So the enemy is the one who grieves at your happiness and rejoices at your sorrow. This is the enemy.

He said: ﴿Clear﴾, meaning clear in enmity, evident in enmity. He was an enemy to our father Adam, peace be upon him, and his enmity has not ceased until the Hour comes, until Allah brings His command. Allah, the Exalted, said about him: ﴿Allah has cursed him, and he said, "I will surely take from Your servants an appointed portion. And I will surely mislead them, and I will surely arouse in them desires, and I will surely order them so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will surely order them so they will alter the creation of Allah"﴾ [An-Nisa' 118–119].

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever takes Satan as a guardian other than Allah has certainly suffered a clear loss﴾. We ask Allah for safety and well-being.

**Student:** An example of the conditional "law" (...), an example of the conditional?

**Shaykh:** Yes. Like: ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another﴾ [Al-Baqarah 253]. ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one nation﴾ [Hud 118].

(...) and the ḍamma of the mīm. And what exists now?

**Student:** This is what exists.

**Shaykh:** This is what exists. There is a reading with kasra of both (letters): ﴿bihimi al-asbāb﴾. In a third reading, with ḍamma of both: ﴿bihumu al-asbāb﴾.

**Student:** It exists, Shaykh: ﴿bihumu al-asbāb﴾.

**Shaykh:** No, it does not exist. The readings now are three: ḍamma of both, and the second? Kasra of both, and the third: kasra of the hā' and ḍamma of the mīm.

**Student:** The reading of Ḥafṣ?

**Shaykh:** Likewise. By Allah, I do not know who recited it as one of the seven readings. ﴿Thus Allah shows them﴾ also has three similar readings: kasra of the hā' and the mīm, ﴿yurīhimi Allāhu a'mālahum﴾; ḍamma of both, ﴿yurīhumu Allāh﴾; and kasra of the hā' with ḍamma of the mīm, ﴿yurīhimu Allāh﴾.

Discussion of ﴿O mankind, eat﴾: it is in the context of expressing divine favor, not in the context of obligation. That a person must eat what sustains him is understood from another evidence; otherwise, a person would be obligated to eat only what sustains him.

**Student:** How was it stated for explanation?

**Shaykh:** For the explanation of favor, the favor of Allah, the Exalted, upon us, in that He permitted for us everything on the earth.

**Student:** Is this a rule?

**Shaykh:** Yes. What is stated to explain favor does not carry obligation.

**Student:** Does it not indicate obligation?

**Shaykh:** No, no. It does not indicate obligation.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** No, no. Do you mean that "eat" applies to "good"? No. "Good" will come, Allah willing, in the benefits that follow, which are addressed to the believers.

**Student:** It does not exclude the obligation of favor?

**Shaykh:** Yes. Alright, His saying: ﴿of what is in the earth﴾. Is "min" here partitive, or is it explanatory of the kind?

**Student:** Explanatory of the kind.

**Shaykh:** And what is the evidence? The evidence?

**Student:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿of what is in the earth﴾, because "earth" is explanatory of the kind.

**Shaykh:** Yes, but does the meaning mean "eat some of what is in the earth"?

**Student:** No, it is explanatory of the kind; it is not partitive.

**Shaykh:** And what is the evidence?

**Student:** His saying, the Exalted (...).

**Shaykh:** I want evidence for this position.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** For both of them together?

**Student:** Yes (...).

**Shaykh:** There is a difference between them.

**Student:** Evidence for the kind is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 29].

**Shaykh:** Yes, good. This is evidence that it is explanatory of the kind: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth﴾. So this is general. Alright.

His saying: ﴿lawful and good﴾. What is the difference between "lawful" (ḥalālan) and "good" (ṭayyiban)?

**Student:** "Good" is an emphasis of "lawful."

**Shaykh:** How is it an emphasis of "lawful"? And what is the aspect of it being an emphasis of "lawful"?

**Student:** Because lawful (...) good.

**Shaykh:** The evidence?

**Student:** The evidence is the saying of the Messenger ﷺ: "Allah has permitted for the believers what He permitted for the prophets," and as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat﴾ [Al-Baqarah 172].

**Shaykh:** "Indeed, Allah has commanded" [Narrated by Muslim (1015/65)]. No, we want something other than this. We want evidence that every lawful thing is good. Who knows?

**Student:** ﴿And He makes lawful for them the good things﴾.

**Shaykh:** The saying of Allah, the Exalted, describing the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And He makes lawful for them the good things﴾ [Al-A'raf 157].

His saying: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾. What are the "steps"?

**Student:** His steps are his paths and his ways.

**Shaykh:** And among them?

**Student:** Among them is commanding indecency and wrongdoing.

**Shaykh:** Good. In the word "Shayṭān," is the nūn original or additional?

**Student:** Its origin is sh-ṭ-n?

**Shaykh:** Yes, so I am asking whether the nūn is original or additional.

**Student:** Original, because it is sh-ṭ-n.

**Shaykh:** From sh-ṭ-n, meaning what?

**Student:** Shaṭaṭ, which is distance?

**Shaykh:** From distance. Good, because he is far from the mercy of Allah, the Exalted.

Can you bring us a witness from the Qur'an that shows the nūn is original?

**Student:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he is not the word of an accursed Satan﴾ [At-Takwir 25]. It is declined, which shows it is original. If it were not original, it would be diptote.

**Shaykh:** It is diptote when it is intended as a proper name.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾. What is the place of this sentence in meaning relative to what precedes it?

**Student:** We said a second opinion: that it is from (sh-y-ṭ), "Shayṭān."

**Shaykh:** From (sh-y-ṭ).

**Student:** From (sh-y-ṭ), meaning hidden.

**Shaykh:** The nūn is additional, and it is also declined, because the feminine of shayṭān is shayṭāna.

I say: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾. What is the place of this sentence in meaning relative to what precedes it?

**Student:** It is emphasizing what precedes it.

**Shaykh:** Emphasizing.

**Student:** Explaining the state of Satan, approximately.

**Shaykh:** Explaining the state of Satan? That is, emphasizing the reality, as if it were emphasizing.

**Student:** Causal.

**Shaykh:** Causal.

**Shaykh:** His saying: "mubīn."

**Student:** That means "clear."

**Shaykh:** Yes, clear. From? The verb from it is what?

**Student:** The verb from it is from (abāna).

**Shaykh:** From abāna. And abāna means what?

**Student:** "Manifested."

**Shaykh:** It means "manifested." So "mubīn" means "making manifest"?

**Student:** From (bāna).

**Shaykh:** From (bāna yabīnu), so it is bayyin. But this is mubīn.

**Student:** Bayyin and mubīn.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** From (abāna), only the intransitive, not the transitive.

**Shaykh:** Correct. From intransitive (abāna). Because we told you that (abāna) comes both intransitive and transitive. It is said: abāna al-shay', meaning he manifested it; and it is said: abāna al-ṣubḥ, meaning it appeared and became clear.

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. O Allah, make it easy.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When those who were followed disassociate themselves from those who followed, and they see the punishment﴾, to the end.

* From this verse is derived: those who are followed in falsehood do not benefit their followers, because of His saying: ﴿When those who were followed disassociate themselves﴾. If they benefited them, they would not have disassociated from them.

* Among its benefits also: the matter is not limited to lack of benefit, but extends to disassociation from them and distancing from them: ﴿When those who were followed disassociate themselves﴾. This is more painful for the followers than if their position had been passive.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of punishment, and from it follows the establishment of resurrection, because of His saying: ﴿And they see the punishment﴾.

* Among them: Allah, the Exalted, gathers the followers and the followed, as rebuke and reproach for them, because there is no doubt that this is the greatest regret when the one they followed, whom they honored in the world, disassociates from them even more. So Allah gathers them and some of them disassociate from others.

* Among the benefits of the verse: all false causes are cut off and vanish on the Day of Resurrection. Every false cause that does not please Allah and His Messenger does not benefit its holder on the Day of Resurrection.

We mentioned that this verse is intended for those who were followed in what?

**Students:** In falsehood.

**Shaykh:** In falsehood, unlike those followed in truth. The messengers do not disassociate from their followers. We supported this by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 67].

* Among the benefits of the following verse: ﴿And those who followed will say, "If only we had another return, so we could disassociate from them as they have disassociated from us."﴾ [Al-Baqarah 167].

* Among the benefits of this verse: these followers wish to return to the world so they can disassociate from those (they followed), as those (leaders) disassociated from them in the Hereafter. Is this possible or not possible?

**Student:** Not possible.

**Shaykh:** Not possible. And this only increases their regret. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Thus Allah shows them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾.

* Among its benefits also: the regret of these people and those like them, who missed righteous deeds in this world. They will regret in the Hereafter with a regret that has no equal, and it does not occur to their imagination today, nor to the imagination of others, because it is remorse that cannot be remedied. In this world, you may regret what you missed, but you strive to repair it. But there, there is no such thing.

* Among them: the establishment of Allah's punishment upon them, because of His saying: ﴿Thus Allah shows them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾.

* Among them: their eternal abiding in the Fire, because of His saying: ﴿And they will never emerge from the Fire﴾.

* Among them: the establishment of the Fire, and that it is true, because of His saying: ﴿from the Fire﴾. And it is so. It exists now, does it not?

**Student:** It exists.

**Shaykh:** Yes, it exists now.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth [that is] lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ [Al-Baqarah 168].

**Student:** O Shaykh, some texts mention that the Fire is in the earth?

**Shaykh:** Yes.

**Student:** How is it reconciled, this and that it exists?

**Shaykh:** We say: Allah knows best. We have not encompassed the earth. It may be in a place unknown to us, meaning in a lower direction, but it is not in the earth itself. Allah knows best.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the manifestation of Allah's favor upon His servants, in that He permitted for them all that is on the earth: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on earth, lawful and good﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse also: the basic principle regarding what is on the earth is permissibility and goodness until it is clear that it is forbidden. Can it be derived from this verse that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia, or not?

**Students:** It is derived.

**Shaykh:** It is derived?

**Students:** It is derived.

**Shaykh:** What is the basis for that?

**Students:** ﴿O mankind﴾.

**Shaykh:** From His saying: ﴿O mankind﴾, and they are included in this address. So they are addressed with the branches of the Sharia. This is the correct view. The correct view is that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia. But being addressed with them does not mean they are bound by them while in disbelief. No. Because we first call them to what? To Islam, and then we bind them with its rulings. And being addressed with them does not mean they are commanded to make up for them afterward. The evidence for the first point is His saying: ﴿And nothing prevented their contributions from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah﴾ [At-Tawbah 54]. So how could we bind them with a command that does not benefit them? This is futility and injustice!

As for the second point, that being addressed means we do not bind them to make up for it, the evidence is His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve, if they cease, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [Al-Anfal 38].

For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ did not command anyone who embraced Islam to pay his past zakat, or to fast the month of Ramadan, or to make up the prayers. So what is the benefit then?

The people of knowledge said: the benefit of our saying that they are addressed with them is increasing their punishment in the Hereafter. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Except the companions of the right, in gardens, they will ask each other about the criminals: "What put you into Saqar?" They will say, "We were not of those who prayed, and we did not feed the poor, and we used to engage in vain discourse with those who engaged, and we used to deny the Day of Recompense, until there came to us the certainty"﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 39–47].

So this verse may be cited as evidence that disbelievers are addressed with the branches (of Sharia), just as they are addressed with the foundations (of belief), by consensus.

**Student:** The whole verse, Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** Yes, the whole (...) the whole verse. The verse contains a command and a prohibition.

**Student:** A follow-up.

**Student:** Regarding a Muslim who is negligent in zakat, is he commanded to make it up or not?

**Shaykh:** There is a difference among the scholars. Some said he is commanded, because it has no set time. The beginning of its time is defined, but its end is not defined. This is the correct view.

**Student:** So he is commanded.

**Shaykh:** That he is commanded. Unlike what has a defined time at its beginning and its end, which is not commanded to be made up. According to the preferred view.

**Student:** But there is a follow-up on the mention of (...) in the verses (...). It says: ﴿He has only forbidden you dead animals and blood﴾. Here, when He mentioned the general people, He also mentioned...

**Shaykh:** We have not reached this yet.

* One of the benefits of the verse is the prohibition of following the footsteps of Satan (khutuwat al-shaytan), based on His saying: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. Is that right?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Does that include prohibiting eating with the left hand and drinking with the left hand?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, based on the saying of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "None of you should eat with his left hand or drink with his left hand, for Satan eats with his left hand and drinks with his left hand."[[Narrated by Muslim (2020/105) and al-Tirmidhi (1799) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, and the wording is that of al-Tirmidhi.]]
* Also among that: disobedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for disobedience to Allah and arrogance towards His command are from the footsteps of Satan. Or not?
Among the following of Satan's footsteps is corrupt analogical reasoning (qiyas fasid).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And what is its basis?
* The Student: The first one to use qiyas was Iblis.
* The Shaykh: They say: the first one to use corrupt qiyas was Iblis, because when Allah commanded him to prostrate to Adam, he opposed this command with corrupt reasoning. He said: ﴿I am better than him: You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf 12]. That is, he thought it would have been better for him to be the one prostrating to Me. So this is qiyas against a clear text, and it is invalid in its consideration.
And also among the following of Satan's footsteps is envy, for envy is from the footsteps of Satan, because Satan only said that out of envy for Adam. So envy is from following the footsteps of Satan, and it is also a habit of the Jews: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief, out of envy from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 109]. Every blameworthy trait or evil deed is from the footsteps of Satan.
* One of the benefits of the verse: the emphasis on Satan's enmity towards the children of Adam. From where do we take it? ﴿Indeed, he﴾ — the sentence is emphasized with (inna): ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾.
* And one of its benefits: the eloquence of the Qur'an is manifest, by coupling a ruling with its cause. Coupling a ruling with its cause has benefits, among them: reassurance, encouragement, and encouragement or warning. In short, it has benefits that we mentioned previously. We mentioned previously three benefits, and perhaps you remember them. Coupling a ruling with its cause has three benefits. Who will explain them?
* Student: Emphasis.
* The Shaykh: Emphasis?
* Student: Yes, or intensity, I mean (...).
* The Shaykh: No, perhaps your thought went to something else.
* Student: First: reassurance of the listener.
Second: the perfection of the Islamic Shariah.
* The Shaykh: And that is the perfection of the Islamic Shariah.
* Student: Yes. Third: analogy based on this generality, the generality of the ruling.
* The Shaykh: The generality of the ruling based on the generality of the cause. ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, except that it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure﴾ [al-An'am 145]. The phrase ﴿for indeed it is impure﴾ is a cause (ta'lil). Three benefits are derived from it:
First: the listener's reassurance that this thing is forbidden, and that it is forbidden because it is impure and foul.
Second: the manifestation of the exalted nature of the Shariah, its rulings and its wisdoms, and that it does not establish a ruling except for a cause.
Third: the generality of the ruling based on the generality of the cause, that is, qiyas. So everything that is impure, even if it is not one of these three, is forbidden.
* One of the benefits of the verse: caution, or strong warning, against the footsteps of Satan, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾. I do not think anyone who believes in another's enmity would ever follow him, or not? Every sensible person who believes in enmity from any soul would not be able to follow it. In it there is a warning against following the footsteps of Satan. So if it is asked: what are the footsteps of Satan?
We say: all sins are the footsteps of Satan, all sins are indeed the footsteps of Satan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 169–171 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, he only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:169]. "Innama" (indeed, only) is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr). Restriction means affirming the ruling for what is mentioned and negating it for everything else. This is restriction, and I think we have already gone over it in rhetoric (balaghah), or not? When you say "innama al-qa'imu Zaydun" (only Zayd is standing), you affirm standing for Zayd and deny it of anyone else. The meaning here is: he commands you only to that, only to evil, and so on.

His saying ﴿innama yamurukum﴾ means "al-Shaytan" (the Devil). To whom is the address? To mankind in general, because all the verses in this context are addressed to people.

﴿bil-su' wal-fahshā'﴾. "Al-su'" (evil) is everything that harms, from the minor sins, since they are evil deeds. This is "al-su'."

"Al-fahshā'" (immorality) is the major sins. So is fornication (zina) among the immoralities, or not?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: And likewise a man marrying the women his father married, is that among the immoralities?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: It is among the immoralities. And likewise withholding zakat is among the immoralities. ﴿The Shaytan promises you poverty and commands you to immorality﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:268]. The main point is that "al-su'" is the minor sins and "al-fahshā'" is the major sins. He commands both this and that. Although minor sins are expiated by good deeds, he still commands them, because when a person commits them again and again, he becomes corrupt and his heart hardens. Then also, we do not know that every prayer expiates. Some prayers may only clear one's obligation, let alone expiate sins. The prayers that expiate are those a person performs completely, to the best of his ability.

His saying ﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ [And that you say about Allah what you do not know]. ﴿Wa an taqūlū﴾ (and that you say) is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿al-su'﴾. That is, "and by your saying." "An" and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun in the genitive, coordinated with his saying ﴿bil-su'﴾, meaning "and your saying."

﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāh﴾: "taqūlū ʿalayhi" means you attribute speech to Him. ﴿mā lā taʿlamūn﴾: "mā" is the object of "taqūlūn" (you say).

His saying ﴿mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ includes everything said about Allah concerning attributes, actions, rulings, and names. Whoever says about Allah anything among these four categories is included in this verse. Whoever affirms for Allah a name that he does not know to be one of His names has said about Allah what he does not know. Whoever affirms for Allah an attribute that he does not know Allah described Himself with has said about Allah what he does not know. Whoever attributes to Allah an action He did not do has said about Allah what he does not know. Whoever attributes to Allah a ruling He did not legislate, saying "this is lawful and this is unlawful" when Allah did not legislate it that way, has said about Allah what he does not know. So it includes what? For names, attributes, actions, and rulings. Whoever says about Allah what he does not know is included in this verse, and doing so is one of the commands of the Shaytan: ﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾. The coordination of ﴿an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ with ﴿al-su' wal-fahshā'﴾ is the coordination of the specific with the general, since it is included either under "evil" or under "immorality." And it is closer to immorality.

His saying ﴿an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾: we said the verses include these four categories. Speaking about Allah divides into three types:

The first type: to say about Allah what one knows Allah said. What is its ruling?

* Student: Permissible.

* Shaykh: Is this obligatory or permissible?

* Student: Obligatory.

* Shaykh: The point is that it is permissible, and it reaches the level of obligation when there is need for it.

The second: to say about Allah what one knows Allah said the opposite of. This is forbidden, the most severe type.

The third: to say about Allah what one does not know Allah said. This is also forbidden. So speaking about Allah becomes forbidden in two states. What are they?

To say what one does not know, or to say what one knows Allah said the opposite of. This principle has many branches, which Allah willing we will mention in the future.

(...) and His names, attributes, actions, and rulings; all of this is included in (...). The Shaytan commands his allies to do so.

If someone says: "I do not hear the Shaytan commanding me, so how do I deduce or know that he has commanded?"

* Student: (...) the whispering. He whispers into people's ears, and likewise that they do evil and immorality. So every command that involves disobedience to Allah and His Messenger is from the command of the Shaytan.

* Shaykh: That means that when a person commits a sin or speaks about Allah what he does not know, he knows that the Shaytan commanded him to it. Not that one hears the Shaytan saying "do this, do that, say that," but when he does or says these things that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned, it is known that the Shaytan commanded him to them.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾. I think we were discussing it?

His saying ﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ includes speaking about Allah concerning His essence. Those who say that He, glorified and exalted, is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither connected nor separate, neither above the world nor beneath it, have spoken about Allah without knowledge. Rather, they spoke with what is known to be contrary to the truth. Likewise, it includes speaking about Allah concerning His names and attributes, such as one who says: "The names of Allah, glorified and exalted, do not indicate attributes. He is Hearing without hearing, Seeing without sight, Knowing without knowledge. He is knowing by His essence, not by His knowledge and attribute." These are the Mu'tazilah and the Jahmiyyah, who do not affirm attributes; they affirm names that do not indicate their meanings.

It also includes those who affirm some attributes but not others, like the Ash'ariyyah, who said: "He intended such-and-such by it," negating what they negated, and said He intended such-and-such and did not intend such-and-such. They spoke about Allah without knowledge in two respects. The first respect: they negated what Allah intended without knowledge. The second: they affirmed what they did not know Allah intended. For example, they said "istawā" (He established Himself) means "istawlā" (He took control). ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:54], meaning He took control of it. They spoke about Allah without knowledge in two respects. The first: negating the reality of "istiwa'" without knowledge. The second: affirming that its meaning is "istīlā'" (taking control) without knowledge. So they spoke about Allah without knowledge in two respects.

Likewise, those who speak about Allah without knowledge concerning His actions, such as affirming causes that Allah did not make causes, like the astrologers, the fortune-tellers, and those like them. These have spoken about Allah without knowledge concerning His actions and His creation. They say: "The cause of this existing is such-and-such," while it is not known to be a cause, neither by creation nor by law. So they speak about Allah without knowledge. For example, the dubbah (a ring). They say it is the cause of a husband's love for his wife. These have spoken about Allah without knowledge, because we do not know that this is a cause, neither by law, nor by sense, nor by decree.

Likewise, those who speak about Allah without knowledge concerning His rulings, and they are very numerous. Among them are the common people, and among them are the pretenders to knowledge who say, "We are scholars," or imagine themselves to be scholars while they have no knowledge. These also speak about Allah without knowledge. Among the strange things that came to me recently: a man went to an imam of a mosque to have him write his divorce document. The imam said to him: "Divorce your wife twice. I will not write one divorce, because Allah says: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:229]."

He said: "I do not know, he is an imam, the imam of a mosque." So I thought the matter was as he said. I said: "Yes, write: I have divorced my wife with two divorces," even though this is forbidden. It is not permissible for a person to divorce with two divorces. This is playing with the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning of the verse is clear: divorce in which the husband has the right of return is twice, because He said after that: ﴿But if he divorces her [a third time], then she is not lawful to him﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:230]. But this is great ignorance, a compound ignorance.

The donkey of the wise man said one day:
"If fate were just, I would be the one who rides.
Because I am a simple ignorant,
and my companion is a compound ignorant."

Is this donkey telling the truth?!

In any case, this, may Allah protect us, is speaking about Allah without knowledge. Speaking about Allah without knowledge concerning His essence, or His names and attributes, or His actions, or His rulings, all of this is from the commands of the Shaytan. Usually, nothing drives a person to it except love of status, leadership, and rank. If a person had taqwa, he would observe proper manners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and would not go ahead of Allah and His Messenger. He would only speak about Allah what he knows Allah said, either in His Book or in the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, which is by His command. The conclusion is that this is speaking about Allah what one does not know.

What is your opinion about one who speaks about Allah what he knows Allah's speech is contrary to?

* Students: This is worse.

* Shaykh: This is worse?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Yes. He says about Allah what he knows Allah said the opposite of, and this is worse. So the levels are three. The levels of speaking about Allah are three: to say what one knows Allah said, and to say what one knows Allah did not say, these are two levels. The third: to say what one does not know Allah said. Did you understand?

Is there a difference between the second and the third?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: Yes, there is a difference. The third: one knows Allah said the opposite, which is the second. And the third: one does not know that Allah said it, so he speaks about Allah what he does not know, and this is forbidden. If someone says: "Do you not permit giving fatwa based on conjecture (ẓann) or on the predominance of conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann)? What is the answer?"

* Students: Yes.

* Students: Indeed.

* Shaykh: Indeed. The answer is "indeed," not "yes." So what is the answer regarding the verse: ﴿that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾?

The answer to the verse is that in reality, if we issue a fatwa based on conjecture, we have spoken about Allah what we do not know, because Allah, glorified and exalted, permitted us to issue fatwas with that in His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [Al-Taghabun 64:16], and in His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:286].

It is known that the predominance of conjecture is better than suspension of judgment. Many of the issues of jurisprudence that scholars speak about and rule upon are, I would not say all of them or most of them, but many of them are based on the predominance of conjecture and probability, and are not definitive matters either in the indication or in the thing indicated by the evidence. Neither in the indication nor in the evidence.

* Student: Shaykh, is every fatwa speaking about Allah?

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: I mean, like one who says to someone: "This is unlawful and this is lawful," it is clearly speaking about Allah. But if someone asks, for example, about a matter that is ambiguous and has disagreement, and the matter is simple, and he says to him: "Just do such-and-such," meaning he says: "Do such-and-such," without saying "this is unlawful or lawful," is this speaking about Allah?

* Shaykh: Yes, because he asked him about a religion by which he worships Allah, and Allah, Exalted, is not worshipped except by what He legislated.

* Student: But this is closer to the well-known meaning, that he says to him: "Do such-and-such"?

* Shaykh: No, no. The well-known (matter), may Allah bless you, is in non-religious issues. What is well-known and purely based on opinion is other than religious issues. As for religious issues, I did not command him except on the basis that the Shari'ah is like this. So this is speaking about Allah.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:170].

﴿idhā qīla lahum﴾: "qīla" is in the passive voice. Its original form is?

* Student: (qāla).

* Shaykh: No, its original form?

* Student: (qawala).

* Student: (qawala), or (quwila).

* Shaykh: (qawala). "Qawala" is the original of "qāla." 

* Student: (qūila).

* Shaykh: (qūila), or not? Like "ḍuriba." This is its original form, but there was a change (iʿlāl) in it, namely that the waw was kasra, so it was changed to yā', then the letter before it was made kasra for harmony, so it became "qīla." ﴿idhā qīla lahum﴾ means: to whom?

* Student: Those who spoke about Allah.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: The disbelievers.

* Shaykh: The disbelievers. ﴿When it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down"﴾. "Ittabiʿū" (follow) means: take it, actually doing what is commanded and abandoning what is forbidden.

His saying ﴿mā anzala Allāh﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun that conveys generality. Allah, the Exalted, sent down to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ the Book and the Wisdom. Many scholars have said that what is meant by the Wisdom is the Sunnah.

In ﴿mā anzala Allāh﴾, we said it is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun needs a relative clause (ṣilah) and a returning pronoun (ʿāʾid). The relative clause is His saying ﴿anzala Allāh﴾. Where is the returning pronoun?

* Student: It is omitted.

* Shaykh: The returning pronoun is omitted. Its estimate is: "mā anzalahu Allāh" (what Allah sent down). When this statement is said to them, they do not soften or accept, but rather they are arrogant. ﴿They said: "Rather, we follow"﴾. "Bal" here is a particle of refutation (idrāb ibṭālī), meaning they said, refuting what was said to them: ﴿Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon﴾. "Mā" here, meaning "alladhī" (that which), is a relative pronoun. "Alfaynā" means "wajadnā" (we found), as Allah said in another verse: ﴿They said: "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ [Luqman 31:21].

The Qur'an explains part of itself by part of itself. We mentioned earlier in the principles of tafsir that we refer to the Qur'an for interpreting the Qur'an, then the Sunnah, then the statements of the Companions, then after that the statements of the senior Successors who were devoted to tafsir, such as Mujahid, Qatadah, and similar, with differences of opinion on this in the second issue, the issue of the Successors.

His saying ﴿mā alfaynā ʿalayhi ābāʾanā﴾: that is, what did we find them upon, guidance or misguidance?

* Students: Misguidance.

* Students: Action.

* Shaykh: Action, whether it was true or false.

His saying ﴿mā alfaynā ʿalayhi ābāʾanā﴾: "ābāʾanā" (our fathers) refers to biological fathers and grandfathers. Also included is what was inherited from their grandfathers. This is the answer, and it is an unsound answer, indeed a false and wrong answer. For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, refuted it in His saying: ﴿Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ ﴿Awa-law kāna﴾: let us see if Mustafa can parse for us ﴿awa-law kāna﴾?

* Student: The hamzah is for interrogation, all of it. The "aw" (or).

* Shaykh: "Aw" all of it is for interrogation?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Yes. And "law"?

* Student: "Law" is a particle of impossibility (imtinā').

* Shaykh: A particle of impossibility?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: A particle of impossibility due to existence.

* Shaykh: Due to existence?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: What do you say about the grammar? The hamzah?

* Student: The hamzah is for interrogation.

* Shaykh: "Aw" ("awa")?

* Student: No, the hamzah only.

* Shaykh: Only?

* Student: Yes, and the waw is for coordination, and the interrogation was placed before the coordination. There are two opinions among grammarians: either one makes the figurative usage in the verb...

* Shaykh: There is no figurative usage in it. Either one makes...

* Student: Yes?

* Shaykh: There is no figurative usage.

* Student: That is, either we estimate a verb, for example: either we estimate a verb and say: either it is, according to the first opinion, that the interrogation was placed before its original position ("awa-law kāna"), so the interrogation was placed before the coordination.

* Shaykh: This is an opinion.

* Student: This is an opinion, and the second opinion: we estimate a suitable verb after the hamzah.

* Shaykh: And the waw is a coordinating particle with this verb. According to that, which verb is estimated here according to this opinion?

* Student: "Fa-yattabiʿūn" (so do they follow?).

* Shaykh: "A-yattabiʿūn" (do they follow)?

* Student: "A-yattabiʿūn, wa-law kāna ābāʾuhum" (do they follow even if their fathers...).

* Shaykh: "Even if their fathers..." Good. And "law"?

* Student: "Law" here is conditional.

* Shaykh: Good. Where is the protasis verb?

* Student: The protasis verb is omitted.

* Shaykh: And what is the estimate?

* Student: The estimate is "fa-ittabiʿūhu" (then follow him) or "kamā hadāhum" (as he guided them).

* Student: The protasis verb is "kāna" (was).

* Shaykh: The protasis verb is "kāna," correct.

* Student: The apodosis is omitted.

* Shaykh: The apodosis is omitted, according to what is well known.

* Student: Or it does not need it.

* Shaykh: Or it does not need it, according to the second opinion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 169–171 (part 2 of 3):

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Nay, we will follow what we found our fathers upon,﴾ even though their fathers were in this state, in which they did not deserve to be followed, ﴿though their fathers understood nothing, nor were they guided﴾. The intended meaning of "understanding" here is the understanding of conduct (ʿaql al-taṣarruf), not the understanding of perception (ʿaql al-idrāk). This is because we mentioned earlier that intellect is of two kinds: intellect of conduct and intellect of perception. The intellect of perception is the basis of legal responsibility (manāṭ al-taklīf), which the jurists speak of when they say, "It is a condition for the obligation of such-and-such that the person be sane (ʿāqil)." As for the intellect of conduct, it is the object of praise and commendation, meaning that a person has an intellect which restrains him from what harms him. So which of the two intellects is meant here?
* The students: Conduct.
* The Shaykh: The intellect of conduct. Their fathers were clever, and their fathers perceived what benefits and harms them, but they did not have sound conduct.
His saying ﴿they understood nothing﴾ means they do not conduct themselves (...) with intelligence such that they perceive what benefits and harms them, so that they would follow what benefits them and abandon what harms them.
His saying ﴿nothing﴾ is an indefinite noun in a context of negation, and an indefinite in a context of negation is general. So if someone says: If it is general, then this means they do not understand anything, even matters of this world, although in worldly affairs they conduct themselves well, is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: They buy and sell, and they seek what is best and most suitable for them. It is said: This is nothing in comparison with matters of the Hereafter, it is nothing in comparison with what relates to the affairs of the Hereafter. Or it is said: The generality here is meant as particularity, because the context here is one of method and action, a context of religion and deeds, not a context of worldly trade and buying and selling. ﴿Follow what Allah has sent down.﴾ They said: ﴿Nay, we will follow.﴾ So the intended meaning of the word ﴿nothing﴾, which is general, is what?
* The students: Matters of the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: Nothing of the matters of the Hereafter. Both matters return to one meaning, or both possibilities return to one meaning. But do we say there is a difference? Do we say that ﴿nothing﴾ is originally meant in its generality, but worldly matters have been excluded from it because they are trivial and count as nothing; or do we say that worldly matters were never intended at all, because the context here is one of action and the Hereafter?
His saying ﴿nor were they guided﴾: they do not understand and they are not guided. It may be said: If you interpret intellect as the intellect of right guidance, then that is guidance; how then do you combine the two? We say: The combination is that understanding relates to conception and the soundness of intention, while guidance relates to action and conduct. That is, they are not guided, so they do not act in a way that is guidance, and neither do they understand, so they do not perceive in a way that leads them to conduct beneficial to themselves. Those who bear this description, who neither understand nor are guided, do they deserve to be followed?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No. For this reason the interrogative hamza of denial came in His saying: ﴿Even though their fathers understood nothing, nor were they guided?﴾ We will, Allah willing, discuss the benefits of this verse, which show that many of the people of misguidance who hold fanatically to their leaders are included in this verse: ﴿When it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down."﴾
They say: ﴿Nay, we will follow what we found our fathers upon,﴾ even if their fathers were in this state in which they neither understand nor are guided. They follow them, and do not say: Is it beneficial or harmful? They follow him in every state. So what is the closest likeness to these people? The closest likeness is the verse that follows: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying out﴾ [al-Baqarah 171], meaning like the shepherd who calls out, calling to that which hears nothing but calling and crying out. What is it that hears nothing but calling and crying out and does not understand?
* The students: Animals.
* The Shaykh: Animals, livestock. So these people are like a person who calls to animals that understand only the voice. ﴿Calling and crying out.﴾ Duʿāʾ (calling) is when one calls a specific thing by its name, and nidāʾ (crying out) is the general call, which is for the general. Among animals there are those which a person names by their name, such that when he calls them by that name they come to him. And there is the general cry for all animals, which is not specific to one over another. I think it is not necessary to illustrate this, since it is known to you. For example, the camel herder calls out to camels with "dūh" (a cry to camels). Is the "dūh" a nidāʾ or a duʿāʾ?
* The students: A nidāʾ.
* The Shaykh: A nidāʾ, because it is general, and for this reason all the camels come to him. But if, for example, he has a she-camel which he has named with a specific name, and he says to her, "O so-and-so," she comes to him from among all the other camels. This is well known. But even so, do they come on the basis that they understand and comprehend and are guided? Perhaps he calls her in order to slaughter her; she sees the knife with him and he calls her and she comes. Is that not so?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: These are like them. The disbelievers are like them in that they follow their fathers without understanding this meaning, this state in which their fathers are.
﴿Like the one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying out.﴾ How many are the ones who resemble the disbelievers in this! How many follow the caller and the one who cries out, while they are like animals that neither understand nor reflect. Is calling to fanaticism, to nationalism, and what is similar to them of this kind or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Of this kind. The callers to it do not consider what follows from it, namely the division of the Muslims and the tearing apart of their unity, and making the bond to be what?
* A student: Language (...).
* The Shaykh: Language and nationalism. But the religious bond, about which Allah said: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt 10], and He did not say: "The Arabs are but brothers." He said: ﴿The believers are but brothers.﴾ This includes for you all the believers, even if they are not Arabs, or not? And it excludes whoever is not a believer, even if he is Arab. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to his father and his people: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who originated me, for indeed He will guide me﴾ [al-Zukhruf 26–27]. Likewise: ﴿There has already been for you an excellent example in Ibrahim and those with him, when they said to their people﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 4]. See: to their people! ﴿Indeed, we are free from you and from what you worship besides Allah﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 4], to the end of the verse. See, this is the real bond. So people being swept away by this call to nationalism falls within a verse like this one, that they are like the one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying out.
* A student: Does not hear (...) animals.
* The Shaykh: Yes, the animals which hear only mere calling and crying out, and do not understand or comprehend.
﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand.﴾ ﴿Deaf﴾ is the plural of (aṣamm), and the aṣamm is one who does not hear. ﴿Blind﴾ is the plural of (aʿmā), and the aʿmā is one who does not see.
﴿Dumb﴾ is the plural of (abkam), one who does not speak. Here, from the standpoint of the Arabic language, the position of His saying ﴿deaf﴾ is what?
* A student: A predicate.
* The Shaykh: A predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimated form is (they are deaf). There is also a difficulty with ﴿ʿumyun﴾. We have said that the ḍamma is not manifest on the yāʾ. When you say "jāʾa al-qāḍī" (the judge came), you say "al-qāḍī" is a subject, marked nominative by an estimated ḍamma on the yāʾ, prevented from appearing by the heaviness. Here ﴿ʿumyun﴾ has two ḍammas after which there is one ḍamma. So what is the answer to this difficulty?
* A student: From (aʿmā).
* The Shaykh: (...) We see that it is a yāʾ and the ḍamma appeared on it.
We say: The yāʾ which is a weak letter, what is manifest on it is the kasra, when the letter before it is kasra, and the wāw is ḍamma when the letter before it is ḍamma. As for a yāʾ with a sukūn before it, or a wāw with a sukūn before it, the ḍamma is manifest on it, and the kasra is manifest on it. Do you understand?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The yāʾ on which neither the ḍamma nor the kasra appears is the one whose preceding letter is kasra, and the wāw on which neither the ḍamma nor the kasra appears is the one whose preceding letter is ḍamma. But when the letter before it is quiescent, the ḍamma and kasra appear on it. You say: "ishtaraytu dalwan" (I bought a bucket), and this is "dalwun": the ḍamma appeared on the wāw? 
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Because the letter before it is quiescent. And you look at "dalwin," the kasra appeared on it?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And likewise "ghazwun" and "ghazwin," and here "ʿumyun," and you look at "ʿumyin." And likewise "ẓabyun" and you look at "ẓabyin." So the difficulty is resolved.
His saying ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾: deaf to what?
* The students: To hearing the truth.
* The Shaykh: To hearing the truth, even though they hear other things, but hearing other things is of no benefit, so it is like nonexistence. For this reason He said ﴿deaf﴾. ﴿Dumb﴾ means they do not speak. Is it true that they do not speak?
* The students: They do not speak.
* The Shaykh: They do not speak. Perhaps they are eloquent, but they do not speak the truth, and Allah forbid. Their speech other than the truth is as nothing, because it benefits nothing. Likewise ﴿blind﴾: they do not see. This is so, but the reality of the matter is that their eyes may be among the finest eyes, yet they do not see the truth, and Allah forbid. They do not see the signs, nor do they see those who speak by the signs either, and they do not benefit from them.
His saying ﴿so they do not understand﴾: the fāʾ is for consequence (tafrīʿ), meaning this sentence is a consequence of what precedes it. That is, because they are blind, dumb and deaf, they do not understand, that is, they do not understand with the understanding of right guidance, even though they have the intellect of perception, but they do not have the intellect of right guidance. Because they did not benefit from their minds, Allah negated from them the intellect which is the true essence of intellect. For this reason intellect was called ʿaql, because it restrains (yaʿqilu) its possessor from what harms him, and it is also called ḥijr, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding (dhī ḥijr)?﴾ [al-Fajr 5], meaning for one of intellect, because it likewise restrains (yuḥjiru) its possessor from what harms him.
﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand.﴾ And what is the grammatical analysis of ﴿duʿāʾan﴾ in ﴿that which hears nothing but duʿāʾan﴾?
* A student: An exception after (illā)?
* The Shaykh: An exception after (illā). What is your view?
* A student: Correct.
* Another student: A direct object in the accusative.
* The Shaykh: A direct object in the accusative?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: These are two opinions. What is your view?
* A student: No, correct, it is an exception.
* The Shaykh: Correct, it is an exception.
* A student: A direct object in the accusative of ﴿yasmaʿu﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct, because the exception here is a "mufarragh" (emptied) exception, since "lā" is a negation particle and ﴿yasmaʿu﴾ is a present-tense verb, and no object has come, so the direct object is then ﴿duʿāʾan﴾. And if you want to know the mufarragh, delete the negation and delete "illā," and say: "yasmaʿu duʿāʾan," for example. In "mā qāma illā Zayd" (none stood but Zayd), say "qāma Zayd," which is what clarifies the grammar for you.
Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality, and that you say about Allah what you do not know.﴾
* From the noble verse it is derived: that Satan has a will and a command, as His saying shows: ﴿He only commands you.﴾
* Among its benefits: that Satan commands only evil, and does not command good. That Satan does not command good: from where do we take that he does not command good?
* The students: From the restriction (ḥaṣr).
* The Shaykh: From the restriction: ﴿He only commands you to evil.﴾
* A student: The hadith of Abu Hurayra, that Abu Hurayra said..
* The Shaykh: Yes, "he spoke the truth, though he is a liar" (ṣaddaqa wa huwa kadhūb). This is rare, this is rare.
* Among its benefits: that when a person is inclined toward an evil deed or an immoral act, let him know that it is one of the commands of Satan, so let him beware of it, because we have no clear sign. Satan does not stand before us and say: Do it. But when the matter we are inclined to is evil and immoral, we know it is one of Satan's commands.
* Among its benefits: that speaking about Allah without knowledge is one of Satan's commands, because of His saying: ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know.﴾
* Among its benefits: the prohibition of issuing fatwas without knowledge. From where do we take it? ﴿And that you say about Allah what you do not know.﴾ For the mufti speaks on behalf of Allah and expresses the law of Allah.
* Among them: the misguidance of the people of ta'wil (interpretation) regarding the names and attributes of Allah. From where do we take it?
* The students: ﴿And that you say about Allah.﴾
* The Shaykh: Because they said about Allah without knowledge. It has already been mentioned that they said about Allah without knowledge in two respects. One of them: they said that Allah did not intend such-and-such, thereby negating what is the apparent meaning of the speech, and they said that He intended such-and-such, thereby affirming what contradicts the apparent meaning of the speech. This is saying about Allah without knowledge.
* A student: Shaykh, did the people of ta'wil say, or the people of taḥrīf (distortion)?
* The Shaykh: No, they are now known as the people of ta'wil. Or the reality is that what they called ta'wil is taḥrīf.
* A student: When is ta'wil praiseworthy, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No. Now, what is well known among the scholars is that the people of ta'wil, when mentioned, are meant to be those who distort words from their places. It is famous among them: the people of ta'wil and the people of literal application. 
* A student: The people of tafsīr; so they are called the people of ta'wil?
* The Shaykh: They are called that, but ta'wil among the later scholars is known only as turning a word away from its apparent meaning. And when the people of ta'wil are mentioned, do not imagine they mean the people of tafsīr at all, except in the terminology of the earlier scholars such as Ibn Jarir and others. As for the later scholars, when you hear "the people of ta'wil," they are those who interpret the attributes, the verses and hadiths about the attributes, and in reality this is taḥrīf. We do not agree with them that this falls under ta'wil; we say it is in fact taḥrīf, because ta'wil without evidence is distortion and changing the meaning from what Allah intended. This is what is known among the scholars: the people of ta'wil are those who turn the apparent meanings of the texts of the Book and the Sunnah away from their intended sense concerning the names and attributes.
* Among its benefits: the obligation to exalt Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that if saying about others were permissible, saying about Him would not be permissible. The reasoning is that He specified after generalizing. Where is the specification after the generalization?
* The students: ﴿And that you say.﴾
* The Shaykh: ﴿And that you say﴾ is a specification after His saying ﴿with evil and immorality﴾, for saying about Allah without knowledge is without doubt among evil and immorality.
﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Nay, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers understood nothing, nor were they guided?﴾
* From the benefits of the verse: the condemnation of partisanship without guidance, by His saying: ﴿They say, "Nay, we will follow what we found our fathers upon,"﴾ even though their fathers had no intellect or guidance, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Even though their fathers...﴾
* Among them: that whoever holds fanatically to a school of thought while opposing the evidence has a resemblance to these people, or not? They say: We will follow what we found our fathers upon, and the one who holds fanatically to his school says: What we found our shaykhs upon. This has a resemblance to them, and it is obligatory that when a person is told, "Follow what Allah has sent down," he should say: "We hear and we obey."
* Among its benefits: that submission is not obligatory except to what Allah has sent down, or not? ﴿Follow what Allah has sent down.﴾ As for submission to the saying of a scholar or what is similar to it, no; there is no submission except to what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has sent down, which is the Book and the wisdom. It has already been mentioned that the scholars differed concerning the saying of a Companion, and that the position of Imam Ahmad is that it is a proof so long as it does not contradict the evidence or conflict with the saying of another Companion. If it contradicts the evidence, it is discarded and the evidence is followed. If it conflicts with the saying of another Companion, weighing is required, and one considers which of them is closer to the Book and the Sunnah, and that is taken. If we do not know which of them is closer to the Book and the Sunnah, we consider which of them is closer to the truth in terms of knowledge, and the Companions differed in this.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the demonstration of the obstinacy of these people. It is said: ﴿Follow what Allah has sent down,﴾ and it is not said: "Follow what we are upon," what Allah has sent down; so they become obstinate and say: "Nay, we will follow what we found our fathers upon."
* Among its benefits: that everyone who opposes the truth and what Allah has sent down is not intelligent and has no guidance, from His saying: ﴿They understood nothing, nor were they guided.﴾
* A student: Shaykh, we said: the Successor (...) there is a difference (...) Qatada..

Shaykh: Yes indeed, and Mujahid. There is a difference of opinion among the scholars regarding this, and it has not become clear to me that the correct view is that following them is obligatory; the obligation of following them is open to question.

And His saying: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts to that which hears nothing except a call and a cry﴾, to the end of the verse.

It is derived from this: that these people, in following their forefathers, are like the cattle that respond to the one who calls them, and they hear nothing but a sound, a call and a cry. They do not understand anything that they can reason about, grasp its benefit, or recognise the harm in opposing it.

Among its benefits also, according to the other interpretation: that these people, may Allah protect us, have had a seal set upon their hearts by Allah, so they do not hear what they are being called to of the truth. ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind; so they do not understand.﴾

And among it, according to the third interpretation: that these idols cannot respond to them. However, this view, as you know, although Ibn Jarir chose it, is weak, because idols do not hear, so the comparison does not apply to them, given that it says: "to that which hears nothing except a call and a cry."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 169–171 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, he only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:169]. "Innama" (indeed, only) is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr). Restriction means affirming the ruling for what is mentioned and negating it for everything else. This is restriction, and I think we have already gone over it in rhetoric (balaghah), or not? When you say "innama al-qa'imu Zaydun" (only Zayd is standing), you affirm standing for Zayd and deny it of anyone else. The meaning here is: he commands you only to that, only to evil, and so on.

His saying ﴿innama yamurukum﴾ means "al-Shaytan" (the Devil). To whom is the address? To mankind in general, because all the verses in this context are addressed to people.

﴿bil-su' wal-fahshā'﴾. "Al-su'" (evil) is everything that harms, from the minor sins, since they are evil deeds. This is "al-su'."

"Al-fahshā'" (immorality) is the major sins. So is fornication (zina) among the immoralities, or not?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: And likewise a man marrying the women his father married, is that among the immoralities?

* Students: Yes.

* Shaykh: It is among the immoralities. And likewise withholding zakat is among the immoralities. ﴿The Shaytan promises you poverty and commands you to immorality﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:268]. The main point is that "al-su'" is the minor sins and "al-fahshā'" is the major sins. He commands both this and that. Although minor sins are expiated by good deeds, he still commands them, because when a person commits them again and again, he becomes corrupt and his heart hardens. Then also, we do not know that every prayer expiates. Some prayers may only clear one's obligation, let alone expiate sins. The prayers that expiate are those a person performs completely, to the best of his ability.

His saying ﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ [And that you say about Allah what you do not know]. ﴿Wa an taqūlū﴾ (and that you say) is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿al-su'﴾. That is, "and by your saying." "An" and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun in the genitive, coordinated with his saying ﴿bil-su'﴾, meaning "and your saying."

﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāh﴾: "taqūlū ʿalayhi" means you attribute speech to Him. ﴿mā lā taʿlamūn﴾: "mā" is the object of "taqūlūn" (you say).

His saying ﴿mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ includes everything said about Allah concerning attributes, actions, rulings, and names. Whoever says about Allah anything among these four categories is included in this verse. Whoever affirms for Allah a name that he does not know to be one of His names has said about Allah what he does not know. Whoever affirms for Allah an attribute that he does not know Allah described Himself with has said about Allah what he does not know. Whoever attributes to Allah an action He did not do has said about Allah what he does not know. Whoever attributes to Allah a ruling He did not legislate, saying "this is lawful and this is unlawful" when Allah did not legislate it that way, has said about Allah what he does not know. So it includes what? For names, attributes, actions, and rulings. Whoever says about Allah what he does not know is included in this verse, and doing so is one of the commands of the Shaytan: ﴿wa an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾. The coordination of ﴿an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ with ﴿al-su' wal-fahshā'﴾ is the coordination of the specific with the general, since it is included either under "evil" or under "immorality." And it is closer to immorality.

His saying ﴿an taqūlū ʿalā Allāhi mā lā taʿlamūn﴾: we said the verses include these four categories. Speaking about Allah divides into three types:

The first type: to say about Allah what one knows Allah said. What is its ruling?

* Student: Permissible.

* Shaykh: Is this obligatory or permissible?

* Student: Obligatory.

* Shaykh: The point is that it is permissible, and it reaches the level of obligation when there is need for it.

The second: to say about Allah what one knows Allah said the opposite of. This is forbidden, the most severe type.

The third: to say about Allah what one does not know Allah said. This is also forbidden. So speaking about Allah becomes forbidden in two states. What are they?

To say what one does not know, or to say what one knows Allah said the opposite of. This principle has many branches, which Allah willing we will mention in the future.

(...) and His names, attributes, actions, and rulings; all of this is included in (...). The Shaytan commands his allies to do so.

If someone says: "I do not hear the Shaytan commanding me, so how do I deduce or know that he has commanded?"

* Student: (...) the whispering. He whispers into people's ears, and likewise that they do evil and immorality. So every command that involves disobedience to Allah and His Messenger is from the command of the Shaytan.
