That is: if you truly humble yourselves before Him, then eat of His provision and be grateful to Him, and do not be like those who are ungrateful, or like those who forbid some provision, as in the Jahiliyyah when people forbade things, saying: "This is forbidden." Whoever forbids some foods or drinks without evidence resembles the people of Jahiliyyah who forbade things without evidence, such as the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila, and the ham, and what is in the bellies of livestock; they said: "It is exclusive to our males and forbidden to our wives," and "if it is dead, they all share in it." This is ignorance.

* A student: If there is doubt about it, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: If it is doubtful, the original ruling is permissibility. On this occasion, a notice was published and distributed among people from the Muslim World League that this cheese, the "Laughing Cow" cheese, is haram. The cow is not laughing, despite what they say!
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: I don't know. No, apparently it is written on it "the laughing one."
* A student: "The laughing one."
* The Shaykh: Likewise "al-Kiri," I think, and some soap, "al-Kami." In any case, they wrote to them with a clarification, saying this is forbidden. Since Shaykh 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Baz, may Allah preserve him, is the president of the League in its meetings, I contacted him and asked. He said: "By Allah, I don't know, but they have written to the League; we will ask it where this report came from, and they have also written to the Ministry of Commerce, and they are awaiting a reply." It is not unlikely that this comes from some companies, because you see some companies promote themselves: if they see that a product is successful, they insert a fabricated defect in order to repel people from it. It is possible that other companies compete with this cheese company and say: "This has international fame, and people are taking from it; so let us place a calamity on it." And Allah knows best. Now, the question has been asked a great deal these days. We said: "By Allah, we have no knowledge; you may eat until its prohibition is clarified." We are now awaiting the Shaykh's reply, God willing, and we will see. Perhaps later it will be published in the newspapers.
* A student: So, for example, leaving these things, meaning that a person doubts them and abstains out of scrupulousness, is it not better, O Shaykh, until it becomes clear to him?
* The Shaykh: My brother, no.
* A student: The hadith: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt" [narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2518) from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali].
* The Shaykh: Yes, but the problem now is that there is no doubt (shubha) regarding an established principle. There is no doubt regarding an established principle. Likewise, the uncertainty concerning imported slaughtered meat has also become uncertain, with much discussion. Yes, regarding slaughtered animals the original ruling is prohibition, so we may say: it is better to leave them. Praise be to Allah, there are plenty of other things without much doubt. But for cheese and the like, what is the original ruling?
* A student: Permissibility.
* The Shaykh: Permissibility, and even if it is from a Christian, a Jew, or a Magian, the original ruling is permissibility until prohibition is clarified.
* A student: They said that a company (...) five or seven years ago announced that it puts pork or pork fat in it. What do they mean?
* The Shaykh: In any case, it will be looked into now, and we, God willing, are awaiting the reply.

﴿...If it is Him you worship (172). Indeed, He has forbidden for you only the carrion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:172–173]. Because He commanded eating of the good things. Know before we pass this verse that what we have been commanded, we the believers, praise be to Allah, was also commanded to the Messengers, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah commanded the believers with what He commanded the Messengers, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾, and He said: ﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾" [narrated by Muslim (1015/65) from Abu Hurayrah].

By this meaning, or by this hadith, the meaning of gratitude becomes entirely clear to us, because the Messenger ﷺ compared the two verses. In the verse about the Messengers he said: ﴿O Messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds﴾, which shows that the gratitude commanded to the believers is righteous action.

﴿He has forbidden for you only the carrion﴾: "innama" is a particle of restriction (hasr), and restriction means what? Affirming the ruling for what is mentioned and negating it for anything else. So prohibition is restricted to these things. The meaning of ﴿He has forbidden for you only the carrion﴾ is: He has forbidden you nothing but carrion; He has forbidden only carrion.

﴿has forbidden for you﴾: tahrim here means prohibition (al-man'), so "harrama 'alaykum" means "prevented you."

As for His saying ﴿has forbidden for you the carrion﴾: what is the meaning of "forbidden for us"? Does it mean forbidden for us to look at it?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No. It means forbidden for us to eat it. What is the evidence that the intended meaning is prohibition of eating? The evidence is the verse before it: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾, then He said: ﴿He has forbidden for you﴾, as though He said: "Eat," then He made an exception, saying: ﴿He has forbidden for you only the carrion﴾.

What is "the carrion" (al-maytah)? Linguistically, maytah is what dies of its own accord (hatf anfihi), meaning without any act on its part: an animal that is struck by illness and dies, falls from a height and dies, and similar. Legally, carrion is what dies without legal slaughter (dhakah shar'iyyah). This is a case where the technical usage is more general than the linguistic usage, which is rare as mentioned before; usually the technical term is more specific than the linguistic. But sometimes the technical term is more general. So here, legally, carrion is what dies without legal slaughter, which includes what dies of its own accord, which is called carrion?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is slaughtered but blood is not drained, is it called carrion?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is slaughtered but over which the name of Allah was not pronounced?
* The students: Carrion.
* The Shaykh: Carrion. What is slaughtered by anyone other than a Jew, a Christian, or a Muslim?
* The students: Carrion.
* The Shaykh: Carrion, even though it was slaughtered. Therefore, legally, carrion is what is slaughtered without legal slaughter.

As for His saying ﴿the carrion﴾: the "al" here is for generality. That is, if "al" is for generality, it means that if you removed it and put "kull" (all) in its place, the sentence would be correct: "He has forbidden for you every carrion." Is this verse general in its scope? The answer is no. Something in the Sharia specifies it, as in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us: as for the two carrions, locusts and fish" [narrated by Ibn Majah (3314) from Ibn 'Umar]. So what is excepted from this? Locusts and fish. Locusts are well known, and fish: all sea fish, small and large alike, so their carrion is lawful, is it not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence for this exception from the general ruling?

The evidence is His saying: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:96]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The game of the sea is what is caught alive, and its food is what is caught dead" [narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (9/255) from Ibn 'Abbas]. This is from the Qur'an, and from the Sunnah we recited just now: the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us..." [previously cited]. That is one. Is the carrion of a human excepted from this?
* The students: No (...) there is a difference.
* The Shaykh: Or is this in the matter of impurity? In the matter of impurity. As for permissibility, no, nothing is excepted except locusts and fish.

Does His saying ﴿Prohibited to you is the carrion﴾ encompass all ways of benefiting from it, so that nothing may be benefited from it, not its hide, sinew, hair, or anything else?
* The students: Its apparent meaning is no.
* The Shaykh: However, the context shows that the intended meaning is eating. For this reason it came in al-Bukhari: "What is forbidden from carrion is only its eating" [agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1492) and Muslim (363/100) from Ibn 'Abbas]: what is forbidden is only its eating. For this reason, if it is benefited from in other than eating, it is permissible. But the hide in particular, when tanned, becomes pure according to the preponderant view, pure like the hide of a non-carrion animal. That is, if a sheep died and we took its hide and tanned it, it is permissible to use it in the water we drink, in milk, in oil, in honey, and in other things, because it is pure. Its flesh, its fat, and its sinews may be made into cords, meaning ropes; we may make them into ropes. Likewise its fat may be used as fuel; we may make it fuel. If someone says: did not the Messenger ﷺ say, when he was told of this, "Indeed Allah has forbidden the sale of wine, carrion, pork, and idols." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what about the fats of carrion, for they are used to coat ships, people use them for lamps, and hides are oiled with them?" He said: "No, it is forbidden" [agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2236) and Muslim (1581/71) from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah]. So what is the answer?

The answer: his saying ﷺ "it is forbidden" means the sale of these things, because what is the discussion about? It is about sale: "Indeed Allah has forbidden the sale of wine." This is supported by his saying: "What is forbidden from carrion is only its eating" [previously cited], and this is not eating.

﴿the carrion and the blood﴾: meaning blood is also forbidden to you. Does "blood" here include every blood, even human blood?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Even human blood, even the blood of a camel, or not?
* A student: Yes.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 172–174 (part 2 of 6):**

* The Shaykh: "Even the blood of a camel?" Yes. It remains to be said that the word "blood" here is unrestricted, but it is restricted in the verse of Al-An'am to being "poured forth," where He says: ﴿unless it be carrion or blood poured forth﴾ [al-An'am 145]. So what is meant is the blood poured forth that flows from the animal before its soul leaves it. As for what remains after the soul has left, it is not forbidden if the animal was properly slaughtered (mudhakkah) in fact. So whatever blood remains in a properly slaughtered animal after its soul has left is pure and lawful, even if it flows onto the ground. On this basis, what about the blood that is in the heart?
* Student: Lawful.
* The Shaykh: Lawful? Congealed blood that you can take in your hand is lawful?
* The students: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: Why?
* The students: Because it is not poured forth.
* The Shaykh: Because it is not poured forth. And likewise what remains in the veins and vessels.
* Student: After the animal's soul has left (...).
* The Shaykh: It is possible.
* Student: But is this lawful or not?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Does it not fall under the same issue?
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: But it is the same reason, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No. The reason is the flesh from which this blood comes out; that flesh is not lawful.
* Student: Lawful (yes).
* The Shaykh: That is it.
* Student: But this is excused because of necessity.
* The Shaykh: No, even this. The principle is that everything that comes out after the soul of the slaughtered animal has left is pure.
* Student: Even if a person licks it, it is lawful.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. How?!
* Student: Shaykh, what is the exception in his saying: "Except the liver and the spleen"?[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3314) and Ahmad (5723) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]]
* The Shaykh: No, he did not say "except the liver and the spleen." He said: "Lawful for us." And it does not prevent that other things are also lawful.
* Student: What does our brother say, the Messenger (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, no. This is a special matter. This is Abu Qatadah. But this is a special matter.
* Student: (...) Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: No, this is a special matter that is considered.
﴿And blood and the flesh of swine﴾ [al-Baqarah 173]. "The flesh of swine": the swine is well known, and what is meant by its flesh is all of its parts. It was forbidden because it is an abomination (rijs). Thus Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is an abomination﴾ [al-An'am 145].
Rijs is more severe than najs (impurity), and it includes both physical and moral impurity. For this reason they say that the swine is notorious for eating excrement and filth, and that it is also notorious for lacking jealousy: it sees the male mounting its female and it does the same (it copulates with her in that manner). Whoever feeds on something is affected by it. For this reason, the Europeans are devoid of jealousy: a man comes, walks with his wife, takes hold of her head and kisses her while her husband watches, and it is as if he had not kissed her, nor his small child. Whether this is the reason or not, it is enough for us that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿for indeed it is an abomination﴾.
(...) Exalted is He, rather He restricted the prohibition to these things: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked. And it was mentioned earlier that there is an exception to carrion. Is that so?
* Student: Carrion? There are two carrions: locusts, the carrion of locusts, and fish.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is in terms of the categories of carrion. And what is excepted from carrion itself?
* Student: Carrion itself. When the Prophet ﷺ forbade carrion...
* The Shaykh: Yes. Benefiting from it? That is: benefiting from it in matters that do not affect a person's worship is not objectionable. And what is the meaning of our saying "in matters that do not affect worship"? That if he anoints himself with its grease, it is not permissible, because that entails that his body and clothing become impure, and this undermines his worship. But if one uses its fat or tallow to oil leather, to coat ships, or for lighting, then there is nothing wrong with that, as has been mentioned. What is the evidence for the exception of the two carrions?
* Student: The hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us. As for the two carrions: the locust and the fish. As for the two bloods: the spleen and the liver."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (3314) and Ahmad (5723) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]]
* The Shaykh: And from the Qur'an?
* Student: Allah mentioned it in this verse, restricting the prohibited things in this verse.
* The Shaykh: Restricting them in this verse?!
* Student: He said regarding the carrion of the sea, in His saying: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 96].
* The Shaykh: ﴿The game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers﴾, yes. The evidence?
* Student: Its food.
* The Shaykh: Its food. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And what is found dead."[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir, no. (12693), ed. Mu'assasat al-Risalah, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (20007) from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi with a similar wording.]] Blood: what is meant by it?
* Student: The blood meant is the poured-forth blood that flows while the animal is alive.
* The Shaykh: What is the evidence that it is poured forth?
* Student: Its restriction in the other verse: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾ [al-An'am 145].
* The Shaykh: Yes, its restriction by His saying: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾. Is anything excepted from the blood?
* Student: What comes out after the soul has left.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And what is mixed with the sinews.
* The Shaykh: Yes. That is, what is not poured forth, which is what comes out after the soul has left, which is in the animal after it is slaughtered, after it is slaughtered necessarily; because after the soul has left, it comes to include carrion, after it is slaughtered.
* Student: Shaykh, does the soul leave the self when the throat is cut?
* The Shaykh: Yes, because it is not possible for the soul to leave unless the blood stops.
* Student: Does one not distinguish the blood after the soul has left?
* The Shaykh: This does not appear clearly. It is not considered poured forth, because it is dead.
* Student: (...) Meaning what is its ruling?
* The Shaykh: No, this is not what happens. Just as what falls into the flesh of the veins (...).
* Student: How did we distinguish between two identical things?
* The Shaykh: Which ones?
* Student: The blood. We said: its beginning is impure and its end is pure?
* The Shaykh: We did not distinguish between them, because its beginning and its end are all impure as long as it is poured forth. And what is not possible to flow out after death is not what flows. This flows from the veins after death, like what remains. For this reason, a sign of life in the strangled animal, the one beaten to death, the one fallen from a height and the like, is that if it is slaughtered, red blood flows from it. Red blood flows from it. But this is not poured-forth blood. His saying: ﴿or the flesh of swine﴾: what is meant by its flesh?
* Student: All of it.
* The Shaykh: All that its body contains. And if it is cooked?
* Student: Cooked, it is not permissible.
* The Shaykh: General?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: Is anything excepted from it?
* Student: Nothing is excepted.
* The Shaykh: Never?
* Student: Never.
* The Shaykh: Good, correct. Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]. The (wa) is a conjunctive particle, and (ma) is a relative pronoun in a accusative position, conjoined to what?
* Student: "Forbidden."
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: "Carrion."
* The Shaykh: To carrion. Because conjunction is made to the first element governed by the governing word. And why is it not made to the last element conjoined? Because the conjoined element is a branch, and a branch does not have anything branching from it. So if you say, for example: "I honored Zayd, 'Amr, Bakr and Khalid," then Khalid is not conjoined to Bakr, and Bakr to 'Amr, and 'Amr to Zayd, correct? All are conjoined to Zayd, because he is the origin upon which the governing word acted. So the conjoined element is conjoined to this origin, not to the branch. 'Amr and Bakr: are they branch or origin?
* The students: Branch.
* The Shaykh: Branch. So Khalid is not conjoined to Bakr.
﴿and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]. (uhilla): al-ihlal means raising the voice. From it is the hadith: "When a newborn cries out loudly, he inherits."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (2920) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] ﴿that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-Baqarah 173]. This happens when the name of other than Allah is mentioned over it, even if it is slaughtered for Allah, such as saying: "In the name of the Messiah," or "In the name of Muhammad ﷺ," or "In the name of Gabriel," or "In the name of Michael," or "In the name of the homeland," or "In the name of nationalism," or "In the name of President So-and-so," or "In the name of King So-and-so." All of this is that over which other than Allah has been invoked, or it is slaughtered for a jinn, or for a devil, or the like.
* Student: Even if the name of Allah is mentioned?
* The Shaykh: Even if the name of Allah is mentioned along with it. ﴿That over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾: by saying "In the name of so-and-so." This is forbidden, because it is shirk (association of partners with Allah). Whatever is shirk is forbidden, not upon the command of Allah and His Messenger. And whatever is not upon the command of Allah and His Messenger is rejected and void, so it is not lawful. If it is invoked for other than Allah, and also for Allah, by saying: "In the name of Allah and the name of His Prophet"?
* The students: It is not lawful.
* The Shaykh: It is also not lawful, because it was invoked for other than Allah. Allah, Exalted, said in the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi): "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in regard to association. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association."[[Narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] Accordingly, what is invoked for other than Allah and for Allah is not lawful. What is invoked for Allah with the intention of something other than Allah, by being slaughtered for an idol while saying: "In the name of Allah"?
* Student: It is not permissible.
* The Shaykh: It is not lawful. But what is derived from this verse is derived from His saying: ﴿and what is slaughtered on the altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]. It is possible that it means, though this is far-fetched, that what is slaughtered on the altars is what is invoked for other than Allah. But this is far-fetched, because Allah joined them in one verse, and joining implies difference. Allah said in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that over which other than Allah has been invoked, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen from a height, the gored, what a beast of prey has eaten except what you slaughter, and what is slaughtered on the altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3].
Even though He said in the middle of the verse: ﴿and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾. So whatever is slaughtered for other than Allah, even if the name of Allah alone is mentioned over it, is forbidden. Is it included if I slaughter this animal for a guest?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: How?
* Student: Yes, for other than Allah.
* The Shaykh: You slaughtered it for other than Allah, for your guest!
* Student: No (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, I am slaughtering it for him.
* Student: If he intends by it to honor the guest, it is not included.
* The Shaykh: If the intention is to honor the guest, then there is no doubt it is not included. Just as if one slaughters this animal for his children to eat, is it forbidden?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No. But if by it one intends drawing near to him and glorifying him with the glorification of worship, then it is forbidden, exactly like what is slaughtered on the altars. Some people, may Allah protect us, used to slaughter sacrifices before their chief or their elder, as a glorification of him, not so that he would eat them, but they are slaughtered in front of him and then left for the world. This is slaughtered on the altars, and even if the name of Allah is mentioned, it is forbidden.
* Student: One who believes as he did (...)?
* The Shaykh: It has been mentioned to us in the chapter on tawhid that one does not slaughter for Allah in a place where slaughter is made for other than Allah. But if one slaughters in a place because it is specific for a particular reason, such as if it is where most of the poor are, or if it was slaughtered here for a relative of his there, meaning it is not specific to the spot, nor specific to an idol or the like, then there is no harm.
* Student: Does al-hajr (abandonment) fall under this?
* The Shaykh: Al-hajr what?
* Student: Al-hajr is not present among you. That is, if some people quarrel, and another person reconciles between them, and the second one wants to slaughter an animal for him as well, that is, he drives it to his house and slaughters it at the house?
* The Shaykh: No, there is nothing wrong with it.
* Student: (…)?
* The Shaykh: There is nothing wrong with it.
* Student: Shaykh, among us, if for example something is delayed in happening, they slaughter and bring people so that they may forgive one another, so that our Lord may send down provision. Is this sound?
* The Shaykh: As charity, meaning?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: By Allah, there is nothing wrong with this, but it is a bid'ah (innovation).
* Student: And they are for the dead?
* The Shaykh: No, this innovation is not praiseworthy.
* Student: Even if, Shaykh, it is for a close relative?
* The Shaykh: No, this is among the innovations. As for charity, there is no doubt that it brings good. But that he slaughters animals and that it becomes, meaning, something of fame and a call (to it); this is among the innovations. But that a person gives charity secretly, for example, there is nothing wrong with that, and it is among the causes of good.
* Student: Shaykh, the last word of his is: "and for the dead."
* The Shaykh: No, this is not beneficial for the dead.
* Student: Meaning the dead gain the reward? One slaughters for the dead?
* The Shaykh: No. This is if it is for the dead as a form of worship and glorification, and that is not permissible, to draw near to them by it. But if it is for the dead, so that he benefits from it by its reward...
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, by its reward. This is not objectionable.
(...) From this noble verse: the excellence of faith, since Allah directed the address to the believers. They are the people for whom the address is directed, by His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾.
* And among its benefits: the obligation to eat from the good things Allah has provided, by His saying: ﴿Eat﴾.
* And among its benefits also, which is indicated by implication: that foul things may not be eaten from, by His saying: ﴿of the good things We have provided for you﴾. And foul things are forbidden, by His saying: ﴿and he makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾ [al-A'raf 157].
* And among its benefits: that whatever food a person obtains is from the provision of Allah, and a person has in it only the means. From where is this derived?
* Student: ﴿what We have provided you﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿what We have provided you﴾.
* And among its benefits: directing a person to seek provision from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From where is this derived?
* Student: "Eat."
* The Shaykh: No. Directing a person to seek provision from Allah, by His saying: ﴿what We have provided you﴾. So if this provision is from Allah, Glorified and Exalted, then let us seek it from Him along with taking the means that He commanded us to take.
* And among them: the obligation to give thanks to Allah, by His saying: ﴿and give thanks to Allah﴾.
* And among them: the obligation of sincerity toward Him in that, from where is it derived? From the lam in His saying: ﴿to Allah﴾.
* And among them: that thanksgiving is part of realizing worship, by His saying: ﴿if it is Him you worship﴾.
* And among them: the obligation of sincerity to Allah in worship, derived from the fronting of the object in His saying: ﴿it is Him you worship﴾.
* And among them: the mercy of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, toward His servants in two respects.
First: from His command to them to eat, because in eating there is preservation of their health.
Second: from His saying: ﴿what We have provided you﴾, for provision is undoubtedly from the mercy of Allah. So from this verse is derived the affirmation of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Student: The two respects, what are they?
* The Shaykh: The two respects: the command to eat, for what it contains of preserving the body, and His saying: ﴿what We have provided you﴾.
And among them: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists)?
* Student: ﴿Eat﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿Eat﴾, ﴿and give thanks﴾, and ﴿you worship﴾. All of these are attributed to the act of the servant, and this indicates that the servant has an act toward which the address is directed for its performance. And if the servant had no act, then directing the address to the servant to perform it would be imposing what cannot be borne (taklif ma la yutaq).
Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿He has only forbidden to you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ [al-Baqarah 173].
His saying: ﴿and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾: what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) position of (ma)?
* Student: A relative pronoun, subject (mubtada').
* The Shaykh: Subject? Do you agree?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: In both respects?
* Student: No, the first is a relative pronoun.
* The Shaykh: And the second?
* Student: It is conjoined to what came before.
* The Shaykh: And that is?
* Student: To His saying: "carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine."
* The Shaykh: To all three?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Another student: To the first. Conjunction is to the first.
* The Shaykh: The first, yes indeed. It is conjoined to the first, so it is then in an accusative position. What is the meaning of ﴿that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾?
* Student: From ihlal, which is raising the voice. And ﴿that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ is slaughtering, or everything done with something for other than Allah, Glorified and Exalted.
* The Shaykh: Yes. And what is the meaning of ﴿that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 2, Verses 172–174 (Part 3 of 6)**

* Student: That means the animal over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked.
* Shaykh: Yes. The name of other than Allah was invoked over it, by saying, "In the name of the Messenger," "In the name of the Prophet," "In the name of Jibril," "In the name of Mika'il," or something similar.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever is compelled﴾. In my view, there are two readings of ﴿فَمَنِ﴾ in His words: ﴿فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ﴾ and ﴿فَمَنُ اضْطُرَّ﴾ with a damma on the nun. As for ﴿فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ﴾ with this reading, the matter is clear: the kasra is to avoid the meeting of two sukūns. As for the damma, it is for the sake of assimilation to the damma on the ṭā'. ﴿فَمَنُ اضْطُرَّ﴾ is easier than ﴿فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ﴾. So there are two readings.

His words ﴿مَنْ﴾ here are conditional (shartiyyah), and the verb after it is a past-tense verb in the jussive position as the conditional verb (fi'l al-shart). His words ﴿اضْطُرَّ﴾ are a passive participle (ism maf'ūl). In a context like this one, only the passive form is used. It is not correct to say ﴿اضْطَرَّ﴾ (active), because iḍṭarra (active) means "he put another into necessity," whereas uḍṭirra (passive) means "he fell into necessity." So the meaning of uḍṭirra is: necessity compelled him. Necessity is above need: need is a matter of completeness, while necessity is unavoidable.

His words ﴿فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ﴾ mean: necessity compelled him to what? To eating. This is because it comes after His words ﴿إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ﴾ [Allah has only forbidden you]. So the meaning is: whoever is compelled by necessity to eat this forbidden thing.

But this is conditional on two conditions, or rather three conditions, if we take necessity as the condition. The three conditions are: that necessity exists; that he is not a rebel (bāghin); and that he is not a transgressor (ʿādin). ﴿غَيْرَ بَاغٍ وَلَا عَادٍ﴾ [neither rebellious nor transgressing]. We want to parse (ghayra) as: it is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the deputy of the subject in His words ﴿اضْطُرَّ﴾. And we want Rashad to parse for us ﴿بَاغٍ﴾.

* Student: Genitive attribute (muḍāf ilayh).
* Shaykh: Complete it.
* Student: A genitive attribute, marked in the genitive by a kasra.
* Shaykh: Genitive by the mudāf construction. What is the sign of its genitive case?
* Student: The kasra.
* Shaykh: An apparent kasra on its final letter. Do you agree with him on this?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: They do not agree.
* Student: There is a deleted yā' in it; its original form is bāghiy.
* Shaykh: Then the sign of its genitive case is a presumed kasra on the deleted yā', which was prevented from appearing by the heaviness, because of the meeting of two sukūns. The tanwīn here is called tanwīn ʿiwaḍ (nunation as compensation for a letter). The same applies to ﴿عَادٍ﴾.

His words ﴿غَيْرَ بَاغٍ وَلَا عَادٍ﴾: the exegetes have differed about "the rebellious" (al-bāghī) and "the transgressor" (al-ʿādī). It was said: the rebellious is the one who rises against the imam, and they are the rebels (bughāh). The transgressor is the one who is disobedient through his journey, the aggressor who disobeys by his travel, who travels on a forbidden journey. Did you all understand this, O group?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: The rebellious is the one who rises against the imam. The transgressor is the one who is disobedient through his journey. These two are not permitted to eat carrion even if they are compelled, because both conditions are necessary: necessity, and the absence of rebellion and the absence of aggression. If he is rebellious or aggressive, it is not permissible for him to eat, even if he dies, because Allah the Exalted made the condition "neither rebellious nor transgressing." Also, he is not deserving of compassion and mercy so that he may be shown mercy, because rising against the imam is forbidden, and a journey of disobedience is also forbidden. Moreover, he is able to rid himself of this forbidden act, so that eating becomes permissible for him by means of what?

By repentance and giving it up. He intends that he is repentant and abandons this, and that becomes the cause that permits him to eat carrion. Do you understand?

Some scholars said: what is meant by the rebellious is the one who seeks to eat carrion, and the transgressor is the one who exceeds the limit permitted to him, that is, the one who eats more than the necessity. So the transgressor is one who exceeds, and the rebellious is one who seeks. The meaning of ﴿غَيْرَ بَاغٍ﴾ is: not seeking to eat carrion, and not transgressing in eating it by eating more than his need. According to this opinion, the circumstantial state here is like an emphasizing state for its governing verb, because in reality there is no necessity unless he does not desire to eat carrion and does not exceed what he needs. If a person is not compelled and goes to eat carrion, we say: this one is rebellious. If he is compelled and eats more than his necessity, we say: this one is transgressing. This opinion is weakened by the fact that the default for a circumstantial state is that it is informative (ta'sīs, adding new information), and it is strengthened by the fact that the Qur'an explains itself. Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿Whoever is compelled by hunger, not inclining toward sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:3]. Because His words ﴿فِي مَخْمَصَةٍ﴾ [in a state of hunger] explain His words ﴿غَيْرَ بَاغٍ﴾, since the one who eats only in hunger has not sought to eat carrion. And the one who is "not inclining toward sin" is known to be the one who did not fall into transgression, so it cannot be permitted to him. This opinion, with this support from the other verse, is more correct: that what is meant by "not seeking" is—

* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: No, "not seeking" means: not seeking to eat carrion. You might say: does anyone seek to eat carrion? We say: yes, it is possible. It is possible for someone whose good, meaty sheep has died, and he grieves over it and sorrows for it, and guests come to him and he serves it to them. It is possible. We, praise be to Allah, by our nature and by our faith, praise be to Allah, dislike this. But there are people who eat carrion. In the Jahiliyyah they ate carrion. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they say: what is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾ [al-An'am 6:139]. ﴿And if it is dead, they are partners in it﴾ [al-An'am 6:139]. I have also heard that there are people now, these disbelievers in the countries, who eat carrion, eat donkeys, eat dogs, eat cats, and this is not strange. So, the point is, this thing may happen. Allah, glorified and exalted, has permitted us carrion, then, under three conditions: necessity. The second: that he is not seeking it, desiring it. The third: that he does not exceed the limit by which necessity is averted.

Based on this, is it permissible for him to eat until he is full?

* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No. It was also said: he may eat until he is full if he thinks it likely that he will not find anything else nearby. This is the correct view. Even if it were said that in this situation he should take some of it with him, eating now only enough to keep himself alive and taking some with him to carry, so that if he is compelled he eats it, and otherwise leaves it, that too would be a good opinion.

It remains for us to say: when a person eats carrion in a state of necessity, how does it become good, even though it is filth, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Except that it be carrion, or flowing blood, or the flesh of swine, for it is an abomination﴾ [al-An'am 6:145]? How does it become good merely because of the necessity for it?

The answer is from two aspects, or from one of the two aspects. The first aspect: we say, ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾. The One who made it impure by death, after it was pure during life, is capable of making it pure at the time of necessity for it. Just as donkeys were good to eat, then they became impure, impure and not to be eaten. And just as grape juice before it fermented was good to eat and drink, but when it fermented it became impure, although its substance is the same. So Allah, glorified and exalted, is the Creator of things, of their attributes, and the One who changes them as He wills. He is capable of making it good if His servant is compelled to it. This is one aspect.

The second aspect: we say, it remains in its state of impurity, but at the time of necessity for it, this impure thing is permitted because of necessity, and the necessity protects against its harm. So dealing with it under necessity is permitted, and its anticipated harm is averted by the necessity.

And I think there is a difference between the two aspects, or not?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: There is a difference between them, because according to the first aspect it has changed from filth to purity, and according to the second aspect it remains, but there is something that protects against its harm. This is perhaps closer to what is rationally understood: that its impurity remains, but the necessity for it has permitted it, and protected from the harm of it. This meaning is supported by the sensory experience: the more a soul is eager for something, the faster it digests it, so the body is not harmed by it. Consider yourself: when you eat food on top of food, you digest the second slowly, and the first is delayed, along with the harm that occurs from it. But if you eat food while hungry, it is digested quickly and the soul accepts it, and because of the strength of the soul's desire, this impurity's harm disappears. What also confirms this is what is narrated from Suhayb al-Rumi, that he had an eye inflammation. Dates were brought to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was present, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ate some of them. Suhayb wanted to eat some, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You eat them while you have an eye inflammation?" [Narrated by Ibn Majah (3443) and Ahmad (16591, 23480) from Suhayb, with similar wording.] Because it is known that one with eye inflammation does not eat dates, as it increases the pain in his eye. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I chew them on the other side," that is, for example, if the right is affected, I chew on the left. So the Prophet (ﷺ) laughed and allowed him.

Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the wisdom in the Messenger (ﷺ) allowing him, although he was a mujtahid, is that the harm is removed by the strength of the soul's desire for it. It is digested quickly and interacts with the body, and its harm passes away.

So what we have now understood is that if a person is compelled to carrion, not seeking it and not transgressing, then whose answer is it? ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾. This is the answer to (man, whoever), and it is joined with the fā' because the sentence is a nominal sentence, and when the answer of the condition is a nominal sentence, it must be joined with the fā'. ﴿no sin upon him﴾. Do we not remember that (lā) puts the noun in the accusative?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And what is it?
* Students: It is the negation of the genus (lā al-nāfiyah lil-jins).
* Shaykh: The negation of the genus? It makes it accusative, and it is built on what it is accusative with if it is singular. Its predicate here is ﴿فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾, that is: then there is no punishment upon him, or: then there is no blame.

His words ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ [Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful]: this is the cause (ta'līl) of the ruling. The ruling is the absence of sin, and the reason is ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. ﴿غَفُورٌ﴾ may be an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha). It has been reported that it is among the intensive forms: fa'ūl?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Where is the evidence in the words of Ibn Malik?
* Student: His words:
"Fu'ūlah and fa'ālah are for fa'ula, as in sahula al-amr (the matter was easy) and zaydun jazula (Zayd was firm)."
* Shaykh: Yes. You are in one valley, and this verse is in another.
* Student: It is close to this.
* Shaykh: No, it is not this. These are the patterns of verbal nouns (maṣādir). He did not say this about the patterns of the active and passive participles. He said:
"Fa''āl, or mif'āl, or fa'ūl, are substitutes for fā'il in frequency."
The evidence is his words: "or fa'ūl." ﴿غَفُورٌ﴾ may be said to be an intensive form because of the abundance of His forgiveness, glorified and exalted, and the abundance of those whom He forgives. So the abundance here applies both to the act and to the object. How is it in the act and in the object? The act is the act of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the abundance of His repentance toward His servant; and in the object, the abundance of those who are forgiven. It may also be an attributive adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah). And His words ﴿رَحِيم﴾ are likewise. ﴿الْغَفُور﴾ is derived from (al-ghafr), which is covering together with protection. It is not merely covering, but covering together with protection. From it the helmet (al-mighfar), which covers the head in battle, is named, because it includes covering and protection. This is supported by the words of Allah, glorified and exalted, when He is alone with His believing servant and calls him to account: "I have concealed it for you in this world, and today I forgive it for you." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52) from Ibn 'Umar.]

His words ﴿رَحِيم﴾ are an intensive form, or an attributive adjective, from mercy. Mercy is one of the essential attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted; it is essential in its origin and active in its renewal. Regarding the fact that it is established for Allah, it is an essential attribute, and regarding the renewal of whom Allah has mercy on, it is an active attribute. For this reason Allah linked it to His will in His words: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:21].

So it is a true attribute established for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The people of ta'wīl, and the more correct thing is to call them the people of taḥrīf (distortion), say that mercy is not literal, and that what is meant by Allah's mercy is His kindness, or the intention of kindness. So they interpret it either as will or as action. This is without doubt an error. Their argument is that they say: mercy is tenderness and softness, and tenderness and softness are not suitable to the greatness of the Creator, glorified and exalted. So we say to them: whose mercy is this mercy?

* Students: The created being's.
* Shaykh: The created being's. It is the mercy of the created being. As for the mercy of the Creator, it is befitting to Him, glorified and exalted.

* Student: Shaykh, is the impurity (...) sensory or moral?
* Shaykh: Sensory. Its impurity is sensory.
* Student: The moral one that (...) applies to the compelled and the non-compelled.
* Shaykh: No. The impurity of donkeys is sensory, and if a person is compelled to them, he eats them.
* Student: As for frogs, if they are dead?
* Shaykh: Frogs are not permitted.
* Student: No, other than frogs. If they live on land and sea, and are found dead on land?
* Shaykh: They are given the ruling of land animals. What lives on land and in the sea is given the ruling of land animals, by giving precedence to the side of the land.
* Student: They say, Shaykh, for example, about the "mermaid" (ʿarūsat al-baḥr)?
* Shaykh: Who is her husband?!
* Student: She has no husband. Scholars mention that she is found in the Caspian Sea. Shaykh, what about this?
* Shaykh: If you find this, keep it and eat it.
* Student: So she is human-like, like fish?
* Shaykh: Yes, we have heard this way. We have heard that there are fish in the shape of human beings, in the shape of human women, and that they are very beautiful.
* Student: Do you eat her?
* Shaykh: Yes, you eat her.
* Student: Does she resemble a human?
* Shaykh: And what about her?
* Student: If one is compelled to her?
* Shaykh: If one is compelled to her, the scholars differed about her. This raises benefits. The well-known view among the Hanbalis is that it is not permissible to eat her even if one is compelled. The Shafi'is said that it is permissible to eat her in necessity, and this is the correct view.
* Student: I say: even forbidden things like dogs and donkeys?
* Shaykh: Is that not the flesh of swine?
* Student: Is the flesh of swine permitted?
* Shaykh: Permitted?! This is what we have: ﴿Allah has only forbidden you carrion and blood﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:173]. And what comes after it?
* Students: ﴿and the flesh of swine﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿and the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:173].
* Student: I think it refers back to the first, all of it, as conjoined to the first?
* Shaykh: Yes? That they are all forbidden things.
* Student: No, I mean: "neither desiring nor transgressing" is not specific to carrion only, or does it apply to all of them?
* Shaykh: No. Even in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿whoever is compelled﴾, and the flesh of swine is included there. In short, all forbidden things, if necessity is removed by them, are permitted. And my saying "if necessity is removed by them" is a precaution against what does not remove necessity. For example, if a person is compelled to eat poison, is it permissible for him to eat it?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: It is a means to killing and death. And if a person is compelled by thirst to wine, while he has a jar of wine?
* Students: He drinks it.
* Other students: He does not drink it.
* Shaykh: He does not drink it. They say he does not drink it, because wine increases thirst, so he does not drink it. But if he is compelled to wine to push down a morsel he is choking on, see how the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, judged! They say: if he chokes on a morsel and has nothing to drink except a jar of wine, he drinks it only to push down the morsel. When it is pushed down, he stops.
* Student: Shaykh, if I see a choking person drinking?!
* Shaykh: No, I seek refuge in Allah! I fear that if he starts to choke and drinks, he chokes and it no longer benefits him!
* Student: Your Eminence, fornication: if one is compelled?
* Shaykh: There is no necessity for this. Fornication has no necessity at all. The most that can be said is that desire is aroused, and it can be reduced by other means.
* Student: Is it permissible to reduce desire by other means?
* Shaykh: Yes, in necessity, yes, in necessity.
* Student: Shaykh, what is the implication of qualifying the swine with "flesh"?
* Shaykh: It was mentioned before.
* Student: When it is unrestricted, it includes all.
* Shaykh: It was mentioned before: when "flesh" is unrestricted, what is meant by it is everything in this body of animals.
* Student: And what is the meaning of the restriction?
* Shaykh: There is no restriction.
* Student: (...) carrion is better?
* Shaykh: Carrion?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Carrion, because its origin is permitted.
(...) Ansari and Ansar, because the one attributed to Abu Hanifah is called Hanafi, and the Hanafi...
* Student: They say: he is not Ahnaf (one with bow legs), meaning the Ahnaf?

**Shaykh:** No, that is not correct. *Ahnaf* is like *Ansari* and *Ansar*, or *Hanafi* and *Ahnaf*. There is nothing wrong with it.

**Student:** In His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿غَيْرَ بَاغٍ وَلَا عَادٍ﴾ (*neither rebellious nor transgressing*), where is the explanation? Is it the first opinion or the second?

**Shaykh:** No, the stronger view is the second.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and exchange it for a small price, those - they consume not into their bellies except the Fire.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 174].

The phrase ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ﴾ consists of *inna* (إن), which denotes emphasis, and *alladhina* (الذين), which is its subject. ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (*ula'ika*, "those") is the subject (*mubtada'*). ﴿مَا يَأْكُلُونَ﴾ is the predicate, and the subject together with its predicate is the predicate of *inna*.

﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْتُمُونَ مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾: *yaktumuna* means "they hide," and concealment may occur when one is asked and when one is not asked. Therefore, whenever the need arises to make knowledge clear, whether by a question or otherwise, it is obligatory upon the one who possesses that knowledge to explain it and make it manifest.

His saying, ﴿يَكْتُمُونَ مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ﴾: as for the word "the Book" (*al-kitab*), the definite article *al-* (أل) is either for a specific known reference (*al-'ahd*) or for the generic nature (*al-jins*). If we say it is for a known reference, then what is meant is the Torah, and "those who conceal" refers to the Jews, because they concealed the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). If we say that *al-* is for generality (*al-'umum*), it includes all the books: the Torah, the Gospel, and others. Then "those who conceal" includes the Jews, the Christians, and others. This second view is stronger because of its generality. His saying, ﴿مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ﴾ means that He sent it down to His messengers, for Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book﴾ [Al-Hadid 25]. Every messenger has with him a Book from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by which he guides the people.

His saying, ﴿وَيَشْتَرُونَ بِهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا﴾ [Al-Baqarah 174]: *yashtarun* means "they take." ﴿بِهِ﴾ refers to what Allah has revealed. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers back to the concealment, meaning they exchange this concealment for it. As for ﴿ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا﴾, what is this price? Is it wealth or position? In reality, either of them may be a price, and either may be intended, were it not that His saying, ﴿they consume not into their bellies except the Fire﴾ [Al-Baqarah 174] indicates that what is meant is wealth.

His saying, ﴿وَيَشْتَرُونَ بِهِ ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا﴾ means that they are given wealth, and it is said: "Conceal this knowledge, do not explain it, be silent about explaining it." This occurs among the Jews and the Christians, and among this Ummah as well, for among the people of knowledge there are those who conceal knowledge for the sake of this world and exchange it for a small price. Now, what if one exchanges it for a large price?

**Students:** Then it is small.

**Shaykh:** Then it is small. In comparison with the Hereafter, it is small. Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿So the enjoyment of this worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is but little﴾ [At-Tawbah 38]. The punishment of these people is: ﴿they consume not into their bellies except the Fire.﴾ *Ma ya'kulun ilia al-nar*: *al-nar* (النارَ) is the object of *ya'kulun*, because the exception here is *al-istithna' al-mufarragh* (the exclusive exception with no stated object); meaning these people consume nothing but the Fire. Reflect on how the punishment came in a nominal sentence. And what is the term?

The establishment and permanence of this punishment is as if it were repeated twice. Had the verse been: "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and exchange it for a small price, they consume into their bellies nothing but the Fire," the sentence would be sound. But with ﴿أُولَئِكَ مَا يَأْكُلُونَ﴾, the subject is mentioned a second time, so the sentence is as if repeated.

His saying, ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾: is the demonstrative for the distant or for the near?

**Students:** For the distant.

**Shaykh:** For the distant. Is it because of their high rank, or because of their low rank and the repulsion from them?

**Students:** Because of their low rank.

**Shaykh:** Yes, because of their distance from good and to repel people from them, not because of their elevated status, as in His saying, ﴿That is the Book﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2]. No, that one is for nearness of rank and closeness to them. And His saying, ﴿إِلَّا النَّارَ﴾: how is it "except the Fire"?

We say: Yes, this wealth they swallow as fire, and we seek refuge in Allah. It is not now fire; now it is eating and drinking, but on the Day of Resurrection it will be fire. Allah, Exalted is He, often describes some actions by means of fire. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "He who drinks from silver vessels only swallows the Fire of Hell into his belly."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5634) and Muslim (2065/1), from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]] And he said concerning the man who wore gold, and he was a man: "One of you deliberately takes a live coal and places it in his hand."[[Narrated by Muslim (2090/52), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] And he said: "Woe to the heels from the Fire."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (60) and Muslim (241/26), from the hadith of Ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]] (This was said) because they neglected washing them. And he said: "What is below the two ankles is in the Fire."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5787), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] Because this action is opposition to the command of Allah and His Messenger and disobedience, so it deserves the punishment of the Fire.

His saying, ﴿مَا يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ إِلَّا النَّارَ﴾ means that these things will be made to swallow as fire on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿وَلَا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ﴾ (*Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection*): He will not speak to them; meaning, speech of pleasure. So the negation here is not a negation of speech in general, but of the speech of good pleasure. It does not prevent Him from speaking to them with speech of reproach, as in His saying, ﴿Remain in it and do not speak to Me﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 108].

﴿وَلَا يُكَلِّمُهُمُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وَلَا يُزَكِّيهِمْ﴾: yes, they will not be purified on the Day of Resurrection, because the believers are purified and testified to with purification. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, purifies them and says: "I concealed it for you in the world, and I forgive it for you today."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2441) and Muslim (2768/52), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]] So he is forgiven. Likewise, they are purified by being given their book in their right hands, because taking the book in the right hand, or being given it in the right hand, is a purification. But those who are not believers are not purified; they take their books in their left hands, and it is called out before all creation: ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 18].

His saying, ﴿وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾: here *fa'il* (فَعِيل) means *mu'fil* (مُفْعِل), "painful," that is, causing pain. Punishment (*al-'adhab*) is retribution and penalty (...).

﴿إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْمَيْتَةَ وَالدَّمَ وَلَحْمَ الْخِنْزِيرِ وَمَا أُهِلَّ بِهِ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ غَيْرَ بَاغٍ وَلَا عَادٍ فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ إِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 173].

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is clear, because He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat from the good things We have provided you and be grateful to Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 172]. When He commanded eating from the good things, He then explained what is forbidden to us from the foul things. From this noble verse, the following is derived: the prohibition of eating carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than Allah. These are four things, and the prohibition of these four things.

* One of its benefits: prohibition belongs to Allah, as in His saying, ﴿He has only forbidden you﴾. The one who forbids is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and He is the one who makes lawful.

* From this noble verse is derived the restriction of the forbidden things to these four: carrion, blood, pork, and what has been dedicated to other than Allah. From where is this taken?

**Students:** ﴿إِنَّمَا﴾ (*innama*, "only").

**Shaykh:** ﴿إِنَّمَا﴾, because it is a particle of restriction. But this restriction has been shown not to be intended, because Allah forbade in another verse things other than these. Is that so or not? He forbade what is sacrificed on stone altars (*nusub*), which is not included among these things. And the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade every animal with fangs among beasts of prey,[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5530) and Muslim (1932/12), from the hadith of Abu Tha'labah.]] and every bird with talons,[[Narrated by Muslim (1934/16), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] and this is not included among these things. And the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade domestic donkeys,[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5527) and Muslim (1936/23), from the hadith of Abu Tha'labah.]] which is not included among these things. Thus the restriction has been shown in the Qur'an to be not absolute. What else?

**Students:** And the Sunnah.

**Shaykh:** And the Sunnah.

* From the benefits of this verse: the prohibition of all carrion, based on His saying, ﴿الْمَيْتَةَ﴾, and this *al-* is for generality. However, this is excepted for fish and locusts, that is, the carrion of the sea and locusts, based on the narrations reported concerning them. And is something excepted from carrion?

**Student:** The hide.

**Shaykh:** The hide?! But the correct view is that it is not excepted, because it is not included in that, it is not included in the prohibition. The thing forbidden here is what?

**Students:** Eating.

**Shaykh:** Eating, because He said: ﴿Eat from the good things﴾, then He said: ﴿He has only forbidden you﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Only the eating of carrion is forbidden."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1492) and Muslim (363/100), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] Based on this, is anything excepted from it or not? No, nothing is excepted.

From this verse is derived the prohibition of blood, based on His saying, ﴿وَالدَّمَ﴾ (*and blood*). It is unrestricted here, but in Surah al-An'am it is restricted to "flowing blood." Based on this, the unrestricted wording of this verse is qualified by Surah al-An'am, meaning flowing blood. And based on this restriction, it is derived that blood remaining after the soul has left a slaughtered animal is lawful. Is it lawful or not?

**Students:** Lawful.

**Shaykh:** Lawful.

* From this noble verse: the prohibition of pork, based on His saying, ﴿وَلَحْمَ الْخِنْزِيرِ﴾. It includes its fat and all its parts. This is not by general meaning (*al-'umum al-ma'nawi*), but by lexical generality (*al-'umum al-lafdhi*), because "flesh" (*lahm*) applies to everything of an animal that is eaten. Though some of it may be excluded when it is mentioned alongside something else, when you say "flesh and fat," the flesh becomes other than the fat, and when you say "flesh and liver," the liver becomes other than the flesh. But when mentioned absolutely, it includes everything.

* From the benefits of the verse: the prohibition of what has had the name of other than Allah pronounced over it. From where?

**Students:** ﴿مَا أُهِلَّ بِهِ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿مَا أُهِلَّ بِهِ لِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ﴾.

* Also from its benefits: the prohibition of what is slaughtered for other than Allah, even if the name of Allah is mentioned over it, such as one who says, "In the name of Allah, Allah is greatest; O Allah, this is for such-and-such idol." Because it was dedicated to other than Allah, or not?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** * From the benefits of the verse: that shirk affects even physical things. It is a spiritual impurity, but it affects even physical things. This animal that was dedicated to other than Allah, what does it become?

**Student:** Impure, forbidden.

**Shaykh:** Impure, foul, forbidden. And that over which the name of Allah was mentioned is good and lawful. Reflect on the extent of shirk, and that it passes from the meanings to the tangible, and it is worthy of being so. This is why Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The polytheists are only impure, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their year﴾ [At-Tawbah 28].

Even if it is not a physical impurity, their bodies are not impure; but because of the strength of its spiritual foulness and the corruption of their creed and inner intention, it affects even perceptible matters.

* From the benefits of the verse: the virtue of sincerity to Allah. From where do we take it?

**Student:** ﴿فَمَنِ اضْطُرَّ غَيْرَ بَاغٍ﴾.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** When sincerity is present, the slaughtered animal is good; when shirk is present, the slaughtered animal is foul.

**Shaykh:** Yes, correct.

* From the benefits of the verse: necessity permits what is forbidden, based on His saying, ﴿So whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him﴾. From His saying, ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾.

* And among them: but notice that this necessity permits what is forbidden under two conditions:
The first condition: the necessity must be genuine, such that harm cannot be averted except by consuming it.
The second condition: the necessity must be removed by it, such that the harm is averted. Do you understand?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Two conditions are required. The first: the necessity must be genuine, such that harm cannot be averted except by it. The second: the necessity is removed by it.

We said this so that the case of seeking treatment with what is forbidden would not be brought against us. Some scholars or some common people think that seeking treatment with what is forbidden falls under necessity, and that if a person is compelled to treat himself with the forbidden, it becomes lawful for him. We say: this is not correct, for two reasons, because both conditions are absent, or not? All of these conditions are absent in the matter of treatment. How so?

Because the genuineness of necessity is not present, since one can treat himself with something permissible, and one can be cured without treatment. Is this not apparent?

Second: if he treats himself with this forbidden thing, is his necessity averted? He may be cured, or he may die, in any case. And this is not like the case of one who has nothing except this carrion and nothing else. In that case we know that if he eats it, his necessity is averted. And we know that as long as he has nothing else, he is compelled. So there is a difference between them.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or not?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes, because it is among the mercy of Allah toward the servant that He permitted him what is forbidden to avert his necessity.

* And among them: that impure substances become pure when the Shariah rules them lawful. From where do we take this?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** During the explanation we mentioned two views: are these substances transformed into purity, or do they remain impure but are permitted out of necessity, and because the soul, due to its great need for them, digests and accepts them so that it is not harmed by them? We mentioned two opinions or two views among the people of knowledge, and we said that both are true. Just as donkeys, after they were lawful and pure, became forbidden through their prohibition, becoming filth and impure. Yesterday this donkey was lawful and pure, and today it has become forbidden and foul. And Allah is capable of all things.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, which are: *al-Ghafur* (the Forgiving) and *al-Rahim* (the Merciful).

* And among them: the affirmation of what the Imams of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah stated, that the transitive names of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, convey the rulings derived from them. Did we not say that the transitive names include the name, the attribute, and the effect, which is the ruling? The scholars derive from such a verse the establishment of the effect, which is the ruling, because He is Forgiving and Merciful; He forgave the one who consumed this carrion out of necessity, and had mercy on him by making it lawful. Therefore, this is clear evidence that the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, indicate the essence, the attribute, and the ruling: the name indicates the essence, and the attribute and the ruling, as the people of knowledge, may Allah have mercy on them, have affirmed.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever consumes the forbidden thing without excuse is sinful. From where do we take it?

**Students:** ﴿فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾. From it we know that if he is not compelled, then he bears sin.

* And among its benefits, according to some scholars: the one who travels in disobedience does not receive the concessions of travel. From where is this taken according to this opinion? From His saying, ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾. They said: what is meant by "desiring" is the one who rebels against the ruler, and "transgressing" is the one who travels in disobedience. They said: the one who travels in disobedience, or the one who rebels against the ruler, is not granted any of the concessions of travel. He does not shorten the prayer, does not wipe over leather socks for three days, and does not eat carrion; none of the concessions of travel are lawful for him, and he does not break the fast in Ramadan. This question is one on which the scholars differ, and we have already pointed to it earlier.

**Student:** Shaykh, is the prohibition of killing a soul, such as a person who must eat (...) to relieve his necessity?

**Shaykh:** It is not clear-cut, because the verse only grants permission. But it may be said that from the permissibility of something forbidden one derives the obligation to partake of it, since a prohibited thing is only violated for an obligatory reason. This is a principle (qa'idah) that some scholars adopted. They said: when something prohibited is violated, that is evidence of obligation. However, it is not consistently applied in reality. Some scholars derived the obligation of circumcision (khitan) from this principle. They said: the basic ruling is that cutting a part of a person's body is permitted or not?

**Student:** Forbidden.

**Shaykh:** Forbidden. Circumcision is cutting a part of the body, and a prohibition is only violated for an obligation. So they established the obligation of circumcision from this principle. But the principle is not applied with complete consistency. For example, it is permissible for a traveller to break his fast, and breaking the fast is a violation of a prohibition, even though breaking the fast is not obligatory. So it is not clearly applied consistently.

**Student:** I say: do they have evidence for whether a sinner on a journey may shorten prayers and take concessions?

**Shaykh:** We mentioned this previously, brother. We said that Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) holds that there is no difference between a sinner on a journey and one who is not sinning, because these rulings are attached to travel, and the sinner is sinful, while the rulings of travel remain in effect.

**Student:** Regarding the slaughter of the People of the Book, in what manner is it lawful for Muslims, and for whom?

**Shaykh:** By the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5].

**Student:** Regarding their slaughter, I mean, they have a method different from the Muslims' method.

**Shaykh:** "Their food is their slaughtered animals," as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said.[[Recorded by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (9/578).]]

**Student:** I mean, if they slaughter in a manner other than the Islamic method?

**Shaykh:** If the blood is made to flow and the name of Allah is mentioned over it, it is lawful.

**Student:** Is mentioning the name of Allah over it a condition?

**Shaykh:** The name of Allah must be mentioned, yes.

**Student:** What if, for example, they strike it with a particular blow?

**Shaykh:** If they strike it with a particular blow, and when it loses consciousness they slaughter it, it is lawful.

**Student:** They did not slaughter it; they did not perform the well-known slaughter?

**Shaykh:** And what kind of slaughter did they perform? How did they slaughter it?

**Student:** With a fingernail, for example.

**Shaykh:** With a fingernail? With a fingernail it is not lawful, because the Messenger (ﷺ) excepted it, saying: "What makes the blood flow and over which the name of Allah is mentioned is lawful, except a tooth and a nail."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2488) and Muslim (1968/20), from the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij.]]

**Student:** Even if this is their method?

**Shaykh:** It is not lawful. But do they slaughter a sheep with their fingernails?

**Student:** No, not a sheep, a chicken.

**Shaykh:** It is not lawful.

**Student:** O Shaykh, what if a Muslim forgets to mention the name of Allah?

**Shaykh:** It is not lawful.

**Student:** The donkey: is there evidence that it was good before its prohibition?

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed, its permissibility indicates that it was good.

**Student:** Then could this not be among the practices of the Jahiliyyah, like their eating of carrion? Should we not say that it was lawful before?

**Shaykh:** No. This was made lawful by the Law, and they ate it openly.

**Student:** Carrion: shall we say that it was good?

**Shaykh:** Carrion was good, but it became impure by death.

**Student:** But you say it was good and carrion, so it became impure.

**Shaykh:** No, it is not lawful. The Law did not establish its permissibility.

**Student:** What is the difference between it and the donkey?

**Shaykh:** The donkey was lawful and they ate it, but they did not eat carrion at all. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, held that the donkey remained lawful even after the prohibition. He said: because Allah says: ﴿Say, "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it..."﴾ [al-An'am 6:145], and where is the donkey?

Some scholars forbid it if there is a need to preserve it. So in our time, according to the opinion of some scholars, it is permissible to eat it. But the correct view is that it is filth and is not lawful.

**Student:** Drinking wine: was it not impure?

**Shaykh:** Wine was also prohibited. But the correct view is that wine is not impure in its essence; its impurity is not intrinsic.

**Student:** Of impurity?

**Shaykh:** The impurity is practical. So the impurity of wine is moral (ma'nawi). This is the correct view, and therefore it does not render garments impure.

**Student:** But, O Shaykh, it affects the intellect.

**Shaykh:** It affects the intellect, usually. Most of what is prohibited is prohibited for this reason. That is why Allah stated the reason for the prohibition: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:91].

**Student:** So you do not judge wine to be impure?

**Shaykh:** Moral impurity.

**Student:** O Shaykh, the foetus of a sheep that is found in its belly without having been slaughtered?

**Shaykh:** Yes, its slaughter is the slaughter of its mother. The main point is that we say: O brothers, regarding slaughter, hunting and similar matters there are specific chapters, but what is in the womb of the mother, if the mother is slaughtered, its slaughter is the slaughter of its mother.

**Student:** Shaykh, the hadith of 'A'ishah: "They bring us meat and we do not know whether the name of Allah was mentioned over it or not." Is there some contradiction?

**Shaykh:** Did he say: "Mention the name yourselves and eat"?[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3174), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]]

**Student:** The meaning is different now. How can it be reconciled between it and them?

**Shaykh:** There is no contradiction between them, no conflict that would require reconciliation.

**Student:** But this concerns slaughter.

**Shaykh:** That is about slaughter. But the basic principle is that what a Muslim slaughters, he has mentioned the name of Allah over it. This is the basic principle. You do not doubt the action of another if the people who asked the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "Some people bring us meat over which they do not mention the name of Allah." Then there is some element of conflict.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and exchange it for a small price – those consume not into their bellies except the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:174].

Allah, the Exalted, mentions in this verse: ﴿Those who conceal﴾, meaning, those who hide. And His saying: ﴿what Allah has revealed﴾.

From this noble verse is derived: the obligation to disseminate knowledge, from His saying: ﴿Those who conceal﴾. Its obligation becomes more emphatic when there is a need for it, when it is asked about, either by the language of the situation or by the language of speech. What is the language of speech? A person comes and asks you. And the language of the situation is when people fall into a matter in which they need to be told that it is prohibited, or they neglect a matter in which they need to be told that it is obligatory.

* Also derived from this noble verse: that the Books were sent down from Allah, from His saying: ﴿what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾. And it is derived from it that they are the speech of Allah. From where is this taken?

**Student:** ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:159].

**Shaykh:** ﴿of the Book and exchange it for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:174].

**Student:** ﴿And We sent down﴾.

**Shaykh:** It is derived that they are the speech of Allah.

**Student:** His saying: ﴿what Allah has revealed﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾. Good. So it is His speech.

* Also derived from it: the highness (`uluww) of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿has revealed﴾. Whenever it is mentioned that things descend from Him, He is High, glorified and exalted.

* Also derived from this verse: that this threat is upon the one who combines two things: concealing and exchanging it for a small price. As for the one who conceals without exchanging, or exchanges without concealing, the ruling for him differs. If he conceals without exchanging, Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance after We have made it clear to the people in the Book – those are cursed by Allah and cursed by the cursers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:159].

As for those who exchange without concealing, Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment – We will fully repay them for their deeds therein, and they therein will not be deprived﴾ [Hud 11:15].

So people are of three categories. One category conceals not for the sake of worldly gain, but out of stinginess with knowledge or something similar. Another category makes it clear, but not for Allah, rather for worldly gain. This one intended his deed for the world, like a person who teaches people for pay, or who intends to spread knowledge for pay. Otherwise, the correct view is that teaching for a wage is permissible. But he learns for the sake of the world, and there is no doubt that his intention is invalid. The third category conceals for some worldly purpose, for example, concealing in order to preserve his leadership, as the Jews did when they concealed the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) so that their leadership would remain. Or a person who says something, then it becomes clear to him that the truth is otherwise, yet he conceals the truth, thinking with his limited view that if he retracts his first statement his standing among the people will fall. So he wishes to maintain his position by his own assumption, and does not retract his statement whose error has become clear to him. This too is concealment, and for what? In order to exchange it for a small price. The ignorant person says: everything desired for the sake of this world is a small price, whether it is status, leadership, administration, wealth, a wife, or anything else. Everything desired for the world is little, so it is part of the small price. Is it clear now? So people in this matter are divided into how many?

**Students:** Three categories.

**Shaykh:** Three categories, all of them blameworthy. As for the one who makes it manifest for Allah and learns for Allah, this is the best of the categories, and it is the fourth category: the one who makes clear with his tongue and pen what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has sent down. This is the fourth category, and it is the best of the categories.

**Student:** O Shaykh, what about the one who conceals out of fear? Is he not included among them?

**Shaykh:** As for one who conceals out of fear, if he will make it clear in another place, there is no harm. But if he conceals absolutely, this is not permissible. He must make it clear even if he is killed.

**Student:** And out of laziness, meaning he has no bad opinion, but is lazy and does not make it clear? That is, he has knowledge and does not make it clear?

**Shaykh:** Yes. If there is a need to make it clear, he must make it clear, and it is not permissible otherwise. But if there is no need... suppose he is in a place where there are people who make knowledge clear and spread it among the people, and he has knowledge but says: "My knowledge has not been needed and no questioner has asked me." This is not obligatory for him. If he makes it clear, he is without doubt better, because he adds strength to the strength of others. If he remains silent, I think he is free from blame as long as the matter has been taken up by others.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that all of this world is little, from His saying: ﴿and exchange it for a small price﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:174]. This is one aspect of the verse. It is also possible that they exchange it for a small price even in the eyes of people.
