This one says: "It is metonymy (majaz mursal)," that one says: "It is intellectual metaphor (majaz 'aqli)," another says: "It is a figure of speech (isti'arah)," and similar things, until they pass judgment on it by this distortion. This is their method; the way of the people of innovation is never free of this. But the People of the Sunnah and the Community say: "What is our business with the matter? Who informed us about Himself? Allah. He knows Himself best and is more truthful in speech than anyone else. Does He want to make clear to His creation, or to obscure things from them?"

* The students: To make clear.
* The Shaykh: To make clear: ﴿يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ أَنْ تَضِلُّوا﴾ [al-Nisa' 176]. So how much more so when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, wants only to make clear to His creation, and He, Glorified and Exalted, is the most truthful of speakers and the most knowing of whoever has spoken? How can we say: "This is metaphor, this is not true, this must be redirected"? Our obligation is to believe in it and take it according to its apparent meaning.

However, as we have established and often reaffirm, we must be cautious about two things: tamthil (likening) and takyif (specifying the modality). We do not say: "This apparent meaning is like what we know of ourselves," or "the modality of this thing is such-and-such." All of this is false and not permissible to believe. My brothers, if we adopt this principle, we will be at ease, both in its inclusiveness and its exclusiveness. We are at ease in its inclusiveness: nothing falls outside it. We apply all the hadiths and verses that come about the attributes of Allah in this way, and we say: "They are established for Allah, but without likening (tamthil) or specifying modality (takyif)." This is the inclusiveness. As for its exclusiveness: no one can object to us saying, "Why did you interpret this and leave that uninterpreted?" For some people are alarmed by certain attributes, being very alarmed by them, though they affirm others with a submissive soul.

Many people, for example, accept the attributes of meaning (sifat al-ma'ani) readily and easily submit to them, but when they encounter some attributes that belong to the category of parts (al-abʿad), and we do not say that they are parts of Allah because it is forbidden to say such a thing, they hesitate, shudder, put one foot forward and draw back the other in affirming them. Our obligation, what is our obligation? To submit to Him. We say: "There is no difference between this and that," and we believe that what Allah has reported about Himself does not resemble or equal the attributes of created beings. In this way we find rest. Praise be to Allah, that whatever is unbefitting to Allah is made clear by Allah and His Messenger; whatever is unbefitting to Him is clarified and not left as it is. When Allah said to His servant: "I asked you for food and you did not feed Me, I asked you for drink and you did not give Me drink, I fell ill and you did not visit Me" [Muslim 2569/43, from Abu Hurayrah], what is its apparent meaning? Its apparent meaning is that it is unbefitting for Allah to ask someone for food while He is the One who feeds and is not fed, or to ask someone for drink, or to be ill. Is this not its apparent meaning?

* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: For this reason, since this is its apparent meaning, Allah, Exalted, made clear that it is not what is intended. When His servant says: "How could I visit You when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He says: "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so fell ill? Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. How could I feed You when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He says: "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so asked you for food? Had you fed him, you would have found that with Me. How could I give You drink when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He says: "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so asked you for drink and you did not give him drink? Had you given him drink, you would have found that with Me." See now, it made clear. What is unbefitting to Allah is made clear, and what Allah affirmed for Himself remains as it is.

This principle, which is the fourth matter of belief in Allah, has been disputed among the people of the religion. Among them are the Salaf, who are alone the People of the Sunnah and the Community, who affirmed it for Allah according to its apparent meaning, befitting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and negated from it likening and specifying modality. Some people rejected it and believed in the names but not the attributes; some believe in the names and some of the attributes but not others; some reject both names and attributes; and some do not describe Allah with either affirmation or negation. This is well known among those who discuss these matters. In sum, belief in Allah includes four matters: belief in His existence, His lordship, His divinity, and His names and attributes. Yes.

The second: ﴿وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾ (and the Last Day). ﴿يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: the Last Day is the Day of Resurrection, and it is called "the last" because there is no day after it; it is a day that continues, in which there is no night or day, no sun or moon, nothing; it is a lasting, continuous day. Therefore it is called the Last Day.

Belief in the Last Day includes belief in everything the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed of that occurs after death, as Shaykh al-Islam said in al-ʿAqidah al-Wasitiyyah. It includes belief in everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that occurs after death: therein is included the trial of the grave, the punishment of the grave, the bliss of the grave, the gathering of people barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, the reckoning, the balance, the bridge, the Pool, the intercession, and whatever else Allah informed will occur on the Day of Resurrection. Everything Allah informed will occur after death is included in belief in the Last Day. And belief in the Last Day, just as it includes this, means that whoever believes in something prepares for it, does he not? So whoever says he believes in the Last Day but does not prepare for it, his claim is deficient, and the measure of its deficiency is the measure of his neglect of preparing for it.

As well as, for example, if someone were told: "Rain will fall today, so cover the grain." A person who has grain wheat and is told, "Rain will fall today, so cover the grain," it is known that whoever does not believe this statement will not cover it. Likewise, if it was said: "An enemy will come today, so tighten the guard." If he believes that an enemy will come, he tightens the guard with everything possible. If he does not believe it, he does not care. There is no doubt that a person who opposes what Allah and His Messenger have commanded has a deficiency in faith in the Last Day. For this reason, Allah, glorified and exalted be He, very often links faith in the Last Day with faith in Him in the Qur'an. He links them very frequently, which indicates that faith in the Last Day necessitates faith in the signs of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

(...) The intercession, the Sirat (the bridge over Hell), Paradise and Hellfire, all of this is included in the Last Day.

He said: ﴿وَالْمَلَائِكَةِ﴾ (and the angels). Faith in the angels. The word malā'ikah is the plural of malak (angel), and the origin of malak is mal'ak, and the origin of mal'ak is ma'lak, because it is derived from al-alūkah, which means message. This is what the linguists say. So it underwent i'lāl (morphological alteration) by deletion and by transposition (qalb). It was pluralized as what? Malā'ikah. The angels are servants among the servants of Allah, glorified and exalted be He. Allah created them from light and subjected them to His worship night and day: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never slackening﴾ [al-Anbiyā' 20]. They are bodies possessing intellects. The proof of that is the saying of Allah, exalted be He: ﴿Who made the angels messengers having wings﴾ [Fāṭir 1]. And wings are bodies, or not? They are bodies. Gabriel, peace be upon him, the Prophet ﷺ saw him in his own form and he had six hundred wings that filled the horizon.[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3232) and Muslim (174/280) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and the wording is that of at-Tirmidhi (3278) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] He also came in the form of a man,[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] and in the form of Dihyah al-Kalbi.[[Related by Ahmad in al-Musnad (5857) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]] All of this indicates that they are bodies, and that they have intellects?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Without doubt, yes. For this reason, "They glorify Him night and day, never slackening" [al-Anbiyā' 20]. And if they had no intellects, as some deviants have said, this would be the greatest blemish upon the messengers of all of them, since the intermediary between them and Allah would be a madman with no intellect. There is no greater blemish, may Allah protect us, upon the messengers and upon the One who sent them as well. Isn't that so? How can one entrust His revelation to someone who has no intellect? So it is a blemish upon Allah, a blemish upon the angels, and a blemish upon the messengers, may Allah protect us.
Among the strange things is that this view has spread among some people, and they said: "They are not bodies and they have no intellects." This is without doubt a false statement, among the most false of statements. The correct view, without any doubt, is that they have intellects and that they are bodies. But Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has given them strength and power far greater than the power of the jinn. The jinn have strength and power. The devil flows through the son of Adam like the flow of blood, and the angel is stronger. ﴿An 'ifrīt of the jinn said: I will bring it to you before you rise from your place﴾ [an-Naml 39], and ﴿The one who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾ [an-Naml 40]. So the angels brought it from Saba' to al-Sham before his glance returned to him: a mighty throne. This is evidence that the angels are stronger and more powerful than the jinn, even though the jinn have power. Whoever sees their speed, as they ascend to the heaven and take seats for eavesdropping... The conclusion is that the angels are without doubt bodies, that they have intellects, that they carry out the command of Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and that they prostrate to Him: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant﴾ [an-Nahl 49].
* Student: Do they have desire, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Yes, they have laws (sharā'i').
* The Student: Do they have desire?
* The Shaykh: Yes, I do not think so.
Know that among the angels, peace be upon them, some have been specified for us and we know them by name, and some have not been specified. As for those specified for us, it is obligatory upon us to believe in their names, such as?
* Student: Gabriel, peace be upon him.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Isrāfīl.
* The Shaykh: Isrāfīl, and what else?
* Student: Mālik.
* The Shaykh: Mālik, the keeper of the Fire.
* Student: Munkar and Nakīr.
* The Shaykh: Munkar and Nakīr, if the hadith is authentic with this wording, and there is room for discussion.
* Student: Mīkāl.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is Mīkāl, that is Mīkā'īl.
* Student: Is he the same as Mālik?
* The Shaykh: No, no, Mālik is the keeper of the Fire.
* Student: And the Angel of Death.
* The Shaykh: And the Angel of Death, but we do not know his name. Some people say 'Azrā'īl, but this has not been authenticated.
* Student: Hārūt and Mārūt, two angels.
* The Shaykh: Yes: ﴿And what was sent down upon the two angels at Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt﴾ [al-Baqarah 102]. It is authentic, yes, correct.
* Student: You say Mālik is the keeper of the Fire, Shaykh, and not Mīkāl. But there is a hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked Gabriel: "Why do I not see Mīkāl laughing?"[[Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (13343) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, and its wording is: "Why have I never seen Mīkā'īl laughing at all?" He said: "Mīkā'īl has not laughed since the Fire was created."]] Because he has never laughed at all.
* The Shaykh: Yes, verify it, verify it. Is this understood? Good. As for those whom we know by name, it is obligatory upon us to believe in them by name. Likewise, as for their deeds, some of them we know their deeds and some we do not know. But we must believe absolutely that they are honoured servants who obey the command of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. Good. Do they have any share in the management of creation without Allah's permission? No. But with Allah's permission, yes. There is one entrusted with rain and plants, one entrusted with blowing the Trumpet, and there are angels entrusted with embryos, and angels entrusted with recording the deeds of the children of Adam, and angels entrusted with protecting the children of Adam: ﴿For him are successive angels before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah﴾ [ar-Ra'd 11]. But all of this is by the command of Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and by His permission. They have no share at all in the universe, whether in rivalry with Allah, mighty and majestic is He, or in assistance. ﴿Say: Call upon those you claim besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have a share in them, nor is there for Him from among them any supporter (22). And intercession with Him does not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba' 22, 23]. So He negated everything the polytheists attach to them: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight﴾ individually; ﴿nor do they have a share in them﴾ in partnership; ﴿nor is there for Him from among them any supporter﴾ as an aide; ﴿nor does intercession with Him benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ as intercession and mediation. Then He said: ﴿Until, when terror is removed from their hearts﴾ [Saba' 23]. Who are they? The angels. And the angels, when they hear the revelation, are struck senseless. So they have no share at all in disposing of the universe, but they carry out the command of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.
* Student: Shaykh, who said that we must believe that some of the angels are not bodies?
* The Shaykh: It is not permissible.
* Student: For example, the angel entrusted with recording your deeds, saying we do not see him, and the angels who...?
* The Shaykh: Even Gabriel, we do not see him, and other than Gabriel we do not see. Gabriel comes and delivers the revelation to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and they do not see him. Do you see everything that is not seen is not a body?
* Student: No, we say: it is possible that...
* The Shaykh: No, we do not say "it is possible." All the angels are bodies.
* Student: Can they not change their form?
* The Shaykh: No, it is possible. By Allah's permission they change. This Gabriel transformed into the form of a man.
* Student: So it is possible that they change, and they say they are not...
* The Shaykh: By Allah's permission.
* Student: By Allah's permission.
* The Shaykh: I do not know about this, but I do not think it is possible.
* Student: Because the angels who are with us in the mosque are not bodies?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. It is not necessary that you see them. Now the jinn are bodies; they eat, drink and urinate, and they urinate upon the one who does not get up to pray Fajr. Yet you see them?
* Student: We say: perceptible bodies?
* The Shaykh: Perceptible bodies, but you do not see them. Now, in what is between our hands, as the doctors say, in this it is full; the air is full of germs and other things, and we no longer know whether to believe them or deny them.
* Student: No, this we see with our eyes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but do you see it with the naked eye?
* Student: If you let the sun's opening enter a dark room.
* The Shaykh: No, they are not that; this is not germs, this is dust particles. In any case, they are concealed from us. The Messenger ﷺ went out from among Quraysh, and they were looking at him: ﴿And We placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and covered them, so they do not see﴾ [Yā-Sīn 9].
* Student: But, Shaykh, do you not hold that a body must be perceptible?
* The Shaykh: Yes, we say it is perceptible, but it does not follow from being perceptible that we must see it.
* Student: So then it is not a body?
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah, glory be to Allah. It may be a body but we do not see it. Allah is capable of all things.
* Student: Shaykh, the saying of Allah: ﴿qa'īd﴾ [Qāf 17], does it not indicate the meaning of a body? Qa'īd means sitting.
* The Shaykh: Without doubt. The evidences are clear, very clear, there is no difficulty in them. Nor perhaps does the saying of the Messenger ﷺ trouble us more than the fact that they are with us and we do not see them: "It flows in the son of Adam as the blood flows." And how does it enter the human being, flowing through him like blood, while he does not feel it? But we must believe and say: now your soul flows through you like blood, every bone, every sinew and every flesh, and it is taken from you at death, yet do you see it or not?
* Student: Yes, we see it.
* The Shaykh: If the person dies, he sees it. But before that he does not see it nor feel it when it enters upon awakening, and he does not feel it when it leaves during sleep.
* Student: Do we not attribute that to the weakness of sight relative to the creature?
* The Shaykh: No, no. It may be weakness. The main point is that they are concealed from us and they are bodies. The main point is that they are concealed from us. If the strongest-sighted person came with the largest magnifying glass and microscope, he would never see them.

Now, we have learned that the angels were created from light, and by this we know that Satan is not among them, because Satan was created from fire, not from light, by the explicit text of the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims (ijmā'). Allah, exalted be He, said about Iblīs that he said to his Lord: ﴿I am better than him; You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾ [al-A'rāf 12]. And Allah, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿And the jinn We created before from the fire of scorching wind﴾ [al-Ḥijr 27]. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed that "the angels were created from light, and the jinn were created from fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to us"[[Related by Muslim (2996/60) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] from clay.

There remains the difficulty in the saying of Allah, exalted be He: ﴿And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, they prostrated except Iblīs. He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah 34]. It has already been mentioned to us in the tafsīr (exegesis) that this exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), and that Iblīs was among them in the gathering, associated with them. So the address was directed to the angels, and they are too numerous to be counted except by Allah, and Satan is one of them. A singular may be addressed within a group while being one of them even if he is not of their kind. The Arabs say: "The people came except a donkey," although the donkey is not of the kind of the people. The point is that speech is directed to a group even if among them is one from a number that only Allah can count, mighty and majestic is He.

And His saying: ﴿and the angels and the Book﴾. The Book here refers to the genus, so it includes every book that Allah, mighty and majestic is He, has sent down. Know that there is no messenger except that he has a book with him. The evidence is: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 25]. We sent down with them, with these messengers who were sent with clear proofs, the Book. So there is no messenger except that he has a book with him. As for the prophet, he may not have a book with him; rather, the apparent position is that he has no book with him, because he judges by the law of one before him: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light, by which the prophets who submitted judged﴾ [al-Mā'idah 44]. ﴿By it﴾: by the Torah. ﴿The prophets who submitted to those who were Jews﴾. And the well-known books that we have are five.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Four? Let us count: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms (Zabūr), the Qur'an, the scrolls of Ibrāhīm, and the scrolls of Mūsā. The scholars differed over whether the scrolls of Mūsā are the Torah or something else. Some said they are something else, and some said they are it. In any case, the five present no difficulty. And the sixth?
* Student: The Psalms (Zabūr).
* The Shaykh: We have counted it.
* Student: The Mazāmīr.
* The Shaykh: The Mazāmīr are sections of the Zabūr.
Good. As for what we do not know of, we believe in it how?
* The students: In general.
* The Shaykh: In general. So you say in your heart and with your tongue: "I believe in every book Allah has sent down upon every messenger." Then, what is meant is that you believe that Allah sent down to Mūsā a book called the Torah, and to 'Īsā a book called the Gospel, and to Dāwūd a book called the Zabūr. As for believing in what exists of them now, it is not obligatory upon you, why? Because it has been altered, changed and distorted. But you believe that it has an origin that was sent down to these prophets. And secondly...
* Student: Do we say: it is not obligatory to believe in them, or it is not appropriate not to believe in them?
* The Shaykh: Yes, we believe in the origin.
* Student: No, the ones that exist now.
* The Shaykh: The ones that exist now, yes. Those that exist now, it is not obligatory for us to believe in them. But we believe that they have an origin. As for everything in them, no: there is alteration in them. That is why we say: we believe that Allah sent down to Mūsā a book called the Torah. As for the Torah that is in the hands of the Jews now, it is altered and changed. Otherwise, its origin is without doubt true. Good. Does this belief in these books oblige us to act by what is in them, or ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Mā'idah 48]?
* The students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The second. The second is what is obligatory upon the believer. So we believe that they are true, and that acting by them is obligatory and imposed as long as the message of the prophet who was sent with them remains. When it is abrogated (naskh) by another law, acting becomes by the second law. Then if the second is abrogated, acting becomes by the third, and so on. This is why some of the Christians now, some of their simple folk, say: "Which is first?" We had a lecture with them and they raised this question: "Which is first, the Gospel or the Qur'an?" And what is the answer?
* The students: The Gospel.
* The Shaykh: The Gospel. But what is the purpose of this question? They say: "Then act by the first." This is possible. So acting by the first. We say, quite simply...
* Student: Acting by the Torah.

**Shaykh:** Yes, exactly as you said. Simply put, if you establish this principle, then there is no obligation to act upon the Gospel either, nor upon the Torah. We would then go back until we reach Adam. The main point, in any case, is that the matter is in fact the reverse: the later revelation abrogates (*naskh*) the earlier one, not the other way around. The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed regarding what is found in these books of valid legislation when our Law does not contradict it. If our Law does contradict it, then by the consensus (*ijma'*) of the Muslims, what our Law has brought is to be acted upon. But if something is found in the Torah or the Gospel that our Law does not contradict, is it obligatory for us to act upon it, and that it is law for us, or is it not obligatory?

Some scholars said that it is not obligatory, because Allah, the Exalted, said in the Qur'an: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what came before it of the Scripture and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:48]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 16:89]. Therefore we have no need of their law, and it is not binding upon us to act upon it, as long as there is nothing in the Qur'an for us to act upon, even if it does not contradict the Qur'an. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Every condition that is not in the Book of Allah is void, even if it were a hundred conditions.»[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (456), Muslim (1504/6), and Ibn Majah (2521) from the hadith of 'Aishah, and the wording is his.]]

Others said: Rather, it is obligatory upon us to act upon what is in the Torah, the Gospel, and other earlier books, when our Law does not contradict them. They argued with the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am 6:90]. They said: Allah commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to follow their guidance. Indeed, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, pointed to this, to something of this kind, when he said: «The best fasting is the fasting of Dawud: he would fast one day and break his fast one day. And the best night prayer is the night prayer of Dawud: he would sleep half the night, stand in prayer for a third of it, and sleep a sixth of it.»[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3420) and Muslim (1159/189) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, with the wording: «The most beloved fasting to Allah is... and the most beloved prayer to Allah is...».]] The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did this most of the time, sleeping in the last part of the night and standing in prayer for a third of it. They said: The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, guided to this. Furthermore, if it is not contradicted by our Law, it does not become opposed to our Law, and it is from Allah, so it is obligatory for us to act upon it. This view is more sound from the standpoint of reasoning. But the difficulty remains concerning what exists now of the earlier books. What is the difficulty?

**Student:** It has been altered (*muharrafah*).

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed. The doubt about its authenticity. This is what obliges a person to hold back. From here we know the error of those who sometimes bring something from the Torah, the Gospel, or the Psalms, wishing to encourage people to act upon it. This is a mistake, especially at this time when the matter has become confused for some people. Some people now cite passages from the Gospel. If they bring them as an argument against the Christians, there is no harm. But sometimes they bring them to establish what is in the Qur'an, as if the Qur'an needed the earlier books to bear witness to it. It does not need that, especially among the common people. Scholars may benefit from this in reality, especially in debates, the debates with the Christians. But one should never place in the hearts of the common people anything except one thing: the Qur'an, and the Sunnah of course, because it explains and clarifies the Qur'an. Introducing things of this kind to the common people confuses them, and they think that this matter, or that this religion, is still in force, the religion of the non-Muslims. The danger of this is great, and we have now witnessed its danger. Some people have come to say: Religions are nothing but ideas, like the thought of Aristotle and other such philosophers. They are ideas, and everyone has his own thought and his own opinion, and one should not object to anyone. You see this as something we have learned from these ignorant people, who do not know that the Islamic religion is a religion from Allah, by which Allah has made us worship Him, and in which we have no opinion. Right? Is it a thought? No. It is something Allah has sent down to His servants, by which they worship Him in belief, word, and deed, all of the servants. There is no room for independent reasoning (*ijtihad*) that contradicts this religion.

﴿the Book and the prophets﴾. The prophets, peace be upon them: do they include the messengers here or not? They undoubtedly include the messengers. ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:163], and so on. So when the term "prophets" is used absolutely, the messengers are included in it. But the messengers do not necessarily include the prophets. The phrase ﴿the prophets﴾ encompasses the messengers. It has been reported in a hadith, which Ibn Hibban authenticated: «The number of messengers is three hundred and some more than ten, and the number of prophets is one hundred and twenty-four thousand.»[[Related by Ahmad in al-Musnad (22288) from the hadith of Abu Umamah.]] If the hadith is authentic, it is an infallible report that we must believe in. And if it is not authentic, Allah says: ﴿And We did send messengers before you; of them are those We have related to you, and of them are those We have not related to you﴾ [Ghafir 40:78]. We are not obligated to believe except in what has reached us. So those messengers whom we know, we must believe in them by name. And those whom we do not know, we believe in them in general: ﴿Each believes in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers; we make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:285].

**Student:** Does the hadith not contradict the verse, Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** No, it does not contradict the verse.

**Student:** (...) ﴿of them are those We have not related to you﴾?

**Shaykh:** Yes. They were not related to us, but their number is known. Knowing the number does not indicate the story. Now, let us see if we can look in the Qur'an. How many messengers are in the Qur'an?

**Student:** Fifteen.

**Student:** Eighteen.

**Shaykh:** Or twenty-five.

**Student:** Twenty-five.

**Shaykh:** Twenty-five? Yes.

**Student:** Twenty-five prophets.

**Shaykh:** Twenty-five messengers, or not? ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and each We guided. And Noah We had guided before, and among his descendants David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron. Thus do We reward the doers of good. And Zechariah, John, Jesus, and Elias, all of them were among the righteous. And Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot, and each We preferred over the worlds﴾ [al-An'am 6:84–86]. So how many is that?

**The students:** Eighteen.

**Shaykh:** Eighteen. Then who remains?

**Student:** Adam.

**Shaykh:** Adam is a prophet and not a messenger.

**Student:** Shu'ayb and Salih.

**Shaykh:** Shu'ayb and Salih, Hud, and Muhammad.

**Student:** And Idris.

**Shaykh:** Idris is present.

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** Idris is not present?

**Student:** He is not present in the verse.

**Shaykh:** He is not present in the verse? Then Idris and Dhu al-Kifl.

**Student:** And Elias.

**Shaykh:** Elias is present. He is present, we counted him. They are twenty-five. And Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

**Student:** We counted him.

**Shaykh:** Muhammad? No, we did not count him.

﴿gives wealth﴾: *ātā* with a long vowel means "gave." So it takes two objects. The first object is ﴿the wealth﴾, and the second object?

**Student:** ﴿despite loving it﴾.

**Shaykh:** No. It is ﴿the near of kin﴾ and what is conjoined to it.

As for His saying ﴿gives wealth﴾: "wealth" is every item whose benefit is permissible, without need. This is wealth. Or if you wish, say: with need as well. Every item whose benefit is permissible is wealth, whether this wealth is cash, clothing, food, real estate, or anything else.

As for His saying ﴿despite loving it﴾: this prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the subject of ﴿gives﴾. That is, while he loves it, loves it because of his need for it, or because his soul is attached to it even without need. Which one?

**Student:** The attachment of his soul to it.

**Shaykh:** Or because of need. But all of them, because you may love wealth because you need it. For example, if a person has a blanket in the winter, he loves it because he needs it. Or a car, a 1973 model.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** No, 1973, a 1973 model. Its tires have started to crack, and it only moves when it is pushed. But he needs it. This is not because of his desire for it. What made him desire it, made him love it? What is it?

**Student:** The need.

**Shaykh:** The need. Or a person who has a car of the 1985 model, one of the most luxurious cars in the world, and he has many other cars. He loves this one for what reason? Because his soul is attached to it. Right or not? Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, whenever something pleased him from his wealth, would give it in charity, and he said: Allah says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:92].[[Related by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah (1/294) from the hadith of Nafi' from him, with the wording: Ibn 'Umar, whenever his admiration for something of his wealth intensified, would draw near to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, by it.]] This matches the verse we have: ﴿and gives wealth despite loving it﴾. Allah speaks in this verse about righteousness: ﴿and gives wealth despite loving it﴾. He loves it for his need of it, or because his soul is attached to it, so he gives it to these needy people. Abu Talhah, as everyone knows, what did he do when he heard this verse? He gave his orchard in charity, which was the most valuable thing he owned, as I think, not only because it was his orchard, but because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, used to come to it and drink from its sweet water. It was near the Mosque of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. I believe that a person whose orchard the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, visits and drinks from its sweet water, how valuable does that orchard become to him? Cheap or expensive?

**The students:** Expensive.

**Shaykh:** Very expensive. That is, the Messenger coming to this orchard is something that makes the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, come to us. This is dearer to us than everything of wealth. Nevertheless, "when this verse was revealed, he went to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and said: O Messenger of Allah, it is a charity for the sake of Allah and His Messenger, so place it where Allah shows you. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to him: «Bakh, bakh! That is profitable wealth, that is profitable wealth!»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1461) and Muslim (998/42), from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: «Bakh! That is profitable wealth, that is profitable wealth.»]] The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke the truth. This is the profit. If he bought it for a million and sold it for ten million, is that a profit or not?

**The students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** But which is more profitable, this or that? This is far more profitable, by seven hundred times, by many multiples. Then he said: «I think you should give it to the nearest relatives.»

The point is: why did He stipulate ﴿despite loving it﴾? Because one who gives without loving it, everyone gives what does not matter to him...

**Student:** But there is hardship in it.

**Shaykh:** No, there is no hardship. Everyone gives. Furthermore, it also includes in His saying ﴿despite loving it﴾ that it be in a state of health and in a state of being anxious about wealth, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said regarding the best and most excellent charity: «That you give charity while you are healthy and miserly.»

**Student:** «Fearing poverty and hoping for wealth.»

**Shaykh:** «Fearing poverty and hoping for long life.» That is the correct wording. Or does it contain «wealth»?[[Related by Muslim (1032/93) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] "Hoping for long life" is the correct wording. But with «wealth» it is also reported.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1419) and Muslim (1032/92), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] But «hoping for long life» is the true locus of real miserliness: he fears poverty and assumes he will remain alive (...) the young man. But someone who has reached a hundred years of age and has millions upon millions, does he fear poverty and hope for long life?

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** No. But the young man who has only a little, he is the one who fears poverty and hopes for long life. Wealth becomes precious to him. So the main point is that love here reveals a new meaning in His saying ﴿despite loving it﴾: the attachment of his desire to wealth, his need for it, and his fear of poverty and hope for long life.

﴿despite loving it﴾ for whom? ﴿the near of kin﴾. Glory be to Allah, the Mighty. ﴿The near of kin﴾: He began with them before all the other categories. Whereas the matter is reversed among us now. You find a person, if he finds a poor man far from him, he thinks he has more right to charity than his relative, his cousin. But no. The near of kin, even if they are rich, give to them. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to one of his wives, I think Juwayriyah, when she had freed a slave woman of hers, he said: «As for you, if you had given her to your maternal uncles, it would have been greater for your reward.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2592) and Muslim (999/44), from the hadith of Kurayb, the freed slave of Ibn 'Abbas, from Maymunah bint al-Harith, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her; the wording is al-Bukhari's.]] The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, made maintaining kinship better than manumission. He made it better than manumission.

As for His saying ﴿the near of kin﴾: whom is meant by the near of kin? The kinship of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or the kinship of the giver?

**The students:** The kinship of the giver.

**Shaykh:** The kinship of the giver. Know that when a ruling is linked to an attribute, it increases in strength with the strength of that attribute. So when it is linked to kinship, whoever is closer is more deserving. And the people nearest to you and most entitled to kindness are your father and your mother.

Second: ﴿the orphans﴾. "Orphans" is the plural of "orphan" (*yatim*), and it is one whose father died before reaching puberty, male or female. As for one whose mother died, he is not an orphan. And one who has reached maturity is not an orphan. He was called an orphan from *yutm*, which means isolation. For this reason, when a poem becomes beautiful or powerful, they say: this is a *yatimah*, "the unique pearl," meaning it has no peer, standing alone. So what do we say about "the orphans"? It is the plural of "orphan," one whose father died and who has not reached maturity, whether male or female. Are they given even if they are rich? Yes, they are given even if they are rich, to console their hearts. But note that giving to a wealthy orphan is not like giving to a poor one. To a poor one I give a garment, or a piece of bread, or something similar, which benefits him. But to a wealthy orphan I do not give such a thing. What do I give him? Now we want (...) about him. What do I give him?

**The students:** Whatever suits his condition.

**Shaykh:** Whatever suits his condition. A general expression.

**Student:** A car.

**Shaykh:** No, a car. A car is large. I could give him a pen, perhaps I could give him a watch for example, perhaps I could give him something to make him happy. But to an orphan I give a car? (..) fourteen (...). He does not even have a driver's license. In any case, one gives what suits him.

﴿and the needy﴾. "The needy" (*al-masakin*) is the plural of "miskin," and it is the poor person, the one whom poverty has made still (*askanahu*). He was called *miskin* because poverty stilled him. And poverty, may Allah protect us and you from it, does not make a person speak with fluency. This is generally the case, because he sees himself as not being at the level that would enable him to speak, and he sees himself as having no word. As the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Many a disheveled, dusty person, turned away at doors, if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfill it.»[[Related by Muslim (2622/138) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] So the main point is that the *miskin* is the poor person, and he was named so because poverty stilled him and humbled him. Know that "the poor" (*faqir*) means "the needy" (*miskin*), and "the needy" means "the poor," except when both are mentioned together. When both are mentioned together, each one has a meaning different from the other. As in the verse on charity: ﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:60]. Which of them is worse off?

**Student:** The poor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 177–179 (part 4 of 6):

* The Shaykh: The correct view is that the one in greater need is the *faqir* (the poor person), because Allah began with him, and in the matter of giving one begins with the most entitled and the most needy. Some scholars said that the *miskin* (the destitute) is in greater need, because poverty has made him *iskan* (still), unlike the *faqir*. The correct view is that the *faqir* is in greater need, because it matches *qafr* (desolation): *faqr* and *qafr*. What does *qafr* mean?
* A student: Drought.
* The Shaykh: *Qafr* means emptiness. *Ard qafr* means an empty land.
*Wa qabru Harbin bi-makanin qafrin* ∗∗∗ *wa laysa qurba qabri Harbin qabru*
(And the grave of Harb is in a desolate place, / and no grave is near the grave of Harb.)
This has a clash of words (*tanafur*).
*Wa al-masakin wa ibn al-sabil* (...). *Al-sabil* means the road, and *ibn al-sabil* (the wayfarer, lit. "son of the road") refers to one who keeps to the road, that is, the traveller. The traveller is usually in need, so he needs someone to support him and give him money. For this reason Allah assigned him a share, from what? From the *zakat* (obligatory almsgiving). *Ibn al-sabil* is the traveller, but the scholars added a condition. They said: the traveller who has been cut off, meaning one whose journey has been cut off, so he has nothing with which to reach his homeland. For if he has what will take him home, he is not in need, and he is on the same footing as a resident. His need is therefore only established when his journey has been cut off.
He says: *Wa al-sa'ilin*. *Al-sa'ilin* is the plural of *sa'il*. Does *sa'il* mean one who asks for information or one who begs?
* The students: One who begs.
* The Shaykh: How, one who begs?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: (...) What is the difference between one who asks for information and one who begs?
* The students: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: The one who asks for information says: "Where is the money?" The one who begs says: "Give me money." So the intended meaning in the verse is the beggars, i.e., those who beg and say: "Give us." The beggar has a right, not on his own account, because he may ask while not being in need, but because of the quality of generosity and modesty, on the part of the giver. When a person is asked and has generosity, he cannot say no. When a person is asked and has modesty, and modesty is part of faith, he cannot say no. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not be asked for anything for the sake of Islam without giving it. A man asked him one day, and he gave him sheep between two mountains.[[Recorded by Muslim (2312/57), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him).]] A cloak was given as a gift to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he was in need of it. A man asked for it, and he gave it to him. It was said to the man: "Why did you do that when the Prophet (ﷺ) needed it?" He said: "I want it to be my shroud." And it became his shroud.[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (1277), from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: A woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a woven *burda* (a cloak) that had a border. Do you know what a *burda* is? They said: a *shamla* (a wrap). He said: Yes. She said: I wove it with my own hand and came to clothe you with it. The Prophet (ﷺ) took it because he needed it, and came out to us wearing it as his waist-wrap. A man admired it and said: "Give it to me, how fine it is!" The people said: "You have not done well. The Prophet (ﷺ) took it because he needed it, then you asked him for it, and you knew he would not refuse." He said: "By Allah, I did not ask him for it to wear. I asked him for it so that it would be my shroud." Sahl said: "And it became his shroud."]] So the Prophet (ﷺ), because of his generosity and modesty, would not be asked for anything without giving it. The beggar has a right. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), but it is not authentic: "The beggar has a right, even if he comes on a horse."[[Recorded by Abu Dawud (1665), from the hadith of al-Husayn ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him).]] However, this hadith is not authentically traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).
Know that asking for money is in principle prohibited and forbidden. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) warned against asking for money and informed us that "a man will keep on asking people until he comes on the Day of Resurrection with no flesh on his face."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (1474) and Muslim (1040/104), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), with the wording: "A man will not cease to ask people..." the hadith.]] He will come with his face stripped, may Allah protect us. Since he debased his face before the servants of Allah, he is punished with this severe punishment in this great gathering. The Prophet (ﷺ) took the pledge from his companions, and among what he took the pledge on was: "That they would not ask people for anything." So one of them would drop his whip from his camel, get down and pick it up, and would not say to his brother: "Give me my whip."[[Recorded by Muslim (1043/108), from the hadith of 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "And do not ask people for anything. I saw some of those men whose whip would fall, and they would not ask anyone to hand it to them."]]
There is no doubt that refraining from asking carries self-restraint, dignity and honour. Asking, however, carries humiliation before the creature. A person who asks, no doubt, however generous, modest and bountiful the one asked may be, his standing falls in the eyes of the one asked and he is lowered in his esteem. For this reason asking is not permitted except in pressing need, the need that cannot be avoided, when a person asks. It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever asks people for their wealth in order to increase it, is only asking for live coals. So let him ask for little or let him ask for much."[[Recorded by Muslim (1041/105), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]
Then know that asking is of two kinds: asking by the tongue of speech and asking by the tongue of state. As for asking by the tongue of speech, it is obvious: a person comes to you and says: "Give me such and such." As for asking by the tongue of state, it is that you see a person who is chaste and does not ask, but you know his need, or you find him, for example, hanging about in front of you and circling around you. This person has not asked with the tongue of speech, but he has asked with the tongue of state.
If someone says: If giving wealth to the beggars is from the people of righteousness, and you have warned against asking, against people asking, how does this agree with that?
The answer: there is no contradiction, because the aspect is separate. The one praised is the giver, and the one warned against is the asker who receives. When the aspect is separate, there is no contradiction. So if you see someone afflicted with this trade, which is the trade of asking people, then give to him when he asks you, then advise him and warn him. Thus you are giving wealth because of the request and advising the asker. You give wealth because of the request, and you advise the asker, because some people, may Allah protect us, you know with certainty, or your strong assumption is, that he is wealthy and only asks people for their money in order to increase it. If you give him, you will certainly encourage him, and he will go and ask others. But give to him so that you are among those who give wealth to the beggars, and advise him so that you are among the advisers.
As for His words: *Wa fi al-riqab* (and for the freeing of slaves). Notice that He did not say "and gave to the slaves," but He said *wa fi al-riqab*, because the wealth spent on the necks is not given to the neck itself. To whom is it given? It is given to the owner of the neck. That is why He used *fi*, which indicates location.
Know that the scholars mentioned that *riqab* (necks) are of three kinds: a slave owned by another whom you buy and free; a *mukatab* (a slave who has contracted to buy his own freedom from his master), whom you help in paying his contract; and a Muslim captive among the disbelievers, whom you ransom. Likewise, if he is captured by people other than disbelievers, such as those who kidnap nowadays, may Allah protect us, if the kidnappers demand a ransom and say: "We will not release him except for this," then he is ransomed from the *zakat*, because there is in it the freeing of a neck, the freeing of a neck from being killed.
* A student: The killer?
* The Shaykh: No, the killer is not included.
His words: *wa fi al-riqab*, up to His words: *wa aqama al-salah*.
We return once more to *ata al-mal 'ala hubbihi* (gives wealth out of love for it). If he gives wealth not out of love for it, would he be righteous? That is: a wealthy person gives charity and does not mind losing a hundred thousand or a hundred riyals. Is he from the righteous or not?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, but he is not like the first. He is incomplete in righteousness. Complete righteousness is that a person gives wealth out of love for it: *Lan tanalu al-birra hatta tunfiqu mimma tuhibbun* ("You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love." [Al 'Imran 92]). The apparent meaning of the verse is that complete righteousness is not attained except by this, when one gives wealth out of love for it.
If someone says: The phrase *ala hubbihi* (out of love for it) has no meaning, because all wealth is loved by a person, due to His saying: *Wa innahu li-hubbi al-khayri lashadid* ("And indeed he is intensely devoted to wealth" [al-'Adiyat 8]), and *Wa tuhibbuna al-mala hubban jamma* ("And you love wealth with immense love" [al-Fajr 20])?
We say, in answer: the love of wealth in general is in every soul. But what is meant here is: he gives a specific wealth out of love for that specific wealth. Do you understand? *Ata al-mala 'ala hubbihi*: that specific wealth, not all wealth being loved by a person. But, for example, I have ten notes of one hundred. Which of them do I love more?
* The students: They are all the same.
* The Shaykh: They are all the same, but is their totality beloved to me or not?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Beloved to me, no doubt. But I have goods that are not cash. For example, I have a recorder of this type, a watch of this type, and a car of this type that I love. Is this a special love or not? This is a special love, other than the general love of wealth. This is what is meant by this noble verse and by His words: "You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love." That is why Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), when something of his wealth pleased him, would give it in charity.
Once more, back to the verse: *Dhawi al-qurba wa al-yatama wa al-masakin wa ibn al-sabil wa al-sa'ilin wa fi al-riqab.*
The apparent meaning of the verse is unrestricted, and the ruling is linked to the attribute. So a relative, even if a disbeliever, if you give him wealth, you are praised for that. Likewise the orphan, the destitute, the wayfarer, the beggar, and those in bondage. The apparent meaning of the verse is general, because it has no restriction. In reality, however, it is not on its general terms, but it is specific to the Muslim and to the non-combatant disbeliever, due to His saying: "Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being righteous to them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly" [al-Mumtahanah 8]. Scholars have differed over whether this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*) or established (*muhkamah*). The correct view is that it is established, and that the default is no abrogation. However, on the condition that they are not fighting us, whether they fight us in person, by the man himself being a fighter, or fight us in their ruling, meaning that they fight us in ruling. For example, if they are from a state that fights the Muslims, because someone from a state that fights the Muslims is ready to fight in ruling. Isn't that so?
* The students: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: If his state orders him to fight, does he respond or not?
* The students: He responds.
* The Shaykh: He responds. On this basis, if the disbeliever is from a state at war with the Muslims, it is not permitted to be righteous to him or to give him wealth. For as long as he is at war with the Muslims, the Muslim wants to destroy him just as he wants to destroy and kill the Muslim. This is a requital in kind and this is justice.
One word remains for us: *fi al-riqab*. We mentioned that there are three kinds: the *mukatab*, the owned slave, and the captive. But the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, restricted the captive to the Muslim. As for a non-Muslim, one does not praise the one who frees his captivity, because the authority of a Muslim is stronger than the authority of a non-Muslim. It is possible to say that the scholars' restriction of this to a Muslim applies to *zakat*, because *zakat* is not given to a non-Muslim, unlike voluntary charity, in which it is permissible to free from it a captive who is a *dhimmi* (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection). Suppose there is a captive *dhimmi*, and that if he does not benefit the Muslims, he does not harm them. Then there is no harm in freeing him.
Then Allah the Exalted said: *Wa aqama al-salah* (and established prayer). *Aqama al-salah* is connected to what?
* The students: *Man amana* (whoever believed).
* The Shaykh: To *man amana*?
* The students: Yes indeed. So *wa aqama* is connected to *amana*, which is the relative clause's predicate.
*Wa aqama al-salah*: *Al-salah* here means both the obligatory and the voluntary prayer. Establishing it means performing it upright, in the sense that one makes a thing stand upright and straight. It does not mean the *iqamah* (the second call to prayer) with "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar" that is well known. What is meant by it is: performing the prayer correctly, as you say: I straightened the wall, I straightened the staff, I straightened so-and-so: I made him stand until he was straight.
As for His words, *al-salah*, the "al" here: is it for specific reference or for generality?
* The students: For generality.
* The Shaykh: For generality, because it includes the obligatory and the voluntary. Know that *salah* is one of the words that the Lawgiver transferred from its linguistic meaning to a technical meaning. Its linguistic meaning is supplication. Allah the Exalted said: *Wa salli 'alayhim* ("And pray for them" [al-Tawbah 103]), meaning: supplicate for them. So say: "May Allah bless you." This is the meaning of *salli 'alayhim*. But in the Sharia it is the well-known prayer: an act of worship with known statements and actions, opened with *takbir* (saying Allahu akbar) and closed with *taslim* (the salam). We must say: an act of worship with statements, though many of those who define it say: it is known statements and actions, opened with the *takbir* and closed with the *taslim*. This is certainly deficient. Rather, we must say: an act of worship. That is why, if a person comes playing around, says the takbir, recites, bows, prostrates and gives the salam, does he become a worshipper in the Sharia sense?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: He is not a worshipper. Rather, it must be an act of worship opened with the takbir and closed with the taslim.
*Wa aqama al-salah wa ata al-zakah* (and paid zakat). *Ata* means "gave." The *zakah* is also one of the words that the Lawgiver transferred from its linguistic meaning to a technical meaning. In language, *zakah* comes from *zaka yazku*, meaning it grew and increased, and also it became good and sound. Zakah in language also means soundness, and from it is His saying: "He has succeeded who purifies it" [al-Shams 9], meaning: he who sets it right and straightens it.
But in the Sharia, *zakah* is: worship through giving up a mandatory amount of wealth from a specific kind of property to a specific category of people. This is zakat, and it was called *zakah* because it develops character, develops wealth and develops reward. How does it develop character?
* A student: A person becomes generous.
* The Shaykh: Yes, through it a person becomes generous, one of the people of giving, bounty and kindness. No doubt this is one of the best characters in the Sharia and in custom. It develops wealth. How does it develop wealth? I have one hundred riyals; I took two and a half riyals from them. Ninety-seven and a half remain with me. Wealth has decreased. How does it develop?
* The students: Through blessing.
* The Shaykh: We say: Yes, it develops through blessing, protection and preservation. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity has never decreased wealth."[[Recorded by Muslim (2588/69), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]] It cannot diminish it. That is, if you do not give out this amount of wealth, perhaps calamities will come to it. You buy and sell and lose. Perhaps you or your family will be struck by illnesses that need treatment, and everything you have will be consumed. Perhaps a thief will come and steal it. Perhaps you will deposit it with someone who will deny it. Isn't that so?
* The students: Indeed.
* The Shaykh: But zakat is a protection for it, a preservation and a blessing. From the blessing of wealth, you buy a garment for ten riyals. If you do not pay zakat, it may tear quickly, but if you pay zakat, Allah sends blessing upon it, and it lasts two or three years, depending on the circumstances.
* A student: I have a garment that is four years old, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: We will not say anything. That is from the blessing. The point is that the kinds of blessing that come upon wealth are many. That is why we said: zakat purifies wealth. Does it purify reward or not?
* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Does it purify the reward? Yes. ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain of corn that grows seven ears, and in every ear is a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies [His reward] for whom He wills.﴾ And beyond that, ﴿Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:261]. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed us, and it is authentically related from him: "Whoever gives in charity the equivalent of a date from good earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, Allah, the Exalted, takes it in His right hand and nurtures it for him just as one of you nurtures his foal, until it becomes like a mountain."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1410) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Whoever gives in charity the equivalent of a date from good earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, Allah receives it with His right hand, then nurtures it for its giver just as one of you nurtures his foal, until it becomes like a mountain."]] So the equivalent of a date becomes like a mountain. Is this not purification?

* Students: Indeed.

* The Shaykh: Indeed, by Allah, it is purification. This is true purification. Is there anything purer than this? When you give a person your money to trade with, how much profit does he make? Let him earn ten, a hundred, or let him lose. But this charity falls into the right hand of the Most Merciful, the Mighty and Majestic, and what a right hand it is, the right hand of the Lord. He nurtures it, the Glorified and Exalted, and increases it for you until it becomes like a mountain. This is the great profit. ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan so that He may multiply it for him many times over? And Allah withholds and extends [provision].﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:245]. Thus it is called zakah, because it purifies wealth, character and reward.

﴿And establishes prayer and gives zakah.﴾ Here we have (ātā, "gave"), which takes two objects. Where is its first object?

* Students: Zakah.

* The Shaykh: Zakah. Where is the second object?

* Students: It is omitted.

* The Shaykh: It is omitted. And what is the implied term?

* A student: "Its deserving recipients" (mustahiqqahā).

* The Shaykh: Its deserving recipients, excellent, its deserving recipients. Look at ﴿gave wealth, despite loving it, to relatives﴾, where the second object is stated: ﴿relatives﴾. Here, ﴿gives zakah﴾ does not state the second object, but it is known and implied. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has taken charge of its distribution to its recipients, saying: ﴿Charity is only for the poor, the needy, those who work to collect it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, to free captives, to those in debt, for the cause of Allah, and for the traveller﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:60]. These eight categories alone are entitled to it, and it is not lawful for anyone else.

﴿And those who keep their promises when they make them﴾. Here He did not say "and he fulfilled his covenant", but used a nominal sentence, because fulfilling covenants is an innate disposition and a character trait. But did the previous items not consist of actions a person performs? Yet this is an innate disposition and a character trait, that a person be faithful, faithful to the covenant when he makes one. ﴿When they make a covenant﴾: here (idhā, "when") is stripped of its conditional sense and is purely temporal. That is, ﴿those who keep their promises﴾ at the time of the covenant, meaning in the state in which they make it. So when they make a covenant, they fulfil it.

Know that covenants are of two kinds: a covenant with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and a covenant with the creatures. So what is the covenant with Allah?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, it is believing in Him. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." [This was] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ [al-A'raf 7:172]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:40]. So the covenant Allah has made with us is that we believe in Him as Lord, and are content with His legislation, and indeed with His decrees, both cosmic and legislative. This is the covenant between us and our Lord.

As for the covenant between you and people: its types are many, numerous indeed. Among them are contracts. Contracts are among the covenants. That is, any contract between you and someone, a contract of sale, a contract of hire, a contract of pledge, any contract at all, is considered a covenant, because...

* A student: The marriage contract, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: And the marriage contract. Because when I contract with you, and what is meant by "I contracted with you"? I have bound myself to what this contract requires. Thus every contract is a covenant. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:1], and He said: ﴿And fulfil the covenant, for the covenant will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra' 17:34].

Among the covenants between you and the creatures is the well-known covenant, which is that you conclude an agreement between you and the disbelievers, for example, that neither side transgresses against the other, like what took place between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists in...?

* Students: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

* The Shaykh: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah is called a covenant. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:4], and ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant at al-Masjid al-Haram. So as long as they are upright towards you, be upright towards them. Indeed, Allah loves those who are mindful of Him﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:7]. This covenant between us and the enemies of Allah and our enemies has three situations: either they remain upright towards us, or they betray, or we fear treachery from them. If they remain upright towards us, it is obligatory for us to remain upright towards them, and we must never betray them in any way. If we fear treachery from them, we must throw back to them [the covenant] on equal terms: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their covenant] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal 8:58].

* A student: Shaykh, do we fight them?

* The Shaykh: No. You say: (...) covenant. You inform them that there is no covenant between us, so that they may be aware.

As for those who betray, what do we do with them? We fight them, because they are the ones who broke the covenant, just as the Quraysh did in the covenant concluded between them and the Messenger (ﷺ) at Hudaybiyyah, since they broke it by aiding their allies against the allies of the Prophet (ﷺ). That is, they, the Quraysh, betrayed by aiding their allies against the allies of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is undoubtedly a breach of the covenant, because the allies of the Messenger means that the Messenger stands with them against whoever opposes them. So when they broke the covenant, the Prophet (ﷺ) fought them. Among the covenants is also what occurs between a person and others in obligations other than contracts and covenants, such as a promise. A promise is indeed part of the covenant. For this reason the scholars differed: is it obligatory to fulfil a promise or not? The correct view, chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, is that fulfilling a promise is obligatory, because it falls under the covenant. When I say, "I will come to you tomorrow at such-and-such a time," this means I have bound myself to that, so fulfilling the promise is obligatory. Also, breaking a promise is one of the signs of hypocrisy. If that is so, can we say that it is permissible for the believer to adopt the characteristics of the hypocrites? If we say no, then fulfilling a promise becomes obligatory. The question now is: are we actually doing this?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: What? We ask Allah for pardon.

* A student: Not at all.

* The Shaykh: Not at all, at no time and by no one. Rather, it is regrettable that it is well known among people that Muslims are the least faithful to their promises. Some of the deceived, may Allah protect us, when they want to emphasise a promise, say: "Look, it's an English promise." Look, I seek refuge in Allah. That is, the English never break a promise even for a minute. The correct thing to say is: "It's a believer's promise, not an English one." The Englishman only took these characteristics from the believers, and otherwise he is a disbeliever. We do not mean all the English, meaning the disbelievers among them. But unfortunately, among us, breaking a promise is a trivial matter, and being late is generally the norm, except what Allah wills. He promises you at twelve o'clock and comes at half past twelve, my brother (...). He says, "It was only half an hour." This is wrong. Try to arrive at the appointed time, because some business may have come up or something similar. And Allah knows best.

(...) ﴿in adversity and affliction and at the time of battle﴾.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿the patient﴾. There is a difficulty here from the standpoint of i'rab (grammatical parsing), because the preceding words are in the nominative case, and this one is not. Why is that?

* A student: For specification (ikhtisas).

* The Shaykh: What is the implied construction?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Some scholars say it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose meaning is: "And I specify the patient." Then we ask: why was it diverted from coordination, unlike the preceding items? We say the wisdom or eloquence behind this is that when the style of speech changes, this draws attention. When a person reads speech in one uniform pattern, he becomes heedless and drowsy, as if he were passing over something without noticing it. But when the style changes, it compels attention. This is similar to what we have often mentioned, namely iltifat (shift of discourse), because by changing the style, the addressee or reader is obliged to pay attention.

Furthermore, ﴿the patient in adversity﴾: patience is in reality not giving something up, but enduring something. Everything that preceded is an act of giving, and differs in kind. Look at: believing, establishing prayer, giving wealth, fulfilling the covenant. All of these are actions. But ﴿the patient﴾ is not an action in which a person gives something; rather he endures.

As for the word ﴿the patient﴾: patience (ṣabr) linguistically means restraint. From it comes the expression "so-and-so was killed ṣabran," that is, restrained (confined). In the Shariah, it means restraining the self upon obedience to Allah, or restraining it from disobedience, or upon His decrees. Do you understand? So patience is of three kinds: patience in obedience, patience in refraining from sin, and patience upon painful decrees. Is that not so?

* Students: Indeed.

* The Shaykh: Which of them is best? The best of them is patience in obedience. It is the most excellent, because it involves striving and action, for a person strives against his self to be patient in obedience, persevering in it and acting. Next comes patience in refraining from sin, because it is restraint, restraint of the self, and does not involve bringing something into being. Although at times patience in refraining from sin is more difficult than patience in obedience (...) it slips from a person. Why? Because it is a decreed matter that occurs by compulsion upon you, whether you are content or not. But restraining your self from wickedness is by your choice: if you wish, you restrain it, and if you wish, you do not. Patience of the self in obedience is likewise by your choice. So the best is patience in obedience, then patience in refraining from sin, then patience upon decrees. For this reason the scholars said: the patience of Yusuf in refraining from indecency with the wife of the ruler is stronger than his patience in what befell him from his brothers, or is it not? What befell him from his brothers was that they threw him into the bottom of a well, and what happened to him happened.

﴿the patient in adversity and affliction and at the time of battle﴾. Ba'sa' (adversity): severe poverty, and from it comes bu's, meaning poverty. Ḍarrā' (affliction): sickness. Ḥīn al-ba's (the time of battle): the intensity of fighting. They are patient in matters where they have capacity, and in matters where they have no capacity.

﴿in adversity﴾, that is, in the state of poverty: their poverty does not drive them to covet people's wealth. Rather, they are patient in refraining from sin. They do not steal, betray, lie or cheat. This is patience in refraining from what?

* A student: From sin.

* The Shaykh: From sin. And affliction, sickness and whatever harms their bodies, does not drive them to become resentful of Allah's decree and destiny. Rather, they always say with their tongues and hearts: "We are content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Messenger."

* A student: Is this (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

Likewise ﴿at the time of battle﴾, the time of severe fighting: they remain patient and do not turn their backs. This is patience in what? In obedience. Patience in obedience. Thus this verse encompasses the three kinds of patience: patience in refraining from sin, patience upon painful decrees, and what else? And patience in obedience.

﴿the patient in adversity and affliction and at the time of battle﴾. It has already been mentioned that the one afflicted by painful decrees has four stages. Which of you can mention them? Whoever is struck by something that harms and pains him has four stations, or four levels?

* A student: First: he rejoices, just rejoices (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

* The student: He is content.

* The Shaykh: Good.

* The student: Second: he is patient, that is...

* The Shaykh: He is patient. Leave "that is", leave the explanation for later. And third?

* The student: And third...

* The Shaykh: Yes?

* A student: He is grateful.

* The Shaykh: Third: he is grateful. And fourth?

* A student: He is patient.

* The Shaykh: Mention it.

* The student: He is distressed.

* The Shaykh: He is distressed and resentful. The one afflicted by decrees has four states or four stations. First: that he is resentful and does not endure. He is resentful. The second: that he endures. The third: that he is content. The fourth: that he is grateful. Four stations. Resentment is forbidden, patience is obligatory, contentment is disputed, and the correct view is that it is recommended, and gratitude is recommended.

What is the difference between contentment and patience? Patience: he dislikes this thing and feels pain from it, and finds it bitter, but he endures, does not express resentment by his tongue, his action or his heart. Do you understand? But he dislikes it. Contentment: he does not dislike this thing. Rather, there is no difference between being afflicted by this harm or not being afflicted; he is accepting, content and at peace. There is no doubt that this is higher than patience, or not? Is it not higher than patience? Because it includes patience and more.

As for gratitude, it is higher than that too. But it may be asked: how can one be grateful when one has been afflicted? We say: yes, he is grateful even though he has been afflicted, because when he sees the fruit of this affliction through being content with it, he thanks Allah for this blessing. Furthermore, he thanks Allah also because he sees that he might have been afflicted with something greater. Is the affliction you have suffered not the lightest affliction in this world, or not? That is why the common people say: "Measure your affliction against something greater, and its ease will become clear to you." Is this correct?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: ﴿the patient in adversity and affliction and at the time of battle﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones who have been truthful﴾. Masha' Allah. This is a testimony from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, a testimony and the highest of testimonies, because it is a testimony from the greatest of witnesses, the Glorified and Exalted. ﴿Those﴾ refers to everyone who has these characteristics. ﴿Who have been truthful﴾: truthful in what?

* A student: In Allah.

* The Shaykh: They were truthful to Allah and truthful to His servants by their fulfilment of covenants, giving zakah, and other things. So they were truthful, they were truthful to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Truthfulness, as you know, is the correspondence of a thing to reality. Thus the one who reports something is truthful when his report corresponds to reality, and the worker who performs an act of obedience, if it proceeds from sincerity, his action is truthful, because it reveals what is in his heart truthfully. The hypocrite is a liar, and the hypocrite who shows off in his deeds is a liar, because his deeds do not reveal what is in his heart. Its outward appearance is sincerity, while he is not sincere but the opposite. These are the ones who have been truthful: they were truthful in what they concealed in their hearts, in what they uttered with their tongues, and in what they carried out with their limbs. Truthfulness, the highest truthfulness. Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Ahzab: ﴿That Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:24]...

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿That He may question the truthful﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:8]. This is ﴿That Allah may reward the truthful for their truthfulness﴾. And He said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and be with the truthful﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:119]. And this truthfulness is in what they manifested and proclaimed.

Then He said: ﴿And those are the mindful﴾, that is, those who establish mindfulness. Taqwa (mindfulness of Allah) is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is the most comprehensive of the definitions of taqwa: taking a shield against Allah's punishment by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Reflect on how this sentence came as a emphatic nominal sentence: ﴿Those are the mindful﴾. The sentence is nominal in indicating what?

* Students: Permanence.

* The Shaykh: Permanence and continuity, because a nominal sentence indicates that the attribute is constant for the one who possesses it. And this sentence is emphasised by what?

* A student: By "they" (hum).

**Shaykh:** With the separating pronoun (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*, the pronoun that separates the predicate from the qualifier), *hum* ("they"). The separating pronoun has three benefits: one that relates to grammatical inflection (*i'rāb*), and two that relate to meaning. What is the verbal benefit that relates to *i'rāb*?

**Student:** That it is emphatic.

**Shaykh:** No, that is a benefit of meaning.

**Student:** (...) a predicate, indicating that it...

**Shaykh:** That it separates the predicate from the attribute.

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** It separates the predicate from the attribute, and shows that what follows it is a predicate, not an attribute. The two benefits of meaning are: first, it conveys emphasis (*tawkīd*), that is one. Second, it conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*), which is affirming the ruling for what is mentioned and negating it for anything else. Let us give an example. If you say: "Zayd al-Fāḍil" (Zayd the virtuous), in this context must the word *al-Fāḍil* be a predicate?

**Students:** No.

**Shaykh:** No, because the meaning could be: "Zayd the virtuous, the best of people," for example. Is that not so?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** So *al-Fāḍil* here can be an attribute, not a predicate. But if you say: "Huwa al-Fāḍil" (He is the virtuous one), "Zayd huwa al-Fāḍil" (Zayd is the virtuous one), is it not more emphatic than your saying "Zayd al-Fāḍil," or not? It is more emphatic in affirming virtue for him. If you say "Zayd huwa al-Fāḍil," it indicates that no one else shares this attribute with him, because you are saying "he, he and no other, is the virtuous one." These are the benefits of the separating pronoun.
