Neither Allah the Exalted nor His Messenger specified a distance or a duration for this journey, neither a distance nor a duration. Whoever wishes to clarify this should refer back: the Qur'an does not state that the journey is defined by a distance a person covers. There were no surveyors at the time of the Messenger ﷺ who measured the land down to the cubit, the span, the fingertip, the grain of barley, or the hair of a horse's mane. For those who define it by distance go down to the hair of a horse's mane, meaning: with this grain of sand one differentiates between the traveller and the non-traveller; whoever is short of the grain is not a traveller, and whoever is beyond it is a traveller. Shaykh al-Islam says this is not reported; nothing of this was transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and there were no surveyors who knew this measurement by this distance, and this is correct. Likewise, the journey was not restricted by a time period. For this reason the opinions of the scholars on this question have varied into about ten views: is the journey defined by a time, or by a distance, or by custom?

Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) has a well-known principle: every matter that the Lawgiver stated without defining its limit is referred back to custom ('urf). What people customarily regard as travel, so that it is said "so-and-so has travelled," such as one who prepares provisions and riding supplies and makes ready for it, is a journey; what is not so regarded is not. He mentioned among such matters the journey. Some scholars said: if one leaves a distance of three miles, regardless of whether it is called a journey, one shortens the prayer. Others said: if one leaves a distance of three farsakh, based on the hadith of Anas ibn Malik: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he went out three miles or farsakh (the doubt is from Shu'bah), would pray two rak'ahs."[[Reported by Muslim (691/12), from the hadith of Anas.]] So on this view one says: since the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, would pray two rak'ahs when he left this distance, we adopt it. But Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said: this is a report of an event that occurred; we do not know what would be the case if one left a lesser or greater distance. A greater distance certainly requires shortening, a fortiori. As for a lesser distance: if you reflect on the wording of the hadith, you find that it implies no shortening for less, because it says "if he went out three," "if he went out," so its implication is that if one goes out less, there is no shortening. We say: the minimum is three miles or farsakh; which is more cautious? Three farsakh. However, the majority of scholars hold it to be sixteen farsakh; they hold that the duration of the distance for shortening is sixteen farsakh, so whatever reaches it is shortening and whatever is less is not shortening. Based on this we say: since the matter has no clear legal limit, when one leaves this distance in which the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, would pray two rak'ahs, one shortens. What is less is a matter of doubt, and the basic principle is—what is the basic principle? Completion. The basic principle is completion, so one completes. Whoever leaves beyond three farsakh shortens, except that it is not counted as a journey. For example, a man who goes out a distance of three farsakh and returns the same day is not regarded as a traveller, even by custom, so the rulings of travel do not apply to him. But if a man goes out three farsakh and stays for a period in that place, he is regarded as a traveller. So the journey is now either defined by a distance or by time, according to custom.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾. The expression differs: in the case of the sick it says ﴿مَنْ كَانَ مِنْكُمْ مَرِيضًا﴾ (whoever among you is sick), while for the journey it says ﴿أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾ (or on a journey). What is the wisdom? It may be said—and Allah knows best—that the traveller may be in a state resembling residence, a state resembling residence, such as if he stays in a town at ease, reassured, and shaded. In reality he is not like a traveller, but he is on a journey. His intention is not to settle, like what happened to the Messenger ﷺ during the Conquest, when he stayed in Makkah for nineteen days, shortening the prayer, and he broke his fast until the month ended, as in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in al-Bukhari.[[Reported by al-Bukhari (1080), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] The Messenger ﷺ here, being in a town, what is considered? He is as if resident; he and the residents are on equal footing. Yet in reality he is on a journey, since his intention is not to settle; his intention is to remain in this place for a period according to his need, then return. So here we say: he is on a journey. This is one benefit. Another benefit, according to the view of some scholars: one who is preparing for a journey is like one who has departed on it. For example, a person who has resolved to set out after noon in Ramadan, who is readying his belongings, carrying his goods, and the like—they say: even if he is in his own town, it is permissible for him to break the fast. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) used to do so and would say: "It is from the Sunnah."[[Reported by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (4/247), from the hadith of Anas.]] However, this hadith has some criticism directed at it. Yet according to those who affirm it, one says: when a person resolves to travel, he becomes one who breaks the fast, and they said this is better than that he fasts and then breaks it when he departs, since he has not entered into the act of worship at all. But the majority of scholars, including the four Imams, hold contrary to this view: that he is not entitled to break the fast unless he actually departs, with a difference among them as well over whether one who travels during the day while fasting may break the fast. The correct view is that he may break it, because the Sunnah indicates this.
* A student: Does he break the fast if he is preparing?
* The Shaykh: No, I do not hold this, I do not hold this; because the hadith is subject to criticism, and in my own mind I have some reservation about it. The basic principle is the obligation of fasting. Praise be to Allah, if he sets out, since he is permitted to break the fast once he has departed, he departs fasting, and if he wishes he breaks it.
* A student: It is possible for the journey to be delayed due to an external cause.
* The Shaykh: It may be delayed, especially in our time now, because now a person is tied to others (...) journeys. In the past a man would load his camel and set off; but now, especially with aircraft, one is bound to others.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿فَعِدَّةٌ مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ (then a number of other days). It is known that the majority of scholars, apart from the Zahiriyyah (literalists), say that the verse has an implied omission, which is: "so he breaks the fast, and upon him is a number [of days]." The Zahiriyyah said: there is no omission, because the basic principle is its absence; when speech is between omission and non-omission, the basic principle is non-omission. On this view, ﴿فَمَنْ كَانَ مِنْكُمْ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾ (so whoever among you is sick or on a journey), then his obligation is ﴿عِدَّةٌ مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ (a number of other days). So if he fasts, it does not suffice him, because Allah only obligated upon him a number of ﴿أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ (other days). ﴿أُخَرَ﴾ means different from these days; so if he fasts, it does not suffice him. This view, were it not for the existence of the Sunnah, would be strong because of the strength of its reasoning. But the Sunnah has clarified that the verse must include an omission: "so he breaks the fast." That is because it is established that the Companions, with the Prophet ﷺ, included those who fasted and those who broke the fast; the fasting person did not reproach the one who broke the fast, nor did the one who broke it reproach the fasting person. Had fasting been unlawful, the Companions would not have done it in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. Indeed, the Prophet ﷺ himself used to fast in Ramadan, as in the hadith of Abu al-Darda: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ in Ramadan in the intense heat, and the one most shaded among us was the owner of the cloak; some of us would shield the sun with his hand; and none of us was fasting except the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah."[[Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (1945) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda, and Muslim (1119/100) from the hadith of Anas with nearly this wording.]]
* A student: During a journey?
* The Shaykh: During a journey, during a journey. This is evidence for the permissibility of fasting while travelling. Furthermore, "the Messenger ﷺ also fasted until people came to him and said: O Messenger of Allah, the people find fasting burdensome, and they are waiting to see what you will do. He then called for a vessel of water after the 'Asr prayer, drank it while on his camel, and the people were watching him."[[Reported by Muslim (1114/90-91), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]] He broke the fast during the day. This is evidence for what? For the permissibility of fasting while travelling; and breaking the fast is the truth, and it is not obligatory—praise be to Allah.
* A student: The permissibility of this, O Shaykh, the permissibility of breaking the fast during the day.
* The Shaykh: (...) the permissibility of breaking the fast during the day.

As for his words: ﴿فَعِدَّةٌ مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾, look: ﴿أَيَّامٍ﴾ is not qualified as "the other days" (al-ayyam al-ukhar); ﴿أَيَّامٍ﴾ is indefinite (nakirah). From this we derive that if he fasts, making up days of summer with days of winter, it suffices. Is that correct? Yes, it suffices, because ﴿أَيَّامٍ﴾ is indefinite and ﴿أُخَرَ﴾ means "different." ﴿مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾. In the benefits, God willing, we will touch on the point that what is obligatory is the days, not the whole month.

﴿وَعَلَى الَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ﴾ (and upon those who are able to fast, a ransom: feeding a poor person). ﴿وَعَلَى الَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾: when He made fasting obligatory, He said: ﴿وَعَلَى الَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 184]. It is as if this sentence is an elaboration of His words ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ﴾ (fasting has been prescribed for you): that for the one who is able, fasting is either to be ransomed or to be fasted, and fasting is better for him.

As for ﴿وَعَلَى الَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾: "ṭāqah" means capability, that is, they are able to do it. This is the correct view, as will come God willing. Some scholars said ﴿يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾ means: it reaches their capacity to the point that it becomes burdensome for them, so the meaning of "yuṭīqūnahu" is "yutawwaqūnahu," that is, they force it upon themselves and it is hard for them. Others said: there is an omission in the verse, and the meaning is: "and upon those who are unable to do it, a ransom; and upon those who cannot bear it." This view is the weakest of them, because it requires explaining an affirmative by its negation: Allah says ﴿يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾ and this says "they are unable to," which is explaining a thing by its opposite, and it does not hold. As for the one who says "yuṭīqūnahu" means it reaches their capacity to the point of hardship, this has a basis; but what is established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa' indicates its weakness. Indeed the apparent wording of the verse also indicates its weakness, since His words at its end ﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 184] indicate that these people are able to fast, and that it was addressed to one who is able. The hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa' in the two Sahihs[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4507), and Muslim (1145/149).]] says that when fasting was first prescribed, a person had the choice between fasting and ransoming, until Allah made fasting obligatory in the verse that follows: ﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ الَّذِي أُنْزِلَ فِيهِ الْقُرْآنُ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 185]. This is the preferred view: that the meaning of ﴿يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾ is that they are able to do it. ﴿فِدْيَةٌ﴾: is "fidyah" here the predicate or the subject?
* The students: The subject, postponed (mubtada' mu'akhkhar).
* The Shaykh: The postponed subject, whose predicate is: ﴿وَعَلَى الَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾.

As for his words ﴿فِدْيَةٌ﴾: it means a ransom in place of fasting, by which one ransoms oneself from fasting. The basic principle is that fasting is binding upon you and you are charged with it, so you ransom yourself from this obligation with what? With feeding a poor person: ﴿فِدْيَةٌ﴾. As for ﴿طَعَامُ﴾, it is an explanatory apposition (‘atf bayan) to ﴿فِدْيَةٌ﴾, because it clarifies it: this ransom is ﴿طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ﴾ (feeding a poor person). Is it distributed among individuals or over the whole group? It is distributed among individuals: for each day, a poor person is fed; the meaning is not that they feed one poor person for the whole month, but for each day. The second reading of the verse supports this: ﴿طَعَامُ مَسَاكِينُ﴾ (food for poor people, in the plural). Do you understand? "Masakin" is plural, so just as the days they owe are plural, so too the poor who are fed are plural; they must be a group. As for ﴿فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ﴾, there are readings. Let us look at the first reading: ﴿فِدْيَةُ طَعَامِ مَسَاكِينَ﴾ (look at the Mushaf and see the construct form and the plural of "masakin"). ﴿فِدْيَةُ طَعَامِ مَسَاكِينَ﴾, that is one. The second reading: ﴿فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مَسَاكِينَ﴾, which matches what is in the Mushaf except that it is in the plural. Yes, except that it is in the plural. So there are also three readings: ﴿فِدْيَةُ طَعَامِ مَسَاكِينَ﴾, which is the attribution of a thing to its type, as when I say "a ring of iron," meaning made of iron: ﴿فِدْيَةُ طَعَامِ﴾, that is, a ransom of food for poor people. As for the second reading, which differs from the Mushaf: ﴿فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مَسَاكِينَ﴾, on the reading of the Mushaf the word "ṭa'ām" is an explanatory apposition, but it shows that what is meant by "miskīn" is the genus, and that it is distributed among individuals, and that what is meant is a ransom for each day for one poor person.

As for ﴿طَعَامِ مَسَاكِينَ﴾ ("ṭa'ām"): has its type been specified?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Has it been specified as to its quantity?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Has its genus been specified?
* A student: Its genus is food.
* The Shaykh: Yes, its genus is food, good. But its type has not been specified, nor its quantity. So we return to the meaning of "food." Whatever is called food suffices. So if we are in a town where they eat only meat, and people have nothing but meat and fish on the seashore, eating birds and some fish, what becomes the food?
* The students: Fish and meat.
* The Shaykh: Fish and meat, is that right or not? If we are in a town where they eat only maize, what is the food?
* A student: Maize.
* The Shaykh: Maize. If we are in a town where they do not feed barley?
* A student: Feeding does not suffice.
* The Shaykh: It does not suffice?
* A student: It does not suffice.
* The Shaykh: Thus it becomes clear the weakness of those who restrict the food to what suffices in the Fitrah (alms of breaking the fast); then they say the things that suffice in the Fitrah are how many kinds? Only five kinds: wheat, dates, barley, raisins, and dried curd. But the correct view is that the generality of the verse applies: whatever is called food is sufficient. As for the quantity, it has not been specified. Based on this, if he gives the poor a lunch or an evening meal, does it suffice them? It suffices them. For this reason, "Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), when he grew old, would prepare food and invite thirty poor people to it."[[Reported by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (12335), Abu Ya'la (4194), and al-Daraqutni (2390).]] And does this suffice him for what? For the fast of Ramadan; because Allah stated "food" without restriction. Some scholars said: the food must be one mudd of wheat or half a sa' of other things. Fine—what is their evidence for half a sa'? They say: the evidence for half a sa' is that the Messenger ﷺ said to Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, when he permitted him to shave his head while in ihram: "Feed six poor people, half a sa' for each poor person."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1816), and Muslim (1201/85), from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah.]] Half a sa' for each poor person. They said: this is a determination by the Messenger ﷺ of something stated in general in the Qur'an, namely ﴿فَفِدْيَةٌ مِنْ صِيَامٍ أَوْ صَدَقَةٍ أَوْ نُسُكٍ﴾ [Al-Baqarah 196].

So whoever says: the unrestricted verses are to be read in light of this verse, just as we read the unrestricted verse on freeing a slave in light of the verse restricting it to a believing slave—they say: applying the unrestricted verse to a restricted verse by a description is like applying the unrestricted verse to a restricted verse by a quantity, because the reality of quantity is a description (...). For when I say: "I have wheat whose quantity is ten sa's," have I described it or not?
* A student: Yes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 183–184 (part 3 of 4):

* The Shaykh: Its description, as when you say: "I have good wheat." They said: the absolute (al-mutlaq, unrestricted) is carried over to all kinds of food when he wants to distribute it to them without inviting them to it, it is carried over to this restricted (al-muqayyad) case. As for the evidence for the mudd of wheat, their evidence is that Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, came to Madinah and wheat had become abundant there, so he said: "I see that one mudd of this is equivalent to two mudds of barley." So the people, in his time, switched from giving the fitrah (the obligatory charity at the end of Ramadan) at a sa' (a measure of about 2.5 kg/three liters) to half a sa'. But Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, was opposed by those among the Companions who opposed him, such as Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I will not stop giving it as I used to give it in the time of the Prophet ﷺ."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1508), and Muslim (985 / 18).]] There is no doubt that what Abu Sa'id adopted is the truth in the matter of the fitrah, because the Messenger ﷺ specified the fitrah from different types: dates and barley, as in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "The Prophet ﷺ made the zakat al-fitr obligatory: a sa' of dates or a sa' of barley."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1503), and Muslim (984 / 12).]] And Abu Sa'id said: "We used to give it as a sa' of food, and the food at that time was dates, barley, raisins and aqit (dried curd)."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1510).]] Wheat was not mentioned because in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, it was very scarce, and it was not their common food. For this reason, nothing in the authentic Sunnah mentions wheat in the matter of the fitrah. Based on this, we say: those who said that a mudd suffices took it from the action of Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him. Alright, what do you say about rice: does it join barley or wheat?
* Student: Food in general.
* The Shaykh: No. Those who restrict it to a mudd of wheat, or half a sa' of dates or barley?
* Student: It is joined to wheat, because barley is cheap.
* The Shaykh: Yes, I see that it is joined to wheat and is more deserving of it, because it is easier. Wheat is easier, and more abundant, I think.
* Student: No, they are all average, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: (...) Let's see. Now, if I put a mudd of rice in a pot and cooked it, how much would it become from the mudd?
* Student: It would become two mudds.
* The Shaykh: It becomes two mudds, or more than two mudds, more than two mudds, yes. But put for you a grain of wheat, which does not amount to this much, even if you grind it, it would not reach this amount. Then it also needs expense. This wheat cannot be eaten unless you grind it and knead it, right? And bake it, or not? But this (rice)?
* Student: It does not need that.
* The Shaykh: (...) There is nothing wrong with it.
* Student: O Shaykh, in some places a person cannot find people who benefit from various kinds of food. If he gives him even an ardab of wheat, he does not benefit from it?
* The Shaykh: How does he benefit from it?
* Student: He benefits by money, he wants to take money.
* The Shaykh: Riyals, you mean.
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What use are these riyals?
* Student: I mean he benefits from them, and food for him is not...
* The Shaykh: What does he want?
* Student: I mean, you do not find poor people in a place, for example.
* The Shaykh: Food is most important. For this reason, a person gives priority to warding off hunger over covering nakedness.
* Student: I mean a person, for example, is not in his own country, a foreigner, for example, in foreign lands and so on, and he does not find poor people to give food to. How does he pay the expiation, I mean?
* The Shaykh: Would he give them riyals, which would benefit them?
* Student: They would be shy and would not take the food.
* Another student: It would be difficult for them to find poor people.
* The Shaykh: (...) The food that they eat (...).
* Student: It would be difficult for them to find poor people. I mean, most of the people of the country are not Muslims.
* The Shaykh: Alright, suppose he eats a sandwich, (...) and gives it. Sheikh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) holds that it is permissible to feed from bread.
* Student: Yes, but he does not feed anyone except Muslims, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: No, no, not non-Muslims.
* Student: Alright, it is difficult for him to find (poor people), there are people in foreign lands...
* The Shaykh: In such a case we say: like zakat, you pay it in other lands of the Muslims to those in need. You appoint someone, then...
* Student: The food of wheat, (...) there is a big difference.
* The Shaykh: In what respect?
* Student: In respect of the food (...) many starches (...).
* The Shaykh: The point is that as for common food, common food, there is no doubt (...).
* Student: O Shaykh, can it be taken from the report of Anas that making up the fast is thirty days?
* The Shaykh: No, it is to be understood as: the month in which he used to feed (people) was thirty days.
* Student: (...) The month is twenty-nine days.
* The Shaykh: No, not in every case.
* Student: (...) Which is stronger?
* The Shaykh: Which?
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Which one, which one? In the matter of feeding?
* Student: In the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, on the verse..?
* The Shaykh: What appears to me, regarding the matter of feeding, is that the absolute remains in its absoluteness. The absolute remains in its absoluteness, because the verse about the ransom in Hajj has high substitutes, which are, for example, the sacrifice (nusuk). The sacrifice undoubtedly feeds more than ten needy people. The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that these remain as they are, in their absoluteness.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿مَسَاكِينَ﴾ (masakina, plural) or ﴿مِسْكِينٍ﴾ (miskin, singular)? There are two readings. What is meant by the miskin is one who does not find what is sufficient for him for a year. Included in this definition is the faqir (poor person). Likewise, when the miskin is mentioned alone, he includes the faqir, and when the faqir is mentioned alone, he includes the miskin. But when both are mentioned together, the people of knowledge have said that there is a difference between them: the faqir is worse off than the miskin, in greater need. The faqir is one who does not find half (of his needs), and the miskin is one who does not find the whole, meaning he finds half but does not find the whole.

﴿فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾ [al-Baqarah 184].
* Student: O Shaykh, before you go into the verse, many people ask: does the (feeding for) days suffice all at once? I mean, would thirty days suffice for them, so that they give it in one lump, or to one person?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not suffice for one person, because it is (plural) "days".
* Student: Because many people would find it difficult to go around every day to a needy person, and not find one.
* The Shaykh: No, no, it is not necessary. Because he can look at, for example, three houses or four houses that have this number (of needy people), and give to them. Suppose there is a large house, for us in Saudi Arabia, this is a house of workers, in which there are thirty poor people, all of them poor. We give them food, we cook for them and deliver it to them to eat.
* Student: No, many, O Shaykh, it is difficult for you to find needy people.
* Another student: There will be a problem, will the workers not pray (...)?
* Another student: In some places, O Shaykh, we have people who do not know any needy people at all.
* Another student: (...) a group of workers (...).
* The Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know, but the default for a Muslim is uprightness (al-'adalah), and that he prays, unless it becomes clear otherwise.

﴿تَطَوَّعَ﴾ is the conditional verb, and its answer is ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾. And His saying ﴿خَيْرًا﴾, what is its grammatical position and what governs it in the accusative?
* Student: It is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), or a direct object postponed, or a circumstantial accusative (hal).
* Another student: It is a direct object, O Shaykh.
* Another student: The third is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi).
* The Shaykh: Yes, alright. Now: "whoever volunteers (tatawwa'a) a good deed" (taṭawwu'an khayran), or ﴿مَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا﴾ with the meaning that we make ﴿تَطَوَّعَ﴾ mean "did" (fa'ala), so ﴿خَيْرًا﴾ is a direct object. Or we make ﴿فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ﴾ mean "seeking good," so it is an object of purpose. The meaning in all these possibilities is one: whoever performs the obedience, intending by it the good, then it is good for him.

It is known that an act is not an act of obedience unless it agrees with the pleasure of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by being sincerely for His sake and conforming to His law. If it is not sincere it is not accepted, and if it is sincere but not according to the law it is not accepted, because the first is shirk (associating partners with Allah), and the second is bid'ah (innovation).

And His saying: ﴿فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾: "it is good for him" in comparison to what? Meaning: do we take (khayr) as a comparative (ism tafdil), i.e., "better for him than other than it"? Or do we say that this (khayr) is a word indicating virtue in the absolute, without comparison? Because there is no comparison and compared-to here. It may be said: ﴿فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾ compared to what? Compared to not doing it. But this meaning is weak, because that the one who volunteers good is better for him than not doing it is a known matter. It is like the saying of one who says: "The sky is above us, and the earth is beneath us," and the other's saying:

"As if we, with water around us, were a people sitting with water all around them."

But the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it is an explanation, because this is good in the absolute, and it is free of the sense of preference.

﴿فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَهُ﴾. Included in this goodness is that he is rewarded tenfold, up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples.

Then He said: ﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. It is clear that the meaning of "good" here is comparison: that your fasting is better for you than the ransom. The grammarians use this as an example of the disguised subject (al-mubtada' al-mu'awwal), because His saying ﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا﴾: (an) is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), and (taṣūmū) is a present-tense verb, and the subject (mubtada') is only a noun. But here it is disguised (mu'awwal), isn't it?
* The students: It is disguised.
* The Shaykh: And the estimate?
* The students: Your fasting.
* The Shaykh: And your fasting is better for you. What is your question?
* Student: A direct object absolute (maf'ul mutlaq) in ﴿فَمَنْ تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا﴾.
* The Shaykh: And what did I say?
* Student: An object of purpose.
* The Shaykh: Yes, a direct object and an absolute object.

﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ means: than the ransom. And His saying: ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, and the meaning is: if you are among those of knowledge, then understand. And (in) here is not a conditional particle relating to what precedes it. That is, it is not a conjunctive one, as they say. That is, the meaning is not that it is better for us if we know, and if we do not know, then there is no good. Rather it is an independent sentence. For this reason, you should pause and say: ﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾.

(...) He used it as evidence for the ruling on the elderly: the old man and the old woman who cannot bear fasting, he said: they feed a needy person for each day. Ibn 'Abbas used this verse as evidence that the elderly person who cannot bear fasting feeds a needy person for each day. The basis of his inference, may Allah be pleased with him, is that when Allah, glory be to Him, made feeding equivalent to fasting and gave the choice between them, the inability to fast is what? It specifies feeding, because Allah, exalted is He, made feeding equivalent to fasting when one is able to do it. So it is known from this that whoever is not able to fast, and is unable to do so permanently, then he does what has been made its equivalent, which is feeding. And this is from his understanding, may Allah be pleased with him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾. As for its grammar, how do we parse it? And how do we parse ﴿أَنْ تَصُومُوا﴾ in detail?
* Student: (an)...
* The Shaykh: (an) is a particle of the verbal masdar that puts the verb in the accusative?
* Student: It puts the present verb in the accusative.
* The Shaykh: It puts the present verb in the accusative. ﴿تَصُومُوا﴾?
* Student: ﴿تَصُومُوا﴾ is a present verb in the accusative by deletion of the nun.
* The Shaykh: In the accusative by (an), and the sign of its accusative?
* Student: The sign of its accusative is the deletion of the nun.
* The Shaykh: Yes, and the waw?
* Student: The waw is the subject.
* The Shaykh: And (an) and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun as subject. ﴿خَيْرٌ﴾?
* Student: ﴿خَيْرٌ﴾ is the predicate.
* The Shaykh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾, is it a restriction on the goodness, or what?
* Student: They know that fasting is good for them.
* The Shaykh: I mean: if you do not know, then it is not good for you?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: How?
* Student: If they are not able to fast...
* The Shaykh: No. Allah said: ﴿وَأَنْ تَصُومُوا خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. That is, if we say this condition refers to the sentence before it, then the meaning becomes: it is good for us if we know, and if we do not know, then it is not good for us.
* Student: Yes, the condition of goodness.
* The Shaykh: The condition of goodness. That is, if we do not know, then it is not good?
* Student: In reality, whether they know or do not know, it is good.
* The Shaykh: Then how do we say, in this sentence, that it is conditional?
* Student: If fasting is realized, and they fast, then it is good for them. If they do not fast...
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: It is an independent sentence.
* The Shaykh: An independent, self-standing sentence. Correct. It is not a restriction on what precedes it. It is not a restriction, but independent. That is: if you are among those of knowledge, then know that fasting is good. It does not mean: if you are among those of knowledge, then fasting is good. No.

﴿تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. Now let us look at the verse and what benefits it contains. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ﴾ and so on to the end.

From this noble verse are derived: the importance of fasting, because Allah, exalted is He, opened it with the address, and that it is one of the requirements of faith, because He directed the address to whom?
* Student: To the believers.
* The Shaykh: To the believers. And that neglecting it damages it, because if it is one of its requirements, then neglecting it damages it and is a deficiency in it.

And from the noble verse is derived: the obligation of fasting. From where?
* Student: ﴿كُتِبَ﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying ﴿كُتِبَ﴾.

And from it is derived: that earlier nations also fasted, from His saying: ﴿كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ﴾.

And from it is derived: the use of consoling a person with what was imposed on others, to make it easier for him to carry it out. Is that taken? ﴿كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ﴾.

And from the verse also: the virtue of this nation, in that Allah prescribed for it what He prescribed for those before it, so that it may rise to degrees of perfection, as those before it rose to them.

And from this verse: the wisdom in prescribing fasting, His saying: ﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ﴾ (so that you may attain taqwa, God-consciousness).

And from the noble verse: the virtue of taqwa, and that one should pursue the means that lead to it, because Allah prescribed fasting for this purpose. So this purpose is a great purpose, and a person should pursue the paths that lead to taqwa.

From this there follows another benefit: the consideration of dhara'i' (means leading to an end; blocking the means). That is, whatever is a means to a thing takes the ruling of that thing. Since taqwa is obligatory, its means are obligatory. For this reason, a person must keep away from places of temptation. He should not look at a non-related woman, nor speak to her in a way that he enjoys with her. Why? Because it leads to it and becomes a means to immorality, so it is obligatory to avoid that. Even the Prophet ﷺ commanded whoever hears about the Dajjal to keep away from him,[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4319), from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him.]] so that he would not fall into his trial.

And from this noble verse is derived: the wisdom of Allah, glory be to Him, in diversifying the acts of worship. Because when we reflect on acts of worship, we find that they are diverse. Some are purely financial, some are purely physical, some are combined of both physical and financial, and some are acts, and some are abstentions. So what is fasting?
* Student: Abstention.
* The Shaykh: Abstention from what is loved. Abstaining from what is loved may be harder than seeking to do something. Isn't that so? Perhaps some people, if you ask them to do things, they will do them, but they cannot abstain from what they love. So this is from the wisdom of Allah, glory be to Him, in the obligations and His servants' worship of Him, glory and praise be to Him: He varied the acts of worship for them in order to test them. Perhaps a person is generous, so giving zakat is among the easiest things for him, or not? Then the complete test is not achieved by imposing zakat alone. Perhaps a person has psychological discipline, so praying, performing ablution, and bathing on cold nights, and the like, become easy for him. Perhaps a person has patience with what he loves, so fasting is easy for him. He says: "I will fast a month rather than pay thirty riyals, because I love my money very much. And fasting (...) is only that you eat lunch a bit earlier and delay dinner. It is simple. But beware that you take thirty riyals from me." Clear?

So people differ. For this reason, whoever gave a fatwa to someone who owed an expiation that involved fasting and manumission (freeing a slave) was in error, when he said to him: "Fast two consecutive months and do not free a slave." Why, when manumission takes precedence over fasting? He said: "Because if we told this king: 'Free a slave,' he would free ten slaves and not fast one day, and that is dearer to him than fasting one day. We imposed this on him because it is more severe for him." But this reasoning is not correct, because it stands against the explicit text, so it is not accepted.

I have come with this to show that Allah, glorified and exalted, is wise in varying the obligations of worship. For example, this man is a king who can easily spend large amounts of wealth on zakat, but fasting is hard for him; for this reason I give the ruling that he should fast instead of freeing a slave. In reality, however, Allah, mighty and majestic, made worship a test for the servant. Among the wonders of our time is that we are patient with fasting, while some of us are not patient with prayer. You find him fasting Ramadan but not praying, praying only from Ramadan to Ramadan if he prays in Ramadan. This is without doubt an error in thinking. But because prayer recurs every day, it has become easy for a person, while fasting is difficult for him. For this reason, when they want to blame someone, they say, "This one neither fasts nor prays," and they begin with abandoning the fast. And this is from (...).

* Student: Shaykh, does ﴿so that you may become righteous﴾ not imply that fasting is accepted only from the righteous (al-muttaqun)?
* Shaykh: No. From ﴿O you who have believed﴾ it is understood that only the believer fasts, because it is a requirement of faith.
* Student: Taqwa?
* Shaykh: No, that is the wisdom of the legislation. Yes, the wisdom of the legislation is also derived from it, from what we mentioned; we mentioned it earlier.
* Student: Shaykh, they said the story of this king is from the category of al-maslahah al-mursalah (unrestricted public interest). Is that correct?
* Shaykh: No, that is not correct. We do not accept al-maslahah al-mursalah as evidence, because if it is a genuine benefit, Islam has already taken it into account, and if it is not a benefit, Islam has not taken it into account. This man—notice—you considered obligating him to fast, but you did not consider that freeing a neck from slavery is among the best deeds. ﴿But he has not attempted the ascent (11). And what can make you know what is the ascent? (12)﴾ [al-Balad 11–12]. What is it? ﴿The freeing of a neck﴾ [al-Balad 13].
* Student: But it seems to him that it is more effective in restraining himself.
* Shaykh: No, not at all. Rather, this is more beneficial.
* Student: Many people have this view, that it restrains themselves more.
* Shaykh: Correct, but this is more beneficial. If he restrains himself only through punishment or expiation, what is the benefit? But this is more beneficial, and Allah is wise, exalted is He, so this is more beneficial for the servant.
The essential point is that the unrestricted public interests which some people cite as evidence have no meaning. In reality, if it is a recognized benefit, the Shari'ah has already brought it, and if it is not a benefit, the Shari'ah has nullified it, and there is no benefit at all in opposing the Shari'ah.

The statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿a number of prescribed days. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days﴾.

From this verse is derived: that fasting is for a few days, prescribed days.
And also derived from it: adopting methods that make easy for a person what he expects to be hardship for him. How? By adopting methods that make easy for a person what he expects to be difficult for him. But ﴿prescribed days﴾ means that they are limited, not difficult, and involve no burden or hardship.
And from the noble verse is derived: the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic toward His servants. First, because the days are few, He did not prescribe a month, nor two, nor three; rather He prescribed prescribed days which are a month, the month of Ramadan, as will come, Allah willing.
And also among them: the affirmation of mercy in His statement ﴿so whoever among you is ill﴾.
And also derived from the noble verse: the permissibility of breaking the fast due to illness.
Is it not also derived from it: an indication that breaking the fast is better?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: From where do we take it?
* Student: ﴿then an equal number﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾. Allah opened the door and did not say: "then he should not fast." Rather He said: ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾, so it is as if He opened a door for the sick person to break the fast.
Know that the sick person, with respect to breaking the fast, is divided into three categories:
First: he is not affected by fasting at all, and fasting does not burden him despite his illness. Here he fasts or breaks the fast? He fasts; he must fast.
Second: fasting burdens him but does not harm him. Here fasting is disliked; it is disliked to fast with hardship, because a person should not burden himself with what Allah has permitted him. This burdening of oneself despite Allah's concession indicates that the person is not receptive to this concession, and it has been said: "The base person is one who rejects the noble." The noble person loves that people take his concessions, as came in the hadith: «Indeed Allah loves that His concessions be taken»[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (5866), from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him.]].
Third: fasting harms him. The sick person is harmed by fasting, such as one who has kidney disease requiring constant water. Here fasting is forbidden for him; he is not permitted to fast, due to the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾ [an-Nisa' 29].
* Student: Shaykh, your statement: "the noble one rejects..."?
* Shaykh: "The base person is one who rejects the noble."
* Student: Then how do we reconcile this with the fasting of the Messenger and some of the Companions during travel?
* Shaykh: No, we have not yet come to travel.
* Student: This is about the sick?
* Shaykh: This is about the sick.
From the noble verse is derived: the permissibility of breaking the fast while traveling. Is the indication from the verse clear?
* Student: God willing.
* Shaykh: Good.
And also derived from it: an indication that breaking the fast is better, from His statement ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah 184]; but this is not explicit in the verse. Therefore the Sunnah reports fasting during travel: the Messenger ﷺ used to fast during travel, and «the Companions included those who fasted and those who broke the fast, and the one who broke the fast did not blame the one who fasted, nor the one who fasted blame the one who broke the fast»[[Narrated by Muslim (1117/97), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah, may Allah be pleased with them.]].

Then we say: fasting during travel is also divided into three categories:
The first: that there is no hardship at all, meaning there is no hardship exceeding that of fasting at home. This is what is intended; otherwise there is some hardship in hot days, but not a hardship exceeding that of fasting at home. In this case we say: fasting is better, and if one breaks the fast there is no blame. Its evidence: «The Messenger ﷺ used to fast during travel»[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3813), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]].
This is the view of Imam ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. However, the well-known position of Imam Ahmad is the disliking of fasting during travel even in this state, and they said: one should not fast, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾.
The position of the Zahiriyyah (literalists) is the prohibition of fasting, and that if one fasts it does not suffice him, because Allah said: ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾, making the obligation an equal number of other days. But this view is very weak, and likewise the well-known position of Imam Ahmad is weak.
The second state: fasting burdens him but with a tolerable hardship. Here breaking the fast is better, and the evidence for this: «that the Prophet ﷺ was on a journey and saw a crowd and a man over whom shade had been cast. He asked about him, and they said: "He is fasting." He said: "It is not righteousness to fast during travel."»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1946) and Muslim (1115/92), from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Have you understood?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Good. The Prophet, peace be upon him, negated righteousness from it.

Here we pause at this evidence and this state. It is known in the principles of jurisprudence that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said here, and what did he say? "It is not righteousness to fast during travel", a general statement with a specific cause, and it is known that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. So what is the answer to this principle with this hadith, while we say that fasting during travel is better if it is not burdensome?
We say: the meaning of "the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause" is that the intended specificity is the specificity of the individual, not the specificity of the attribute. As for specificity of attribute, it is undoubtedly considered. For example, this man over whom shade was cast: we do not say, "It is not righteousness for you, O man, to fast during travel" only; if we said that, we would be restricting the general by its cause. Rather we say that specificity of attribute must restrict the generality, so the meaning is: "It is not righteousness to fast during travel for one whose state is like this." So if Zayd, 'Amr, Khalid, Bakr and so on all come, all of whom find fasting burdensome like this man, we say: it is not righteousness for you to fast. If someone says: "Did the Messenger say it only for this man?" we say: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. Ibn Daqiq al-'Id alerted to this principle in his commentary on this hadith in al-'Umdah.
This is truly a principle for whoever reflects upon it: generality is of two kinds, generality of attribute and generality of person. Here the consideration is the generality of the wording with respect to the person; as for the attribute, the ruling is tied to its cause for which the ruling was legislated.
* Student: So with this principle, even if the evidence does not indicate its reality (...), or we say: if the evidence indicates that it does not apply...
* Shaykh: In any case, the origin is that it cannot be restricted except by evidence. If it is said: "It is not righteousness to fast during travel"?
* Student: It is not general except by evidence.
* Shaykh: Here we know the cause for which this generality was issued, which is hardship. So it is as if the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "It is not righteousness to fast during travel in a state of hardship."
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, even if we do not find it. As long as we know that the reason for the ruling is this meaning, we restrict it by it.

And ﴿ill or on a journey﴾.
From this noble verse is also derived: that the ruling is linked to what is called travel without restriction. From where do we take it?
* Student: You mentioned two opinions: that there is no hardship, and that there is a tolerable hardship?
* Shaykh: The third state is not a third opinion. The third state: fasting is burdensome to the traveler with severe hardship that cannot be borne. Here breaking the fast is required, and its evidence is what is established in the Sahih: «that the Messenger ﷺ was in the campaign of Makkah, and his companions came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, people have found fasting difficult, and they are waiting to see what you do." He called for water after the 'Asr prayer and drank it while the people looked on. Then it was told to the Prophet, peace be upon him, that some people had fasted, and he said: "Those are the disobedient, those are the disobedient."»[[Narrated by Muslim (1114/90), from the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].
Disobedience occurs only in committing what is prohibited. So if this man found fasting during travel severely difficult, it is obligatory for him to break the fast. Why would he not break it, why would he exhaust himself and burden himself while the matter is spacious?
From this noble verse is derived: that the travel in which breaking the fast is permitted is not restricted by time or distance. From where do we take it?
* Students: From its generality.
* Shaykh: From its generality, ﴿or on a journey﴾.
But some scholars said: his journey must extend over a day, because the least breaking of the fast possible is what? The day. The least breaking of the fast possible is the day, so the journey must extend over the day. So whoever wishes to travel, for example, to Riyadh early in the day and return at the end of the day, we say to him: do not break the fast, because this is less than what is permitted to you. You are permitted to break the fast in Ramadan, and this is part of a day which is not called fasting.
This ruling is quite clear according to the view of the Hanbali jurists, who say: whoever knows that he will arrive tomorrow is obligated to fast. They say, may Allah have mercy on them: if a person knows that he will arrive tomorrow—for example, suppose you are in Makkah and you know that tomorrow you will travel to your country and will not reach it before sunset—it is obligatory for you to fast while in Makkah, because you will be arriving in your country. This is in fact the opposite of those who say you may break the fast even if you arrive in the country, because there is an opinion of some scholars that a traveler who arrives while breaking the fast may continue in his breaking of the fast. This is one of the two narrations from Imam Ahmad and the position of Malik and ash-Shafi'i: that if a person arrives at his country while having broken the fast, he remains upon his breaking. They cited in this a report from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Whoever eats at the beginning of the day, let him eat at its end," meaning: whoever is permitted to eat at the beginning of the day is permitted to eat at its end.
Likewise, a woman who becomes pure from menstruation during the day is not obligated to abstain. Accordingly, if the traveler arrives at his town having broken the fast and finds that his wife has become pure from menstruation on that day, it is permissible for him to have intercourse with her, because abstention is not obligatory on him or on her.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿prescribed days. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 183–184 (part 1 of 4):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 183].

First: The address by the call "﴿O you who﴾" has already been explained to indicate alerting the addressee to a matter of great importance. For this reason the call was directed to them with ﴿O you who﴾, as if He were saying: "Pay attention!"

Second: Linking this command to the attribute of faith contains three benefits. The first is encouragement to attach oneself to it. The second is that this is a requirement of faith. The third is that abandoning it is a deficiency in faith. As for how it serves as encouragement: addressing a person with this attribute, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, necessitates urging them to do this thing on account of their faith. For this reason, if I say to you, "O man, do such-and-such," this encourages you to do it, as if, were you not to do it, you would miss the attribute of manliness. This is the reason it serves as encouragement. As for it indicating that it is a requirement of faith: it is addressed to the believers, so this is because of the requirement of their faith. As for its being a deficiency if it is neglected: since it is specific to the believer, it is known that it is one of his characteristics, and if the characteristics of faith, or any part of them, are lost, that becomes a deficiency in faith. Thus we conclude from this that fasting is among the matters that are given care and attention.

﴿It has been prescribed for you﴾: meaning it has been obligated, and the one who obligated it is Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

﴿Fasting﴾: this is the substitute subject (nā'ib al-fā'il). In ﴿it has been prescribed for you fasting﴾, it is the substitute for the agent, in the nominative case.

Fasting (al-siyam) linguistically means abstention, and from it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam 26], meaning abstention from speech, as evidenced by her saying: ﴿So I will not speak today to any human being﴾ [Maryam 26]. As for in the Sharia, it is: worship of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, by abstaining from the things that break the fast, from the appearance of dawn until sunset.

And His saying: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 183]. The kāf here is a prepositional particle and indicates comparison, but it is a comparison of the prescribing with the prescribing, not of the thing prescribed with the thing prescribed: ﴿as it was prescribed﴾. This type of comparison with the verb, without reference to the one upon whom the act falls, is a consistent matter. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed you will see your Lord just as you see the moon on the night of the full moon" [narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2554) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah; its origin is in al-Bukhari (806) and Muslim (182/299) and (2968/16)]. Is the comparison here to the seeing or to the thing seen with the thing seen? To the seeing with the seeing, because the kāf has entered upon the verb which reverts to the verbal noun. So His saying ﴿as it was prescribed﴾: do we say here that it is a comparison of the thing prescribed with the thing prescribed, or of the prescribing with the prescribing? Of the prescribing with the prescribing; that is, like His prescribing. For this reason we say that (mā) here is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), not a relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl).

And His saying: ﴿on those before you﴾: from whom? From the earlier nations. It includes the Jews and Christians and those before them. All of them had fasting prescribed upon them, but it does not necessarily follow that it was like our fasting in timing and period.

And His saying: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾: this comparison has two benefits for us. The first benefit is consolation and taking example from those who came before. Lest this nation say, "Allah has laid upon us burdens and heavy loads by this fast, especially in the summer days," it is said: be reassured, for this matter was something that those before you were also subjected to. Without doubt, when a person is told of someone who shared with him in a difficult matter, it eases it for him. The evidence for this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [Al-Zukhruf 39]. That is, your sharing in the punishment will not benefit you. Rather, in this world, when people share a punishment, it becomes easier for them. For this reason al-Khansa said in lamenting her brother Sakhr:

"Were it not for the multitude of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
And they do not weep like my brother, but I console the soul concerning him with consolation."

Those in the Fire, sharing the punishment does not benefit them by making it easier. Likewise here: when Allah mentioned that He had prescribed fasting for us, He clarified that it was prescribed for those before us, so that we would be reassured and not say, "We have been burdened with what the earlier nations were not burdened with." This is the first benefit.

The second benefit for us in mentioning its prescription for those before us: it shows that this nation has been perfected in virtues just as the earlier nations were perfected. There is no doubt that fasting for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is among the greatest virtues: a person abandons his desire, his food and his drink, the most appealing of what (...) to him, for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. For this reason Allah reserved their reward for Himself. He singled it out for Himself, saying: "Every deed of the son of Adam is for him, the good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundred times, except fasting, for it is for Me and I will reward it, he leaves his food, his drink and his desire for My sake" [agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1894) and Muslim (1151/164) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, the wording being Muslim's].

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Who?
* Student: The earlier nations (...).
* Shaykh: Good, this is one of the blessings of Allah upon us; for we say: when Allah prescribed it for us, He made clear that it was prescribed for those before us, so that we would not say it is among the burdens placed upon us.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, and also we take example by it: since this is prescribed for others besides us, it becomes easier for us. Now the people..
* Student: (...) even if it was not written.
* Shaykh: (...). Allah, Mighty and Majestic, makes the matter easy for us by its coming in "a number of days" (...) "We hear and we obey", God willing (...) and reminds the servants of things so that the matter becomes easy for them and they submit completely.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: "So that you may be God-conscious" (taqwa) of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is the legal, devotional wisdom of fasting. Whatever other benefits come, whether bodily or social, they are a consequence; and yet there are bodily and social benefits in it. It saddens me greatly that some people focus on the bodily and social benefits of fasting. I do not say they should not be mentioned; they may be mentioned, but one should not focus on them, as if it was only legislated for them, for this removes the spirit of fasting, which is worship of Allah through it. If a person is told, "If you fast, this removes the waste in your body from excessive eating, and this brings such-and-such medical benefits, and this also reminds you of your poor brothers so that you may console them with your wealth," and similar matters, and we do not say it this way, but forget the foundation for which fasting was prescribed, which is God-consciousness (taqwa) of Allah. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ said: "Whoever does not give up false speech, acting upon it, and ignorance, Allah has no need that he give up his food and his drink" [narrated by al-Bukhari (6057) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. This is the wisdom of fasting, and the God-consciousness in it is very evident. There is no need for me to bring you evidence while you fast Ramadan and feel what arises in your souls of God-consciousness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, during the days of fasting. A person, as soon as he tells himself, or makes himself feel, that he has left his pleasures for Allah, there is no doubt that he says: "If I leave these pleasures which are part of my nature, and my nature urges me strongly towards them, then this without doubt wins for my heart the love of Allah, the veneration of Him, light, faith and tranquility." This is the secret in His saying: ﴿so that you may be God-conscious﴾.
* Student: Shaykh, ﴿so that you may be God-conscious﴾ here is unrestricted (...) what is its meaning?
* Shaykh: No, the correct understanding is that you may be God-conscious of Allah; because taqwa, when stated without qualification, means the taqwa of Allah, like: ﴿and cooperate in righteousness and God-consciousness﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 2], and similar.
* Student: Someone may say: taqwa is often greater during breaking the fast than during fasting, because when the body is energetic it is more humble before Allah, and if it is otherwise, it will certainly weigh down remembrance and worship?
* Shaykh: I have not tried it, my son. Fullness is what calls to arrogance and exultation.
* Student: And to sleep.
* Shaykh: And to sleep: a person who is full (...).
* Student: Especially if the weather is hot.
* Shaykh: True, he becomes tired; there is no doubt he becomes tired, do you understand? But this tiredness and this humbling has an effect on the heart, an effect known to the people of spiritual discipline (ahl al-suluk). We do not know it; we are closer to the material than to the spirit. But in any case the people of spiritual discipline know this, so it has great reformative effect on the heart, provided it is within the legal limits. I am not saying: let your spirit die of hunger while you are fasting. No: ﴿Eat of the good things that We have provided for you and give thanks to Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 172]. But it has an effect, especially when combined with the person feeling that he is worshipping Allah, and this has great benefit.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good. Then He said: ﴿for a certain number of days﴾ [Al-Baqarah 184]. "Days" here is the object (maf'ul) of His saying ﴿fasting﴾, because fasting is a verbal noun (maṣdar) which operates like a verb, or not? Has Ibn Malik's statement passed by us here? What does he say?
* Student:
"To its verb-like verbal noun attach its action, whether annexed, bare, or with al,"
* Shaykh: Or with (al).
* Student:
"If a verb with (an) or (ma) takes its place, and for a verbal noun of the nominal type, action."
* Shaykh: The point now is with al, do you understand? So "fasting" operates in His saying ﴿days﴾, meaning: it has been prescribed for you to fast for certain days.

His saying ﴿for a certain number of days﴾ is indefinite (nakirah), and the indefinite indicates fewness, and indicates abundance, and indicates greatness, and indicates contempt according to context. When it is joined here with His saying ﴿counted﴾ (ma'dudat), it indicates fewness: this fasting is not months, not years, not weeks, but what? Days, certain few days.

And it is not hidden from you that ﴿ma'dudat﴾ is among the forms of the plural of paucity (jam' al-qilla), because the sound masculine plural and the sound feminine plural are among the forms of the plural of paucity. So they are few days; and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, spoke the truth: few, when thirty days are compared to three hundred and sixty days.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Few; and yet there is this great virtue in ﴿a certain number of days﴾. Then He said, the exception from His saying ﴿it has been prescribed for you﴾, because ﴿O you who have believed, it has been prescribed for you﴾ includes the sick and the traveler, the able and the unable. But He said: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾. ﴿Whoever﴾ is a conditional particle, ﴿was﴾ is the conditional verb, and ﴿then a number﴾ is the response of the condition. ﴿A number﴾ is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and the estimate is: upon him is a number of other days. It is also permissible that it be a predicate whose subject is omitted, and the estimate is: the obligation is a number.

His saying ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾: ill. Some scholars took its apparent meaning and said: any illness that afflicts a person allows him to break the fast; any illness that afflicts a person allows him to break the fast. But there is consideration in this, and its basis is that the ill person is excepted only because of the hardship of fasting upon him. On this basis we say: ﴿whoever among you is ill﴾, an illness that makes fasting hardship for him, or delays his recovery, meaning: it does not cause hardship but delays recovery, or causes the treatment to be lost, such as if the doctor tells him: take pills every four hours and similar. The point is: if fasting has an effect on this illness, by hardship, or delay of recovery, or difference in treatment, then it is permissible for him to break the fast. But a person with a toothache, for example, who becomes lethargic because of the pain of the tooth, yet bears the fast without hardship, we do not tell him: break your fast. Or one who has a thorn in his finger, which causes some lassitude because of it, but fasting does not burden him: we do not tell him this either: break your fast, because there is no need to break the fast; the illness will not affect him at all. If someone says: we need evidence for this specification. We say: the specification is understood from the cause (al-'illah).

His saying ﴿or on a journey﴾: "on a journey", and He did not say "traveling" (musafiran), though He said in the first part "ill" (mariḍan) and did not say "in illness". So there must be a wisdom in the variation of expression. What is the wisdom? The wisdom, according to those who say that whoever resolves to depart may break the fast even if he is in the middle of his city, as is related from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "It is the Sunnah" [narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (4/247) from the hadith of Anas]. The meaning of His saying ﴿or on a journey﴾ becomes fully clear, because one who is preparing to travel and setting out, if he has not left and is not actually on a journey, he is on a journey. For this reason the poet says:

"The locust passed over my crop, so I said to it: do not eat, and do not strive to corrupt it.
Then a speaker among them stood upon an ear of grain: we are on a journey, there must be provision for it."

The proof is his saying: "we are on a journey." (...) ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ [Al-Baqarah 184]. His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ is on the estimate of an omitted thing, and the estimate is: so he breaks the fast, then a number of other days.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: So he breaks the fast, then a number of other days.
Then: ﴿a number﴾ either is a subject whose predicate is omitted, the estimate: upon him is a number; or it is a predicate whose subject is omitted, the estimate: the obligation is a number; or: what is prescribed is a number of other days.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It has been prescribed for you fasting as it was prescribed﴾: this comparison is for what purpose?
* Student: A comparison of writing with writing.
* Shaykh: And not the thing prescribed with the thing prescribed?
* Student: No, not the thing prescribed with the thing prescribed.
* Shaykh: What is its parallel? Or is there evidence in a similar construction that supports what you said?
* Student: Like the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed you will see Allah just as you see the moon on the night of the full moon" [narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2554) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah; its origin is in al-Bukhari (806) and Muslim (182/299) and (2968/16)].
* Shaykh: "Indeed you will see your Lord just as you see the moon." Here, certainly, the comparison is of the seeing with the seeing, not of the thing seen with the thing seen. His saying ﴿as it was prescribed﴾: (mā) here?
* Student: It is maṣdariyyah.
* Shaykh: Maṣdariyyah?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And it cannot be relative (mawṣūlah)?
* Student: It cannot.
* Shaykh: Yes, yes, correct. His saying ﴿so that you may be God-conscious﴾: what does "la'alla" mean?
* Student: The meaning of la'alla? Causation (ta'līl).
* Shaykh: Causation; that is, in order that you may be God-conscious. ﴿Days﴾: what is its grammatical analysis (i'rab)?
* Student: Days is an object.
* Shaykh: Object of what?
* Student: Object of ﴿prescribed﴾.
* Shaykh: Object of ﴿prescribed﴾; that is, (prescribed) is in the passive voice.
* Student: Fasting.
* Shaykh: Object of what?
* Student: Object of fasting.
* Shaykh: Object of fasting? And does this fasting govern an object in the accusative?
* Student: It does not govern, because it is a noun.
* Shaykh: It does not govern because it is a noun.
* Student: An object of an omitted verb.
* Shaykh: And what is the estimate?
* Student: Then upon him.
* Shaykh: Then upon him?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Days would be?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And here the verb takes its place:
"If a verb with (an) or (ma) takes its place..."
That is: it has been prescribed for you that you fast certain days. So it is the object of fasting. Now, what is the wisdom in His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿certain days﴾?
* Student: Clarifying that these days (...) Allah, Exalted, that these days do not include the whole year, but are a small thing relative to the whole year.
* Shaykh: What is the wisdom in it: merely that it shows they are only counted days?
* Student: Lightening for the servants.
* Shaykh: Correct, lightening the matter for the one obligated. I am not asking why they were days; I am asking why He expressed it as days. We say: this is for lightening the matter for the obligated, so that he accepts it; as if I said to you: they are only a few days, or they are only a few nights, or similar.

His saying ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey﴾: is the meaning absolute illness?
* Shaykh: Is the meaning absolute illness?
* Student: Yes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 183–184 (part 2 of 4):

* The Shaykh: What kind of illness is meant?
* A student: Any illness.
* The Shaykh: What kind of illness is meant?
* A student: Yes, any illness.
* The Shaykh: Any illness. Alright, do you agree?
* A student: The apparent wording is like this, but the correct view is otherwise.
* The Shaykh: But what is intended? Who holds the correct view?
* A student: What is intended is an illness that makes fasting burdensome, or whose cure would be delayed by it, or that conflicts with taking treatment.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well said, excellent. And this restriction we have placed on the apparent meaning, where is it drawn from?
* A student: It is drawn from the cause ('illah).
* The Shaykh: From the cause and the wisdom (hikmah), precisely.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾ (or on a journey). What is the journey?
* A student: The journey? We took it up, we stopped at it.
* The Shaykh: Alright. The word "journey" (safar) occurs in the Qur'an and in the Sunnah. It occurs in the Qur'an in the phrase ﴿أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾, and in the phrase ﴿وَإِذَا ضَرَبْتُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [An-Nisa 101], and in the phrase ﴿وَآخَرُونَ يَضْرِبُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ [Al-Muzzammil 20], and what is similar to that. Neither Allah the Exalted nor His Messenger specified a distance or a duration for this journey, neither a distance nor a duration. Whoever wishes to clarify this should refer back: the Qur'an does not state that the journey is defined by a distance a person covers. There were no surveyors at the time of the Messenger ﷺ who measured the land down to the cubit, the span, the fingertip, the grain of barley, or the hair of a horse's mane. For those who define it by distance go down to the hair of a horse's mane, meaning: with this grain of sand one differentiates between the traveller and the non-traveller; whoever is short of the grain is not a traveller, and whoever is beyond it is a traveller. Shaykh al-Islam says this is not reported; nothing of this was transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and there were no surveyors who knew this measurement by this distance, and this is correct. Likewise, the journey was not restricted by a time period. For this reason the opinions of the scholars on this question have varied into about ten views: is the journey defined by a time, or by a distance, or by custom?

Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) has a well-known principle: every matter that the Lawgiver stated without defining its limit is referred back to custom ('urf). What people customarily regard as travel, so that it is said "so-and-so has travelled," such as one who prepares provisions and riding supplies and makes ready for it, is a journey; what is not so regarded is not. He mentioned among such matters the journey. Some scholars said: if one leaves a distance of three miles, regardless of whether it is called a journey, one shortens the prayer. Others said: if one leaves a distance of three farsakh, based on the hadith of Anas ibn Malik: "The Prophet ﷺ, when he went out three miles or farsakh (the doubt is from Shu'bah), would pray two rak'ahs."[[Reported by Muslim (691/12), from the hadith of Anas.]] So on this view one says: since the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, would pray two rak'ahs when he left this distance, we adopt it. But Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said: this is a report of an event that occurred; we do not know what would be the case if one left a lesser or greater distance. A greater distance certainly requires shortening, a fortiori. As for a lesser distance: if you reflect on the wording of the hadith, you find that it implies no shortening for less, because it says "if he went out three," "if he went out," so its implication is that if one goes out less, there is no shortening. We say: the minimum is three miles or farsakh; which is more cautious? Three farsakh. However, the majority of scholars hold it to be sixteen farsakh; they hold that the duration of the distance for shortening is sixteen farsakh, so whatever reaches it is shortening and whatever is less is not shortening. Based on this we say: since the matter has no clear legal limit, when one leaves this distance in which the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, would pray two rak'ahs, one shortens. What is less is a matter of doubt, and the basic principle is—what is the basic principle? Completion. The basic principle is completion, so one completes. Whoever leaves beyond three farsakh shortens, except that it is not counted as a journey. For example, a man who goes out a distance of three farsakh and returns the same day is not regarded as a traveller, even by custom, so the rulings of travel do not apply to him. But if a man goes out three farsakh and stays for a period in that place, he is regarded as a traveller. So the journey is now either defined by a distance or by time, according to custom.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾. The expression differs: in the case of the sick it says ﴿مَنْ كَانَ مِنْكُمْ مَرِيضًا﴾ (whoever among you is sick), while for the journey it says ﴿أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾ (or on a journey). What is the wisdom? It may be said—and Allah knows best—that the traveller may be in a state resembling residence, a state resembling residence, such as if he stays in a town at ease, reassured, and shaded. In reality he is not like a traveller, but he is on a journey. His intention is not to settle, like what happened to the Messenger ﷺ during the Conquest, when he stayed in Makkah for nineteen days, shortening the prayer, and he broke his fast until the month ended, as in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in al-Bukhari.[[Reported by al-Bukhari (1080), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] The Messenger ﷺ here, being in a town, what is considered? He is as if resident; he and the residents are on equal footing. Yet in reality he is on a journey, since his intention is not to settle; his intention is to remain in this place for a period according to his need, then return. So here we say: he is on a journey. This is one benefit. Another benefit, according to the view of some scholars: one who is preparing for a journey is like one who has departed on it. For example, a person who has resolved to set out after noon in Ramadan, who is readying his belongings, carrying his goods, and the like—they say: even if he is in his own town, it is permissible for him to break the fast. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) used to do so and would say: "It is from the Sunnah."[[Reported by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (4/247), from the hadith of Anas.]] However, this hadith has some criticism directed at it. Yet according to those who affirm it, one says: when a person resolves to travel, he becomes one who breaks the fast, and they said this is better than that he fasts and then breaks it when he departs, since he has not entered into the act of worship at all. But the majority of scholars, including the four Imams, hold contrary to this view: that he is not entitled to break the fast unless he actually departs, with a difference among them as well over whether one who travels during the day while fasting may break the fast. The correct view is that he may break it, because the Sunnah indicates this.
* A student: Does he break the fast if he is preparing?
* The Shaykh: No, I do not hold this, I do not hold this; because the hadith is subject to criticism, and in my own mind I have some reservation about it. The basic principle is the obligation of fasting. Praise be to Allah, if he sets out, since he is permitted to break the fast once he has departed, he departs fasting, and if he wishes he breaks it.
* A student: It is possible for the journey to be delayed due to an external cause.
* The Shaykh: It may be delayed, especially in our time now, because now a person is tied to others (...) journeys. In the past a man would load his camel and set off; but now, especially with aircraft, one is bound to others.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿فَعِدَّةٌ مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ (then a number of other days). It is known that the majority of scholars, apart from the Zahiriyyah (literalists), say that the verse has an implied omission, which is: "so he breaks the fast, and upon him is a number [of days]." The Zahiriyyah said: there is no omission, because the basic principle is its absence; when speech is between omission and non-omission, the basic principle is non-omission. On this view, ﴿فَمَنْ كَانَ مِنْكُمْ مَرِيضًا أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ﴾ (so whoever among you is sick or on a journey), then his obligation is ﴿عِدَّةٌ مِنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ (a number of other days). So if he fasts, it does not suffice him, because Allah only obligated upon him a number of ﴿أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ (other days). ﴿أُخَرَ﴾ means different from these days; so if he fasts, it does not suffice him. This view, were it not for the existence of the Sunnah, would be strong because of the strength of its reasoning. But the Sunnah has clarified that the verse must include an omission: "so he breaks the fast." That is because it is established that the Companions, with the Prophet ﷺ, included those who fasted and those who broke the fast; the fasting person did not reproach the one who broke the fast, nor did the one who broke it reproach the fasting person. Had fasting been unlawful, the Companions would not have done it in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. Indeed, the Prophet ﷺ himself used to fast in Ramadan, as in the hadith of Abu al-Darda: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ in Ramadan in the intense heat, and the one most shaded among us was the owner of the cloak; some of us would shield the sun with his hand; and none of us was fasting except the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah."[[Agreed upon; reported by al-Bukhari (1945) from the hadith of Abu al-Darda, and Muslim (1119/100) from the hadith of Anas with nearly this wording.]]
* A student: During a journey?
* The Shaykh: During a journey, during a journey. This is evidence for the permissibility of fasting while travelling.
