The word "now" (الآن), as we have already explained, is a demonstrative of present time (اسم إشارة إلى الزمن الحاضر), indeclinable in the fatha (مبنية على الفتح) and in the place of an accusative (في محل نصب). As for His words ﴿have relations with them﴾, the intended meaning of mubashara (المباشرة) is intercourse (الجماع), and it was called mubashara because of the meeting of the two skins (البشرتين) in it: the skin of the woman and the skin of the man. As for His words ﴿have relations with them﴾, it is, as we all know, an imperative verb (فعل أمر). So what is the intended meaning of this command?
* Student: Permission (الإباحة).
* Shaykh: Permission, or the lifting of the prohibition (رفع التحريم)?
* Student: Or that.
* Shaykh: "Or that" no; there is a difference between them.
* Student: It is permission.
* Shaykh: No, no, there is a difference between them. For this reason the scholars of usul al-fiqh (الأصوليون) differed concerning a command that follows a prohibition (الأمر بعد الحظر): is it for permission, or is it a lifting of the prohibition? Some of them said: it is for permission, and some said: it is a lifting of the prohibition, and there is a difference between them. If we say it is for permission, the meaning is that this act after the prohibition has become merely permissible. If we say it is a lifting of the prohibition, the meaning is that this thing has returned to its ruling before the prohibition: if it was obligatory, it is obligatory; if it was recommended, it is recommended; if it was permissible, it is permissible. Now has the difference between the two statements become clear, or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: The argument of those who say it is for permission: they say that when the prohibition came upon the original ruling it abrogated it and it became as though it had never been. So when the command comes after it, its meaning is that it has become permissible, having been forbidden and now becoming permissible. This is a strong argument.
And those who said it is a lifting of the prohibition said: because the original ruling, when the prohibition came upon it, became forbidden, so when the prohibition was removed it returned to what it was. It is as if the prohibition were a veil placed over something covered; when the veil is lifted, what is covered is as it was. For this reason they said, regarding the words of the Exalted, ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2], is hunting permissible, or does it follow its previous ruling? It follows the previous ruling. This is what appears more likely, although the matter is not, in my view, so clear-cut, because both justifications are strong. But what appears closer is that a command after a prohibition is a lifting of the prohibition.
﴿So when the prayer has been concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 10]. This is a command after a prohibition, because He said: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 9]. Then He said: ﴿So when the prayer has been concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty.› Shall we now say that trade, which had been forbidden, has become merely permissible now, or has become recommended, or what? We say it has returned to what it was, and trade, as is known, may be obligatory, may be recommended, and may be permissible.
* Student: We say it indicates permission, but there is another proof in this verse; what is permission here? There are other proofs (...).
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: For example, in this verse.
* Shaykh: No, we are speaking of the general rule: is the abrogation of a prohibition a lifting of it, or does it imply permission, a command after a prohibition?
* Student: I think it implies permission, for example, but other proofs have indicated (...) in other places.
* Shaykh: No, there is a difference between them.
* Student: According to our statement that the permissible is subject to the five rulings, does the difference between the two expressions apply?
* Shaykh: Yes, because if we say it returns to what it was, or that it lifts the prohibition, we look at this thing that was forbidden now: was it recommended before the prohibition? Then it is recommended, and if it was recommended before the command, it remains recommended.
* Student: But, Shaykh, like trade, what is its ruling...?
* Shaykh: No, trade's ruling is permissibility, without doubt.
* Student: O Shaykh, (...) do both matters come to permissibility?
* Shaykh: Which?
* Student: The return of what Allah cast upon...
* Shaykh: Yes, because hunting is originally permissible. But if something is of a kind that is sought, like if I said to you: do not visit so-and-so, who is your relative for example, and then I said to you: when the sun rises, visit him, this command does not mean permission. If we say it lifts the prohibition, the visit has become recommended again; and if we say it is for permission, the visit remains permissible. This is the meaning.
* Student: What about His words ﴿and He has pardoned you﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿Have relations with them﴾: I said the intended meaning is intercourse, and what is less than that is, a fortiori, not prohibited.
﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾. ﴿Seek﴾: ask for, ﴿what﴾: that which, ﴿Allah has decreed for you﴾: has written for you. Is the writing here the universal decree (الكتابة الكونية) or the legislative prescription (الكتابة الشرعية)? That is, does it mean what Allah has destined for you, or what Allah has legislated for you? We say it may bear both meanings, and including both is preferable. So the meaning is: seek what Allah has legislated for you, i.e., seek what He has legislated for you of enjoyment of women and its permissibility, or what He has legislated for you of night prayer in the nights of Ramadan, or what He has legislated for you of the pre-dawn meal (السحور); all of this is included. Or: seek what Allah has decreed for you by way of destiny (كتابة قدرية), such as seeking offspring through this intercourse, as some exegetes said: "seek offspring," meaning: do not let your intercourse be for the sake of attaining desire only, but for the sake of obtaining offspring and progeny. So I say: the verse includes both meanings, ﴿and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾, and the benefits, Allah willing, will come to us.
﴿And eat and drink﴾ is conjoined to ﴿have relations with them﴾, according to the first reading, on ﴿have relations with them﴾. ﴿Eat and drink﴾: what is the meaning of eating and drinking? What about eating and drinking?
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: But it does not become clear to us, and so it is: at the first appearance of dawn, there is no doubt that it does not become clear all at once; it appears gradually, but we are responsible for what we can do until it becomes clear and evident to us.
As for His words ﴿the white thread from the black thread﴾: we understood, when He said ﴿from the thread﴾, that ﴿becomes distinct﴾ means becomes distinguished, one distinguished from the other, as He said: ﴿until Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [Al 'Imran 179]. So "min" (مِن) does not come after yatabayyana here except when distinction is intended; meaning: until the white thread is distinguished from the black thread of dawn. ﴿From the dawn﴾ explains what is meant by the thread: the thread of what? The whiteness of the day; and the black thread? The blackness of the night. In describing them as two threads there is evidence that they alternate, and that this may be in one direction and that in another direction, for they are two threads, and two threads must alternate; otherwise they would be only one thread.
As for His words ﴿until the white thread from the black thread from the dawn becomes distinct to you﴾: the Messenger ﷺ explained that dawn is of two kinds: true and false. He explained that the true dawn is that which appears spread across the horizon (معترضًا في الأفق), spreading like a bird or like a bird's wing from north to south. As for the false dawn, it is that which appears as an elongated streak (مستطيلًا) on the horizon, like the tail of a wolf (كذنب السرحان), i.e., the tail of a wolf.
The scholars mentioned three differences between them. The first: the true dawn is spreading and crosswise, while the other is elongated. The second: after the true dawn there is no darkness, whereas after the other there is darkness. The third: the true dawn is joined to the horizon, while the other has darkness between it and the horizon (...).
﴿until the white thread from the black thread from the dawn becomes distinct to you﴾: we said that ﴿becomes distinct﴾ means becomes apparent, but it implicitly carries the meaning of manifestation and distinction. From where? From His words ﴿the white thread from the thread﴾, meaning: one is distinguished from the other.
His words ﴿from the dawn﴾ are an explanation of ﴿the white thread﴾. He did not say "in the black thread of the night," being content with the first, as in His words: ﴿And He made for you garments to protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 81], meaning: and the cold, since garments protect from both heat and cold; ﴿and garments to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Nahl 81], like armor. The point is that this is from the figure of speech of mentioning one of two opposites and omitting the other: meaning, until the white thread from the dawn from the black thread of the night becomes distinct to you. Do you understand? But "from the night" is omitted, being content with His words ﴿from the dawn﴾, because a thing becomes distinct by mentioning its opposite. A parallel to this? ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾, meaning: and the cold.
His words ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: "then" (ثم) refers to after the distinction becomes clear. This is from the vastness of the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He used "then" after the distinction, to give latitude to the servants. For this reason Imam Ahmad narrated with a chain that is acceptable: "If the dawn call is heard while the vessel is in your hand, do not put it down from your hand until you have fulfilled your need." (Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (10629), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.) This is to ease matters for those who are responsible. For this reason "Ibn Umm Maktum would not call the adhan until dawn had broken, and it would be said to him: You have entered the morning, you have entered the morning." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (617) and Muslim (1092/36), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar; the wording is al-Bukhari's.)
His words ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: ﴿complete﴾ (أتموا) means finish, finish it completely. As for ﴿the fast﴾ (الصيام): it was mentioned earlier that in language it means abstention (الإمساك), and from it the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam 26], meaning abstention from speech, as evidenced by His words: ﴿so I will not speak today to any human being﴾. The term fasting in the Sharia is worship of Allah, the Exalted, by abstaining from what breaks the fast from the emergence of the second dawn until sunset.
As for His words ﴿until the night﴾: what is meant by the night? Its darkness? The answer: No, but its beginning. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained this when he said: "When the night approaches from here," and he pointed to the east, "and the day withdraws from here," and he pointed to the west, "and the sun sets, the fasting person has broken his fast." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1941) and Muslim (1100/51), from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, may Allah be pleased with them.) And with the mere setting of the sun, that is, the setting of its disc, the fast is broken; it is not a condition that the redness disappear, as some common people think.
﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: so the fast is bounded by "from" and "until," so do not add to it or subtract from it. The ruling on continuous fasting (الوصال) will come in the benefits, Allah willing.
His words ﴿And do not have relations with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques﴾: when He said ﴿It has been made lawful for you to go to your wives during the night of fasting; they are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾, He excepted one state from this, which is: when a person is secluded in the mosques while fasting, he does not have relations with his wife. For this reason He said ﴿And do not have relations with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques﴾. The pronoun in "them" refers to the women, and the clause ﴿while you are devoting yourselves to worship﴾ is a circumstantial clause (حال) from the waw in ﴿do not have relations﴾. The word ﴿devoting yourselves﴾ (عاكفون) is an active participle from ʿakafa (عَكَفَ يَعْكُفُ), and devotion to a thing (العكوف على الشيء) means staying with it and persisting in it. From it is the words of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to his people: ﴿What are these statues to which you are devoted?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 52], meaning: persisting and constant. For this reason we say: i'tikaf (الاعتكاف) in language means remaining with a thing; in the Sharia it is worship of Allah, the Exalted, by remaining in the mosques in obedience to Him: remaining in the mosques for the sake of obedience to Allah. This is i'tikaf.
I'tikaf was known in the pre-Islamic period and is known in Islam. ʿUmar said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I vowed to devote one night in the Sacred Mosque during the pre-Islamic period?" The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Fulfill your vow." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2032) and Muslim (1656/27), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them.) It is prescribed in Ramadan, and the Messenger ﷺ used to seclude himself seeking the Night of Power (ليلة القدر); for this reason he secluded himself in the first ten nights, then he was told: the night is not in this ten, so he secluded himself in the middle ten, then it was shown to him in the last ten, until he went out to the people and said: "I was shown that night, so whoever was secluded, let him seclude himself in the last ten nights." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2016) and Muslim (1167/216), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him.) So i'tikaf in Ramadan was for the sake of seeking the Night of Power. Later, Allah willing, the ruling on i'tikaf will come to us in the benefits: is it a sunnah? Is fasting a condition for it or not?
From the mention of i'tikaf after the verses on fasting, some scholars deduced that i'tikaf is only in Ramadan and at its end, since Allah mentioned it following the verses on fasting after concluding the discussion of fasting. And Allah knows best whether this inference holds or does not hold.
Then the Exalted said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾. ("Tilka" (تلك): what is "ti"? What is its meaning? "Ti" tilka?)
* Student: A demonstrative (اسم إشارة).
* Shaykh: "Ti" is a demonstrative, the "la" indicates distance, and the "ka" is a particle of address (حرف خطاب). It was previously mentioned that this "ka" is according to the addressee, and the demonstrative according to the thing pointed to, and that the most eloquent form is for the "ka" to follow the addressee: for masculine singular one says dhalika, for feminine dhalik, for dual dhalikuma, for masculine plural dhalikum, for feminine plural dhalikunna. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that is your assumption which you assumed﴾ [Fussilat 23]; ﴿And they are called out: That is the Garden which you have been made to inherit﴾ [al-A'raf 43]; and He said: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ [Yusuf 32]; and for the dual He said: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾; and for the singular: "dhalika," and it is frequent. This is the well-known classical dialect. There is a second dialect: that the "ka" is always singular and open, according to the interpretation of the addressee as singular. And there is a third dialect: its fatha for the masculine in all cases, and its kasra for the feminine in all cases.
Here, is "tilka" for the masculine singular, or not? The meaning is: that, O addressee, even if he addresses all people, since "people" is a genus, so it is valid to refer to it with the addressee form.
* Student: Shaykh, in His words ﴿And those days﴾ [Al 'Imran 140], while observing the addressee in the "ka," why is the pronoun not plural?
* Shaykh: Yes, often the plural is omitted; in the Qur'an the majority is singular, as if He addresses humankind in general through the Qur'an, addressing the human being; meaning: that, O human being, are the limits of Allah. And this is frequent; even the addresses without the "ka" in the demonstrative you will find in the singular.
He said: and ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾: "limits" (حدود) is the plural of "limit" (حد).
* Student: You said: with a waw.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ has no waw. ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾: the "hudud" (الحدود) is the plural of "hadd" (حد), and hadd in language means prevention, as in "the boundaries of the house" (حدود الدار), because they prevent others from entering it. So the meaning of ﴿the limits of Allah﴾ is His prohibitions (موانعه).
Know that the limits of Allah are of two kinds: limits that prevent, i.e., they keep whoever is outside from entering, and these are the barriers to entry, which concern the prohibited things; and other limits that prevent whoever is within from leaving, and these are the limits of the commands. The limits of Allah the Exalted are prohibitions and commands. The prohibitions: what is their nature? They keep whoever is outside from entering. The commands keep whoever is within from leaving. For this reason, when commands come, Allah says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah 229], meaning: do not go out of them; and when prohibitions come, He says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah 187]. This is the difference, and all of them are called limits, because commands have a limit you do not go beyond, and prohibitions have a limit you do not enter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 186–188 (part 4 of 7):

His saying: ﴿Those are the limits of Allah﴾ is an instance of attributing what is prescribed to the one who prescribed it. ﴿So do not approach them﴾: the fa' is for consequence (al-tafri'), and (lā) is a prohibitive particle. What is the evidence?
* A student: The deletion of the nūn.
* The Shaykh: It is jussive, by the deletion of the nūn. ﴿So do not approach them﴾: he did not say "so do not do them." Rather, He forbade approaching them, so that we keep far from the prohibited thing and from the means to the prohibited thing, because means have the rulings of the ends. How many a person has hovered around the sanctuary (al-hima) and then fallen into it! For this reason He said ﴿so do not approach them﴾. Thus, it is obligatory to keep away from the prohibitions and not to draw near to them.
﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾: this occurs frequently in the Qur'an, and we have previously pointed out its i'rab (grammatical analysis), and we said that the kāf is a noun meaning "like," and that it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: like that clarification, Allah makes clear. It occurs frequently in the Qur'an, and this is its i'rab: we say that the kāf is a noun meaning "like," and it is in the accusative as an absolute object, and its governing element is what follows it. His saying ﴿thus﴾ refers to what preceded of clarification. I think there is much clarification in these verses, or not? There is much clarification: Allah, glorified and exalted, has made clear the ruling on eating and drinking at night, the ruling on intimacy with women, the ruling on i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), its place, what is forbidden in it, and so on. The point is that these are a number of rulings which Allah has made clear.
His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear His signs to the people﴾: āyāt (signs) is the plural of āya, which linguistically means "sign" or "indicator." Its meaning in the Sharia is the proofs that indicate what is required of the attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted. Some of them indicate wisdom, some indicate mercy, some indicate knowledge, and some indicate comprehensiveness. The point is that they are diverse. The āyāt are the plural of āya, which linguistically means "sign," and the meaning here in the Sharia is the proofs that indicate what is required of the attributes of Allah.
The scholars have mentioned that the signs are divided into two kinds: cosmic (kawniyya) and legislative (shar'iyya). The cosmic signs are the created beings: all created beings, their essences, their attributes and their conditions, are among the cosmic signs. ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat 37]; ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed in them of living creatures﴾ [al-Shura 29]; ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you from yourselves spouses﴾ [al-Rum 21]; ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust, and then, behold, you are human beings dispersed﴾ [al-Rum 20], and so on. So all created beings, their essences, attributes and conditions, are all among the cosmic signs of Allah, and each is a sign of Allah, because none of the created beings can make the like of them. The sign of a thing is its indication, so none of the created beings can ever make the like of these signs, or not?
The second kind of signs: the legislative signs, which are what Allah, exalted, revealed to His messengers and prophets of revelation. They are legislative signs indicating the One who sent them down, glorified and exalted. The reason: when you reflect upon their reports, you find them in utmost truthfulness, clarity and benefit: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 3]. So the best reports are the reports of the Qur'an, and of revelation generally. When you reflect upon their rulings, you find them the best of rulings: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'ida 50]. Were all of creation to gather to produce the like of the rulings Allah revealed to His messengers, they would not be able to do so. By this they are a sign, is it not? They are a sign of what is required of the attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted. Our saying "of what is required" is because the signs differ: some indicate greatness, some indicate mercy, some indicate knowledge, and some indicate majesty. The point is that they differ.
His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear His signs to the people so that they may become righteous﴾: this (la'alla, "so that") is for causation. Become righteous (yattaqun) toward whom? They become righteous toward Allah, mighty and majestic. Taqwa of Allah, glorified and exalted, is: taking a protection from His punishment by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is taqwa: taking a protection from the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa. Some say that taqwa is that you act in obedience to Allah, upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and that you leave what Allah has forbidden, upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah. Some say that taqwa is abandoning sins, but the most comprehensive of what has been said is what we mentioned at the beginning: taking a protection from His punishment by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. It is true that when it is paired with birr (righteousness), such as ﴿and cooperate in righteousness and taqwa﴾ [al-Ma'ida 2], taqwa means avoiding sins and birr means doing acts of obedience. A poet says:
Leave sins, the small of them and the great of them; that is taqwa.
And act like one walking over a field of thorns, wary of what he sees.
What does the one walking on a field of thorns do? Does he stamp with his foot and not mind? No.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.
Do not belittle a small sin; indeed the mountains are made of pebbles.
This is correct. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, likened the trivial sins to a group of people who descended upon a land and wanted to light a fire. They went and one brought a stick, and another a stick, and another a stick, until they gathered a great amount of firewood and kindled a great fire. And what do they bring? Stick by stick; it is nothing. Yes indeed. So we say: the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa is taking a protection from the punishment of Allah, exalted, by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.
* A student: Could this be a level near to taqwa? That is, taqwa is not something higher than doing the obligations, but rather doing the recommended acts?
* The Shaykh: The commands are recommended acts; the recommended is a command, because a command may be obligatory and may be recommended, and a prohibition may be reprehensible and may be forbidden.
* A student: Should we not say that the verse ﴿Thus Allah makes clear His signs﴾ covers from the beginning of the surah and is not specific to the rulings of fasting?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not apparent, because you know that the verses are separate sections.
* The student: Yes, but the surah is connected?
* The Shaykh: No. And even if it were connected, it could only be in the subject under discussion, and also in what preceded it with verses about it before.
* A student: (...) fasting, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: It includes, and Allah knows best, some scholars said: it includes the four rulings that follow it, from His saying ﴿It has been made lawful for you to go to your wives on the night of the fast﴾ to the end, only. And if it were said that it is from His saying ﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqara 183], it would be good. Then know that His saying ﴿His signs﴾ is a plural construct, so it is general, meaning that this kind of clarification which we have made clear to you in these verses is a clarification of all the signs.
* A student: You know the limit linguistically, but not legally?
* The Shaykh: Yes, I know it.
* The student: No.
* The Shaykh: We said: the limits in the Sharia are the commands and prohibitions of Allah. As for the definition (had) according to the logicians, it is other than this. The logicians' definition we covered earlier in our explanation of the Safarini creed.
* The student: So it differs from what was at...
* The Shaykh: Yes, it differs, according to the terminologies.
* A student: Shaykh, if someone said: the clarification of the signs seems to a person to have as its benefit faith?
* The Shaykh: Faith?
* The student: Faith. Perhaps you, for example, will believe, because then when one believes he becomes righteous.
* The Shaykh: No. Originally there is no taqwa except after faith. So when the signs are made clear to a person, he becomes righteous toward Allah, mighty and majestic, so faith occurs first.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: There is no taqwa, brother, except after faith. Does a person guard against something he does not believe in? He does not.

Then He said: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth by false means﴾. The connection of this verse to what preceded is clear, because what preceded in the verses of fasting was the prohibition of specific things at a specific time. The verse after it, ﴿And do not consume﴾, is a general prohibition: general in what is judged, in its time, and in its place. This is the aspect of connection: when He mentioned the specific prohibition that occurs with fasting, He clarified the general prohibition that occurs both in fasting and outside fasting. So He said: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves by false means﴾. ﴿Do not consume﴾: the intended meaning of consuming is something broader than eating, but He specified eating because it is the strongest way of benefiting. The strongest way of benefiting from wealth is eating. A person benefits from wealth by building a dwelling for himself. The building is attached to him, is it not? But it is not as close to him as clothing. Which is closer to him?
* The students: Clothing.
* The Shaykh: Clothing. Likewise, one spends wealth on garments before spending it on furnishings, and furnishing is more specific than the house, or not? Because furnishing is what is adjacent to him when sleeping, sitting and the like. He spends it on clothing, which is more specific than furnishing. He spends it on food and drink, which is the most specific of things; nothing comes after it. For this reason some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, mentioned that if a person has doubtful wealth, he should spend it on fuel, not on food and drink, because the body is nourished by food and drink, and they are the most specific benefit of wealth.
If Allah says ﴿do not consume your wealth﴾, and this is the most specific benefit, and one who does not do it would perish, for if he did not eat he would die, how then would He return to other than it?
His saying: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves﴾: how does He say ﴿your wealth﴾ ﴿your wealth among yourselves﴾ (...)? We say: we have an eater and something eaten from. If you, the eater, do not accept that your wealth be consumed, how would you accept consuming the wealth of another? Consider the wealth of another as if it were your own wealth. And why? So that you do not consume it, just as you do not accept that someone wrongs you and consumes your wealth. You must place your brother's wealth in the position of your own. So we say: the benefit of attributing the wealth to the one who consumes it, which is consumed belonging to another, is that he should reflect that the wealth of another must be protected by him just as he protects his own wealth.
His saying: ﴿among yourselves﴾ means: in contracts, such as leases, sales, pledges and others, because these occur between two parties. It is all the more fitting that you should not consume it through plunder and usurpation, where there is no transaction between you and another person. That is: if you are forbidden to consume it in contracts, then it is all the more so forbidden to consume it through usurpation, coercion and the like.
His saying: ﴿by false means﴾: the word ﴿bil-batil﴾ (by false means). This bā' is a particle of genitive, but what is its meaning? Is its meaning accompaniment, that is, eating accompanied by falsehood? Or is its meaning instrumental, that falsehood is like a tool with which one eats, as when you say "I slaughtered with the knife," or "I threw it with the stone"? We say that the bā' is suitable for both together. It is not permitted that you take another's wealth by falsehood, by making falsehood a means to take wealth, nor that you consume wealth in a manner accompanied by falsehood. So it includes what is forbidden in itself and what is forbidden because of its attribute.
His saying: ﴿and send it as a bribe to the rulers﴾: ﴿tudlū bihā﴾ (and send it): the pronoun refers either to wealth, or it refers to litigation. The root of idlā' is from adlā dalwahu (he lowered his bucket), and it is known that one who lowers his bucket wants to reach the water. So the meaning of ﴿and send it to the rulers﴾ is that you reach toward the rulers through it, so that you make the rulers a means to consuming it. How does it become a means to consuming it? You deny the right that is upon you when there is no evidence for it, then you dispute with him before the judge. What does the judge say to the accused? He says: bring evidence. If the claimant has no evidence, the oath is directed at you, and if you swear, you are cleared. Do you understand? Now I have sent it to the rulers, meaning I made the ruler a means to consuming wealth. This is one view on the matter. The second view: the meaning of ﴿tudlū bihā ilā al-ḥukkām﴾ is that you convey it to them by bribing the rulers so that they rule in your favor. So the meaning of ﴿tudlū bihā ilā al-ḥukkām﴾ is that you convey it to them for the purpose of what? That they rule for you. Both meanings are correct.
* A student: Does not "the fallāsa" enter into it, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: The fallāsa?
* The student: Yes, the one who makes the rulers bankrupt in order to take wealth unjustly.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but you would not be the one who consumed it.
* The student: Yes, but you sent it to the rulers?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but the verse says ﴿do not consume﴾ and ﴿and send﴾. If we consider the two clauses separate from each other, then yes, it enters as you said, and the prohibition becomes about two things: ﴿do not consume your wealth among yourselves by false means﴾ is an independent clause, and ﴿and send it to the rulers﴾ is an independent clause. But the apparent structure of the wording, meaning the apparent sense of the speech, is that the two clauses are one; for this reason He said ﴿and send it﴾ and did not say ﴿and do not send it﴾, so He made it conjoined with His saying ﴿and do not consume﴾, and so it is built upon it.
* A student: Where does the pronoun return?
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* The student: In the second view, the bribing?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it returns to the wealth.
* The student: Is the wealth with which the judge was bribed different from the wealth...?
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no contradiction, but its meaning would be: do not consume your wealth among yourselves by falsehood, and do not send your wealth so that you may consume this.
* The student: So it is other wealth?
* The Shaykh: Other wealth, in order that by it you may consume the wealth of others, when they rule for you by it.
* A student: Shaykh, does the fallāsa we mentioned not fall under bribery?
* The Shaykh: No, no, the fallāsa is not this. The fallāsa is when one informs the ruler that so-and-so has wealth in order that he may take it from him.
* A student: With us, in (...), we say "upon it (...)," meaning he bribes, so the matter became confused for him?
* The Shaykh: No, he points the rulers to people's wealth so that they may consume it.
* A student: Are the rulers judges, or rulers...?
* The Shaykh: The rulers are the princes. If we say the meaning is as Ghanim said, that is one case; but if we say the meaning is "at the time of litigation," then it includes both princes and judges who rule.

He said: ﴿and send it to the rulers so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people﴾. His saying ﴿so that you may consume﴾: someone may say there is a difficulty in it, because He said ﴿and do not consume﴾ and then said ﴿so that you may consume﴾; how does He give a reason for the ruling by the same ruling? We say: the lām here is not for causation, but the lām here is for consequence, meaning that when you do it, the consumption occurs for you, the consumption of a portion of the wealth of people. So the lām here is for consequence, and the lām comes for consequence as in His saying, exalted: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. Did the family of Pharaoh pick him up for this cause, or was the consequence so? The consequence was so. So the lām in His saying ﴿li-ta'kulū﴾ is the lām of consequence.
His saying ﴿li-ta'kulū﴾: why was the nūn deleted?
* A student: It is in the accusative.
* The Shaykh: It is in the accusative by an implied "an" after the lām according to one view, or by the lām itself according to whose view?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct. ﴿li-ta'kulū farīqan min amwāl al-nās﴾: farīq means a group or party, and it was called farīq because it separates from others. So this is a group of people, meaning a party of them that has separated and split off.
His saying ﴿farīqan min amwāl al-nās﴾: if someone said, "He might consume all the wealth of the defendant?"
* A student: Then it is all the more so.
* The Shaykh: All the more so? Yes, all the more so. Or we say that the wealth of the defendant is a portion of people's wealth in the general sense, because however much wealth a person may have, others also have wealth. Yes indeed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 186–188 (part 5 of 7):

﴿مِنْ أَمْوَالِ النَّاسِ بِالْإِثْمِ﴾ ﴿لِتَأْكُلُوا فَرِيقًا مِنْ أَمْوَالِ النَّاسِ بِالْإِثْمِ﴾ The bāʾ here is for accompaniment (muṣāḥabah), meaning: eating accompanied by sin (ithm), which is wrongdoing; and that is because it is false (bāṭil). From this we know that bāṭil means ithm. But is bāṭil always ithm? No. Bāṭil may refer to that which has no benefit in it, as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): «Every diversion with which the son of Adam diverts himself is bāṭil, except his playing with his bow, his playing with his wife, or his training of his horse» [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (1637), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (17300), from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir (may Allah be pleased with him).]].
* * *
﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ﴾.
* Several benefits are derived from this verse. First: fasting is a occasion for the answering of supplication, because Allah the Exalted mentioned this verse in the midst of the verses on fasting, and especially since He mentioned it at the end of the discussion of the verses on fasting. Some scholars said: from it another benefit is derived, that it is recommended to supplicate at the end of the day of fasting.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed; because it was mentioned after we spoke about fasting and abstaining.
* Student: It may be said: it is more fitting on the ʿĪd?
* Shaykh: No, but every day counts as one act of worship.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah the Exalted has knowledge of the unseen, because His saying ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ﴾ is in the future.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the compassion (raʾfah) of Allah the Mighty and Majestic in His saying ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي﴾, where He attributed them to Himself as an honour and as tenderness toward them.
* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of the nearness of Allah the Exalted, from His saying ﴿فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾; and all the pronouns refer to Allah: ﴿إِنِّي قَرِيبٌ أُجِيبُ﴾ ﴿إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾ ﴿فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي﴾, six pronouns all referring to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. So from this noble verse is derived His nearness, the Exalted.
Is the nearness of Allah general or specific? The discussion of this matter has already preceded us, and we explained that the nearness of Allah is only specific, and that His saying ﴿وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ الْوَرِيدِ﴾ [Qāf 16] means: by His angels; and likewise His saying ﴿فَلَوْلَا إِذَا بَلَغَتِ الْحُلْقُومَ (٨٣) وَأَنْتُمْ حِينَئِذٍ تَنْظُرُونَ (٨٤) وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْكُمْ﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah 83–85], also means: by His angels.
Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Nearness (qurb) is not reported in a general sense as companionship (maʿiyyah) is. Companionship is reported in both general and specific senses, but as for nearness, Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that it is reported only in a specific sense, specific to the one who calls upon Him or the one who worships Him. The one who calls upon Him is as in this verse: ﴿أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾, and as in the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): «O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you do not call upon one who is deaf or absent, but you call upon One who is Hearing and Near, and He is with you»[[Previously cited.]]. As for His nearness to the worshipper, it is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating»[[Narrated by Muslim (482/215), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]; because this is worship." It has also preceded us that His nearness to His servants does not negate what has been mentioned of His exaltedness and His being above; for He, the Exalted, is not like anything in all His attributes. A created being cannot be near while being far, but the Creator can be near while being far. On this basis, this verse does not indicate that Allah the Exalted is not above, because there is no contradiction between the two in regard to the Creator.
* Student: Companionship (...) is more specific than nearness, or nearness is more specific (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the apparent view is that nearness is more specific, more specific than it; and for this reason it did not come in a general sense, unlike companionship.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of Allah's hearing, from where is it taken? From His saying ﴿أُجِيبُ﴾; for one is not answered except after his supplication is heard.
* And among them: affirmation of Allah's power, because answering the supplicant requires power.
* And among them: affirmation of Allah's generosity, from His saying ﴿أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾.
* And among the benefits of the verse also: that one of the conditions for the answering of supplication is that the supplicant be sincere in his calling upon Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such that he is sincerely devoted, aware of his neediness toward his Lord, and aware of the generosity and bounty of Allah. From where is this benefit taken? From where is this benefit taken?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From His saying ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي﴾ to His saying ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ﴾, or not? Do we want the specific word?
* Student: ﴿إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾; because we alerted to this in the tafsir. So then, what is required for the answering of supplication? That the supplicant be sincere in his supplication, such that he is devoted to Allah, and that he has a sense of his neediness toward Allah the Mighty and Majestic; for a person does not supplicate except while feeling need; and that he has a sense of what? Of the self-sufficiency of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and His answering; from His saying ﴿إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that turning (inābah) to Allah the Mighty and Majestic and carrying out His obedience is a cause of right guidance, from His saying ﴿فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ﴾.
* And among its benefits also: that responding must be accompanied by faith, because Allah joined the two; so whoever worships Allah while his faith is weak, meaning that he has doubt, may Allah protect us, or uncertainty, it does not benefit him; or he also has denial, as the hypocrites do, for they worship Allah the Mighty and Majestic outwardly but they have no faith, so it does not benefit them.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of causes and means.
The Jahmiyyah are Jabriyyah, and so are the Ashʿariyyah; that is, we have already said that the Ashʿariyyah affirm causes only as formal causes, saying that causes do not act by themselves, but the act occurs with them.
Then the Exalted said: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكُمْ لَيْلَةَ الصِّيَامِ الرَّفَثُ إِلَى نِسَائِكُمْ هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَهُنَّ﴾ [al-Baqarah 187] and so on to the end.
When we know the occasion of revelation, we benefit from this noble verse, we benefit the mercy of Allah the Exalted toward His servants. How so?
* Student: By abrogation (naskh), meaning the abrogation of the first ruling.
* Shaykh: By abrogation; the first ruling was one of severity, as they used to be, if they slept or prayed ʿIshāʾ, women, food and drink were forbidden to them.
* From this verse is derived: permissibility of speech between a husband and his wife concerning what is shameful, from where is it taken?
* Student: From ﴿الرَّفَثُ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿الرَّفَثُ إِلَى نِسَائِكُمْ﴾; because it includes the meaning of intimacy (ifḍāʾ).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: permissibility of a man's enjoyment of his wife from the moment of the marriage contract; from where is it taken?
* Students: ﴿إِلَى نِسَائِكُمْ﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿إِلَى نِسَائِكُمْ﴾.
I have been asked several times about a man who contracts marriage with a woman but the consummation is after a month, two months, or three; is it permissible for him to enjoy her or not?
* Students: It is permissible.
* Shaykh: It is permissible; but among people, some ignorant people think it is not permissible until the marriage is announced, until it is announced, is on the wedding night. But here there is something to be feared, which is that a pregnancy may occur, and if a pregnancy occurs, especially if the consummation is delayed, suspicion may arise. So if a person fears this matter, then, praise be to Allah, he can control himself and enjoy her without intercourse, so as to avoid suspicion among the common people. As for students of knowledge, no suspicion arises for them; because by the mere contract the woman becomes a bed (firāsh) for him, and the child is attributed to him according to the school, even if he has not been with her, while it is possible to be with her, as long as we do not know that he was with her; so the child is his child. I think this has passed over us before: by what the woman becomes a bed. So the matter has no difficulty for students of knowledge, but among the common people there is difficulty; yet from the legal standpoint there is no harm in her being his wife from the day he contracts with her.
* Student: Based on the obligation of announcing the marriage.
* Shaykh: No, they do not mean this, but they only mean custom; otherwise they do not know whether announcing the marriage is obligatory or not.
* Student: (...) shyness (ḥayāʾ) in the woman?
* Shaykh: No no, shyness among women today has begun to diminish.
* Student: There is no longer blame on the common people in this, from the aspect of (...) shyness and so on.
* Shaykh: But now it has gone...
* Student: As for the dowry (mahr), O Shaykh, the dowry was not paid; among them there are people who contracted and did not receive the dowry.
* Shaykh: No, with us the dowry is paid before the contract; in our custom here it is paid before the contract.
* Student: Some people did not take the dowry; there are people who contracted and did not take the dowry.
* Shaykh: Perhaps, perhaps there are people...
* Student: They refuse.
* Shaykh: It is not necessary.
* Student: But there is nothing wrong, I mean, if the dowry is left at the marriage... at, I mean.
* Shaykh: The consummation.
* Student: The consummation.
* Shaykh: Yes, there is nothing wrong.
* Student: If he consummated...
* Shaykh: It passed over us in the chapter on the dowry that it is permissible to postpone it or to postpone part of it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is the custom of the people.
* Student: It is written in the contract.
* Shaykh: There is nothing wrong.
* Student: (...) if the dowry is presented as is our custom, is it then specified (musammā)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not valid (...).
* Student: He handed it over.
* Shaykh: Yes, even if we say he handed it over, because it is not specified at the contract; with us it is not specified at the contract.
* Student: So if he dies, for example, or divorces her, is it affected?
* Shaykh: If he divorces her before the consummation?
* Student: Yes, if it is handed over (...).
* Shaykh: Even if he handed it over.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: (...) because it is known among them.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse is this meaning derived from His saying ﴿هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَهُنَّ﴾, namely that the woman is a covering for the man's nakedness just as the man is a covering for the woman's nakedness.
* Second: that there is between them the closeness of garments and those who wear them: ﴿هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَكُمْ وَأَنْتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَهُنَّ﴾.
In it also is protection of the private parts (...).
* And from it is derived, from His saying ﴿هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَكُمْ﴾, the affirmation of causes in rulings; because this clause is for causation, the causation of permissibility.
* From the noble verse is derived: the knowledge of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; from it is derived the affirmation of Allah's knowledge of what is in the souls, from His saying ﴿عَلِمَ اللَّهُ أَنَّكُمْ كُنْتُمْ تَخْتَانُونَ أَنْفُسَكُمْ﴾.
* And among its benefits: that a person, just as he betrays others, may betray himself, and that is when he brings it into the disobedience of Allah; for this is betrayal, and on this basis a person's self is a trust (amānah) with him.
* This is a benefit branching from His saying ﴿أَنَّكُمْ كُنْتُمْ تَخْتَانُونَ أَنْفُسَكُمْ﴾: that a person's self is a trust with him which he must safeguard; and His Exalted saying confirms this: ﴿وَمَا ظَلَمُونَا وَلَكِنْ كَانُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ يَظْلِمُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 57]; so just as a person wrongs others, he also wrongs himself.
* From this noble verse is derived: the affirmation of repentance from Allah; the attribute of Allah as one who repents, from His saying ﴿فَتَابَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾. Is it one of the essential attributes or the active attributes?
* Student: Active.
* Shaykh: Active, yes.
* Student: Do we say in describing Him: repentance, or is the correct form "Oft-Returning" (tawwāb)?
* Shaykh: No, repentance: repentance is among His attributes, and His name is at-Tawwāb.
* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of Allah's pardon, from His saying ﴿وَعَفَا عَنْكُمْ﴾.
* And among its benefits: permissibility of abrogation, or the affirmation of abrogation, contrary to whoever denies it; and in this verse it is explicit. From where is it taken? From His saying ﴿فَالْآنَ﴾, ﴿فَالْآنَ بَاشِرُوهُنَّ﴾; meaning that before now it was not lawful.
And among its benefits: permissibility of intimacy with the wife in an unrestricted sense without qualification; from where is it taken? From His saying ﴿بَاشِرُوهُنَّ﴾. But this generality is restricted in certain states and restricted in certain places: it is restricted in states, in the state of menstruation, one cannot have intercourse with her, because of the Exalted saying: ﴿فَاعْتَزِلُوا النِّسَاءَ فِي الْمَحِيضِ وَلَا تَقْرَبُوهُنَّ حَتَّى يَطْهُرْنَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 222]; and it is also restricted in the case of the rear passage, in the place of the rear, for it is not lawful for a person to have intercourse with a woman in her rear.
It has been mentioned of Imam al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, a debate, which I used to find strange, that he engaged in a discussion permitting intercourse with a woman in her rear; but it has come to my attention that this is not authentically from al-Shafiʿi, and that al-Shafiʿi explicitly stated the prohibition of intercourse in the rear, and this is most befitting to him. There is no doubt that the prohibition of intercourse in the rear, even though the ahadith that came concerning it contain something and have some discussion, their collection at least requires that they be ḥasan, to be relied upon. Then, if we reflect on the Exalted saying: ﴿فِي الْمَحِيضِ﴾, ﴿قُلْ هُوَ أَذًى فَاعْتَزِلُوا النِّسَاءَ فِي الْمَحِيضِ﴾ [al-Baqarah 222], ﴿أَذًى فَاعْتَزِلُوا﴾, we find that harm and filth in the rear are greater and more severe, so the verse indicates by allusion the prohibition of intercourse in the rear. Moreover, His saying ﴿فَأْتُوا حَرْثَكُمْ أَنَّى شِئْتُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah 223] shows that the place of enjoyment is the place of tilth, which is the vagina, but not the rear. However, a person may still enjoy his wife by other than tilth, such as enjoying between the thighs; this is not objectionable.
* Student: For example, "touched" (...).
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: The enjoyment.
* Shaykh: Between the thighs?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, touching. ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger (ﷺ) used to order me, so I would wrap a waist-wrap, and he would be intimate with me while I was menstruating."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (300).]]
* Student: We said: since she is menstruating, touching her is not permissible.
* Shaykh: The touching intended is intercourse.
So then, His saying ﴿فَالْآنَ بَاشِرُوهُنَّ﴾: is this unrestricted act restricted or not? It is restricted by what the Shariʿah has forbidden in a state or place.
* Student: Is it authentic what is attributed to Ibn ʿUmar and others, that they permitted this kind of approach?
* Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know whether it is authentically from them or not; I do not think it is authentic; this is far-fetched.
* Student: Al-Shaykhayn mentioned it (...), al-Bukhari for example, if he permitted this thing.
* Shaykh: Verify it for us, and it is upon you, God willing.
* Student: Yes, meaning from the rear into the front in some ahadith?
* Shaykh: Yes, behold, this is the Sunnah: from her rear into her front, this is permissible; it may be that it is understood in this sense; there is doubt in it, and by Allah we will see whether it is authentic from them.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that a person should intend by his intercourse the seeking of offspring, from His saying ﴿وَابْتَغُوا مَا كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ﴾.
"And it is mentioned from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he would not have intercourse except when he desired a child"[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah (19479), and Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-ʿIyal (390), in which: "Were it not for children, I would not desire them," from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him).]]; but nevertheless this does not prevent a person from acting merely out of desire; there is no prohibition in this.
* Among the benefits of the verse: that a person should not divert himself with enjoyment from performing acts of obedience; from where is it taken?
* Students: ﴿وَابْتَغُوا مَا كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah 187].
* Shaykh: According to one of the two interpretations, in which it was explained that the meaning of ﴿وَابْتَغُوا مَا كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ﴾ is seeking the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) and standing in prayer[[See what al-Tabari recorded in his tafsir (3/246), and Ibn Abi Hatim in his tafsir (1683) (1/317), from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both).]].
* Student: Is it authentic from ʿUmar (...)?
* Shaykh: Perhaps it is, perhaps it is authentic.
* And among them, among the benefits of the verse: permissibility of eating and drinking during the nights of fasting; because of His saying ﴿كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا حَتَّى يَتَبَيَّنَ﴾.
Some scholars took from this the recommendation of suḥūr, or suḥūr with a ḍammah, so what is your opinion?
* Student: (...) the exact place of the verse.
* Shaykh: From this verse is it there, or not?
* Student: Because the lām is for emphasis?
* Shaykh: There is no lām.
* Student: Even for the limit (ḥattā lil-ghāyah).

The Shaykh: "Until" (ḥattā, *lil-ghāyah*, the particle of limit).

* Student: (...)

* The Shaykh: Some scholars derived a ruling from this, and this derivation has depth. What is its basis? They say: the permission to eat and drink on the night of fasting was granted out of consideration for the one who is obligated. The later one delays it, until near the break of dawn, the kinder it is to him. Do you all agree?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: There is no need to pause. The later you eat, until the break of dawn, the easier it is for you, or not? They said: since the text of the permission is for the sake of ease for the one obligated, it implies that eating at the break of dawn is better than before it, because it is easier.

This derivation is sound, and the ḥadīth supports it too. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Take the pre-dawn meal (*taṣaḥḥarū*), for in the *suḥūr* there is blessing." Or: "in the *suḥūr*."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (300) from ʿĀʾishah.]] The *suḥūr* with a *ḍammah* refers to the act (of eating), and with a *fatḥah* refers to what is eaten; both readings are permissible. There is blessing in the *suḥūr*. For this reason, one meal suffices a person in place of two meals during the day, and one drink suffices him in place of how many? In place of six drinks. A person who breaks his fast in the summer may drink six times during the day.

* Student: (...) If someone is awake, for example, and delays his sleep, so that he eats his pre-dawn meal at the beginning of the night, or in (...) the night, and then sleeps, is that easier for him?

* The Shaykh: No, no. It is not easier for him in terms of assistance in fasting, not at all. It is easier in terms of rest for the body. That is outside (...). But in terms of fasting, there is no doubt that this is more helpful for fasting.

In any case, I have presented this derivation to you so that you know that some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have depth in deriving rulings. At first glance you would say: "He did not say: eat and drink at the time of *saḥar*."

* Student: O Shaykh, where do we take (...) the permission? Because it was prohibited and then He permitted it?

* The Shaykh: How is it permitted? For what reason was it permitted?

* Student: This is good, so that it may be obtained...

* The Shaykh: No, no. It was permitted for facilitation, and Allah loves ease, as in His saying: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 185].

* Student: So how do we say that the scholars take the recommendation (*istiḥbāb*)...

* The Shaykh: This is the reason. We said it is recommended, because it was permitted only for the sake of facilitating the one who is obligated, may Allah bless you. Since it is for the sake of facilitation, and facilitation for him is to eat near the break of dawn, it is recommended.

* From this noble verse is derived: is the permission to eat, drink and have intercourse until the break of dawn, or not? Correct, or not? Or until the call to dawn prayer (*adhān al-Fajr*)?

* Students: Until the break of dawn.

* The Shaykh: Until the break of dawn, because of His saying: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you﴾, until it becomes distinct.

* Student: (...) The call to prayer, O Shaykh (...) has risen.

* The Shaykh: No (...). Before dawn. Some of them delay after dawn. For this reason, we attach the ruling to the clear appearance of dawn, not to the call to dawn prayer, except for one who knows that the muezzin calls at the proper time. As the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls the adhān, for he does not call until dawn has risen."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1919), and the wording is his, and Muslim (1092/36), from ʿĀʾishah.]]

* Student: A layperson, for example, does not know, meaning he cannot...

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. They know this by asking the muezzin. If the muezzin is known for care and precision, they follow him.

* From this noble verse is derived a matter on which the scholars differed: if dawn rises while a man is having intercourse with his wife, then if he remains, it is prohibited for him, and if he withdraws, he is obligated to expiate (*kaffārah*). So what is your opinion? The school in our region is the Ḥanbalī school, which holds that if a person has intercourse when dawn rises and then withdraws, he is obligated to expiation: to free a slave, and if he cannot find one, to fast two consecutive months, and if he cannot do that, to feed sixty needy persons. So what do you think of this view? Does the noble verse support it, or does it weaken it?

* Student: It weakens it.

* The Shaykh: The verse weakens it, without doubt. The verse weakens it, because Allah permitted us this until when?

* Students: Until it becomes distinct.

* The Shaykh: Until it becomes distinct to us. Until it becomes distinct. So if a man has intercourse with his wife and has not seen the dawn, he has done something permitted, and what is permitted cannot be punished.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of fasting while in a state of *janābah* (ritual impurity from intercourse), that is, the permissibility of a fasting person beginning the morning in a state of *janābah*. From where is this derived? The permission of intercourse until it becomes distinct. Its meaning is that it is permitted for you to have intercourse until the last moment. It follows from this that you will begin the morning in a state of *janābah*, or not? Yes. It is established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that "he would begin the morning in a state of *janābah* from intercourse with his wives while fasting."[[Reported by Muslim (1109/75) from ʿĀʾishah and Umm Salamah.]] Is that clear?

* Student: We say: whoever begins the morning in a state of *janābah* has nothing against him. What is the evidence for its permissibility?

* The Shaykh: No. We say: it is permissible, because some scholars say that if he begins the morning in a state of *janābah*, his fast is invalidated.

* From the benefits of the verse: the permissibility of eating while in doubt about the break of dawn. The permissibility of eating and drinking while in doubt about the break of dawn. If he says: "By Allah, I now have doubt, I do not know whether what we see is dawn or not, I have doubt." We say: eat, because of His saying: ﴿until it becomes distinct﴾.

* From the noble verse: the refutation of the view of those who say that a fasting person may eat and drink until sunrise, because of His saying: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn﴾. Likewise, the refutation of those who say that one may eat and drink until the *ghalas* (the dim darkness before dawn) (...).

* Student: Who said this?

* The Shaykh: They mentioned it.

* Student: O Shaykh, a ḥadīth from the Prophet (...) is established.

* The Shaykh: This is weak (...).

* Student: Ḥasan.

* The Shaykh: In recitation it is correct, but in (...) it is weak.

* Student: Ḥasan (...).

* The Shaykh: It is never sound. Anything that contradicts the Qur'an is not sound at all.

We are still on the question: if the muezzin who calls the dawn adhān has a vessel in his hand and is drinking, must he lower the vessel and abstain, or may he satisfy his need from it?

* The students: (...)

* The Shaykh: No, that is not permitted according to the school of Imam Ahmad. According to the school of Imam Ahmad, it is not permitted. It is obligatory: if there is water in his mouth, he must spit it out.

* Student: (...) if it is known that he left it.

* The Shaykh: The same applies to food, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. However, it is recorded in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from the ḥadīth of Abu Hurayrah, with a chain that Ahmad Shakir declared sound, "that if the muezzin calls while the vessel is in your hand, do not put it down until you have satisfied your need from it."[[Reported by Abu Dawud (2350) from Abu Hurayrah.]] If this ḥadīth is sound, it is interpreted as meaning that the muezzin does not call until... that is, he may be cautious, not calling the adhān until dawn has actually risen. It may be that he calls while the matter has not become very clear to him, so the person is given leniency. Otherwise it would contradict the sound ḥadīths and the Qur'an too, for Allah says in it: ﴿until it becomes distinct﴾, and the Messenger ﷺ says: "Eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls the adhān, for he does not call until dawn has risen."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1919), and the wording is his, and Muslim (1092/36), from ʿĀʾishah.]]

* Student: Some of the common people (...) dawn (...) before dawn (...) ﴿until it becomes distinct﴾?

* The Shaykh: No, this is trickery (...) the verification. No, this is trickery. Likewise, what some of the common folk narrate from the Messenger ﷺ, that he used to shelter his she-camel from the dawn, this is a lie and trickery.

* Student: The Ḥanbalīs' view that if the adhān for dawn is called while he is having intercourse, and then he withdraws, he owes expiation: on what is this based?

* The Shaykh: It is based on the premise that withdrawal is intercourse, that they regard withdrawal as intercourse, like the beginning of intercourse. This is not correct (...) let him do it.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No. As for the muezzins nowadays, they cannot call with true precision, they do not call with precision. But we do not issue a ruling on this, for we fear trickery, so we do not issue it.

* Student: He advances (...).

* The Shaykh: By Allah, most of them advance it.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: it is not proper to be overcautious regarding the dawn adhān during fasting. That is, some people nowadays, especially the ignorant, say: "We call the adhān before dawn out of caution, so that people abstain." We say: this caution is misplaced, because true caution is to follow the Sharīʿah. Do you understand? Yes. If there were conflicting evidences, that would be different, but here the evidences are clear, even in the verse: ﴿becomes distinct﴾. There is no caution in it. So caution in adherence to the Sharīʿah is that you eat and drink until it becomes distinct. Moreover, if you are cautious in regard to fasting, you neglect something more important than fasting, which is prayer, because some people, when they hear the dawn adhān, say: "Come, let us pray immediately." Thus we would have deceived people regarding prayer, which is more important.

* Student: The benefit (...)

* The Shaykh: Which one?

* Student: The last one.

* The Shaykh: The last one? That it is not proper to be overcautious regarding the dawn adhān during the days of fasting by calling it before dawn.

* Student: (...) five minutes.

* The Shaykh: Who?

* Student: (...) a person (...) the time (...).

* The Shaykh: No, do not be overcautious, for if you are overcautious, you prevent the servants of Allah from what Allah has made lawful to them.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know. I see that caution lies in following the Sharīʿah. Do not be strict with yourself.

* Student: Until it becomes distinct.

* The Shaykh: Until it becomes distinct.

* Student: Now, if I am in a place and know that people follow the false dawn, not the true dawn, and some people call the adhān at the false dawn.

* The Shaykh: You cannot know about them. Do not rely on them.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: if a person eats believing that dawn has not yet become distinct to him, and then it becomes clear that it was after dawn had risen, he owes no make-up fast.

* Student: That is, he says: ﴿until it becomes distinct﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿until it becomes distinct﴾. So his eating was permitted, or not? It was permitted. And what is permitted does not entail sin, liability for damages, or anything else. We have already encountered in the legal maxims (*qawāʿid al-fiqh*): what results from what is permitted is not liable for compensation.

So we say: whoever eats while dawn has not become distinct to him, and then it becomes clear that it was after dawn had risen, owes no make-up fast.

This is what the general texts support, such as the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make a mistake﴾ [al-Baqarah 286], and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you did in error, but what your hearts intended﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 5]. It is also supported by specific texts on this very matter, and by the ḥadīth of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim (may Allah be pleased with him), who used to place two cords under his pillow, one black and one white, and eat until the white thread became distinct from the black. He informed the Prophet ﷺ of this, and the Prophet did not order him to make up the fast.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4509), and Muslim (1090/33), from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim. The wording is: ʿAdī took a white cord and a black cord, and when part of the night had passed he looked, but could not distinguish them. When he woke in the morning he said: "O Messenger of Allah, I placed two cords under my pillow." He said: "Your pillow must be wide, if the white thread and the black thread are under your pillow."]]

So we have specific evidences and general evidences. The well-known view of the school of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, is that if a person eats and then it becomes clear that dawn had risen, he must make up the fast, because he ate after dawn had risen. But this view is weak.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the lawful fast begins at dawn and ends at sunset, because of His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾.

Be attentive, my brothers, to this question. In the sentence before it, we forgot a benefit: an indication of the disliked nature of *waṣāl* (continuous fasting). From where is it derived? From His saying: ﴿Eat and drink until it becomes distinct﴾.

*Waṣāl* means that a person joins the fast of two days together, not breaking it between them. Continuous fasting was once permitted, then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade it and said: "Whoever wishes to continue fasting, let him continue only until the pre-dawn meal (*saḥar*)."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (1963) from Abu Saʿīd al-Khudrī.]] Even though he encouraged hastening the breaking of the fast.

This is one of the matters I had previously pointed out: that a thing may be permitted without being legislated (*mashrūʿ*). Or not? So continuous fasting until the pre-dawn meal is permitted, but it is not legislated. We encountered another example earlier. Such as what?

* Student: Worship on behalf of the dead.

* The Shaykh: Yes, like giving charity on behalf of the dead. It is permitted but not legislated. And such as?

* Student: Concluding the prayer with the recitation of Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ.

* Student: Concluding the prayer with the recitation of Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ.

* The Shaykh: Concluding the prayer with the recitation of Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ: this is permissible but not legislated.

* From the benefits of the verse, as we said: the lawful fast ends.

* Student: At sunset.

* The Shaykh: At sunset. Not at night, because He said: ﴿until the night﴾. The phrase ﴿until the night﴾: now let us examine it. Is the intended meaning until the night covers the earth, or the intended meaning ﴿until the night﴾ is until the night becomes distinct? Or is there some other meaning beyond that?

We say: there is no doubt that the most correct interpretation, after the interpretation of Allah, the Exalted, is the interpretation of the Messenger ﷺ. It is established from him that he said: "When the night approaches from here" (and he pointed to the east) "and the day turns its back from here" (and he pointed to the west) "and the sun sets, the fasting person has broken his fast."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1954), and Muslim (1100/51), from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.]] This ḥadīth is a decisive ruling that clarifies this general statement in His saying: ﴿until the night﴾. For this reason, the Rāfiḍa (Rāfiḍah, a Shīʿī sect) held that one does not break the fast until the night covers the earth, and therefore they do not break their fast until the stars appear, clinging to the apparent meaning of the verse. But it is said: the Messenger ﷺ explained it, and he is the one who explains the Qur'an: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may explain to people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Naḥl 44]. No one among mankind may be referred to for its interpretation, and it is obligatory to refer to the Messenger's interpretation.

So if we attach the ruling merely to the approach of the night, it is not correct (...), it is not correct.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: I say: (...) it is not correct?

* Student: Because He said: ﴿until the night﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes, fine. Let it approach, so that we see it dark. We say: because the beginning of the night, as we see and witness now, the beginning of the night occurs while the sun has not yet set, or not? Have you never seen it? Now look at the sky from the east: darkness begins there while the sun has not set.

To say: ﴿until the night﴾ means until the night extends to the farthest horizon, this too is not correct; it is not what the verse intends. What the verse intends is what the Messenger ﷺ explained: "When the night approaches and the sun has set."

If someone said: what if the sun sets before the night approaches?

* Students: That cannot happen.

* The Shaykh: We say: this cannot happen except according to the opinion of the teacher of Abu Ḥanīfah. Yes, they say that Abu Ḥanīfah... Although I, by Allah, do not wish to relate matters that cause laughter in the recitation of the Qur'an, its interpretation, or its *iʿrāb* (grammatical analysis), they say: Abu Ḥanīfah was sitting with his companions when a man of dignified appearance came in. He had stretched out his leg among his brothers and companions. This man came in, and Abu Ḥanīfah honored him, drew in his own leg, and began speaking to his companions. He was speaking to them, I think, during the times when prayer is prohibited, and he said: "The prohibited times are from the break of dawn until sunrise." In any case, the man said to him: "O my master, what do you say if the sun rises before dawn breaks?" He said: (...). In any case, it is impossible for the sun to set before the night becomes distinct; that is among the impossibilities, on the horizon (...).

* From the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the legislation of *iʿtikāf* (retreat in the mosque).

* And among them: *iʿtikāf* is only valid in mosques, because of His saying: ﴿while you are devoted to worship in the mosques﴾ [al-Baqarah 187].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 186–188 (part 7 of 7):

If someone says: "﴿while you are staying in the mosques for worship (i'tikaf)﴾ indicates that there is i'tikaf outside them. So what is the answer?"
The answer: When He made a ruling for i'tikaf in the mosques, this indicates that if i'tikaf outside them were prescribed, the ruling would be general. Also, Allah says in another verse: ﴿that you purify My House for those who circumambulate it and those who stay in it for worship﴾ [al-Baqarah 125].
* Among the benefits of the verse: intercourse invalidates i'tikaf. We mentioned the prohibition of physical contact. What did we mention? Good, then leave aside what comes before it: the prohibition of intimacy with women during i'tikaf; that intimacy with women invalidates i'tikaf, or that i'tikaf is nullified by it. What is the reason it is invalidating? What is the basis for it being invalidating?
* Student: The prohibition.
* The Shaykh: The prohibition; because it is specifically forbidden, and whatever is specifically forbidden in an act of worship is one of the things that invalidates it. We mentioned during the explanation that some scholars derived from it that i'tikaf is only in fasting and at the end of the month, because Allah mentioned it right after the verse on fasting.
* Among its benefits: what some scholars have deduced, that i'tikaf takes place in the last part of the month of Ramadan.
Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿These are the limits set by Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah 187].
* Student: If he performs i'tikaf in the middle (of the month)?
* The Shaykh: He was waiting for Laylat al-Qadr entirely, until he was told that it is in the last ten nights, so he settled on the last ten nights.
* Student: Did he perform i'tikaf once in the first ten of Shawwal?
* The Shaykh: A makeup (qada'). He made it up as a qada', because when he went out on the morning of his i'tikaf he found that his wives had pitched tents, so he said: «Do they intend righteousness?»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2041), and Muslim (1173/6), whose wording it is, from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] Then the Prophet ﷺ ordered these tents to be taken down and left off i'tikaf that year, then made it up in Shawwal.
* Student: (...) contrary to what some scholars stipulated, that he must have had intercourse; he stated it absolutely...
* The Shaykh: Yes, yes, it is not stipulated that he must have had intercourse, yes.
* Student: Even if he prays some of the prayers in it.
* The Shaykh: No, he must pray the five daily prayers in it, so that he does not leave and so that his leaving is not repeated; because either he abandons congregational prayer, which is haram, or he goes out frequently, and in reality he is as if he were not in i'tikaf.
* Student: Shaykh, i'tikaf outside Ramadan?
* The Shaykh: As for us, we said: it is permissible but not prescribed (mashru'), permissible but not prescribed.
* Student: Some mosques do not hold the five prayers at all (...).
* The Shaykh: The hadith of 'Umar: "a day or a night"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2032), which has the wording "a night", and Muslim (1656/28), which has the wording "a day", from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]].
* Student: What is the reasoning for it being in the last ten from the verse (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿So do not approach them. Thus does Allah make clear His signs to the people that they may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 187].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the commands of Allah, may He be exalted, are limits set by Him, and likewise His prohibitions. The evidence: ﴿These are the limits set by Allah﴾. But if it is a limit on leaving, then they are commands; and if it is a limit on an act, then they are prohibitions. That is why it says about prohibitions: ﴿so do not approach them﴾, and about commands: ﴿so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah 229].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that one should keep away from what is forbidden. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿so do not approach them﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, makes the signs clear to people, both the cosmic and the legislative signs; by His words: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear His signs to the people﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the people of ta'til (denial of divine attributes) who distort words from their places regarding the names and attributes of Allah. What is the basis for that?
For example, when they say: "By 'hand' is meant blessing or power, by 'istiwa' is meant domination, and by such-and-such is meant such-and-such," which contradicts the apparent meaning of the wording and has no evidence, does the Qur'an become a clarification for people, or not a clarification? Not a clarification; because as long as the clarification is contrary to what is apparent, there is no clarification.
So it is derived from this noble verse: the refutation of the people of ta'til and others who distort words from their places and say that Allah intended such-and-such without evidence.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that knowledge is a cause of righteousness. From where is this taken?
* Students: ﴿that they may become righteous﴾.
* The Shaykh: What is the reasoning? Because He followed it with it, that is, He placed it right after His words: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear His signs to the people﴾. This indicates that whenever the signs become clear, righteousness is attained. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir 28]. So the more a person knows the signs of Allah, the more he becomes God-fearing. That is why it is said: whoever knows Allah best fears Him most.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the high rank of righteousness (taqwa). From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿that they may become righteous﴾. Had righteousness not been a high rank, for the sake of which the signs are made clear in order to attain it, Allah would not have made the signs clear for its sake, and for the sake of people being God-conscious toward their Lord.
