Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor send it [as bribes] to the rulers, so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people sinfully while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah 188].
First: the connection of this verse with the one before it is quite clear; because when He mentioned the things forbidden due to fasting, He mentioned the things forbidden due to making up the fast. The things forbidden due to fasting were previously explained to us: eating and drinking from the break of dawn until sunset. He followed that with the prohibition of consuming wealth in general due to making up the fast.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of consuming wealth unjustly. What is the meaning of "unjustly"? "Unjustly" is everything to which you have no legitimate right by the Law; everything to which you have no legitimate right is unjust.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the eagerness of the Lawgiver to preserve wealth, by His words: ﴿nor consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾.
Also among its benefits: the prohibition of bribery, according to one of the two interpretations mentioned earlier, by His words: ﴿nor send it to the rulers﴾, meaning: you give them some of your wealth so that they will rule in your favour unjustly.
* Among its benefits: that the judge rules by what is apparent, meaning he judges by what he hears, as the Messenger ﷺ said: «I only judge according to what I hear»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6967), and Muslim (1713/4), from the hadith of Umm Salamah.]]. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿nor send it to the rulers﴾.
This applies to one who claims what is not his, and disputes and produces a false proof, or who denies what he owes, disputes and swears falsely; all of this is "sending it" to the rulers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, glory be to Him, facilitates things for rulers among people, in that He does not hold them accountable for inner matters, does He not? Allah's facilitation for rulers is that He does not make them sinful for hidden matters, nor does sin attach to them through them; otherwise people would be in hardship and difficulty.
* Student: What is the basis for that?
* The Shaykh: The basis for that from the verse is that if the ruler rules by what appears to him, even if it contradicts the reality, there is no sin upon him; because if these people claim what is not theirs and send it to the rulers, and the rulers rule by it, then the sin rests on the one in whose favour the ruling was made.
* Student: Meaning it is also derived from ﴿and send it﴾?
* The Shaykh: It is derived from ﴿nor send it to the rulers﴾ and from what follows it: ﴿so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people sinfully﴾. So He placed the sin on the one who consumes, not on the judge.
* Student: And bribery, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: And bribery is forbidden.
* Student: But if the judge takes a bribe?
* The Shaykh: Then he is sinful; that is not our question, because the verse has two opinions, and it includes all of them. If the judge takes a bribe, it is forbidden for him. But if he does not take a bribe, yet the opponent is brought before the judge in order to deny the claim, then the judge bears no burden.
* Student: Doesn't it confirm that it is other than bribery? He said: ﴿nor send it to the rulers﴾; could bribery be given to rulers?
* The Shaykh: No, even the sending of it, that is, of the bribe, the wealth, to the rulers; the sending of it to the rulers is undoubtedly an overt bribe. He sent it to the rulers, because it is taken from "adla dalwahu" (he lowered his bucket), meaning he lowered it into the well. Likewise, ﴿you send it to the rulers﴾ means you send (...).
There is no sin without knowledge. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿while you know﴾: ﴿so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people sinfully while you know﴾.
So if it is supposed that a person does not know, there is no sin on him. For example, if his creditor has paid him back but he forgets, and swears that he has not been repaid, and judgment is made in his favour, there is no sin on him; but as soon as he remembers that he has been repaid, it becomes obligatory for him to return the money to its owner (...).
It is the moon at the beginning of the month, and it is called hilal because of its appearance; from it come istihlal and ihlal, which means raising the voice, as in the hadith of Khallad ibn al-Sa'ib from his father that the Prophet ﷺ said: «Jibril came to me and commanded me to order my companions to raise their voices with the ihlal»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1814) and Ibn Majah (2922), from the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Khallad.]], meaning with the talbiyah.
From it also is their saying: "istahalla al-mawlud" (the newborn cried out) when he shouted after being born. This is why the crescent is called hilal, because of its appearance; and the hilal is the moon when it appears on the first night.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 186–188 (part 1 of 7):

﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186] To whom does the address in His words ﴿And when they ask you﴾ refer?
* Student: To the Messenger.
* Shaykh: To the Messenger ﷺ, because he is the intermediary between us and Allah, the Exalted, in conveying the revelation. It does not refer to everyone, it does not refer to everyone. We have already mentioned that an address directed by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may be specific to the Messenger, and may be general to him and to the Ummah, according to the context.
﴿When My servants ask you concerning Me﴾: "servants" (ʿibād) is the construct, and the "ya" (my) is the possessive pronoun. The intended meaning of "servants" here is the believing servants, as evidenced by His words: ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾, for the disbelievers do not call upon Allah; they call upon others along with Him.
And His words: ﴿When My servants ask you concerning Me﴾: concerning what? Concerning the essence of Allah, His attributes, His nearness, His generosity? The answer is what determines the meaning of the question. The answer is what determines its meaning. Let us look at the answer: ﴿indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant﴾. So what are they asking about? About nearness and responding. For the word ﴿concerning Me﴾ can bear many meanings, but the answer determines it, and as it is said: the answer is according to the measure of the question.
﴿When My servants ask you﴾: does this indicate that they have asked him, or that they will ask him, or that it is on the assumption and supposition of this matter? We have three possibilities: does the verse indicate that they have asked him, or that they will ask him, or that if they ask you, say such-and-such?
* Student: The third.
* Another student: The second and third.
* Another student: It includes all of them.
* Shaykh: The third; the second and third. But I mentioned these three possibilities to you because a hadith is mentioned at this point: "The Companions said: O Messenger of Allah, is our Lord near that we may whisper to Him, or far that we should call out to Him?' So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse."[[Recorded by ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in al-Sunnah (522), from the hadith of ʿUyaynah ibn Abi ʿImran, as a mursal report.]] Scholars have spoken about this hadith and declared it weak, but some cite it as evidence, and among those who cite it as evidence is Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him. When he cites it here as evidence, this indicates that he considers it a proof, and at the least its status is good (hasan). But many of the hadith scholars have declared this hadith weak, and the context of the verse does not indicate that it is its occasion of revelation, because if the occasion of revelation of the verse were this statement, it would have said, as is expressed in many verses: ﴿They ask you concerning orphans. Say: Reforming them is best﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220], ﴿They ask you concerning menstruation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], and what is similar to that. It would use the present tense that indicates occurrence, not the past tense conditioned by a condition, for the past tense conditioned by a condition indicates that the thing has not occurred.
But does it indicate that it will occur, or on the assumption that it occurs? The scholars of rhetoric said: both (idha) and (in) are conditional particles, but (in) does not indicate occurrence; it may be attached to a matter that is utterly impossible, unlike (idha), which indicates occurrence.
An example of that: you say to someone: "If Zayd comes, honour him." What is the meaning of this? That he is expected to come, and your honouring him should be at his coming. But if you say: "If Zayd comes, honour him," this indicates that he may come or may not come.
So in this verse, ﴿When they ask you﴾, its apparent meaning is that their asking is expected. Accordingly, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given a ruling concerning a matter that may occur, and this is closer to occurrence. As for (in), I told you that it does not indicate the occurrence of a thing; rather it may be attached to a thing that is utterly impossible, as in His words, exalted is He, concerning Himself: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81]. Is this condition possible?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: It is not possible. And His words concerning the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿If you should associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely become worthless﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. Is this possible? It is not possible, yes indeed.
As for His words: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child. But if they have a child, then for you is one-fourth of what they leave﴾ [al-Nisa': 12], the (in) here indicates something whose occurrence is not impossible; rather its occurrence is possible..
This question concerns what? Concerning His nearness and His responding: ﴿concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾.
Who asks?
* Student: If we say that (in) is used when occurrence is unlikely (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it may be attached to what is neither impossible nor unlikely, but the difference is that (idha) indicates that the matter will occur, unlike (in).
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Must he have a son? Is it necessary that he has one?
* Student: It may be.
* Shaykh: It may be, and it may not be; but (idha) indicates that this thing will be.
﴿When My servants ask you concerning Me﴾: note that in ﴿My servants﴾ the "ya" refers to Allah, ﴿concerning Me﴾ refers to Allah, and ﴿indeed I am near﴾ does not say "then say: indeed I am near." Some have said that it is on the assumption of an implied "say": "When My servants ask you concerning Me, then say: indeed I am near," so the answer of (idha) is omitted, and ﴿indeed I am near﴾ is the content of that omitted verb, i.e., the object of the speech: "say: indeed I am near." But the correct view is that it needs no such supposition, for two reasons:
First: the original principle is its absence, and as long as the speech is sound without the supposition, that is preferable.
Second: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿indeed I am near﴾, as though the matter is too clear to require a question. ﴿Indeed I am near﴾, ﴿When they ask you﴾, ﴿indeed I am near﴾. This is more eloquent than saying: "say: indeed I am near."
As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿indeed I am near﴾, the "ya" we say refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Thus Allah informs that He Himself is near: ﴿indeed I am near﴾, because the pronoun refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But what is the meaning of the nearness that Allah affirmed for Himself? Does it mean that He is located in a place? What is the answer? No, this is impossible, and the verse cannot be understood as something impossible; rather it is understood according to a meaning fitting for Him, glorified and exalted is He, and it is, as Shaykh al-Islam said: near with His loftiness, with His loftiness above His Throne, since He encompasses everything, and whoever encompasses everything is near, even though He is far in His loftiness, glorified and exalted is He.
This nearness does not entail any deficiency; rather it is evidence of perfection. The reason: if He is above the highest heavens, established on His Throne, and yet near, what does that indicate? It indicates the perfection of His greatness and His encompassing, glorified and exalted is He. Otherwise, a person, in relation to creatures, cannot conceive that something so distant could be near, for Allah is above everything. So by His perfection, glorified and exalted is He, and the perfection of His greatness, He is near while being lofty. For this reason, in the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, he mentioned that when they ascended a height or descended into a valley they would glorify Allah and raise their voices. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to them: "O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent, but you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and Near, and He is with you. Indeed the One you call upon is nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2992) and Muslim (2704/4), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him.]] So the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, explained that there is no need for a person to weary himself by raising his voice in supplication and glorification, because Allah, Majestic and Exalted, is near, near even though He is above His Throne.
Know that some, indeed the Hulūliyyah among the Jahmiyyah and others, use such ambiguous texts to support their falsehood. Their hearts are not expansive enough to combine the evidences, nor expansive enough to distinguish between the Creator and the created. They take up some texts and abandon their like. Strangely, Satan has deceived them, may Allah protect us, so they adopted the texts which, by their claim, imply deficiency regarding the Creator, and abandoned the texts which are perfection regarding the Creator. They abandoned the texts of loftiness, which is perfection, and adopted these ambiguous texts, which by their claim imply deficiency, that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is encompassed by His creatures, and that He is not exempt from places from which the generality of creation are exempt.
So the conclusion is that we say: this nearness does not permit us to imagine that He, glorified and exalted is He, is in the places where we are. Every text of this kind that reaches you, know that it indicates the greatness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His encompassing. Among them is what came in the hadith: "My servant, I was ill and you did not visit Me." He said: "How can I visit You when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He said: "Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was ill, and if you had visited him, you would have found Me with him."[[Recorded by Muslim (2569/43), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] "You would have found Me with him." Do the Hulūliyyah rejoice in this or not?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: They make a great fuss over it; this is very clear to them. It is said to them: you looked with one eye; you took one aspect of the texts and neglected another aspect. You ignored the rational, innate and transmitted evidences that Allah, the Exalted, is above His Throne, established upon it, and you adopted these ambiguous texts. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, those are the ones Allah has named, so beware of them." And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4547) and Muslim (2665/1), from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her.]] Those are the ones Allah named.
We know with certainty that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in what he related from his Lord in the words "you would have found Me with him," did not intend that He was found in the room where the sick person was. Rather, since the sick person, especially a believer, usually has a state of brokenness of heart, turning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and humility that he does not have in a state of health, and since Allah, the Exalted, is with those whose hearts are broken for His sake, it is correct to express it in this manner.
So these texts, O my brothers, do not think that they contradict the texts of knowledge, for, as I told you, they indicate the greatness of the Creator, Majestic and Exalted, and that He, with His essential loftiness above His Throne, is near to His creation; He draws near to His creation as He wills, and there is no contradiction. This is correct regarding the created: one cannot be at the highest thing and be said to be near. But Allah, the Exalted, ﴿there is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11].
Similarly His words, exalted is He, in the Hadith Qudsi: "Whoever draws near to Me a handspan, I draw near to him a cubit; whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; and whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7405) and Muslim (2675/2), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] And what is similar to that of the hadiths which the intellects of some people may fail to grasp, so they try to interpret them. We say: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, draws near to His creation as He wills, as the early scholars said, and we do not ask how. We say: Allah knows best the modality of this, but we know that He, glorified and exalted is He, though He draws near to His creation and descends to the lowest heaven, still remains lofty; He still remains lofty, glorified and exalted is He.
* Student: Shaykh, may we say: "I found with him reward or forgiveness"?
* Shaykh: No, that is not appropriate, because in the case of feeding, when He said: "My servant asked you for food and you did not feed him. He said: Had you fed him, you would have found that with Me," Allah, Mighty and Majestic, distinguished between feeding and visiting the sick.
* Student: "He plunges into mercy"[[Recorded by Ahmad in al-Musnad (12782), from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "Whoever visits a sick person, he is only plunging into mercy; when he sits by the sick person, mercy covers him."]] — shall we take it as its literal meaning?
* Shaykh: Yes, we take it literally: "he plunges into the mercy of Allah," meaning he is immersed in it.
* Student: Yes, meaning in reward and recompense?
* Shaykh: In reward and recompense, yes indeed, there is no difficulty.
* Student: But how do we say "you would have found Me with him" (...) do we not take it as (...)?
* Shaykh: We do not take it so, because this is a single hadith in which the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, differentiated between them in what he related from his Lord.
* Student: We cannot conceive (...)?
* Shaykh: No, we can conceive it; one conceives it. Being "with" does not contradict loftiness with respect to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for the created, yes, you cannot be with something while it is on the roof. But with respect to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His attributes are not like our attributes. The hadith which mentions food says: "Had you fed him, you would have found that with Me," in this wording, and in the visit it says: "you would have found Me with him," so he distinguished between them.
* Student: Shaykh, the innate disposition in supplication does not favour this statement, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not near either in His essence or in modality. Or does the innate disposition say that Allah is far, not near?
* Shaykh: Allah is in the heaven, but with His loftiness He is near.
* Student: But the innate disposition says: not near?
* Shaykh: No, that is not possible.
* Student: Yes, that Allah, Mighty and Majestic..
* Shaykh: No. If you say "not near," meaning that Allah, glorified and exalted, is in a place here (...), but He is near with a nearness fitting to Him. We do not know the reality of how He is near; we affirm that He is near, but we do not know how this nearness is.
(...) This does not necessarily apply to the Creator, because He, glorified and exalted, "there is nothing like unto Him in all His attributes," as Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "He is high in His nearness, near in His loftiness." So He is not measured by His creation.
His words, exalted is He: ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾. He said: ﴿indeed I am near﴾. ﴿Near﴾ is the predicate of ﴿indeed﴾ (inna). ﴿Indeed I am near, I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾. You have now understood that He is near with His loftiness, and that there is no contradiction between them, because Allah is not measured by the created things. He is near in His loftiness, lofty in His nearness, glorified and exalted is He.
﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant﴾: His words ﴿I respond﴾ form a second predicate of (inna), so its predicate is a noun and a sentence: its predicate is a singular noun, and the second predicate is a sentence: ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾. Supplication (du'a') here means request. The phrase ﴿the invocation of the supplicant﴾ originally was "al-dā'ī" with a "ya," like "al-qāḍī" and "al-hādī," but the "ya" was dropped for lightness. A parallel is His words, exalted is He: ﴿the Great, the Exalted﴾ [al-Ra'd: 9], originally "al-muta'ālī." This is with "al" (the definite article); it may also be dropped in what does not have "al," as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they have no protector besides Him﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], originally "min wālī." All of this is for lightness.
﴿the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾: look, He said ﴿when he calls upon Me﴾, although one is not a supplicant except when he calls. So someone may ask: what is the benefit of the condition in His words ﴿when he calls upon Me﴾? The one who calls is only a caller when he calls, so what is the benefit of the condition?
We say its benefit is an indication of matters, indeed of three matters:
The first matter: sincerity, that one calls upon Allah, the Exalted, Himself, without taking intermediaries between himself and Him, so that he does not say: "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah for me" after the death of the Messenger ﷺ, or "O such-and-such saint" after the death of the saint, "pray to Allah for me," or what is similar to that. Its benefit is sincerity: that one be sincere to Allah in supplication.

Second benefit: believing that Allah, glorified and exalted, will certainly grant what one asks of Him. For you do not sincerely call upon anyone unless you are confident of his response; for this reason the hadith says: "Call upon Allah while you are certain of being answered"[[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi (3479), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Its benefit is therefore: ﴿when he calls upon Me﴾, meaning truly, one who calls upon Me truly, knowing that I will give him what he asks.

The third thing: it indicates the soundness of one's need of Allah, and that one is truly in need of Him, since no one calls upon another except one who is in need of him. Thus the benefit of this is the realization of this supplication in three aspects: sincerity, ... what remains? Certainty of being answered, trust in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and third, the soundness of need of Allah, such that one calls only while in need; for the one who is self-sufficient does not call upon Allah, the self-sufficient does not supplicate.

And His saying ﴿when he calls upon Me﴾: its original form is "daʿānī" with a yā', and the yā' was dropped for lightness.

And His saying ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾. Notice that He did not say "I grant his request," but said "I respond to his invocation." Responding to the invocation does not necessarily entail fulfilling the request, for Allah may not grant his request but respond to him either by turning away from him an evil greater than it, or by storing it up for him. So if He does not give him precisely what he asked and stores it for him, or turns away from him an evil greater than it, can it be said that He has answered the supplication or not?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: He has answered the supplication, without doubt; but out of His wisdom and His mercy toward this supplicant He chooses for him what He chooses. It may be in the supplicant's interest that his invocation be granted, I mean that his specific request be granted, and it may not be in his interest.

And His saying ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ is followed by ﴿so let them respond to Me﴾, meaning: let them obey Me. For "istajāba" means "ajāba" (to respond), as Allah says: ﴿Then their Lord answered them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 195], meaning responded; and as He says: ﴿And those who responded to their Lord﴾ [al-Shūrā 38], meaning responded to Him. Here His saying ﴿so let them respond to Me﴾ does not say "fa-yastajībūnanī" ... (...) "ajāba" is said as "ajābahu," but here it is construed with "lām": "istajāba lahu," because it has been given the sense of submission (inqiyād); otherwise "ajāba" would take its object directly. A parallel is the Prophet's ﷺ saying in the hadith of Muʿādh: «If they respond to you in that» ("fa-in hum ajābū laka bi-dhālika")[[Agreed upon; recorded by al-Bukhari (2346) and Muslim (19/29) with the wording: "fa-in hum aṭāʿū li-dhālika," and in a narration of Ibn Khuzaymah (2346) with the wording: "fa-in hum ajābū li-dhālika."]], "ajābū laka," and he did not say "ajābūka," so the responding was given the sense of submission.

﴿so let them respond to Me﴾ means: let them submissively comply with Me, a response that is grounded in what follows, ﴿and let them believe in Me﴾, grounded in faith. Here He said ﴿and let them believe in Me﴾ rather than "li" (to Me), because faith in Allah includes tranquillity, complete acknowledgment, and is not merely assent; it is assent with the tranquillity of the heart. For this reason one says "his heart was reassured by it" (iṭmaʾanna qalbuhu bihi): he assented and was reassured. And in His saying ﴿and let them believe in Me﴾ and ﴿so let them respond to Me﴾, the lām in both verbs is the lām of command; for this reason it is vowel-less (sukūn) after the conjunction.

﴿so let them respond to Me and let them believe in Me, that they may be guided﴾. "La'alla" (that they may): what is it?

* Student: For causation.

* The Shaykh: For causation, yes. Whenever "la'alla" appears in the Book of Allah, it is for causation; for expectation (tarajjī) only pertains to one who needs and hopes to remove what has befallen him soon, whereas for the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, this is impossible. So whatever such expression occurs in the Qur'an means causation for the sake of guidance.

"Rushd" is used in the sense of good conduct and in the sense of gain; for this reason one says, "O Rāshid," meaning, "O one who gains." As for rushd in the sense of good conduct, it is frequent, as in His saying: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them rushd (maturity), hand over to them their property﴾ [al-Nisā' 6]. What does "rushdan" mean here? It means good conduct. And He says: ﴿But Allah has endeared to you faith and made it beautiful in your hearts, and made hateful to you disbelief, defiance and disobedience; those are the rāshidūn﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt 7], meaning the ones who gain, so it is close in meaning to "the successful." In this verse, ﴿that they may be guided (yarshudūn)﴾ admits both meanings: rushd as good conduct, and the second: gain by which they are rightly guided. There is no doubt that whoever believes in Allah and responds to Him is the best of people in conduct, he is granted success, guided, and his affairs are made easy: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him ease in his affair﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 4]; ﴿As for he who gives and fears (Allah) and affirms the best (reward), We will ease him toward ease﴾ [al-Layl 5–7]. And there is also no doubt that whoever believes in Allah and responds to Him is a gainer and a winner, and none is more profitable than him.

If someone says: if you take rushd here in both senses together, then you have used the homonym in two meanings, so what do we say? We say: there is no objection. The correct view is that it is permissible when the two meanings do not contradict each other, and what prevents the speaker from intending what the speech indicates, both this and that?

* Student: Do the two meanings make it more eloquent in this way?

* The Shaykh: Yes. A man said: "Thieves entered the house of so-and-so and destroyed his eye." What is meant by "eye"?

* Student: Goods.

* Student: Wealth.

* The Shaykh: Wealth. And his eye also: the spring that flows, water; or not? And his eye: his seeing eye; each is possible. If we know that these thieves destroyed all three, there is no objection to saying that they entered his house and destroyed his eye. What is the objection? The only requirement is that there be evidence that this shared term is used in both meanings; when evidence indicates it, there is no objection.

* Student: Al-Shawkānī says: in the sense of guidance?

* The Shaykh: Yes, guidance is part of good conduct.

* Student: Shaykh, the saying ﴿when he calls upon Me﴾ — is there no benefit in the fact that supplication divides into two kinds: supplication of asking and supplication of worship (...)? Did it specifically mention supplication of asking?

* The Shaykh: No, there is no evidence for that; because this too — it will come to us, God willing, in the benefits — is suitable for both matters.

* Student: In another verse, ﴿He will remove that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾ [al-An'ām 41]: does this restrict the text here?

* The Shaykh: It will come to us, God willing, in the benefits.

* Student: Regarding "la'alla," is it not for expectation when it concerns created beings?

* The Shaykh: No, regarding Allah it does not apply.

* Student: No, regarding...

* The Shaykh: For created beings it is for expectation, for causation, for anticipation, and for apprehension; and it also comes, as we passed in rhetoric, for wishing (tamannī).

* Student: Shaykh, (...) "la'alla" (...)?

* The Shaykh: Because there is nothing previously causing it.

* Student: Regarding this verse, as regards the speech of Allah?

* The Shaykh: Because its intent here is causation; we say: for causation.

* Student: Is this addressed to created beings: ﴿that they may be guided﴾?

* The Shaykh: Yes, but who said ﴿that they may be guided﴾?

* Student: Yes, Allah, glorified and exalted, said it; the entire Qur'an is the speech of Allah.

* The Shaykh: Meaning: do you hope that they will be guided?

* Student: No, it is truly (...) differs.

* The Shaykh: No, it is not fitting; since Allah has given a cause for one of His acts...

* Student: So we say that the servants vary: some are guided and some are not...

* The Shaykh: Not at all. If they respond to Allah and believe, they will undoubtedly be guided; it is necessary: if they respond to Allah and believe in Him, they must be guided.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in to your wives﴾. The word ﴿uḥilla﴾ is passive, because it is known who holds the power of making lawful and making unlawful, namely Allah. His saying ﴿uḥilla﴾ indicates that the matter had been unlawful before; otherwise there would be no need for a text on making lawful, since the default is permissibility. This contrasts with ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Mā'idah 3], which does not indicate that it had been lawful, for example, since the default is not prohibition. So here we say that ﴿uḥilla﴾ indicates that it had been unlawful before, and that is so.

His saying ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast﴾: which fast? The fast previously described, which is the fast of Ramadan.

His saying ﴿al-rafath﴾ (the sexual relation): "al-rafath" is the deputy subject, the agent of ﴿uḥilla﴾, and therefore it is in the nominative. "Rafath" is used of intercourse, and it is also used of the words exchanged between husband and wife during intercourse, since between husband and wife during intercourse there are words that are shameful to say, and these are called rafath; but here it is meant as intercourse, as evidenced by its being governed by "ilā" (to): ﴿al-rafath ilā nisā'ikum﴾, meaning the going in to your women. "Ifḍā'" (going in) means intercourse, as Allah says: ﴿And how can you take it back when you have gone in to one another and they have taken from you a solemn covenant?﴾ [al-Nisā' 21].

Then He said: ﴿ilā nisā'ikum﴾. "Nisā'" is the plural of "niswah," and "niswah" is a collective noun with no singular of its own; its singular is "imra'ah," just as "ibil" (camels) is a collective noun with no singular of its own, its singular being "baʿīr."

His saying ﴿ilā nisā'ikum﴾ means: your wives and your slave-women, and this is clear, since no one else is lawful in any way, neither on the night of fasting nor otherwise: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Mu'minūn 5–6].

﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾: this sentence is a resumptive explanation for the causation of the permission, meaning: this was made lawful for you because you cannot do without them, nor can they do without you; you are a garment for them and they are a garment for you. Note the expression "garment" (libās), for in it is the preservation of chastity: a garment covers the nakedness, and marriage secures the chastity, and in it there is covering, protection and safeguarding: ﴿And He made for you garments to protect you from the heat, and garments to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Naḥl 81].

This meaning of "libās" extends beyond being a covering, protection and safeguard; it includes the closeness between husband and wife, as the poet said:

When the bedfellow turns his side, she turns, and becomes a garment upon him.

The conclusion is that this expression "garment" gives the strongest evidence of what exists between the spouses of what? Of closeness, of guarding and protection, and that neither can do without the other; and this is part of the wisdom and mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from yourselves that you may find tranquillity in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [al-Rūm 21]. This which Allah has placed between the spouses of His mercy: He made lawful for us going in to our women during the nights of fasting.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained another wisdom requiring this permission, namely His saying: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you﴾ — praise be to Allah — ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾: in what? In going in to them, such that you could not be patient and so betrayed yourselves. The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that this betrayal consists in a person deceiving himself that the matter is minor, or that he has come into a state in which his wife is not forbidden to him, and the like. The origin of this was that at first, if a person prayed the late evening prayer ('ishāʾ), or if he slept before the 'ishāʾ prayer, it became forbidden to him to enjoy a woman, or to eat and drink, until sunset of the following day. This was a tremendous hardship for them, so much so that some of them did not endure it. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained His wisdom and His mercy toward us in making this matter lawful for us; and for this reason He said: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying﴾, and did not say "takhūnūn" (betray); because in His saying "takhtānūn" there is an addition of letters indicating an addition of meaning, since they say: an increase in form indicates an increase in meaning. This is correct, is it not? It is correct, but it is mostly a general tendency, not always: "baqarah" and "baqar," which has more letters? "Baqarah." And which has less meaning? The single cow is less in meaning; which is more numerous: the single cow or cattle? Cattle are more numerous. Yes. So the matter is one of general tendency.

He said: ﴿you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you﴾: "He turned to you" — does the meaning mean He turned to you before you repented, or that Allah abrogated this ruling, and abrogation is a repentance, since had there been no abrogation, falling into it would have been sinful? Which is the meaning?

* Student: The latter.

* The Shaykh: But this last meaning is the more sound. A parallel is His saying in Surat al-Muzzammil: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you﴾ [al-Muzzammil 20], after He had made standing in the night obligatory upon us: ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little — half of it, or reduce from it a little, or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in slow, measured recitation﴾ [al-Muzzammil 2–4]. He said: ﴿He knew that you would not keep count of it, so He turned to you﴾, meaning by abrogating the obligation, since had there been no abrogation, abandoning it would have been abandoning an obligatory act, and thus sinful. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, expresses abrogation by repentance, indicating that had there been no abrogation, the person would have been sinful, either by committing what is prohibited or by abandoning what is obligatory.

* Student: Shaykh, is the addition of letters not consistent in derived forms?

* The Shaykh: We cannot judge anything definitively. We say: a general tendency; we cannot do more, because confining these matters is difficult. Someone may come and refute your example, and then you will be forced to say "generally," (...).

* Student: You said: "It is made lawful" indicates that it had been forbidden before — is this general throughout the Qur'an?

* The Shaykh: But here, in this verse, there is evidence.

* Student: And is it not general?

* The Shaykh: In the Qur'an... 

* Student: ﴿Today the good things are made lawful for you﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5].

* The Shaykh: In the Qur'an, this either serves as a preface to what follows, or removes a misconception, or the like, or expresses favour. We do not fix them; but in this verse it indicates that it was forbidden before.

* Student: ﴿takhtānūn﴾: its meaning is between two parties, i.e., the verb in the reciprocal sense; a person does not betray himself, it occurs between them. Is this the intended meaning?

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is undoubtedly among the intended meanings: that each of you betrays the other, is that what you mean?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Like "tuqātilūn" (you fight)? No, but the word "ikhtān" is like "ikhtār" (to choose); it does not indicate reciprocity. Yet this may be among what is gained from the addition of letters in the form; it may be among its component meanings. But to say that this is the benefit, we cannot say that, because the form "iftaʿala" does not indicate participation.

He said: ﴿so He turned to you﴾. By what did He turn? We said: by abrogation, since had there been no abrogation, his act would have been forbidden and entailed sin.

﴿so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾. Pardon (ʿafw) occurs in response to wrongdoing, as Allah says: ﴿Whether you disclose a good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent﴾ [al-Nisā' 149]. What is the wrongdoing that occurred? It is what some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did, going in to their wives on nights of fasting before the prohibition was abrogated; for this reason He said: ﴿and pardoned you﴾. The root of pardon is abandoning blame for a sin. Among Allah's names is al-ʿAfuww (the Pardoner), and ʿafw is also used in the sense of increase, as in His saying: ﴿until they multiplied (ʿafaw)﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 95], meaning they increased; and from it is the saying of the Messenger ﷺ: «Let the beards grow» (aʿfū al-liḥā), meaning let them grow and make them abundant.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 186–188 (part 3 of 7):

﴿So now, have relations with them﴾ and so on to the end. ﴿So now﴾: the fa' (فاء) is a conjunctive particle (حرف عطف) that implies sequence (الترتيب), meaning: so now, after the prohibition and after repentance and pardon have been confirmed, have relations with them. The word "now" (الآن), as we have already explained, is a demonstrative of present time (اسم إشارة إلى الزمن الحاضر), indeclinable in the fatha (مبنية على الفتح) and in the place of an accusative (في محل نصب). As for His words ﴿have relations with them﴾, the intended meaning of mubashara (المباشرة) is intercourse (الجماع), and it was called mubashara because of the meeting of the two skins (البشرتين) in it: the skin of the woman and the skin of the man. As for His words ﴿have relations with them﴾, it is, as we all know, an imperative verb (فعل أمر). So what is the intended meaning of this command?
* Student: Permission (الإباحة).
* Shaykh: Permission, or the lifting of the prohibition (رفع التحريم)?
* Student: Or that.
* Shaykh: "Or that" no; there is a difference between them.
* Student: It is permission.
* Shaykh: No, no, there is a difference between them. For this reason the scholars of usul al-fiqh (الأصوليون) differed concerning a command that follows a prohibition (الأمر بعد الحظر): is it for permission, or is it a lifting of the prohibition? Some of them said: it is for permission, and some said: it is a lifting of the prohibition, and there is a difference between them. If we say it is for permission, the meaning is that this act after the prohibition has become merely permissible. If we say it is a lifting of the prohibition, the meaning is that this thing has returned to its ruling before the prohibition: if it was obligatory, it is obligatory; if it was recommended, it is recommended; if it was permissible, it is permissible. Now has the difference between the two statements become clear, or not?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: The argument of those who say it is for permission: they say that when the prohibition came upon the original ruling it abrogated it and it became as though it had never been. So when the command comes after it, its meaning is that it has become permissible, having been forbidden and now becoming permissible. This is a strong argument.
And those who said it is a lifting of the prohibition said: because the original ruling, when the prohibition came upon it, became forbidden, so when the prohibition was removed it returned to what it was. It is as if the prohibition were a veil placed over something covered; when the veil is lifted, what is covered is as it was. For this reason they said, regarding the words of the Exalted, ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [al-Ma'idah 2], is hunting permissible, or does it follow its previous ruling? It follows the previous ruling. This is what appears more likely, although the matter is not, in my view, so clear-cut, because both justifications are strong. But what appears closer is that a command after a prohibition is a lifting of the prohibition.
﴿So when the prayer has been concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 10]. This is a command after a prohibition, because He said: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 9]. Then He said: ﴿So when the prayer has been concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty.› Shall we now say that trade, which had been forbidden, has become merely permissible now, or has become recommended, or what? We say it has returned to what it was, and trade, as is known, may be obligatory, may be recommended, and may be permissible.
* Student: We say it indicates permission, but there is another proof in this verse; what is permission here? There are other proofs (...).
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: For example, in this verse.
* Shaykh: No, we are speaking of the general rule: is the abrogation of a prohibition a lifting of it, or does it imply permission, a command after a prohibition?
* Student: I think it implies permission, for example, but other proofs have indicated (...) in other places.
* Shaykh: No, there is a difference between them.
* Student: According to our statement that the permissible is subject to the five rulings, does the difference between the two expressions apply?
* Shaykh: Yes, because if we say it returns to what it was, or that it lifts the prohibition, we look at this thing that was forbidden now: was it recommended before the prohibition? Then it is recommended, and if it was recommended before the command, it remains recommended.
* Student: But, Shaykh, like trade, what is its ruling...?
* Shaykh: No, trade's ruling is permissibility, without doubt.
* Student: O Shaykh, (...) do both matters come to permissibility?
* Shaykh: Which?
* Student: The return of what Allah cast upon...
* Shaykh: Yes, because hunting is originally permissible. But if something is of a kind that is sought, like if I said to you: do not visit so-and-so, who is your relative for example, and then I said to you: when the sun rises, visit him, this command does not mean permission. If we say it lifts the prohibition, the visit has become recommended again; and if we say it is for permission, the visit remains permissible. This is the meaning.
* Student: What about His words ﴿and He has pardoned you﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿Have relations with them﴾: I said the intended meaning is intercourse, and what is less than that is, a fortiori, not prohibited.
﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾. ﴿Seek﴾: ask for, ﴿what﴾: that which, ﴿Allah has decreed for you﴾: has written for you. Is the writing here the universal decree (الكتابة الكونية) or the legislative prescription (الكتابة الشرعية)? That is, does it mean what Allah has destined for you, or what Allah has legislated for you? We say it may bear both meanings, and including both is preferable. So the meaning is: seek what Allah has legislated for you, i.e., seek what He has legislated for you of enjoyment of women and its permissibility, or what He has legislated for you of night prayer in the nights of Ramadan, or what He has legislated for you of the pre-dawn meal (السحور); all of this is included. Or: seek what Allah has decreed for you by way of destiny (كتابة قدرية), such as seeking offspring through this intercourse, as some exegetes said: "seek offspring," meaning: do not let your intercourse be for the sake of attaining desire only, but for the sake of obtaining offspring and progeny. So I say: the verse includes both meanings, ﴿and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾, and the benefits, Allah willing, will come to us.
﴿And eat and drink﴾ is conjoined to ﴿have relations with them﴾, according to the first reading, on ﴿have relations with them﴾. ﴿Eat and drink﴾: what is the meaning of eating and drinking? What about eating and drinking?
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: But it does not become clear to us, and so it is: at the first appearance of dawn, there is no doubt that it does not become clear all at once; it appears gradually, but we are responsible for what we can do until it becomes clear and evident to us.
As for His words ﴿the white thread from the black thread﴾: we understood, when He said ﴿from the thread﴾, that ﴿becomes distinct﴾ means becomes distinguished, one distinguished from the other, as He said: ﴿until Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [Al 'Imran 179]. So "min" (مِن) does not come after yatabayyana here except when distinction is intended; meaning: until the white thread is distinguished from the black thread of dawn. ﴿From the dawn﴾ explains what is meant by the thread: the thread of what? The whiteness of the day; and the black thread? The blackness of the night. In describing them as two threads there is evidence that they alternate, and that this may be in one direction and that in another direction, for they are two threads, and two threads must alternate; otherwise they would be only one thread.
As for His words ﴿until the white thread from the black thread from the dawn becomes distinct to you﴾: the Messenger ﷺ explained that dawn is of two kinds: true and false. He explained that the true dawn is that which appears spread across the horizon (معترضًا في الأفق), spreading like a bird or like a bird's wing from north to south. As for the false dawn, it is that which appears as an elongated streak (مستطيلًا) on the horizon, like the tail of a wolf (كذنب السرحان), i.e., the tail of a wolf.
The scholars mentioned three differences between them. The first: the true dawn is spreading and crosswise, while the other is elongated. The second: after the true dawn there is no darkness, whereas after the other there is darkness. The third: the true dawn is joined to the horizon, while the other has darkness between it and the horizon (...).
﴿until the white thread from the black thread from the dawn becomes distinct to you﴾: we said that ﴿becomes distinct﴾ means becomes apparent, but it implicitly carries the meaning of manifestation and distinction. From where? From His words ﴿the white thread from the thread﴾, meaning: one is distinguished from the other.
His words ﴿from the dawn﴾ are an explanation of ﴿the white thread﴾. He did not say "in the black thread of the night," being content with the first, as in His words: ﴿And He made for you garments to protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 81], meaning: and the cold, since garments protect from both heat and cold; ﴿and garments to protect you from your violence﴾ [al-Nahl 81], like armor. The point is that this is from the figure of speech of mentioning one of two opposites and omitting the other: meaning, until the white thread from the dawn from the black thread of the night becomes distinct to you. Do you understand? But "from the night" is omitted, being content with His words ﴿from the dawn﴾, because a thing becomes distinct by mentioning its opposite. A parallel to this? ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾, meaning: and the cold.
His words ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: "then" (ثم) refers to after the distinction becomes clear. This is from the vastness of the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He used "then" after the distinction, to give latitude to the servants. For this reason Imam Ahmad narrated with a chain that is acceptable: "If the dawn call is heard while the vessel is in your hand, do not put it down from your hand until you have fulfilled your need." (Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (10629), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.) This is to ease matters for those who are responsible. For this reason "Ibn Umm Maktum would not call the adhan until dawn had broken, and it would be said to him: You have entered the morning, you have entered the morning." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (617) and Muslim (1092/36), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar; the wording is al-Bukhari's.)
His words ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: ﴿complete﴾ (أتموا) means finish, finish it completely. As for ﴿the fast﴾ (الصيام): it was mentioned earlier that in language it means abstention (الإمساك), and from it the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam 26], meaning abstention from speech, as evidenced by His words: ﴿so I will not speak today to any human being﴾. The term fasting in the Sharia is worship of Allah, the Exalted, by abstaining from what breaks the fast from the emergence of the second dawn until sunset.
As for His words ﴿until the night﴾: what is meant by the night? Its darkness? The answer: No, but its beginning. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained this when he said: "When the night approaches from here," and he pointed to the east, "and the day withdraws from here," and he pointed to the west, "and the sun sets, the fasting person has broken his fast." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1941) and Muslim (1100/51), from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, may Allah be pleased with them.) And with the mere setting of the sun, that is, the setting of its disc, the fast is broken; it is not a condition that the redness disappear, as some common people think.
﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: so the fast is bounded by "from" and "until," so do not add to it or subtract from it. The ruling on continuous fasting (الوصال) will come in the benefits, Allah willing.
His words ﴿And do not have relations with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques﴾: when He said ﴿It has been made lawful for you to go to your wives during the night of fasting; they are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾, He excepted one state from this, which is: when a person is secluded in the mosques while fasting, he does not have relations with his wife. For this reason He said ﴿And do not have relations with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques﴾. The pronoun in "them" refers to the women, and the clause ﴿while you are devoting yourselves to worship﴾ is a circumstantial clause (حال) from the waw in ﴿do not have relations﴾. The word ﴿devoting yourselves﴾ (عاكفون) is an active participle from ʿakafa (عَكَفَ يَعْكُفُ), and devotion to a thing (العكوف على الشيء) means staying with it and persisting in it. From it is the words of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to his people: ﴿What are these statues to which you are devoted?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 52], meaning: persisting and constant. For this reason we say: i'tikaf (الاعتكاف) in language means remaining with a thing; in the Sharia it is worship of Allah, the Exalted, by remaining in the mosques in obedience to Him: remaining in the mosques for the sake of obedience to Allah. This is i'tikaf.
I'tikaf was known in the pre-Islamic period and is known in Islam. ʿUmar said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I vowed to devote one night in the Sacred Mosque during the pre-Islamic period?" The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Fulfill your vow." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2032) and Muslim (1656/27), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them.) It is prescribed in Ramadan, and the Messenger ﷺ used to seclude himself seeking the Night of Power (ليلة القدر); for this reason he secluded himself in the first ten nights, then he was told: the night is not in this ten, so he secluded himself in the middle ten, then it was shown to him in the last ten, until he went out to the people and said: "I was shown that night, so whoever was secluded, let him seclude himself in the last ten nights." (Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2016) and Muslim (1167/216), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him.) So i'tikaf in Ramadan was for the sake of seeking the Night of Power. Later, Allah willing, the ruling on i'tikaf will come to us in the benefits: is it a sunnah? Is fasting a condition for it or not?
From the mention of i'tikaf after the verses on fasting, some scholars deduced that i'tikaf is only in Ramadan and at its end, since Allah mentioned it following the verses on fasting after concluding the discussion of fasting. And Allah knows best whether this inference holds or does not hold.
Then the Exalted said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾. ("Tilka" (تلك): what is "ti"? What is its meaning? "Ti" tilka?)
* Student: A demonstrative (اسم إشارة).
* Shaykh: "Ti" is a demonstrative, the "la" indicates distance, and the "ka" is a particle of address (حرف خطاب). It was previously mentioned that this "ka" is according to the addressee, and the demonstrative according to the thing pointed to, and that the most eloquent form is for the "ka" to follow the addressee: for masculine singular one says dhalika, for feminine dhalik, for dual dhalikuma, for masculine plural dhalikum, for feminine plural dhalikunna. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And that is your assumption which you assumed﴾ [Fussilat 23]; ﴿And they are called out: That is the Garden which you have been made to inherit﴾ [al-A'raf 43]; and He said: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ [Yusuf 32]; and for the dual He said: ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me﴾; and for the singular: "dhalika," and it is frequent. This is the well-known classical dialect. There is a second dialect: that the "ka" is always singular and open, according to the interpretation of the addressee as singular. And there is a third dialect: its fatha for the masculine in all cases, and its kasra for the feminine in all cases.
Here, is "tilka" for the masculine singular, or not? The meaning is: that, O addressee, even if he addresses all people, since "people" is a genus, so it is valid to refer to it with the addressee form.
* Student: Shaykh, in His words ﴿And those days﴾ [Al 'Imran 140], while observing the addressee in the "ka," why is the pronoun not plural?
* Shaykh: Yes, often the plural is omitted; in the Qur'an the majority is singular, as if He addresses humankind in general through the Qur'an, addressing the human being; meaning: that, O human being, are the limits of Allah. And this is frequent; even the addresses without the "ka" in the demonstrative you will find in the singular.
He said: and ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾: "limits" (حدود) is the plural of "limit" (حد).
* Student: You said: with a waw.
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ has no waw. ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾: the "hudud" (الحدود) is the plural of "hadd" (حد), and hadd in language means prevention, as in "the boundaries of the house" (حدود الدار), because they prevent others from entering it. So the meaning of ﴿the limits of Allah﴾ is His prohibitions (موانعه).
Know that the limits of Allah are of two kinds: limits that prevent, i.e., they keep whoever is outside from entering, and these are the barriers to entry, which concern the prohibited things; and other limits that prevent whoever is within from leaving, and these are the limits of the commands. The limits of Allah the Exalted are prohibitions and commands. The prohibitions: what is their nature? They keep whoever is outside from entering. The commands keep whoever is within from leaving. For this reason, when commands come, Allah says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah 229], meaning: do not go out of them; and when prohibitions come, He says: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqarah 187]. This is the difference, and all of them are called limits, because commands have a limit you do not go beyond, and prohibitions have a limit you do not enter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 186–188 (part 4 of 7):

His saying: ﴿Those are the limits of Allah﴾ is an instance of attributing what is prescribed to the one who prescribed it. ﴿So do not approach them﴾: the fa' is for consequence (al-tafri'), and (lā) is a prohibitive particle. What is the evidence?
* A student: The deletion of the nūn.
* The Shaykh: It is jussive, by the deletion of the nūn. ﴿So do not approach them﴾: he did not say "so do not do them." Rather, He forbade approaching them, so that we keep far from the prohibited thing and from the means to the prohibited thing, because means have the rulings of the ends. How many a person has hovered around the sanctuary (al-hima) and then fallen into it! For this reason He said ﴿so do not approach them﴾. Thus, it is obligatory to keep away from the prohibitions and not to draw near to them.
﴿Thus Allah makes clear﴾: this occurs frequently in the Qur'an, and we have previously pointed out its i'rab (grammatical analysis), and we said that the kāf is a noun meaning "like," and that it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning: like that clarification, Allah makes clear. It occurs frequently in the Qur'an, and this is its i'rab: we say that the kāf is a noun meaning "like," and it is in the accusative as an absolute object, and its governing element is what follows it. His saying ﴿thus﴾ refers to what preceded of clarification. I think there is much clarification in these verses, or not? There is much clarification: Allah, glorified and exalted, has made clear the ruling on eating and drinking at night, the ruling on intimacy with women, the ruling on i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), its place, what is forbidden in it, and so on. The point is that these are a number of rulings which Allah has made clear.
His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear His signs to the people﴾: āyāt (signs) is the plural of āya, which linguistically means "sign" or "indicator." Its meaning in the Sharia is the proofs that indicate what is required of the attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted. Some of them indicate wisdom, some indicate mercy, some indicate knowledge, and some indicate comprehensiveness. The point is that they are diverse. The āyāt are the plural of āya, which linguistically means "sign," and the meaning here in the Sharia is the proofs that indicate what is required of the attributes of Allah.
The scholars have mentioned that the signs are divided into two kinds: cosmic (kawniyya) and legislative (shar'iyya). The cosmic signs are the created beings: all created beings, their essences, their attributes and their conditions, are among the cosmic signs. ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat 37]; ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed in them of living creatures﴾ [al-Shura 29]; ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you from yourselves spouses﴾ [al-Rum 21]; ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust, and then, behold, you are human beings dispersed﴾ [al-Rum 20], and so on. So all created beings, their essences, attributes and conditions, are all among the cosmic signs of Allah, and each is a sign of Allah, because none of the created beings can make the like of them. The sign of a thing is its indication, so none of the created beings can ever make the like of these signs, or not?
The second kind of signs: the legislative signs, which are what Allah, exalted, revealed to His messengers and prophets of revelation. They are legislative signs indicating the One who sent them down, glorified and exalted. The reason: when you reflect upon their reports, you find them in utmost truthfulness, clarity and benefit: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories by what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf 3]. So the best reports are the reports of the Qur'an, and of revelation generally. When you reflect upon their rulings, you find them the best of rulings: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'ida 50]. Were all of creation to gather to produce the like of the rulings Allah revealed to His messengers, they would not be able to do so. By this they are a sign, is it not? They are a sign of what is required of the attributes of Allah, glorified and exalted. Our saying "of what is required" is because the signs differ: some indicate greatness, some indicate mercy, some indicate knowledge, and some indicate majesty. The point is that they differ.
His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear His signs to the people so that they may become righteous﴾: this (la'alla, "so that") is for causation. Become righteous (yattaqun) toward whom? They become righteous toward Allah, mighty and majestic. Taqwa of Allah, glorified and exalted, is: taking a protection from His punishment by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is taqwa: taking a protection from the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, and this is the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa. Some say that taqwa is that you act in obedience to Allah, upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and that you leave what Allah has forbidden, upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah. Some say that taqwa is abandoning sins, but the most comprehensive of what has been said is what we mentioned at the beginning: taking a protection from His punishment by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. It is true that when it is paired with birr (righteousness), such as ﴿and cooperate in righteousness and taqwa﴾ [al-Ma'ida 2], taqwa means avoiding sins and birr means doing acts of obedience. A poet says:
Leave sins, the small of them and the great of them; that is taqwa.
And act like one walking over a field of thorns, wary of what he sees.
What does the one walking on a field of thorns do? Does he stamp with his foot and not mind? No.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed.
Do not belittle a small sin; indeed the mountains are made of pebbles.
This is correct. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, likened the trivial sins to a group of people who descended upon a land and wanted to light a fire. They went and one brought a stick, and another a stick, and another a stick, until they gathered a great amount of firewood and kindled a great fire. And what do they bring? Stick by stick; it is nothing. Yes indeed. So we say: the most comprehensive of what has been said about taqwa is taking a protection from the punishment of Allah, exalted, by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.
* A student: Could this be a level near to taqwa? That is, taqwa is not something higher than doing the obligations, but rather doing the recommended acts?
* The Shaykh: The commands are recommended acts; the recommended is a command, because a command may be obligatory and may be recommended, and a prohibition may be reprehensible and may be forbidden.
* A student: Should we not say that the verse ﴿Thus Allah makes clear His signs﴾ covers from the beginning of the surah and is not specific to the rulings of fasting?
* The Shaykh: No, that is not apparent, because you know that the verses are separate sections.
* The student: Yes, but the surah is connected?
* The Shaykh: No. And even if it were connected, it could only be in the subject under discussion, and also in what preceded it with verses about it before.
* A student: (...) fasting, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: It includes, and Allah knows best, some scholars said: it includes the four rulings that follow it, from His saying ﴿It has been made lawful for you to go to your wives on the night of the fast﴾ to the end, only. And if it were said that it is from His saying ﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqara 183], it would be good. Then know that His saying ﴿His signs﴾ is a plural construct, so it is general, meaning that this kind of clarification which we have made clear to you in these verses is a clarification of all the signs.
* A student: You know the limit linguistically, but not legally?
* The Shaykh: Yes, I know it.
* The student: No.
* The Shaykh: We said: the limits in the Sharia are the commands and prohibitions of Allah. As for the definition (had) according to the logicians, it is other than this. The logicians' definition we covered earlier in our explanation of the Safarini creed.
* The student: So it differs from what was at...
* The Shaykh: Yes, it differs, according to the terminologies.
* A student: Shaykh, if someone said: the clarification of the signs seems to a person to have as its benefit faith?
* The Shaykh: Faith?
* The student: Faith. Perhaps you, for example, will believe, because then when one believes he becomes righteous.
* The Shaykh: No. Originally there is no taqwa except after faith. So when the signs are made clear to a person, he becomes righteous toward Allah, mighty and majestic, so faith occurs first.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: There is no taqwa, brother, except after faith. Does a person guard against something he does not believe in? He does not.

Then He said: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth by false means﴾. The connection of this verse to what preceded is clear, because what preceded in the verses of fasting was the prohibition of specific things at a specific time. The verse after it, ﴿And do not consume﴾, is a general prohibition: general in what is judged, in its time, and in its place. This is the aspect of connection: when He mentioned the specific prohibition that occurs with fasting, He clarified the general prohibition that occurs both in fasting and outside fasting. So He said: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves by false means﴾. ﴿Do not consume﴾: the intended meaning of consuming is something broader than eating, but He specified eating because it is the strongest way of benefiting. The strongest way of benefiting from wealth is eating. A person benefits from wealth by building a dwelling for himself. The building is attached to him, is it not? But it is not as close to him as clothing. Which is closer to him?
* The students: Clothing.
* The Shaykh: Clothing. Likewise, one spends wealth on garments before spending it on furnishings, and furnishing is more specific than the house, or not? Because furnishing is what is adjacent to him when sleeping, sitting and the like. He spends it on clothing, which is more specific than furnishing. He spends it on food and drink, which is the most specific of things; nothing comes after it. For this reason some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, mentioned that if a person has doubtful wealth, he should spend it on fuel, not on food and drink, because the body is nourished by food and drink, and they are the most specific benefit of wealth.
If Allah says ﴿do not consume your wealth﴾, and this is the most specific benefit, and one who does not do it would perish, for if he did not eat he would die, how then would He return to other than it?
His saying: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves﴾: how does He say ﴿your wealth﴾ ﴿your wealth among yourselves﴾ (...)? We say: we have an eater and something eaten from. If you, the eater, do not accept that your wealth be consumed, how would you accept consuming the wealth of another? Consider the wealth of another as if it were your own wealth. And why? So that you do not consume it, just as you do not accept that someone wrongs you and consumes your wealth. You must place your brother's wealth in the position of your own. So we say: the benefit of attributing the wealth to the one who consumes it, which is consumed belonging to another, is that he should reflect that the wealth of another must be protected by him just as he protects his own wealth.
His saying: ﴿among yourselves﴾ means: in contracts, such as leases, sales, pledges and others, because these occur between two parties. It is all the more fitting that you should not consume it through plunder and usurpation, where there is no transaction between you and another person. That is: if you are forbidden to consume it in contracts, then it is all the more so forbidden to consume it through usurpation, coercion and the like.
His saying: ﴿by false means﴾: the word ﴿bil-batil﴾ (by false means). This bā' is a particle of genitive, but what is its meaning? Is its meaning accompaniment, that is, eating accompanied by falsehood? Or is its meaning instrumental, that falsehood is like a tool with which one eats, as when you say "I slaughtered with the knife," or "I threw it with the stone"? We say that the bā' is suitable for both together. It is not permitted that you take another's wealth by falsehood, by making falsehood a means to take wealth, nor that you consume wealth in a manner accompanied by falsehood. So it includes what is forbidden in itself and what is forbidden because of its attribute.
His saying: ﴿and send it as a bribe to the rulers﴾: ﴿tudlū bihā﴾ (and send it): the pronoun refers either to wealth, or it refers to litigation. The root of idlā' is from adlā dalwahu (he lowered his bucket), and it is known that one who lowers his bucket wants to reach the water. So the meaning of ﴿and send it to the rulers﴾ is that you reach toward the rulers through it, so that you make the rulers a means to consuming it. How does it become a means to consuming it? You deny the right that is upon you when there is no evidence for it, then you dispute with him before the judge. What does the judge say to the accused? He says: bring evidence. If the claimant has no evidence, the oath is directed at you, and if you swear, you are cleared. Do you understand? Now I have sent it to the rulers, meaning I made the ruler a means to consuming wealth. This is one view on the matter. The second view: the meaning of ﴿tudlū bihā ilā al-ḥukkām﴾ is that you convey it to them by bribing the rulers so that they rule in your favor. So the meaning of ﴿tudlū bihā ilā al-ḥukkām﴾ is that you convey it to them for the purpose of what? That they rule for you. Both meanings are correct.
* A student: Does not "the fallāsa" enter into it, Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: The fallāsa?
* The student: Yes, the one who makes the rulers bankrupt in order to take wealth unjustly.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but you would not be the one who consumed it.
* The student: Yes, but you sent it to the rulers?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but the verse says ﴿do not consume﴾ and ﴿and send﴾. If we consider the two clauses separate from each other, then yes, it enters as you said, and the prohibition becomes about two things: ﴿do not consume your wealth among yourselves by false means﴾ is an independent clause, and ﴿and send it to the rulers﴾ is an independent clause. But the apparent structure of the wording, meaning the apparent sense of the speech, is that the two clauses are one; for this reason He said ﴿and send it﴾ and did not say ﴿and do not send it﴾, so He made it conjoined with His saying ﴿and do not consume﴾, and so it is built upon it.
* A student: Where does the pronoun return?
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* The student: In the second view, the bribing?
* The Shaykh: Yes, it returns to the wealth.
* The student: Is the wealth with which the judge was bribed different from the wealth...?
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is no contradiction, but its meaning would be: do not consume your wealth among yourselves by falsehood, and do not send your wealth so that you may consume this.
* The student: So it is other wealth?
* The Shaykh: Other wealth, in order that by it you may consume the wealth of others, when they rule for you by it.
* A student: Shaykh, does the fallāsa we mentioned not fall under bribery?
* The Shaykh: No, no, the fallāsa is not this. The fallāsa is when one informs the ruler that so-and-so has wealth in order that he may take it from him.
* A student: With us, in (...), we say "upon it (...)," meaning he bribes, so the matter became confused for him?
* The Shaykh: No, he points the rulers to people's wealth so that they may consume it.
* A student: Are the rulers judges, or rulers...?
* The Shaykh: The rulers are the princes. If we say the meaning is as Ghanim said, that is one case; but if we say the meaning is "at the time of litigation," then it includes both princes and judges who rule.

He said: ﴿and send it to the rulers so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people﴾. His saying ﴿so that you may consume﴾: someone may say there is a difficulty in it, because He said ﴿and do not consume﴾ and then said ﴿so that you may consume﴾; how does He give a reason for the ruling by the same ruling? We say: the lām here is not for causation, but the lām here is for consequence, meaning that when you do it, the consumption occurs for you, the consumption of a portion of the wealth of people. So the lām here is for consequence, and the lām comes for consequence as in His saying, exalted: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. Did the family of Pharaoh pick him up for this cause, or was the consequence so? The consequence was so. So the lām in His saying ﴿li-ta'kulū﴾ is the lām of consequence.
His saying ﴿li-ta'kulū﴾: why was the nūn deleted?
* A student: It is in the accusative.
* The Shaykh: It is in the accusative by an implied "an" after the lām according to one view, or by the lām itself according to whose view?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct. ﴿li-ta'kulū farīqan min amwāl al-nās﴾: farīq means a group or party, and it was called farīq because it separates from others. So this is a group of people, meaning a party of them that has separated and split off.
His saying ﴿farīqan min amwāl al-nās﴾: if someone said, "He might consume all the wealth of the defendant?"
* A student: Then it is all the more so.
* The Shaykh: All the more so? Yes, all the more so. Or we say that the wealth of the defendant is a portion of people's wealth in the general sense, because however much wealth a person may have, others also have wealth. Yes indeed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 186–188 (part 5 of 7):

﴿مِنْ أَمْوَالِ النَّاسِ بِالْإِثْمِ﴾ ﴿لِتَأْكُلُوا فَرِيقًا مِنْ أَمْوَالِ النَّاسِ بِالْإِثْمِ﴾ The bāʾ here is for accompaniment (muṣāḥabah), meaning: eating accompanied by sin (ithm), which is wrongdoing; and that is because it is false (bāṭil). From this we know that bāṭil means ithm. But is bāṭil always ithm? No. Bāṭil may refer to that which has no benefit in it, as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): «Every diversion with which the son of Adam diverts himself is bāṭil, except his playing with his bow, his playing with his wife, or his training of his horse» [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (1637), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (17300), from the hadith of ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir (may Allah be pleased with him).]].
* * *
﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ﴾.
* Several benefits are derived from this verse. First: fasting is a occasion for the answering of supplication, because Allah the Exalted mentioned this verse in the midst of the verses on fasting, and especially since He mentioned it at the end of the discussion of the verses on fasting. Some scholars said: from it another benefit is derived, that it is recommended to supplicate at the end of the day of fasting.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed; because it was mentioned after we spoke about fasting and abstaining.
* Student: It may be said: it is more fitting on the ʿĪd?
* Shaykh: No, but every day counts as one act of worship.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah the Exalted has knowledge of the unseen, because His saying ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ﴾ is in the future.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the compassion (raʾfah) of Allah the Mighty and Majestic in His saying ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي﴾, where He attributed them to Himself as an honour and as tenderness toward them.
* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of the nearness of Allah the Exalted, from His saying ﴿فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾; and all the pronouns refer to Allah: ﴿إِنِّي قَرِيبٌ أُجِيبُ﴾ ﴿إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾ ﴿فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي﴾, six pronouns all referring to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.
