For three days: ﴿during appointed days﴾. That is, whoever delays until the third day, there is no sin upon him. Thus He removed sin from both the one who hastens and the one who delays, from both of them together. Insha'Allah, the question of which of the two is better, hastening or delaying, will come in the discussion of the benefits of the verse.

His saying ﴿for whoever has taqwa﴾: this is a prepositional phrase serving as the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: "That," meaning the removal of sin is for whoever has taqwa. That is, the removal of sin in either hastening or delaying is for whoever has taqwa, meaning the one who accompanies taqwa in his pilgrimage. This is because when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said ﴿So whoever hastens, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾, the one who is mistaken might imagine that there is no sin upon him absolutely, even if he sins in his pilgrimage or opposes taqwa. So He said:
* A student: ﴿for whoever has taqwa﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿For whoever has taqwa﴾, in order to remove the misconception that arose from the negation of sin, because the negating la of genus negates every sin. But Allah restricted it: ﴿for whoever has taqwa﴾. "Ittaqa" is a past-tense verb derived from taqwa. And what is taqwa?
* A student: Taqwa is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.
* The Shaykh: Well said, may Allah bless you. Taqwa: taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is taqwa, because it is derived from wiqaya (protection). Its original form, according to what the grammarians say, is "waqwa."

Then He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in all your circumstances, during the pilgrimage and after the pilgrimage. Taqwa is not only for one who is engaged in obedience, like the state of the heedless. The heedless have taqwa only while they are engaged in obedience: if he is fasting, he has taqwa; if he is on pilgrimage, he has taqwa. But when he finishes this act, some people do not fear Allah and return to heedlessness, forgetting this obligatory matter, which is taqwa. For this reason He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾. Thus He reminded us of the return to Him. It is as if, when we finish the rites, we are reminded that we will also finish with the whole world. He said: ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾. Al-hashr means gathering and joining together, that is, you will be gathered to Him, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and He will repay you for your deeds. The purpose of this final sentence, ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾, is: threat and warning against disobedience and sin, because whoever knows that he will be gathered to Allah fears Allah, does he not? Yes, he fears Allah. If he knows that he will be gathered to Him and recompensed for his deeds, he fears Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

His saying ﴿And know﴾: beginning it with the command to know indicates that this knowledge has importance in reforming a person's heart, his method, and his conduct.

His saying ﴿that you will be gathered to Him﴾ contains the fronting of the complement (al-muta'allaq) before the complemented (al-muta'allaq bihi): ﴿to Him you will be gathered﴾. So what does the fronting convey?
* A student: Restriction.
* The Shaykh: It conveys restriction: you will be gathered to Him and not to other than Him. The return is to Him, just as the origin is from Him.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech may please you in worldly life﴾ and ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾. In the previous verses, He divided people in the pilgrimage into two categories: some say, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world,' and for him in the Hereafter there is no share﴾, and others say, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾, and these ﴿will have a share from what they have earned﴾. Here He also divides people into two categories: believer and hypocrite. He spoke of the hypocrite, saying: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech may please you in worldly life﴾. ﴿Among the people﴾: the (min) here is partitive, and it means "some of the people." For this reason some grammarians parsed it as the subject (mubtada'), saying that it is a particle with the meaning of a noun, since it means "some of the people." So (min) would be the subject, and ﴿whose speech may please you﴾ its predicate. But the well-known view is that (min) is a preposition, and the prepositional phrase is connected with an omitted predicate placed first, and ﴿whose speech may please you﴾ is the delayed subject. That is, "among the people is the one whose speech pleases you."

In His saying ﴿among the people is one whose speech may please you﴾, the address in ﴿may please you﴾ is either to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone who can be addressed. Which of these is preferable?
* A student: The second.
* Another student: The generality.
* The Shaykh: The second, the generality. That is, whoever pleases you, O addressee: the Messenger (ﷺ) and others. ﴿Among the people is one whose speech pleases you﴾.

His saying ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾: some grammarians mentioned that when one says "I was pleased by such-and-such" (a'jabanī kadhā), it refers to what is found admirable, and when you say "I marvelled at such-and-such" ('ajibtu min kadhā), it refers to what is disapproved. So you say, for example, "The speech of so-and-so pleased me" if it is good speech, and "I marvelled at his speech" if it is bad, objectionable speech. So His saying ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾ means: whose speech you find admirable.

His saying ﴿in worldly life﴾ means: when he speaks about matters connected with worldly affairs, such as speaking in a way by which he reaches safety from killing, captivity, and similar things. This is because we have said that this verse concerns whom? The hypocrites. The evidence for this is the Almighty's saying: ﴿And when you see them, their physiques please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:4], because of its beauty and eloquence. But they are people of deception, delusion, and lying. The sign of the hypocrite is threefold, among which: "When he speaks, he lies." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (33) and Muslim (59/107), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him); and al-Bukhari (2459) and Muslim (58/106), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both).]

He said: ﴿whose speech pleases you in worldly life﴾. The phrase ﴿in worldly life﴾ is connected with an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) of (qawl, speech): that is, his speech while it is in worldly life, meaning concerning matters connected with this world, because he does not speak in a way that pleases regarding religious matters. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿whose speech pleases you in worldly life﴾, that is, speech that pleases even concerning religion, but does not benefit him in the Hereafter; it benefits him only in this world.

He said: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾. Scholars differed in its meaning, with two views:
The first view: ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ refers to hypocrisy: his inner state contradicts his outward state. The one who is witnessed against, namely his inner state, is who? Allah. So by concealing hypocrisy, he is one whom Allah witnesses concerning what is in his heart of hypocrisy. This is one view.
The second view: ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ means he swears by Allah and takes an oath that he is a believer and sincere, and that what is in his heart is this, so he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of love for faith and adherence to it, while he is lying. Is he lying or truthful?
* A student: Lying.
* The Shaykh: Lying. This is supported by the Almighty's saying: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We testify that you are the Messenger of Allah." Allah knows that you are His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:1]. Are they lying about your being the Messenger of Allah, or in their claim that they testify to it?
* The students: In their claim.
* The Shaykh: In their claim that they testify to it.

The Almighty said: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾. This... there are two views. I say:
The first view: he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of hypocrisy, meaning that his heart is folded over with this, firmly rooted in his heart, and none witnesses it except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because it is inward.
The second view: ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ means that he swears and openly testifies before the people that he is a believer, loves faith, and is committed, while in that he is lying. In my view, the two meanings are not contradictory; both are true. He is folded over with disbelief and hypocrisy, and he also declares to the people and calls Allah to witness that he is a believer.

As for his reality, Allah said about him: ﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾. ﴿The most contentious of opponents﴾ means: the most crooked and the most lying of them. ﴿Opponents (khisam)﴾ may be a verbal noun (masdar) or a plural. If it is a verbal noun, its verb is khasama, yukhasimu, khisaman, like jadala, yujadilu, jidalan, and qatala, yuqatilu, qitalan. The principle is that fi'al forms come as the verbal noun of fa'ala. Ibn Malik gave us that rule in his saying:
* A student: "And fa'ala."
* The Shaykh: No, for fa'ala, not "and fa'ala."
[For fa'ala comes the fi'al and the mufa'alah...]
So here, khasama has: al-khisam and al-mukhasamah. Accordingly, ﴿the most contentious of opponents﴾ is an idafah that is verbal (lafziyyah), because it is an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah) added to its modified noun: that is, "his opposing is the most contentious of oppositions."

If we say that khisam is the plural of khasm, meaning khusum (opponents), its meaning is: he is the most crooked of opponents and the most lying of them. This is also correct, and it is also an idafah of an attribute to its modified noun, because the meaning is: he is among the strong and vehement opponents in their disputation. It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the most contentious opponent." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2457) and Muslim (2668/5), from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).] So the person who disputes and argues falsely in order to refute the truth thereby, this is the most hateful of men to Allah.

Generally, no person who is given to disputation is spared the loss of the blessing of knowledge. The person who is given to argument loses the blessing of knowledge, because most of those given to argument, in most cases, intend only to support their own position, and thereby they lose knowledge.

As for one who seeks the truth, the truth is easy and near and does not require great argument, because it is clear. For this reason you find the people of innovation who dispute about their innovations: you find their knowledge lacks blessing, lacks any good, and you find that they dispute and argue and end up with nothing. They do not reach the truth, because they intended only to support what they are upon. So every person who argues, may Allah save us and grant us well-being, every person who argues in order to have his position prevail, most likely will not be granted success and will not find the blessing of knowledge. But whoever argues in order to reach knowledge, this is praiseworthy and commanded: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125].

But review what is reported from the people of innovation in their disputes with the people of the Sunnah and the community, and you will find long, wide argument, logic, and philosophy, yet you reach nothing through them. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) informed us: "People will not cease asking: who created such-and-such? Who created such-and-such? Until they say: who created Allah?" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3276) and Muslim (134/214), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).] When one reaches this point, what should a person say?
* A student: He seeks refuge in Allah.
* The Shaykh: He seeks refuge in Allah and stops. But if you go to these philosophers or logicians, look at what kinds of proofs, premises, and many other things they bring, and in the end they do not reach what the hadith reached.

So the point is: the contentious opponent who prevails, and I do not say every disputant, most often is deprived of the blessing of knowledge, because he only intends by it to crush his opponent and to make his own position prevail, and this is deprivation of blessing.

His saying ﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾: look at this man, now he has become the most contentious of opponents, because his speech is good and clear, it has clarity and eloquence, and it pleases you. Because he relies on his eloquence and clarity, you find him to be the most contentious of opponents, disputing and arguing.
* A student: Shaykh, does the statement of the grammarians (...) not apply to it?
* The Shaykh: Yes. This should not come from them. It is not fitting for them to despair of him, although He, glory be to Him, is quick to change.
* The student: So this is a command, meaning...
* The Shaykh: It is not praiseworthy. It is not praiseworthy for creatures to despair of Allah's mercy, while He, glory be to Him, is quick to change.

* Student: Shaykh, (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny, and Allah does not like corruption.﴾
* Student: So there is no variant reading (qira'a)?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿wa-yashhadu Allah﴾.
* Shaykh: No, there is no reading from the Seven, no.
* Student: There is a reading.
* Shaykh: It is not one of the Seven.
* Student: Yes, it is one of the Seven, one of the Seven.
* Shaykh: I have no answer; it is not written down for me.
* Student: Yes, Hamzah al-Zayyat recited it with the report form (ʿalā al-khabar).
* Shaykh: I do not know. In any case, verify it, because I have not recorded it, and my general practice is to follow the Seven recitations (qirāʾāt al-sabʿ).
* Student: He says Hamzah.
* Shaykh: Nothing beyond that. Just verify it.
* Student: From one source.
* Shaykh: I say: verify it. Verification is good.

He said: ﴿When he turns away﴾ is in my copy ﴿wa-huwa﴾. This is a known matter with a rule: ﴿wa-huwa﴾ with the ha silent (sukūn) occurs throughout the Qur'an. It is recited as wa-huwa and as wa-hwa.

* Student: According to the reading (...)?
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: ﴿wa-yashhadu﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes. You say: ﴿and Allah bears witness to what is in his heart﴾? This favours the second meaning, that he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of hypocrisy.

He said: ﴿When he turns away, he strives throughout the land﴾. ﴿When he turns away﴾ means: he turns away from you and leaves. ﴿He strives throughout the land﴾: the meaning of striving (saʿy) here is general movement, not running on foot. The meaning is that he moves about to cause corruption. ﴿He strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾: is the lām here a lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) or a lām of consequence (lām al-ʿāqiba)?

* Student: Causation.
* Shaykh: Causation. That is, he seeks corruption, is eager for it, and strives for it to the extent he is able.

﴿to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny﴾. How does he destroy crops and progeny? Some exegetes (mufassirūn) said: the verse was revealed about a specific person, al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who went to a group of the Anṣār, burned their crops, and killed their donkeys, the ḥumur (donkeys).

But the correct view is that the meaning of ﴿destroys crops and progeny﴾ is that, because of his corruption on earth, blessings are diminished and calamities descend, and thus he is the cause of the destruction of crops and progeny. The correct view, as we said, is that the verse is general and not about one specific person; it applies to everyone who has this description. Allah says: ﴿Among people is he whose speech impresses you...﴾. Accordingly, ﴿destroys crops and progeny﴾ means: he becomes a cause of the destruction of crops and progeny.

﴿The crops (al-ḥarth)﴾ means what is sown, the cultivated produce, just as one says al-ghars for what is planted. And His saying ﴿progeny (al-nasl)﴾ is similar: al-nasl means what is begotten, i.e., children and offspring. So his striving becomes a cause of corruption of the earth and of the corruption of animals. When disobedience occurs, and we seek refuge in Allah, blessings are diminished and removed from the earth, calamities descend, and rains decrease. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:96]. And: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and been mindful, We would have expiated their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss. And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:65–66]. ﴿They would have eaten from above them﴾: from the fruits of the trees. ﴿And from beneath their feet﴾: from the crops.

﴿And destroys crops and progeny, and Allah does not like corruption﴾. Is this a statement that his action is beloved to Allah or hateful to Him? It is hateful to Him, because Allah does not like corruption. If He does not like this act, He does not like the one who is characterised by it. For this reason, another verse says: ﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:64]. Allah does not love corruption nor the corrupters; corruption itself is hateful to Allah, and the corrupters are also hateful to Him; He does not love them.

When the negation of love is attached to a description, it may be inferred that love is affirmed for its opposite description. Since He does not love corruption, He loves righteousness. Likewise the reformers (al-muṣlihūn), to the point that Allah says: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hūd 11:117]. So Allah the Exalted loves the reformer and loves righteousness as well.

﴿And when he is told, "Fear Allah," pride (al-ʿizza) takes hold of him with sin﴾. We seek refuge in Allah. ﴿When he is told "Fear Allah"﴾: who says it? Any speaker; because qīla is a passive verb, and the original form of qīla is qūila, on the pattern ḍuriba, since it is a triliteral passive. But a morphological alteration (iʿlāl) occurred by changing the waw into a yāʾ, and then the preceding letter was given a kasra: qīla.

﴿When he is told "Fear Allah"﴾ means: he is commanded to fear Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and to avoid what he strives for in the land of corruption, which is the cause of the destruction of crops and progeny. His response, we seek refuge in Allah, was: ﴿pride takes hold of him with sin﴾. ﴿Pride (al-ʿizza)﴾ here means haughtiness, zeal, and arrogance.

Pride may be a praiseworthy trait and may be a blameworthy trait. The one who takes pride in his religion is praiseworthy: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 63:8]. But the one who takes pride in his lineage and ancestry, to the point that he has an aversion to being commanded in religion, this is blameworthy. So pride takes hold of him with sin, meaning it drives him to sin. The bāʾ here is said to be causal (sababiyya): pride, i.e., haughtiness, took hold of him because of his sin; because of his sin he was not granted guidance and was not enabled to accept the command to be mindful. It is also said that the bāʾ is transitive (taʿdiya), meaning "took hold of him with such-and-such," i.e., it carried him to it. This is the closer view.

And His saying ﴿with sin (bi-l-ithm)﴾: what is the meaning of ithm? It means a sin that brings about punishment. Every sin that brings about punishment is ithm.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Hell will suffice him, and surely it is a wretched resting place﴾. ﴿Hell will suffice him (ḥasbuhu jahannamu)﴾ means: it is enough for him, and it is a threat to him with it, we seek refuge in Allah. Ḥasb means sufficient. Allah says: ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:129], meaning sufficient for me. ﴿And they said: "Allah is sufficient for us"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:173], meaning sufficient for us. ﴿Hell will suffice him﴾, meaning it is enough for him, and the meaning is that he will be among its people, we seek refuge in Allah. ﴿And surely it is a wretched resting place﴾.

(Jahannam) is one of the names of the Fire. It is said that it is a loanword (ism muʿarrab), i.e., it is not from classical Arabic but is Arabized. It is also said that it is from classical Arabic, and that its origin is al-juhmah, which means darkness, but the letter nūn was added to it for intensification: jahannam. Either way, Jahannam is the name of the Fire that Allah the Exalted prepared for the disbelievers. It is named so because of the depth of its bottom and its darkness, we seek refuge in Allah.

And His saying ﴿and surely it is a wretched resting place﴾: how do we parse the lām here?

* Student: It is the lām of initiation (lām al-ibtidāʾ).
* Shaykh: The lām of initiation, for what?
* Student: A lām introducing an oath (mūṭiʾa lil-qasam).
* Shaykh: Or a lām introducing an oath, meaning: "And by Allah, it is a wretched resting place." This is closer.

And His saying ﴿wretched (biʾsa) resting place﴾: this is a rigid verb (fiʿl jāmid) used to express dispraise (inshāʾ al-dhamm). Biʾsa is a rigid verb used to express dispraise, and its subject (fāʿil) is? ﴿al-mihād (the resting place)﴾. These are among the verbs that require a specified object of dispraise (makhṣūṣ bil-dhamm). Where is the specified object?

* Student: al-mihād.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿al-mihād﴾ is the subject.
* Student: Omitted.
* Shaykh: Omitted. That is: "and surely it is a wretched resting place, its resting place, since it is Hell."

(...) ﴿on two days﴾ and so on to the end.

* Benefits derived from these noble verses: the excellence of remembrance during these counted days, as indicated by ﴿and remember Allah﴾; because remembrance of Allah in general is performed at all times, but this is remembrance in a specific manner.
* Another benefit of these noble verses: it is permissible during these three days to hasten or delay, as indicated by ﴿whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾.
* Another benefit: the breadth of Allah the Mighty's favour and His facilitation in His rulings, in that He made the person free to remain three days or to hasten on the second day.
* Another benefit: he must leave Mina before the sun sets, because "in" (fī) denotes containment, and a container encompasses what is contained, so hastening must occur within the two days.
* Another benefit: it is not permissible to hasten on the eleventh day, because if he hastened on the eleventh day, he would have hastened on one day, not on two days. Is this clear?

I warn you here that many common people think that the two days refer to the day of ʿĪd and the eleventh day, and they think it is permissible to hasten on the eleventh day. This is not correct, because Allah says: ﴿And remember Allah during numbered days﴾, and these are the days of tashrīq (the days of drying meat). The days of tashrīq begin?

* Student: On the eleventh.
* Shaykh: On the eleventh.
* Another benefit of the verse: actions for which there is a choice do not incur sin unless the person performs them out of mindfulness of Allah the Mighty, and not with negligence toward His commands; as indicated by ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾. So whoever does what is optional out of mindfulness of Allah the Mighty and by taking His facilitation, there is no sin upon him. But whoever does it out of negligence and indifference, he bears sin for abandoning mindfulness and for neglecting the commands of Allah.

Can it be inferred from the verse that it is permissible to delay until the fourteenth and fifteenth days, or not?

* Students: No.
* Shaykh: The verse says ﴿whoever delays﴾; it did not say "in three days". Is it unrestricted? But the basis of the remembrance is in three days, in counted days, so the meaning is: whoever delays during these counted days, which are the three days.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Because Allah restricted it by saying ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾.
* Student: How is that conceived?
* Shaykh: Conceived?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: It is conceived that a man does this out of negligence and indifference, not in the sense that Allah has facilitated it for him and granted him a concession in it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the obligation of mindfulness, as indicated by ﴿and fear Allah﴾. We have already mentioned that mindfulness (taqwā) and righteousness (birr), when both are mentioned together, are?

* Student: Distinct.
* Shaykh: When both are mentioned together?
* Student: Distinct.
* Shaykh: They are distinct in meaning; and when one is mentioned alone, the other is included in it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation of resurrection, as indicated by ﴿and know that you will be gathered to Him﴾.
* Another benefit: combining admonitions with warning, as indicated by ﴿and fear Allah and know that you will be gathered to Him﴾. When a person knows that he will be gathered to Allah the Mighty and that He will recompense him, he will fear Allah and perform what Allah has obligated. From this we understand the wisdom behind Allah the Mighty joining faith in the Last Day with faith in Allah in many verses. In many verses, faith in the Last Day is paired with faith in Allah, without the other things in which one must believe; this is because faith in the Last Day entails acting for that day, and that is?—to carry out the obedience of Allah and His Messenger.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And among people is he whose speech impresses you in the life of this world﴾ to the end.

* From this noble verse it is derived that people are divided into types: some are of this description, and others come with a description as well.
* It is also derived that a person should not be deceived by outward appearances. From where is this taken? ﴿whose speech impresses you﴾. Likewise, among people there is one whose action impresses you, but he conceals disbelief, we seek refuge in Allah. So do not be deceived by his outward condition. But there is no doubt that for us, we are not permitted to judge except by what?

* Student: The apparent.
* Shaykh: The apparent, because we do not know what is in hearts, and it is impossible for us to hold people accountable for what is in their hearts; we only hold them accountable according to outward appearances.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: this category of people calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, either regarding what he displays or what he conceals. For we said there are two meanings: either regarding what he displays, meaning it appears to you that he speaks words by which he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of his outward condition; or that he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of disbelief and hypocrisy, for he conceals it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: an indication of abandoning contention and quarrelling, as indicated by ﴿yet he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾. Disputes generally contain no blessing. But this verse, as we said earlier, is restricted to what Allah commanded regarding argument, which is arguing with falsehood using truth, since this is a matter that cannot be avoided.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: affirmation of the knowledge of Allah the Mighty regarding what is in breasts, as indicated by ﴿and calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾; because what is in the heart is known only to Allah the Mighty and to the one who has that thing in his heart.

* Another benefit of the following verse: this man whose speech impresses you and who calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, when he turns away, strives throughout the land to corrupt it, by what?

* Student: By sins.
* Shaykh: By sins, for sins are a cause of the destruction of crops and progeny, we seek refuge in Allah. The evidence? ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:96]. And: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and been mindful, We would have expiated their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss. And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:65–66].

* Another benefit of the verse: this man whose speech impresses you turns away; he does not stay or remain; as indicated by ﴿when he turns away﴾. It has already passed in us at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah that the Arabic language distinguishes between ʾin and idhā: ʾin, the conditional particle, is used for a matter that may be impossible or unattainable, and usually does not occur; whereas idhā is used for what is possible and expected. For this reason, regarding His saying ﴿Every time it lights for them, they walk therein; but when darkness falls upon them, they stand still﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:20], scholars note that He did not say "if darkness falls upon them". When He said ﴿when darkness falls upon them﴾, it is known that it must occur. Here, ﴿when he turns away﴾ is not like "if he turns away, he strives". Rather, "when he turns away" means turning away will certainly happen from him, because it is not fixed.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: affirmation of Allah the Mighty's love, as indicated by ﴿does not like corruption﴾.
If you say: this is a negation and not an affirmation, we say: His negating love for corruption is evidence of the existence of the basic love. Had He not loved at all, there would be no difference between corruption and righteousness, would there? Since He negated love from corruption, it is known that He loves righteousness, and so it is.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: a warning against corruption on earth, as indicated by ﴿and Allah does not like corruption﴾. It is well known that every person must be wary of exposing himself to a matter that Allah does not love.

If He does not love corruption, does He not love the corrupter?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is known; because if a description is not beloved to Allah, whoever is characterised by it is not beloved to Allah. Moreover, it appears in other verses: ﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:64].

Then He said: ﴿And when he is told, "Fear Allah," pride takes hold of him with sin; so Hell will suffice him, and surely it is a wretched resting place.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 203–206 (part 3 of 3):

* It is derived from this noble verse that this man, described with these attributes, is disdainful of being commanded to fear Allah; this is shown by His saying: ﴿Pride seized him﴾. He is disdainful, as if he were saying to himself: "I am too exalted to be told to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." This is without doubt injustice. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded by Allah, the Exalted, to fear Allah; He commanded His Prophet, who was the most God-fearing of people, to fear Allah: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah, and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab 1], and He said in the story of Zaynab: ﴿And fear Allah, while you concealed within yourself that which Allah was to disclose, and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab 37]. This was said to the Prophet (ﷺ). So how about you, O human, are you not told: "Fear Allah"? Yet, may Allah protect us, this is evidence that he has within him an aversion to the truth, arrogance, and haughtiness.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete eloquence in omitting the agent in His saying: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah"﴾. He did not say: "When so-and-so or so-and-so says to him," so as to include everyone who says this to him, because his rejection of this command is not directed at the person of the speaker, but at his dislike of what he is commanded to do. For if he had said: "When the Messenger says to him," it would be as if he were saying: "This one is too proud to accept that the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), though he was not sent?" Or if the one who said it to him were a poor man, he would say: "What does this poor man think he can say to me?" But when the agent is omitted, his rejection of the truth is due to— 

* Student: Dislike.

* The Shaykh: Due to dislike of the truth itself: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against rejecting those who give advice, since Allah, the Exalted, made this one of the attributes of these hypocrites. Whoever rejects one who commands him to fear Allah has in him a resemblance to the hypocrites. It is obligatory for a person, when he is told, "Fear Allah," to say: "We hear and we obey." Whoever commands you to fear Allah, you must say: "We hear and we obey," not for the sake of this man, but because of the obligation of fearing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that disdain may lead its possessor into sin; this is shown by His saying: ﴿Pride seized him with sin﴾. We have previously mentioned that the scholars gave it two meanings, both of which are valid: either the meaning is that, because of his sin, pride seizes him and he does not submit to the command to fear Allah; or the meaning is that his pride led him into sin, i.e., did sin precede the pride, so that pride seized him because of it, or did pride precede and drive him to sin? We mentioned two opinions on this, and we said that both are valid.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that he—i.e., this man—is among the people of the Fire; this is shown by His saying: ﴿Hell is sufficient for him﴾.
And among them: the praise of the Fire by way of censure; this is shown by His saying: ﴿And what an evil resting place﴾, and there is no doubt that Hell is an evil resting place..

The Almighty said: ﴿And remember Allah during appointed days﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:203]. Here Allah commands remembering Him. ﴿Remember﴾ ( udhkuru) is an imperative verb, and the imperative, as already explained, implies obligation, though it may be shared between obligation and recommendation according to what other evidence indicates.

His saying ﴿remember Allah﴾ encompasses every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. That is, the intended meaning is not only that we say "there is no god but Allah." Rather, it includes every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah.

If someone asks: "What is your evidence for what you say, and what is the basis for it?" I reply: my evidence is the Almighty's saying: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer. Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing. And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:45]. That is, the remembrance of Allah contained in this prayer is greater. Also from the Sunnah is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The circumambulation of the House, and between as-Safa and al-Marwah, and the throwing of the pebbles, were only prescribed to establish the remembrance of Allah." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (1888) and al-Tirmidhi (902), from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).]

As for the basis for it, namely why every statement and act that brings one closer to Allah is considered remembrance of Him: every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah is accompanied by the intention that it be for whom? For Allah. And this is remembrance of Allah. When you do something by which you draw near to Allah, or say something by which you draw near to Allah, there is in your heart the intention that you have intended (...), because by it you seek the Face of Allah. This is remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (...).

His saying ﴿during appointed days﴾: the appointed days are said to be the days of at-Tashriq (the days of drying meat), which are the three days: the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. Remembering Allah during them encompasses, as I said a moment ago, every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah. Accordingly, the unrestricted and restricted takbir enters into this. Also included is the throwing of the pebbles at the jamarat, and the circumambulation of the House and the sa'y between as-Safa and al-Marwah if they fall during these days.

The Almighty said: ﴿So whoever hastens in two days﴾ (...). So, ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ hastens what? The scholars said: "hastens" means he leaves Mina. ﴿In two days﴾ means within this period, within two days. There is no sin upon him if he hastens. It should not be said that one must remain until the thirteenth day, because Allah said ﴿appointed days﴾, and "days" is plural, so someone might understand that staying for the three days is obligatory. Therefore He said: ﴿whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, meaning there is no blame upon him.

His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ is the answer of the conditional clause. As we all know, it is connected with the linking fa' (fa' al-jawab) because the clause is nominal, and the answer must be connected with the fa'.

Nominal, imperative, and what is rigid (jamid) with ma, qad, la, and the future particle [i.e., the seven positions where the answer of the conditional must be introduced by fa'], these are the seven positions in which, when they occur as the answer of a conditional, they must be connected with fa'. What are the ones in our present example?
* The students: Nominal.
* The Shaykh: Nominal. Is it fitting for us to say "nominal" or "connected with la"? Or no?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And with la. It is connected with la and it is also nominal.
* A student: In the verse (la) or (ma)?
* The Shaykh: And with ma, yes, with ma.
[Nominal, imperative, and with the rigid, and with ma...]
What about (la)? So this is nominal. This is nominal only.
﴿So there is no sin upon him﴾. His saying ﴿upon him﴾ is the predicate.
﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾. Delays until when? The verse does not specify ﴿delays﴾, but we know that ﴿delays﴾ refers to these appointed days, meaning until the third day. So if anyone remains until the fourth day, we say: this is not legislated. If someone argues against us with the verse, saying that Allah said ﴿and whoever delays﴾ without restriction, we say: but the basic remembrance is legislated for when? For three days: ﴿during appointed days﴾. That is, whoever delays until the third day, there is no sin upon him. Thus He removed sin from both the one who hastens and the one who delays, from both of them together. Insha'Allah, the question of which of the two is better, hastening or delaying, will come in the discussion of the benefits of the verse.

His saying ﴿for whoever has taqwa﴾: this is a prepositional phrase serving as the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: "That," meaning the removal of sin is for whoever has taqwa. That is, the removal of sin in either hastening or delaying is for whoever has taqwa, meaning the one who accompanies taqwa in his pilgrimage. This is because when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said ﴿So whoever hastens, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾, the one who is mistaken might imagine that there is no sin upon him absolutely, even if he sins in his pilgrimage or opposes taqwa. So He said:
* A student: ﴿for whoever has taqwa﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿For whoever has taqwa﴾, in order to remove the misconception that arose from the negation of sin, because the negating la of genus negates every sin. But Allah restricted it: ﴿for whoever has taqwa﴾. "Ittaqa" is a past-tense verb derived from taqwa. And what is taqwa?
* A student: Taqwa is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.
* The Shaykh: Well said, may Allah bless you. Taqwa: taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. This is taqwa, because it is derived from wiqaya (protection). Its original form, according to what the grammarians say, is "waqwa."

Then He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in all your circumstances, during the pilgrimage and after the pilgrimage. Taqwa is not only for one who is engaged in obedience, like the state of the heedless. The heedless have taqwa only while they are engaged in obedience: if he is fasting, he has taqwa; if he is on pilgrimage, he has taqwa. But when he finishes this act, some people do not fear Allah and return to heedlessness, forgetting this obligatory matter, which is taqwa. For this reason He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾. Thus He reminded us of the return to Him. It is as if, when we finish the rites, we are reminded that we will also finish with the whole world. He said: ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾. Al-hashr means gathering and joining together, that is, you will be gathered to Him, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and He will repay you for your deeds. The purpose of this final sentence, ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾, is: threat and warning against disobedience and sin, because whoever knows that he will be gathered to Allah fears Allah, does he not? Yes, he fears Allah. If he knows that he will be gathered to Him and recompensed for his deeds, he fears Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

His saying ﴿And know﴾: beginning it with the command to know indicates that this knowledge has importance in reforming a person's heart, his method, and his conduct.

His saying ﴿that you will be gathered to Him﴾ contains the fronting of the complement (al-muta'allaq) before the complemented (al-muta'allaq bihi): ﴿to Him you will be gathered﴾. So what does the fronting convey?
* A student: Restriction.
* The Shaykh: It conveys restriction: you will be gathered to Him and not to other than Him. The return is to Him, just as the origin is from Him.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech may please you in worldly life﴾ and ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾. In the previous verses, He divided people in the pilgrimage into two categories: some say, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world,' and for him in the Hereafter there is no share﴾, and others say, ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good﴾, and these ﴿will have a share from what they have earned﴾. Here He also divides people into two categories: believer and hypocrite. He spoke of the hypocrite, saying: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech may please you in worldly life﴾. ﴿Among the people﴾: the (min) here is partitive, and it means "some of the people." For this reason some grammarians parsed it as the subject (mubtada'), saying that it is a particle with the meaning of a noun, since it means "some of the people." So (min) would be the subject, and ﴿whose speech may please you﴾ its predicate. But the well-known view is that (min) is a preposition, and the prepositional phrase is connected with an omitted predicate placed first, and ﴿whose speech may please you﴾ is the delayed subject. That is, "among the people is the one whose speech pleases you."

In His saying ﴿among the people is one whose speech may please you﴾, the address in ﴿may please you﴾ is either to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone who can be addressed. Which of these is preferable?
* A student: The second.
* Another student: The generality.
* The Shaykh: The second, the generality. That is, whoever pleases you, O addressee: the Messenger (ﷺ) and others. ﴿Among the people is one whose speech pleases you﴾.

His saying ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾: some grammarians mentioned that when one says "I was pleased by such-and-such" (a'jabanī kadhā), it refers to what is found admirable, and when you say "I marvelled at such-and-such" ('ajibtu min kadhā), it refers to what is disapproved. So you say, for example, "The speech of so-and-so pleased me" if it is good speech, and "I marvelled at his speech" if it is bad, objectionable speech. So His saying ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾ means: whose speech you find admirable.

His saying ﴿in worldly life﴾ means: when he speaks about matters connected with worldly affairs, such as speaking in a way by which he reaches safety from killing, captivity, and similar things. This is because we have said that this verse concerns whom? The hypocrites. The evidence for this is the Almighty's saying: ﴿And when you see them, their physiques please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:4], because of its beauty and eloquence. But they are people of deception, delusion, and lying. The sign of the hypocrite is threefold, among which: "When he speaks, he lies." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (33) and Muslim (59/107), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him); and al-Bukhari (2459) and Muslim (58/106), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both).]

He said: ﴿whose speech pleases you in worldly life﴾. The phrase ﴿in worldly life﴾ is connected with an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause (hal) of (qawl, speech): that is, his speech while it is in worldly life, meaning concerning matters connected with this world, because he does not speak in a way that pleases regarding religious matters. It is also possible that the meaning is: ﴿whose speech pleases you in worldly life﴾, that is, speech that pleases even concerning religion, but does not benefit him in the Hereafter; it benefits him only in this world.

He said: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾. Scholars differed in its meaning, with two views:
The first view: ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ refers to hypocrisy: his inner state contradicts his outward state. The one who is witnessed against, namely his inner state, is who? Allah. So by concealing hypocrisy, he is one whom Allah witnesses concerning what is in his heart of hypocrisy. This is one view.
The second view: ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ means he swears by Allah and takes an oath that he is a believer and sincere, and that what is in his heart is this, so he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of love for faith and adherence to it, while he is lying. Is he lying or truthful?
* A student: Lying.
* The Shaykh: Lying. This is supported by the Almighty's saying: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We testify that you are the Messenger of Allah." Allah knows that you are His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun 63:1]. Are they lying about your being the Messenger of Allah, or in their claim that they testify to it?
* The students: In their claim.
* The Shaykh: In their claim that they testify to it.

The Almighty said: ﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾. This... there are two views. I say:
The first view: he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of hypocrisy, meaning that his heart is folded over with this, firmly rooted in his heart, and none witnesses it except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because it is inward.
The second view: ﴿he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ means that he swears and openly testifies before the people that he is a believer, loves faith, and is committed, while in that he is lying. In my view, the two meanings are not contradictory; both are true. He is folded over with disbelief and hypocrisy, and he also declares to the people and calls Allah to witness that he is a believer.

As for his reality, Allah said about him: ﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾. ﴿The most contentious of opponents﴾ means: the most crooked and the most lying of them. ﴿Opponents (khisam)﴾ may be a verbal noun (masdar) or a plural. If it is a verbal noun, its verb is khasama, yukhasimu, khisaman, like jadala, yujadilu, jidalan, and qatala, yuqatilu, qitalan. The principle is that fi'al forms come as the verbal noun of fa'ala. Ibn Malik gave us that rule in his saying:
* A student: "And fa'ala."
* The Shaykh: No, for fa'ala, not "and fa'ala."
[For fa'ala comes the fi'al and the mufa'alah...]
So here, khasama has: al-khisam and al-mukhasamah. Accordingly, ﴿the most contentious of opponents﴾ is an idafah that is verbal (lafziyyah), because it is an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah) added to its modified noun: that is, "his opposing is the most contentious of oppositions."

If we say that khisam is the plural of khasm, meaning khusum (opponents), its meaning is: he is the most crooked of opponents and the most lying of them. This is also correct, and it is also an idafah of an attribute to its modified noun, because the meaning is: he is among the strong and vehement opponents in their disputation. It is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the most contentious opponent." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2457) and Muslim (2668/5), from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).] So the person who disputes and argues falsely in order to refute the truth thereby, this is the most hateful of men to Allah.

Generally, no person who is given to disputation is spared the loss of the blessing of knowledge. The person who is given to argument loses the blessing of knowledge, because most of those given to argument, in most cases, intend only to support their own position, and thereby they lose knowledge.

As for one who seeks the truth, the truth is easy and near and does not require great argument, because it is clear. For this reason you find the people of innovation who dispute about their innovations: you find their knowledge lacks blessing, lacks any good, and you find that they dispute and argue and end up with nothing. They do not reach the truth, because they intended only to support what they are upon. So every person who argues, may Allah save us and grant us well-being, every person who argues in order to have his position prevail, most likely will not be granted success and will not find the blessing of knowledge. But whoever argues in order to reach knowledge, this is praiseworthy and commanded: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125].

But review what is reported from the people of innovation in their disputes with the people of the Sunnah and the community, and you will find long, wide argument, logic, and philosophy, yet you reach nothing through them. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) informed us: "People will not cease asking: who created such-and-such? Who created such-and-such? Until they say: who created Allah?" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3276) and Muslim (134/214), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).] When one reaches this point, what should a person say?
* A student: He seeks refuge in Allah.
* The Shaykh: He seeks refuge in Allah and stops. But if you go to these philosophers or logicians, look at what kinds of proofs, premises, and many other things they bring, and in the end they do not reach what the hadith reached.

So the point is: the contentious opponent who prevails, and I do not say every disputant, most often is deprived of the blessing of knowledge, because he only intends by it to crush his opponent and to make his own position prevail, and this is deprivation of blessing.

His saying ﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾: look at this man, now he has become the most contentious of opponents, because his speech is good and clear, it has clarity and eloquence, and it pleases you. Because he relies on his eloquence and clarity, you find him to be the most contentious of opponents, disputing and arguing.
* A student: Shaykh, does the statement of the grammarians (...) not apply to it?
* The Shaykh: Yes. This should not come from them. It is not fitting for them to despair of him, although He, glory be to Him, is quick to change.
* The student: So this is a command, meaning...
* The Shaykh: It is not praiseworthy. It is not praiseworthy for creatures to despair of Allah's mercy, while He, glory be to Him, is quick to change.

* Student: Shaykh, (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny, and Allah does not like corruption.﴾
* Student: So there is no variant reading (qira'a)?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: ﴿wa-yashhadu Allah﴾.
* Shaykh: No, there is no reading from the Seven, no.
* Student: There is a reading.
* Shaykh: It is not one of the Seven.
* Student: Yes, it is one of the Seven, one of the Seven.
* Shaykh: I have no answer; it is not written down for me.
* Student: Yes, Hamzah al-Zayyat recited it with the report form (ʿalā al-khabar).
* Shaykh: I do not know. In any case, verify it, because I have not recorded it, and my general practice is to follow the Seven recitations (qirāʾāt al-sabʿ).
* Student: He says Hamzah.
* Shaykh: Nothing beyond that. Just verify it.
* Student: From one source.
* Shaykh: I say: verify it. Verification is good.

He said: ﴿When he turns away﴾ is in my copy ﴿wa-huwa﴾. This is a known matter with a rule: ﴿wa-huwa﴾ with the ha silent (sukūn) occurs throughout the Qur'an. It is recited as wa-huwa and as wa-hwa.

* Student: According to the reading (...)?
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: ﴿wa-yashhadu﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes. You say: ﴿and Allah bears witness to what is in his heart﴾? This favours the second meaning, that he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of hypocrisy.

He said: ﴿When he turns away, he strives throughout the land﴾. ﴿When he turns away﴾ means: he turns away from you and leaves. ﴿He strives throughout the land﴾: the meaning of striving (saʿy) here is general movement, not running on foot. The meaning is that he moves about to cause corruption. ﴿He strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾: is the lām here a lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) or a lām of consequence (lām al-ʿāqiba)?

* Student: Causation.
* Shaykh: Causation. That is, he seeks corruption, is eager for it, and strives for it to the extent he is able.

﴿to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny﴾. How does he destroy crops and progeny? Some exegetes (mufassirūn) said: the verse was revealed about a specific person, al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, who went to a group of the Anṣār, burned their crops, and killed their donkeys, the ḥumur (donkeys).

But the correct view is that the meaning of ﴿destroys crops and progeny﴾ is that, because of his corruption on earth, blessings are diminished and calamities descend, and thus he is the cause of the destruction of crops and progeny. The correct view, as we said, is that the verse is general and not about one specific person; it applies to everyone who has this description. Allah says: ﴿Among people is he whose speech impresses you...﴾. Accordingly, ﴿destroys crops and progeny﴾ means: he becomes a cause of the destruction of crops and progeny.

﴿The crops (al-ḥarth)﴾ means what is sown, the cultivated produce, just as one says al-ghars for what is planted. And His saying ﴿progeny (al-nasl)﴾ is similar: al-nasl means what is begotten, i.e., children and offspring. So his striving becomes a cause of corruption of the earth and of the corruption of animals. When disobedience occurs, and we seek refuge in Allah, blessings are diminished and removed from the earth, calamities descend, and rains decrease. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:96]. And: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and been mindful, We would have expiated their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss. And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:65–66]. ﴿They would have eaten from above them﴾: from the fruits of the trees. ﴿And from beneath their feet﴾: from the crops.

﴿And destroys crops and progeny, and Allah does not like corruption﴾. Is this a statement that his action is beloved to Allah or hateful to Him? It is hateful to Him, because Allah does not like corruption. If He does not like this act, He does not like the one who is characterised by it. For this reason, another verse says: ﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:64]. Allah does not love corruption nor the corrupters; corruption itself is hateful to Allah, and the corrupters are also hateful to Him; He does not love them.

When the negation of love is attached to a description, it may be inferred that love is affirmed for its opposite description. Since He does not love corruption, He loves righteousness. Likewise the reformers (al-muṣlihūn), to the point that Allah says: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hūd 11:117]. So Allah the Exalted loves the reformer and loves righteousness as well.

﴿And when he is told, "Fear Allah," pride (al-ʿizza) takes hold of him with sin﴾. We seek refuge in Allah. ﴿When he is told "Fear Allah"﴾: who says it? Any speaker; because qīla is a passive verb, and the original form of qīla is qūila, on the pattern ḍuriba, since it is a triliteral passive. But a morphological alteration (iʿlāl) occurred by changing the waw into a yāʾ, and then the preceding letter was given a kasra: qīla.

﴿When he is told "Fear Allah"﴾ means: he is commanded to fear Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and to avoid what he strives for in the land of corruption, which is the cause of the destruction of crops and progeny. His response, we seek refuge in Allah, was: ﴿pride takes hold of him with sin﴾. ﴿Pride (al-ʿizza)﴾ here means haughtiness, zeal, and arrogance.

Pride may be a praiseworthy trait and may be a blameworthy trait. The one who takes pride in his religion is praiseworthy: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn 63:8]. But the one who takes pride in his lineage and ancestry, to the point that he has an aversion to being commanded in religion, this is blameworthy. So pride takes hold of him with sin, meaning it drives him to sin. The bāʾ here is said to be causal (sababiyya): pride, i.e., haughtiness, took hold of him because of his sin; because of his sin he was not granted guidance and was not enabled to accept the command to be mindful. It is also said that the bāʾ is transitive (taʿdiya), meaning "took hold of him with such-and-such," i.e., it carried him to it. This is the closer view.

And His saying ﴿with sin (bi-l-ithm)﴾: what is the meaning of ithm? It means a sin that brings about punishment. Every sin that brings about punishment is ithm.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Hell will suffice him, and surely it is a wretched resting place﴾. ﴿Hell will suffice him (ḥasbuhu jahannamu)﴾ means: it is enough for him, and it is a threat to him with it, we seek refuge in Allah. Ḥasb means sufficient. Allah says: ﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:129], meaning sufficient for me. ﴿And they said: "Allah is sufficient for us"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:173], meaning sufficient for us. ﴿Hell will suffice him﴾, meaning it is enough for him, and the meaning is that he will be among its people, we seek refuge in Allah. ﴿And surely it is a wretched resting place﴾.

(Jahannam) is one of the names of the Fire. It is said that it is a loanword (ism muʿarrab), i.e., it is not from classical Arabic but is Arabized. It is also said that it is from classical Arabic, and that its origin is al-juhmah, which means darkness, but the letter nūn was added to it for intensification: jahannam. Either way, Jahannam is the name of the Fire that Allah the Exalted prepared for the disbelievers. It is named so because of the depth of its bottom and its darkness, we seek refuge in Allah.

And His saying ﴿and surely it is a wretched resting place﴾: how do we parse the lām here?

* Student: It is the lām of initiation (lām al-ibtidāʾ).
* Shaykh: The lām of initiation, for what?
* Student: A lām introducing an oath (mūṭiʾa lil-qasam).
* Shaykh: Or a lām introducing an oath, meaning: "And by Allah, it is a wretched resting place." This is closer.

And His saying ﴿wretched (biʾsa) resting place﴾: this is a rigid verb (fiʿl jāmid) used to express dispraise (inshāʾ al-dhamm). Biʾsa is a rigid verb used to express dispraise, and its subject (fāʿil) is? ﴿al-mihād (the resting place)﴾. These are among the verbs that require a specified object of dispraise (makhṣūṣ bil-dhamm). Where is the specified object?

* Student: al-mihād.
* Shaykh: No, ﴿al-mihād﴾ is the subject.
* Student: Omitted.
* Shaykh: Omitted. That is: "and surely it is a wretched resting place, its resting place, since it is Hell."

(...) ﴿on two days﴾ and so on to the end.

* Benefits derived from these noble verses: the excellence of remembrance during these counted days, as indicated by ﴿and remember Allah﴾; because remembrance of Allah in general is performed at all times, but this is remembrance in a specific manner.
* Another benefit of these noble verses: it is permissible during these three days to hasten or delay, as indicated by ﴿whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾.
* Another benefit: the breadth of Allah the Mighty's favour and His facilitation in His rulings, in that He made the person free to remain three days or to hasten on the second day.
* Another benefit: he must leave Mina before the sun sets, because "in" (fī) denotes containment, and a container encompasses what is contained, so hastening must occur within the two days.
* Another benefit: it is not permissible to hasten on the eleventh day, because if he hastened on the eleventh day, he would have hastened on one day, not on two days. Is this clear?

I warn you here that many common people think that the two days refer to the day of ʿĪd and the eleventh day, and they think it is permissible to hasten on the eleventh day. This is not correct, because Allah says: ﴿And remember Allah during numbered days﴾, and these are the days of tashrīq (the days of drying meat). The days of tashrīq begin?

* Student: On the eleventh.
* Shaykh: On the eleventh.
* Another benefit of the verse: actions for which there is a choice do not incur sin unless the person performs them out of mindfulness of Allah the Mighty, and not with negligence toward His commands; as indicated by ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾. So whoever does what is optional out of mindfulness of Allah the Mighty and by taking His facilitation, there is no sin upon him. But whoever does it out of negligence and indifference, he bears sin for abandoning mindfulness and for neglecting the commands of Allah.

Can it be inferred from the verse that it is permissible to delay until the fourteenth and fifteenth days, or not?

* Students: No.
* Shaykh: The verse says ﴿whoever delays﴾; it did not say "in three days". Is it unrestricted? But the basis of the remembrance is in three days, in counted days, so the meaning is: whoever delays during these counted days, which are the three days.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Because Allah restricted it by saying ﴿for whoever fears Allah﴾.
* Student: How is that conceived?
* Shaykh: Conceived?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: It is conceived that a man does this out of negligence and indifference, not in the sense that Allah has facilitated it for him and granted him a concession in it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the obligation of mindfulness, as indicated by ﴿and fear Allah﴾. We have already mentioned that mindfulness (taqwā) and righteousness (birr), when both are mentioned together, are?

* Student: Distinct.
* Shaykh: When both are mentioned together?
* Student: Distinct.
* Shaykh: They are distinct in meaning; and when one is mentioned alone, the other is included in it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: the affirmation of resurrection, as indicated by ﴿and know that you will be gathered to Him﴾.
* Another benefit: combining admonitions with warning, as indicated by ﴿and fear Allah and know that you will be gathered to Him﴾. When a person knows that he will be gathered to Allah the Mighty and that He will recompense him, he will fear Allah and perform what Allah has obligated. From this we understand the wisdom behind Allah the Mighty joining faith in the Last Day with faith in Allah in many verses. In many verses, faith in the Last Day is paired with faith in Allah, without the other things in which one must believe; this is because faith in the Last Day entails acting for that day, and that is?—to carry out the obedience of Allah and His Messenger.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And among people is he whose speech impresses you in the life of this world﴾ to the end.

* From this noble verse it is derived that people are divided into types: some are of this description, and others come with a description as well.
* It is also derived that a person should not be deceived by outward appearances. From where is this taken? ﴿whose speech impresses you﴾. Likewise, among people there is one whose action impresses you, but he conceals disbelief, we seek refuge in Allah. So do not be deceived by his outward condition. But there is no doubt that for us, we are not permitted to judge except by what?

* Student: The apparent.
* Shaykh: The apparent, because we do not know what is in hearts, and it is impossible for us to hold people accountable for what is in their hearts; we only hold them accountable according to outward appearances.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: this category of people calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, either regarding what he displays or what he conceals. For we said there are two meanings: either regarding what he displays, meaning it appears to you that he speaks words by which he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of his outward condition; or that he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of disbelief and hypocrisy, for he conceals it.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: an indication of abandoning contention and quarrelling, as indicated by ﴿yet he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾. Disputes generally contain no blessing. But this verse, as we said earlier, is restricted to what Allah commanded regarding argument, which is arguing with falsehood using truth, since this is a matter that cannot be avoided.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: affirmation of the knowledge of Allah the Mighty regarding what is in breasts, as indicated by ﴿and calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾; because what is in the heart is known only to Allah the Mighty and to the one who has that thing in his heart.

* Another benefit of the following verse: this man whose speech impresses you and who calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, when he turns away, strives throughout the land to corrupt it, by what?

* Student: By sins.
* Shaykh: By sins, for sins are a cause of the destruction of crops and progeny, we seek refuge in Allah. The evidence? ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:96]. And: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and been mindful, We would have expiated their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss. And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:65–66].

* Another benefit of the verse: this man whose speech impresses you turns away; he does not stay or remain; as indicated by ﴿when he turns away﴾. It has already passed in us at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah that the Arabic language distinguishes between ʾin and idhā: ʾin, the conditional particle, is used for a matter that may be impossible or unattainable, and usually does not occur; whereas idhā is used for what is possible and expected. For this reason, regarding His saying ﴿Every time it lights for them, they walk therein; but when darkness falls upon them, they stand still﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:20], scholars note that He did not say "if darkness falls upon them". When He said ﴿when darkness falls upon them﴾, it is known that it must occur. Here, ﴿when he turns away﴾ is not like "if he turns away, he strives". Rather, "when he turns away" means turning away will certainly happen from him, because it is not fixed.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: affirmation of Allah the Mighty's love, as indicated by ﴿does not like corruption﴾.
If you say: this is a negation and not an affirmation, we say: His negating love for corruption is evidence of the existence of the basic love. Had He not loved at all, there would be no difference between corruption and righteousness, would there? Since He negated love from corruption, it is known that He loves righteousness, and so it is.

* Another benefit of the noble verse: a warning against corruption on earth, as indicated by ﴿and Allah does not like corruption﴾. It is well known that every person must be wary of exposing himself to a matter that Allah does not love.

If He does not love corruption, does He not love the corrupter?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, that is known; because if a description is not beloved to Allah, whoever is characterised by it is not beloved to Allah. Moreover, it appears in other verses: ﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:64].

Then He said: ﴿And when he is told, "Fear Allah," pride takes hold of him with sin; so Hell will suffice him, and surely it is a wretched resting place.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 203–206 (part 3 of 3):

* It is derived from this noble verse that this man, described with these attributes, is disdainful of being commanded to fear Allah; this is shown by His saying: ﴿Pride seized him﴾. He is disdainful, as if he were saying to himself: "I am too exalted to be told to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." This is without doubt injustice. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded by Allah, the Exalted, to fear Allah; He commanded His Prophet, who was the most God-fearing of people, to fear Allah: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah, and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab 1], and He said in the story of Zaynab: ﴿And fear Allah, while you concealed within yourself that which Allah was to disclose, and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab 37]. This was said to the Prophet (ﷺ). So how about you, O human, are you not told: "Fear Allah"? Yet, may Allah protect us, this is evidence that he has within him an aversion to the truth, arrogance, and haughtiness.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete eloquence in omitting the agent in His saying: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah"﴾. He did not say: "When so-and-so or so-and-so says to him," so as to include everyone who says this to him, because his rejection of this command is not directed at the person of the speaker, but at his dislike of what he is commanded to do. For if he had said: "When the Messenger says to him," it would be as if he were saying: "This one is too proud to accept that the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), though he was not sent?" Or if the one who said it to him were a poor man, he would say: "What does this poor man think he can say to me?" But when the agent is omitted, his rejection of the truth is due to— 

* Student: Dislike.

* The Shaykh: Due to dislike of the truth itself: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning against rejecting those who give advice, since Allah, the Exalted, made this one of the attributes of these hypocrites. Whoever rejects one who commands him to fear Allah has in him a resemblance to the hypocrites. It is obligatory for a person, when he is told, "Fear Allah," to say: "We hear and we obey." Whoever commands you to fear Allah, you must say: "We hear and we obey," not for the sake of this man, but because of the obligation of fearing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that disdain may lead its possessor into sin; this is shown by His saying: ﴿Pride seized him with sin﴾. We have previously mentioned that the scholars gave it two meanings, both of which are valid: either the meaning is that, because of his sin, pride seizes him and he does not submit to the command to fear Allah; or the meaning is that his pride led him into sin, i.e., did sin precede the pride, so that pride seized him because of it, or did pride precede and drive him to sin? We mentioned two opinions on this, and we said that both are valid.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that he—i.e., this man—is among the people of the Fire; this is shown by His saying: ﴿Hell is sufficient for him﴾.
And among them: the praise of the Fire by way of censure; this is shown by His saying: ﴿And what an evil resting place﴾, and there is no doubt that Hell is an evil resting place..

The Almighty said: ﴿And remember Allah during appointed days﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:203]. Here Allah commands remembering Him. ﴿Remember﴾ ( udhkuru) is an imperative verb, and the imperative, as already explained, implies obligation, though it may be shared between obligation and recommendation according to what other evidence indicates.

His saying ﴿remember Allah﴾ encompasses every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. That is, the intended meaning is not only that we say "there is no god but Allah." Rather, it includes every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah.

If someone asks: "What is your evidence for what you say, and what is the basis for it?" I reply: my evidence is the Almighty's saying: ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer. Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing. And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:45]. That is, the remembrance of Allah contained in this prayer is greater. Also from the Sunnah is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The circumambulation of the House, and between as-Safa and al-Marwah, and the throwing of the pebbles, were only prescribed to establish the remembrance of Allah." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (1888) and al-Tirmidhi (902), from the hadith of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).]

As for the basis for it, namely why every statement and act that brings one closer to Allah is considered remembrance of Him: every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah is accompanied by the intention that it be for whom? For Allah. And this is remembrance of Allah. When you do something by which you draw near to Allah, or say something by which you draw near to Allah, there is in your heart the intention that you have intended (...), because by it you seek the Face of Allah. This is remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (...).

His saying ﴿during appointed days﴾: the appointed days are said to be the days of at-Tashriq (the days of drying meat), which are the three days: the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. Remembering Allah during them encompasses, as I said a moment ago, every statement or act that brings one closer to Allah. Accordingly, the unrestricted and restricted takbir enters into this. Also included is the throwing of the pebbles at the jamarat, and the circumambulation of the House and the sa'y between as-Safa and al-Marwah if they fall during these days.

The Almighty said: ﴿So whoever hastens in two days﴾ (...). So, ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ hastens what? The scholars said: "hastens" means he leaves Mina. ﴿In two days﴾ means within this period, within two days. There is no sin upon him if he hastens. It should not be said that one must remain until the thirteenth day, because Allah said ﴿appointed days﴾, and "days" is plural, so someone might understand that staying for the three days is obligatory. Therefore He said: ﴿whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, meaning there is no blame upon him.

His saying ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ is the answer of the conditional clause. As we all know, it is connected with the linking fa' (fa' al-jawab) because the clause is nominal, and the answer must be connected with the fa'.

Nominal, imperative, and what is rigid (jamid) with ma, qad, la, and the future particle [i.e., the seven positions where the answer of the conditional must be introduced by fa'], these are the seven positions in which, when they occur as the answer of a conditional, they must be connected with fa'. What are the ones in our present example?
* The students: Nominal.
* The Shaykh: Nominal. Is it fitting for us to say "nominal" or "connected with la"? Or no?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And with la. It is connected with la and it is also nominal.
* A student: In the verse (la) or (ma)?
* The Shaykh: And with ma, yes, with ma.
[Nominal, imperative, and with the rigid, and with ma...]
What about (la)? So this is nominal. This is nominal only.
﴿So there is no sin upon him﴾. His saying ﴿upon him﴾ is the predicate.
﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾. Delays until when? The verse does not specify ﴿delays﴾, but we know that ﴿delays﴾ refers to these appointed days, meaning until the third day. So if anyone remains until the fourth day, we say: this is not legislated. If someone argues against us with the verse, saying that Allah said ﴿and whoever delays﴾ without restriction, we say: but the basic remembrance is legislated for when? For three days: ﴿during appointed days﴾. That is, whoever delays until the third day, there is no sin upon him. Thus He removed sin from both the one who hastens and the one who delays, from both of them together. Insha'Allah, the question of which of the two is better, hastening or delaying, will come in the discussion of the benefits of the verse.

His saying ﴿for whoever has taqwa﴾: this is a prepositional phrase serving as the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: "That," meaning the removal of sin is for whoever has taqwa. That is, the removal of sin in either hastening or delaying is for whoever has taqwa, meaning the one who accompanies taqwa in his pilgrimage.
