* And it is derived from it: that the disbelievers are infatuated with it, and that it is their concern and their aim, because what is made attractive to a person must be something that he is concerned with and seeking.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: that the world is not worth anything in the eyes of the believers, since He says: ﴿to those who disbelieve﴾. Is it clear? For this reason, when the Messenger ﷺ saw something in the world that pleased him, he would say: "Here I am (labbayka), indeed life is the life of the Hereafter."[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (16038), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn al-Harith.]] It is a great statement. Whenever he saw something that pleased him, of any kind, he would say: "Labbayka, indeed life is the life of the Hereafter." Why? Because the soul, when it sees what pleases it by its nature, seeks that thing, so he says "Labbayka," to direct the soul toward answering whom? Toward answering Allah, not toward answering its desire. Otherwise the soul, this worldly thing being made attractive in the hearts of people except those whom Allah protects, seeks it and turns toward it, so he says "Labbayka." Then he also persuades the soul that I have only turned you away and answered the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, for a good reason. Why? "Indeed life is the life of the Hereafter." The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke the truth: life is the life of the Hereafter. And the wonder is that whoever seeks the life of the Hereafter, the life of this world becomes good for him, and whoever seeks the life of this world, both this world and the Hereafter are lost to him.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Az-Zumar 15]. This is the loss: they lost themselves, because they were ruined for them. Their destiny is the Fire, and we seek refuge in Allah. Their families who are in the Fire also do not care for one another. Each one, we seek refuge in Allah, is wretched in what he is in. The conclusion is that we say: this is part of the wisdom of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, which every person should follow. We see in this world what pleases us, without doubt: we see what pleases us of vehicles, palaces, and other things. But place this in your mind: "Labbayka, indeed life is the life of the Hereafter." You will find that everything before you diminishes. If you say it with sincerity, devotion, and following the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, you will see all of that before you, which pleases you, appearing diminished, as if it were nothing.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the baseness of the world. From where do we take it? From its description as such: "the world" (al-dunya), "the life of this world" (al-hayah al-dunya). It has already been mentioned that it derives from nearness (al-dunuww) in time and rank: in time, because it comes before the Hereafter; in rank, because it is little compared to the Hereafter.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the disbelievers never cease to impose themselves upon the believers, since He says: ﴿and they ridicule﴾. But I say: they never cease to impose themselves. From where did I take "never cease"? From His saying: ﴿and they ridicule﴾, in the present tense. Look: ﴿has been made attractive﴾, ﴿and they ridicule﴾. He did not say "and they ridiculed." ﴿And they ridicule﴾, because the present tense indicates continuity, the present, and the future. They are always mocking those who believe, saying: "What are these, ... (...)?! A car like (...) and a house of mud," and similar things. You see they mock, but the outcome is what matters: ﴿and those who fear Allah will be above them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212]. And when? On the Day of Resurrection, when there is no return backward, nor descent to the earth. For this reason He said: ﴿and those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212].

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the strengthening of the believers and the firming of their feet in their faith, since He says: ﴿they ridicule those who believe﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212]. That is: be patient, be patient, for this is their custom and their way, that they mock you. But as long as you know that this is the nature of the disbelievers, or something like a nature, a person will be patient. Indeed, when a person knows that this thing is unavoidable, he becomes prepared for it, accepting it, and unaffected by it.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the good news for the believers, for those who fear Allah, that they will be above the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. Recite the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed (29) And when they passed by them, they winked at one another (30) And when they returned to their own people, they returned jesting (31) And when they saw them, they said: Indeed, these are misguided﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29-32]. Backward-looking, meaning they have nothing (...), they are not fit for this age. Then after it: ﴿But they were not sent as guardians over them (33) So today those who believe﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 33-34]. Today is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Those who believe will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 34]. By Allah, this is a laughter after which there is no weeping, but the laughter of those criminals is followed by weeping.

﴿Upon couches, they will look﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 35]. Look at what? They will look at what Allah has prepared for them of bliss, and among it is looking at the Face of Allah, the Exalted. May Allah make me and you among them. They will look at the Face of Allah, and they will also look at what Allah did to those people: ﴿A speaker among them will say: Indeed I had a companion (51) Who used to say: Are you really among those who affirm? (52) When we die and become dust and bones, will we truly be recompensed? (53) He will say: Would you like to look? (54) So he looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [As-Saffat 51-55]. His companion in the world, he saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire. He said to him: Speak to him. This one is in the highest of the ʿIlliyyin, and that one is in the lowest of the low. He said to him: ﴿By Allah, you almost brought me to ruin﴾ [As-Saffat 56]. Look at this wicked companion trying to misguide this man. ﴿Inna﴾ here is a lightened form of the heavy one, for emphasis, and ﴿kidta﴾ means "you came close," meaning: you came close to ruining me. ﴿And if not for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth﴾ [As-Saffat 57]. So, do they look down on them or not? They look down on them, and they ask those with them in Paradise to look: ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ [As-Saffat 54]. For this reason He said: ﴿But those who feared Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212].

Affirmation of the acts of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, that are connected to His will, since He says: ﴿and Allah provides for whom He wills﴾. These acts are called in the books of creed "voluntary acts" (al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyyah), that is, those connected to the will of Allah, and they are affirmed for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in their true sense. Their examples in the Qur'an are numerous.

His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾ contains affirmation of will for Allah, and everything in the universe occurs by the will of Allah. Will (mashi'ah) differs from volition (irada) in that it is not divided, whereas volition is divided into two kinds: legislative volition (irada shar'iyyah) and universal volition (irada kawniyyah). Will is not divided like this; rather, what He wills is necessarily realized. That is, if Allah, the Exalted, wills something, it comes to be. For this reason it is a common saying among Muslims: "What Allah wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur."

Is it connected to what He loves and what He does not love? Yes. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to misguide, He misguides him﴾ [Al-An'am 39], and this He does not love. ﴿And whomever He wills to place upon a straight path﴾ [Al-An'am 39], and this He loves. So it is connected to what He loves and what He does not love.

It has already been mentioned for us that every act to which Allah attaches will is accompanied by wisdom, since it is not merely will by itself, but will accompanied by wisdom. The evidence for this is both textual and rational. The textual evidence is His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30]. The rational evidence is that Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, described Himself as Wise, indeed named Himself the Wise, and the Wise does not produce anything except what agrees with wisdom.

So this verse indicates: the affirmation of will for Allah, and its unrestricted application is restricted by what is known, that every will is accompanied by wisdom.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the abundance of the provision of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since He says: ﴿without account﴾. Its meaning is that He gives a gift that does not reach a reckoning, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is Expansive and Knowing﴾ [Al-Baqarah 261].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 207–212 (part 1 of 7):

(...) When He mentioned the state of the hypocrites, "those whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and they are the most contentious of opponents, and when they turn away, they strive in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals, and Allah does not like corruption," He mentioned the state of a people opposite to them. This is how the Qur'an is, as has been mentioned to us many times: the Qur'an is *mathani* (oft-repeated), in which matters are repeated in pairs. Thus the Garden is mentioned and then the Fire, and the righteous (al-muttaqun) are mentioned and then the wicked (al-fujjar). This is so that a person remains in a varied garden, never growing weary or bored. Then a person remains between fear and hope: fear when he sees the Fire, its threat and its punishment, and hope when he sees the Garden, its bliss and its reward. Then he continues to look at the condition of all people, the people of good and the people of evil, as if they were before him in a mirror, unlike if the contexts were all uniform. Then the discussion of the states of all these people ended, and then it began to speak about the states of others. So the arrangement of the Qur'an is undoubtedly from the One who is All-Wise, All-Aware, glory be to Him and exalted, and it is the arrangement that suits the reform of hearts. For this reason we see that it is not commendable, rather we see it as forbidden, that those who gathered the Qur'an's corresponding verses, bringing some of them together with others, as is found in the "Tafsil Ayat al-Quran al-Hakim" by the author of the "al-Mu'jam al-Mufahras li-Alfaz al-Quran" (the indexed lexicon of the Qur'an's words). The indexed lexicon is sound and unobjectionable, but he wrote another book, "Tafsil Ayat al-Quran al-Hakim," and gathered all the verses on tawhid together, all the verses on prayer together, all the verses on zakat together, all the verses on the righteous together, and so on. This is an arrangement of the Qur'an in the Mushaf, but arranged according to meanings. In reality this is not accepted, and we see it as closer to prohibition, because it removes the Book of Allah, glory be to Him, from the arrangement upon which it was ordered. Is the arrangement of the verses an ijtihadi matter or tawqifi (divinely fixed)?
* Students: Tawqifi.
* Shaykh: Tawqifi. Here He said, "And among the people is one who pleases you" [al-Baqarah 2:204], then He said, "And among the people is one who sells himself" [al-Baqarah 2:207].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: This is a compiled book.
* Student: He gathered the verses..
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: He gathered, arranged them to the end of the Mushaf.
* Shaykh: Yes, to the end of the Mushaf.
* Student: Originally there are many works in it that come out..
* Shaykh: There are many works in it, for example as we see in the verses of prayer (...) the rulings, there is nothing wrong with these.
* Student: (...) the Qur'an (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, this (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: In any case, it is not permissible to take the Qur'an out, meaning to compile it entirely according to this detailed arrangement, except in the way that Allah's Book came.
* Student: There is now a thematic tafsir, meaning each topic gathers all the verses that came on this topic..
* Shaykh: There is no objection to this, because it is partial, meaning it takes a unified topic and places it in an independent book. There is nothing wrong with this, and the scholars have continued to do it, such as the book "Tafsir Ayat al-Ahkam" by al-Jassas and others, which exist, and al-Qurtubi. This is collecting the whole Qur'an in one Mushaf and leaving these verses for this situation, these for that situation, and these for another situation.
* Student: Like re-arranging it.
* Shaykh: If it is arranged anew.
* Student: (...) the Qur'an (...).
* Shaykh: Each one, my brother. As long as the whole Qur'an exists in this arrangement, that means there is something like an objection to the divine arrangement.
* Student: (...) if he wants to return, he wants to look (...) like he finds something..
* Shaykh: This is a problem.
* Student: It is necessary (...).
* Shaykh: It does not contradict. We say: if he excepts a part in the story of Musa and writes one word in the story of Musa, there is no harm, he partitions it separately. But that he writes it all vocalized as if it were a Mushaf (...) this is not valid, it is not permissible. What is the meaning of saying the arrangement is tawqifi?
* Student: No, originally (...) not that he did it as if it were the Qur'an.
* Shaykh: What is the difference then? Just a name?
* Student: No, it is (...).
* Shaykh: No, my brother, I do not think at all (...).
* Student: They call this tafsil..
* Shaykh: Yes, it is not permissible. Make, for example, a specific topic, there is no harm, we agree with you in this. But that you arrange the entire Qur'an from its beginning to its end according to what you want, this is forbidden, call it whatever you wish.

The important point is His saying, "And among the people is one who sells himself." This is the second division, the first division being His saying, "And among the people is one who pleases you." Accordingly, *min* (مِن) is partitive, "from among the people," and *man* (مَن) is the subject (mubtada'), and the prepositional phrase before it is its predicate. Some grammarians said that the partitive *min* is a noun, since it means "some of," and accordingly it would be the subject, and "man yashri" would be its predicate.

His saying, "man yashri nafsahu," means: sells it, for *shara* (شَرَى) means *baa* (باع, sold), as in His saying, "And they sold him for a meager price" [Yusuf 12:20], *sharawhu* meaning they sold him for a meager price. As for *ishtara* (اشترى), it comes meaning *ibtaa'* (to buy). When the *ta'* appears, it is for the buyer, the one who takes, and when the *ta'* is dropped, it is for the seller, the one who gives.

"Man yashri nafsahu ibtigha'a mardat Allah," meaning his self, meaning he sells his self. *Ibtighaa'* (ابتغاء) is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), meaning seeking. *Mardat Allah* means His good pleasure (ridwan), meaning he sells his self seeking the pleasure of Allah, glory be to Him. Thus he has sold his self sincerely for Allah, glory be to Him, in this sale.

Then He said, "And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants." Does the phrase "min al-nas" refer to a specific person or is it general?

Some exegetes said it refers to a specific person, namely Suhayb al-Rumi: when he wanted to emigrate from Makkah, the Makkan disbelievers prevented him and said, "You cannot emigrate at all unless you leave for us all that you possess, and then we will permit you to emigrate." So he agreed to that and saved himself by emigrating seeking the pleasure of Allah.[[Narrated by Ibn Hibban (7082) from the hadith of Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi.]]

Other scholars said: rather it is general, and they are the majority of exegetes, general to all the believing mujahidin in the path of Allah. They said: the evidence for this is His saying, "Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their selves and their wealth in exchange for that they will have Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed" [al-Tawbah 9:111]. This view is more correct, that it is general, and even if it is established that the occasion of revelation was the story of Suhayb, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.

Allah, the Exalted, said, "And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants," meaning: those who sold their selves seeking the pleasure of Allah, Allah, the Exalted, encompasses them with His compassion, by His saying, "And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants." The scholars said: *ra'fa* (رأفة, compassion) is the most tender mercy, meaning the highest degrees of mercy in tenderness. So it is a mercy in the utmost degree of tenderness, and so it is *ra'fah*. Among Allah's names is *al-Ra'uf* (the Most Compassionate), and among His attributes is compassion, because every name of Allah indicates one attribute or two or more, as has passed.

His saying, "bil-'ibad": the *al* (ال) here is for generality, it substitutes for *kull* (all), meaning toward all the servants. By "servants" here is meant those who are servants to Him in the sense of destiny (al-ma'na al-qadari), not in the legal sense (al-ma'na al-shar'i). So Allah's compassion and mercy encompass everyone, but whoever is a believer obtains both special and general compassion, and whoever is not a believer has the general compassion. Know that servanthood has two meanings: specific and general, and the specific has a more specific sense, which is the specific of the specific. From the general is His saying, "There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant" [Maryam 19:93], and from it His saying, "Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided" [al-Hijr 15:42], according to the view that the exception here is connected. If it is said that it is disconnected, then His saying, "Indeed My servants," belongs to the specific category.

As for the specific, such as His saying, "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan 25:63]. Who is meant by them, all servants? No, the servants of the Most Merciful are those characterized by these attributes, so whoever is not characterized by them is excluded.

And the more specific, such as His saying, "Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant" [al-Furqan 25:1]. This is a servanthood more specific: the servanthood of prophethood.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says, "O you who have believed, enter into Islam completely" [al-Baqarah 2:208]. His saying "ra'uf": I have another reading of it, which is "ra'uf" without the waw, "wa-Allahu ra'fun bil-'ibad."

He says: "O you who have believed, enter into Islam completely and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy" [al-Baqarah 2:208]. "Al-silm" has two readings: "al-salm" and "al-silm," and "khutuwat" has two readings: "khutuwat" with a dammah on the ta', and "khutwat" with a sukun on the ta'.

He says: "O you who have believed, enter into Islam completely." "Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu": the address is to the believers. It has been mentioned before that when Allah begins a ruling with a call, it is a sign of concern for it, because the purpose of a call is to alert the addressee, and alerting is only required for what is important. If I say, "Pay attention," it is less than if I say, "O so-and-so, pay attention," because the address to him is for alerting. So the ruling introduced by a call indicates by that introduction that it is important. For this reason the call that necessitates alertness was introduced. Then, when the address is to those who have believed, there are three benefits in that, as has passed. The first benefit?
* Student: That this one pointed to is of its nature, or of (...) characterized by it.
* Shaykh: That carrying out this command is among the requirements of faith. The second benefit?
* Student: What He forbids them from is evil, or not..
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Urging and enticing.
* Shaykh: Yes, correct, urging and enticing. Because if you say, "O believer," you urge him, because by the requirement of his faith he will act, just as if you say, "O generous one, give to the poor," the intent is to entice him with his generosity so that he remembers his attribute, which is generosity. This is so that he remembers his attribute, which is faith.
The third benefit: that doing this, if it is a command, is from the perfection of faith, and abandoning it is from the deficiency of faith, and doing it (...) diminishes faith, and abstaining from it for Allah increases faith. Now let us see, is the verse before us a command or a prohibition? "Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu," and what follows? A command, "udkhulu" (enter). So entering into Islam is among the requirements of faith, entering into Islam completes faith, and not entering into Islam diminishes faith. We have learned all of this from the address "Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu."

He said, "udkhulu fi al-silm." *Al-silm* and *al-salm* mean Islam, which is submission to Allah, the Exalted, outwardly and inwardly. If someone says: how does He say, "O you who have believed, enter into Islam," when we already know that faith is more complete than Islam, by His saying, "The Bedouins say, 'We have believed.' Say, 'You have not believed; but say, "We have submitted," for faith has not yet entered your hearts'" [al-Hujurat 49:14]? How then does He say, "O you who have believed, enter into Islam"? We say: this command is restricted by what follows "fi al-silm," which is His saying, "kaffah" (completely). Here the command is directed, or up to "kaffah" the command is directed, meaning: implement all the rulings of Islam, do not neglect any of them, because this is the requirement of the perfection of faith. So is the command focused on mere entry into peace, or on His saying "kaffah"? On His saying "kaffah."

As for His saying "kaffah": *kaffah* is an active participle used for one who restrains others, and the *ta'* in it is for emphasis, like *rawiyah*, *saqiyah*, *allamah*, and the like. The *ta'* in these three examples, saqiyah, rawiyah, allamah, is for emphasis. So "kaffah" means *kaff* (restraining), and the *ta'* is for emphasis. They said: from it is His saying, "And We have not sent you except as a messenger to all mankind" [Saba' 34:28], "kaffatan lil-nas," meaning restraining them, restraining them from what harms them, "to bring mankind out of darknesses into the light" [Ibrahim 14:1]. So the meaning of *kaffah* is restraining them from what harms them, and the *ta'* here is for emphasis. They also gave as an example His saying, "And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together" [al-Tawbah 9:36]. They said: "fight them all together" means restraining them from shirk, as they fight you restraining you from Islam, as in His saying, "Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah" [al-Nisa' 4:167], "They are those who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque" [al-Fath 48:25]. They fight us to restrain us from our religion, so we fight them to restrain them from shirk and disbelief. The word *kaffah* is also used meaning the community, like *al-'ammah* (the general public), as one says "kaffat al-nas," meaning their general public and community. The connection to its original meaning, which is restraint, is that a community has strength and power, and by its gathering it restrains whoever intends harm against it. For this reason the community was named *kaffah*.
* Student: Kaffat al-nas..
* Shaykh: Like kaffat al-nas and 'ammat al-nas, meaning their community. They said: from it is the hadith, "I was sent to the people..."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (335) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah with the wording, "And I was sent to the people in general (ʿāmmatan)," and also narrated from his hadith (438) with the wording, "And I was sent to the people entirely (kaffatan)."]] Is it *kaffah* or *'ammah*?
* Student: Kaffah.
* Students: 'Ammah.
* Shaykh: 'Ammah. But "wa-arsalnaka kaffatan lil-nas."
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: "wa-arsalnaka."
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) In any case it is said: the Prophet ﷺ was sent to mankind entirely. *Kaffah* means all together. Here, "udkhulu fi al-silm kaffah": is the meaning "enter into peace all together," so that *kaffah* is a circumstantial clause (hal) of *al-silm*, or "you all enter into peace," so that *kaffah* is a circumstantial clause of the waw in His saying "udkhulu"? Which is closer? The first meaning is closer, because if we said the second meaning, "enter all together into peace," it would mean that some believers had not entered Islam, and then the address could not be directed to them with the description of faith. The second meaning is the correct one: that *kaffah* is a circumstantial clause of *al-silm*, meaning: enter into all of Islam, all together, do not leave any of its rites, and this is the correct meaning of the verse, and it is what fits the requirement of faith, because the requirement of faith is that a person performs all the laws, not taking one law and leaving another.
* Student: They say whoever reads "al-salm" it means reconciliation, and I read it in the explanation of "al-salm" as meaning reconciliation?
* Shaykh: Yes, the correct view is that all their meanings are one, that what is meant by it is Islam, but it does come meaning reconciliation, correct, like His saying, "So do not weaken and call for peace while you are the superior" [Muhammad 47:35]. This is correct.

The Shaykh says: ﴿Enter into submission (Islam) completely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:208]. A command is followed by a prohibition, because following the footsteps of Satan contradicts entering into submission completely. ﴿Do not follow﴾: the meaning is clear, that is, do not follow them. ﴿Footsteps﴾ is the plural of khutwah (step), and it may be read as خُطْوَاتِ or خُطُوَاتِ. A khutwah is the distance covered by the foot in walking, the extent of one movement of the foot. When you walk, moving your foot from one place to another is called a khutwah. The meaning is evident: we do not follow Satan in his course. Why? Because Allah has explained in another verse that Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing, and what is like that cannot be followed. Would anyone agree to follow indecency and wrongdoing? No. Also, Satan is an enemy to us, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you both﴾ [al-A'raf 7:22], then He said: ﴿So take him as an enemy﴾. If he is an enemy to you, then take him as an enemy. So, does any intelligent person follow his enemy?

*Students:* No.

*The Shaykh:* I hear only two weak voices, as if you were seeking Allah's guidance in answering? 

*Students:* No.

*The Shaykh:* No one follows his enemy. No one follows his enemy. Is it clear? Now, if Satan commands indecency and wrongdoing, and he is an enemy to us, then it is not reasonable, let alone in keeping with faith, for a person to follow him in his steps. Now, what are the footsteps of Satan? If someone says: explain to us the footsteps of Satan? We say: Allah the Mighty and Majestic has explained them. He commands indecency, which is grave sins, and wrongdoing. So every act of disobedience is one of the footsteps of Satan, whether that disobedience is committing what is forbidden or abandoning what is commanded; it is among the footsteps of Satan. However, there are things the Messenger (ﷺ) explicitly stated to be the actions of Satan, such as eating with the left hand, drinking with the left hand, taking with the left hand, and giving with the left hand. The Messenger (ﷺ) stated that these are the actions of Satan. Likewise, turning around in prayer is a snatching that Satan snatches from the prayer of the servant. These are explicitly mentioned and clear. For what is not explicitly mentioned, we say: every act of disobedience is among the footsteps of Satan.

As for His words ﴿Satan﴾: it was previously mentioned whether it is derived from (shaṭana), meaning to be far away, because he is distant from Allah's mercy, or from (shāṭa), meaning to be angry and foolish, because he is undoubtedly the most foolish of Allah's servants.

*A student:* (...) Is he from the footsteps of Satan?

*The Shaykh:* No. He is undoubtedly from the whisperings of Satan. As for saying that he is from the footsteps of Satan, the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that he is not, because He said: ﴿Do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Whoever follows the footsteps of Satan, indeed, he commands indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-Nur 24:21].

As for His words ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:168]: this verse is emphasized by two emphasizers: (inna) and the lam. Is that correct?

*Students:* Yes.

*The Shaykh:* Are you sure?

*Students:* Emphasized by two emphasizers other than the lam.

*The Shaykh:* Emphasized by two emphasizers, which are inna and the lam.

*Students:* No.

*The Shaykh:* (inna) what?

*Students:* Inna and the lam.

*The Shaykh:* No.

*A student:* Fronting of the predicate.

*The Shaykh:* No, that is not present. It has one emphasis, which is (inna). But there is a semantic emphasis other than the emphatic particles, which is His words ﴿a clear enemy﴾.

As for His words ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾: ﴿Indeed, he is to you﴾. It is as if Satan was only made an enemy to us, to the children of Adam. There is no doubt that he is an enemy to us by the report of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This is clear from the textual evidence (naql) and from rational reasoning (nazari), because Satan only deserved the curse by not submitting to our father by Allah's command. This one who was expelled and removed from Allah's mercy because of our father, because he did not prostrate to our father, becomes an enemy to us, or not? Yes, because here he says: these are the ones who were the cause of the expulsion and removal from Allah's mercy and deserved the curse. Therefore he was an enemy to us according to the textual evidence (sam'i). What else? And the rational evidence.

As for His words ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾: the word (mubīn) is a form of (af'ala), and it may be derived from (abāna), meaning to make clear, and from (abāna) meaning (bāna), because (bāna yabīnu) gives (bayyin), and (abāna yubīnu) gives (mubīn), with one meaning. However, the quadriliteral (abāna) comes with the meaning of (aẓhara), to make manifest, not with the meaning of (ẓahara).

*A student:* (...).

*The Shaykh:* ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:77].

*A student:* (...).

*The Shaykh:* No. Is it in Surah Yasin? ﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an, to warn whoever is alive﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:69–70]. ﴿A clear Qur'an﴾ here, does it mean clarifying (bayyin) or making manifest (muzhir)? ﴿A clear Qur'an﴾ means making manifest. The evidence is His words: ﴿to warn whoever is alive and that the word may be justified against the disbelievers﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:70]. As for (mubīn) meaning clear (bayyin), it is like His words: ﴿And indeed, they had been before in manifest error﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:164], meaning clear. Good. And the word (mubīn) here, ﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾: does it mean clear (bayyin) or make manifest (muzhir)? That is, does it mean apparent (ẓāhir) or making manifest?

*Students:* Apparent.

*A student:* (...).

*The Shaykh:* Apparent and also making manifest, apparent and making manifest. Because his commanding us to indecency and wrongdoing means that he has made enmity manifest. Likewise, his not prostrating to our father and saying that he is better than him, this also makes his enmity manifest. So it is suitable for both meanings. Now, who is the enemy? What is the enemy? The enemy comes from enmity (mu'adah), which is distance and hostility. The jurists said: whoever is pleased by another's harm, or grieved by another's joy, is his enemy. That is, your enemy is one who grieves at your happiness and rejoices at your sorrow. This is an enemy. Yes, this is the enemy. Is Satan like that? Yes. The evidence: ﴿Secret conversation is only from Satan, to grieve those who believe, but it cannot harm them at all except by permission of Allah﴾ [al-Mujadilah 58:10]. In His words: ﴿Do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾, concluding this prohibition with this sentence has two benefits. The first benefit: explaining the reason for the previous ruling. The second benefit: warning against following the footsteps of Satan.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:209]. Regarding ﴿if you slip﴾, some scholars said: that is, if you deviate. Others said: that is, if you incline. This latter is closer to the meaning of the wording, because (zallal) is like (zalaq) in slipping; his foot slipped with him, meaning he fell down, from a slippery place or from a height on a stairway and the like. This is more forceful than (you deviated). That is, if you incline away from the truth and follow the footsteps of Satan ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:209]. The clear proofs (al-bayyinat) is a description of an omitted noun, meaning the clear verses and the manifest admonitions. If you slip away from the truth and incline, and Allah the Exalted called that a slip, because in inclining and deviating from the truth there is ruin, or not?

*A student:* Yes.

*The Shaykh:* Yes, like if a person slipped and fell into a well for example, or slipped and fell down in the street.

As for His words ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾: this is the response to the conditional, the response to (in) is (then know). The intended knowledge is not merely that it reaches our hearts, but that we beware of the One who has might. ﴿Know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾. Ending with these two names shows that the person is exposed to punishment or has fallen into punishment. Here, is he exposed to punishment or not? Yes. If he slips after the proof has come to him, he has exposed himself to punishment. As for the ending of the verse being a punishment, it is like His words: ﴿And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands as recompense for what they earned, as a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:38]. It is said that a bedouin was with a reciter who was reciting this verse, and the reciter was saying: ﴿as recompense for what they earned, as a deterrent from Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. He said to him: No, this is not correct, recite it. He recited it: ﴿cut off their hands as a deterrent from Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. He said: That is not right. I say: The bedouin said: That is not possible. When he recited it a third time, ﴿as a deterrent from Allah, and Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾, he said: Now you are correct, because He is Exalted in Might and judged, so He cut off. If He had forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off. This is a correct inference. For this reason, Allah the Exalted said regarding those who spread corruption in the land: ﴿except for those who repent before you gain power over them, so know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:34]. For this reason the scholars said: if highway robbers repent before they are captured, the punishment owed to Allah is dropped from them. Here He says: ﴿so know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾. So you have exposed yourselves, after the slip with which you slipped, after the clear proofs came to you, to destruction.

Then He said: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210]. ﴿They await﴾: that is, the deniers who slipped after the clear proofs came to them.

﴿Do they await﴾: (hal) is an interrogative used in the sense of negation, meaning they do not await. ﴿Yanzurun﴾ means await, and it may also mean to look with the eye. If it is followed by (ilā), it is looking with the eye; if it is not followed by it, it means waiting. An example of the form followed by (ilā) is His words: ﴿Allah will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them﴾ [Ali 'Imran 3:77]. Also His words (ﷺ): "Three will not be spoken to by Allah, nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them" [Agreed upon; Bukhari (2672), Muslim (108/173), from Abu Hurayrah; the wording is Muslim's]. Also His words: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:22–23]. The first is with the ḍād (nāḍirah, radiant), and the second is with the ẓā' (nāẓirah, looking), because the first, nāḍirah, means beautiful, and the second is looking with the eye. As for the form that does not take (ilā), it means await, like this verse: ﴿Do they await only that it come to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210], meaning: these only await that it come to them. Also His words: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:104], meaning: wait for us.

﴿Only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾: ﴿Allah should come to them in canopies﴾. Does the meaning of the verse, ﴿Allah should come to them in canopies﴾, mean that canopies from Allah come to them?

*A student:* No, it does not...

*The Shaykh:* Like if you said: unless Allah should bring them punishment from Him?

*A student:* No (...).

*The Shaykh:* Like His words: ﴿And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with punishment from Him or by our hands﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:52]. Is it like this verse? No, because it is followed by (fī, in), ﴿unless Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210], so the meaning is not that canopies from Allah come to them. No.

As for His words ﴿that Allah should come to them﴾: He attributed the action to Allah, and this is according to the path of the people of the Sunnah and the community (ahl al-sunnah wal-jama'ah), upon its apparent and literal meaning, meaning that Allah Himself comes. As for the people of distortion (ahl al-tahrif), they say that its meaning is that the command of Allah comes to them in canopies of clouds. This is a distortion of the Qur'an from its apparent meaning without any evidence except an evidence they claim is rational, while it is actually imaginary (wahmi) and not rational. So we say: Who attributed the act of coming to Himself? Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and He knows Himself best. Does He want to make clear to His servants, or to mislead His servants?

*Students:* To make clear to His servants.

*The Shaykh:* To make clear. Far be it from Him to want misguidance: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:176]. If Allah wants to make clear, and He knows Himself best, is there any incapacity or inability in His speech to express what is in Himself? No. Is there any deficiency in the eloquence of His speech? No. Therefore His speech is at the utmost of knowledge, the utmost of desire for guidance, and the utmost of eloquence and rhetoric. Can we after this say that its apparent meaning is not intended? Never, it is not possible, unless Allah Himself says that He did not intend that, then yes.

He said: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds﴾, meaning: those who deny the Messenger (ﷺ) await only this day, which is the Day of Resurrection, on which Allah the Mighty and Majestic comes to judge between His servants. He says: ﴿unless Allah should come to them﴾. Here (ya'tī, comes) is an imperfect verb, and the subject is (Allah). It is attributed, and the verb here is attributed to whom? To Allah. That is, it is attributed in meaning, not in grammatical case. So the verb is attributed to Allah: ﴿unless Allah should come to them﴾. Everything that Allah attributed to Himself, its intended meaning is the reality of His essence. ﴿He rose over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 7:54], meaning in His essence. (istawā, He rose) is a past verb referring to Allah. Does He descend to the lowest heaven?

*A student:* In His essence.

*The Shaykh:* In His essence. Since it is attributed to Allah, the intended meaning is His essence, glory be to Him and exalted. Likewise, He laughs, meaning He Himself. He is pleased, He Himself. He comes, He Himself. He walks, He Himself. "I come to him running" [Agreed upon; Bukhari (7405), Muslim (2675/2), from Abu Hurayrah]. He comes running, and so on. So everything Allah attributed to Himself, its intended meaning is His essence, unless evidence establishes that another meaning is intended, like what is in the authentic hadith: "O My servant, I was hungry and you did not feed Me, or I asked you for food and you did not feed Me" [Muslim (2569/43), from Abu Hurayrah]. Here Allah the Mighty and Majestic made clear that what is intended is asking for food from one of His servants, from His righteous servants. If you say: what do you say about the holy hadith: "When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, and his sight with which he sees," and so on. It is known that the predicate is attributed to the subject. (kuntu, I was) is the subject of (kāna, was), and in origin it is the subject (mubtada'), and (sam'ahu, his hearing) is the predicate of (kāna), which in origin is the predicate. It is known that the predicate is attributed to the subject. So when you say: Zayd is standing, to whom does standing belong?

*Students:* To Zayd.

*The Shaykh:* To Zayd. So how do you say regarding this holy hadith: "I was his hearing"? Do you say that Allah the Mighty and Majestic, that the intended meaning is that Allah Himself was hearing for this?

*Students:* No.

**The Shaykh:** We say, "He was his hearing," in accordance with the rule. However, the meaning of what Allah said does not make the hearing itself Allah. Rather, He said, "He was his hearing," and the meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, guides his hearing, his sight, and his limbs: "I was his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely protect him." The whole hadith, from its beginning to its end, indicates that this is impossible. "My servant does not draw near to Me" (to Me, my servant). It is well known that the worshipper cannot be the one worshipped. "With what I have made obligatory upon him" (I made it obligatory upon him): the one who makes obligatory cannot be the one upon whom it is made obligatory. "And My servant continues to draw near to Me": here, "My servant" continues, so the servant is not the one worshipped. "Draws near to Me": the one drawing near cannot be the one drawn near to. "Until I love him": there is a lover and a beloved. "When I love him, I am his hearing": it is impossible that Allah is the hearing of this created being, it is impossible. As for the hand, He said, "his hand with which he strikes," because action is done by the hand, "and his foot with which he walks"[[Related by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. So it becomes clear that the rule is the rule, but what prevents this thing from being Allah is the pronouns, which all indicate that these are two distinct things.

So then, ﴿يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ (that Allah should come to them). Do we apply the rule to it or not?

**The students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** Who is the one who comes?

**The students:** Allah.

**The Shaykh:** Allah Himself. Those who say, "The command of Allah comes," we say: this is wrong. You have said about Allah what you do not know, and you have turned the words of Allah away from their apparent meaning without any evidence. Allah says ﴿يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾, and you say, "The command of Allah comes to them"?! It is a grave offense against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. How can He affirm for Himself a coming, while you say: He does not come, rather it is only His command that comes? If the matter were as you say, it would follow that the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is an impossibility for Allah, and the Qur'an, which was a clarification for people, would become a confusion for people and a misguidance for them. Is that not so? Because when a person hears that ﴿يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ and recites it, he says: Allah Himself, the Mighty and Majestic, comes. But if you say, "His command comes," you have turned the Qur'an, which is a clarification, into a deception and misguidance, and you have made it, after it was an admonition and a reminder, a confusion for the creation. If these interpreters had reflected on the consequences of this interpretation of theirs, their feet would never have stood firm upon it, because no believing, sensible person says it. As my shaykh said in his tafsir: no one says it while there is in his heart a grain of mustard seed of faith. This is a great misguidance, and it entails consequences among the most invalid of consequences. And al-Shinqiti, may Allah have mercy on him, also said in his tafsir: no one turns such verses away from their apparent meaning except one whose heart has been defiled with the filth of likening (tashbih, attributing to Allah the likeness of created things). Just as Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: these interpreters (mu'awwilah) only interpreted because they believed that the apparent meaning of these verses was likening, so they likened first and then denied second. As for us, we believe that what Allah said about Himself is true, because He, the Exalted, is most knowing about Himself, most truthful in speech, and best in narration, and He wants to make things clear to His servants. The evidence for this is: ﴿يُبَيِّنُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ أَنْ تَضِلُّوا﴾ (Allah makes clear to you so that you do not go astray) [an-Nisa' 176]. He does not want to conceal the matter from His servants and to show them a statement that contradicts what He intended, for that would be obstinacy.

If someone says, "How does He come?" We say: "How" here. This question is either a rejection on the part of the person, and then he must repent to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because he has denied it. That is, he says: "What way does He come? How does He come?" A question may come for the purpose of disbelief and denial, and this is a serious matter. Or he asks about the modality (kayfiyyah), meaning: "I believe that He comes, but how does He come, in what manner?" We say: this is an innovative question (bid'ah, an innovation in religion). I think the difference between the two questions is clear? The first: the one who says, "How does He come?" as a denial. This means denial or doubt. But if he says, "How does He come?" believing in the principle and its meaning, asking only about the modality, what do we say to him? We say: this is an innovation, and it is not permissible to ask about the modality, because it is a question about something that cannot be answered. Is it clear? No one can answer it. For this reason, it is well known that Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said about the istiwa' (settling) upon the Throne: "The istiwa' is not unknown, the how (kayf) is not conceivable, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation"[[Related by al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (867).]]. So he, may Allah have mercy on him, made clear that the how is not conceivable, that is, our minds do not grasp it and no revealed evidence has come concerning it. So when both the revealed and the rational evidence are absent regarding it, our position is to refrain from that.

He also said: asking about it is an innovation, because this was not known in the time of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The Companions were more eager for good than we are, more understanding than we are, and more intelligent. Allah gathered for them eagerness, understanding, and intellect. For this reason they did not ask, because they knew that this is a matter that cannot be encompassed, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا﴾ (and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge) [Ta-Ha 110]. The same applies to the rest of the attributes: one should never ask about their modality. For this reason some of the scholars said: if a Jahmi (a follower of Jahm ibn Safwan, who denied Allah's attributes) says to you, "How does He descend?", then say, concerning the descent (i.e., in the hadith of the descent): Allah has informed us that He descends, and He has not informed us how He descends. That is a complete answer. So we stop at what He has informed us of, and we remain silent about what we have not been informed of.

Others said: if a Jahmi says to you, "What is the attribute of such and such of Allah's attributes?", then say to him: "What is His essence? Can you describe His essence (modality)?"

**A student:** No.

**The Shaykh:** No. We say: if you do not know the modality of His essence, then the modality of an attribute is a branch of the modality of the essence. Knowledge of the modality of an attribute cannot be attained except after knowledge of the modality of the essence. Just as you do not know the modality of His essence, we do not know the modality of His attributes. The matter in this is clear. So we believe in the coming in truth, and that He, glorified and exalted, truly comes. But in what manner? Allah knows best. Is He in a manner?

**The students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, in a manner, but it is unknown. For this reason Imam Malik said: "the how is not conceivable." He did not say: He has no how.

﴿إِلَّا أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ فِي ظُلَلٍ مِنَ الْغَمَامِ﴾ (unless Allah comes to them in canopies of clouds) [al-Baqarah 210]. The "fi" (in) in its meaning is "ma'a" (with). That is, He comes accompanied by these canopies. We have taken it out of its original meaning, which is the sense of enclosure (zarfiyyah), because if we took it as enclosure, Allah would be encompassed by them, and Allah, the Exalted, is not encompassed by anything of His creation. He is greater and more majestic than to be encompassed by anything of His creation. A comparable example is that you say: "So-and-so came in such-and-such a group," meaning with them. Yet this comparison is not exact in every respect, because a person can be encompassed by the group, but Allah cannot be encompassed by the canopies.

As for His saying ﴿فِي ظُلَلٍ مِنَ الْغَمَامِ﴾ (in canopies of clouds), this cloud comes as a preface before the coming of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as He said in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿وَيَوْمَ تَشَقَّقُ السَّمَاءُ بِالْغَمَامِ﴾ (And the day the sky will split open with clouds) [al-Furqan 25]. So the sky splits. Notice that He did not say "tanshaqq" (it is split), He said "tashaqqaq" (it is split open), as if it bursts forth from every side, split open with the clouds. The cloud, they said, is the white, thin cloud, but it is not like the clouds of this world. The name is the same, but the reality is not the same, because the named things in the Hereafter, although they share names with the named things of this world, differ just as this world differs from the Hereafter. Is that not so?

**A student:** Indeed.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, ﴿فِي ظُلَلٍ مِنَ الْغَمَامِ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ﴾ (in canopies of clouds, and the angels). The word ﴿وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ﴾ is in the nominative (raf'), as a conjunction (ataf) upon His saying ﴿يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾. That is: the angels also come to them, surrounding them, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿كَلَّا إِذَا دُكَّتِ الْأَرْضُ دَكًّا دَكًّا (٢١) وَجَاءَ رَبُّكَ وَالْمَلَكُ صَفًّا صَفًّا﴾ (No! When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded and crushed, and your Lord comes with the angels, rank upon rank) [al-Fajr 21–22]. In the long hadith of the Trumpet, which Ibn Jarir and others cited, the heavens are split: the lowest heaven is split open with the clouds, and the angels descend and surround the people of the earth. Then the second heaven, the third, and the fourth, each one after the other. For this reason He said ﴿صَفًّا صَفًّا﴾ (rank upon rank), meaning row after row. Then the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, descends to judge between His servants, a descent that befits His greatness and majesty, and no one encompasses Him, because He, the Exalted, cannot be encompassed, as Allah said: ﴿لَا تُدْرِكُهُ الْأَبْصَارُ وَهُوَ يُدْرِكُ الْأَبْصَارَ﴾ (No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision) [al-An'am 103], and He said: ﴿وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِهِ عِلْمًا﴾ (and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge) [Ta-Ha 110]. So the angels surround the creatures, then the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, descends and judges among the servants. But when will this be? It will only be after people are overtaken by grief and distress that they cannot bear. Then they go to someone who will intercede for them with Allah, that He may judge between them and relieve them from this station. They come to Adam and mention to him some of his virtues, but he excuses himself, saying that he ate from the tree and disobeyed. He excuses himself even though he repented to Allah, and his Lord chose him and guided him. But the station of intercession is not an easy matter. The intercessor cannot come forward for intercession while he remembers that he has sinned against the one to whom he intercedes, because, as the common people say, his face cannot meet him. How could he disobey Him yesterday and come today to intercede for another? For this reason he excuses himself. Then they come to Noah, who is the first of the messengers. That one is the first of mankind, and this one is the first of the messengers. They come to him, but he also excuses himself. With what? With the fact that he asked about what he had no knowledge of: ﴿فَقَالَ رَبِّ إِنَّ ابْنِي مِنْ أَهْلِي﴾ (He said: My Lord, my son is of my family) [Hud 45]. Did Noah seek forgiveness?

**A student:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** He sought forgiveness?

**The students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** What did He say?

**The students:** (...)

**The Shaykh:** ﴿قَالَ يَا نُوحُ إِنَّهُ لَيْسَ مِنْ أَهْلِكَ إِنَّهُ عَمَلٌ غَيْرُ صَالِحٍ فَلَا تَسْأَلْنِ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ إِنِّي أَعِظُكَ أَنْ تَكُونَ مِنَ الْجَاهِلِينَ (٤٦) قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَسْأَلَكَ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ وَإِلَّا تَغْفِرْ لِي وَتَرْحَمْنِي أَكُنْ مِنَ الْخَاسِرِينَ﴾ (He said: O Noah, he is not of your family; he is one whose conduct is not righteous. So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant. He said: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about what I have no knowledge of. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers) [Hud 46–47]. This is a seeking of forgiveness, a seeking of forgiveness by way of acknowledging that he must be forgiven by Allah, or else he would be among the losers. Then they come to Abraham, and he excuses himself. With what? With the fact that he lied three lies, which were lies but were equivocation (tawriyah), an equivocation that is a lie with respect to the one addressed, or is it not a lie in reality? Then they come to Moses, and he excuses himself. With what? With the fact that he killed a soul that he had not been commanded to kill. Then they come to Jesus, and he mentions no sin. He does not excuse himself with any sin, but he excuses himself by the grace of Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. He says: "Go to Muhammad, a servant whom Allah has forgiven his past and future sins"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4712) and Muslim (194/327) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. There is no doubt that this is from the great praiseworthy station of the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace. The prophets excuse themselves. Some of them mention a fault that makes them ashamed to be intercessors, and some of them mention nothing, but they see that there is in that place one who is more worthy than they are, and he is Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace. So they come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and ask him to intercede with Allah. Yet even so, he does not intercede with Allah, despite being the most honored of creation before Allah. He does not intercede except after Allah's permission. Likewise with kingship, majesty, and authority: the one closest of creation to the king cannot speak of intercession for another, nor even for his own benefit, except after the king's permission. Can the greatest king's wife, who is the one he has intimacy with, intercede or not?

**The students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** Without asking permission? But the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, because of His greatness and authority, no one intercedes until He gives permission. So he asks permission from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He grants him permission, and he prostrates a long prostration, and Allah opens for him praises and glorification of Allah that He had not opened for him before. Then He says to him: "Raise your head, speak and you will be heard, intercede and your intercession will be accepted, and ask and you will be given." So he intercedes with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and then the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, comes as is mentioned here.

﴿فِي ظُلَلٍ مِنَ الْغَمَامِ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ﴾ (in canopies of clouds, and the angels) [al-Baqarah 210]. We have already discussed the angels when we came to His saying: ﴿وَلَكِنَّ الْبِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَالْمَلَائِكَةِ وَالْكِتَابِ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ﴾ (But righteousness is in one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets) [al-Baqarah 177], and we explained that the angels are an unseen world, that they are created messengers whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created for His worship, and that they glorify Allah night and day. Is it at night and in the day, or in the night and the day?

**The students:** Night and day.

**The Shaykh:** Is there a difference between them? "Night and day" means always, continuously. But "fi" (in) for enclosure allows for part of the night. Night and day.

﴿وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ وَقُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ﴾ (and the angels, and the matter is decided). The grammarians (al-mu'rabun, those who analyze the grammatical case of words) differed about the phrase ﴿وَقُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ﴾. Some of them said that it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ﴾, so it falls within the scope of the awaited matter: "Do they await anything except that He comes to them, or that the matter is decided?" But it came in the past tense to emphasize that it will certainly occur. This is what some of them said. On this view, the clause is in the accusative case, because ﴿أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ is in the accusative with ﴿يَنْظُرُونَ﴾. That is: "Do they await anything except the coming of Allah in canopies of clouds, the coming of the angels, and the decision of the matter?" This is one view. The second view is that His saying ﴿وَقُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ﴾ is a new independent clause: "Do they await anything except that Allah comes to them in canopies of clouds?" And the matter has ended, meaning: the matter has ended, and they will have no excuse or argument after that. The word ﴿الْأَمْرُ﴾ means "the affair." As we mentioned earlier, "al-amr" is the singular of "al-awamir" (commands) and of "al-umur" (affairs). So here it is the singular of what? "Al-umur" (affairs) or "al-awamir" (commands)?

**The students:** Al-umur (affairs).

**The Shaykh:** Affairs. That is, the matter is decided and everything has ended, and the people of the Fire have gone to the Fire and the people of Paradise to Paradise. For this reason He said after it: ﴿وَإِلَى اللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾ (And to Allah all matters are returned), and in one reading: ﴿تَرْجِعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾ (matters return). Here, the complement is placed before what it complements, because ﴿إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾ is related to what?

**Students:** To "tarji'u" (returns).

**The Shaykh:** To "tarji'u" (returns). Placing the object before the verb conveys restriction and exclusivity: to Allah alone, not to anyone else. ﴿تَرْجِعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾: the affairs of this world and the Hereafter. Is that so? All their affairs, religious, worldly, retributive, and everything. As Allah, the Exalted, said in Surat Hud: ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ يُرْجَعُ الْأَمْرُ كُلُّهُ﴾ (and to Him the whole matter is returned) [Hud 123]. All the matter. So all affairs return to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Among them is that people will return on the Day of Resurrection to their Lord, and He will hold them to account. This verse, as will come in the benefits (al-fawa'id), if Allah wills, serves to threaten these deniers.

**A student:** Shaykh, in the verse ﴿أَوْ يَأْتِيَ أَمْرُ رَبِّكَ﴾ (or the command of your Lord comes) [an-Nahl 33], meaning "or His command comes."

**The Shaykh:** Yes, what about it?

**The student:** Some of them used it as evidence that this (verse) explains that...

**The Shaykh:** That is not correct. The argument is invalid, because we must say that every verse is interpreted according to what is in it.

**The student:** So what is the meaning of the verse here?

**The Shaykh:** His command to punish them.

**A student:** That is, after (...).

**The Shaykh:** No, no. That is, His command that Allah orders their punishment in this world, the punishment of this world.

**A student:** And the angels?

**The Shaykh:** The angels are to seize their souls. That is the difference between them.

**A student:** (...) with this meaning?

**The Shaykh:** Which of them?

**A student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** No, it is not far off.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 207–212 (part 4 of 7):

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [al-Baqarah 211]. ﴿Sal﴾ (ask) originally was (isal). The vowel of the hamza was moved to the unvowelled sin, and then the hamza was dropped for ease of pronunciation. Then the hamza of connection (hamzat al-wasl) was dropped because there was no need for it. So we now have two dropped hamzas: the hamza of connection at the beginning of the word, and the hamza that is the root letter of the verb ('ayn al-fi'l). As for the hamza of connection, it was dropped because it is only brought in to facilitate pronouncing a sakin (unvowelled letter). Why did we bring a hamza to (isal)? Because it is not possible to pronounce an unvowelled letter at the start of speech unless a hamza precedes it: (isal). As for the second, which is the 'ayn of the verb, it was dropped for ease after its vowel had been moved to the sin, so it became (sal). So, what is the pattern (wazn) of (sal) in morphological measure?

* Students: (fal).

* The Shaykh: Its pattern is (fal).

* A student: Its original form is not (fa'il)?

* The Shaykh: Its original form is (if'al), so the 'ayn was dropped, the hamza of connection was dropped, and it became (fal).

* * *

(...) "Children" (banī) of Israel. We have already covered the rule that (banī), when it is added to a tribe, includes males and females, and when it is added to an individual, it refers to males. So you say, for example: "Banū Muhammad", if Muhammad is the name of a person who is not a tribe, and you say "Banū Tamīm" for males and females.

﴿Sal banī Isrā'īl﴾: here it is added to what? It is added to a tribe.

* A student: Or to a person (...).

* The Shaykh: No. It has become the name of a tribe, just as Tamīm was originally one person, so it became the name of a tribe. It is now the name of a tribe.

﴿Sal banī Isrā'īl﴾. As has already been mentioned, Isrā'īl is Ya'qūb ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. It is said that (Il) in Hebrew means God, so the meaning of Isrā'īl is "servant of God" (ʿabd Allāh).

And His saying: ﴿how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [al-Baqarah 211]. ﴿Kam ātaynāhum﴾ is an interrogative (istifhāmiyyah) that has suspended the verb (sal) from acting (ta'līq). So it, along with its clause, is in the accusative position (fi maḥall naṣb). The original was: "Ask so-and-so about such and such", so the verb was suspended from its second object.

And His saying: ﴿how many clear signs﴾. You know that (kam) requires a tamyīz (specifying noun, which clarifies the vague quantity). (Kam) is a vague noun that indicates a number. So what is the counted item? The counted item is His saying ﴿clear signs﴾. Is (kam) here a kathrah (indicating abundance) or a khabariyyah (informative)?

* A student: Kathrah.

* The Shaykh: Kathrah. That is, it means "many signs We gave them".

And His saying: ﴿We gave them﴾: We gave them. As we have learned, (ātā) takes two objects. The first object is the pronoun (hā', "them"), and the second object is omitted. The estimated form is: "how many clear signs We gave them." The omitted pronoun refers to something that comes later in wording, because in rank it comes first. The original order was for "min āyah" (of signs) to come after (kam): kam min āyah.

And His saying: ﴿how many signs We gave them﴾. The giving here includes both the legislated giving (al-īttā' al-shar'ī) and the universal, predestined giving (al-īttā' al-qadarī al-kawnī). They were given clear legislated signs that the Torah brought, and they were given universal signs such as the staff and the hand. His saying: ﴿clear sign﴾: (āyah) means a sign of a thing; all of these are called āyāt. His saying ﴿clear﴾ means evident as a sign. Like what?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: In the Qur'an: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isrā' 101].

Among them: Allah sent down to them the manna and the quails.

Among them: Allah raised Mount Sinai above them so that they would take what they were given with strength. And there are many other signs. Also, Allah informed them that He had preferred them over the worlds. Moses, peace be upon him, said to them: ﴿O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you, when He made among you prophets, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given anyone else in the worlds﴾ [al-Mā'idah 20]. And Allah said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah 47]. How many signs and blessings Allah gave the Children of Israel, yet they disbelieved in them and denied them! Even after Allah rescued them from Pharaoh, they passed by a people devoted to their idols, and ﴿they said: "O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods"﴾ [al-A'rāf 138]. This is without doubt great ignorance. That is why ﴿he said: "Indeed you are a people who behave ignorantly"﴾. ﴿How many clear signs We gave them﴾ [al-Baqarah 211].

Is the address in His saying ﴿Ask﴾ directed to the Messenger ﷺ alone, or to everyone who can be addressed?

It has already been established for us that such addresses are sometimes shown by evidence to be specific to the Messenger ﷺ, and so they are specific to him. Sometimes evidence shows that they are general to him and to others, and so they are general. And sometimes no evidence exists either way. The apparent meaning in that case is that it is general, because the Qur'an was revealed for the Ummah until the Day of Resurrection. What is an example of an address shown by evidence to be specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him?

* A student: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Inshirāḥ 1].

* The Shaykh: Yes, like: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast? And We removed from you your burden, which had weighed down your back, and raised high for you your mention﴾ [al-Inshirāḥ 1–4]. This is specific to the Messenger ﷺ.

An example where evidence shows it is general is His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 1]. Here He said "O Prophet", but He addressed them with a general ruling: ﴿when you divorce﴾ (plural). He did not say "when you divorce" (singular). As for what is ambiguous, it is common in the Qur'an, and this verse is one of them.

﴿Sal-hum﴾: is the intention to ask for information (istiʿlām), or is the intention to ask in order to rebuke and reproach (tabkīt wa-tawbīkh)? Which one?

* A student: The last.

* Another student: The second.

* The Shaykh: The last. The apparent meaning is the last, in order to establish the proof against them by showing the blessings of Allah, which it was their duty to thank Him for, but they changed them into disbelief. Otherwise, the apparent meaning is that the Messenger ﷺ already knew what Allah had revealed to him, including the clear signs Allah had given them.

He said: ﴿of a clear sign. And whoever replaces the blessing of Allah after it has come to him, indeed Allah is severe in penalty﴾ [al-Baqarah 211]. The ending of the verse with this clause shows that the signs are blessings, and that the Children of Israel disbelieved in them and changed them. They disbelieved in them and changed them into disbelief. That is why He said: ﴿And whoever replaces the blessing of Allah after it has come to him, indeed Allah is severe in penalty﴾.

﴿Man﴾ is a conditional noun (ism sharṭ jāzim), which is why it jussed the verb (yubaddil). Where is its answer? Its answer is understood from His saying: ﴿indeed Allah is severe in penalty﴾. So this clause indicates the answer, but it is not the answer itself, because the severity of Allah's punishment is established whether they changed or not. But it indicates the answer to the conditional.

And His saying: ﴿whoever replaces the blessing of Allah﴾. What is the meaning of (yubaddil)? It means "changes". On this basis, (baddala) here does not need an object, and their change of Allah's blessing is that they disbelieved in it, so it was removed from them. Its removal became a curse, so it became a replacement. How did they replace the blessing of Allah? ﴿And whoever replaces the blessing of Allah﴾. We said: (yubaddil) means "changes". How do they change it? If they disbelieve in it?

* A student: It was removed from them.

* The Shaykh: It was removed from them. This is the replacement. Now they have replaced it with a curse, by making it lead to a curse, through their disbelief. So the meaning is: whoever replaces it with a curse. This implies that those who disbelieve in blessings are content that curses should take their place. But if we take the meaning as in the verse of Ibrahim: ﴿Have you not seen those who replaced the blessing of Allah with disbelief?﴾ [Ibrahim 28], then we say: the second object of (yubaddil) is omitted, and the estimate is: "whoever replaces the blessing of Allah with disbelief, indeed Allah is severe in penalty". Here the meaning is that replacing the blessing is replacing gratitude: whoever makes disbelief a substitute for gratitude, indeed Allah is severe in penalty. Both meanings are correct, and both are inseparable, because disbelief necessarily involves changing the blessing. So both meanings amount to the same thing: whoever does actions that contradict gratitude will be punished.

And His saying: ﴿indeed Allah is severe in penalty﴾ [al-Baqarah 211]. (Shadīd) means "strong". (ʿiqāb) means recompense through punishment. The recompense was called punishment (ʿuqūbah) and ʿiqāb because it comes after (ʿaqib) the sin, following it and seizing one for it.

And His saying: ﴿severe in penalty﴾ is an example of an attribute being added to the one it describes, like when you say: "good of face", meaning "the one with a good face". It is an attribute-like adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah).

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 212]. (Zuyyina) means tazyīn: making a thing beautiful in a person's sight, or in his hearing, or in his taste, or in his thinking. The main point is that the original meaning of tazyīn is making a thing beautiful, pleasing, and attractive.

His saying: ﴿zuyyina﴾ is in the passive voice, and the deputy subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil) is ﴿the life of this world﴾. Here a grammarian among you may ask: why is the verb not feminine, although "life" is feminine and is the deputy subject? The answer has two parts. The first part: the feminine here is not real (ghayr ḥaqīqī). Ibn Malik says:

*And the feminine marker is only obligatory on a verb whose subject is a connected pronoun or a feminine that is real (having sex).*

Yes, this is the first point. The second point is separation (al-faṣl). Ibn Malik says "connected", meaning the ta' is obligatory only when the feminine is real and connected.

*And the feminine marker is only obligatory on a verb whose subject is a connected pronoun or a feminine that is real (having sex).*

And here, I do not mean "a feminine that is real".

﴿Zuyyina lil-ladhīna kafarū﴾: the subject of (zuyyina) is omitted. So who makes it attractive? Is it Satan, or Allah, Mighty and Majestic?

* A student: Allah decrees it, and Satan...

* The Shaykh: There are two verses: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter—We have made their deeds attractive to them, so they wander blindly﴾ [al-Naml 4]. And in another verse: ﴿And Satan made attractive to them what they used to do﴾ [al-An'ām 43]. Here (zuyyina) is in the passive voice, so it is interpreted in light of these two verses. Is there a contradiction between the two verses?

The answer: there is no contradiction between the two verses. Allah, the Exalted, made their evil deeds attractive to them because of their evil deeds, as indicated by His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Ṣaff 5]. The attractiveness is from Allah in terms of decree, while the one who directly carried out the adornment and whispered it to them is Satan.

His saying: ﴿zuyyina lil-ladhīna kafarū al-ḥayāh al-dunyā﴾. He did not say "zuyyina lil-nās" (made attractive to people), as in another verse: ﴿Made attractive to people is the love of desires: of women and sons and heaped-up sums of gold and silver﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 14], and so on to the end. So shall we take ﴿the people﴾ to refer to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ and say that there is general wording intended as specific? Or shall we say that there is a difference between the two verses? Or shall we say that mentioning some individuals of a general category does not require specification? We say: it was made attractive to people in general, and here Allah mentioned His making it attractive to some members of this category, namely those who disbelieve.

﴿Al-ḥayāh al-dunyā﴾. Al-ḥayāh is the opposite of death, and what is meant is this abode. (Al-dunyā) is on the pattern fuʿlā, meaning it is a feminine superlative (ism tafḍīl). It is derived from what? From (al-dunuww), which is the opposite of (al-ʿulūw), height. It was named this for two reasons: because of the nearness of its rank, and the nearness of its time. As for the nearness of its time, it is because it comes before the Hereafter; it is closer to the Hereafter, and we are living in it now. As for the nearness of its rank, it is obvious, yes indeed, very obvious and clear. The Messenger ﷺ informed us that the place of a whip of one of us in Paradise is better than the world and everything in it. The place of the whip; you know the place of the whip, an approximate length of a meter, is better than the world and everything in it. Not the world in which you are now, but the world from its beginning to its end and everything in it. So there is a difference between this and that. It is near in time and near in rank, because it is far removed from the Hereafter. That is why, glory be to Allah the Mighty, you will not find a state of joy in it except mixed with turbulence before and after it. But this turbulence, for the believer, is good, even if there is disturbance, pain, and harm in it, because it is good for him, as the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "How wondrous is the affair of the believer, for all of his affairs are good. If adversity befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him. If ease befalls him, he is grateful, and that is good for him." [Reported by Muslim (2999/64) from the hadith of Suhayb.] When the believer is tested with a physical or psychological trial, he says: "This is a blessing from Allah by which Allah expiates my sins." When he feels this, the pain becomes a blessing, because a person constantly errs. Without doubt, these things, praise be to Allah, are expiation for sins. If he is patient and seeks reward, it becomes an increase in ranks. So pains, afflictions, worries, and grief are expiation in every case, but with patience and seeking reward, it becomes a righteous deed for which he is rewarded and recompensed.

So the world is indeed the world, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic described it. Whatever bliss it contains, it is still the world. That is why I always mention to you the story of the Hafiz Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, with the Jewish oil merchant in Egypt. Ibn Hajar was the chief judge there, and they called him "Qāḍī al-Quḍāh" (Judge of Judges). He was passing through the market with his carriage drawn by mules in a procession. A Jewish oil merchant, dirty from the oil, stopped him and said: "How does your Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ, say: 'The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever' [reported by al-Bayhaqī in al-Zuhd (452) from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him], while you are now in bliss in this world?" And this Jew, with what he has of harm and affliction in this world, how can this be?

So he replied to him immediately, saying: "What I am in of bliss, compared to the bliss of the Hereafter for the believer, is a prison; it is nothing. And what you are in of misery, compared to the punishment of the Hereafter that you will meet, is a paradise. Is that correct or not?"

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: At once the man said: "I testify that there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." The matter became clear to him. The point is that the world remains called what it is, "the life of this world". Allah the Exalted named it "the world" only so that we would not raise our heads because of it, nor be preoccupied with it, but that we would strive and make our highest aim and supreme goal the Final Abode. It is enough for a sensible person, when he hears this description, to call it "the world".

* A student: Shaykh, we mentioned "zuyyina", that Allah made their evil deeds attractive to them because of their evil deeds. So we say: Allah made their evil deeds attractive to them (...).

* The Shaykh: No, no. Because tazyīn is of two kinds: an initial tazyīn and a continuing tazyīn. The continuing tazyīn is built on the first, and the first is built on intention. Their intention went bad, then their action went bad, then they were increased in evil, may Allah protect us.
