* The Shaykh: It means the greatness of this day. It does not mean that it lasts fifty thousand years. It explains the greatness of this day, and this does not necessarily mean that it lasts that long.

* Student: But there would not be in it, it would be fifty thousand years.

* The Shaykh: If it were not for the phrase "until judgment is made among the servants," the apparent meaning of the hadith would be that his punishment is from its beginning to its end. But since the phrase "until judgment is made among the servants" is restricted, and we say that judgment among the servants is made at midday, based on His saying: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that day will be better in residence and finer in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan 24], it becomes clear that their punishment lasts until midday. How long that is: twenty-five thousand years.

* Student: Shaykh, what is the point of evidence from this verse that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, completes the reckoning in part of the day?

* The Shaykh: Yes?

* Student: You said: it is said (...) glorified and exalted be He, since this matter is decided in part of a day?

* The Shaykh: No, we did not say that. This is not derived from it. It is derived from the verse of al-Furqan.

* Student: Shaykh, is the day meant in this verse the day as reckoned by Allah, glorified and exalted be He?

* The Shaykh: Yes, the Day of Resurrection, "whose measure is fifty thousand years" [al-Maʿarij 4].

* Student: Meaning, is the time period what we count as our days?

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is the apparent meaning.

* Student: Fifty thousand?

* The Shaykh: Fifty thousand years.

* Student: Allahu Akbar!

* The Shaykh: Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ to the end [al-Baqarah 211].

* It is derived from this verse: the explanation of the abundance of Allah's blessings upon the Children of Israel, based on His saying: ﴿how many clear signs We gave them﴾.

* Among its benefits: the rebuke and reproach of the Children of Israel who disbelieved in Allah's blessing. Is the question here a question of inquiry or a question of rebuke? A question of rebuke.

The fruits of the verse include: a warning against changing the blessing of God, the Mighty and Majestic, since He says: ﴿And whoever substitutes the favor of Allah after it has come to him...﴾ [Al-Baqarah 211].

Another is establishing the severity of God's punishment, since He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in penalty﴾ [Al-Baqarah 211].

Is punishment, when it is in its proper place, praiseworthy? Yes, it is praiseworthy, indeed commanded: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress, lash each one of them with a hundred lashes, and do not let pity for them detain you in the religion of Allah﴾ [An-Nur 2]. Flog them. Stoning is a punishment. A punishment of what?

* Students: Adultery.

* The Shaykh: The later scholars call it (execution) (i'dam), and this is an error. It is a punishment of killing, and there is a difference between killing and execution. When we kill someone, have we executed him? No, his body remains, but...

(...) with what is not named by it, because the category of reporting (ikhbar) is broader than the category of naming (tasmiyah). For example, is it permissible for us to report that Allah is speaking (mutakallim)? Is it permissible?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Do we name Him by it?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: We do not name Him by it. It is permissible to say that Allah is willing (murid), or not? We report that He is willing, but we do not name Him by it. For this reason He said: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [Al-Hijr 49]. What follows it? ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [Al-Hijr 50]. So the severity of punishment: "severe in punishment" (shadid al-iqab). In reality, this is an adjective of quality (sifah mushabbahah) attributed to its agent: Allah is severe in punishment, the severity is in His punishment. But "the Forgiving, the Merciful" is among His names, as in the verse: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful (49) And that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [Al-Hijr 49-50].

* A student: Shaykh, is there now a criterion for applying names and attributes to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic? What is the criterion for reporting about Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?

* The Shaykh: Yes, the criterion for reporting about Allah is that you report about Allah every attribute with which Allah has described Himself. Every attribute with which Allah has described Himself, you report it about Him. But if it is unrestricted, it is unrestricted, and if it is restricted, it is restricted. There are things it is not valid to report about Allah, because they do not befit Him, such as sleeping, for example, or being incapable, or ignorant, or what is similar to that, because they do not befit Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But there are things by which you do not name Allah, yet He is reported as having them, because they are not valid to be names. The Most Beautiful Names contain no possibility of evil at all. All the names are beautiful; there is no evil in them, not even by possibility. But what is reported about Him may, at certain times, include evil, yet for Allah it includes no evil. For example, "the speaker" (al-mutakallim): the speaker may speak good, and may speak evil, so not all speech is good. And "the one who wills" (al-murid) likewise has willing good and willing evil. For this reason it did not come as a name, but it came as a report, because the category of reporting is broader. "The maker" (al-sani'), for example, may be reported about Allah, but He is not named by it.

* A student: Shaykh, "the physician" (al-tabib), meaning the physician.

* The Shaykh: As a report, there is no harm.

* A student: The saying "Engineer of the Greatest Universe," the saying of some?

* The Shaykh: By Allah, this is "engineer" (muhandis).

* A student: What?! (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, there are those who say it like this, being bold. I do not dare to say it. Yet its meaning is correct, because what is the meaning of engineering (al-handasah)?

* Students: Mastery and design.

* The Shaykh: Design and mastery, design with mastery. But I do not dare to say it of Allah. As for the physician, it was narrated from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he fell ill, and it was said to him: "Shall we not call the physician for you?" He said: "The physician has seen me and said: I do what I will."[[See Kitab al-Zuhd of Ahmad ibn Hanbal (588), and Hilyat al-Awliya' of Abu Nu'aym (1/34).]] As for the matter of the engineer, you may feel that "engineer," if my understanding is not mistaken, may be understood as one who has learned, meaning one who has acquired the craft by acquisition. Someone may say: the physician too, by his attribution to human beings, is also one who has acquired it. But I do not dare to say "Engineer of the Universe." I cannot.

* A student: Shaykh, "inventor" (mukhtari')?

* The Shaykh: "Inventor" is acceptable; it may be applied to Him, because the inventor is like the originator (mubdi'). For this reason this term occurs in the speech of some scholars, that He is capable of invention and similar things.

Then He said: ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they ridicule those who believe﴾ and so on to the end [Al-Baqarah 212].

* The following is derived from this noble verse: the deception of the disbelievers by worldly life, since He says: ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve﴾.

* And it is derived from it: that the disbelievers are infatuated with it, and that it is their concern and their aim, because what is made attractive to a person must be something that he is concerned with and seeking.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: that the world is not worth anything in the eyes of the believers, since He says: ﴿to those who disbelieve﴾. Is it clear? For this reason, when the Messenger ﷺ saw something in the world that pleased him, he would say: "Here I am (labbayka), indeed life is the life of the Hereafter."[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf (16038), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn al-Harith.]] It is a great statement. Whenever he saw something that pleased him, of any kind, he would say: "Labbayka, indeed life is the life of the Hereafter." Why? Because the soul, when it sees what pleases it by its nature, seeks that thing, so he says "Labbayka," to direct the soul toward answering whom? Toward answering Allah, not toward answering its desire. Otherwise the soul, this worldly thing being made attractive in the hearts of people except those whom Allah protects, seeks it and turns toward it, so he says "Labbayka." Then he also persuades the soul that I have only turned you away and answered the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, for a good reason. Why? "Indeed life is the life of the Hereafter." The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke the truth: life is the life of the Hereafter. And the wonder is that whoever seeks the life of the Hereafter, the life of this world becomes good for him, and whoever seeks the life of this world, both this world and the Hereafter are lost to him.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Az-Zumar 15]. This is the loss: they lost themselves, because they were ruined for them. Their destiny is the Fire, and we seek refuge in Allah. Their families who are in the Fire also do not care for one another. Each one, we seek refuge in Allah, is wretched in what he is in. The conclusion is that we say: this is part of the wisdom of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, which every person should follow. We see in this world what pleases us, without doubt: we see what pleases us of vehicles, palaces, and other things. But place this in your mind: "Labbayka, indeed life is the life of the Hereafter." You will find that everything before you diminishes. If you say it with sincerity, devotion, and following the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, you will see all of that before you, which pleases you, appearing diminished, as if it were nothing.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the baseness of the world. From where do we take it? From its description as such: "the world" (al-dunya), "the life of this world" (al-hayah al-dunya). It has already been mentioned that it derives from nearness (al-dunuww) in time and rank: in time, because it comes before the Hereafter; in rank, because it is little compared to the Hereafter.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the disbelievers never cease to impose themselves upon the believers, since He says: ﴿and they ridicule﴾. But I say: they never cease to impose themselves. From where did I take "never cease"? From His saying: ﴿and they ridicule﴾, in the present tense. Look: ﴿has been made attractive﴾, ﴿and they ridicule﴾. He did not say "and they ridiculed." ﴿And they ridicule﴾, because the present tense indicates continuity, the present, and the future. They are always mocking those who believe, saying: "What are these, ... (...)?! A car like (...) and a house of mud," and similar things. You see they mock, but the outcome is what matters: ﴿and those who fear Allah will be above them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212]. And when? On the Day of Resurrection, when there is no return backward, nor descent to the earth. For this reason He said: ﴿and those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212].

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the strengthening of the believers and the firming of their feet in their faith, since He says: ﴿they ridicule those who believe﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212]. That is: be patient, be patient, for this is their custom and their way, that they mock you. But as long as you know that this is the nature of the disbelievers, or something like a nature, a person will be patient. Indeed, when a person knows that this thing is unavoidable, he becomes prepared for it, accepting it, and unaffected by it.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the good news for the believers, for those who fear Allah, that they will be above the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. Recite the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed (29) And when they passed by them, they winked at one another (30) And when they returned to their own people, they returned jesting (31) And when they saw them, they said: Indeed, these are misguided﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 29-32]. Backward-looking, meaning they have nothing (...), they are not fit for this age. Then after it: ﴿But they were not sent as guardians over them (33) So today those who believe﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 33-34]. Today is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Those who believe will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 34]. By Allah, this is a laughter after which there is no weeping, but the laughter of those criminals is followed by weeping.

﴿Upon couches, they will look﴾ [Al-Mutaffifin 35]. Look at what? They will look at what Allah has prepared for them of bliss, and among it is looking at the Face of Allah, the Exalted. May Allah make me and you among them. They will look at the Face of Allah, and they will also look at what Allah did to those people: ﴿A speaker among them will say: Indeed I had a companion (51) Who used to say: Are you really among those who affirm? (52) When we die and become dust and bones, will we truly be recompensed? (53) He will say: Would you like to look? (54) So he looked and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [As-Saffat 51-55]. His companion in the world, he saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire. He said to him: Speak to him. This one is in the highest of the ʿIlliyyin, and that one is in the lowest of the low. He said to him: ﴿By Allah, you almost brought me to ruin﴾ [As-Saffat 56]. Look at this wicked companion trying to misguide this man. ﴿Inna﴾ here is a lightened form of the heavy one, for emphasis, and ﴿kidta﴾ means "you came close," meaning: you came close to ruining me. ﴿And if not for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth﴾ [As-Saffat 57]. So, do they look down on them or not? They look down on them, and they ask those with them in Paradise to look: ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ [As-Saffat 54]. For this reason He said: ﴿But those who feared Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾ [Al-Baqarah 212].

Affirmation of the acts of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, that are connected to His will, since He says: ﴿and Allah provides for whom He wills﴾. These acts are called in the books of creed "voluntary acts" (al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyyah), that is, those connected to the will of Allah, and they are affirmed for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in their true sense. Their examples in the Qur'an are numerous.

His saying: ﴿whom He wills﴾ contains affirmation of will for Allah, and everything in the universe occurs by the will of Allah. Will (mashi'ah) differs from volition (irada) in that it is not divided, whereas volition is divided into two kinds: legislative volition (irada shar'iyyah) and universal volition (irada kawniyyah). Will is not divided like this; rather, what He wills is necessarily realized. That is, if Allah, the Exalted, wills something, it comes to be. For this reason it is a common saying among Muslims: "What Allah wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur."

Is it connected to what He loves and what He does not love? Yes. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to misguide, He misguides him﴾ [Al-An'am 39], and this He does not love. ﴿And whomever He wills to place upon a straight path﴾ [Al-An'am 39], and this He loves. So it is connected to what He loves and what He does not love.

It has already been mentioned for us that every act to which Allah attaches will is accompanied by wisdom, since it is not merely will by itself, but will accompanied by wisdom. The evidence for this is both textual and rational. The textual evidence is His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Insan 30]. The rational evidence is that Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, described Himself as Wise, indeed named Himself the Wise, and the Wise does not produce anything except what agrees with wisdom.

So this verse indicates: the affirmation of will for Allah, and its unrestricted application is restricted by what is known, that every will is accompanied by wisdom.

* And among the fruits of the noble verse: the abundance of the provision of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, since He says: ﴿without account﴾. Its meaning is that He gives a gift that does not reach a reckoning, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is Expansive and Knowing﴾ [Al-Baqarah 261].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 213–214 (part 1 of 6):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213]. Let us look at the i'rab (grammatical analysis). First: ﴿أُمَّةً﴾ (ummatan), what put it in the accusative?

* Students: It is the predicate (khabar) of (kana).
* The Shaykh: It is the khabar of (kana). ﴿مُبَشِّرِينَ﴾ (mubashshirin), what is its i'rab?
* Students: It is a circumstantial accusative (hal).
* The Shaykh: A hal. Is it a hal from the subject or from the object?
* Students: From the subject.
* The Shaykh: From the subject? You mean Allah is the one who gives good tidings?
* A student: It can be either.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: From the object.
* The Shaykh: From the object, because it is plural, referring back to ﴿النَّبِيِّينَ﴾ (the prophets) in His saying ﴿so Allah sent forth the prophets﴾.

And His saying: ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ مَعَهُمُ الْكِتَابَ﴾ (and sent down with them the Book). Here, what is al-kitab? It is a singular noun used to denote the category, so it covers every Book. Good, what is its i'rab?

* Students: It is the object of (anzala).
* The Shaykh: The object of (anzala)? Good. And His saying: ﴿بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (bil-haqq), the ba'?
* A student: It indicates accompaniment (musahabah).
* The Shaykh: Accompaniment. And His saying: ﴿لِيَحْكُمَ﴾ (liyahkuma), the pronoun refers to what?

* Students: To the Book.
* Other students: To the prophets.
* The Shaykh: To the Book, to the prophets, or to Allah?
* A student: To the Book, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Good, let us now look at it. ﴿So Allah sent forth the prophets, bearing good tidings and warning, and sent down with them the Book﴾ ﴿لِيَحْكُمَ﴾ means: He, that is Allah, because judgment belongs to Him; or: that the Book may judge, in that it is the means of judgment; or: that the prophet may judge, in that he is the one who has the Book with him. But there is a difficulty here, namely that (yahkuma) is singular while (al-nabiyyin) is plural. However, they said: since the prophets are a plural, and a plural has individuals, (liyahkuma) means that each individual of them judges, each one of them, by what Allah has sent down.

His saying: ﴿وَمَا اخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ إِلَّا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ﴾ (And none differed over it except those who were given it) [al-Baqarah 2:213]. ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ (alladhina), what is its i'rab? ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of (ikhtalafa), because the exception here is an exhaustive exception (mustathna mufarragh).

And His saying: ﴿إِلَّا الَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا جَاءَتْهُمُ الْبَيِّنَاتُ بَغْيًا بَيْنَهُمْ﴾ (except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of animosity among themselves). His saying ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا جَاءَتْهُمُ﴾ (after clear proofs had come to them), what is it connected to?

* A student: ﴿أُوتُوهُ﴾ (were given it), O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: "Were given it"? No, because that corrupts the meaning. Rather, it is connected to His saying ﴿وَمَا اخْتَلَفَ﴾ (and none differed), meaning: "and none differed over it after the clear proofs had come to them, out of animosity among themselves, except those who were given it."

﴿بَغْيًا﴾ (baghyan), what is its i'rab? It is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). I assume the rest of the verse is clear.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213]. Here ﴿أمّة﴾ (ummah) means a group (ta'ifah). In former times, before the messengers were sent to them, they were one community, that is, one group upon one religion. What is this one religion?

* A student: Islam.
* The Shaykh: It is the religion of Islam, because Adam was a prophet to whom a law was revealed, by which he worshipped, and his children followed him in that. Then after a period of time, people multiplied and whims (ahwa') diverged, so they differed. At that point they needed the sending of messengers, so Allah sent the messengers. Now, we have already been told that the word (ummah) comes in how many senses?

* A student: Three.
* Another student: Four.
* The Shaykh: Four?
* Students: Three.
* The Shaykh: Five? Good, let us enumerate now. (Ummah) meaning a group: its example is this verse. (Ummah) meaning a leader (imam): ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a ummah﴾ [al-Nahl 16:120]. (Ummah) meaning a period of time: He said, ﴿and after a period (ummah) he remembered﴾ [Yusuf 12:45], meaning after a time. That is three. The fourth: (ummah) meaning a way or path, as in: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a ummah, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:22]. And the fifth?

* A student: One who follows a path.
* The Shaykh: One who follows a path. How is that an example?
* The student: "Allah will raise some of the prophets as a single ummah on the Day of Resurrection."
* The Shaykh: Yes, no, that is meaning "group." What is the fifth? I can only recall four right now.
* A student: Meaning a generation (qarn).
* The Shaykh: Meaning what?
* The student: A generation, that is, a generation of people.
* The Shaykh: Meaning a generation? The ummah is a group of people...
* A student: The term (ajal).
* The Shaykh: The term (ajal), example?
* The student: The verse of Hud.
* The Shaykh: Example?
* The student: An example from the verses in Surat Hud.
* The Shaykh: Which is it?
* The student: ﴿Until a limited period (ummah), they will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾ [Hud 11:8], meaning its term.
* The Shaykh: (...).
* The student: (...) until an ummah.
* The Shaykh: Until an ummah... So yes, yes. But can (ummah) not refer to...?
* The student: The term (...).
* The Shaykh: Until a period of time.
* The student: The term.
* The Shaykh: Until a period of time.
* The student: The term.
* The Shaykh: I am saying: can I not take (ummah) to mean (time), as in ﴿and after a period (ummah) he remembered﴾ [Yusuf 12:45]?

Here (ummah) means a group. ﴿ummatan wahidah﴾ (one community): upon one religion, which is Islam.

﴿So Allah sent forth the prophets﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213]. The fa' here is conjunctive (atifah). Is there an implied antecedent that is being connected to, or is there no need to presume one because it is understood from the context? Because their being one community is not the cause of the sending; the cause of the sending is the disagreement. Some of them said that it is based on an implied omitted clause: "Mankind were one community, then they differed, so Allah sent forth [prophets]." They cited for this His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And mankind were not but one community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus 10:19], and so on to the end. They also cited that the context indicates it, from His saying: ﴿so that He might judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213].

Others said: it does not need to be presumed, because it is understood from the verse itself. In any case, it does not matter, for there is no doubt that the meaning must be that they differed, so the messengers were sent. A parallel to this, where the context specifies what is meant, is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is ill or on a journey, then [an equal number of] other days﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185]. Is the sick person or the traveler obliged to make up the days even if he fasted? No. Therefore we must presume: "then he broke his fast, and then he must make up the days."

He said: ﴿So Allah sent forth the prophets﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213]. (Ba'atha) means (arsala), sending. Its root is in bringing out and stirring up. There is no doubt that the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, is a stirring up and a bringing out, for Allah the Exalted brought them into existence from among these nations, until through them Allah guided whomever He guided.

﴿So Allah sent forth the prophets﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213]. There is a reading ﴿al-nabi'in﴾ with a hamzah, and both or both of them are canonical readings (sab'iyyah).

﴿Allah sent forth the prophets, bearing good tidings and warning﴾: the prophets here mean the messengers, because of His saying ﴿bearing good tidings and warning﴾. And His saying ﴿al-nabiyyin﴾ (the prophets): I said that it includes the messengers. Is there a difference between a nabi and a rasul?

The answer: Yes, there is a difference, and the proof of the difference is that Adam was a nabi, while the first of the messengers was Nuh. If there were no difference, who would the first of the messengers have been? Adam.

So there is a difference between them. What is the difference between the nabi and the rasul? It has been said: the difference is that the nabi is one to whom a law (shar') is revealed but who is not commanded to convey it; rather he is made to worship by it for himself, and he serves as a renewer (mujaddid) of the previous religion. As for the rasul, he is one to whom a law is revealed and who is commanded to convey it. This is the view of the majority (jumhur), and it is a very good distinction, because the nabi is from naba', which is news, so he is one who is informed. And the rasul is from irsal, which is sending, meaning dispatching someone to a destination. You say: "I sent so-and-so," meaning I dispatched him to convey on my behalf. Isn't that so?

* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Some scholars said: the difference is that if the one who brings the revelation completes a previous message, that is, renews it, then he is a nabi; but if he is independent with a message, then he is a rasul. But this is refuted against us by what? By Adam, because Adam was not a renewer. So the view of the majority is good on this issue.

His saying: ﴿mubashshirin﴾ is a hal. ﴿mubashshirin wa-mundhirin﴾: bearing good tidings of what? Of Allah's reward for whoever deserves it, and ﴿and warning﴾ of Allah's punishment for whoever opposes the command of Allah. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿to warn of a severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾ [al-Kahf 18:2]. Here the verse explains the one who receives the good tidings and the thing given as good tidings. Who is the one given good tidings? ﴿the believers who do righteous deeds﴾. And what is the good tidings? ﴿that they will have a good reward, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Kahf 18:2–3], ﴿and to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son." They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Great is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but falsehood﴾ [al-Kahf 18:4–5]. So the one warned are the disbelievers, and what they are warned of is the punishment.

His saying: ﴿mubashshirin wa-mundhirin﴾: are these two hals combined (murakkabani) or separate (munfaridani)?

The answer: They are combined, because the messenger comes with good tidings and warning at the same time, is that not so? That is, no one of the messengers was a bringer of good tidings while another was a warner. Rather, each one combined giving good tidings and warning.

In His saying ﴿mubashshirin wa-mundhirin﴾ there is evidence that what is now called the call of the Christians to their religion by the term "tabshir" (evangelism) is a mistaken, false, and hostile designation, which burns in a blazing fire. Who is most deserving of this term? Those who call to the religion of Islam. And the messenger, peace be upon him, says to those whom he sends: «Give good tidings and do not repel, make things easy and do not make things hard»[[Recorded by Muslim (1732/6) from the hadith of Abu Musa, with the wording: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent one of his companions on some errand, he would say: 'Give good tidings and do not repel, make things easy and do not make things hard.'"]]. So it is obligatory upon us, the Muslim community, to be vigilant regarding such designations. We must not take them in isolation and say: "By Allah, this country has been flooded with tabshir, the missionaries are many," and similar things. This is not permitted. It is not permissible for us to strip this beloved description from our own souls, taking it from ourselves, which is ours, and give it to our enemies. The parallel to this is none other than the parallel of one who is deceived by calling the Christians "Masihiyyun" (Messianists). The term (Masihiyyun) means that you have now acknowledged that they follow the Messiah, just as when you say: "So-and-so is a Tamimi," meaning he belongs to Banu Tamim. So he is a Masihi, upon the religion of the Messiah. But the Messiah, son of Maryam, disavows this religion, because it is disbelief. Such words, therefore, require the student of knowledge to be vigilant about them, and he must not say: "This is a customary convention." He should not say this. A customary convention that changes meanings is not acceptable. If the Prophet ﷺ said: «Do not let the Bedouins overcome you regarding your 'Isha' prayer, which they call 'al-Atamah,' for Allah has named it 'al-'Isha' in the Qur'an, and they only delay it because of their camels»[[Recorded by Muslim (644/228) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, with the wording: "Do not let the Bedouins overcome you regarding the name of your prayer. Indeed it is 'al-'Isha', but they delay it because of their camels."]].

The Messenger ﷺ commanded us not to change this name, even though it carries no danger like the danger of this designation of the Christians, that they are "mubashshirun" (missionaries) and "Masihiyyun." I think that if someone said of the Jews, "They are Musawiyyun" (Mosaists), what would people say? They would reject it, saying: "Musa is innocent of them, peace be upon him." So the matter is exactly the same, with no difference. ﴿mubashshirin wa-mundhirin﴾.

* A student: Shaykh, regarding the majority's view when they distinguished between the nabi and the rasul, some object to them that the believer, meaning the callers (du'at), convey the message, and by this they would be more complete than the prophets who do not convey?

* The Shaykh: No, because they lost revelation.

* The student: But the callers convey, and the prophets, according to this definition and this distinction, do not convey?

* The Shaykh: Yes, they do not convey, because they were not commanded to do so. They are obedient. The essence of perfection in worship is in carrying out the command, even if you are commanded to associate partners with Allah, to kill, and you do it, you are still a worshipper. For this reason the angels were worshippers of Allah the Mighty and Majestic in their prostration to Adam, which is shirk, and Abraham, peace be upon him, was a close friend (khalil) of the Most Merciful, because he was commanded to slaughter his son and he complied.

* A student: Shaykh, but regarding His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet﴾ [al-Hajj 22:52], the message is attributed to the prophet. How is that?

* The Shaykh: No, this is the application of the term "messenger" to the prophet by way of precedence (taghlib), because He said ﴿messenger﴾ first, just as we say "al-qamarani" (the two moons) and "al-'umarani" (the two 'Umars).

* A student: What is the evidence that Adam was a prophet who was sent?

* The Shaykh: The evidence is the hadith of Abu Dharr in Ibn Hibban and others, that the Messenger said: «He is a prophet who was spoken to»[[Recorded by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (361) from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, in his question about Adam, peace be upon him, with the wording: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, was he a prophet who was sent? He said: Yes. Allah created him with His own hand, breathed into him of His spirit, and spoke to him directly."]]. This is with respect to the hadith, and it is explicit. As for the Qur'an, it is clear that Allah spoke to him, commanded him, and forbade him, and this is revelation. Furthermore, he must have worshipped, so how did he worship? Worship is not established by reason; it requires revelation.

* A student: O Shaykh, also, if we say "Nasara" instead of "Masihiyyun," they will say: "Yes, we are the helpers (ansar) of Isa." What do we say?

* The Shaykh: No, the origin of "Nasara" is a relation to the town of Nazareth (al-Nasirah). "Nasara" is not the plural of "nasir" (helper). No, it is a relation to this place.

* A student: Some (...) in defining the messenger say that he is commanded to wage jihad (...) by law (...). Is that correct?

* The Shaykh: No.

* The student: What is the basis for that?

* The Shaykh: Because it is not correct, since some messengers were commanded to wage jihad, and some were not commanded to wage jihad.

* A student: Shaykh, regarding your statement that it is not permissible to describe the Christians as "mubashshirun," because tabshir (...), but Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21].

* The Shaykh: What is the answer to this? The answer is that when tabshir is restricted, it is what it is restricted to. But to say "these are the mubashshirun" without qualification! I agree with you if you say: "These are the missionaries of punishment."

* A student: Shaykh, you know that some call the Rafida (Shi'a) "Ja'fariyyun" (Ja'faris). Is this a relation to Ja'far al-Sadiq, who is innocent of them?

* The Shaykh: In any case, whoever attributes himself to a prophet, a messenger, a believer, or a saint while opposing him, his attribution to him is false.

He says here: ﴿So Allah sent forth the prophets, bearing good tidings and warning, and sent down with them the Book in truth﴾. ﴿أَنْزَلَ مَعَهُمُ﴾ (sent down with them): the preposition (ma'iyyah) here indicates accompaniment, and the "ma'iyyah" whenever used without qualification indicates accompaniment, but in every context it is according to what fits that context. ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ مَعَهُمُ الْكِتَابَ﴾: al-Kitab here, as I said a little while ago, is meant as a category, that is, the category of Book, for otherwise each messenger had a Book. Some exegetes claimed that His saying ﴿and sent down with them﴾ means "with some of them," and said that not all the messengers had a Book. But this contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and Allah, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-Hadid: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Hadid 57:25]. The apparent meaning of the verse is that with every messenger there is a Book. This is what the situation requires, so that the Book he has can be conveyed to the people. And it is not an objection to this that some laws agree in their principles and even in their methods, with only minor differences, as in the law of the Torah and the Gospel, for this does no harm. The important point is that, according to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, every messenger had a Book.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 213–214 (part 2 of 6):**

His saying, "Kitab" (Book) means "maktub" (written). Some of it we know Allah wrote, and some of it we do not know that Allah wrote, but He spoke it. The Tawrah (Torah) was written by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything﴾ [al-A'raf 145]. Likewise the Zabur (Psalms): ﴿And We certainly wrote in the Zabur, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya' 105]. As for the Noble Quran, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention that He wrote it. He only mentioned that He sent it down upon Muhammad (ﷺ). So it is a revelation from Allah, which He spoke and conveyed to Jibril, then Jibril conveyed it to the Prophet (ﷺ). But in every case, all of it is sent down from Allah, whether it is written or spoken. That is, whether its path of descent is in the manner of writing or in the manner of speech and revelation, which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, inspires to Jibril, and then Jibril brings it down to the one whom Allah sent it to.

His saying: ﴿He sent down with them the Book﴾. Is the Quran one of the books or not? We have mentioned previously that it is called a "Kitab" because it is written in the Lawh al-Mahfuz (the Preserved Tablet), and because it is written in the scrolls that are in the hands of the angels, and because it is written in the scrolls that are in our hands. We have also previously explained that "Kitab" is on the pattern of "fi'al" in the sense of "maf'ul" (passive participle), and that "fi'al" comes in the sense of "maf'ul" very often in the Arabic language. We gave examples of this with words such as: firash (bed/carpet), bina' (building), ghiras (planting), kisa' (covering), and what resembles them.

His saying: ﴿bil-haqq﴾ (with truth). Is it connected to "anzala" (He sent down), so that ﴿He sent down with them the Book with truth﴾, meaning the Book came with the truth? Or is it a circumstantial phrase (hal) of the Book, meaning accompanied by truth? The latter is the more apparent, although the two are mutually implying: since it is accompanied by truth, these books are all true, so they are indeed sent down from Allah in truth, because Allah is the Truth, and nothing descends from Him except truth, glorified and exalted is He.

His saying: ﴿bil-haqq﴾ means: the established, the established and beneficial. Its opposite is falsehood, which passes away and benefits nothing. So what is the truth that is established for the books sent down from Allah? We say: as regards reports (akhbar), the truth in them is sincerity (sidq), because a report, when you say "this report is true," means it is sincere and corresponds to reality. As for truth in rulings (ahkam), it is justice (adl) and benefit. On this basis, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿And the word of your Lord is fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]. The books that come from other than Allah contain contradiction, and contradiction is the cancelling of one thing by another: ﴿And had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [an-Nisa' 82]. For this reason, in the field of debate in knowledge, they say: among the greatest things by which you defeat your opponent is to show that his statement is self-contradictory. If a statement is contradictory, it is not correct, because the true statement cannot be contradictory. It is impossible for it to be contradictory at all; rather it is consistent. Indeed, you yourself, if you wish to choose one of the opinions and then find that the opinion you lean toward is contradictory, know that it is not correct, even if at first it appears to you to be correct. But when you know that it is contradictory, know that it is not true, because the truth cannot be contradictory.

So here we say: ﴿bil-haqq﴾ (with truth). Does the meaning mean that its descent was with truth, so it is connected to "anzala," meaning it is true and from Allah and not from other than Him? Or does the meaning mean accompanied by truth, that is, it contains truth in its writing?

* Students: Both.
* The Shaykh: We said both. Both are true. As for the first, it is clear, because the books that the messengers brought from Allah are beyond doubt. As for the second, it is likewise, because whoever reflects on what these books brought finds it to be sincere in reports and just in rulings.

Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾. ﴿liyahkum﴾ (that he may judge). I mentioned that there are three opinions regarding it: is the agent Allah, or the Messenger, or the Book?

Some said: the agent is Allah, meaning "that Allah may judge." They said: because the pronouns should be consistent in one manner: ﴿so Allah sent﴾, ﴿and sent down with them﴾, ﴿that He may judge﴾. All the pronouns refer to whom? To Allah, so that the context is consistent. It is well known that Allah is the Judge, and even the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, judge only by His judgment. The books are a sign and evidence of the judgment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Otherwise, the origin is that judgment belongs to whom? To Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Those who said ﴿liyahkum﴾ means "the Book" said: because it is the means of judgment, and we do not know that this is the judgment of Allah except through the sent-down Book, so it is the judge, because it is the revelation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. In reality, even according to this opinion, the ultimate reference is to whom? To Allah. The reference is to Allah.

As for His saying ﴿liyahkum﴾ meaning "the Prophet," we raised an objection to it: that "al-nabiyyin" (the prophets) is plural while this is singular, and if it referred to the prophets, it would say "liyahkumu" (that they may judge). We answered this by saying that "al-nabiyyin" is plural, and the plural indicates individuals, so the meaning is: that each one of them may judge between the people. On one opinion, this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And make us an imam for the muttaqin (God-fearing)﴾ [al-Furqan 74]. He did not say "a'immah" (imams) for the God-fearing, even though "na" (us) indicates plurality. He said "ij'alna" (make us), meaning make each one of us an imam for the God-fearing.

* Student: Shaykh, the first opinion, that ﴿liyahkum﴾ refers to Allah, ﴿that He may judge between the people﴾, is this correct regarding Allah's judgment through the Book?
* The Shaykh: It is known from the legal perspective. Legal judgment is only known through the Book that Allah sent down. As for the predestined judgment (al-hukm al-qadari), that is not the subject of this verse.

He said: ﴿that He may judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾. The people differed: some of them said, "The truth is such-and-such," and went with it. Others said, "The truth is such-and-such," and went with it.

The noble verse: ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 212]. This affirms the actions of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, that are connected to His will. His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾ shows that these actions are called in the books of creed "al-af'al al-ikhtiyariyyah" (acts linked to His will), because they are connected to Allah's will, and they are established for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in their true sense. Examples of them in the Quran are numerous.

His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾ contains the affirmation of will for Allah. Everything in the universe occurs by the will of Allah. Will (mashi'ah) differs from volition (iradah), because will is not divided, whereas volition is divided into two types: legislative volition (al-iradah al-shar'iyyah) and universal/cosmic volition (al-iradah al-kawniyyah). Will is not divided in this way, but rather what He wills is necessarily brought about. That is, if Allah, exalted is He, wills something, it happens. For this reason, it is said commonly among the Muslims: "Whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur."

Is it connected to what He loves and what He does not love? Yes. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to mislead, He misleads﴾ [al-An'am 39]; this He does not love. ﴿And whoever He wills, He places him on a straight path﴾; this He loves. So it is connected to what He loves and to what He does not love.

We have previously explained that every act that Allah has linked to His will is accompanied by wisdom, since it is not merely will alone, but will accompanied by wisdom. The evidence for this is both textual (sam'i) and rational ('aqli):

The textual: His saying: ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30]. What comes after it? ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ This shows that His will is accompanied by wisdom.

The rational: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, described Himself as Wise, indeed named Himself "al-Hakim" (the Wise). And the Wise does not produce anything except what is in accordance with wisdom.

So it is derived from this verse: the affirmation of will for Allah, and its unrestricted application is restricted by what is known, that every will is accompanied by wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the abundance of the provision of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying ﴿without account﴾. Its meaning is that He gives a gift that no reckoning can reach, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing and All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 261].

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah 213]. Let us look at the i'rab (grammatical analysis). First: ﴿ummatan﴾ (a community): what made it accusative?

* Student: It is a predicate.
* The Shaykh: It is the predicate of "kana" (was). ﴿mubashshirin﴾ (bringers of good news): what is its i'rab?
* Student: It is a circumstantial phrase (hal).
* The Shaykh: A circumstantial phrase of the subject or of the object?
* Students: Of the subject.
* The Shaykh: Of the subject? Meaning Allah is the one giving good news?
* Student: It can apply to both.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Of the object.
* The Shaykh: Of the object, because it is plural. And His saying...
* Student: (...)
* The Shaykh: From His saying ﴿the prophets﴾: ﴿So Allah sent the prophets﴾.

His saying: ﴿And sent down with them the Book﴾. "al-Kitab" (the Book) here, what is it? It is singular, intended as a genus, so it includes every book. Now, its i'rab?

* Student: It is the object of "anzala" (sent down).
* The Shaykh: The object of "anzala"?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: His saying ﴿bil-haqq﴾ (with truth), the "ba'" (with)?
* Student: Accompaniment.
* The Shaykh: Accompaniment. His saying ﴿liyahkum﴾ (that he may judge), the pronoun refers to what?
* Student: The Book.
* Another student: To the prophets.
* Another student: To the Book.
* The Shaykh: To the Book, to the prophets, or to Allah?
* Student: To the Book.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Good. Let us look at the verse: ﴿So Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾. ﴿liyahkum﴾ (that he may judge): either it is He, Allah, because judgment belongs to Him; or the Book, because it is the means of judgment; or the Prophet, because he is the one with whom the Book is. But there is a difficulty here, which is that "yahkum" is singular while "al-nabiyyin" is plural. But they said: since "al-nabiyyun" is plural, and the plural has individuals, it means "that each individual of them may judge," that each one of them judges by what Allah sent down.

His saying: ﴿And none differed over it except those who were given it﴾. ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who): what is its i'rab? "Alladhina" is the subject of "ikhtalafa" (differed), because the exception here is "mufarragh" (an exception where the excluded element is absent and the sentence is governed by what precedes the exception).

His saying: ﴿except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves﴾. His saying: ﴿min ba'di ma ja'athhumu﴾ (after what had come to them): what is it connected to?

* Student: To ﴿utuhu﴾ (were given it), Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: With "utu" (were given)? No, because that corrupts the meaning. But it is connected in His saying ﴿and differed﴾. That is: and they differed concerning it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves, except those who were given it.

﴿baghyan﴾ (out of envy): what is its i'rab? It is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and I think the rest of the verse is clear.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾. "Ummah" here means a group (ta'ifah). Kana (was): in the past, before the messengers were sent to them, they were one community, that is, one group, upon one religion. What is this one religion? It is the religion of Islam, because Adam was a prophet to whom revelation was given with a law by which he worshipped, so he worshipped by it, and his descendants followed him in that. Then after a period of time, the people multiplied and their desires differed, so they differed. At that point they needed the sending of messengers, so Allah sent the messengers.

"Ummah": it was previously mentioned that it comes in how many senses?

* Student: Three.
* Another student: Four.
* The Shaykh: Four?
* Students: Three.
* The Shaykh: Five? Good, let us count now. "Ummah" in the sense of a group: an example?
* Student: The verse.
* The Shaykh: This verse. "Ummah" in the sense of an imam: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾ [an-Nahl 120]. "Ummah" in the sense of a period of time: His saying ﴿And he who was saved of them remembered after a period (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45], meaning after a period of time. These are three. The fourth: "ummah" in the sense of a way or method, like: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion (ummah), and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [az-Zukhruf 22]. The fifth?

* Student: Following the path.
* The Shaykh: Following the path. How? Like what?
* Student: Allah will raise some of the prophets as one ummah on the Day of Resurrection.
* The Shaykh: No, that is in the sense of a group. The fifth, where is it? I do not remember now except four?
* Student: In the sense of a generation (qarn).
* The Shaykh: In the sense of what?
* Student: Qarn: a generation of people.
* The Shaykh: In the sense of a generation. "Ummah" is a group of people.
* Student: The term (ajal).
* The Shaykh: The term like what?
* Student: The verse of Hud.
* The Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: Like one of the verses in Surat Hud.
* The Shaykh: And which is it?
* Student: ﴿Until a specified term (ummah ma'dudah), they will surely say: what holds it back?﴾ [Hud 8]; its term.
* The Shaykh: (...).
* Student: (...) until a term.
* The Shaykh: Until a term... So yes, yes. But "ummah" cannot be made to refer to...?
* Student: The term (...).
* The Shaykh: To a period of time.
* Student: The term.
* The Shaykh: To a period?
* Student: The term.
* The Shaykh: I am saying: I cannot make "ummah" mean "period (zaman)," like: ﴿And he who was saved remembered after a period (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45]?

Here, "ummah" means a group. ﴿ummatan wahidatan﴾ (one community): upon one religion, which is Islam.

﴿fa-ba'atha Allahu al-nabiyyin﴾ (So Allah sent the prophets): the "fa" here is conjunctive. So is the thing it conjoins to implied? Or is there no need to posit an implied element, because it is understood from the context? Because their being one community is not the cause of the sending. What is the cause of the sending? Difference. Some of them said: it is based on an omitted element: "The people were one community, then they differed, so Allah sent." They cited as evidence His saying: ﴿And mankind was not but one community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus 19], ﴿And mankind was not but one community, then they differed,﴾ and so on. They also cited that the context indicates it, by His saying ﴿to judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾. Others said: it does not need a supposed element, because it is understood from the verse.

In any case, it does not matter. There is no doubt that the meaning must be: they differed, so the messengers were sent. An example of something the context determines is His saying: ﴿And whoever is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah 185]. Is the sick or the traveler obligated to make up the days even if he fasted? No. Therefore we must supply: "and he broke his fast, so he must make up the days."

He said: ﴿fa-ba'atha Allahu al-nabiyyin﴾. "Ba'atha" means "arsala" (sent), and its origin is removal and stirring up. There is no doubt that the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, is a stirring up and bringing out, because Allah, exalted is He, brought them forth from among these nations until Allah guided through them whomever He guided.

﴿fa-ba'atha Allahu al-nabiyyin﴾: there is also a reading ﴿al-nabiyyin﴾ with hamza (al-nabi'yin), and both are among the seven canonical readings. ﴿ba'atha Allahu al-nabiyyin mubashshirina wa-mundhirin﴾ (Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good news and warners). The intended meaning of "al-nabiyyin" here is the messengers, based on His saying: ﴿bringers of good news and warners﴾.

His saying: ﴿al-nabiyyin﴾. I said that it includes the messengers. Is there a difference between a prophet (nabi) and a messenger (rasul)? The answer: yes, there is a difference. The evidence for the difference is that Adam was a prophet, and the first of the messengers was Nuh. If there were no difference, the first of the messengers would have been Adam. So there is a difference between them. What is the difference between the prophet and the messenger?

It has been said: the difference between them is that the prophet is one to whom a law (shar') is revealed but who is not commanded to convey it. Rather, he worships by it himself, and he is like a renewer (mujaddid) of the previous religion. As for the messenger, he is one to whom a law is revealed and who is commanded to convey it. This is the opinion of the majority, and it is a very good distinction, because the "nabi" is from "naba'" (news), which is information, so he is an informant. The "rasul" is from "irsal" (sending), which is dispatching to someone. You say: "I sent so-and-so," meaning I dispatched him to convey on my behalf. Is that not so?

* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Some scholars said: the difference is that if the one who brings the revelation completes a previous message (i.e., renews it), he is a prophet; but if he is independent with a message, he is a messenger. But this is refuted against us by what?

* Student: By Adam.
* The Shaykh: By Adam, because Adam was not a renewer. So the majority's opinion on this issue is good.

His saying: ﴿mubashshirin﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal). ﴿mubashshirin wa-mundhirin﴾: bringing good news of what? Of the reward of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for whoever deserves it. ﴿wa-mundhirin﴾ (and warning) of whom? Of the punishment of Allah for whoever opposes the command of Allah. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, said: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾ [al-Kahf 2]. Here the verse has clarified the one who receives good news and what he receives. Who is the recipient of good news?

* Student: The believers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 213–214 (part 3 of 6):

* The Shaykh: the believers who do righteous deeds, and the good news is: ﴿that for them is a good reward, (2) abiding therein forever (3) and to warn those who say, "God has taken a son." (4) They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Enormous is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie.﴾ [al-Kahf 2–5]. So the ones being warned are the disbelievers, and what they are warned of is the punishment; the thing warned of is the punishment.
And His saying: ﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾. These two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl), are they compound or separate? The answer?
* A student: Separate.
* The Shaykh: Compound, because the Messenger comes with good news and warning at one and the same time, right or not? I mean, it is not that one of the messengers is a bearer of good news and the other a warner, rather each one combines, between...?
* Student: The good news...
* The Shaykh: The giving of good news and warning, between giving good news and warning.
And in His saying: ﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾ there is evidence that what is now called the missionary work of the Christians to their religion (tabshīr, "evangelism") is a mistaken and false designation, ﴿toiling, burning in a scorching Fire﴾. Who is most deserving of this term? Those who call to the religion of Islam. The Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, said to those he sent: "Give good news and do not make people run away." [Reported by Muslim (1732/6) from the hadith of Abu Musa, may God be pleased with him, with the wording: When the Messenger of God ﷺ sent one of his companions on some matter, he would say: "Give good news and do not repel; make things easy and do not make them difficult."] So it is incumbent upon us, the Muslim community, to be alert to such designations. We must not take them in their bare form and say: "By God, this land has seen the spread of tabshīr, there are many missionaries here," and similar things. This is not permissible. It is not permissible for us to strip this beloved description from the souls, to strip it from ourselves while it belongs to us, and give it to our enemies.
The parallel to this is none other than that of one who is deceived by calling the Christians "Masihiyyun" (Messianists). Masihi means that you have now acknowledged that they follow the Messiah. It is like saying: "So-and-so is a Tamimi," meaning he is from the Banu Tamim. A "Masihi" on the religion of the Messiah, while the son of Mary disavows this religion, because it is disbelief. Therefore, a student of knowledge should be alert regarding such words, and he should not say: "This is a customary usage (iṣṭilāḥ 'urfī)." He should not speak like this. A customary usage that changes the meanings is not acceptable. If the Prophet, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, said: "Do not let the Bedouins overcome you regarding your night prayer, al-'Atamah (the late night), for God has named it al-'Ishā' in the Qur'an, and they only call it al-'Atamah because of their camels" [Reported by Muslim (644/228), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, with the wording: "Do not let the Bedouins overcome you regarding the name of your prayer. Indeed it is al-'Ishā', but they call it al-'Atamah because of their camels."], the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, commanded us not to change this name, even though the danger in it is not like the danger of this designation for the Christians, that they are "missionaries" and that they are "Masihiyyun."
I think that if someone were to say about the Jews that they are "Musawiyyun" (Mosaists), what would people say? They would respond to him, saying: Moses is innocent of them, peace be upon him. So the matter is the same, there is no difference.
﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾..
* A student: The majority view, when they differentiated between the Prophet (nabī) and the Messenger (rasūl), some object to them, saying that the believing callers (du'āh) convey (the message), and by this they would be more complete than the prophets who do not convey?
* The Shaykh: No, because they have lost revelation.
* The student: But the callers convey, and the prophets, according to this definition, this difference, do not convey?
* The Shaykh: Yes, they do not convey, because they were not commanded to do so. They are obedient. The origin of it is that the perfection of worship lies in carrying out the command. Even if you are commanded to associate partners with God and to kill, and you do it, you are still a worshipper. This is why the angels were servants of God, the Mighty and Majestic, by their prostration to Adam, which is shirk. And Abraham, peace be upon him, was the Friend (khalīl) of the Most Merciful, because he was commanded to slaughter his son and he complied.
* Student: Shaykh, but regarding His saying: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet﴾ [al-Ḥajj 52], how is "messenger" applied to a prophet, how is that?
* The Shaykh: No, this is the application of the term "messenger" to the prophet by way of prevalence (taghlīb), because He said: ﴿messenger﴾, just as we say "al-qamarān" (the two moons) and "al-'umarān" (the two 'Umars).
* Student: What is the evidence that Adam was a prophet and not a messenger?
* The Shaykh: The evidence is the hadith of Abu Dharr in Ibn Hibban and others, that the Messenger said: "He was a prophet who was spoken to" [Reported by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (6190), from the hadith of Abu Umamah, may God be pleased with him. As for the hadith of Abu Dharr, it was reported by Ahmad in al-Musnad (21546).]. This is regarding the hadith, and it is explicit. As for the Qur'an, it is clear that God, the Exalted, spoke to him, commanded him and forbade him, and this is revelation. Furthermore, he must worship, so by what does he worship? Worship cannot be known by reason; it necessarily requires revelation.
* Student: Shaykh, also, if we say "Nasara" instead of "Masihiyyun," would the Christians say: "Yes, we are the helpers (anṣār) of Jesus"?
* The Shaykh: No. The origin of (Naṣārā) is a relative noun to the town of Nazareth (al-Nāṣira), because "Naṣārā" is not the plural of "nāṣir" (helper). No, it is a relative to this place.
* Student: Some (...) in their definition of the Messenger say that he was commanded to wage jihad, he was commanded to it by the Law, whereas the Prophet is not obligated to wage jihad. Is this correct?
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: So what is the reasoning behind this?
* The Shaykh: Because it is not correct, since some messengers were commanded to wage jihad, and some of them were not commanded to wage jihad.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding your statement, which he supports: it is not permissible to describe the Christians as "bearers of good news," because good news (...), but God, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 21]?
* The Shaykh: What is the answer to this? The answer is that when good news is qualified, it is by what it is qualified with. But if you say: "These are the bearers of good news" without qualification, I agree with you if you say: "These are the bearers of good news of punishment."
* Student: Shaykh, you know that the leaders of the Rawafid are called "Ja'fariyyun," so is there an answer to this? "Ja'fariyyun" is a relative to Ja'far al-Sadiq, and he is innocent of them?
* The Shaykh: In any case, whoever claims affiliation to a prophet, a messenger, a believer, or a saint, while opposing him, his claim of affiliation to him is false.
He says here: ﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book with truth﴾. ﴿sent down with them﴾: the "ma'iyyah" (with) here is for accompaniment, and "ma'iyyah," whenever it is used without qualification, indicates accompaniment, but it is in each place according to its context. ﴿sent down with them the Book﴾: "the Book" here, I said a little while ago, is intended as a genus, meaning the category of Book. Otherwise, each messenger had a book. Some exegetes claimed that His saying ﴿and sent down with them﴾ means "with some of them," and said that not all messengers had a book with them. But this contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and God, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Hadid: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 25]. So the apparent meaning of the verse is that with every messenger there is a book, and this is what the situation requires, so that this book he has conveys it to the people.
It is not an objection to this that some laws agree, some laws agree in their legislative matters and even in their methods, with only slight differences, as in the law of the Torah and the Gospel. This does no harm. The important point is that, in the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, every messenger had a book with him.
And His saying "Kitāb" (Book) means "maktūb" (written). Some of them we know God wrote, and some of them we do not know God wrote, but He spoke them. The Torah, God, the Mighty and Majestic, wrote it: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning all things﴾ [al-A'rāf 145]. Likewise the Psalms (Zabur): ﴿And We have written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiyā' 105]. The Noble Qur'an, God did not mention that He wrote it; rather He mentioned that He sent it down upon Muhammad ﷺ. So it is a revelation from God, He spoke it and cast it to Jibril, then Jibril cast it to the Prophet ﷺ. But in any case, all of it is sent down from God, whether it was written or spoken. That is, whether its mode of sending down was by way of writing or by way of speech and revelation that God reveals to Jibril, then Jibril sends it down to the one God sent it to.
And His saying: ﴿sent down with them the Book﴾: is the Qur'an among the books or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned previously that it was called a "Kitāb" because it is written in the Preserved Tablet, and because it is written in the scrolls that are in the hands of the angels, and because it is written in the scrolls that are in our hands. We have also previously explained that "kitāb" is a form (fi'āl) in the meaning of maf'ūl (passive participle), and that fi'āl comes in the meaning of maf'ūl in the Arabic language often, and we gave examples of this, such as firāsh (bedding), binā' (building), ghirās (planting), kisā' (cloth/covering), and what resembles them.
And His saying: ﴿with truth﴾: is it connected to "sent down," so that "﴿and sent down with them the Book with truth﴾" means the Book came with truth; or is it a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the Book, meaning clothed with truth? The latter, although the two are mutually implicative. As long as it is clothed with truth, these books are all truth, so they are indeed sent down from God in truth, because God is the Truth, and nothing descends from Him except truth, glory be to Him.
And His saying: ﴿with truth﴾ means the established, the established and beneficial. Its opposite is falsehood, which passes away and does not benefit. So what is the established truth in the books sent down from God? We say: As for reports, the truth in them is truthfulness, meaning if you say, "This report is true," it means truthful and conforming to reality. As for truth in rulings, it is justice and benefit. On this basis God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'ām 115]. The books that are not from God contain contradiction, and contradiction is the nullification of one thing by another: ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisā' 82]. Therefore, they say in the field of debate in knowledge that among the greatest things by which you can refute your opponent is that his statement is self-contradictory. If a statement is self-contradictory, it is not correct, because a true statement cannot be self-contradictory. It can never be self-contradictory; rather it is consistent.
Indeed, if you yourself want to choose one of the sayings, then you find that this saying you incline toward contradicts itself, know that it is not correct. If you find it contradicts itself, know that it is not correct, even if at first it appears to you to be correct. But if you know that it is self-contradictory, know that it is not true, because truth cannot be self-contradictory.
So here we say: ﴿with truth﴾: is the meaning that its descent is with truth, so it is connected to "sent down," meaning it is true from God and not from other than Him; or the meaning is clothed with truth, that is, it contains truth, the Book?
* The students: Both meanings.
* The Shaykh: We say: both meanings. Both are true. As for the first, it is clear, for the books that the messengers brought from God are beyond doubt. And as for the second, likewise, because whoever reflects on what these books brought finds them truthful in reports and just in rulings.
Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿that He might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. ﴿that He might judge﴾: I mentioned that there are three opinions regarding it: Is the agent God, or the agent the Messenger, or the agent the Book? Some said the agent is God, meaning "that God might judge," and they said: because pronouns should be consistent in one direction: ﴿So God sent﴾, ﴿and sent down with them﴾, ﴿that He might judge﴾, so all the pronouns return to whom? To God. So the context is consistent. And it is known that God, the Exalted, is the Judge. Even the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, do not judge except by His judgment, and the books are a sign and evidence of the judgment of God, the Mighty and Majestic. Otherwise, the origin is that judgment belongs to whom? To God, glory be to Him.
As for those who said: ﴿that He might judge﴾ means the Book, they said: because it is the means of judgment, and we do not know that this is the judgment of God except through the sent-down Book, so it is the judge, because it is the revelation of God, the Mighty and Majestic. In reality, even on this view, the return is to what? To God. The return is to God.
As for His saying ﴿that He might judge﴾ meaning the Prophet, we raised an objection to this, that "the prophets" is plural and this is singular. If it returned to the prophets, it would say: "that they might judge between people." And we answered that "the prophets" is plural, and the plural indicates individuals, and the meaning is: that each one of them might judge between people. And this is, in the opinion of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqān 74], where He did not say "and make us leaders for the righteous," even though "na" (us) indicates plurality. They said: ﴿and make us﴾, meaning make each one of us a leader for the righteous.
* Student: Shaykh, the first opinion, ﴿that He might judge﴾, that it returns to God, that He might judge between people, is this true for God's judgment through the Book?
* The Shaykh: It is known in the legal sense that the legal ruling is only known through the Book which God sent down. As for the divine decree (qadarī) judgment, that is not the subject of this verse.
He said: ﴿that He might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. People differed, so some said: The truth is such-and-such, and went with it, and some said: The truth is such-and-such, and went with it. Two adversaries must have a judge between them, so what is the judge? It is what the messengers brought. Therefore He said: ﴿that He might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. And His saying ﴿concerning that over which they differed﴾: ﴿that﴾ (mā) here is a relative pronoun, and relative pronouns are among the words of generality, so it includes everything over which people differed, from the minute to the major, in matters of religion.
Perhaps you are saying: Why did you not say: "from the fundamentals of religion and its branches"? This division that became famous among the scholars has been refuted by Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah), and Ibn al-Qayyim says: There is no evidence that religion is divided into fundamentals (uṣūl) and branches (furū'), nor is there a sound criterion for it, and this division is an innovation. In religion there are things that are fundamentals by consensus, which you consider branches, such as prayer, pilgrimage, zakat, and fasting. The pillars of Islam are fundamentals, and they are called branches by these people. And among the matters of knowledge there are things that are not considered fundamentals of religion, and whoever opposes them is not declared a disbeliever or misguided. This indicates that this division is not correct, despite it being famous among the scholars, to the extent that they built branches upon it, among them: that one who opposes the fundamentals is declared misguided, and one who opposes the branches is not declared misguided; and among them: that the fundamentals are only accepted with certain report, and the branches are accepted with speculative report, and similar things they mentioned as derivatives of this. Whoever wants more research on it should refer to the book of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, and likewise his student Ibn al-Qayyim in the Mukhtasar al-Sawa'iq al-Mursalah, where he mentioned the refutation of this view from multiple angles.
The important point is that His saying ﴿concerning that over which they differed﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun that indicates generality: everything over which they differed, from the minute and the major in religion, its reference is to God and His messengers. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisā' 59], and God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment is with God﴾ [al-Shūrā 10].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 213–214 (part 4 of 6):

﴿None differed concerning it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves.﴾ ﴿None differed concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning the Book, meaning its kind, ﴿except those who were given it﴾, i.e., were granted it. Here He said ﴿those who were given it﴾, and what is meant here is the nations, not the messengers. Why? Because the giving (ītā') directly applies to whom? To the messengers: ﴿and We gave him the Gospel﴾ [al-Ma'idah 46], ﴿and We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Nisa' 163]. But the reality is that it is given to the messengers and then it returns to the nation. So His saying ﴿those who were given it﴾ means: those who were given the Book. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah 4]. Those who differed concerning it differed without excuse, because they were given it, they knew it, and despite that, they differed about it.

﴿None differed concerning it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves.﴾ As for His saying ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, they said: it is connected to ﴿differed﴾, meaning: none differed concerning it after the clear proofs had come to them except those who were given it. And ﴿out of rebellion﴾ (baghyan) is an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi, i.e., the object showing the reason for an action), whose governing verb is what? ﴿differed﴾ also. That is, they differed out of rebellion. Its governing verb is not ﴿were given it﴾, because the meaning would be corrupted. If you said, "they were given it out of rebellion," would Allah have given it to them so that they might rebel with it? No. Rather, they differed out of rebellion. Accordingly, the sense becomes clear: none differed concerning it after the clear proofs had come to them out of rebellion except those who were given it.

In His saying ﴿except those who were given it﴾, the use of this description in particular contains clear rebuke and blame. This is because it was most fitting and proper for those who were given it to be what? Not to differ about it. It was most fitting that they agree upon it. Yet they differed about it despite Allah's bounty upon them in granting it to them, so this is more severe in blame and rebuke.

(..) The Exalted said: ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed, by His permission.﴾ (Guided) Here, guidance means the guidance of tawfīq (divine enablement), preceded by the guidance of knowledge and direction, because guidance is divided into two kinds: guidance of indication and direction (hidāyat dalālah wa irshād), and guidance of tawfīq. Consider His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. What is the meaning of "We guided them"? That is, We made clear to them and directed them, but they did not become guided. And consider His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas 56], meaning you cannot grant him enablement to be guided. So this is the guidance of tawfīq. Here, ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to that concerning which they differed﴾: is the intended meaning the guidance of tawfīq, because all of them were guided by the indication of what the Books brought with the messengers, or is it both the guidance of indication and that of tawfīq together?
* Student: Tawfīq.
* Shaykh: Tawfīq, because all of them were brought the messengers with the Books and they were made clear to them. But none of them became guided except those whom Allah guided.

﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed.﴾ ﴿Those who believed﴾: Faith (īmān, a technical term) linguistically means affirmation (taṣdīq). But in the religious law, it means affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. Mere affirmation is not faith. If mere affirmation were faith, Abu Talib would have been a believer, because Abu Talib used to acknowledge that Muhammad (ﷺ) was truthful, and he would say:

"They surely know that our son is not one accused of lying among us, nor is he one who is concerned with false words."

But he did not accept, nor did he submit, so he was not a believer. Therefore, faith in the religious law is affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission, not merely affirmation.

As for His saying ﴿those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed﴾, it means: to that which they differed about. The pronoun in ﴿they differed﴾ refers to ﴿the people﴾. That is, Allah guided the believers to the truth about which they differed, since people differed concerning the truth: some of them accepted it, and some of them rejected and denied it. The believers were guided by Allah to this truth about which they differed. On this basis, His saying ﴿from the truth﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial description (ḥāl), clarifying what? ﴿lima﴾, which is the relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl). And what shows that the prepositional phrase clarifies it is that if you said, "So Allah guided those who believed to the truth that they differed about," would the meaning be sound? Yes, the meaning is sound. From this we know that His saying ﴿from the truth﴾ is not partitive, but explanatory, i.e., clarifying the vagueness contained in the relative ﴿mā﴾ in ﴿to that which they differed about from the truth﴾.

As for His saying ﴿from the truth﴾, we have previously mentioned several times the meaning of "truth" (ḥaqq): that it originally means the established thing that contradicts falsehood. We said that if it describes a report, the intended meaning is truthfulness (ṣidq), and if it describes a judgment, the intended meaning is justice ('adl). On this basis, His saying the Exalted: ﴿The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115].

As for His saying the Exalted ﴿by His permission﴾, it means by His will. He guided them by His will and decree. But He, glory be to Him, does not will anything except with a will joined with wisdom, since the will of Allah the Glorified is not a bare will, but is joined with wisdom. What is the evidence for this?
