* The Shaykh: Compound, because the Messenger comes with good news and warning at one and the same time, right or not? I mean, it is not that one of the messengers is a bearer of good news and the other a warner, rather each one combines, between...?
* Student: The good news...
* The Shaykh: The giving of good news and warning, between giving good news and warning.
And in His saying: ﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾ there is evidence that what is now called the missionary work of the Christians to their religion (tabshīr, "evangelism") is a mistaken and false designation, ﴿toiling, burning in a scorching Fire﴾. Who is most deserving of this term? Those who call to the religion of Islam. The Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, said to those he sent: "Give good news and do not make people run away." [Reported by Muslim (1732/6) from the hadith of Abu Musa, may God be pleased with him, with the wording: When the Messenger of God ﷺ sent one of his companions on some matter, he would say: "Give good news and do not repel; make things easy and do not make them difficult."] So it is incumbent upon us, the Muslim community, to be alert to such designations. We must not take them in their bare form and say: "By God, this land has seen the spread of tabshīr, there are many missionaries here," and similar things. This is not permissible. It is not permissible for us to strip this beloved description from the souls, to strip it from ourselves while it belongs to us, and give it to our enemies.
The parallel to this is none other than that of one who is deceived by calling the Christians "Masihiyyun" (Messianists). Masihi means that you have now acknowledged that they follow the Messiah. It is like saying: "So-and-so is a Tamimi," meaning he is from the Banu Tamim. A "Masihi" on the religion of the Messiah, while the son of Mary disavows this religion, because it is disbelief. Therefore, a student of knowledge should be alert regarding such words, and he should not say: "This is a customary usage (iṣṭilāḥ 'urfī)." He should not speak like this. A customary usage that changes the meanings is not acceptable. If the Prophet, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, said: "Do not let the Bedouins overcome you regarding your night prayer, al-'Atamah (the late night), for God has named it al-'Ishā' in the Qur'an, and they only call it al-'Atamah because of their camels" [Reported by Muslim (644/228), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, with the wording: "Do not let the Bedouins overcome you regarding the name of your prayer. Indeed it is al-'Ishā', but they call it al-'Atamah because of their camels."], the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of God be upon him, commanded us not to change this name, even though the danger in it is not like the danger of this designation for the Christians, that they are "missionaries" and that they are "Masihiyyun."
I think that if someone were to say about the Jews that they are "Musawiyyun" (Mosaists), what would people say? They would respond to him, saying: Moses is innocent of them, peace be upon him. So the matter is the same, there is no difference.
﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾..
* A student: The majority view, when they differentiated between the Prophet (nabī) and the Messenger (rasūl), some object to them, saying that the believing callers (du'āh) convey (the message), and by this they would be more complete than the prophets who do not convey?
* The Shaykh: No, because they have lost revelation.
* The student: But the callers convey, and the prophets, according to this definition, this difference, do not convey?
* The Shaykh: Yes, they do not convey, because they were not commanded to do so. They are obedient. The origin of it is that the perfection of worship lies in carrying out the command. Even if you are commanded to associate partners with God and to kill, and you do it, you are still a worshipper. This is why the angels were servants of God, the Mighty and Majestic, by their prostration to Adam, which is shirk. And Abraham, peace be upon him, was the Friend (khalīl) of the Most Merciful, because he was commanded to slaughter his son and he complied.
* Student: Shaykh, but regarding His saying: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet﴾ [al-Ḥajj 52], how is "messenger" applied to a prophet, how is that?
* The Shaykh: No, this is the application of the term "messenger" to the prophet by way of prevalence (taghlīb), because He said: ﴿messenger﴾, just as we say "al-qamarān" (the two moons) and "al-'umarān" (the two 'Umars).
* Student: What is the evidence that Adam was a prophet and not a messenger?
* The Shaykh: The evidence is the hadith of Abu Dharr in Ibn Hibban and others, that the Messenger said: "He was a prophet who was spoken to" [Reported by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (6190), from the hadith of Abu Umamah, may God be pleased with him. As for the hadith of Abu Dharr, it was reported by Ahmad in al-Musnad (21546).]. This is regarding the hadith, and it is explicit. As for the Qur'an, it is clear that God, the Exalted, spoke to him, commanded him and forbade him, and this is revelation. Furthermore, he must worship, so by what does he worship? Worship cannot be known by reason; it necessarily requires revelation.
* Student: Shaykh, also, if we say "Nasara" instead of "Masihiyyun," would the Christians say: "Yes, we are the helpers (anṣār) of Jesus"?
* The Shaykh: No. The origin of (Naṣārā) is a relative noun to the town of Nazareth (al-Nāṣira), because "Naṣārā" is not the plural of "nāṣir" (helper). No, it is a relative to this place.
* Student: Some (...) in their definition of the Messenger say that he was commanded to wage jihad, he was commanded to it by the Law, whereas the Prophet is not obligated to wage jihad. Is this correct?
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: So what is the reasoning behind this?
* The Shaykh: Because it is not correct, since some messengers were commanded to wage jihad, and some of them were not commanded to wage jihad.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding your statement, which he supports: it is not permissible to describe the Christians as "bearers of good news," because good news (...), but God, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 21]?
* The Shaykh: What is the answer to this? The answer is that when good news is qualified, it is by what it is qualified with. But if you say: "These are the bearers of good news" without qualification, I agree with you if you say: "These are the bearers of good news of punishment."
* Student: Shaykh, you know that the leaders of the Rawafid are called "Ja'fariyyun," so is there an answer to this? "Ja'fariyyun" is a relative to Ja'far al-Sadiq, and he is innocent of them?
* The Shaykh: In any case, whoever claims affiliation to a prophet, a messenger, a believer, or a saint, while opposing him, his claim of affiliation to him is false.
He says here: ﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book with truth﴾. ﴿sent down with them﴾: the "ma'iyyah" (with) here is for accompaniment, and "ma'iyyah," whenever it is used without qualification, indicates accompaniment, but it is in each place according to its context. ﴿sent down with them the Book﴾: "the Book" here, I said a little while ago, is intended as a genus, meaning the category of Book. Otherwise, each messenger had a book. Some exegetes claimed that His saying ﴿and sent down with them﴾ means "with some of them," and said that not all messengers had a book with them. But this contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and God, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Hadid: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Book and the Balance﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 25]. So the apparent meaning of the verse is that with every messenger there is a book, and this is what the situation requires, so that this book he has conveys it to the people.
It is not an objection to this that some laws agree, some laws agree in their legislative matters and even in their methods, with only slight differences, as in the law of the Torah and the Gospel. This does no harm. The important point is that, in the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, every messenger had a book with him.
And His saying "Kitāb" (Book) means "maktūb" (written). Some of them we know God wrote, and some of them we do not know God wrote, but He spoke them. The Torah, God, the Mighty and Majestic, wrote it: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning all things﴾ [al-A'rāf 145]. Likewise the Psalms (Zabur): ﴿And We have written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiyā' 105]. The Noble Qur'an, God did not mention that He wrote it; rather He mentioned that He sent it down upon Muhammad ﷺ. So it is a revelation from God, He spoke it and cast it to Jibril, then Jibril cast it to the Prophet ﷺ. But in any case, all of it is sent down from God, whether it was written or spoken. That is, whether its mode of sending down was by way of writing or by way of speech and revelation that God reveals to Jibril, then Jibril sends it down to the one God sent it to.
And His saying: ﴿sent down with them the Book﴾: is the Qur'an among the books or not?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: We mentioned previously that it was called a "Kitāb" because it is written in the Preserved Tablet, and because it is written in the scrolls that are in the hands of the angels, and because it is written in the scrolls that are in our hands. We have also previously explained that "kitāb" is a form (fi'āl) in the meaning of maf'ūl (passive participle), and that fi'āl comes in the meaning of maf'ūl in the Arabic language often, and we gave examples of this, such as firāsh (bedding), binā' (building), ghirās (planting), kisā' (cloth/covering), and what resembles them.
And His saying: ﴿with truth﴾: is it connected to "sent down," so that "﴿and sent down with them the Book with truth﴾" means the Book came with truth; or is it a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the Book, meaning clothed with truth? The latter, although the two are mutually implicative. As long as it is clothed with truth, these books are all truth, so they are indeed sent down from God in truth, because God is the Truth, and nothing descends from Him except truth, glory be to Him.
And His saying: ﴿with truth﴾ means the established, the established and beneficial. Its opposite is falsehood, which passes away and does not benefit. So what is the established truth in the books sent down from God? We say: As for reports, the truth in them is truthfulness, meaning if you say, "This report is true," it means truthful and conforming to reality. As for truth in rulings, it is justice and benefit. On this basis God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'ām 115]. The books that are not from God contain contradiction, and contradiction is the nullification of one thing by another: ﴿Had it been from other than God, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisā' 82]. Therefore, they say in the field of debate in knowledge that among the greatest things by which you can refute your opponent is that his statement is self-contradictory. If a statement is self-contradictory, it is not correct, because a true statement cannot be self-contradictory. It can never be self-contradictory; rather it is consistent.
Indeed, if you yourself want to choose one of the sayings, then you find that this saying you incline toward contradicts itself, know that it is not correct. If you find it contradicts itself, know that it is not correct, even if at first it appears to you to be correct. But if you know that it is self-contradictory, know that it is not true, because truth cannot be self-contradictory.
So here we say: ﴿with truth﴾: is the meaning that its descent is with truth, so it is connected to "sent down," meaning it is true from God and not from other than Him; or the meaning is clothed with truth, that is, it contains truth, the Book?
* The students: Both meanings.
* The Shaykh: We say: both meanings. Both are true. As for the first, it is clear, for the books that the messengers brought from God are beyond doubt. And as for the second, likewise, because whoever reflects on what these books brought finds them truthful in reports and just in rulings.
Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿that He might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. ﴿that He might judge﴾: I mentioned that there are three opinions regarding it: Is the agent God, or the agent the Messenger, or the agent the Book? Some said the agent is God, meaning "that God might judge," and they said: because pronouns should be consistent in one direction: ﴿So God sent﴾, ﴿and sent down with them﴾, ﴿that He might judge﴾, so all the pronouns return to whom? To God. So the context is consistent. And it is known that God, the Exalted, is the Judge. Even the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, do not judge except by His judgment, and the books are a sign and evidence of the judgment of God, the Mighty and Majestic. Otherwise, the origin is that judgment belongs to whom? To God, glory be to Him.
As for those who said: ﴿that He might judge﴾ means the Book, they said: because it is the means of judgment, and we do not know that this is the judgment of God except through the sent-down Book, so it is the judge, because it is the revelation of God, the Mighty and Majestic. In reality, even on this view, the return is to what? To God. The return is to God.
As for His saying ﴿that He might judge﴾ meaning the Prophet, we raised an objection to this, that "the prophets" is plural and this is singular. If it returned to the prophets, it would say: "that they might judge between people." And we answered that "the prophets" is plural, and the plural indicates individuals, and the meaning is: that each one of them might judge between people. And this is, in the opinion of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and make us leaders for the righteous﴾ [al-Furqān 74], where He did not say "and make us leaders for the righteous," even though "na" (us) indicates plurality. They said: ﴿and make us﴾, meaning make each one of us a leader for the righteous.
* Student: Shaykh, the first opinion, ﴿that He might judge﴾, that it returns to God, that He might judge between people, is this true for God's judgment through the Book?
* The Shaykh: It is known in the legal sense that the legal ruling is only known through the Book which God sent down. As for the divine decree (qadarī) judgment, that is not the subject of this verse.
He said: ﴿that He might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. People differed, so some said: The truth is such-and-such, and went with it, and some said: The truth is such-and-such, and went with it. Two adversaries must have a judge between them, so what is the judge? It is what the messengers brought. Therefore He said: ﴿that He might judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. And His saying ﴿concerning that over which they differed﴾: ﴿that﴾ (mā) here is a relative pronoun, and relative pronouns are among the words of generality, so it includes everything over which people differed, from the minute to the major, in matters of religion.
Perhaps you are saying: Why did you not say: "from the fundamentals of religion and its branches"? This division that became famous among the scholars has been refuted by Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah), and Ibn al-Qayyim says: There is no evidence that religion is divided into fundamentals (uṣūl) and branches (furū'), nor is there a sound criterion for it, and this division is an innovation. In religion there are things that are fundamentals by consensus, which you consider branches, such as prayer, pilgrimage, zakat, and fasting. The pillars of Islam are fundamentals, and they are called branches by these people. And among the matters of knowledge there are things that are not considered fundamentals of religion, and whoever opposes them is not declared a disbeliever or misguided. This indicates that this division is not correct, despite it being famous among the scholars, to the extent that they built branches upon it, among them: that one who opposes the fundamentals is declared misguided, and one who opposes the branches is not declared misguided; and among them: that the fundamentals are only accepted with certain report, and the branches are accepted with speculative report, and similar things they mentioned as derivatives of this. Whoever wants more research on it should refer to the book of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, and likewise his student Ibn al-Qayyim in the Mukhtasar al-Sawa'iq al-Mursalah, where he mentioned the refutation of this view from multiple angles.
The important point is that His saying ﴿concerning that over which they differed﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun that indicates generality: everything over which they differed, from the minute and the major in religion, its reference is to God and His messengers. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisā' 59], and God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its judgment is with God﴾ [al-Shūrā 10].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 213–214 (part 4 of 6):

﴿None differed concerning it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves.﴾ ﴿None differed concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning the Book, meaning its kind, ﴿except those who were given it﴾, i.e., were granted it. Here He said ﴿those who were given it﴾, and what is meant here is the nations, not the messengers. Why? Because the giving (ītā') directly applies to whom? To the messengers: ﴿and We gave him the Gospel﴾ [al-Ma'idah 46], ﴿and We gave David the Psalms﴾ [al-Nisa' 163]. But the reality is that it is given to the messengers and then it returns to the nation. So His saying ﴿those who were given it﴾ means: those who were given the Book. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah 4]. Those who differed concerning it differed without excuse, because they were given it, they knew it, and despite that, they differed about it.

﴿None differed concerning it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves.﴾ As for His saying ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, they said: it is connected to ﴿differed﴾, meaning: none differed concerning it after the clear proofs had come to them except those who were given it. And ﴿out of rebellion﴾ (baghyan) is an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi, i.e., the object showing the reason for an action), whose governing verb is what? ﴿differed﴾ also. That is, they differed out of rebellion. Its governing verb is not ﴿were given it﴾, because the meaning would be corrupted. If you said, "they were given it out of rebellion," would Allah have given it to them so that they might rebel with it? No. Rather, they differed out of rebellion. Accordingly, the sense becomes clear: none differed concerning it after the clear proofs had come to them out of rebellion except those who were given it.

In His saying ﴿except those who were given it﴾, the use of this description in particular contains clear rebuke and blame. This is because it was most fitting and proper for those who were given it to be what? Not to differ about it. It was most fitting that they agree upon it. Yet they differed about it despite Allah's bounty upon them in granting it to them, so this is more severe in blame and rebuke.

(..) The Exalted said: ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed, by His permission.﴾ (Guided) Here, guidance means the guidance of tawfīq (divine enablement), preceded by the guidance of knowledge and direction, because guidance is divided into two kinds: guidance of indication and direction (hidāyat dalālah wa irshād), and guidance of tawfīq. Consider His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. What is the meaning of "We guided them"? That is, We made clear to them and directed them, but they did not become guided. And consider His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas 56], meaning you cannot grant him enablement to be guided. So this is the guidance of tawfīq. Here, ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to that concerning which they differed﴾: is the intended meaning the guidance of tawfīq, because all of them were guided by the indication of what the Books brought with the messengers, or is it both the guidance of indication and that of tawfīq together?
* Student: Tawfīq.
* Shaykh: Tawfīq, because all of them were brought the messengers with the Books and they were made clear to them. But none of them became guided except those whom Allah guided.

﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed.﴾ ﴿Those who believed﴾: Faith (īmān, a technical term) linguistically means affirmation (taṣdīq). But in the religious law, it means affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. Mere affirmation is not faith. If mere affirmation were faith, Abu Talib would have been a believer, because Abu Talib used to acknowledge that Muhammad (ﷺ) was truthful, and he would say:

"They surely know that our son is not one accused of lying among us, nor is he one who is concerned with false words."

But he did not accept, nor did he submit, so he was not a believer. Therefore, faith in the religious law is affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission, not merely affirmation.

As for His saying ﴿those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed﴾, it means: to that which they differed about. The pronoun in ﴿they differed﴾ refers to ﴿the people﴾. That is, Allah guided the believers to the truth about which they differed, since people differed concerning the truth: some of them accepted it, and some of them rejected and denied it. The believers were guided by Allah to this truth about which they differed. On this basis, His saying ﴿from the truth﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial description (ḥāl), clarifying what? ﴿lima﴾, which is the relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl). And what shows that the prepositional phrase clarifies it is that if you said, "So Allah guided those who believed to the truth that they differed about," would the meaning be sound? Yes, the meaning is sound. From this we know that His saying ﴿from the truth﴾ is not partitive, but explanatory, i.e., clarifying the vagueness contained in the relative ﴿mā﴾ in ﴿to that which they differed about from the truth﴾.

As for His saying ﴿from the truth﴾, we have previously mentioned several times the meaning of "truth" (ḥaqq): that it originally means the established thing that contradicts falsehood. We said that if it describes a report, the intended meaning is truthfulness (ṣidq), and if it describes a judgment, the intended meaning is justice ('adl). On this basis, His saying the Exalted: ﴿The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115].

As for His saying the Exalted ﴿by His permission﴾, it means by His will. He guided them by His will and decree. But He, glory be to Him, does not will anything except with a will joined with wisdom, since the will of Allah the Glorified is not a bare will, but is joined with wisdom. What is the evidence for this?

The evidence is what we pointed to earlier, namely His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30]. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made clear that His will follows His wisdom. So it is not a mere will, but a will joined with wisdom, to be the most perfect will.

As for His saying ﴿by His permission﴾: the permission by which Allah is described is of two kinds: cosmic (kawnī) and legislative (shar'ī). The cosmic is that which relates to predestination and decree, and the legislative is that which relates to the law. An example of the cosmic is His saying: ﴿And they could not harm anyone with it except by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 102], meaning: sorcery. So ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾ here means what? The cosmic permission, not the legislative permission, because Allah cannot permit sorcery and the harm that results from it. Rather, this is cosmic permission. An example of the legislative permission is His saying: ﴿Or do they have partners who have legislated for them of religion that for which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 21]. This must be the legislative permission. Why? Because it was permitted cosmically: it occurred. So it is, cosmically, permitted, because they legislated for themselves from religion, but legislatively, He did not permit it. Therefore, His saying ﴿they legislated for them of religion that for which Allah has not permitted﴾ must mean what? The legislative permission. First, because it is joined with legislation: ﴿they legislated for them of religion﴾, they legislated from religion, so the intended meaning is the legislative permission. Second, it cannot mean the cosmic permission, because that has already occurred, so what they legislated is permitted cosmically, not legislatively. Here, in His saying the Exalted ﴿from the truth by His permission﴾, which of the two meanings is intended?
* Student: The legislative.
* Shaykh: ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed, by His permission﴾.
* Student: The cosmic.
* Shaykh: The cosmic is intended, yes.

The Exalted said: ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. In ﴿ṣirāṭ﴾ there are two readings: with ṣād and with sīn, both canonical (sab'iyyah). His saying ﴿And Allah guides﴾ is a sentence composed of a subject and predicate, and the predicate within it is a sentence.

His saying ﴿guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾: does ﴿guides﴾ mean: directs and indicates, or means: directs, indicates, and grants tawfīq? All of them. So it is cosmic and legislative guidance: ﴿guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾.

As for His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾, it means: among those who deserve guidance. Since we have established that everything tied to Allah's will follows His wisdom, then He guides whom He wills if he is deserving of guidance. He, glory be to Him, just as He places the message with those who are fit for it, likewise He places guidance with those who are fit for it, as Allah said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 124]. Likewise, He knows best where to place His law and His enablement.

As for His saying ﴿to a straight path﴾: the ṣirāṭ in the Arabic language is the wide road. It is called ṣirāṭ, and it is said zirāṭ with a zāy. They said that is because it swallows its traveler. Just as when you swallow a morsel quickly, what is said?
* Student: Zaraṭahā.
* Shaykh: Zaraṭahā, yes. Because it is wide, it swallows the traveler who walks quickly on it. So it is called ṣirāṭ. Thus, the ṣirāṭ is the wide road. Some said: the wide, straight road, because a crooked road does not allow easy passage. And they made His saying ﴿straight﴾ an emphasizing adjective.

In any case, the straight path that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned is explained by Allah, glory be to Him, in Surat al-Fatihah in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have evoked [Your] anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah 6–7]. It is the path that combines knowledge and guidance, and if you wish, say: combines guidance and right direction, unlike the crooked path, in which the traveler is deprived of guidance, like the path of the Christians, or deprived of right direction, like the path of the Jews.

﴿guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. Then He said..
* Student: Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: What is the difference between permission (idhn) and decree (qaḍā')?
* Shaykh: From what aspect?
* Student: From the aspect of meaning.
* Shaykh: Both are close in meaning. Even decree is divided into: legislative decree and cosmic decree.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, they are close.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: All of these meanings are close and mutually implicative, because when Allah, glory be to Him, decrees, He permits, meaning He commands, and His permission is a judgment, and His command is a judgment. They are close meanings, like anger and wrath, or contentment and acceptance.
* Student: (...), not directly?
* Shaykh: No, it is not necessarily direct.

Then He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed away before you has not yet come to you?﴾ and so on to the end. Here, ﴿am﴾ (or) is one of the conjunctive particles. But is it here connected (muttaṣilah) or disconnected (munqaṭi'ah)?
* Student: Disconnected.
* Shaykh: Disconnected? Good. Whoever says "disconnected," we want to ask him: what is the difference between them? Otherwise, he would be like a child. If you say to a child, "Do you love your father or your mother?" he says, "My mother." If you say, "Do you love your mother or your father?" he says, "My father." He makes the last one the choice. So now let us see: you said "disconnected"?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Good, what is the reason?
* Student: Because the counterpart (mu'ādil) is not mentioned with it. A disconnected ﴿am﴾ is one where the counterpart is not mentioned.
* Shaykh: When ﴿am﴾ is not accompanied by its counterpart, it is disconnected. Good. Another difference?
* Student: It means ﴿bal﴾ (rather).
* Shaykh: It means ﴿bal﴾, and the connected one means?
* Student: It means the conjunction ﴿aw﴾ (or).
* Shaykh: It means ﴿aw﴾. Correct. The difference between connected and disconnected is from two aspects: the connected one has its counterpart mentioned, as in His saying: ﴿It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 6]. And the disconnected one has no counterpart mentioned. Second: the disconnected one means ﴿bal﴾, and the connected one means ﴿aw﴾.

Here, ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾: they said it is disconnected, and an interrogative hamzah is to be understood after it, meaning: "Rather, did you think...?" So it is for idrāb (a transition from one topic to another). Is the idrāb here annulling (ibṭāl) or transitional (intiqāl)?
* Student: Transitional.
* Shaykh: Transitional, a transition from one speech to another: "Rather, did you think?"

And ﴿ḥasibtum﴾ means ẓanantum (you supposed). Accordingly, it governs two objects, but where are its two objects? Some grammarians said: ﴿an﴾ and what follows it fill the place of both objects. Others said: rather, ﴿an﴾ and what follows it fill the place of the first object, and the second object is omitted. Is the statement clear?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Good. If we say that ﴿an﴾ and what follows it fill the place of both objects, the matter is clear and needs no other supposition. If we say that ﴿an﴾ and what follows it fill the place of the first object, then how do we supply the second? The supposition would be: "Did you think your entering Paradise was established while Allah had not yet known..."

Then He said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾ [al-Baqarah 214]. The address in ﴿Or did you think﴾ refers to whom? To everyone who is addressed: to the Prophet (ﷺ), to the Companions, and to those who came after them.

As for His saying ﴿that you would enter Paradise﴾: Paradise (jannah), we have mentioned many times, linguistically means a garden with many trees, and it was named that because it covers (yajunnu) whoever is in it, meaning it conceals and shelters him. The root of this word is jīm and nūn, and its origin is concealment. From it comes the word jinn, and from it the shield (junnah) with which a fighter protects himself, as in His saying: ﴿They took their oaths as a shield, and so they averted [people] from the way of Allah﴾ [al-Mujadilah 16]. So we have jannah, jinnah, and junnah, all present in the Quran or not? ﴿they took their oaths as a shield [junnah]﴾, ﴿of the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-Nas 6], ﴿and they have made between Him and the jinn a relationship﴾ [al-Saffat 158]. As for jannah, it is frequent.

But do we say, regarding the Paradise that Allah promised to the righteous, that it is a garden with many trees?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: We have told you: we do not say this, because if you said it, it would belittle its matter and diminish its status. But if you say: it is the abode that Allah prepared for the righteous, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not occurred to the heart of any human, which of the two is greater in the soul: that you say such words, or that you say, "It is a garden with many trees"? In my view, the first is more eloquent, because if you say "a garden with many trees," someone will say, "This exists. Go to so-and-so's garden, it has many trees." But if you say, "It is the abode that Allah prepared for the righteous, in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not occurred to the heart of any human," that is greater in souls.
* Student: Shaykh?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The hadith in which "Inform them that Paradise (...), and that its plants are: Subhan Allah"[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3462), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "And inform them that Paradise has good soil and sweet water, and that it is flat plains (qī'ān), and that its plants are: Subhan Allah..." until the end of the hadith.]]?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is authentic.
* Student: So does this suggest that it is, like, a garden such as...?
* Shaykh: Yes, but its plants are not these plants, because many people do not imagine, when you say "a garden with many trees," anything other than what is seen in this world.

Then He said: ﴿And the example of those who passed away before you has not yet come to you. Adversity and hardship touched them﴾ and so on to the end. Is ﴿lammā﴾ here jussing the verb, or not?
* Student: It jusses it.
* Shaykh: What is the evidence?
* Student: The deletion of the yā'.
* Shaykh: The deletion of the yā', yes.

﴿And has not yet come to you﴾: if it did not jussify, it would say ﴿yaʾtīkum﴾. ﴿And has not yet come to you the example of﴾: is ﴿lammā﴾ here in its own meaning and literal sense, or does it mean ﴿lam yaʾtikum﴾ (has not come to you)? Some grammarians said: it means ﴿lam﴾, and others said: rather, it is in its literal sense as ﴿lammā﴾, because the original principle is to keep the speech in its apparent sense. Is there a difference between the two views?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. If we say ﴿lam﴾, it only indicates the negation of that thing, or the negation of that thing without it being expected. But if it is said ﴿lammā yaʾtikum﴾ (it has not yet come to you), the matter becomes one that is expected, so that souls may be prepared for its occurrence. What is expected may occur or may not occur, is that not so? But when it is presented as something expected, souls prepare for it. This view, that it is in its apparent sense, is more correct.

It has already been mentioned that if you say, "I travelled to the town but did not enter it," this is a negation of entering, but it does not imply that you were expected to enter. However, if you say, "I travelled to the town and have not yet entered it" (*wa-lamma adkhulha*), you have come close to it, and your entering it is expected.

He says: ﴿Yet there has not come to you the like of those who passed away before you; adversity and hardship touched them﴾. *Mathal* ("the like," "the description") here means the description of what happened to them. The word *mathal* is used to mean a description, as in His saying, ﴿The description of Paradise which the righteous have been promised﴾ [al-Ra'd 35], meaning its description is such and such. So ﴿the like of those who passed away before you﴾ means the description of what befell them.

As for His saying, ﴿those who passed away before you﴾, *khalaw* means "passed on." What is the benefit of ﴿before you﴾ when ﴿passed away﴾ already means "passed on"? We say: this is a case of emphasis (*tawkid*), and emphasis may come with the same meaning but with different wording, as in His saying, ﴿and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief﴾ [al-Baqarah 60]. Corruption (*ifsad*) is the same as transgression (*'utuw*), yet it came as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the *waw*, so it emphasises its verb by its governing verb. Likewise, ﴿before you﴾ emphasises His saying, ﴿passed away before you﴾.

Then, since *mathal* is vague (*mubham*), ﴿the like of those who passed away before you﴾: what is this like? Allah, the Exalted, clarified it by His saying: ﴿adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken﴾. *Massat-hum* ("touched them"): *mass*, as you know, is direct contact with something. You say, for example, "I touched it with my hand," or "his garment touched the ground," and similar things. ﴿Massat-hum﴾ means that affliction struck them directly. This sentence is a resumptive clause (*isti'nafiyyah*, a new clause that begins anew) explaining the *mathal* mentioned in His saying, ﴿the like of those who passed away before you﴾. ﴿Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken﴾: there are three things. *Al-ba'sa'* (adversity), they said, is severe poverty, derived from *bu's*, which means extreme poverty. *Al-darra'* (hardship), they said, is illness and bodily calamities. ﴿They were shaken﴾ by fears and anxiety. So the afflictions here occur in three places: in wealth, in the body, and in the soul.

﻿﴿Zulzilu﴾ (they were shaken): shaken by what? Does it mean the earth was shaken beneath them? No. They were shaken by great fears and trials. Consider the story of the People of the Ditch: were they shaken or not? Yes, they were shaken and tested. As He said, ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and believing women and then did not repent will have the punishment of Hell, and they will have the punishment of the Burning﴾ [al-Buruj 10]. So the shaking here is not the shaking of the earth, but the shaking of hearts through what occurs to them of fears, trials, doubts, and desires. This did happen to the believers, in the Battle of the Trench. Or not?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Recite the verse? ﴿There the believers were tested, and they were shaken with a severe shaking﴾ [al-Ahzab 11]. This also actually occurred. From this we know that His saying, ﴿Yet there has not come to you﴾, the correct view is to keep it on its apparent meaning.

﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: When is the help of Allah?﴾ There are two recitations of ﴿yaqula﴾: ﴿yaqulu﴾ and ﴿yaqula﴾. The recitation with *raf'* (*yaqulu*, nominative) is based on *hatta* being treated as not governing (*ilgha'*, cancelling its effect). The recitation with *nasb* (*yaqula*, accusative) is based on *hatta* governing it. It has already been discussed whether *hatta* governs by itself, or whether an implied *an* follows it, but it does not govern, and it governs only in the future. Or not?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Good. Here, ﴿until the Messenger says﴾: this saying was uttered by those who passed away before us, so how can it be in the accusative when they have already passed away? Pay attention: how can it be in the accusative? The grammarians (*mu'rabun*) said it is in the accusative by the narration of the state (*hikayat al-hal*, relating a situation as if it were present). If we consider the narration of a past state, then *yaqulu* becomes future relative to it. So is *yaqulu* future relative to the shaking, the adversity, and the hardship, or not future?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken, until he says﴾: it is future relative to what precedes it. But relative to us, it is not future, because it is past. However, considering the narration of the state, it becomes future. On this basis, we say that it is future relative to what precedes it, but the states that occurred are all past relative to us.

As for the recitation with *raf'*, ﴿hatta yaqulu﴾, it is based on the narration of a past state. What is the meaning of "based on the narration of a past state"? It means that Allah, the Exalted, is relating this to us as something that has already passed, that is, "so much so that the Messenger and those with him said," and so on. So there are two recitations in the verse: the accusative, and what else? The nominative. As for the accusative, it is based on the reckoning of the narration of a present state, as if it were a present situation now, so we say ﴿hatta yaqula﴾ with *nasb*. As for the second, it is based on the narration of a past state; that is, as if Allah is informing us of this saying.

His saying, ﴿until the Messenger says﴾: who is the Messenger?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is meant is the category (*jins*), that is, until the Messenger from among those who were shaken, afflicted, and touched by adversity and hardship says it.

His saying, ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾: *mata* is an interrogative particle, and it is used to express denial (*inkar*), remoteness (*istib'ad*), urging for haste (*istibta'*), and hope (*raja'*), and several other meanings. So here, is it for denial?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: No. For remoteness?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: No. Then for denial, what is an example? ﴿And they say: When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ [Yunus 48]. This is for denial. But this cannot be for denial, nor for remoteness. Why? They said: it is for urging for haste (*istibta'*), meaning they were slow to see the help come. They were not slow in its occurrence, as in (...) it will occur, but they wanted it hastened, like the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, at Badr: "O Allah, fulfil for me what You promised me" [Reported by Muslim (1763/58), from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him]. So they want it hastened; that is, they say: O our Lord, Your help has been slow to reach us, so hasten it for us. This shows the severity of what befell them, so much so that they say this supplication, the supplication of one distressed who seeks relief: When is the help? When is the help? When is the help? That is, they are in hardship and in urgent need of this help because of the severity of the matter that struck them.

﴿Until the Messenger and those who believed with him say﴾: is the phrase *ma'ahu* ("with him") connected to ﴿yaqulu﴾ or to ﴿amanu﴾?

* A student: ﴿Amanu﴾.

* The Shaykh: Until they say together with him, or "until the Messenger and those who believed with him"? If we say "says with him," then their saying is all together, as if they all say: When is the help of Allah? If we say "and those who believed with him," its meaning is that their faith was accompanied by their being with him, that is, they did not believe and then abandon him, but believed with him. This indicates that they are believers accompanying this Prophet. This does not mean that it is not understood that they say it; rather they do say it, because the conjunction ﴿and those who﴾ requires that the conjoined and the conjoined-to share in the ruling, which is the saying. But its connection to His saying ﴿amanu﴾ is closer than its connection to His saying ﴿yaqula﴾.

﴿And those who believed with him: when is the help of Allah?﴾ Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾. Where does this answer come from?

* A student: From Allah.

* The Shaykh: From Allah. That is, Allah says: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾. But is He saying this to those who said: When is the help of Allah? Or is Allah informing us now that the help of Allah is near? His informing us that the help of Allah is near is more emphatic, meaning that the matter reached ﴿adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken﴾ to this extent, even though ﴿the help of Allah is near﴾. I think we have already discussed this in Bukhari's *Tafsir*, and we said that some exegetes say that His saying ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ is part of the speech of the Messengers, and that the meaning is that ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him say: when is the help of Allah?﴾ is what the believers say, and the Messenger says ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾. But it has already been established that this view is far from correct, because it requires scattering the verse (...) its meaning. The correct view is that it is part of the speech of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and that the saying of the Messenger and the believers is ﴿When is the help of Allah?﴾.

(...) ﴿one community, so Allah sent the Prophets as bearers of good news and warners﴾.

* From this noble verse it is derived that the religion of Islam is the *fitrah* (innate nature); from His saying, ﴿Mankind was one community﴾. Before what would test them occurred, they were upon one religion, the religion of Islam.

* From this it is derived that there is wisdom in sending Messengers, which is giving good news and warning; from His saying, ﴿so Allah sent the Prophets as bearers of good news and warners﴾.

And from this it is derived that prophethood is not attained by acquisition, but is a bounty from Allah; from His saying, ﴿so Allah sent﴾. Al-Saffarini said in his creed:

*Prophethood's rank is not attained by effort, refinement, or chivalry,*
*but it is a bounty from the Lord, the Mighty, to whomever He wills among His creation, until the appointed term.*

The evidence for this is ﴿so Allah sent the Prophets﴾.

* From this noble verse it is derived that the most deserving description of "bearing good news" belongs only to the followers of the Messengers; from His saying, ﴿bearers of good news﴾. As for the Christians, may Allah destroy them, taking this description for their missionaries now, calling a person who preaches Christianity "a bearer of good news (*mubashshir*)," this is aggression and injustice on their part, and heedlessness and sleep on the part of the Muslims. Otherwise, the Muslims who follow the Messengers are the most deserving of people of this description. As for those others, the most fitting description for them is that we say they are missionaries (proselytisers) or misleaders.

* From the noble verse it is derived that the laws brought by the Messengers are divided into commands and prohibitions. From where are they taken?

* The students: ﴿bearers of good news and warners﴾.

* The Shaykh: How? Because warning is against falling into transgression, and good news is for those who comply and obey.

* From the noble verse it is derived that the Books are sent down from Allah; from His saying, ﴿and He sent down with them the Book﴾.

* From it is also derived the exaltedness of Allah, Glorified and Exalted; because if the Books are sent down from Him, it follows that He must be exalted, or not?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Because descending is from? From above to below.

* A student: The mercy of Allah toward His servants.

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* From the noble verse it is also derived that it is obligatory to return to the heavenly Books when there is dispute; from His saying, ﴿that He might judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾. Otherwise, the benefit of the revealed Books would be lost.

* From the verse it is also derived the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, toward His servants, in that He did not leave them to their own minds; for if they were left to their minds, the heavens and the earth would be corrupted, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿If the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Mu'minun 71]. Every person says: "The intellect is with me, and the right is with me." But Allah, the Exalted, sent the Prophets and sent down with them the Book, to judge between people concerning that over which they differed.

* From the noble verse it is derived that disagreement among people is inevitable; from His saying, ﴿between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾. Supporting this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has had mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together"﴾ [Hud 118–119], and His saying: ﴿He is the One who created you, and among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun 2]. Were it not for this, the world would not stand, nor would jihad stand, nor would enjoining good and forbidding evil stand, nor would the truthful be distinguished from the liar.

* From the noble verse it is derived that those who differed over the law had already been given the Book; from His saying, ﴿and those who differed concerning it were none but those who had been given it﴾.

* It follows from this benefit that the proof has been established against them; from His saying, ﴿except those who were given it﴾, and since they had been given the Book, it was obligatory upon them not to differ.

* From this noble verse is derived the refutation, or the showing of the weakness, of the hadith narrated from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: "The difference of my community is a mercy." [Al-'Iraqi said in his takhrij of the Ihya' (1/106): al-Bayhaqi mentioned it in his *Risalah al-Ash'ariyyah* without a chain, in this wording.] This hadith is not authentic from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and difference is not a mercy; for this reason He said: ﴿And they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has had mercy﴾. Yes, the inclusion of all of them under the pardon of Allah is a mercy, since Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not punish the one who erred. So those who differ are encompassed by mercy if they were striving (*mujtahidin*), because "whoever strives and is correct has two rewards, and whoever strives and errs has one reward" [Reported by Abu Dawud (3574) and Ibn Majah (2314), from the hadith of 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "If a judge judges and strives and is correct, he has two rewards; and if he judges and strives and errs, he has one reward."]. But as for our saying that the disagreement within the Ummah is a mercy, no.

* From the noble verse it is derived that those who differed and rejected the truth, their action is transgression and aggression; from His saying, ﴿out of insolence among themselves﴾. So the Jews who knew the truth and differed concerning the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: some of them believed in him and some disbelieved. Those who disbelieved, disbelieved out of insolence and aggression. Likewise, those to whom the Qur'an was sent down from Quraysh and others differed concerning it, and those who opposed it only opposed it out of insolence and aggression.

* From this it is derived that every opponent of the truth, after it has become clear to him, is a transgressor. Even if he says, "I do not want transgression and I do not want aggression," we say: you are a transgressor. When the truth has become clear to you, it is obligatory upon you to follow it and not oppose it; otherwise you are a transgressor.

On this occasion, I would like to point out that for whatever rulings are attached to a specific description, intention is not a condition. So if transgression occurs, it is transgression even if the doer did not intend it. If someone wears the clothing of Christians or the clothing of polytheists and says, "I did not intend to imitate them," what do we say to him? We say: imitation has occurred; the imitation itself has occurred, whether you intended it or not. For this reason, imitation does not require the intention of purpose, as long as the doer knows that this is one of their practices. But if he does not know, then once he knows, he must remove what he imitated.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse is the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, toward the believers; from His saying, ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed, by His permission﴾.

* Among its benefits: it is obligatory upon a person whom Allah has guided not to be conceited about himself, nor to think that this came from his own strength; from His saying, ﴿So Allah guided﴾, then He said, ﴿by His permission﴾ as well, by His cosmic and decreed command. Were it not for that, they would not have been guided, and they would have been like those people who rejected the truth out of insolence and aggression.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse is the indication that a person should ask for guidance from whom? From Allah; from His saying, ﴿So Allah guided those who believed﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 213–214 (part 6 of 6):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the more a servant's faith is strong, the closer he is to attaining the truth. From where is this taken? Because Allah tied guidance to faith with this description, so whenever a person's faith is stronger, he is closer to attaining the truth. ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾. For this reason the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) were closer to the truth than those after them, not in the interpretation of the Qur'an, nor in the rulings on the actions of the responsible persons, nor in matters of belief either. The Companions are the people closest to the truth, because the guidance to the truth was tied to faith, and there is no doubt that the Companions were the strongest of people in faith. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "The best of people are my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2652) and Muslim (2533/212), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him).]] For this reason Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) held that the statement of a Companion is a proof so long as it does not contradict the explicit text; if it contradicts the text, it is not a proof, or if another Companion contradicts it, then if another Companion contradicts it, one considers which of the two is closer to correctness by way of preference.
* And benefiting from this noble verse: the affirmation of the attribute of permission, by His saying ﴿by His permission﴾, meaning: by His command. What is the attribute of permission? The permission is ﴿by His permission﴾.
* And benefiting from it: the affirmation of Allah's voluntary actions, by His saying ﴿So He guided﴾ ﴿So Allah guided﴾, and likewise ﴿by His permission﴾.
* And benefiting from it: the refutation of the Qadariyya, by His saying ﴿So Allah guided﴾ and also ﴿by His permission﴾. Guidance is evident in their actions. So if that is from the action of Allah, it shows that Allah is the One who created their actions, and if it is by His permission, that indicates that Allah is the One who willed their actions. The Qadariyya say that the servant's action is never connected to Allah in any state; rather, he is the one who willed his action and he is the one who brought his action into existence independently of Allah, glorified and exalted is He.
* And benefiting from it: the refutation of the Jabriyya as well, by His saying ﴿concerning which they differed﴾, so to whom did He attribute the action? To them. The Jabriyya say: man has no action; man is compelled in his action. He is in his movements like the movement of the branches of a tree by the wind; he has no choice in them. Have you understood? You are now writing against your will; you are compelled to take the pen and write. If you stopped writing against your will... Now you place the tape in the recorder against your will. Now I am speaking to you against my will. This is the doctrine of the Jabriyya, and in reality it is madness.
And those who say that you speak and act without Allah's will or power, this too is a kind of madness. You are a creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; your attributes are created by Allah. Yes indeed.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's will: ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills﴾. The affirmation of will.
And I have a question: is will divided like volition?
* A student: Yes.
* Another student: It is not divided.
* The Shaykh: It is not divided, because will is one category: what Allah wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur, and it relates to what Allah loves and to what He does not love.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that everything other than the Sharia is a crooked path, ﴿to a straight path﴾.
* And it is also derived from it: that the Sharia has no narrowness, no crookedness, and no hardship, because it is a path that is broad and straight.
* And it is derived from it: the indication to the three paths mentioned by Allah the Exalted in Surat al-Fatiha, which are: the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, the path of those who have earned anger, and the path of those who are astray. Those upon whom Allah bestowed favour are the messengers and their followers; those who earned anger are the Jews and their like; and those who are astray are the Christians and their like.
This statement, namely that those who are astray are the Christians and their like, is said before the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent. As for when the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent and they denied him, they became among those who earned anger, of the category of the Jews; for the Jews were those who earned anger when Jesus came, so they denied him after they had known the truth. And after Jesus was sent and the Christians followed him, and time lengthened, they innovated what they innovated in religion, and went astray, so they became those who are astray. But when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent and they denied and rejected him, they became of the category of the Jews, among those who earned anger.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed away before you has not yet come to you?﴾ ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise﴾ to the end.
* Benefiting from this noble verse: the care of Allah the Mighty and Majestic for this Ummah, in that He consoles it with what befell others. Is that not so? Yes. And likewise, as it came in the Qur'an, it came in the Sunnah. The Messenger (ﷺ), when his Companions came to him complaining in Makkah, informed them that those before us had a saw placed upon their heads, and it would be used to comb between their flesh and bones, yet that would not turn them from their religion.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3612), from the hadith of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (may Allah be pleased with him).]] This was to firm up the believers.
* And benefiting from this noble verse: that faith is not by wishful thinking nor by adornment. You do not say, "I am a believer, so let me enter Paradise." No, there must be an affliction.
* And benefiting from this noble verse: the wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, in that He tests the believers with such great calamities, and for what purpose? As a trial, until it becomes clear: ﴿And We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and the patient, and We will test your reports﴾ [Muhammad 31].
I suppose we do not know the fakeness of gold except when we melt it in fire, do we? And we do not know the fragrance of oud except when we burn it in fire. Likewise, the sincere person is not known except through trial and affliction. So, my brother, hold fast to patience. You may be harmed for your religion, you may be mocked, perhaps pursued, perhaps watched. But be patient and sincere. Be patient and look at what befell the steadfast messengers, upon them be prayer and peace. The Messenger (ﷺ) was prostrating to Allah in the safest place on earth, prostrating, harming no one and nothing, in the safest place on earth, which is the Sacred Mosque. Then the tyrants of mankind came with harm and filth, the entrails of a she-camel, and placed them on him while he was prostrating, upon him be prayer and peace. This is a great matter; none bear it except those of resolve. It remained so until his young daughter Fatimah came and removed it from his back, while the people kept laughing and guffawing.[[Narrated by Muslim (1794/107), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him).]]
I believe that a person, psychologically, unless Allah protects and strengthens him, will grow weary and tired, and say: "Why does he do this to me?" At the very least he will hide his religion. But be patient, seek reward, and know that whatever the matter is, the utmost that can happen is death, and if you die upon patience for the sake of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, you have moved from one abode to a better one. ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he considers the trial of people as the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-Ankabut 10]. Do not be like that. Be patient and seek reward, and know that ﴿Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [an-Nahl 128], and that Allah is with the patient, and that you have people among your brothers who watch what happens to you; when you are patient, you encourage them and make them patient. And you know that the Ummah is individuals: if one individual is righteous, then one and one and one and one, become a community.
And what is this word? "Al-Rakiyya" is the well; if one of its pebbles falls out, it becomes unbalanced and everything falls.
The point is that Allah the Mighty and Majestic consoles the believers with such things, and informs them that He afflicted those before us: adversity, scarcity of wealth and great want, poverty, harm to their bodies; they were beaten, wounded, and perhaps killed, as the Children of Israel used to kill the prophets without right, and great fears came upon them and they were shaken.
And benefiting from this noble verse: that a person should not seek victory except from the One who is able to grant it, who is Allah; by His saying ﴿When will the help of Allah come?﴾ [al-Baqarah 214].
And benefiting from that: the virtue of following the messengers; by His saying ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him say﴾, they agree upon this statement that calls for victory: ﴿When will the help of Allah come?﴾
And benefiting from this verse: the completeness of the power of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; by His saying ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾
And benefiting from it: the wisdom of Allah, in that He withholds victory for a specific period of time even though it is near: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾
And benefiting from this noble verse: that patience upon affliction for the sake of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is among the causes of entering Paradise, because the meaning of the verse is: be patient until you enter Paradise.
And benefiting from this noble verse: the indication to what came in the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (6487) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and Muslim (2822/1) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, and the wording is his.]] Is it not so? Because these are hardships, but they are the path to Paradise.
And benefiting from the noble verse: that there is no arrival at perfection except after drinking the cup of patience, which is from His saying ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed away before you has not yet come to you?﴾ to the end.
And benefiting also from the noble verse: the affirmation of Paradise, by His saying ﴿that you would enter Paradise﴾. It has already been mentioned that the end of creation is one of two abodes with no third: either Paradise or Hellfire. Paradise is for the God-fearing, and Hellfire is for the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 215–218 (part 1 of 7):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾. Let us see: ﴿They ask you﴾ — is the sentence a verb, subject and object, or not? "Yas'aluna" (they ask) is a verb, "waw" is the subject, and "ka" (you) is the object. And the pronoun in His saying ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to whom? It refers to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

As for His saying ﴿what they should spend﴾: "ma" is an interrogative noun, and "dha" is a relative noun, and the clause ﴿they spend﴾ is the relative clause. On this basis we say: "ma" is an interrogative noun, a subject (mubtada'), and "dha" is a relative noun serving as its predicate (khabar), and "yunfiqun" (they spend) is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: "what they spend it."

This is if "dha" is not treated as redundant (mulgha). If it is treated as redundant, another parsing arises, which is to say: "madha" is an interrogative noun built on sukun in a position of accusative, as a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) of His saying ﴿they spend﴾, and ﴿yunfiqun﴾ is an imperfect verb, its subject is the "waw," and the object is what has preceded. Do you understand? The meaning does not differ between the two parsings.

The question they asked was: what is it that they spend, and what do they spend? Do they spend food, do they spend garments, do they spend dirhams, what do they spend? Is the question here about the one who spends, not about the one spent upon, or not? About the one who spends: about its kind, or about its quantity, or about both together?

* The students: About both.

* The Shaykh: Apparently it is about both together, about the kind and the quantity.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: whatever good you spend is for the parents﴾. This is the answer. ﴿Whatever you spend﴾: "ma" here is a relative pronoun, though if you wish you may make it conditional. ﴿Then it is for the parents﴾: if you make "ma" relative, then this is the predicate; if you make it conditional, then this is the answer of the condition.

﴿Whatever you spend of good, then it is for the parents﴾. It may appear to a person at first glance that Allah, glory be to Him, answered them about what they should spend it on, not about what they should spend, that is, on what they should spend it. He said: ﴿Whatever you spend of good, then it is for the parents﴾, because the reality of the matter is that the whole concern is that your spending should be in its proper place. So you should not be concerned with what you spend; be concerned with where you spend it, right? Some people spend on evil, some spend on something with neither good nor evil in it, and some spend on good.

﴿Then it is for the parents, the near relatives, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. I say: it may appear to a person at first glance that the answer does not correspond to the question, because the question was about what? ﴿What they should spend﴾, and the answer came: ﴿Then it is for the parents﴾. So is this from the style of the wise (uslub al-hakim), well known in rhetoric, where this answer in this form is an indication that they ought to have asked: on whom should they spend? That is how it appears. But upon reflection it becomes clear to you that Allah, mighty and majestic, answered the question with a corresponding answer and added to it, or went beyond it; for the answer to the question is understood from His saying ﴿whatever you spend of good﴾: of good. So what is it that is spent? Good. Since what is spent is good, it may be good in food, and it may be good in garments, and it may be good in bedding, and it may be good in dirhams. It varies, does it not? If you come to a person who is in dire need once, hungry, who will die if you do not feed him, and who is naked with no garments at all, then what is the good here? Garments or food? Food. It is known: begin with food first, it is better than garments. And if you come to a person who has not reached the level of necessity for food but is in need of clothing, because the weather is cold and he has only a thin garment, then what is the good at that time? In garments. Is it clear?

Thus Allah, mighty and majestic, has answered ﴿what they should spend﴾ by His saying ﴿whatever you spend of good﴾, and He added to the answer by mentioning the one spent upon in His saying ﴿then it is for the parents﴾.

You may say: is adding to the question a case of prolixity and lengthening? We say: if the addition is something the need calls for and the state of the questioner requires, then it is not prolixity or lengthening, but rather it is part of the complete answer. For this reason, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the water of the sea, "Can we perform ablution with it?", what did he say? He said: «It is pure in its water, and lawful is its dead animal»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (83) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Although he was not asked about carrion, nor was he asked about fish, he said: «Its water is pure and its dead animal is lawful», because the one who rides the sea needs that.

"The parents" means the mother and the father, and the grandmother and the grandfather; for the grandmother and grandfather, though they are not parents directly, are parents of your parents: they are the cause of your parents' existence, and your parents are the cause of your existence. So "the parents" includes the nearer and the more distant ancestors.

As for His saying ﴿and the near relatives﴾: "al-aqrabin" is the plural of "aqrab" (nearer), and it refers to whoever is closer than others to the one spending. A brother and a nephew: who is nearer? The brother. An uncle and a paternal cousin: who is nearer? The uncle. A nephew and an uncle: who is nearer? The nephew is nearer. For this reason the scholars agreed that if a nephew and an uncle come together in a question of inheritance shares, the nephew is given precedence, on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «What remains goes to the nearest male man»[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (6737) and Muslim (1615/3) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]], and the scholars agreed that the nephew has priority over the uncle.

Do those who are more distant than the nearest have a right? The answer: yes, since they are among the kin, but the nearer has priority over the more distant; otherwise, all have a right, and a person is rewarded for spending on all of them.

As for His saying ﴿then it is for the parents and the near relatives﴾: does it include children? Yes, it includes children. But the spending on children has been restricted by the Sunnah to justice, when the Prophet ﷺ said: «Fear Allah and be just among your children»[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2587) and Muslim (1623/13) from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]]. So it is not permissible to give the male and withhold from the female, or to give the female and withhold from the male, or to give one and withhold from the other.

﴿And the orphans﴾: "al-yatama" is the plural of "yatim," and who is the orphan? The scholars said: it is derived from "yutm," which is solitude, and what is meant by it is: one whose father has died before reaching maturity. That is, the young child whose father has died; this is the orphan. Allah has enjoined concern for him in many verses, as a restoration for what he has suffered of brokenness through the death of his father while still young. For this reason, when he reaches maturity and becomes independent, he is no longer an orphan.

As for His saying ﴿and the needy﴾: "al-masakin" is the plural of "miskin," and it is the destitute person who has no wealth. He was called "miskin" because poverty has made him still (askanahu) and humbled him; for this reason he is called "miskin." The "miskin" here includes the "faqir" (poor), because we have already mentioned several times that when "miskin" is mentioned alone, the "faqir" is included in it, and when "faqir" is mentioned alone, the "miskin" is included in it; and when the two are combined, the "faqir" is in greater need than the "miskin," so they are differentiated. You will find in the Qur'an that "faqir" may come alone and "miskin" may come alone, and "faqir" and "miskin" may come together. In His saying: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their wealth﴾ [al-Hashr 8], it includes the "masakin." In His saying: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nur 32], it includes the "masakin." In His saying: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah﴾ [Fatir 15], does it include?

* A student: All people, all people, even the rich.

* The Shaykh: All people, even the rich, for he is poor toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason I restricted it: ﴿You are the poor toward Allah﴾.

And in His saying: ﴿Then its expiation is feeding ten needy persons﴾ [al-Ma'idah 89], the "faqir" is included, and likewise here.

﴿And the wayfarer﴾: who is the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil)? The scholars said: he is the traveler whose journey has been cut off. He was called "son of the way": "al-sabil" is the road, and he was called its son because he is constant with it; and everything that constantly accompanies something is its son. For this reason it is said: "ibn al-ma'" (son of the water) for the water bird that constantly stays in it; a bird called "son of the water" because it constantly stays with it. Allah singled out the wayfarer because he is a stranger in his place, and may need something while no one knows of his need. For this reason, if anyone wishes to draw near to Allah through spending, he gives to the wayfarer. But do you give him if he asks, or do you give him even if he does not ask?

We say: this is in two ways. One: you know that he does not need it, such as when he is rich, and you know he is rich, and he is passing through this town as a traveler; there is no need for you to give him, and even if you gave him, he would see that as a deficiency in himself. Another: you know he is needy and bears the traces of need; you give him without doubt. A third: you doubt his situation. If you give him after he asks, you say: "Are you in need?" That is good; otherwise, there is no blame on you. And if you give him, thinking he is in need, then you are upon good.

He said: ﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾. This last sentence encompasses every good. They asked what they should spend for the sake of good, so Allah generalized: ﴿whatever good you do﴾, and "ma" here is conditional, and ﴿you do﴾ is the condition verb; for this reason the nun is dropped from it, and the sentence ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾ is the answer of the condition.

As for His saying ﴿of good﴾: "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining what?

* A student: For the one spending.

* The Shaykh: No, no.

* A student: For the spending.

* The students: It is an imperative of incitement (fi'l igra').

* The Shaykh: ﴿And whatever good you do﴾: "of good" explains "ma," because we have already mentioned several times that the relative is vague, and likewise conditional nouns are vague; so ﴿whatever you do of good﴾, "of good" explains "ma." For this reason, if you deleted "ma" and said: "Whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it," the sentence would be sound, right? The sentence is sound. So His saying ﴿of good﴾ explains "ma."

As for His saying ﴿and whatever good you do﴾, He did not say: "and whatever you spend of good," so that it would include spending, physical action, speech, and everything: everything you do of good, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.

As for His saying ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾: that is, of this good you do, whether little or much, Allah knows it, whether secret or public.

What is the benefit of the answer here together with the condition? If someone says: ﴿Whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾; what is the benefit of Allah informing us that He knows it? The benefit is that we know He must reward us for it, because Allah is just and does not wrong; so when we do good, Allah knows it, and He will... what? He will reward us for it.

Do not say: the answer does not correspond to the condition, since there is no benefit for us in Allah knowing it. We say: rather there is a benefit for us, which is that when we know Allah knows it, Allah the Exalted is just and does not waste it; rather, He must reward us for it.

And there is also a benefit in it, as will come, Allah willing, in the benefits: it is incitement and encouragement.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you..﴾

* A student: Shaykh (...) is this here come in the form of (...)?

* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾. The prepositional phrase in ﴿of it﴾ is attached to what?

* A student: To ﴿Knowing﴾.

* The Shaykh: To ﴿Knowing﴾, yes.

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you﴾. ﴿Prescribed﴾ means obligated; and "kataba" in origin means obligation, and from it is His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 183], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers as a decree of specified times﴾ [al-Nisa 103]. And the prescribing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is divided into two kinds: a legislative prescription (kitab shar'i) and a cosmic prescription (kitab kawni). The cosmic prescription must occur and cannot fail; the legislative prescription may be performed by the one on whom it is prescribed, or may not be performed. So ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 183]: people may fast and may not fast; ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾: they may fight and may not fight. But ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya 105] is this cosmic, divine decree, which must be. ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadilah 21]: prescribing of what? Cosmic; it must be.

So prescribing is then of two types: cosmic prescribing and legislative prescribing. The difference between them: in cosmic prescribing, the occurrence of what is prescribed is necessary, unlike legislative prescribing.

The second difference: cosmic prescribing relates to what Allah loves and what He does not love, whereas legislative prescribing is only in what Allah loves. It is not possible for Allah to prescribe on His servants what He does not love; rather everything He prescribes is beloved to Him.

As for His saying ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾: what kind of fighting is it? The fighting against the enemies of Allah, the disbelievers. And ﴿al-qital﴾ (fighting) is the verbal noun of "qatala," and this form generally does not come except between two parties: "qatala," "shara" and the like.

As for His saying ﴿and it is hateful to you﴾: the pronoun in ﴿and it﴾ refers to the fighting, not to the prescribing; for the Muslims do not dislike what Allah has prescribed upon them, but they dislike fighting according to human nature. There is a difference between our saying that we dislike what Allah has prescribed of fighting, and our saying that we dislike fighting. Disliking fighting is a natural matter, for a person dislikes fighting anyone among people and killing him, and thus becoming one who is killed.
