[Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (6912) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.] This is the general meaning. The specific meaning: that a person leaves his city and homeland for the sake of Allah and His Messenger, when that city or homeland does not let him practice his religion, so he emigrates in order to establish the religion of Allah, protecting his own religion and supporting the religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as in the authentic hadith: "Whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger, and whoever's emigration was for worldly gain he would obtain or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155) from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and the wording is al-Bukhari's.]

﴿Those who have believed﴾ and ﴿emigrated﴾: what is meant by emigration here encompasses both meanings, the general and the specific.

His saying ﴿and those who emigrated and strove﴾: observe. The relative pronoun was repeated after ﴿those who have believed﴾, He said ﴿and those who emigrated﴾, but in the case of striving He did not repeat it; He did not say "and those who strove." This is because emigration and jihad are deeds built upon iman, whereas iman is the root of roots; for this reason He mentioned it alone: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾. As for emigration and jihad, they are deeds branching from it.

His saying ﴿strove﴾: jihad is exerting effort for a sought-after matter. Juhd means capacity, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who find nothing but their effort [to give]﴾ [al-Tawbah 79], meaning except their capacity. It is predominantly used for exerting effort in fighting the enemies; this is the predominant sense. Otherwise, every arduous matter in which capacity is expended is jihad. For this reason, the jihad of the self is called jihad. The jihad of the self is jihad without doubt. But there is no authenticity to the report that the Prophet ﷺ, when he returned from Tabuk, said: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad," meaning the jihad of the self. This has no basis. Yet there is no doubt that the self requires striving.

As for jihad in its specific sense, it is exerting effort in fighting whom? In fighting the disbelievers. And it depends on what motivates it. If the motive is partisanship, zeal, bravery, or showing off, then it is not in the way of Allah. If the motive is that the word of Allah be supreme, then it is in the way of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said this when he was asked about a man who fights out of zeal, fights out of bravery, and fights to be seen in his position: "Which of these is in the way of Allah?" He said: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the way of Allah." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7458) and Muslim (1904/150) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]

Thus the meaning of His saying ﴿and strove in the way of Allah﴾ is defined. ﴿Strove﴾: its object is omitted for knowledge of it, i.e., strove against whom? Against the disbelievers or the enemies of Allah. ﴿In the way of Allah﴾: that the word of Allah be supreme.

Know that it is said: "fi kadha," "li-kadha," and "bi-kadha." For example, one says: "jahadtu li-Allah" (I strove for Allah), "jahadtu bi-Allah" (I strove with Allah), and "jahadtu fi Allah" (I strove in Allah). The lam in "li-Allah" indicates purpose, so it indicates sincerity. The ba' in "bi-Allah" is for seeking help, so it indicates that you did that seeking help from Allah. The fi is for location, so it indicates that that jihad is within the framework of Allah's law, which does not transgress its limits, as you say: "I prayed for Allah," and what else? "And by Allah," and "in Allah," meaning: you did not go out of His religion.

His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾: we mentioned not long ago that sabil means path, and that it is sometimes attributed to Allah and sometimes attributed to creation. Examples of attribution to Allah are many, as in this verse: ﴿in the way of Allah﴾. An example of its attribution to creation is His saying: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows other than the way of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa' 115], where ﴿sabil﴾ is attributed to ﴿al-mu'minin﴾. As for when you say "ibn al-sabil," the sabil is the mudaf ilayhi (the attributed-to term) and not the mudaf (the term attributed).

﴿And follows other than the way of the believers﴾: observe that the way of the believers is sometimes attributed to them. Its attribution to them is because they travel it; its attribution to Allah is because Allah is the One who legislated it and because it leads to Allah. It is attributed to Allah from two aspects.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾. The phrase ﴿Indeed, those who﴾ requires a predicate. Since ﴿alladhina﴾ is its subject, where is the predicate? ﴿Those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾: this predicate is the clause, because ﴿ula'ika﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿yarjuna﴾ is a clause serving as predicate of the second subject, and that clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. So we have two clauses: a major clause and a minor clause, and the minor clause contains two clauses: a major and a minor, is that not so? The major clause is ﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾ and its predicate, this major clause. The minor clause is ﴿Those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾: this is minor with respect to the first, and ﴿yarjuna﴾ is minor with respect to the second subject.

﴿Those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾: if someone asks, what is this structure? Why did He not say: "Indeed, those who believed and emigrated and strove in the way of Allah hope for the mercy of Allah"? We say: because the reference with a new subject indicates the elevation of their rank, especially since He used the demonstrative that indicates distance, ﴿ula'ika﴾. Furthermore, repetition of the subject makes the single clause like two clauses, as if He said: "Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah hope for the mercy of Allah; those hope for the mercy of Allah." So there is in this a honoring of their mention from two aspects:

First: the reference to them with what indicates elevation and exaltation.

Second: that repetition of the subject makes one clause like two clauses, so it becomes emphasis upon emphasis.

His saying ﴿those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾: the meaning of hope here is expectation (tama'). ﴿Hope for the mercy of Allah﴾: hope (raja') in the sense of seeking the attainment of what is near; this is hope. Wish (tamanni) is expectation of what is distant or unattainable. It is known that raja' is expectation of what is near, and it is not near except by doing what makes it near. These people did what makes mercy near to them: iman, hijrah, and jihad. If these do not hope for the mercy of Allah, who does? Iman, hijrah, and jihad. For this reason He said: ﴿Those hope﴾. These are the people of hope. But a negligent man with no hijrah, no jihad, and little deed, whose hope is what? They say: "Wishing is the capital of the bankrupt." The bankrupt, meaning those who have nothing; he wishes but has nothing. These are the people of hope. As for one who commits sins, and is warned and guided, and says "Allah's mercy is vast," this is not the place of hope. Hope must have its causes; good opinion of Allah must also have its causes.

So: ﴿they hope for the mercy of Allah﴾ on account of what they did; but nevertheless...

Allah did not say "those have the mercy of Allah," as in another verse. He said only ﴿hope for the mercy of Allah﴾, because they are not deceived by their deeds and do not rely upon them before Allah, but perform them while hoping, not that they are dependent on them and certain of their reward.

His saying ﴿Those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾: is the mercy here meant as His attribute, or is the mercy meant as what results from His mercy, which is the reward?
* Students: It allows both meanings.
* The Shaykh: It allows both meanings. It allows: "those hope that Allah will have mercy upon them." In that case, ﴿yarjuna﴾ is what, the attribute or the reward? The attribute: they hope that He will show them mercy. As for the possibility that it is the mercy of Allah, meaning what results from His mercy, the authentic hadith has established that Allah said regarding Paradise, indeed He said to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whom I will." So He made the created thing a mercy of His, because it is one of the effects of Allah's mercy. For this reason He said: "I show mercy through you" (arhamu bik), making it like an instrument. As for the mercy which is His attribute, that is something else. Thus the verse admits both meanings, and both are mutually entailing, because when Allah shows mercy to a servant, He admits him into where? Into His Paradise, which is His mercy.

He said: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. Consider this: Allah is Forgiving. Someone may ask: what is the purpose of mentioning Allah's name al-Ghafur (the Forgiving) here, given that these people performed righteous deeds?

The answer: the one who performs righteous deeds may still fall short in some respect. This is why, when we finish the prayer, having been conversing with Allah in it, what do we say first upon finishing? "Astaghfir Allah" (I seek Allah's forgiveness). A person is never free of shortcoming. Allah, the Exalted, also said, when mentioning the departure from 'Arafah: ﴿Then seek forgiveness from Allah﴾.

The point is that here He mentioned the name al-Ghafur, because even though these noble deeds are performed by a person, shortcoming may still occur from him. Therefore He said: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾. As for ﴿Merciful﴾, its relevance is clear, because all these deeds that they performed are among the effects of His mercy. For the one who does a righteous deed, Allah has three great blessings:

The first blessing: He made clear to him the righteous deed from the unrighteous deed. By what means did He make it clear? By what He revealed through revelation to His messengers. What do you think would be the case if people remained blind and did not know? This is a blessing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that Allah the Exalted sent messengers to you. Indeed, it is the greatest of blessings, that they explain it to you.

Second: another great blessing is that He guided you to it. Allah the Exalted led many nations astray from Islam. He led astray people who were stronger than you in purity and more resolute than you, He led them astray from Islam, while Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, guided you. This is a great blessing.

Third: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has ordained for the blessing He bestowed upon you, which is guidance, an abundant reward. Therefore all of this is part of the requirement of His mercy, the Exalted and Majestic. Yet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, who bestowed these blessings upon us, says: ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman 55:60]. Glory be to Allah! You are the one who does good to us, first and last, and then you say: "Is the reward of your good anything but that I do good to you?!" Is the reward of good (the deed) anything but good (the reward)? This indicates the perfection of Allah's mercy toward creation, that He bestows blessings and then thanks the one upon whom the blessing was bestowed. ﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insan 76:22]. Glory be to Allah, how great is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic! He bestows and rewards, He bestows guidance, indeed He bestows clarification, then guidance, then reward. Then He says: ﴿And your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insan 76:22]. Allah is greater! All of these are requirements of His mercy, may He be exalted. Faith, emigration, and striving in jihad, all of them are from the requirement of His mercy. Were it not for Allah's mercy, this would not have occurred for those who believed, emigrated, and struggled.

(...) ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire﴾ is an independent sentence. ﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾ is an independent sentence, a subject and predicate.

* Student: So there is no connection between them?
* The Shaykh: No, the connection means that this one is built only upon that one.
* Student: So there is no relationship?
* The Shaykh: No, grammatically, no.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting therein﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is the reference for the Companions in knowledge, as indicated by His words: ﴿They ask you﴾.
* And from its benefits: the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, does not know all the rulings; rather, he knows only what Allah has taught him. This is why Allah answered this question: ﴿Say: fighting therein is a grave matter﴾.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were concerned about any violation that occurred from them, and they would feel regret and ask about their situation regarding that violation, as indicated by His words: ﴿They ask you﴾, because they asked the Messenger after they had fought, when the disbelievers began to reproach them, and so they began to ask.
* And from the benefits of this noble verse: fighting in a sacred month is among the major sins, as indicated by His words: ﴿Say: fighting therein is a grave matter﴾. Scholars differed regarding this noble verse, whether it is abrogated (mansukh) or still in force (muhkam). The majority of scholars held that it is abrogated, and that fighting in the sacred months was forbidden and then abrogated. However, the second view is that the verse is muhkam, and that fighting in the sacred months is not permissible; rather it is forbidden. The evidence of those who say it is abrogated is His saying: ﴿And fight against the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:36], ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:73], and similar general texts indicating the obligation to fight the disbelievers. Among their proofs is that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, fought the Thaqif, and when? In Dhu al-Qa'dah, in the month of Muharram.
And among them: when was the Battle of Tabuk? In Muharram or in Rajab? In Rajab, which is a sacred month. But what appears to me is that fighting in the sacred months remains, and that the verse is muhkam. The evidence of those who say it is abrogated is answered by saying: general verses are like other general texts, which are specified (takhsis), are they not?
﴿Kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:5], ﴿Strive against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:73] is general, and it is specified by His saying: ﴿Say: fighting therein is a grave matter﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:217]. As for the fighting of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, it is answered that this was not initiated fighting, but rather defensive fighting, and defensive fighting is not a problem even in these sacred months, if they fight us, we fight them. The Thaqif had gathered against the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, so the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, went out to them to fight them. Likewise, the Byzantines gathered against him at the Battle of Tabuk, so he went out to them to defend against them. Therefore, the correct position on this issue is that the verse is muhkam, and that it is not permissible to initiate fighting against the disbelievers, but if they transgress against us, we fight them, even in the sacred month.
* And it is derived from the noble verse, ﴿about the sacred month﴾, that months are of two kinds: sacred months and non-sacred months. From this benefit it follows that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, specifies among His creation whomever He wills. There are sacred places and non-sacred places, sacred times and non-sacred times, is that not so? There are messengers and there is one to whom they are sent, there are the truthful (siddiqun), and there are those below them, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as He gives preference among human beings, also gives preference among times and places.
* And it is derived from the noble verse that sins are divided into two kinds: minor sins (saghair) and major sins (kaba'ir). Are the major sins all at one level and the minor sins all at one level? No, there are degrees. This is why the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about the greatest of the major sins; the greatest of the major sins. This shows that among the major sins there is one that is greater and one that is lesser than the greatest, otherwise they would all be simply major sins. Associating partners with Allah is the greatest of the major sins, and it is shirk that takes one out of the religion. Disobedience to parents is among the major sins, but it does not take one out of the religion. False testimony is among the major sins, but it does not take one out of the religion. Killing a soul is likewise. So major sins have degrees, and minor sins likewise. But what is the definition of a major sin?

The definition of major sins: people's opinions differed about it. Some said: the major sins are enumerable, and went about tracing every text in which the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said that this is a major sin, and listed them one by one. Others said: the major sins are bounded, and what does "bounded" mean? It means that they have a limit; they are not specifically this and this and this. No, they are bounded, with a limit, and a great deal falls within this limit. Then they differed about the limit: by what do we define major sins?

Some of them said: every sin whose doer is cursed is a major sin. Some said: every sin that has a prescribed penalty (hadd) in this world is a major sin. Others said: everything that carries a threat of punishment in the Hereafter is a major sin. However, Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said in some of his statements: a major sin is anything for which a specific punishment has been prescribed. Sins, when it is said: do not do such-and-such, or such-and-such is forbidden to you, or something similar, without making a specific punishment for that sin, are minor. But if a punishment has been prescribed for it, whatever punishment it is, then it is a major sin. So cheating, for example, is a major sin, or not?

* Students: A major sin.
* The Shaykh: Because a specific punishment has been prescribed for it, which is disassociation from the one who does it: "Whoever cheats is not one of us." [Narrated by Muslim (102/164) and al-Tirmidhi (1315), whose wording it is, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] Is that so? A person not loving for his brother what he loves for himself is a major sin, because a specific punishment has been prescribed for it: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (13) and Muslim (45/71), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.]

A person not honoring his neighbor is a major sin: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6019) and Muslim (48/77), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from Abu Shurayh, may Allah be pleased with him.] And his wronging his neighbor is even greater. This is why the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "By Allah, he does not believe, by Allah, he does not believe, by Allah, he does not believe." They said: "Who, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The one whose neighbor is not safe from his evil." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (6016) from Abu Shurayh, may Allah be pleased with him.] This definition is, in reality, a reasonable definition, because you cannot distinguish between what has a prescribed penalty in this world, such as adultery and theft, and what carries a threat in the Hereafter, or a negation of faith, or wrath, or curse, or something similar. Yet despite this, we do not say that these major sins are equal. Rather, among the major sins there are some that come close to being minor sins, according to the punishment prescribed for them. Those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger are not like those who merely steal. This is why the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger is ﴿that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:33]. And what Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said about the definition of a major sin is the closest and most consistent, meaning it is consistent (mutarrid).

* And it is derived from the noble verse that barring from the way of Allah is greater than fighting in the sacred months. From where is this taken? ﴿And hindering from the way of Allah﴾, until He said: ﴿is greater than killing﴾.
* Student: In the sight of Allah?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Finally: fitnah (persecution and discord) is greater than killing.

From this benefit it follows that one of the greatest sins is for a person to bar others from the truth. You may come across a person who, for instance, is devoted to worship and is a student of knowledge, and you say to him: "What do you want from this? What do you want from reading? What do you want from seeking knowledge?!" People have now advanced, he says: "We have reached the moon, we have reached space," and similar things. Is the one who does such a thing barring from the way of Allah? Yes, he is barring from the way of Allah. Whoever discourages from good is barring from the way of Allah. But this barring differs according to what it is barring from. Whoever bars from faith is committing the greatest thing, like what the polytheists of Quraysh did. Whoever bars from something lesser, like someone who bars from voluntary acts, is lighter. But there is no doubt that this is a wrong. Forbidding what is good is a wrong without doubt, and it is barring from the way of Allah.

* And from the benefits of the verse: is disbelief in Allah greater than killing in the sacred month, or not? Based on His saying: ﴿and disbelief in Him and the Sacred Mosque﴾, and so on to the end.
* And it is derived from the verse: the great gravity of barring from the Sacred Mosque. Is it derived from this that it is not permissible to prevent people from Hajj or not?
* It is derived from it that it is not permissible to prevent people from Hajj. But if the ruler says: "I do not prevent them, but I organize them," because people would kill one another if they all gathered together, would we say that this is among permissible administrative policy, like the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, preventing from jihad those who were not fit for it, or do we say there is consideration in this?
* Students: The first.
* Student: Like our saying, O Shaykh (...), our saying "organization" is permissible.
* The Shaykh: In any case, this matter, meaning, requires far-reaching consideration, and does the consideration of public interests (maslahah) for the general public override the consideration of interests for particular cases, or not?

﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾. Some benefits are derived: among its benefits is the eagerness of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, to ask about knowledge, since they asked the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Many questions were put to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, by the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, more than twelve times.

* And it is derived from it: that it is part of good answering that the one being asked adds to what the question requires, when there is need for it. From where is this taken?
From His saying: ﴿Say: whatever good you spend is for parents﴾. For they did not ask about whom to spend on; they only asked "what should they spend," and they were answered by stating whom to spend on. Were they answered regarding the question?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: Where?
* Student: ﴿of good﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿of good﴾, yes.
* And it is derived from the noble verse: the virtue of spending on parents and relatives, and that it takes precedence over the poor and needy. What is the reason? That Allah began with it: ﴿for parents and relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾, and one begins only with what is most important, then what is next in importance.
* And from the benefits of the noble verse: orphans have a right in spending even if they are wealthy. The reason: He singled them out, then followed them with His words: ﴿and the needy﴾. If they are orphans and needy, two entitlements are combined in them: orphanhood and need. And if they are relatives too? Relatives, orphans, and needy? Three entitlements. And if they are also wayfarers? Four? Can an orphan become a wayfarer?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: He may travel with him.
* And it is derived from the noble verse: the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah: ﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾.
* And it is also derived from it: that every good act, whether financial spending, a physical act, teaching knowledge, striving in the way of Allah, or otherwise, Allah, the Exalted, knows it, and will reward it, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do﴾. The phrase ﴿min khayr﴾ ("of good") is an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional, "whatever you do," so it is general. When is an indefinite noun general? When it is in the context of negation, or prohibition, or condition, or rhetorical interrogation, like His saying: ﴿Do you perceive any of them?﴾ [Maryam 19:98]. In these four contexts it is general. But in an affirmative statement, as when you say, "Strike a man," it is for generality in the sense of non-specificity (itlaq), not general (umum). What is the difference between non-specificity (itlaq) and generality ('umum)?
The difference: non-specificity has a distributive generality, while generality has an inclusive generality. A speech in a non-Arabic language. Is it clear?
* Student: In Arabic.
* The Shaykh: In Arabic, but not understood. I say: the difference between non-specificity and generality is: non-specificity has a distributive generality, while generality has an inclusive generality. Is it clear? The detail: its generality is distributive, meaning that it includes all individuals by way of substitution, one of them suffices for all. This is the meaning. Its generality is distributive, that it includes all individuals by way of substitution, that is, one of them suffices in place of all. As for the general (the 'amm), its generality is inclusive, meaning that it covers all individuals by specific designation, not by substitution. So if you say, for example: "Honor the students," it includes all of them, you must honor all of them. If you say: "Honor a student," one suffices, but not by specific designation, by substitution. Whether you honor the first one, the last one, or one in between, it suffices. Do you understand?
An indefinite noun in an affirmative context is for non-specificity, and in a negative context it is for generality. So if you say: "Free a slave," whichever slave you free suffices. If you say: "Do not free a slave," then you must not free any slave at all. Clear?

* And it is derived from the noble verse: that a person should not belittle any good. Because of His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, do not belittle any good. Do not say: "By Allah, this is a little, this is small, this is trivial." "Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date."[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7512) and Muslim (1016/67), from 'Adi ibn Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him.]

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you while it is hateful to you﴾, and so on to the end.

* It is derived from the noble verse: the obligation of jihad, because of His saying: ﴿has been prescribed﴾, meaning (made obligatory).

* It may be deduced from this noble verse that a person is not blamed for disliking something prescribed for him, not in terms of the Lawgiver having commanded it, but in terms of its nature, as Allah says: ﴿Fighting has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you﴾. However, in terms of the Lawgiver having commanded it, what is obligatory? The obligation is contentment and the opening of the chest toward it.

* It may be deduced from this noble verse that human beings do not know the unseen: ﴿Perhaps you dislike a thing while it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing while it is bad for you﴾.

* It may be deduced from the verse that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may decree upon His servant, whether by legislation or by creation, something he dislikes while it is good for him. A person may be struck by a calamity that turns out to be good for him. Suppose, for example, that you are traveling and your car breaks down. You dislike this, do you not? You dislike it. But it becomes clear that a few miles ahead there are highway robbers, and this breakdown has become good for you, though you did not know it. Allah may decree for a person something he dislikes, and it is good for him. Therefore, one should not dislike it.

* It may be deduced from the noble verse that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has comprehensive knowledge, as in His words: ﴿And Allah knows﴾. But from where do we derive the generality?

* Student: From the negative particle "lā", O Shaykh.

* Shaykh: No. How do we derive the generality?

* Student: From the present-tense verb.

* Shaykh: The present-tense verb does not indicate generality. The omission of the object indicates generality. This principle has passed us before: does the omission of the object indicate generality or not? ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And He found you lost and guided you? And He found you in need and made you self-sufficient﴾ [Ad-Duha 6–8]. All of these have omitted objects. (He sheltered you), and He sheltered through you as well. ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾: did He guide you, or did He guide through you also? He guided you and guided through you. ﴿And He found you in need and made you self-sufficient﴾: had He said "and made you self-sufficient" [with a direct object], we would not have learned that He enriched others through him as well. Rather, He enriched him and enriched others through him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: "Did I not find you astray and Allah guided you through me? And in need and Allah enriched you through me?" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4330) and Muslim (1061/139), from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Zayd (may Allah be pleased with him)]. So we derive the generality from His words: ﴿And Allah knows﴾. And what is the way of knowing that? The omission of the object. Yes, the omission of the object indicates generality.

* It may be deduced from the noble verse that human beings are weak, as in His words: ﴿And you do not know﴾. The default for a human being is ignorance. This is why Allah, exalted is He, said to His Messenger, reminding him of His favor: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know, and the bounty of Allah upon you has been great﴾ [An-Nisa 113]. Thus the default for a human being is that he does not know. ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing﴾ [An-Nahl 78].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is a great [sin]﴾, and so on to the end. From ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ we derive what preceded regarding the eagerness of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to ask and to learn. This is why it is said: the key to knowledge is asking.

* It may be deduced from the noble verse that fighting in the sacred months is prohibited. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿Say: fighting in it is a great [sin]﴾, meaning it is one of the major sins. The sacred months are four, and I think they are known to you.

* It may be deduced from the noble verse that what indicates causation is given precedence, in His words: ﴿about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾. The thing asked about is fighting in the sacred month, but He mentioned the month first because it is the cause of the prohibition of fighting. That is, what is the matter with fighting in it?

* It may be deduced from the noble verse that the Messenger (ﷺ) does not know any of Allah's rulings except what Allah has taught him.

* Student: "They ask."

* Shaykh: No. The answer. From Allah's answer to him: ﴿Say: fighting in it is a great [sin]﴾. Is it so? This is based on the question of whether the Prophet (ﷺ) was permitted to exercise ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) or not. The answer: Yes, he was permitted to exercise ijtihad. Then, if he exercised ijtihad and Allah approved it, his ijtihad takes the status of revelation, just as when the Prophet approved something a Companion did, that Companion's act takes the status of Sunnah (the prophetic example). Do you understand? If Allah does not approve it, it becomes clear that the ijtihad was not correct, as in His words: ﴿Allah pardon you! Why did you give them permission until it became clear to you who were truthful and you knew the liars?﴾ [At-Tawbah 43].

* Student: O Shaykh, how do we reconcile this with His words: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ [An-Najm 3]?

* Shaykh: Yes. Most exegetes hold that what is meant in ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾ is the Qur'an: ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾. That is, the Qur'an is revelation from Allah.

* Student: O Shaykh, the Christian's action... the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it. Is this the principle?

* Shaykh: No. We have mentioned that the Prophet's approval of a thing does not necessarily mean it is a legislated Sunnah; it means it is permissible. The Prophet approved it, meaning it is not forbidden, but it is not a Sunnah. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) did not do it. We also mentioned some parallel examples. Do you remember any of them?

* Student: Like giving charity on behalf of the dead (...).

* Shaykh: This is permissible but not prescribed. It is not legislated for every person whose dead relative has passed to give charity on his behalf.

* It may be deduced from the noble verse that sins vary. From where? ﴿Say: fighting in it is a great [sin]﴾. This first indicates that sins vary. And from the variation of sins it follows that faith varies, because the greater the sin, the greater the deficiency of faith through it. Thus there is a refutation of those who denied that faith increases and decreases. Regarding this, the scholars hold three opinions. Some said: faith neither increases nor decreases. Some said: faith increases and decreases. Some said: faith increases and does not decrease. Those who said it neither increases nor decreases are two groups: the Murji'ah, and the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij. Why did the Murji'ah say it neither increases nor decreases? They said: because faith is affirmation in the heart, and affirmation in the heart neither increases nor decreases; because actions, in their view, are not included in the definition of faith. The Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij said: faith is affirmation in the heart, utterance with the tongue, and action with the limbs. If any one of these three is lost, all of them are lost. So according to this, it neither increases nor decreases. Either all of it remains, or all of it is gone. Is it clear?

Some scholars said: faith increases and does not decrease, because Allah explicitly stated in the Qur'an that it increases: ﴿And that those who believe may increase in faith﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 31]. But nowhere in the Qur'an is it stated that faith decreases. Do you understand? The correct view is that it increases and decreases, and that it increases and decreases in terms of the heart's belief, the tongue's utterance, and the limbs' action. Even in terms of the heart's belief it increases and decreases. Did not Abraham (peace be upon him) say: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Have you not believed? He said: Yes, but that my heart may be at ease﴾ [Al-Baqarah 260]? Does it increase or not? It increases. Now, when a trustworthy man informs you that so-and-so has come to town, you believe him. If another comes, does your belief increase or not? It increases. If a third comes, it increases. If a fourth comes, it increases. When it reaches the level of tawatur (mass transmission), knowledge is established. So belief in the heart increases. A person himself may, at certain times and in certain hours, find in his heart a firm faith, as if he were witnessing the Throne, as if he were seeing Allah, exalted is He, as the Messenger said: "[It is] that you worship Allah as if you see Him" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him)]. At other times he becomes heedless and his faith completely or largely declines. As for the increase of faith through the utterances of the tongue, speak of it without blame. The one who glorifies Allah a hundred times is not like the one who glorifies Him ten times. Which is greater? A hundred times. And just as it varies in quantity, it also varies in quality. Worship built on sincerity and complete adherence to the Sunnah is not like worship lacking in sincerity and complete adherence. Likewise with the limbs: the action of the limbs varies. The one who prays four units is not like the one who prays eight units. Is it clear? So, does it increase or not? It increases by belief, by speech, and by action. As for those who said it increases and does not decrease, we say to them: Subhan Allah! We refute them in two ways.

First: The Prophet affirmed deficiency when he said: "I have not seen anyone more deficient in intellect and religion, who takes away the intellect of a prudent man, than one of you women" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (304) and Muslim (80/132), and the wording is al-Bukhari's, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him)].

Second: We say that if increase is established, decrease is necessarily established. What does "this is more than that" mean, except that the second is lacking compared to the first? They are mutually implied: whenever increase is established, decrease is established; and whenever decrease is established, increase is negated. Is it clear?

So the correct view, then, is that faith increases and decreases in terms of the heart's affirmation, the tongue's utterance, and the limbs' action. This is an established matter, known by necessity from the variation of major sins or sins in general, and from the variation of righteous deeds as well, for the variation of deeds entails the variation of the doer.

* Student: O Shaykh, is it correct to say: the scholars among the Khawarij and the Mu'tazilah? Do we call them "scholars"?

* Shaykh: Yes, "scholars." Yes, what?

* Student: They are misguided, O Shaykh.

* Shaykh: Scholars. But whether we say they are misguided or not, that is a separate matter. We say they are scholars. They are scholars of the religion. Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, says in al-Hamawiyyah: "The people of the qiblah (those who face the Ka'bah in prayer) divided, in matters of the divine attributes, into six sects." He counted among them the Jahmiyyah and the Mu'attilah, because they claim to be Muslims and are counted among the Islamic sects, though they oppose the truth.

* Student: Do they disbelieve?

* Shaykh: There is no doubt that some innovations amount to disbelief. But as for the specific individual, no. That requires that the proof be established against him.

* Student: O Shaykh, there is someone who says about (...): the faith of the angels neither increases nor decreases, the faith of the prophets increases and does not decrease, and the faith of ordinary people increases and decreases?

* Shaykh: This is an error. We say: faith, as faith, increases and decreases, regardless of the one who is characterized by it. The prophets (peace be upon them) may do some things by which they wrong themselves. Here is Adam, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said of him: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray. Then his Lord chose him﴾ [Ta-Ha 121–122]. And here is Moses, who killed a soul without right, and many other things. But they returned to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, repented, and after their repentance they became better than they were before it.

* Student: So his statement is wrong?

* Shaykh: Yes, wrong.

* Student: What about the angels, O our Shaykh? Do they do pure good?

* Shaykh: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [At-Tahrim 6]. Yes. We cannot say anything about it. We say nothing.

* Student: We refrain from it?

* Shaykh: We refrain from it. We do not say anything. We say: faith, as faith, increases and decreases. As for the believer himself, some people are blessed by Allah and always increase in their faith and righteous deeds, while some people, on the contrary, are always in decline.

* Student: So the views are three? That it increases and decreases?

* Shaykh: There are three views: it increases and decreases; it neither increases nor decreases; it increases and does not decrease.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, is among the Murji'ah, but he includes speech within the definition of faith. He includes it.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the gravity of barring people from the way of Allah, as in His words: ﴿And hindering from the way of Allah﴾, and so on to the end. Barring from the way of Allah has many and varied forms, which cannot be enumerated. It may be by preventing people from performing acts of worship. It may be by occupying and distracting them from performing acts of worship. It may be by belittling acts of worship in their own souls. It may be by casting doubts into people's hearts until they doubt their religion and abandon it. The point is that the ways of barring people from Allah's religion are innumerable and very many.

* It may be deduced from the noble verse: Is disbelief in Allah greater than fighting in the sacred month, or not? It may be deduced from this that barring people from al-Masjid al-Haram is greater than fighting in the sacred month, from His words: ﴿And al-Masjid al-Haram﴾.

* It may also be deduced from the noble verse that expelling the people of Makkah from it is greater than fighting in the sacred month.

* It may be deduced from the noble verse that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, consoles the believers with what the disbelievers did in response to the believers' action of fighting in the sacred month. This is consolation. From where is it taken? (...) Who is characterized by it? The polytheists who criticized the Muslims for killing that man in the sacred month. That is, "If you did this, they did something greater." There are four matters, each one greater than this.

* It may be deduced from this noble verse that whoever is more diligent in obedience to Allah has more right to al-Masjid al-Haram, as seen in His words: ﴿Its expulsion of its people﴾. Although the polytheists were residing in Makkah, they were not its rightful people, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said in Surah al-Anfal: ﴿And they were not its guardians. Its guardians are only the righteous﴾ [Al-Anfal 34].

* It may be deduced from this that fitnah (trial, persecution, and turning people from faith) is greater than killing. Fitnah is greater than killing. And what is fitnah? Shirk. Shirk is greater. We said earlier that it includes shirk, and it also includes turning people away from their religion through various kinds of doubts or various kinds of desires.

* It may be deduced from it: a warning against fitnah, as in His words: ﴿And fitnah is greater than killing﴾. If it is greater, then the obligation is to be cautious of it. Many people go to places of fitnah believing they will not be tested by it, but matters keep on until they fall into it. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said regarding the Dajjal: "Whoever hears of him should keep away from him, for by Allah, a man may come to him thinking he is a believer, and he follows him because of the doubts he brings." Or "because of the doubts he brings." [Abu Dawud (4319), from the hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "Whoever hears of the Dajjal, let him keep away from him, for by Allah, a man may come to him thinking he is a believer, and so he follows him, because of the doubts he brings." This is the hadith, or its meaning.] The point is that a person should not expose himself to trials. How many people have fallen into places of trial while thinking they would escape, and then they did not escape. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like a shepherd who grazes around the sanctuary, close to falling into it" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107), with his wording, from the hadith of al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir (may Allah be pleased with him)].

* It may be deduced from the noble verse: the eagerness of the polytheists to make the believers apostatize, as in His words: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion﴾. To this extent: to fighting, in order to turn us back from our religion. And if apostasy occurs without fighting?

* Student: I would love that for them.

Shaykh: "Do they like it?" Liking it is known: if it happens that Muslims apostatize without fighting, that is what they love more. For this reason, the intellectual invasion and the moral invasion are greater than the military invasion, aren't they? Because this enters the Ummah without it being aware, whereas that is an armed clash that people naturally recoil from; they cannot fight anyone. But this, may Allah protect us, is a deadly weapon, and so how much has it corrupted the Ummah! The root of the trials that occurred in the Islamic Ummah stems from things like this: the innovation of the Rafidah, the innovation of the Khawarij, and what is similar to that. And what are their causes? It is this: they corrupt thought until they bring people into fighting.

From the benefits of this noble verse: caution against the disbelievers, based on His saying: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion﴾. And the word "lā yazālūn" (they will not cease), I think we all understand, indicates continuity, and that it is not confined to a particular time: they will not cease doing this until they turn you back from your religion.

It is derived from the noble verse: despairing the disbelievers of turning all the believers away from the religion, in His saying: ﴿if they are able﴾. But they will not be able, until the command of Allah comes, and at the end of time a wind will blow that seizes the soul of every believer, so that none remain except the most wicked of creation.

It is derived from the noble verse: that apostasy nullifies deeds, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾.

It is also derived from it: that it nullifies the deed only if one dies in disbelief, based on His saying: ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾. Accordingly, we say: if someone apostatized, may Allah protect us, apostatized from Islam, began not to pray, abandoned prayer entirely, then Allah guided him and he returned to Islam and began to pray, do his previous deeds return or are they lost? They return, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made it a condition that he die upon his disbelief. Now, if he was a Companion (ṣaḥābī), does his companionship return? Yes, according to the more correct view, as Ibn Hajar said, according to the more correct view, it returns. Now, if he had performed Hajj, then returned to disbelief, then returned to Islam, is he obligated to perform Hajj again? No, the first Hajj suffices.

It is derived from the noble verse: that the apostate is eternally in the Fire, based on His saying: ﴿their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾.

It is derived from the noble verse: that the apostate is not treated in this world by the rulings applicable to believers, based on His saying: ﴿their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾. So he is not washed, not shrouded, not prayed over, and not buried with the Muslims. And does he inherit and is he inherited from? Is there a difference of opinion? As for his not inheriting, the apparent position is that this is by consensus, though I am not certain, but it is apparent. As for his being inherited from, Shaykh al-Islam chose that his Muslim relatives inherit from him. But the correct view is that there is no inheritance, due to the general statement of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in the hadith of Usama: «A Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, nor does a disbeliever inherit from a Muslim»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6764), and Muslim (1614/1) from the hadith of Usama ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. A man has millions in dirhams, hundreds of properties, thousands of cars, but he does not pray and dies, and he has children and wives; we say: this wealth is not yours, the wealth goes to the public treasury (bayt al-māl). This is very difficult, but nevertheless it has great benefit, because some people may be moved by imagining that their children will be left destitute after them, and they will have no entitlement to his wealth beyond what they receive from the public treasury. Perhaps this matter moves him to return to Islam and repent, and if he returns to Islam and repents, Allah accepts his repentance and he becomes an heir.

Student: Likewise, it moves his family to (...).

Shaykh: And it also moves his family to press him strongly in advice.

It is derived from the noble verse: that apostasy nullifies the deed whoever that apostate may be, whether from the Companions, or the Successors, or those after them, based on His saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts﴾, and the address first includes the Companions: ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless﴾. And one of them did apostatize during the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, such as Abdullah ibn Khatal. He embraced Islam, then apostatized, may Allah protect us, and went back to Mecca, and took slave-girls who would sing, mocking the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. For this reason, when the conquest of Mecca came, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «Whoever enters the Masjid is safe, and whoever enters his house is safe, and whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe»[[Abu Dawud (3022) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. They came to him and said: O Messenger of Allah, Abdullah ibn Khatal is clinging to the curtains of the Kaaba inside the Masjid, or outside? Inside the Masjid, clinging to the curtains of the Kaaba. He said: «Kill him, kill him»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1846) and Muslim (1357/450) from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. So he was killed, even though he was in the most secure place on the face of the earth, and even though the Messenger had said: "Whoever enters the Masjid is safe," yet he said: "Kill him." The scholars said: because disbelief, may Allah protect us, is grave; for he had reviled the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, through those slave-girls who would sing disparaging the Messenger ﷺ.

Student: So this "man" (man) — whoever enters his house is safe?

Shaykh: This is general.

Student: Does it not include him?

Shaykh: Except; but it is permissible to specify a general statement. This involves specifying the general; that is, Abdullah ibn Khatal was excluded by the hadith.

Student: And expelling his family from it is greater, so what prompted them to exile the adulterer?

Shaykh: No, this is lawful; exiling the adulterer is lawful.

Student: O Shaykh, I say: this story of Ibn Khatal does not support the words of Shaykh al-Islam, that is, he says: whoever reviles the Messenger must be killed?

Shaykh: Yes, it is cited as evidence for it.

Student: But Ibn Khatal?

Shaykh: Yes, but he was not killed; he repented and remained.

Student: Does shirk not nullify the deed?

Shaykh: Shirk, if one dies, if one dies in disbelief, his deed is nullified.

Student: The sorcerer who is on Hajj, they say his Hajj is nullified; do you agree with this sorcerer?

Shaykh: Who says?

Student: They say his Hajj is nullified.

Shaykh: No. If he believes he knows the unseen, he becomes a disbeliever, because none knows the unseen except Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And if he disbelieves and dies in his disbelief, [it is nullified]; and if he repents, Allah accepts his repentance.

Student: If the pilgrim is a polytheist, does his Hajj not need to be repeated?

Shaykh: How, if he is a polytheist, and what color?

Student: He apostatized, I mean..

Shaykh: If he apostatized after Hajj, then returned to Islam, he does not repeat the Hajj.

Student: If he performed Hajj and then embraced Islam?

Shaykh: Then embraced Islam.

Student: Then embraced Islam, meaning he performed Hajj, I mean the Hajj?

Shaykh: It does not nullify the Hajj, no, it does not nullify it. That is, if he apostatized after Hajj, we say: if he did not die in disbelief, then it is valid; that is, his deed is not nullified.

Student: Shaykh, regarding his words: «Whoever goes to a soothsayer or a fortune-teller and believes what he says»[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (9536) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him.]], does it say: his prayer is not accepted for forty days?

Shaykh: That one, he asked him; merely asking him, his prayer is not accepted for forty days.

Student: If he performs Hajj within those forty days, is it accepted or not?

Shaykh: It is accepted, it is accepted.

Student: And the prayer is not accepted?

Shaykh: No, the prayer is accepted, but the meaning of "not accepted" is not that the obligation is not discharged by it; the obligation is discharged by it. Rather, its meaning is that his evil deed cancels the reward of the prayer, so it is as though he had not prayed; by consensus his prayer is valid.

﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the cause of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah﴾.

It is derived from the noble verse: the virtue of faith and emigration, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the cause of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 218].

It is also derived from it: that jihad is of a rank below emigration. From where is this taken?

Students: From the order.

Shaykh: Because He said: ﴿those who believed and those who emigrated and strove﴾, so He made jihad coordinated (ma'tūf) upon emigration, and did not give it a separate independent relative clause.

It is derived from this: observing sincerity in emigration and jihad, based on His saying: ﴿in the cause of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah﴾. As for without sincerity, his emigration is to what he emigrated to.

It is derived from the noble verse: that a person should not be certain that his deed is accepted, but rather should be hopeful, yet his hope should lead him to a good opinion of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 215–218 (part 1 of 7):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾. Let us see: ﴿They ask you﴾ — is the sentence a verb, subject and object, or not? "Yas'aluna" (they ask) is a verb, "waw" is the subject, and "ka" (you) is the object. And the pronoun in His saying ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to whom? It refers to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

As for His saying ﴿what they should spend﴾: "ma" is an interrogative noun, and "dha" is a relative noun, and the clause ﴿they spend﴾ is the relative clause. On this basis we say: "ma" is an interrogative noun, a subject (mubtada'), and "dha" is a relative noun serving as its predicate (khabar), and "yunfiqun" (they spend) is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: "what they spend it."

This is if "dha" is not treated as redundant (mulgha). If it is treated as redundant, another parsing arises, which is to say: "madha" is an interrogative noun built on sukun in a position of accusative, as a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) of His saying ﴿they spend﴾, and ﴿yunfiqun﴾ is an imperfect verb, its subject is the "waw," and the object is what has preceded. Do you understand? The meaning does not differ between the two parsings.

The question they asked was: what is it that they spend, and what do they spend? Do they spend food, do they spend garments, do they spend dirhams, what do they spend? Is the question here about the one who spends, not about the one spent upon, or not? About the one who spends: about its kind, or about its quantity, or about both together?

* The students: About both.

* The Shaykh: Apparently it is about both together, about the kind and the quantity.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: whatever good you spend is for the parents﴾. This is the answer. ﴿Whatever you spend﴾: "ma" here is a relative pronoun, though if you wish you may make it conditional. ﴿Then it is for the parents﴾: if you make "ma" relative, then this is the predicate; if you make it conditional, then this is the answer of the condition.

﴿Whatever you spend of good, then it is for the parents﴾. It may appear to a person at first glance that Allah, glory be to Him, answered them about what they should spend it on, not about what they should spend, that is, on what they should spend it. He said: ﴿Whatever you spend of good, then it is for the parents﴾, because the reality of the matter is that the whole concern is that your spending should be in its proper place. So you should not be concerned with what you spend; be concerned with where you spend it, right? Some people spend on evil, some spend on something with neither good nor evil in it, and some spend on good.

﴿Then it is for the parents, the near relatives, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. I say: it may appear to a person at first glance that the answer does not correspond to the question, because the question was about what? ﴿What they should spend﴾, and the answer came: ﴿Then it is for the parents﴾. So is this from the style of the wise (uslub al-hakim), well known in rhetoric, where this answer in this form is an indication that they ought to have asked: on whom should they spend? That is how it appears. But upon reflection it becomes clear to you that Allah, mighty and majestic, answered the question with a corresponding answer and added to it, or went beyond it; for the answer to the question is understood from His saying ﴿whatever you spend of good﴾: of good. So what is it that is spent? Good. Since what is spent is good, it may be good in food, and it may be good in garments, and it may be good in bedding, and it may be good in dirhams. It varies, does it not? If you come to a person who is in dire need once, hungry, who will die if you do not feed him, and who is naked with no garments at all, then what is the good here? Garments or food? Food. It is known: begin with food first, it is better than garments. And if you come to a person who has not reached the level of necessity for food but is in need of clothing, because the weather is cold and he has only a thin garment, then what is the good at that time? In garments. Is it clear?

Thus Allah, mighty and majestic, has answered ﴿what they should spend﴾ by His saying ﴿whatever you spend of good﴾, and He added to the answer by mentioning the one spent upon in His saying ﴿then it is for the parents﴾.

You may say: is adding to the question a case of prolixity and lengthening? We say: if the addition is something the need calls for and the state of the questioner requires, then it is not prolixity or lengthening, but rather it is part of the complete answer. For this reason, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the water of the sea, "Can we perform ablution with it?", what did he say? He said: «It is pure in its water, and lawful is its dead animal»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (83) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Although he was not asked about carrion, nor was he asked about fish, he said: «Its water is pure and its dead animal is lawful», because the one who rides the sea needs that.

"The parents" means the mother and the father, and the grandmother and the grandfather; for the grandmother and grandfather, though they are not parents directly, are parents of your parents: they are the cause of your parents' existence, and your parents are the cause of your existence. So "the parents" includes the nearer and the more distant ancestors.

As for His saying ﴿and the near relatives﴾: "al-aqrabin" is the plural of "aqrab" (nearer), and it refers to whoever is closer than others to the one spending. A brother and a nephew: who is nearer? The brother. An uncle and a paternal cousin: who is nearer? The uncle. A nephew and an uncle: who is nearer? The nephew is nearer. For this reason the scholars agreed that if a nephew and an uncle come together in a question of inheritance shares, the nephew is given precedence, on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «What remains goes to the nearest male man»[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (6737) and Muslim (1615/3) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]], and the scholars agreed that the nephew has priority over the uncle.

Do those who are more distant than the nearest have a right? The answer: yes, since they are among the kin, but the nearer has priority over the more distant; otherwise, all have a right, and a person is rewarded for spending on all of them.

As for His saying ﴿then it is for the parents and the near relatives﴾: does it include children? Yes, it includes children. But the spending on children has been restricted by the Sunnah to justice, when the Prophet ﷺ said: «Fear Allah and be just among your children»[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2587) and Muslim (1623/13) from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.]]. So it is not permissible to give the male and withhold from the female, or to give the female and withhold from the male, or to give one and withhold from the other.

﴿And the orphans﴾: "al-yatama" is the plural of "yatim," and who is the orphan? The scholars said: it is derived from "yutm," which is solitude, and what is meant by it is: one whose father has died before reaching maturity. That is, the young child whose father has died; this is the orphan. Allah has enjoined concern for him in many verses, as a restoration for what he has suffered of brokenness through the death of his father while still young. For this reason, when he reaches maturity and becomes independent, he is no longer an orphan.

As for His saying ﴿and the needy﴾: "al-masakin" is the plural of "miskin," and it is the destitute person who has no wealth. He was called "miskin" because poverty has made him still (askanahu) and humbled him; for this reason he is called "miskin." The "miskin" here includes the "faqir" (poor), because we have already mentioned several times that when "miskin" is mentioned alone, the "faqir" is included in it, and when "faqir" is mentioned alone, the "miskin" is included in it; and when the two are combined, the "faqir" is in greater need than the "miskin," so they are differentiated. You will find in the Qur'an that "faqir" may come alone and "miskin" may come alone, and "faqir" and "miskin" may come together. In His saying: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their wealth﴾ [al-Hashr 8], it includes the "masakin." In His saying: ﴿If they are poor, Allah will enrich them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nur 32], it includes the "masakin." In His saying: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah﴾ [Fatir 15], does it include?

* A student: All people, all people, even the rich.

* The Shaykh: All people, even the rich, for he is poor toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason I restricted it: ﴿You are the poor toward Allah﴾.

And in His saying: ﴿Then its expiation is feeding ten needy persons﴾ [al-Ma'idah 89], the "faqir" is included, and likewise here.

﴿And the wayfarer﴾: who is the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil)? The scholars said: he is the traveler whose journey has been cut off. He was called "son of the way": "al-sabil" is the road, and he was called its son because he is constant with it; and everything that constantly accompanies something is its son. For this reason it is said: "ibn al-ma'" (son of the water) for the water bird that constantly stays in it; a bird called "son of the water" because it constantly stays with it. Allah singled out the wayfarer because he is a stranger in his place, and may need something while no one knows of his need. For this reason, if anyone wishes to draw near to Allah through spending, he gives to the wayfarer. But do you give him if he asks, or do you give him even if he does not ask?

We say: this is in two ways. One: you know that he does not need it, such as when he is rich, and you know he is rich, and he is passing through this town as a traveler; there is no need for you to give him, and even if you gave him, he would see that as a deficiency in himself. Another: you know he is needy and bears the traces of need; you give him without doubt. A third: you doubt his situation. If you give him after he asks, you say: "Are you in need?" That is good; otherwise, there is no blame on you. And if you give him, thinking he is in need, then you are upon good.

He said: ﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾. This last sentence encompasses every good. They asked what they should spend for the sake of good, so Allah generalized: ﴿whatever good you do﴾, and "ma" here is conditional, and ﴿you do﴾ is the condition verb; for this reason the nun is dropped from it, and the sentence ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾ is the answer of the condition.

As for His saying ﴿of good﴾: "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining what?

* A student: For the one spending.

* The Shaykh: No, no.

* A student: For the spending.

* The students: It is an imperative of incitement (fi'l igra').

* The Shaykh: ﴿And whatever good you do﴾: "of good" explains "ma," because we have already mentioned several times that the relative is vague, and likewise conditional nouns are vague; so ﴿whatever you do of good﴾, "of good" explains "ma." For this reason, if you deleted "ma" and said: "Whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it," the sentence would be sound, right? The sentence is sound. So His saying ﴿of good﴾ explains "ma."

As for His saying ﴿and whatever good you do﴾, He did not say: "and whatever you spend of good," so that it would include spending, physical action, speech, and everything: everything you do of good, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.

As for His saying ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾: that is, of this good you do, whether little or much, Allah knows it, whether secret or public.

What is the benefit of the answer here together with the condition? If someone says: ﴿Whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾; what is the benefit of Allah informing us that He knows it? The benefit is that we know He must reward us for it, because Allah is just and does not wrong; so when we do good, Allah knows it, and He will... what? He will reward us for it.

Do not say: the answer does not correspond to the condition, since there is no benefit for us in Allah knowing it. We say: rather there is a benefit for us, which is that when we know Allah knows it, Allah the Exalted is just and does not waste it; rather, He must reward us for it.

And there is also a benefit in it, as will come, Allah willing, in the benefits: it is incitement and encouragement.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you..﴾

* A student: Shaykh (...) is this here come in the form of (...)?

* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾. The prepositional phrase in ﴿of it﴾ is attached to what?

* A student: To ﴿Knowing﴾.

* The Shaykh: To ﴿Knowing﴾, yes.

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you﴾. ﴿Prescribed﴾ means obligated; and "kataba" in origin means obligation, and from it is His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 183], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers as a decree of specified times﴾ [al-Nisa 103]. And the prescribing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is divided into two kinds: a legislative prescription (kitab shar'i) and a cosmic prescription (kitab kawni). The cosmic prescription must occur and cannot fail; the legislative prescription may be performed by the one on whom it is prescribed, or may not be performed. So ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 183]: people may fast and may not fast; ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾: they may fight and may not fight. But ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya 105] is this cosmic, divine decree, which must be. ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujadilah 21]: prescribing of what? Cosmic; it must be.

So prescribing is then of two types: cosmic prescribing and legislative prescribing. The difference between them: in cosmic prescribing, the occurrence of what is prescribed is necessary, unlike legislative prescribing.

The second difference: cosmic prescribing relates to what Allah loves and what He does not love, whereas legislative prescribing is only in what Allah loves. It is not possible for Allah to prescribe on His servants what He does not love; rather everything He prescribes is beloved to Him.

As for His saying ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾: what kind of fighting is it? The fighting against the enemies of Allah, the disbelievers. And ﴿al-qital﴾ (fighting) is the verbal noun of "qatala," and this form generally does not come except between two parties: "qatala," "shara" and the like.

As for His saying ﴿and it is hateful to you﴾: the pronoun in ﴿and it﴾ refers to the fighting, not to the prescribing; for the Muslims do not dislike what Allah has prescribed upon them, but they dislike fighting according to human nature. There is a difference between our saying that we dislike what Allah has prescribed of fighting, and our saying that we dislike fighting. Disliking fighting is a natural matter, for a person dislikes fighting anyone among people and killing him, and thus becoming one who is killed. But when this fighting is prescribed upon us, it becomes beloved to us in one respect and hateful to us in another: by considering that Allah has prescribed it upon us, it is beloved to us; by considering that the soul recoils from it and dislikes it, it is hateful to us. And because the soul recoils from it and dislikes it, and it is heavy upon it, there is in it this great reward; the martyrs with their Lord have their reward and their light: ﴿And never think of those who have been killed in the cause of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for, rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them—that there is no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve. They rejoice in a favor from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 169–171].

Attention. So does the dislike of fighting contradict the sincerity of worship? No. A person can dislike fighting in itself while loving it because Allah has prescribed it for him. This is why the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, would come to the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, insisting that they fight. He would sometimes turn them back because they were too young, and they would be saddened. At Uhud, he turned back some of the young Companions. One of them said: "O Messenger of Allah, how can you turn me back when you have permitted so-and-so, and I can now wrestle him?" He said: "You want to wrestle? Let him wrestle with me." So he wrestled him, threw him down, and he was permitted.[[Narrated by al-Tahawi in Sharh Ma'ani al-Athar (5034), from the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub.]] All of this was from their love of fighting. Likewise, 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, may Allah be pleased with him, was lame, and he insisted on going out to fight. His sons said to him: "Do not go out, for Allah has excused you." He came with them to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and they informed him. The Prophet said to him: "Allah has excused you." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I want, or I love, to step with this lameness of mine into Paradise."[[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (9/24), via Ishaq ibn Yasar.]] Allahu Akbar. When the Prophet saw that he was attached to fighting, he permitted him and said to his sons a statement, meaning that if he loves to go out, do not prevent him. The conclusion is that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, did not dislike fighting after Allah had prescribed it. Rather, they loved it because Allah prescribed it. How many things a person dislikes, yet he loves them because Allah commanded them. Now, is the Hajj burdensome or not? In terms of being a hardship, a person may dislike it, but if he knows that in it is the pleasure of Allah, he loves it. Spending wealth in zakat, for example: a person is naturally inclined to love wealth, ﴿and you love wealth with an intense love﴾ [al-Fajr 20], but if he knows that in this is the pleasure of Allah, it becomes easy for him. This is the wisdom of the test in the acts of worship that the servant is charged with.

As for His saying ﴿and it is hateful to you﴾: ﴿hateful﴾ (kurh) is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, meaning "disliked by you" (makruh lakum). The verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle occurs often, such as His saying ﴿and if they are pregnant, then spend on them﴾ [al-Talaq 6], meaning "burden" (hamal) in the sense of what is carried in the womb. And the Messenger's, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected,"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/18) from the hadith of 'A'ishah; the wording is Muslim's.]] meaning "mardud," rejected.

Here, ﴿kurh﴾ means "makruh," disliked. And the clause ﴿and it is hateful to you﴾: what is its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis)? It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). The circumstance is that fighting is disliked by you. But look at the consolation from Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾. ﴿'Asa﴾ here means hope, or apprehension, or expectation, or causation, since it has four meanings.

* Student: Causation.
* Shaykh: Causation? No, I do not know that. Does it fit causation? If I said, for example: "Take all this medicine, perhaps you will be cured," that is clearly causation, or hope.

But here, in ﴿and it may be that you dislike﴾, the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is closest to expectation or to encouragement. It is not hope in the sense of Allah hoping, since nothing is uncertain for Allah, and everything is easy for Him. Rather it is encouragement, meaning that He wants the addressee to hope for this. That is, the meaning is: do what is disliked by you, perhaps it will be good.

﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾. Is what Allah mentioned here real or not? It is real, even in matters other than acts of worship. Sometimes a person does an ordinary thing and says: "I wish I had not done it," or "I wish this had not happened." Then the outcome turns out to be praiseworthy, and at that point he dislikes something that is good for him.

Fighting is disliked by us, but its outcome is good, because the fighter, as Allah said, commanding His Prophet to say: ﴿Say: Do you await for us except one of the two best things?﴾ [al-Tawbah 52], meaning that there must be a good outcome: ﴿one of the two best things.﴾ What are they? Either victory and triumph, or martyrdom, is it not so? Therefore the fighter in the cause of Allah is in good.

﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing while it is bad for you﴾. This also often occurs: a person loves something and insists on it, then the outcome is bad. By this noble verse, a person consoles himself for everything he misses of what he loves, and steadies himself for everything he gets of what he dislikes. Whatever reaches you that you dislike, you steady yourself with ﴿it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾. And whatever escapes you while your soul seeks it, you console yourself, saying: ﴿it may be that you love a thing while it is bad for you﴾. This is the reality. If a person reflects on the events of his daily life, he will find much of this.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah knows while you do not know﴾. Glory be to Him, He does not decree for the believer anything except that it is good for him, does not obligate on the believer anything except that it is good for him, and does not forbid him anything except that it is good for him. Do not say: "I wish this had not been forbidden, I wish this had not been obligated, I wish this had not happened." Do not say this, because your knowledge is limited. ﴿And Allah knows while you do not know.﴾ And what does He know? Everything, even the future that you think is evil, Allah knows the good in it.

His saying ﴿and you do not know﴾ is an absolute negation of human knowledge. So do we say that this absolute negation is meant to refer to something specific, or do we say it is an absolute negation according to the basic principle, and that the basic principle regarding a human being is lack of knowledge in absolute terms?

The answer: It is the latter. Just as the basic principle regarding Allah's attributes is absolute knowledge, Allah has absolute knowledge. That is why He said ﴿He knows﴾ without restricting this knowledge to a known object. And ﴿you do not know﴾ does not restrict this negation to a known object. He did not say "you do not know the future," nor "you do not know the present," nor anything else; it is ﴿you do not know.﴾ So the basic principle regarding us is: lack of knowledge. This is why Allah said: ﴿And man carried it. Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab 72], and He said: ﴿And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing, sight, and hearts that you may be grateful﴾ [al-Nahl 78].

﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting therein﴾. The i'rab of this sentence: ﴿about the sacred month﴾ is in the genitive after ﴿'an﴾ ("about"). ﴿Fighting therein﴾: what is it that puts it in the genitive? It is a substitute (badal). Of what kind of substitution?

"Corresponding, or part, or that which includes it is found / or like a conjunct with 'bal'" which of the five is it?
