If He willed, He would have put us in difficulty, because He is Mighty and possesses authority; and because He is Wise, He is the possessor of judgment: ﴿Surely, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf 54], ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ [al-An'am 57]. But together with His being Mighty and Wise, He is Forgiving and Merciful; for this reason He was gentle with His servants in this matter and in other matters: ﴿He has not placed upon you any difficulty in religion﴾ [al-Hajj 78].

Then the Most High said: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾. Nikah in its origin means joining and gathering, and from it is the poet's saying:

O you who would join al-Thurayya to Suhayl, may Allah preserve you, how can the two come together?

O you who would join al-Thurayya to Suhayl... (...)

That is: O you who wish to bring together al-Thurayya and Suhayl.

So His saying "how can they come together" shows that nikah in origin is joining and gathering. As for in the law, it is a contract to make lawful the enjoyment of a woman and the guarding of the private parts, and so on, and the other benefits connected with marriage. It is a contract on a woman made lawful for the purpose of the benefits that follow from marriage: guarding chastity, procreation, enjoyment, and other things.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says here: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾.

* A student: What is the meaning of (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, He is gathering them together. ﴿al-Mushrikat﴾ is the plural of mushrikah. The mushrikah or mushrik is one who ascribes a partner to Allah the Most High in what is specific to Him, whether in lordship, or in divinity, or in His names and attributes. So whoever takes a god with Allah to worship is a mushrik, even if he believes that Allah is the creator of the heavens and the earth. And whoever believes that there is a creator of the universe besides Allah, or one who independently has some part of the universe, or a helper of Allah the Most High in creation, in creating some part of the universe, is a mushrik. Three things: what are they?

* A student: Whoever takes a god with Allah. (...)

* The Shaykh: The creation of the universe, then he is a mushrik.

* A student: But did He forbid saying "mutasarrifan" (one who disposes)? (...)

* The Shaykh: Even the women of the People of the Book. If we take the commonly known usage, it does not include Jews and Christians, because: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾ [al-Bayyinah 6], where He conjoined the polytheists to the People of the Book, which shows that they are?

* A student: Other than them.

* The Shaykh: Other than them. This difference bears on whether this verse remains general or is specified by the verse of al-Ma'idah, which will come, Allah willing. (...)

In this noble verse, Allah the Mighty and Majestic forbids...

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 219–221 (part 4 of 5):

(...) to idolatresses ﴿until they believe﴾: until they enter the Islamic religion and believe in Allah and His Messenger. A believing man may not marry idolatresses, as Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Mumtahanah: ﴿Do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. His saying ﴿Do not marry the idolatresses﴾ includes those who associate partners with Allah in His worship, or who associate partners with Him in His lordship. So whoever believes that there is a creator besides Allah, it is not permissible for a believer to marry her. And whoever worships something alongside Allah, it is not permissible for a believer to marry her.

His saying ﴿Do not marry the idolatresses until they believe﴾: Does this include the women of the Christians, who say that Allah is the third of three and make the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, a god alongside Allah? The scholars have differed on this. The correct view is that the women of the People of the Book are not included, even if they claim that 'Isa is a god alongside Allah. This is because Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them; and [lawful for you are] the chaste women from among the believers and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you give them their compensation﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5]. Surah al-Ma'idah is among the last to be revealed. For this reason some scholars said that there is no abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one) in it; everything in it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). And in the same surah in which Allah permitted the women of the People of the Book, He said: ﴿Those who said, "Indeed, Allah is the third of three," have certainly disbelieved﴾ [al-Ma'idah 73]. So He described them as disbelievers and made their women lawful. Nevertheless, even though it is permissible, the better course is that he not marry her, because it affects his children from her. And it may also affect him, if he is impressed by her and by her beauty, and she takes away his reason, so that it may lead him to disbelieve. Some people have related to me that a man travelled to a disbelieving land and was impressed by a girl, and he proposed to her. She said to him: "It is not possible unless you come with me to the church and say that Allah is the third of three." He tried to refrain, but, may Allah protect us, her beauty had taken over his mind and he became infatuated with her. Finally he went with her to the church and testified that Allah is the third of three. We ask Allah for well-being. But I give you good news: this man who did such a thing repented. He turned to Allah and regretted what he had done, and came asking what should be upon him in this state in which this woman had enticed him. Our answer to him was: if he repents, Allah will accept his repentance. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins"﴾ [al-Zumar 53].

And His saying ﴿until they believe﴾: Someone may say: Why did He not say "until they affirm the oneness of Allah (yuwahhidna)", since the opposite of shirk is tawhid? And why did He say ﴿until they believe﴾? We say: because belief (iman) is more general, as it includes belief in everything that must be believed in: affirming the oneness of Allah, belief in His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and destiny, its good and its evil. So if she has stopped associating partners with Allah but has not believed in everything that must be believed in, she is still not lawful. This is the reason for the shift from expressing the opposite to expressing belief.

And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, explained the reason and the wisdom behind this, saying: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than an idolatress, even though she may please you﴾. Allah has spoken the truth: a believing slave-woman is better than an idolatress, even if she pleases the person in her beauty, or pleases him in her wealth, or pleases him in her knowledge, or pleases him in her grace and the like. The believing woman is better than the idolatress. Then He said ﴿a slave-woman (amah)﴾. Do not think that by this He means a enslaved woman. We will explain, Allah willing, in Surah al-Nisa' that it is not permissible to marry slave-women except under conditions. Rather, what is meant by "amah" here is the servant of Allah, that is, one who worships Allah the Mighty and Majestic. A male is called "slave of Allah ('abd Allah)", and a female is called "servant of Allah (amat Allah)", as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (900) and Muslim (442/136), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar]. He, ﷺ, said in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "the son of your maidservant" [recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad (3712), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud], mentioning the mother and the father. For the father he said "your slave ('abd)" and for the mother he said "your maidservant (amah)". By this we know that what is related in the hadith of Sayyid al-Istighfar, which is: "O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your slave ('abduka)" [recorded by al-Bukhari (6306), from the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws], is for a male. As for a female, she says: "I am Your maidservant (amatuka)". This was the view of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him. Some scholars said that in the hadith of Sayyid al-Istighfar she should say "wa-ana 'abduka" (and I am Your slave), interpreting it as a person. A person, is that masculine or feminine?
* The students: Masculine.
* The Shaykh: Masculine. But what Shaykh al-Islam held is more eloquent in humility and servitude. For when a woman says "wa-ana 'abduka", it is as if she feels she is a man. But when she says "wa-ana amatuka", that is more eloquent in expressing her humility. So His saying, glorified be He, ﴿and a slave-woman (amah)﴾ here, and what is the meaning of "amah"? A woman. ﴿is better than an idolatress (mushrikah)﴾. It does not mean a comparison between the one preferred and the one it is preferred over, i.e., it is not a comparison. It means explaining that she possesses good, only. Like prayer is good, and charity is good, and enjoining good and forbidding evil is good: good, which is the opposite of evil. But if the one compared with is mentioned, either explicitly or implicitly, then "khayr" (better) is used for comparison. Here is a question on this verse (...) and the rule concerning the elative (ism al-tafdil, the comparative form) is that the one preferred and the one it is preferred over agree in the basic attribute and differ in its degree, like the hadith: "The congregational prayer is better (khayr) than the prayer of the solitary one" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (645) and Muslim (650/249), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar]. Here the two prayers agree in being good, but the congregational prayer is distinguished by greater excellence. This is what is known among scholars as (af'al al-tafdil, the comparative form): when a preferred item and the item it is preferred over are mentioned, they agree in the basic attribute, and the preferred one is distinguished from the other in its degree.

Here Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than an idolatress﴾. It is known that there is no good in an idolatress, and there is no good in an idolater. So how did He say ﴿better than an idolatress﴾? The answer is one of two ways. The first: the elative may be used between two things (...) where one of the two sides has nothing of that attribute, and it is meant as absolute preference, like His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden, that Day, are better in residence and finer in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan 24]. By Allah, there is no good among the people of the Fire, but this is a case where the elative indicates preference and the other side has no share of it at all. The second: we say that the one who marries an idolatress may think there is good in her, for example because she is beautiful. That is why He said ﴿even though she may please you﴾. A person may think that his connection to this idolatress is good. So Allah, glorified and exalted, explained that what a person believes to be good in marrying an idolatress, we say to him: marrying a believing slave-woman is better, on the basis of what he believed to be good in marrying the idolatress.

Then He said: ﴿And do not marry (tunkihu) the idolaters﴾. Is "tunkihu" in the active or the passive voice?
* A student: Passive.
* The Shaykh: No. Why?
* The student: It is active.
* The Shaykh: If we say it is not passive, then it does not say to you that it is active... (...) built on what basis?
* The student: .(...)
* The Shaykh: The present tense passive is formed by raising its first letter and opening the letter before its last. Ibn Malik said about this:
"And make it from a present verb with its vowel opened, as in yantahi, the passive of which is yuntaha."
So "tunkihu" is not passive; it is active, but it comes from a quadriliteral (rubai) verb. The first is from nakaha, yankihu, and the second is from ankaha, yunkihu. That is why in the first he said ﴿and do not marry (tankihu)﴾ and in the second ﴿and do not marry off (tunkihu)﴾. The first is for the husband who conducts the contract himself for himself, with no guardian, and a wife does not marry herself; her guardian marries her off. So this is from the quadriliteral ankaha. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not marry off (tunkihu) the idolaters until they believe﴾. The prohibition on marrying an idolater, or marrying off an idolater, has no exception, even if he is from the People of the Book. It is not permissible for him to be married to a Muslim woman. If a Christian proposes to a Muslim woman to us, should we marry her to him?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: It is not permitted. ﴿And do not marry off the idolaters﴾ is general, with no exception, unlike ﴿And do not marry the idolatresses﴾, which excepts those who are People of the Book. Two men in Egypt, a Copt and a Muslim, debated. The Copt argued against the Muslim, saying: "Why do you make our women lawful for you, while you do not make your women lawful for us? This is unjust." He said: "Because we acknowledge the religion of the Christians before us. So when a Muslim marries a woman whose religion is Christianity, she increases in goodness, as he acknowledges her religion and the religion of Islam. But if he is a disbelieving Christian man who wants to marry a Muslim woman, he does not acknowledge her religion, because the Christian does not acknowledge Muhammad, ﷺ."
* A student: If he says, "I acknowledge"?
* The Shaykh: It is not enough. He has not entered the religion of Muhammad, ﷺ. The Messiah gave them good news of the final Messenger, and commanded them to abandon their religion and follow him.

﴿And do not marry off the idolaters until they believe﴾. It has already been stated that there is a contrast in wording, where He said ﴿the idolaters until they believe﴾ and did not say "until they affirm the oneness of Allah". This is because belief in everything that must be believed in is necessary. So the shift from mentioning the opposite to mentioning something that is not its direct opposite is for a purpose. This is found frequently in the Qur'an, and it is generally found only for a benefit. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah judges with truth, while those they call upon besides Him do not judge with anything﴾. Does it say "they do not judge with truth", or "they do not judge with anything"?
* The students: ﴿They do not judge with anything﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿They do not judge with anything﴾ [Ghafir 20]. Why did He not say "they do not judge with the truth"? Because ﴿they do not judge with anything﴾ is more eloquent, more eloquent in exposing the deficiency of these idols: they judge with nothing, neither truth nor falsehood. Pay attention to this point from the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When one shifts from mentioning the opposite to something else, there must be a benefit in that, so reflect on it.

He said: ﴿And a believing servant (abd) is better than an idolater, even though he may please you﴾. A believing servant is better than an idolater, even if he pleases you. Allah has spoken the truth. The believing servant who believes in Allah and His messengers and in what must be believed in is better than the idolater. If there is an idolater who is an expert in building airplanes, rockets, and spacecraft, something genius, and a Muslim man who knows nothing of this, which of them is better?
* A student: The Muslim.
* The Shaykh: The believing servant. So if a woman says she wants to marry this disbeliever because he has knowledge of the natural sciences that the Muslim does not have, we say to her: ﴿And a believing servant is better than an idolater, even though he may please you﴾. He did not say "even though he may please you (feminine plural)". Nor did He say "even though she pleases her". This is because the contract of marriage is in the hand of a guardian, so the address is to the guardians. So if the idolater pleases you and gains your admiration through his wealth or otherwise, it is not permissible for you, but giving him in marriage is your responsibility.

Then the Mighty and Majestic explained the aspect of this superiority, saying: ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾. ﴿Those﴾: the pronoun refers to the idolaters, male and female. ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾ by their words and their actions, and perhaps their outward appearance is good for us. May Allah humiliate them and curse them (...) they spread the call to their religion and their polytheism with everything they can: with wealth, speech, and action. Indeed, we hear that they build schools and build hospitals and treat the sick until they recover, in order to win us over to their religion. They have not ceased calling to the religion of the Christians until our day, but, praise be to Allah, it has no acceptance. (...) The words they say on their broadcasts (...) then they send them to the address of some organizations (...) experience and research into the conditions of the Muslims (...). He does not know except that a cassette has come to him (...). Praise be to Allah, they are defeated in everything to which they call, however much they call. They only call to the Fire, or are these among the causes of entering the Garden? And why is it not said of their charitable works: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good﴾ [al-Baqarah 195]? Because these charitable works do not benefit them at all, and Allah would accept them if they came from a Muslim. Allah the Exalted said about the disbelievers: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 23]. So is there any good in that or not?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: No. Why? Because their deeds are a call to the Fire. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert from the way of Allah. They will spend it; then it will be for them a regret; then they will be overcome. And those who disbelieve will be gathered to Hell﴾ [al-Anfal 36]. So the young Muslims must pay attention to this point, which is the activity of the missionaries in calling to their religion through the ways of spending. Allah informs us that they spend it only to avert from the way of Allah. The purpose of their expenditure is war against the Most Merciful and enmity toward Him. So we must be attentive to this and not be deceived by them and their deeds. That is why He said: ﴿Those invite to the Fire, while Allah invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His permission﴾. A call to the Fire, and a call to the Garden and forgiveness. Yet we find that the matter does not involve a direct opposition. If it did, He would have said: "Those invite to the Fire, while believers invite to the Garden and forgiveness." But He shifted from "the believer invites" to "Allah invites", because the believer may fall short in calling to the Garden of Allah and His forgiveness. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, invites to the Garden and forgiveness, and the more a person grows in faith in Allah, the more he calls to the Garden of Allah and His forgiveness. Here He says: ﴿He invites to the Garden and forgiveness﴾. The Garden is the reward for righteous deeds, and forgiveness is the reward for bad deeds when a person seeks forgiveness for them. This is because a person in his actions is between two things: either a purely righteous deed, which is a cause of entering the Garden, or a deed that is not righteous but for which he repents. So this is a call to forgiveness.

And the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿by His permission (idhnihi)﴾. ﴿He invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His permission﴾. The permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is divided into legislative permission (idhn shar'i) and existential permission (idhn kawni). So His permission, glorified be He, when it relates to created beings and decrees, is existential permission, and when it relates to legislation, it is legislative permission. His permission in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]: what do you say about the permission here? Is it legislative or existential? It is existential; that is, Allah permits intercession. ﴿Or do they have partners who have legislated for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura 21]: this is legislative. And His saying: ﴿Say, "Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made from it [some that is] unlawful and lawful?" Say, "Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent [lies] against Allah?"﴾ [Yunus 59]: is the permission here existential or legislative? Now let us see: is the interrogative here for denial and rebuke, or for affirmation? It is for denial and reproach. So is the permission of Allah to these people existential?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Is it established or not established?
* The student: Established.
* The Shaykh: It is established. But His permission to them is legislative, not (...). Now the verse we have here: ﴿He invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His permission﴾. Do you see it as legislative permission or existential permission?
* A student: Legislative.
* The Shaykh: Or both?
* The students: Both.
* The Shaykh: Or legislative? Or existential?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 219–221 (part 5 of 5):

* Students: Both.
* The Shaykh: When a child is asked about something, he answers with the last option. You say to him, for example: "Is today Saturday or Sunday?" He says: "Sunday." "Is today Sunday or Saturday?" He says: "Saturday." In this verse before us, the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it includes both the cosmic (kawni) and the legislated (shar'i). That is because a person's entering into what becomes a cause for Paradise and forgiveness is cosmic, while the legislating of what becomes a cause for Paradise and forgiveness is legislated (shar'i).

And His saying: ﴿And He makes His signs clear to the people, that they may remember﴾. ﴿Yubayyin﴾ means "He makes clear, manifests." ﴿Ayatihi﴾ is the plural of ayah, which is the decisive sign, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day, and at once they are in darkness﴾ [Ya-Sin 37], and His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin 41]. So the decisive sign is that which necessitates inferring from it the existence of Allah. ﴿He makes His signs clear﴾: the signs are divided into two kinds: legislated and cosmic. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made both clear. He made clear to His servants the legislated signs and He also made clear the cosmic signs, so nothing remains that people need in the matters of their religion or the matters of their worldly life except that He has made it clear. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [An-Nahl 89]. Abu Dharr said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away, and there was no bird flapping its wings in the sky except that he reminded us of knowledge about it."[[Narrated by al-Bazzar in al-Musnad (3897) from the hadith of Abu Dharr with similar wording.]] Some people may find something unclear to them; some legislated signs may remain hidden from them, the face of the sharia in them not becoming apparent to them, and then it becomes apparent to them afterwards. So what we take from the verse is that when the legislative ruling becomes clear to a particular person, this does not mean that the legislative ruling in itself was hidden. Rather, it may be hidden from a person either because of the scarcity of his knowledge, or the deficiency of his understanding, or his negligence in seeking the truth. These are three causes that make something hidden: either the scarcity of his knowledge, or that he has deficient understanding in many things, or that he is not concerned, and the issue comes to him as a problem, and he says: "I will hold off on this and not investigate." But the truth in itself has been made clear by Allah, Exalted is He, with complete clarity. The ways of clarification in the legislated signs are many. Among them is the generality of the wording and its comprehensiveness, and among them is their inclusion within its generality when the two share the same reason; then the meaning encompasses both, so the ruling encompasses both.

So there is no deficiency in it. Look at the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the verses on inheritance: He said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [An-Nisa 176].

The cosmic signs are what relates to the created things, and it is a sign of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. A sign of what? Of knowledge or of power? Of all of this. For example, the alternation of night and day is among the signs of Allah that point to what?

* Students: To power.
* The Shaykh: To power, knowledge, mercy and sovereignty. Because its indicating power is clear, since none of the people can bring forward the rising of the sun or delay it for himself. But its Creator, who commanded it to proceed by His permission, is a proof of His knowledge of it and His power over it. There is no effect except that it is preceded by knowledge and power. Suppose you made a garment: you would not sew it except while knowing how to sew it, and also being able to sew it, otherwise it would not be possible for you to sew it. Likewise, the alternation of night and day cannot occur except from the knowledge of Allah and His power by which night and day alternate. And it is, as a proof of His sovereignty, a sign of His sovereignty, because the alternation of night and day includes sensory and non-sensory alternation (...). The sensory is that of which Allah said: ﴿And these days We alternate among the people﴾ [Ali 'Imran 140]: He makes a poor man rich and makes a rich man poor, guides one who is astray and leads astray one who is guided. The conclusion is that the cosmic signs are a sign of their Creator, Mighty and Majestic (...). It is not that you say: "It points to power or mercy, or what is similar." Rather, you say: it is a sign of every meaning that fits that sign, and it varies according to the signs.

Has Allah made the cosmic signs clear to us? Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made clear, and what is the reason for the length of the day (...)? He has made clear to us that this is by His power: ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it phases until it returns like the old dry palm stalk﴾ [Ya-Sin 39]. Then, if there is a sensory cause, or if there is (...) that a person studies astronomy to benefit, to benefit from what (...). The legislated signs are made clear and the cosmic signs are made clear. But my question now is: is the clarification of the legislated signs more eloquent and precise, or the clarification of the cosmic signs? The first: the legislated signs are more eloquent, more precise and more comprehensive, because a person is in the greatest need of them, a necessary need, on them depends his happiness in this world and the Hereafter. For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made clear to His servants from the legislated signs even the manners of sitting and seeking permission: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek permission and greet their people﴾ [An-Nur 27]. ﴿O you who believe, when it is said to you, "Make room in the assemblies," then make room; Allah will make room for you﴾ [Al-Mujadila 11]. Allah made clear even this matter. A man from among the polytheists said to Salman al-Farisi: "Your Prophet has taught you everything, even teaching you how to go to the toilet." He said: "Yes, and that we should not cleanse ourselves with dung or bone."[[Narrated by Muslim (262/57) from the hadith of Salman al-Farisi.]] (...) The clarification of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is from the clarification of Allah, because ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 80]. The clarification of revelation for the legislated signs is more comprehensive than the clarification for the cosmic signs. The cosmic signs come in a general manner, unlike the legislated ones, because the sharia must be received from revelation (...). ﴿Allah makes His signs clear to you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 242]. If you believe in this sentence, a matter may come before you that you do not find in the words of the jurists nor in the words of the scholars of hadith. When you reflect upon the Qur'an, you find it clear and explicit, or when you reflect upon the Sunnah, you find it clearly explained in it. This is a known matter. For this reason I urge you, students of knowledge, that your constant practice in reaching the depths of issues should be returning to the Book and the Sunnah. There is no harm in seeking help from the words of the people of knowledge, because a person's reliance on himself in understanding the Book and the Sunnah may involve much error. So he must know the principles that the early generations, from the Companions and the Successors, established, deriving them from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: When we speak, we speak about its clarification in itself. As for whether they are blinded or are made blind to some people, this is possible. The disbelievers may perceive from the cosmic signs what the Muslims do not perceive, but it does not benefit them, because they do not derive from them proof of Allah's mercy or of His existence. When we speak, what do we speak about? The legislated signs as signs, regardless of the one who acts upon them. For this reason, now we all know that some of us understand from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger what another does not understand. It is said that Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, hosted Imam Ahmad one night, and when the dinner was brought to him, he ate all of it (...).
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh: 'Umar wanted to prevent it as a matter of policy, but he did not prevent it as a legislated ruling. It was his own ijtihad, but he was not successful in it. He, may Allah be pleased with him, did not cite any evidence; rather, he feared for those who married Kitabiyyat, he feared only for himself.
* The student: Is the fear present now?
* The Shaykh: This belongs to the ruler: if he sees that policy requires preventing marriage, he has the right to prevent it, as currently exists in the Saudi government, may Allah grant it success, which prevents marriage to foreigners except under conditions it approves and agrees to. So if the ruler sees that people should be prevented from marrying foreigners, even if they are Muslim women, for a matter related to the interests of the country, he may do so. This is because if we said that you do only what is commanded and forbid only what is forbidden, the ruler's authority would have no effect. So the ruler must have some discretion: he may prohibit what he sees the truth lies in prohibiting, or permit what he sees the truth lies in permitting, provided it does not contradict a text.
* Student: Shaykh, what if public interest takes precedence in the system of legislated rule? (...)
* The Shaykh: No. The legislated ruling is permissibility. So the ruler may prohibit if he sees that the interest lies in prohibition, just as the remarriage (raj'ah) after three divorces was permitted during the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and Abu Bakr, and two years of the caliphate of 'Umar. 'Umar saw that the interest required prohibition, so he prohibited it. The interest he saw was that people hastened in a matter in which they had had patience, and that one of them would, at every slight anger toward his wife, pronounce the final divorce. So he, may Allah be pleased with him, saw that she should be prevented from being taken back in this situation. This returns to the ijtihad of the ruler, and between him and Allah, if he intends the truth, he is rewarded whether he is right or not. If he intends something else, his Lord will hold him to account.
* Student: Allah, Exalted is He, gave a reason at the end of the verse: ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾, although this reason exists among the People of the Book?
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: What is its aspect?
* The Shaykh: Its aspect is that in the case of the People of the Book there is another interest that counterbalances this reason, which is that the knowledge a woman has, which may call her to Islam, is greater and larger than the ignorance in which she may continue in polytheism.
* Student: We say: the People of the Book have shirk. How do we exclude them from the polytheists?
* The Shaykh: Because Allah excluded them. He said: ﴿And the chaste women from the believers and the chaste women from those who were given the Book﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5].
* The student: So we say that this verse of al-Ma'idah abrogates the verse of al-Baqarah?
* The Shaykh: It specifies (mukhassisah). This is if we say that the verse before us is general, although some scholars say that what is meant by it is the polytheists, and the People of the Book enter into it from the origin, or they did not enter it, so it is a general expression intended in a specific sense.

In this noble verse: the prohibition of marrying polytheist women to believing men. From where do we derive it? ﴿And do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾.

And in it: the ruling revolves with its cause in existence and non-existence. From where? From His saying: ﴿until they believe﴾. This indicates that whenever shirk is removed, marriage becomes permissible, and whenever it is absent, marriage is absent.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the husband is the guardian of himself. From where is this taken? ﴿And do not marry polytheist women﴾: the address is directed to the husband.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the believer is better than the polytheist even if the polytheist has qualities that please him, due to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist even though he should impress you﴾. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Not equal are the evil and the good, even if the abundance of the evil impresses you"﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 100]. So do not be deceived by abundance, do not be deceived by skill, nor by excellence, nor by eloquence, nor by anything else. Return to the legislated descriptions to which praiseworthy attributes are attached.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that people differ in their conditions and are not on the same level, due to His saying: ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾. In it is a clear refutation of those who said, or who asserted, that the religion of Islam is a religion of equality. How so? Because preference contradicts equality. Strangely, the word "equality" has never come in Islam, neither in the Book nor in the Sunnah, at all, nor did Allah command it or encourage it, because it is not sound. If you say "equality," it includes the wicked and the just, the disbeliever and the believer, the male and the female, and this is what the enemies of Islam want for Muslims: that they make the religion of Islam a religion of equality with no distinction. But Islam came with a word that is better than that word and has no ambiguity at all, which is: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice﴾ [An-Nahl 90]. The word "justice" requires that we equate the two when they agree in the attributes that require equating, and that we differentiate between them when they differ in the attributes that require differentiating. Is that not so? Most of what is found in the Qur'an is the negation of equality in this respect: ﴿Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal, or are the darknesses and the light equal?"﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 16]. ﴿Not equal are those believers who sit [at home], other than those with a disability, and those who strive in the way of Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 95]. ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾ [Al-Hadid 10], and many verses of this kind: ﴿Are they equal in example?﴾ [Hud 24], and what is similar to them. The conclusion is that this word was introduced by the enemies of Islam into the Muslims, and most Muslims, especially those with general culture, have no verification or precision in matters and no distinction between expressions. For this reason you find them regarding this word as a light carried on the heads: "Islam is a religion of equality." We say: you have lied. Islam is a religion of justice. Bring us a single letter from the Book of Allah or from the Sunnah of His Messenger that commands equality at all. Rather, the entire Qur'an is justice and commands justice: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾ [An-Nahl 90]. ﴿And act justly; indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾ [Al-Hujurat 9]. ﴿And weigh with the just balance﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 182], and what is similar to that. So this word and many others must be taken heed of.
* Student: Shaykh, some have restricted it, saying: equality in rights and obligations. Is this correct?
* The Shaykh: Even this is wrong, it is not correct. Does one who has no wealth equal one who has wealth in zakat? And is one whose wealth is a million the same as one whose wealth is a thousand? No. And is one who is able to pray standing the same as one who is not able? (...)

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 219–221 (part 1 of 5):

The subject of His saying ﴿They ask you﴾ refers to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and the object pronoun in ﴿they ask you﴾ refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). Allah revealed four verses concerning wine (khamr, intoxicant). The first permits it: His saying, ﴿And from the fruits of the date palm and the grapes you take from them intoxication and good provision﴾ (An-Nahl 16:67). The second hints at its prohibition, which is this verse we have before us. The third prohibits it at certain times and not others: the verse of An-Nisa, ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾. The fourth prohibits it absolutely: the verse of Al-Ma'idah, which was revealed in the eighth year after the Hijrah. Thus the definitive prohibition of wine was delayed until the eighth year after the Hijrah.

As for His saying, ﴿They ask you﴾, the reason for their question is that when a sensible person sees the harms that result from wine and gambling, which contradict human nature (fitrah), he will inevitably have a difficulty with it. This is why they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about them, asking about their ruling and not their meaning, because the meaning is known; rather, they asked about the ruling. It has already been mentioned to us that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, asked the Prophet (ﷺ) many questions. But how many questions did they ask the Messenger in the Qur'an?

* A student: Thirteen.
* Another student: Twelve.
* The Shaykh: Twelve or thirteen? It is well known that they are twelve questions.

As for His saying, ﴿They ask you about wine﴾: from what is khamr derived? It was said: it is derived from (خَمَرْتُه أخْمِرُه), meaning "I covered it," so it comes from covering. It was also said: it is derived from (خَامَره يُخامِره), meaning "he mixed with it." The correct view is that it is derived from both meanings together, because wine mixes with the intellect and also covers the intellect. It mixes with it, and then afterward it covers it, until it places its drinker among the insane, who have no intellect.

Then what is khamr? Is khamr only what intoxicates from grape wine, or is khamr whatever intoxicates, of any kind?

The correct view is that khamr is whatever intoxicates, of any kind. We do not say this is a matter of technical juristic terminology (istilah fiqhi); rather, it is a matter of the linguistic meaning. The evidence for this is that the Prophet (ﷺ), who was the most eloquent of the Arabs, said: «Every intoxicant is khamr, and every intoxicant is forbidden».[[Recorded by Muslim (2003/73) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] So in this statement the Prophet (ﷺ) explained both the definition and the ruling. «Every intoxicant is khamr» is the definition, and «every intoxicant is forbidden» is the ruling. On this basis, it is not restricted to any particular substance: not grapes, not dates, not barley, not honey, not wheat, nor anything else. Whatever intoxicates is khamr.

But what is the meaning of intoxication (al-iskar)?

The scholars said: the meaning of intoxication is the covering of the intellect for the sake of pleasure and elation (tarab). It is not merely that a person loses his consciousness, becoming drunk. For example, (al-bang) covers the intellect, but not for the sake of pleasure and elation, so it is not intoxicating. Rather, khamr covers the intellect for the sake of pleasure and elation. That is why the drunkard sees himself in comfort and luxury, as if he were one of the kings, as if he owned everything. As Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

"We drink it, and it leaves us as kings ∗∗∗ ......................."

That is, it leaves us like kings in a person's imagination of himself. The reality also testifies to this. When the Messenger (ﷺ) came to Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, after he had drunk and become intoxicated, his slave-girl sang to him:

"Oh Hamz, to the high-humped she-camels ∗∗∗ ......................."

Two water-camels belonging to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib had passed by him. Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him (that is, Hamzah), rose, cut off their humps, and I think he also split open their bellies. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to complain. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Hamzah, he found him very drunk and not yet sober, so he spoke to him. Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "Are you not but slaves of my father?"[[Agreed upon: Al-Bukhari (3091) and Muslim (1979/1) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]] This shows that at that moment he had exuberance, elation, exaltation, and rising arrogance. This is why he said: "Are you not but slaves of my father?"

This is khamr and this is its derivation. As for its ruling, it will be explained in this verse.

As for His saying, ﴿and gambling (al-maysir)﴾: maysir has been said to be derived from (al-yusr), meaning ease, and it was said to be derived from (al-iysar), meaning wealth. As you see, the root contains the letters ya, sin, and ra. The truth is that it is derived from both together: there is ease in it and there is becoming wealthy in it, just as there is also impoverishment in it. Maysir is contesting and gambling for a stake (al-mughalabat wal-muqamarat bil-iwad). Contesting for a stake is maysir. It is derived from (al-yusr) because the person gains much wealth with ease and facility. It is derived from (al-iysar) because the winner, after poverty, becomes wealthy. So it is derived from both meanings together.

The Arabs in the pre-Islamic period (al-jahiliyyah) used this contesting and gambling. They used arrows (al-aqdah) and divining arrows (al-azlam), and sometimes other means. What matters is the meaning, not the form. So if we gamble over some money in any manner whatsoever, this is considered maysir. Among this is what is called luck and chance (al-hazz wal-nasib), which is maysir. Among it also are insurance policies on money, on cars, on goods, on houses, on souls, or the like. These are from maysir, meaning that in reality there is contesting in them, because the person who pays for insurance may profit or may lose. For if he is safe, he becomes a loser. If he is safe, he is a loser?!

* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How is the one who is safe the loser?! Because he has taken the payment without a corresponding return. If he is safe, he is a loser, and if he loses, he is a winner. If an accident occurs that is greater than what he paid, such as if he paid the insurance premium of five hundred riyals and then an accident occurred for five thousand riyals, he becomes a winner, meaning he took more than he paid. This is the basis of maysir: that it is built on luck and chance, where a person gains something without right. This is forbidden, and its ruling will come, God willing.

* A student: And among it is betting, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Yes, betting is among it, from maysir. If he says, "I say such and such," and the second says, "I say such and such," and the first says, "Come on, whoever is defeated by us will owe such and such," this is from it. It will come to us, God willing, in the lessons that the Shari'ah has excepted three matters from this: the arrowhead (al-nasl), the camel's hoof (al-khuff), and the horse's hoof (al-hafir).

Allah the Most High said in response: ﴿Say﴾. Here, that means: say to the questioners, or say to all people?

* Students: To all people.
* A student: Not everyone.
* The Shaykh: Yes. ﴿Say: in them is great sin﴾, meaning: say to the entire community, just as He said, for example, ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower some of their gaze﴾ (An-Nur 24:30). Here we may derive a principle: the answer may be directed to more than the questioner, as the scholars said regarding rulings: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. So here we may say: the questioners were specific people, but the answer is for them and for others.

﴿Say: in them is great sin and benefits for people.﴾ In another reading: ﴿great sin﴾ (ithmun kathir), ﴿in them is much sin﴾. ﴿In them﴾ refers to wine and gambling. ﴿Sin (ithm)﴾: what is sin? Sin is punishment, or that which is a cause of punishment. Allah the Most High said: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:2). It is said: so-and-so is ithim, meaning deserving of punishment.

As for His saying, ﴿in them is great sin﴾, the other reading is ﴿kathir﴾ (much). The difference between them is that greatness (kibar) refers to the quality, and abundance (kathrah) refers to the quantity. The meaning is that in them is much sin according to how a person deals with them. A person afflicted with this, may Allah protect us, hardly escapes it, and this necessitates that his action is repeated, and repetition of the action necessitates an abundance of sin. Likewise, the sin in them is great, meaning enormous, because they contain many corruptions in the intellect, religion, body, society, and conduct. Muhammad Rashid Rida, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned many very numerous harms of these two in this place. Whoever reads these harms will understand how Allah expressed this with His saying: ﴿great sin﴾ or ﴿much sin﴾. Are these two readings contradictory? No. Why would they not be contradictory? We say: because it is possible for both to be combined, so the sin is much in terms of its individual instances and great in terms of its nature. You may have ten pigeons and twenty camels; twenty camels surpass ten pigeons in both quantity and quality, and this is not impossible.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and benefits for people﴾. Manafi' is the plural of (manfa'ah), and it is of the form of the plural of excess (sighat muntaha al-jumu'), which is why He said ﴿manafi'﴾ and did not say manafi'un (with nunation), because it is a diptote (ism la yansarif). The form of the plural of excess indicates abundance, because it is the form of the plural of excess. So in them there are many great benefits. If you say: how did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say ﴿benefits for people﴾ with this great plurality? Does this not necessitate that people would turn toward them? Since He mentioned the sin in the singular, even though it was described as great or abundant, while the benefits were mentioned in the plural?

We say: this may occur to the minds of some people, but there is great eloquence in it: despite the abundance of their benefits, their sin is greater and more severe. For if there were a single benefit, we could say the sin might be greater. But even if the benefits are numerous and abundant, the sin is greater and more severe. This is why He said: ﴿their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, even if there are many benefits. What are these benefits?

Among the benefits of wine: exuberance and joy, even if it is a joy followed by sorrow, but in that moment a person rejoices and is elated, and perhaps his chest expands. Among them: they mentioned that it may be a cause of digesting food. Among them: it is traded, so it becomes an economic source. Likewise regarding gambling: if a person gains a million, having entered with ten riyals, what happens? He rejoices? He rejoices, even if his joy is with what harms him. The point is that he benefits from it. If at first he had only two hundred riyals and entered the arena of gambling and won a million riyals, he goes and buys a villa for himself, takes a car, takes a wife, for example, and takes things from the splendor of this world. This is a benefit in his view. In them there are benefits. Consider His saying: ﴿benefits for people﴾ and He did not say "benefits for the believers," because these benefits are purely material benefits suitable for people as people, and they are not benefits of goodness by which believers benefit. Rather, they are benefits for people insofar as they are people.

﴿And benefits for people﴾: where is the predicate of the subject in His saying ﴿benefits for people﴾?

* A student: "In them."
* The Shaykh: Is it omitted, do you say?
* The student: No.
* The Shaykh: Where?
* The student: Fronted.
* The Shaykh: ﴿In them﴾ is fronted? Is ﴿in them﴾ not the predicate of ﴿sin﴾?
* The student: Conjoined.
* The Shaykh: Correct, conjoined. When you say: Zayd and 'Amr are standing (qa'imani), then "standing" is the predicate of both. When you say: Zayd and 'Amr are in the house, then "in the house" is the predicate of both. When you say: in the house are Zayd and 'Amr, then "in the house" is the predicate of both. In ﴿in them is great sin and benefits﴾, the predicate ﴿in them﴾ is fronted.

Allah the Most High said: ﴿and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. Their sin, meaning the punishment that results from them, is greater than their benefit. Why? Because the punishment is in the Hereafter, while the benefit is in this world, and harm is in general greater in effect than benefit, because benefit is perfection and harm is deficiency. Perfection may be dispensed with, but deficiency, when does it get rebuilt once something is diminished or destroyed? For this reason He said: the sin is greater, for two reasons. The first: it is an otherworldly deficiency, and perhaps also a worldly one. The second: deficiency is a breach, while benefit is completion and perfection. Thus, when something is diminished, it is only restored with difficulty.

His saying: ﴿their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. Even if we suppose that the benefit in them is abundant and covers the worldly harm, we say: the otherworldly harm is more severe. Consider His saying: ﴿their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, when He said: ﴿in them is great sin and benefits for people﴾. Now we need a comparison, because we now have two things: sin and benefits. Which of them do we prefer?

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, clarified the preferred option by saying: ﴿their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. Then it becomes clear that weighing these two requires us to keep away from them, or from what is in them of benefits, as long as the sin is greater than the benefit. This is why many of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, refrained from wine and gambling when this verse was revealed, and they said: since the sin is greater than the benefit, why would we do it? But this does not necessitate prohibition; rather, it requires presenting the matter to the sensible person. And what does the sensible person prefer?

* A student: He prefers the benefits.
* The Shaykh: How? No, he does not prefer the benefits; he prefers avoiding the sin.

﴿And they ask you what they should spend﴾. Look: there are two questions in one verse. ﴿And they ask you what they should spend.﴾ Does the question here take one object or two objects? It was already established for us that if the question means requesting money, it takes two objects. Or is that not so? "Whoever asks Allah for something, He gives him." Look: (Allah) is the first, and (something) is the second. This applies when the question means requesting money. But when the question is an inquiry (istifham), it takes one object, and the second is introduced by the preposition (عن) 'an, and what do you say? You say: "I asked him about such-and-such." ﴿They ask you about wine﴾, ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:187), ﴿They ask you about menstruation﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:222), and the like. It governs one object, and the second is introduced by (عن) 'an. Sometimes the second is dispensed with by an interrogative clause, as in the verse before us: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾. The difference between its taking an interrogative clause and its taking the second object with a preposition is this: when it takes the second with the interrogative form, that form is the very wording of the questioner. It is exactly the questioner's own words. When it takes (عن) 'an, it may be the questioner's exact wording, or it may be something else. But if it comes in interrogative form, it is exactly the questioner's own wording. As if they said: "What should we spend, O Messenger of Allah? What should we spend?" Then Allah said: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, meaning: they say, "What should they spend?" Do you understand?

As for His saying: ﴿what they should spend﴾, we have already had a parallel to this structure. We explained that two possibilities are allowed: either (ما) or (ماذا) is a fronted object of (يُنْفِقُونَ) ﴿they spend﴾, or (ما) is an interrogative noun and (ذا) is a relative noun. On this second analysis, (ما) is the subject (mubtada'), and (ذا) is its predicate (khabar). On this analysis there must be a pronoun referring back to the relative, and here it is omitted. The sense is: "What is it that they spend?" Do you understand?

So in its grammatical analysis there are two possibilities. The first: we make (ماذا) a fronted object, or (ما) alone with (ذا) as an extra element, a fronted object of (ينفقوا) "they spend." In that case, does ﴿they spend﴾ need an object? No, because its object is this fronted element, so it needs no pronoun.

The second: we make (ما) an interrogative noun, a subject, and (ذا) a relative noun, its predicate. The clause ﴿they spend﴾ is the relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted. The sense is: "What is it that they spend?"

﴿And they ask you what they should spend﴾. A parallel to this wording has already passed us in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever good you spend is for the parents﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:215).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: That which is surplus.﴾ ﴿Say: That which is surplus.﴾ ﴿Al-'afw﴾ has two readings: the accusative (naṣb) and the nominative (raf'). The nominative is based on taking (mā) as an interrogative noun in the nominative as subject (mubtada'), and (dhā) as a relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl) serving as its predicate: "What is it that they spend?" The answer: al-'afw, meaning "it is the surplus." As for the accusative, it is based on taking (mādhā) as a fronted object (maf'ūl muqaddam), so that al-'afw means: "Say: spend the surplus," or "Say: you spend the surplus."

We said that the nominative or accusative depends on the parsing of the sentence preceding it, because the answer is built upon the question. Here, is the word (mā), whether relative or interrogative, the one that is explained by the word al-'afw or not? Because now the one asked about is: what is it that is spent? Answer! The surplus. So when it is an explanation of it, it takes its grammatical ruling: if you put (mādhā) in the accusative, then put al-'afw in the accusative, and if you put (mādhā) in the nominative, then put al-'afw in the nominative.

As for His saying ﴿al-'afw﴾: do not think that it means forgiveness of an aggression against you. Rather, the intended meaning of al-'afw is the excess, the surplus; that is, spend the surplus, i.e., what exceeds your need and necessity. This is because al-'afw is sometimes used to mean overlooking, as in His saying: ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ [al-Baqarah 109], and His saying: ﴿And whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾. It is also used to mean increase and abundance, as in His saying: ﴿Take what is given freely (al-'afw) and enjoin what is good﴾ [al-A'raf 199]; that is: take what is extra from people and what they bring, and do not demand the full measure of the right. From this is His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: «Let the beards grow (a'fū al-liḥā)» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5893), Muslim (259/52), from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both]. What is the meaning of al-'afw here, or of al-i'fā'? It is increase.

So His saying ﴿Say: al-'afw﴾ means: what exceeds your need. As for what falls within your need, do not spend it, because a person begins with himself, then with those he supports. For someone to go and give charity to a stranger while his own family are hungry is contrary to wisdom and also contrary to the Shari'ah. The cause of this is that some people think that spending on themselves and their families carries no reward and is not charity, but this is ignorance on their part, for your spending on yourself and your family is charity, and when it is charity, spending your wealth on relatives is more fitting than spending it on distant people.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you the signs, that you may reflect﴾. The parsing of ﴿thus (kadhālika)﴾?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...); that is, Allah makes clear to you a clarification like that clarification. The one indicated by ﴿that (dhālika)﴾ is what has preceded: the explanation of the ruling on wine and gambling and the explanation of what is spent. Allah the Exalted has explained to the utmost degree of clarity.

If you say: how did Allah explain it when there is no detail in it? That is, Allah did not detail the benefits, nor did He detail the sin? The answer is that Allah the Exalted indicated that the sin is great or abundant, and this is an explanation: the more a person drinks, the more sin he accumulates, and this is an explanation. The benefits also Allah summarized, because enumerating them has no benefit, and perhaps enumerating them would be an incitement for the shortsighted. Likewise His saying ﴿Say: al-'afw﴾ is clear and plain, with no difficulty in it: that is, what exceeds your need and necessity, and there is no ambiguity in it.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾. ﴿Yubayyinu﴾ means: it makes manifest. We say "bayyantuhu fatabayyana," meaning it became manifest, and from this is His saying: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ [al-Baqarah 187]; ﴿yatabayyana﴾ means: becomes manifest. So the meaning of ﴿Yubayyinu Allahu lakumu al-ayat﴾ is: He makes them manifest until they are clear and evident.

﴿Al-ayat﴾ is the plural of āyah, and we have often come across that the signs are divided into two types?
* Student: Legislative (shar'iyyah) and cosmic (qadariyyah).
* Shaykh: Yes, legislative and cosmic. Is there another term besides "cosmic" (qadariyyah)?
* Student: Kawniyyah.
* Shaykh: Kawniyyah. The legislative signs are what?
* Student: They are the created beings.
* Shaykh: The legislative signs are the created beings?!
* Student: The legislative signs are those in the books.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 219–221 (part 3 of 5):

* The Shaykh: (...) He explained them, neither the cosmic signs nor the legislative signs, He explained them with complete clarity. However, the legislative signs Allah the Most High explained in detail because of our need for worship, for we are in need of worship in general and in particular. For this reason the legislative signs came in detail, as Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away, and there was no bird flapping its wings in the sky except that he gave us knowledge of it."[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (21361), from the hadith of Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him).]] A man said to Salman al-Farisi: "Has your Prophet taught you everything, even how to relieve yourself?" He said: "Yes. He forbade us to face the qiblah when defecating or urinating, to clean ourselves with the right hand, and to clean ourselves with less than three stones, or with dung or bone."[[Narrated by Muslim (262/57), from the hadith of Salman (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

So the legislative signs are explained in detail, in the manner of detail that we need. As for the cosmic signs, the detail in them is by kinds or types, not by individuals. You find, for example, ﴿And of His signs is the night and the day﴾ [Fussilat 37]. In what? And what does it indicate to us? But search for yourselves and you will find much. ﴿And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [ar-Rum 22]. Of what is it a sign? Search and you will find out. And measure everything else by this. Allah the Most High made the cosmic signs general and summarized, and did not explain them in detail, because people do not need them in detail. Also, they are observable, perceptible signs, and people can know what is in them in detail according to their capacity.

As for His saying: ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ (la'alla) here expresses purpose. Its subject is the kaf (the pronoun "you"), and its predicate is the clause ﴿you reflect﴾. ﴿So that you may reflect﴾ — in my view this is a station (for pause), but reflect on what? Or about what?

He said: ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾. ﴿So that you may reflect upon this world﴾ — it is clear that reflection is upon this world. But His saying ﴿and the Hereafter﴾: do people reflect on the Day of Resurrection?

* The students: (...).

* The Shaykh: So you reflect on this world and the Hereafter in their affairs. The meaning is not that reflection takes place in the Hereafter; no, we reflect in this world, in our life, regarding what relates to the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter. This supports that the signs in His saying ﴿Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾ include both the legislative signs and the cosmic signs, because what relates to the matter of the Hereafter is mostly from the legislative signs, and what relates to the matter of this world is mostly from the cosmic signs. That is, he reflects upon their affairs.

When a person reflects upon this world, he finds it as Allah the Most High said: ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is only like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it﴾. Why did it mingle? Because of its abundance and its spreading; it spread and became intertwined, grew and became interwoven: ﴿and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, [such as] that which people and livestock eat. Until, when the earth takes on its adornment﴾, meaning its full beauty, ﴿and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it﴾, and that nothing remains but to harvest it and profit from it, ﴿there comes to it Our command by night or by day, and We make it as stubble, as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus 24]. And Allah the Most High said: ﴿Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion and adornment and boasting among you and competition in wealth and children — like a rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers; then it dries and you see it turned yellow; then it becomes debris. And in the Hereafter is severe punishment and forgiveness from Allah and approval﴾ [al-Hadid 20].

* * *

(...) ﴿And they ask you about the orphans﴾. ﴿They ask you﴾ — see, they are all joined by "and," as if they are successive questions. They first asked about wine and gambling, then they asked what they should spend. The connection between the two questions is very clear, because in wine and gambling there is the destruction of wealth without benefit, and in spending there is the expenditure of wealth with benefit. Then He said: ﴿And they ask you about the orphans﴾; for when you know the cause, you know the connection of the third question with the two before it.

﴿They ask you about the orphans﴾. The orphans (al-yatama) is the plural of yatim (orphan), which is one whose father has died before reaching maturity. It is derived from al-yutm, which means solitude. Since the orphan's father has died, he needs more care and attention; for this reason, the Qur'an has repeatedly enjoined concern for them. So His saying ﴿And they ask you about the orphans﴾: the reason for this is that when Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume into their bellies a fire﴾ [an-Nisa 10], and revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ [al-An'am 152], the two verses confused the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), so they began to set apart the food of the orphans and their own food, meaning that if food was cooked for the orphan, they made it for him alone. Such cooking either would spoil and be unfit to eat, or would be fit to eat but not in the most complete manner. They found this burdensome, and it was hard for them to make separate food for the orphans and separate food for themselves. They were also confused about whether they could mix their food with the food of the orphans, while Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume into their bellies a fire﴾. So they asked the Prophet (peace be upon him) about this, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic answered them with a response of the utmost eloquence, brevity and clarity, saying: ﴿Say: Improving their condition is best﴾. The word ﴿improving﴾ means that a person follows what is most beneficial for them in all matters, whether in upbringing or in property, and whether by commanding or by prohibiting. Whatever is an improvement for them is good.

As for the word "good" (khayr): is it a comparative of general preference or a restricted comparison? That is, is the meaning: "improving them is better than corrupting them," or is it an absolute goodness? The answer: it is absolute goodness. Improvement is good in every respect. This is like His saying: ﴿And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion, there is no blame upon them if they make settlement between them a settlement, and settlement is best﴾ [an-Nisa 128]. This sentence in its comprehensiveness, generality and clarity is like the second sentence.

﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾. This second sentence is part of what the answer contains, because I said earlier that the answer contains two sentences: the first is ﴿Say: Improving their condition is best﴾, and the second is ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾. That is: if you mix with them in eating and drinking and combine your food with theirs, they are not strangers to you; rather, are they your brothers in religion or in lineage?

* The students: In religion.

* The Shaykh: In religion, or in lineage, or in both together. It may be that a young brother whose father has died is your brother, so he is a brother to you in religion and in lineage. And it may be that the orphan is a son of your paternal uncle and he is a believer, so he is a brother to you?

* A student: In religion and lineage.

* The Shaykh: In religion. And he may be a brother to you but not a believer, so he is a brother to you in lineage.

The point is that they are our brothers, whether in religion, or in lineage, or in both. It is well known that a brother's mixing with his brother is something one does not shun or fear, so when you feel while mixing with them that they are your brothers, you will be keen not to mix with them except in a way that benefits them. For this reason He said: ﴿then they are your brothers﴾, and it is known that a brother is compassionate toward his brother.

By this the difficulty is lifted. Consider that Allah the Mighty and Majestic began with improvement before mixing, as if to indicate that if there is no improvement in mixing, then what is better?

* A student: Not mixing.

* The Shaykh: Not mixing. And if there is improvement in it, then it is good and they are your brothers; you cannot harm them in anything. So is mixing now permissible or not?

It is permissible; it is understood from His saying ﴿then they are your brothers﴾, as if you are branches of one root. But there must be improvement in it.

* A student: Shaykh, how is there hardship upon themselves (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...) ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾. His saying ﴿knows﴾: the knowing here is knowledge of recognition, because it takes only one object. Ibn Malik said:

For knowledge of recognition and for supposition of accusation, [it takes] a transitive to one object that is obligatory.

That is, He, glorified and exalted, recognizes the corrupter from the reformer in this matter and in others, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

His saying ﴿knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ did not say "knows the corrupter and the reformer," but said ﴿the corrupter from﴾, as if knowledge has been given the meaning of distinguishing, meaning: He knows him and distinguishes between this one and that one, and recompenses each person according to what he deserves, because distinguishing between this and that requires distinguishing between them also in reward and recompense.

His saying ﴿knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ includes religious and worldly corruption and religious and worldly reformation. Do you understand? Or is it only in worldly matters? It is in matters of religion and of this world. He, the Mighty and Majestic, knows the corrupter from the reformer among people. The words "corrupter" and "reformer" mean not only one who has actually corrupted, but also include one who intends corruption or reformation. Whoever's intention is corruption, Allah knows him, and he may not achieve his aim. There may be a person who is a corrupter who loves to corrupt people but is not able to; and there may likewise be a reformer, but he is prevented from his reform. But whoever Allah knows to have this or that intention, He will recompense him according to what he deserves.

Does this include the corrupter from the reformer in matters of orphans? It includes it, it is known; because the scholars of legal theory say that the cause of a revelation is decisive regarding what is meant, meaning that it is certain to be included. So when we say He knows the corrupter from the reformer in all affairs, the first thing included in this is what? Reform and corruption regarding orphans, because it is the cause, and what is a cause is certainly included in the generality.

Allah the Most High said: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He could have put you in difficulty. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾. (Law) is conditional; its condition is His saying ﴿if Allah had willed﴾. And its answer?

* A student: ﴿He could have put you in difficulty﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿He could have put you in difficulty﴾. And is the lam in the answer of law obligatory or frequent?

* A student: Frequent.

* The Shaykh: Frequent. Among its omissions is the Most High's saying: ﴿If We willed, We would have made it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 70]. Most often the lam is present in its answer.

﴿If Allah had willed, He could have put you in difficulty﴾, that is: He would have burdened you. In what? He would have burdened you in two matters regarding orphans:

The first: that you make their food and drink separate.

The second: that you measure that food and drink such that nothing remains that is subject to spoiling and decay. This is something hard for people, but Allah, in His mercy, negated that.

As for al-'ANAT, I said it means hardship. Among its uses is the Most High's saying: ﴿That is for whoever fears hardship among you﴾ [an-Nisa 25]. What is the meaning of 'anat? That is, hardship.

﴿If Allah had willed, He could have put you in difficulty; indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾. This sentence is a reason for what preceded. But is it a reason for what preceded in the last verse, ﴿And they ask you about the orphans﴾ to the end, or even for what preceded it from His saying ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾? Because all these verses are joined to one another by conjunction. It allows both, but if we take the generality, there is no obstacle.

As for al-'Aziz (the Mighty), it was previously explained to us that it is one of the names of Allah, and that it has three meanings:

* A student: Qadar (power, decree).

* The Shaykh: Qadar or qadari? What is the difference between them?

* The student: Qadr.

* The Shaykh: Qadr with a sukun, yes.

* The student: Qahr (dominion).

* The Shaykh: The might of qadr, the might of qahr, and the might of imtina' (inaccessibility). The might of qadr: no one comes near Him in the loftiness of His station. The might of qahr: no one overcomes Him; rather He is the Overcomer. The might of imtina': every deficiency and defect is withheld from Him; He is Mighty, no deficiency touches Him, Mighty, no humiliation touches Him, but He is the Dominant, the Subduer, glorified and exalted. Al-'Aziz means that He has a lofty rank and an exalted station.

As for al-Hakim (the Wise), it was previously explained to us that it is derived from al-hukm (judgment) and al-hikmah (wisdom), and that judgment is of two kinds: cosmic and legislative; and wisdom is of two kinds: final (teleological) and formal. That is, the thing being in this form is wisdom, and its purpose is also wisdom. So if you multiply two by two you get four: wisdom in the decree, its form and its purpose; wisdom in the law, its form and its purpose.

The reason for concluding the noble verse with might and wisdom is that He, glorified and exalted, holds judgment. If He willed, He would have put us in difficulty, because He is Mighty and possesses authority; and because He is Wise, He is the possessor of judgment: ﴿Surely, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf 54], ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ [al-An'am 57]. But together with His being Mighty and Wise, He is Forgiving and Merciful; for this reason He was gentle with His servants in this matter and in other matters: ﴿He has not placed upon you any difficulty in religion﴾ [al-Hajj 78].

Then the Most High said: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾. Nikah in its origin means joining and gathering, and from it is the poet's saying:

O you who would join al-Thurayya to Suhayl, may Allah preserve you, how can the two come together?

O you who would join al-Thurayya to Suhayl... (...)

That is: O you who wish to bring together al-Thurayya and Suhayl.

So His saying "how can they come together" shows that nikah in origin is joining and gathering. As for in the law, it is a contract to make lawful the enjoyment of a woman and the guarding of the private parts, and so on, and the other benefits connected with marriage. It is a contract on a woman made lawful for the purpose of the benefits that follow from marriage: guarding chastity, procreation, enjoyment, and other things.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says here: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾.

* A student: What is the meaning of (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, He is gathering them together. ﴿al-Mushrikat﴾ is the plural of mushrikah. The mushrikah or mushrik is one who ascribes a partner to Allah the Most High in what is specific to Him, whether in lordship, or in divinity, or in His names and attributes. So whoever takes a god with Allah to worship is a mushrik, even if he believes that Allah is the creator of the heavens and the earth. And whoever believes that there is a creator of the universe besides Allah, or one who independently has some part of the universe, or a helper of Allah the Most High in creation, in creating some part of the universe, is a mushrik. Three things: what are they?

* A student: Whoever takes a god with Allah. (...)

* The Shaykh: The creation of the universe, then he is a mushrik.

* A student: But did He forbid saying "mutasarrifan" (one who disposes)? (...)

* The Shaykh: Even the women of the People of the Book. If we take the commonly known usage, it does not include Jews and Christians, because: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists﴾ [al-Bayyinah 6], where He conjoined the polytheists to the People of the Book, which shows that they are?

* A student: Other than them.

* The Shaykh: Other than them. This difference bears on whether this verse remains general or is specified by the verse of al-Ma'idah, which will come, Allah willing. (...)

In this noble verse, Allah the Mighty and Majestic forbids...

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 219–221 (part 4 of 5):

(...) to idolatresses ﴿until they believe﴾: until they enter the Islamic religion and believe in Allah and His Messenger. A believing man may not marry idolatresses, as Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Mumtahanah: ﴿Do not return them to the disbelievers; they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. His saying ﴿Do not marry the idolatresses﴾ includes those who associate partners with Allah in His worship, or who associate partners with Him in His lordship. So whoever believes that there is a creator besides Allah, it is not permissible for a believer to marry her. And whoever worships something alongside Allah, it is not permissible for a believer to marry her.

His saying ﴿Do not marry the idolatresses until they believe﴾: Does this include the women of the Christians, who say that Allah is the third of three and make the Messiah, 'Isa son of Maryam, a god alongside Allah? The scholars have differed on this. The correct view is that the women of the People of the Book are not included, even if they claim that 'Isa is a god alongside Allah. This is because Allah the Exalted said in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them; and [lawful for you are] the chaste women from among the believers and the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you give them their compensation﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5]. Surah al-Ma'idah is among the last to be revealed. For this reason some scholars said that there is no abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one) in it; everything in it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated).
