* Among them: the affirmation of these two noble names and what they include of attributes: the Forgiving and the Forbearing.
* Among them: that the heart has earning and action, because of the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿for what your hearts have earned﴾. The hearts have actions and have speech. The speech of the heart is its affirmation and acknowledgment. The actions of the heart are its movements, such as love, intention, fear, dread, and what is similar to that.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿For those who swear abstinence from their wives is a waiting period of four months﴾ [al-Baqarah 226].

﴿For those who﴾ is the predicate placed first, and ﴿waiting period﴾ (*tarabbuṣ*) is the postponed subject. After this, Allah clarified the situation after this waiting period.

Regarding His saying ﴿For those who swear abstinence from their wives﴾: the *lām* here is either for permission or for entitlement. That is, they deserve a waiting period of four months, or a waiting period of four months is permitted for them.

His saying ﴿swear abstinence﴾ (*yu'lūn*): *al-īlāʾ* (vowing abstinence from marital relations) means swearing an oath. So the meaning of *yu'lūn* is "they swear."

His saying ﴿swear abstinence from their wives﴾: the *min* (from) has been said to mean *'an* (concerning), that is, they swear to abstain from having relations with their wives. It has also been said that it retains its original sense: he swore an oath from it, and so it clarifies the place of the oath, that is, the swearing.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿from their wives﴾, that is, from their spouses, because a man's wives are his women. A woman becomes his wife by the marriage contract alone, even if consummation has not occurred.

His saying ﴿waiting period﴾ (*tarabbuṣ*) means waiting (*intiẓār*). It is similar to patience (*ṣabr*) because it shares its letters, although it differs in order. Patience means restraining the self and waiting for it.

His saying ﴿a waiting period of four months﴾ begins from the time of their vow, not from the wife's demand of him. So they wait for a period of four months.

﴿And if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. ﴿They return﴾ means they went back to their wives after they had sworn abstinence from them.

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: that is, He forgives them for what they dared to do, namely swearing to deprive the wives of their rights. Because swearing not to have relations for a period of four months is a violation of the woman's right, since a man is obligated to live with his wife in kindness. It is not part of living with kindness for a person to swear that he will not have relations with his wife for four months. If he does so, he has exposed himself to punishment. But if he returns, Allah forgives him.

His saying ﴿And if they return﴾ includes whether they return before four months or after them. If they return before four months, the matter is clear. If they return after them, it is likewise, but their return must come immediately after, because after four months it is said to him: either you return or you divorce.

His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: in this is the affirmation of the two noble names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, the Forgiving and the Merciful. The Forgiving is the one possessing forgiveness, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd 6]. The Merciful is the one possessing mercy, as Allah said: ﴿And your Lord is the Free of need, the Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-An'ām 133].

Forgiveness (*maghfirah*) is: covering the sin and overlooking it. It is derived from *al-mighfar*, which is what is placed on the head during battle to protect against arrows. In the *mighfar* there is covering and protection.

His saying ﴿Merciful﴾ is derived from mercy, which entails tenderness, compassion, kindness, and averting calamities. So mercy is an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is other than kindness and other than the will to be kind. Rather, kindness and the will to be kind are among its requirements and implications.

﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾ [al-Baqarah 227], that is, they intended it with firm determination. That the resolve here means intention is indicated by the fact that it is transitive directly to *ṭalāq* (divorce) without a preposition. If "resolve" had its original meaning, it would have said "and if they resolve upon divorce," as some commentators explained, and they said: *ṭalāq* is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (*naṣb bi-naz' al-khāfid*), and the implied meaning is "and if they resolve upon divorce."

But it has already passed for us that the accusative by removal of the preposition is not consistent with *anna* and *an*. As for other than these two, it is restricted to what is heard (*al-samā'*). But we can get out of this by saying: ﴿if they resolve﴾ means they intended with firm determination, so the meaning of "resolve" here has included the meaning of "intend": ﴿if they resolve upon divorce﴾, that is, that they divorce their wives.

﴿Then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: that is, He hears their statements, including divorce, and knows their conditions, including separation from wives. In concluding this sentence with His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, there is an indication that Allah, Exalted, does not desire divorce. Because concluding it with these two names contains some form of warning, unlike the first. The first: He said ﴿And if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 226], and here He said ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 227]. And *al-samī'* (the All-Hearing) is one of the names of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and it has two meanings:

The first: answering.

The second: perceiving what is heard.

As for answering, an example is His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrāhīm 39], and the worshipper's saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." His saying ﴿the Hearer of supplication﴾ means the one who answers it. And "Allah hears whoever praises Him" means He responds. This is why it is followed by *lām* and not said as "Allah hears whoever (*man*)."

As for *al-samī'* in the sense of the one who perceives what is heard, and hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard, the scholars divided it into categories:

Among them is what is meant as a warning.

Among them is what is meant as reassurance.

Among them is what is meant as encompassing.

An example of what is meant as a warning: His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed Allah is poor, and we are rich"﴾ [Āl 'Imrān 181]. This is meant as a warning, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿We will record what they have said and their killing of the prophets without right﴾ [Āl 'Imrān 181].

An example of what is meant as reassurance: His saying to Mūsā and Hārūn: ﴿Do not fear. Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 46].

An example of what is meant as encompassing: His saying: ﴿Allah has heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [al-Mujādilah 1].

So the first hearing is among the active attributes (*ṣifāt fi'liyyah*), which is answering the supplication. The second meaning of hearing is among the essential attributes (*ṣifāt dhātiyyah*), because Allah has not ceased and will not cease to be characterized by hearing. But what is renewed is what is heard. As for Allah's hearing, Mighty and Majestic, He has not ceased and will not cease to be characterized by it.

His saying ﴿All-Knowing﴾: knowledge is perceiving a thing as it truly is with certainty. This is knowledge. If one does not perceive the thing, one is ignorant of it. If one perceives it other than as it is, one is also ignorant of it. If one perceives it without certainty, this is not knowledge, but is either supposition (*ẓann*), doubt (*shakk*), or delusion (*wahm*). So knowledge, then, what is knowledge?

**Student:** Perceiving a thing as it is, with certainty.

**Shaykh:** Yes, well done. So whoever does not perceive a thing is ignorant. Whoever perceives it other than as it is, is ignorant, but this is compound ignorance (*jahl murakkab*), that is, ignorant with compound ignorance. And if one perceives it as it is but without certainty, one is not knowledgeable. Rather, one is either doubtful, or supposing, or deluded. These are five categories. Whoever does not perceive it at all is in simple ignorance (*jahl basīṭ*). For example, someone asks you, "When was the Battle of Badr?" And you say, "By Allah, I do not know." Yes, what is this?

**Students:** Simple ignorance.

**Shaykh:** This is simple ignorance. Someone says to you: "There is a wound on one of the limbs of ablution. Is it permissible for me to perform tayammum (dry ablution) for it?" And you say, "I do not know."

**Student:** Simple ignorance.

**Shaykh:** Simple ignorance. A questioner asked: "When was the Battle of Badr?" He said: "The Battle of Badr was on Monday, corresponding to the fifteenth of Jumādā al-Ākhirah in the seventh year after the Hijrah."

**Student:** Compound.

**Shaykh:** How? Do you want more precision than this? He mentioned the day, the month, and the year to you?

**Student:** It is not as it is.

**Shaykh:** It is not as it is. This is called compound ignorance. Why compound? It is composed of being ignorant and being ignorant that one is ignorant. Ignorant, and ignorant that he is ignorant. So it is composed of two ignorances. Someone asks you: "When was the Battle of Badr?" He says: "I suppose it was in Ramadan, in the second year of the Hijrah." Is this knowledge? It is not knowledge, it is supposition.

Someone asks: "When was it?" He says: "By Allah, I have doubt about it, whether it was in the second year or the third year." It is not knowledge, it is doubt.

Now, the one who said the first, "I suppose it was in the second year," has another side: he suspects it was in something else. The second side, that he suspects it was in something else, is called delusion (*wahm*). The weaker side is called delusion.

Now, they say that a man called Tawma the Sage, whom I mentioned to you earlier, claimed that he was a wise scholar. He had a donkey, and the donkey said, singing:

*The donkey of the sage Tawma said: "If time were just, I would be the one riding."*
*Because I am simply ignorant, but my companion is compound-ignorant.*

That is, the donkey says: if time were just, I would be the one riding my companion, mounting on his back and placing loads on him and walking. But it is the opposite.

As for the story of this sage, the poet said about him:

*Whoever seeks the sciences without a shaykh will go astray from the straight path.*
*The sciences will become confused for him until he becomes more lost than Tawma the Sage.*
*He gave charity in daughters to men, desiring by that the gardens of bliss.*

Charity to the needy with money: is there merit in it?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** There is merit in it, and it may lead to entry into the gardens. But this one said: instead of going to give them money and having them toil in the sermon, "Come, we will give you daughters. We will give charity to these bachelors directly with daughters. What do you want, O Tawma?"

He said: "This is better. I want by that the gardens of bliss." And what do you say about these charities?

**Students:** Sin and ignorance.

**Shaykh:** This is fornication, may Allah protect us. This is fornication.

In sum, knowledge is perceiving a thing as it is, with certain and corresponding certainty. This is knowledge. The Lord, Mighty and Majestic, perceives things as they are. For this reason, some scholars said: if you were to say to a person while you are lying, "Allah knows that I did not do such-and-such," while you did it, then if you say this, you may become a disbeliever. Why?

He said: because if you say, "Allah knows that I did not do it," while you did it, you have attributed to Allah what? You have attributed to Him ignorance, that He does not know. This is disbelief. Although some people nowadays do this, saying, "Allah knows that I did not do it," and you did it. This is extremely dangerous.

He says: ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 227]. Then He said: ﴿For those who﴾... yes.

**Student:** We said: the waiting period is four months (...).

**Shaykh:** The *īlāʾ*.

**Student:** It does not begin from...

**Shaykh:** From the demand.

**Student:** The wives' demand. Does the verse indicate that?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it will come to us in the benefits.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And the divorced women﴾.

**Student:** Is it correct that whoever says this statement becomes a disbeliever?

**Shaykh:** If he intends the meaning, he is a disbeliever. But most people do not intend the meaning.

**Student:** ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾ O Shaykh, what is meant? Does it mean that your wives, if they are determined, divorce them? Is that its meaning?

**Shaykh:** No, it means if they intend divorce.

**Student:** Here "أرادوا" is better than (...).

**Shaykh:** It did not happen to him. Insha'Allah, the benefits will come to us.

He said, Exalted is He: ﴿وَالْمُطَلَّقَاتُ يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah 228]. ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ is general, or not?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** And what is the basis of its generality? It is from the relative nouns (al-asma' al-mawsulah). ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ is from the relative nouns.

**Student:** It is not like that.

**Shaykh:** It is not like that? Subhan Allah! It is correct, it is from the relative nouns.

**Student:** (The "ال")?

**Shaykh:** Good. This is the relative noun, and its clause (ṣilah, the relative clause that completes it):

*"A clear descriptive, the ṣilah of 'al' ∗∗∗ ...................*
*And man, ma and al equal what has been mentioned ∗∗∗ ...................."*

So it is a relative noun, because ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ is a relative noun, and so it is general, meaning every woman who has been divorced.

His words ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ are restricted by an exception, as will come, Insha'Allah: the woman who has not been consummated with, because the one not consummated with has no waiting period ('iddah).

﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ means they wait. His words ﴿بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ mean with what is in their selves; they are trusted regarding their own circumstances. Also, ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ means in a secure place in which she protects herself, which is the husband's house, as will be mentioned, Insha'Allah, in the chapter on divorce.

﴿ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾: here ﴿ثَلَاثَةَ﴾ is a substitute for the adverb of time, or it is a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), meaning a waiting of three periods. Is that so or not?

The word قُرُوء is the plural of قَرْء (qar', with a fatha). The scholars differed about the meaning of qar': is it menstruation (ḥayḍ) or the purity (ṭuhr)? There was a long and wide dispute. Whoever wishes to look into it will not find it explained as fully as it is in *Zad al-Ma'ad* by Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him.

The correct view is that qurū' means menstruation, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the mustaḥāḍah (a woman with irregular bleeding) that she should sit "for as long as her qurū' used to hold her back."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (325) with the wording: "But leave prayer for the days in which you used to menstruate," and Muslim (334/65) with the wording: "Remain for the period that your menstruation used to hold you back," from ʿĀʾishah; and Abu Dawud (297) and al-Tirmidhi (126) from Dinar with the wording: "She leaves prayer during the days of her aqrā'."]] That is, her menstrual periods. So "three qurū'" means three menstrual periods. How long is its duration usually?

Three months, based on the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿وَاللَّائِي يَئِسْنَ مِنَ الْمَحِيضِ مِنْ نِسَائِكُمْ إِنِ ارْتَبْتُمْ فَعِدَّتُهُنَّ ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْهُرٍ﴾ [al-Talaq 4].

But a woman may menstruate for less than that, and she may menstruate only for more than that. In fact, I heard that a woman would be pure for four months, and then her menstruation would come for one full month, a full month, as if (...). This is rare, but the usual case is once in every month.

He said: ﴿وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ﴾, meaning for these divorced women, ﴿أَنْ يَكْتُمْنَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ﴾. From where? From the pregnancy. It is not lawful for her to conceal the pregnancy. But how would she conceal the pregnancy? What is her purpose in concealing it? What is her purpose in concealing the pregnancy?

**Student:** Lengthening the 'iddah?

**Shaykh:** Lengthening the 'iddah, or shortening the 'iddah.

**Student:** To remarry.

**Shaykh:** Yes. But does she conceal what is in her womb and say that she menstruated three times, to lengthen the 'iddah, or to shorten it?

**Student:** On the contrary, to shorten it.

**Shaykh:** To shorten the 'iddah. Perhaps she conceals it in order to shorten the 'iddah so that she can be rid of her husband. So it is not lawful for her to conceal what Allah has created in the womb. Rather, it is obligatory upon her to make it clear, like anyone else who has dealings with another, for it is obligatory upon him to be clear and truthful, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not parted. If they are truthful and make it clear, their sale will be blessed for them. But if they lie and conceal, the blessing of their sale will be erased."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2097) and Muslim (1532/47), from Hakim ibn Hizam.]]

His words ﴿وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ أَنْ يَكْتُمْنَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ﴾: the womb is called a *raḥim* (womb) because it encloses the fetus and protects it. So it is like the relatives (dhawu al-arḥām), in that they gather around their kin, show compassion toward them, and are tender toward them.

His words ﴿فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ﴾: because the fetus, by the permission of Allah, is in the womb, not in the belly. And this womb, Allah has described it as a "firm lodging," as He said: ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهُ فِي قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ (٢١) إِلَى قَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ﴾ [al-Mursalat 21-22].

And Allah, Exalted is He, described it as being in three darknesses: ﴿يَخْلُقُكُمْ فِي بُطُونِ أُمَّهَاتِكُمْ خَلْقًا مِنْ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ فِي ظُلُمَاتٍ ثَلَاثٍ﴾ [al-Zumar 6]. They are: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (al-mashīmah), the membrane around the fetus. This membrane around the fetus, Glory be to the One who created it: it is a membrane of viscous water, very, very soft. Because the fetus, as you know, is a lump of flesh with no skin, and very delicate. If this water were not there, through which it moves with great movement, it would tear. But Allah made this water so that it moves in every direction until it grows. When it grows, by the permission of Allah, its face is toward its mother's back and its back is toward her belly. Look at the wisdom. Why?

Because if its face is toward the back, the back has strong bony vertebrae that protect it. If its back were toward the mother's belly, its back would bear the pressure, the shock, and the like. When the Great Lord wants to bring it out, it moves and turns over on its head. It turns over on its head in the womb, and it turns until it takes its path. For this reason, the scholars said: if a pregnant non-Muslim woman dies while carrying a Muslim child, where do we bury her?

They say: if a separate place can be found, she is buried in a separate place. If none is found, she is buried among the Muslims, out of respect for the one in her belly. But how is she buried?

They say: is she buried on her left side, facing away from the qiblah, or on her right side?

**Student:** The left.

**Shaykh:** On her left side, facing away from the qiblah, so that the child will be on the right side, facing the qiblah. See, Subhan Allah the Great.

**Student:** Is prayer offered over her, O Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** Yes, prayer is offered over what is in her belly. Prayer is offered over her, and the intention is made to pray over what is in her belly. And on this occasion I want to alert you: if a pregnant woman is brought for the funeral prayer and her child has had the soul breathed into it, it is obligatory that we intend the prayer for it and for its mother. If we pray only for the mother, it means we have not fulfilled the obligation of praying for what is in her belly. This is an issue I think many people do not know. Most people, when a pregnant woman is brought, pray only for this woman, although the scholars say: it is obligatory that the prayer be intended for the woman and for what is in her belly, both together.

**Student:** They do not tell us.

**Another student:** They do not tell the worshippers.

**Shaykh:** But sometimes, as with us here in al-Qassim, the pregnancy becomes apparent and the mother's belly is large.

**Student:** It is not necessary that there be a pregnancy.

**Shaykh:** Yes, perhaps there is no pregnancy.

In any case, the matter at least should be publicized. Even if her family alone intends it, that is sufficient. That is, it is not necessary that all the followers intend it; if one of the people intends it, it is enough.

He said: ﴿وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ أَنْ يَكْتُمْنَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾. If they do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, is there no sin upon them for concealing what Allah has created in their wombs?

**Students:** No, there is still sin upon her.

**Shaykh:** No? Then this condition is meant to incite and to stir up. That is: if she is truthful in that she believes in Allah and the Last Day, she will not conceal that.

﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: the Last Day is meant as the Day of Resurrection. But Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said that belief in it includes everything the Prophet (ﷺ) informed about that happens after death, so it includes the trial of the grave, the punishment or bliss of the grave, and everything that will happen.

﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: what is appropriate for belief in Allah here? Belief in what He has of attributes of grace, mercy and kindness, or belief in what He has of attributes of punishment, anger and retribution?

**Student:** All of them together.

**Shaykh:** But the woman, what do you notice now? Do you notice fear of Allah's punishment, so she does not conceal, or do you notice hope in His grace, so she makes it clear?

**Student:** Both?

**Shaykh:** Both. But usually, when it occurs here in the context of prohibition, the prohibited matters take into account the aspect of fear, unlike the commanded matters, for in commands the aspect of grace and hope is taken into account. As for prohibitions, usually the aspect of fear is taken into account.

﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: He mentioned the Last Day because there is no day after it. When people are resurrected on the Day of Resurrection, there is no more death in it; there is only eternal abiding, either in Paradise or in Hellfire.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: He mentioned the Last Day because belief in it moves a person to do acts of obedience and avoid what is forbidden, because he knows that before him is a day on which a person will be recompensed for his deeds. So you find him eager to do what is commanded and to abandon what is forbidden.

He said: ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ﴾. Bu'ūlah is the plural of ba'l, which is the husband, as Allah said about the wife of Ibrahim: ﴿أَأَلِدُ وَأَنَا عَجُوزٌ وَهَذَا بَعْلِي شَيْخًا﴾ [Hud 72], meaning: my husband.

﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ﴾, that is, the husbands of the divorced women, ﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in that time, or in that waiting period, and so on.

﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ﴾: from where? It is unrestricted. He did not say "more entitled to take them back than their own people," nor "than their families," nor "than other husbands," so that it is general. So the right belongs to the husband as long as she is in the waiting period: ﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾.

His words ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ﴾ referring back to ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ may give the impression that "the divorced women" is a general term used to mean a specific group. Which group is meant?

**Student:** The revocable ones (al-rajʿiyyāt).

**Shaykh:** The revocable ones, because the right of taking back applies only to them. As for the irrevocable ones (al-bawā'in), those irrevocable by annulment (faskh) or divorce, such as divorce for compensation or a triple divorce, their husbands have no right to take them back. This matter will be explained later in the benefits, Insha'Allah.

He said: ﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾. What does "that" refer to? The waiting period. ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾, ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾.

If someone says: how do you say it refers back to the waiting period? Where is the waiting period?

We say: because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) understood from His words ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾, and a verbal noun understood from the verb may be referred back to by a pronoun, as in His words: ﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8]: "Be just; it is nearer to righteousness." "It" means justice, which is understood from ﴿اعْدِلُوا﴾. Likewise, "that" refers to the waiting period understood from ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾.

But Allah made the husbands' right to take them back conditional. He said: ﴿إِنْ أَرَادُوا إِصْلَاحًا﴾ [al-Baqarah 228].

If they, that is the husbands, intend reconciliation in taking them back. If they intend harm, the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that they have no right in that, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There shall be no harming nor reciprocating harm."[[Reported by Ibn Majah (2341) and Ahmad (2865) from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Majah (2340) from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit.]] How would he intend harm to her?

He waits until she is near the end of her 'iddah, then takes her back. Then he divorces her. When he divorces her and her 'iddah begins again, he waits until she is near the end of her 'iddah. When she is near the end of her 'iddah, he takes her back, then divorces her again. Sharia has limited this now: there is no more taking back in that manner. But in the pre-Islamic period he would leave her until she was near the end, then take her back, then divorce her, then leave her until she was near the end, then take her back, then divorce her, and so on, until Allah limited that to three divorces.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ فَإِنْ فَاءُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾.

* From the noble verse we derive: the establishment of the ruling on *īlā'* (an oath of abstinence from one's wife, the *īlā'*), that the ruling is established, because Allah set four months for it.
* And from it: that *īlā'* is not valid except regarding a wife, based on His words: ﴿مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ﴾ ("from their wives").
* And from this verse: that the one who makes an *īlā'* (the *mūlī*) is given four months from his *īlā'*, based on His words: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ﴾.
  Here He said ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ﴾ and then said ﴿تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ﴾, which indicates that the beginning of the period is from when? From the *īlā'*.
* And from it: the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His mercy toward His servants in protecting rights, whose rights? The wife's, based on His words: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ﴾. In reality, just as it is a right of the wife, it is also in the husband's interest, so that the wife's right is not lost at his hand, and he does not become an oppressor.
* And from the noble verse: the *mūlī* is held in place when the four months have passed, and it is said to him: either you return, or you divorce, based on His words: ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا﴾ ("if they return") and His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا﴾ ("but if they are determined," [al-Baqarah 227]).
* And from it: divorce is in the hand of the husband, based on His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 227]. To whom does the pronoun refer? To ﴿الَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ﴾.
* And from it: the validity of *īlā'* from a wife not yet consummated with. From where? From His words: ﴿مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ﴾, and a woman becomes one's wife by the contract alone.
* And from it: that *īlā'* for four months or more is forbidden, based on His words: ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾, for forgiveness only occurs in exchange for what? A sin.
* And from the verse: a person's returning from what he is upon of disobedience is a cause of forgiveness. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾. A person's turning back from persisting in disobedience is one of the signs of repentance, so it is a cause of forgiveness.
* And from it: that Allah, Glory be to Him, does not love divorce, based on His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqarah 227].
* And also from the verse: divorce does not take effect merely by the completion of the period. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾.

Is it derived from the verse that if he refuses to return and refuses to divorce, he is compelled? If he says: "I will neither return nor divorce"?

**Student:** Divorce is pronounced against him.

**Another student:** He is compelled.

**Shaykh:** Let us see whether it is derived from the verse.

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** It does not contradict it. ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا﴾ and ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾. Is it derived from it that if he does not return and does not divorce, he is compelled?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Good. Who is ready to show me the basis of the indication?

**Student:** The threat, because at the end of the verse He said: ﴿فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾.

**Shaykh:** That is in the verse, that divorce is not beloved to Allah.

**Student:** Shaykh, here the two matters are an option, that is correct. The first matter: it is not possible for the ruler or anyone else to compel him to it. The second matter remains: either he divorces or he returns to her.

**Shaykh:** If he says, "I am not divorcing"? And Allah says: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾, so the matter is returned to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 225–230 (part 3 of 3):

* Student: We cannot compel him to return to his wife.
* Shaykh: That is not correct. Regarding return (ruju'), we can say: we do not compel him to return.
* Student: Nothing remains but divorce. If he does not pronounce divorce, and there is no third situation to which we can resort, we compel him to it.
* Another student: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a waiting period of four months﴾, so He specified four months. Within those four months, either we compel him to return, or she becomes divorced; he divorces her outright.
* Shaykh: And the evidence?
* Student: Allah the Exalted gave the believer a choice between two matters, and the context is one of detailed explanation. If there were a third situation, Allah would have mentioned it.
* Shaykh: And what is it? So its meaning is: if there were a third situation, namely compelling him to divorce, He would have mentioned it?
* Student: No, (...) he is obliged.
* Shaykh: They are working on it.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿If they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: wherever they return, they are compelled to divorce.
* Shaykh: ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾?
* Student: Apparently it is not derived from this.
* Shaykh: As we say, for example: Allah mentioned that he has only two states, so he is compelled to one of the two states, because Allah mentioned the two states for the sake of whose rights?
* Student: The wife's.
* Shaykh: The wife's. So if we say he may refrain from both, the wife's right is lost. In that case, the ruler's compelling him is an application of the wife's right, because if we said: if he wishes he divorces, and if he wishes he returns, and if he wishes he neither divorces nor returns, then the woman's right would be lost. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made this choice for him only for the sake of the wife's right, so it cannot be lost. For this reason the scholars said: if he refuses both, then the ruler either obliges him to divorce, detaining him until he divorces, and this was mentioned to us, I think, in the Qawa'id of Ibn Rajab, or the ruler obliges him, saying: you must divorce, and he detains him and disciplines him until he divorces, or the ruler divorces on his behalf.
This is clear, and this is the correct view, and it can be derived from the verse, because He only mentioned these two states to protect the wife's right, and this protection is indispensable. If there is no alternative to protecting it, he is compelled to one of the two matters. Fay'ah (return) may be difficult to compel, because it relates to a person's own inclination and desire, and one cannot be compelled to incline toward something. Yes.
* Student: Is it derived from the verse that whoever turns back from a sin, even without pronouncing repentance, has repented?
* Shaykh: Yes, this return, turning back from disobedience, is repentance.
* Student: I say: even if he did not say it?
* Shaykh: Even if he did not say: "I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him." Its mention is not among the conditions of repentance.
Also here: Can it be derived from the verse that ila' (oath of abstention from one's wife) is not valid from a minor?
* Student: It is not derived.
* Another student: He cannot.
* Shaykh: Or not?
* Student: It is general.
* Shaykh: How so? ﴿For those who swear abstention from their wives﴾, and the minor...
And His saying: ﴿and if they resolve upon divorce﴾. Can it be derived from this wording that divorce must be in a lawful manner?
Answer: Yes, because divorce here is unrestricted, and whatever is unrestricted in the Book and the Sunnah is understood according to its sharia meaning. Marriage, sale, prayer, fasting, and others are all used for what? For the legal (sharia) realities. Accordingly, divorce must be in a manner that is lawfully permitted.
If he divorces during menstruation, then according to the preponderant view, the divorce does not take effect. According to the view of the majority, it takes effect, but he is told: take back your wife, as the Prophet ﷺ commanded Abdullah ibn Umar to take back his wife.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5252) and Muslim (1471/11) from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "Command him to take her back; then, when she becomes pure, let him divorce her during her purity."]]
* From the noble verse is derived: the affirmation of four of Allah's names, namely: the Forgiving (al-Ghafur), the Merciful (al-Rahim), the All-Hearing (al-Sami'), and the All-Knowing (al-Alim), along with the attributes these names contain.
* From the noble verse is derived: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, from His saying: ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 227].
[[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]]

**Shaykh:** "Yu'akhidhu" (﴿يُؤَاخِذ﴾) has two possible meanings. The first is *mu'akhadha* in the sense of punishment. The second is *mu'akhadha* in the sense of obligating someone to make expiation (*kaffārah*). Both meanings are correct. So the idle oath (*laghw*) is one for which Allah does not hold you accountable, neither with sin nor with expiation. His saying ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths﴾ [al-Mā'idah 89]. What is *laghw*?

*Laghw* linguistically originally means "the thing that falls off." Here it means what a person did not intend in his heart. This is the meaning of *laghw* in oaths: what a person did not intend in his heart. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, Exalted, in Sūrat al-Mā'idah: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have deliberately bound by oaths﴾ [al-Mā'idah 89]. This indicates that the idle oath is the one whose what was not intended?

**Shaykh:** Its binding was not intended. This is the idle oath. An example: a person says in the course of his speech, "No, by Allah," "Yes, by Allah," "By Allah, I did not see so-and-so," "By Allah, that is not so about so-and-so," "Well, come with me." He says, "No, by Allah, I am not leaving," and then, "Man, he went away." Is there an expiation for him or not?

**Students:** No.

**Shaykh:** Why?

**Students:** Because he did not intend an oath.

**Shaykh:** Because he did not intend an oath. So if he did not intend an oath, there is no expiation for him, because of the noble verse: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what you have deliberately bound by oaths﴾. And because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the foundational hadith, the great principle of Islam: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155), with his wording, from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

So this is the idle oath. Some scholars said that the idle oath is when a person swears to something he believes to be so, and it turns out otherwise. This is what the Hanafi jurists (*al-Aḥnāf*, may Allah have mercy on them) mentioned. But the correct view is that it is not included in idle oaths, except that it has no ruling. It has no ruling not because it is idle, but because a person swore to something he believed to be so. And his oath on what was established in his soul as belief is truthful, or not?

**Student:** Truthful.

**Shaykh:** Truthful. Therefore, even if the matter is otherwise, there is nothing upon him. There is no difference whether this concerns the future or the past. In the past, for example, he says, "By Allah, so-and-so did not come," which is what he believed, but he had come. In the future, for example, he says, "By Allah, so-and-so will not come tomorrow," and he comes; or he says, "By Allah, he will surely come," and he does not come.

As for when he swears upon himself, intending to bind himself, for example, he says, "By Allah, I will surely do such-and-such tomorrow," and then he does not do it, then here there is expiation for him, if the conditions are fulfilled.

So there are two opinions among the scholars regarding the interpretation of *laghw*:

The first is that it refers to the oath whose binding was not intended. The second is what?

**Student:** That a person swears to what he thinks is likely, like this.

**Shaykh:** The second is that a person swears to something he thinks is likely to be as he swore, and then it becomes clear that it is otherwise.

He says: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾ [al-Baqarah 225]. Praise be to Allah, He did not say "what has settled in your hearts" or "what was." Rather, He said ﴿for what your hearts have earned﴾. This is a general principle. It is not only about oaths. Whatever the hearts have earned, we are held accountable for it. It is known that earning requires action. So merely what occurs in the heart does not make a person accountable, unless there is an action and movement of the heart. Then here expiation is required.

﴿But He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾ [al-Baqarah 225].

When He mentioned the idle oath and the binding oath, He concluded the verse with these two noble names. They are what?

**Student:** The All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.

**Shaykh:** No. The Almighty, the Most Great, or the All-Wise? The Almighty, the All-Wise, is that correct?

**Student:** No.

**Shaykh:** Beware of blind imitation. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾.

(...) with the idle oath; because of His saying: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the criterion is what is in the hearts, because of His saying: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾.
* Among its benefits: that swearing to what is likely in one's estimation does not make one accountable, even if it becomes clear that it was otherwise, according to one of the two interpretations. This is correct, because Allah does not hold us accountable except for what the hearts have earned, and what the hearts have earned is that in which one has deliberately committed sin.
* Among them: the affirmation of these two noble names and what they include of attributes: the Forgiving and the Forbearing.
* Among them: that the heart has earning and action, because of the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿for what your hearts have earned﴾. The hearts have actions and have speech. The speech of the heart is its affirmation and acknowledgment. The actions of the heart are its movements, such as love, intention, fear, dread, and what is similar to that.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿For those who swear abstinence from their wives is a waiting period of four months﴾ [al-Baqarah 226].

﴿For those who﴾ is the predicate placed first, and ﴿waiting period﴾ (*tarabbuṣ*) is the postponed subject. After this, Allah clarified the situation after this waiting period.

Regarding His saying ﴿For those who swear abstinence from their wives﴾: the *lām* here is either for permission or for entitlement. That is, they deserve a waiting period of four months, or a waiting period of four months is permitted for them.

His saying ﴿swear abstinence﴾ (*yu'lūn*): *al-īlāʾ* (vowing abstinence from marital relations) means swearing an oath. So the meaning of *yu'lūn* is "they swear."

His saying ﴿swear abstinence from their wives﴾: the *min* (from) has been said to mean *'an* (concerning), that is, they swear to abstain from having relations with their wives. It has also been said that it retains its original sense: he swore an oath from it, and so it clarifies the place of the oath, that is, the swearing.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿from their wives﴾, that is, from their spouses, because a man's wives are his women. A woman becomes his wife by the marriage contract alone, even if consummation has not occurred.

His saying ﴿waiting period﴾ (*tarabbuṣ*) means waiting (*intiẓār*). It is similar to patience (*ṣabr*) because it shares its letters, although it differs in order. Patience means restraining the self and waiting for it.

His saying ﴿a waiting period of four months﴾ begins from the time of their vow, not from the wife's demand of him. So they wait for a period of four months.

﴿And if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. ﴿They return﴾ means they went back to their wives after they had sworn abstinence from them.

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: that is, He forgives them for what they dared to do, namely swearing to deprive the wives of their rights. Because swearing not to have relations for a period of four months is a violation of the woman's right, since a man is obligated to live with his wife in kindness. It is not part of living with kindness for a person to swear that he will not have relations with his wife for four months. If he does so, he has exposed himself to punishment. But if he returns, Allah forgives him.

His saying ﴿And if they return﴾ includes whether they return before four months or after them. If they return before four months, the matter is clear. If they return after them, it is likewise, but their return must come immediately after, because after four months it is said to him: either you return or you divorce.

His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: in this is the affirmation of the two noble names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, the Forgiving and the Merciful. The Forgiving is the one possessing forgiveness, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Ra'd 6]. The Merciful is the one possessing mercy, as Allah said: ﴿And your Lord is the Free of need, the Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-An'ām 133].

Forgiveness (*maghfirah*) is: covering the sin and overlooking it. It is derived from *al-mighfar*, which is what is placed on the head during battle to protect against arrows. In the *mighfar* there is covering and protection.

His saying ﴿Merciful﴾ is derived from mercy, which entails tenderness, compassion, kindness, and averting calamities. So mercy is an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is other than kindness and other than the will to be kind. Rather, kindness and the will to be kind are among its requirements and implications.

﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾ [al-Baqarah 227], that is, they intended it with firm determination. That the resolve here means intention is indicated by the fact that it is transitive directly to *ṭalāq* (divorce) without a preposition. If "resolve" had its original meaning, it would have said "and if they resolve upon divorce," as some commentators explained, and they said: *ṭalāq* is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (*naṣb bi-naz' al-khāfid*), and the implied meaning is "and if they resolve upon divorce."

But it has already passed for us that the accusative by removal of the preposition is not consistent with *anna* and *an*. As for other than these two, it is restricted to what is heard (*al-samā'*). But we can get out of this by saying: ﴿if they resolve﴾ means they intended with firm determination, so the meaning of "resolve" here has included the meaning of "intend": ﴿if they resolve upon divorce﴾, that is, that they divorce their wives.

﴿Then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: that is, He hears their statements, including divorce, and knows their conditions, including separation from wives. In concluding this sentence with His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, there is an indication that Allah, Exalted, does not desire divorce. Because concluding it with these two names contains some form of warning, unlike the first. The first: He said ﴿And if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 226], and here He said ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 227]. And *al-samī'* (the All-Hearing) is one of the names of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and it has two meanings:

The first: answering.

The second: perceiving what is heard.

As for answering, an example is His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrāhīm 39], and the worshipper's saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." His saying ﴿the Hearer of supplication﴾ means the one who answers it. And "Allah hears whoever praises Him" means He responds. This is why it is followed by *lām* and not said as "Allah hears whoever (*man*)."

As for *al-samī'* in the sense of the one who perceives what is heard, and hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard, the scholars divided it into categories:

Among them is what is meant as a warning.

Among them is what is meant as reassurance.

Among them is what is meant as encompassing.

An example of what is meant as a warning: His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed Allah is poor, and we are rich"﴾ [Āl 'Imrān 181]. This is meant as a warning, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿We will record what they have said and their killing of the prophets without right﴾ [Āl 'Imrān 181].

An example of what is meant as reassurance: His saying to Mūsā and Hārūn: ﴿Do not fear. Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 46].

An example of what is meant as encompassing: His saying: ﴿Allah has heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [al-Mujādilah 1].

So the first hearing is among the active attributes (*ṣifāt fi'liyyah*), which is answering the supplication. The second meaning of hearing is among the essential attributes (*ṣifāt dhātiyyah*), because Allah has not ceased and will not cease to be characterized by hearing. But what is renewed is what is heard. As for Allah's hearing, Mighty and Majestic, He has not ceased and will not cease to be characterized by it.

His saying ﴿All-Knowing﴾: knowledge is perceiving a thing as it truly is with certainty. This is knowledge. If one does not perceive the thing, one is ignorant of it. If one perceives it other than as it is, one is also ignorant of it. If one perceives it without certainty, this is not knowledge, but is either supposition (*ẓann*), doubt (*shakk*), or delusion (*wahm*). So knowledge, then, what is knowledge?

**Student:** Perceiving a thing as it is, with certainty.

**Shaykh:** Yes, well done. So whoever does not perceive a thing is ignorant. Whoever perceives it other than as it is, is ignorant, but this is compound ignorance (*jahl murakkab*), that is, ignorant with compound ignorance. And if one perceives it as it is but without certainty, one is not knowledgeable. Rather, one is either doubtful, or supposing, or deluded. These are five categories. Whoever does not perceive it at all is in simple ignorance (*jahl basīṭ*). For example, someone asks you, "When was the Battle of Badr?" And you say, "By Allah, I do not know." Yes, what is this?

**Students:** Simple ignorance.

**Shaykh:** This is simple ignorance. Someone says to you: "There is a wound on one of the limbs of ablution. Is it permissible for me to perform tayammum (dry ablution) for it?" And you say, "I do not know."

**Student:** Simple ignorance.

**Shaykh:** Simple ignorance. A questioner asked: "When was the Battle of Badr?" He said: "The Battle of Badr was on Monday, corresponding to the fifteenth of Jumādā al-Ākhirah in the seventh year after the Hijrah."

**Student:** Compound.

**Shaykh:** How? Do you want more precision than this? He mentioned the day, the month, and the year to you?

**Student:** It is not as it is.

**Shaykh:** It is not as it is. This is called compound ignorance. Why compound? It is composed of being ignorant and being ignorant that one is ignorant. Ignorant, and ignorant that he is ignorant. So it is composed of two ignorances. Someone asks you: "When was the Battle of Badr?" He says: "I suppose it was in Ramadan, in the second year of the Hijrah." Is this knowledge? It is not knowledge, it is supposition.

Someone asks: "When was it?" He says: "By Allah, I have doubt about it, whether it was in the second year or the third year." It is not knowledge, it is doubt.

Now, the one who said the first, "I suppose it was in the second year," has another side: he suspects it was in something else. The second side, that he suspects it was in something else, is called delusion (*wahm*). The weaker side is called delusion.

Now, they say that a man called Tawma the Sage, whom I mentioned to you earlier, claimed that he was a wise scholar. He had a donkey, and the donkey said, singing:

*The donkey of the sage Tawma said: "If time were just, I would be the one riding."*
*Because I am simply ignorant, but my companion is compound-ignorant.*

That is, the donkey says: if time were just, I would be the one riding my companion, mounting on his back and placing loads on him and walking. But it is the opposite.

As for the story of this sage, the poet said about him:

*Whoever seeks the sciences without a shaykh will go astray from the straight path.*
*The sciences will become confused for him until he becomes more lost than Tawma the Sage.*
*He gave charity in daughters to men, desiring by that the gardens of bliss.*

Charity to the needy with money: is there merit in it?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** There is merit in it, and it may lead to entry into the gardens. But this one said: instead of going to give them money and having them toil in the sermon, "Come, we will give you daughters. We will give charity to these bachelors directly with daughters. What do you want, O Tawma?"

He said: "This is better. I want by that the gardens of bliss." And what do you say about these charities?

**Students:** Sin and ignorance.

**Shaykh:** This is fornication, may Allah protect us. This is fornication.

In sum, knowledge is perceiving a thing as it is, with certain and corresponding certainty. This is knowledge. The Lord, Mighty and Majestic, perceives things as they are. For this reason, some scholars said: if you were to say to a person while you are lying, "Allah knows that I did not do such-and-such," while you did it, then if you say this, you may become a disbeliever. Why?

He said: because if you say, "Allah knows that I did not do it," while you did it, you have attributed to Allah what? You have attributed to Him ignorance, that He does not know. This is disbelief. Although some people nowadays do this, saying, "Allah knows that I did not do it," and you did it. This is extremely dangerous.

He says: ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 227]. Then He said: ﴿For those who﴾... yes.

**Student:** We said: the waiting period is four months (...).

**Shaykh:** The *īlāʾ*.

**Student:** It does not begin from...

**Shaykh:** From the demand.

**Student:** The wives' demand. Does the verse indicate that?

**Shaykh:** Yes, it will come to us in the benefits.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And the divorced women﴾.

**Student:** Is it correct that whoever says this statement becomes a disbeliever?

**Shaykh:** If he intends the meaning, he is a disbeliever. But most people do not intend the meaning.

**Student:** ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾ O Shaykh, what is meant? Does it mean that your wives, if they are determined, divorce them? Is that its meaning?

**Shaykh:** No, it means if they intend divorce.

**Student:** Here "أرادوا" is better than (...).

**Shaykh:** It did not happen to him. Insha'Allah, the benefits will come to us.

He said, Exalted is He: ﴿وَالْمُطَلَّقَاتُ يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah 228]. ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ is general, or not?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** And what is the basis of its generality? It is from the relative nouns (al-asma' al-mawsulah). ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ is from the relative nouns.

**Student:** It is not like that.

**Shaykh:** It is not like that? Subhan Allah! It is correct, it is from the relative nouns.

**Student:** (The "ال")?

**Shaykh:** Good. This is the relative noun, and its clause (ṣilah, the relative clause that completes it):

*"A clear descriptive, the ṣilah of 'al' ∗∗∗ ...................*
*And man, ma and al equal what has been mentioned ∗∗∗ ...................."*

So it is a relative noun, because ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ is a relative noun, and so it is general, meaning every woman who has been divorced.

His words ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ are restricted by an exception, as will come, Insha'Allah: the woman who has not been consummated with, because the one not consummated with has no waiting period ('iddah).

﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ means they wait. His words ﴿بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ mean with what is in their selves; they are trusted regarding their own circumstances. Also, ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ﴾ means in a secure place in which she protects herself, which is the husband's house, as will be mentioned, Insha'Allah, in the chapter on divorce.

﴿ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾: here ﴿ثَلَاثَةَ﴾ is a substitute for the adverb of time, or it is a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), meaning a waiting of three periods. Is that so or not?

The word قُرُوء is the plural of قَرْء (qar', with a fatha). The scholars differed about the meaning of qar': is it menstruation (ḥayḍ) or the purity (ṭuhr)? There was a long and wide dispute. Whoever wishes to look into it will not find it explained as fully as it is in *Zad al-Ma'ad* by Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him.

The correct view is that qurū' means menstruation, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the mustaḥāḍah (a woman with irregular bleeding) that she should sit "for as long as her qurū' used to hold her back."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (325) with the wording: "But leave prayer for the days in which you used to menstruate," and Muslim (334/65) with the wording: "Remain for the period that your menstruation used to hold you back," from ʿĀʾishah; and Abu Dawud (297) and al-Tirmidhi (126) from Dinar with the wording: "She leaves prayer during the days of her aqrā'."]] That is, her menstrual periods. So "three qurū'" means three menstrual periods. How long is its duration usually?

Three months, based on the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿وَاللَّائِي يَئِسْنَ مِنَ الْمَحِيضِ مِنْ نِسَائِكُمْ إِنِ ارْتَبْتُمْ فَعِدَّتُهُنَّ ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْهُرٍ﴾ [al-Talaq 4].

But a woman may menstruate for less than that, and she may menstruate only for more than that. In fact, I heard that a woman would be pure for four months, and then her menstruation would come for one full month, a full month, as if (...). This is rare, but the usual case is once in every month.

He said: ﴿وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ﴾, meaning for these divorced women, ﴿أَنْ يَكْتُمْنَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ﴾. From where? From the pregnancy. It is not lawful for her to conceal the pregnancy. But how would she conceal the pregnancy? What is her purpose in concealing it? What is her purpose in concealing the pregnancy?

**Student:** Lengthening the 'iddah?

**Shaykh:** Lengthening the 'iddah, or shortening the 'iddah.

**Student:** To remarry.

**Shaykh:** Yes. But does she conceal what is in her womb and say that she menstruated three times, to lengthen the 'iddah, or to shorten it?

**Student:** On the contrary, to shorten it.

**Shaykh:** To shorten the 'iddah. Perhaps she conceals it in order to shorten the 'iddah so that she can be rid of her husband. So it is not lawful for her to conceal what Allah has created in the womb. Rather, it is obligatory upon her to make it clear, like anyone else who has dealings with another, for it is obligatory upon him to be clear and truthful, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not parted. If they are truthful and make it clear, their sale will be blessed for them. But if they lie and conceal, the blessing of their sale will be erased."[[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2097) and Muslim (1532/47), from Hakim ibn Hizam.]]

His words ﴿وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ أَنْ يَكْتُمْنَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ﴾: the womb is called a *raḥim* (womb) because it encloses the fetus and protects it. So it is like the relatives (dhawu al-arḥām), in that they gather around their kin, show compassion toward them, and are tender toward them.

His words ﴿فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ﴾: because the fetus, by the permission of Allah, is in the womb, not in the belly. And this womb, Allah has described it as a "firm lodging," as He said: ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهُ فِي قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ (٢١) إِلَى قَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ﴾ [al-Mursalat 21-22].

And Allah, Exalted is He, described it as being in three darknesses: ﴿يَخْلُقُكُمْ فِي بُطُونِ أُمَّهَاتِكُمْ خَلْقًا مِنْ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ فِي ظُلُمَاتٍ ثَلَاثٍ﴾ [al-Zumar 6]. They are: the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta (al-mashīmah), the membrane around the fetus. This membrane around the fetus, Glory be to the One who created it: it is a membrane of viscous water, very, very soft. Because the fetus, as you know, is a lump of flesh with no skin, and very delicate. If this water were not there, through which it moves with great movement, it would tear. But Allah made this water so that it moves in every direction until it grows. When it grows, by the permission of Allah, its face is toward its mother's back and its back is toward her belly. Look at the wisdom. Why?

Because if its face is toward the back, the back has strong bony vertebrae that protect it. If its back were toward the mother's belly, its back would bear the pressure, the shock, and the like. When the Great Lord wants to bring it out, it moves and turns over on its head. It turns over on its head in the womb, and it turns until it takes its path. For this reason, the scholars said: if a pregnant non-Muslim woman dies while carrying a Muslim child, where do we bury her?

They say: if a separate place can be found, she is buried in a separate place. If none is found, she is buried among the Muslims, out of respect for the one in her belly. But how is she buried?

They say: is she buried on her left side, facing away from the qiblah, or on her right side?

**Student:** The left.

**Shaykh:** On her left side, facing away from the qiblah, so that the child will be on the right side, facing the qiblah. See, Subhan Allah the Great.

**Student:** Is prayer offered over her, O Shaykh?

**Shaykh:** Yes, prayer is offered over what is in her belly. Prayer is offered over her, and the intention is made to pray over what is in her belly. And on this occasion I want to alert you: if a pregnant woman is brought for the funeral prayer and her child has had the soul breathed into it, it is obligatory that we intend the prayer for it and for its mother. If we pray only for the mother, it means we have not fulfilled the obligation of praying for what is in her belly. This is an issue I think many people do not know. Most people, when a pregnant woman is brought, pray only for this woman, although the scholars say: it is obligatory that the prayer be intended for the woman and for what is in her belly, both together.

**Student:** They do not tell us.

**Another student:** They do not tell the worshippers.

**Shaykh:** But sometimes, as with us here in al-Qassim, the pregnancy becomes apparent and the mother's belly is large.

**Student:** It is not necessary that there be a pregnancy.

**Shaykh:** Yes, perhaps there is no pregnancy.

In any case, the matter at least should be publicized. Even if her family alone intends it, that is sufficient. That is, it is not necessary that all the followers intend it; if one of the people intends it, it is enough.

He said: ﴿وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَهُنَّ أَنْ يَكْتُمْنَ مَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ فِي أَرْحَامِهِنَّ إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾. If they do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, is there no sin upon them for concealing what Allah has created in their wombs?

**Students:** No, there is still sin upon her.

**Shaykh:** No? Then this condition is meant to incite and to stir up. That is: if she is truthful in that she believes in Allah and the Last Day, she will not conceal that.

﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: the Last Day is meant as the Day of Resurrection. But Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said that belief in it includes everything the Prophet (ﷺ) informed about that happens after death, so it includes the trial of the grave, the punishment or bliss of the grave, and everything that will happen.

﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: what is appropriate for belief in Allah here? Belief in what He has of attributes of grace, mercy and kindness, or belief in what He has of attributes of punishment, anger and retribution?

**Student:** All of them together.

**Shaykh:** But the woman, what do you notice now? Do you notice fear of Allah's punishment, so she does not conceal, or do you notice hope in His grace, so she makes it clear?

**Student:** Both?

**Shaykh:** Both. But usually, when it occurs here in the context of prohibition, the prohibited matters take into account the aspect of fear, unlike the commanded matters, for in commands the aspect of grace and hope is taken into account. As for prohibitions, usually the aspect of fear is taken into account.

﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: He mentioned the Last Day because there is no day after it. When people are resurrected on the Day of Resurrection, there is no more death in it; there is only eternal abiding, either in Paradise or in Hellfire.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿إِنْ كُنَّ يُؤْمِنَّ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ﴾: He mentioned the Last Day because belief in it moves a person to do acts of obedience and avoid what is forbidden, because he knows that before him is a day on which a person will be recompensed for his deeds. So you find him eager to do what is commanded and to abandon what is forbidden.

He said: ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ﴾. Bu'ūlah is the plural of ba'l, which is the husband, as Allah said about the wife of Ibrahim: ﴿أَأَلِدُ وَأَنَا عَجُوزٌ وَهَذَا بَعْلِي شَيْخًا﴾ [Hud 72], meaning: my husband.

﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ﴾, that is, the husbands of the divorced women, ﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾, that is, in that time, or in that waiting period, and so on.

﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ﴾: from where? It is unrestricted. He did not say "more entitled to take them back than their own people," nor "than their families," nor "than other husbands," so that it is general. So the right belongs to the husband as long as she is in the waiting period: ﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾.

His words ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ﴾ referring back to ﴿الْمُطَلَّقَاتُ﴾ may give the impression that "the divorced women" is a general term used to mean a specific group. Which group is meant?

**Student:** The revocable ones (al-rajʿiyyāt).

**Shaykh:** The revocable ones, because the right of taking back applies only to them. As for the irrevocable ones (al-bawā'in), those irrevocable by annulment (faskh) or divorce, such as divorce for compensation or a triple divorce, their husbands have no right to take them back. This matter will be explained later in the benefits, Insha'Allah.

He said: ﴿أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾. What does "that" refer to? The waiting period. ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنْفُسِهِنَّ ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ﴾, ﴿وَبُعُولَتُهُنَّ أَحَقُّ بِرَدِّهِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾.

If someone says: how do you say it refers back to the waiting period? Where is the waiting period?

We say: because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) understood from His words ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾, and a verbal noun understood from the verb may be referred back to by a pronoun, as in His words: ﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8]: "Be just; it is nearer to righteousness." "It" means justice, which is understood from ﴿اعْدِلُوا﴾. Likewise, "that" refers to the waiting period understood from ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾.

But Allah made the husbands' right to take them back conditional. He said: ﴿إِنْ أَرَادُوا إِصْلَاحًا﴾ [al-Baqarah 228].

If they, that is the husbands, intend reconciliation in taking them back. If they intend harm, the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that they have no right in that, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There shall be no harming nor reciprocating harm."[[Reported by Ibn Majah (2341) and Ahmad (2865) from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Majah (2340) from ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit.]] How would he intend harm to her?

He waits until she is near the end of her 'iddah, then takes her back. Then he divorces her. When he divorces her and her 'iddah begins again, he waits until she is near the end of her 'iddah. When she is near the end of her 'iddah, he takes her back, then divorces her again. Sharia has limited this now: there is no more taking back in that manner. But in the pre-Islamic period he would leave her until she was near the end, then take her back, then divorce her, then leave her until she was near the end, then take her back, then divorce her, and so on, until Allah limited that to three divorces.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ فَإِنْ فَاءُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾.

* From the noble verse we derive: the establishment of the ruling on *īlā'* (an oath of abstinence from one's wife, the *īlā'*), that the ruling is established, because Allah set four months for it.
* And from it: that *īlā'* is not valid except regarding a wife, based on His words: ﴿مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ﴾ ("from their wives").
* And from this verse: that the one who makes an *īlā'* (the *mūlī*) is given four months from his *īlā'*, based on His words: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ﴾.
  Here He said ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ﴾ and then said ﴿تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ﴾, which indicates that the beginning of the period is from when? From the *īlā'*.
* And from it: the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His mercy toward His servants in protecting rights, whose rights? The wife's, based on His words: ﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ﴾. In reality, just as it is a right of the wife, it is also in the husband's interest, so that the wife's right is not lost at his hand, and he does not become an oppressor.
* And from the noble verse: the *mūlī* is held in place when the four months have passed, and it is said to him: either you return, or you divorce, based on His words: ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا﴾ ("if they return") and His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا﴾ ("but if they are determined," [al-Baqarah 227]).
* And from it: divorce is in the hand of the husband, based on His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 227]. To whom does the pronoun refer? To ﴿الَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ﴾.
* And from it: the validity of *īlā'* from a wife not yet consummated with. From where? From His words: ﴿مِنْ نِسَائِهِمْ﴾, and a woman becomes one's wife by the contract alone.
* And from it: that *īlā'* for four months or more is forbidden, based on His words: ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾, for forgiveness only occurs in exchange for what? A sin.
* And from the verse: a person's returning from what he is upon of disobedience is a cause of forgiveness. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾. A person's turning back from persisting in disobedience is one of the signs of repentance, so it is a cause of forgiveness.
* And from it: that Allah, Glory be to Him, does not love divorce, based on His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqarah 227].
* And also from the verse: divorce does not take effect merely by the completion of the period. From where is this taken? From His words: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾.

Is it derived from the verse that if he refuses to return and refuses to divorce, he is compelled? If he says: "I will neither return nor divorce"?

**Student:** Divorce is pronounced against him.

**Another student:** He is compelled.

**Shaykh:** Let us see whether it is derived from the verse.

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** It does not contradict it. ﴿فَإِنْ فَاءُوا﴾ and ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾. Is it derived from it that if he does not return and does not divorce, he is compelled?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Good. Who is ready to show me the basis of the indication?

**Student:** The threat, because at the end of the verse He said: ﴿فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾.

**Shaykh:** That is in the verse, that divorce is not beloved to Allah.

**Student:** Shaykh, here the two matters are an option, that is correct. The first matter: it is not possible for the ruler or anyone else to compel him to it. The second matter remains: either he divorces or he returns to her.

**Shaykh:** If he says, "I am not divorcing"? And Allah says: ﴿وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ﴾, so the matter is returned to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 225–230 (part 3 of 3):

* Student: We cannot compel him to return to his wife.
* Shaykh: That is not correct. Regarding return (ruju'), we can say: we do not compel him to return.
* Student: Nothing remains but divorce. If he does not pronounce divorce, and there is no third situation to which we can resort, we compel him to it.
* Another student: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿a waiting period of four months﴾, so He specified four months. Within those four months, either we compel him to return, or she becomes divorced; he divorces her outright.
* Shaykh: And the evidence?
* Student: Allah the Exalted gave the believer a choice between two matters, and the context is one of detailed explanation. If there were a third situation, Allah would have mentioned it.
* Shaykh: And what is it? So its meaning is: if there were a third situation, namely compelling him to divorce, He would have mentioned it?
* Student: No, (...) he is obliged.
* Shaykh: They are working on it.
* Student: From His saying: ﴿If they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: wherever they return, they are compelled to divorce.
* Shaykh: ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾?
* Student: Apparently it is not derived from this.
* Shaykh: As we say, for example: Allah mentioned that he has only two states, so he is compelled to one of the two states, because Allah mentioned the two states for the sake of whose rights?
* Student: The wife's.
* Shaykh: The wife's. So if we say he may refrain from both, the wife's right is lost. In that case, the ruler's compelling him is an application of the wife's right, because if we said: if he wishes he divorces, and if he wishes he returns, and if he wishes he neither divorces nor returns, then the woman's right would be lost. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made this choice for him only for the sake of the wife's right, so it cannot be lost. For this reason the scholars said: if he refuses both, then the ruler either obliges him to divorce, detaining him until he divorces, and this was mentioned to us, I think, in the Qawa'id of Ibn Rajab, or the ruler obliges him, saying: you must divorce, and he detains him and disciplines him until he divorces, or the ruler divorces on his behalf.
This is clear, and this is the correct view, and it can be derived from the verse, because He only mentioned these two states to protect the wife's right, and this protection is indispensable. If there is no alternative to protecting it, he is compelled to one of the two matters. Fay'ah (return) may be difficult to compel, because it relates to a person's own inclination and desire, and one cannot be compelled to incline toward something. Yes.
* Student: Is it derived from the verse that whoever turns back from a sin, even without pronouncing repentance, has repented?
* Shaykh: Yes, this return, turning back from disobedience, is repentance.
* Student: I say: even if he did not say it?
* Shaykh: Even if he did not say: "I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him." Its mention is not among the conditions of repentance.
Also here: Can it be derived from the verse that ila' (oath of abstention from one's wife) is not valid from a minor?
* Student: It is not derived.
* Another student: He cannot.
* Shaykh: Or not?
* Student: It is general.
* Shaykh: How so? ﴿For those who swear abstention from their wives﴾, and the minor...
And His saying: ﴿and if they resolve upon divorce﴾. Can it be derived from this wording that divorce must be in a lawful manner?
Answer: Yes, because divorce here is unrestricted, and whatever is unrestricted in the Book and the Sunnah is understood according to its sharia meaning. Marriage, sale, prayer, fasting, and others are all used for what? For the legal (sharia) realities. Accordingly, divorce must be in a manner that is lawfully permitted.
If he divorces during menstruation, then according to the preponderant view, the divorce does not take effect. According to the view of the majority, it takes effect, but he is told: take back your wife, as the Prophet ﷺ commanded Abdullah ibn Umar to take back his wife.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5252) and Muslim (1471/11) from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "Command him to take her back; then, when she becomes pure, let him divorce her during her purity."]]
* From the noble verse is derived: the affirmation of four of Allah's names, namely: the Forgiving (al-Ghafur), the Merciful (al-Rahim), the All-Hearing (al-Sami'), and the All-Knowing (al-Alim), along with the attributes these names contain.
* From the noble verse is derived: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, from His saying: ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 227].
[[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]]

**Shaykh:** "Yu'akhidhu" (﴿يُؤَاخِذ﴾) has two possible meanings. The first is *mu'akhadha* in the sense of punishment. The second is *mu'akhadha* in the sense of obligating someone to make expiation (*kaffārah*). Both meanings are correct. So the idle oath (*laghw*) is one for which Allah does not hold you accountable, neither with sin nor with expiation. His saying ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths﴾ [al-Mā'idah 89]. What is *laghw*?

*Laghw* linguistically originally means "the thing that falls off." Here it means what a person did not intend in his heart. This is the meaning of *laghw* in oaths: what a person did not intend in his heart. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, Exalted, in Sūrat al-Mā'idah: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have deliberately bound by oaths﴾ [al-Mā'idah 89]. This indicates that the idle oath is the one whose what was not intended?

**Shaykh:** Its binding was not intended. This is the idle oath. An example: a person says in the course of his speech, "No, by Allah," "Yes, by Allah," "By Allah, I did not see so-and-so," "By Allah, that is not so about so-and-so," "Well, come with me." He says, "No, by Allah, I am not leaving," and then, "Man, he went away." Is there an expiation for him or not?

**Students:** No.

**Shaykh:** Why?

**Students:** Because he did not intend an oath.

**Shaykh:** Because he did not intend an oath. So if he did not intend an oath, there is no expiation for him, because of the noble verse: ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what you have deliberately bound by oaths﴾. And because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the foundational hadith, the great principle of Islam: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1) and Muslim (1907/155), with his wording, from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

So this is the idle oath. Some scholars said that the idle oath is when a person swears to something he believes to be so, and it turns out otherwise. This is what the Hanafi jurists (*al-Aḥnāf*, may Allah have mercy on them) mentioned. But the correct view is that it is not included in idle oaths, except that it has no ruling. It has no ruling not because it is idle, but because a person swore to something he believed to be so. And his oath on what was established in his soul as belief is truthful, or not?

**Student:** Truthful.

**Shaykh:** Truthful. Therefore, even if the matter is otherwise, there is nothing upon him. There is no difference whether this concerns the future or the past. In the past, for example, he says, "By Allah, so-and-so did not come," which is what he believed, but he had come. In the future, for example, he says, "By Allah, so-and-so will not come tomorrow," and he comes; or he says, "By Allah, he will surely come," and he does not come.

As for when he swears upon himself, intending to bind himself, for example, he says, "By Allah, I will surely do such-and-such tomorrow," and then he does not do it, then here there is expiation for him, if the conditions are fulfilled.

So there are two opinions among the scholars regarding the interpretation of *laghw*:

The first is that it refers to the oath whose binding was not intended. The second is what?
