* From the noble verse is derived: the affirmation of four of Allah's names, namely: the Forgiving (al-Ghafur), the Merciful (al-Rahim), the All-Hearing (al-Sami'), and the All-Knowing (al-Alim), along with the attributes these names contain.
* From the noble verse is derived: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, from His saying: ﴿All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 227].
[[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 231–232 (part 1 of 6)**

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them with kindness or release them with kindness.﴾

His words ﴿When you divorce﴾: the address here is to people in general, meaning: when one of you divorces. ﴿the women﴾ means the wives. For this reason Allah did not attach the word to anyone. He said ﴿the women﴾ with the definite article (al-), which indicates generality, as in His words ﴿Men are the protectors of women﴾ [an-Nisa' 34]. So the meaning is: when any one of you divorces his wife and she reaches her term, then retain her with kindness.

Some scholars said: ﴿they reach their term﴾ means they are close to reaching it, because once she reaches the term the 'idda (waiting period) has ended and there is no retention at that point. But the correct view is that "reaching" here means actually reaching. The principle is that speech is to be understood in its apparent and literal sense until there is evidence that it is not meant that way. This is a general rule for all the texts of the Book and the Sunnah, and even for people's speech with one another, in contracts, transactions and other matters: speech is understood in what sense? In its apparent and literal sense, until there is evidence that diverts it. On this basis, ﴿they reach their term﴾ means that their 'idda has ended. This is because a man may take his wife back (raj'a, revocation) after her third menstrual period as long as she has not performed ghusl (the major ritual bath), as has been reported from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. So when a woman has had three menstrual periods after the divorce, she has reached her term, but he may still take her back as long as she has not bathed. On this basis the verse is taken in its apparent sense: they have completed the 'idda, so retain them.

However, His words ﴿then retain them﴾ indicate sequence and immediacy, and that it should not be delayed. Some scholars have said that the apparent sense of what was reported from the Companions is that if she delayed the ghusl for many years, he may still take her back as long as she has not bathed. But this is open to question. He may take her back as long as she has not bathed, provided she has not neglected an obligatory ghusl. If a prayer has passed while she has not bathed, hoping that her husband will take her back, then she is prevented from that.

* Student: Shaykh, does His words ﴿then retain them﴾ not indicate that the meaning of ﴿reach﴾ is "come close to"?
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: Otherwise, how would he retain her after she has...?
* The Shaykh: Yes, he may take her back as long as she has not bathed. This is what was reported from the Companions. Although the 'idda ends with the cessation of menstruation, for this reason, if he or she dies after the third menstrual period has ended, the other does not inherit from them.
* The student: But he may need to travel with her?
* Another student: If she is a Christian (kitabiyya), she does not bathe.
* The Shaykh: The apparent view is that for a Christian woman who does not bathe, it ends with the completion of the menstrual period.
* The student: Perhaps her family is not present in the town where he is, so when the 'idda ends he is compelled to travel with her, and she is not a maḥram (a permanently unmarriageable relative) for him, if...(...)?
* The Shaykh: No, no. As long as it has been reported from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that a person may take her back as long as she has not bathed, even after the 'idda is complete, this is considered an explanation of the noble verse by the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.
* The student: But does it not differ if her family is in a town (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, no, it does not differ, because it is his right.
* The student: He travels with her and she is not a maḥram?
* The Shaykh: No, he does not travel. Leave her where she is and ask her family to come and travel with her.
* The student: She is not a maḥram for him?
* The Shaykh: Yes. If the 'idda has ended and he has not taken her back, and she has bathed, then he may not keep her in his house unless there is no seclusion (khalwa, being alone together). For example, if there is someone else in the house, then there is no objection.

So we say: there are two views among the scholars regarding this verse. The first is that the meaning of ﴿they reach their term﴾ is that they are close to reaching it. We have already noted that the verb may be used to mean what is close to occurring. But the stronger view is that the verse is to be taken in its apparent sense, based on what was reported from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

His words ﴿then retain them with kindness or release them﴾: ﴿retain them﴾ means take them back into your marital bond, which is revocation (muraja'a). ﴿or release them﴾ means leave them. Tasrih means release, so the meaning is: release them, and they will be free, or free to choose, regarding themselves. Here He said ﴿retain them with kindness or release them with kindness﴾, and there He said ﴿Divorce is twice; then either retain with kindness or release with good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah 229]. Here He said ﴿release them with kindness﴾. What, then, is the difference? It may be said that this is the obligatory minimum, while release with good treatment is recommended and preferable, because good treatment is not obligatory but is encouraged. Allah willing, this will be discussed further in the benefits (al-fawa'id) later on.

He said: ﴿And do not retain them to harm them, to transgress﴾. Here (la) is a prohibitive particle, and the verb after it is jussive by the omission of the final nūn. ﴿Ḍirāran﴾ (to harm) is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Ibn Malik said about the object of purpose:

*The verbal noun is put in the accusative as an object of purpose when it clearly gives the reason, like "generosity out of gratitude" and "religion".*

And here, does it clearly give the reason? Yes. Do not retain them for the sake of harm. In the Jahiliyya, men used to take their wives back during the 'idda for the purpose of harm: he would take her back and keep her, then divorce her again so that she would begin the 'idda anew. Then when she was close to the end, he would take her back and divorce her again, so she would begin the 'idda anew, and so on. We have already noted that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, limited this to how many? To three. After the third, there is no revocation. Here He said ﴿And do not retain them to harm them﴾. In the previous verse He said ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back during that period if they desire reconciliation﴾ [al-Baqarah 228]. So revocation is conditional on the desire for reconciliation, and its prohibition is conditional on what? On the intention to harm. If he intends harm, it becomes forbidden. If he does not intend reconciliation, he has no right of revocation. But if he takes her back without intending harm, he does not sin.

He said: ﴿to transgress﴾. The lām here is the lām of causation (lām al-ta'līl), but it is meant here in the sense of consequence (lām al-'aqiba). That is: do not retain them to harm them, so that your outcome or condition becomes that of transgressors.

The lām known to some grammarians as lām kay (the lām of purpose) is sometimes used for causation, sometimes is extra (zā'ida), and sometimes indicates consequence. It is causative, as in your saying: "I came in order to read," and as in His words ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them and enjoy themselves﴾ [al-'Ankabut 66]. It is extra, as in His words ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [an-Nisa' 26]. When it comes after "intends", it is extra, because the intention is itself the causation: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ means Allah intends to make clear to you. It indicates consequence when the speaker knows that what follows is not intended, but the result turns out to be so, such as His words ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas 8]. Did the family of Pharaoh pick him up for this purpose? Never. Had they thought so, they would have killed him. But the consequence was that he became for them an enemy and a grief.

In which of these three senses does this verse apply? It applies to consequence. It may be said that whoever intends harm has intended transgression, so it is as if He said: do not retain them to harm them and to transgress, because intending harm is without doubt transgression.

He said: ﴿And whoever does that has certainly wronged himself﴾. ﴿Whoever does﴾ is a conditional sentence, and its answer is ﴿has certainly wronged himself﴾. Why is the answer linked with the particle fa'? Because it cannot stand in place of the condition. Ibn Malik said:

*Link with fa' as an obligatory answer whatever cannot be made a condition with "in" or others.*

So whatever cannot be a conditional clause must be linked with fa' when it occurs as an answer. Some people have versified this, to help the student of knowledge: the answer to the condition that must be linked with fa' is what? 

* Student: I do not know.
* The Shaykh: This question keeps coming up for us, and it is difficult.
* Student: 

*Nominal, imperative,*
*and with the frozen forms, and with "mā", "qad", "lan", and with the future particles.*

* The Shaykh: 

*Nominal, imperative,*
*and with the frozen forms, and with "mā", "qad", "lan", and with the future particles.*

In this verse, which of the seven cases applies? His words "qad" (certainly): do you know it? So if the answer to the condition is one of these seven things, it must be linked with fa'. This brings it closer to the beginning student, although the rule stated by Ibn Malik is not open to criticism.

His words ﴿whoever does that has certainly wronged himself﴾: the root meaning of ẓulm (wrong) in the language is deficiency. From it is His words ﴿Each of the two gardens brought its produce and did not fall short therein at all﴾ [al-Kahf 33], meaning it did not diminish. Then it came to be used for everything in which there is deficiency, whether physical or non-physical. Whoever neglects what is due to him, or what is obligatory upon him, or violates what is forbidden to him, has diminished, has diminished his own soul's right. This is because the soul is a trust with you, and you must care for it with proper care. You must not expose it to what Allah has forbidden you, and you must perform what Allah has obligated upon you. Otherwise you are a wrongdoer to yourself.

His words ﴿has certainly wronged himself﴾: He did not say "has wronged the wife", even though in reality he is a wrongdoer toward his wife. But because a person's zeal for himself is stronger than his zeal for others, He said ﴿has wronged himself﴾. If He had said "has wronged the wife", then he, from the outset, retained her for what purpose? For harm and transgression. But what moves a person and makes him leave off is to be told: you are wronging yourself. This wronging of the self may not be felt by a person in this world. He may even think he has taken his revenge, but in truth it becomes clear to him in the Hereafter, when his good deeds are taken from him and given to this wronged person. If he has some good deeds, they are taken. If not, some of the wronged person's sins are taken and cast upon him, and then he is cast into the Fire.

Allah the Most High says: ﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in mockery﴾. There is a reading: ﴿huz'an﴾ (﴿هَزْءًا﴾). ﴿Huzuwan﴾ and ﴿huz'an﴾ are two canonical readings (qira'atan sab'iyyatan). ﴿Do not take them﴾ means: do not make them objects of ridicule and mockery. The signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are the plural of āya, which means a sign of something. But it is not an āya unless it is a clear and compelling proof; then it is an āya, a sign.

The signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are divided into two kinds: legislative signs (āyāt shar'iyya), which are what the messengers brought of revelation, and cosmic signs (āyāt kawniyya), which are these created beings that we witness. As for why what the messengers brought is a sign: it is speech that no human can produce the like of, neither in its organization, nor in its style, nor in its aim, nor in anything else, especially the noble Qur'an. As for why existing things are cosmic signs, it is obvious: no one can create the like of these creatures. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, challenged those idol-worshippers that their deities could create any of these signs. He said: ﴿O mankind, a parable is presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah could never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should steal from them a thing, they could not recover it from him. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [al-Hajj 73]. Could they create the heavens and the earth? No. Could they create a human? No. Could they create a camel? No. So these creatures, in their order and beauty, are all signs indicating that Allah, the Most High, is the Creator and is One, glorified and exalted:

*And in everything there is a sign*
*indicating that He is One.*

Taking the legislative signs of Allah in mockery is evident: a person mocks and scorns the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, whether he scorns the whole law or a part of it. Even if he mocks the washing of the face in wuḍū' (ablution), he has mocked all the signs of Allah and ridiculed all of them, because ridiculing part of the sharī'a is ridiculing the whole sharī'a. How much more so for one who mocks the whole sharī'a, or its great pillars, by mocking prayer, zakat, fasting, the hajj, or what is similar to these. This is greater and greater still. Whoever mocks any part of the sharī'a of Allah is mocking the whole sharī'a, just as whoever disbelieves in any part of the sharī'a of Allah is a disbeliever in the whole sharī'a, and whoever disbelieves in any one of the messengers is a disbeliever in all the messengers. Is this clear?

If a person does not take the signs of Allah in mockery but does not act upon them, is he like one who mocks? The answer: No, he is not like one who mocks, because there is a difference between one who abandons action while still venerating the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and one who scorns the law and mocks it, considering it futile and vain or similar. The first has the ruling of a disobedient person. If his disobedience reaches the level of disbelief, he is a disbeliever; otherwise he is a sinner (fāsiq); otherwise he is below the level of the sinner, such as if his sins are minor and he does not persist in them. As for the second, the one who mocks and considers the law to be futile, or that it belongs to people who have passed away, or that this age is not fit for acting upon this law, this is without doubt disbelief (kufr).

If a person mocks something other than the sharī'a but mocks the bearer of the sharī'a, is he a disbeliever?

* The students: Yes, there is detail.
* The Shaykh: Yes, there must be detail. Disbelief is not a small matter. Disbelief is not trivial. Is every matter disbelief, disbelief, disbelief? If he mocks the bearer of the sharī'a because of his bearing the sharī'a, he is a disbeliever. For example, if he mocks a man who has grown his beard, intending to mock the growing of the beard, whether it is on this man or on another man, this is disbelief, because he has mocked one of the laws of Allah. For this reason Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said about those group who said: "We have never seen the like of these reciters of ours, more gluttonous in their stomachs, more lying in their tongues, and more cowardly at the encounter"—meaning the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions—Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿And if you asked them, they would surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?" Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief﴾ [at-Tawbah 65–66]. And whoever says about the bearers of the law and those who act upon it, "these are dervishes who do not understand, and do not know society or the world," and similar words, these too are disbelievers, because Allah says: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crime used to laugh at those who believed. And when they passed by them, they would exchange winks﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 29–30]. Look, look at this poor fellow, this dervish! They exchange winks among themselves. ﴿And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 32]. In our age we have replaced "misguided" with "reactionary": when they see them they say, "These are reactionaries." ﴿And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 31], meaning enjoying themselves; they consider that they have obtained something great by mocking these so-called dervishes. Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 34]. This shows that those who mock the believers are disbelievers. As for one who mocks a bearer of the sharī'a other than the Messenger, peace be upon him, because of his clothing, or his gait, or his appearance, then this is...

How does one take the cosmic signs in mockery?

* Student: By denying a blessing (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).
* Student: He says: what is the benefit of these signs, if it were placed (...)?
* The Shaykh: For example, if rain falls, if it falls in the summer, when it is not customary for rain to fall, (...) what is this arrangement? When people need rain, and it did not come in winter, and now it comes! For example, this may exist. Some of the wicked say such things.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 231–232 (part 2 of 6):

Or like a people from among the Arabs who are defeated, and the Jews overcome them, and they say: "What is this? What could this be? Will victory go to the Jews over the Arabs, over the Banu Kan'an, 'Adnan and Qahtan?! How can this be, when the state belongs to the Children of Israel?" and the like. This is mockery and ridicule of God's decree and destiny, whether it is from His action in which no human has any hand or involvement, or from matters in which a human does have involvement. But the believer submits to the cosmic command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, just as he submits to His legislated command, and he sees that it is in the utmost wisdom and the utmost perfection, and that it is in its proper place, and that whoever is defeated, whether Arab or non-Arab, wisdom requires that he be defeated, that it be so; because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is All-Wise, and does nothing except for a wisdom. So the point is that mocking the cosmic signs may occur, and God, exalted is He, has forbidden us to take these signs in jest, whether the signs are cosmic or legislated; but since the verse is in the context of the legislated signs, it applies more specifically to the legislated signs than to the cosmic signs.

He said: ﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in jest, and remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah 231].

Remember with what? With the tongue? With the heart? With the limbs? With all of them?

* The Shaykh: With all of them. Remember the favour of Allah upon you, so that you may be thankful for it, for heedlessness of remembering blessings is a cause of failing to be thankful. Remember them with the tongue, by praising Allah for them; you say: "Allah has bestowed upon me such-and-such," ﴿But as for the favour of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha 11]. You praise Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for them; you say: "O Allah, to You be praise for what You have bestowed upon me of such-and-such wealth, or wife, or children, or the like."

And His saying: ﴿the favour of Allah﴾ is a singular noun in construct form (mufrad mudaf), and a singular noun in construct form indicates generality; it is among the forms of generality, as in His saying: ﴿And if you count the favours of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim 34]. If the intended meaning of "favour" were its singular referent, would counting it be possible?

* The students: No, and it has no number.

* The Shaykh: Because it has no number. The people of language differ over whether one is a number or not a number.

The point is that the favour of Allah here is general; favours whose kinds cannot be counted, let alone their individual instances. So His saying: ﴿the favour of Allah upon you﴾ includes all favours, however small; because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And whatever favour you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 53].

Know that "ni'mah" (favour) is good, while "na'mah" (luxury) is evil, because the meaning of "na'mah" is comfort and affluence. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They left behind gardens and springs, and crops and a noble station, and luxury in which they had been delighting. Thus; and We bequeathed them to another people﴾ [al-Dukhan 25–28], and He said: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil 11].

As for "ni'mah," it comes from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is goodness and benevolence. So it is obligatory upon a person to remember the favour of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by praising Him for it with the tongue, by fulfilling its due with the limbs, and by believing with the heart that it is from Allah, as a bounty and a kindness; so that by this he is disassociated from his own power and strength, because all favour is from the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.

He said: ﴿and what was sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom, with which He admonishes you﴾ [al-Baqarah 231].

﴿and what was sent down﴾: the "wa" is a conjunction particle, and "ma" is a relative pronoun built on sukun in a position of nasb, in coordination with what? With Allah, or with "favour"?

* The students: With "favour."

* The Shaykh: With "favour." That is, remember what was sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom, with which He admonishes you. The coordination here is of the specific upon the general, because what Allah sent down to them of the Book and the Wisdom is among the favours; rather, it is among the greatest of favours: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3]; ﴿Allah has certainly conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses and purifying them and teaching them the Book and the Wisdom﴾ [Al 'Imran 164]. Why was it coordinated with the favours, which are general?

Because coordinating the specific with the general indicates its importance and its elevated status; for this reason it was singled out from the general, to make explicit mention of it. And that is because the general term's indication of all its individual instances is definitive or speculative?

It is speculative. Pay attention to this rule: the indication of a general term over all its individual instances is speculative; because the general term is sometimes intended to be specific, and sometimes it is general but restricted. The difference between the two is clear. Is the difference between "general but restricted" and "general intended as specific" clear or not clear?

* A student: Not clear.

* The Shaykh: Not clear. Well done. This is how a student of knowledge is when it is not clear to him; he says: it is not clear. The difference between the general restricted is that the expression is general and intended over all its instances, then some instances are excluded from it, such as: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-'Asr 2–3]. The word "al-insan" (mankind) — do we say of it: general restricted?

﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them with eighty lashes and do not accept their testimony ever after, and those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Nur 4]. This is general, but restricted for the husband if he accuses his wife, for he has a special ruling.

﴿And those who accuse their spouses and have no witnesses except themselves, the testimony of one of them is four testimonies by Allah﴾ [al-Nur 6]. We gave this example alongside the first one only so that we may illustrate connected specification and separated specification. Is this known or not known?

* The students: Known.

* The Shaykh: Connected specification is when it is within a single speech: the general and the specifier, ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe﴾.

Separated specification is when the specification is in another speech, separate from the first. The verse of accusation was revealed before the verse of mutual cursing (li'an), because when the verse of accusation was revealed, "Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I find that if I found my wife with a man, I would have to go and seek four witnesses? By Allah, if I found him, I would strike him with the sword, without striking with the flat."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6846), and Muslim (1498/16), from the hadith of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, and the wording of Muslim: Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah said: O Messenger of Allah, if I found a man with my family, would I not touch him until I brought four witnesses? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes." He said: "No, by the One who sent you with truth, I would have struck him with the sword before that."]]. Then Allah revealed the verse of mutual cursing: ﴿And those who accuse their spouses and have no witnesses except themselves﴾ [al-Nur 6].

The point is, this is an example of what? Of the general restricted by a connected or a separated specifier. The general intended as specific is, originally, one whose generality was not intended at all; rather it was intended for something specific, such as His saying: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you"﴾ [Al 'Imran 173]. Is the intended meaning all the people?

* A student: No..

* The Shaykh: First: ﴿the people said to them﴾ — only one person said it; the speaker is one.

Second: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ — who? Abu Sufyan and those with him, not all the people. This they call general intended as specific.

It has become clear to you now that the general term does not indicate all its individual instances definitively; rather its indication is speculative, as proven by the fact that it may be specified or that it may originally be intended as specific. So when one individual instance of the general term is mentioned, is the indication of the generality over this individual definitive or speculative?

* The students: Definitive... speculative.

* The Shaykh: One individual instance of the general term has been mentioned? Definitive, may Allah bless you. ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you and what was sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah 231] — is it included in the favour or not? Certainly it is included in the generality, and for this reason it was singled out.

﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr 4].

* A student: Definitive (...)

* The Shaykh: Now we know with certainty that Gabriel, the Spirit, is included among the angels without doubt. But Israfil and Mika'il, and the like?

* The student: Speculative.

* The Shaykh: We say: yes, the generality indicates their inclusion, but we do not definitively affirm their inclusion. However, when an individual instance of the general term is mentioned, we are certain of its inclusion.

Then we say: after its mention, is it still included in the generality, or does singling it out exclude it from the generality?

* The students: It excludes it from the generality.

* The Shaykh: With the speed of your answers, I do not know whether it is understanding or not understanding. Does singling it out by mention exclude it from the generality?

* A student: It excludes it from the generality.

* The Shaykh: Or do we say it is included in the generality and was mentioned specifically to elevate its status, and thus it is mentioned twice?

* The students: (...)

* The Shaykh: (...) The first?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: This too is a matter of difference among the scholars. Some of them say: singling it out indicates that it was not intended within the generality; as if he said: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you," and he intends other than what was sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom; then he said: ﴿and what was sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom﴾. These people base their view on the principle that coordination requires difference. But the correct view is that it is included in the generality, and that singling it out is to elevate its status, as if it were mentioned twice, and that difference has occurred in the coordination, because we have coordinated the specific upon the general, and this is a kind of difference. Difference occurs in essence as it occurs in attribute, as is well known, as in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who decreed and guided, and who brought out the pasture﴾ [al-A'la 1–4]. Who is it that decreed and guided, and who brought out the pasture?

* The students: Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

* The Shaykh: No. Does coordination require difference?

* The students: No..

* The Shaykh: Fine, and what do you say about this rule? Coordination requires difference, what do you do with it?

* The students: Difference..

* The Shaykh: Difference of attributes. Here the difference is by descriptions, is it not?

Without doubt, each of the attributes of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is other than the rest: the One who created and proportioned is the One who decreed and guided, and He is the One who brought out the pasture; but these are one attribute and those are another attribute.

So what Allah has sent down to us of the Book and the Wisdom is undoubtedly a favour of Allah, and it is obligatory upon us to remember that. But how do we remember it?

We do not go to people and say: "O people, do you see that Allah has sent down to us a Book and Wisdom?" No. Remember it in your hearts, and implement what it contains of directives, by doing or abstaining, with your limbs. This is the remembrance of the Qur'an. How can one who does not act by it be one who remembers the Qur'an? Where is his remembrance of the Qur'an?

So remember it with your hearts, acknowledging to Allah, exalted is He, the favour in sending it down; then believe what it indicates of creedal matters, and carry out what it requires of commands and prohibitions. Is this understood or not?

And His saying: ﴿and what was sent down to you of the Book﴾: the intended meaning of "the Book" is the Qur'an, and it is on the pattern "fi'al" in the sense of "maf'ul," like "firash" meaning "mafrush" (spread), "bina'" meaning "mabni" (built), "ghirас" meaning "maghrus" (planted); so "fi'al" always comes in the sense of "maf'ul," and among them is "al-kitab," meaning "maktub" (written). Written where?

Written in the Preserved Tablet: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [al-Buruj 21–22]. Written by the hands of the angels: ﴿No! Indeed, it is a reminder, so whoever wills may remember it, in scriptures honoured, exalted, purified, by the hands of scribes﴾ [Abasa 11–15]. Written in the pages in our hands? So it is written.

And His saying: ﴿and the Wisdom﴾: is the intended meaning of wisdom knowledge? That is, what Allah has sent down to you of the Book and what knowledge you have acquired from it; because this Book contains many sciences. Or is the intended meaning of wisdom knowing the secrets of the Sharia? For Allah, exalted is He, has sent down wisdom to us in the Qur'an, and how numerous are the rulings with their reasons in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is it not so? And we have explained many times that the reasoning attached to legal rulings serves what purpose?

It serves three benefits:

* A student: Four.

* The Shaykh: Let us see. First: showing the exaltedness and greatness of the Sharia, and that there is no ruling among its rulings except that it has a reason consistent with reason.

Second: the tranquillity of the person, for whenever he knows the wisdom he becomes more at ease with it, is that not so? This is why people always ask: "Why is this so? Why is that so?" in order to be reassured.

Third: that by it the ruling is analogized to — i.e., the ruling — whatever shares that same reason; these are three.

We ask the brother to bring the fourth, either from his own pocket or from his heart.

* The student: There is none.

* The Shaykh: There is none, then.

* The student: The fourth: the submission of the one obligated.

* The Shaykh: That is tranquillity itself; this is a branch of tranquillity. When one is at ease, one submits. This is one opinion.

Or we say: the intended meaning of wisdom is the Sunnah. Or we say: the intended meaning of wisdom is what includes these three?

* A student: The last.

* The Shaykh: The last; because we have a principle in tafsir: if the verse can bear the mentioned meanings without conflict among them, then it is obligatory to take them all.

﴿and what was sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom, with which He admonishes you﴾ [al-Baqarah 231].

﴿He admonishes you﴾: admonition (maw'izah) is the mention of rulings accompanied by encouragement or warning. Among the encouragement toward them is mentioning their reasons, because the soul becomes at ease with them and grows more attached to them when they are commanded; and it recoils from them and grows more hatred for them when they are forbidden. So admonition is the mention of rulings accompanied by encouragement and warning.

It has been said that admonition is more general: it is the mention of rulings in general, because when a person adheres to them, he has been admonished. But the first is more apparent, because what is meant by admonition is that which produces in the hearts desire or fear, and this only occurs when rulings are accompanied by their reasons. In the hadith of al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) admonished us with an admonition from which hearts trembled and eyes shed tears."[[Related by Abu Dawud (4607), and al-Tirmidhi (2676).]]

This must be something that moves the heart; and all of Allah's rulings are an admonition, because most rulings are accompanied by their reasons, either concluded with one of Allah's names or one of His attributes, or a mention of His punishment or reward, or the like.

The clause ﴿He admonishes you with it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), a circumstantial clause from the subject of "anzala" (sent down), which is Allah; is it not so? That is: what was sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom while He is admonishing with it. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from "the Book," meaning the Book while being admonished with; these two are mutually implied. So the Book and the Wisdom are an admonition from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a cure for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [Yunus 57].

﴿He admonishes you with it, and fear Allah﴾. How often Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commands taqwa, because the righteousness of hearts lies in it.

Among the scholars of tafsir there are many differing opinions on taqwa, and the most comprehensive of them is that taqwa is: taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. The etymology supports this, for it is derived from wiqayah (protection). On this basis, taqwa is taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Some of them said regarding it:

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 231–232 (part 3 of 6)**

Abandon sins, both the small and the great,
for that is taqwa (God-consciousness).
Act like one walking over a field of thorns,
who watches carefully where he steps.
Do not belittle any small sin,
for mountains are made of pebbles.

Some of the scholars said: Taqwa is that you act in obedience to God upon a light from God, hoping for God's reward, and that you abandon what God has forbidden upon a light from God, fearing God's punishment. All of these are expressions, but they converge on one meaning, which is what we pointed to first, and it is the most comprehensive of them.

As for His words, ﴿Fear God﴾, it is clear that there is an explicit indication of the obligation of sincerity (ikhlas) in the taqwa of God, the Exalted. A person does not fear anyone, but he fears the One who created him, namely God, the Mighty and Majestic. He does not avoid sins out of fear of people's blame, nor does he perform acts of obedience hoping for people's reward for them. This applies whether the acts of obedience are bodily acts of worship, knowledge-based acts, or other kinds. All acts of worship must be sincerely for God, the Exalted. For this reason, it was mentioned to Imam Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, that a man said to a people: "I will not lead you in the Ramadan taraweeh prayers unless you give me such-and-such." He said: "We seek refuge in God. Who would pray behind this man?"[[Masa'il al-Imam Ahmad, narration of Abu Dawud (p. 91).]]

He sought refuge from him, may God have mercy on him, and said: "How? Who would pray behind this man?"

However, what people take from the stipend from the public treasury (bayt al-mal) should not confuse you. This is not objectionable, provided the person takes it while not being greedy for it and not begging for it. But if he is begging, as when someone writes, for example: "I have prayed in this mosque for two months, three, and the salary has not come," or he writes: "Increase the salaries," or the like, then I fear that it is not lawful for him. Likewise, regarding those who asked for an increase in salary, such as teachers and others, I fear that this may nullify their rewards. This is because everything you do for God must have as its intention only the Hereafter, only the reward of God, the Mighty and Majestic. As for going to argue for worldly matters while you are working for the Hereafter, this contradicts both reason and the Sharia.

He said: ﴿And fear God, and know that God is Knower of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:231].

﴿Know﴾ is a command to knowledge, the knowledge that must bear fruit. It is not merely knowledge; it must bear fruit. When you know that ﴿God is of all things﴾...

﴿All﴾ is one of the forms of generality (umum), and ﴿thing﴾ is likewise. The word "thing" (shay') is one of the most general of words, to the point that it is used even of non-existence, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿He was not a thing worth mentioning﴾ [al-Insan 76:1]. So "thing" is among the most general of words, and when it is qualified by "all," it encompasses everything: the existent and the non-existent, the small and the great, what relates to God's own action, what relates to the actions of the servants, what is secret and what is open. Even what is in the heart, God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows it.

﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾ [Qaf 50:16]. In the mention of His words, ﴿And know that God is Knower of all things﴾, following the command to taqwa, there is an indication that you should not make your taqwa contrary to what is in your inner self. God, the Exalted, knows what is in your conscience and in your heart. Beware of obeying God openly while disobeying Him in secret, even if only in your heart. God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows what is in a person's heart, and what will be in a person's heart. Does He not? And what will be in his heart. Therefore He knows you better than you know yourself.

He said: ﴿And know that God is Knower of all things﴾. His knowledge, the Mighty and Majestic, encompasses everything, eternally and everlastingly, the small and the great, the present and the future.

He said: ﴿And know that God is Knower of all things﴾.

As for His words, ﴿of all things﴾, it is the fronted object of ﴿Knower﴾, or not? It is the fronted object of "knower," a prepositional phrase connected to "knower." So do we say that the benefit of fronting here is restriction (hasr)?

*Student:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* How is that? What is the benefit of fronting it?

*Student:* Restriction.

*Shaykh:* Observing the verse-endings (fawasil) is undoubtedly part of this. Observing the verse-endings is intended in the Noble Quran, because when the verse-endings follow one rhythm, they are undoubtedly more pleasing to the ear.

Then we say: The apparent meaning, and God knows best, is that the specification here is in the sense that the one specified with this general knowledge is God. Or is the phrase ﴿of all things﴾ not restrictive at all? But there is no one who knows all things except God, the Exalted. As for the created being, his knowledge is limited, limited in every respect: in its beginning, its end, and its scope. As for its beginning, because human knowledge is preceded by ignorance: ﴿And God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [al-Nahl 16:78]. Or not? And the knowledge you have today, before yesterday, means that yesterday you were ignorant of it. Likewise, it is surrounded by forgetfulness. So it is preceded by ignorance and followed by forgetfulness.

Then, it is also not comprehensive. It is not comprehensive; it is narrowly limited. Even a person does not know what he will earn tomorrow. But God, the Mighty and Majestic, knows all things.

Then He said: ﴿And when you divorce women and they have reached their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:232].

There is a difficulty in this verse regarding the pronouns. Let us see:

﴿When you divorce﴾: to whom is the address?

*The students:* To the husbands.

*Shaykh:* To the husbands. ﴿Do not prevent them﴾: the address is to the guardians (awliya'). This is the well-known view. There is no objection to shifting pronouns (tashtit al-damair) when the meaning is clear. Just as there is no objection to a pronoun referring to the nearest preceding noun rather than the one immediately adjacent, when this is known. Like His words: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham. He named you Muslims before, and in this [revelation]﴾ [al-Hajj 22:78]. The pronoun ﴿He﴾ refers to whom? To God, not to Abraham.

The conclusion is that shifting pronouns is not objectionable when the intended meaning is understood. It may even have a benefit. What is it?

It is to awaken attention. Because it is known that when speech follows one rhythm, the mind flows along with it and may forget and not reflect. But when the pronouns differ, or the form differs, as in the device of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), the listener becomes attentive, thinks, and reflects on whom the pronoun refers. If it refers to what came before, the meaning changes.

So there are several views on the verse:

The first view: what you have pointed out, that His words ﴿When you divorce﴾ are addressed to the husbands, and His words ﴿Do not prevent them﴾ are addressed to the guardians. There is no objection to shifting the pronouns, since the meaning is clear.

The second view: ﴿When you divorce women﴾ is addressed to the husbands. ﴿Do not prevent them﴾ is addressed to the husbands, ﴿from marrying their husbands﴾.

Based on this view, is His words ﴿from marrying their husbands﴾ taken in regard to the past or the future?

*Student:* The future.

*Shaykh:* In regard to the future. And according to the first view, ﴿their husbands﴾ is in regard to the past. Is that clear?

*Student:* Yes, regarding the pronouns.

*Shaykh:* It is not about the pronouns. The word "husbands" also has two meanings for us. Does the word ﴿their husbands﴾ refer to the past or the future? If we say ﴿do not prevent them﴾ is addressed to the husbands, then "husbands" means the future. If we say the address is to the guardians, then "husbands" means those who had been [husbands] in the past.

How can the divorcing husband be preventing the divorced wife from marrying someone else?

We say: Yes, this existed in the period of ignorance (jahiliyyah), when a man was noble and had standing. If he divorced a woman, no one could approach her to marry her after him. If anyone did so, woe to him. In that case, what did God forbid in this verse? He forbade a practice they used to commit in the jahiliyyah: that when a husband divorced his wife, he would not allow her to marry after him. This is undoubtedly an injustice. But it did occur. I think you have studied the hadith of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, when he found a man with his wife and said: "I will strike him with the sword, not with the flat of it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do you wonder at the jealousy of Sa'd? By God, I am more jealous than Sa'd, and God is more jealous than I."[[Already cited.]]

His companions informed him that Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah was jealous, to the point that if he divorced a woman, no one would marry her after him. But he, may God be pleased with him, did not prevent people [from marrying].

In any case, this was a practice existing in the jahiliyyah, so God forbade it. According to this view, are the pronouns scattered or in one consistent pattern? In one consistent pattern.

There is a third aspect to the verse: that the address is to people in general: "When you divorce, O people." The address is not to the husbands. So "do not prevent them, O people." On this view, the meaning is directed to whoever it is appropriate to address. This view is strong insofar as the community is one entity, so address to it is like address to each individual. This meaning has great strength: God addresses all the servants, saying: "When you divorce women, do not prevent them." He addresses people collectively, not individually, meaning each person in particular. That is, the verse is addressed to all people regardless of Zayd and 'Amr. The meaning is: when you divorce, do not prevent; the divorce is attributed to the husband, and the prevention to whoever among the guardians or the husbands may commit it. This meaning has its strength.

In any case, let us return to the verse: ﴿When you divorce women﴾. What is divorce (talaq)?

Linguistically, it is the untying of a fetter. One says "aṭlaqtu al-naqah" and "ṭallaqtuha," meaning I unfastened her shackle.

Legally, it is the dissolving of the bond of marriage, or part of it. The part is dissolved in the revocable divorce (raj'iyyah).

﴿When you divorce women and they have reached their term﴾: the term (ajal) here is the completion of the 'iddah (waiting period) by agreement, unlike the term in the preceding verse. The term in the previous verse means approaching the end, according to many scholars, or the reaching of the term before bathing. But here, ﴿they have reached their term﴾ means: they have completed their 'iddah, by agreement.

﴿They have reached their term, so do not prevent them﴾: the fa' here is the connective of the response. For what reason is it the connective of the response?

*Student:* Imperative?

*Shaykh:* No. Imperative? The fa' is imperative. What is it?

*Student:* It is the prohibitive lam (lam al-nahy).

*Shaykh:* No. Prohibitive? Is it prohibitive or negative? It is negative with the fa', or prohibitive with the ha'?

*The students:* With the ha'?

*Shaykh:* With the ha'. What is the evidence that it is prohibitive?

*Student:* The verb is apocopated (jazm).

*Shaykh:* The verb is apocopated, because the nun has been dropped. He did not say ﴿fa-la ta'dulunahunna﴾ with the nun. So it is imperative: ﴿fa-la ta'dulūhunna﴾. And al-'adl (preventing) means prohibition, that is, do not prevent them.

His words ﴿an yankiḥna﴾: this ʾan is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, and it and what follows it are interpreted as a verbal noun in the accusative by removal of the preposition. The estimate is: "from [that] they marry," that is, from the marriage of their husbands. Is the accusative here by removal of the preposition regular (muṭṭarid) or only by hearing (samā'i)?

*Student:* Regular.

*Shaykh:* What is the evidence from the words of Ibn Malik?

*Student:* [recites]

"Count it intransitive with a preposition, and if it is omitted, the accusative belongs to the genitive-marked [noun], by transmission. But with 'anna and 'an it is regular, provided there is no ambiguity, as in 'ajibtu an yadū."

*Shaykh:* ﴿yankiḥna azwājahunna﴾: here He attributed marriage (nikah) to the women, because what is meant is the contract ('aqd), and the contract takes place from both parties. One says: "The woman married the man" and "the man married the woman." As for sexual intercourse (wat'), they say... one says: "The man married his wife," and one says: "He married so-and-so's daughter," meaning he contracted with her. When nikah means the contract, it is correct to apply it to both the man and the woman.

His words ﴿azwājahunna﴾ are the plural of zawj (spouse). The husband was called zawj because by the contract he makes the single one two. The husband makes his wife a pair, and she does likewise for him.

His words ﴿when they agree among themselves in a proper manner﴾: ﴿when they agree﴾ here: He said ﴿when they agree﴾ and did not say "when they (feminine) agree," giving precedence to the masculine. Otherwise, the husband usually is content with this, because he is a suitor, whether he is the divorcing husband or a new man. But since consent in the contract of marriage is required of both the man and the woman, the masculine was given precedence, so He said: ﴿when they agree among themselves in a proper manner﴾.

His words ﴿tarāḍaw﴾ are of the form tafā'ala, meaning that consent occurred from both parties.

His words ﴿baynahum﴾ mean between the husbands and the wives.

﴿bil-ma'rūf﴾: the bāʾ here is either transitive or accompaniment. That is, when they agree in a manner that is known, not objectionable according to the Sharia or custom. So when the husband and wife agree, whether the husband is the divorcing husband or a suitor, in the sharia-approved and customary manner, it is not permissible to prevent the women from marrying.

﴿That is admonished by it whoever among you believes in God and the Last Day﴾: to whom is the address of ﴿that﴾?

To everyone who can be addressed. One might ask: why did He not say "dhālikum"? Because He addresses a group in His words ﴿when you divorce women﴾?

It is said: when a demonstrative pronoun is addressed to a group, it is permissible to mention it in the singular, even if they are a group, and it is permissible to observe the addressee. The particle "ka" attached to the demonstrative has three permissible forms in the language:

The first form: observing the addressee. If it is masculine, it is masculine; if feminine, feminine; if singular, singular; if plural, plural; if dual, dual.

The second form: that it is always fixed on the opening vowel, singular and masculine, "dhālika," whatever the addressee may be. It is as if the speaker says: "I point out, addressing this one before me, to such and such."

The third form: that "ka" is mentioned as a single consonant, kasra in addressing a feminine, fatḥa in addressing a masculine. An example of this: you have, for instance, a group of women, and you want to point to something masculine, addressing them. What do you say?

*The students:* "Dhālikunna."

*Shaykh:* "Dhālikunna," as the wife of the 'Aziz said: ﴿She said: That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ [Yusuf 12:32]. Because she points to one masculine, Joseph, and addresses a group of women, so she made the pronoun the pronoun of the group of women: ﴿dhālikunna﴾.

It is permissible for me to say, addressing women, "dhālika" with kasra and singular, because I am addressing women. It is also permissible to say "dhālika" with fatḥa and singular. All of this is attested in the language, but the more eloquent is observing the addressee. This is the more eloquent. Therefore, when it comes contrary to observing the addressee, it must be interpreted.

Here He said ﴿that is admonished by it﴾. The thing referred to is singular and masculine, but the addressee ﴿when you divorce﴾ is a group of males, which requires saying what?

*The students:* "Dhālikum."

*Shaykh:* "Dhālikum," as also came in Surat al-Talaq in His words: ﴿That is admonished by it whoever believes in God and the Last Day, and whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out﴾ [al-Talaq 65:2].

Here it came in the singular, because both forms are correct.

His words ﴿admonished by it whoever was﴾: admonition (maw'izah) has already been explained to us as the mention of rulings combined with encouragement for commands and warning against prohibitions. This is admonition, because a person is admonished by it.

Admonition may also be applied to the mere mention of rulings, because in adhering to them there is admonition and remembrance, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent is that which God instructs you. Indeed, God is ever Hearing and Seeing﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:58].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 231–232 (part 4 of 6):

Moreover, this verse ﴿How excellent is that with which He admonishes you﴾ [an-Nisa' 58] points to what? ﴿How excellent is that with which He admonishes you﴾ means: the command to render trusts. The upshot is that this is the meaning of admonition (maw'izah). No admonition is greater than the Quran for one who has a heart, or who gives ear while he is a witness. As for one who turns away from it and pays it no heed, it does not benefit him, but rather becomes a sickness for him. For this reason, the condition here is ﴿whoever among you is admonished by it, who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. He specified this for those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, because they are the ones who are admonished and benefit. ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [Yunus 57]. So it is the believers who benefit.

As for His saying ﴿who believes in Allah﴾ (...), all of this is necessary. As for belief in the Last Day, what is meant by it is belief that this Day will certainly occur. Shaykh al-Islam [Ibn Taymiyyah] mentioned in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah [the Creed of Wasitiyyah] that belief in the Last Day includes everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will happen after death. Accordingly, the trial of the grave (fitnat al-qabr), and the bliss or punishment of the grave, fall under belief in the Last Day.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always pairs belief in Allah with belief in the Last Day, because belief in the Last Day is the greatest incentive for a person to act. Whoever believes in this Day, on which he will meet his Lord, who will call him to account for his deeds and recompense him for them, will work for that Day. As for one who denies it, will he act? One who denies this Day and says, ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world; we die and we live﴾ [al-Jathiyah 24], such a person is not an doer of good.

So belief in the Last Day is the strongest driver for a person and the thing that moves him to act, by performing what is commanded and abstaining from what is forbidden.

Allah called it the Last Day because there is no day after it. This Day is one with no night, because the sun and the moon will be wound up and cast into the Fire. So there is only day, and for this reason Allah called it the Last Day, for there is no day after it.

Belief in the Last Day. I said: Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, says that belief in it includes everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will happen after death. It includes the trial of the grave, its punishment, its bliss, the standing of people barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, the setting up of the scales, the weighing of deeds, the taking of the records, the Sirat (the bridge over Hell), the drawing near of the sun to people, the sweat, the Basin (al-hawd), and intercession. Everything that the Messenger, peace be upon him, informed of in this regard is included in belief in the Last Day.

Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿That is purer for you and more purifying﴾ [al-Baqarah 232]. ﴿That﴾ — look now, He has addressed it in a way that takes the one addressed into account: ﴿that﴾ (dhalikum).

﴿Purer for you (azka lakum)﴾ is a comparative form from zaka' (growth). Zaka' originally means growth, and from it comes zakah (obligatory charity), because it causes wealth to grow by bringing blessing into it, and it causes character to grow by moving a person from the group of the stingy to the group of the generous. So zakah linguistically means increase.

﴿Purer for you﴾ in what respect? Purer for you in your deeds: their growth and their multiplication. When you heed this admonition, you obey Allah and His Messenger, so deeds increase and faith increases too, because faith, even the faith in the heart, increases by carrying out the command and avoiding the prohibition for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying ﴿that﴾, what is the thing pointed to? Is it the admonition, or the rulings that were mentioned, or the necessary consequence of the admonition, which is taking heed?

We now have rulings: ﴿when you divorce women, do not prevent them﴾, and we have an admonition, and we have a ruling, and we have taking heed. So to what does this demonstrative refer? Does the meaning of ﴿that﴾ mean your not preventing them is purer for you? Or does it mean your taking heed of this admonition is purer for you?

* The students: It includes all of them.

* The Shaykh: It includes all of them. That is, what has been mentioned of rulings and admonition, and heeding it, is purer for you, as I said: it is a comparative from zaka', which is growth.

﴿And more purifying (atharr)﴾. More purifying from what? From immorality (fahshaa'). Because if you prevent her from her husband, who has come back and proposed to her, and there was some relationship between them before, perhaps Satan will whisper to them and what happens in immorality will happen between them. For he only proposed to her and she only consented because there was affection and love between them. So if you prevent them, what happens of immorality may happen. For this reason He said ﴿more purifying﴾.

Reflect on how Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when speaking about matters related to immorality and abstaining from it, mentions that this is purer, because of the chastity it contains and the purity of heart by which deeds and faith grow and flourish.

﴿That is purer for you and more purifying﴾. More purifying from what?

* A student: From sins.

* The Shaykh: From sins, or from accusations, or whatever is similar to that.

﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. The sentence here is nominal, in ascribing knowledge to Allah Himself and negating knowledge from His servants.

He said ﴿And Allah knows﴾. This is a nominal sentence beginning with a noun.

As for His saying ﴿knows﴾, the object has been omitted to convey generality. Because when the object of a transitive verb is omitted, it becomes inclusive of everything it could refer to. He knows the present, the future and the past, what benefits you and what does not benefit you, what you obey and who among you obeys and who does not. In sum, it is general.

As for His saying ﴿while you do not know﴾, this is the original state of a human being, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing and sight﴾ [an-Nahl 78].

So the original state of a human being is ignorance. For this reason He said ﴿while you do not know﴾. Then he gradually acquires knowledge from those around him, from what he hears and what he witnesses, until his knowledge grows. Accordingly, the negation of knowledge here is considered in terms of what? In terms of the original state of the human being, that he is not a knower. Otherwise, a human being does know, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is Knower of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah 282].

There is no doubt that a human being knows. But the original state of a human is non-knowledge, unless Allah, glorified and exalted, teaches him. There is no difference in this between what is known through revelation, what is known through the senses, and what is known through the natural disposition (fitrah), because the ways of knowledge are many. Revelation is one of the ways of knowledge, is it not? And the senses are a way of knowledge: what a person witnesses with his eye, or hears with his ear, or feels with his hand, or smells, or tastes. These are ways of knowledge. Also among the ways of knowledge is the natural disposition, for a human being is created upon the disposition of monotheism toward Allah, glorified and exalted, and turning to Him in repentance.

* * *

The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them in kindness (ma'ruf) or release them in kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah 231].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that every divorce has a term (ajal). This is shown by His saying ﴿and when you divorce women and they reach their term﴾. And what is this term?

The term here is general, but it is specified in His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual periods (quru')﴾, and in other verses that indicate the waiting period ('iddah).

From this benefit it follows that the Quran sometimes comes in general terms and sometimes in detail. His saying supports this: ﴿A Book whose verses have been perfected and then explained in detail from One who is Wise and Acquainted﴾ [Hud 1].

The benefit of presenting something in general and then in detail is this: when a text comes in general terms, the soul looks forward to knowing what is general and the clarification of what is ambiguous, so it becomes more eager to seek knowledge, does it not? But if the matter came clearly and in detail from the beginning, the soul would have no eagerness to reach knowledge. So when it is mentioned in general terms, the soul seeks to reach the clarification of this general matter, and this becomes one of the ways of firmly establishing knowledge.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of taking the wife back after the waiting period is complete. This is because of His saying ﴿and when they reach their term, then either retain them in kindness or release them﴾. The basis of the inference is that His saying ﴿then retain them﴾ is the answer to the condition in His saying ﴿when you divorce﴾ and ﴿they reach﴾. This implies that retaining or releasing is after the term is reached.

It is necessary that the conditioned thing occurs after the condition, and the conditioned thing, which is the answer, occurs after the condition. Scholars have differed on this matter. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the husband may retain her until she performs ghusl (the full bath) after the third menstruation. So if she became pure in the morning after dawn, after the sun had risen, and then did not perform ghusl until the noon prayer, and her husband took her back in the interval between her becoming pure and her ghusl, this is permissible according to Imam Ahmad, and he may take her back. However, many scholars hold that the time for taking her back ends with purity from the third menstruation. According to this view, they need to interpret His saying ﴿they reach their term﴾ to mean that they are close to reaching the term, so that the husband can take her back.

But what Imam Ahmad held is correct, because it is what is reported from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. It also represents a broadening (tawsi'ah) in favour of the husband, because he may regret and then return. This is similar to the establishment of the option between the two parties to a sale as long as they remain in the session, since the contract is complete by offer and acceptance. But they have the option as long as they are in the session, as a broadening in their favour. This is a known matter in the natural disposition and character of a human being: when he is prevented from something, he longs for it, and when he obtains it he may lose interest in it. For example, if this commodity is with so-and-so, you find yourself longing and eager to obtain it, but when it enters my possession, my longing for it is not as it was before. Accordingly, what Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said is the correct view.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of treating one another with kindness even after divorce, because of His saying ﴿so either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness﴾, so that a person does not harm his wife by words, by deeds, by withholding rights, or anything similar.

From this we know that what sometimes happens between spouses, such as disputing and the husband's claim to what his wife has of the goods he gave her as dowry or afterwards, you may find him at the time of divorce quarrelling with her, saying to her: give me everything. Some even demand back the jewellery he gave her, may Allah protect us. This is contrary to the kindness (ma'ruf) that Allah has commanded.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's care for His servants that they should deal with one another in what way?

In kindness (ma'ruf), whether in a state of agreement or a state of disagreement, because that is what preserves the unity of the community. If the community does not deal with one another in kindness but in wrongdoing, it becomes divided and divergent, and does not truly represent the Islamic community. The Islamic community is one community, as Allah said: ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favour, brothers﴾ [Ali 'Imran 103].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of retaining a divorced woman for the purpose of harm, because of His saying ﴿and do not retain them to harm them﴾.

Is it deduced from this that everyone who treats his brother harmfully is committing sin? Yes, by analogy with this matter. From this one deduces by analogy that it is not lawful for anyone to treat his Muslim brother in a harmful manner. It has come in a hadith from the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever harms, Allah will harm him, and whoever causes hardship, Allah will cause hardship for him"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3635) and at-Tirmidhi (1940), from the hadith of Abu Sirmah.]] and in another hadith: "There is no harming and no reciprocating harm"[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (2341) and Ahmad (2865), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]. So harming among Muslims is forbidden, and for this reason Allah said: ﴿and do not retain them to harm them﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that harm is aggression, because of His saying ﴿so that you transgress (li-ta'taduu)﴾, whether the lam is of consequence (al-'aqibah) or of purpose (at-ta'lil). That is, whether the person intends aggression in causing harm or does not intend it, it is aggression in itself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the soul is a trust (amanah) with a person, which he must guard as it deserves to be guarded, because of His saying ﴿and whoever does that has wronged his soul﴾.

Among them: the prohibition of a person wronging himself, because Allah forbade it and then said: whoever does that has wronged his soul.

* Among its benefits: that committing sins is wronging oneself. A person should not say: "I am free, I will do what I like, what is it to you? I am patient with punishment." We say to him: this is a mistake. It is not lawful for you to wrong yourself. If the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Begin with yourself" [[Narrated by Muslim (997/41), and the rest of it: "Begin with yourself and give charity to it."]] in attaining what is sought, then likewise in being saved from what is feared: begin with yourself. Just as you know that wronging others is aggression and forbidden, so wronging yourself is also aggression and forbidden. ﴿And whoever does that has wronged his soul﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strong warning against aggression toward others, in that He said ﴿has wronged his soul﴾, because one who wrongs another may imagine in his mind that he is wronging the one he attacks, while in reality he is wronging himself.

Can we derive from it that a person must love for his brother what he loves for himself?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: How so?

Because He made wronging others a wronging of oneself. Accordingly, just as you do not like to wrong yourself, you must not wrong others. And just as, when it becomes clear to you that you are transgressing against others by wronging them, you are likewise transgressing against yourself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of taking the signs of Allah in mockery, because of His saying ﴿and do not take the verses of Allah in mockery﴾.

Among them: that opposition is a form of mockery. This is a very serious matter: opposing the command of Allah and falling into what He has forbidden is a kind of mockery. How so?

Because if you believe that Allah, the Mighty, is the Lord who has the rule and to whom judgement belongs, and then you disobey Him, it is as if you mock that greatness and treat it lightly. If a king, and to Allah belongs the highest example, forbade you from something, and then you opposed that command in his presence, or did what he forbade you in front of him, would he not say to you: "You are mocking me! I commanded you and you opposed me in front of me!"?

So disobedience is a kind of mockery of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, although it is not the kind of mockery that takes a person out of Islam. The kind of mockery that takes a person out of Islam is mocking in actual earnest, such as ridiculing the adhan, saying: "What is the adhan for? In the past people had no clocks, but now there is no need for the adhan; it is a redundancy and unnecessary," or mocking the muezzin, how he stands and raises his voice with this call, or mocking those who pray. This takes one out of the religion. So mocking a ruling of Allah's rulings is different from opposing the ruling. Opposing the ruling is a kind of mockery, just as it is a kind of shirk, but it is not the shirk that is termed as such, nor is it the mockery that takes one out of the religion. Rather, opposition is undoubtedly a kind of mockery, as He said: ﴿and do not take the verses of Allah in mockery﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of remembering the favour of Allah: ﴿and remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾.

Is what is meant remembering it within yourself, by recalling it, reflecting upon it and contemplating it, or remembering it before people by speech, or remembering it before people by action?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 231–232 (part 5 of 6):

It encompasses everyone. However, mentioning it before people, whether by speech or by action, must not be done in a manner of boasting over them. If it is done in a manner of boasting over them, then "Allah does not love everyone who is arrogant and boastful." It must be done as a means of showing the favour of the one who has favour, and that Allah the Mighty and Majestic has bestowed this blessing upon him. For example, if a person is strong and displays the blessing of Allah upon him through strength, through courage, through defending others, through helping a man with his animal, and the like; or he speaks of the blessing of Allah, saying: "Praise be to Allah, I am strong and healthy, Allah the Most High has given me wealth, has given me a child," and the like, as a display of the blessing of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, not for boasting over creation. This falls under the verse: ﴿And remember the blessing of Allah upon you﴾.

As for remembering it in the heart, it is evident: a person should always regard himself as lowly before the blessings of Allah, knowing that they are purely a gift from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. He should not be like the one who said: ﴿I was only given it on account of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas 78], but rather he should say it with his heart, and likewise speak of it with his tongue, that this is purely a favour from Allah, glorified and exalted is He; for if Allah wished, He could strip you of this blessing, just as He has stripped many people you know or do not know.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah's favour upon us in sending down the Book and the wisdom is greater than every blessing. From where is this derived?
From its singling out after the general mention; for singling out after generalisation indicates the excellence of what is singled out. Accordingly, what Allah has sent down to us of the Book and the wisdom is the greatest favour Allah has bestowed upon us and the greatest blessing. And the mention of the blessing of Allah in what He has sent down to us has already preceded: the intent is that you praise Allah for it and that you carry out what He has commanded you and what He has forbidden you.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And remember the blessing of Allah upon you, and what He has sent down to you of the Book and the wisdom, He admonishes you thereby.﴾
We have said that the noble verse indicates that what has been sent down to us of the Book and the wisdom is greater than every blessing; its basis is the singling out after generalisation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Quran is the speech of Allah; due to His words: ﴿what He has sent down to you﴾, because what Allah sends down is either a self-subsisting entity, or an attribute subsisting in an entity. In the former case it is created. As for when "sending down" is used without it being a self-subsisting entity, nor an attribute in a self-subsisting entity, then it is one of the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.
Example of an entity: the words of the Most High: ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah 22]; ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is mighty strength﴾ [al-Hadid 25].
Example of an attribute in a subsisting entity: ﴿It is He who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers that they might increase in faith﴾ [al-Fath 4].
So "He sent down tranquillity": tranquillity is an attribute in the heart of the believer, and the believer is a self-subsisting entity; so here it is created. Tranquillity is created, and likewise iron and the water that descends from the sky are created. But here the Book: the Book is the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and speech is an attribute of the speaker. So when Allah says that He has sent down the Book to us, it is known that this Book is among the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; thus it is part of His speech.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Law of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is entirely wisdom; due to His words: ﴿what He has sent down to you of the Book and the wisdom﴾.
Another benefit branches from this: that there is no need for us to ask about the wisdom in the legislation of some rulings whose wisdom we do not know; for among the legislated matters are some whose wisdom we do not know. If someone said: What is the wisdom in the noon prayer being four rakahs, not eight or six? What is your answer?
* The student: We do not know the wisdom.
* The Shaykh: We do not know the wisdom; well, does it have wisdom?
Yes, it has wisdom, but we do not know it. Therefore it is obligatory upon the Muslim, regarding the states of the legal rulings, to submit to them absolutely, whether he knows the wisdom or not. As for one who does not submit and is not reassured by a ruling until he knows its wisdom, in reality he has not worshipped Allah by His Law, but rather worshipped what? By his whim. Mu'adhah asked 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, saying: "What is the matter with the menstruating woman that she makes up the fast but does not make up the prayer?" She did not say: "The wisdom is such and such." She said: "This used to befall us, and we were ordered to make up the fast and were not ordered to make up the prayer."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (321), and Muslim (335 / 69) with his wording, from the hadith of Mu'adhah al-'Adawiyyah.]] This is the wisdom.
So the rulings of Allah the Mighty and Majestic are not for us to ask about their wisdom on the basis that our submission is not complete unless we know the wisdom. As for asking about the wisdom for the sake of seeking guidance, this is not objectionable; for this is why the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to ask the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, about the wisdom of some matters: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are times set for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah 189].
So asking about the wisdom for guidance is not objectionable; rather it is part of seeking knowledge. But asking about the wisdom in such a way that a person does not submit to the ruling and does not comply unless he knows it, this is an error.
From the noble verse it is derived: that what comes in the Book of Allah is an admonition by which the servant is admonished. Being admonished means that a person turns away from what is harmful to what is beneficial; "I admonished him and he was admonished," meaning he benefited and left what was harmful for what was beneficial. This is derived from the words: ﴿He admonishes you thereby﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; and that Allah the Most High is possessor of vast mercy. From where is this derived?
From the sending down of the Book and the wisdom. Why?
For our benefit, so that we may be admonished by it; the mercy of Allah is known by its effects.
From the noble verse is derived: the obligation of taqwa; due to His words: ﴿And fear Allah﴾. Its definition has already preceded: it is carrying out the command of Allah and avoiding His prohibition.

* Among its benefits: the comprehensiveness of the knowledge of Allah for everything; due to His words: ﴿that Allah is Knower of all things﴾.
Among its benefits also: warning; warning a person against opposition. What is its aspect?
* A student: That Allah is Knower of all things.
* The Shaykh: That when he knows that Allah is Knower of all things, he will beware of opposing Him. Therefore He followed it after the command to taqwa, saying: ﴿And fear Allah and know﴾, and He prefaced it with ﴿and know﴾ for alerting, because when it is said "know that such-and-such," it is an added alert.
