Moreover, this verse ﴿How excellent is that with which He admonishes you﴾ [an-Nisa' 58] points to what? ﴿How excellent is that with which He admonishes you﴾ means: the command to render trusts. The upshot is that this is the meaning of admonition (maw'izah). No admonition is greater than the Quran for one who has a heart, or who gives ear while he is a witness. As for one who turns away from it and pays it no heed, it does not benefit him, but rather becomes a sickness for him. For this reason, the condition here is ﴿whoever among you is admonished by it, who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. He specified this for those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, because they are the ones who are admonished and benefit. ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [Yunus 57]. So it is the believers who benefit.

As for His saying ﴿who believes in Allah﴾ (...), all of this is necessary. As for belief in the Last Day, what is meant by it is belief that this Day will certainly occur. Shaykh al-Islam [Ibn Taymiyyah] mentioned in al-'Aqidah al-Wasitiyyah [the Creed of Wasitiyyah] that belief in the Last Day includes everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will happen after death. Accordingly, the trial of the grave (fitnat al-qabr), and the bliss or punishment of the grave, fall under belief in the Last Day.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, always pairs belief in Allah with belief in the Last Day, because belief in the Last Day is the greatest incentive for a person to act. Whoever believes in this Day, on which he will meet his Lord, who will call him to account for his deeds and recompense him for them, will work for that Day. As for one who denies it, will he act? One who denies this Day and says, ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world; we die and we live﴾ [al-Jathiyah 24], such a person is not an doer of good.

So belief in the Last Day is the strongest driver for a person and the thing that moves him to act, by performing what is commanded and abstaining from what is forbidden.

Allah called it the Last Day because there is no day after it. This Day is one with no night, because the sun and the moon will be wound up and cast into the Fire. So there is only day, and for this reason Allah called it the Last Day, for there is no day after it.

Belief in the Last Day. I said: Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, says that belief in it includes everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will happen after death. It includes the trial of the grave, its punishment, its bliss, the standing of people barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, the setting up of the scales, the weighing of deeds, the taking of the records, the Sirat (the bridge over Hell), the drawing near of the sun to people, the sweat, the Basin (al-hawd), and intercession. Everything that the Messenger, peace be upon him, informed of in this regard is included in belief in the Last Day.

Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿That is purer for you and more purifying﴾ [al-Baqarah 232]. ﴿That﴾ — look now, He has addressed it in a way that takes the one addressed into account: ﴿that﴾ (dhalikum).

﴿Purer for you (azka lakum)﴾ is a comparative form from zaka' (growth). Zaka' originally means growth, and from it comes zakah (obligatory charity), because it causes wealth to grow by bringing blessing into it, and it causes character to grow by moving a person from the group of the stingy to the group of the generous. So zakah linguistically means increase.

﴿Purer for you﴾ in what respect? Purer for you in your deeds: their growth and their multiplication. When you heed this admonition, you obey Allah and His Messenger, so deeds increase and faith increases too, because faith, even the faith in the heart, increases by carrying out the command and avoiding the prohibition for the sake of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

As for His saying ﴿that﴾, what is the thing pointed to? Is it the admonition, or the rulings that were mentioned, or the necessary consequence of the admonition, which is taking heed?

We now have rulings: ﴿when you divorce women, do not prevent them﴾, and we have an admonition, and we have a ruling, and we have taking heed. So to what does this demonstrative refer? Does the meaning of ﴿that﴾ mean your not preventing them is purer for you? Or does it mean your taking heed of this admonition is purer for you?

* The students: It includes all of them.

* The Shaykh: It includes all of them. That is, what has been mentioned of rulings and admonition, and heeding it, is purer for you, as I said: it is a comparative from zaka', which is growth.

﴿And more purifying (atharr)﴾. More purifying from what? From immorality (fahshaa'). Because if you prevent her from her husband, who has come back and proposed to her, and there was some relationship between them before, perhaps Satan will whisper to them and what happens in immorality will happen between them. For he only proposed to her and she only consented because there was affection and love between them. So if you prevent them, what happens of immorality may happen. For this reason He said ﴿more purifying﴾.

Reflect on how Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, when speaking about matters related to immorality and abstaining from it, mentions that this is purer, because of the chastity it contains and the purity of heart by which deeds and faith grow and flourish.

﴿That is purer for you and more purifying﴾. More purifying from what?

* A student: From sins.

* The Shaykh: From sins, or from accusations, or whatever is similar to that.

﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. The sentence here is nominal, in ascribing knowledge to Allah Himself and negating knowledge from His servants.

He said ﴿And Allah knows﴾. This is a nominal sentence beginning with a noun.

As for His saying ﴿knows﴾, the object has been omitted to convey generality. Because when the object of a transitive verb is omitted, it becomes inclusive of everything it could refer to. He knows the present, the future and the past, what benefits you and what does not benefit you, what you obey and who among you obeys and who does not. In sum, it is general.

As for His saying ﴿while you do not know﴾, this is the original state of a human being, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing and sight﴾ [an-Nahl 78].

So the original state of a human being is ignorance. For this reason He said ﴿while you do not know﴾. Then he gradually acquires knowledge from those around him, from what he hears and what he witnesses, until his knowledge grows. Accordingly, the negation of knowledge here is considered in terms of what? In terms of the original state of the human being, that he is not a knower. Otherwise, a human being does know, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is Knower of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah 282].

There is no doubt that a human being knows. But the original state of a human is non-knowledge, unless Allah, glorified and exalted, teaches him. There is no difference in this between what is known through revelation, what is known through the senses, and what is known through the natural disposition (fitrah), because the ways of knowledge are many. Revelation is one of the ways of knowledge, is it not? And the senses are a way of knowledge: what a person witnesses with his eye, or hears with his ear, or feels with his hand, or smells, or tastes. These are ways of knowledge. Also among the ways of knowledge is the natural disposition, for a human being is created upon the disposition of monotheism toward Allah, glorified and exalted, and turning to Him in repentance.

* * *

The words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them in kindness (ma'ruf) or release them in kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah 231].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that every divorce has a term (ajal). This is shown by His saying ﴿and when you divorce women and they reach their term﴾. And what is this term?

The term here is general, but it is specified in His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual periods (quru')﴾, and in other verses that indicate the waiting period ('iddah).

From this benefit it follows that the Quran sometimes comes in general terms and sometimes in detail. His saying supports this: ﴿A Book whose verses have been perfected and then explained in detail from One who is Wise and Acquainted﴾ [Hud 1].

The benefit of presenting something in general and then in detail is this: when a text comes in general terms, the soul looks forward to knowing what is general and the clarification of what is ambiguous, so it becomes more eager to seek knowledge, does it not? But if the matter came clearly and in detail from the beginning, the soul would have no eagerness to reach knowledge. So when it is mentioned in general terms, the soul seeks to reach the clarification of this general matter, and this becomes one of the ways of firmly establishing knowledge.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of taking the wife back after the waiting period is complete. This is because of His saying ﴿and when they reach their term, then either retain them in kindness or release them﴾. The basis of the inference is that His saying ﴿then retain them﴾ is the answer to the condition in His saying ﴿when you divorce﴾ and ﴿they reach﴾. This implies that retaining or releasing is after the term is reached.

It is necessary that the conditioned thing occurs after the condition, and the conditioned thing, which is the answer, occurs after the condition. Scholars have differed on this matter. Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the husband may retain her until she performs ghusl (the full bath) after the third menstruation. So if she became pure in the morning after dawn, after the sun had risen, and then did not perform ghusl until the noon prayer, and her husband took her back in the interval between her becoming pure and her ghusl, this is permissible according to Imam Ahmad, and he may take her back. However, many scholars hold that the time for taking her back ends with purity from the third menstruation. According to this view, they need to interpret His saying ﴿they reach their term﴾ to mean that they are close to reaching the term, so that the husband can take her back.

But what Imam Ahmad held is correct, because it is what is reported from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. It also represents a broadening (tawsi'ah) in favour of the husband, because he may regret and then return. This is similar to the establishment of the option between the two parties to a sale as long as they remain in the session, since the contract is complete by offer and acceptance. But they have the option as long as they are in the session, as a broadening in their favour. This is a known matter in the natural disposition and character of a human being: when he is prevented from something, he longs for it, and when he obtains it he may lose interest in it. For example, if this commodity is with so-and-so, you find yourself longing and eager to obtain it, but when it enters my possession, my longing for it is not as it was before. Accordingly, what Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said is the correct view.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of treating one another with kindness even after divorce, because of His saying ﴿so either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness﴾, so that a person does not harm his wife by words, by deeds, by withholding rights, or anything similar.

From this we know that what sometimes happens between spouses, such as disputing and the husband's claim to what his wife has of the goods he gave her as dowry or afterwards, you may find him at the time of divorce quarrelling with her, saying to her: give me everything. Some even demand back the jewellery he gave her, may Allah protect us. This is contrary to the kindness (ma'ruf) that Allah has commanded.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's care for His servants that they should deal with one another in what way?

In kindness (ma'ruf), whether in a state of agreement or a state of disagreement, because that is what preserves the unity of the community. If the community does not deal with one another in kindness but in wrongdoing, it becomes divided and divergent, and does not truly represent the Islamic community. The Islamic community is one community, as Allah said: ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favour, brothers﴾ [Ali 'Imran 103].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of retaining a divorced woman for the purpose of harm, because of His saying ﴿and do not retain them to harm them﴾.

Is it deduced from this that everyone who treats his brother harmfully is committing sin? Yes, by analogy with this matter. From this one deduces by analogy that it is not lawful for anyone to treat his Muslim brother in a harmful manner. It has come in a hadith from the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever harms, Allah will harm him, and whoever causes hardship, Allah will cause hardship for him"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3635) and at-Tirmidhi (1940), from the hadith of Abu Sirmah.]] and in another hadith: "There is no harming and no reciprocating harm"[[Narrated by Ibn Majah (2341) and Ahmad (2865), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]. So harming among Muslims is forbidden, and for this reason Allah said: ﴿and do not retain them to harm them﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that harm is aggression, because of His saying ﴿so that you transgress (li-ta'taduu)﴾, whether the lam is of consequence (al-'aqibah) or of purpose (at-ta'lil). That is, whether the person intends aggression in causing harm or does not intend it, it is aggression in itself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the soul is a trust (amanah) with a person, which he must guard as it deserves to be guarded, because of His saying ﴿and whoever does that has wronged his soul﴾.

Among them: the prohibition of a person wronging himself, because Allah forbade it and then said: whoever does that has wronged his soul.

* Among its benefits: that committing sins is wronging oneself. A person should not say: "I am free, I will do what I like, what is it to you? I am patient with punishment." We say to him: this is a mistake. It is not lawful for you to wrong yourself. If the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Begin with yourself" [[Narrated by Muslim (997/41), and the rest of it: "Begin with yourself and give charity to it."]] in attaining what is sought, then likewise in being saved from what is feared: begin with yourself. Just as you know that wronging others is aggression and forbidden, so wronging yourself is also aggression and forbidden. ﴿And whoever does that has wronged his soul﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the strong warning against aggression toward others, in that He said ﴿has wronged his soul﴾, because one who wrongs another may imagine in his mind that he is wronging the one he attacks, while in reality he is wronging himself.

Can we derive from it that a person must love for his brother what he loves for himself?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: How so?

Because He made wronging others a wronging of oneself. Accordingly, just as you do not like to wrong yourself, you must not wrong others. And just as, when it becomes clear to you that you are transgressing against others by wronging them, you are likewise transgressing against yourself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of taking the signs of Allah in mockery, because of His saying ﴿and do not take the verses of Allah in mockery﴾.

Among them: that opposition is a form of mockery. This is a very serious matter: opposing the command of Allah and falling into what He has forbidden is a kind of mockery. How so?

Because if you believe that Allah, the Mighty, is the Lord who has the rule and to whom judgement belongs, and then you disobey Him, it is as if you mock that greatness and treat it lightly. If a king, and to Allah belongs the highest example, forbade you from something, and then you opposed that command in his presence, or did what he forbade you in front of him, would he not say to you: "You are mocking me! I commanded you and you opposed me in front of me!"?

So disobedience is a kind of mockery of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, although it is not the kind of mockery that takes a person out of Islam. The kind of mockery that takes a person out of Islam is mocking in actual earnest, such as ridiculing the adhan, saying: "What is the adhan for? In the past people had no clocks, but now there is no need for the adhan; it is a redundancy and unnecessary," or mocking the muezzin, how he stands and raises his voice with this call, or mocking those who pray. This takes one out of the religion. So mocking a ruling of Allah's rulings is different from opposing the ruling. Opposing the ruling is a kind of mockery, just as it is a kind of shirk, but it is not the shirk that is termed as such, nor is it the mockery that takes one out of the religion. Rather, opposition is undoubtedly a kind of mockery, as He said: ﴿and do not take the verses of Allah in mockery﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of remembering the favour of Allah: ﴿and remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾.

Is what is meant remembering it within yourself, by recalling it, reflecting upon it and contemplating it, or remembering it before people by speech, or remembering it before people by action?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 231–232 (part 5 of 6):

It encompasses everyone. However, mentioning it before people, whether by speech or by action, must not be done in a manner of boasting over them. If it is done in a manner of boasting over them, then "Allah does not love everyone who is arrogant and boastful." It must be done as a means of showing the favour of the one who has favour, and that Allah the Mighty and Majestic has bestowed this blessing upon him. For example, if a person is strong and displays the blessing of Allah upon him through strength, through courage, through defending others, through helping a man with his animal, and the like; or he speaks of the blessing of Allah, saying: "Praise be to Allah, I am strong and healthy, Allah the Most High has given me wealth, has given me a child," and the like, as a display of the blessing of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, not for boasting over creation. This falls under the verse: ﴿And remember the blessing of Allah upon you﴾.

As for remembering it in the heart, it is evident: a person should always regard himself as lowly before the blessings of Allah, knowing that they are purely a gift from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. He should not be like the one who said: ﴿I was only given it on account of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas 78], but rather he should say it with his heart, and likewise speak of it with his tongue, that this is purely a favour from Allah, glorified and exalted is He; for if Allah wished, He could strip you of this blessing, just as He has stripped many people you know or do not know.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah's favour upon us in sending down the Book and the wisdom is greater than every blessing. From where is this derived?
From its singling out after the general mention; for singling out after generalisation indicates the excellence of what is singled out. Accordingly, what Allah has sent down to us of the Book and the wisdom is the greatest favour Allah has bestowed upon us and the greatest blessing. And the mention of the blessing of Allah in what He has sent down to us has already preceded: the intent is that you praise Allah for it and that you carry out what He has commanded you and what He has forbidden you.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And remember the blessing of Allah upon you, and what He has sent down to you of the Book and the wisdom, He admonishes you thereby.﴾
We have said that the noble verse indicates that what has been sent down to us of the Book and the wisdom is greater than every blessing; its basis is the singling out after generalisation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Quran is the speech of Allah; due to His words: ﴿what He has sent down to you﴾, because what Allah sends down is either a self-subsisting entity, or an attribute subsisting in an entity. In the former case it is created. As for when "sending down" is used without it being a self-subsisting entity, nor an attribute in a self-subsisting entity, then it is one of the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.
Example of an entity: the words of the Most High: ﴿He sent down water from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah 22]; ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is mighty strength﴾ [al-Hadid 25].
Example of an attribute in a subsisting entity: ﴿It is He who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers that they might increase in faith﴾ [al-Fath 4].
So "He sent down tranquillity": tranquillity is an attribute in the heart of the believer, and the believer is a self-subsisting entity; so here it is created. Tranquillity is created, and likewise iron and the water that descends from the sky are created. But here the Book: the Book is the speech of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and speech is an attribute of the speaker. So when Allah says that He has sent down the Book to us, it is known that this Book is among the attributes of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; thus it is part of His speech.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the Law of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is entirely wisdom; due to His words: ﴿what He has sent down to you of the Book and the wisdom﴾.
Another benefit branches from this: that there is no need for us to ask about the wisdom in the legislation of some rulings whose wisdom we do not know; for among the legislated matters are some whose wisdom we do not know. If someone said: What is the wisdom in the noon prayer being four rakahs, not eight or six? What is your answer?
* The student: We do not know the wisdom.
* The Shaykh: We do not know the wisdom; well, does it have wisdom?
Yes, it has wisdom, but we do not know it. Therefore it is obligatory upon the Muslim, regarding the states of the legal rulings, to submit to them absolutely, whether he knows the wisdom or not. As for one who does not submit and is not reassured by a ruling until he knows its wisdom, in reality he has not worshipped Allah by His Law, but rather worshipped what? By his whim. Mu'adhah asked 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, saying: "What is the matter with the menstruating woman that she makes up the fast but does not make up the prayer?" She did not say: "The wisdom is such and such." She said: "This used to befall us, and we were ordered to make up the fast and were not ordered to make up the prayer."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (321), and Muslim (335 / 69) with his wording, from the hadith of Mu'adhah al-'Adawiyyah.]] This is the wisdom.
So the rulings of Allah the Mighty and Majestic are not for us to ask about their wisdom on the basis that our submission is not complete unless we know the wisdom. As for asking about the wisdom for the sake of seeking guidance, this is not objectionable; for this is why the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to ask the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, about the wisdom of some matters: ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are times set for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah 189].
So asking about the wisdom for guidance is not objectionable; rather it is part of seeking knowledge. But asking about the wisdom in such a way that a person does not submit to the ruling and does not comply unless he knows it, this is an error.
From the noble verse it is derived: that what comes in the Book of Allah is an admonition by which the servant is admonished. Being admonished means that a person turns away from what is harmful to what is beneficial; "I admonished him and he was admonished," meaning he benefited and left what was harmful for what was beneficial. This is derived from the words: ﴿He admonishes you thereby﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; and that Allah the Most High is possessor of vast mercy. From where is this derived?
From the sending down of the Book and the wisdom. Why?
For our benefit, so that we may be admonished by it; the mercy of Allah is known by its effects.
From the noble verse is derived: the obligation of taqwa; due to His words: ﴿And fear Allah﴾. Its definition has already preceded: it is carrying out the command of Allah and avoiding His prohibition.

* Among its benefits: the comprehensiveness of the knowledge of Allah for everything; due to His words: ﴿that Allah is Knower of all things﴾.
Among its benefits also: warning; warning a person against opposition. What is its aspect?
* A student: That Allah is Knower of all things.
* The Shaykh: That when he knows that Allah is Knower of all things, he will beware of opposing Him. Therefore He followed it after the command to taqwa, saying: ﴿And fear Allah and know﴾, and He prefaced it with ﴿and know﴾ for alerting, because when it is said "know that such-and-such," it is an added alert. This is like His words at the end of the surah: ﴿And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is Knower of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah 282]. So the command to taqwa is followed by the statement of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of everything, so that we may be warned and not be negligent.
In the verse there is a refutation of the extreme Qadariyyah who say that Allah does not know the actions of the servants until they occur. This is what the extremists used to say in the past. Shaykh al-Islam said: Those who deny it today are few; the denial of knowledge is rare. But they, as you know, that is the Qadariyyah, say that the servant has a will and power independent of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Then the Most High said: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term﴾ to the end. From this verse and what precedes it is derived: the great care of Allah the Most High for the matter of marriage and divorce; for it is among the most important and most serious contracts. For this reason there came in it details that did not come in other matters.
From the noble verse is derived: that there is no marriage before the completion of the waiting period; due to His words: ﴿and they reach their term, then do not prevent them﴾. Indeed, marriage during the waiting period is void, except by one for whom the waiting period is owed. Is that possible?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: It is possible. How so?
* The student: A revocable divorce.
* The Shaykh: No, that is not marriage. If he divorced her in exchange for compensation, a khul'; in that case she is separated from him, and he cannot take her back by merely saying: "I have taken back my wife." Rather a contract is necessary. And the contract here is permissible, is it not?
Yes, it is permissible, because he is one for whom the waiting period is owed.
As for anyone else, the contract is not lawful. And does a woman become lawful by it?
The answer: she becomes lawful by a contract after the completion of the waiting period. Some scholars said: she does not become lawful, even after the completion of the waiting period, to the one who married her during the waiting period. The correct view is that this is referred to the judgment of the judge; if he sees fit to deprive this man who married her during her waiting period of her permanently, then he may do so, as is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.[[Related by Ibn Abi Shaybah (19006).]] For the well-known legal principle is: whoever hastens something before its time in a prohibited way is punished by being deprived of it.
So the judge may prevent him from marrying her permanently, saying: he cannot marry her. However, the majority of the people of knowledge hold that she is lawful to this man who contracted with her after the completion of the waiting period.
From the noble verse is derived: the prohibition of a guardian preventing his ward from marrying one whom she has agreed to; due to His words: ﴿do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾.
It is also derived from it: that marriage must have a guardian, and that a woman does not marry herself; what is its basis?
* The students: ﴿and do not prevent them﴾.
* The Shaykh: Its basis from this clause is that if she held the power of contract over herself, the prevention of her guardian would have no effect; whether he prevents or does not prevent, she wishes to marry herself. So had his prevention not been effective, Allah would not have said: ﴿do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾.
This is how many people of knowledge have derived evidence from this verse. Yet someone may dispute its indication of this, because he may say: Allah forbade preventing them, and a person may, according to custom and convention, prevent his daughter or his ward from marrying another husband, even though she could marry herself, because she does not want to oppose him, for fear of disgrace and blame from people; it is said: her father prevented her, and so she went and married herself. In other words, the verse is not clear and explicit that marriage is impossible without a guardian; for it is possible that she has the right to marry herself, but her father comes and says: if you marry yourself I will kill you; it is possible that he prevents her while she could still marry. Just as if he said to her: if you sell your house I will kill you, for example; has he prevented her from selling the house or not? But if she sells it, the sale is valid and it is hers to do.
* A student: And what is the answer to that, O Shaykh?
* The Shaykh: The answer is that when the possibility exists, the inference falls away. But there are other verses that indicate the condition of a guardian, such as His words: ﴿And do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 221].
Also among the benefits of the verse: the application of a thing to what is past or what is future, even though at the present moment it does not possess that description; His words: ﴿that they marry their husbands﴾ [al-Baqarah 232]. For if the intent is those who were divorced and then their husband wished to return to them, then "their husbands" is by reference to what was past; and if the intent is the addressees, then "their husbands" is by reference to the future.
And the expression of the past and future has come in the Quran: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [an-Nisa 2], although by the time of giving them the property they have reached maturity and the description of orphanhood has ceased from them.
﴿Indeed I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf 36], and he is not pressing wine, but he is pressing grapes which will become wine.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the consideration of consent in the contract of marriage, whether from the husband or from the wife; due to His words: ﴿when they agree among themselves in an acceptable manner﴾.
Consent is a condition for the validity of marriage, whether the wife is young or mature, and whether the one contracting is her father or another, according to the preferred view; the father or anyone else has no right to compel the woman into marriage, based on the general statement of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "A previously married woman is not to be married until she is consulted, and a virgin is not to be married until her permission is sought." They said: "How is her permission, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "That she remains silent."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (5136), and Muslim (1419 / 64) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And it is reported in Sahih Muslim: "A virgin's father must seek her permission."[[(1421 / 68).]] This is explicit that it is not lawful for anyone to marry off his daughter while she is unwilling; rather her consent is necessary. The meaning also requires it: for if the father cannot sell a grain of her wealth except with her consent, how could he possess the right to sell her person without her consent?!
If a man forced his daughter to buy this house, what is the ruling on the contract?
It is invalid; even though, if she bought the house while unwilling, she could sell it after a day or two. So how could he have the right to force her to marry a man she does not want?!
It is not possible for the Law to permit this while forbidding sale; that is far-fetched, for we know that the Law came from the All-Wise, the All-Aware, may He be exalted. So the correct view, beyond doubt, is that it is not lawful for anyone to compel his adult daughter into a marriage she does not want, whatever the circumstances. But if she wants a man who is not acceptable in his religion and character, then the guardian may prevent it; and in that case, if she remains unmarried her whole life, there is nothing upon him, for he is commanded to do so, and what results from a command is not forbidden. If you say: an objection to what you have said is the marriage of 'Aishah by Abu Bakr to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when she was six years old? What do you say to this?
We say: bring a wife like 'Aishah and a husband like the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and we will say: he married her when she was two years old; but where is this?!
Is it conceivable that 'Aishah would object, had she reached twenty years of age, to her marriage to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him?
* The students: It is not possible.
* The Shaykh: Never; rather, when he gave her the choice by the command of Allah, she was the first of his wives to be given the choice, and what did she say?
She said: "I choose Allah and His Messenger." When he said: "Consult your two parents," he, peace and blessings be upon him, feared that she would hasten and say: "I choose myself." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, am I to consult my parents about this?"[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (4785), and Muslim (1475 / 22) from the hadith of 'Aishah.]] The story is well known.
﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the worldly life and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you in a graceful release﴾ [al-Ahzab 28]: I will give you provision, and release you with a gentle word, and in the protection of Allah. ﴿But if you desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode﴾ [al-Ahzab 29], this is a great kindness; ﴿Indeed, Allah has prepared for the good-doers among you a great reward﴾. He, peace and blessings be upon him, was the first to begin; see his obedience to the command of his Lord, may He be exalted. He did not begin except with the dearest of women to him and the most beloved of women to him.
She was also the youngest of his wives; that is, she might choose the life of this world and its adornment, so the cause that calls for choosing the world came together in her case, and the matter would have been severe for the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, had she chosen the world. Yet when he gave her the choice, he said, for her benefit: "There is no harm for you in consulting your two parents," meaning seeking their counsel; he feared she would be hasty and rash. But she, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "O Messenger of Allah, am I to consult my parents about this? I desire Allah and His Messenger and the Last Abode."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (4786), and Muslim (1475 / 22) from the hadith of 'Aishah.]] Observe what occurred: that a woman, even after the contract remains, can be given the choice. The point is that a woman cannot be compelled into marriage with one she does not want, and the use of the hadith of 'Aishah as evidence is misplaced; for 'Aishah, as you see, was given the choice and chose what?
* The students: Allah and His Messenger.

Shaykh: She chose Allah and His Messenger. Whoever chooses Allah and His Messenger after being given the choice, can it be that the Messenger ﷺ would object to marrying her? Never. Yet jealousy is common among women. If she is given the choice and her husband says to her, "Do you want to stay with me in frugality and in the living I have, or do you want the world and go to so-and-so?", a woman is generally seized by jealousy and becomes upset. She says: "Whoever does not want us, we do not want him, and whoever sells us cheaply, we sell him for nothing." But in any case, the correct view, without doubt, is that the wife's consent is necessary, and the evidence for this from the Qur'an and the Sunnah is clear.

It is derived from the noble verse that if a woman consents to a suitor in a manner that is not known, rather in a manner that is objectionable and not approved by the Shari'ah, she is not to be enabled to do so, because of His saying: ﴿in a known manner﴾. So if a woman consents to this suitor despite his immorality and his having departed from the religion, but without reaching the level of disbelief, may her guardian (wali) prevent it? Yes, he may prevent it, because of His saying: ﴿when they agree among themselves in a known manner﴾.

And if she says: "I consent to him without a dowry, I want him without a dowry, she takes nothing from him," may he prevent her? He may prevent her, because the dowry is among the conditions for the validity of the marriage. For this reason, if it is stipulated that there is no dowry, the correct view is that the marriage is invalid. But if the matter of the dowry is left unmentioned, the marriage is valid and she is due the customary dowry (mahr al-mithl). ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligatory payment﴾, and ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, while you have already specified for them an obligatory payment﴾. Here there is a difference between leaving the dowry unmentioned and stipulating that there is no dowry.

It is also derived from the noble verse that the wise rulings, or rather all the rulings, are admonitions, because of His saying: ﴿with it you are admonished﴾. The demonstrative ﴿that﴾, as we have already explained in the tafsir, refers to everything mentioned before of the rulings. It is admonition for whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day.

Among its benefits as well: the admonitions of the Qur'an do not benefit those who are not believers, because of His saying: ﴿for whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. So if I find that I am not admonished by the admonitions of the Qur'an, I must suspect myself, I must suspect myself. How? You say: "Why? What is the evidence?" Because Allah has made clear that the believer in Allah and the Last Day must be admonished by the rulings of the Qur'an. So if you find in yourself that you are not admonished, then suspect yourself. Examine yourself. There may be something in the heart that you have neglected. Do not rely on outward forms. Do not rely on correcting the prayer outwardly through movements and words, nor on abundant remembrance with the tongue, because this sometimes does not reach the heart, and so it does not benefit. We may pray while our hearts are absent, and then we gain nothing from the prayer. It is like a solid stone that stands between the water and the roots of the tree, so the water cannot penetrate from behind it. We feel this when we recite the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 45]. By Allah, when you finish the prayer, do you feel that you hate immorality and wrongdoing more than you hated it before you prayed? The answer?

Student: No.

Shaykh: The answer is no. Let us be frank. The answer is no, unless Allah wills. Sometimes Allah, Mighty and Majestic, places in the heart a light, and the heart becomes so present in the prayer that it is as if you are addressing Allah, the Exalted, and you are indeed addressing Him without doubt. The heart is present, so the person finds in this prayer a pleasure he does not forget, and after finishing he finds an aversion to immorality and wrongdoing and a love of good, and he wishes to remain with Allah always in this state. Therefore I say: we must hold ourselves accountable by such measures. Do the admonitions of the Qur'an benefit us? Let us look. Whenever we benefit more from the admonitions of the Qur'an, we are more complete in faith, and whenever we fall short, our faith is deficient.

In the verse there is evidence for affirming the Last Day, which is the Day of Resurrection: ﴿whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. Belief in the Last Day includes belief in everything that is mentioned about that day: the resurrection, the reckoning, the Sirat (bridge), the Hawd (the Pool), the drawing near of the sun, the sweat, and other matters mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah, sometimes in summary and sometimes in detail. Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said: belief in the Last Day includes all that the Prophet ﷺ informed of that occurs after death, including the trial of the grave, the punishment of the grave, and the bliss of the grave. That day is called the Last Day. We have passed this, yes: ﴿whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that taking admonition from the rulings of Allah is a purification of the soul, because of His saying: ﴿That is purer for you﴾. It is a purification that develops the soul, develops faith, develops morals, develops manners. Here He said ﴿purer for you﴾ and did not restrict the place of purity, so that it would be general in everything, and every person seeks purity: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [Ash-Shams 9-10]. So it is derived from this that whenever a person is more diligent in applying the rulings of Allah, that is purer for him.

It is also derived from this: that applying the rulings is purer for the person. Purer for his heart or for his body?

* Students: For his heart.

Shaykh: For his heart. Because some rulings have no connection with purifying the body. Wudu' and ghusl have a connection with purifying the body, but some rulings do not. Yet it is purer for the heart. But be assured that whenever the heart is purified, the body is purified too. For this reason you find in the truly faithful person a vitality, energy, joy and happiness that others do not have, which is recognized in his face. The person, and Allah forbid, who is a people of sins has a dark face and a downcast state. If he rejoices at what he rejoices in of the flower of this world, sometimes, it is a deceptive joy. But the believer whom Allah has expanded his chest for Islam, and whose heart is filled with the light of Allah and His guidance, is not like that. So we may also say: the purity of the heart, indeed we say it: the purity of the heart undoubtedly purifies the body, and the happiest people in this world are the purest of heart.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the human being's deficiency in knowledge, because of His saying: ﴿and Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. The deficiency is established in two ways: affirming knowledge for Allah and negating it from the human being, because negation alone only indicates a great deficiency, but negation together with affirmation is more severe. For example, if I say to you: "I know and you do not know," my statement "you do not know" has a stronger impact. For this reason, among the good manners of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, with his father, he said: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 43]. He did not say: "I know more than you," or "you have no knowledge." There are three levels. Sometimes a person says: "I have knowledge that you do not have." This is the gentlest form, because it implies that the other party has some knowledge, but I have what you do not have. And saying to someone, "I have knowledge that you do not have," does not necessarily mean that I am more knowledgeable than him, because I may have knowledge of carpentry while you do not, but you have other fields of knowledge more than carpentry. Is that not so?

* Students: Yes.

Shaykh: Second, he says: "You do not know this thing." This is stronger than the first, because he has negated knowledge from him. Sometimes he says: "I know and you do not know." This is stronger still, because it affirms the superiority of the speaker over the addressee, and it contains a belittling of... what? The addressee. Here He said: ﴿and Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. So if Allah knows and we do not know, the consequence of that is that we submit completely to His rulings, the Exalted, and that we do not oppose them with our intellects, however much the intellects may be, if they contradict the Shari'ah, they are not truly intellects. For this reason, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, reproaches the disbelievers and polytheists, condemning them for lacking intellect. So everything that contradicts the Shari'ah is not intellect. We call it cleverness and intellect of perception, but it is not the intellect of right conduct and guidance. How excellent is the expression of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) about the people of kalam (speculative theology). He said: "They were given understandings but were not given knowledge. They have comprehension but they do not have knowledge. They were given cleverness but were not given purification (zaka')." They were given cleverness; they have cleverness, they have understanding, but they were deprived of knowledge and of purification, which is the fruit of knowledge. You see, "they were not given purification." From where? From self-purification, zaka'. In sum, Allah has clarified for us in this verse His perfection and our deficiency. How excellent it is to combine the two: to show the deficiency of the human being and the perfection of the Creator, to show the deficiency of the created and the perfection of the Creator. Read: ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away. And there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾ [Ar-Rahman 26-27]. Therefore ﴿and there remains the Face of your Lord﴾, though it is an independent verse, is closely connected to what precedes it, so that the perfection of this and the deficiency of that become clear. ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away. And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not intend from this verse to show merely that people are mortal, or that people perish. Rather He intends to show the deficiency of mankind or the deficiency of creation and the perfection of the Creator. ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away. And there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour.﴾ Here He says: ﴿and Allah knows, while you do not know﴾. The negation here, one might ask: is it an absolute negation or a relative negation?

* Student: Relative.

Shaykh: Yes, relative, comparative, and not an absolute negation, because we do have knowledge, but it is deficient, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [Al-Isra' 85]. So we have knowledge, but it is little, and it cannot be compared to the knowledge of Allah, Glorified and Exalted. Then Allah, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿And the mothers...﴾

* Student: (...) the first?

Shaykh: Or the reasonable? Reasonable provision is obligatory, and good conduct is recommended. We mentioned this.

* Student: What does the fa' in His saying, Exalted: ﴿So when they have fulfilled their term, then retain them﴾ indicate?

Shaykh: Upon what is it conjunctive?

Student: What does it indicate?

Shaykh: It indicates that from the moment she reaches her term, it is either retention or release.

* * *

(...) So that we know what we are saying.

The mufawwidah (those who delegate the meaning of the divine attributes to Allah) are those who say: we recite the verses and hadiths about the attributes, and we say nothing about them. We affirm no meaning contrary to the apparent sense, nor any meaning that agrees with the apparent sense. Rather we delegate their matter to Allah, and we say: all we have to do is recite, that is all. They are like the letters alif, ba, ta, tha, jim, ha, kha, and so on to the end, as if they were letters of the alphabet with no meaning. However, some of the mufawwidah contradict themselves and say: "We do not know what Allah intended by them, but we know that He did not intend their apparent meaning." Fine, then how can you delegate first and then contradict yourselves? You say: He did not intend their apparent meaning. Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) has explained the contradiction of this group among them. For the mufawwidah, can we say that this verse refutes them: ﴿And know that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾? Because if we do not know that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has a knowledge by which He perceives what we do, there is no benefit in His saying: ﴿know that Allah﴾. Yes, there can be a refutation from it. There is no doubt, my brothers, that the doctrine of the mufawwidah is more corrupt than the doctrine of the ahl al-tahrif (those who distort the meanings of the attributes). It is more corrupt, and it is the worst of the statements of the people of innovation and atheism, as Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his book Ar-Radd 'ala al-Mantiqiyyin (Refutation of the Logicians). He says: this statement is among the worst of the statements of the people of innovation and atheism. He says: with it the philosophers who deny the attributes, indeed those who deny the Last Day, indeed those who deny the Creator, have gained boldness. What did the people of imagination (ahl al-takhyil) say? They said: "You go on (...), you are ignorant like children. You do not know what Allah intended. But we are the masters who know what Allah intended." What did Allah intend, according to them? They said: Allah intended imagination, which has no reality. There is no Lord, no Paradise, no Fire, no reckoning, nothing. It is mere imagination. They said: "We are more worthy than you, O mufawwidah." How are they more worthy than us? Because we know the intended meaning and you do not know the intended meaning. Although their statement regarding the intended meaning is certainly wrong, as we will explain shortly, Allah willing, the point is that the doctrine of the mufawwidah makes people illiterate, indeed makes them children. How can Allah send down to us verses about ablution, purification, and prayer and similar matters, and we understand their meanings, while what relates to His names and attributes we do not know? Is this reasonable? It is not reasonable, and we cannot worship a Lord with true worship unless we know from His names and attributes that by which worship is established. As for refuting the people of imagination, it is impossible to silence them and put them to shame except by the way of whom? The Salaf, who say: we know what our Lord intended by His speech, and that it is true in its reality. But the modality (kayfiyyah) and the reality in which these attributes exist, we do not perceive.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 233 (part 1 of 3):

(...) The clause ﴿yur'ḍna﴾ (they suckle) is its predicate (khabar), so the clause is declarative in form but carries the meaning of an imperative (inshā'iyya), i.e., the meaning of a command. The scholars said: a declarative clause is used with the meaning of a command for emphasis on its certainty and on its being carried out, as if the matter is already settled and unavoidable.

His saying ﴿al-wālidāt﴾ (the mothers) is an active participle (ism fā'il), meaning: those who have given birth. ﴿Yurḍi'na awlādahunna﴾ (they suckle their children): "awlād" (children) includes males and females, because we mentioned earlier that the word walad in the Arabic language applies to both male and female. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [An-Nisa' 11].

His saying: ﴿yurḍi'na awlādahunna ḥawlayni kāmilayn﴾. Al-ḥawl means a year, and it is twelve lunar months. So when it is said ﴿ḥawlayn﴾ (two years), the meaning is two years, twenty-four months. Then Allah emphasised these two years with His saying ﴿kāmilayn﴾ (complete), so the description here is of completeness, lest someone imagine that what is meant by the two years is their completion or something close to completion. So He said ﴿ḥawlayni kāmilayn﴾. A parallel to this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So fasting three days during the Hajj and seven when you have returned; those are ten complete﴾ [Al-Baqarah 196]. He emphasised it with "kāmila" (complete), although it is ten, lest someone imagine that once the three were separated from the seven they would not be ten. So Allah made clear that they are ten complete.

His saying: ﴿li-man arāda an yutimma al-raḍā'a﴾ (for whoever wishes to complete the suckling). The prepositional phrase here necessarily has an object of attachment (muta'alliq), as in all other places, as was said:
"The prepositional phrase must have an attachment, to a verb or what carries its meaning..."

Regarding ﴿li-man arāda﴾: what is this prepositional phrase attached to? It was said that it is attached to ﴿yurḍi'na awlādahunna﴾, so that ﴿man﴾ refers to the husbands, because they are the ones for whom suckling is done, as Allah, the Exalted, said in Surat at-Talaq: ﴿If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment﴾ [At-Talaq 6]. On this view, the prepositional phrase is attached to the verb ﴿yurḍi'na awlādahunna﴾, meaning they suckle the children for the one who wishes to complete the suckling. For whom? For the husbands. It was also said that the prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted element whose estimate is: "that", i.e., that ruling, which is the mother's suckling of her child for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the suckling. Then ﴿man﴾ would refer to the nursing wives, or would include them and the father of the child, unlike the first estimate.

His saying: ﴿li-man arāda an yutimma al-raḍā'a﴾ means that he wishes to bring it about in its complete form, for it is not less than two years. Can it exceed that?
* The students: Two years.
* The Shaykh: Yes, two years. Can it exceed that? One looks at the state of the child: if he still needs milk, it is extended by the amount needed; if he does not need it, it ends.

His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿li-man arāda an yutimma al-raḍā'a﴾ is in the accusative case, with ﴿an﴾ being a verbal particle (maṣdariyya). It was read irregularly (shādhdh) as ﴿an yutimma al-raḍā'a﴾, with ﴿an﴾ being the lightened form of the heavy ﴿inna﴾. He said: ﴿li-man arāda an yutimma al-raḍā'a﴾. His saying: ﴿al-raḍā'a﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) or a noun of the verbal noun, meaning the suckling that the child needs.

He said: ﴿wa-'alā al-mawlūdi lahu rizquhunna wa-kiswatuhunna bil-ma'rūf﴾ (and upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing according to what is reasonable). I think the grammar is clear: ﴿'alā al-mawlūdi﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), ﴿rizquhunna﴾ is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and ﴿lahu﴾ is attached to ﴿al-mawlūdi﴾.

﴿wa-'alā al-mawlūdi lahu﴾: who is "the one to whom the child is born"? It may be the husband, and it may be the master if the mother is a slave-woman, is it not? It may be otherwise if supposed, but it is only conceivable as the husband or the master. His saying ﴿al-mawlūdi lahu﴾ and he did not say "wa-'alā al-wālid" (upon the father). Some said this is for two benefits: one is verbal, and the other is conceptual. As for the verbal benefit, it is variety in expression: wālida (mother) and mawlūd lahu (the one to whom the child is born). As for the conceptual benefit, the father is the one to whom the child is given as a gift, since the child is a gift to his father. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "You and your wealth belong to your father" [Abu Dawud (3530) and al-Bayhaqi in al-Kubra (7/480), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, and the wording is his]. So it is as if this child is given to him as a gift. Zakariyya said: ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ [Maryam 5]. Therefore He expressed it as ﴿wa-'alā al-mawlūdi lahu﴾.

﴿rizquhunna wa-kiswatuhunna﴾: "rizq" means what a person sustains himself with, of food and other things. "Kiswa" means what a person clothes his body with. It has passed us that clothing is of two kinds: necessary clothing that cannot be dispensed with, and ornamental clothing. Both were mentioned in His saying: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts, and as adornment (rīsh)﴾ [Al-A'raf 26]. So the rīsh is the clothing of beauty and adornment, and that which covers the private parts is the necessary clothing. We also explained earlier the wisdom in Allah making for the human an external clothing, not attached to him, like the clothing of animals for example. What is it? That a person feels he is naked unless he does what covers his nakedness. At that point he moves from physical nakedness to spiritual nakedness, and from physical clothing to spiritual clothing, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the clothing of piety, that is best﴾ [Al-A'raf 26].

﴿wa-kiswatuhunna bil-ma'rūf﴾: ﴿bil-ma'rūf﴾ is attached to what? To ﴿rizq﴾, meaning that he provides for them and clothes them according to what is reasonable, i.e., what people have known among themselves and what the Shari'a has approved. Among acts of worship, what is reasonable is what the Shari'a approved; among customs, what is reasonable is what people of custom approved. Here, feeding and clothing the wife: is it from worship or from customs, or both?
* The students: Both.
* The Shaykh: Both together. For this reason Allah obligated a person to provide for his wife and clothe her. It is from worship, but it is a right of a human being, not a right of Allah. It is also from customs, since the custom operates with it. So ﴿bil-ma'rūf﴾: according to what people know among themselves and what the Shari'a knows and approves.

His saying here: ﴿wa-'alā al-mawlūdi lahu﴾ includes the husband who is separated and the husband who is still married, meaning that he is obliged to spend on the nursing woman, whether she is in his marriage or not. But if she is in his marriage, it is called maintenance (nafaqa); if she is not in his marriage, it is called a wage (ujra), as Allah said concerning divorced women: ﴿If they breastfeed for you, give them their payment, and consult among yourselves in reasonableness﴾ [At-Talaq 6]. If you say: the verse here includes, as we mentioned, the divorced and the non-divorced, and the feeding and clothing of a non-divorced woman is obligatory in every case, can you not say that we obligate him, in addition to the maintenance required by marriage, to pay a wage for the suckling? We say: the sounder opinion is that we do not obligate him to that; we do not obligate him to a wage for suckling. So when Allah said ﴿wal-wālidātu yurḍi'na awlādahunna﴾, it is as if a questioner asked: then what is incumbent upon the father? So He clarified that upon the father is their provision and clothing. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, made clear that the husband's or the father's provision and clothing is in exchange for the woman's suckling of her child. Then, can a woman be with her husband while maintenance is not obligatory for her? When?
* A student: When she is disobedient (nashaza).
* The Shaykh: When she is disobedient. In that case, he must spend on her in exchange for the suckling.

﴿wa-'alā al-mawlūdi lahu rizquhunna wa-kiswatuhunna bil-ma'rūfi. Lā tukallafu nafsun illā wus'ahā﴾: ﴿tukallafu﴾: taklif means imposing what involves hardship. That is why, when you carry something heavy, you say: "this burdens me" (yukallifunī) or "this has burdened me" (kallafanī). So taklif in the language means imposing what involves hardship. That is, Allah, mighty and majestic, does not impose upon a soul except what it can bear, i.e., its capacity. This is general in what is obligatory from Allah and what is obligatory by Allah's command upon His servants, for Allah does not burden a soul except with what it can bear. Is the taklif here legal (shar'i) or predestined (qadari)?
* The students: Legal.
* The Shaykh: Legal. For Allah does not legally obligate or impose upon anyone a thing that the person cannot do and that does not fall within his capacity. As for predestined taklif, Allah, mighty and majestic, may burden a person with what is hard upon him in order to test him, whether he will be patient or not, and this is known.

His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul except with its capacity﴾: what is it that put ﴿wus'ahā﴾ in the accusative? ﴿yukallifu﴾ is the second object of ﴿yukallifu﴾, and the first object is ﴿nafsan﴾. This type of exception is called the "emptied exception" (istithnā' mufarragh), because the governing word is left free to act on what follows ﴿illā﴾: ﴿lā tukallafu nafsun illā wus'ahā﴾. This rule is a general rule in everything, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul except with its capacity. It has what it earned, and it bears what it earned﴾ [Al-Baqarah 286]. Later, if Allah wills, in the benefits, the mention of what is derived from this general legal rule will come.

﴿lā tuḍārra wālidatun bi-waladihā﴾: there are two readings: ﴿lā tuḍārra﴾ and ﴿lā tuḍārru﴾. On the reading with a fatha, ﴿lā tuḍārra﴾, we say: ﴿lā﴾ is a prohibitive particle, and ﴿tuḍārra﴾ is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive after the prohibitive ﴿lā﴾, and the sign of its accusative is an apparent fatha at its end, correct?
* The students: Wrong.
* The Shaykh: No?
* The students: It is jussive (majzūm).
* The Shaykh: Now the verb is pronounced with a fatha.
* A student: ﴿lā tuḍārr﴾.
* The Shaykh: With a kasra?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Fine, then we say: ﴿lā﴾ is prohibitive, and the prohibitive does not put in the accusative. Nothing in the language, ever, puts the imperfect in the accusative with ﴿lā﴾. On this basis we say: ﴿lā﴾ is prohibitive, ﴿tuḍārra﴾ is an imperfect verb in the jussive after the prohibitive ﴿lā﴾, and the sign of its jussive is a sukūn, but it was given a fatha because of the meeting of two sukūns. If you say: why was it not given a kasra? Because giving a kasra is the common way to resolve the meeting of two sukūns, as in ﴿lam yakuni alladhīna kafarū﴾ [Al-Bayyina 1]. The answer: the fatha is lighter, so the fatha was chosen. As for the reading with a damma, ﴿lā tuḍārru﴾, then ﴿lā﴾ is negative, and therefore it does not govern the verb. ﴿Tuḍārru﴾ is an imperfect verb in the nominative with an apparent damma. But what do you say: is ﴿tuḍārru﴾ in the active or the passive voice? If you say it is active, that is wrong; if you say it is passive, that is wrong. Can it fit both? It can, like (mukhtār): is it an active participle or a passive participle? It fits both, and what determines one of them is the context. Here, ﴿lā tuḍārra﴾: if we say that ﴿tuḍārra﴾ is active, the unassimilated form becomes: lā tuḍārirru wālidatun bi-waladihā, is it so? ﴿lā tuḍārir﴾, or not? Like: lā tuḍārib, lā tujāhid, lā tuqātil, lā tuḍārir. And if we say that it is passive, the unassimilated form becomes: lā tuḍārar, like: lā tuḍārab, lā tuqātal, lā tujāhad, and what is similar. So the word is shared between the active participle and the passive participle. We mentioned earlier among the benefits of tafsir that if a verse can bear two or more meanings that do not contradict each other, it is taken as bearing both, and that this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an. If they contradict, the stronger is taken. Here they do not contradict. Let us explain it as active: lā tuḍārir wālidatun bi-waladihā. Who is the one harmed? The one to whom the child is born. That is, the mother must not harm the father of the child, by making him bear what he cannot bear, by asking him for a large wage or provision that he cannot afford, or by refusing to suckle her child so as to embarrass the father by demanding wet nurses, even though she has milk, saying: "let him tire, let him go look for wet nurses." Is this harm or not? It is harm, and harm in the Shari'a is forbidden and prohibited. So: "a mother must not harm her child's father", the one harmed is the father of the child. We mentioned two examples of harm: one is that she asks for a wage or provision that he cannot bear; the second is that she refuses to suckle so as to embarrass his father, though she has milk but says: "I want to constrict this man," and Allah, mighty and majestic, forbade that.

As for if we explain it as passive: lā tuḍārar wālidatun, then the prohibition is directed at whom? At the father of the child: the father of the child must not harm the mother. How does he harm her? By preventing her from suckling her child, when she asks to suckle her child and he says: "No, I do not want you to nurse him." This is harm to her, since a mother has compassion and tenderness that require her to suckle the child. Likewise he harms her through the child, by obligating her to a burden she cannot manage, whether because of an illness in her breast, or lack of milk, or the like. The point is that he obligates her to what she cannot bear. This is among harm. Also among harm is that he delays her rights of maintenance or wage, for that is harm.

His saying: ﴿wālidatun﴾: how do we parse it? If we say that ﴿tuḍārra﴾ is passive, then it is?
* The students: Subject (fā'il).
* The Shaykh: No. If we say that ﴿tuḍārra﴾ is passive, then it is a deputy subject (nā'ib fā'il). And if we say it is active, then it is a subject (fā'il). Fine. His saying ﴿wālidatun﴾ is indefinite in the context of prohibition or negation, on both readings, and indicates generality: it is not lawful for any mother to be harmed through her child. Even if there is personal enmity between the husband and this mother, it is not permitted for him to harm her through her child, because this is a right of whom? Of her and of her child, so he cannot harm her by means of it. For this reason ﴿wālidatun﴾ came indefinite, to encompass every mother. Does this include animals?
* A student: No, it does not include them.
* The Shaykh: It does not include what? That is, is it permitted for a person to harm an animal through its offspring?
* The student: No.
* The Shaykh: Then what is it?
* A student: It is not derived from this verse.
* The Shaykh: It is not derived from this verse, because the verse is in the context of the children of Adam. It is derived by another route, from other hadiths, which is the obligation of mercy toward animals.

He said: ﴿wa-lā mawlūdun lahu bi-waladihi﴾: that is, "and the one to whom a child is born must not be harmed through his child." The waw is a conjunction, the ﴿lā﴾ is negative, and ﴿mawlūdun﴾ is conjoined to ﴿wālidatun﴾. So how do we parse ﴿mawlūd﴾?
* A student: In both ways.
* The Shaykh: In both ways. But if you parse ﴿wālidatun﴾ as the subject, then this is the deputy subject, and if you parse ﴿wālidatun﴾ as the deputy subject, then this is the subject. It is strange for something to be conjoined to something that matches it only in grammatical case and not in meaning. But if it differs in meaning, the better view is to estimate for the conjoined word a verb suited to it, since it is known that the conjoined elements share the meaning indicated by the governing word; if they differ, a verb suited to the conjoined word must be estimated, as in the poet's verse:
"I fed her straw, and cold water..."
We do not say "cold water" is conjoined to "straw" because the meaning does not hold; rather we say: "and I gave her to drink." On this basis, after ﴿lā﴾ we must estimate a verb of which ﴿mawlūd﴾ is the object.

His saying: ﴿wa-lā mawlūdun lahu bi-waladihi﴾: how is the one to whom a child is born harmed through his child? It was explained in both forms: the woman harms him by embarrassing him over the maintenance of her child, by demanding suckling for her child, or by increasing the maintenance or wage. If it is he who harms, then he harms the mother to whom the child is born, by what? By preventing her from suckling, or by obligating her to what she cannot bear, or by delaying her rights.
* A student: Reducing the wage.
* The Shaykh: Or reducing the wage. That is among delaying. ﴿wa-lā mawlūdun lahu bi-waladihi﴾. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿wa-'alā al-wārithi mithlu dhālik﴾ (and upon the heir is the like of that). ﴿'alā al-wārith﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a fronted predicate, and ﴿mithlu dhālika﴾ is a delayed subject. It has passed us in the principles of jurisprudence that ﴿'alā﴾ is among the particles that indicate obligation. When one says "'alayka kadhā" (upon you is such-and-such), it means "it is obligatory upon you." So ﴿wa-'alā al-wārithi mithlu dhālika﴾ means: and it is obligatory upon the heir?
* A student: (...).

* **The Shaykh:** It is possible to say this as well: the likeness (*mithlīyah*) here refers to nursing, and to provision and clothing. Its reference to provision and clothing is quite clear. But what about His saying ﴿upon the heir﴾? Does it mean the heir of the one to whom the child is born, or the heir of the nursing infant? On this there are two opinions among the exegetes, and the preferred view is that it refers to the heir of the infant. Note that He said ﴿and upon the heir﴾ here, whereas earlier He said ﴿upon the one to whom the child is born﴾, because the heir is not like the father, who is granted to him, unlike the parent, who is granted to him.

﴿upon the heir the like of that﴾: Is this from the heir by a fixed share (*fard*), by agnatic inheritance (*ta'ṣīb*, the heir who takes the residue), or by kinship (*raḥim*)? This too is a point of disagreement. If we look at the apparent meaning of the verse, it covers everyone who inherits, whether by fixed share, agnatic inheritance, or kinship. Some scholars restricted it to the agnatic heir by analogy with bearing the blood money (*diyah*). They said: the ones held liable for financial obligations are the agnates (*'aṣabah*). Just as the holders of fixed shares do not bear any part of the blood money, so they do not bear any part of the maintenance. The same applies to the kindred (*dhawū al-arḥām*). But the preferred view is that it covers everyone who inherits by fixed share or by agnatic inheritance, except what the evidence specifies. What the evidence specifies must be restricted according to that evidence. We have made this exception so that there is no objection to what some people have held: that a wife must be supported by her husband if he is poor. Some scholars derived from the general wording of the verse the obligation of a wife's maintenance upon her husband if he is poor. They said: because the husband is an heir. But this is refuted by specific evidence, namely the statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage, when he said: "They have a right to their provision and their clothing in a reasonable manner" (narrated by Muslim, 1218, from Jabir), without detail.

His saying ﴿But if the two of them desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them both﴾. ﴿if the two of them desire weaning﴾: *fiṣāl* means weaning (*fiṭām*). The subject of *arādā* refers to the mother and the one to whom the child is born. The desire here is not the desire of mere whim, as shown by His saying ﴿by mutual consent and consultation﴾. This weaning must occur by mutual consent of both. *Tarāḍin* (mutual consent) is a reciprocal form (*tafā'ul*) from *raḍiya*, so it must come from both sides. If the mother consents but the father does not, the weaning is prohibited. If the father consents but the mother does not, the weaning is prohibited.

His saying ﴿and consultation﴾: *tashāwur* is also a reciprocal form. Its root is from *shāra al-'asal*, meaning when one extracts honey, as in "I extracted the honey," meaning I separated it from the wax in it until it appeared pure and clear. So it is a reciprocal form of *shāra*. What then is the meaning of *tashāwur*? *Tashāwur* is the exchange of opinions in order to extract the correct one. Two people exchange opinions so that they arrive at the correct opinion that is suitable and beneficial. Therefore, there must be what? There must be consultation. If the two agreed without consultation, and the mother came and said to her husband, "I want to wean the child so that he does not tire me in carrying and nursing him, and so on," and he said, "Very well, rely upon Allah," without any consultation, this is not permissible. There must be consultation. Now, what is the locus and place of consultation? Is its locus the interest of the father and mother in terms of the child's custody and the burden upon them? Or is its place the interest of the child? The interest of the child. They must consult about his interest. Is it in his interest to be weaned before the two years, or is it in his interest to remain until he completes the two years, or is it in his interest to remain even beyond the two years, since he may need nursing even after two years? There must be consultation on this matter. And whose interest is to be considered? The child's.

His saying ﴿there is no blame upon them both﴾: upon whom? Upon the two parents for weaning him before completing the two years. *Junāḥ* (blame) is the subject of *lā* (there is no), built upon the fatḥah with it, and its predicate is the prepositional phrase ﴿upon them both﴾. We have already mentioned that *junāḥ* means sin.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you wish to seek wet-nurses for your children, there is no blame upon you provided you pay what you agreed, in accordance with what is reasonable﴾. In a reading: ﴿mā ataytum﴾. The difference between *ataytum* and *ātaytum* is that *ataytum* without the madd means "you came," and *ātaytum* with the madd means "you gave." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And give the relative his right﴾ (al-Isrā' 26). Here it is *ātī* with the madd. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then bring a surah like it﴾ (Yūnus 38), here ﴿fa'tū﴾ and He did not say *ātū*, meaning "come." So when it is hamzated, i.e. the hamzah carries the madd, it means "give," and when it is without the madd, it means "come." Here He, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And if you wish to seek wet-nurses for your children﴾. To whom is the address?

* **Student:** To the parents.

* **The Shaykh:** How to the parents? To the one to whom the child is born. And at that point you must raise the difficulty: how did He say ﴿if you wish﴾ when earlier He said ﴿upon the one to whom the child is born﴾? He said "the one to whom the child is born," not "those to whom the children are born." So it is said: *al-mawlūd* is a generic noun. If you wish, you may say: *al-mawlūd* is a relative noun by virtue of the definite article (*al*), because when the definite article is followed by a descriptive, it becomes a relative noun from the shared nouns, which can be used for the singular and for others. At that point, the singularity of the pronoun referring back to it is in view of the wording, and its plurality is in view of the meaning, if you wish. Good. The Qur'an has used these shared designations, observing both wording and meaning. We have already mentioned a verse in which the wording is observed, then the meaning, then the wording. Do you remember it?

* **The Students:** Yes.

* **The Shaykh:** What is it?

* **Student:** In Surat al-Ṭalāq, in His saying: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness – He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah has certainly perfected for him provision﴾ (al-Ṭalāq 11).

* **The Shaykh:** Yes. ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness – He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. All the rivers, in view of what?

* **Student:** The wording.

* **The Shaykh:** The wording is singular. ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ is in view of the meaning. ﴿Allah has certainly perfected for him provision﴾ is in view of the wording. So here, ﴿if you wish﴾, the address to the ones to whom the children are born is in view of the meaning.

﴿to seek wet-nurses for your children﴾: *arāda* (to wish) requires a direct object. So where is the object of ﴿arādtum﴾?

* **Student:** *An* (that) and what follows it.

* **The Shaykh:** *An* and what follows it, in the sense of a verbal noun, is the direct object. Now, ﴿awlādakum﴾ is in the accusative. What made it accusative? Would you say *istarḍi'a waladahu* (he sought a nurse for his child), or *istarḍi'a li-waladihi* (he sought a nurse for his child, with a preposition)?

* **Student:** The latter.

* **The Shaykh:** The latter. Then where is the object of *istarḍa'a*? Because *istarḍa'a* requires an object. The meaning of *istarḍa'a* is to request nursing. Here, one is requested to nurse, for a nursing person. So ﴿awlādakum﴾ is the nursing person, and where is the one from whom nursing is requested? It is omitted, and its implied form is: to seek wet-nurses (*marāḍi'*) for your children. We parse ﴿awlād﴾ as accusative by the removal of the preposition, and the preposition is omitted here because the meaning is clear. It is also said that it is accusative by the verb through transitivity by metaphor (*tajawwuz*). In any case, its first object is omitted. The implied sense: wet-nurses for your children. That is, if you wish to seek someone to nurse the children, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, i.e., there is no sin upon you. But is it desirable for a person to seek wet-nurses for his children, or is it better not to? Or is there detail in that? There is detail, which, God willing, will be mentioned in the benefits.

﴿there is no blame upon you provided you pay what you agreed, in accordance with what is reasonable﴾. Allah, mighty and majestic, stipulated that there is no blame upon us to seek wet-nurses on the condition that we fulfill what we committed to. So His saying ﴿provided you pay﴾ means: you give ﴿what you agreed, in accordance with what is reasonable﴾. Know that His saying ﴿provided you pay what you agreed﴾ necessarily requires an implied element, because ﴿provided you pay what you agreed﴾ might lead someone to say: what we give, we have already paid, so what is the benefit of His saying ﴿provided you pay﴾? But the meaning is: provided you pay what you were obligated to give. What you were obligated to give. The verb is used to express the intention to fix it, as though it were an event that had already happened and been accomplished. That is, this matter that you have committed yourselves to and imposed on yourselves, the wage for the wet-nurses, is as though it had already been paid and given. Therefore He said: ﴿provided you pay what you agreed, in accordance with what is reasonable﴾. ﴿in accordance with what is reasonable﴾ is connected to ﴿you pay﴾.
