We now have two things: ﴿qatilu﴾ and ﴿fi sabili﴾. Does the command apply to His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, or to His saying ﴿fight﴾? Would it be a command to fight restricted by sincerity?

The apparent meaning is this: it is a command to fight restricted by sincerity, and not merely a command to be sincere in fighting. Otherwise He would have said: "If you fight, then fight in the way of Allah." On this basis the verse indicates the command to fight, and that it be in the way of Allah.

Is this command for obligation or for recommendation? And is it a collective obligation (fard kifaya) or an individual obligation (fard 'ayn)?

This varies. It may be an individual obligation, it may be a collective obligation, and it may be recommended.

Jihad in the way of Allah is the pinnacle of the hump of Islam, and in terms of the love of Allah for deeds it is in the third rank, as Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ): Which deed is most beloved to Allah? He said: 'Prayer at its appointed time.' I said: Then which? He said: 'Kindness to the two parents.' I said: Then which? He said: 'Jihad in the way of Allah.' And if I had asked more, he would have increased it for me."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (527) and Muslim (85/139), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]] Based on this, we say that fighting in the way of Allah is divided into three categories: obligatory upon individuals, obligatory as a collective duty, and voluntary.

The scholars mentioned that it becomes an individual obligation in four situations:

The first situation: when he is present in the battle line, it becomes obligatory on him at that time, and it is not permissible for him to withdraw, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing [in battle], do not turn to them your backs. And whoever turns his back to them on such a day, unless it is maneuvering for [another] battle or joining [another] company, has certainly returned with anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [al-Anfal 8:15-16].

And because the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned fleeing on the day of the advance as one of the major sins.[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2766) and Muslim (89/145), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

The second: when the enemy besieges his land, meaning encircles it, then it becomes obligatory on him to defend, because of the obligation to rescue the Muslim. A siege of a land means preventing things from entering it or leaving it, and in this there is harm to the Muslims, because if the siege lasts, the end is surrender.

Likewise, when the leader calls him to march forth, meaning he says: "March forth, so-and-so, go out," it becomes obligatory on him, and here it is an individual obligation, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ [an-Nisa 4:59].

The fourth: when he is needed personally, specifically, then it is obligatory on him. It may be a collective obligation for others, but for him it is an individual obligation, because people are in need of him, such as if he is a man of opinion and planning, or if he has knowledge of using the instruments of jihad that no one else knows how to use. In this case it becomes incumbent upon him, and jihad becomes an individual obligation for him.

It is a collective obligation, and this is the original ruling: the original ruling is that jihad is a collective obligation. Muslims are obligated to strive in the way of Allah as an obligation, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded it with an unrestricted command, as in this verse, and the original ruling of a command is obligation.

We do not say that it is an individual obligation outside the four situations that preceded, because the purpose of fighting is to humiliate the disbelievers, so if someone sufficient for the task undertakes it, it is dropped from the rest.

This is the rule for acts of worship that are commanded and whose purpose is to bring about the act itself: they are a collective obligation. Every act of worship whose purpose is to bring about this act is a collective obligation. For example, the call to prayer (adhan): is it an individual or collective obligation? It is a collective obligation, because the aim is to have the adhan performed, so when it is performed it is dropped from the rest. Likewise jihad: Muslims are obligated to strive in the way of Allah. But it should be known that jihad has conditions.

Among its conditions is capability. Among the conditions of jihad is capability. If the Muslims are unable to carry it out, Allah, the Exalted, does not obligate them to it, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:286], and His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [at-Taghabun 64:16], and because the Prophet (ﷺ) was not commanded to fight except when he had a state, power and strength.

It is neither reasonable nor wise for us to fight when we are unable to fight, because that would mean giving our enemy power over us until he destroys us. For example, if a man went out with his sword, dagger and spear against a man who has intercontinental missiles, aircraft and similar things, and said: "I am fighting in the way of Allah," would we agree to this? We would not agree to it, because it would mean that you exposed yourself to the enemy. Rather, wait for him until Allah brings about His command, and Allah is over all things competent.

From the noble verse it is derived: the obligation of sincerity to Allah, due to His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained this sincerity by his saying: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme."[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (123) and Muslim (1904/150), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]]

It is also derived from it: that it is forbidden for a person to fight out of zeal, or to fight out of bravery, or to fight for show. This is because commanding a thing is a prohibition of its opposite. So if Allah commands this great act of worship to be purely for Him, then whatever is other than that is prohibited, and it is not permissible for a person to endanger himself for these aims, which are, in relation to being in the way of Allah, extremely base.

But if a man says: "I fight out of zeal for my homeland, because it is an Islamic homeland, and I want to defend it," is this a sincere intention? Yes, it is a sincere intention, because he says: "I do not distinguish between my homeland and another homeland, as long as I am fighting for the lands of the Muslims." This is a sincere intention, and there is no harm in it.

Does the noble verse indicate the obligation of sincerity in every act of obedience? By analogy, by analogy to fighting, because fighting has causes and motives other than sincerity. If Allah obligates sincerity in it, then all the more so for other acts of worship that do not have motives like those of jihad.

From the noble verse it is also derived: the obligation to proceed in jihad according to what the Sharia requires, in advancing and holding back, and in taking and leaving, due to His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: caution against opposition, due to His saying ﴿and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, for the purpose of that is warning against opposition.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of these two names for Allah, namely: As-Sami' (the All-Hearing) and Al-'Alim (the All-Knowing).

Also from it: affirmation of these two attributes, namely: hearing (sam') and knowledge ('ilm). Hearing is applied to perceiving what is heard, and to the result of this perception, which is responding.

So hearing is of two kinds: hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard, and hearing in the sense of responding to what is heard, responding to what is heard, which is answering a supplication. From the second meaning, responding, is the worshipper's saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah). What does it mean?

* The students: He responds.

* The Shaykh: So? So? What did you say?

* The student: I said: the worshipper's saying "Allah hears whoever praises Him."

* The Shaykh: But what comes before it?

* The student: Hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard, and in the sense of responding.

* The Shaykh: Good. "Allah hears whoever praises Him" means He responds to whoever praises Him. And His saying about Abraham: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Hearing of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 14:39], meaning: Responding.

As for the first, which is hearing together with perception, it is common. Then this hearing that accompanies perception is of three kinds. The hearing that accompanies perception may intend a warning, may intend affirmation, and may intend an indication of comprehensive encompassment.

From the first, intending a warning, is His saying: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor, and we are rich"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:181]. And what is meant by the report? A warning. Allah only reported this to warn those people.

From the second is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:46]. What is meant is affirmation: the affirmation of Musa and Harun.

From the third is His saying: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of the one who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [al-Mujadila 58:1]. What is meant here is the indication of Allah's encompassing of everything, the Exalted.

Here is a question before we move past this point: is hearing one of the essential attributes (sifat dhatiyya) or of the attributes of action (sifat fi'liyya)?

* The students: Essential.

* The Shaykh: Wrong.

* A student: Of action.

* The Shaykh: Wrong.

* A student: Essential and of action.

* The Shaykh: Wrong.

* The student: Shaykh, in terms of the basic attribute it is essential, and in terms of its individual instances, in terms of His act, it is of action.

* The Shaykh: Wrong.

* A student: Hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard is essential and of action.

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is an essential attribute, and in the sense of responding it is an attribute of action, because Allah, if He wills, acts, and if He wills, does not act. And in terms of perceiving what is heard it is an essential attribute. Does Allah, if He wills, hear, and if He wills, not hear? Allah is described as hearing from eternity without beginning and forever without end.

Knowledge is perceiving a thing as it is, with certainty. This is knowledge. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is described with knowledge from eternity without beginning and forever without end, in totality and in detail. Nothing is hidden from Him, glory be to Him, in the earth or in the heaven, neither in totality nor in detail, neither past nor present. For this reason, human knowledge is surrounded by two afflictions along with its deficiency: the first affliction is ignorance, and the second is forgetfulness. And it is itself limited; it does not extend beyond, meaning it includes only what surrounds the person. It does not go beyond what is around him and does not perceive, unlike the knowledge of Allah, glory be to Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 245:

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ There is a reading, another reading: ﴿fayuḍa'ifahu﴾ (fayuḍa'ifahu), a third reading: ﴿fayuḍa'ifuhu﴾, a fourth reading: ﴿fayuḍā'ifahu﴾. So there is doubling and single letter, opening and vowelling, four readings: ﴿fayuḍa'ifahu﴾, ﴿fayuḍa'ifuhu﴾, ﴿fayuḍā'ifahu﴾, ﴿fayuḍā'ifuhu﴾.

Now look at its written form. Do the four readings fit the rasm (the consonantal script)? If we wrote it according to the rules known to us, the four readings would not fit, because according to the known rules ﴿fayuḍā'ifahu﴾ requires an alif, and it differs from ﴿fayuḍa'ifahu﴾ because there is no alif in it. But the 'Uthmani script contains the readings; it contains them according to the rasm.

﴿Who is it that will lend Allah﴾: such a construction has already come before us, and in such a construction dhā is treated as redundant (mulghāh).

So ﴿man dhā﴾ is an interrogative noun, or "man" is an interrogative noun, "dhā" is superfluous, and ﴿alladhī﴾ is the predicate of the subject; that is, ﴿man﴾ is the subject.

﴿Man dhā alladhī yuqriḍu Allāh﴾ is an interrogation carrying the sense of encouragement and urging, meaning: where is the one who will lend to Allah? Let him come forward.

As for His saying ﴿yuqriḍu Allāh﴾: al-qarḍ in the language (lexically) means "cutting," and from it comes al-miqrāḍ, do you know the miqrāḍ? What is it? The scissors; because it cuts cloth. Al-qarḍ in the language is cutting, and the meaning of "aqraḍtu fulānan" is that I cut off for him a portion of my wealth and gave it to him. Is that right?

﴿yuqriḍu Allāh﴾ means: he cuts off a portion of his wealth for Allah. This is the meaning. Because when He said ﴿Fight in the way of Allah﴾, and fighting is with the self, He said ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah﴾, and this is jihad with wealth.

As for His saying ﴿yuqriḍu Allāh﴾: generally the borrower borrows only out of need, so is this possible with regard to Allah?

* The students: It is not permissible.

* The Shaykh: It is not possible, except among the most wicked of Allah's creatures, the Jews. "When this verse ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah﴾ was revealed, they said: O Muhammad, your Lord has become poor and so He asks us to lend to Him."[[See Tafsir Ibn Abi Hatim (2429, 4588), al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul (377), and al-Durr al-Manthur (4/161).]] We seek refuge in Allah. May Allah fight them. This is not strange of them, for they said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor﴾ [Al 'Imran 181], and they said: ﴿The hand of Allah is chained up; their own hands are chained﴾ [al-Ma'idah 64], and they said that Allah became tired when He created the heavens and the earth, so He rested on the day of Saturday. They are well known as the most audacious of Allah's servants toward the rights of Allah.

So ﴿yuqriḍu Allāh﴾: we have said that a loan, generally, is only for the need of borrowing. Does that mean Allah is in need? Never, by Allah. Indeed Allah, the Exalted, is the Rich, the Enricher. But He, glorified and exalted, likened spending for Him to a loan, because the lender is confident of repayment and the borrower is bound to repay. So Allah, the Exalted, made His dealing like a loan, to reassure whoever spends in His way that what you have spent will, what? It will be returned to you.

Now listen to the manner of repayment. The manner of repayment is not the manner in which you deal with people; the manner of repayment is in what you deal with the servants of Allah. What you deal with the servants of Allah may be delayed, may be denied, may be reduced: delayed, denied, reduced. But the right of Allah, mighty and majestic, opposes all of that, rather it is increased. For this reason He said ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah﴾, but Allah, mighty and majestic, stipulated, saying: ﴿a good loan﴾.

What is the meaning of a good loan? A good loan is that which conforms to the Shariah: that it be from lawful wealth. If it is from unlawful wealth, it is not a good loan, because Allah is Good and accepts only what is good.

Second: that it be sincerely for Allah. If it is for show and reputation, it is not a good loan. The evidence is His saying in the hadith qudsi: "Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his association."[[Related by Muslim (2985/46), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

Third: that it be placed in its proper place, by giving to a poor person or a needy person, or in public welfare. As for spending it in what angers Allah, that is not a good loan.

Fourth: that his soul be content with it, not resentful, nor believing it to be a burden and a tax, as some people think about zakat; they think it is a tax, to the extent that some writers use this expression, saying: "the tax of zakat, the tax of zakat," and Allah forbid. It is obligatory that your soul be content with what you give for the sake of Allah, the Exalted; because the best of what you spend from your wealth is what you spend for Allah. If you are content to buy oranges and apples for your family to eat, which then rot in their bellies and then go out to the toilet, how is it that your soul is not content to give charity to Allah, the Exalted, with charity which you will find stored for you with Allah?! "When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, entered upon his family, he said: 'What have you left for us of the sheep?' What did they say? 'They said: Nothing remains except its shoulder. He said: All of it remains except its shoulder.'"[[Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2470), from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] Why? Because what is spent is what remains. For this reason Allah made that an advancing of the self, and He said in Surah al-Muzzammil: ﴿And lend to Allah a good loan. And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward﴾ [al-Muzzammil 20].

It is true that a person is stingy in spending wealth in obedience to Allah, he is stingy; because before him are two enemies: Satan and the self. ﴿Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to immorality﴾ [al-Baqarah 268]. With stinginess, meaning: he threatens you with poverty, he says: look (...) you will go begging from people, right or not? Yes, your wealth diminishes, your dependents go hungry, and you find nothing (...) for the house. Do not spend, is that right?

﴿He threatens you with poverty and commands you to immorality﴾, he says: hold back, hold back your wealth, it is better for you. ﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾: forgiveness, because charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire; and bounty. ﴿And whatever you give in zakat, seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ [al-Rum 39].

﴿A good loan﴾: we said that it has four matters, let us repeat them: that it be from lawful earnings; second, sincerity to Allah; third, that it be placed in its proper place; fourth, that the soul be content with it.

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿so that He may multiply it for him many times over﴾. ﴿Many times over (adl'āfan)﴾ here is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and we may say that it specifies the kind; because He said ﴿adl'āfan﴾, since the bare notion of doubling (ḍiʿf) could be in one unit, but when He says "many times over," it becomes more than one, so it is a verbal noun specifying the type. How are these multiples?

Allah, mighty and majestic, said in this same surah: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾ [al-Baqarah 261]. How much is the multiplication? Seven hundred.

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 261]: perhaps even more multiples will come. So we say: the multiples mentioned here are those mentioned in the same surah: ﴿like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 261].

As for His saying ﴿Allah withholds and extends﴾: ﴿yaqbiḍu wa yabsuṭu﴾. Qabḍ is the opposite of basṭ, and basṭ is expansion, so the meaning of qabḍ is restriction. He is the One in whose hand is withholding and in whose hand is extending. The benefit of this, or of mentioning withholding and extending, after the encouragement to spend, is: to indicate that the spender should not think that his spending is a cause of narrowing his provision, for withholding and extending are in the hand of Allah, the Exalted. A person may give charity and spend, and Allah widens his provision; and he may hold back and be stingy, and Allah narrows it for him. How many a person has held back and not spent in the way of Allah, so Allah set afflictions upon his wealth: in the wealth itself, such as loss, burning, theft and the like, or afflictions that reach this man in his body or his family, requiring large sums of money. This is from the category of withholding. And a person may spend and give charity in the way of Allah in the manner that pleases Allah, so Allah blesses his wealth and provision comes to him from where he does not expect.

His saying ﴿yaqbiḍu wa yabsuṭu﴾ encompasses everything: He withholds in provision and extends, He withholds in knowledge and extends, and likewise He withholds in everything connected to the life of this world and the life of the Hereafter. Withholding and extending all belong to whom? To Allah, the Exalted. He withholds lifespans and lengthens them; this is from the withholding and extending.

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾. He concluded the verse with His saying ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, which is to make one disinclined to the world. Its benefit: disinclining one from the world. It is as if He says: this wealth which you covet and are stingy with, and do not spend, you will move away from it and return to Allah, glorified and exalted. For this reason the verse was concluded with ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾.

The fronting of the object in His saying ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ has two benefits: a verbal benefit and a semantic benefit. The verbal benefit: it agrees with the ends of verses (ru'ūs al-āyāt). The second is restriction, the semantic benefit is restriction. ﴿ilayhi﴾ means not to other than Him, ﴿turja'ūn﴾: so the return is all to Allah, just as the origin is all from Allah, glorified and exalted.

Among the benefits of this noble verse, I think the preceding ones have been written down? Among its benefits: encouragement.

* A student: Before the benefits, is there a reading in it?

* The Shaykh: Yes, in ﴿yabsuṭu﴾ there is a reading with sīn, ﴿yabsuṭu﴾, and ﴿yabṣuṭu﴾ with ṣād.

* A student: In the first reading, ﴿fayuḍā'ifahu﴾, what is its justification?

* The Shaykh: Its justification?

* The student: The i'rab, the accusative?

* The Shaykh: Yes, from the standpoint of i'rab. He said: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan, so that He may multiply it for him﴾ [al-Baqarah 245]. As for the reading in the accusative, its basis is that it has become a response to the interrogative in His saying ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah﴾.

The fa' of causation after an interrogative puts the following present verb in the subjunctive, with an implied "an" after the fa' of causation, and Ibn Malik alluded to this in his saying:

"And after fa' that answers a negation or a command, purely, an is implied and its concealment is obligatory in the subjunctive."

As for the reading in the nominative, the fa' here is for resumption and not for causation, meaning: "so He multiplies it," so the sentence here is a new resumed clause.

Among the benefits of the verse: encouragement to spend in the way of Allah, mighty and majestic, by His saying ﴿Who is it that﴾, and the interrogation here is for urging and encouragement.

Also among its benefits: that Allah, mighty and majestic, obligated Himself to recompense the one who lent Him a good loan. The basis of the obligation: He named spending a loan, and a loan obligates the borrower to repay it.

* Among its benefits: attention to sincerity, and that a person be a lender to Allah, mighty and majestic, with sincerity, contentment of soul, and from lawful wealth, and that his spending not be followed by reproach or harm, by His saying ﴿a good loan﴾.

Does the verse imply that a loan involving interest (ribā) is forbidden?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: From where is it derived?

* A student: ﴿a good loan﴾.

* The Shaykh: From ﴿a good loan﴾. If someone says: this is with regard to Allah, ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan?﴾ We say: true, this is with regard to Allah, but it may be cited as indicating that a loan must be good, with nothing departing from the Shariah; and it may be cited for this by His saying: ﴿And whatever you give as ribā so that it increases within people's wealth, it does not increase with Allah; and whatever you give in zakat, seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ [al-Rum 39].

Look: He contrasts zakat with what? With ribā. In any case, deriving from this verse carries some weight.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the generosity and giving of Allah, mighty and majestic, is vast, and that His recompense to the good-doer is recompense of bounty, not recompense of justice. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿so that He may multiply it for him many times over﴾; because if it were recompense of justice, he would be given only its equivalent. But His recompense, glorified and exalted, to the obedient good-doers is recompense of bounty.

As for His recompense to the disobedient, it lies between justice and bounty: if the disobedience is disbelief, its recompense is justice; and if it is less than that, its recompense lies between bounty and justice. How between bounty and justice? Because Allah, if He wills, punishes for it, and if He wills, forgives; so this lies between bounty and justice.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the completeness of the lordship of Allah, mighty and majestic, from His saying: ﴿And Allah withholds and extends﴾.

And among them: an indication that spending is not itself the cause of constriction and poverty. How?

Because He mentioned this sentence after the encouragement to spend, which indicates that spending does not necessitate destruction or narrowing; because the matter is in whose hand? In the hand of Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Among the benefits of the verse: affirmation of the return and resurrection, from His saying: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾.

And among its benefits also: a warning to a person against opposing, and encouragement to obey Allah, from His saying: ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾; because when a person knows that he will certainly return to his Lord, he must necessarily do what he is commanded and abandon what he is forbidden, because he fears this return. As if a king of the kings of this world said to you: go, and your return is to me; how would you deal with that king? You would deal with him as one who believes that the king will hold him accountable for his good deeds and for his bad deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 246 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah"?﴾

﴿Have you not considered﴾: the address is either to the Messenger (ﷺ), and addressing the leader of the nation is an address to him and to the nation, since they follow him; or it is an address to everyone to whom address may be directed, so that it is general in its original form.

The difference between the two meanings: the first is general by way of the nation being followers of the one addressed first, who is the Messenger (ﷺ).

The second aspect: it is general by way of its original form; that is, "Have you not considered, O addressee?"

And the verb ﴿tara﴾: does it mean "look" (tanzur), or "hear" (tasma'), or "know" (ta'lam)? Here the verb is followed by (ila) "to", and when it is followed by (ila), it is determined to be sight with the eye. You say: "ra'a ila kadha" or "nathara ila kadha". Had it been used without a preposition, it would be possible for the intended meaning of seeing to be knowing. In that case the meaning would be: "Have you not known of the affair of the chiefs of the Children of Israel?" because it is well known that neither we nor even the Messenger (ﷺ) witnessed it.

It may be said that it is followed by (ila) while meaning "looking", because the report of it came from Allah, and what comes from Allah is like what is seen with the eye, indeed stronger and more eloquent.

Regarding ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs﴾: is the interrogative here for confirmation (taqrir) or for arousing interest (tashwiq)?

The apparent view is that it is for arousing interest; that is, it stirs us to look at this story so that we may take a lesson from it. Confirmation, brethren, occurs only in a matter that was known to the addressee, so that he is made to affirm it, like: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1]. But this is a matter not known to the addressee except after it is reported to him, so here it is for arousing interest.

That is, like His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction?﴾ [al-Saff 10], and His saying: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 1], and what is similar to them. So the meaning is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, stirs us to look at this story in order that we may take a lesson from it. But if He were addressing one who already knew it, we would say the interrogative is for confirmation.

﴿Ila al-mala'﴾ and ﴿al-mala' min bani Isra'il﴾: when it is idafa (annexed) to someone, the intended meaning is the notables, like: ﴿The chiefs of his people said﴾ [al-A'raf 60], meaning the notables and the elders.

It may also be used to mean a group in general, whether they are of the notables of the people or not. These are a group ("mala'") of the Children of Israel: ﴿when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah."﴾

﴿Idh﴾ here is temporal.

* A student: ﴿min ba'di Musa﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿to the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses﴾.

﴿Min bani Isra'il﴾: (banu) is originally for males, but when a tribe is described by it, it becomes general for males and females, as we say "Banu Tamim", which includes their males and females.

As for His saying ﴿Isra'il﴾: who is Israel? He is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq, and the meaning of Israel is "servant of Allah" or something similar of the attributes that are annexed to Allah.

As for His saying ﴿after Moses﴾: after He mentioned their tribe, that they are of the Children of Israel, He mentioned their era, saying ﴿after Moses﴾, Musa ibn 'Imran (peace be upon him), who is the most excellent of the prophets of the Children of Israel.

﴿Idh qalu﴾: this is a temporal adverb, and it is built on sukun in a place of nasb, meaning: at the time of their saying.

﴿Idh qalu li-nabiyyin lahum﴾: and in ﴿nabiyyin﴾ there are two readings: "li-nabiyyin" (...) its original form is "nabi'" but the hamza was lightened, so there is no disagreement. And if we say "nabi'" is from prophethood (nubuwwah) and not from news (naba'), then there is a disagreement between them. ﴿To a prophet of theirs﴾, belonging to these chiefs, ﴿"Appoint for us a king"﴾.

According to the majority of scholars, a prophet (nabi) is one to whom Allah revealed a law but who was not obligated to convey what he was commanded. He is thus in the position of a renewer who corrects what has become corrupt among the people, even though he is not obligated to convey this revelation to others. The closest parallel to him in this nation is the scholar, though the scholar is commanded to convey, but he is commanded to convey a message from before him.

It is said that the prophet is one who is commanded to convey a message from before him and to whom a special revelation is given, conveying a message from before him. This is the apparent view of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and he cites as evidence His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which was guidance and light, by which the prophets who submitted judged﴾ [al-Ma'idah 44]. (By which they judged.) He did not make for these prophets a special revelation, meaning an independent revelation, but made them judge by the Torah. This view is good, were it not refuted by the prophethood of Adam, for Adam was a prophet and no law preceded him. Were it not for this refutation, the view of the Shaykh would be preferable.

It may be said that if a prophet is revealed a law but is not commanded to convey it, then the law revealed to him is only the earlier law, to affirm that law and renew what has faded from it. But the well-known view among scholars is the first meaning.

As for His saying ﴿to a prophet of theirs﴾: if someone asks, "Who is this prophet?" we say: Allah the Exalted left him unspecified, so let us leave unspecified what Allah left unspecified. Had there been any benefit in knowing his name, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, would have explained it to us; He would have made his name clear to us. But there is no benefit for us in it. The important thing is that he is a prophet among the prophets.

﴿Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾: the meaning of "appoint" (u'th) is: command a king, and establish for us a king. ﴿That we may fight in the way of Allah﴾: it is as if their affair at that time was disorderly, having no king to manage their affairs and arrange their concerns. When people have no guardian of affairs, their affairs become chaos, as it is said:

"People do not thrive in chaos without a leader for them..." ...............

And for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) "commanded the people, when they travel, to appoint one of them as leader, so that their affairs are not in chaos."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (2609), and Abu 'Awanah (7539), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

He says: ﴿Appoint for us a king﴾, that is, establish for us a king, ﴿that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾. The word ﴿nuqatil﴾ is jussive because it is the answer to the imperative ﴿u'th﴾.

This is evidence that they were determined to have a guardian of affairs who would lead them to fight in the way of Allah.

As for His saying ﴿that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾: we have already discussed the meaning of ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, and that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it in the best explanation. And what was it? How did the Messenger (ﷺ) explain it?

* The student: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the way of Allah."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (123) and Muslim (1904/150), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]]

* The Shaykh: "Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the way of Allah." This is "in the way of Allah." Then the Prophet, wishing to strengthen them and to examine their resolve, said to them: ﴿Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?﴾

﴿'Asaytum﴾ has two readings: with kasra and with fath.

* A student: The nasb.

* The Shaykh: No, the nasb is a matter of i'rab. The kasra and fath: ﴿'Asiytum﴾ and ﴿'Asaytum﴾. It means: "Is it to be expected of you that if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?"

They said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, while we have been expelled from our homes and our children?﴾ So the meaning here is: is it expected? Thus ('asa) here is for expectation; that is, if fighting is prescribed for you, is it expected of you that you will not fight?

The clause ﴿if fighting is prescribed for you﴾ is a conditional clause inserted between the subject of ('asa) and its predicate, because the subject of ('asa) is the pronoun "ta'" (you). And ﴿that you will not fight﴾ is its predicate. ('Asa) is often followed by (an), as in the Alfiyyah. The conditional clause ﴿if fighting is prescribed for you﴾ is an inserted conditional whose answer is omitted. It may be said that it does not need an answer because the context makes it known, but some grammarians estimated it, saying: "then do not fight": is it expected of you that you will not fight if fighting is prescribed for you, so do not fight?

The answer: yes, this is the omitted answer. And if we say that since it is known from context it does not need to be mentioned, as in its counterparts, that would have some merit.

As for His saying ﴿if fighting is prescribed for you﴾: "kutiba" means "furidha", that is, fighting was made obligatory upon you, that you not fight.

What was their answer? ﴿They said, "And what is [the matter] with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, while we have been expelled from our homes and our children?"﴾ As for His saying ﴿wa-ma lana alla nuqatil﴾: is (an) here extra (za'idah) or not extra?

The correct view is that it is not extra, because this construction permits both the presence of (an) and its omission. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not rely upon Allah, while He has guided us to our ways?﴾ [Ibrahim 12], and He said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not believe in Allah and in what has come to us of the truth?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 84]. In the first verse (an) appears, and in the second it is omitted. Both are well-known Arabic usages; that is, (an) in this construction may be present or may be omitted.

﴿Wa-ma lana alla nuqatil fi sabili Allah﴾: meaning, what is there for us in not fighting? That is, what obstacle prevents us from fighting in the way of Allah, when the reason for it exists? What is the reason? ﴿While we have been expelled from our homes and our children.﴾ When a person is expelled from his home and his sons, he must fight to liberate the lands and free the captives.

As for His saying ﴿wa-ma lana﴾: we return to its i'rab. ﴿Ma﴾ is an interrogative noun built on sukun in a place of raf'. ﴿Lana﴾ is a prepositional phrase related to an omitted predicate of ma, and ﴿alla nuqatil﴾ is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the original is: "wa-ma lana fi alla nuqatil" (and what is there for us in not fighting).

It has passed with us that when (an) the verbal particle enters upon a negative particle, the particle is estimated as a word. Is it "fi" (in)?

* Students: "Fi."

* The Shaykh: No, it is estimated as the word "'adam" (absence). The meaning then is: "and what is there for us in the absence of fighting", that is, what is there for us in not fighting? Any obstacle? The answer: is there an obstacle? No obstacle.

﴿Wa-ma lana alla nuqatil fi sabili Allah.﴾ ﴿Wa-qad ukhrijna﴾: the clause here is circumstantial (hal), so it is in the accusative place.

﴿Wa-qad ukhrijna min diyarina wa-abna'ina﴾. Their saying: ﴿We have been expelled from our homes and our children﴾. The exegetes said: the intended meaning is the expulsion of some of them, because these who spoke to their prophet were in their homes, but there were people before them who were overcome by the enemy, who expelled them from their homes and from their children.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away﴾. We ask Allah for safety. They had now asked that their prophet send them a king who would fight in the way of Allah, so that they might fight in the way of Allah. When their prophet asked them for assurance, what did they say?

They said: "We are resolute, determined upon that, and steadfast in it." But when fighting was prescribed for them and made obligatory upon them, they turned away, so what their prophet had feared came true: they did not fight. It will come to us in the benefits that some questioning becomes a calamity for the questioner, as Allah said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you; but if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 101].

Here Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away﴾, that is, they turned away from this obligation and did not carry it out.

﴿Except a few of them﴾. The few is usually less than half, is it not? Or we may say: less than a third as well, due to the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "A third is much."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (5668) and Muslim (1628/5, 7, 8), from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.]] So they all turned away except a few; it is possible to say: less than a third. It is in the accusative as an exception.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: Knowing of the wrongdoers, and the requirement of His knowledge of them is that He will recompense them for their wrongdoing. The wrongdoing here is not for committing a forbidden act, but for abandoning an obligation, because abandoning an obligation is like committing a prohibited act, containing wrong to oneself and a deficiency in its right.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: encouragement to reflect and to take heed, from His saying ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel﴾ and so on to the end.

And among the benefits of this noble verse also: that in this story there are lessons for this nation, since these people upon whom fighting was prescribed turned away except a few of them. In it is a warning to this nation against turning away from fighting when it is prescribed for them.

* And among its benefits: that armies must have a commander who takes charge of leading them, from their saying: ﴿Appoint for us a king that we may fight in the way of Allah.﴾

And among them: that the rank of prophethood is higher than the rank of kingship, from their saying: ﴿Appoint for us a king﴾, addressing the prophet. So the prophet has the authority to appoint for them a king who manages their affairs and governs them.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: mention of what encourages the granting of a request, when a person asks something from another, to mention what encourages him to grant the request, from their saying: ﴿that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾, for this stirs the prophet and encourages him to appoint for them the king.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the indication of sincerity in their saying: ﴿in the way of Allah﴾.

* And among its benefits: testing the one addressed regarding what is asked of him to be done, testing whether he will fulfill what is incumbent upon him toward it, from His saying: ﴿Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?﴾ So if someone asks you to send him on an errand, or to assign him a task, there is no harm in your mentioning to him the things by which his steadfastness and his carrying out of this task become evident, by this verse.

And among the benefits of this noble verse also: that a person by nature is prepared to fight whoever fights him, from their saying: ﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, while we have been expelled from our homes and our children?﴾

For this reason you find the coward, who is among the most cowardly, when he is cornered, brings out whatever courage he has, exhausting everything, even if he is more cowardly than an ostrich, for when he is gathered he has the strength to defend himself.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the causes of fighting is the expulsion of a person from himself and his family, I mean the expulsion of a person from his land and his people, from their saying: ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes and our children.﴾

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person may think he can be patient in abstaining from what is forbidden or in performing what is commanded, but when he is tested by it, he recoils. From where is this taken? ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them,﴾ even though at first they had been eager to fight.

* A student: Shaykh, would you repeat the last benefit?

* The Shaykh: I say: and among them: a person may think that he is able to do what is commanded and to abstain from what is forbidden, but when he is tested with it, he recoils and is unable. These people thought they were able to fight, but when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away except a few of them.

And it follows from this: there is an indication in it to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not wish to meet the enemy, but ask Allah for well-being. When you do meet them, then be patient, for Paradise is under the shade of the swords."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2965, 2966) and Muslim (1742/20), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa.]] So a person may wish for something among the matters that befall him, and then be unable to bear it.

This benefit is indicated by the words of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Whoever hears of the Dajjal (the Antichrist) should keep away from him, for a person may come to him thinking he is a believer, and he will not cease to be pulled along by him until he follows him because of the doubts that he casts."[[Abu Dawud recorded it in Sunan Abi Dawud (4319), with the wording: "Whoever hears of the Dajjal should keep away from him, for by Allah, a man may come to him thinking he is a believer, and so he follows him, because of the doubts that he brings," or "because of the doubts that he brings," from the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn.]] This is the hadith or its meaning.

Another benefit that branches from this: many people make vows (nadhr) while thinking they will fulfil them, and then they do not fulfil them. This is as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and surely be among the righteous." (75) But when He gave them of His bounty, they became miserly with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ [at-Tawbah 75, 76].

Can it be deduced from the verse that trials are assigned to speech? Because he said to them: ﴿Is it likely that if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?﴾ They said... So what their prophet anticipated came to pass, for when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of fighting in defence of oneself. From where is this taken? Because when he said: ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes﴾, he then said: ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them﴾. "Prescribed" means obligated, so that they would defend themselves, liberate their lands from their enemy, and likewise their sons from captivity.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: warning the wrongdoer against wrongdoing, due to His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning any wrongdoing whatsoever.
And among them, i.e., among its benefits: the vastness of the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, in that He knows even the wrongdoing of a wrongdoer, even if he is one person, due to His words: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾.
And from that also, among the benefits of the verse: the prohibition of wrongdoing, because a threat has been made concerning it.
* And among its benefits: that abandoning an obligation is a form of wrongdoing, due to His words: ﴿They turned away, except a few of them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: those who turned away, who were obligated to fight but did not undertake it. This shows that wrongdoing is divided into two kinds: either committing a prohibited act, or abandoning an obligatory duty.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾.

* Student: Shaykh, there is a benefit here.
* Shaykh: And what is it?
* Student: The ruling on asking the people for a commander who would lead them to jihad. That is, if the conditions of the Muslims are, for example, troubled, and some people say, for example: "By Allah, if only a commander would lead us to jihad (...)." Is this from this verse or not?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. What do you all say? Is it that if the affairs of the Muslims are in disarray, it is recommended to supplicate Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that He prepare for them a commander who unites their word? Is this derived from it?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: How?
* Students: ﴿Appoint for us a king﴾.
* Shaykh: Because they asked their prophet to raise up for them a king who would fight in the way of Allah.
* Student: Shaykh, why did they not ask their prophet to lead them in war?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Perhaps they wanted their prophet to devote himself to calling to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and for this commander to be someone else.
* Student: Here, Shaykh, there is a benefit.
* Another student: Shaykh, was the Prophet (ﷺ) not the commander of the Muslims?
* Shaykh: Muhammad, yes indeed.
* Student: Alright, then what is the difference between here and there?
* Shaykh: We cannot say. We say: that is what happened. What appears to us is that they wanted their prophet to remain in calling to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and with those among them who did not fight, who were not obligated to fight.
* Student: We said in the tafsir that it will come to us that some questioning may be a calamity for others?
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: We said in the tafsir that some questioning may be a calamity upon the rest?
* Shaykh: We have touched on this in His words: that a person may ask for something while thinking that he will carry it out, but he does not carry it out, and so he errs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 247:

He said: ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾. In it, you find a reading ﴿nabi'uhum﴾, just as His saying ﴿a prophet for them﴾ has a reading ﴿li-nabi'in lahum﴾.

﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as a king."﴾ Notice the good manners toward Allah. They said to their prophet: ﴿Appoint for us﴾, and did not say "I have appointed," but said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you﴾. It is as if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to this prophet that he should make so-and-so a king over them, or a king for them, so he said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as a king.﴾ In his turning away from the word ﴿appoint﴾, while it is good manners toward Allah, there is an indication of the strength of the obligation for them to accept it. Why? Because the one who designated him is who? Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as a king.﴾ Talut (Talut) is a proper name of a person, and it is not as some have said: that it is derived from (al-tul, height). Some said it is derived from height, because Allah increased him in breadth of knowledge and body, so they said: Talut is from (al-tul). That is not so; rather it is a proper name like other proper names. But you know that this is a name in whose language? In the language of the Children of Israel. It is possible that some Arabization has entered it.

And His saying: ﴿has sent to you Talut as a king﴾. ﴿Malikan (as a king)﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from ﴿Talut﴾. The king (malik) is the one who has the management that is not disputed, but in relation to the created, it is according to what legitimate or customary authority requires; this is the king, who has the power of disposal, unlike the owner (malik/mālik). The owner is the one who has disposal over a specific, defined property.

They objected to this, saying: ﴿How can he have kingship over us, when we have more right to kingship than him, and he has not been given abundance of wealth?﴾ That is, they said: how can he have kingship? ﴿Anna (how)﴾ means "how," so it is interrogative.

﴿He has kingship over us﴾. Look at the expression: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut﴾, and did not say "over you," because sending from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is not intended merely as authority, but it is intended as disposal with what contains good and benefit. For this reason it is said: kingship is a responsibility, not an honour. In the first, He said: ﴿has sent to you Talut﴾, and here they began speaking about authority: they said: ﴿How can he have kingship over us﴾, and they did not say: how can he have kingship for us, over us. So they made the matter one of authority only, not one of considering benefit.

Then they said, strengthening their improbability of this matter: ﴿and we have more right to kingship than him﴾. Why? It is as if they saw that kingship does not occur except from great man to great man, and that this had not been granted to any of his forefathers, unlike us, for the kings were from among us. So how did kingship come to him?

Also, ﴿he has not been given abundance of wealth﴾. So he is what? Poor, having no abundant wealth. It may be said: he is not poor, but he does not have abundant wealth, and there is a difference between the destitute poor and one who finds something but is not of abundance; that is, he is not rich, so that we may benefit from his wealth, and he may govern us with his wealth, and gather armies and troops with his wealth. So they mentioned two reasons: one of them in terms of his standing in his community, and the second in terms of wealth. That is, the power of lineage and the power of wealth. They said: this man is lacking; he has no lineage, so he is not of the sons of kings, and he has no wealth, so he is not of the rich wealthy ones who subdue people with their money.

Their prophet answered: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you﴾. ﴿Istafahu (has chosen him)﴾ means: he selected him, and its root is from (safwa, purity/choice), so the origin of ﴿istafahu﴾ would be (istatafah) with the reflexive ta of the form, but it was changed to a ta' (ṭāʾ) as will come, Allah willing, in the chapter on morphology (ṣarf).

His saying: ﴿has chosen him over you﴾, and did not say "has chosen him for you." Here, and in the first, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you﴾, and here He said: ﴿has chosen him over you﴾, indicating that He preferred him over them, choosing him because he is better than them. So he is preferred over them by what Allah, glory be to Him, has given him, which will be mentioned.

﴿And He has increased him broadly in knowledge﴾. Basṭah (breadth) means abundance, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah withholds and extends﴾ [al-Baqarah 245]. ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts﴾ [al-Ra'd 26].

That is: He gave him abundance in knowledge. Which knowledge? We are speaking now about kingship, so the intended knowledge is the knowledge of governing the kingdom, and he has in it such wisdom and judgment that made him chosen over them by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Also "and body": He increased him in breadth of body along with knowledge, so two strengths gathered in him: the moral and the physical. Breadth of body is not only in height but in height and strength as well; he is strong and mighty and tall too. So when there gathered in him the two strengths: the moral, which is knowledge, and the second, the bodily or sensory, which is that Allah, exalted is He, increased him in breadth of body.

The third reason: ﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills﴾. "Yu'ti" means gives, His kingship to ﴿whom He wills﴾. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty from whom You will, and You honour whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are over all things competent﴾ [Aal 'Imran 26].

And His saying: ﴿to whom He wills﴾: it has passed us many times that every act that Allah attributes to will is restricted by wisdom. So He gives His kingship to whom He wills from among those whom divine wisdom requires should be given kingship. Therefore, since the giving, the giving of kingship, is joined with wisdom, Allah does not give kingship except to one who is worthy of it. The intent of this is not to repel their objection by mentioning mere will in general.

It is true that the matter belongs to Allah, He does what He wills, but the intent is to make clear that Allah is the One who gives kingship to whom He wills, and along with this He gives it only to one who is worthy of it.

It has become clear from what was mentioned, that Allah gave him breadth in knowledge and body, that this man is worthy to be given kingship.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. ﴿Wasi'un (All-Encompassing)﴾ is unrestricted. He did not say "vast in knowledge, in wisdom, in grace," so it includes all His attributes: vast in His knowledge, grace, generosity, power, strength, and all His attributes and actions as well.

His saying: ﴿'Alim (All-Knowing)﴾ means: knowing of whoever deserves to be a king or other than that, of the grace which Allah, exalted is He, gives to whom He wills. Here, their prophet, peace be upon him, mentioned several matters that qualify this man to be a king over them:

First: that Allah chose him over them and preferred him; in that there are virtues whose knowledge is with Allah, for nothing of them was mentioned, nothing was mentioned.

Second: that Allah increased him in breadth of knowledge, and in the management of the community, and in wars, and other things.

Third: that Allah increased him in breadth of body, which includes strength and height.

Fourth: that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the One who gives His kingship to whom He wills, joined with wisdom. Were it not that wisdom requires that Talut be the king, Allah would not have given him the kingship.

Fifth: that Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing; He is the possessor of grace which He extends to whomever of His servants He wills, so He may bestow grace upon whom He wills. "Allah knows best where to place His message" [al-An'am 124], and He is also best aware of where to place His guardianship.

From the benefits of this noble verse: their prophet responded to them, for they asked him to send them a king, and he complied, but what was his response? By asking Allah, exalted is He, for that, and Allah's answering him.

And among them: kingship is not obtained by inheritance, but is obtained by entitlement and superiority.

And also among them: the pillars of kingship are firmly established when a person has distinction in his lineage, his descent, his knowledge, or his strength. From where is this taken?

* Student: From the qualities that were mentioned.

* The Shaykh: Yes. It is taken first from their saying: ﴿How can he have kingship over us, when we have more right to kingship than him, and he has not been given abundance of wealth?﴾

And the second from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him broadly in knowledge and body﴾.

And among the benefits of this noble verse: the interrogation of these people ﴿How can he have kingship over us﴾ may be intended as objection, and it may be intended as seeking to understand: how was he a king when we have more right to kingship than him, and he was not given abundance of wealth? If it is the first, then their state requires what? Blame; for how can they object when they are the ones who asked that a king be sent to them?!

If it is the second, does their state require blame or not? That is, their intent is seeking clarification and inquiring about the cause without objection; in this case there is no objection against them and no blame upon them.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration that the acts of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are beyond every conception, by His saying: ﴿He said: Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you﴾, although they disparaged him on two grounds: that they had more right to kingship than him, and that he was poor. So their prophet clarified that Allah, exalted is He, chose him over them by what wisdom requires.

Also among its benefits: whenever the ruler has greater breadth in knowledge, in managing affairs, and in body and strength, he is more suited to his kingship and more complete in his command, by His saying: ﴿and increased him broadly in knowledge and body﴾.

And among them: that human kingship is a kingship of Allah, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills﴾. So this king in his kingdom, in reality, has not ruled except by the permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; sovereignty belongs to Allah alone, who gives it to whom He wills.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that our ownership of what we possess is not in the sense of true ownership, nor is it absolute ownership, but it is under the ownership of Allah, exalted is He. For this reason we do not dispose of what we own except according to what Allah has legislated. If a person wanted to dispose of his property as he wished, destroying it, burning it, torturing it, or harming it, if it were an animal, we would say: No, because your ownership is subordinate to what? To the ownership of Allah, exalted is He.

And among them: the affirmation of will for Allah by His saying: ﴿to whom He wills﴾, and the affirmation of voluntary acts by His saying: ﴿gives His kingship﴾, for a person's receiving of kingship we see as renewing, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty from whom You will, and You honour whom You will and You humble whom You will﴾ [Aal 'Imran 26]. So Allah, exalted is He, has voluntary acts, meaning that He performs them whenever He wills.

Many of the Ash'aris and the theologians (mutakallimun) have denied that voluntary acts subsist in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, arguing that voluntary acts are originated events (hawadith), and originated events subsist only in something originated, as they claimed. So if we affirm that voluntary acts subsist in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He does what He wills and renews His acts, exalted is He, it would follow that He is originated, while it is well known that Allah, exalted is He, is the First, before whom there is nothing.

We say to them: this necessary consequence you have mentioned is false, for renewal of acts does not entail renewal of the agent, and origination of acts does not entail origination of the agent. We, now, are undoubtedly originated, and our acts are renewed. Do we say it is necessary that our existence is concurrent with our acts, or that our existence precedes our acts? There is no doubt that our existence precedes our acts, and this is in the case of the created. So the existence of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, precedes His acts, and it does not follow from the renewal of His acts that He Himself is originated, exalted is He; rather He is the First, before whom there is nothing. Hence, because of their denial of originated events subsisting in Him, they said: Allah, exalted is He, does not speak with a speech He originates, so that He speaks little by little; and they said: the speech of Allah is the eternal meaning subsisting in His self.

There is no doubt that interpreting speech in this way leads to the conclusion that speech is what? It is knowledge. When they say: speech is the meaning subsisting in the self, and this is the doctrine of the Ash'aris, the meaning of this is that it is knowledge, because they hold that speech is the meaning subsisting in the self, and that these letters and sounds that are heard are what? Created, which Allah, exalted is He, created to express what is in His self.

For this reason some scholars said: in reality there is no difference between them and the Mu'tazilah, since all agree that what we now read in the mushafs is created; but those say it is the speech of Allah, and these say it is an expression of the speech of Allah.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names: Wasi' (All-Encompassing) and 'Alim (All-Knowing). Al-Wasi' is the One who encompasses everything; the Vast whose attributes have no end in perfection; the Vast whose richness has no limit. Likewise, whatever meaning this word comprises enters into the word "wasi'"; for this reason this name and attribute are considered comprehensive of all the names and attributes, for Allah, exalted is He, is vast in everything He is described with.

And 'Alim means: encompassing everything in knowledge. For this reason the word "wasi'" is always paired with the word "'alim," because each of them contains comprehensiveness and encompassing.

It has already passed for us that a divine name, when it is transitive (muta'addi), includes how many things?

Three things: the name, the attribute, and the judgment, meaning the effect that results from it. So 'Alim includes the name Al-'Alim, includes the attribute, which is knowledge, and includes the judgment, which is that He knows; He knows everything. When the name is not transitive, it includes two things: the name and the attribute, like Al-Hayy (the Living) and Al-'Azim (the Great) and the like.

So the attributes are more numerous and broader than the names, for there is no name except that it includes an attribute, and there are attributes from which no names are derived. Thus the attributes are broader and more general than the names. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that there will come to you the chest (al-tabut)﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:248].

"Ayah" (آية) means a sign, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel knew it?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:197], meaning a sign indicating that it is true, that the Children of Israel would know this Qur'an and that it would be sent down.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that there will come to you the chest﴾, "an-" (أنْ) and what follows it are in a place of nominative case, as the predicate of "inna" (إنَّ).

﴿That there will come to you the chest, in it is tranquility (sakinah) from your Lord﴾. The "tabut" (التابوت) is an object of wood or ivory resembling a chest; it was brought down and they took it along with them, and in it was tranquility (sakinah). That is, it was like something that calms them and in which they find reassurance, and this is one of the signs of Allah, glorified and exalted.

﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun had left behind﴾. "A remnant of what he left behind": what did the family of Musa and the family of Harun leave behind? They were prophets who left behind knowledge and wisdom, because "The prophets did not bequeath dinars or dirhams; they only bequeathed knowledge"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3641), al-Tirmidhi (2682), and Ibn Majah (223), from the hadith of Abu al-Darda'.]]. So this chest, by the permission of Allah, had been lost, and this king whom Allah had sent to them came and brought it, and it remained with them; they took it along on their campaigns, and in it was tranquility from Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. That tranquility meant that when they saw this chest their hearts were calmed and their chests were expanded.

And in it also..

And in it also: a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind of knowledge and wisdom. "The family of Musa and the family of Harun": because Musa and Harun, upon them be prayers and peace, were brothers, from the father, or from the mother?

* Student: From both.

* The Shaykh: From the father and the mother. Why did Harun say to Musa: ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head﴾ [Taha 20:94]?

* Student: To soften his heart.

* The Shaykh: Yes, this is for appeal and softening; its meaning is that he sought to soften him so that perhaps he would be gentle with him.

﴿The angels carry it﴾: meaning this chest, with this king, is carried by the angels. The angels, as we have mentioned often, are an unseen world, created from light. The root of "malà'ika" (ملائكة) is "ma'alika" (مآلِكَة), because it is derived from "al-alukah" (الألوكة), which in the language means message, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Making the angels messengers﴾ [Fatir 35:1]. But there is an alteration (i'lal) by transposition of letters. The angels are an unseen world created from light; they do not eat or drink, but they are inspired to glorify Allah; they glorify night and day without ceasing. As we have often noted, the angels have functions and tasks, both transitive and specific. Jibril, for example, has a transitive task and a specific task: the specific task is that by which he worships Allah, and the transitive one is that he is entrusted with revelation. Israfil is entrusted with blowing the Trumpet, and he is also one of the bearers of the Throne. Mika'il is entrusted with rain and plants. The Prophet ﷺ, when he began the night prayer, used to mention these three, saying: "O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning what they differed about. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth in what they differed about, for You guide whom You will to a straight path"; because each of them is entrusted with what life depends upon: Jibril with what gives life to hearts, Israfil with what gives life to the earth, right? 

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: Mika'il with what gives life to the earth: rain and plants; and Israfil with what gives life to bodies, for when he blows into the Trumpet the spirits come out and enter their bodies. There are other angels entrusted with other things, such as Malik, who is in charge of the Fire, as the people of the Fire say: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:77]; and among them is the keeper of Paradise; and among them is the Angel of Death, whom the common people call "Azra'il", but that is not so. This name has no basis in the authentic Sunnah; it is mentioned only from the Isra'iliyyat, and it is not mentioned in the Qur'an except as "the Angel of Death." If it were his name, he would have been mentioned by it, either in the Book or the Sunnah.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: why is it in the accusative? Or why did it come in the accusative?

* Student: The subject of "inna" is delayed.

* The Shaykh: Because it is the delayed subject of "inna", and the lam is the lam of emphasis, which enters on the delayed element of the subject or predicate of "inna". So His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you﴾ means: indeed in the bringing of the chest carried by the angels is a sign for you, indicating that this man sent among them, Talut, has more right than them to kingship. But He said: ﴿if you are believers﴾, and if you are not believers, Allah says: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 10:101]. So the one who benefits from signs, is admonished by them, and builds his belief and action upon them is only the believer. As for the non-believer, he never benefits from signs; rather, signs only increase the non-believer in transgression, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is disease, it adds to their filth, upon their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:124-125]. The point is that the believer is the one who benefits from signs, both the cosmic signs and the legislative signs. As for the legislative signs, his faith increases by them, because they are righteous deeds, and faith increases by righteous deeds; and because when he reflects upon them he recognizes what they contain of wisdom, goodness and reform, and so his faith increases. As for the cosmic signs, the increase of faith by them is clear, because when he sees this cosmos and what is in it of wondrous order, wisdom, harmony, absence of contradiction and absence of discord, there is no doubt that he will increase in faith.

From the benefits of this noble verse: ﴿Indeed the sign of his kingship﴾ and to the end of it.

From the benefits of this noble verse: the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward His servants, in that He supports matters with signs so that the proof is established, as in His saying: ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed the sign of his kingship"﴾. Had Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed, He would have done what He does without a sign and would have punished the deniers and the arrogant. But by His mercy, Mighty and Majestic, He sends signs so that hearts may be reassured and the proof may be established. For this reason, no messenger was sent except that he was given what is like it by which mankind believes. And the agreement of signs with wisdom is evident, for if a man came out from among us and said, "I am the messenger of Allah to you; do what I command you, leave what I forbid you, or else your blood and your wealth are lawful to me," would we obey, or not obey?

* The students: We would not obey.

* The Shaykh: Of course we would not obey. But by the mercy and wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, He made for them a sign, for the messengers, so that the proof is established and people respond.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the great signs in the chest, for this chest contained, in one respect, what the family of Musa and the family of Harun had left behind of knowledge and wisdom, and it was also tranquility for the people, in which their souls and hearts found rest, and they grew stronger in their pursuits.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that tranquility has an effect upon hearts, by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord﴾. Consider how He attributed it to His Lordship, indicating that in this there is great care for these people. When tranquility descends into the heart, a person becomes reassured, at ease, and his chest is expanded to accept the commands of the Shari'ah with complete acceptance.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of angels, by His saying: ﴿The angels carry it﴾. Can we derive from this verse that the chest is great and large?

* Student: It is possible.

* The Shaykh: Possible?

* Another student: It is not necessary.

* The Shaykh: Let us see. ﴿The angels carry it﴾: the word ﴿the angels﴾ is plural, and that it is carried by the angels indicates that it is large. Someone might say that what is meant by "the angels" is the category, and it does not necessarily follow that those who carry it are many. And Allah knows best.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that signs benefit only the believer, by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾.

Also from its benefits: the emphasis of a matter by means of emphatic particles and by repetition. That is, emphasizing a matter is done by emphatic particles and it is done by repetition, and in this verse both repetition and particles are combined. Where is that?

* Student: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾.

* The Shaykh: That is one. Where is the repetition?

* Student: At the beginning of the verse.

* The Shaykh: Yes, at the beginning of the verse: ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed the sign of his kingship is that there will come to you the chest"﴾, then He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you﴾. So this is emphasized by repetition, and also emphasized by "inna". What else?

* Student: And the lam.

* The Shaykh: With "inna" and the lam: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of faith, and that faith is the greatest factor in benefiting from the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you﴾.

Can it be derived from it that when a person's faith in Allah increases, his understanding of the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger increases?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes; because it has already been established for us that when a thing is tied to a attribute, or conditioned upon an attribute, it increases with the increase of that attribute and decreases with its decrease. So whenever faith is complete, the person's benefit from the signs of Allah is greater and his understanding of them is greater.

And perhaps we may also say that it indicates another new benefit: that faith is a cause of preservation, because if it is a sign, then when it is forgotten its being a sign ceases, and when it remains, its being a sign continues. The necessary consequence is that the believer is quick in understanding, strong in understanding, and slow to forget. We have mentioned many times that faith and piety increase knowledge, in memorization and in understanding, so they gain what is absent and firm up what is present.

Shall we derive from it that the angels are bodies?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: From where?

* The students: From ﴿carries it﴾.

* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿The angels carry it﴾. As for the saying of one who says they are intellects only, or that they are spirits and have no bodies, his saying is weak, indeed false; because Allah says: ﴿Making the angels messengers, possessing wings﴾ [Fatir 35:1], and the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his created form, with six hundred wings that filled the horizon. Allahu Akbar.

* Student: Shaykh, is it established that the keeper of Paradise is named Ridwan?
* Shaykh: No, but it is well known. It is well known, though its authenticity is not established. It is well known among the scholars.
(...) and he establishes among them commanding and forbidding.

﴿Their prophet said to them: "Indeed, God has sent Talut (Saul) to you as king."﴾ They found it strange that Talut should be king over them, because he was not of a distinguished lineage among them, nor did he have wealth among them, and he was also below them in rank, so they had a better claim to the kingship than he did. Their prophet explained to them that God's bounty is given to whomever He wills, and that God, exalted is He, had chosen him over them and increased him in breadth of knowledge and of physique. In knowledge: knowledge of statecraft (siyasa) and knowledge of the Sharia. In physique: the strength needed to carry out what he knows of the knowledge of the Sharia and of statecraft. Then God, mighty and majestic, gave them a sign of his kingship, which is the Ark (al-tabut) carried by the angels, containing a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron had left. It also contained, after the sign was completed for them, what indicates that he has the better claim to kingship and that he is fit to rule them, and to "arrange their ranks" (rattaba-hum), meaning to arrange the armies for fighting the enemies who had driven them from their homes and their wealth.

He said: ﴿When Talut set out with the armies﴾, meaning he departed with them, that is, he went forth with them and left his place.

﴿With the armies﴾: the plural of "jund," and they are the fighting army, on the basis that they fight in the way of God to save their homes and their sons. He said: ﴿When Talut set out with the armies﴾. He was an intelligent and sensible man, because God had increased him in breadth of knowledge and of physique, and he had knowledge of their circumstances beforehand, and that when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away except for a few of them. He made clear to them that God would test them with a river. The river is well known: it is flowing water. The people were thirsty, so he said: ﴿Indeed God will test you with a river﴾, meaning He will examine you by it, so that God, mighty and majestic, may know who is patient and who is not patient, since jihad requires hardship and patience. So God tested them with this river, to know who is patient and who is not. This is one purpose. And to know who obeys among those who do not obey.
