The scholars are extremely careful regarding what is attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, so they do not rule on a matter except when all possibilities are excluded; that is, they do not rule that it is traced to the Prophet except when all the possibilities that could prevent them from ruling that it is traced to the Prophet have been excluded.

In any case: the People of the Sunnah and the Community, the majority of them, hold that the Kursi is the place of the feet of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and this was affirmed by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim, and other scholars and leading verifiers.

It has been said that the Kursi is the Throne, but this is not correct, for the Throne is greater, broader, and more encompassing than the Kursi. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "its Kursi is its knowledge"[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (5787), from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.]], but I do not think this report is authentic from Ibn 'Abbas, because this is not the meaning of this word in the Arabic language nor in its customary usage, so it is very far from being authentically from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

The Kursi is the place of the two feet, and there has come a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The seven heavens and the earths, in comparison to the Kursi, are nothing but like a ring thrown into a desert of the earth, and the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the desert over that ring"[[Narrated by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih (361), from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]. This indicates the vastness of these great creations, which are, relative to us, from the realm of the unseen. For this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it?﴾ [Qaf 6], and He did not say: "Have they not seen the Kursi or the Throne?", because that is not visible to us. Had Allah not informed us of it, we would not have known of it.

His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾ supports what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and other verifiers have held, that the heavens and the earths are all spherical in shape, because this is a matter known through the senses, and likewise known through report, although its knowledge through report has been hidden from many of the earlier people; yet in reality it is clear that these creations are spherical in shape. The evidence for this in the Qur'an is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the sky is split open, and it listens to its Lord and is obligated to, and when the earth is stretched out﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 1-3]. And when is this?

* The students: On the Day of Resurrection.

* The Shaykh: On the Day of Resurrection. His saying: ﴿when the earth is stretched out﴾ implies that it is not stretched out now. Likewise the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed: "It will be stretched out on the Day of Resurrection like the stretching of a leather mat (adim)"[[Narrated by Ibn Majah in his Sunan (4081), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]. This is by way of emphasis. The adim means the hide, i.e., just as a hide is stretched so that it becomes one flat surface. Also among the evidence is His saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ [al-Zumar 5]. Takwir (wrapping) means tadwir (turning around), and from it our saying: akwar al-'imamah (the folds of the turban), because they go around.

We know that the night and the day alternate over the earth, and if they alternate over the earth, it necessarily follows that the earth is spherical, because a thing is not wrapped around something that is not round. This is a matter observed: that it is spherical now.

If the Kursi has encompassed the heavens and the earth, this is evidence that it is round. As for the Throne, the Prophet, peace be upon him, reported: "Indeed His Throne above His heavens is like a dome (qubbah)"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4726), from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im.]], and a dome is not wrapped (round), but it is also not flat: it is like the dome of a tent, whose middle is raised.

Then he said: ﴿And their preservation does not weary Him﴾. ﴿Does not weary Him﴾ means: does not burden Him or cause Him difficulty. ﴿Their preservation﴾ means the preservation of the heavens and the earth. This attribute, as you see, is an attribute of what? It is a negative, negating attribute: ﴿their preservation does not weary Him﴾. What does preservation require, so that we know this negation is for the perfection of that thing which preservation necessitates? Knowledge? Yes. Life, knowledge, power, strength, mercy, and perhaps other attributes as well. The point is that this negation includes the perfection of Allah's knowledge, power, strength, mercy, and what else of the attributes that His preserving Himself, glorified and exalted, necessitates.

Then he said: ﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾. ﴿And He is the Most High﴾: a sentence like this, whose two parts are definite, conveys restriction (hasr), meaning He alone is the Most High, i.e., possessor of absolute highness. As for relative highness, it is established for humans. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Do not weaken and do not grieve, for you will be superior if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 139]. Are the believers superior with absolute superiority, or over the disbelievers?

* The students: Over the disbelievers.

* The Shaykh: Over the disbelievers. But absolute highness belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, alone. He, glorified and exalted, is above everything. Furthermore, the highness of Allah, according to the People of the Sunnah and the Community, is divided into: the highness of His essence (dhat) and the highness of His attributes (sifah). As for the highness of essence, it means that He is high in His essence above everything; all things are beneath Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and Allah, exalted, is above them in His essence. If you say: why did you make this division? Do you have evidence for it from the Book or the Sunnah? And have you seen this in the statements of the Companions? The answer: No, but I was compelled to it when the negators, the People of Ta'til, restricted highness to the highness of attributes only, and said: He is high with a highness of attributes, not a highness of essence. Then those negators of the highness of essence split into the following groups.

The point is that the Imams of the early generations (salaf), may Allah have mercy on them, and those who came after them, were compelled to these divisions, which may be confusing to some people, because they were afflicted with a people who used to negate them. So they were compelled to affirm them by such means. If we only said: "And He is the Most High," and then a negating, denying opponent came and said: "The highness is of His attributes," what would the common people understand? The common people would understand from this only the highness of attributes. But if we say: He is high in His essence and His attributes, the common people understand this meaning. Indeed, the first thing that comes to the common person's mind is the highness of essence, there is no doubt about this. The strange thing is that these negating Ta'til deny what comes immediately to the mind, and affirm a matter that is undoubtedly included in its meaning, but does not come to the minds of many people. The point is that we were compelled to this division in opposition to these negating Ta'til. When these Ta'til negated Allah's highness in His essence, they split into two groups:

One group said: He is in His essence in every place; in every place Allah is present in His essence. And if Allah is in a place in His essence, then either He occupies a space (according to their claim) or He does not occupy one. If He occupies a space, it necessarily follows that He fills places and there is no room in them for anyone. And if He does not occupy a space, then He is non-existent. Nor can they say that He is like the air and the like, because that is not consistent for them.

The second group, who denied His highness in His essence, said: He, glorified and exalted, is neither in highness nor in lowness, neither inside the world nor outside the world, neither right nor left, neither connected nor separated. This is pure ta'til, because this is the description of non-existence.

Some scholars said: If we were told, "Describe nothingness," we would find no description more comprehensive than this. Observe how ta'til, the negation of what is established by reason and transmission, led them to say what neither sense, reason, nor transmission accepts. But thus is falsehood, and Allah forbid, it hurls its people into the abyss.

So we believe that Allah, exalted, is knowing in His essence and knowing in His attributes. We have previously established that the highness of Allah in His essence is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason, and innate nature (fitrah), and that the textual evidence from the Book and the Sunnah on this is varied in several respects: sometimes by mentioning highness ('uluw), sometimes by mentioning being above (fawqiyyah), sometimes by mentioning the ascent of things to Him, and sometimes by mentioning their descent from Him, and other things that are well known.

Likewise the Sunnah came in statement, act, and tacit approval, all establishing the highness of Allah in His essence. The statement is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Our Lord is Allah, who is in the heaven"[[Narrated by Muslim (1436/121), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (3892), from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', and the wording is his.]]. The act is like his gesturing toward the sky on the Day of 'Arafah at the greatest Islamic gathering, when "he raised his hand to the sky and said: 'O Allah, bear witness'"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1741), from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, and Muslim (1218/147), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]]. As for tacit approval, he said to the slave girl: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the sky." He said: "Free her, for she is a believer"[[Narrated by Muslim (537/33), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami.]].

As for consensus, all the early generations agree that Allah, exalted, is above the Throne, and none of them ever said that He is in His essence in every place, nor did any of them say that He is neither above the world nor below it, nor right nor left, nor connected nor separated, never.

As for reason, its indication of this is from two aspects. The first aspect: highness is an attribute of perfection, is it not?

* The students: Indeed.

* The Shaykh: If it is an attribute of perfection, it necessarily follows that it is established for Allah, since Allah has been established as possessing attributes of perfection in every respect.

The second aspect: suppose we set this aspect aside, and we say: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is either above the world or beneath it, or to the right or left. Which of these indicates perfection?

* The students: Above.

* The Shaykh: Above. For if He were beneath, He would be more deficient than the creation; and if He were mingled with it, He would be equal to it in perfection. So it necessarily follows that He is above everything.

As for innate nature (fitrah), every human being is innately disposed to know that Allah, exalted, is above the heavens. For this reason, when a person calls upon his Lord, you find him turning toward the sky. When al-Juwayni, Abu al-Ma'ali, may Allah have mercy on him, who denied the istiwa' (settling) over the Throne and the essential highness, used to affirm that Allah, glorified and exalted, was before the Throne, and He is now as He was. Wishing to deny the istiwa' over the Throne, he would say: Allah was and nothing was with Him, and He is now as He was. Therefore He did not settle upon the Throne. Abu al-'Ala' al-Hamadhani, may Allah have mercy on him, said to him: "O Master, leave aside mention of the Throne"—meaning and the istiwa' upon it—"for the evidence of Allah's istiwa' upon the Throne is auditory, established by hearing, and were it not for hearing we would not know it. But tell us about this necessity, for no knower has ever said 'O Allah' without finding within himself a necessity to seek highness. Is this correct?"

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: A necessity. Tell us about this necessity. So he began striking his head and cried out at the top of his voice: "Hamadhani has bewildered me! Hamadhani has bewildered me!" And he was unable to answer, because the innate matter cannot be denied. The man was refuted and unable to respond to this necessity that Abu al-'Ala', may Allah have mercy on him, had put to him.

In sum: the highness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His essence is established by the Book, the Sunnah, the consensus, reason, and innate nature. The strange thing is that those who deny Allah's highness, when they themselves call upon Allah, what do they say?

* A student: They raise their hands toward the sky.

* The Shaykh: They raise their hands toward the sky. You will not find one of them saying "O Allah" and placing his hands here at all; all of them raise their hands to the sky, because their innate nature refuses to be otherwise. Yet despite this they deny it. We ask Allah for well-being.

I do not know how this man will face his Lord on the Day of Resurrection! How will he face Him while he believes that He is in His essence in every place, or that He is not present inside the world nor outside it, nor above it nor beneath it? A man stood with another, and this other—who was a stranger (akhir; the word is spoken akhir, meaning another)—said: "Allah is in His essence in every place." He said to him: "Open your pocket, let us look in it." He found nothing in his pocket but a pen. The one who had denied was struck dumb, struck dumb.

There is no doubt that whoever believes in his heart that Allah is in His essence in every place—I have no doubt he is a disbeliever, unless I doubted the existence of the sun at midday, we seek refuge in Allah—because there is no doubt that he would be placing his Lord in toilets, in filthy places, in the bellies of donkeys, in the bellies of dogs, in every place. No sensible person who knows what he is saying could say this. We ask Allah for well-being and safety. O Allah, guide us to the straight path.

* * *

(...) the Kursi; for it is a verse, the greatest verse in the Book of Allah, as was authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (8659), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.]].

* A student: The Mighty.

* The Shaykh: Yes. First, the names: the names in this verse are five: Allah, al-Ilah, al-Hayy, al-Qayyum, al-'Ali, al-'Azim: six if we include al-Ilah with them, otherwise five.

* From it is derived, then: the affirmation of these five or six names for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Every name of Allah, exalted, includes an attribute, but not conversely: not every attribute yields a name; but every name yields an attribute. For example: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾ [al-Sajdah 5]: we do not derive from it the name "al-Mudabbir" (the Arranger) for Allah. ﴿They plot, and Allah plots﴾ [al-Anfal 30]: we do not derive from it the name "al-Makir" (the Plotter) for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And ﴿Allah does what He wills﴾ [Ibrahim 27]: we do not derive from it the name "al-Fa'il" (the Doer), nor "al-Sha'i" (the Willer). ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa with speech﴾ [al-Nisa' 164]: we do not derive from it the name "al-Mutakallim" (the Speaker), and so on. But every name includes an attribute, so from Allah we derive what? Divinity (uluhiyyah). From al-Hayy: life (hayah). From al-Qayyum: self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah). From al-'Ali: highness ('uluw). From al-'Azim: greatness ('azamah).

The point is that if they describe Him with this description, it means nothingness, and that He is non-existent.

What is the argument of those who say He is in His essence in every place? Is their evidence for them or against them?

* A student: Against them.

* The Shaykh: Against them. How so? Who knows?

* A student: (...)

* The Shaykh: No. I say: how can He be on the earth in His essence? We now refute them, saying: Allah said: ﴿Then He settled upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf 54]. So He is above, and this becomes evidence against them.

But such falsifiers look at the texts like the one-eyed man who sees with only one eye while the other is closed. Whoever looks at the texts from every aspect knows the falsity of their statement.

As for those who say: "We do not describe Him with highness, nor lowness, nor right, nor left, nor connection, nor separation," there is no need to argue with them, for they have described Him with non-existence. It is as if they are saying: "He has no Lord."

﴿The Mighty (al-'Azim)﴾ means: possessor of greatness. Greatness is an expression of majesty (jalal), and it means the modality of the attributes: all His attributes are great. The great, in relation to anything, is the majestic one who reaches the utmost of attributes, as Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾ [al-Naml 23], and ﴿I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾ [al-Naml 22]. Thus greatness of anything is the thing that is of utmost importance and utmost attributes; that is, it is an expression of perfection, perfection with greatness.

This is the end of the verse, and we return to explaining the names and attributes in it. In this verse we said there are five names, or six, because I am uncertain whether to count ilah (God) as a name, since He says: ﴿There is no god except Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 35], where ilah is indefinite here. In any case, the five are certain, and each name indicates an attribute. Our principle in this is: every name indicates an attribute, but not every attribute gives rise to a derived name.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that Allah, may He be exalted, is alone in divinity (uluhiyyah); due to His saying: ﴿There is no god except Him﴾.

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the polytheists who affirmed another god alongside Allah, indeed gods, more than one, and who say: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [Sad 5]. We say: you have made the gods many; indeed, this is a strange thing. This is the strange thing; as for one God, it is not strange, but rather this is the truth and the correct position.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the attribute of life (hayah) for Allah, may He be exalted, and that it is a complete life, not preceded by non-existence, not followed by cessation, and not described by any deficiency. Is that not so?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Our life is preceded by non-existence, followed by cessation, accompanied by deficiency. All our life is deficient; for this reason Allah described it as "the worldly life" (al-dunya). But the life of Allah, may He be exalted, is complete in every respect. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿the Ever-Living (al-Hayy)﴾; because al-Hayy is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq), meaning the one who gathers the meanings of the attributes of complete life. Do you understand? It is as if He says: there is no living one except Him, and that is so: there is no one with complete life except Allah, may He be exalted.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting Sustainer) for Allah; due to His saying: ﴿the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyum)﴾. The meaning of al-Qayyum is: the one who subsists by Himself and sustains others.

* A student: The one you are facing (...).

* The Shaykh: The one who subsists by Himself and sustains others. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is He then who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who have no partners]?﴾ [al-Ra'd 33].

* A student: (...)

* The Shaykh: No, we explained it; why is there a need for (...)? We explained it and clarified the evidence for "subsisting by itself" and "sustaining others."
Can this description apply to a human being? Not at all. No human being subsists by himself at all, nor does a human sustain others in the absolute sense. Is that correct?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: No human subsists by himself, because there is no human who is not in need of others. Is that not so? We are in need of workers, and workers are in need of us; we are in need of women, and women are in need of us; we are in need of children, and children are in need of us; we need wealth, and wealth needs us. Is that not so?

* Students: No (...) wealth does not need us.

* The Shaykh: How does it need us? Have you not heard the cry of the dirham and the dinar? When we exchange money, I exchange dirhams and dinars, and you can hear a sound from them. It may be that the dinar I am exchanging cries out at parting from me, and that one cries out at parting from its companion. But it is in need of us in another respect: its preservation and its growth. Is that not so?
Is there anyone who sustains another in an absolute sense? No; I may sustain others, but sustaining is limited, is it not? It is limited sustaining. For this reason Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is He then who stands over every soul in what it has earned...﴾. Who is He?

* Students: Allah.

* The Shaykh: He is Allah; no one stands over every soul in what it has earned except Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that it contains the Greatest Name of Allah, which is established in His saying: ﴿the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. These two noble names are mentioned in three places in the Qur'an: in the two luminous (al-Zahrawayn) and in a third surah.

* Students: Ta-Ha.

* The Shaykh: Ta-Ha. In the two luminous ones and in Ta-Ha. What are the two luminous ones?

* Students: Al-Baqarah and Al-'Imran.

* The Shaykh: Al-Baqarah and Al-'Imran. Here in al-Baqarah, and in Al-'Imran: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Allah! There is no god except Him, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ [Al-'Imran 1-2]; and in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ [Ta-Ha 111]. The people of knowledge said: the Greatest Name is in these two names because they comprise all the Most Beautiful Names: the attribute of perfection is in al-Hayy, and the attribute of beneficence (al-ihsan) is in al-Qayyum.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of Allah's attributes, the perfection of His life and His self-subsistence. From where is this taken?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: Also the perfection of His life and His self-subsistence, such that no least deficiency afflicts them, from His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾. Why? Because perfection may be applied on the basis of what is most prevalent, even if some deficiency may affect it in some respects. But when deficiency is negated, its meaning is that the perfection is absolute perfection, is it not? Absolute perfection, to which no deficiency ever attaches.

To clarify this meaning: perfection may be applied to a thing as absolute perfection, because that is most of its attributes, even though some deficiency may still afflict it. When the possible deficiency in this perfection is negated, the meaning becomes: it is absolute perfection, which no deficiency afflicts in any respect. Here the negation occurred with His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of negative attributes; due to His saying: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ and ﴿and their preservation does not tire Him﴾.

* Among its benefits also: the comprehensiveness of Allah's dominion; due to His saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

* Among its benefits also: the exclusivity of this dominion to Allah, may He be exalted; from which saying?

* A student: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾.

* The Shaykh: No, it is not from His saying ﴿To Him﴾; it is from the fronting of the predicate: ﴿To Him belongs...﴾. Why? Because the predicate should be placed later, so when it is placed first it conveys restriction (hasr); because we have the principle that when something that should be postponed is placed first, that is evidence for restriction.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the heavens and the earth; due to His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾, and that the heavens are plural. From where is it taken that they are plural?

* Students: From the plural form.

* The Shaykh: From the plural form: "the heavens" (al-samawat). As for whether they are seven, or fewer, or more, that is from another evidence.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the completeness of Allah's sovereignty; from His saying: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾. This is other than the comprehensiveness of dominion: the strength and completeness of authority is greater than the comprehensiveness of ownership.
Among it: the affirmation of intercession by Allah's permission; due to His saying: ﴿except by His permission﴾. Were it not that intercession is established by His permission, the exception would not be valid. Were it not that intercession is established by His permission, the exception would not be correct. Is that known?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Were it not that intercession is established by Allah's permission, the exception would not be correct; He would have said: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him?﴾ only. But when He said ﴿except by His permission﴾, it is known that it is established by Allah's permission, glorified and exalted is He.
Among it: the affirmation of permission (idhn), which is command; due to His saying: ﴿except by His permission﴾. We have already been told in the exegesis that permission is of two kinds: cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i), and we gave an example of each kind. What is an example of legislative permission?

* Students: (...)

* The Shaykh: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾ [Yunus 59]; ﴿They have instituted for them of the religion what Allah has not permitted﴾ [al-Shura 21], meaning what He did not legislate. As for permission in the sense of decree (qadari), He has permitted it, and so it was legislated and occurred. What is an example of cosmic permission?

* A student: (...)

* The Shaykh: Like this verse; this is cosmic permission: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge, from His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾; and that it is general across past, present and future. His saying ﴿what is before them﴾ refers to the future, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ refers to the past. Is that clear?

* Among its benefits: a refutation of the extreme Qadariyyah. The affirmation of comprehensive knowledge refutes them, because the extreme Qadariyyah denied Allah's knowledge of the actions of His creatures, saying: Allah does not know the actions of creatures until they occur; before that He has no knowledge of them, and once they occur He knows them.
Also in it: a refutation of the Kharijites and the Mu'tazilah regarding the affirmation of intercession. The Kharijites and the Mu'tazilah deny general intercession, the general intercession that belongs to the Messenger and others, which is intercession for the people of sins. They say: there is no intercession for them, because their doctrine is that the perpetrator of a major sin is eternal in the Fire. We are now speaking of the Mu'tazilah and the Kharijites. The doctrine of both groups is that the perpetrator of a major sin is eternal in the Fire. If an adulterer dies without repenting, he is eternal in the Fire even if he prays and fasts. But they differed: is he a disbeliever, or neither believer nor disbeliever? The Kharijites, out of a boldness, which is boldness for the truth but not with the truth, declared that the perpetrator of a major sin is a disbeliever who has left Islam.
As for these, the Mu'tazilah vacillated; they were too timid to oppose the People of the Sunnah and to oppose the Kharijites, and they said: we will sit in the middle of the road and say: the perpetrator of a major sin is in an intermediate position between two positions. We do not say he is a believer, nor do we say he is a disbeliever. He has traveled from one country to another, but stopped in the middle of the road; he has left Islam but has not reached disbelief; he is in an intermediate position between the two positions. Whose doctrine is this?

* Students: The Mu'tazilah.

* The Shaykh: The Mu'tazilah. But all agree that he is eternal in the Fire in the Hereafter. Therefore, on the basis of this opinion, they denied intercession, and said: it is impossible for Allah to permit anyone to intercede for the people of major sins, because they are eternal. The verse in its generality ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him...﴾ refutes them, does it not?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: It refutes them, in its generality.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, may He be exalted, cannot be encompassed in knowledge, just as He cannot be encompassed by hearing or sight: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him, but He perceives vision﴾ [al-An'am 103]; ﴿and they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha 110], as in Surah Ta-Ha. Here He said: ﴿and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾.

So we do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills. Whatever He wills us to encompass, we encompass. For example, we now know that Allah is described by the attributes He has made known to us in His Book; were it not that He made them known to us, we would not have encompassed them. But He made them known to us, so we knew them, although some of these attributes can be known by reason, the details are known only through revelation.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that we know nothing of His creation, nor of His essence, except what He has made known to us. From where do we take this?

* Students: (...).

* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿and they encompass nothing of His knowledge﴾, according to one of the two interpretations of it that we have already gone through.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of asking about the modality (takyif) of Allah's attributes; the prohibition of takyif. What is its basis?

* Students: (...)

* The Shaykh: That we do not know the modality of His attributes except what Allah has made known to us. Allah, may He be exalted, did not inform us of the modality of His attributes. So if He did not inform us of them, then if we claim to know them we are liars, because Allah says: ﴿and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾.
Also in it: a refutation of the Mu'attilah (those who deny attributes). How?

* A student: ﴿of His knowledge﴾.

* The Shaykh: Those who say ﴿of His knowledge﴾ is not established; so that we may debate him, how does he derive evidence from it?

* A student: The Mu'attilah?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* The student: The Knowing (al-'Alim).

* The Shaykh: No, ﴿of His knowledge﴾.

* The student: ﴿of His knowledge﴾?

* The Shaykh: ﴿and they encompass nothing of His knowledge﴾; there is a refutation of the Mu'attilah in it. This same verse, not the whole verse; this sentence contains a refutation of the Mu'attilah.

* A student: (...) they deny knowledge.

* The Shaykh: Because they say, for example, that Allah has no real hand. That means they claim to have encompassed the negation of something of what? Of His attributes. But they lied in that, because Allah affirmed this for Himself. Their claim that this does not befit Allah, for example that a real hand does not befit Allah, or a real face does not befit Allah, or an eye does not befit Allah, and the like, is a false claim. We say: knowledge is of two kinds, affirmation and negation. It is not possible to negate something of something except by knowledge, just as it is not possible to affirm something of something except by knowledge. So if you negate the realities of these attributes, then bring your proof, if you are truthful. They have no proof. Allah, may He be exalted, did not negate a hand for Himself in any verse of the Qur'an, nor did His Messenger negate it in any hadith, nor did the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) negate it, and yet they say: we negate it. Where is their knowledge? Is there also in it a refutation of the Mu'attilah?

Is there in it a refutation of the Mumaththilah (those who liken Allah to creation)? Yes, all the more so. Since there is a refutation of the one who asks about modality, there is all the more a refutation of the one who likens. Likening is also prohibited in other verses that we have already gone through.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of Allah's will: ﴿except what He wills﴾.
Shall we derive from it a refutation of the moderate Qadariyyah? Because from ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ we understood how to refute the extreme Qadariyyah. But can we derive from the verse ﴿and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾ a refutation of the moderate Qadariyyah?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: How so?

* The student: They deny (...)

* The Shaykh: No, they deny the actions of the servant.

* The student: ﴿except what He wills﴾ (...)

* The Shaykh: No, it is not apparent.

* A student: (...)

* The Shaykh: A person's encompassing of a thing is among his attributes, among the attributes of a human being. They say that Allah, may He be exalted, does not will anything connected with a human being: neither will, nor desire, nor anything at all. So there is in it also a refutation of the moderate Qadariyyah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the greatness of the Throne: ﴿His Throne encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾.
And among them: the greatness of its Creator, because the greatness of a created thing indicates the greatness of the Creator. For this reason, if we see, for example, a made thing that is strong, of good craftsmanship, or well constructed, and the like, we infer from it the skill of its maker. So this great Throne we infer from it the greatness of its Creator, because the Throne is great, is it not?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: * Among its benefits: the affirmation of the heavens and the affirmation of the earth. Is that so? From where is it taken?

* A student: (...)

* The Shaykh: No, it has passed us in discussion. What is (...)

* Students: (...).

* Among its benefits: the disbelief of one who denies the heavens. How so? Because it entails denying the report of Allah. As for the earth, I do not think anyone denies it, but the heaven, some have denied it, and said: there are no heavens; above us is an infinite and boundless space, and there are only [stars and] stars and the like. This is undoubtedly disbelief in the Mighty God, whether a person believes it by himself and in his delusion, or by imitating someone he imitates whom he venerates; this is disbelief.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the affirmation of Allah's strength: ﴿and their preservation does not tire Him﴾.
And among its benefits: the negation of hardship from Him, may He be exalted, due to His saying: ﴿and does not tire Him﴾. This is a negative attribute, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38].

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of what this sentence comprises: ﴿and their preservation does not tire Him﴾, namely?

* A student: Knowledge.

* The Shaykh: Knowledge? And what else? The one for whom preserving a thing is not burdensome, what does that indicate? This sentence indicates what? That Allah, meaning, the preservation of the heavens and the earth is not burdensome for Him?

* A student: Knowledge and power.

* The Shaykh: Knowledge and power, correct. And what else?

* A student: Mercy.

* The Shaykh: And mercy.

* A student: And greatness.

* The Shaykh: And wisdom.

* A student: And strength.

* The Shaykh: And strength.

* Among its benefits: that the heavens and the earth need preservation.

* A student: (...)

**Sheikh:** So they both need preservation. This preservation does not burden Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, nor does it... (...). Right? And do the heavens and earth truly need preservation? Yes. Were it not for Allah's preservation, they would be corrupted. ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:251]. ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned would have been demolished﴾ [al-Hajj 22:40].

**Student:** (...)

**Sheikh:** All of them, yes. ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth, except by His permission﴾ [al-Hajj 22:65]. ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him﴾ [Fatir 35:41].

* Among its benefits is the affirmation of Allah's exaltedness, ﴿And He is the Most High﴾. Is it the Exaltedness of His Essence and Attributes, or the Exaltedness of His Essence and Attribute (singular)?

It also contains a refutation of the Hulūliyyah (those who believe that Allah indwells His creation) and of the Mu'aṭṭilah (those who deny the attributes). The Hulūliyyah said that He is not high above, but rather He is in every place. The Mu'aṭṭilah, who deny attributes, said that He cannot be described as high or low, nor as right or left, nor as connected or separate. Here He said: ﴿And He is the Most High﴾.

* Among its benefits is the warning against tyranny toward others. From where does this come?
* **Student:** From ﴿the Most Great﴾.
  **Another student:** From ﴿the Most High﴾.
* **Sheikh:** From ﴿the Most High﴾, and from ﴿the Most Great﴾ as well, from both of them together. For this reason Allah the Exalted said in Surat an-Nisa': ﴿Then if they obey you, do not seek a way against them. Indeed, Allah is ever Most High and Great﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:34]. So if you are arrogant within yourself, remember the exaltedness of Allah the Exalted. If you are great in yourself, remember the greatness of Allah. If you are proud in yourself, remember the pride (kibriyā') of Allah the Exalted.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of greatness for Allah, from His saying ﴿the Most Great﴾.
  And among them: the affirmation of a perfect attribute that results from the combination of the two attributes, namely exaltedness and greatness, for combining these two yields a more perfect attribute in both. Although all of Allah's attributes are perfect, this is more emphatic.

**Student:** His saying, Exalted is He, (...) indicates the absence of (...) of the human being regarding what (...)

**Sheikh:** From the saying of Allah ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ it is derived that dominion belongs to Allah the Exalted. Have we mentioned this?
* **Students:** Yes.
* **Sheikh:** It follows from this that we should not dispose of His dominion except in what pleases Him. Right?
* **Students:** Yes.
* **Sheikh:** Accordingly, this verse contains an indication that the legal judgment among people and the settling of disputes among them must be based on what? On the ruling of Allah. And that a person's reliance on the rulings of created beings and man-made laws is a form of associating partners with Allah the Exalted, because dominion belongs to Allah the Exalted.
* It is also derived from it that one should be content with the decree and destiny of Allah the Exalted. For when you know that a thing belongs to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, you say: this is the disposition of the Owner over His property, and He may do as He wills. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:23]. This is why, when the Prophet (ﷺ) consoled his daughter, he said: "Indeed, to Allah belongs what He took, and to Him belongs what He left, and everything with Him has a specified term." [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (1284) and Muslim (923/11) from the hadith of Usama ibn Zayd.] Thus there is in this consolation for a person in calamities and his contentment with the decree and destiny of Allah.

**Student:** (...) the refutation of the Mu'aṭṭilah necessarily entails the refutation of the Mumaththilah (anthropomorphists), since by their likening (Allah to creation) they negated the attributes?

**Sheikh:** Yes, look: every anthropomorphist is a negator, and conversely, every negator is an anthropomorphist, and every anthropomorphist is a negator. Glory be to Allah, this combines two contradictories. Yes, indeed. So: every negator is an anthropomorphist, and every anthropomorphist is a negator.

**Student:** (...)

**Sheikh:** (...)

**Student:** Every negator is an anthropomorphist, because he only negated after (...)

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 256 (part 1 of 3):

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become distinct from error.﴾

First: The grammatical analysis (i'rab). ﴿لَا إِكْرَاهَ فِي الدِّينِ﴾: ﴿لَا﴾ is a negation of the genus (la nafiyah lil-jins), which operates like ﴿إنَّ﴾ (inna). ﴿إِكْرَاهَ﴾ is its noun, and ﴿فِي الدِّينِ﴾ is its predicate.

And His saying: ﴿قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ الرُّشْدُ مِنَ الْغَيِّ﴾. ﴿تَبَيَّنَ﴾ means تميَّز (tamayyaz, to be distinguished). This clause is connected in meaning to what precedes it as a causal explanation (ta'lil); that is, it serves as the justification for what came before.

And His saying: ﴿فَمَنْ يَكْفُرْ بِالطَّاغُوتِ﴾: (مَنْ) is a conditional particle, and ﴿يَكْفُرْ﴾ is the verb of the condition, jussive because of it. The clause ﴿فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ﴾ is the response of the condition. The fa' (فاء) is attached to the response because it is not suitable to be a condition itself. Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, says in the Alfiyya:

"Attach with fa' necessarily the response, if it is made
a condition for 'in' or other than it, and it is not made so."

Here, (قد) cannot be a conditional; if you said "in qad," it would not be suitable. Therefore the response must be attached with the fa'. We have previously passed a verse listing the clauses that take the fa' when they are a response to a condition. Will one of the brothers recite it for us?

That is (qad).

And His saying: ﴿لَا انْفِصَامَ لَهَا﴾: its parsing is as already mentioned: ﴿لَا﴾ is a negation of the genus, ﴿انْفِصَامَ﴾ is its noun, and the prepositional phrase ﴿لَهَا﴾ is its predicate.

Now we begin with the meanings. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. This clause, as we observe, is a negation. But is it meant as a prohibition (nahy), or is it a pure report (khabar mahd)?

It has been said that it means a prohibition: do not compel anyone to the religion of Allah. On this view it has been said that it is abrogated (mansukhah), and it has been said that it is rather specified (makhsusah). It was said it is abrogated by the verses of jihad, and it was said it is specified by the verses of the jizyah (poll tax). Those who said it is specified differed over whether it is general or only concerns the People of the Book. This is on the view that the negation here means a prohibition.

As for if we say the negation is a pure report, meaning that Allah informs that no one will be compelled into the religion, because he will enter the religion by choice, based on His saying: ﴿قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ الرُّشْدُ مِنَ الْغَيِّ﴾, then the matter is clear. A person, whenever he looks at the religion with a examining gaze, with knowledge and justice, will choose the religion, the religion of Islam, over others. On this, it is a pure report whose meaning is: people will not enter the religion of Allah, the Exalted, under compulsion, but they will enter by choice, because the right course is clear and error is clear, and every intelligent person will be on the right course rather than error, for this is what reason and natural disposition (fitrah) require. Which of the two matters is more fitting?

* A student: The second.
* Another student: The last.
* The Shaykh: The apparent view is that the second is more fitting, because it clearly shows that the religion of Islam is the religion of natural disposition, which no one can choose under compulsion; rather, one only chooses it while submitting to it and convinced of it.

As for the first view, I told you that the scholars differed over whether the verse is abrogated, or decisive (muhkamah), or specified. On the view of specification, is it specific to the People of the Book or general? The evident conclusion from the evidences, on the view that it is a prohibition, is that it is specified, because non-Muslims are compelled either to embrace Islam, or to pay the jizyah, or to be fought: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not adopt the religion of truth from those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah 29]. So we say: the verse is general but specified; that is, we say: compel the disbelievers to Islam or to paying the jizyah, without exception. If they refuse, they are fought. Thus the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he appointed a commander over an army or a detachment, would instruct him with these three matters: Islam; if they refuse, the jizyah; if they refuse, fighting [[See what Muslim transmitted (1731/3) from the hadith of Buraydah al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him.]], without fail, because the disbeliever, whatever he is, if he remains in his disbelief, will be against Islam to the extent he is able.

We have now explained the word ﴿al-rushd﴾ (right guidance), and we have explained the word ﴿al-ghayy﴾ (error), and we have shown the ways of distinguishing right guidance from error. You know that the position of this sentence relative to what precedes it is causal in meaning.

He, exalted is He, says: ﴿So whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut and believes in God has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾. This too is guidance and error. ﴿Whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut﴾. Disbelief (al-kufr) in the language is derived from concealment (al-satr), and from it is named al-kufurra. I think Yasir knows al-kufurra?

**A student:** The farmers (al-zurrā').

**The Shaykh:** No. Al-kufurra is what the common people call al-kafur (the sheath of the palm flower).

**A student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** After what, what?

**The student:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** No, shaykh. You are from Najd, you know this. Don't you know the date palm when it first comes out? Is there not a (kim)? ﴿And the palm tree with its sheaths﴾ [al-Rahman 11]. The (kim) that conceals the fruit is called this kufurra, right?

**A student:** (...), shaykh?

**The Shaykh:** Because it conceals. So disbelief originally derives from concealment, because the disbelieving person conceals God's blessing upon him. Here He says: ﴿whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut﴾. Disbelief in al-Taghut is to reject and deny al-Taghut, rejecting and denying it in such a way that one accepts from it neither compensation (ṣarf) nor ransom ('adl).

What is al-Taghut? Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, explained it with a comprehensive definition. Its root is from transgression (al-ṭughyān), which is exceeding the limit. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah 11]. That is, it increased beyond the limit. The water with which God drowned the disbelievers in the time of Noah exceeded its limit until it reached above the mountain peaks. So transgression is excess.

Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, said: al-Taghut is everything by which the servant exceeds his limit, whether a deity worshipped, a figure followed, or an authority obeyed. Everything by which the servant exceeds his limit in worship (of it) as a deity. So idols are therefore taghut, because a person exceeds his limit with them in worship as a deity.

As for a figure followed: the rabbis and monks, because a person exceeds his limit with them in declaring lawful what God has forbidden or forbidding what God has made lawful.

Or an authority obeyed: the rulers who command by their executive power, not by their legislative power. The scholars (have authority) by the authority of the Sharia, and the rulers by the authority of influence. Yes, or execution. These are three. Every person whom one exceeds the limit regarding them has worshipped al-Taghut.

So ﴿whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut﴾ means: whoever disbelieves in idols, right?

**A student:** All of them.

**The Shaykh:** Wait. Whoever disbelieves in idols. ﴿Whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut﴾: whoever disbelieves in the evil rabbis and monks, right?

**A student:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** ﴿Whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut﴾: whoever disbelieves in the evil rulers who command disobedience to God, right?

**A student:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** So this is disbelief in al-Taghut: disbelief in whatever is worshipped besides God, disbelief in every evil scholar who commands what opposes the Sharia of God, disbelief in every evil ruler who compels what? 

**The students:** What opposes the Sharia of God.

**The Shaykh:** What opposes the Sharia of God, mighty and majestic. This is al-Taghut.

The one who disbelieves in this, yet disbelief alone is not sufficient, because disbelief is emptying and absence, and there must be establishing. The establishing is His saying: ﴿and believes in God﴾. "Yu'min" (believes) is in the jussive (majzūm) by coordination (ʿaṭf) with His saying ﴿yakfur﴾ (disbelieves).

Faith in God includes four matters: belief in His existence, belief in His divinity (ulūhiyyah), belief in His lordship (rubūbiyyah), and belief in His names and attributes. This is necessary.

Belief in His existence, lordship, divinity, names and attributes, a belief that necessitates acceptance and submission: acceptance of the report and submission to the command, whether it is a command or a prohibition. So faith is composed of four matters that entail two things. What are the four matters? Belief in the existence of God, His lordship, His divinity, and His names and attributes. And this belief necessitates acceptance and submission: accepting the report and affirming it, and submitting to the command by doing what is commanded and abstaining from what is forbidden.

Then know that when we say belief in the existence of God, His lordship, His divinity, and His names and attributes, what is meant is belief in His singularity in these things: in lordship, divinity, names and attributes, and in necessary existence. He, glory be to Him, is singular in this, being the one of necessary existence, the Lord, the God, and the One possessing great names and attributes. This is belief in God.

So whoever believes in God's existence and lordship but associates others with God, he is not a believer in God, even if he says with full mouth that he believes in God. We say to him: You have not believed in God. If you had believed in Him, you would not have associated anything with Him, because you have not disbelieved in al-Taghut. There must be disbelief in al-Taghut and belief in God, mighty and majestic.

If someone believes in God's existence, lordship and divinity but not His names and attributes, he has not believed in God. And they are in degrees: his denial may reach the level of disbelief, and it may be less than that.

Someone who believes in God's existence, lordship, divinity, names and attributes, but denies one single report of His reports?

**The students:** He is a disbeliever.

**The Shaykh:** He is a disbeliever. If he says, "I am a believer," we say: You are lying. How do you believe in God, mighty and majestic, as Lord, and yet deny His reports?!

If he does not deny, but does not submit, then he has not believed in God. Yet they are in degrees. Abandoning submission may be disbelief, and it may be less than that, according to what the legal evidences require.

But now look: God, exalted is He, made two conditions: ﴿whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut and believes in God﴾. He began with the negative before the positive. What is the negative?

**The students:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** ﴿So whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut﴾ is the negative. The positive is ﴿and believes in God﴾, because clearing comes before adorning. Clean the place first, then spread the carpet. If a person wanted to place a carpet on a spot full of thorns, nails, pebbles and such, would that be suitable or not?

**The students:** It would not be suitable.

**The Shaykh:** What do we say? Clean it first, then spread. So here: disbelieve in al-Taghut first, and after your heart is empty of al-Taghut, put in faith.

**A student:** Belief in God.

**The Shaykh:** Belief in God. So empty first, then adorn second. There is a well-known expression among the scholars: "takhliyah before tahliyah" (emptying before adorning). Tahliyah means putting on ornaments. If a person wanted to adorn his wife, and she had just gotten up from sleep, covered in filth and all kinds of things, frightening, and he put ornaments on her, would that be suitable?

**The students:** It would not be suitable.

**The Shaykh:** What do we say? Let her wash first and clean herself, and then put on the ornaments.

﴿So whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut and believes in God﴾. The answer, which is the inevitable result: ﴿then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾. See, glory be to God the Mighty, the great eloquence: ﴿has grasped﴾ and not ﴿has held fast﴾ (tamassaka). ﴿Istamsaka﴾ is more emphatic, because an increase in the form indicates an increase in meaning, generally, though not always.

﴿Istamsaka﴾ means that his grip has become firm. Moreover, it suggests there is a peril: a person grasped this handhold and held fast to it, and that is the case, for the origin is ruin, except whom God protects. ﴿And I do not acquit myself; indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon whom my Lord has mercy﴾ [Yusuf 53].

So here ﴿istamsaka﴾ indicates the intensity of gripping, and that there is something from which he tries to escape until he reached this handhold. The handhold (ʿurwah) originally is the grip of a thing, like the handle of a pitcher, the handle of a bucket, and many things of this kind. It is only the grip by which a person takes hold.

﴿Al-Wuthqā﴾ is the feminine of (awthaq, most firm), and it is derived from what? From trust (al-thiqah), which is the tranquility regarding a thing. That is, by the handhold which is the most firm thing with which a person is reassured, meaning that when he holds fast to it, he becomes certain with complete certainty of what?

**A student:** Of salvation.

**The Shaykh:** Of salvation. Because a person may hold on to a rope out of fear of drowning, but is he confident? He is not confident. He fears it may slip from his hand, fears it may break. He is not in confidence. But here He said ﴿al-wuthqā﴾, meaning the feminine of (awthaq), the most firm there can be. Then, in addition, ﴿there is no severing for it﴾. See three attributes: holding fast, a handhold, the most firm, and third: ﴿there is no severing for it﴾, meaning it cannot be broken. Therefore He used (lā), the negation of the genus, which cannot occur: it is impossible for it to be severed.

A handhold may be firm, but could it, over a long time?

**A student:** Be severed.

**The Shaykh:** Be severed. It may, with heavy load, be severed. But this handhold is not severed: ﴿by the most trustworthy handhold, there is no severing for it﴾, never.

So whoever holds fast to it is saved without doubt. How easy the matter is: emptying, then adorning with something the soul is at rest with, content with, and accepts. Then the result is that you are saved by this handhold you have held fast to.

I told you: (istamsaka, held fast) is more emphatic than (tamassaka, grasped). A person may grasp a thing without holding it fast; that is, the holding fast does not happen for him. Unlike (istamsaka).

His saying ﴿there is no severing for it﴾ is the third attribute, meaning that it is secure from what?

**A student:** From severing.

**The Shaykh:** Yes, from severing, which is cutting off.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. He concluded the verse with this, as a warning from one aspect and a glad tidings from another aspect. A warning from what? From opposition. And a glad tidings in conformity: if you conform, your deed will not be lost, for God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. And if you oppose, your deed will not be hidden from God, because God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

It has come to our attention many times that the scholars, may God have mercy on them, (...).

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. We repeat what we always repeat: (samī', All-Hearing) is one of God's names, and every name of God includes one or more attributes. It must include one or more attributes.

It has been mentioned not long ago that the name (al-Ḥayy, the Living) includes the life indicated by the root (ḥ-y-y) and other perfect attributes. We said: al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm (the Living, the Self-Subsisting), the two together encompass all of God's beautiful names. Therefore they are the Greatest Name.[[See what Abu Dawud (1496) and al-Tirmidhi (3478) reported from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Greatest Name of God is in these two verses: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, and the opening of Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. God, there is no deity except Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾."]] So every name... the rule: every name of God includes one attribute or more, but not every attribute includes a name. Is it clear?

For example: ﴿Your Lord has come﴾ [al-Fajr 22]. This is an attribute. Must we say that among God's names is "the One who comes"?

**The students:** No.

**The Shaykh:** ﴿God spoke to Musa with speech﴾ [al-Nisa' 164]. It is not necessary, or it is not permissible (...) based on establishing the attribute of speech for Him. But (samī') we say: it includes the attribute, which is hearing. The scholars say hearing (...) has two main divisions: one meaning perception of what is heard, that is, the sound even if faint. This too is sometimes intended for affirmation (ta'yīd, support), sometimes for threat (tahdīd), and sometimes to show the all-encompassing scope of God's hearing over everything. This hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard is sometimes intended for affirmation, sometimes for threat, and sometimes to show the encompassing of God's hearing, exalted is He, over everything. In His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha 46], what is meant?

**The students:** Affirmation.

**The Shaykh:** Affirmation. That is, along with affirming hearing, it means affirmation (support). And in His saying: ﴿God has heard the saying of those who said, "Indeed, God is poor and we are rich"﴾ [Al 'Imran 181], what is meant?

**The students:** Threat.

**The Shaykh:** Threat. And likewise: ﴿Do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation? Yes﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80].

**The students:** (...).

**The Shaykh:** And sometimes... for threat. For threat, this meaning: ﴿that We do not hear their secret and their private conversation? Yes, and Our messengers with them are writing﴾ [al-Zukhruf 80].

And sometimes it is intended to show the encompassing of God's knowledge of everything heard, like: ﴿God has heard the speech of the one who argues with you about her husband and complains to God﴾ [al-Mujadila 1]. It is also perhaps said that every occurrence of the name (samī') is indicative of and includes that.

As for the second type, or second main division of hearing, it means response (istijābah). From it is His saying about Ibrahim: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Ibrahim 39]. (Samī' al-du'ā', Hearer of supplication) means: the Responder to supplication. Because the intended meaning is not seeking a means through God's hearing of the supplication without answering it. Rather, the intended meaning is seeking a means through His being, exalted is He, one who answers supplication, that He answer the supplication of this supplicant.

They said: From it is the saying of the one praying: "God hears whoever praises Him," meaning: He responds to whoever praises Him. Is there a contradiction between these two divisions?

**A student:** There is no contradiction between them.

**The Shaykh:** There is no contradiction between them, because this is for one thing and that is for another thing. Contradiction occurs only if both meanings apply to one thing and it is impossible to combine them. Thus it is clear that God's hearing divides into two divisions: hearing in the sense of perceiving what is heard, meaning perceiving sounds even if faint, and hearing in the sense of response, the response to supplication. The first is sometimes intended as threat, sometimes as affirmation, and sometimes to show encompassing.

As for His saying ﴿All-Knowing﴾, it is also one of God's names, exalted is He, which is among the widest of names, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That you may know that God is over all things competent, and that God has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq 12].

The scholars said knowledge is the encompassing of a thing in a manner that is certain and corresponds to its reality. This is knowledge: perceiving a thing as it is, with certain, corresponding perception. Whoever does not perceive a thing is ignorant of it. Whoever perceives it contrary to what it is, is also ignorant of it. Whoever perceives it without certainty is doubtful about it, not knowing. Doubt is not knowledge. God, mighty and majestic, knows all things, the subtle and the great, what relates to His action and the action of His servants, and what is past, present and future. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾ [al-Baqarah 255]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "Its knowledge is with my Lord, in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets"﴾ [Ta-Ha 52]. ﴿Neither errs﴾: does not ignore what will come. ﴿Nor forgets﴾: what has passed.

The reason the verse ends with these two noble names is that it speaks of religion, and of the one who holds fast to it and the one who deviates from it. For that reason, these two names are most suitable to end with. For whoever knows that God is All-Hearing of his words and All-Knowing of his states, what does he choose for himself? He chooses right guidance for himself and avoids error. He chooses right guidance because he knows that God hears him if he speaks, and knows him in whatever state he is, and he fears the punishment of God. In his state of guidance he hopes for good from his Lord, due to his knowledge of his condition and His hearing of his speech. In a state of error, he fears from his Lord and so abandons error.

As for the benefits of this noble verse, it contains many benefits. I do not know, before I begin on the benefits of this verse, whether you have actually finished counting the benefits of Ayat al-Kursi?

**The students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** How many did they reach?

**The students:** Forty-two.

**The Shaykh:** They recite it in the morning and evening litanies. If its benefits are gathered, and also its explanation is added to this, it might come to two or three pages.

**A student:** A booklet.

**The Shaykh:** More than two?

**The student:** Thirty-five pages.

**The Shaykh:** Thirty-five pages!

**The student:** (...).

The Shaykh: "What contradicts it? We say: thirty-five leaves, but (...) what the Sunnah has brought."

Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is obligatory upon the scholars of the Muslims to explain to people the right guidance from error, because this reasoning is, as it were, a settled matter in the religion of Islam. Who is able to explain the right guidance from error? Who?

The students: The scholars.

The Shaykh: The scholars. On this basis, the scholars are obligated to explain to people the right guidance from error, so that no one has an argument against them.

Can it be deduced from the verse that the coercion ruling is negated for the one coerced mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who has been forced while his heart is at peace with faith﴾ [an-Nahl 106]?

A student: Far-fetched.

The Shaykh: We have said that a speaker might say so, but His saying ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right path has become clear from error﴾ [al-Baqarah 256] refutes it, since this reasoning does not fit that meaning.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: there is only guidance and error; for if there were a third, it would have been mentioned, because the context is one of restriction. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is there after the truth except error?﴾ [Yunus 32].

Among the benefits of this noble verse: sincerity is not complete except by negating all association with Allah, because of His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the false deities (taghut) and believes in Allah﴾. So whoever believes in Allah but does not disbelieve in the taghut, his faith is not complete.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: everything worshipped besides Allah is taghut (false deity, transgressing object of worship), because of His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the taghut and believes in Allah﴾. The reasoning is this: He, glory be to Him, made disbelief in the taghut the counterpart of what? Of belief in Allah. And the counterpart of a thing is other than the thing, separate from it.

Can it be deduced from this that disbelief and belief do not combine in the heart?

A student: It can be deduced.

The Shaykh: Let us see: what is the answer of the conditional? Is the answer of the conditional "then he is a believer," or is the answer of the conditional ﴿then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾?

A student: ﴿Then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾.

The Shaykh: This is the answer. So we do not deduce that a person cannot have both faith and disbelief in his heart, because the answer is not that he is not a believer; rather the answer is that he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold. On this basis, it is possible for a person to have both faith and disbelief, and this is the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah). But whoever wants to grasp the most trustworthy handhold, let him disbelieve in the taghut. "Grasping" means that which cannot fall away or be broken.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: there is no salvation except by disbelieving in the taghut and believing in Allah, because of His saying: ﴿then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾.

Among its benefits also: actions vary in merit. From where is this taken?

A student: (...).

The Shaykh: How?

A student: The comparative (tafdil).

The Shaykh: From the comparative form, because preference requires one preferred and one preferred over. There is no doubt that actions vary in merit, by the text of the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [Hud 7]. And "best" (ahsan) is a comparative form, so this is evidence that actions vary in goodness. "The Prophet ﷺ was asked: Which deed is most beloved to Allah? He said: 'Prayer at its time'" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (527) and Muslim (85/139), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him]. And Allah, exalted is He, said in the Hadith Qudsi: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him" [al-Bukhari (6502), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him].

If actions vary in merit, does it follow that the doer varies in merit? Yes, indeed, it follows that the doer varies in merit: whenever the action is more excellent, the doer is more excellent.

By what does the variation of actions occur?

A student: (...).

The Shaykh: By several matters. First: according to the doer; according to the time; according to the place. Time is the period; according to the manner and following (of the Sunnah); according to sincerity to Allah, mighty and majestic; according to the kind or type. What remains with us?

A student: The quantity (qadr).

The Shaykh: The quantity. Is there variation in this?

The student: Following (of the Sunnah).

The Shaykh: We have already said it: the manner is following.

The student: The quantity.

The Shaykh: The quantity is the amount. Now we return once more; perhaps it will become clear to us (...).

According to the doer. Its example is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not revile my companions. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to (the mountain of) Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him; and Muslim (2540/221), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. This is according to the doer.

According to the kind and type of action: obligatory acts are better than voluntary acts of the same kind. Each obligatory act is better than the voluntary act of its type. So the obligatory prayer is better than what?

The students: Than the Sunnah.

The Shaykh: Than the Sunnah prayer.

It also varies according to type: prayer is better than zakat, and zakat is better than fasting. This is considered in terms of type.

Third: considered in terms of time. Its evidence is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There are no days in which righteous action is more beloved to Allah than these ten days" [al-Bukhari (757), and al-Tirmidhi (969) with this wording, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him]. And: "Whoever fasts one day in the cause of Allah, Allah will distance his face from the Fire by seventy autumns" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2840), and Muslim (1153/168), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him].

According to place, its evidence is: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except the Sacred Mosque" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1190), and Muslim (1394/506), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him].

According to manner: meaning that the manner of worship is better than another manner, such as humility (khushu') in prayer for example. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Certainly will the believers have succeeded, who are during their prayer humbly submissive﴾ [al-Mu'minun 1, 2]. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 31]. So whenever a person follows the Messenger more closely, his action is better, because we have mentioned a principle: a ruling attached to an attribute grows strong in proportion to the strength of that attribute. Is this clear? Therefore, whenever a person follows more closely in his worship, his worship is better.

Sincerity. This is among the most important things; the variation according to sincerity is among the most important. An action into which showing off (riya') enters, there is no doubt that it is greatly diminished compared to an action free of showing off. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf 110]. Indeed, if association (shirk) accompanies it from its beginning, it is nullified, as in the Hadith Qudsi: "I am the most independent of partners from association. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another along with Me, I abandon him and his association" [recorded by Muslim (2985/46), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].

Shall we say, considering the state? Quantity, what is this? That is, quantity is not considered in reality; what is considered is an increase in quantity, not an increase in merit in something related to the act itself. But quantity, I think we mentioned that in the increase of faith.

Considering the state: worship in a time of turning away and heedlessness is better than worship in a time of attentiveness. For this reason, the days of patience for the doer carry the reward of fifty of whom? Of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. The reward of fifty of the Companions. Why? Because of the great turning away from Allah, mighty and majestic, and from His religion, so he finds no one to help him and assist him; rather he may find only someone who mocks him and ridicules him.

A student: Does this not fall under time?

The Shaykh: No, this is under state, because it is not specific to one time over another.

Perhaps we also say: it varies. Among its variation considering state is that the chastity of a young man is better than the chastity of an old man. That is, the chastity of a youth is better than the chastity of an elder. Why?

A student: Because the desire of the young man is stronger.

The Shaykh: Because the desire of the young man is stronger than the desire of the old man. So the impulse toward lack of chastity in his case is stronger than the impulse in the case of the old man. For this reason, the punishment of an old adulterer is greater, or more severe, than the punishment of a young one. This is also among the variations of actions according to the state of the person. So now, what are the causes of excellence?

The students: Seven.

The Shaykh: Seven? We (...) entered (...) into state, and you insist that variation also occurs by the number of instances.

A student: Why would the variation not be (...) in (...).

The Shaykh: Second: because a report may be multiple, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Owner of the Throne, the Glorious﴾ [al-Buruj 14, 15]. And it may also be a state (hal), meaning that He is the one bringing them out of darkness into light.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 257 (part 1 of 2):

And His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Taghut (false deities/transgressors); they bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah 257]. ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿their protectors﴾ is another subject (mubtada' thani, a second subject); ﴿the Taghut﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of the second subject, and the clause made of the second subject and its predicate is the predicate of the first subject.

And His saying: ﴿they bring them out﴾ — as for its i'rab (grammatical analysis), we say: ﴿their protectors, the Taghut, they bring them out﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to ﴿the Taghut﴾.

And His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire﴾ is a subject and predicate as well, and ﴿they therein are abiding forever﴾ is a subject and predicate as well.

In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Allah is the Protector (Wali) of those who believe﴾. The wali means the one who takes charge, the helper, the one who manages their affairs and supports them.

And His saying: ﴿the Protector of those who believe﴾ is a special protection, because Allah, Exalted is He, is the Wali of every person; but in the specific sense, His protection is for the believers. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail (in their duty) (61). Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am 61-62]. This is the general protection, and it includes the believer and the disbeliever, for every person is under Allah's protection by virtue of His lordship (rububiyyah). As for this (verse), it is a special protection.

And His saying: ﴿those who believe﴾ — what is faith (iman)?

Faith (iman), linguistically, has been said to be affirmation (tasdiq), and it has been said to be acknowledgment (iqrar), and this is the closer view; because tasdiq is transitive by itself, whereas iman is transitive by a preposition, for you say: "saddaqtu Zaydan" (I believed Zayd), but you do not say: "amantu Zaydan" (I had faith in Zayd, without a preposition). And when a word has the meaning of another word, it must be transitive by what the other word is transitive by; and if it is transitive by itself, it is transitive by itself, or if by a preposition, it is transitive by a preposition.

Also, it is said: "amana bi-kadha" (he believed in such-and-such), just as it is said: "aqarra bi-kadha" (he acknowledged such-and-such). Yet a speaker may still say that tasdiq is also transitive with the letter ba' (bi), so one says: "saddaqtu bi-kadha", as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and affirmed it﴾ [al-Zumar 33]. But the first difference is that (saddaqa) is transitive by itself while (amana) is not transitive by itself.

In any case, faith in the Sharia is other than faith in the language; rather, it is more specific. It is more specific than faith in the language, since it is acknowledgment or affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission: acceptance of the report, and likewise of the rulings; and submission (idhan) is yielding to them. It therefore includes belief in the heart, speech with the tongue, and action with the limbs; all of this is part of faith.

We have mentioned earlier the evidences indicating this. Among the evidences that faith includes belief in the heart is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels..." to the end [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah; Muslim (8/1) from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab]. This is the belief of the heart. And the evidence that it includes speech with the tongue and action with the limbs is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Faith has seventy-some branches; the highest of them is the saying 'there is no god but Allah,' and this is speech; and the lowest of them is removing harm from the road, and modesty is a branch of faith" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (9), Muslim (35/58), and the wording is his, and in it: "Then the best of them is the saying..." from the hadith of Abu Hurairah].

So whenever faith is mentioned to you in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, what is meant by it is acknowledgment that necessarily entails what?

* The students: Acceptance and submission.
* The Shaykh: Acceptance and submission. It thus includes these three things: belief in the heart, speech with the tongue, and action with the limbs. Some also said: the actions of the heart, which is also correct. The actions of the heart are its love, its intention, its aversion, its hatred, and the like, as well as its fear and its hope; all of these are actions of the heart.

And His saying: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾. What are the ﴿darknesses﴾? Are they sensory darknesses, in the sense that a person comes out of a dark room into a lit corridor?
