No; rather, what is meant by the darknesses is the darknesses of ignorance, the darknesses of disbelief, and the darknesses of sins. All of these are darknesses. Ignorance is undoubtedly darkness. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Is he who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose likeness is in darknesses, from which he does not emerge?﴾ [al-An'am 122]. And Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisa' 174]. The manifest light is the Qur'an, and by it knowledge is attained; this is the light of knowledge.

Also the light of faith: when Allah expands a person's breast for faith, his heart is illuminated by faith, so much so that some believers show that light of their faith in their intuition, their assumption, and their estimation; this is what is called firasa (discernment). For this reason it came in the hadith: "Beware of the discernment of the believer" [al-Tirmidhi (3127) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]; because the light that Allah casts into a person's heart may guide him to things hidden from others, as if it were a lamp illuminating what is before him.

The third: the light of guidance and uprightness, which is opposite to the darknesses of wickedness; because wickedness (fisq), which is sins, becomes darkness, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "When a man commits a sin, a black spot is marked on his heart" [al-Tirmidhi (3334), Ibn Majah (4244), al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (10179), and Ahmad (7952) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah]. This blackness causes darkness of the heart.

So the darknesses are three: the darkness of ignorance, and what else? And disbelief, and sins. Light corresponds to these: against the darkness of ignorance is the light of knowledge; against the darkness of disbelief is the light of faith; and against the darkness of wickedness is the light of uprightness and steadfastness. For this reason Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them﴾ [Fussilat 30]. And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, when a man said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me something about Islam about which I will not ask anyone other than you," meaning a statement that would cut off every question to people: "Say: I believe in Allah, then be steadfast" [Muslim (38/62) from the hadith of Sufyan ibn 'Abdullah al-Thaqafi, with the wording: "fa-istaqim"].

And His saying: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Taghut﴾: you now see a difference between the first and second constructions in order. There he said: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾, and he did not say: "Those who believe, Allah is their protector"; rather he said: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾, because when this noble name first comes upon the heart, it brings joy. That is one point, unlike if he had said: "Those who believe, Allah is their protector."

Second: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾ conveys blessing through mentioning the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, first: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾.

Third: to show favor to these people, that Allah is the One who first bestowed favor upon them, bringing them out of darknesses into the light. But here he said: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾. If he had made the second clause follow the pattern of the first, what would he have said?

* The students: "And the Taghut are the protectors of those who disbelieve."
* The Shaykh: "And the Taghut are the protectors of those who disbelieve." But he did not say it that way. It has been said that the wisdom behind this is so that the Taghut is not placed opposite the name of Allah; for if the two clauses were balanced, the Taghut would be in opposition to the name of Allah.

Second: the Taghut is too lowly and contemptible to be mentioned first and given precedence.

Third: these disbelievers are blameworthy for taking the Taghut as protectors; they are the ones who initiated and chose the Taghut over uprightness. They chose the Taghut over uprightness, so they became the ones who began with what necessitates reproach and blame; therefore beginning with them is more fitting.

﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ — disbelieved in whom? They disbelieved in everything that must be believed in, whether their disbelief was in Allah, or in His Messenger, or in His Book, or in His angels, or in the Last Day, or in predestination.

﴿Those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Taghut﴾. Here he said ﴿their protectors (awliya'uhum)﴾, and there he said ﴿the Wali﴾ (singular). The difference is clear: the taghuts are many, and the callers to misguidance are many, whereas Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is one; He is the one Protector. Then he said: ﴿their protectors, the Taghut﴾. We have already mentioned that the taghut is a comprehensive name for everything by which a servant transgresses his limit, whether a deity, a figure to be followed, or one to be obeyed: a deity like an idol, a figure followed like scholars, or one obeyed like rulers. These are the ones through whom whoever goes astray among people goes astray: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Tawbah 31].

He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Taghut; they bring them out﴾. Here the word taghut, we said earlier, is derived from transgression (tughyan), and the taa' in it is for emphasis (mubalaghah), like the emphasis in "'allamah" and "fahhamah" and the like; and on this basis the waw is the final letter of the word.

And His saying: ﴿they bring them out of the light﴾ uses the plural because he said: ﴿their protectors, the Taghut; they bring them out﴾. Thus taghut is a generic noun including every transgressor, and ﴿they bring them out﴾ is plural in consideration of the generic noun and in agreement with the second subject, which is ﴿their protectors﴾.

And His saying: ﴿they bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾ has been found problematic, because its apparent meaning is that those who disbelieve are those who first believed and entered the light, then disbelieved and left it; yet it also includes the original disbeliever who had not believed before. So what is the answer to this?

* A student: We say: the origin is faith in Allah, Glorified and Exalted.
* The Shaykh: That is an answer. It is indicated by the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Every child is born upon the fitrah; then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1385), Muslim (2658/22) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah]. So the origin of a person's birth is upon the fitrah and the light; but what necessitates disbelief may befall him, and so he disbelieves. This is one answer. As for the apostate disbeliever, it is clear how the matter applies. But as for the original disbeliever...

* A student: Perhaps, for example, a man upon whom Allah bestowed guidance, and then there came upon him (...).

* * *

* The Shaykh: (...) And the light that is with him, what may arise in his mind or soul of love of good, perhaps. But Allah said concerning Shu'ayb: ﴿It is not for us to return to it﴾ [al-A'raf 89], ﴿We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it﴾ [al-A'raf 89], although Shu'ayb and those who believed with him had not been upon their religion, especially Shu'ayb, since the prophets never associated partners with Allah. The meaning, then, is that they bring them out because they were disposed to guidance, but they expelled them and eliminated that disposition.

So we now have three possibilities: either what is meant is those who were first upon faith and then were expelled, as is the apparent meaning of the wording. Or we say that this is in consideration of what?

* The students: The fitrah.
* The Shaykh: The fitrah. So the fitrah is sound and upon faith, and then they expelled them. Or it is said: they expelled them because they were disposed to acceptance; their souls may have tempted them toward it, but they dominate them so that they do not enter the light from the outset.

He said: ﴿they bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾. The plural of darknesses and the singular of light have also been discussed before, because light is the path of truth, which is one, while darknesses are the paths of falsehood, which are many.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire, therein they abide forever﴾. ﴿Those are the companions (ashab) of﴾: the companion (sahib) is one who is constantly attached to a thing, so no one is called a companion except the constant one. Except for one companion: who?

* A student: The companions of the Prophet ﷺ.
* The Shaykh: The companionship (suhbah) of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is applied to whoever met him while believing in him, even for a moment, and died upon that; this is among the special privileges of the Prophet ﷺ. Otherwise, whoever met you and parted from you is not called a companion. So the companions of the Fire are its people, those constantly attached to it. On this basis, there is in this an indication of their eternal abiding therein, as He said, as an emphasis on that: ﴿they therein are abiding forever﴾. ﴿They﴾ is a subject, and ﴿abiding forever﴾ is—

* The students: The predicate.
* The Shaykh: And ﴿therein﴾ is related to what?

* The students: To ﴿abiding forever﴾.

* The Shaykh: To ﴿abiding forever﴾. It was placed first to indicate restriction (hasr) and to accommodate the rhyme (fawasil); that is, for a meaningful benefit and a verbal benefit.

* * *

(...) ﴿That Allah gave him the kingship﴾.

* A student: We have not taken the benefits of the verse.

* The Shaykh: Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾, and so on to the end.

* Several benefits are derived from this verse:

* First: the virtue of faith, and that by it the protection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is attained; by His saying: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾.

* Second: the affirmation of protection for Allah, Mighty and Majestic; that is, He, Glorified and Exalted, protects His servants. But do the servants also take Him as protector?

The answer: yes, they do take Him as protector, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever takes Allah and His Messenger and those who believe as protectors﴾ [al-Ma'idah 56]. But our taking Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as protector is taking up His religion; that is, we support His religion, strive on its behalf, and expend our lives and wealth for it. It is possible that the meaning of His saying: ﴿whoever takes Allah and His Messenger as protectors﴾ is: whoever makes Allah his protector; and the meaning is one.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that among the fruits of faith is Allah's guidance of the believer. From where is this derived?

* A student: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾, and His saying: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾.

* The Shaykh: His saying: ﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light﴾. We have already explained the meaning of the darknesses, and that they are the darknesses of ignorance, disbelief, and sin.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that the disbelievers have the taghut as their protectors, whether they are those who are followed, worshipped, or obeyed; because taghut derives from transgression, which is what a servant transgresses his limit by, whether a deity, a figure followed, or one obeyed, as Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, defined it.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the freedom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from those who disbelieve, derived from the explicit and the implicit meaning. The implicit meaning is in His saying: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾, whose implication is: not those who disbelieve; and the explicit meaning is from His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Taghut﴾. This corresponds to His saying: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the evil fruits of disbelief, and that it leads to misguidance, and we seek refuge with Allah; by His saying: ﴿they bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾. This bringing out may be a bringing out after falling into darknesses, or a bringing out at the moment of falling into disbelief; that is, it may be after their disbelief or at the time of their desire for disbelief.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: that it is fitting for the believer, indeed for every intelligent person (and "fitting" here means "obligatory") to choose that in which there is the protection of Allah. And what is that?

* A student: Faith.

* The Shaykh: Faith, and it is faith; for every intelligent person, if asked: "Would you prefer that Allah be your protector, or that the taghuts be your protectors?" would say: "Allah." So it is obligatory upon every intelligent person to strive to attain the protection of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that is by faith. Know that this protection is a great protection with many fruits, among which is what we have already pointed to.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse is that disbelief is the opposite of faith, as His saying shows: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾ ﴿while those who disbelieve have the Taghut (false deities, anything worshipped besides Allah) as their protectors﴾.
But does this mean that the two cannot coexist in one person?
* Students: (...)
* The Shaykh: According to the sound opinion, which is the view of Ahl as-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), a person may have qualities of faith and qualities of disbelief together. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Two things among people are acts of disbelief: slandering a person's lineage and wailing over the dead." [Reported by Muslim (67/121) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] This does not take a person out of faith. Consider that a person may be given to lying, and lying is a trait of the hypocrites; he may be treacherous, and treachery is a trait of the hypocrites; he may be envious, and envy is a trait of the Jews. Similar examples are many. So a person may combine faith and disbelief in himself. But absolute disbelief, which takes a person out of Islam, cannot coexist with faith.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse is the affirmation of the Fire, as His saying shows: ﴿They are the companions of the Fire﴾. Does the Fire exist now?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And be wary of the Fire, which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Aal 'Imran 131]. He said ﴿has been prepared﴾ in the past tense, and "preparation" means readying. It is also established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in more than one hadith that he saw it. In the eclipse prayer (salat al-kusuf), the Fire was shown to him, and he saw 'Amr ibn Luhayy dragging his intestines in the Fire. [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3521) and Muslim (2856/50) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] He saw in it the woman who was punished because of a cat she had confined until it died of hunger. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "She neither fed it nor released it to eat from the creatures of the earth." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3482) and Muslim (2242/151) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar; al-Bukhari (3318) and Muslim (2242/152, 2619/135) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah; and al-Bukhari (745) from the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr.] He also saw in it the owner of the muhjan (a staff with a curved head) being punished. [Reported by Muslim (904/10) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.] Who is the owner of the muhjan? He was a man who used to steal from pilgrims with his muhjan. The muhjan is a staff with a curved head, by which one grabs goods. If the owner of the goods noticed, he would say that the muhjan had pulled them; if he did not notice, the thief took them and left. The Prophet saw him being punished with his muhjan in the Fire of Hell, and we seek refuge in Allah.
The point is that the Fire exists. Is it everlasting or not? Yes, it is everlasting without doubt. It is not pre-eternal, because it was created after it did not exist, but it is everlasting and does not perish. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, for them is the fire of Hell; it will not be decreed upon them so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them. Thus We recompense every ungrateful disbeliever﴾ [Fatir 36].
Allah the Exalted mentioned the everlasting abode of its people in three places in the Qur'an:
In Surat an-Nisa': ﴿Allah would never forgive them nor guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [an-Nisa' 168-169]. In Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever; they will find no protector or helper﴾ [al-Ahzab 64-65]. In Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 23].
By this, the falsehood of those who say that the Fire will perish is known, and that this is a false view contrary to the textual evidences of the Shari'ah.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse is that the disbelievers abide forever in the Fire. From where is this derived?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From where did you derive it? From which word of ﴿Those﴾?
* The student: No, ﴿abiding﴾ (khalidun).
* The Shaykh: From ﴿abiding﴾?
* The student: ﴿Companions﴾ (ashab).
* The Shaykh: From ﴿companions﴾; because the companion (sahib) is?
* The student: The one who is constant with something.
* The Shaykh: The one who is constant with something.
* Among its benefits: abiding forever is specific to them, and whoever among the believers enters the Fire is not made to abide in it, as His saying shows: ﴿They therein are abiding﴾, meaning, exclusively them and not others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 258 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:258]. ﴿Have you not considered﴾: the hamzah is an interrogative particle, and it is meant here as taqrir (affirmation, confirming that the matter is established) and ta'ajjub (wonderment, calling the addressee to marvel at this strange matter: that someone would dispute the existence of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic).

And ﴿tara﴾ means "look at." Is it with your eye or with your heart?
* A student: With your eye.
* Another student: With your heart.
* The Shaykh: With your heart, brother, with your heart; because he did not live to see it with his eye. With the heart. The alif has been dropped from ﴿tara﴾ for the jussive, due to the entry of (lam), which is a jussive particle.

The address in His words ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is either to the Prophet ﷺ, or to everyone who can be addressed among those to whom the Qur'an was revealed, and this is more general. We have mentioned before that whatever comes in address form in the Noble Qur'an has three situations: either evidence indicates that it is for the Messenger (peace be upon him) and his community; or evidence indicates that it is specific to the Messenger ﷺ; or neither of these applies, and the ruling on it is that it is general, general to the Messenger (peace be upon him) and to others. But is this specific address one that is meant for the community, with its leader being addressed because they follow him, or is it meant for the Prophet (peace be upon him) with others doing it by way of following his example?
There are two opinions among the scholars, and their implications are one. Among the examples of what evidence shows is specific to the Messenger (peace be upon him) is His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast? And We removed from you your burden﴾ [al-Sharh 94:1-2]. This is undoubtedly specific to the Messenger (peace be upon him).
Among the things that indicate it is for the Messenger and others is: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq 65:1]. He addressed the Prophet (peace be upon him), then said: ﴿when you divorce﴾, which is general; this shows that the intended meaning is generality.
Among what admits of both is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It has been revealed to you and to those before you: if you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar 39:65].
This may be for the Messenger (peace be upon him) alone, with his community following him, and this is the apparent wording, although such shirk will never occur from him; because (in) does not indicate that a thing occurred, it indicates the supposition of its possibility, whether it is possible that this thing be supposed or not.
Here, ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾ admits both meanings, or not?
* A student: It admits both.
* The Shaykh: It admits both meanings: meaning, "Have you not considered, O Muhammad?" or "Have you not considered, O addressee?" ﴿the one who argued with Abraham﴾: (Abraham) is mentioned twice.
* A student: Three times.
* Another student: In this verse, four times.
* The Shaykh: Three times. There are two readings: ﴿Ibrahim﴾ and ﴿Ibraham﴾, which is a Sab'i (canonical seven-reading) reading: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibraham about his Lord﴾, and ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord﴾; both are correct.
* A student: In all three places?
* The Shaykh: Yes, three places, in all three. ﴿Hājja﴾ (argued) is in the form mufā'ala, (fā'ala), and the mufā'ala form is in most cases only between two; like qātala (fought), nāẓara (debated), ḥājja (argued), dāfa'a (repelled), and what is similar to that. And (ḥājja) here is a mufā'ala form, and the mufā'ala comes from two, and its examples in the Arabic language are many, and it comes from two mostly. I say: mostly; so that you do not object to me with your saying: "safara" (he travelled), is it from one or from two?
* The students: From one.
* The Shaykh: From one. So (ḥājja) means argument from two, and the meaning of ḥājjahu is: he debated him, and each one presented his proof, and the ḥujja is the evidence and demonstration. This was a man, a king, whom Allah gave kingship, a kingdom that lasted a long time, and he ruled wide lands. It does not concern us to know his name, whether he was Nimrod ibn Canaan or someone else; it does not matter, what matters is the story. This was a man whom Allah gave kingship, a complete kingship that no one contested, and his reign lasted, and as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The likeness of the life of this world is like water which We send down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingle with it, of which men and livestock eat, until when the earth takes on its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it a harvest as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus 10:24].
When Allah gave this man kingship and his reign lasted, he became arrogant, may Allah protect us, and became haughty, exalted himself, and denied the existence of the Most High, and said: there is no Lord. Because he had been given a kingship with no rival and it lasted a long time, he denied Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, just as Pharaoh after him denied Him, saying: there is no Lord. Abraham (peace be upon him) called him to belief in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and he said: Never, there is no Lord; where is the proof of your Lord?
﴿Abraham said: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾. This is undoubtedly, as we know from the context of the wording, an answer to a question, as if he had said: What is your Lord? Or who is He? Or what is His affair? Or what is His action? So he said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾, just as Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?* He said: The Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Shu'ara 26:23-24].
﴿argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾, that is: about His divinity and His existence; Abraham calls to the worship of Allah alone, without partner, and this one denies Allah outright.
So ﴿about his Lord﴾ means: about His existence. What else?
* The students: (...).
* The Shaykh: And His divinity; because Abraham was called to both matters.
As for His words ﴿that Allah had given him the kingship﴾: (that, *an*) here is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle that entered upon the present-tense verb, and when it enters upon the present-tense verb it does not put it in the subjunctive; it does not govern it, but it does not prevent it being converted into a verbal noun, and it is on the estimate of (lam), i.e. "because Allah gave him the kingship," meaning "for the giving of kingship by Allah to him." So it is in the accusative by omission of the preposition, and is the omission of the preposition here regular or transmitted?
* A student: Regular.
* The Shaykh: From where is this taken from the words of Ibn Malik? His saying?
* The student: His saying:
"Transmitted and with inna and an it is regular, ..........................."
* The Shaykh: Yes.
"...With inna and an it is regular, with safety from ambiguity, like 'I was amazed that they should...'"
So ﴿an ātāhu Allāhu al-mulk﴾ is in the accusative by omission of the preposition, and the preposition is the lam of causation; i.e. "because Allah gave him the kingship," meaning he disputed with Abraham about his Lord out of his tyranny, because Allah had given him kingship. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nay, indeed man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-Alaq 96:6-7]. When a person sees himself as self-sufficient, he may transgress and his obstinacy and stubbornness increase, may Allah protect us. For this reason, sometimes sicknesses are a blessing from Allah upon the servant, and poverty is a blessing, and calamities are a blessing; because when a person remains in blessing, in comfort and in ease, he may transgress and forget Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
This man to whom Allah gave kingship: look what this blessing produced in him. He denied Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and said: ﴿that Allah had given him the kingship﴾. Here, (al) apparently indicates the totality of perfection, not the totality of inclusion; because Allah did not give him the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, nor even the kingdom of the whole earth. By this we know that what is reported from some of the Successors, that four people ruled the earth: two believers and two disbelievers, there is room for scrutiny in this; and Allah did not give the whole earth to any one human being, but He gives some of it to some: ﴿And were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others, the earth would be corrupted﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:251]. As for one human being possessing the whole earth, this is impossible in the sunnah of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as far as we know.
He said: ﴿that Allah had given him the kingship﴾, but here (al) is for the totality of what?
* The students: Perfection.
* The Shaykh: Perfection, not inclusiveness; meaning a complete kingship that no one contests in his kingdom.
﴿When Abraham said: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾. ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾. What is the grammatical analysis of ﴿Rabbiya (my Lord)﴾?
* A student: Predicate.
* The Shaykh: No, subject (mubtada'). And ﴿alladhi (He who)﴾?
* A student: And ﴿alladhi﴾ is its predicate.
* The Shaykh: Its predicate. ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾, meaning: it is He who gives life and causes death.
As for His words ﴿Rabbi (my Lord)﴾: the meaning of Rabb has been explained many times before, that He is the Creator, the Owner, the One who disposes of affairs; this is the Lord, and these attributes are established in their perfection and totality only for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
As for His words ﴿yuhyi wa yumit (gives life and causes death)﴾: that is, He creates, brings into existence, annihilates and destroys. Whereas we see a human being who was nothing worth mentioning, suddenly he becomes something worth mentioning: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ [al-Insan 76:1]. So man before his existence was not a thing worth mentioning, then he comes into existence, then he remains on the earth as long as Allah wills, then he is annihilated and perishes.
*As though there had not been, between al-Ḥajūn and al-Ṣafā, / a companion, nor had a nighttime talker conversed in Mecca.*
That is, as if he had not found...
*While a man is seen therein, informing, / until he is seen as news among the news.*
So who is able to bring these existing things into being and then annihilate them?
* The students: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* The Shaykh: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. No one can give life; even your father, from whose water you were created, cannot bring you into existence, nor can your mother, by whose blood and milk you were nourished, bring you into existence. Rather, the One who gives life and causes death is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
Abraham said these words as if saying to him: He is the One who brings into existence and annihilates; then he gave an example, which is giving life and causing death, which no one can do. But this stubborn, arrogant man said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾. How?
He said it either as deception or as arrogance: either as deception, as most exegetes said, and they said: he brought two men, killed one of them and spared the other, and said: I caused the first to die and I gave life to the second. This is the well-known view of many exegetes; according to this, his saying ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ is what? Deception. In reality he neither gave life nor caused death here; because the life of the one he spared was already existing, and the death of the one he killed is not from him; rather he performed an act that was a cause for death, but death itself is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But he said that as deception. This is the well-known view of many exegetes.
Others said: rather he said it out of arrogance, meaning he knew that he neither gives life nor causes death, but he said it out of arrogance, meaning he said: if your god is able to do that, then I am able; and he did not bring an example; meaning he did not bring two men and kill one and spare the other, but he said it as a matter of arrogance.
Based on these two opinions, there follows the second transition: ﴿Abraham said﴾, and there is a reading here:
* The students: ﴿Ibraham﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Ibraham﴾. ﴿Abraham said: Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾. Look: this fa' shows that what follows is built upon what precedes it: ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾.
If we say that he first spoke as deception, and that he brought two men deserving of death, killed one and spared the other, then his saying ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east﴾ is a transition from the proof in which deception is possible to a clearer proof, namely that Allah brings the sun from the east, which is a great power; so if you are truthful that you are a lord, then bring it from the west. ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾. Accordingly, this is a transition from a hidden proof to a clearer proof. But if you reflect, you may find room for scrutiny here, from two aspects:
The first aspect: the first proof is clear, that Allah gives life and causes death, and that other than Him does not give life or cause death; it is clear. And the deception is simple.
The second aspect: moving from one argument to another before completing the debate is considered a failure; for Abraham could have said: your act is neither giving life nor causing death; so how did he move from the proof before completing it?
They say: perhaps he moved from the proof before completing it because the second is clear and undisputed, unlike the first, and there is no harm in a person moving from a proof in which argument is possible to a proof in which argument is absolutely not possible, for the sake of what? For the sake of ending the dispute. As for the view that it was arrogance, they said: when Abraham, peace be upon him, confronted that man and he claimed that he gives life and causes death, this is a claim that he owns everything and is able over everything; so it is as if he held him to what he had acknowledged and claimed. He held him to what? To what he had acknowledged and claimed; because his saying ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ implies that he is a lord. So he said: Yes, you now give life and cause death; but if you give life and cause death, then the One who gives life and causes death is able to bring the sun from the west, just as Allah, who gives life and causes death, made it come from? 
* The students: The east.
* The Shaykh: From the east. Then in this debate there is no transition; there is no transition in it, but there is the building of part of the proof upon part of it. And to this last view Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, went, and he refuted the first view and said: it is the method of the logicians, the Mantiqiyyin or the philosophers. As for what he, may Allah have mercy on him, established, he does not see a transition in the matter, but he sees the building of part of the proof upon part. As if Abraham said: I have granted to you that you give life and cause death; meaning, did I grant you this as a fact or as a debating assumption?
* The students: As a debating assumption.
* The Shaykh: As a debating assumption. Then bring the sun from the west, as the One who gives life and causes death, who is my Lord, brings it from the east.
He said: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾. ﴿Buhita﴾: he was bewildered and dumbfounded and did not find an answer; he was incapable.
He said: ﴿alladhi kafara (the one who disbelieved)﴾, an indication that this argument of his was an argument in falsehood; because those who disbelieve are the ones who argue with a false proof. Allah said about them: ﴿Their argument is void before their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is severe punishment﴾ [al-Shura 42:16].
So the one who disbelieved was confounded, bewildered and incapable. So did Abraham overcome him, or equal him?
* The students: He overcame him.
* The Shaykh: He overcame him; because an opponent's standing still in a debate is incapacity; as soon as he does not answer you, that is evidence of his incapacity and cessation.
If someone says: why did this wicked disbeliever not say: if your Lord brought it from the east, let Him bring it from the west Himself? You asked me to bring it from the west, so why does not your god bring it from the west?
Some said: Allah silenced him by a miracle of Abraham; otherwise he could have made such a claim. But in my view there is clear room for scrutiny in this, because what Abraham, peace be upon him, sought was a counterpart; the One who brought it from the east is able to bring it from the west, and there is no need for further argument in it or for repeating the proof. For this reason, and without doubt he was wicked and was either arrogant or deceptive, if he had thought, even one in a hundred or one in a million, that this was a proof for him, he would have said it. But he knew there was no proof in it, because he said that Abraham had argued with him, wanting to bring what corresponds to the act of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is bringing it from the west. This is even though it is possible that in his inner self he feared that if he said that, Abraham would supplicate his Lord and He would bring it from the west, just as the sun was held back for Yusha' ibn Nun: it was held back, did not move, and did not travel its usual course; and as it will rise from the west at the end of time. But in my view this may be said to be a hypothetical matter; meaning he feared that Abraham would supplicate his Lord and He would bring it from the west, which would be a greater disgrace and clearer for him. So the first possibility is more correct: that he could not say, "Let him bring it from the west," because the matter is in counterpart to what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did, and this cannot be turned back upon the one holding the proof.

**Shaykh:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. I seek refuge in Allah. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not guide the wrongdoing people. Why?

* **Students:** Because of their wrongdoing.
* **Shaykh:** Because of their wrongdoing. Attaching a ruling to a descriptive attribute is evidence of its causation (*ʿillah*, causal reason). The more wrongdoing a person commits, the further he is from guidance, whether he wrongs himself in what lies between him and his Lord or wrongs himself in what lies between him and the servants. Wrongdoing is darkness, and we seek refuge in Allah from it. So whenever a person does wrong, he is further from guidance, and whenever a person is guided, he is closer to guidance. ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

Here He says: ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. He did not say "the disbelieving people." What is the appropriate wording? It is appropriate because this kind of disbelief is a great wrongdoing, in that he claimed what was not his and denied what belonged to another. What did he claim that was not his, in his statement?

* **Students:** ﴿I give life and cause death﴾.
* **Shaykh:** ﴿I give life and cause death﴾. He denied what belongs to another, namely the sole right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to that. Allah the Exalted alone gives life and causes death. Thus the wrongdoing appears more clearly in this disbelief. Therefore He said: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. Every disbeliever is a wrongdoer. And is every wrongdoer a disbeliever?

* **Students:** Not every wrongdoer is a disbeliever.
* **Shaykh:** Not every wrongdoer is a disbeliever.

* **The benefits:**
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord...﴾ to the end.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the eloquence of the Noble Qur'an in presenting marvelous matters in the form of affirmation and interrogation. Affirmation (*taqrir*) compels the addressee to acknowledge, and interrogation arouses a person's attention. Here it combines interrogation and affirmation. Then, as we said, what is the primary purpose?

* **Student:** Affirmation and wonderment.
* **Shaykh:** Wonderment at this state.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: it clarifies how a person's condition can reach the level this tyrant reached, namely denying the truth to its rightful owner and claiming it for himself. How?

* **Students:** He said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾.
* **Shaykh:** He said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that argumentation to refute falsehood and establish truth is one of the stations of the messengers, as His saying shows: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord﴾.

* Among them: an indication that a person should learn the methods of debate (*munazarah*) and argumentation (*muhajjah*), because they are a ladder and a means. Many people have much knowledge but are defeated when it comes to argumentation; they are weak. And many people have no knowledge but, when it comes to argumentation?

* **Students:** Strong.
* **Shaykh:** Strong, because he trained himself. I recall that once I said to a man in a public gathering, a gathering of common people, when we were speaking about some people and I said that they say that ﴿Istawa ʿala al-ʿArsh﴾ means "He seized (*istawla*) the throne." This man, who was an utterly unlearned commoner who had never studied knowledge, said: "May Allah bring him to ruin! He seized it! Who had it before him? Look, Subhan Allah, by his natural disposition."

This is a clear argument without having learned debate. Therefore learning debate is truly obligatory for the student of knowledge. Many scholars present themselves in the station of argumentation, meaning that they assume they choose a certain view, for example, and that another person chooses the opposite view. Then they themselves say: "This is objected to with such-and-such, and it is answered with such-and-such; and this is objected to with such-and-such, and it is answered with such-and-such." This is very common in the words of Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him; he very often speaks this way, because this is extremely important in the realm of knowledge and defending the truth.

* **Student:** What are the means of debate?
* **Shaykh:** Among the means is training. There are also books written on this subject. But the most important thing is training. It is important that a person train himself in debate.
* **Student:** The method of teaching?
* **Shaykh:** Teaching. By Allah, I do not recall a specific book. There is a book called *Adab al-Bahth wa al-Munazarah* (The Etiquette of Inquiry and Debate), by an Egyptian whose name I have forgotten.
* **Student:** Contemporary or one of the later scholars?
* **Shaykh:** A recent one, among the later scholars, but I have forgotten his name. However, you do not need to know it. The most important thing is that you yourself train, present matters, and answer them. Shaykh al-Islam, for example: whoever studies his books learns debate. If you study the books of Shaykh al-Islam, even if you do not study them as a discipline, you will know how to debate.

* * *

(...) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord, because Allah had given him kingdom...﴾ to the end.

Let us take the benefits; read them to me so they are not repeated.

* **Student:** The benefits.
* **First benefit:** The eloquence of the Noble Qur'an in presenting marvelous matters in the form of affirmation and interrogation.
* **Shaykh:** * From the benefits of the noble verse: that some blessings may be a cause of tyranny, or that blessings may be a cause of tyranny, because this man did not transgress and deny the Creator except because Allah gave him kingdom.

* Also among its benefits: the correctness of attributing sovereignty (*mulkiyyah*) to other than Allah, as in His saying: ﴿that Allah had given him kingdom﴾. But from this it is learned that a person's dominion is not intrinsic dominion from himself, but is something bestowed upon him: ﴿that Allah had given him kingdom﴾. This verse is like His saying: ﴿You give kingdom to whom You will﴾ [Al ʿImran: 26].

* From the benefits of the verse: the virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said, proudly and with pride before this tyrant: ﴿My Lord﴾, attributing Lordship to himself, as if he were proud that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is his Lord. This is a noteworthy point: how excellent it is for a person to attribute the Lordship of Allah to himself and to say "I am a servant of my Lord." Here he said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of voluntary acts (*af'al ikhtiyariyyah*) for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿gives life and causes death﴾. Pay attention, because many scholars of kalam denied this and said: Allah is not characterized by voluntary acts. They justified this with feeble reasons, indeed dead reasons that have no basis, because they said: "Temporal events (*hawadith*) do not subsist except in a temporal thing. And if temporal events are a perfection, why were they not pre-existent? And if they are a deficiency, why would Allah be characterized by them?" Do you understand? Is the last point known?

* **Students:** (...).
* **Shaykh:** Yes. Regarding temporal events they said: if they are a perfection, why were they not pre-existent? That is, why was Allah not characterized by them before? And if they are a deficiency, why is He characterized by them? Therefore they must be impossible for Him, because they are a deficiency in every case: their absence is a deficiency and their presence is a deficiency. Thus He must be declared free of them, and they must be impossible for Him. Do you understand now?
* **Students:** Yes indeed.
* **Shaykh:** Good. We have answered both of these false arguments, or both of these false proofs. We said: your claim that temporal events do not subsist except in a temporal thing is an assertion, a mere assertion. Who said this? We know that temporal events occur from us, but they are not pre-existent by our pre-existence, are they?
* **Students:** Yes indeed.
* **Shaykh:** Temporal events occur from us and are not pre-existent by our pre-existence, and this is not considered a deficiency in us or in Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Temporal events occur after the one who brings them about, and there is no objection to that. It is possible that the one characterized by them is eternal while the events are temporal.

As for your statement: if they are a perfection, why were they not pre-existent, and if they are a deficiency, why is He characterized by them?

We say: they are a perfection at the time of their occurrence, because we say that the acts of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are not acts of mere will but acts accompanied by wisdom. If they are acts accompanied by wisdom, then in the state of their existence they are a perfection, and in the state of their non-existence they are a perfection. Then they do not necessarily imply deficiency absolutely. Do you understand, everyone?

* **Student:** An example.
* **Shaykh:** Like the istiwa' over the Throne. Istiwa' over the Throne is one of the attributes of action (*sifat fi'liyyah*). They say: if istiwa' is a perfection, why was it not eternal? And if it is a deficiency, why is He characterized by it?
* **Student:** (...).
* **Shaykh:** The response is: it is a perfection in the state of its occurrence. We do not say that He does it merely by will; rather, by a will accompanied by wisdom. If it is a perfection in the state of its occurrence and not a perfection in the state of its non-occurrence, then its occurrence is a perfection and its non-occurrence is a perfection.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that giving life and causing death are in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿gives life and causes death﴾. Therefore rely upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and do not fear, and do not imagine imaginary causes. For example: you are invited to a righteous deed, any deed, and you say: "I fear that if I do this deed I will die." We say: if this is merely an illusion, then this fear should not be made a basis for a ruling that prevents you from something in which lies your benefit and good.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that the disputing person may stubbornly claim something he knows with certainty he does not possess, as in the statement of the tyrannical man?

* **Students:** ﴿I give life and cause death﴾.
* **Shaykh:** ﴿I give life and cause death﴾. It is known that he said this only under the pressure of argumentation. A person under the pressure of argumentation, that is, of disputation and debate, may commit himself to things that, if he returned to himself, he would know are not correct. But in the heat of debate a person may claim a claim or deny things, knowing that his claim or his denial is not correct; yet the narrowness of the debate and dispute compels him to say this, whether affirming or denying.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the wisdom and excellence of Abraham, peace be upon him, in debate, whether we say that this is a transition from one proof to a clearer one, or that it is the derivation of one proof from another, in that he moved him to a matter he could never oppose. He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings up the sun from the east, so bring it up from the west﴾.

Within the noble verse there is a refutation of the astronomers (*ʿulamaʾ al-hayʾah*) who say that the sun's coming is not its coming in itself, but that the earth revolves until it comes upon the sun. Because Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings up the sun from the east﴾; therefore Allah brought it from the east. But they say: no, Allah did not bring it from the east; rather, we turned and came to it. We turned and the earth revolved with us, so we came to it. As for the sun, it is a king on his yacht or on his throne, not moving. You are the one who (...); the earth turns you around like this and then you come to it.

We, Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings up the sun from the east, so bring it up from the west﴾. He did not say: "Indeed, Allah turns the earth until the sun is seen from the east, so turn it until it is seen from the west." He did not say that. Rather He said: ﴿brings up the sun from the east﴾. I say this, and I say: we must in this matter take the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and not turn to anyone's words while the apparent meaning of the Qur'an exists, because we are obligated to act according to what the Qur'an indicates. This is one reason; another is that He who revealed the Qur'an knows best what He created. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk: 14]. If He repeatedly tells us in His speech that the sun rises, sets, moves away, inclines, and hides, attributing all these actions to the sun, why do we reverse this and attribute them to the earth?! We say: the sun that rises, the earth that rises.

On the Day of Resurrection Allah will say to us: ﴿And the day He will call them, and say: "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65]. He will not say: "What was your response to such-and-such engineer, or such-and-such astronomer?" Moreover, astronomers, ancient and modern, disagree on this; they have not agreed on anything. They have not agreed that the earth is what by its rotation produces night and day. Since the matter is subject to disagreement among the astronomers themselves, we say, as we say to the scholars of the Sharia when they disagree: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa: 59].

Indeed, we also say: even if the astronomers came all together, every one of them, complete and entire, we would not turn away from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an until a sensory matter becomes clear to us, which we perceive ourselves. We would say to our Lord when we meet Him: You said, and Your word is the truth: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and You said: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. We cannot do otherwise than say that Your saying: ﴿and you see the sun when it rises﴾ [al-Kahf: 17] means: when it rises in the view of the eye, not in the reality of the fact; because we know by our senses and sight that what causes the alternation of night and day is the rotation of the earth.

I say: if (...) is something sensed beyond any doubt, then it is permissible to turn the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from its apparent meaning to an interpretation, because a sensed matter that we cannot deny indicates that. But as for the case where the senses have not indicated this, and it is merely conjectures and theories, I am of the view that it is not permissible for anyone to depart from the apparent meaning of the speech of his Lord, who created and who revealed the Qur'an as an explanation of all things, and who said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa: 176]. I say: it is not permissible to depart from the apparent meaning of His speech merely because of the words of these people. If a person sees, by his certain sensation, something that justifies altering the words of Allah from their apparent meaning, then he has the right to say so.

He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings up the sun from the east, so bring it up from the west﴾. We say: and among the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of the sun?

* **Students:** (...) clear.
* **Shaykh:** A known fact?
* **Students:** (...) its naming (...).
* **Shaykh:** The affirmation that its name is the sun? Apparently it is not appropriate to take it as a benefit. Therefore some grammarians said that the saying of the speaker "the sky is above us and the earth is beneath us" is not, by convention, a proper statement.
* **Student:** Because it is not beneficial.
* **Shaykh:** Because it is not beneficial. Everyone knows this is the reality, do they not?

And it is like the saying of the poet:
*As if we, with the water around us, are a people sitting around whom is water.*
What is this?! This is nothing.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: that the truth cannot be disputed; as His saying when Abraham made this statement?

* **Student:** ﴿was confounded﴾.
* **Shaykh:** ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾.
* Also among its benefits: the affirmation that whoever denies Allah is a disbeliever. From where is this derived?
* **Students:** ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾.
* **Shaykh:** ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾. This is the point of using the explicit noun ﴿the one who disbelieved﴾ in place of a pronoun, so that we may say: everyone who argues as this man argued is a disbeliever.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: a refutation of the Qadariyyah (the sect who deny divine predestination).
* **Students:** ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.
* **Shaykh:** ﴿does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, because the Qadariyyah say: man is free; he guides himself and goes astray by himself, with no disposal of Allah over it. This verse clearly shows that guidance is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the warning against wrongdoing, as in His saying: ﴿does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

Among wrongdoing is that the truth becomes clear to you and you argue to defend your own position (we ask Allah for well-being). The truth becomes clear to you, and you argue to defend your view. This is wrongdoing, because justice is that you submit to the truth and do not stubbornly resist when it becomes clear. Therefore, (we ask Allah to grant us and you safety) those among the people of kalam who went astray did so because the truth became clear to them, but they argued and remained in the error they were in.

* Among them: that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, never withholds His bounty from anyone without that withheld thing being the cause.
* **Students:** ﴿does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.
* **Shaykh:** His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. So because of their wrongdoing, Allah does not guide them. This is like His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5].

* Among them: that whoever adopts justice is deserving of guidance. From the explicit statement or from the implicit implication?
* **Students:** From the implicit implication.

The Shaykh: This is from the argument of contrary implication (mafhum al-mukhalafa, the reasoning that what a statement does not state carries the opposite meaning). If Allah does not guide the wrongdoer, then the one who upholds justice is more deserving of being guided by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is indeed the case. The person who seeks the truth and follows it, and the truth is justice, is generally guided and granted success. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his creed, al-Wasitiyya, a phrase among the finest expressions: "Whoever reflects upon the Qur'an seeking guidance from it, the path of truth will become clear to him." This statement is derived from the Qur'an, from its verses both explicitly (manṭūq) and by implication (mafhūm).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 4):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or like one who passed by a town, while it lay in ruins upon its roofs﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:259]

Grammatical analysis (i'rab, the analysis of the grammatical case and function of words): ﴿أَوْ﴾ (aw, "or") is a conjunction. As for the kaf (ك) in ﴿كَالَّذِي﴾, it is said to be an extra particle for emphasis, and it is said to be a noun meaning "like" (مثل). On both views it is conjoined to ﴿الَّذِي﴾ (alladhi, "the one who") in His saying ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:258]. The meaning is: "or [have you considered] someone like the one who passed by." If we take the kaf to mean "like" (مثل), the implied sentence is: "or [have you considered] something like..." That is, "or have you not considered something like the one who passed by a town?" If we take the kaf as extra, the implied sentence is: "or [have you considered] the one who passed by a town," that is, "have you not considered the one who passed by a town," and so on.

The clause ﴿وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَى عُرُوشِهَا﴾ (wa-hiya khawiyatun 'ala 'urushiha, "while it lay in ruins upon its roofs") is in a place of accusative case as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿أَنَّى﴾ (anna) is an interrogative particle, and what is meant by it is astonishment or disbelief. It is also said that what is meant by it is urgency and hope.

His saying ﴿يُحْيِي هَذِهِ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا﴾ (yuhyi hadhihi Allahu ba'da mawtiha, "Will Allah bring this back to life after its death?") contains a fronting of the object before the subject, because ﴿هَذِهِ﴾ (hadhihi, "this") is a fronted object, and ﴿اللَّهُ﴾ (Allah) is a delayed subject.

His saying ﴿مِائَةَ عَامٍ﴾ (mi'ata 'amin, "a hundred years") is in place of an adverb of time (ẓarf), since it is annexed to what follows it, so it is in the accusative case as a substitute for an adverb of time. So what is the adverb of time then? Is it a word?

* A student: ﴿عَامٍ﴾ (‘āmin, "year").

* The Shaykh: The word ﴿عَامٍ﴾. It is connected to ﴿أَمَاتَهُ﴾ (amatahu, "caused him to die"). It is also said that it is connected to a verb that is omitted, whose estimated form is: "then He kept him alive for a hundred years." Why?

They say: because death is not postponed. Death is death. What is postponed is his remaining dead for a hundred years.

His saying ﴿كَمْ لَبِثْتَ﴾ (kam labithta, "How long have you remained?"), ﴿قَالَ بَلْ لَبِثْتُ﴾ (qala bal labithtu, "He said: 'I have remained'") and ﴿قَالَ بَلْ لَبِثْتَ﴾ (qala bal labith, "He said: 'Rather, you have remained'") differ in the vowel on the taa' depending on who is being addressed. As for His saying ﴿كَمْ لَبِثْتَ﴾, this is a fronted object of what? Of ﴿لَبِثْتَ﴾ (labithta, "you remained"). That is, how long of a period did you remain?

His saying ﴿فَانْظُرْ إِلَى طَعَامِكَ وَشَرَابِكَ لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾ (fa-nzur ila ta'amika wa-sharabika lam yatasannah, "Look at your food and your drink, they have not spoiled") has two readings: ﴿لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾ with the hā' (ه), and ﴿لَمْ يَتَسَنَّ﴾ when connected to what follows. The two readings differ only in the state of connected speech (waṣl), not in pause (waqf). In pause, it is always ﴿لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ﴾ with the hā'. In connected speech there is a reading of the seven readers that drops the hā': ﴿لَمْ يَتَسَنَّ وَانْظُرْ﴾.

His saying ﴿وَلِنَجْعَلَكَ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ﴾ (wa-li-naj'alaka ayatan lil-nas, "and that We may make you a sign for the people") – the waw is a conjunction, and the conjoined element is omitted, indicated by the context. Its estimated form is: "so that you may know the power of Allah, and that We may make you a sign for the people."

His saying ﴿فَلَمَّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ قَالَ أَعْلَمُ﴾ (falamma tabayyana lahu qala a'lamu, "When it became clear to him, he said: 'I know'") – in one reading it is ﴿قَالَ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ (qala i'lam anna Allaha 'ala kulli shay'in qadir, "He said: 'Know that Allah is over all things capable'"). The one who says it to him is Allah.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says in the context of what He has shown us of His signs that indicate His oneness and the perfection of His power: ﴿Or like one who passed by a town﴾. That is, "Or have you not seen like the one who passed by a town," meaning, "like the one who passed by a town while it lay in ruins upon its roofs." You now see that the one who passed by is unspecified, and the town is also unspecified. So who is this passer-by? And what is this town?

The exegetes have differed: What is the town? And who is the passer-by? This disagreement has no basis. That is, it is built on matters taken from the Children of Israel, whom we were commanded not to believe or disbelieve.

What is intended is not the specific identity of the passer-by or the town he passed by. What is intended is the lesson and admonition in this story. For if we do not know who passed by or what the town was, does that cause us to miss any of the admonition from it?

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: Not at all. For this reason, in many verses Allah mentions such stories, and people start asking: "Who is this? What is his name?" Just as they differed about the name of the dog of the People of the Cave and its color, and other such matters whose ignorance does not harm us, and knowing them is not obligatory.

His saying ﴿كَالَّذِي مَرَّ عَلَى قَرْيَةٍ﴾ (ka-alladhi marra 'ala qaryatin, "like one who passed by a town"): the word qarya (town) is derived from (al-qary), which means gathering. It is used for the people gathered in a city, and it is used for the city itself, according to context. For example, in His saying, ﴿They said: "We are going to destroy the people of this town"﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 29:31]. What is meant by it here?

* The students: (...), the town of the people of Lot, the people of Lot, (...).

* The Shaykh: O brothers! I do not mean in ﴿We are going to destroy the people of this town﴾, what is meant by "town"?

* The students: (...).

* The Shaykh: The dwellings, brother, because He said "people." If we say that "town" here means "people," it becomes "the people of this people," and that is not sound. ﴿The people of this town﴾ means the city, the people of this city. Is it clear?

* A student: It is not clear.

* The Shaykh: It is not clear. ﴿We are going to destroy the people of this town﴾, what is meant by "town"?

* The student: Our point is that we say (...), the intended meaning of the matter.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the city, you mean?

* The student: The city.

* The Shaykh: The city, and it does not mean its people, because He said: ﴿the people of this town﴾, He explicitly said "people." So "people" is annexed, and "town" is what?

* A student: Annexed to.

* The Shaykh: (...) after the entry of (...). Is it clear?

* A student: There is a contradiction, one might say...

* Another student: (...) confusion occurs (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) so the word (...), what is meant by it?

* The students: The dwellings.

* The Shaykh: This matter: the people are the inhabitants, but my speech now is about the town. Who?

* The students: The dwellings.

* The Shaykh: These dwellings. The proof is that He annexed "people" to it. He said ﴿the people of this town﴾, so it is impossible for "town" here to mean its people, it is not possible. Why? Because the meaning becomes corrupt. If you say ﴿the people of this town﴾ as "the people of these people"?

* A student: It is not sound.

* The Shaykh: It is not sound. ﴿So how many a town We destroyed while it was wrongdoing﴾ [Al-Hajj 22:45].

* The students: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is meant is its people. What is the proof?

* The students: "Wrongdoing" (...).

* The Shaykh: His saying ﴿We destroyed﴾ and His saying ﴿wrongdoing﴾: this is not something a city is described by. So it is now clear that "town" is sometimes meant as the city, which is the place where people gather, and sometimes meant as the gathered people, according to what?, according to context.

The sons of Jacob said to their father: ﴿Ask the town in which we were, and the caravan in which we came﴾ [Yusuf 12:82].

* The students: The people of the town.

* The Shaykh: How do you know?

* A student: Majaz (metaphor).

* Another student: "Ask."

* The Shaykh: Majaz. Leave this majaz, the majaz is not permissible. ﴿Ask the town﴾, what is meant?

* The students: The people of the town.

* The Shaykh: What is the proof?

* The students: ﴿Ask﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Ask﴾. Because a question cannot be directed to a town. And if "town" is applied to the people of the town by the explicit text of the Qur'an, ﴿So how many a town We destroyed while it was wrongdoing﴾, as you heard, then there is no need to say this is a majaz, and the original is: "Ask the people of the town." Because we have seen in the Noble Qur'an that "town" is meant as...?

* The students: The inhabitants.

* The Shaykh: The inhabitant. It means the inhabitants. And then we say in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or like one who passed by a town, while it lay in ruins upon its roofs﴾, the clause ﴿وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ﴾ (while it lay in ruins), we said what?

* A student: A circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

* The Shaykh: A circumstantial clause. ﴿Khawiyah﴾ means fallen, with some of it piled upon the rest. And the ʿurūsh (roofs) are the ceilings. How can a town be in ruins upon its ceilings? Someone may say: what comes to mind is that the ceilings are the upper parts.

It is said: the ceiling falls first, then the walls fall second. Is this clear or not?

* The students: It is clear.

* The Shaykh: It is clear. ﴿Khawiyah﴾, that is, collapsed and falling down upon what?

* The students: Its roofs.

* The Shaykh: What?

* The students: Its ceilings.

* The Shaykh: Its ceilings. So the ceiling falls, then the wall falls upon it. So ʿurūsh is the plural of ʿarsh, which is the ceiling. For this reason the Throne of the Most Merciful, may His majesty be exalted, is the ceiling of the creation (...) the ceiling.

﴿Ruined upon its roofs﴾. And where are its people?

* The students: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, they are dead. Its people are dead, or its people have left it. It is possible they have perished and are beneath the rubble, and it is possible they have departed from it.

This man, when he passed by this town, which was (and Allah knows best) a town flourishing with inhabitants and trade, passed by it briefly. He saw it in this state and said: how...

Having passed by briefly and seen it in this state, ﴿He said: "How will Allah bring this back to life after its death?"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:259]. ﴿How (anna)﴾ is an interrogative particle, and we said it is for astonishment. Some of them said it is for urgency and wishing, as if he were saying: "When will Allah bring this town back to life after its death, when it was yesterday a town flourishing with inhabitants, trade and other things? When will what it had before return to it?" Or the meaning is that he found it unlikely, according to his own conception, that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would restore to this town what it had before, and he said: "How will Allah bring this town back to life after its death?" He called it dead because it had previously been populated, populated with inhabitants. It will become clear to us later that life and death may be attributed to inanimate things, even though in principle they are not capable of life or death.

﴿He said: "How will Allah bring this back to life after its death?"﴾ But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, showed mercy to this man. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, may prepare and bring about for a person from among the cosmic matters that which increases his faith. Either He causes him to call upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and Allah answers his supplication, and he knows without doubt that this is an answer to a supplication. Or he sees other matters that are made easy and facilitated for him, and his faith increases thereby. Indeed, perhaps his faith increases when he sees his affairs become difficult for him and fall apart. How?

He realizes that he has been heedless of the remembrance of his Lord. When he sees his affairs being undone, and he repairs something but there is no point in repairing it, he toils over it and then the benefit lies in not doing so. Thus he knows that Allah has made his heart heedless of His remembrance, because Allah says: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who followed his desire and whose affair was ever in neglect﴾ [Al-Kahf 18:28]. So when you realize that your affairs are wasteful, that you gain nothing, that you adorn something and then demolish it, know that there is heedlessness in your heart regarding the remembrance of Allah. And this increases a person's faith.

The point is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestowed this honor upon this man. Allah may cause miracles (karamat) to occur at the hands of His friends, either to strengthen their faith, or to establish the truth, meaning to make firm this person, or to establish a truth that people need to have established, which is general. For example, what happened to Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may God be pleased with him, after he died. He saw a companion of his in a dream, who said: a man passed by me, took my armor, and placed it under a cooking pot at the edge of the people's camp, and there was a horse neighing beside it. When morning came, the man (this was at the Battle of Yamama) went to Khalid ibn al-Walid and informed him of what he had seen. Khalid said: "Go, go to the place he described to you." He went to the place and found the matter as Thabit had described. This is a kind of miracle, with no doubt that Allah preserved Thabit's property after his death.

It may also occur out of necessity, because of the Muslims' need for such a miracle, like what happened to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may God be pleased with him, when he was conquering the lands of Persia, one city after another, until he reached the Tigris River. When he reached the Tigris, he found that the Persians had broken the boats and the bridges, they had sunk the boats and destroyed the bridges, and he could not cross. It is said that he called out to Salman al-Farisi, may God be pleased with him, and said to him: "Give us some of your cunning," because Salman al-Farisi was the one who advised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the Trench. He said: "By Allah, I have nothing. What can I say? It's a sea, a river flowing. I have nothing. But let me look at the army to see whether they are upright and on the truth, for Allah will surely grant victory to this community, and this community is not inferior to the Children of Israel, for whom Allah split the sea. But let me be, give me time." Salman went to inspect the army, and what did he find? What? They were monks by night and knights by day. At night, they were standing in prayer, humble, weeping, and by day, their only concern was to attend to the affairs of war and jihad. He returned to him and said: "By Allah, I saw the people in the best condition, but rely upon Allah." Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may God be pleased with him, thought, and decided to cross the river. He ordered the army to prepare, and said: "I will stand at the river and say the takbir three times. When I say the third takbir, cross in the name of Allah." When he said the takbir three times, they crossed the river. They crossed the river, which was flowing, a river and not a sea, flowing as it does. The horsemen, camels and men crossed on foot, and not one of them drowned. It is even reported that when a horse became tired, Allah made a mound appear for it, and it stood upon it to rest, because Allah is capable of all things. They crossed the river.

When they crossed the river, and the Persians saw them, they said: "By Allah, you are not fighting men, but jinn, and you have no strength against them. Come on, flee!" So they fled. Then the Islamic armies entered the Persian capital, Ctesiphon (al-Mada'in), and came upon the crown of Khosrow, the crown which, when he sat, was raised above his head. It was enormous, and they could not carry it except on two camels until they brought it to the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him. From where? From beyond the river to Medina. They said: they carried it on two camels, two camels tied together, and they lifted it, because there were no cars there and no ships, until it was placed before the Commander of the Faithful 'Umar, may God be pleased with him. This man, who wore nothing but a patched garment and rested on nothing but sand in the mosque or pebbles, the crown of Khosrow is placed before him? Look at the might belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers. It is not by the multitude of armies nor their strength, but by the permission of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And might belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, but the hypocrites do not know﴾ [Al-Munafiqun 63:8]. When 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, saw this crown, with its pearls and jewels set in it, not one of them was missing. He said: "By Allah, a people who could return this are trustworthy!" Allahu akbar! But we say: they became trustworthy because you were trustworthy. When you were trustworthy, they became trustworthy, and when you were just, they became just. The point is that what happened to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may God be pleased with him, is a miracle. What does he intend by it?

* The students: Strengthening the Muslims.

* The Shaykh: Yes, the Muslims' need for it, meeting their need. Because they had no boats or bridges, so they needed this. Something similar happened to al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami, may God be pleased with him, when he invaded Bahrain. So this miracle occurred for this man who said: ﴿How will Allah bring this back to life after its death?﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:259]. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, caused him to die for a hundred years. He caused him to die a real death, not sleep, a real death, and then resurrected him.

His saying ﴿a hundred years﴾: it was mentioned a little while ago that some scholars say that "a hundred years" is not connected to ﴿amatahu﴾ (He caused him to die), because death is a state that comes upon a person and does not extend over time. What extended is the remaining (al-ibqā'), which Allah caused.

In any case, the meaning is clear, whether we say it is connected to an implied verb or that it is connected to ﴿amatahu﴾: ﴿Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾. "A hundred years": in my view, there is an alif (ا) between the mīm and the hamza, and the mīm is kasrah, and the alif has a small circle over it. The small circle over it indicates that this alif is written but not pronounced. By this we know the error of those who lost their walk and the walk of the dove, the crow. They say that he wanted to imitate the dove's walk. One day he tried to imitate the dove and could not do it, so he went back to his original walk, having lost it. Neither this nor that. Some people now say: how do they pronounce "mi'a" (a hundred)?

* The students: "Mā'a."

* The Shaykh: "Mi'a," glory be to Allah! The mīm is kasrah, and you say "mā'a"? What language is this? It is not the Arabic language. "Mi'a 'ām," and whoever says "mā'a" in the Qur'an has committed a grammatical error and must correct it.

As for some scholars and some contemporary writers, they said: since the matter has become confusing, let us write "mi'a" like "fi'a" (group), meaning mīm, hamza and tā' marbūṭa, "mi'a 'ām." This is correct, because as long as we let people make mistakes just to avoid writing the alif!

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 2 of 4):

And His saying: ﴿a hundred years﴾. The word ʿāmin (year): is it derived? Some said it is derived from al-ʿawm (swimming), because the sun "swims" through it across the four seasons. Some of them said this, and it is clear on this view: the year necessarily involves the sun moving through the four seasons, which are spring, summer, autumn and winter. Each of these seasons contains three of the constellations (burūj) mentioned in the verse:

*Ḥamal, then Thawr, then Jawzāʾ, then Sarṭān, then Asad, then Sunbula, then Mīzān, then ʿAqrab, then Qaws, then Jadi, then Dalw, and the last of them is the Ḥūtān.*

These are twelve constellations for the four seasons, and each season has three.

It was also said that the word ʿāmin is not derived, and that it is like the words bāb (door) and sāj (a type of tree) and similar words that have no derivation. It is like sana (year), meaning it has no derivation. Whichever is the case, the meaning is known: ﴿a hundred years, then He raised him﴾, that is, He caused him to die for a hundred years and then raised him. You might say that one would expect "then He revived him" to match "caused him to die," but al-baʿth (raising) is more eloquent, because baʿth carries the idea of rapid and forceful movement. This is why we say "the dust was raised (infabaʿatha) by the wind" and similar expressions that indicate a thing arrives swiftly and with force. So this man was raised by Allah with a single word: He said "Be," and he was alive, so he was alive.

﴿Then He raised him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ [al-Baqara 2:259]

As for His saying ﴿He said﴾, there is no doubt that there is a hidden pronoun referring to Allah, because He said: He caused him to die, then raised him, and He said, "How long have you remained?" So who is the speaker: is it Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or is it an angel among His angels?

The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that the speaker is Allah. There is no obstacle to Allah speaking this way, making him hear His speech without seeing Him, just as He made Mūsā (Moses) hear His speech without seeing Him, and just as He made Muḥammad (ﷺ) hear His speech during the Miʿrāj (the Night Ascent) without seeing Him. As for the one who says that "He said" means that Allah said it through an angel, there is no doubt that this is a departure from the apparent meaning, and it is acceptable only if there is a text from an infallible source (maʿṣūm) to that effect. Otherwise, it is obligatory to keep it on its apparent meaning. Because if we said, "The angel said to him," our Lord would say to us on the Day of Resurrection, "Who told you that the angel said it to him?"

The Qur'an says ﴿Allah caused him to die﴾: the doer is Allah. ﴿Then He raised him﴾: who? 
* Student: Allah.
* Shaykh: Allah. ﴿He said﴾?
* Student: Allah.
* Shaykh: Yes, Allah. How can we say "an angel"?! So it is obligatory to keep the text on its apparent meaning until there is evidence that requires departing from it.

﴿He said, "How long have you remained?"﴾ That is: how long have you remained, in terms of the duration? And the duration was a hundred years. ﴿He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ How is it "a day or part of a day"? Is it that one of these is certain and the other not, or is it a case of two possibilities (tanwīʿ)?
* Students: It is uncertainty.
* Shaykh: It is uncertainty. The scholars said: he only said that because Allah caused him to die at the beginning of the day and revived him at the end of the day. So he said, "I have remained a day," if this was the second day since his death, or "part of a day," if this was the first day.
