Allah said to him: ﴿Nay﴾. Is this bal (nay) for idrāb (a rhetorical retraction), meaning cancelling what came before, or for intiqāl (transition to a new matter)?
* Students: For cancelling.
* Shaykh: For cancelling. That is: nay, you did not remain a day or part of a day. ﴿Nay, you have remained a hundred years.﴾ Allahu Akbar, a hundred years! He did not know how long that period had passed. It was not short. But we can give an example of a sleeper. When a person stays up on winter nights, how long does the night seem to him?
* Student: Very long.
* Shaykh: Very long. He says, "How long the night is!" But if someone sleeps from the time he prays ʿIshāʾ and does not wake up until the call to Fajr, it seems like nothing; it is like a single glance, especially if Allah, glory be to Him, has protected him from the satanic or psychological dreams that his soul would produce. So by the will of Allah the night passes for him in an instant.

The point is that this shows that the separation of the soul from the body makes the time seem short. Allah the Exalted said to him: ﴿Look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled﴾. Allahu Akbar! Look at the food and drink: food and drink that remained a hundred years, with the night and day, the winds and rains, the heat and cold passing over them, and yet they did not change. Is this according to the usual custom?
* Student: It is contrary to the usual custom.
* Shaykh: It is not according to the usual custom. When does food normally change?
* Students: On the second or third day.
* Shaykh: It is possible on the second or third day, depending on the weather. But a hundred years and it did not change. It was said that what he had was figs and date wine, or grapes, but we do not care about that. What matters is that he had food and drink, and they remained all these hundred years without changing.

﴿lam yatasannah﴾: is it from al-sana (year) or from al-sanan (change)?

Some said: ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ means "it did not change," because sanan means change, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿black mud altered (masnūn)﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:26], meaning changed. But the nūn was replaced by an alif, because in ﴿lam yatasannah﴾ there is undoubtedly a deleted alif, and the original form was lam yatasannā. The alif was deleted, and then the nūn was replaced with an alif, just as the ṭāʾ is replaced by an alif when it repeats with its counterpart, as in His saying: ﴿then he went to his family, strutting (yatamaṭṭā)﴾ [al-Qiyāma 75:33], meaning yatamaṭṭaṭ. This is its origin. This is an explanation or a morphological analysis of yatasannah, is it not? And what did we say?
* The student: Sanan.
* Shaykh: The one before it. ﴿lam yatasannah﴾.

He said: ﴿And look at your donkey﴾. He looked at his donkey and found that the donkey was bones showing, with no flesh or sinew, scattered bones on the ground. Is there not in this a greatest lesson: that the donkey died, and its flesh, sinews and skin went away, while the food, which was about to change within a day and a night, did not change?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: In this is a great sign of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He is able to preserve what changes so that it does not change, as with the food and drink, in contrast to what is customarily more durable than food and drink, which changed.

He said: ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. The waw here is a conjunctive particle, as we said just now, and the element it conjoins is omitted. The implied meaning is: "so that you may know Our power, and that We may make you a sign for the people." He looked at the donkey.

He says: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾ [al-Baqara 2:259].
* Students: ﴿nunshizuhā﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿nunshizuhā﴾, yes. There is a reading ﴿nunshiruhā﴾, yes. ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾, or ﴿nunshizuhā﴾. Nunshizuhā means We assemble some of them upon others, from al-nashaz, which is elevation, as in His saying: ﴿And if a woman fears ill-treatment (nushūz) or aversion from her husband﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:128]. So ﴿nunshizuhā﴾ means We raise some of them above others. He looked at the bones; the bone came and was fitted onto the second bone in its place, until the donkey became bones, each bone fitted in its place upon the others. Then after that Allah clothed them with flesh. Allah clothed these bones with flesh after some of them had been fitted to others in the sinews, and then He clothed them with flesh. As for the reading ﴿nunshiruhā﴾, it was said its meaning is: We give them life, because the bones had dried and become like crumbled dust, with no substance of life in them. Then they were revived so that they became able to have some of them fitted onto others. As for the view of some that there is a reordering in the verse, because the bringing to life occurs after the covering with flesh, we say: no, the bringing to life of each thing is according to its nature. So Allah gave life to the bones until they became, what? Able to have some fitted to others, so that they would be prepared for the life of the whole donkey. Allah did not say "We raise (nunshir) the donkey," so that it could be said that the raising of the donkey is resurrection.

He said: ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾. So he witnessed this with his own eyes. Thus there gathered before him two signs of Allah: the preservation of what changes, and the revival of what was dead, whose parts had scattered, leaving only lifeless bones with no life in them. He says: ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾.
* Student: O Shaykh (...)
* Shaykh: Look, brother, the strength of reliance on Allah and good opinion of Him led them to do this. They had good opinion of Allah. They said: the One who gave victory to the Children of Israel is able to give victory to this Ummah. Rather, this Ummah is more entitled to victory. So they had trust in Allah and knowledge that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said in the ḥadīth qudsī: "I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me." [Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhārī, no. 7405, from Abū Hurayra, and the wording is his; and by Muslim, no. 2675, from Abū Hurayra.]
* Student: He says: is it okay to deny what some Sufis claim about waiting for the fire?
* Shaykh: No, no, may Allah bless you. The Sufis, they lost a condition of their claim, which is: they say that the karāmāt (miraculous gifts) of what?
* Student: The awliyāʾ (saints).
* Shaykh: The awliyāʾ. And they are not awliyāʾ of the Merciful. The awliyāʾ of the Merciful are those who follow the Sunna of the Messenger, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him.
* Student: People who follow the Sunna of the Messenger (ﷺ).
* Shaykh: Such a matter may have occurred; perhaps they exaggerate, perhaps. But in my opinion this is now impossible, because the Messenger said: "The best of people are my generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them." [Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhārī, no. 2652, and Muslim, no. 2533/212, both from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.] This excellence does not come to anyone other than them, does not come to anyone other than them.
* Student: An example: the Qur'an addresses a human, as when We said, "O Nūḥ," and also: ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me"﴾ [Ṣād 38:35], he spoke directly. So is there here a special selection?
* Shaykh: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾ [al-Baqara 2:253], of the Messengers in general. But those who were addressed with the message through direct speech: apparently it was Mūsā, peace be upon him. Even Muḥammad, peace be upon him, was not addressed with the message through direct speech; the angel came to him.
* Student: Was he not addressed in the heavens?
* Shaykh: Yes, but the angel came to him. However, as far as we know, no one was addressed with the message in direct speech except Mūsā.
* Student: When Allah addressed the Messenger (ﷺ) in the heavens regarding the prayer, did it become (...) something, then?
* Shaykh: Yes, but that was not the beginning of the revelation. All the Messengers were spoken to, all of them were spoken to. But the beginning of revelation, the beginning of the message: we know of no one who was addressed with the message in direct speech except Mūsā. There were more karāmāt among the Tābiʿūn than among the Companions. It is explained that among the Companions these karāmāt came as signs of the Messenger, peace be upon him, because they came through the hand of the Prophet, peace be upon him, so they were a sign for him. Moreover, every karāmah granted to a people is a sign of their prophet, because its purpose is that what this man was upon is true. So if he followed the Messenger, that karāmah was a testimony, because the Messenger whom this man followed was followed upon the truth.
* Student: Shaykh, it may come (...)
* Shaykh: That is why we say: every karāmah of a walī is a miracle (muʿjizah) of that prophet whom he followed. This is a principle.
* Student: Is the speech of Shaykh al-Islām correct, or is it rejected?
* Shaykh: No, there is nothing wrong with that statement. Whoever reflects on this finds that it is more common outside the Companions. Among the Companions too they did not become numerous except after the death of the Messenger (ﷺ). (...) They exist, but they are not apparent. They exist.
* Student: Only now these stories have multiplied among the Ikhwān, the mention of these stories; much more than about the Tābiʿūn and...?
* Shaykh: By Allah, nothing of the sort. Every report needs authentication. Each person says he will bring an isnād (chain of transmission). Have you not heard of the man who came to the mosque of al-Rusāfa in Baghdad and stood up to narrate a ḥadīth that whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ will have Allah give him, for each letter, so-and-so many tongues, and for each tongue so-and-so many languages, and many angels will glorify Allah for him by night and day? And the chain said: "Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn narrated to me from so-and-so, from so-and-so, from so-and-so." And the people, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn are reliable transmitters for them. When the people dispersed, Imam Aḥmad called him and said: "Come here. Who narrated this to you?" He said: "Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn." He said: "I am Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and this is Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn, we did not narrate this to you." He said: "By Allah, I thought you were a sensible man, O Aḥmad! Is there anyone in the world named Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal other than you? I have narrated from seventeen men named Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal!" He put his hand over his face and went off laughing at him!
* Student: After that?
* Shaykh:
*"Indeed, the one who was a master, then his father was a master, then after that his grandfather was a master."*
It is known that the father is above the son who is a master, and the grandfather is above the father.
* Student: Before and after?
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: "Then he was a master after that."
* Shaykh: "After that" means what? It is an order of mention too, that is, from what follows that.
* Student: "After"? Does it not prevent the order of the grandfather?
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: Does it not prevent the order of the grandfather?
* Shaykh: Which of them?
* Student: "After"?
* Shaykh: No, not at all, it does not prevent it, because his grandfather was not a master after him. His grandfather must have been a master before him.
* Student: Shaykh.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And from it (...) our children.
* Shaykh: No, this contains only inversion (taqdīm wa taʾkhīr).
* Student: ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾.
* Shaykh: The phrase ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾, that is, it became clear to this man who passed by the village and considered it unlikely that Allah would revive it after its death, or he was impatient and considered it slow that Allah would revive it after its death, and what happened of Allah's signs with regard to him, his donkey and his food occurred. ﴿It became clear to him﴾: the matter by which the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, was established became clear to him. ﴿He said, "I know that Allah is over all things capable."﴾ In another reading: ﴿Know (iʿlam) that Allah is over all things capable.﴾ The benefit of the two readings is that it is as if he was commanded to know, so he knew and acknowledged, and said: "I know." So there is a benefit in both readings: he was commanded to know with a knowledge from which he would benefit, so he said: ﴿I know that Allah is over all things capable.﴾

As for His saying ﴿I know﴾: we have mentioned many times that knowledge (ʿilm) is the perception of a thing as it actually is, a firm perception that corresponds to reality. The phrase "as it actually is" means that: the perception of a thing as it actually is, firm perception. So the absence of perception is?
* Students: Ignorance.
* Shaykh: Ignorance. And what type of ignorance is this?
* Students: Simple (basīṭ).
* Shaykh: Simple ignorance. And perceiving it other than as it actually is?
* Students: Compound (murakkab).
* Shaykh: Compound ignorance. And absence of firmness: doubt (shakk), or conjecture (ẓann), or illusion (wahm). Absence of firmness is doubt, or conjecture, or illusion. If the two possibilities are equal, it is doubt; if one of them is more likely, the more likely is conjecture and the less likely is illusion. A person's standing in this matter requires knowledge; that is, he must know that Allah is over all things capable. His saying ﴿that Allah is over all things capable﴾: "thing," "all things": Allah is capable of it. Power (qudra) is an attribute by which one is able to act without incapacity. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿Nothing in the heavens or the earth can ever overcome Him. Indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾ [Fāṭir 35:44]. Notice that when He negated that anything could overcome Him, He said: what? ﴿Indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾. So if someone asks, "Define power (qudra)?" I say: an attribute by which one is able to act without incapacity.
"Define strength (quwwa)?" An attribute by which one is able to act without weakness, because Allah set weakness opposite to strength, saying: ﴿Allah is He who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength﴾ [al-Rūm 30:54]. He did not say "after weakness, power," but said "strength." So what is the difference between them? Which is more complete?
* Students: Power.
* Shaykh: Power is more complete?
* Students: Yes, more comprehensive.
* Shaykh: No.
* Students: Strength is more complete.
* Shaykh: Strength is more complete, is that correct or not?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: So strength is more complete. This is made clear by an example: here before me is a large stone, and I say: "Lift it." You lift it, but you lift it while grunting, and what does "grunting" mean? It means "Yā Allah, yā Allah, ih ih ih!" "Help me lift it, help me lift it!" But you lifted it, you raised it. What is this?
* Students: Weakness; this is power.

* Shaykh: This is power (qudrah), not strength (quwwah), right? It is power because when you cannot lift something, you have carried it. It is not strength because you became weak, meaning after "the first and the second" attempts. Suppose another man, and you say to him: "Lift this stone." He says, "This stone?" You say, "Yes." He says, "In the name of God," and he lifts it as if it were a feather. What is this?
* Students: Strength.
* Shaykh: Strength. So which of the two is more complete?
* Students: Strength.
* Shaykh: Strength is more complete, but strength is broader in one respect, since it is attributed both to one who has a will and to one who has no will. It is attributed to one who has a will and to one who has no will. You say: "The man is strong" and "the iron is strong," right?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Power (qudrah), however, is attributed only to one who has a will. You say: "The man is able (qadir)," and you do not say: "The iron is able." Do you now understand the difference?
* A student: This is another aspect.
* Shaykh: Yes, this is another aspect. So ﴿I know that God has power over all things﴾ means: possessor of power, which is an attribute by which one is enabled to act without incapacity. And here He said ﴿over all things﴾. "All things" is inclusive, isn't it?
* Students: Inclusive.
* Shaykh: It is inclusive and general. Some of them said: "The intellect has excluded His essence, so He is not able over Himself." That is, the meaning is that this generality has been affected by rational specification (takhsis 'aqli), namely the Essence of God. In other words, He is able over everything except His own essence, so He is not able over it. They claim that the intellect is what specified this. The author of Tafsir al-Jalalayn, may God have mercy on him, said this regarding the verse of God, Exalted, in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ma'idah 120]. He said: "The intellect excluded His essence, so He is not able over it." This statement is a great error, even if the intention of its speaker is correct. But it is an error in expression, because denying power over something while the generality is affirmed in God's saying ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾ [al-Baqarah 284] is an error and an objection against God, Mighty and Majestic. The intellect does not specify what God has said. If by his saying "the intellect excluded His essence, so He is not able over it" he meant that He cannot act, as some of the Ash'arites and others said, that the attachment of voluntary acts to God is impossible, saying: God, Mighty and Majestic, does not act by His will, because a voluntary act requires occurrence (huduth), and what is originated subsists only in what is originated, according to their claim. If he means by this that God cannot do anything in His own self, then this is true, right? But this is wrong, this is false. Because saying that God is able to do what He wills by a voluntary act, that He istawa over the Throne, descends to the lowest heaven, speaks to whom He wills, comes on the Day of Resurrection to judge between the servants, and similar things, is true. And if by his saying "the intellect excluded His essence, so He is not able over it" he meant that He cannot annihilate Himself, or cannot create His like, or cannot cause His hand to cease to exist, even though He does not have a hand in the sense of creation, but we say by way of illustration: if he meant that, then his meaning is correct and his wording is wrong. His meaning is correct but his wording is wrong. The meaning of our saying "his meaning is correct" is that God, Mighty and Majestic, does not annihilate Himself, and does not destroy any of His attributes. But we do not say that this is because He is unable to do it; rather we say that this is an impossible thing. It is impossible that God should perish, impossible that God, Exalted, should destroy any of His attributes. This is an impossible thing. Power relates only to what is possible. As for the impossible, its true description is that it is "not a thing" (la shay'). Note that the true description of the impossible is that it is not a thing, because it is impossible. If it is impossible, then its conception is impossible and its existence is impossible. So it is nothing. Therefore whoever says, "God is able to create His like, but He does not will it," errs with a gross, heavy, great error. I seek refuge in God. If the person saying this were not ignorant, he would be an unbeliever by this statement, because this matter is impossible, and the created cannot be like the Creator in any way at all. Even if the only distinction between them were that the first is eternal (azali) and this is originated, then similarity can never exist at all. We do not say: "He is able to create a likeness but He does not want to," just as He is able to do injustice but does not want to, because God said: ﴿And God does not want injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir 31], and He said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [ash-Shura 11]. He did not say: "He does not want anything like Him." He said ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. And there is a difference between one expression and another expression.
The point is that we say: Exalted is God, the power does not relate to such impossible matters, because the impossible is not a thing, not a thing that could be supposed to exist. If the mind supposes it, where is it in external reality? It does not exist. It is said that Satan, the sultan of the devils, the greatest of them, once said to his soldiers: "Why do you rejoice at the death of a scholar and not rejoice at the death of a worshipper, although the worshipper may be more devoted in worship than the scholar?" He said: "Because the worshipper has no effect; his worship benefits only himself. But the scholar benefits, benefits the people, and defends the religion of God." And if you wish, I will give you an example. They said: "Fine." He said: "I will send to the worshipper first, we begin with the worshipper. I send a devil to the worshipper, and he says to the worshipper: 'Can your Lord create its like?' He says: 'Yes, He can, for God is over all things competent.'" The worshipper rejoiced at this answer. So the soldier returned to his master and said: "He said such-and-such." He said: "He has disbelieved, he has disbelieved by that, because now he has denied the saying of God, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, and he believed that God, Mighty and Majestic, is originated, meaning created, because only what is created resembles what is created."
He said: "We send him a second time." He sent to him a second time and said to him: "Can God make the heavens and the earth into an egg?" An egg of a hen, the heavens and the earth all of them. The worshipper said: "What is this?" No, He cannot; He cannot make them into an egg. He said: "This is another calamity." Then he sent to the scholar and said to him: "Can God create its like?" He said: "This is an impossible thing. ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾." He said: "He was saved, wasn't he?"
* Students: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: He said: "Can God make the heavens and the earth into an egg?" He said: "Yes, ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82]." Of course, if God, Mighty and Majestic, wills something, He makes this egg large and the heavens and the earth small, and enters them into it. And God is over all things competent.
The point is that we say: this generality admits no exception whatsoever. As for the intellect which whoever claimed it said specifies this generality, we say that this is not even included in the first place, let alone being excluded by specification. If someone says: "We often hear people say: 'He is competent over whatever He wills' (...)," this implies restriction, as if He is able over a thing only if He wills it, and what He does not will He is not able over. For this reason some scholars said that this expression suggests the view of the Qadariyyah (a sect that denied God's predetermination of human acts). And what is the view of the Qadariyyah? Do you know the view of the Qadariyyah? They say: the acts of servants are not within God's power, and a person performs an act independently, and God is not able to prevent him or to urge him. If He is not able over the servant's act, it follows that He does not will it. Because if we say "He is competent only over whatever He wills," and the will of God does not relate to the act of the servant, then He is not able over it. If you say: "It has been transmitted from the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the story of the man whom God addressed, and he is one of the people of Paradise, that God said to him: 'Indeed I am able over what I will'" [Recorded by Muslim, no. 187/310, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud]. The answer is that this statement was made by God, Mighty and Majestic, after the act had been done. It is as if He said: "This act happened by My will, and I am able over it." This is not like the unrestricted absolute attribute as in the saying of many people: "He is competent over whatever He wills." For this reason, when you want to conclude a supplication, do not say "He is competent over whatever He wills." Say: "He is over all things competent," as He said: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites... The Prophet and those who believed with him, their light running before them and on their right hands, they say: "Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed You are over all things competent"﴾ [at-Tahrim 8]. They did not say, "Indeed You are competent over whatever You will." And it is not for us to depart from the expression God chose for Himself as a description, nor from the expression chosen by the Prophet, peace be upon him, and those with him as a means, because their saying ﴿Indeed You are over all things competent﴾ is a means of seeking nearness to God, Mighty and Majestic, by His power, that He complete their light on the Day of Resurrection. And they chose the means of power because the hypocrites' light will be extinguished on the Day of Resurrection and the disbelievers have no light, so they chose the attribute of power, by which the difference between the state of the believers and the state of the disbelievers is achieved.
* A student: And the answer regarding the verse?
* Shaykh: Which verse?
* A student: "He is competent over whatever He wills"?
* Shaykh: There is no verse with this wording. It is a hadith.
* A student: Yes, roughly it exists.
* Shaykh: No, it does not. ﴿So when it became clear to him, he said: "I know that God is over all things competent."﴾
God, Exalted, said: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town while it was fallen upon its roofs﴾ and so on to the end.
In this there is the eloquence of the Qur'an, in that it varies the proofs and evidences for great matters, because the three verses before it and after it are all in the context of God's power over the revival of the dead. For Abraham, in the first verse, what did he say? ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. In this is the eloquence of the Qur'an, in that it repeats what? The meanings, as much as repetition is needed in important matters.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: an indication that a person should not be preoccupied with the identities of the people of the story, for if this were an important matter, God would have explained it, saying "so-and-so," and would have specified the town.
Also among the benefits of the verse: that consideration (i'tibar) is given to meanings and purposes rather than to individuals.
* And among its benefits also: the application of the word "qaryah" (town) to what?
* Students: To dwellings.
* Shaykh: To dwellings, because of His saying ﴿while it was fallen upon its roofs﴾. Although there is a possibility that in this verse it means the dwellings and their inhabitants, because its being fallen upon its roofs indicates that its people are also lost and perished.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the limitation of human vision, and that a person looks at matters by the standard of what is visible and observed before him. This is shown by the saying of this man: ﴿He said: "How will God revive this after its death?"﴾. So the fact that you find things changed does not mean you should deem it unlikely that God, Mighty and Majestic, removes this change. How many things people estimated would never cease, and then they ceased! How many people hoped for lasting wealth, lasting security, and lasting happiness, and then the opposite followed! And how many people were in hardship of life, fear, worries and sorrows, and then God, Exalted, replaced them with something else new.
* A student: (...)?
* Shaykh: One does not judge a thing as always so. A person considers something unlikely. It does not mean that he thinks God is unable; rather, he considers it unlikely according to his view that this town would return to what it was before.
* A student: Is it not proper for a person to say this statement?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. He says: "It is far-fetched that God, Exalted and Majestic, would do such-and-such." The Messenger said: "How could that be answered for that?" [Recorded by Muslim, no. 1015/65, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. He considered it unlikely that God would answer this man whom he described.
Yes, read the verse: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed within them of living creatures, and He is, when He wills, over their assembly competent﴾ [ash-Shura 29].
﴿when He wills﴾ is connected to "assembly"; that is, "and He is, over their assembly, when He wills, competent." It is a parallel to the hadith we pointed out: the power is attached to a specific thing. It is said, for example: "If God wills it, it comes to be and occurs." This differs from when power comes as an unrestricted attribute of God, Mighty and Majestic, which is not restricted by will. When power is attached to a specific act, there is no objection to saying: Yes, God willed this thing and He is able over it, and the meaning is that He does not fail to do it, and only the absence of will prevents its existence. When will exists, power is present. Yes indeed.
* A student: And what is the difference?
* Shaykh: And what is the difference? He says: what is the difference between His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [ash-Shura 11] and ﴿God does not want injustice for the servants﴾ [Ghafir 31]?
* A student: (...) impossible.
* Shaykh: Impossible.
* The student: Injustice is not impossible for God?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is not impossible.
* The student: We said, I mean, where do we place it, when He says ﴿God does not want injustice for the servants﴾?
* Shaykh: He wants injustice? He does not want it, but if He willed it, He would do it.
* The student: But He has negated it from Himself.
* Shaykh: Yes, He negated His will.
* A student: But there is evidence, Shaykh: "I have forbidden injustice to Myself" [Recorded by Muslim, no. 2577/55, from the hadith of Abu Dharr]?
* Shaykh: Well said. Forbidding injustice to Himself: does this imply that He is able over it, or that He is not able over it?
* The student: It implies that He is able, but (...).
* Shaykh: Enough. Now it cannot occur, not because it is impossible, but because God does not will it, owing to His perfect justice.
* The student: But does it not fall under the impossible, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: It is impossible by God's report, not impossible in its essence. It is impossible by God's report that He does not will it, and by the perfection of God's justice. But ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [ash-Shura 11] is impossible absolutely; it cannot be.
* A student: For example, the disbelief of Abu Jahl: if God had willed it, would He have guided him?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, if God had willed it, He would have guided him. The hadith (of the man whom God addressed after his entry into Paradise) shows this: that man considered it unlikely that this thing should be, and God said, "I am able over what I will"; that is, since I willed it, I am able over it.
* A student: But why not interpret the general phrase "He is competent over whatever He wills" as applying to this?
* Shaykh: No, it is not like that. If a man recounted to us a story and said: "God did such-and-such," and we said: "How is this?" and he said: "Yes, God is able over whatever He wills," we would say: "This is a sound expression." But if he brings it as a general attribute of God and then says, "He is competent over whatever He wills," this is not correct.
* A student: So we restrict it in a particular context?
* Shaykh: In a specific thing. When we want to describe God by it in an absolute sense, we do not restrict it by will. When we attach it to a specific thing that occurs by His will, we say: "What God wills, He cannot be incapable of."
* A student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, but they hold that reason indicates the will through specification, and reason indicates creation through bringing into existence, or power.
* A student: Is this statement sound?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: Then will specifies?
* Shaykh: No, that is not their intention. They do not mean that it acts by itself without God, because the attributes of God do not act; God is the one who acts by these attributes. Yes. The context of the verse favors that he considered it unlikely.
* A student: (...)?
* Shaykh: By God, it is not apparent. The apparent sense is that the man considered it unlikely, but without doubting. He considered it unlikely, but a person may consider a thing unlikely and then the thing happens, and then he knows that God is over all things competent.
If you say: "Zayd came, then 'Amr," this order is factual: Zayd came first, then 'Amr. Do you understand? But:
"Indeed, whoever rules, then his father rules after him..." ∗∗∗ ........................
His father—what?
* The student: Dhikri (mentioned).
* Shaykh: Dhikri. Because his father does not rule after him.
* The student: I mean in the verse, in the verse.
* Shaykh: This verse: ﴿How We raise them﴾, ﴿How We raise them﴾ [kayfa nunshizuha / nunshiruha]. If we say ﴿how We raise them﴾, meaning how We give them life, then the giving of life occurs after the clothing of the bones. In the verse there is an order: "dhikri," because the clothing comes before the giving of life. But it is mentioned here after. Or was it before in the verse?
* A student: After.
* Shaykh: Yes. Is the clothing now mentioned before the raising, or after it?
* The student: After?
* Shaykh: And is it after or before, if ﴿nunshiruha﴾ means We give them life?

**Student:** No, it is not before it. It is before the revival, if the verb is ﴿نُنْشِرُهَا﴾ (We raise them up).

**Shaykh:** It is before the revival, and it is mentioned after it according to the order of mention (*al-tartib al-dhikri*). But what about ﴿نُنْشِزُهَا ثُمَّ نَكْسُوهَا﴾ (We raise them, then We clothe them with flesh)? Is the order then real?

**Student:** Natural.

**Shaykh:** Real. In the course of the lesson I mentioned that someone may say: ﴿نُنْشِرُهَا﴾ means "We raise the bones", that is, "We bring the bones to life," because the bones were at first dead, with no life in them at all. When they are raised, meaning brought to life, after some of them are raised over others and interlocked, life enters them. On this view, is the order real?

**Student:** Real.

**Shaykh:** Real.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town while it was fallen upon its roofs. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 259], and so on to the end.

In it is a clarification of the limited vision of man, since he sees or looks at what is visible and observed, as indicated by His words: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power by determining the duration of death, as in His words: ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾.

* Another of its benefits: the affirmation that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks and says, and that His speech is with letters and sound, as in His words: ﴿He said, "How long have you remained?"﴾. We have already noted that it is better to take the Qur'an at its apparent meaning, and that the speaker is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

In it is also a refutation of the Ash'ariyyah (the Ash'arite school), who say that the speech of Allah is the meaning subsisting in His essence, and that these sounds that are heard, which Moses, Muhammad (ﷺ), and others whom Allah addressed heard, are sounds that Allah created to express what is in His self. This view, they say, amounts to denying speech in reality, denying that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, speaks.

* Another of the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in that He caused this man to die and then raised him, so that the complete power of Allah would become clear to him.

* Another of its benefits: it is permissible for a person to report what he thinks likely, and if it contradicts reality he is not considered mistaken. From where do we take this?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Yes: ﴿I have remained a day or part of a day﴾, although the reality, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, is that he remained a hundred years.

* Another of its benefits: Allah, Glorified and Exalted, may bestow on His servant the sight of some of His signs, which increases his certainty, as in His words: ﴿Look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled﴾, and so on to the end.

* Another of its benefits: the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is beyond what is customary in the nature of things, since this food and drink remained how long? A hundred years, without changing.

In it is also a refutation of the naturalists (*ahl al-tabi'ah*), who say that the cosmic laws do not change. From where is this derived? From the fact that this food and drink did not change for a hundred years, while the winds passed over it, and the sun and the heat, and yet it did not change for all that time. This shows the invalidity of the view of the scientists of nature who say that natural laws do not change.

* Another of its benefits: it is permissible to benefit from donkeys, as in His words: ﴿And look at your donkey﴾.

* And among them: the establishment of ownership in them, since Allah attributed the donkey to him, saying: ﴿your donkey﴾. If you say: how do you reconcile this with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, when Allah forbids something, He forbids its price"[[Narrated by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, no. (4938), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]? Does the establishment of ownership necessitate the permissibility of its price?

**Student:** Before the prohibition (...) the domestic donkeys.

**Shaykh:** So the meaning is that we may not sell domestic donkeys?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** It is not permitted? It is not permitted to sell domestic donkeys?

**Student:** Yes, because "Indeed, when Allah forbids something, He forbids its price."

**Shaykh:** We say: if they are sold for eating, then they are forbidden, because it is He who forbade them. But if they are sold for benefit, then this is lawful, because benefiting from them is clearly lawful?

So this does not contradict the hadith "Indeed, when Allah forbids something, He forbids its price." If a donkey is bought for eating, its price is forbidden; if it is bought for its benefit, the benefit is lawful and its price is lawful.

* Another of the benefits of this noble verse: a person may be a lesson to others. That is, Allah may place in a person something that happens to him which becomes a lesson for others, as in His words: ﴿and that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. Similar is the saying of Allah, Exalted, about Jesus son of Mary: ﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit and made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 91].

* Another of its benefits: one should reflect on what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created and brought into being in the cosmos, because that increases faith, since this thing is a sign of Allah's signs, and "sign" means a token. Therefore we should contemplate this cosmos and reflect on it, because of the signs of Allah in it, which increase us in faith and certainty.

* Another of the benefits of this noble verse: one should look at the signs in both a general and a detailed way. He said at first: ﴿And look at your donkey﴾, unrestricted, then He said in the second: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾. This requires that we reflect first on the cosmos in general, then in detail, for that also increases us in faith.

* Another of the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made the flesh on an animal like a garment, indeed a garment in reality, as in His words: ﴿then We clothe them with flesh﴾. For this reason you find that flesh protects the bones from breakage and harm, since harm to bones is more severe than harm to flesh. If something strikes you on the thigh and affects it, you find that it heals quickly and the pain goes away quickly. But if it strikes you on the knee or the shin? It is delayed; it can take a long time, perhaps months or even years, and whenever you touch it you feel pain, because flesh is a garment for the bones. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 14], and here He said: ﴿then We clothe them with flesh﴾.

* Another of the benefits of this noble verse: by reflection, contemplation, and observation, a person comes to understand from the signs of Allah what he would not have understood had he been heedless, as in His words: ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾.

* Another of its benefits: the demonstration of the all-encompassing power of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, as in His words: ﴿that Allah is Able to do all things﴾. All things.

* Another of the benefits of the verse: a refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine decree). In which word?

**Student:** ﴿that Allah is Able to do all things﴾.

**Shaykh:** ﴿Able to do all things﴾. How so? Because among things is the act of the servant, and Allah, Exalted, is capable of the acts of the servant. But according to the Qadariyyah and the Mu'tazilah, Allah, Exalted, is not capable of the acts of the servant, because the servant, in their view, is independent and creates his own act, and Allah, Exalted, did not create his acts.

* Another of the benefits of the verse: a refutation of those who deny voluntary acts, or who deny that voluntary acts subsist in Allah, Mighty and Majestic. From where is this derived?

**Student:** ﴿Allah is Able to do all things﴾, ﴿all things﴾, ﴿knows﴾.

**Shaykh:** No. You see, we may sometimes bring a benefit after the end of the verse, while the place of the benefit is in the middle of the verse, and that is not necessary in order.

**Student:** Allah caused him to die, then raised him.

**Shaykh:** Allah caused him to die, then after that. This is one of the voluntary acts, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is described by it: He does what He wills at any time; when He wills He acts, and when He wills He does not act; when He wills He creates, and when He wills He causes to die; when He wills He humbles, and when He wills He exalts. The Ash'ariyyah and those who follow their path say that these acts are impossible for Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and that acts do not subsist in Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Why? They say: because whatever events subsist in something is itself originated. But this is not correct. Rather, we say: whoever has events subsisting in him and acts proceeding from him is more perfect than whoever does not act and has no events subsisting in him, and cannot bring anything into being. So if you say that Allah does none of the acts that occur by His will, this means you have attributed deficiency to Allah. Whoever acts by his will is more perfect than whoever acts without will, or whoever does not act at all, without doubt. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has all perfection.

As for your saying that events subsist only in an originated thing, from where do you get this principle? This is a false principle, and it does not follow that when an act comes into being, the agent must be originated at the moment the act comes into being. Look, for example, we are now doing an act. Were we created before we acted, or not?

For example, let us suppose one of us is twenty years old. If he does an act today, does his doing this act today imply that he was not created until today?

**Students:** No.

**Shaykh:** Certainly not. So if a newly arising act subsists in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it does not entail that Allah was non-existent and then came into existence. Events: this principle they established is a false principle, for Allah has sent down no authority for it.

* Another of the benefits of the verse: that the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is with letters.

**Students:** He said, he heard.

**Shaykh:** No, these are with sounds, and we have said this before.

**Student:** It is the object of speech (*maqul al-qawl*).

**Shaykh:** With letters, because the object of speech consists of letters. Say: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾, ﴿He said, "Rather you remained a hundred years. So look﴾, and so on to the end. All of these are letters, and Allah attributed them to Himself with the word "said." So the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, consists of letters. But do these letters change or not? The answer: they change, because the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the Qur'an is in the Arabic tongue, and when He addresses Moses, for example, He addresses him in his tongue, the Hebrew tongue, because Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is capable of all things.

Is the audible sound of the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic like the sounds of created beings?

**Students:** No.

**Shaykh:** No. The letters are the letters with which people express themselves, but the sound is not, because sound is an attribute of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, says: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [Ash-Shura 11].

**Student:** Shaykh, the skin (...) is it clothed over the flesh?

**Shaykh:** And what do you say? Is skin part of the flesh?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** I think if I told him: go buy me flesh, and he brought me skin, would I accept it or not?

**Students:** You would not accept it.

**Shaykh:** I would not accept it.

**Student:** Do they eat it?

**Shaykh:** In hunger they eat even the leather socks; they eat anything when hungry. The point is, skin is not flesh. But in reality skin does not protect the bone the way flesh does. That is why, when an animal becomes emaciated and nothing remains on it but its skin over its flesh, as the common people say, "skin over bone," you find that the animal has such weakness, lack of resistance, and sensitivity to pain from the slightest cause, which is evident. So the true clothing is indeed the flesh.

**Student:** There are benefits in it.

**Shaykh:** What are they?

**Student:** There is no question.

**Shaykh:** No, complete the benefits; there is no objection.

**Student:** If a person understands from Allah's signs upon him, he must acknowledge it: ﴿He said, "I know that Allah is Able to do all things"﴾.

**Shaykh:** Like this? Shall we take this benefit?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Or it is necessary; this is the correct view: from considering the signs there necessarily follows knowledge and certainty.

**Student:** Praise (...) praised.

**Shaykh:** This is possible, and it is also possible that Allah established the proof against him. For this reason, in the other reading He said: ﴿Know that Allah is Able to do all things﴾. What is derived from it is what we earlier pointed out: the demonstration of Allah's blessing upon this man, since He did not leave him to wander in his error and doubt, or what is similar to that.

**Student:** Shaykh, is it derived from it that a person should not generalize, from His words: ﴿I have remained a day or part of a day﴾?

**Shaykh:** And what do you say?

**Students:** This is a strong presumption.

**Shaykh:** They say the indication is that Allah caused him to die at the beginning of the day and revived him at the end of the day. Or the indication is taken from his seeing the town fallen upon its roofs, when he said: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾. This is possible.

**Student:** Shaykh, the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It has not spoiled﴾, mean there is a benefit that the food and drink are still fit for use as long as they have not spoiled. The benefit of His words ﴿It has not spoiled﴾ is that this food is still in its state, fit for eating and drinking; "has not spoiled" indicates that no change occurred in it.

**Shaykh:** But if it said "so eat and drink," we would say the same.

**Student:** He said: look at it, it was...

**Shaykh:** Yes. But it does not necessarily mean that he eats and drinks it. However, if it said "so eat it and drink it," we would say: the "fa" (so) is a consequence of what precedes it, and its meaning is that if it had changed, it should not be eaten or drunk, because the purpose is to look at this wondrous matter, namely that its non-change contradicts the cosmic laws. And this donkey, which is more patient with atmospheric changes than the food and drink, is the one that died, and its bones became what he witnessed.

**Student:** The power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in keeping the food in its state, meaning, indicates that it changed without his perceiving it (...)?

**Shaykh:** Yes, we have mentioned this power before.

**Student:** I say, in His words: ﴿I know that Allah is Able to do all things﴾, one may derive from it the difference between man and animals, since an animal, if it sees many things, does not, let us say, comprehend them, and even if it knows them, let us say, even if it sees them with its eyes.

**Shaykh:** I do not know. Apparently this is a benefit that walks on your head after the day ends.

**Student:** The refutation of the Jabriyyah (those who deny human choice) (...).

**Shaykh:** By God, I do not know. Perhaps? The refutation of the Jabriyyah.

**Student:** Yes, Shaykh.

**Shaykh:** But apparently the Jabriyyah do not deny that a person can reach knowledge. However, on the reading ﴿Know﴾, this is what may be used to refute the Jabriyyah, because if a person were compelled, the address directed to him with a command and obligation would be pointless and vain.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be at rest."﴾ [al-Baqarah 260] and so on to the end.

Regarding ﴿Ibrahim﴾ there are two readings: ﴿Ibrahim﴾ and ﴿Ibraham﴾. Regarding ﴿arini﴾ there are also two readings: ﴿arini﴾ and ﴿arni﴾ with the ra' sukun. In His saying ﴿fasurhunna﴾ there are also two readings: ﴿surhunna﴾ with a damma, and ﴿sirhunna﴾ with a kasra. In ﴿juz'an﴾ there are also two readings: ﴿juzuan﴾ and ﴿juz'an﴾ with the zay sukun. So how many words is this? One, two, three, four words, and in each word there are two seven-canonical readings.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Abraham said﴾. ﴿Idh﴾ (when) is an object of a verb omitted, its estimate being: "Remember when Abraham said." And ﴿arini kayfa﴾: the seeing here is visual, so it takes one object; but when the transitive hamza entered upon it, it came to take two objects. The first is the ya' (the pronoun "me"), and the second is the clause ﴿kayfa tuhyi al-mawta﴾ (how You give life to the dead).

﴿Awalam tu'min﴾ has two well-known grammatical analyses. One: the hamza has entered upon an implied element to which the phrase "wa-lam tu'min" is conjoined, and this implied element depends on the context; on this view the hamza is in its proper place. The second analysis: the hamza is placed first while the conjunction is placed after it, and the original is "wa-alam"; thus this clause is conjoined to what precedes it. We have mentioned that this analysis is safer and easier: safer, because a person may estimate a verb that is not the intended one; and easier, so that a person does not tire himself seeking a verb that would be suitable.

In His saying ﴿surhunna﴾ with a damma, it is from (sara yasuru), and with a kasra it is from (sara yasir). In His saying ﴿ya'tinaka sa'yan﴾: the verb here is marfu' or majzum?
* Student: Majzum.
* Shaykh: It is indeclinable in any case, but is it in a place of jazm or a place of raf'?
* Student: In a place of jazm.
* Shaykh: Being?
* Student: The answer to a command.
* Shaykh: The answer to a command. This is the fifth story in this surah in which the dead are brought to life, is it not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: This is the fifth. And the first?
* Student: In the Children of Israel.
* Shaykh: In the Children of Israel. And the second?
* Students: In Abraham.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: In the slain man.
* Shaykh: In the slain man of the Children of Israel, in the story of the cow. And the third?
* Student: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes...﴾
* Shaykh: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, while they were thousands, fearing death?﴾ [al-Baqarah 243]
* Student: ﴿And when Abraham raised the foundations﴾ [al-Baqarah 127]?
* Shaykh: No, my brother, it is not in it. The fourth is in the story of the one who passed by a town fallen upon its roofs, and the fifth is this verse. All of them contain the giving of life to the dead in this world, so there is a clear sign in them refuting those who deny resurrection.

He said: ﴿And when Abraham said﴾. Abraham, upon him be peace, is the third father of the prophets, since the first is Adam, the second Noah, and the third Abraham, as Allah said: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾, and He said of Noah: ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [al-Saffat 77]; and Adam is known to be the father of mankind.

He said: ﴿Rabbi arini kayfa tuhyi al-mawta﴾. [The word] ﴿Rabbi﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), if I err, correct me.
* Student: No, O Shaykh.
* Shaykh: ﴿Rabbi﴾ a subject?
* Students: A vocative, a vocative.
* Shaykh: ﴿Rabbi﴾ is a vocative. Where is the vocative particle?
* Students: Omitted, it is omitted.
* Shaykh: Omitted because it is known. ﴿Rabbi﴾: we know that the vocative is in the accusative and sometimes is built on a damma; this one is neither accusative nor built on a damma?
* Student: The vocative has six grammatical cases, and this is a noun added to a ya', so the ya' was omitted.
* Shaykh: This is the vocative of a noun added to the ya' of the speaker, and the ya' of the speaker here is omitted and the kasra remained.
* Student: As a substitute for it.
* Shaykh: It is not a substitute for it.
* Student: As an indication.
* Shaykh: As an indication of it. So how do we say its i'rab? We say: ﴿Rabbi﴾ is a vocative in the accusative with a fatha estimated on what precedes the omitted ya' of the speaker, for lightness; its appearance was prevented by the occupation of the position by the harakah of harmony. And His saying ﴿Rabbi arini﴾ means: show me with my eye so that I may see; in our colloquial language we say (warrin), we say: show me, meaning make me look and see with my own eye. ﴿Kayfa tuhyi al-mawta﴾: the question here is about the how, not about the possibility, because Abraham did not doubt the power, but he wished to know the modality: how Allah gives life to them after He caused them to die and they became dust and bones, how He revives them?

So the question is about the modality, not about the meaning of giving life, because the meaning of giving life is known to him, and the question is about the how. And His saying ﴿kayfa tuhyi al-mawta﴾: is the intended meaning of Abraham, upon him be peace, any dead that may be, or is the intended meaning the dead of the children of Adam, so Allah struck for him an example with the four birds?

If we look at the word ﴿al-mawta﴾ we find that it is general; that is, anyone or anything that Allah the Mighty and Majestic gives life to before him, He has shown him. Allah the Exalted said to him: ﴿Awalam tu'min﴾, meaning: are you not a believer? This interrogation is for affirmation, not for denial or negation; it is like His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1], meaning: We have indeed expanded for you. ﴿Awalam tu'min﴾ means: or have you not already believed? So this is for affirmation, affirming Abraham's faith, upon him be peace, and he said: ﴿Yes﴾, affirming this matter. As for His saying ﴿tu'min﴾: many people explained faith linguistically as assent (tasdiq), and said: faith in language is assent. This explanation is not precise, but it is an explanation by something close, like their explanation of doubt (rayb) as skepticism, their explanation of pledge (rahn) as detention, and their explanation of His saying ﴿lest a soul be delivered up﴾ [al-An'am 70] as "be detained," and what is similar to that, which they explain by a close meaning that brings it near to understanding; otherwise, in reality there is a difference between faith and assent, and what shows this is transitivity. Assent is transitive by itself and by a preposition, and its meaning differs when it is transitive by itself and when it is transitive by a preposition; but faith is transitive only by a preposition and is not transitive by itself. Is it clear?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Let us return to assent. Assent is transitive by itself and by a preposition, and yet its meaning differs. You say: "saddaqtuhu," meaning I considered the informant truthful; and you say: "saddaqtu bihi," meaning I considered the information true, or by the informant? 
* Students: By the information.
* Shaykh: By the information. So its meaning changes between its transitivity by a preposition and its transitivity by itself, and this change of meaning and difference in the verb's transitivity indicates that there is a difference between them, since if there were no difference, the two verbs would be equal, or the two roots would be equal in transitivity and intransitivity, for what reason? Because the explainer must match the explained. Does "amana" transitive by itself or by a preposition?
* Students: By a preposition.
* Shaykh: It is transitive by a preposition, and it is transitive by the preposition lam and by the preposition ba', and its meaning differs. You do not say "amantuhu" as you say "saddaqtuhu"; never, this does not exist in the Arabic language. But you say: "amantu bihi" and "amantu lahu." "Amantu bihi" conveys the meaning of acknowledgment and tranquility, and for this it is said: "aqarartu bihi" and "itmanantu bihi." Do you understand?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: But "amantu lahu" conveys the meaning of submission: I submitted to him and yielded to him together with acknowledgment, because amana in terms of acknowledgment is not transitive by lam; but when it includes the meaning of submission it is transitive by lam. For this reason, faith in the Sharia necessarily includes tranquility, which is acceptance, and submission, which is surrender. So it is now established that faith cannot be taken to mean assent in an absolute sense, for the meaning we have indicated; but there is no harm in explaining it as assent for a person whom we wish to bring closer to the meaning. However, in terms of precision and verification, the difference between them..
But in terms of precision and verification, the difference between them is clear, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, alluded to something of this in the book of Faith; his book on Faith is well known. The sum is that Abraham, upon him be peace, believed in the sense that he acknowledged, was reassured, and confessed without any doubt that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, gives life to the dead. ﴿He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes"﴾. (Balaa) is a particle used to answer a negation, the negation affirmed by interrogation in order to establish it. So if you say: "Are you not present with us at the lesson, O Abdullah?" what do you say?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, meaning present. And if you say: "Are you not present with us at the lesson?" what do you say?
* Student: Na'am (yes).
* Student: This is negation.
* Shaykh: Then you were not present! If you say "na'am," it means you were not present.
* Student: He was present in heart.
* Shaykh: Then if you answer with "na'am," it is to affirm the negation, and if you answer with "bala," it is to affirm the affirmation. Many important issues follow from this: "Do you not owe so-and-so such-and-such?"
* Students: Yes.. bala.. if you want the details.
* Shaykh: Let us see: if you answer with bala or na'am, is it clear? If you say "na'am," it is affirmation of what?
* Students: Of the negation.
* Shaykh: And if you say "bala," it is for affirmation. For this reason it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord?  They said, "Yes [bala]"﴾ [al-A'raf 172] that he said: "If they had said 'na'am,' they would have disbelieved" [al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran (2/12)]; because the meaning, if they had said "na'am," would be: You are not our Lord. Is it clear?
* Students: Clear.
* Shaykh: Good. Nevertheless, it may be answered with "na'am" intending "bala," as in the saying of the poet:
"Does not the night gather the mother of 'Amr / and us, so that is what brings us near,
Na'am, and you see the crescent as I see it / and the day covers her as it covered me."
Now this man...
"Does not the night gather the mother of 'Amr / and us, so that is what brings us near"
And what did he say?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, meaning bala: "does it not gather," and he does not intend negation. Look, the poor man is satisfied with this gathering: "and you see the crescent as I see it"; as long as I see the crescent and she sees the crescent, this is togetherness. But the bankrupt... says thus, "and the darkness covers her" or "the day covers her as it covered me"; I forgot this word. The point is that in his saying "na'am, and you see the crescent as I see it," here he answered "does it not?" with "na'am," intending "bala."

So the answer to ﴿Awalam tu'min﴾ in affirmation is "bala," and for this He said: ﴿Yes, but that my heart may be at rest﴾, meaning that it may increase in tranquility; otherwise he was already at rest from His saying: ﴿Have you not believed? He said, "Yes, but [I ask] that [my heart] may be at rest"﴾, meaning that it may increase in tranquility. Tranquility, as we all know, is stability, as the Prophet, upon him be peace, said: "Bow until you are at rest in bowing, prostrate until you are at rest in prostration" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (757) and Muslim (397/45) from Abu Hurayrah], meaning, you settle and remain. ﴿But that my heart may be at rest﴾. So Allah the Exalted showed him the sign.

﴿He said, "Take four birds and make them incline toward you, then place on every hill a portion of them, then call them; they will come to you in haste."﴾ [al-Baqarah 260]. His saying ﴿Take four of the birds﴾: which birds are these?
* Students: It was not specified.
* Shaykh: Allah the Mighty and Majestic did not specify them, and therefore the attempt of those exegetes who tried to specify them is considered a fruitless attempt, because it does not concern us whether these birds were geese, or doves, or crows, or any kind of bird, since Allah did not explain them to us.

﴿Four of the birds, then make them incline toward you﴾: ﴿surhunna﴾ is from (sara yasir) or from (sara yasur); ﴿surhunna﴾ means: incline them to you; and as-sawr is inclination, and from it comes the man al-aswar, whose eye inclined toward one side of his eyelid, the asvar meaning the one whose eye inclined to one side of his eyelid, and he is called al-ahwal (squint-eyed). For this reason, even in people's custom now, if someone looks intently, they say: "he sawwara with his eye," looking at the sun, looking at the moon, and what is similar; so the meaning of ﴿surhunna﴾ is: incline them to you, gather them to you. So he did: he took four birds, gathered them to himself, slaughtered them, and divided them into parts.

He said: ﴿Then place on every hill a portion of them﴾: the hills around him. ﴿Place on every hill of them﴾, that is, of these four, ﴿a portion﴾, so that the observer does not think that your act is sorcery, because when you move them away from you, the suspicion disappears, while remaining at a distance from you. ﴿Place on every hill of them a portion, then call them﴾. So he, upon him be peace, did: he gathered the four, slaughtered them, cut them into parts, placed on every hill a portion, and then called them, saying: "O birds, come to me." So what happened? The birds came to him, coming to him in haste.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be at rest." He said, "Take four of the birds and make them incline toward you, then place on every hill of them a portion, then call them"﴾.

﴿Call them﴾, that is, summon them, because calling is called du'a'; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among you like the summoning of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nur 63], meaning: do not call him as some of you call others, saying "O Muhammad," but say "O Messenger of Allah," "O Prophet of Allah," and what is similar. So ﴿ud'uhunna﴾ means: summon them, that is, say: "Come."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will come to you in haste﴾. ﴿Ya'tinaka﴾ is said to be an answer to His saying ﴿ud'uhunna﴾, and it is said to be an answer to an omitted conditional verb whose estimate is: "If you call them, they will come to you." On the first view it is an answer to ﴿ud'uhunna﴾, because it is necessarily implied in Allah's command to him to call them that he should call them; so the condition is known from the command. On the second view there is no difficulty: if we make ﴿ya'tinaka﴾ an answer to an omitted conditional verb, meaning: "if you call them, they will come to you." ﴿Ya'tinaka﴾ is an answer whether we say it is an answer to the imperative verb in ﴿ud'uhunna﴾ or say it is an answer to an estimated condition, "if you call them." It is built on quiescence and is not jussive; it is built on quiescence in a place of jazm. It was built on quiescence because it is attached to what?
* Students: The feminine plural nun.
* Shaykh: The feminine plural nun, ﴿ya'tinaka﴾.

His saying ﴿ya'tinaka﴾ is from the pattern (ata ya'ti), not from the pattern (ata yu'ti). The difference between the two patterns is that (ata), with the long vowel, means "gave," as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and you had given one of them a heap of gold﴾ [al-Nisa' 20], meaning you had given one of them; but (ata) means "came," as He said: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl 1]: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, meaning the command of Allah has come.

So if you want to report that a person came, you say: "ata"; and if you want to report that a person gave, you say: "ata" (with the long vowel). Is it clear?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: So ﴿ya'tinaka﴾ is from the pattern (ata ya'ti) in the sense of "came," meaning they will come to you.

﴿Sa'yan﴾ may be an infinitive in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal); because sa'yan has no difficulty in being an infinitive, and its verb is (sa'a). But is it accusative as an infinitive, its agent omitted, its estimate being: "they will come to you, striving, striving"; or is it an infinitive in the position of a circumstance, meaning "they will come to you as strivers"? Which is more preferable?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: The second is more preferable. Why?
* Students: Because of the absence of estimation.

**The Shaykh:** For lack of a specified referent. We have a rule that we established earlier: when it is unclear whether a statement is emphatic (ta'kid) or introduces something new (ta'sis), it is taken as introducing something new. And when it is unclear whether something has been omitted from it or not, it is taken as not omitted. These are two useful rules. When it is unclear whether a statement is emphatic or new, it is new. When it is unclear whether something is omitted or not, nothing is omitted. So we say: ﴿sa'yan﴾ (striving, hastening) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

The statement ﴿sa'yan﴾: Should we interpret sa'y (striving) according to each context, or should we say it means walking on the feet? Some of them said: sa'y is interpreted according to each thing, meaning that the sa'y of birds is flying. So the meaning is: they come to you flying, with no deficiency in them. Or it means striving on foot, that is, on their feet, walking but quickly. There are two opinions among the exegetes on this. One: that sa'y here means flying, because the striving of each thing is according to its nature. The second: that what is meant by sa'y is walking quickly. But which of them is preferable, as it appears to us?

**The students:** Flying.

**The Shaykh:** Flying. Because their walking on their feet does not indicate their perfection, since a bird whose wing is broken begins to walk. But their flying is more eloquent, as if they had come to the fullest form of life and existence.

Then He said: ﴿And know that Allah is Almighty, Wise﴾. To whom is the address of ﴿And know﴾?

**The students:** To Ibrahim.

**The Shaykh:** To Ibrahim. ﴿And know that Allah is Almighty, Wise﴾. When you know this, you know the perfection of His power, Mighty and Majestic, due to the perfection of His might and the perfection of His wisdom, because He is Wise. Allah, glorified and exalted, always links these two names: al-'Azīz (the Mighty) and al-Ḥakīm (the Wise). Do you know why? Because a mighty created being may lose wisdom due to his might, so he sees himself as overpowering and dominant, and he acts recklessly and without wisdom. And the wise person, when his wisdom is joined with might, gains authority and strength, and matters do not escape him, and he does not wait to see whether this action is wise or not. So Allah combined the Mighty and the Wise.

What is the meaning of al-'Azīz? Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in his Nuniyyah (his poem) that it has three meanings: the might of rank (ʿizzat al-qadr), the might of subjugation (ʿizzat al-qahr), and the might of invincibility (ʿizzat al-imtināʿ).

The meaning of the might of rank: Allah, exalted, has a lofty rank, far removed from every deficiency; rank and nobility are known to us.

The meaning of the might of subjugation: Allah, exalted, is dominant and cannot be overcome; rather He is the Subduer (al-Qāhir). From it is His saying, exalted: ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ [Ṣād 23], meaning: he overcame me and prevailed over me in the argument.

The third: the might of invincibility, meaning strength, and that He, glorified and exalted, is not harmed by anything because of His strength. From it is the Arabic expression: arḍ ʿazāz (ʿazāz land), meaning hard and strong ground. So al-'Azīz has three meanings: the might of rank, the might of subjugation, and the might of invincibility.

Al-Ḥakīm is derived from ḥukm (judgment, decree) and ḥikmah (wisdom). Judgment is of two kinds: cosmic (kawnī) and decreed (qadarī). Wisdom is of two kinds: form (ṣūrah) and purpose (ghāyah). So the divisions are four. From where is al-Ḥakīm derived?

**The students:** From ḥukm (judgment) and ḥikmah (wisdom).

**The Shaykh:** Al-Ḥakīm is from ḥukm and ḥikmah. Judgment is of two kinds, and wisdom is of two kinds. Judgment is of two kinds: cosmic judgment and legislative judgment. Is it correct for me to say: decreed judgment and legislative judgment?

**The students:** It is correct.

**The Shaykh:** It is correct. Cosmic judgment is binding on everyone in every situation, correct?

**The students:** Correct.

**The Shaykh:** Whether people wish it or refuse. Legislative judgment is not binding on everyone. It is established, but not everyone implements it; rather, some people are arrogant towards it. Is it clear, everyone?

**The students:** Clear.

**The Shaykh:** We need an example that supports what we said. One of the brothers of Yusuf said: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me﴾ [Yūsuf 80]. "Allah decides for me" is a cosmic, decreed judgment. That is, I will not leave the land of Egypt for the land of Shām until my father permits me, saying "Come," or until Allah decides that for me, and He, glorified and exalted, decrees it.

Legislative judgment: when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the rulings concerning emigrant women in Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah, He said: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 10]. This is a legislative judgment. From it is His saying, exalted: ﴿Then do they seek the judgment of the time of ignorance? And who is better in judgment than Allah for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Māʾidah 50]. Although this may also include the decreed judgment.

Wisdom: first, what is wisdom? Wisdom is placing a thing in its proper place, such that sound reason does not say that this is in an unsuitable place, but rather says that this is in a fitting place, whether it is cosmic or legislative. We said that wisdom is form and purpose. Form means that a thing is in a specific form; this is wisdom. For example, prayer being in this specific form is wisdom, is it not?

**The students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** That zakāh is obligatory only on specific wealth, in a specific amount, and for specific people, is wisdom, is it not?

**The students:** Wisdom.

**The Shaykh:** These are in legislative matters.

Decreed matters: a human being being in this form, upright, standing straight, walking on two legs, is wisdom, is it not?

**The students:** Yes.

**The Shaykh:** And a donkey walking on four is wisdom. If it walked on two legs, what would we load on its head? It is not suitable; rather on its back. Measure everything by this. This wisdom is what?

**A student:** Decreed.

**The Shaykh:** Cosmic and decreed. This wisdom is form; that is, a thing being in a specific form, and this is in a specific form that accords with wisdom.

Is it necessary that we know the wisdom of every thing in its form? Not at all, it is not necessary. For example, if someone said: Why did prayer become four rak'ahs at Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr and ʿIshāʾ, and two rak'ahs at Fajr? You cannot know the wisdom, can you not?

**The students:** Certainly.

**The Shaykh:** The purposive wisdom: what is the aim of bringing this thing into existence? That is one. And what is the aim of its being in this quality? You understand. So does wisdom include purposive wisdom?

**A student:** Form and the aspect of form.

**The Shaykh:** That is, why it was in this specific form. That is wisdom. And why it was legislated, or why it occurred if it is cosmic? That too has wisdom. If someone said: What is the wisdom of drought? The land being barren and plants not growing, the drought of rain, corruption on the earth, and what is the wisdom of this?

**The students:** So that one may take heed.

**The Shaykh:** Yes. ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, so that He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾ [al-Rūm 41]. And what is the wisdom of creating harmful things like scorpions and snakes, and intense heat and intense cold, and similar things?

**The students:** So that they may take heed.

**The Shaykh:** Wisdom has several purposes. We mentioned earlier six wisdoms for the creation of these harmful things. We call this purposive wisdom.

**The Shaykh:** Purposive wisdom. The wisdom of the legislations: first, tawḥīd (affirmation of Allah's oneness) is the fundamental root for the creation of all creatures, humans and jinn. Then these branching legislations are, to it, like watering. When you pray, it is as if you are watering your heart with the substance of life, because you connect with whom? With Allah, Mighty and Majestic. You confide in Him and address Him. But you see, I want the prayer in which the heart and tongue address Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and most of our prayer has only the tongue addressing. The heart addresses whom?

**The students:** The person seeks the gain of the world.

**The Shaykh:** It differs. This one addresses his car, this one his building, and this one his companion. People differ, so that when a person remembers that he was distracted and made a mistake and turned his prayer around, Satan comes, opening a second door: "Leave this, behind you, the second one comes." The person notices and turns to his prayer, and Satan opens a third door. You find such doors opening, all of which contain no benefit for the person. Sometimes, when the prayer ends, after the thoughts from "Allahu Akbar" until "wa raḥmatullāh" have passed, not a single word remains of it, and sometimes he goes on, planning, changing, advancing and delaying in his prayer, and when he finishes his prayer and all the thoughts have passed (...) all of it (...) it does not become clear. This matter is clear.

So the wisdom of these acts of worship branching from tawḥīd is nourishing the heart: nourishing the heart by connecting with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and increasing faith. For this reason Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 45]. Thus the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His cosmic and legislative rulings has become clear.

Now let us return to the noble verses to take their benefits. First: Ibrahim said to his Lord: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾.

From this noble verse it is derived that addressing Allah by His lordship (rubūbiyyah) is among the etiquettes of supplication by which the messengers invoked Him ("My Lord"). The reason: answering supplication is one of the requirements of lordship, since it is an act, and everything related to the acts of the Lord belongs to the requirements of lordship. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ said, when mentioning the man who travels far, disheveled, stretches his hands to the sky and says: "O Lord, O Lord": [Narrated by Muslim, no. (1015/65), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] And if you reflect more on the supplications of the Qur'an, you will find most of them begin with "Lord": ﴿And they contemplate the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vanity; exalted are You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire. (191) Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced; and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers. (192) Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, 'Believe in your Lord,' and we believed﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 191–193], and so on to the end. ﴿And their saying was only that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs, and make firm our feet, and give us victory over the disbelieving people"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 147]. ﴿Our Lord, forgive us﴾, because answering supplication is one of the requirements of lordship. So we derive from this: that among the etiquettes of supplication is that the one supplicating invokes Allah by His lordship.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: there is no harm for a person to ask for what increases his certainty, from His saying: ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾, because if he sees with his eyes, there is no doubt that it increases.

* And from it: the report of certainty is not like the sight of certainty: ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾; because Ibrahim had the report of certainty that Allah is capable, but he wanted the sight of certainty.

* And from it: the sight of certainty is more complete than the report of certainty. For this reason a hadith says: "The report is not like the witnessing" [Narrated by Aḥmad (1842, 2447), and Ibn Ḥibbān (6213 – Iḥsān), from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās]. The scholars say: certainty has three degrees: knowledge (ʿilm), sight (ʿayn), and truth (ḥaqq). All are present in the Qur'an, and I think in one sūrah, not in two sūrahs: ﴿No! If you knew with the knowledge of certainty﴾ [al-Takāthur 5]. What comes after it?

**The students:** ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takāthur 6].
