The good (tayyib) of earnings is lawful earnings, and the wicked (khabith) is unlawful earnings. Every unlawful earning is wicked, and every lawful earning is good. ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned﴾, not from its wicked things. Do you understand? The word khabith may be meant as unlawful, being wicked due to its acquisition, and it may be meant as bad, being wicked in its own essence, and its explanation will come, Allah willing.

He said: ﴿spend from the good things you have earned﴾, meaning what you have acquired through earning, such as dirhams, trade, the yield of an endowment (waqf), rent, and other things. Everything obtained through your own work is from your earnings.

He said: ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾. Some of them said: His saying ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾ is conjoined to "what" (ma) in His saying ﴿what you have earned﴾, meaning "and from the good things of what We have produced for you from the earth." But the correct view that appears is that it is conjoined to His saying ﴿good things﴾, meaning: spend from the good things We have provided you with, and spend from what We have produced for you from the earth, because everything Allah has produced for us from the earth is good and is ours: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾.

His saying: ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾. Here is "min" (from) for partitioning (tab'id) or for explanation (bayan)?
* The students: For partitioning.
* The Shaykh: ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned﴾: spend some of the good things you have earned and some of what We have produced for you from the earth, or spend from what We have produced for you from the earth even if you spend all of it?
* The students: The first.
* The Shaykh: There is a possibility that "min" is for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins), and the meaning is: ﴿spend from this,﴾ even if a person spends all his wealth. Or that the intended meaning is partitioning, and the command to spend is a command to spend a part, not the whole. But in my view, that it is for the kind is better, because being for the kind encompasses the little and the much.

He said: ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾. And Allah produces for us from the earth what?
* A student: Plants and minerals.
* The Shaykh: Palm trees, grapes, crops, fruits, minerals, and many other things. So what Allah has produced for us from the earth, we must spend from it.

He said: ﴿And do not aim at the wicked part of it to spend from it﴾. ﴿Tayammamu﴾ means: intend, because tayammum in the language means intention, and from it is His saying: ﴿then aim at clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 6].

His saying: ﴿al-khabith﴾: the wicked here is meant as the bad, meaning: do not intend the bad to bring out and leave the good for yourselves, for this is not justice. For this reason He said: ﴿And do not aim at the wicked part of it to spend from it﴾. Is the word ﴿minhu﴾ linked to ﴿al-khabith﴾ as a circumstantial clause (hal), or linked to ﴿tunfiqun﴾?

There are two views. It is said: ﴿minhu﴾ is linked to ﴿al-khabith﴾ as a circumstantial clause: the wicked, while being from what We have produced for you from the earth. On this view, there is an omitted pronoun in ﴿tunfiqun﴾, its estimate being "tunfiquhu" (you spend it). ﴿And do not aim at the wicked part of it﴾, meaning from what We have produced for you, that you spend.

It is said: rather it is linked to His saying ﴿tunfiqun﴾, meaning: do not intend the wicked to spend from it. And he placed it before its governing word for what reason?
* A student: For restriction (hasr).
* The Shaykh: For restriction. The two views do not differ in meaning, for their meaning is that Allah forbids us from intending the wicked, which is the bad, to spend from it.

He said: ﴿And you would not accept it yourselves except with closed eyes﴾. Let the good ones among you parse for us ﴿bi-akhidhihi﴾? ﴿And you would not accept it yourselves﴾.
* A student: It is the predicate of "laysa."
* The Shaykh: Parse ﴿lastum﴾ entirely, the whole clause, parse it.
* The student: ﴿bi-akhidhihi﴾ is a prepositional phrase.
* The Shaykh: I did not ask you to parse ﴿lastum﴾.
* The student: "Laysa" is a past verb built on the fatha.
* The Shaykh: "Laysa" is a defective past verb.
* The student: A defective past verb.
* The Shaykh: What does it do?
* The student: It puts the object in the accusative, and raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative.
* The Shaykh: Good. ﴿Lastum﴾.
* The student: The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) built on the damma in a place of nominative... as subject.
* The Shaykh: Subject?
* The student: No, it is in a nominative place (not a subject).
* The Shaykh: A noun?
* The student: The noun of "laysa."
* The Shaykh: The noun of "laysa," and the mim?
* The student: The mim of the plural.
* The Shaykh: ﴿bi-akhidhihi﴾?
* The student: The ba' is an extra preposition.
* The Shaykh: Extra? Either qualify it or just say extra, extra.
* A student: Just extra?
* The Shaykh: Just extra. Is that not acceptable?
* A student: We say: the ba' is an extra preposition in wording, meaning not extra in meaning.
* The Shaykh: Yes, good, correct.
* A student: And ﴿akhidh﴾ is the predicate of "kana" in the accusative, its sign of accusative is the ya', and ﴿akhidh﴾ is in construct.
* The Shaykh: Where is the ya'?
* The student: The ya' in "akhidhihi."
* The Shaykh: Is it not a preposition?
* The student: But it is presumed.
* The Shaykh: And its sign of accusative?
* A student: The kasra.
* The Shaykh: The ya' or the kasra?
* The student: The ya'.
* The Shaykh: The ya' presumed upon the ya' that was brought in for the extra preposition. Look at the philosophy of this. But these are the rules of grammar. And the nun?
* The student: Dropped for the construct.
* The Shaykh: For the construct. Good. And the meaning?
* A student: Extra in meaning or not extra, sir?
* The Shaykh: The meaning.
* A student: Neither extra nor not extra?
* The Shaykh: No, in meaning it is not extra; it conveys emphasis.

His saying: ﴿And you would not accept it yourselves﴾. The parsing is as you heard, and the ba' is an extra preposition in wording but not extra in meaning. "In wording" means the parsing is valid without it; but it is not extra in meaning because it conveys what?
* The students: Emphasis.
* The Shaykh: It conveys emphasis, meaning that Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: how do you aim at the wicked to spend from it, while you would not accept it yourselves if it were given to you? If you had a right with a person and he gave you the bad part of common property, would you accept it or not?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: You would not accept it except with closed eyes, meaning you would take it with indulgence and leniency. Let us give an example: between me and you is a shared batch of dates; in it are bad, medium, and good dates. I wanted to divide them, and I gave you the bad side of these dates. Would you accept it?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: You may say: I will not accept it, and you have the right in this. Perhaps you have modesty and shame, so you take it with closed eyes. The meaning of closing the eyes is leniency and overlooking a thing, like a man who closes his eyes to something to avoid seeing it, but out of embarrassment. As the proverb says: "Take it while you do not look." So we say: if you were given from common property between you and another some of the bad of that property, would you accept it? No, except with closed eyes. So how would you be content to give someone deserving of spending from your wealth from the side of the bad? Is this justice?

It is not justice. Know that if you give him from the bad, you are only giving to yourself, and if you give him from the good, you are only giving to yourself. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran 92]. Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) used to give in charity whatever pleased him of his wealth.[[Recorded by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah (1/294), from the hadith of Nafi' from him with the wording: Ibn 'Umar, when his admiration for something of his wealth intensified, would bring it near to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic.]] And Abu Talhah (you know his story, may Allah be pleased with him): "When this verse was revealed, he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of Allah, Allah says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran 92], and the dearest of my wealth to me is Bayruha'." Bayruha' was an orchard facing the Prophet's Mosque, which the Prophet ﷺ used to visit and drink from its water, which was sweet, pure, and clean; that orchard's value increased by the Messenger ﷺ coming to it and drinking from it. He said (may Allah be pleased with him): "The dearest of my wealth to me is Bayruha', and I wish to offer it as charity, so place it, O Messenger of Allah, where Allah shows you." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Bakh, bakh! That is profitable wealth, that is profitable wealth," Allahu Akbar, this is profitable wealth. "I think you should make it for your relatives."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (1461) from the hadith of Anas.]] Because he said: place it where Allah shows you. The proof is that the person who spends the good in reality spends for himself, and the one who spends the wicked also spends for himself.

Here He says: ﴿And do not aim at the wicked part of it to spend from it﴾, and the good, meaning we spend the good.

He said: ﴿And know﴾.
* A student: The clause, sir.
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* The student: ﴿lastum bi-akhidhihi﴾.
* The Shaykh: In what respect?
* The student: In respect of parsing, it has a place in the accusative as a circumstantial clause.
* The Shaykh: Which one?
* The student: ﴿lastum bi-akhidhihi﴾ ﴿min tayyibat ma kasabtum﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿min tayyibati ma kasabtum﴾ may be suitable as a circumstantial clause.

He said: ﴿And know that Allah is Rich, Praiseworthy﴾. ﴿And know that Allah is Rich﴾, so He did not ask you to spend due to His poverty or need. ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ means hamid (praising) and mahmud (praised), because fa'il comes in the sense of fa'il and in the sense of maf'ul. Its coming in the sense of fa'il, like what?
* A student: Subhanahu.
* The Shaykh: No, the coming of fa'il in the sense of fa'il, like what?
* A student: Rahim in the sense of rahim (merciful).
* The Shaykh: Sami' in the sense of sami' (hearing), basir in the sense of mubsir (seeing). Its coming in the sense of maf'ul is like qatil (slain), jarih (wounded), dhabih (slaughtered), and the like. Here ﴿Hamid﴾ may be in the sense of hamid and in the sense of mahmud. As for Allah being praised, that is clear; as for His being one who praises, how is that?

Because He praises, the Mighty and Majestic, those among His servants who deserve praise, and for this He commended His prophets, messengers, and righteous servants. This shows that He, the Mighty and Majestic, is one who praises those deserving praise, and He is also praised. The relevance of mentioning "Praiseworthy" after "Rich" is that His richness, the Mighty and Majestic, is a richness for which He is praised, unlike the richness of creatures, for which they may be praised or not. When is a creature not praised for his richness?
* The students: When he is stingy.
* The Shaykh: When he is stingy. When he is stingy, he is not praised for his richness, and he is praised if he gives. Allah the Mighty and Majestic is Rich and Praiseworthy; He did not ask this of you because He needs it, but for your own benefit.
* A student: (...) the words of Allah: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not feel shy from the truth﴾ [Al-Ahzab 53]. He says: give me from the good.
* The Shaykh: What? Yes, he may say this, but if he says to his partner, "Give me from the good," the partner says, "No, I will not give you from the good; let me and you divide the good, and I will give you your right from it; let us divide the medium, and I will give you your right from it; let us divide the lowest, and I will give you your right from it."
* A student: We mentioned at the start of the verse that the one who imitates, like one who imitates people's voices (...) a voice, and stops to attract people with it?
* The Shaykh: Does he attribute it to a specific person?
* The student: Yes, some attribute it to a specific person.
* The Shaykh: No, this is like backbiting, because not everyone is pleased that people imitate his voice.
* A student: Also, it is not loved.
* The Shaykh: So your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes. We want, for example, imitating a seller, someone narrating a person who behaves rudely.
* A student: So what is the answer regarding the hadith, sir?
* The Shaykh: A person who behaves rudely toward his dealer, a person who behaves rudely in his conduct in markets and mosques, and the like.
* A student: The hadith, sir: "Whoever imitates a people is one of them" [[Recorded by Abu Dawud (4031) from the hadith of Ibn Umar.]]. We said: the first, meaning if, for example, he imitates the role of a disbeliever, how do we answer the hadith?
* The Shaykh: Because he does not play the role of a disbeliever.
* The student: No, you said we said: he does not become a disbeliever, for example, but if he is pleased with this and imitates him?
* The Shaykh: No, not at all, he does not become a disbeliever, because he does not attribute disbelief to himself.
* A student: But the hadith "Whoever imitates"?
* The Shaykh: Yes, whoever imitates intends the act, meaning a man goes and wears the clothes of disbelievers, for example; this is undoubtedly imitation, because he attributed the act to himself. Then this hadith does not mean disbelief that expels one from the religion; for this reason, whoever imitates the disbelievers is not a disbeliever. Rather some scholars said: it is disliked, and some said: it is forbidden, and the correct view is that imitating the disbelievers is forbidden.
* A student: Shaykh, we said: imitating the voices of animals is forbidden, but if he imitates, for example, the voice of a rooster?
* The Shaykh: And what about the rooster?
* A student: Meaning it has not come in the Shari'ah as being blamed; meaning we say: the rooster is not blamed in the Shari'ah, is it not like the dog?
* The Shaykh: What do you say about this?
* A student: It is not an animal at all.
* The Shaykh: The question says: if he imitates the call of the rooster? Will it become a custom or not? No, correct. And what do you say: if he imitates the sound of an animal that has not been mentioned in the Shari'ah as blameworthy, and is not something blamed?
* A student: Let us see if the rooster is an animal.
* Another student: Shaykh, we say, the hadith: "Woe to the one who speaks to make the people laugh, woe to him, then woe to him"?
* The Shaykh: He lies, he lies: "Woe to the one who lies" [[Recorded by Abu Dawud (4990) from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah.]].
* A student: He does not speak?
* The Shaykh: He speaks and lies.
* A student: Shaykh, what is his name... the animal, as such, is blameworthy, because when Allah the Exalted honored the children of Adam He said: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾ [Al-Isra 70], and a human's descent to the animal includes everything that is disliked for a human, because it is a descent?
* The Shaykh: This is a good point. He says: even if it is in the rooster or in the...
* A student: Rejected, Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: Is it established from the Messenger ﷺ that he placed him on his shoulder and walked with them, saying: "What excellent riders you both are"? [[Recorded by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (2677) from the hadith of Salman al-Farisi.]]
* A student: Al-Hasan and al-Husayn.

*Shaykh:* Yes, meaning he made him like a camel, or so? Fine, let us look now. Some people think that Allah, glorified and exalted, preferred the human being over everything, and this is not so, because Allah says: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam and carried them on land and sea and provided for them of the good things and preferred them over much of what We have created[[Al-Isra 70]]. It does not say over everything. Likewise, the human being is not preferred over everything. Correct. ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, they are the best of creation[[Al-Bayyinah 7]]. Therefore, among the children of Adam there are those who are worse than animals, or not?

*Students:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding eternally therein. They are the worst of creation[[Al-Bayyinah 6]].

Some people say, "This is my brother in humanity," and similar things. This is forbidden. Humanity is not a quality for which a person is praised unless he fulfills the requirements of that humanity. As for being a human while being more corrupt than an animal, there is no good in that.

*Student:* Shaykh, what about imitating the voices of reciters?

*Shaykh:* There is nothing wrong with it.

*Student:* What if he deliberately imitates a reciter?

*Shaykh:* Yes, indeed. This reciter may have a good recitation, so people enjoy it and find comfort in it. There is nothing wrong with it.

*Student:* The rooster (...).

*Another student:* Someone who plays the role of a disbeliever, if he utters words of disbelief jokingly, such as insulting the religion, or insulting the people, meaning insulting the Muslims, or insulting Allah?

*Shaykh:* Yes, but he does not insult while attributing it to himself. He insults while attributing it to the one whose role he is playing, not to himself. If he mocks the religion of Allah or the Muslims, even if joking, for example if someone wants to speak mocking one of the Sunnahs, if it is one of the Sunnahs of the Messenger (ﷺ) and he attributes the statement to himself, it is disbelief. As I explained to you, the example will become completely clear: a man who divorced his wife jokingly, and played the role of a man who divorces his wife. In the first example the wife is divorced; in the second example, yes, she is not divorced.

*Student:* Shaykh, we say there is a difference, that this matter relates to, but mockery of Allah relates to.. ?

*Shaykh:* No, he says: I am not mocking.

*Student:* Words of disbelief.

*Shaykh:* He does not say "I mock." This word he said, he attributes it to another. It is as if he says: this man whose role I am playing said such and such. One who imitates disbelief is not a disbeliever.

So there is a difference between a person who mocks the religion and attributes the mockery to himself, and if he says, "By Allah, I did not intend it," we say: if you did not intend it, that is even worse. But if he relates about a man that he mocked the religion, he does not become a disbeliever.

*Student:* Shaykh, more than this, especially the viewers, is it that this matter becomes lenient, this mockery of the religion?

*Shaykh:* We have said this is forbidden. But the discussion is not about that; the discussion is about disbelief: does he become a disbeliever or not? Because leaving the religion is not a trivial matter. Removing a person from the religion is not like removing him from the mosque or from the house. It is a serious matter. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who believed, spend from the good things you have earned[[Al-Baqarah 267]].

From this verse is derived the virtue of faith, due to His saying: ﴿O you who believed﴾, for this is a description that requires compliance with Allah's command, and this indicates the virtue of faith.

Second: that among the requirements of faith is compliance with Allah's command and avoidance of His prohibition. Its explanation: Allah said: ﴿O you who believed, spend﴾. Had faith not had an effect, it would be pointless to introduce the command with this description, with no benefit in it.

Third: the obligation of spending from the good things we have earned, due to His saying: ﴿Spend﴾. The default in a command is obligation until there is a diverting indicator, or until there is evidence diverting it from obligation.

Among the benefits of the verse: the obligation of zakat on trade goods, due to His saying: ﴿what you have earned﴾, and there is no doubt that trade goods are earnings, for they are earned through transactions.

Among its benefits: that unlawful wealth (...).

If someone says: what should I do with it if I repent? That is, a man acquired unlawful wealth and then repented, what should he do with it?

We say: he gives it in charity to be free of it and to clear his obligation, not seeking nearness to Allah through it. For if he gives it in charity seeking nearness to Allah, it will not be accepted from him and his obligation will not be cleared. It will not be accepted because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, Allah is good and accepts only what is good"[[Recorded by Muslim (1015) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. And his obligation is not cleared because he gave it in charity as his own property, not as one who is freeing himself from it and disowning it. Unlike one who gives it in charity to free himself from it, he will be rewarded for that. So if he gives it in charity to disown it, will he be rewarded for the charity itself or for the disowning and repentance?

*Students:* For the disowning and repentance.

*Shaykh:* For the disowning and repentance.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the refutation of the Jabriyyah (the determinist sect), due to His saying: ﴿Spend﴾ and ﴿what you have earned﴾. The indication from ﴿Spend﴾ is that if a person were compelled in his actions, it would not be correct to direct to him a command to spend, because he would say: I cannot. If I wanted to spend while being compelled to act, I would not be able to. Likewise His saying: ﴿you have earned﴾, He attributed the earning to them, which is evidence that a person is credited with the act and is not compelled to it.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of zakat on what comes out of the earth. From where is it taken?

﴿O you who believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾.

*Student:* ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾ is this the evidence?

*Shaykh:* His saying: ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾. In it is the obligation of zakat on what comes out of the earth. Do you understand?

The apparent meaning of the verse is the obligation of zakat on what comes out of the earth without restriction, whether it is little or much, and whether it is measured by weight or volume or not. Some scholars held this view: that zakat is obligatory on what comes out of the earth without restriction, due to the generality of the verse. But the correct view is otherwise, because the Sunnah indicates detail in this. First: zakat is not obligatory on a small amount, because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no charity in what is less than five wasq"[[A hadith agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1484) and Muslim (979), the wording is Muslim's, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]]. So if a person gathers from the crops less than five wasq, and the wasq is the load, and five wasq equals three hundred sa' by the sa' of the Prophet (ﷺ), then if a person gathers from the crops only what equals two hundred sa', if we returned to the apparent meaning of the verse?

*Students:* It would be obligatory on him.

*Shaykh:* It would be obligatory on him. But the Sunnah clarified that nothing is due on him for what is less than that, of the two hundred.

Second: the Sunnah indicates that what is not measured by volume is not subject to zakat. How is that?

From his saying: "There is no charity in what is less than five wasq," and the wasq, as I said, is the load, which is sixty sa'. Accordingly, zakat is not obligatory on vegetables such as apples, oranges, citrons and the like, because the Sunnah clarified that it is necessary for that thing to be of what is measured by wasq.

Third: the amount to be spent is left general in the verse: ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾. The Sunnah indicates for what comes out of the earth that the obligation for what is irrigated with labor is half a tenth, that is five percent, and for what is irrigated without labor a tenth, that is ten percent. Is it clear?

*Students:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* ﴿from the good things you have earned﴾. Did the Sunnah clarify what is due on trade goods? We say yes, because trade goods are valued in gold and silver, and the Sunnah has clarified that for each of them, what is due is what? A quarter of a tenth. A quarter of a tenth is how much?

*Students:* Two and a half.

*Shaykh:* One in forty, and it is so.

Among the benefits of the verse: what becomes clear from the difference in expression in His saying: ﴿from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾. Why did He express the first in a way indicating that it is the action of the servant, and the second in a way indicating that it is not the action of the servant?

The matter here is clear, because the growth of trade through earning is mostly the action of the servant: he sells, buys, and earns. As for what comes out of the earth, it is not in reality the action of the servant: ﴿Have you considered what you plant? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the ones who make it grow?[[Al-Waqi'ah 63-64]].

Also among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation of zakat on mines, on minerals.

*Students:* ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾.

*Shaykh:* Because it enters into the generality of ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾. But the scholars say: if the mineral is gold and silver, zakat is obligatory on it in every case. If it is other than gold and silver, such as copper, lead and the like, zakat is due on it if he prepared it for trade, because zakat is not obligatory on these minerals in themselves; zakat is obligatory on them by intention. That is, if he intends them for trade, zakat becomes obligatory on them.

Fine. Is it derived from it that zakat is obligatory on buried treasure (rikaz)?

*Students:* It is not derived.

*Shaykh:* There is disagreement. Some said it is derived from it: zakat is obligatory on rikaz. And we must know what rikaz is.

Rikaz: what is found of the buried treasure of the Jahiliyyah, that is, the buried property of the pre-Islamic era, meaning what is found of old currency attributed to a distant time, such that it is strongly presumed that it has no people today. These dirhams and dinars, if found, are rikaz. Is zakat obligatory on them or not? There is disagreement among the scholars. This disagreement is based on what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "And in rikaz is the khums (one-fifth)"[[A hadith agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1499) and Muslim (1710), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

Some said: what is meant by the khums is one out of five.

Others said: what is meant by the khums is the "al" of familiar reference in the Sharia, which is the khums that is spent in the manner of fay' (public revenue). They said: there is nothing from the zakat wealth and the khums. Those who said the khums means one out of five said: it was made obligatory in it, one-fifth, because it is easy to obtain. That is, for example, dirhams and dinars or trade goods involve hardship, while what Allah brings out of the earth is less hard to obtain, and rikaz is easier than all of them, so for each of them what wisdom requires was made obligatory.

*Student:* No one searches for rikaz, Shaykh. No one looks for buried treasure.

*Shaykh:* No, it exists. There are people who stumble upon it, it exists, either through excavations, or someone is alerted in a dream and told: in such and such a place there is such and such.

*Student:* Which opinion is stronger, Shaykh?

*Shaykh:* The stronger opinion is the obligation of one-fifth.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of intending the inferior in giving zakat, due to His saying: ﴿and do not intend the bad from it to spend, while you would not take it yourselves except with closing your eyes to it﴾.

Also among its benefits: if it is combined with the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Mu'adh to Yemen and said: "Beware of the choicest of their property"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1496) and Muslim (19), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]]. If you combine the hadith with the verse, the justice in the Sharia becomes clear to you. Because his saying: "Beware of the choicest of their property": if the zakat collector intended the choicest of the property, this would be an injustice to whom?

*Students:* To the owner of the property.

*Shaykh:* To the people of the property. And if he intended the inferior, it would be an injustice to the people of zakat. So the obligation becomes moderate: we do not oblige the owner of property to give the best, nor do we enable him to give the worst. He gives the middling.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication to a general principle of faith, which is the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ), may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (13) and Muslim (45), from the hadith of Anas, the wording is al-Bukhari's.]], due to His saying: ﴿and you would not take it yourselves except with closing your eyes to it﴾. What is the indication? Who knows?

*Student:* That if a person himself would not be pleased with this for himself, then all the more so he would not be pleased with it for others.

*Shaykh:* Then why would he be pleased with it for others? I think it is clear.

*Students:* Yes, indeed.

*Shaykh:* If you yourself, if I gave you from this property, you would not take it except with leniency and ease and overlooking some of its defects, then why would you choose it for your fellow? This is what a person should adopt as a rule in how he treats others: to deal with them in the way he loves to be dealt with. For this reason, the authentic hadith says: "Whoever loves to be drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise, let his death come while he believes in Allah and the Last Day, and let him treat people as he loves to be treated"[[Recorded by Muslim (1844) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr.]].

Look at this rule in dealing with people. With great regret, many people today do not deal with one another in this way. Most people consider deception a gain, and lying a gain, to the extent that some common people say: "The false oath in buying and selling is the nails of goods," the nails of goods. What is the meaning of this?

That is, he says that what fixes and secures goods, like a nail for wood, is the false oath, may Allah protect us. He did not know that "Oath-taking promotes sales but erases profit"[[Recorded by al-Nasa'i (4461) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the use of analogy (qiyas), or the establishment of analogy. I say, among the benefits of the verse is the establishment of analogy?

*Student:* The verse?

*Shaykh:* The verse: ﴿O you who believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth, and do not intend the bad from it to spend, while you would not take it yourselves except with closing your eyes to it. And know that Allah is Rich, Praiseworthy﴾.

*Student:* The proof of analogy?

*Shaykh:* Do you not know it?

*Another student:* His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not intend the bad from it to spend, and you would not take it yourselves﴾.

*Shaykh:* From which of the two sentences? From ﴿do not intend﴾ or from ﴿and you would not take it yourselves except with closing your eyes to it﴾?

*Student:* From ﴿do not intend﴾.

*Shaykh:* Do you agree with it from His saying: ﴿do not intend﴾?

*Students:* No.

*Shaykh:* We want another guest. Go ahead.

*Student:* ﴿and you would not take it yourselves﴾.

*Shaykh:* But I think he will know right away, since the first sentence has been excluded. Fine. Explain to me the basis of analogy, so we know that you (...) who? No, if it comes from the guests, I would like that more.

*Student:* Yes, ﴿and you would not take it yourselves except with closing your eyes to it﴾.

*Shaykh:* Good. The basis of the analogy?

*Student:* ﴿except with closing your eyes to it﴾.

*Shaykh:* I am saying, what is the basis of the analogy? This is the wording of the verse, but we want the basis for establishing analogy from this verse.

*Student:* What one does not accept for himself, he does not accept for others.

*Shaykh:* That is, if you do not accept it for yourself, how would you accept it for others? That is, analogize this to that. Is it clear?

*Students:* Yes.

*Shaykh:* Fine. Is it analogy by priority?

*Shaykh (continuing):* Among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, and they are: Rich (Ghani) and Praiseworthy (Hamid), is that right?

And the affirmation of two of Allah's attributes: richness (ghina) and praise (hamd).

*And also in it:* the affirmation of a third attribute from the combination of both together, which is the perfection of His richness, namely that it is a richness for which He is praised, glorified and exalted.

Are these two names among the transitive names, so that faith in them is not complete except by affirming three matters, or among the intransitive names, so that faith in them is complete by affirming the two matters?

*Student:* Al-Ghani is intransitive, and al-Hamid is transitive.

*Shaykh:* Good. Al-Ghani is intransitive. By what is faith in it completed?

*Student:* Faith in it is completed by believing that it is one of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and likewise you must believe that it is an attribute that includes an attribute, which is richness.

* The Shaykh: It includes an attribute, which is richness (al-ghina). Al-Hameed. I said that it is transitive (*muta'addi*), so faith in it is not complete except with three matters. Tell me them.
* The student: You mean you believe that it is a name, and that we believe that...
* The Shaykh: In the attribute, which is praise (*al-hamd*).
* The student: Which is praise. Third, we believe
* The Shaykh: In the ruling or the effect, which is that He
* The student: Is praised by the believers.
* The Shaykh: That is if we take *hameed* in the sense of *hamid* (one who praises). But if we take it in the sense of *mahmood* (one who is praised)?
* Student: *Mahmood* is intransitive (*lazim*).
* The Shaykh: So it is intransitive, and faith in it is completed by two matters: affirming the name and affirming the attribute. Well done.
* Student: The first is transitive?
* The Shaykh: No, it is not transitive.
* Student: Even the first, that it suffices (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, no. He is self-sufficient (*ghani*) by Himself.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 268–270 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Shaytan promises you poverty and orders you to immorality.﴾ ﴿Al-Shaytan﴾ (the Shaytan) is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is the clause ﴿yaʿidukúmu﴾ (promises you). The word ﴿wa-yaʾmurukum﴾ (and orders you) has two readings: with a damma on the ra' (wa-yaʾmurukum) and with a sukun (wa-yaʾmurkum). The reading with the damma presents no difficulty, since it is coordinated (maʿtuf) with the nominative ﴿yaʿidukúmu﴾.

As for the reading with the jazm (apocopation, the sukun on the ra'), it presents a difficulty, because according to the known rules of grammar, the present-tense verb (fiʿl muḍāriʿ) is nominative when no jussive particle (jāzim) or subjunctive particle (nāṣib) precedes it. Here it is jussive. They said: its jazm here is for lightening (takhfīf) the pronunciation, because his saying ﴿wa-yaʾmurkum﴾ is lighter on the tongue than his saying ﴿wa-yaʾmurukum﴾.

However, this rule is not generalizable (ghayr mutaʿaddiyah). It is only used to explain what has been transmitted. This is a non-generalizable cause, and it is only used to explain what has been established. Why do we say it is not generalizable?

Because if we said it was generalizable, the analogy would be that every word in the Qur'an that is heavy on the tongue should be given a sukun, and that is not the case, because the Qur'an is based on transmission (samāʿ). But when a reading is transmitted that is lighter and contrary to the known rules of Arabic, we say: the rule was departed from for lightness.

His saying ﴿wa-Allahu yaʿidukúm maghfiratan minhu wa-faḍlan﴾ (and Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty) is also a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. The subject is ﴿Allah﴾? The subject?

* Student: ﴿wa-yaʾmurkum﴾, the ra' is with a sukun.
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a reading I told you about. There is a canonical reading (qirāʾah sabʿiyyah) of the ra' with a sukun, ﴿wa-yaʾmurkum﴾, and there is a reading ﴿yaʾmurukum﴾. There are two readings.

﴿wa-Allahu yaʿidukúm﴾ is also a nominal sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. The subject is ﴿Allah﴾, and the predicate is the clause ﴿yaʿidukúm﴾ (promises you). ﴿wa-Allahu wasiʿun ʿalim﴾ (and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing) is also a declarative nominal sentence, with the subject ﴿Allah﴾, ﴿wasiʿun﴾ (All-Encompassing) as the predicate, and ﴿ʿalim﴾ (All-Knowing) as a second predicate.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: "Indeed, ﴿al-Shaytan﴾, and the Shaytan is a name of Iblis. It is said that it derives from (sh-ṭ-n), meaning "to be far away," and on this basis the nūn is original (aṣliyyah, part of the root). It is also said that it derives from (sh-ṭ-ṭ) meaning "to become enraged and angry," because its characteristic is rage, anger, folly and ignorance. But the first view is closer: that it is from (sh-ṭ-n), meaning "to be far away," as evidenced by the fact that it is declinable (ṣarf, takes nunation and inflection), as Allah says: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed Shaytan﴾ [al-Ḥijr 17].

Its declension is evidence that the nūn is: original or added?

* The students: Original.
* The Shaytan: Original. That is so because Allah distanced him in His saying: ﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Ḥijr 35].

He says: the Shaytan promises the children of Adam poverty and orders them to immorality. He promises them poverty: he says "Do not spend, do not spend, because if you spend you will become poor." If you have a hundred riyals and you spend ten, how much remains?

* The students: Ninety.
* Shaykh: Ninety. If you spend another ten, eighty remains. If you spend fifty, thirty remains. If you spend twenty, ten remains. If you spend ten, you have become poor. So he tells you: "Do not spend, for if you spend you will become poor." So he promises you poverty. But is this correct or not?

* The students: No, it is not correct.
* Shaykh: No. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity does not decrease wealth." [Reported by Muslim (2588) from Abu Hurayrah.] Charities do not diminish wealth.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whatever you give in usury so that it may increase the wealth of people, it does not increase with Allah. And whatever you give in zakat, seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who receive multiplied (reward).﴾ [al-Rūm 39] That is, they are the ones who attained the degree of multiplication.

He says: ﴿promises you poverty﴾, and poverty is emptiness, and it agrees in the greater derivation (al-ishtiqāq al-akbar, shared root letters) with (al-qafr), which is an empty land. That is, emptiness of one's hand. ﴿And orders you to immorality﴾. So he promises and frightens you with poverty, and orders you to immorality. What is meant by immorality (fawāḥish) here?

Immorality here is stinginess (bukhl), because fāḥishah (immorality) differs in each context according to what is appropriate to it. The context here is spending, and what is considered most shameful in spending is stinginess. So the Shaytan orders stinginess. And the stinginess to which the Shaytan orders is of two kinds: stinginess regarding an obligation, such as withholding zakat, and withholding obligatory maintenance from a wife and relatives; and stinginess regarding what is recommended. This is what the Shaytan orders. As for stinginess regarding what is permissible (mubāḥ), the Shaytan does not order it, because it does not benefit a person whether he spends or does not spend. Indeed, not spending in what is permissible may be preferable.

Allah the Exalted says: "Immorality." I said that what is meant here is stinginess. Does it come with a meaning other than stinginess? Yes, it comes to mean any sin that is considered shameful in general, such as His saying: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾ [al-Najm 32]. It also comes to mean fornication, sodomy, and marriage with those within the prohibited degrees (dhawāt al-maḥārim).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an immorality﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 32].

And Allah the Exalted says regarding marriage with those within the prohibited degrees: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an immorality﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 22]. And regarding sodomy, He said about Lot: ﴿Do you commit the immorality?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 80]. ﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾. Notice the difference between this and that.

﴿promises you forgiveness﴾, because charities expiate sins. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Charity extinguishes sin just as water extinguishes fire, and a man's prayer in the depths of the night." [Reported by al-Tirmidhi (2616) from Muʿādh, with the wording: "and a man's prayer in the depths of the night."]

﴿wa-faḍlan﴾ (and bounty) means increase. So charity increases forgiveness, the opposite of "he orders you."

﴿He promises you poverty﴾, is that right or not?

* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Do not follow me until you are certain.
* The students: Bounty is the opposite of poverty.
* Shaykh: Bounty is the opposite of poverty, and forgiveness is the opposite of immorality, because immorality earns sins and forgiveness erases sins. So there is a difference between this and that.

As for His saying ﴿wa-faḍlan﴾: if someone says, "How can charity or spending from wealth be a bounty when we see that it decreases? If one spends a dirham out of ten, it becomes nine. So what is the sense of increase? Or at least, what is the sense of no decrease?"

* A student: It is on two aspects. The first aspect: this is blessing and increase in the Hereafter, and Allah will reward him with good deeds. The second: the blessing that is given may be a blessing in meaning, and sometimes it is tangible, so his wealth increases. So what is the rational explanation of this?

* Shaykh: We say: there is an increase! As for the increase in reward in the Hereafter, the matter is clear. If you spend a dirham, you will receive in the Hereafter ten dirhams up to seven hundred dirhams. That is an increase. But if we want a tangible increase in this world, how can it be? We say the increase comes in several aspects:

The first aspect: a person may find that Allah opens to him a door of provision, so he earns and his wealth increases. Is that not so?

* The student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: Second: this wealth may be protected by Allah from calamities that would have struck it had there been no charity. This is observed. That is why people commonly say now, if something of a person's is lost and then found later: "This wealth was purified (muzakkā)," meaning among the common people, if wealth has been purified by zakat, the zakat protects it from calamities. Clear?

The third thing that increases it is blessing. The blessing in spending: if blessing is removed from spending, a person may spend twenty dirhams on things that do not benefit him. But when blessing descends, a small amount of spending suffices a person for many needs. This is something observed. I think I have related to you a story that happened to two men who shared out a date-palm harvest, and that was during Ramadan. One of them said: "I will harvest the fruit during the day in Ramadan so that the poor will not come and eat from it."

* The students: At night?
* Shaykh: No, during the day. At night they come and eat.

The second said: "I will delay the harvesting of the palms until after the Fitr (the end of Ramadan), and I will harvest during the day so that people come and eat." Notice. The fruit was divided, and one of them said to the other: "Choose, take whichever you want." So he took what he saw as the larger share. Who took it? The stingy one. He took the share he saw as more (...). When they harvested the palms, the share of the generous one, which he harvested after the Fitr and from which the poor ate much, became larger than the other. So the two men took their dispute to the judge. The stingy one claimed the division was a mistake, even though the generous one had given him the choice. When they came before the judge, he said: "Alright, did he give you the choice?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did you choose your share?" He said: "Yes." "Why?" He said: "Because I saw it was more." He said: "You have acknowledged against yourself now, how can you claim?" Then the generous one said: "The story is this and that: he harvested during the day in Ramadan and no poor person came to eat. I delayed it. When the day of the Eid came, I told the people: we will harvest the palms on such-and-such a day, so whoever among you wishes to attend, let him attend." Many of the needy attended and ate. The shaykh said to him: "This is the fulfillment of the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): 'Charity does not decrease wealth.'" [Reported by Muslim (2588) from Abu Hurayrah.] Notice, glory be to Allah the Mighty. This matter is well known in our town (...).

﴿yu'tī﴾ means "gives," and in this sense it takes two objects. Originally, are these two objects a subject and predicate or not?

* The students: No.
* Shaykh: They are not originally a subject and predicate. It is also said: ﴿yaʾtī﴾ and ﴿yaʾtī﴾ meaning "comes," and in this sense it takes one object: ﴿Say: Have you considered if it came to you﴾ [Yūnus 50]. But if it is from (ā-t-ā) meaning "gave," it takes two objects. The first object here is ﴿yu'tī al-ḥikmah man yashāʾ﴾ (He gives wisdom to whom He wills): the first object is "wisdom" (al-ḥikmah), and the second is (man) in His saying ﴿man yashāʾ﴾ (whom He wills).

As for His saying: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾. We might say that this second clause indicates that the first object of ﴿yu'tī al-ḥikmah﴾ is (man), and ﴿al-ḥikmah﴾ is the second object, because he made the one who is given, in His saying ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah﴾, the conditional particle ﴿man yu'ta﴾ (whoever is given). And His saying ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah﴾. ﴿yu'ta﴾ is a present-tense verb in the passive voice (mabnī li-ayy shay'?)

* The students: Passive.
* Shaykh: In the passive voice (lil-mafʿūl), and its subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil, the deputy of the agent) is the first object, and ﴿al-ḥikmah﴾ is the second object. The clause ﴿fa-qad ūtiya﴾ (then he has been given) is the answer to the conditional. And ﴿ūtiya khayran kathīran﴾ (he has been given much good) we say of it as we said of ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah fa-qad ūtiya khayran kathīran﴾.

He says: ﴿wa-mā yadhdhakkaru illā ulū al-albāb﴾ (And none will be reminded except the people of understanding). What is ﴿ulū﴾ in this construction?

﴿wa-mā yadhdhakkaru illā ulū﴾? ﴿ulū﴾, and what is its grammatical position (iʿrāb)?

* The student: It is the agent (fāʿil).
* Shaykh: ﴿ulū﴾ is the agent of ﴿yadhdhakkaru﴾, because the exception here is "detached" (mufarragh, where the exception is from an unstated general noun). ﴿ulū﴾ means "possessors of" and it is attached to the sound masculine plural, and for this reason it is raised with the waw.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says in this verse: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾, meaning that Allah the Exalted gives wisdom to whomever He wills of His servants, because the whole matter is in His hand, glory be to Him and exalted be He.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will; You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will. In Your hand is all good. Indeed, You are Competent over all things﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 26].

Wisdom is in the hand of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, He gives it to whom He wills of His servants. We have often mentioned that an act of Allah that is tied to His will is referred back to wisdom, as the wisdom requires. We have cited as evidence for this His saying: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ [al-Insān 30]. So Allah, glory be to Him and exalted be He, gives wisdom to whoever He knows is worthy of it, just as He gives prophethood to whoever He knows is worthy of it: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-Anʿām 124].

And Allah the Mighty and Majestic's act is not merely a matter of will, that He gives this and withholds that, simply because He willed this or willed that. Rather, it is for a wisdom.

As for His saying ﴿al-ḥikmah﴾, what is it? Wisdom (al-ḥikmah) is a noun of the form ﴿fiʿlah﴾ from ﴿aḥkama yuḥkimu iḥkāman﴾, meaning "to perfect." There is no perfection of anything except through two things: knowledge and right judgment (rushd). It is not possible for perfection of anything to occur except through two things: knowledge and right judgment, because how can someone who lacks knowledge perfect a thing when he does not know?

If someone told you that this man will make a clock and perfect it and do it well, but he has not learned how to make it, could he make it or not?

* The students: No, impossible.
* Shaykh: It is not possible. If someone told you that this man will build a building, and he knows about construction, but he is foolish and does not handle matters well, he does not know how to place the columns, nor the beams, nor the floors, nor anything of this. He is good and has knowledge, but he does not have good management, he does not have sound conduct. Could he perfect it or not?

* The students: No.
* Shaykh: It is not possible. So wisdom goes back to two things: knowledge and right judgment. That is why Allah the Mighty and Majestic said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 113]. By the Book is knowledge, and by wisdom is right judgment. And if you wish, say: wisdom also includes knowledge and right judgment, and it is the Sunnah.

In any case, Allah the Mighty and Majestic bestows wisdom on whomever He wills. You will find some people whom Allah has given knowledge and right judgment. They have knowledge, they have right judgment; they place things in their proper positions. They give when giving is more beneficial, they withhold when withholding is more beneficial, they speak when speech is more beneficial, and they stay silent when silence is better, and so on. We say: what is this? It is wisdom and right judgment: knowledge, because he knows that this is more beneficial, and right judgment, because he follows what is beneficial.

If Allah bestows this matter of wisdom upon a person, then Allah says: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾. That is, whoever Allah grants wisdom, knowledge and right judgment, he is given much good, because he has knowledge and right judgment; nothing escapes him, he does not waste an opportunity, and he knows the matters of good and the matters of evil.

His saying ﴿fa-qad ūtiya khayran kathīran﴾ (then he has been given much good) and He did not say, glory be to Him and exalted be He, "then he has been given all good," because no matter what a person is, he is deficient. No matter how far he reaches in knowledge and right judgment, he is still deficient. Ignorance can overtake him, and poor judgment can overtake him. That is why a person should always ask Allah for success, guidance and rectitude, because no matter how capable he is, he is deficient. Sometimes a person speaks, believing while speaking that he is correct, and then it becomes clear to him that he was wrong. Why?

Because he lacked either knowledge or right judgment. Indeed, even the diligent scholar (mujtahid, one who exerts effort in deriving rulings), sometimes strives to seek the truth, investigates and studies the texts, then says: "the ruling is such-and-such." After a period of time his reasoning changes, and he sees that the ruling is different from the first ruling. Is this deficiency or perfection?

* The students: Deficiency.
* Shaykh: This is deficiency, but it becomes perfection if he returns to the truth and does not defend himself and remain in his error. He says: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾. You may ask: why did the wording change between His saying ﴿yu'tī al-ḥikmah﴾ and then ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah﴾? Why did He not say ﴿wa-man yu'tihi al-ḥikmah﴾ (whoever He grants wisdom)? Because He said at the beginning ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah﴾, so why did He say ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah﴾?

The answer, and Allah knows best: wisdom may be innate and may be acquired. That is, a person may gain, through practice and mixing with people, wisdom and good conduct that he would not gain if he were isolated from people. That is why He used the present-tense verb in the passive voice, to encompass all the means by which wisdom comes, whether one is given wisdom from Allah the Mighty and Majestic or through practice and experience. And what is gained of wisdom through practice and experience is also from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. It is He who has arranged for you someone who opens for you the doors of wisdom and the doors of good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 268–270 (part 2 of 3):

He says: ﴿And none will be mindful except those of understanding.﴾ ﴿Mindful (yadhdhakkaru)﴾ means being admonished and taking lesson from matters, their courses, their outcomes and their fruits. ﴿None except those of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾ means the people possessing ﴿al-albab﴾, that is, the intellects; for al-albab is the plural of (lubb) (kernel, i.e., the core of the mind), which is the intellect ('aql). The people of intellect are those who take heed, whether that concerns the established precedents God has applied to His servants in punishing the deniers and destroying the criminals, or what occurs in the experiences of life in their own time. As it is said: "The intelligent person is one who learns from others." Every intelligent person draws lessons and studies from events; that is why you find him looking, reflecting, and comparing the past with the present and the future with the present in order to reach a conclusion. As for one who has no intellect, he is heedless, heedless and not mindful: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 10:101].

If someone asks: Is lubb intelligence (dhaka') or something else?
* A student: It is intelligence.
* The Shaykh: No. We have said that lubb is 'aql (intellect), and 'aql is other than dhaka' (intelligence). A disbeliever may be extremely intelligent yet extremely foolish, and for this reason God described the disbelievers as ﴿deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171].
﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but calls and cries: deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171].
Therefore, however much we see of the politics and cleverness of disbelieving nations, we should never say they are people of intellect. How can God say ﴿so they do not understand﴾ while you say they are intelligent?! Rather we say: they are clever (adhkiya'), and intelligence does not necessarily entail intellect. Intellect is good conduct, and it is called 'aql because it restrains (ya'qilu) its possessor from what harms him. Intelligence (dhaka') is sharpness of perception and understanding, which may be praised or not praised. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Fatwa al-Hamawiyya concerning the theologians (mutakallimun): "They were given dhaka' but were not given dhaka'." Is this a complete pun (jinas tam) or an incomplete one?
* The students: Incomplete.
* The Shaykh: An incomplete pun. Apparently you do not yet know what jinas is...
And the transmitted sciences, and they are the ones who claim that they are...? That they are the intelligent ones, the people of intellect. The point is that ﴿al-albab﴾ is the plural of lubb, which is 'aql, and 'aql is something other than dhaka', is it not?
* The students: Yes, other than it.
* The Shaykh: Other than dhaka'. For this reason I tell you that the geniuses of disbelievers in intelligence should never be called intellectuals, not at all. What do we call them?
* The students: Clever.
* The Shaykh: Clever. But intellectuals, no.

Several benefits are derived from this noble verse.
* A student: The previous verse.
* The Shaykh: Good, the verse before it: ﴿The Satan promises you poverty and commands you to indecency﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:268], and so on to its end.
* From this noble verse is derived: the affirmation of devils, from His saying ﴿the Satan﴾. It has already been mentioned that what is meant by "Satan" here is the genus, not a specific individual by his person; specific by what? By his kind, i.e., the genus of devils.
* Among the benefits of the verse: Satan has an influence on the children of Adam, whether to proceed or to refrain. When he promises poverty and commands stinginess, the implication of that is refraining and not giving.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the doors of pessimism (tasha'um) are opened only by devils, from His saying ﴿He promises you poverty﴾. Satan is the one who opens the door of pessimism for you. He says: If you spend, and you now have twenty riyals, you spend ten today, and the next day five, how much remains? Five; and tomorrow three; two riyals remain, and after that two more, and you have become poor. Do not spend. A human being is human, and perhaps he does not spend, perhaps he forgets the saying of God Most High: ﴿Whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba' 34:39], and the saying of His Messenger (ﷺ): "Charity does not diminish wealth"[[Narrated by Muslim (2588/69) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of Satan's enmity toward man, for in reality he is an enemy to him in information and an enemy in command. In information he promises him what? Poverty. In command he orders him to indecency. So he is an enemy both in information and in command, and we seek refuge with Allah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: stinginess is among the indecencies, is it not? Why? Because the context is the context of spending, so what Satan commands us to do is not spending. But is stinginess itself the indecency, or is it part of the indecency? It is part of the indecency. We mentioned during the tafsir that indecency (fahsha') comes in other senses in several verses.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Satan commands after whispering, exaggeration, and pessimism. He commands, saying: Do not spend, or does he say: Withhold?
* A student: Do not spend.
* A student: Withhold.
* The Shaykh: Be attentive.
* A student: The same thing.
* The Shaykh: One and two. Shall we say: Withhold, or do not spend?
* Students: Withhold.
* Students: Do not spend.
* A student: He says "do not spend," shaykh.
* The Shaykh: ﴿He commands you﴾?
* The students: "Withhold"?
* The Shaykh: Withhold, which? Withhold; because if we say "do not spend," it is a prohibition, and so the command becomes of the type of the necessary. But if we say "withhold"?
* A student: It becomes congruent.
* The Shaykh: It becomes congruent. Then the word "withhold" is stronger than "do not spend," as if he says: do not spend, and emphasize in retention: withhold.
Is there anyone other than Satan who commands this?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And what is he?
* A student: The self (nafs).
* The Shaykh: The self: ﴿And I do not absolve myself; indeed the self is ever commanding to evil﴾ [Yusuf 12:53].
Can we say: it is derived from the verse that whoever commands a person to withhold from spending is similar to Satan?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is that so? Correct. One who commands people to withhold from lawful spending, and not from unlawful spending, is similar to whom? To Satan. One who commands another to lavish spending?
* A student: He is a brother of Satan.
* The Shaykh: The squanderer is a brother of Satan: ﴿Indeed the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isra' 17:27]. And the one who commands him to squander? Apparently he is a devil, for everyone who commands evil commands indecency, so he is a devil.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: look at this promise, the generous and delightful promise: ﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾. Allahu akbar! How far apart are the two promises: Satan promises you poverty, ﴿and Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾.
Someone may say: Is there correspondence (tatabuq) in the two verses, or, more precisely, antithesis (taqabul)? ﴿He promises you poverty﴾, but God says ﴿He promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾. Did He add or not add?
* The students: He added.
* The Shaykh: That is, He promises us two things: forgiveness and bounty. Forgiveness for sins, and bounty for the increase of wealth in its blessing and growth. Is that clear or not? So we gain through spending these two matters which God Most High has promised: forgiveness and bounty.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this forgiveness with which God promises us is great forgiveness. ﴿From Himself﴾, why? Because the greatness of the gift follows the greatness of the Giver. For this reason it came in the hadith which the Prophet (ﷺ) advised Abu Bakr with, he said: "So forgive me with forgiveness from Yourself, and have mercy on me"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (834) and Muslim (2705/48) from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.]]. It is known that a gift is according to the giver: ﴿forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that optimism (tafa'ul) from Allah. From where?
* The students: "He promises you" — God promises you.
* The Shaykh: ﴿He promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty.﴾ So when a person is optimistic toward his Lord when he spends, and he thinks well of God the Mighty and Majestic, that God will forgive his sins and increase him from His bounty, this is among the best of what the inner heart holds.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of God's names, which are al-Wasi' (the All-Encompassing) and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), and the affirmation of two of His attributes: vastness (sa'a) and knowledge ('ilm). If someone says: From where did you affirm vastness?
* The students: From "Wasi'."
* The Shaykh: From "Wasi'." And does the name indicate the attribute?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Certainly?
* Students: Yes, certainly.
* The Shaykh: I do not know, certainly? Certainly?
* The students: Shaykh, certainly, shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Does "al-Sami'" indicate hearing?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And "al-'Alim"?
* The students: It indicates knowledge.
* The Shaykh: It indicates knowledge. Every name of God necessarily indicates an attribute, and it has already passed us that faith in a name is not complete until you believe that it is a name of God and that it includes an attribute of His which that name indicates, and you believe in its effect where it is from a transitive attribute. Is that clear? And there is no need, brothers, to say: Bring evidence for affirming the attribute, for the Arabic language is the evidence. The Qur'an was revealed in what language? In the Arabic language. It is impossible in Arabic to say "al-Sami'" of one who has no hearing, nor "al-Wasi'" of one who has no vastness, nor "al-Hakim" of one who has no wisdom. Whoever claims that Arabic uses such names without affirming the meaning they include is either a liar against the Arabic language or ignorant of it, is it not? Either a liar or ignorant. But a man who knows the Arabic language and is truthful about what he says about it must say that every derived name indicates the attribute it includes, without exception. If I saw a blind man and said, "Masha' Allah, this man is the seeing one," what would you say?
* The students: Optimism.
* The Shaykh: No, not optimism at all, truly.
* The students: Wrong.
* The Shaykh: You would say, how is this man "the seeing one," when he is blind and cannot see? You would call him seeing?!
A man who has cannons next to him and does not hear; masha' Allah, the man came to me, "the hearing one." What do you say? You say: this speech is madness; how is he hearing when he has no hearing?! Is that clear? Yes. Some of the brothers present now told me that someone says: What is the evidence that God has hearing? What do you say to this? We say: Bring the evidence that you have intellect before we give you the evidence that God has hearing. Is it possible, by intellect or language or custom, to say "al-Sami'" of one who has no hearing?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: Never, it is not possible. But some people have had the door of ijtihad opened to them, and I say: I thank and praise Allah that He, glorious and exalted, has made it easy for us, or opened for us, the seeking of evidence. But seeking evidence for everything, even where the evidence is clear, and saying "What is the evidence?" Is this correct? This is extravagance (israf); this is extravagance, not seeking evidence.
* A student: The third attribute, shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Yes?
* A student: The breadth of knowledge.
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is also derived from the two names and the two attributes: the affirmation of a third attribute by their combination. For we have said previously, the rule is that a name of God may, when joined with another, include another attribute: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Forgiving﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:43]. Look at the combination of pardon and power; it has the distinction that His pardon is not mixed with incapacity at all. Why? Because some people pardon out of incapacity. A man snatched another's turban and fled with it; the one robbed ran after him, and when he could not catch him, he said: "I forgive you." What is this pardon?
* The students: Incapacity.
* The Shaykh: Is this praiseworthy or not?
* The students: No, not praiseworthy.
* The Shaykh: God knows best. In any case, he is weak; perhaps he will benefit from it in the Hereafter, that he will not be held to account for it, but he is weak without doubt. But that God is "Pardoning, Capable": this is perfection.
So ﴿All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: what is the third attribute that arises from this? That His knowledge is all-encompassing, and all His attributes are all-encompassing. This is derived from His name al-Wasi': His knowledge, His hearing, His sight, His power, all His attributes.
Then He said: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:269], to its end.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of God's actions that are connected with His will?
* A student: In His saying ﴿All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾, that the vastness of God Most High (...)
* The Shaykh: No, everything.
* A student: That charity increases wealth.
* The Shaykh: What do you say? Charity increases wealth, derived from His saying ﴿and bounty﴾.
From the second verse is derived: the affirmation of God the Mighty and Majestic's actions that are connected with His will, from His saying ﴿He gives wisdom﴾, and this is among the attributes of what?
* The students: The active ones.
* The Shaykh: The active attributes, among the active attributes.
* Among its benefits: that what is in a human being of knowledge and right guidance is a bounty from God the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾. So if God has favored you with knowledge, right guidance, strength, power, hearing and sight, do not be elevated by them as if they were from yourself. Had God willed, He would have taken them from you after He gave them to you. God the Glorified and Exalted may take knowledge from a person after He has given it to him, we seek refuge with Allah from that, and perhaps He takes wisdom from him, so that all his conduct becomes frivolity, misguidance and waste.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of will. From where do we take it?
* A student: ﴿to whom He wills﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿to whom He wills﴾, good. And do we say in it the affirmation of wisdom for God?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, in it is the affirmation of wisdom for God the Mighty and Majestic, for wisdom is perfection, and the giver of perfection is more worthy of it; the giver of perfection is more worthy of it, the Mighty and Majestic. So from the verse we take: the affirmation of wisdom for God by this way.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the great honor for the one to whom God has given wisdom, from His saying ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of gratitude upon the one whom God the Most High has given wisdom, for this abundant good requires what? Gratitude.
Also among its benefits: wisdom may have known paths, that is, the paths of wisdom may be many, from His saying ﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾. This is an observed matter: a person acquires wisdom according to his disposition, and acquires it through experiences and practice, is that not so? For this reason, sometimes you accompany a man of virtuous character and you acquire from his character without him teaching you. Sometimes you acquire manners from an ignorant man while you are more knowledgeable than him, is that correct?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is correct and occurs, for manners are other than knowledge.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the excellence of intellect, from His saying ﴿And none will be mindful except those of understanding﴾; for mindfulness is without doubt praiseworthy for a person, so if it occurs only from the possessor of intellect, that indicates the excellence of intellect.
Also among its benefits: that failing to be mindful is foolishness, or not? One who does not take mindfulness and does not take lesson from what has passed and what is present, is in reality not intelligent, or not? Rather we say: he is dead, as al-Mutanabbi said:
"Whoever is humiliated, humiliation becomes easy for him; there is no pain for a wound that is dead."
And this is true; the person who does not take lesson and does not remember is in reality dead, gaining nothing.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that a person without intellect is husks. From where do we take it? From His saying ﴿except those of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾, where He named intellect lubb.

It has passed for us that God the Mighty and Majestic explained that He gives wisdom to whom He wills. So is this will an absolute, bare will, or what?
* A student: A will coupled with wisdom.
* The Shaykh: A will coupled with wisdom? Good. Do we extend this to everything? Whenever a will is mentioned, do we say it is coupled with wisdom?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Good, what is the evidence?
* A student: The evidence is His saying, glorified and exalted, in Surat al-Insan: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾ [al-Insan 76:30].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾ Good, you are correct.
He says: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills.﴾ What is wisdom?
* A student: It is putting a thing in its place.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but only that?
* A student: Knowledge and right guidance.
* The Shaykh: Knowledge and right guidance, good. The evidence that wisdom means knowledge? Here "mā" is conditional (shartiyya), and the evidence that it is conditional?
* A student: It requires a response (talzamuhu).

**The Shaykh:** It is composed of a condition and an answer, ﴿Whatever you spend of expenditure or vow of vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:270]. This answer is ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾.

Second: He says, ﴿whatever you spend of expenditure﴾. The *min* here is *za'idah* (additional), *za'idah*. What is the meaning of "additional, additional"? It means additional in *i'rab* (grammatical case-marking, syntax) and additional in meaning. It is a superfluous preposition in terms of *i'rab*. Therefore we parse ﴿of expenditure﴾ as the direct object: "Whatever you spend, expenditure, or you vow, a vow, indeed Allah knows it."

It is also permissible for the *min* to be explanatory (*bayaniyyah*) of *ma* in His saying ﴿whatever you spend﴾, because the conditional *ma* is vague, and the vague requires clarification.

His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ is the answer of the condition. The *fa'* here falls in the answer of the condition obligatorily. The evidence for this is from the words of Ibn Malik:

*"And join with fa' decisively the answer, if it is made the condition for in or other than it, it will not be made so."*

"Join with fa' decisively" means obligatorily. "The answer, if it is made the condition for *in* or other than it, it will not be made so": here *in* (if) — if *law* were made a condition for *in*, it would not be correct. Therefore it is obligatory to join it with *fa'*. The cases are seven, collected in a line of verse. Who will recite it to us?

**A student:** His saying:

*"Nominal and imperative, and with the rigid, and with ma, qad, la, and with the future (tanfis)."*

**The Shaykh:** *"Nominal and imperative, and with the rigid, and with ma, qad, la, and with the future."*

That is: when the condition clause begins with one of these seven matters, it is obligatory to join it with *fa'*.

Now, ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ — is it an affirmative sentence or a negative one?

**A student:** Negative.

**The Shaykh:** Negative; that is, a sentence of negation, and its subject is His saying ﴿helpers﴾, and the *min* in it is superfluous, superfluous in *i'rab* and superfluous in meaning — that is, it adds to the meaning although it is superfluous in *i'rab*. Therefore we parse ﴿helpers﴾ as a postponed subject, nominative by the inception, and the sign of its nominative is a presumed *damma* at its end, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the vowel of the superfluous preposition.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addresses His servants: Whatever expenditure you spend and whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it. The purpose of the information about knowledge is to clarify what follows from knowledge of recompense. So His saying ﴿whatever you spend of expenditure﴾ includes obligatory expenditures, foremost among them *zakah*, and expenditure is called *infaq* because it goes out (*yakhruj*): a person takes this spent wealth out of his possession. It also includes recommended expenditure, such as charities and spending in acts of righteousness of charitable works and others. Whatever expenditure a person spends, Allah knows it. If he spends it seeking the Face of Allah, he is rewarded for it, even if it is on himself or on his family. The Prophet ﷺ said to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him): *"And know that you will not spend an expenditure"* — *nafaqah* is indefinite in a negative context, so it is general — *"an expenditure by which you seek the Face of Allah, except that you will be rewarded for it, even what you place in the mouth of your wife."* [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (56) and Muslim (1628/5) from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas with the wording: "... even what you place in the mouth of your wife."]

Although a man's spending on his wife is obligatory, it is an exchange (*mu'awadah*) which he can be compelled to. How is it an exchange? Because it is in return for enjoyment of the wife. Even this obligatory matter, from whose return I benefit, if I do it for Allah, I am rewarded for it. Expenditure now includes the obligatory, foremost among it *zakah*, and the recommended, which is everything a person spends for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without obligation upon him, of acts of goodness.

﴿or you vow a vow﴾: a vow means obligating oneself, and what is meant by it is what a person vows upon himself of obedience. ﴿Indeed Allah knows it﴾. The scholars have divided the vow into five categories, and the basic ruling on making it is disliked (*makruh*), because the Prophet ﷺ forbade it. [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6608) and Muslim (1639/4) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.] Whether a person makes it outright or conditionally, it is disliked. Therefore you find many vowing people regretting, and sometimes they go to the people of knowledge, perhaps they find a concession or a release from this vow. As long as a person is in health, he should not obligate himself with what Allah has not obligated him with. Your duty is to clarify to people that making a vow is disliked, so that they do not obligate themselves with it. Then, failing to fulfil it is very grave, for Allah says: ﴿And among them are those who covenanted with Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous." (75) But when He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:75–76]. So what is the punishment? ﴿He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they used to lie﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:77]. But if he vows, and if it is a vow of obedience, it is obligatory upon him to fulfil it, whether it was made outright or conditioned upon a condition, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him."* [Related by al-Bukhari (6696) from the hadith of Aisha.]

﴿or you vow a vow﴾: Does entering into obligatory acts of worship fall under the vow?

Apparently it does, because when a person begins an obligatory act of worship, he is obligated to complete it, even if it is a make-up (*qada'*). If a man fasts a day of making up Ramadan, may he break it? No, because he has begun an obligation, and beginning an obligation is entering into it as something binding upon him and obligatory for him. Therefore the scholars said: whoever begins an obligation, whether it is flexible (*muwassa'*) or restricted (*mudayyaq*), is obligated to complete it.

Fine. Also included in this are conditions (...), for he has imposed it upon himself. This is supported by the saying of the Most High: ﴿Then let them end their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj 22:29].

Then He said: ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:270] — He knows it; that is, He knows whatever you spent or whatever you vowed, whether that thing was apparent and open or hidden and concealed. Why did we say: "whether it is thus or thus"?
