Why did He not say ﴿wa-man yu'tihi al-ḥikmah﴾ (whoever He grants wisdom)? Because He said at the beginning ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah﴾, so why did He say ﴿wa-man yu'ta al-ḥikmah﴾?

The answer, and Allah knows best: wisdom may be innate and may be acquired. That is, a person may gain, through practice and mixing with people, wisdom and good conduct that he would not gain if he were isolated from people. That is why He used the present-tense verb in the passive voice, to encompass all the means by which wisdom comes, whether one is given wisdom from Allah the Mighty and Majestic or through practice and experience. And what is gained of wisdom through practice and experience is also from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. It is He who has arranged for you someone who opens for you the doors of wisdom and the doors of good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 268–270 (part 2 of 3):

He says: ﴿And none will be mindful except those of understanding.﴾ ﴿Mindful (yadhdhakkaru)﴾ means being admonished and taking lesson from matters, their courses, their outcomes and their fruits. ﴿None except those of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾ means the people possessing ﴿al-albab﴾, that is, the intellects; for al-albab is the plural of (lubb) (kernel, i.e., the core of the mind), which is the intellect ('aql). The people of intellect are those who take heed, whether that concerns the established precedents God has applied to His servants in punishing the deniers and destroying the criminals, or what occurs in the experiences of life in their own time. As it is said: "The intelligent person is one who learns from others." Every intelligent person draws lessons and studies from events; that is why you find him looking, reflecting, and comparing the past with the present and the future with the present in order to reach a conclusion. As for one who has no intellect, he is heedless, heedless and not mindful: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus 10:101].

If someone asks: Is lubb intelligence (dhaka') or something else?
* A student: It is intelligence.
* The Shaykh: No. We have said that lubb is 'aql (intellect), and 'aql is other than dhaka' (intelligence). A disbeliever may be extremely intelligent yet extremely foolish, and for this reason God described the disbelievers as ﴿deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171].
﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but calls and cries: deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171].
Therefore, however much we see of the politics and cleverness of disbelieving nations, we should never say they are people of intellect. How can God say ﴿so they do not understand﴾ while you say they are intelligent?! Rather we say: they are clever (adhkiya'), and intelligence does not necessarily entail intellect. Intellect is good conduct, and it is called 'aql because it restrains (ya'qilu) its possessor from what harms him. Intelligence (dhaka') is sharpness of perception and understanding, which may be praised or not praised. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Fatwa al-Hamawiyya concerning the theologians (mutakallimun): "They were given dhaka' but were not given dhaka'." Is this a complete pun (jinas tam) or an incomplete one?
* The students: Incomplete.
* The Shaykh: An incomplete pun. Apparently you do not yet know what jinas is...
And the transmitted sciences, and they are the ones who claim that they are...? That they are the intelligent ones, the people of intellect. The point is that ﴿al-albab﴾ is the plural of lubb, which is 'aql, and 'aql is something other than dhaka', is it not?
* The students: Yes, other than it.
* The Shaykh: Other than dhaka'. For this reason I tell you that the geniuses of disbelievers in intelligence should never be called intellectuals, not at all. What do we call them?
* The students: Clever.
* The Shaykh: Clever. But intellectuals, no.

Several benefits are derived from this noble verse.
* A student: The previous verse.
* The Shaykh: Good, the verse before it: ﴿The Satan promises you poverty and commands you to indecency﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:268], and so on to its end.
* From this noble verse is derived: the affirmation of devils, from His saying ﴿the Satan﴾. It has already been mentioned that what is meant by "Satan" here is the genus, not a specific individual by his person; specific by what? By his kind, i.e., the genus of devils.
* Among the benefits of the verse: Satan has an influence on the children of Adam, whether to proceed or to refrain. When he promises poverty and commands stinginess, the implication of that is refraining and not giving.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the doors of pessimism (tasha'um) are opened only by devils, from His saying ﴿He promises you poverty﴾. Satan is the one who opens the door of pessimism for you. He says: If you spend, and you now have twenty riyals, you spend ten today, and the next day five, how much remains? Five; and tomorrow three; two riyals remain, and after that two more, and you have become poor. Do not spend. A human being is human, and perhaps he does not spend, perhaps he forgets the saying of God Most High: ﴿Whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba' 34:39], and the saying of His Messenger (ﷺ): "Charity does not diminish wealth"[[Narrated by Muslim (2588/69) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of Satan's enmity toward man, for in reality he is an enemy to him in information and an enemy in command. In information he promises him what? Poverty. In command he orders him to indecency. So he is an enemy both in information and in command, and we seek refuge with Allah.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: stinginess is among the indecencies, is it not? Why? Because the context is the context of spending, so what Satan commands us to do is not spending. But is stinginess itself the indecency, or is it part of the indecency? It is part of the indecency. We mentioned during the tafsir that indecency (fahsha') comes in other senses in several verses.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Satan commands after whispering, exaggeration, and pessimism. He commands, saying: Do not spend, or does he say: Withhold?
* A student: Do not spend.
* A student: Withhold.
* The Shaykh: Be attentive.
* A student: The same thing.
* The Shaykh: One and two. Shall we say: Withhold, or do not spend?
* Students: Withhold.
* Students: Do not spend.
* A student: He says "do not spend," shaykh.
* The Shaykh: ﴿He commands you﴾?
* The students: "Withhold"?
* The Shaykh: Withhold, which? Withhold; because if we say "do not spend," it is a prohibition, and so the command becomes of the type of the necessary. But if we say "withhold"?
* A student: It becomes congruent.
* The Shaykh: It becomes congruent. Then the word "withhold" is stronger than "do not spend," as if he says: do not spend, and emphasize in retention: withhold.
Is there anyone other than Satan who commands this?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And what is he?
* A student: The self (nafs).
* The Shaykh: The self: ﴿And I do not absolve myself; indeed the self is ever commanding to evil﴾ [Yusuf 12:53].
Can we say: it is derived from the verse that whoever commands a person to withhold from spending is similar to Satan?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Is that so? Correct. One who commands people to withhold from lawful spending, and not from unlawful spending, is similar to whom? To Satan. One who commands another to lavish spending?
* A student: He is a brother of Satan.
* The Shaykh: The squanderer is a brother of Satan: ﴿Indeed the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isra' 17:27]. And the one who commands him to squander? Apparently he is a devil, for everyone who commands evil commands indecency, so he is a devil.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: look at this promise, the generous and delightful promise: ﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾. Allahu akbar! How far apart are the two promises: Satan promises you poverty, ﴿and Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾.
Someone may say: Is there correspondence (tatabuq) in the two verses, or, more precisely, antithesis (taqabul)? ﴿He promises you poverty﴾, but God says ﴿He promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾. Did He add or not add?
* The students: He added.
* The Shaykh: That is, He promises us two things: forgiveness and bounty. Forgiveness for sins, and bounty for the increase of wealth in its blessing and growth. Is that clear or not? So we gain through spending these two matters which God Most High has promised: forgiveness and bounty.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: this forgiveness with which God promises us is great forgiveness. ﴿From Himself﴾, why? Because the greatness of the gift follows the greatness of the Giver. For this reason it came in the hadith which the Prophet (ﷺ) advised Abu Bakr with, he said: "So forgive me with forgiveness from Yourself, and have mercy on me"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (834) and Muslim (2705/48) from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.]]. It is known that a gift is according to the giver: ﴿forgiveness from Himself and bounty﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that optimism (tafa'ul) from Allah. From where?
* The students: "He promises you" — God promises you.
* The Shaykh: ﴿He promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty.﴾ So when a person is optimistic toward his Lord when he spends, and he thinks well of God the Mighty and Majestic, that God will forgive his sins and increase him from His bounty, this is among the best of what the inner heart holds.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of two of God's names, which are al-Wasi' (the All-Encompassing) and al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), and the affirmation of two of His attributes: vastness (sa'a) and knowledge ('ilm). If someone says: From where did you affirm vastness?
* The students: From "Wasi'."
* The Shaykh: From "Wasi'." And does the name indicate the attribute?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Certainly?
* Students: Yes, certainly.
* The Shaykh: I do not know, certainly? Certainly?
* The students: Shaykh, certainly, shaykh.
* The Shaykh: Does "al-Sami'" indicate hearing?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And "al-'Alim"?
* The students: It indicates knowledge.
* The Shaykh: It indicates knowledge. Every name of God necessarily indicates an attribute, and it has already passed us that faith in a name is not complete until you believe that it is a name of God and that it includes an attribute of His which that name indicates, and you believe in its effect where it is from a transitive attribute. Is that clear? And there is no need, brothers, to say: Bring evidence for affirming the attribute, for the Arabic language is the evidence. The Qur'an was revealed in what language? In the Arabic language. It is impossible in Arabic to say "al-Sami'" of one who has no hearing, nor "al-Wasi'" of one who has no vastness, nor "al-Hakim" of one who has no wisdom. Whoever claims that Arabic uses such names without affirming the meaning they include is either a liar against the Arabic language or ignorant of it, is it not? Either a liar or ignorant. But a man who knows the Arabic language and is truthful about what he says about it must say that every derived name indicates the attribute it includes, without exception. If I saw a blind man and said, "Masha' Allah, this man is the seeing one," what would you say?
* The students: Optimism.
* The Shaykh: No, not optimism at all, truly.
* The students: Wrong.
* The Shaykh: You would say, how is this man "the seeing one," when he is blind and cannot see? You would call him seeing?!
A man who has cannons next to him and does not hear; masha' Allah, the man came to me, "the hearing one." What do you say? You say: this speech is madness; how is he hearing when he has no hearing?! Is that clear? Yes. Some of the brothers present now told me that someone says: What is the evidence that God has hearing? What do you say to this? We say: Bring the evidence that you have intellect before we give you the evidence that God has hearing. Is it possible, by intellect or language or custom, to say "al-Sami'" of one who has no hearing?
* The students: No.
* The Shaykh: Never, it is not possible. But some people have had the door of ijtihad opened to them, and I say: I thank and praise Allah that He, glorious and exalted, has made it easy for us, or opened for us, the seeking of evidence. But seeking evidence for everything, even where the evidence is clear, and saying "What is the evidence?" Is this correct? This is extravagance (israf); this is extravagance, not seeking evidence.
* A student: The third attribute, shaykh?
* The Shaykh: Yes?
* A student: The breadth of knowledge.
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is also derived from the two names and the two attributes: the affirmation of a third attribute by their combination. For we have said previously, the rule is that a name of God may, when joined with another, include another attribute: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning, Forgiving﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:43]. Look at the combination of pardon and power; it has the distinction that His pardon is not mixed with incapacity at all. Why? Because some people pardon out of incapacity. A man snatched another's turban and fled with it; the one robbed ran after him, and when he could not catch him, he said: "I forgive you." What is this pardon?
* The students: Incapacity.
* The Shaykh: Is this praiseworthy or not?
* The students: No, not praiseworthy.
* The Shaykh: God knows best. In any case, he is weak; perhaps he will benefit from it in the Hereafter, that he will not be held to account for it, but he is weak without doubt. But that God is "Pardoning, Capable": this is perfection.
So ﴿All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: what is the third attribute that arises from this? That His knowledge is all-encompassing, and all His attributes are all-encompassing. This is derived from His name al-Wasi': His knowledge, His hearing, His sight, His power, all His attributes.
Then He said: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:269], to its end.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of God's actions that are connected with His will?
* A student: In His saying ﴿All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾, that the vastness of God Most High (...)
* The Shaykh: No, everything.
* A student: That charity increases wealth.
* The Shaykh: What do you say? Charity increases wealth, derived from His saying ﴿and bounty﴾.
From the second verse is derived: the affirmation of God the Mighty and Majestic's actions that are connected with His will, from His saying ﴿He gives wisdom﴾, and this is among the attributes of what?
* The students: The active ones.
* The Shaykh: The active attributes, among the active attributes.
* Among its benefits: that what is in a human being of knowledge and right guidance is a bounty from God the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾. So if God has favored you with knowledge, right guidance, strength, power, hearing and sight, do not be elevated by them as if they were from yourself. Had God willed, He would have taken them from you after He gave them to you. God the Glorified and Exalted may take knowledge from a person after He has given it to him, we seek refuge with Allah from that, and perhaps He takes wisdom from him, so that all his conduct becomes frivolity, misguidance and waste.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of will. From where do we take it?
* A student: ﴿to whom He wills﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿to whom He wills﴾, good. And do we say in it the affirmation of wisdom for God?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, in it is the affirmation of wisdom for God the Mighty and Majestic, for wisdom is perfection, and the giver of perfection is more worthy of it; the giver of perfection is more worthy of it, the Mighty and Majestic. So from the verse we take: the affirmation of wisdom for God by this way.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the great honor for the one to whom God has given wisdom, from His saying ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾.
* Among its benefits: the obligation of gratitude upon the one whom God the Most High has given wisdom, for this abundant good requires what? Gratitude.
Also among its benefits: wisdom may have known paths, that is, the paths of wisdom may be many, from His saying ﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾. This is an observed matter: a person acquires wisdom according to his disposition, and acquires it through experiences and practice, is that not so? For this reason, sometimes you accompany a man of virtuous character and you acquire from his character without him teaching you. Sometimes you acquire manners from an ignorant man while you are more knowledgeable than him, is that correct?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is correct and occurs, for manners are other than knowledge.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the excellence of intellect, from His saying ﴿And none will be mindful except those of understanding﴾; for mindfulness is without doubt praiseworthy for a person, so if it occurs only from the possessor of intellect, that indicates the excellence of intellect.
Also among its benefits: that failing to be mindful is foolishness, or not? One who does not take mindfulness and does not take lesson from what has passed and what is present, is in reality not intelligent, or not? Rather we say: he is dead, as al-Mutanabbi said:
"Whoever is humiliated, humiliation becomes easy for him; there is no pain for a wound that is dead."
And this is true; the person who does not take lesson and does not remember is in reality dead, gaining nothing.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that a person without intellect is husks. From where do we take it? From His saying ﴿except those of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾, where He named intellect lubb.

It has passed for us that God the Mighty and Majestic explained that He gives wisdom to whom He wills. So is this will an absolute, bare will, or what?
* A student: A will coupled with wisdom.
* The Shaykh: A will coupled with wisdom? Good. Do we extend this to everything? Whenever a will is mentioned, do we say it is coupled with wisdom?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Good, what is the evidence?
* A student: The evidence is His saying, glorified and exalted, in Surat al-Insan: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾ [al-Insan 76:30].
* The Shaykh: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾ Good, you are correct.
He says: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills.﴾ What is wisdom?
* A student: It is putting a thing in its place.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but only that?
* A student: Knowledge and right guidance.
* The Shaykh: Knowledge and right guidance, good. The evidence that wisdom means knowledge? Here "mā" is conditional (shartiyya), and the evidence that it is conditional?
* A student: It requires a response (talzamuhu).

**The Shaykh:** It is composed of a condition and an answer, ﴿Whatever you spend of expenditure or vow of vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:270]. This answer is ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾.

Second: He says, ﴿whatever you spend of expenditure﴾. The *min* here is *za'idah* (additional), *za'idah*. What is the meaning of "additional, additional"? It means additional in *i'rab* (grammatical case-marking, syntax) and additional in meaning. It is a superfluous preposition in terms of *i'rab*. Therefore we parse ﴿of expenditure﴾ as the direct object: "Whatever you spend, expenditure, or you vow, a vow, indeed Allah knows it."

It is also permissible for the *min* to be explanatory (*bayaniyyah*) of *ma* in His saying ﴿whatever you spend﴾, because the conditional *ma* is vague, and the vague requires clarification.

His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ is the answer of the condition. The *fa'* here falls in the answer of the condition obligatorily. The evidence for this is from the words of Ibn Malik:

*"And join with fa' decisively the answer, if it is made the condition for in or other than it, it will not be made so."*

"Join with fa' decisively" means obligatorily. "The answer, if it is made the condition for *in* or other than it, it will not be made so": here *in* (if) — if *law* were made a condition for *in*, it would not be correct. Therefore it is obligatory to join it with *fa'*. The cases are seven, collected in a line of verse. Who will recite it to us?

**A student:** His saying:

*"Nominal and imperative, and with the rigid, and with ma, qad, la, and with the future (tanfis)."*

**The Shaykh:** *"Nominal and imperative, and with the rigid, and with ma, qad, la, and with the future."*

That is: when the condition clause begins with one of these seven matters, it is obligatory to join it with *fa'*.

Now, ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ — is it an affirmative sentence or a negative one?

**A student:** Negative.

**The Shaykh:** Negative; that is, a sentence of negation, and its subject is His saying ﴿helpers﴾, and the *min* in it is superfluous, superfluous in *i'rab* and superfluous in meaning — that is, it adds to the meaning although it is superfluous in *i'rab*. Therefore we parse ﴿helpers﴾ as a postponed subject, nominative by the inception, and the sign of its nominative is a presumed *damma* at its end, prevented from appearing by the occupation of the place by the vowel of the superfluous preposition.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, addresses His servants: Whatever expenditure you spend and whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it. The purpose of the information about knowledge is to clarify what follows from knowledge of recompense. So His saying ﴿whatever you spend of expenditure﴾ includes obligatory expenditures, foremost among them *zakah*, and expenditure is called *infaq* because it goes out (*yakhruj*): a person takes this spent wealth out of his possession. It also includes recommended expenditure, such as charities and spending in acts of righteousness of charitable works and others. Whatever expenditure a person spends, Allah knows it. If he spends it seeking the Face of Allah, he is rewarded for it, even if it is on himself or on his family. The Prophet ﷺ said to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him): *"And know that you will not spend an expenditure"* — *nafaqah* is indefinite in a negative context, so it is general — *"an expenditure by which you seek the Face of Allah, except that you will be rewarded for it, even what you place in the mouth of your wife."* [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (56) and Muslim (1628/5) from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas with the wording: "... even what you place in the mouth of your wife."]

Although a man's spending on his wife is obligatory, it is an exchange (*mu'awadah*) which he can be compelled to. How is it an exchange? Because it is in return for enjoyment of the wife. Even this obligatory matter, from whose return I benefit, if I do it for Allah, I am rewarded for it. Expenditure now includes the obligatory, foremost among it *zakah*, and the recommended, which is everything a person spends for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, without obligation upon him, of acts of goodness.

﴿or you vow a vow﴾: a vow means obligating oneself, and what is meant by it is what a person vows upon himself of obedience. ﴿Indeed Allah knows it﴾. The scholars have divided the vow into five categories, and the basic ruling on making it is disliked (*makruh*), because the Prophet ﷺ forbade it. [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (6608) and Muslim (1639/4) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.] Whether a person makes it outright or conditionally, it is disliked. Therefore you find many vowing people regretting, and sometimes they go to the people of knowledge, perhaps they find a concession or a release from this vow. As long as a person is in health, he should not obligate himself with what Allah has not obligated him with. Your duty is to clarify to people that making a vow is disliked, so that they do not obligate themselves with it. Then, failing to fulfil it is very grave, for Allah says: ﴿And among them are those who covenanted with Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous." (75) But when He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:75–76]. So what is the punishment? ﴿He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they used to lie﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:77]. But if he vows, and if it is a vow of obedience, it is obligatory upon him to fulfil it, whether it was made outright or conditioned upon a condition, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Whoever vows to obey Allah, let him obey Him."* [Related by al-Bukhari (6696) from the hadith of Aisha.]

﴿or you vow a vow﴾: Does entering into obligatory acts of worship fall under the vow?

Apparently it does, because when a person begins an obligatory act of worship, he is obligated to complete it, even if it is a make-up (*qada'*). If a man fasts a day of making up Ramadan, may he break it? No, because he has begun an obligation, and beginning an obligation is entering into it as something binding upon him and obligatory for him. Therefore the scholars said: whoever begins an obligation, whether it is flexible (*muwassa'*) or restricted (*mudayyaq*), is obligated to complete it.

Fine. Also included in this are conditions (...), for he has imposed it upon himself. This is supported by the saying of the Most High: ﴿Then let them end their untidiness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj 22:29].

Then He said: ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:270] — He knows it; that is, He knows whatever you spent or whatever you vowed, whether that thing was apparent and open or hidden and concealed. Why did we say: "whether it is thus or thus"?

Because of the generality of His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾. He did not say "He knows its apparent aspect," but rather He knows the apparent and the hidden. And the generality of "He knows it" includes His knowledge in summary and in detail. The benefit of mentioning Allah's knowledge of it is an indication of the recompense that follows from that knowledge. Otherwise, merely knowing that Allah knows it, without being aware of what that knowledge entails, has no benefit.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. That is: there is no one for the wrongdoers to help them, neither from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, nor from creatures. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. But an objection may be raised against us: wrongdoers may find those among the oppressors who help them, isn't that so? We say: yes, there are those among the oppressors who help them, but their final end is all to abandonment, due to the saying of Allah, the Most High: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ [al-An'am 6:21]. The wrongdoer never succeeds, however high the world may raise him, he will surely descend, and however numerous his helpers, he will surely be forsaken. It is impossible for him to be granted success. But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may sometimes enable him so that He may destroy him, as Allah, the Most High, mentioned in the benefits of the defeat at Uhud, for Allah mentioned among its benefits that He might destroy the disbelievers, because the disbeliever, if he feels victory, becomes arrogant and his tyranny increases; when his tyranny increases, his destruction and ruin draw near. So we respond to this objection, or this objection's assertion, that the wrongdoers and their helpers have as their end abandonment, and even if they support one another, they will never succeed.

This verse includes many benefits. The first benefit: that expenditure, whether little or much, a person is rewarded for it. From where is it taken?

**A student:** (...)

**The Shaykh:** In a context of negation?

**A student:** Or the condition.

**The Shaykh:** The condition.

**A student:** Yes indeed.

**The Shaykh:** Better than your saying "or the condition" is to say "rather, the condition." Good. It includes the little and the much.

The stipulation of sincerity in expenditure: can it be derived from the verse? Because expenditure without sincerity is of no benefit. How is it derived?

**A student:** From the saying of Allah, the Most High: ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾.

**The Shaykh:** From His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, for this implies reward for it, and there is no reward for anything in which there is no sincerity.

Among the benefits of the verse: it is appropriate for a person, when he spends an expenditure, to seek the reward from Allah. From where is it taken, that when a person spends an expenditure, he should seek the reward from Allah, Mighty and Majestic?

**A student:** ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾.

**The Shaykh:** From His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, because if you spend while you feel that Allah knows this expenditure, you will seek the reward from Allah.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of vowing?

**A student:** There is no permissibility in it.

**The Shaykh:** There is not, how?

**The student:** Because Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿or you vow﴾; this is a restriction, restricted by the condition, "if you vow..."

**The Shaykh:** That is, it does not give an explanation of the ruling on vowing?

**The student:** It does not give it.

**The Shaykh:** But it does give that Allah knows it; then the person may be punished for it, and he may not be punished. What do you say? The verse is correct: it does not indicate permissibility, just as if someone said, for example: "If you steal, indeed Allah knows your theft." Does this indicate that theft is permissible? No. Therefore we do not say that the verse contradicts the hadith forbidding vowing from the Prophet ﷺ, because it does not indicate its permissibility. But if a person vows, it becomes obligatory upon him to fulfil it if his vow is an act of obedience.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's, Mighty and Majestic, knowledge. From where is it derived?

**A student:** ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾.

**The Shaykh:** What is the aspect of generality?

**The student:** Every expenditure or vow, indeed Allah knows it.

**The Shaykh:** That ﴿whatever you spend﴾ is general, because conditional particles indicate generality.

* And among the benefits of the verse: the refutation of the extreme Qadariyyah (those who deny divine foreknowledge)?

**A student:** They say that Allah, glorified and exalted, does not know the thing (...)

**The Shaykh:** That Allah does not know the thing; and some of them say He does not know things at all, and that a person is independent in his deeds, and Allah has no intervention in them whatsoever. But the verse refutes them. As for whoever among them says that Allah knows a thing after it occurs, the verse does not refute him, because the verse is explicit that Allah knows it after its occurrence.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, does not help the wrongdoer.

**A student:** ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾.

**The Shaykh:** Good. But this is objected to by what occurred at Uhud, that Allah, glorified and exalted, granted victory to the disbelievers.

**A student:** We say: their victory was for a wisdom from Allah, glorified and exalted, which is to discipline the believers for disobeying the Messenger ﷺ, and He had permitted in the battle that they not pursue the Prophet ﷺ, and this (...)

**The Shaykh:** We say in this: Allah's granting victory to those disbelievers was not in order that they should triumph over the Muslims, but for punishment because of what occurred: ﴿until, when you lost heart and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He showed you what you love﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:152]. Then, is this victory a perpetual victory? No, because Allah mentioned that this was to entice the disbelievers in their disbelief and tyranny, so that He might utterly destroy them.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever supplicates against his brother while the latter is wronging him, Allah does not answer his supplication.

**A student:** I say: this one, who supplicated against his brother while he was wronging him, may Allah not grant his brother success apart from him.

**The Shaykh:** Yes; for if it were answered, it would be a victory for him. Based on this, if you testify about a person with a right, and he supplicates against you, saying: "May Allah not profit so-and-so, the one who knew about me," is his supplication accepted or not? No; because he is a wrongdoer, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, never helps the wrongdoers: ﴿and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. Allah, glorified and exalted, is too wise and too just to help the wrongdoer. Many people now fear the supplication of a person even if he is a wrongdoer. But we say: be at ease, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will not help the wrongdoer and will not answer his supplication. But reflect on yourself: are you a wrongdoer or not? For perhaps there is wrongdoing from you, so his supplication is answered because of your wrongdoing, while you are unaware. But if he is a wrongdoer with pure wrongdoing, it will not be answered.

Is there also reward for little and much?

**A student:** He, glorified, says: ﴿whatever expenditure you spend﴾; expenditure includes the little and the much.

**The Shaykh:** Good. Is there anything in the Qur'an that testifies to this?

**A student:** ﴿And they do not spend an expenditure, small or large﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:121].

**The Shaykh:** ﴿This is the wealth of this Book﴾ [al-Kahf 18:49].

**A student:** No, in expenditure.

**The Shaykh:** ﴿And they do not spend an expenditure, small or large﴾. Good. Is there anything else besides it?

**A student:** The verse in Surah al-Kahf, the saying of Allah, the Most High: ﴿This is the wealth of this Book; it leaves nothing small or great but it has counted it, and they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ [al-Kahf 18:49].

**The Shaykh:** Good. And at the end of Surah al-Zalzalah: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it (7), and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:7–8].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 271:

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah 271]

Grammar (al-I'rab): Here there is a conditional sentence (jumlah shartiyyah). I can pose a question to you: is there a conditional sentence here?

* Student: "In" (إن) is a conditional particle.

* Shaykh: Just show me the conditional sentence; I do not want its grammatical analysis.

* Student: ﴿In tubdu al-sadaqat﴾.

* Shaykh: What is the evidence that it is conditional?

* Student: The response of the condition, ﴿fa-ni'immā hiya﴾.

* Shaykh: Good, excellent.

Second: In ﴿fa-ni'immā hiya﴾, why is ni'ma combined with the fa'?

* Student: It is a nominal sentence.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: ﴿Fa-ni'immā hiya﴾ is an invariable verb (fi'l jamid).

* Shaykh: Because it is an invariable verb.

Nominal and imperative [sentences], and with an invariable verb ... [verse-poem incomplete in the source]

There is also another conditional sentence here in which the response is combined with fa'. What is the reason?

* Student: ﴿Fa-huwa khayrun lakum﴾.

* Shaykh: Is ﴿fa-huwa khayrun lakum﴾ combined with the verb because it is a sentence?

* Students: Nominal.

* Shaykh: Nominal.

Here there is a difficulty: ﴿wa-yukaffiru 'ankum min sayyi'atikum﴾ is in the raised form (marfu'), though it is coordinated with the response clause ﴿fa-huwa khayrun lakum﴾, and he did not say "wa-yukaffir" (jussive). Why?

* Student: Because it is coordinated to the place (al-mahall).

* Shaykh: The place?

* Student: The nominal clause's place is raised.

* Shaykh: No, its place is jussive. This nominal clause ﴿fa-huwa khayrun lakum﴾ has a jussive place.

* Student: We say, O Shaykh: the waw is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah).

* Shaykh: Correct. We say: the waw is resumptive. This is according to the reading with the raised form. There is a second and third reading: ﴿wa-nukaffir﴾ and ﴿wa-nukaffiru﴾, and ﴿nukaffir﴾ as jussive, coordinated to the place of the response of the condition, which is jussive. ﴿Wa-nukaffiru﴾ as resumptive. So the readings there are three: ﴿wa-yukaffiru﴾, ﴿wa-nukaffir﴾, ﴿wa-nukaffiru﴾.

Regarding ﴿min sayyi'atikum﴾: Shall we say that min here is superfluous (za'idah)? Because this construction always comes without min, as in His saying: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives; that is better for you, if you knew. He will forgive you your sins﴾ [al-Saff 11-12].

* Student: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion and will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Anfal 29]. ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds﴾ [Al 'Imran 193]. So shall we say that min here is superfluous, or that min is not superfluous?

* Student: The second; the second is the correct analysis.

* Shaykh: The second is the required one, because min is not added in affirmative statements, as Ibn Malik said:

"It is added in negation and what resembles it, so it draws a indefinite noun, as for the fugitive there is no escape (min mafar)."

"Zaida" means min.

So min is for partitiveness (tab'id), and "He will remove from you some of your misdeeds."

Regarding ﴿wa-yukaffiru 'ankum min sayyi'atikum﴾: there is no difficulty in it, and the rest of the verse has no grammatical difficulty.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾, meaning: you make them apparent. Disclosure is of two kinds: general disclosure and specific disclosure. General disclosure is that a person stands in a large gathering and gives charity, or says: "I have given charity." Specific disclosure is that he gives charity to a poor person in a small gathering, or informs others afterward that he has given charity, because "disclosure" (ibda') includes disclosing the charity at the time of giving it and disclosing it afterward by reporting it. The charities here include both obligatory zakat and voluntary charity. Is zakat a sadaqah? Yes, because Allah said in Surat al-Tawbah: ﴿Charities are only for the poor and the needy﴾ [al-Tawbah 60]. It is called sadaqah, they say, because it indicates the truthfulness of faith (sidq al-iman). How does it indicate the truthfulness of faith?

Wealth is among the things most beloved to a person. Allah said: ﴿And you love wealth with immense love﴾ [al-Fajr 20]. When a person displays this beloved thing for a promised reward not yet present, that is, he displays something present for something promised, this indicates the truthfulness of his faith, does it not? Yes, it indicates the truthfulness of faith. A person now has wealth in his hand, and wealth is dear to him, and the common people say a phrase: "Wealth is what?"

* Student: "Equal to the soul" (adl al-ruh).

* Shaykh: "Equal to the soul"? Good. He says: this wealth, which is among the most beloved things to him, he gives out because he was promised reward for it. So whoever gives out the present beloved thing for a promised matter is undoubtedly a believer. Therefore it was called sadaqah.

﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent﴾: this is an expressive sentence (jumlah insha'iyyah) praising them, meaning: they are good, and an excellent charity is one that is disclosed, because it is beneficial. But there is a better state than it, which is His saying: ﴿But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾.

* Student: Shaykh, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows it﴾.

* Shaykh: It may be in the Hereafter, and it may be in both, except misdeeds: if they are recompensed in this world, they are not recompensed in the Hereafter.

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And whatever expenditure you spend or vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. Let us take its benefits.

* Student: The second verse.

* Shaykh: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ Have we completed its explanation?

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: Good. He says: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent﴾, meaning: excellent is a thing; the praise of them is absolute, because charity is a benefit extending to others and a kindness to people, and Allah loves the doers of good. Therefore Allah praised charities whether they were disclosed or concealed. But He says: ﴿But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾.

He said: ﴿And if you conceal them﴾, meaning: do not announce them, but keep them secret.

﴿And give them to the poor﴾, meaning by way of example, because the poor are the people of charity; and if one gives them to others who deserve charity, it is the same.

His saying ﴿give them to the poor﴾ implies that they must reach them. As for a person who intends to give this wealth in charity but it does not reach the poor, he is not recorded as having the reward of charity. Therefore a person is free to either carry out the charity or withhold it.

His saying ﴿it is better for you﴾, meaning: than disclosing and displaying it.

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾. In His saying ﴿wa-yukaffiru﴾ there are three Sab'i readings: ﴿yukaffiru﴾ with ya' and damm on the ra', ﴿nukaffir﴾ with nun and sukun on the ra', ﴿nukaffiru﴾ also with nun and damm on the ra'. As for the jussive reading ﴿nukaffir 'ankum﴾, it is coordinated to the place of His saying ﴿fa-huwa khayrun lakum﴾, because its place is jussive as it is the response of the condition; and as for the raised reading, it is resumptive.

His saying ﴿min sayyi'atikum﴾ may be partitive, meaning that charity does not remove all misdeeds but removes some of them; it may also be explanatory (bayaniyyah), but the first is closer. And misdeeds (sayyi'at) are what distress a person.

Does a misdeed distress a person in this world and the Hereafter, or in the Hereafter only?

The answer: In the Hereafter there is no doubt that it distresses a person, because he finds its reward turned into punishment. In this world, it may also distress him, because the soul's joy in disobedience is followed by sorrow and grief. Disobedient people, even if they appear joyful in practicing these sins that suit the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammarah bi'l-su'), behind the commanding soul there is a self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah) that blames committing sin, and that joy is followed by sorrow. This applies to one in whose heart there is life. As for one whose heart is dead, he does not grieve, even if he commits whatever sin.

Whoever is humiliated, ease comes to him from humiliation; there is no pain for a dead wound.

These are people whose hearts Allah has sealed, so they never grieve over committing sins. But the believer must grieve. Some people even find at times within themselves distress and constriction and do not know a clear apparent cause, but when they remember, they find that they committed a sin or became heedless of remembrance, or the like.

Some people also commit some prohibited acts, and when they finish, they find distress and grief immediately. This is one of Allah's blessings upon His servant, that such emotional reaction occurs when he neglects a duty or violates a prohibition. I think it has passed before you when the Messenger ﷺ finished two rak'ahs of one of his afternoon prayers, then went to a wooden post placed in the mosque and leaned on it as if angry, because his soul was constricted when he had not completed his prayer. And a man whom I trust told me, in our time not long ago, that a man known for piety, who would eat only what he earned with his hand, and who was a camel-driver carrying loads on his camel, went out one day to load his camel with cut acacia wood (athl), do you know the athl? They used to cut it and bring it into houses to be used as firewood. He made the camel kneel beside a pile like a bundle of wood, loaded the wood on it and tied it. The camel stood up, but he struck it, and it refused to rise; whenever he made it rise, it refused to stand, and this was not its habit. He remained silent about it, then returned, then remained silent, then returned; it refused. He reflected, or God opened to him to look, so he turned right and left, and behold, the wood that was his was not loaded, and he had loaded his neighbour's wood. Yes, this is a confirmed and reliable report. So he put the wood down in its place, the camel stood up with complete ease, and he made it kneel there and loaded it. This is from Allah's gentleness toward a person: sometimes Allah prevents him from something that, had he known of it, he would not have done; so Allah comes between him and that thing He does not approve of, were he aware of it. In sum, a misdeed distresses the believer in this world and the Hereafter unless Allah pardons it. As for the disbeliever, it distresses him in the Hereafter, but not in this world; yet even so he may be punished for it.

He said: ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾. His saying ﴿with what you do﴾ is connected to ﴿Acquainted﴾. The Khabir is one of Allah's names, meaning the Possessor of knowledge, and khibrah is knowledge of the inner aspects of matters. Its root is from al-khibar, meaning sowing, because a person places seed in the earth hidden; and from the hadith: he forbade al-mukhabarah [agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2381) and Muslim (1536/82) from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah]. So Khabir means the All-Knowing of inner matters, and we all know that one who knows inner matters knows outer matters all the more. Here there is a question about His saying ﴿bi-ma ta'malun khabir﴾, where ﴿bi-ma ta'malun﴾ is placed first, while sometimes ﴿khabir﴾ is placed before ﴿bi-ma ta'malun﴾, as in: ﴿and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Al 'Imran 153]. It is said that placing it first here is for restriction (hasr), but it is a relative restriction, because Allah is Acquainted with what we do, and Acquainted with what we do not do, and Acquainted with what we humans do, and what other animals do, and Acquainted with everything. But He placed it first for emphasis on it and as a warning against disobedience, as if He says: even if He were acquainted with nothing else, He is acquainted with what you do, so beware.

* Student: The fawasil (verse-endings).

* Shaykh: The fawasil. No, a person may say it is separated by the nun.

[Good, whether he conceals it or displays it; by His saying: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 271].]

Among its benefits: concealing charity is better, by His saying ﴿it is better for you﴾, and by the authentic hadith: "Seven will be shaded by Allah in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade," and among them is mentioned: "a man who gave charity and concealed it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends" [related by al-Bukhari (1423) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. But disclosure may in some cases be better than concealment, as if this poor person asked us to help and assist him, and you displayed the charity to him so that people would follow your example; this would be better.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the superiority of deeds, that some deeds are better than others, by His saying ﴿it is better for you﴾. The superiority of deeds entails the superiority of the doer, does it not? Yes, because a person is honored and distinguished by his deed. The superiority of deeds entails increase in faith, because faith is speech and action; when deeds vary in excellence, faith varies. All this is evidence for the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, that deeds and doers differ in excellence. We mentioned earlier that the excellence of a deed has six or seven causes, which passed before us; review them. So here there is the superiority of deeds, which entails the superiority of faith, and the People of the Sunnah and the Community believe that faith increases and decreases, as will come, Allah willing, in creed (al-'aqidah).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that charity is a cause of the expiation of misdeeds, by His saying ﴿and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾ [al-Baqarah 271] in the reading. This is also supported, indeed confirmed, by the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire, and a man's prayer in the depth of the night," then he recited: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾ [related by al-Tirmidhi (2616) and Ibn Majah (3973) from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of Allah's voluntary actions, as is the position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, the meaning of "voluntary" being what He does by His will and volition. It does not mean that Allah may be compelled to act; no, by His saying ﴿and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the demonstration of the effects of sins, that they distress the servant, by His saying ﴿of your misdeeds﴾.

Among them: affirmation of the name of Allah, the Khabir, and affirmation of the attribute it indicates.

Among them: warning the servant against disobedience, by His saying ﴿and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah 271]; for His informing us of this entails that we should fear His knowledge, so He does not miss us where He has commanded us, and does not see us where He has forbidden us.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272]. The address here is to the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾: the pronoun refers to the children of Adam, and the guidance negated here is the guidance of tawfiq (divine enabling). As for the guidance of bayan (clarification), it is incumbent upon the Messenger ﷺ, due to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:67], and His saying: ﴿Upon you is only the conveyance﴾ [Ash-Shura 42:48], and He said: ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller﴾ [Al-Ghashiyah 88:21-22], and ﴿Upon you is only the conveyance, and upon Us is the account﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 13:40], and other verses that indicate that it is upon the Messenger ﷺ to guide people by the guidance of showing the way and giving direction. As for the guidance of tawfiq, it is neither upon the Messenger nor to the Messenger. It is not obligatory for him to guide them, and it is not within his power and capacity to guide them. Had it been within his power to guide them, he would have guided his uncle Abu Talib, but he cannot do that, because this belongs to Allah alone. And if it is not upon him to guide them, then who takes charge of that? Listen: He said: ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272]. Is this the guidance of showing the way and direction, or the guidance of tawfiq? Yes, both together, but the more precise meaning is the guidance of tawfiq, because it came after the negation of guidance from the Messenger ﷺ.

﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272]. When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained the conditions of those who give charity and the conditions of those who practise usury, and that Allah, glorified and exalted, loves that a servant give charity because of the good and benevolence it contains, He said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾. The preceding verses contain no reference to usury, but they contain a reference to spending and not spending, spending and miserliness. Usury will come, Allah willing, later on.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the guidance whose obligation Allah negated for His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ is the guidance of tawfiq. The Messenger ﷺ is not obligated to make people guided; rather, he is obligated only to convey, while the guidance of people is to Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾. As for their guidance in the sense of conveying the message to them and conveying the revelation, it is obligatory upon the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:67]. But the guidance of tawfiq is not up to the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ means: rather, guidance rests with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He said: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance, and indeed to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾ [Al-Layl 92:12-13]. So Allah, glorified and exalted, is the One who guides whom He wills, guiding with the guidance of tawfiq and the guidance of showing and clarification. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the One who makes clear to His creation and enables whom He wills among His creation to be guided. His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾ has been mentioned to us many times: that linking an action to will, or restricting an action by will, is tied to what? To wisdom; for Allah, the Exalted, does not will anything except that wisdom requires His willing it. On this basis, ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ refers to one who is fit for guidance, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 6:124]. As for one who is not fit for guidance, Allah the Exalted does not guide him, because the word of punishment has become due against him, and because he deviated, so Allah turned his heart away.

He said: ﴿And whatever good you spend is for yourselves﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272], and it is not for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for Allah does not benefit from it. ﴿Whatever good you spend is for yourselves﴾, which you advance; and what you do not spend, you have deprived yourselves of. His saying ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾: "ma" here is conditional, as evidenced by the response being joined with "fa" in His saying ﴿then it is for yourselves﴾. His saying ﴿of good﴾ is an explanation of the conditional "ma", because the conditional "ma" is vague and needs explanation: meaning, whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves. And what is meant by "good"? Good is everything expended for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whether wealth or benefit, and it is mostly in wealth, but it may also be in benefits. His saying ﴿then it is for yourselves﴾: the "fa" links the response, and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of an omitted subject; the estimate is: "it is for yourselves", meaning not for others. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that man has not but what he strives for﴾ [An-Najm 53:39].

﴿And you spend not except seeking the Face of Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272]. Meaning: you spend no spending that benefits you except what you intend by it the Face of Allah. As for what is sought by other than Allah, it does not benefit its doer; rather it is a loss for him. His saying ﴿except seeking﴾ means: seeking, and His saying ﴿seeking the Face of Allah﴾ means the real Face. That is because when a person is among the people of Paradise, he looks at Allah, Mighty and Majestic, looking at Him with a real look with the eye, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [Al-Qiyamah 75:22-23], and as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed you will see your Lord as you see the moon on the night of the full moon."[[Hadith agreed upon; al-Bukhari (806), Muslim (182/299), and al-Tirmidhi (2554), the wording being his, from Abu Hurairah radiyallahu 'anhu.]] So, "except seeking the Face of Allah" means His real Face, which is His attribute; for whoever reaches Paradise looks at the Face of Allah. Thus the highest thing a person seeks in his righteous deed is to look at the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So, what is meant by "the Face"? Brother, is it the real Face or the direction?

* Student: The real one.

* The Shaykh: How does a person seek, how does a person seek the Face of Allah? And what does that mean?

* The student: Looking at the Face of Allah.

* The Shaykh: Looking at His Face which is in the abode of His honour, which is Paradise.

So: "you spend not except seeking the Face of Allah."

If someone says: Do we not see someone spending not for the sake of Allah's Face? The answer: Yes, we see that, but beneficial spending is that which is done seeking the Face of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "Know that you will not spend an expenditure seeking by it the Face of Allah except that you will be rewarded for it, even what you put into your wife's mouth."[[Hadith agreed upon; al-Bukhari (56), Muslim (1628/5), from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas radiyallahu 'anhu.]]

﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272]. "Ma" here is also conditional, as evidenced by the jussive response ﴿yuwaffa﴾, which is jussive by the deletion of the weak letter, the alif. ﴿Whatever good you spend﴾ means: whatever good you spend of wealth, whether little or much. ﴿Will be repaid to you﴾ means: you will be given it. And how is it repaid? "A good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundredfold, up to many multiples."[[Hadith agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6491), Muslim (131/207), from Ibn 'Abbas radiyallahu 'anhuma.]]

He said: ﴿And you will not be wronged﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272]. Meaning: you will not be wronged by any reduction in the reward of what you spent; rather it is given to you in full and complete. Indeed, the matter is not merely that we are not wronged, but we are increased, and our good deeds are multiplied: "A good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundredfold, up to many multiples." A person who gives in charity the equivalent of a date from good earnings, Allah takes it with His right hand and nurtures it as one of you nurtures his foal, meaning his young colt, until it becomes like a mountain.[[Hadith agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7430), Muslim (1014/63), from Abu Hurairah radiyallahu 'anhu.]] A date becomes like a mountain: how much has it been multiplied? By many multiples without limit. If a date becomes like a mountain, it means many multiples without limit. ﴿It will be repaid to you and you will not be wronged﴾: meaning Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not wrong you in your reward, due to the perfection of His justice, not due to incapacity to do wrong; rather, out of the perfection of His justice He has forbidden wrongdoing to Himself.

* This verse contains many benefits, among them: that guiding creation is not obligatory upon the messengers, nor upon others; by His saying ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [Al-Ghashiyah 88:22].

* Among its benefits: that when a person conveys the law of Allah, he is absolved of responsibility; by His saying ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾. Had his responsibility not been discharged, he would be obligated to make them guided, and this is not upon him.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation that all matters, subtle and grand, are in Allah's hand; by His saying ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾.

And in it: a refutation of the Qadariyah; by His saying ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾.

And in it: affirmation of Allah's will; by His saying ﴿whom He wills﴾.

And also in it: that the actions of the servant occur by Allah's will, because the servant's being guided is his action; so when it occurs by Allah's will, it is evidence that the actions of servants are linked to Allah's will.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that a person's deeds do not pass to others; by His saying ﴿And whatever good you spend is for yourselves﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272].

Does the verse imply that the reward of righteous deeds does not benefit others, by His saying ﴿whatever good you spend is for yourselves﴾, making what a person spends of good for himself, meaning it does not extend beyond him to others? The answer: No. Rather, it shows that what a person does is his right, and it does not prevent a person from giving his deed in charity to another. For this reason the Sunnah explicitly permits giving charity on behalf of the dead, as established in Sahih al-Bukhari in the story of the man who said: "O Messenger of Allah, my mother died suddenly, and I think that if she had been able to speak she would have given charity; shall I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes."[[Hadith agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1388), Muslim (1004/51), from 'A'ishah radiyallahu 'anha.]] Likewise the hadith of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, who gave his orchard, al-makhraf, meaning his garden, in charity on behalf of his mother. So the verse does not indicate prohibition of charity on behalf of others; it only indicates that what a person does is not transferred to others.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that spending not sought for the Face of Allah does not benefit the servant; by His saying ﴿And you spend not except seeking the Face of Allah﴾.

* Among its benefits: an alert to sincerity, that a person should be sincere to Allah, the Exalted, in all his deeds; even in spending and giving wealth, he should be sincere in it; by His saying ﴿And you spend not except seeking the Face of Allah﴾. Spending may be driven by love of display, love of praise, saying "So-and-so is generous," and attracting attention to oneself. But all this does not benefit; it benefits only what is sought by the Face of Allah.

And in it: affirmation of the Face of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; by His saying ﴿except seeking the Face of Allah﴾. The People of the Sunnah and the Congregation say: Allah, the Exalted, has a real Face, described with majesty and honour, and it is among the essential attributes that are informative (dhatiyyah khabariyyah). The essential informative attribute is that by which He has always been and will always be characterized; its counterpart in us consists of parts and limbs, but we do not say that they are parts and limbs of Allah, because it is not proper to apply this term to the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The People of Ta'til deny that Allah has a real Face, and they say the meaning of "Face" is reward or direction or the like. This is a distortion by them of the apparent wording and contrary to it, contrary to the consensus of the Salaf that Allah has a real Face, and because reward is not described as majestic and honoured, whereas Allah has described His Face as majestic and honoured, saying: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾ [Ar-Rahman 55:27].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that nothing of a person's deeds is diminished; by His saying ﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:272].

* Among its benefits: an indication that spending from what is unlawful is not accepted, from His saying ﴿of good﴾, and its reasoning: unlawful wealth is not good, but evil.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: negation of wrongdoing in Allah's recompense, Mighty and Majestic; by His saying ﴿and you will not be wronged﴾. This entails the perfection of His justice, because we have often noted that every attribute Allah negates of Himself entails the perfection of its opposite.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿For the poor who are restricted in the way of Allah, who cannot travel about the land. The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their modesty; you will know them by their mark; they do not ask people persistently.﴾ [al-Baqarah 273].

This is an explanation of the recipients of spending. It is as if a questioner asks: where should we direct this good? When He said: ﴿Whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full﴾, it was as if it were said: where should it be directed? So He said: ﴿for the poor﴾. Accordingly, "for the poor" is either connected to ﴿spend﴾ or to an omitted element, its estimate being: the spending or the charities are for the poor. "Poor" (fuqara') is the plural of faqir, and the faqir is the one who is destitute (mu'dam). This is because the root of this word is derived from faqr (need), which corresponds to qafr (barrenness) in the greater derivation (al-ishtiqaq al-akbar), the greater derivation being that which shares the same letters without regard to order. Qafr means an empty thing, an empty land, as the poet said:

"A grave of Harb is in a barren place, and there is no grave near the grave of Harb."

They say that a person who recites this verse seven times will certainly make a mistake in it. The point is that qafr means an empty thing; the faqir means one empty-handed. He is sometimes paired with the miskin (needy). When they are paired, each has its own meaning: the faqir is one who is empty-handed, or who has less than half of his sustenance, while the miskin is in a better condition than him but does not have full sufficiency. When one of them stands alone, their meanings become one. This is among the words that, when combined, become distinct, and when distinct, become combined. ﴿For the poor﴾ means: empty-handed.

﴿Who are restricted in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 273], i.e., prevented in the way of Allah, because ihsar (restriction) means prevention, as in His saying: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah. But if you are prevented﴾ [al-Baqarah 196], i.e., prevented from completing them. ﴿Restricted in the way of Allah﴾ means they are restricted from jihad, either by preparing for it, or by the defects that befell them in jihad which kept them from work. The point is that they are restricted in this path, the way of Allah.

﴿They cannot travel about the land﴾ [al-Baqarah 273] means they cannot journey to seek provision, because they are either occupied with jihad, or unable to travel due to wounds, fractures, or the like.

﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their modesty﴾ [al-Baqarah 273]. There are two readings: ﴿yahsibuhum﴾ and ﴿yahsabuhum﴾. Is "the ignorant" one who lacks knowledge, or one ignorant of their circumstances? The second: ignorant of their circumstances, since the ignorance of each thing is according to its kind. The one ignorant of their circumstances who does not know them thinks them wealthy. Wealthy from what? He says: ﴿because of their modesty﴾, i.e., because of their restraint and their not asking. ﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy﴾ because when you see them you suppose them rich, though they are poor. This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The needy one is not the wanderer who is turned away by a morsel or two morsels, but the needy one is the one who keeps modest, and about whom one is not alerted so as to give him charity, and who does not ask people."[[Agreed upon hadith; al-Bukhari (1479), and Muslim (1039/101) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah radiyallahu 'anhu.]] This is truly the needy one, yet if you see him you say: this one is rich. He does not appear in the appearance of the poor at all, neither in his form nor in his clothing. His saying ﴿because of their modesty﴾ means restraint from what is in people's hands. The word ta'affuf: someone may say its apparent meaning is the feigning of modesty, because ta'affuf is not like 'affa; 'affa means he became chaste, while ta'affafa means he feigned chastity. So it is said, but the correct view is otherwise: rather, the "ta" here is for intensification, not for feigning or seeking. The meaning is that you think them wealthy because of the completeness of their chastity, so they do not ask people.

He said: ﴿You will know them by their mark﴾. In the first part He says: ﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy﴾, and thinking is according to outward condition. But ﴿you will know them by their mark﴾ is by insight, observation and scrutiny. Many people possess insight and keenness of observation by which they know inner conditions. When you see such people, you know them by their mark. The sima means a sign, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "You will be called on the Day of Resurrection with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu', a mark (sima) that is not for others."[[Narrated by Muslim (247/37) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah radiyallahu 'anhu, with the wording: "You have a mark that is not for anyone other than you, you will come to me with bright faces and white limbs from the traces of wudu'."]] That is, a sign not belonging to others. ﴿By their mark﴾ means by their sign. And what is the sign in them? The sign is that a person who sees them thinks them rich, and if he scrutinizes their condition, it becomes clear that they are poor but chaste. How many a person comes to you in the appearance of extreme poverty, with torn clothing, disheveled hair, a grim face, groaning and moaning, yet when you look closely you find him rich. And how many a person, on the contrary, comes to you in the dress of wealth, in the manner of one who has triumphed over himself and needs no one, yet when you scrutinize his condition you learn that he is poor. This is known by one whom Allah has blessed with insight. Allah the Exalted gives many people knowledge through insight, so that they know a person's condition from the features of his face, his glances, and likewise some of his expressions, as He said: ﴿And you will surely recognize them in the tone of speech﴾ [Muhammad 30].

He said: ﴿You will know them by their mark; they do not ask people persistently﴾. Ilhaf is insistence in asking. The saying ﴿they do not ask people persistently﴾: is the negation directed at the restriction, or at both the restriction and the restricted? If we look at the apparent wording, the negation is directed at the restriction: they do not ask people in the manner of persistence, but they ask them with gentleness, modesty and shame; if the one asked refuses them once, they do not return to him again. This is what the apparent wording requires. But the context, and that the setting is one of praise, indicates that the negation is of the restriction, which is persistence, and of the restricted, which is asking; so they do not ask people persistently nor without persistence. The proof is His saying: ﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their modesty﴾; had they been asking, the ignorant man would not have thought them wealthy, but would have thought them poor because of their asking. Accordingly the negation is of the restriction and of the restricted. However, He mentioned the highest kind of blameworthy asking, which is insistence. For this reason you find that when a person insists, even if he is poor, he weighs heavily upon you, and you grow weary of his request, until perhaps pride in sin takes hold of you and you do not give him, though you know he deserves it, because he insisted. And you find that the person who appears in the guise of the wealthy and modest, you feel compassion for him and give him more than you give the one who asks. These are five attributes. He said: ﴿Those restricted in the way of Allah, who cannot travel about the land, the ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their modesty, you will know them by their mark, they do not ask people persistently﴾. These are five, and the sixth is "the poor." These are the ones truly entitled to charity and spending. If one of the attributes is absent, entitlement remains, but not as it is when all these six attributes are present.

﴿And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾ [al-Baqarah 273]. This sentence is a conditional clause appended to the verse explaining those deserving of spending, urging spending; for if Allah knows whatever good we spend, He will reward us for a good deed with ten like it up to seven hundred times, up to many multiples. So reflect on what these verses show of the urging to spend, and that all this spending is restricted to good, and restricted to its deserving recipients. In the verse is an explanation of who deserves spending in the full sense: they are the poor described by these five attributes, since we said they are the poor described by these five attributes which are founded upon poverty.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person's occupation with a work considered part of the way of Allah permits giving to him and spending on him. If someone able to earn is occupied with seeking knowledge, we give him even from obligatory charity so that he may devote himself to seeking knowledge. And if a person devotes himself to jihad in the way of Allah, do we give him or not? Yes, we give him, even from obligatory charity.

Now, if a person devotes himself to worship, he is not given except from voluntary charity; from zakat he is not given, because he has devoted himself to a limited benefit that does not extend beyond himself. There is a difference between limited benefit and general benefit.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that one should not give, indeed it is not permissible to give, to one who is able to earn; because of His saying: ﴿who cannot travel about the land﴾. It is understood from this that if they are able to travel about the land and earn, they are not given. For this reason, when two men came to the Messenger ﷺ asking him for charity, he looked at them intently and then said: "If you wish, I will give you, but there is no share in it for the wealthy or for the strong and able to earn."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1633), and an-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (2598) from the hadith of 'Ubaydullah ibn 'Adi ibn al-Khiyar.]] So if a person is able to travel about the land, trade and earn, he is not given, because although he is poor in wealth, he is not poor in his work.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of chastity (ta'affuf), because of His saying: ﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their modesty﴾.

Also: an alert that a person should be perceptive, possessing firmness and keen observation, because Allah described the one who does not know the condition of these people as ignorant, saying: ﴿The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their modesty﴾. So a person should be perceptive, firm, and observant of affairs.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of causes, because of His saying: ﴿because of their modesty﴾, for min here indicates causation: because of their chastity, the ignorant one who does not know their condition thinks them wealthy.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of insight and perceptiveness, because of His saying: ﴿you will know them by their mark﴾, for the sima is a sign that only those with insight perceive. How many a person of sound heart, without insight or far-sightedness, is deceived by the slightest cause, and how many a person with strength of insight, firmness and consideration of consequences is protected by Allah through his insight from many things.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of one who does not ask people, because of His saying: ﴿they do not ask people persistently﴾. Among what the Prophet ﷺ took as a pledge from his Companions was that they would "not ask people for anything, so that a man's whip would fall from his camel, and he would dismount and take it himself, and would not say to his brother: give it to me."[[Narrated by Muslim (1043/108) from the hadith of Abu Muslim al-Khawlani radiyallahu 'anhu.]] All this is a distancing from asking. Asking for wealth without necessity is forbidden, unless we know that the one asked is pleased and gladdened by it, as when a person asks a friend whom he knows will be gratified by the request; that is not objectionable. The Prophet ﷺ said concerning the meat in the cooking pot: "It is a charity for Barirah, and it is a gift for us."[[Agreed upon hadith; al-Bukhari (5097), and Muslim (1075/171) from the hadith of 'A'ishah radiyallahu 'anha, with the wording: "It is charity for her and a gift for us."]] So if you know that your companion is delighted by your asking and rejoices, and that had you not asked, he would have given it to you as a gift, then there is no harm in asking. But abandoning asking is safer, for who can be certain that his companion loves to be asked?

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, because of His saying: ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾, which is general: whatever good it may be, Allah knows it. It shows the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, and that it encompasses what a person does and what Allah Himself, the Mighty and Majestic, does.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 274:

Then He, the Exalted, said, praising those who spend (in charity), saying: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, for them is their reward with their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:274].

﴿Alladhina﴾ (those who) is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿fa-lahum ajruhum﴾ (then for them is their reward) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. It is joined with the particle fa' (fa) because the subject resembles the conditional (shart) in generality; for the subject here is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), and the relative pronoun resembles the conditional in generality.

He said: ﴿Those who spend their wealth﴾. It may be said that by "wealth" (amwal) here is meant all wealth, and it may be meant as a category (jins), which includes the whole and the part.

His saying: ﴿by night and by day﴾ includes all times, and ﴿secretly and openly﴾ includes all states; that is, in every state and at every time.

His saying: ﴿secretly﴾ means in concealment, and it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of ﴿yunfiquna﴾ (they spend), meaning: spending secretly. ﴿And openly﴾ means publicly. The placing of secrecy before openness and of night before day is an indication that the more hidden the charity is, the better and more deserving it is; however, openness may be better when it brings about a benefit.

He said: ﴿fa-lahum ajruhum 'inda rabbihim﴾ (then for them is their reward with their Lord). ﴿Ajruhum﴾ means their reward with Allah, stored up, which they will find when they are most in need of it. This reward has been explained previously in His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is as the likeness of a grain that grows seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:261].

He said: ﴿And no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:274]. ﴿No fear upon them﴾ concerns what is to come, and ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ concerns what has passed.
