When taqwa is mentioned alone, it encompasses both; and when birr is mentioned absolutely, it encompasses both, encompassing taqwa by implication, because when we are commanded to do good, what necessarily follows or is implied by that is abandoning evil.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of abandoning riba even if the contract concerning it has been concluded, by His saying ﴿give up what remains of riba﴾, and this is in a contract part of which has been fulfilled and part of which remains.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verses 277–280 (part 2 of 5):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permissible to carry out contracts that are forbidden in Islam, even if they were concluded during the state of polytheism (shirk), based on His saying: ﴿Leave what remains of interest (ribā)﴾. Otherwise, if we were to enforce contracts made in polytheism while they are forbidden in Islam, then what remains of interest would be permissible. But we must know that contracts which have already taken place, where the cause of their prohibition no longer exists, are, what? They are carried out according to what has passed and are not annulled. If two people sold something forbidden during disbelief and then embraced Islam while the preventive cause no longer exists, the transaction stands as it was concluded, even if it was interest. If two disbelievers entered into an interest contract and then both received what was due under it, that stands and is enforced, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted, concerning what preceded: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed﴾. What if a disbelieving man married a woman who was in her waiting period ('iddah), and then they both embraced Islam after the waiting period had ended, eh?
* Students: Correct.
* Shaykh: Then the marriage is valid. And if he married his wife's sister, and then the first wife died and he embraced Islam, the marriage remains. And if he had married his sister and then embraced Islam?
* Students: They are to be separated.
* Shaykh: They are separated, because the cause of prohibition still exists. So from the noble verse we derive that if a person embraces Islam while holding something forbidden, and the cause of prohibition still exists, it must be abandoned, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And leave what remains of interest﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of taking what are called "interest payments" (fawā'id) from banks, based on His saying: ﴿Leave what remains of interest﴾. Some people claim that interest payments from banks may be taken so that the bank will not use them to aid in usury, and if the bank is a disbelievers' bank, then so that it will not use them to aid in disbelief. Do you understand? We say: Are you more knowledgeable, or is Allah? Personal preference (istihsan) in the face of a clear text is void. If Allah says: ﴿Leave what remains of interest﴾, and does not say: "Take it and give it in charity," then it is obligatory upon us to leave what remains of interest, to abandon it.
If someone says: If the bank is a non-Islamic bank, a disbelievers' bank, and we leave it to them, they will spend it on churches and on weapons with which Muslims are fought, or they will keep it, and their interest will grow through it. What is the answer? We say: We are addressed with a command, so it is obligatory upon us to do what we have been commanded, and the results are not up to us. If Allah says: ﴿Leave what remains of interest﴾, then we leave it. Whether they spend it on this or that, or their wealth grows through it, this is not up to us. Furthermore, we say: Is this so-called "interest" truly a profit from our wealth? The answer is no. The money you gave them may not earn a profit; it may be lost. So what they give you is not the growth of your wealth, that you should say: "By Allah, this is the growth of my money, so I will take it and want to take it and give it in charity to be rid of it." We say: Whoever claims this is the growth of your wealth, your own wealth may have been used to buy something and they lost money, or it burned. Moreover, it is not the growth of your wealth, because the growth of your wealth is not fixed; rather it is subject to increase and subject to decrease. So it is not the profit of your money, so that you should say: "By Allah, I fear I will sin if I leave it with them, for they will spend it on what Allah has forbidden."
Furthermore, we say: If you take it, where will you spend it? He says: I will spend it on charity, on repairing roads, on building mosques, to be rid of it, or seeking nearness to Allah through it. We say to him: If you do that seeking nearness to Allah, it will not be accepted from you, and you will not be free of its sin, because in this state you spent it as if it were your property, and when you spend it as if it were your property, it is not accepted from you, because it is charity from unlawful wealth, and whoever earns unlawful wealth and then spends it and gives it in charity, it is not accepted from him. And if you take it out to be rid of it, what benefit is there in a thing that, we say, has soiled you, and then you try to wash it from your hand?! What is the benefit?! If you now acknowledge that it is not lawful for you, then why do you take it and then try to get rid of it?!
Furthermore, we say: Does every person guarantee that he will bring it out to be rid of it?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No. Perhaps when he sees a large profit, as they say, it is a profit that overpowers his soul, and he does not bring it out. (...) He says: "By Allah, this is a lot of money. What is this, let me take it out. Boy, open the box, put it in there." When the box is opened, he says: "I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him, I fear Allah." So he takes it out with his hand. If he wants to take it out, his hand feels heavy, and he says: "Put it back in the box." Perhaps in the end it will be in the box.
Also, you took it, and people said: "So-and-so took this interest payment, which they call interest." Do you not fear that people will follow your example? Because not every person knows that you will bring this money out and be rid of it? Indeed, people may follow your example: "By Allah, so-and-so took it." You are not publishing an announcement that you took this and spent it. People do not know, so they follow you. And if they follow you and take it, even if they know that you spend it and get rid of it, there will come back to them what we raised with you earlier, which is stinginess and failure to be rid of it. For this reason we hold that it is not permissible to take any interest at all. And what will your encounter with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, be on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah has said to you: ﴿Fear Allah and leave what remains of interest﴾, and then you take it through your own reasoning?
Furthermore, we say: When a person takes this thing, he hardly ever gives it up. He hardly ever desists from placing money in forbidden, usurious, disbelieving banks. But if we say, "Do not take it," he will continue to calculate a thousand calculations before placing money in the bank, once he knows it is forbidden to him. All these matters indicate the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿Leave what remains of interest﴾, and He did not direct the servants to anything else. He did not say: "Take it and give it in charity."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that engaging in interest (ribā) contradicts faith, based on His saying: ﴿If you are believers﴾. But does a person leave faith for disbelief? The doctrine of the Khawārij (a sect) is yes, it takes him out of faith into disbelief. According to the Khawārij, he is a disbeliever like Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun, a disbeliever, because he committed one of the major sins. The doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamā'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community) is that he is a believer with deficient faith, but he is feared to be at risk of disbelief, especially the one who consumes interest, because the consumer of interest is nourished by what?
* Students: By the unlawful.
* Shaykh: By the unlawful. And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, when mentioning the man who "travels far, disheveled and dusty, stretching out his hands to the sky, saying: 'O Lord, O Lord,' while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished by the unlawful." He said: "How then could his supplication be answered?"[[Narrated by Muslim (1015/65) from Abu Hurayrah.]] We ask Allah for well-being.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the mercy of Allah, glorified and exalted, toward His servants, in that He prohibited for them what involves injustice and emphasized this prohibition, and revealed the Qur'an concerning it in wording that compels abandoning this prohibited thing, based on His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, the second: ﴿Fear Allah﴾, the third: ﴿If you are believers﴾, and the ruling: ﴿Leave what remains of interest﴾.
Then He said: ﴿But if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. Allahu akbar! ﴿If you do not﴾ means if you do not leave what remains of interest. "What remains," how is this one who renews an interest contract? If you do not do it and leave what remains of interest, this is the ruling. Which is worse, this or the one who initiates interest?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: The second is worse. The one who initiates interest is worse than a person who dealt in interest before the verse was revealed and took what remained. Is that not so?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: ﴿If you do not﴾ means if you do not abandon it. ﴿Then be informed﴾, and in another reading: ﴿Then announce a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. ﴿Idhnū﴾ means "be informed" or "know," but it was made to carry the meaning of certainty or assurance; that is, be certain of war from Allah and His Messenger. This is according to the reading ﴿fa-idhnū﴾. As for the reading ﴿fa-ādhinū﴾, it means "inform," "let others know," as in "ādhana bi-kadhā," meaning he informed of it. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to the women who washed a dead woman: «When you have finished, inform me» (idhā faraghtunna fa-ādhinnanī),[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1253) and Muslim (939/36) from Umm 'Atiyyah al-Ansariyyah.]] meaning inform me. In the verse there are two readings: "idhnū" and "ādhinū." "Idhnū" means "know," but it has been made to carry the meaning of certainty: be certain of war, meaning be certain that you are at war. With whom?
* Students: With Allah and His Messenger.
* Shaykh: With Allah and His Messenger. Allahu akbar! Who can confront Allah and His Messenger with war?! Or "inform," meaning inform others that you are at war with Allah and His Messenger.
As for His saying: ﴿Ādhinū bi-harb﴾ or ﴿Idhnū bi-harb﴾, does its meaning mean that a person shouts, saying, "O people, we are now going to war against Allah and His Messenger"? Or is merely his continuing in interest an announcement?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: Yes, the second. The second is what is intended, because the first a person may not do. A person may not stand at the door of his shop and say: "O people, I inform you that I am at war with Allah and His Messenger." He cannot, and he does not speak that way. If he said that at his shop's doorstep, the first to stone him would be the young people with stones. Or not?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: They would say: "We are the soldiers of Allah. Since you are fighting Allah, take a stone to his head and a stone to his chest." But he does not say it with his tongue; he says it with what?
* Students: With his actions.
* Shaykh: With his deed. So his persistence and continuation in consuming interest is an announcement of war against Allah and His Messenger. What punishment is more severe than this punishment, other than the punishment of associating partners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic?! For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the threat concerning interest has come in a form that does not come for any sin short of polytheism. Nothing is worse than fornication. For this reason there is the hadith with multiple chains: «Interest has seventy-some branches, the least of which is like a man committing adultery with his mother».[[Narrated by Ibn Majah in his Sunan (2274) from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (2290) from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud with a similar wording.]] Everyone finds this abhorrent. Interest is no trivial matter. By Allah, a person's limbs tremble when he hears a verse like this, if he is a believer: ﴿Be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. And what are you, O son of Adam?! You wage war against Allah and His Messenger openly, announcing it to the people, because "a'lamū" means "inform the people that you are at war with Allah and His Messenger." ﴿But if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. This is so because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, loves justice and dislikes injustice, and interest is injustice. But because it is an injustice to which souls are strongly drawn, since it does not come by force. Injustice by force, a wrongdoer does not undertake it except after calculating a thousand calculations, and he will find someone who prevents him and opposes him. But this comes by choice. By choice from whom?
* A student: From the one in need.
* Shaykh: From the usurer. From both men: the consumer of interest and the one who pays it. It comes from this one and that one, because the payer of interest is in need, and had he not been in need, he would not have chosen to be overpowered. And the consumer of interest is an oppressor and aggressor, having no mercy in his heart. For this reason we now find those people who devise ways around interest through what they call "debt-financing" (mudāyana). We find that the more needy the debtor, the greater his burden. This is the reality. A person comes to them whom they know will repay, and says: "Come, let us lend you ten, eleven." That is, a hundred for how much?
* Students: For a hundred and ten.
* Shaykh: A hundred and ten. A poor person comes to them whom they know will not repay except after two or three years, unless a rich relative dies for him. And when will a rich relative die for him?! Or if he is greedy, he marries off his daughter and takes her dowry. In any case, if the poor person comes to them, they give him ten for fifteen or more. O son of the lawful, why?! He says: "Because the first is fat, and this one is lean." The first is fat, and what does "fat" mean?
* Students: Wealthy.
* Shaykh: That is, wealthy. Perhaps now he is short of money and will repay. But this one is lean, so bow down to him. Is this transaction one of mercy or one of cruelty?
* Students: A transaction of cruelty.
* Shaykh: A transaction of cruelty. If they had mercy in them, the poor person would be closer to being relieved of the burden than the wealthy one, is that not right?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yet they wipe away crocodile tears. He says: "By Allah, we have mercy on people. A poor man comes to us wanting to marry or wanting to build a house; we have mercy and give him." What should we do?! If we do not give him, he stays unmarried and without a house. Fine, how much did you give him? He says: "I gave him ten for fifteen." Why? He says: "Because he will delay and not repay." And that second person, the one who is fat, as they say, is given ten for eleven.
So I want from these examples to conclude that interest is founded on what?
* Students: Injustice.
* Shaykh: Injustice. It is founded on injustice. For this reason, it was part of the wisdom of the Most Wise of judges and the mercy of the Most Merciful of the merciful that He made these usurers announce war against Allah and His Messenger, declaring it publicly before the people: ﴿But if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾.
Is the door of repentance closed?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No, by Allah, it is not closed, and the Most Merciful of the merciful does not close it. ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾ [Az-Zumar 53]. Whatever sin you have committed, know that before you is One who rejoices at your repentance. "Allah is more pleased with the repentance of His servant than a man who lost his camel in the wilderness, and then, when he was about to perish, found it."[[Narrated by Muslim (2744/3) from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud with a similar wording.]]
﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾.
What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Leave﴾? Abandon. How does He say "abandon what remains" and not say "abandon interest"?
* A student: Because perhaps they had already contracted interest, so He commands them to abandon this interest.
* Shaykh: Even what was already contracted. He says: ﴿Fear Allah and leave what remains of interest﴾. What kind of conjunction is this?
* A student: Because fearing Allah includes abandoning interest.
* Shaykh: Excellent. It is the conjunction of the specific over the general (...) and giving it attention.
* A student: (...)
* Shaykh: Excellent. His saying: ﴿If you are believers﴾, this is a conditional clause. Where is its response? According to the grammarians? I think we have studied this? We did not discuss it. Good, this is the well-known view among the grammarians. Is there another opinion? Who knows? There is another opinion.
* A student: Because such a construction does not need a response.
* Shaykh: Excellent. Because such a construction does not need a response, since once its content has been mentioned, there is no need to estimate it. This is what Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, inclined to: that such a construction does not need a response, since its content has already preceded. So there is no need to say: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and leave what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾, then "fear Allah and leave what remains of interest," what need is there? We say: because the content of the response has already preceded, so there is no need for it.
If someone says: How does He say: ﴿O you who have believed, fear﴾?
* A student: ﴿Fa-ādhinū﴾.
* Shaykh: What does it mean?
* The student: Inform the people that you are at war with Allah and His Messenger.
* Shaykh: Inform the people that you are at war with Allah and His Messenger, excellent. And ﴿Fa-idhnū﴾?
* The student: Then know.
* Shaykh: Then know. Good, and what does "then know war (...) with yourselves" mean? It is derived from the combination of the two readings?
* A student: (...)
* Shaykh: That is, know and inform others of that too?
* A student: (...)
* Shaykh: Good, this is according to the reading "idhnū," meaning know that you are at war with Allah and His Messenger. This is according to the reading "ādhinū." What is derived from the combination of the two readings?
* A student: Know yourselves, and inform others.
* Shaykh: That is, know yourselves and also inform others. And this is worse: a person knows and makes others know.

**Student:** If someone asks: did these usurers give notice to others that they are at war?

**Shaykh:** Good. If someone says: they are at war with Allah. ﴿So be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. If someone asks: the notice of war from Allah is clear, but how can they be warned of war from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he has died? The answer: this is opposing his Sharia, opposing the Sharia of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and opposing the Sharia of the Messenger is opposing him, just as supporting the Sharia of the Messenger is supporting him.

And His saying: ﴿And if you repent, you shall have your principal sums﴾. ﴿Repent﴾ means you return to Allah, Exalted, from disobeying Him to obeying Him. Repentance (tawbah) is of two kinds: absolute repentance and restricted repentance. If you wish, say: general and specific. General repentance is from all sins, such that the person is keeping to the commands of Allah and abstaining from His prohibitions. This is the absolute repentance, not merely any repentance, but complete absolute repentance by which the penitent deserves to be included among those of whom Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 222]. On this basis, the person must be repentant from every sin and not persist in any sin. This is absolute repentance, and among its proofs is His saying, Exalted: ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the wanderers﴾ and so on to the end of the verse [al-Tawbah 112].

The second kind: restricted or specific repentance, which is repentance from a particular, specific sin. This is valid and recognized, and it is accepted from him that he repents to Allah, Exalted, from this specific sin, even if he is persisting in others. So the one who repents from usury has a valid repentance even if he drinks alcohol, for example, and the one who repents from drinking alcohol has a valid repentance even if he deals in usury. This is specific repentance. However, the penitent here does not deserve to be attached to those described by absolute repentance, so that it is said: he is among the penitent. This is because we cannot describe him as penitent while he persists in disobedience. But his repentance from the specific sin is accepted, because this is what justice requires, the justice of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Some scholars held that repentance from one sin is not accepted while persisting in others. Rather, one must do righteous deeds in all acts of worship. Others said: repentance is not accepted from a sin while persisting in its kind (genus), not in others. For example, repentance from looking at non-related women is not accepted if he is conversing with them, because all of this is of one genus. Even if the type differs, this is speech and that is looking, the genus is one and it returns to the desire of the private parts. Likewise, the repentance of one who drinks alcohol is not accepted while he persists in selling alcohol. That is, his repentance from drinking alcohol is not valid while he persists in what? 

**Students:** In selling alcohol.

**Shaykh:** In selling alcohol, because the genus is one. This is a view that has some basis. But the closest of the views to me is the first view: repentance from a specific sin is valid even with persistence in others, because this is what justice requires and what the saying of Allah requires: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422) and Muslim (2751/15) from Abu Hurayrah, and the wording is al-Bukhari's.] The matter, as Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Madarij al-Salikin*, has depth, meaning it has a far depth. This is because true repentance, which is returning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, never exists with persistence in sins, because what occupies the heart of the penitent of the glorification of Allah and fear of Him prevents him from practicing any sin. But this repentance is deficient and incomplete, a repentance from a particular specific sin only.

Then, repentance has conditions. Five conditions, does he count them for us? (...) Regret for what one has done. Good, all these conditions are clear. Sincerity: that the person is not moved to repent by concern for anyone of creation or concern for some worldly matter.

Second: abandoning the sin. If he does not abandon it, he is a liar. How can he say: I repent to Allah from usury while he is practicing usury? This is a liar.

Third: regret for what has occurred from him. Regret means the person feels remorse, sorrow and grief. If you say: regret is an emotion, not an action, so how is a person obligated to it? The answer: psychological emotions are produced by mental reflections. Are love and hatred not emotions? Yet a person can love something when he reflects on its results and fruits with his thought, and he loves it. Likewise, hatred is possible when he reflects and considers its bad results and consequences, and he hates it. Similarly, when he reflects on the consequences of sins and their evil effects, what arises in him is what?

**Students:** Regret.

**Shaykh:** Regret, and sorrow and grief over what has passed.

Fourth: resolve never to return. Pay attention to your words: resolve never to return, rather than saying "that he never returns," because there is a great difference between them. Resolve never to return means that if he returns later, having been overcome by his soul and returning, his previous repentance is not nullified. But if you say the fourth condition is "that he never returns," then if he returns, his repentance would be nullified, and the matter is not so.

Fifth: that it be within the time when repentance is accepted, which is before the sun rises from the west, and before the arrival of death, due to His saying: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue to commit evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented"﴾ [al-Nisa 18]. This one has no repentance. And due to the saying of Allah: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord will come, no soul will benefit from its faith if it had not believed before or had not earned through its faith some good﴾ [al-An'am 158]. Some of the signs here refers to the sun rising from the west.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** Yes, and what is it?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** It falls under abandonment.

**Student:** He abandons (...)

**Shaykh:** It is not possible that he has abandoned it until he gives back to its owner.

**Student:** The principle is that if he has abandoned (...)

**Shaykh:** Good, it is not required. Abandonment in its true meaning, not abandonment with persistence. These are the five conditions of repentance. As for usury, repentance from it applies to this, and these five conditions must be present in it.

﴿And if you repent, you shall have your principal sums﴾. "Principal sums" is the plural of "principal," and "principal" here means the original amount, meaning you have the original amounts of wealth, but as for usury, it is not yours. Usury is not yours.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave the reason for this ruling by His saying: ﴿You do no wrong and you are not wronged﴾. ﴿You do no wrong﴾ because you did not take the excess. ﴿Nor are you wronged﴾ because it did not diminish your principal sums.

So let no one say: the usurer should be treated leniently by having from his principal an amount equal to what he took as usury? 

**Students:** From usury.

**Shaykh:** From usury. For example, if he took interest of twelve, we say: we reduce his principal by ten, we reduce ten to about eight, because the ratio of two to twelve is not the ratio of two to eight or ten.

In any case, we say neither this nor that. He does not wrong others by taking usury, nor is he wronged by having some of his principal reduced because he was emboldened in usury. This is complete justice.

Good. If he has his principal, and he is neither wronging nor wronged, then where does the usury go? Does it remain with the usurer, or is it taken from him and placed in the public treasury (bayt al-mal)? In the noble verse Allah says: ﴿You shall have your principal sums﴾. So the usurer now deserves only his principal, nothing else. We remain with the matter of what was taken from him as usury. If we leave the usury with him, that means he has gained twice: once by having the money in his possession all this time, benefiting from it, and the second time by retaining this profit. We return to the legal principles and say: this profit was given to him by the one from whom it was taken, by his own choice, and he committed to it by his own choice. But since this is a non-lawful commitment, we say: we will take it from you and place it in the public treasury, as we say regarding the wages of prostitution and the payment of a soothsayer. Yes, if it is assumed that the one who was made to pay usury was forced to pay it, such as when at the due date he said to him: either you pay me or you increase the amount and pay interest, and so he paid interest so that the debt would remain on his record because he was insolvent, then we say: the usury is his, and nothing is taken from him.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿But if you do not do so, then be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger﴾.

* From this noble verse is derived: a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists), by His saying: ﴿But if you do not do so﴾. This is because the Jabriyyah say that a person is unable to act, since he is compelled, nor to abstain, since he is compelled. According to their view, the commands and prohibitions become void, because a person cannot do what he is commanded nor abstain from what he is forbidden. This is truly the nullification of commands and prohibitions. The discussion of this and the refutation and debate with them is well known in the science of Tawhid.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the one who persists in usury has declared war on Allah and His Messenger, by His saying: ﴿then be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger﴾.

* Branching from this benefit: if he has declared war on Allah and His Messenger, then he has declared war on the friends of Allah and His Messenger. Who are they? The believers. This is because every believer must support Allah and His Messenger, and every war against Allah and His Messenger is a war against the believers, because these believers are the party of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Then the usurer is declaring war on Allah, His Messenger and the believers. As for Allah and His Messenger, the indication of that is by direct indication (dalalat al-mutabaqah), and as for the believers, it is by implicit indication (dalalat al-iltizam).

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the magnitude of usury. I do not recall that any other sin has reached this rank. Do you recall anything?

* A student: Shirk.

* Shaykh: But shirk has been mentioned, though not in this form: ﴿But if you do not do so, then be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. Look at the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to parents." He had been reclining and then sat up, and said: "Beware, and false speech; beware, and false testimony." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5976) and Muslim (87/143) from Abu Bakrah Nufay' ibn al-Harith, and the wording is al-Bukhari's.] Because it relates to human beings, and the soul is inclined to aggression against others except those whom Allah protects. Therefore, a severe threat like this came concerning the one who consumes usury.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: whoever repents to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from usury must not take anything that he gained through usury, due to His saying: ﴿And if you repent, you shall have your principal sums﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is not permissible to take anything beyond the principal, for any purpose whatsoever, whether you take it to give it in charity, or to spend it on public benefits, or to protect yourself with it, such as saying that it should be spent on churches or on weapons against the Muslims or similar things. The point is that if you are sincere in repentance, do not take more than the principal.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication of the wisdom behind the prohibition of usury, which is injustice, due to His saying: ﴿You do no wrong and you are not wronged﴾.

If you say: in some forms of usury there is no injustice, we say: when the cause is widespread and cannot be controlled, the ruling is not restricted by its absence, or is not negated by its absence. It is true that in some forms of usury there is no injustice, such as when a person buys a sa' of good wheat for two sa's of inferior wheat that is equal to it in value. Here, is there injustice or not?

**Students:** No.

**Shaykh:** There is no injustice at all. Therefore, neither of the two parties says: I am patient with injustice, because there is no injustice. But Muhammad (ﷺ), the Messenger of Allah who brought this Qur'an, when he was informed of such a case, said: "Oh! This is the very essence of usury, this is the very essence of usury." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2312) and Muslim (1594/96) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.] This shows that the absence of injustice in some forms does not take them out of the general ruling on usury, because this cause is widespread and cannot be controlled. A poor person may be content to be given a hundred dirhams for a hundred and twenty, and he says: I am content with this, because I will benefit from these dirhams from now on, and the other party will be deprived of their benefit from now on. So I benefit in exchange for the excess, and he is deprived of the benefit of the money too, in exchange for the excess I give him. So there is no injustice. I have benefited from the money, and I gained an extra amount, and he has been deprived of the benefit of the money and has been given extra.

* A student: Like banks.

* Shaykh: Like banks and other than banks. The point is that when such a cause is widespread and uncontrolled, the ruling becomes what? It becomes general in its application. This has many examples, and we always find in the words of the scholars such reasoning: when a cause is widespread and uncontrolled, the ruling is general and the cause is not considered. The cause for shortening prayer during travel and breaking the fast during travel is hardship. But if a person travels by airplane, there is no cause, there is no hardship at all. Do we say he may not break his fast? No. Do we say he may not shorten his prayer? No. This is based on what we have indicated.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the Prophet's (ﷺ) messengership, due to His saying: ﴿and His Messenger﴾.

* And among its benefits: the mercy of Allah, Exalted, toward His servants, in that He sent Messengers to them, because minds cannot independently comprehend in full detail what benefits them and what harms them, isn't that so?

* The students: Yes.

* Shaykh: Minds know what benefits and harms them in general terms, but in detail they do not know, due to their limitations. ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra 85]. For this reason Allah sent the Messengers, and in this there is great mercy to creation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the repentance of one who has taken people's wealth is not valid unless he returns it to them, due to His saying: ﴿You shall have your principal sums﴾. But if he does not know the owner, sometimes a person steals from someone and does not know him afterward, so what does he do? Yes, we say: he gives it in charity to be free of it, not seeking reward through it, so he intends it for whom?

* The students: For its owner.

* Shaykh: For its owner. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows of that. Then, if the owner comes at some point, he is given the choice: you may have your wealth or its reward. If he says: I want my wealth, then the reward goes to the one who gave charity. If he says: I want its reward, then its reward is for him, since it was given on his behalf.

Then Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾.

* The student: Is it permissible to mix lawful and unlawful wealth (...)?

* Shaykh: No. Mixing lawful and unlawful wealth, if it is in a way that allows distinguishing between them, then yes. That is, distinction is possible, such as wheat mixed with rice, or distinction is possible by parts, such as oil mixed with oil. In these cases, it is possible to distinguish one from another. But if distinction is not possible, there is no way to avoid the unlawful except by avoiding the whole.

He said: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then [let there be] postponement until [a time of] ease﴾. As for His saying, Exalted: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾: "kāna" is well known as one of the defective verbs (al-af'al al-naqisah), which raise the subject and put the predicate in the accusative. Here we seek the predicate and find none in ﴿if the debtor is in hardship﴾. So how do we parse it? We say: this "kāna" is complete (tāmmah), and when it is complete, it is satisfied with its nominative subject. Ibn Malik said in the *Alfiyyah*:

*"...and the complete one is that which is satisfied with the nominative; and what is other than it is defective..."*

"The complete one is that which is satisfied with the nominative": this is complete. Based on this, we say: "kāna" is a past-tense verb, and "dhū" is its subject, raised by the wāw because it is one of the Six Nouns (al-asma' al-sittah). The sentence here is conditional, and the answer is His saying: ﴿then [let there be] postponement until [a time of] ease﴾. And "nazhrah" (postponement) is a subject whose predicate is omitted. How do we estimate this predicate? Do we estimate "fa-'alaykum" or "fa-lahu"?

* A student: "Fa-'alaykum."

* Shaykh: Or "then it is incumbent upon you to grant postponement," or "then upon you is postponement," or "then for him is postponement," any of these is acceptable, because if the right belongs to him, it is obligatory upon me to give him his right.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 277–280 (part 4 of 5):

Regarding His saying: ﴿And that you give charity﴾. I would like us to begin with the grammatical analysis (i'rab) before the explanation. Shall we, or not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And that you give charity is better for you﴾. ﴿Tasaddaqu﴾ here is a present-tense verb preceded by (an) (the verbal particle "that," called al-masdariyyah), so it is converted into a verbal noun, and the estimated meaning is: "your giving charity." It is then the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿is better for you﴾. As for His saying: ﴿if you know﴾, the conditional clause, we say regarding its analysis what was said previously in His saying: ﴿if you are believers﴾.

As for the recitations (qira'at) of this verse, there are variant readings. In ﴿maysarah﴾ there is a reading ﴿maysurah﴾ with a dammah on the sin: ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease (maysurah)﴾. And in His saying ﴿and that you give charity﴾ there is a reading ﴿wa-an tassaddaqu﴾, meaning "that you give charity," but the taa' is assimilated into the saad.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾, meaning: if a person in hardship is found, that is, one who has difficulty and cannot repay. There are then three options: either to overlook it, or to grant respite until a time of ease, or interest (riba). Riba is forbidden, so what remains? Respite and remission, meaning forgiveness. Allah mentioned both, saying: ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease; and that you give charity is better for you﴾. Thus Allah made respite obligatory and recommended remission. He made respite obligatory in His saying ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease﴾; "nazirah" here means "inzar" (granting respite), meaning: it is obligatory upon you to grant him respite. Until when? Until a time of ease. The time of ease is not known: he may become well-off in a year, in two years, in three, or he may never become well-off at all. It is said that a distinction is made between the initial contract and its continuation. If you sell something to a poor person and say, "payable at a time of ease," the view known among most scholars is that this is not valid, why? Because the time is unknown, and the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade gharar (uncertain) sales. But if you sold to him and then his poverty became evident, the obligation is what?
* The students: Granting him respite.
* The Shaykh: Granting him respite until a time of ease, if you do not choose to cancel the contract. If you choose to cancel, there is no harm. But if you do not choose cancellation, the obligation is respite. However, the preponderant view is that if you sell to him on a deferred basis until a time of ease, the sale is valid and the deferral is valid, because this is the requirement of the contract. For whoever sells to a person he knows to be insolvent, the requirement of the contract is what? That he grant him respite, because he knows that he cannot demand payment now. So if he says, "I will buy it from you, and by Allah I have nothing, but I will buy it from you until Allah makes me sufficient," the correct view in this is validity. A hadith has been narrated on this from 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her): "A man had brought some cloth from Syria, and 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Indeed, so-and-so has brought cloth from Syria; if only you sent for him to buy two garments on credit until a time of ease."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in his Jami' (1213) from the hadith of 'Aishah.]] This indicates that such a thing is permissible.
* A student: (...) Does he mean that if he took the benefit of riba, he gives him the same as what he took?
* The Shaykh: Not at all; that is not permissible.
* The student: So it is analogous to banks (...)?
* A student: Shaykh, (...)
* The Shaykh: The point is that this is directed at a specific thing: ﴿Fear Allah and give up what remains of riba﴾. As for the verse in al-Fatiha, there is no doubt that a person needs guidance at all times, even in the very act of work he needs guidance.
* The student: So it does not contradict (...)?
* The Shaykh: I do not think so.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This requires that his debts be examined. If his debts exceed his assets, he is placed under restriction (hajr), and when he is placed under restriction, his property is sold and distributed among the creditors proportionately.
* The student: A benefit from the saying of Allah Most High, in the hadith: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war against him"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]: can this be added to the verse?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, this can be added to the verse, correct.
* The student: There is a benefit... another benefit that the particle (...)
* A student: If the one who dealt in riba repents, must he return all the riba he took in the past, or only the same contract concluded now between the one who takes riba and the one who gave it?
* The Shaykh: No, he must return everything he took.
* The student: Even the past?
* The Shaykh: Even the past.
* The student: If he did not know?
* The Shaykh: If he did not know, we may say that the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has past﴾ means that what has passed is forgiven for him.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it is obligatory upon the Muslims to give it to him.
* The student: If they do not find [him]?
* The Shaykh: They do not find [him]?
* The student: (...)
* The Shaykh: He has the right to take from his property, he is bound by that and does not pay it. That is, the riba is not paid; I mean the excess. The principal must be paid.
* The student: O Shaykh, a person who is an employee in a bank and deals in riba invited me to a meal at his place (...). Should I return his invitation or not (...)? He invited me to a feast; should I refuse or accept?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, did you understand the question?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: He says: Is it permissible to accept the invitation of one who deals in riba, or not? This is the summary; what do you say? What is it?
* A student: The meaning is (...).
* The Shaykh: Not at all. He invited me (...); he has bread, meat and decorative things. I will not go (...) and I will not invite him at all (...).

The forbidden thing's sin falls upon the one who earns it. Accordingly, there is no sin upon you even if you accept his invitation. Moreover, this person who deals in riba must have a principal; does his wealth have a principal or not? His wealth must have a principal. It is not riba all the way; he proceeds with it. For example, he may have a hundred riyals, he began to work with them in riba, and they grew. So his wealth has a principal, and this riba arose from lawful wealth and from forbidden action, lawful wealth and forbidden action. Some scholars have mentioned that if a usurper trades with usurped property, the profit is not entirely for the owner of the property; rather, the usurper, if he repents, is given what corresponds to his labour. In any case, regarding accepting the invitation of one who deals in riba, we say: it is permissible, and leaving it is better; but if accepting it leads to something forbidden, then accepting it is forbidden from that angle.

Allah Most High said: ﴿And if someone is in hardship, then [let there be] postponement until a time of ease﴾. Here the word "kana" (was/is) has a difficulty. What is the difficulty?
* A student: From the standpoint (...)
* The Shaykh: From the standpoint of Arabic grammar; that is, from the standpoint of i'rab there is a difficulty.
* The student: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾: this "kana" is called the complete kana (kana al-tammah), which does not require a predicate.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed; the difficulty is that we have not found its predicate.
* The student: So it is called complete.
* The Shaykh: So we say it is complete. When it is complete, what does that mean?
* The student: It suffices with the noun.
* The Shaykh: It suffices with the agent (fa'il).
* The student: Yes, with the agent.
* The Shaykh: But what does ﴿if someone is in hardship﴾ mean? It means: if a person in hardship is found. Good. Where is the response of the condition in ﴿in kana﴾?
* The student: The response of the condition is ﴿then [let there be] postponement﴾.
* The Shaykh: Is it a clause or a single word?
* The student: No, a clause.
* The Shaykh: A clause. Why is it connected with the particle fa'?
* The student: Because it (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: It is a nominal clause.
* The Shaykh: Because it is a nominal clause. Good, what are the types of clauses that must be joined with fa' when they occur as the response of a condition?
* The student: "Wa-bi-jamidin, wa-bi-qad, wa-bi-l-tanfis..."
* The Shaykh: Repeat the verse.
* The student:
Nominal, imperative,
and with an inert (jamid) one, and with ma, and qad, and with la, and with the future (tanfis)...
* The Shaykh: Seven, they are seven.
Nominal, imperative,
and with an inert one, and with ma, and qad, and with la, and with the future (tanfis)...
Is that so? His saying: ﴿and that you give charity is better for you﴾: what type is this, a single word or a clause? Is it a clause or a single word? This question: ﴿and that you give charity is better for you﴾?
* The student: A clause.
* The Shaykh: A clause, composed of what?
* The student: A verb and an agent.
* The Shaykh: No. A nominal clause composed of what?
* The student: A particle and a verb.
* The Shaykh: A particle and a verb?
* A student: Of a subject and a predicate.
* The Shaykh: Of a subject and a predicate. Where is the subject?
* The student: The verbal noun.
* The Shaykh: The verbal noun formed from "that" and the verb. And the estimate is?
* The student: "Your giving charity is better for you."
* The Shaykh: And what is the estimate?
* The student: "Your giving charity is better for you."
* The Shaykh: "Your giving charity is better for you," perfect. ﴿If you know﴾: this is a conditional clause; where is its response?
* The student: (...)
* The Shaykh: And what is the estimate?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, the response of the condition is an object of the verb: "If you know that, then do it, or give charity." Is that so?

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the repentant one who has taken people's wealth does not have his repentance validated except by returning it to them, based on His saying: ﴿then you shall have your principal﴾. But if he does not know its owner, sometimes a person steals from someone and afterwards does not know him; what does he do? We say: he gives it in charity to rid himself of it, not keeping it for himself. He intends it on behalf of its owner, and Allah, glory be to Him, knows that. Then if its owner comes at some point, he is given the choice: "Either you have your wealth, or your reward." If he says, "I want my wealth," then the reward goes to the one who gave the charity. If he says, "I want its reward," then its reward is for him, since it was intended for him.

Then Allah Most High said: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾.
* A student: (...) mixing of two kinds of wealth (...) the principal of lawful wealth (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. The mixing of forbidden and lawful wealth: if it is in a manner in which distinction between them is possible, then yes, meaning it is possible to distinguish, such that this is, for example, wheat and that is rice; or distinction is possible by parts, such as mixing oil with oil; this can be distinguished from one another. But if distinction is not possible, there is no way to avoid the forbidden except by avoiding the whole.

He said: ﴿And if someone is in hardship, then [let there be] postponement until a time of ease﴾ [al-Baqarah 280].

Allah's saying ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾: "kana" is well known to be one of the defective verbs (al-af'al al-naqisah), which raise the subject and put the predicate in the accusative. Here we seek the predicate and find none: ﴿if someone is in hardship﴾. So how do we parse it? We say: this "kana" is complete (tammah), and when it is complete it suffices with its raised noun. Ibn Malik said in the Alfiyyah:
"...and the complete one is that which suffices with the raised noun; and whatever else is defective..."
"And the complete one is that which suffices with the raised noun": this one is complete. On this basis we say: "kana" is a past verb, and "dhu" is its agent; it is raised by the waw because it is one of the six nouns (al-asma' al-sittah). The clause here is conditional, and the response is His saying ﴿then [let there be] postponement until a time of ease﴾. "Nazirah" is a subject whose predicate is omitted. How do we estimate this predicate? We estimate: "then upon you [is] postponement," or "then the obligation upon you [is] postponement," or "then for him [is] postponement." It is suitable, because if the right is his, it is obligatory upon me to pay him his right.

As for His saying ﴿and that you give charity﴾: I would like us to begin with the grammar before the explanation. So: ﴿and that you give charity is better for you﴾. ﴿Tasaddaqu﴾ here is a present-tense verb preceded by "an" (the verbal particle "that"), so it is converted into a verbal noun, and the estimate is: "your giving charity," which makes it the subject whose predicate is ﴿is better for you﴾. As for His saying ﴿if you know﴾, it is a conditional clause, and we say regarding its analysis what was said in His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 278].

As for the recitations of this verse, there are variant readings: in ﴿maysarah﴾ there is a reading ﴿maysurah﴾ with a dammah on the sin: ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease (maysurah)﴾. And in His saying ﴿and that you give charity﴾ there is a reading ﴿wa-an tassaddaqu﴾, meaning "that you give charity," but the taa' is assimilated into the saad.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if someone is in hardship﴾, meaning: if a person in hardship is found, that is, one who has difficulty and cannot repay. There are three options: either to overlook it, or to grant respite until a time of ease, or interest (riba). Riba is forbidden, so what remains? Respite and remission, meaning forgiveness, and Allah mentioned both, saying: ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease; and that you give charity is better for you﴾. Thus Allah made respite obligatory and recommended remission. He made respite obligatory in ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease﴾; "nazirah" means "inzar" (granting respite), meaning: it is obligatory upon you to grant him respite until a time of ease. The time of ease is not known: he may become well-off in a year, two years, three, or never at all. It is said that a distinction is made between the initial contract and its continuation. If you sell something to a poor person and say "payable at a time of ease," the view of most scholars is that this is not valid, because the time is unknown, and the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade gharar sales. But if you sold to him and then his poverty became evident, the obligation is to grant him respite until a time of ease, unless you choose to cancel the contract, in which case there is no harm. If you do not choose cancellation, the obligation is respite. However, the preponderant view is that if you sell to him on deferred terms until a time of ease, the sale and the deferral are valid, because this is the requirement of the contract. Whoever sells to a person he knows to be insolvent has, by the nature of the contract, to grant him respite, since he knows he cannot demand payment now. If he says, "I will buy it from you, and by Allah I have nothing, but I will buy it from you until Allah makes me sufficient," the correct view is validity. A hadith on this from 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her): "A man had brought cloth from Syria, and 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Indeed, so-and-so has brought cloth from Syria; if only you sent for him to buy two garments until a time of ease."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (1213) from the hadith of 'Aishah.]] This indicates that such a thing is permissible. In any case, this will, God willing, come in the benefits.

﴿And if someone is in hardship, then [let there be] postponement until a time of ease﴾, and in one reading ﴿maysurah﴾ with a dammah, ﴿and that you give charity﴾, and in one reading ﴿wa-an tassaddaqu﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made respite obligatory for one who is in hardship, contrary to what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, when the insolvent debtor had more added to his debt or was compelled to pay. He said: ﴿then let there be postponement until a time of ease﴾. And His saying ﴿until a time of ease﴾, though it is unknown, is the reality, because as long as he is insolvent, the cause for granting respite exists, so it is not permissible to demand the debt from him.

Then Allah Most High said: ﴿And that you give charity is better for you﴾. ﴿Tasaddaqu﴾ with what? It was said: with granting respite, but there is room for doubt in that. It was also said: with remission, meaning that pardoning the debt is better for you. This is the correct view: the meaning of ﴿that you give charity﴾ is: with the remission of the debtor from his debt, it is better for you than granting him respite, because when you remit it, his obligation is cleared, whereas when you grant respite, his obligation remains occupied, though he is given time until he becomes well-off. It is well known that the first is more appropriate and gentler toward the debtor, which is remission, and it is better for the reason we mentioned: clearing the debtor's obligation so that he remains free of debt is better than granting respite while the debt remains.

Then He said: ﴿if you know﴾. This conditional clause is independent, intended to urge. I said "independent," meaning it is not connected to what precedes it, because if it were connected to what precedes it, it would give a corrupt meaning: that charity is better for us only if we know, and if we do not know, it is not better for us. There is no doubt that this meaning is corrupt and is not intended by the verse. Rather, the meaning of ﴿if you know﴾ is: if you are people of knowledge, then do it, that is, give charity. The meaning of the clause here is urging and inciting, because every intelligent person of knowledge will necessarily choose what is better.

This verse contains benefits, among them: the establishment of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Its basis: He made it obligatory upon His servants to grant the insolvent respite, and this is mercy toward whom? Toward the insolvent. So in it is the affirmation of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, among which is that He obliged the creditor to grant the insolvent respite.

Among its lessons: the wisdom of God Almighty in dividing people into wealthy and poor. In this verse, the wealthy one is the creditor (al-da'in), and the poor one is the debtor (al-mu'sir/al-madin). This wisdom of God Almighty is one without which the affairs of worshippers can never be set right. That is why the communists, who want to make people equal, have begun to retreat now. They have come to know that the worshippers cannot be set right except through this difference. God Almighty says: ﴿Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and raised some of them above others in rank, so that some of them may take others in service.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. Were it not for this elevation, could anyone be made to serve us and do what we want? Never. You go to a worker and say, "Come and work for me, and I will pay you money," and what does he say? He says, "(...) I am not a worker; you work for me." You find a merchant, and you say to him, for example, "Supply me with goods and I will give you such-and-such," and what does he say? He says, "What you have is with me... (...) and you, supply me." And so on. Thus the creation cannot be set right except by what the wisdom of God Almighty and His law require of the difference among them: this one is poor and this one is wealthy, so that by this the wisdom of God Almighty becomes clear and the conditions of the worshippers are upheld.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to grant respite to the poor debtor, that is, to give him time. The obligation to grant respite to the poor is shown by His saying: ﴿fa-nazhirah (then let there be postponement)﴾.

Among its benefits, i.e., of the verse: the obligation that the respite extend until he is in ease (al-maysarah), not until a month or a year. Or until a week, until he is in ease. Good. And if the period of ease is long? Yes, even if it is long.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that the ruling revolves around its cause, existing and non-existing. How so? Because when the obligation of granting respite was tied to the cause of hardship, it continues until the cause, which is hardship, is removed, so that it becomes permissible to demand payment from him. And the opposite of that is what the Prophet ﷺ said: «Delay by the wealthy is injustice.» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2287) and Muslim (1564/33) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] The wealthy man is forbidden to delay, and the creditor is forbidden to demand payment if the debtor is poor. If people walked in the fear of God Almighty in this matter, the conditions of people would be free of troubles. But we find the wealthy man delaying: the dirhams are with him in the drawer or in the box. The one who has a right comes to him and says, "Pay me my right." He says, "Tomorrow." He comes to him tomorrow, and he says, "After tomorrow," and so on, even though the Messenger ﷺ said: «Delay by the wealthy is injustice.» [Previously cited.] And we find those stingy people, possessed of greed, who do not grant the poor respite nor show him mercy. He says, "Give me, or else prison," and he actually imprisons him, even though it is not permissible to imprison him if we are certain that he is poor. It is not permissible to imprison him. Rather, the creditor is to be disciplined (ta'zir) if he insists on demanding payment while the debtor is poor. The creditor is to be disciplined. Why? Because his demand while the debtor is in hardship is a sin, and ta'zir (discretionary discipline), according to the scholars, is obligatory for every sin that has no prescribed penalty (hadd) and no expiation (kaffarah).

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of remission (al-ibra'), the virtue of remitting debt; by His saying: ﴿and that you give charity is better for you﴾. Remission is a sunnah, and granting respite is obligatory. Here, the sunnah is better than the obligatory by the text of the Qur'an: ﴿and that you give charity is better for you﴾. Is that not so? The sunnah is now better than the obligatory by the text of the Qur'an. Then a problem arises for us: how do we reconcile the meaning of the Noble Qur'an here with the saying of God the Glorified and Exalted in the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi): «My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him»? [Narrated by al-Bukhari (6502) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] For this implies that obligatory acts (fara'id) are better than voluntary acts (nawafil). Is that not so? There is no doubt that obligatory acts are better than voluntary acts, although the ignorant and foolish among us give more attention to voluntary acts than to obligatory acts. You find him in a voluntary prayer, humble, reflecting on what he says and does, while in an obligatory prayer it is the opposite: he looks at the clock at times, and at the pen at other times, and mentions something he has forgotten, so he takes out the pen and writes it down at ease, so that he does not forget. In the voluntary prayer you find him humble and reflecting on what he says and does. This is without doubt from our ignorance. Otherwise, attention to obligatory acts is more fitting than attention to voluntary acts. The point is: how do we reconcile the meaning of this noble verse with what the sacred hadith indicates? The answer is that the reconciliation between them is that when the voluntary act includes the obligatory, that is, when it contains the obligatory, it is superior, because it has become obligatory plus something extra. It has become obligatory plus something extra; do you understand? Good. Does remission include granting respite, or not? Yes, indeed, there is granting of respite and something extra. Is that not so? There is granting of respite and something extra. So we say it is better only because it includes the obligatory plus something extra. A parallel to that is what some scholars said: washing the limbs three times for wudu' is sunnah, and washing once is obligatory, and three times is better than the obligatory. How is three times better than the obligatory, when it is a sunnah and the obligatory is a fard? The answer: because this sunnah includes the obligatory, so it is obligatory plus something extra. They also said: initiating the greeting of peace is sunnah, and returning it is obligatory (fard), and initiating is better than returning, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «The better of the two is the one who begins with the greeting of peace.» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6077) and Muslim (6237) from the hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.] How is this, when the hadith says: «My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him»? [Previously cited.] They said: yes, because this return is built upon the initiation. So the initiation became legislated both in itself and for something else. Were it not for the initiation, the return would not have occurred. Since the return is built upon the initiation, the initiation here becomes superior, because it became both a cause and a principle. It is an initiatory greeting and a cause of an obligatory act, so it is given the virtue of the obligatory because it is its cause, and the virtue of initiation because it is the initiation. Do you understand?

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the difference of deeds in excellence. How so? By His saying: ﴿better for you﴾. The difference of deeds requires the difference of the doer, and that the doers differ among themselves in excellence. This is a matter known by necessity from both the revealed law and reason, that people of deeds differ: ﴿Those who sit at home, other than the disabled, are not equal to those who strive in the way of God with their wealth and their lives. God has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit at home﴾ [An-Nisa' 95]. Are they equal or not? They are not equal. ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. And to each God has promised the best﴾ [Al-Hadid 10]. From this noble verse there branches out for us now: the difference of deeds, from which branches the difference of the doer, and from which branches the difference of faith (iman). How so? Because deeds are part of faith according to Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (the people of the Sunnah and the community). So if deeds differ, it necessarily follows that faith differs. For this reason, the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah is that faith increases and decreases.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the virtue of knowledge, and that knowledge guides its possessor to good. By His saying: ﴿if you know﴾.

Can it be derived from the noble verse that remitting a debtor suffices for zakat? Pay attention. A person owes one hundred riyals in zakat. He finds a poor man who owes him one hundred riyals, and he says, "I have remitted this poor man, I have remitted him from my zakat." Is that sufficient for him or not? Let us look at the verse. Do you say that the verse indicates that remitting the poor man suffices for zakat? If someone says yes, the verse indicates that it suffices, because God called remission charity, and said: ﴿Alms are only for the poor and the needy﴾ [At-Tawbah 60]. If remission is charity, and you have remitted the poor man, then you have paid zakat. But the correct view is that it does not suffice. The correct view among the statements of the scholars is that it does not suffice. How so? Because God Almighty said: ﴿O you who believe, spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad, of which you spend while you would not accept it yourselves unless you overlook in it﴾ [Al-Baqarah 267]. He made the debt a zakat for the specific property. This is from aiming at the bad to pay it instead of the good. The bad here means the inferior, not what is unlawful. Is that not so? Because the specific property is an existing possession in the hand of its owner, who disposes of it as he wishes. But the debt owed by a poor debtor is, in reality, lost property, lost property. For the basic principle is the continuation of poverty, or its removal? The basic principle is the continuation of poverty. Then this debt is in the position of lost property, so it is not valid to make this lost property a zakat for specific property. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah), may God have mercy on him, said: this does not suffice without any dispute, without any dispute, it does not suffice. And if we said it suffices, then every person who has creditors who cannot pay would say, "I have remitted him and intended it as zakat," and so his wealth would remain with him, while the lost, perished debts that are not expected to be recovered would be the zakat. This is not possible. For this reason, if I gave you the choice, saying: "I will give you ten riyals, or I will transfer you to a poor person for ten," what would you choose?

* Students: Ten.
* Shaykh: You would give me ten?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: May God guide you. Reflect: I said to a person, "I will give you ten riyals in cash, or I will transfer you to a poor person," what does he take?
* Students: Ten.
* Shaykh: Ten?
* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: And he does not hesitate?
* Students: He does not hesitate.
* Shaykh: He does not hesitate. So then the ten riyals, in relation to the debt, become of the category of the good, and that one is of the category of the bad. If you wanted to give a person a fat, healthy sheep, and you gave him a thin, sick sheep, which one would he choose? The first. This is the same thing. So we say it is not permissible to remit the poor man and count that as zakat. Yes. If it were supposed that he would make it zakat for a debt, zakat for a debt: if we say zakat is obligatory on debt, then we might say this is correct, because this debt you have remitted has become of the same kind as the property with which you paid zakat on it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 281 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah.﴾ In another recitation: ﴿You will be returned to Allah therein.﴾ ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾ [al-Baqarah 281].

His saying: ﴿yawman﴾ ("a Day") here is not a time adverbial (zarf), because the action falls upon it, not within it. A time adverbial is one in which the action takes place, not one upon which it falls. So "the Day" is the thing feared (muttaqa), and it is the object (maf'ul bihi). The clause ﴿turja'un﴾ ("you will be returned") is a description of "a Day," because it is indefinite, and clauses following indefinite nouns function as descriptions. His saying ﴿thumma tuwaffa﴾ ("then will be paid in full") is coordinated with ﴿turja'un﴾, meaning: the Day on which you are returned, and on which you are paid in full what you earned. His saying ﴿wa-hum la yuzlamun﴾ ("and they will not be wronged") is a new independent clause (jumla isti'nafiyya). It may also be a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), but the first is more evident.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says, after mentioning many kinds of transactions and usury, that He warns against this Day on which all creatures will be returned to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He made the Day indefinite for the sake of magnifying it, and He did not specify it except by its description, which is His saying ﴿you will be returned to Allah therein﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection. Allah commanded us to fear it, so that we do not transgress against anyone. For if we wrong anyone, then on this Day, when we are in need of reward, the wronged person will take from our reward.

His saying ﴿thumma tuwaffa kullu nafs﴾ means: it is given in full. Tawfiya means istifa' (full payment), which is taking the right from the one who owes it. So ﴿tuwaffa kullu nafs﴾ means: it is given its reward and its wage that was written for it, if its deed was righteous; or, if its deed was evil, it is given the punishment for its deed.

His saying ﴿ma kasabat﴾ ("what it earned"): kasb is what a person does, or what comes to him through an action. What comes to a person through an action is called kasb. If a person trades and makes a profit, we say this is kasb. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the best of what you eat is from your earnings (kasb), and indeed your children are from your earnings."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3530) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As.]]

﴿wa-hum la yuzlamun﴾ ("and they will not be wronged"): zulm (wrongdoing) originally means diminishing. From it is His saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therefrom in anything﴾ [al-Kahf 33], meaning: it did not diminish. This is its original meaning, but it has come to be used in a more general sense, so that zulm occurs through diminishing and through increasing: through diminishing good deeds, and through increasing evil deeds. That is, a person's good deeds are not reduced and his evil deeds are not increased. As Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, he will not fear injustice (zulman) or diminution (hadman)﴾ [Ta-Ha 112]. ﴿Zulman﴾ refers to the increase of evil deeds, and ﴿hadman﴾ refers to the decrease of good deeds.

In this noble verse there is: the obligation to fear this Day, which is the Day of Resurrection, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾. But by what do we fear it? We fear it by carrying out the commands of Allah and avoiding His prohibitions.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: taqwa (fear of Allah, God-consciousness) may be attributed to other than Allah, but when it is not in the form of worship, it is attributed to other than Allah. One says: "Fear so-and-so," "Fear such-and-such." This is abundant in the Qur'an and Sunnah. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And fear Allah that you may receive mercy﴾ [al-Hujurat 10]; ﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran 131]. But there is a difference between the two kinds of taqwa: the first is taqwa of worship, humility and submission; the second is taqwa of protection only, by which one takes what protects him from the punishment of that Day or the punishment of the Fire. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware (ittaqi) the supplication of the one who has been wronged."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2448) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] Here he attributed taqwa to supplication. It is well known among people: "Beware the evil of the one to whom you have done good." But this taqwa attributed to a created being is not the taqwa of worship which is exclusively for Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of resurrection (al-ba'th), based on His saying: ﴿you will be returned to Allah therein﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the return of all creatures is to Allah, by His judgment, His decree and His recompense. The entire return is to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, as He says: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm 42], in all things.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and this is through resurrection. Allah the Exalted resurrects creatures after they had become bones (rumim) and dust.

* Among its benefits: the refutation of the Jabriyya (fatalists, who deny human choice).

* Students: (...)
* The Shaykh: (...) ﴿And fear a Day﴾. For the command to taqwa would be meaningless if the person were compelled, since that would be imposing what cannot be borne. Is that not so? Yes.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a person will not be paid on the Day of Resurrection except for his own deeds, based on His saying: ﴿then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾. Some scholars have used this to argue that it is not permissible to gift acts of worship (ihda' al-qurab) from a person to another. That is, if you do a righteous deed for a specific person, it does not benefit him and he does not gain from it, because Allah said: ﴿every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾, not what another earned. So whatever another earned is for him. Thus if a person does a righteous deed wishing it to go to his brother, his paternal uncle, his maternal uncle, or his friend, it does not benefit that person. But an exception is made for children. They said: because children are from one's earnings, and because it was established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the story of the woman who said: "My father has not been able to ride the mount (for Hajj), may I perform Hajj on his behalf?" He said: "Yes."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1513) and Muslim (1334/407) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] And in another report, the woman said: "My mother vowed to perform Hajj but did not perform it until she died; may I perform Hajj on her behalf?" He said: "Yes."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1852) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] They said: this is because children are from one's earnings, so the righteous deeds of children suffice for their fathers and mothers. As for supplication for others: if the one prayed for is a Muslim, he benefits from it by the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims, by text and by consensus. The text is His saying: ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith"﴾ [al-Hashr 10]. Allah did not mention this of them except that those prayed for benefit from it. As for consensus, all Muslims pray over the dead and say in the prayer: "O Allah, forgive him and have mercy on him." So they are unanimous that he benefits from this.

This matter is one in which the scholars differ, a long and broad disagreement. The preponderant view is that of Imam Ahmad in this matter: it is permissible for a person to do a righteous deed on behalf of whomever he wishes among the Muslims, except for what is obligatory (fard). It is not permissible to make an obligatory act for another, because it is obligatory upon him personally. So if a person performs wudu' for the noon prayer and intends that the wudu' be for his father, it is not valid and does not suffice, because it is obligatory upon you yourself. Obligatory acts are not gifted to anyone. Voluntary acts (nawafil) may be gifted: you do them and intend that the voluntary act is for so-and-so. But is this something required and legislated that a person should do? Or is it among the permissible matters which we do not call a bid'ah (innovation), but which we do not encourage? We say: it is not legislated (mashru') and we do not call it a bid'ah; rather we say it is among the permissible matters, and supplication (du'a') is better than it. Supplication is better than it. The evidence that supplication is better than deeds is that the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except from three: ongoing charity (sadaqah jariyah), or knowledge from which benefit is gained, or a righteous child who prays for him."[[Narrated by Muslim (1631/14) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] He did not say: "who prays for him, or gives charity for him, or fasts for him, or the like." The Prophet's guidance specifically toward supplication is evidence that it is better, and it is so.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a child is recorded to receive reward. From where is this taken? From ﴿kullu nafs﴾ ("every soul"), by generality. If someone says: and is punishment recorded against him?

* Students: (...)
* The Shaykh: We say: ﴿la yuzlamun﴾? Yes indeed. We say: first, that the Sunnah has come with the lifting of the pen from him.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4398) and al-Tirmidhi (1423) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] Is that so? And also He said: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾, and if the child were punished, that would be wronging him.

But if someone says: the sins of the child do not enter here, nor even the sins of the adult, because Allah said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It will have what it has earned, and it will bear what it has earned﴾ [al-Baqarah 286]. He distinguished between good deeds, saying ﴿what it earned (kasabat)﴾, and evil deeds, saying ﴿what it has earned (iktasabat)﴾. If someone says that ﴿kasabat﴾ here excludes ﴿iktasabat﴾, we say this is not correct, it is not valid. For Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So the evil consequences of what they earned (kasabu) befell them, and those who wronged among these will be struck by the evil consequences of what they earned (kasabu), and they cannot escape﴾ [al-Zumar 51]. So He made evil deeds a kasb. But its benefit in the verse of al-Baqarah is said to be verbal: for the sake of varying the wording, kasaba and iktasaba. If the verse were "what it earned and what it earned," there would be some awkwardness; but as it is, ﴿laha ma kasabat wa-'alayha ma iktasabat﴾ [al-Baqarah 286] has the same meaning with different wording.
