It is also said that there is a real difference between them. Kasb may come from a person's own action or from the action of another: if someone gives you a gift, it is kasb. Iktisab, however, is what a person strives to attain, and it is only recorded against him for what he himself did directly, not what came to him from others. That is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another, and if a heavily laden soul calls to [another] to carry its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative﴾ [Fatir 18].

If someone says to his relative: "O so-and-so, did you drink wine?" He says: "Yes." He says: "Your sin is upon me." "O so-and-so, did you steal?" He says: "Yes." "Your sin is upon me." "O so-and-so, did you commit fornication?" He says: "Yes." He says: "Your sin is upon me." "O so-and-so, did you associate partners with Allah?" He says: "Yes." He says: "Your sin is upon me." Fine. But what happens to the one who said this? Is either of these two things transferred to him? No, neither of them. Shirk and what is less than it do not transfer to him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Follow our way, and we will bear your sins." But they will not bear anything of their sins. Indeed, they are liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut 12].

* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: The meaning is that his deed which is his own deed has been cut off. That is why He attributed it to himself, and did not say: "the deed has been cut off from him." If the wording of the hadith were "the deed has been cut off from him," then no deed would reach him. But the Messenger (ﷺ) informed that his deed itself is cut off, except from three.

* Student: (...). His father performed Hajj, and (...) I am an ordinary person (...) after he learned the rites and learned the correct Hajj. Then may he perform Hajj (...)?
* The Shaykh: You mean he doubts whether the obligation was performed?
* Student: He is doubtful, O Shaykh, that his father did not perform the obligation in the correct manner.
* The Shaykh: If he thinks that his father neglected the obligation, then the apparent view here is to favor that he perform Hajj on his behalf. But if he wants to perform Hajj on his behalf while knowing that his father performed the obligation in the most complete manner within his ability, then we say that supplication is better.
* Student: (...)
* The Shaykh: By Allah, ordinary people benefit if they are guided to a righteous, knowledgeable man.
* Student: O Shaykh, regarding some scholars who say: (...) reward, except what has evidence for it. They use as evidence the generality of the saying of Allah, Glorified: ﴿And that man will have only what he strove for﴾ [al-Najm 39], and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/17) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] He says: what is reported is done, and what is not reported (...)?
* The Shaykh: As for the first, ﴿And that man will have only what he strove for﴾, it is correct: he has only what he strove for. The striving of another is not his. But if another wants to make it his, meaning it is not possible that the striving of another be taken from him and given to him. However, if he gives you something that you do not have, just as if you said: "You have only what you own of wealth," and a person came and gave you some wealth. As for restricting oneself to what is reported, it is said that the reports are case-specific events (qada ya a'yan). If they were statements from the Messenger (ﷺ), we would say: yes, we are bound by them. But they are case-specific events: people came to the Messenger and he did something, and he said: "Yes, it suffices." This indicates that righteous deeds on behalf of others do in fact suffice. For we do not know: if a man came and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I prayed two rak'ahs for my mother, or for my father, or for my brother," we do not know what the answer would be. But if they were statements, such as that he said: "Whoever gives charity for his father, mother, brother or the like," we would say this is a statement and we would restrict ourselves to it. As for people who ask us, we do not know. For example, if a thousand people came asking, each asking about a deed, the expected answer, which we assume the Messenger would give, is: "Yes." As for the hadith "Whoever does a deed that is not upon our command, it is rejected,"[[Narrated by Muslim (1718/18) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]] yes, that is for one who does a deed that is not upon the command of Allah and His Messenger. But this one did a deed that is upon the command of Allah and His Messenger, sincerely for Allah and following the Messenger of Allah, but wishing to benefit a Muslim person by it.
* Student: The prayer?
* The Shaykh: The prayer of what?
* Student: Like night prayer (qiyam al-layl), he prays at night with the intention (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, no. Look: it is either a deputation (niyaba) or a gift (ihda'). A gift has no obstacle.
* Student: He prays (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, yes, he prays and says: "O Allah, I intend that this prayer be for my father, its reward is for my father." But as for saying to his father, "Sleep in your bed and I will pray on your behalf by way of agency (wakala)," that is not acceptable.
* Student: O Shaykh, is Hajj better than supplication (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but is it based on being an act of worship, not supplication? For this reason, if you went and said, "Here I am, O Allah, here I am," and circumambulated without speaking any supplication, and performed sa'y without speaking any supplication, and did all the acts with remembrance (dhikr) rather than supplication, does the Hajj suffice or not? It suffices, yes.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, the return is to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Student: The judgment (...)?
* The Shaykh: The judgment is more general. The judgment is more general, meaning that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, judges a matter and it happens, and the decree is in the eternal past.
* Student: The hadith "Supplication is worship" (...). First, a person supplicates for himself. Here the intended meaning of supplication is worship, comprehensive of all worship, based on the hadith "Supplication is worship"?
* The Shaykh: This does not hold up, no, it does not hold up. Undoubtedly supplication is worship, because when a person raises his hands to Allah and asks Him, this is devotion and humility. But when supplication is mentioned without qualification, what is meant is supplication of request (du'a' al-mas'alah). Yet supplication of request is part of worship.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes. This is some of the common people's practice: when the deceased craves this type of food ordinarily, they bring it and place their hands upon it, saying: "O Allah, make its reward for so-and-so." This is without doubt a bid'ah, one of the innovations. For they think, and Allah knows best, that since he loved it, he wants to be given it. If, for example, it is harees (a grain and meat dish) and he loves harees and meat, and they say: "O Allah, make its reward his," then he will be brought harees and meat in his grave.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: I see the common people (...)
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: By Allah, there is no doubt that this formula was not reported from the early generations (salaf). But if they say: "We are doing it, for our eating of it is charity," as the Messenger (ﷺ) said: "When a person spends on himself, it is charity, and when he spends on his wife, it is charity,"[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (1690) from the hadith of Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, with the wording: "Whoever spends on himself and his family."]] then this falls under this category.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, we say this is a reward for him, but this door should not be opened. This door should never be opened before the common people.
* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: Now some people rely on others in this matter. If one of them says, "By Allah, I will not make a bequest," he says, "My dependents are my supper and my general sacrifice (...)"
* * *
* Student: Allah the Most High said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And let a scribe write it between you in justice. And no scribe should refuse to write as Allah has taught him. So let him write, and let the one who has the obligation dictate. And let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything from it. But if the one who has the obligation is of limited understanding, or weak, or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate in justice. And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men. And if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of them errs, the other can remind her. And the witnesses should not refuse when they are called. And do not be weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, for its specified term.﴾ [al-Baqarah 282]
* Shaykh: "Enough. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan." Allah the Most High said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾.
I suppose we have finished with everything in the previous discussion and the benefits? Good.
This noble verse is the longest verse in the Book of Allah, and, as you see, it concerns transactions between people. And the shortest verse in the Book of Allah is ﴿Then he looked﴾ [al-Muddaththir 21], because it has six letters?
* Student: ﴿Ta Ha﴾ [Ta-Ha 1]
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, but these are the alphabetic letters. I think among them there is something shorter than ﴿Ta Ha﴾ [Ta-Ha 1], such as ﴿Nun﴾ [al-Qalam 1] and ﴿Sad﴾ [Sad 1]. But we mean non-alphabetic letters: ﴿Then he looked﴾ [al-Muddaththir 21]. So the longest verse is the verse of debt, and the shortest verse is ﴿Then he looked﴾ [al-Muddaththir 21]. And the verse that comprises all the alphabetic letters: there are only two verses in the Qur'an that have gathered all the alphabetic letters.
* Student: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath 29]
* Shaykh: Yes, that is one. ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath 29], up to the end of the verse, this includes all the alphabetic letters. Yes. The second?
* Student: ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness overcoming a group of you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 154]
* Shaykh: Yes, ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness﴾ [Ali 'Imran 154]. In Ali 'Imran, this verse includes all the alphabetic letters. But the verse we have here, despite its length, does not include all the alphabetic letters.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 1 of 6):

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.﴾ It has already been explained to us that introducing a ruling with the address "O you who..." indicates the importance given to it, because the address (nida') is for alerting, and one does not alert to anything except something significant. It has also been mentioned previously that when the address is directed to the believers, there are benefits in it:
First: encouragement and urging, as if He is calling them by the quality of their faith, which drives them to carry out the command and avoid the prohibition.
Second: that adherence to this is one of the requirements of faith.
Third: that opposing it is among the things that diminish faith. These are three benefits in addressing the believers. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When Allah, the Exalted, says: 'O you who have believed,' then give it your ear" – meaning: listen to it – "for it is either good that you are commanded to, or evil that you are forbidden from."[[Narrated by Ibn al-Mubarak in az-Zuhd (36) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt﴾. Faith (iman) linguistically is more specific than tasdiq (affirmation/belief in the sense of confirming truth), because faith (iman) ... You say: "I believed him (amantu lahu)," and for the one who reports something you say: "I believed in him (amantu bihi)." ﴿O you who have believed﴾: so faith in the Sharia sense is an affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. As for acceptance, it is acceptance of what? Acceptance of the report and acceptance of the ruling too, whether you accept that this is obligatory or that this is recommended or the like. As for submission, it means surrender and compliance. Whoever affirms without acceptance is not a believer. Abu Talib, for example, affirmed the message of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, but he was not a believer, because he did not accept and did not submit.
﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.﴾ ﴿Tadayantum﴾ indicates an action occurring between two parties, like "tusharaka" (they shared), "tuqatila" (they fought), "tusabba" (they reviled one another), "takhasama" (they disputed), and the like. That is: when some of you deal in debt with one another. The word "mudayana" is applied to a known debt and also to recompense: "Whoever does you a kindness, reward him"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (1672) from the hadith of Ibn Umar.]] and "As you judge, so you will be judged"[[Narrated by Ma'mar in al-Jami' (20262) from the hadith of Abu Qilabah.]]. Therefore He emphasized it by saying: ﴿debt﴾ in order to exclude recompense. That is, if I give you something and you give me something, this is not mudayana, because I worked and was rewarded; and the saying "as you judge, so you will be judged" applies to this. But when He said ﴿debt﴾, He removed this possibility, and what is meant is what is fixed in the liability (dhimmah), that is, when you deal in a transaction involving debt. Debt is everything that is fixed in the liability, and its opposite is a specific item ('ayn). So if I sell you this bag for this recorder, is this a debt or not a debt? This is a specific item, not a debt. And if I sell you this bag for ten riyals, without specifying it, then this is both a specific item and a debt: the thing sold is a specific item, and the price is a debt.
He says: ﴿when you contract a debt﴾. Therefore, debt is everything that is fixed in the liability, so the price of an unspecified sold item is a debt, the wage is a debt, the loan is a debt, the dowry is a debt; in short, everything fixed in the liability is a debt. This differs from what is understood by the common people by "debt," for the common people think debt means tawarruq, but that is not so; rather tawarruq is one type of debts. So debt is everything fixed in the liability: the price of a sale, a wage, a dowry, or a loan – a loan meaning salaf – or other than that.
And His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾ means up to a defined end point. The term (ajal) is the end point to which a thing comes to its conclusion. ﴿Specified (musamman)﴾ means determined and defined, such as: "I sold you this item for ten riyals until the month of Rajab." This is a specified term...?
Student: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down, and let a scribe write between you justly, and let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him. So let him write, and let the one who has the obligation dictate, and let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything from it. But if the one who has the obligation is feeble-minded or weak or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate justly. And call upon two witnesses from among your men; but if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses – so that if one of the two errs, the other can remind her. And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called. And be not weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, for its term.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 282].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.﴾
This noble verse is the longest verse in the Book of Allah, and it concerns dealings between people, as you see. And the shortest verse in the Book of Allah? ﴿Then he looked﴾ [al-Muddaththir 21], because it has six letters.
* Student: Ta-Ha.
* The Shaykh: Yes, no – the letters of the alphabet, I think, are shorter in it than Ta-Ha, Nun, Sad, but we want non-alphabetic letters: ﴿Then he looked﴾. So the longest verse is the verse of debt, and the shortest verse is ﴿Then he looked﴾, and the verse that contains all the letters of the alphabet – there are only two verses in the Qur'an that contain all the letters of the alphabet.
* Student: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath 29].
* The Shaykh: Yes, that is one: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him...﴾ to the end of the verse, which contains all the letters of the alphabet. The second?
* Student: ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness overcoming a faction of you﴾ [Ali 'Imran 154].
* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿Then He sent down upon you﴾ in Ali 'Imran, ﴿after distress, security in the form of drowsiness﴾; this contains all the letters of the alphabet. But the verse we have here, despite its length, does not include all the letters of the alphabet.
Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt, write it down.﴾ It has already been explained to us that introducing a ruling with the address "O you who..." indicates the importance given to it, because the address is for alerting, and one alerts only to something significant. It has also been mentioned previously that when the address is directed to the believers, there are benefits in it:
First: encouragement and urging, as if He is calling them by the quality of their faith, which drives them to carry out the command and avoid the prohibition.
Second: that adherence to this is one of the requirements of faith.
Third: that opposing it is among the things that diminish faith. These are three benefits in addressing the believers. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When Allah says: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, then give it your ear" – meaning: listen to it – "for it is either good that you are commanded to, or evil that you are forbidden from."[[Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur in at-Tafsir (50) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt﴾. Faith linguistically is more specific than tasdiq; because faith is ... You say: "I believed him," and for the one who reports something you say: "I believed in him."
﴿O you who have believed﴾: so faith in the Sharia sense is: an affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. As for acceptance, it is acceptance of what? Acceptance of the report and acceptance of the ruling too, whether you accept that this is obligatory or that this is recommended or the like. As for submission, it means surrender and compliance. Whoever affirms without acceptance is not a believer. Abu Talib, for example, affirmed the message of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, but he was not a believer, because he did not accept and did not submit.
﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.﴾ ﴿Tadayantum﴾ indicates an action occurring between two parties, like "tusharaka," "tuqatila," "tusabba," "takhasama," and the like. That is: when some of you deal in debt with one another. The word "mudayana" is applied to a known debt and also to recompense: "Whoever does you a kindness, reward him"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan (1672), and an-Nasa'i in al-Mujtaba (2567) from the hadith of Ibn Umar.]] and "As you judge, so you will be judged"[[Narrated by Ma'mar in al-Jami' (20262), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat (132) from the hadith of Abu Qilabah.]]; therefore He emphasized it by saying: ﴿debt﴾ in order to exclude recompense. That is, if I give you and you give me, this is not mudayana, because I worked and was rewarded, and to this applies the saying "as you judge, so you will be judged." But when He said ﴿debt﴾, He removed this possibility, and what is meant is what is fixed in the liability, that is, when you deal in a transaction involving debt. Debt is everything fixed in the liability, and its opposite is a specific item ('ayn). So if I sell you this bag for this recorder, is this a debt or not a debt? This is a specific item, not a debt. And if I sell you this bag for ten riyals, without specifying it, then this is both a specific item and a debt: the thing sold is a specific item, and the price is a debt.
He says: ﴿when you contract a debt﴾. Therefore, debt is everything fixed in the liability: the price of an unspecified sold item is a debt, the wage is a debt, the loan is a debt, the dowry is a debt; in short, everything fixed in the liability is a debt. This differs from what is understood by the common people by "debt," for the common people think debt means tawarruq, but that is not so; rather tawarruq is one type of debts. So debt is everything fixed in the liability: the price of a sale, a wage, a dowry, or a loan – a loan meaning salaf – or other than that.
And His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾, that is, up to a defined end point. The term (ajal) is the end point to which a thing comes to its conclusion. ﴿Specified (musamman)﴾ means determined and defined, such as: "I sold you this item for ten riyals until the month of Rajab." This is a specified term, is it not? Specified, specified by the month.
And His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾ – does it imply something? It implies two things: that a debt may be without a term, and that a debt may be for an unspecified term. A debt may be without a term, such as if you say: "I sold you this item for ten riyals"; this is a debt but not deferred. An unspecified term: "I sold you this item for ten riyals until the arrival of Zayd." Is this deferred or not deferred?
* The students: Deferred.
* The Shaykh: With a specified term or an unspecified term?
* The students: Unspecified.
* The Shaykh: Unspecified; this is unknown, because we do not know when Zayd will arrive. He may arrive after a day, or after a year, or after ten years, or he may not arrive at all.
"I sold you this item until the time of harvest"?
* The students: Specified.
* The Shaykh: Known?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The harvest is known, the harvest of crops, but is it determined or not determined?
* The students: Determined.
* The Shaykh: The scholars differed on this. Some of them say it is not determined, because harvest contains some uncertainty; between the beginning of the harvest and its end there may be a month or more, so this involves uncertainty and is not valid. But the correct view is that it is valid, and that when people differ in this way, the middle is considered, because this is the apparent meaning of the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The people used to pay in advance for fruits for a year or two years."[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (2253) and Muslim (1604/127) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas. The wording is his.]] And it is known that the seller of fruit, when he delivers the item, does so at the time of picking, and the time of picking is like the time of harvest. Yes.
He says: ﴿so write it down﴾. The fa' here is connective for the answer; the answer to what? The answer of the conditional in ﴿when﴾: ﴿so write it down﴾. As you see, this is a command. Is this command for obligation, recommendation, or guidance? It was explained to us in usul al-fiqh that a command comes for obligation, recommendation, and guidance. Which of these is it to be understood as? The basic position is the first; it was said – and this is the view of the majority – that it is the second; and it was said that it is for guidance, because this is a direction toward a transaction in which the preservation of a person's right is the only aim, and there is no injustice in it. But those who said it is for recommendation said: this is the least we can say about a command, and if it is for preserving a person's right, which Allah has commanded, then it is recommended, and a person is forbidden from squandering wealth.
Those who said it is obligatory said: because in this there is a prevention of what may happen through forgetfulness; for if it is not written, it becomes exposed to forgetting, and if forgetting occurs, disputes and enmity arise that lead to hatred and resentment among Muslims, and hatred and resentment among Muslims is forbidden, so whatever causes it is itself forbidden. For this reason, Allah gave as the reason for prohibiting wine and gambling what?
* Student: That it is an abomination of Satan's handiwork.
* The Shaykh: Then He said: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling﴾ [al-Ma'idah 91].
In any case, the basic position is obligation, but the majority said it is for recommendation, and they cited for this His saying: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted fulfil his trust﴾; and the discussion of this will come, if Allah wills, in the benefits. He says: ﴿so write it down﴾, that is: write the debt.
﴿And let a scribe write between you justly, and let no scribe refuse﴾, and so on to the end. ﴿And let him write﴾: the lam here is the lam of command, but it is well known that the lam of command is kasra-vowelled, as in His saying: ﴿Let the one of wealth spend from his wealth﴾, and here it is not kasra-vowelled, so why?
* Student: Because it came after the waw and after thumma.
* The Shaykh: After the waw; when it comes after waw, thumma, and what else?
* The Student: And the fa'.
* The Shaykh: And the fa'. When the lam of command comes after these three letters, it is sukun-vowelled.
He says: ﴿let a scribe write between you justly﴾. ﴿A scribe (katib)﴾ is indefinite, to show that it is sufficient for one of the scribes to write, that is, anyone among the scribes may write. But He said ﴿justly﴾. Justice ('adl) is uprightness, and uprightness in reporting is truthfulness, and uprightness in ruling is the opposite of oppression, and the scribe is therefore a reporter, since he will write, and in reality he is also a judge. For this reason, this scribe must be trustworthy, possess integrity, and have knowledge of Sharia-compliant writing, because Sharia-compliant writing is justice. It is not enough to bring anyone from the market and say: "Come, write between us." Rather, he must be a just scribe who writes justly, just and writes justly. Accordingly, we say: ﴿justly﴾ is a description that refers to the scribe and to the writing: that the scribe be just and that the writing be just, which means conforming to what the Sharia has brought.
And His saying: ﴿let a scribe write between you﴾ – is this "between" (bayn) a relation of transaction, that is, a figurative "between," or a spatial "between"?
* Student: The first.
* The Shaykh: Apparently it is the first, that is, between you in the transaction, because the transaction is between two parties, so it binds them together. Some people said it also includes the spatial "between," and that the scribe should, at the time of writing, be positioned between the two contracting parties, so that he hears from each of them equally; for if he were on one side, the words of the distant party might be hidden from him, and the one who is near the distant party might murmur – and what does murmuring mean? It means that he disturbs him, mumbles so that the other does not hear well. They said: so "between" here includes the relation of the transaction, which is the bond between the two, and the spatial "between": ﴿let a scribe write between you justly﴾.
﴿And let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him, so let him write﴾: ﴿la﴾ here – how do we parse it? And how do we parse ﴿la﴾?
* Student: Negative.
* The Shaykh: Negative with the fa'?
* Student: A prohibitive la.
* The Shaykh: Yes. What told you it is prohibitive?
* Student: Because the verb came after it.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: Because it put the verb in the jussive.
* The Shaykh: It put the verb in the jussive. Where is the jussive verb?
* Student: ﴿wa la ya'ba﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿ya'ba﴾ is not jussive? It is fatha-vowelled?
* Student: The weak letter was dropped.
* The Shaykh: It is jussive by dropping the weak letter, which is the alif. Is that right?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 2 of 6):

He said: ﴿Let not a scribe refuse﴾. ﴿Yaba'﴾ means: let him refrain. ﴿A scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him﴾. ﴿An yaktuba﴾ ("to write") is a masdariyyah (verbal-noun) clause, interpreted as a verbal noun. What is its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis)? Either: "let not a scribe refuse writing," or "let not the scribe refrain from writing." If it is the first, the verb is transitive by itself. If it is the second, it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid).

He said: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him﴾. The kaf here is for comparison (tashbih). It is also said that it is for causation (ta'lil). On the first reading, Allah, glorified and exalted, forbids him to refuse writing in the manner Allah has taught him, because Allah, glorified and exalted, taught man how to write between contracting parties. So it is not permissible for him to refrain from writing as Allah has taught him; rather it is obligatory for him to write as Allah has taught him. This is if we take it as what? As comparison.

If we take it as causation, the meaning becomes: let not a scribe refuse to write, because Allah taught him writing. So let him remember Allah's favour upon him and His kindness to him, and let him be good to the servants of Allah as Allah was good to him. This is like His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ [al-Qasas 77].

But if someone asks: does the kaf come for causation?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: He is asked to give an example.
* Student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah 198].
* Shaykh: His saying, ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾, meaning: because of His guidance to you.
He is asked to give evidence for that from the words of Ibn Malik.
* Student: His saying:
"Liken it with the kaf; and with it, causation is sometimes intended, and it occurs as an extra particle for emphasis."
* Shaykh: "Liken it with the kaf, and with it causation is sometimes intended," meaning: with it, causation is sometimes meant.

He says: ﴿So let him write﴾. ﴿As Allah has taught him, so let him write﴾. The fa' is for resulting consequence (tafri'), the lam is the imperative lam, and it is sukun-ed because it came after the fa'. What is the position of ﴿so let him write﴾ in relation to what precedes it?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. We said: the fa' is for consequence. But what is its relation in meaning to what precedes it? That is: if someone says that his saying ﴿And let not a scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him﴾ suffices in place of it, since when he is forbidden from refusing to write, it follows that he must write. Do we then say that it is for emphasis (tawkid)? Yes, some scholars said it is for emphasis. Others said: rather it is for establishing a new ruling (ta'sis) and not for emphasis. It has passed before you in Mukhtasar al-Tahrir fi Usul al-Fiqh that when a statement may be either emphasis or establishment, it is taken as establishment, because emphasis is an addition. Some scholars say it is for establishment. How so? He said: because the prohibition on refusing to write does not require hastening to it, whereas the command to write requires hastening, because the command implies immediacy (fawr), as has passed in usul al-fiqh. So it is as if He said: let not a scribe refuse, and let him hasten to write. For example, if the scribe writes after a month, would one say that he refused to write? No, he complied. But when it is said "so let him write," its meaning is that he hastens to write and does not procrastinate. He says to those who come to him: "By God, come tomorrow." They come tomorrow, and he says: "Come after tomorrow." After tomorrow, he says: "Come in two days." After two days, he says: "After a week, I am travelling." After a week, he says: "Come after a month." After a month he writes. We say: this one refused, or did not refuse? In the end he wrote. But ﴿so let him write﴾ is what restricts this command. So it has a benefit; is it emphatic? We say: it has a benefit; it is establishing, not emphatic. He said: ﴿so let him write﴾.

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾. ﴿Yumlil﴾ is also said as yumli. Both are eloquent dialects; al-imlal and al-imla' have the same meaning. Do you understand? So you say, for example, amlaytu 'alayhi, and you say amlaltu 'alayhi. It is standard eloquent Arabic and it is in the Quran.

He said: ﴿And let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾. Why not "the one to whom the right is owed"? It is "the one upon whom it is owed," because the creditor may tell the scribe: "Write that so-and-so owes me a million riyals," when he is owed a hundred. Is that possible? Yes, it is possible for one who does not fear Allah. But the debtor is the one who dictates, because he is the one being claimed against. He dictates and says: "Write that I borrowed from so-and-so such-and-such," that is a debt; "that I bought from so-and-so goods for such-and-such," that is a debt; "that I rented from so-and-so a house for such-and-such," that is a debt. The point is: who dictates? The one upon whom the right is owed.

He said: ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything from it﴾. Glory be to Allah! When Allah, mighty and majestic, commanded that the one who dictates is the one upon whom the right is owed and no other, He directed to him a command and a prohibition. The command: ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, meaning: let him take a shield against the punishment of Allah, so he speaks the truth. ﴿And not diminish from it﴾, meaning: from the right, ﴿anything﴾. Bakhs means: to reduce. Reduction of a right is either in quantity, or in quality, or in both, or in the term. Now we are speaking of a deferred debt. In quantity: the debt's principal is a hundred, and he tells the scribe: "Write fifty," or "write ninety." Or the debt is of a good kind, and he says: "Write medium," that "I owe him a hundred sa' of medium-quality wheat." What is this? Quality. Or the debt falls due after a year, and he says: "Write that I owe him such-and-such, due in two years," for example. All of this is bakhs, so it is not permissible for the one who owes the right to diminish any of the right, neither in quantity nor in quality, nor in ... ? Nor in the term.
Can we say: nor in kind? Or is it included in quality? It is included in quality. So kind, for example: it is wheat, and he makes it barley.
* Student: Barley.
* Shaykh: No, barley is a genus (jins).

﴿If the one who owes the debt is foolish, or weak, or unable to dictate﴾. ﴿Yumilla﴾ means: yumli. ﴿Or is unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate with justice﴾. The one who dictates is the one who dictates, i.e., the one upon whom the right is owed. But Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned that there are three situations in which the one upon whom the right is owed does not dictate, and instead his guardian dictates. He said: ﴿foolish, or weak, or unable to dictate﴾.

﴿Foolish﴾ refers to conduct, meaning he does not manage affairs well. For example, if the creditor says: "Write such-and-such," and he says: "Fine (...)." For example, this foolish person, who does not manage affairs well, the debt owed on him is a hundred riyals. They come to the scribe, and he says: "Write that I owe him a hundred riyals." The creditor says to him: "You are a generous man, a good man, a beloved man," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on a man who is lenient when he sells, lenient when he buys, lenient when he pays, and lenient when he demands payment." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (2076) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.] "Make it two hundred, my friend. Since it is deferred for a year, make it two hundred." He says: "Write two hundred." What would this be? This is foolishness. Or the debt was of a poor kind, and the creditor said: "Write good quality." The foolish person might write it, would he not? Because he does not manage affairs well. So we say: this foolish person does not dictate. Who dictates? ﴿His guardian with justice﴾. The guardian of the foolish person, with justice. The guardian is one who takes charge of his affairs, whether a father, an older brother, a grandfather, a mother, or the like.

﴿Or weak﴾. Is weakness here of the body or of the mind? Both: weakness of body because of youth, and weakness of mind because of madness. The one upon whom the right is owed is a minor who has not reached maturity, or he is an adult but insane or mentally deficient. Such a person does not dictate. Who dictates? His guardian.

﴿Or is unable to dictate himself﴾: he is unable to dictate himself because he is mute or afflicted with a defect, or he is unable to dictate because the situation is one of awe and grandeur, such as being in the presence of a minister, a president, or the like. Suppose a man has a debt owed by the head of state. Is this possible or not?
* Students: It is possible.
* Shaykh: Or is he owed a debt by the head of state?
* Students: It is not possible.
* Shaykh: He is owed a debt by the head of state, and the situation is one of awe, so he is unable to dictate. Who dictates? His guardian. Who is his guardian before the head of state? Yes, we bring someone like him, like the president.

In any case, inability is either due to a defect, like muteness, or due to an accident, like an incident that prevents him from speaking, or because the situation is one of awe, so he cannot dictate as he should.

﴿If the one who owes the debt is foolish, or weak, or unable to dictate himself﴾: in it, ﴿an yumilla﴾ (to dictate). Its place in i'rab?
* Student: Verbal noun.
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: It is an object, interpreted as a verbal noun functioning as an object. ﴿Huwa﴾?
* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: Emphasis, or subject? Can it not be a subject? Yes, ﴿huwa﴾ is not suitable as the subject; rather ﴿huwa﴾ is an emphatic pronoun.

If someone says: you said that when the pronoun can be estimated as huwa or hiya, it is concealed permissibly (mustatir jawazan). And the permissible is that which, if you wish, you conceal, and if you wish, you make it apparent, is it not so? So it is valid for ﴿huwa﴾ to be the subject, and some grammarians said that ﴿huwa﴾ is the subject. But the researching grammarians say: the meaning of our saying "concealed permissibly" is that it is permissible for an apparent noun to take its place, not that it is permissible for the pronoun itself to be made explicit. So when you say "Muhammad stood," for example, it is not valid to say "stood he" and make "he" the subject. Rather "he" is an emphatic for the concealed pronoun. The meaning of our saying "permissibly" is that an apparent noun can take its place. This is the view of the researching grammarians. Others said: it is permissible to make the apparent pronoun the subject. The matter in this is not of great importance; nothing major depends on this disagreement.

He said: ﴿So let his guardian dictate﴾. The lam here is the lam of command, and it is sukun-ed because it came after the fa', as previously explained. ﴿His guardian﴾: we said he is the one who takes charge of his affairs, whether a father, a grandfather, a brother, a mother, or others.

His saying ﴿with justice﴾ is connected to ﴿yumlil﴾, meaning: dictation with justice, such that he does not wrong the one to whom the right is owed out of favouritism toward his relative, nor wrong his relative out of fear of the creditor. Rather it must be with justice. What is justice here? Truthful speech that corresponds to reality, neither adding nor subtracting.

He said: ﴿And call to witness two witnesses from among your men﴾. ﴿Istashhidu﴾: to call to witness whom?
* Student: To the writing.
* Shaykh: To the writing, or to the debt? That is, call witnesses along with the writing.
Istashhada means: he asked someone to bear witness, like istaghfara means: he asked for forgiveness. Istashhada means: he asked another for testimony.

﴿And call to witness two witnesses from among your men﴾. Here He said ﴿istashhidu shahidayn﴾ and did not say "ithnayn" (two). Why? So that our request for these two men is a request for those who are fit to be witnesses. Otherwise He would have said: "and call two men to witness." But ﴿shahidayn min rijalikum﴾ means: those who are of the people fit for testimony. And the people fit for testimony, as we have known previously, must be Muslim, adult, sane, just, able to speak, and retentive, the six conditions that have passed.

His saying ﴿from among your men﴾ is addressed to the believers. The phrase ﴿min rijalikum﴾ ("from among your men") was used instead of "from among your males," because the witness must be adult.

﴿And if they are not two men﴾, meaning: if the witnesses are not two men, ﴿then one man and two women﴾.

* Shaykh: No, it is not permissible. Yes, only the one upon whom the right is owed dictates.

* Shaykh: This will come to us, God willing, in the benefits (fawa'id). But there is no harm in mentioning it now. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, because the Lord, mighty and majestic, has creation, dominion, and management. When He has management and dominion, He is worthy of being feared, like His saying in surah al-Talaq: ﴿And fear Allah, your Lord; do not expel them from their houses﴾ [al-Talaq 1]. Yes.

* Student: This is the principal.
* Shaykh: It is not sufficient.

* Shaykh: In reality, here there is a right of the principal and a right upon him. A right to him, because he may be claimed against, and this one says: "I have witnesses that I am your agent." Do you understand? And a right upon him, because if that man acted (...) he would not say (...). Therefore you must know the one in whose favour and the one against whom the testimony is given. You must know them all.
* Student: What is meant by ﴿and two women﴾? Do the two women testify for a stranger?
* Shaykh: Yes, we will come to it; we have not reached it yet.
* Student: Shaykh, His saying ﴿And let the one upon whom the right is owed dictate﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, because if the one upon whom the right is owed wanted to conceal, that one would not obey him.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but the basic principle is that this is the one whose statement is accepted. That is, in a dispute, for example, whose statement is accepted?
* Student: The one upon whom the right is owed.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed; therefore it is he who dictates.
* Student: Shaykh, the one who dictates is the one upon whom the right is owed. If he himself writes, and no one else who knows writing is available, may he write it himself?
* Shaykh: And what would he write?
* Student: The document (kitab).
* Shaykh: An acknowledgment (iqrar), that is?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no harm, there is no obstacle.

* Shaykh: Can he not write it? Because afterward, if a dispute arises?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Two or three days later, he came to him and said: (...).

* Student: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And let a scribe write it between you with justice. And let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him. So let him write, and let the one who has the obligation dictate.﴾
* Shaykh: ﴿So let him write﴾. Stop here.

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says in the verse of debt, which is the longest verse in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.﴾ This is the beginning of our discussion.

What is meant by "debt" here?

**Student:** (...)

**Shaykh:** That is, what becomes established in the liability (dhimmah).

If I sell you a book for ten dirhams, is this a debt? Is this book, for example, sold for ten dirhams?

**Student:** No, it is not a debt (...).

**Shaykh:** No. A specific book is not a debt for ten dirhams?

**Shaykh:** It falls under it, since ten riyals, the price of the book you bought from me, become established in your liability. Is that clear?

Does this fall under the noble verse, in the sense that this debt must be written down? In the case we mentioned: I sold this book to him for ten dirhams and we separated; I gave him the book and we parted, and he did not take possession of the price. Does it fall under the verse?

**Student:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** How? Read the verse.

**Student:** ﴿for a debt for a specified term﴾.

**Shaykh:** Good. ﴿Then write it﴾. The important point is whether it falls under the verse or not.

**Student:** It does not fall under the verse.

**Shaykh:** It does not fall under the verse. Therefore such a transaction is not to be written down; writing it is not obligatory, because it is not for a term.

What do you say about the salam (advance-payment sale)? Does it fall under this verse?

**Student:** Yes, it falls under the verse.

**Shaykh:** Yes. Do you agree?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes. What is the form of the salam?

**Student:** The form of the salam?

**Shaykh:** Yes, indeed.

**Student:** That money is paid to a craftsman, and he is asked to make something.

**Shaykh:** To the owner of a date-palm orchard, not the craftsman, because the craft (sun'ah) is subject to disagreement.

**Student:** To the owner of a date-palm orchard after a year of such-and-such.

**Shaykh:** That is: he buys from the owner of the palm-trees, for example, dates after a year, and gives him the dirhams now. Does it fall under the verse or not?

**Student:** Yes, it falls under the verse.

**Shaykh:** It falls under this verse? Do you agree?

**Students:** Yes.

**Shaykh:** Yes, it falls under this verse, because it is a debt for a specified term. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed the salam is included in this noble verse"[[Narrated by Ibn Jarir in Jami' al-Bayan (5/70) from a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]].

His saying: ﴿And let a scribe write it between you with justice.﴾ What is the lam in His saying ﴿And let write﴾?

**Student:** It is the lam of command.

**Shaykh:** It is the lam of command. Can it not be the lam of causation (ta'lil)?

**Student:** No, it cannot.

**Shaykh:** Why? We want a verbal barrier that prevents it from being the lam of causation.

**Student:** Because its verb is in the jussive mood (majzum).

**Shaykh:** Well done, correct. Also, it has a sukun after the waw; if it were the lam of causation, it would not have a sukun.

His saying: ﴿And let a scribe write it between you with justice.﴾ Some scholars derived from this that the scribe should be among the two contracting parties, meaning in the middle of them in seating.

**Student:** It could be a spatial "between" (makaniyyah).

**Shaykh:** Spatial, correct. It could also be intended as a figurative "between" (ma'nawiyyah), because in reality the seller and the buyer have a connection between them.

His saying: ﴿with justice﴾: the prepositional phrase depends on what?

**Student:** It depends on ﴿write﴾.

**Shaykh:** It depends on ﴿write﴾? Do you agree with this?

**Student:** No.

**Student:** Yes, shaykh, it depends on ﴿write﴾.

**Shaykh:** So it depends on "write." Do you agree?

**Student:** Yes, I agree with him.

**Shaykh:** You agree. Is there not the possibility that it depends on an omitted element, as a qualifier of "scribe": a scribe who is, or is described as, just?

**Student:** The original rule, shaykh (...), the original is non-existence (...).

**Shaykh:** No, it is valid: "a scribe with justice," meaning a scribe who possesses justice. Does it include that he himself is just, and also that he writes between them with justice, meaning that the writing is not biased toward one of them over the other?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him, so let him write.﴾ In His saying ﴿and let not a scribe refuse﴾, why was it indefinite, although it was previously mentioned?

**Student:** To include any scribe.

**Shaykh:** To include any scribe whatsoever. Here there is a difficulty regarding the verb, since it is in the fatha form although it is preceded by the prohibitive lā, which imposes the jussive.

**Student:** It is jussive by omitting the alif, and the fatha is evidence of it.

**Shaykh:** Correct. The original is ya'ba, and its origin is ya'bā.

His saying: ﴿as Allah has taught him﴾. The kaf here?

**Student:** It is for comparison or for causation.

**Shaykh:** For comparison or for causation? What is its meaning in both cases?

**Student:** For comparison: let him write, as Allah, glorified and exalted, has taught him the form of writing.

**Shaykh:** Yes: let him write as He taught him the form of legislated writing, so that his writing conforms to the rules of the Sharia.

**Student:** As for the kaf being for causation: let him write because Allah, glorified and exalted, has taught him writing.

**Shaykh:** Yes, so let him thank Allah for this blessing, and let him write for the people and be kind to them.

If someone said: we want an example showing that the kaf comes for causation. Bring a proof that the kaf comes for causation.

**Student:** With an example from me, or...

**Shaykh:** No, from you we can say: that is not correct.

**Student:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remember Allah as He has taught you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:239].

**Shaykh:** ﴿So remember Allah as He has taught you﴾; and ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:198], meaning: because of His guidance.

Can you (plural) bring us evidence from the words of Ibn Malik that the kaf comes for causation?

**Student:** His saying:
Express likeness with the kaf, and with it causation is sometimes intended ∗∗∗ ...................

**Shaykh:**
Express likeness with the kaf, and with it causation is sometimes intended ∗∗∗ ...................
That is, it is sometimes meant. Perfect.

What is the benefit of His saying ﴿then let him write﴾ after His saying ﴿and let not a scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him﴾? Because it is known that the opposite of a prohibition is a command; that is, when you are forbidden from something, you are commanded to do its opposite?

**Student:** For emphasis.

**Shaykh:** What?

**Student:** For emphasis.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** For immediacy.

**Shaykh:** Yes. Its benefit is that writing should be immediate, because His saying ﴿and let not a scribe refuse to write﴾ may allow the scribe to delay, saying: come to me tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, after a month, after a year. If he writes after a year, it would be said of him that he did not refuse. But ﴿then let him write﴾ means: immediately.

Who undertakes the dictation in writing a debt?

**Student:** The one who owes the right.

**Shaykh:** The one who owes the right. Why? What is the wisdom?

**Student:** First, the verse.

**Shaykh:** Well done: first, the verse, perfect; because the command of Allah and His Messenger is wisdom.

**Student:** Second: this means that he may not be unjust, like the one who holds the right.

**Shaykh:** Because the statement of a person against himself is accepted, or not? And the statement of a claimant against another is not accepted. So if the one who holds the right were to dictate, would he be dictating a claim or not? And it is not accepted. But if the one who owes the right dictates, he dictates an acknowledgment, and a person's acknowledgment against himself is accepted. Is that correct?

So the noble verse says: ﴿and let him dictate﴾. And what is the meaning of ﴿yumlil﴾?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** From imlal (dictating), I mean: from mall (tiring)? That is, from mall?

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** From mall (tiring) in the hadith: "Indeed Allah does not tire until you tire"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (1970) and Muslim (782/215) from a hadith of 'A'ishah.]].

**Student:** This hadith (...), but the word is from imla', since it comes in two dialects: yumli and yumill.

**Shaykh:** So yumlil means yumli, a second eloquent dialect.

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿and let him not diminish anything from it﴾. What is the meaning of yabkhas in ﴿does not diminish from it﴾?

**Student:** It reduces.

**Shaykh:** It reduces.

**Shaykh:** From?

**Student:** From the debt.

**Shaykh:** From the debt. And the word ﴿shay'an﴾ (anything) is indefinite in the context of prohibition, so it includes the little and the much. Shall we stop here, I think? Or more?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿istashhidu﴾?

**Student:** Seek two witnesses.

**Shaykh:** Seek two witnesses. That is, istishhad is seeking testimony.

Can you give an example showing that istaf'ala means seeking?

**Student:** Taqatala.

**Shaykh:** No, brother, istaf'ala is not tafa'ala.

**Student:** Istaf'ala.

**Shaykh:** Yes indeed, it means seeking.

**Student:** Istashara.

**Shaykh:** No.

**Student:** Istaghfara, meaning he sought forgiveness.

**Shaykh:** Istaghfara means he sought forgiveness. Well done. The sin and the ta' may also come for intensification, not for seeking, like: istakbara.

**Student:** Istasqa.

**Shaykh:** What? Istasqa, he sought rain, yes. Istakbara means he became very proud, not that he sought pride.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿But if there are not two men, then a man and two women﴾.

Here you see in the noble verse ﴿if there are not two men﴾. It might be expected that the phrase would be: "if there are not two men," because ﴿if there are not two men﴾ means: if there are not found two men. One would expect: "if there are not two men," that is, if two men are not found. But the matter is not so. For this reason the expression was changed to His saying: ﴿if they (the two) are not two men﴾. Accordingly, the testimony of a woman is not conditioned on the absence of a man; rather the meaning is: if the two witnesses are not two men, then a man. This indicates choice, with preference for two men over a man and two women. Note the difference: if the wording of the verse had been, "if there are not two men, then a man and two women," the testimony of a man and two women would be conditioned on the absence of two men, meaning: if two men do not exist. But when He said ﴿if they are not two men﴾, that is: if the witnesses are not two men, then a man and two women. That is: if this is not available, then that. This indicates that it is not a condition that two men be absent; therefore the testimony of a man and two women is permissible, as will come, God willing, in the benefits.

﴿then a man and two women﴾: the fa' here is the connective of the apodosis, and "a man" is the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate is: so the witness is a man and two women. In His saying ﴿a man and two women﴾, "man" applies to an adult, and "woman" likewise applies to an adult woman.

But He said: ﴿from among those whom you accept as witnesses﴾. The prepositional phrase depends on an omitted qualifier: that is, a man and two women who are of those whom you accept from among the witnesses. The address in His saying ﴿whom you accept﴾ is directed to the community; that is, the man and the two women should be acceptable to people. For a person may be acceptable to one individual and not to people in general, or to another. Therefore these two witnesses, or these witnesses, the man and the two women, must be known among people as acceptable.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Men whom I accept testified to me, and the most pleasing of them to me was 'Umar: that the Prophet ﷺ forbade prayer after 'Asr until the sun sets"[[Agreed upon; narrated by al-Bukhari (581) and Muslim (826/286) from a hadith of 'Umar.]]. So the criterion is acceptance among people in general, not the acceptance of the one in whose favor testimony is given, because the one in whose favor testimony is given may accept someone who is not acceptable.

His saying: ﴿from among the witnesses﴾. Here "min" is explanatory (bayaniyyah). Explanatory of what? Explanatory of the relative pronoun "man" (whoever), because the relative pronoun is among the vague words. If you say: "I like whoever was clever," this is vague. If you say: "I like whoever was clever among the students," it becomes specified. So His saying ﴿from among the witnesses﴾: "min" is explanatory, and the vague item it clarifies is the word "man," the relative pronoun.

He said: ﴿lest one of them err, so that one of them may remind the other﴾.

First: there are readings for this. There are two readings: ﴿if one of them errs, then one of them reminds the other﴾, where "in" is conditional and the clause ﴿then one reminds﴾ is the apodosis of the condition. The second reading: ﴿lest one of them err, then one of them reminds the other﴾. The third reading: ﴿lest one of them err, then one of them reminds (causes to remember) the other﴾. So the readings are three.

We take the reading that is in the Mushaf: ﴿lest one of them err﴾. Here "an" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and ﴿tadilla﴾ is in the subjunctive after the verbal-source "an." Grammarians differed about this structure, which is frequent in the noble Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:176], that is: out of dislike that you go astray. Here He said: ﴿lest one of them err﴾. Some grammarians said it is an object of purpose, with the estimate: out of dislike that one should err, or fearing that one should err. Others said it is on the omission of the negative "la" and the lam of causation, so the estimate is: so that one of them does not err, and then one of them reminds the other. On either view, the meaning of the noble verse is that Allah obligated that the witness be two women instead of a man, so that if one of them errs, the other reminds her. Who is the one who reminds? The one who remembers. And the other, the one who errs and forgets, is the one reminded. This is because women have less memory than men and less intelligence and perceptiveness. Therefore the testimony of two women equals the testimony of one man. It is established in the Two Sahihs that the Prophet ﷺ addressed the women and said: "I have not seen anyone deficient in intellect and religion who takes away the mind of a resolute man more than one of you." They said: "What is the deficiency of our intellect?" He said: "Is not the testimony of a woman equal to half the testimony of a man?"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (304) from a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Muslim (79/132) from a hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]] This indicates the deficiency of her intellect.

His saying: ﴿so that one of them may remind the other﴾ is from tadhkir (reminding), which is alerting a forgetful person to what he has forgotten. And a strange point in tafsir, which is truly among the strange things of tafsir, is that some said: "tudhakkira" means: makes her like a male (dhakar). Especially on the reading ﴿tudhkir﴾, meaning: makes her like a male, and ﴿tudhkir one of them the other﴾ means: the two women become like a male. This is strange, because it does not agree with His saying ﴿lest one of them err﴾. For what stands opposite to error, in the sense of forgetting, is reminding, that is, alerting a person to his forgetfulness. That is what stands opposite to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 4 of 6):

Here He said: ﴿that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾. In it there is eloquence in the use of an explicit noun where a pronoun would be expected. How so? Because He did not say "then the other will remind her," but said: ﴿then one of them will remind the other﴾. This is because forgetting can vary: one of them forgets one part and the other forgets another part. So this one reminds that one of what she forgot, and that one reminds this one of what she forgot. Therefore He said: ﴿one of them will remind the other﴾, so that the meaning is not restricted to one woman being the forgetful one and the other being the reminder. We say: forgetting may come from both women, and reminding likewise from both of them. For this reason He said: ﴿then one of them will remind the other﴾.

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And the witnesses must not refuse when they are called﴾. There He said: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse﴾, and here He said: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾. "Witnesses" (shuhada') is the subject (fa'il) of "refuse" (ya'ab). In the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿let not refuse﴾ we say what we said in the i'rab of ﴿let not refuse﴾ regarding the scribe.

As for His words: ﴿when they are called﴾, the word ﴿مَا﴾ (ma) here is superfluous (za'ida), and there is a well-known verse about it in which it is said:

*O seeker, take this benefit:*
*What follows "idhā" is superfluous.*

Continue the verse.

Student:
*O seeker, take this benefit:*
*What follows "idhā" is superfluous.*

Shaykh: Correct. The meaning of "what follows idhā is superfluous" is that we want to mention, together with "an" (that), the meanings of "mā," for "mā" has ten meanings, also mentioned in a verse.

Student:
*The meanings of "mā" are ten, if you wish to count them,*
*So memorise this verse, free from poetic defect:*
*You will understand the condition of the conjunction; marvel at its denial*
*With "kāff" (restrictive), and negation; "zīda" (superfluous), and the magnifying of a verbal noun.*

Shaykh: Correct. Shall I repeat it?

Student:
*The meanings of "mā" are ten, if you wish to count them,*
*So memorise this verse, free from poetic defect:*
*You will understand the condition of the conjunction; marvel at its denial*
*With "kāff" (restrictive), and negation; "zīda" (superfluous), and the magnifying of a verbal noun.*

Shaykh: How many have we counted? Ten: "satafham" (you will understand), "sharṭ" (condition), "al-waṣl" (the conjunction), "fa-'jab" (marvel): it is the exclamatory (ta'ajjubiyya); "li-nukrihā": it is a indefinite noun, sometimes descriptive or described; "bi-kaff": restrictive (kāffa); "wa-nafy": negating (nāfiya); "zīd": superfluous (zā'ida); "ta'ẓīm": magnifying (ta'ẓīmiyya), as in His saying: ﴿The Inevitable Reality. What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [Al-Haqqah 1-2]; "maṣdar": verbal (maṣdariyya). These are the ten meanings of "mā."

This is one of the superfluous kinds. But we must know that there is nothing superfluous in the Qur'an in the sense that it has no meaning. Rather it is superfluous in i'rab but not in meaning; it adds to the meaning and to the grammar. If it were removed, the sentence would be sound without it. If it were said: "idhā da'aw" (when they are called), is that correct?

Now His words: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾. Does it mean: when they are called for performing the testimony, or when they are called for bearing it? It includes both. As for its being for performing (al-adā'), there is no difficulty, because the one who has borne testimony is a witness, so it is said: "O witness, come and testify." But the difficulty is how one who has not yet borne testimony can be described as a witness, since until now he was not a witness. If we say that it includes both bearing and performing, then there is a difficulty regarding bearing, since until now he was not a witness. The answer is that this is in view of what will be.

Also, ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾ is clear: that is, the witnesses must not refuse when they are asked to give testimony. So if you call a man for something other than testimony, while he is fit to testify, he may refuse. This is the point of why He did not say, "Let not the man or men refuse when they are called for testimony," but said "the witnesses," meaning those who have been asked to be witnesses should not refuse to testify.

As for His words: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾, who calls them? Usually it is the one who has the right. This is the usual case, but it may also be the one who owes the right, so that the right is not lost. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is not the right of a Muslim man who has something to bequeath that he should spend two nights without his will being written and kept with him" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (2738) and Muslim (1627/1) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar]. It may be that the one who owes the right is the one who calls the witnesses to testify to the right he owes, so that his obligation is discharged.

﴿And do not be weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, up to its term﴾. Allahu akbar! ﴿Do not be weary﴾ means: do not become bored. ﴿Writing it﴾: the pronoun refers to the debt implied by His words ﴿up to its term﴾. ﴿Whether small or large, up to its term﴾: so every deferred debt must be written. Every deferred debt, we say to its creditor: do not be weary of writing it, do not be bored. Even if it were supposed that a man deals with twenty people in a single day on deferred debts, he must write them; he must write and not grow weary. Let him not say: "By God, this is too much, I write twenty documents in one day or one morning." We say: your Lord says: ﴿Do not be weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, up to its term﴾.

How much does the small amount equal? The least that is called a debt, for example one riyal, half a riyal, or less. "Large"? Yes, this too is according to custom. In a past time fifty riyals were considered large; now it is small. Can five hundred riyals perhaps be large? Or small? Medium?

In any case, Allah says: ﴿small or large﴾. Does that mean "or medium"? Is it not so?

His words: ﴿up to its term﴾ mean: one writes up to the term. One does not merely say "a deferred debt," but writes it up to the term and specifies it by what has preceded: a defined, known term agreed upon by both parties.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾. Look at the reason given for these rulings: the writing of deferred debt and the prohibition of weariness. He gave the reasons: ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ — this is one; ﴿and more upright for testimony﴾ — two; ﴿and more likely to prevent doubt﴾ — three. Until this moment I have not found a ruling explained by three explicitly stated reasons. Search if you wish. It is true that a ruling may be explained by one or two reasons, but three reasons together, I have not seen this until now. I cannot deny it, because denial is difficult, but I have not seen it. This shows Allah's care for financial dealings, contrary to those who claim that the Qur'an did not cover financial dealings, and claim that the Qur'an's legislation is only for worship and personal status (al-aḥwāl al-shakhṣiyya), such as marriage and inheritance and the like, while transactions are left to people — and Allah forbid. The ruling on one who holds this belief will come, God willing, and he is refuted by the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims.

He says: ﴿aqsaṭu ʿinda Allāh﴾. ﴿Aqsaṭu﴾ means "more just," derived from ʾiqsāṭ, not from qisṭ, because qisṭ means injustice, while ʾiqsāṭ means justice. So if you were asked: "Are you qāsiṭ (unjust) or muqsiṭ (just)?"

Students: Muqsiṭ.

Shaykh: Muqsiṭ, yes, muqsiṭ... "In what did you wrong, and in what did you oppress? Are you khāṭi' (sinner) or mukhṭi' (mistaken)?"

Students: Mukhṭi'.

Shaykh: Mukhṭi', not khāṭi'.

So we say: ﴿aqsaṭu ʿinda Allāh﴾ is derived from ʾiqsāṭ, meaning: more just and more upright in the sight of Allah the Exalted. Why? Because this is from His law, and all His law is justice, and whatever follows the law more closely is more just.

Second: ﴿and more upright for testimony﴾. Which testimony? The testimony of the witnesses, whether the two witnesses are two men or one man and two women. If it is written, that is more upright for testimony, because a witness who does not write down his testimony may forget and add or subtract.

﴿And more likely to prevent doubt﴾: that is, so that you do not have doubts. For if a thing is not written and witnessed, it will be forgotten and doubt will arise. Doubt disturbs the soul, both for the creditor and for the debtor. The creditor is disturbed because he fears he may forget some part of the right that is his, so he may demand more than the debtor owes. The debtor too fears he may forget, and so he may deny what he owed.

Student: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾ means it has become obligatory for them? It became...

Shaykh: That is, for bearing testimony.

Student: Yes. We do not say that it has become obligatory...

Shaykh: No, but if the speech were: "Let no one refuse to testify when called," then if one is called, there is no harm. But He said: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾, and until now they have not become witnesses. When I called them, were they witnesses or not witnesses?

Student: But it became obligatory for them.

Shaykh: Yes, it became obligatory for them. But on whom did it become obligatory?

Student: On the one I mentioned.

Shaykh: He did not say "let no one refuse." He says: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾. Until now they have not become witnesses. But God willing, we will come to the benefit of this in the lessons: that if a person asks for testimony whose testimony is not accepted, such as if someone came and said: "Testify for your son" — this is not accepted, and what is the benefit of this?

Student: The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write or count..."?

Shaykh: Did you hear his question? You heard the question? He says: how does God command writing when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "We are an unlettered nation; we neither write nor calculate"?

Student: We say: the address in the verse is to the one who writes. As for one who does not write, then...

Shaykh: Indeed, I am amazed how a simple, clear answer from the Qur'an escaped your minds.

Student: The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him﴾...

Shaykh: The one to whom the command was addressed was who?

Student: The one who knows how to write. As for the one who does not know it, there is no blame on him.

Shaykh: The difficulty is still entirely there. Let us take the short answer.

Student: Shaykh, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [Al-'Alaq 1]. This is a command to the Prophet, peace be upon him.

Shaykh: Yes, but he said: "I am not a reader" [Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3) and Muslim (160/252) from the hadith of 'A'ishah].

Student: But he was commanded.

Shaykh: No, now Jibril commanded him, and Jibril perhaps does not know. In any case, the answer to this is: yes, we were an unlettered nation, not reading and not writing, before the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, came. But after he was sent, we became a nation that reads and writes, and the description of unlettered-ness was removed from us: ﴿Allah certainly conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom﴾ [Aal 'Imran 164]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 48]. Before. Look at "before." When the Qur'an was revealed and the nation learned, the description of unlettered-ness was removed from them. Yes.

Student: Shaykh, what is the difference between qāsiṭ and muqsiṭ?

For the one who errs (mukhṭi'): ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make mistakes﴾ [Al-Baqarah 286]. For the sinner (khāti'): ﴿Then let him call his assembly. We will call the guards of Hell﴾ [Al-'Alaq 17-18]. What? In Surah Iqra': ﴿a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [Al-'Alaq 16].

Shaykh: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners﴾ [Yusuf 29].

Student: (...)

Shaykh: It will come, God willing; this is in the benefits. This verse has many benefits (...).

"And if there are not two men..." Yes. Why did He not say: "If there are not two men"?

Student: Because it does not stipulate that there be no two men at all; if there is one man and two women, there is no harm.

Shaykh: If the wording of the verse were: "If there are not two men..."

The words ﴿that if one of them errs﴾: do they have readings (qira'at)? ﴿that if one of them errs, then one of them will remind the other﴾?

Student: "Tadilla" and "tudallil."

Shaykh: No, ﴿tadilla﴾ has a reading, and ﴿tudhakkira﴾ has a reading.

Student: As for "tudhakkira," it has the readings: ﴿tudhakkira﴾, tudhkira, and tudhkira, three. As for "tadilla," the well-known reading is ﴿tadilla﴾, and tadlil.

Student: "Anna" and "in."

Shaykh: "Anna" and "in": ﴿an tadilla﴾ and ﴿in tadilla﴾. What is the difference between the two readings?

Student: "Anna" with a fatḥa is the verbal (maṣdariyya) particle; (...) it is for causation.

Shaykh: No.

Student: It is conditional (shartiyya).

Shaykh: It is conditional: ﴿an tadilla﴾ is verbal, and ﴿in tadilla﴾ is conditional. Does the pronunciation of "tadilla" change?

Student: It does not change.

Shaykh: Why, even though the conditional "in" jazms and the verbal "an" nasbs?

Student: If it were verbal, it would be interpreted.

Shaykh: No, let us leave interpretation aside; this is not about i'rab. But in pronunciation, does "tadilla" differ depending on whether "in" is conditional or verbal?

Student: ﴿in tadilla﴾ (...) if conditional, the lām of tadilla is jazm.

Student: One, Shaykh.

Student: If it is conditional, the lām is sukūn: "in tadilla."

Shaykh: So the pronunciation does not differ?

Student: No, it does not differ.

Shaykh: Yes.

Student: It is built on fatḥa in place of a noun: you say ﴿an tadilla﴾ or ﴿in tadilla﴾ (...).

Shaykh: So it does not differ in pronunciation? Rather the i'rab differs. If it is verbal, "tadilla" is in the accusative with the visible fatḥa; with ﴿in tadilla﴾ it is in the jussive, and it is moved with fatḥa because of the meeting of two sukūns. Yes.

Why did He say ﴿then one of them will remind the other﴾ and not "then will remind her"?

Student: Perhaps one of the two women forgets, and perhaps both women forget.

Student: Perhaps this one forgets one part and that one forgets another part.

* The Shaykh: That means the forgetting would be on both women, correct? That is: if one of them errs, the other reminds her. The meaning is that the forgetting occurred from one of them. So when He says ﴿that if one of them errs, the other of them will remind her﴾, the meaning becomes that forgetting may occur from both women together, and that is indeed so; one of them may forget some parts and the other some parts.
The words ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are summoned﴾ — what is "ma" here? ﴿when they are summoned﴾ — and what is this "ma"?
* A student: "Ma" is extra (ziyadah).
* The Shaykh: "Ma" is extra? What is your proof that it is extra?

* The Shaykh: But what is the proof based on a known rule of the grammarians?

* The Shaykh: This...

* A student: Perhaps this one forgets one sentence and that one forgets another.
* The Shaykh: That means the forgetting would be on both women together; that is: if one of them errs, the other reminds her, the meaning being that the forgetting occurred from one; so when He says: "if one of them errs, one of them reminds the other," the meaning becomes that forgetting may occur from both women together, and that is indeed so, for one may forget some parts and the other some parts.
The words ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are summoned﴾ — what is "ma" here?
* The student: What?
* The Shaykh: ﴿when they are summoned﴾ — what is this "ma"?
* A student: "Ma" is extra.
* The Shaykh: "Ma" is extra?
* A student: No, it is not extra.
* The Shaykh: What is your proof that it is extra?
* A student: It has no meaning in this context.
* The Shaykh: But what is the proof based on a known grammatical rule?
* A student: Because the meaning is "when they are summoned."
* The Shaykh: That meaning is correct, but we want a proof based on a grammatical rule.
* The student: Ibn Malik says:
"O seeker..."
* The Shaykh: Give us the rule first, then cite the verse as evidence.
* The student: The rule is that it came after "idha" (when)?
* The Shaykh: Because it came after "idha," what?
"And O seeker, take this benefit: what comes after 'idha' is an extra (particle)."
You take it, brother. These extra particles in the Noble Qur'an: are they extra in wording and meaning, or in wording only?
* A student: In wording and meaning.
* The Shaykh: In wording and meaning.
* A student: That is, the extra particle in structure yields an extra in meaning and an extra in i'rab.
* The Shaykh: So an extra in meaning differs from an extra in wording. An extra in wording means in i'rab; but an extra in meaning means it adds to the meaning, does it not?
So we say: it is extra, extra, extra, in this way?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Extra in terms of i'rab; extra in terms of meaning, that is, it adds to the meaning; but in i'rab it adds nothing, because if it were removed, the sentence would still stand.

* The Shaykh: Do we want as-sa'amah? In the sense of boredom?

He says: ﴿small or large, to its term﴾. Why did He begin with the small? And what type of transition is this according to the rhetoricians (al-bayaniyyun)?
* A student: He began with the small, meaning: because it is perhaps little that one cares for, so He alerted to it.
* The Shaykh: Well said. He began with the small because it is likely to be neglected. Well said. But according to the rhetoricians, this is called a transition from the lower to the higher.
A parallel to this is beginning with something out of fear of it being neglected, as in His saying: ﴿after a bequest he has bequeathed or a debt﴾ [An-Nisa' 11]. Which is mentioned first? The debt. Yet the bequest was mentioned first, lest it be treated lightly.
We mentioned that this ruling — i.e., writing — Allah explained with three reasons; tell us, brother, what are they?
* The student: Three reasons: ﴿more just in the sight of Allah﴾; ﴿more upright for testimony﴾; ﴿and nearer to preventing doubt﴾.
* The Shaykh: Well said. What does explaining this ruling by these three reasons convey?
* The student: Demonstrating the exalted nature of the Shari'ah and the assurance of the one held accountable.
* The Shaykh: And the importance of this act.
* The student: The rulings of the reasons, this.
* The Shaykh: Good. I say: this is meant to show the care given to this ruling; therefore Allah explained it with three reasons. I told you that I do not know anything about these three reasons, and you cited several examples explained by three reasons; so the earlier negation is not an absolute rule, because something may indeed be explained by three reasons.
* * *
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿except that it be an immediate trade which you conduct among yourselves﴾.
