First: in this sentence ﴿except that it be a trade﴾ there are two readings: ﴿except that it be an immediate trade﴾ with the accusative tijaratan; and the second reading with the nominative: ﴿except that it be an immediate trade which you conduct among yourselves﴾ (tijaratun hadiratun).
On the first reading, ﴿except that it be an immediate trade﴾: where is the subject of kana? The subject of kana is a hidden pronoun. The estimate: except that the transaction be an immediate trade, and so on.
And ﴿which you conduct among yourselves﴾ is a second adjective of ﴿trade﴾, and the first adjective is ﴿immediate﴾.
As for the nominative reading, ﴿except that there be an immediate trade which you conduct﴾: ﴿trade﴾ is the subject of ﴿be﴾, ﴿immediate﴾ is an adjective, and ﴿which you conduct﴾ is the clause that is the predicate of kana.
Allah says: ﴿except that it be an immediate trade﴾, or ﴿except that it be an immediate trade which you conduct among yourselves, then there is no sin upon you that you not write it.﴾
﴿Trade﴾: trade is every transaction intended for profit, so it is trade, clear?
It includes buying and selling, and also rental contracts; for this reason Allah called faith and jihad in His cause a trade: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [As-Saff 10].
As for ﴿immediate﴾: it is the opposite of ﴿when you contract a debt﴾; immediate means not deferred. A transaction is either immediate or deferred; the ruling on the deferred has already been explained, and that it must be written. What is its ruling?
* The students: Its writing.
* The Shaykh: Writing, its writing.
And ﴿which you conduct among yourselves﴾ means that you exchange it among yourselves, such that this one takes his goods and the other takes the price, and so on; so the "conducting" here means exchange, i.e., some of you give to others.
He says: ﴿then there is no sin upon you﴾: this fa' is either coordinating or resultative; meaning: in this case there is no sin upon you if you do not write it, i.e., no wrongdoing in not writing it. We said "in not writing it" because the verb governed by "an" followed by a negation is converted into a verbal noun preceded by "lack of" (ʿadam). What is the meaning of "bi-ʿadam"? I.e., with the word ʿadam.
Now we say: "an" governs the verb, and so He said ﴿alla taktubuha﴾, dropping the nun, followed by the negative "la". When we convert the verb into a noun, we must bring in the word ʿadam to take the place of the negation, because negation is ʿadam; and from where did we estimate "fi"? We estimated it according to the context, so the estimate is: then there is no sin upon you in the lack of writing it.
And ﴿alla taktubuha﴾: the pronoun refers to the trade; so this trade customary among people, there is no sin on a person if he does not write it, because error and forgetting in it are remote, since it is immediate, conducted and handled by people, unlike the deferred.
Then He said: ﴿and call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾. Call witnesses over what? Over the sale.
And ﴿when you conclude a sale﴾ means when a sale takes place between you. Originally, "tabaya'a" (to trade mutually) and "bay'" (sale) properly refer to the giver, while "shira'" (purchase) refers to the taker; but the usage may be generalized, so one says: "the two men traded," instead of "the two men bought."
The seller is called a seller (ba'i'), and the buyer is called a buyer (mubtaʿ); the seller is called shari, and the other is called? 
* The students: A buyer (mushtari).
* The Shaykh: A buyer. Allah says: ﴿And among people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [Al-Baqarah 207], i.e., sells himself.
﴿Call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾: i.e., when some of you sell to others, call witnesses. This command has been said to be recommended (nadb), and said to be guidance (irshad). The difference: if it is taken as recommendation, it belongs to acts of worship; if taken as guidance, it belongs to worldly benefits. That is what has been said; but in my view, when a person complies with what Allah has directed, he is rewarded for this intention, even if we say the command is not recommendation, because a man, so long as his act is compliance with Allah's command, undoubtedly will be rewarded for it.
And ﴿let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾: the word ﴿yudarra﴾ is derived from harm, but it may be read as active or passive, and the i'rab of ﴿katib﴾ and ﴿shahid﴾ differs according to the form of the verb: if it is active, ﴿katib﴾ is the subject; if passive, ﴿katib﴾ is the deputy subject (na'ib al-fa'il).
What makes this clear? It becomes clear when the idgham is unfolded: taking it as active, when we unfold the idgham we say: "wa la yudarrir katibun wa la shahid"; taking it as passive, when unfolded: "wa la yudarrar katibun wa la shahid", like yusharik and yusharak: yusharik is active, yusharak is passive. Also, mukhtar: is it active or passive?
* The students: It fits.
* The Shaykh: It fits both, so: if active, it is mukhtarir; if passive, it is mukhtarar.
Similar is what we have already had: ﴿la tudarra walidatun﴾ [Al-Baqarah 233], i.e., la tudarrir, with the mother as subject; or la tudarrar, with her as deputy subject.
This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an: a word that is suitable for two aspects, neither of which negates the other.
So here, ﴿let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾: if we make it active, the meaning of the verse is that Allah, glorified and exalted, forbade that a scribe harm or that a witness harm, i.e., do an act that harms the one for whom or against whom it is written; this is when it is active, is it not?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Likewise we say of the witness: the witness should not do an act that is harmful to the one he testifies for or against. But if we make it a deputy subject, we say: it is not permissible for the one for whom or against whom it is written to harm the scribe, and it is not permissible for the one for whom or against whom testimony is given to harm the witness.
If you ask: how is harming the scribe? The harm to the scribe is either sensory harm or moral harm. Sensory harm: that we make the student weary when he is asked to write; we make him weary or reluctant to submit to the obligation of writing; they say: "Come, write," and he sits, scratching with the pen, wiping the nib, cleaning it, asking for it, and so on.
The student may become bored and leave; this is sensory harm.
Moral harm: that one neglects something by which the ruling is invalidated, such as omitting some conditions, or bringing descriptions that cause the contract to be invalid, or the like; this is undoubtedly harm, but it is moral harm, because the one for whom it is written may not know these matters, and the scribe is the one who knows; so.
As for testimony: the witness is asked to testify and bear witness; he says: "Fine, go ahead, I'm coming (...)" and he goes, stays ten minutes, twenty minutes, thirty minutes, then comes to him: "Come on, testify." He says: "Wait, this is going ahead and I'm behind you," and he proceeds while the other is behind him, as he says; and he stays half an hour, an hour minus a quarter; then he returns to him and says: "Go ahead, I'll come behind you," and whenever he comes, he goes ahead, "I'll come behind you." The call to noon prayer comes; he says: "We want to pray first." He prays noon; he says: "Lunch has come." Lunch ends; he says: "Sleep has come." In any case, is this sensory harm or moral harm?
* The students: Sensory.
* The Shaykh: Sensory. It may be that from the witness there is moral harm? It may be: he adds to his testimony or subtracts. As for our harming the scribe, it is that we come to him at a time not suitable for coming, such as coming to him at one o'clock at night, an hour after midnight, knocking on his door and asking: "What do you have?" He says: "Walk, write for me between me and so-and-so." Is there harm?
* The students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed; or after lunch or dinner has been served we come and say; or in intense heat, intense cold, rain, or otherwise; this is the harm.
If someone says: how can there be harm? Can he not say: "I will not write"? We say: yes, he can say "I will not write," and he is excused; but he may suffer hardship from it; he himself thinks: "I have erred, I have not complied with Allah's command in His saying: ﴿and let not a scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him; so let him write﴾; I have erred, perhaps I have opposed Allah's saying: ﴿and let not the witnesses refuse when they are summoned﴾," and then some hardship and anxiety enter his soul; this is a type of harm, when we take the scribe and witness as deputy subjects.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if you do it, indeed it is defiance (fusuq) in you﴾. ﴿And if you do it﴾: i.e., the scribe or witness is harmed in both readings.
﴿Indeed it is defiance in you﴾: "it" means the act; how do we know it is the act? From His saying ﴿if you do﴾, because the verb includes the meaning that is the verbal noun and the tense. So ﴿and if you do, indeed it [i.e., your act]﴾.
If someone says: the word "act" has not preceded? We say: it is understood from the word ﴿if you do﴾. A parallel is His saying: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 8]. That is what?
* The students: Justice.
* The Shaykh: That is, the justice understood from the word ﴿be just﴾. So here: ﴿indeed it﴾ means the act understood from the word ﴿do﴾.
And ﴿defiance in you﴾ means departure from you from the straight path and from obedience to Allah. The root meaning of fisq in language is departure; from it the saying: "fasaqat al-thamarah" when the fruit came out of its skin. So fisq is departure from obedience; and this was defiance on the part of the doer, because it is a departure from the obedience of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 6 of 6):

Then he said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾. "Fear Allah" (ittaqu Allah). It has been mentioned several times that taqwa (God-consciousness) means taking a shield against the punishment of Allah, and that this is done by:

* Student: By taking a shield against the punishment of Allah through keeping away from Allah's disobediences.
* Shaykh: Yes, but by what does one take this shield? By what does taking the shield come about?
* Student: Righteous deeds.
* Shaykh: And what else?
* Student: By carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.
* Shaykh: Yes. Taking a shield against the punishment of Allah is by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, so that is the definition.

Some scholars said: Taqwa is that you act in obedience to Allah upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and that you abandon what Allah has forbidden upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah.

Did someone say a third meaning?

* Student: Shaykh, it is that He does not see you where He has forbidden you, and does not find you absent where He has commanded you.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student:
Leave sins, small and great, that is taqwa.
Walk as one who treads on thorny ground, watchful of every step.
Do not belittle any small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, this is a poem (manzumah):
Leave sins, small and great, that is taqwa.
Walk as one who treads on thorny ground, watchful of every step.
Do not belittle any small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles.

But the first meaning is the most comprehensive: taking a shield against the punishment of Allah by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

Then he said: ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾. The waw here is for resumption (isti'naf), and it is not correct for it to be conjoined (ma'tufah) to taqwa; rather it begins a new sentence. The meaning is: fear Allah by doing all that has preceded, then He clarifies that all that has preceded of guidance and direction is teaching from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾. We said this out of caution regarding people who claimed knowledge from the divine presence (al-'ilm al-ladunni) on account of their taqwa, as they alleged. These are the Sufis, who said that their leaders take knowledge directly from Allah without revelation, because they fear Allah, and Allah says: ﴿Fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾. This is without doubt an error, a blunder, and disbelief in the message: whoever claims to receive from Allah instructions other than the instructions of the Messenger ﷺ is a disbeliever in the message of the Messenger ﷺ. But they say: "Taqwa is with us, and Allah says: ﴿Fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾." This is also incorrect in meaning. That is, it is an error in doctrine (al-'aqidah), and an error in grammar and Arabic, because a declarative sentence (khabar) is not conjoined to an imperative sentence (insha'): ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is an imperative, and ﴿Allah teaches you﴾ is a declarative. And it is an error on a third level of meaning: there is no taqwa except with knowledge, for knowledge precedes taqwa, since if you have no knowledge, what would you guard against?

Unless someone claims that His saying ﴿Allah teaches you﴾ means "in addition to what you already have." If he claims this, the two previous points refute it.

Here He said ﴿Allah teaches you﴾ explicitly, and said ﴿And fear Allah﴾ explicitly, and said ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ explicitly.

If it were in other than the Qur'an and it said: "Fear Allah and He teaches you, and He is Knowing of everything," would the sentence be sound?

* Students: It would be sound.
* Shaykh: But Allah, exalted is He, used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun in these clauses, to make clear that each clause is independent of what precedes it, and so it is. Each clause is independent. The address in ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is to us, and taqwa is our action. The teaching in His saying ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾ is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and is for us: from Allah to us, and taqwa from us to Allah. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ belongs to Allah alone.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾, concerning our actions and His actions.

His saying ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ includes everything in the heavens and the earth, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah﴾ [Surah Ali 'Imran 3:5]. The knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, is vast and encompassing of the small and the great, the minute and the grand, and encompassing of the future, the present and the past, and encompassing what relates to His action and the action of His creatures, and encompassing the obligatory (wajib), the permissible (ja'iz) and the impossible (mustahil). Is that so?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: Because of the generality of His saying ﴿of everything﴾. So, from its relation to the obligatory, give an example of its relation to the obligatory.
* Student: That Allah exists.
* Shaykh: How? What is the meaning of "that Allah exists"?
* Student: Allah exists, meaning Allah knows that He exists.
* Shaykh: No, we want an example in which Allah mentions knowledge and which relates to the obligatory.
* Student: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Surah al-An'am 6:124].
* Shaykh: This could be correct, but in a distant sense.
* Student: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him, and so do the angels and those of knowledge, upholding justice﴾ [Surah Ali 'Imran 3:18].
* Shaykh: This one.
* Student: It is obligatory.
* Shaykh: This is obligatory: the oneness of Allah in divinity is obligatory. And with the impossible? The relation of Allah's knowledge to the impossible?
* Student: The saying of Allah: ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor, and we are rich. We will record what they have said"﴾ [Surah Ali 'Imran 3:181]. And recording includes it.
* Shaykh: Another one? Because He said "what they have said," and this has occurred.
* Student: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya' 21:22].
* Shaykh: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾. Here He informs of an impossible thing consequent upon an impossible thing. Good. And the possible?
* Student: The existence of man, the existence of creatures.
* Shaykh: ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature﴾ ﴿in toil﴾ [Surah al-Balad 90:4].

* Student: The other way to refute one who argues, saying ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾ and ﴿And fear Allah﴾: we say that ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is jussive (majzum) and ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾ is marfu'?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Why?
* Shaykh: Because this one, "ittaqu" (fear), is a built (mabni) imperative verb.
* Student: Shaykh, if He says ﴿lā tuḍārra﴾, built on the passive, what would be the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿wa-lā shahīd﴾?
* Shaykh: It is conjoined to "kātib" (scribe). It is conjoined to "kātib" in any case.
* Student: The deputy (nā'ib), if it is built as a direct object (maf'ul bihi)?
* Shaykh: The deputy. When the verb is built for the object, the deputy of the subject is the object in meaning. The deputy of the subject is the object in meaning. So if you say, for example, "ḍuriba Zayd" (Zayd was struck), then Zayd is the deputy of the subject and is the object in meaning, because he is the one struck.
* Student: Shaykh, we said that it is not correct to conjoin a declarative to an imperative. Is the converse also correct, that it is not correct to conjoin an imperative to a declarative?
* Shaykh: The whole issue is disputed, but the well-known view of the Basrans is that it is not correct.
* Student: The discussion of the well-known view is that neither of the two possibilities is correct.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: The preferred view on ﴿wa-ashhidū﴾ (and call to witness) is that it is an imperative here.
* Shaykh: Yes, that will come in the benefits (fawa'id).
* Student: Shaykh, the saying of Allah, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿then there is no blame upon you﴾. Does it imply the obligation of writing? Does it mean (...) that if it is not in trade, this would have (...).
* Shaykh: What is this? This is a benefit.
* Student: ﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah 2:282]. Is the calling of witnesses at the time of writing or at the time of the debt?
* Shaykh: No, at the time of the debt. And if that is not possible, then at the time of writing, because the writing may be delayed.
* Student: Shaykh, ﴿fusūq bikum﴾: what is the meaning of "bikum" here?
* Shaykh: The "bi" here means "fi" (in), that is, "wickedness in you."
* Student: The saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾ [Surah al-Anfal 8:29]. Is there a connection between it and ﴿And fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾?
* Shaykh: No, according to the correct view there is none. But the verse you pointed to indicates that when a person fears Allah, the Exalted, He grants him a criterion between truth and falsehood, and between truthfulness and lying.
* Student: Shaykh, Shaykh al-Islam mentioned that the rank of taqwa may reach, in justice, that in some matters for which the Sharia has brought no evidence, one gives a verdict by his own knowledge?
* Shaykh: No, no. Do you mean that Allah opens it up for him?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: But that is from the evidences of the Sharia.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: Yes, it is known to be from the evidences of the Sharia. That is, Allah, exalted is He, may cast into a person's mind an understanding that is not granted to others, and a person may be granted success, so that he says a statement and the truth bears witness to it. For example, suppose that I, in my reflection, say: "This is forbidden," and I have no text on it, then I come across a text that forbids it. This may happen, as happened to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, when he agreed with Allah in several matters.
* Student: Allah says: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Surah Fatir 35:28]. This verse, and ﴿And fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾: does it mean that taqwa is the result of knowledge?
* Shaykh: Yes, and the result of knowledge is awe and fear.
* Student: That means (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but we said that these clauses are each independent of the other, and for this reason He made it explicit: He said ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾, then He said ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾.
* Student: Shaykh, what supports this meaning is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "What is good (al-hasan) is what the people deem good," meaning the Companions, that because of their taqwa toward Allah, the good that... (...)
* Shaykh: He said: "What the Muslims see as good is good" [narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat (3602) from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him].
* Student: "What the Muslims see as good is good": does this not indicate that Allah, exalted is He, grants success to the servant (...)?
* Shaykh: This indicates consensus (ijma'), that if the Muslims agree that something is good, it becomes good. What the Muslims see as good is good.
* Student: Taqwa of Allah, exalted is He, enters into this matter, so one avoids what Allah dislikes.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, and there is no doubt that when Allah grants a person knowledge and taqwa, He guides him aright: ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾ [Surah al-Talaq 65:2].

[This is an abridgement of the author's words due to their great length.]

I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand﴾. There are two readings of it. ﴿Rihan﴾ has two readings?

* Student: There is the reading ﴿fa-ruhunun﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Fa-ruhunun﴾. And ﴿rihanun﴾, is there a difference between them in terms of form?
* Student: ﴿Fa-ruhunun mqbudatun﴾, meaning they have the same sense.
* Shaykh: In terms of form, I mean. Is each of them singular, or do they not differ?
* Student: ﴿Fa-ruhunun﴾ is not singular, it is more than one.
* Shaykh: Plural. And ﴿rihanun﴾?
* Student: Singular.
* Shaykh: Singular. And ruhn?
* Student: Rihan (...).
* Shaykh: So then it is plural. That is, in form they are the same, both are plurals of rahn.

His saying: ﴿Then if one of you trusts another, let him who is trusted fulfil his trust﴾. What is the meaning of ﴿u'tumina﴾?

* Student: "The one who is trusted" means the one who gives (...) ﴿The one who was trusted with his trust﴾, the one who gives (...), meaning if you are in a settled place and one of you trusts another (...).
* Shaykh: And what is the meaning of ﴿u'tumina﴾, just that, we want nothing more than this?
* Student: That is, he was trustworthy.
* Shaykh: That is, he was made trustworthy. Correct.

His saying: ﴿So indeed his heart is sinful﴾. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis)?

* Student: ﴿Athimun qalbuhu﴾ is a verb and subject.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: We say: the fa' follows what precedes it, or it is a conjunction.
* Shaykh: No, it does not follow what precedes it, nor is it a conjunction. It follows what precedes it, but is it understood?
* Student: It occurs as the answer to the conditional.
* Shaykh: Yes, it occurs as the answer to the conditional.
* Student: Inna is a particle of emphasis that puts the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. The ha' is a attached pronoun, built on damma, in the place of accusative as the noun of inna. ﴿Athimun﴾ is a nominative predicate, and ﴿qalbuhu﴾ is a subject, and it is an annexed noun, and the pronoun is the annexed-to noun.
* Shaykh: Correct. Is there another possibility? There is another possibility.
* Student: A subject and predicate.
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: A subject.
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: ﴿Qalbuhu﴾ is the predicate, ﴿athimun qalbuhu﴾, ﴿athimun﴾ is the subject, ﴿qalbuhu﴾ is its predicate, and the sentence is its predicate.
* Shaykh: ﴿So indeed his heart is sinful﴾.
* Student: Innahu: inna and its noun.
* Shaykh: And ﴿athimun﴾ is its predicate.
* Student: No, ﴿athimun qalbuhu﴾ is the sentence as predicate, it is not a subject and predicate.
* Shaykh: Where is the subject in it?
* Student: ﴿Athimun﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Athimun﴾ is the subject?
* Student: No, ﴿qalbuhu﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Qalbuhu﴾ is the subject, and ﴿athimun﴾?
* Student: Its predicate.
* Shaykh: Its predicate. That is: indeed his heart is sinful.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand﴾, to the end.

From this noble verse it is derived that a journey has rulings that differ from those of residence, and so it is. It has rulings that differ from those of residence in acts of worship, in transactions and in other matters. In acts of worship it differs in prayer, fasting and purification. In transactions, the bequest on a journey has already passed us: if a person cannot find a Muslim to call as a witness, he calls a disbeliever as witness, either a People of the Book or disbelievers in general according to the stronger opinion. In other matters: the traveller has a supplication that is not rejected. That is, travel is among the causes for answering supplication. The main point is that travel has rulings that differ from the rulings of what? Residence. Among them is this verse. It is derived from it that if a person is travelling and gives credit to someone and does not find a scribe, then the way to establish his right is that he takes a pledge, or that he takes a pledge and takes possession of it, that he takes a pledge and takes possession of it. An example of that: you lend someone money while you and he are on a journey and there is no scribe with you both, so you say: give me a pledge that I may hold as security for my right, and he gives you one. Is it clear?

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the care of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for preserving the wealth of His servants. That is, He, glorified and exalted, mentioned even this case: if a person gives credit to another and does not find a scribe, he takes a pledge, to preserve his wealth and out of fear of dispute and discord in the future, so that the one who owes the right denies it and a quarrel and conflict arises.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of pledging, from His saying: ﴿then a pledge﴾. But that is conditioned, according to what is in the verse, on travel, whether it is short or long, and on not finding a scribe. Is this condition binding?

The answer: the Sunnah has shown that it is not binding, neither the absence of a scribe nor travel. For "the Prophet (ﷺ) bought thirty measures of barley for his family and pledged his armour with a Jew until he died"[[Reported by Ibn Majah (2437) and Ahmad (13169) from the hadith of Anas.]], and this shows the permissibility of pledging while resident, even when a scribe is present.

If someone says: if the matter is so, what is the answer regarding the verse?

The answer regarding the verse: Allah, the Exalted, mentioned a case in which a scribe is unavailable, so we have that by which the right is established or secured, which is the pledge. He mentioned this case not as a condition for the ruling. That is, it is as if He said: when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And if you are on a journey and have no scribe, then what? 
* The students: Then take pledges.
* Shaykh: Then take pledges, ﴿then a pledge taken in hand﴾.

We have said: the permissibility of pledging. I think we have already defined the pledge, it was defined in connection with this verse.

Some scholars used this verse to show that possession is a condition for the validity of the pledge. Others used this verse to show that possession is a condition for the binding nature of the pledge. Others did not consider this condition. So now we have three opinions: Is taking possession of the pledge a condition for its validity? Is taking possession of the pledge a condition for its being binding? Is taking possession of the pledge a matter of securing the right, or a matter of adding to the security, and not a condition either for validity or for binding?

These are three opinions. Some scholars say that taking possession of the pledge is a condition for validity, because Allah said: ﴿a pledge﴾, and described it, He did not leave it unqualified, He said: ﴿taken in hand﴾. On this basis, a pledge without possession is not valid. This was said by some scholars, and it is a narration from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him.

The second opinion: the pledge is a condition for being binding. So the pledge is valid, but if the pledgee takes possession of it, it becomes binding, and if he does not take possession of it, it is not binding. If his agent takes possession of it, or someone agreed upon by the pledgor and the pledgee takes possession of it, then the pledge is also binding. If it remains with the pledgor, then the pledge is not binding. This is the well-known position of the school.

The third opinion: possession is not a condition either for binding or for validity. The pledge is valid and binding without possession, if it is specified. This is the correct opinion and it is what is acted upon.

We must examine: which of these opinions does the verse indicate? Those who said that possession is a condition for validity say: if you pledge something and do not hand it over, the pledge is not valid, and the pledged item may be disposed of as you wish, and if you wish to restore the pledge, a new contract is required. They say: Allah said ﴿a pledge taken in hand﴾, so He described it as taken in hand, and the description is a restriction on what is described. If it is not taken in hand, it is not valid.

Those who said it is a condition for being binding said: because the pledge is completed with all its conditions and pillars without possession. So if he says: I have pledged to you this car, and he has seen it and identified it, then the contract is complete because the conditions are fulfilled and the impediments are absent. As for possession, it is a condition for being binding. On this basis, if it remains with the pledgor, and then the pledgee comes in the morning, or at night, or something similar, and takes it, does he need to renew the contract? He does not need to, because the contract is valid, but as long as it is with the pledgor it is not binding. This means that the pledgor may dispose of this pledge as he wishes, by sale, gift, endowment, or otherwise.

These people argued for the validity of the contract by saying that it is a contract complete in its conditions, made by its proper parties, so it must be valid. As for the binding nature of the pledge, it is not binding except by possession, because of His saying: ﴿a pledge taken in hand﴾.

The third opinion: they said that it is not a condition for validity, that is, possession. They said: possession is not a condition for validity nor a condition for being binding, and the pledge is valid and binding without possession, even if it is with the pledgor, if the pledgee has permitted it to remain with the pledgor. We say: this opinion is the correct one. If this opinion is the correct one, then we need an answer regarding what? Regarding the noble verse.

The answer regarding the noble verse: Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned the pledge in a case in which securing the right by it cannot be completed except by taking possession of it, because the matter is presupposed: the two parties to the transaction or the two creditors and debtors are on a journey and have no scribe. How will the creditor secure his debt except by a pledge that is taken in hand? If it is not taken, the one who owes the debt may deny it, may even deny the existence of the pledge, and a dispute arises. So he cannot secure his debt except by taking possession. So the verse is an expression about a specific situation in which possession is part of completing the security, not a condition.

Second: they say: have you not dropped the restriction of travel, even though it is explicit in conditionality? ﴿And if you are on a journey﴾. They will say: yes. And some of them will say: no, because some scholars said: pledging is not permitted except on a journey, and they took the condition and restriction. But whoever did not take it will say: yes, the restriction of being on a journey is dropped, "because the Prophet (ﷺ) pledged while he was resident"[[Reported by Ibn Majah (2437) from the hadith of Anas.]], and this is authentic. But we argue against him with it and say: this is evidence that the conditions mentioned in the verse are not conditions for validity. If they were conditions for validity, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have pledged his armour while resident, he would not have pledged it while resident.

So the stronger opinion is that this is only a matter of completing the security, and not a condition for validity or for being binding. This is what is acted upon. People still pledge the property of debtors while it remains in their hands. Perhaps you hear that a person pays in advance for dates or wheat to the owner of an orchard and pledges the orchard as well, and the owner of the orchard has not handed it over, and it remains with him, he works on it. Now the real estate development fund: houses are pledged, and they are with whom?
* The students: With their owners.
* Shaykh: With their owners, and they continue to regard this as a binding, complete pledge, and it is so.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the word of the pledgee is accepted if they differ about the amount of the debt. This matter is one on which the scholars differ. Some say the word of the pledgor is accepted, some say the word of the pledgee is accepted, and some make a distinction.

The case: I gave you a loan of ten thousand riyals and you pledged the car, your car, and I took it, I held it in custody, I took possession of it, because I feared that if it remained in your hand you would destroy it, so I kept it with me. Then at the time of repayment, the pledgor, the owner of the car, claimed that the loan was only five thousand riyals, and I said it was ten. Whose word is accepted?
* The students: (...)
* Shaykh: There is disagreement, or there is a distinction. Some scholars said: the word of the pledgor is accepted, and this is the school's position. The word of the pledgor is accepted. Of the pledgor?
* Student: The owner of the car.
* Shaykh: The debtor, the owner of the car. Why? They said: because he is the one who pays, and the rule is that the one who pays is the one whose word is accepted. This rule is derived from the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies"[[Reported by al-Tirmidhi (1341) and al-Daraqutni (3191) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]]. Because the one who pays is the one being sued. So in the example we mentioned, did we agree on five thousand or not?
* Student: Ten.
* Shaykh: My brother, on five. We agreed on five. I say ten, and the five is included in the ten, and you acknowledge it. So did we agree on five thousand or not? The additional five beyond the five, I claim it and you, as the one who pays, deny it. So the word of the pledgor is accepted, because he is the one who pays, based on this hadith: "The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies." Is that correct or not?

The second opinion: the word of the pledgee is accepted. They argued that Allah, the Exalted, made the pledge a substitute for writing: ﴿and if you do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand﴾. And if the creditor and the debtor differ over the amount of the debt, we return to what? To writing. Just as the written document is a proof for the creditor, so the pledge is a proof for him. So it has the status of a document for him. This is the apparent meaning of the words of our shaykh Abd al-Rahman in the tafsir.

But the third opinion, a distinction in the matter, which is the correct one. The distinction says: the word of the pledgee is accepted, as long as he does not claim more than the value of the pledge. Do you understand?
* The students: Yes.
* Shaykh: The word of the pledgee is accepted as long as he does not claim more than the value of the pledge. For example, this car is worth ten. And I say: O pledgee, the debt is ten, my word is accepted. You say five and I say ten, my word is accepted, because I have an indication, which is that usually a person does not pledge something unless the amount of his debt is equal to it or more, or less. This is for the pledgor: he gives only the amount of his debt or less, he does not give more than his debt, this is the usual case. So if he claims that the amount is such and such, and it does not exceed the price of what? The pledge, then the word of the pledgee is accepted. And if he claims more, then for the excess the word of the pledgor is accepted. This is the choice of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, and the position of Imam Malik, and it is closer to the two previous opinions.

If we apply this case to the opinion that the word of the pledgor is accepted: this man pledged a car for ten thousand riyals, and when we came to litigation the owner of the car, the pledgor, said: your debt which you demand is ten riyals, whose word is accepted?
* The students: The pledgee.
* Shaykh: No, according to the school the word of the pledgor is accepted. Has it become customary for a person to pledge a car worth ten thousand riyals for ten riyals?
* The students: No.
* Shaykh: Not at all, this is something reality refutes. For this reason we say: the statement of Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, is supported by the indication, and reality also supports it. If we accepted the word of the pledgor absolutely, it would lead us to say what no one would believe.

And if the pledgee also claimed what reality does not confirm, what is more than that is not accepted. If, for example, he gave him the car, whose value was ten thousand riyals, and at the time of collection he said: the debt is a million riyals, is it accepted?
* The students: It is not accepted.
* Shaykh: Why? Because it is not customary for a person to give a million in money and pledge a car for ten thousand riyals. That is far-fetched. Indeed, the apparent meaning of the words of * Shaykh: If he claimed that the debt is fifteen thousand riyals while the pledge is ten, it is not accepted, because he claimed something whose amount is more than the value of the pledge, so it is not accepted.

Can it not be said regarding this matter that the distinction takes another form, and that if he claims something close to it, his word is accepted even if it exceeds the value of the pledge? That is, for example, if he said it was twelve thousand and the pledge is worth ten, is that possible?
* The students: It is possible.
* Shaykh: It is possible, because this sometimes happens, he says: I pledge the car for ten and my whole right is not lost. But in any case, the statement of Shaykh al-Islam is among the best opinions and the strongest, although the second opinion, that it returns to indications as a strong opinion, is also there. But I do not know whether anyone has held it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that when trust is placed by some of us in others, no pledge, no witnessing, and no writing is required. This is from His saying: ﴿Then if one of you trusts another, let him who is trusted fulfil his trust﴾. For this reason many scholars said: this verse abrogates what came before it, His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾, and His saying: ﴿Call witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾, and His saying here: ﴿if you are on a journey﴾ and ﴿then a pledge taken in hand﴾, and that when trust is placed, none of those things is required.

However, to say that it abrogates [previous rulings] in a general sense is questionable. If one were to say that it abrogates [them] only in matters that do not involve significant risk, that would have some basis. That is, in matters where the custom is to exchange without witnesses or writing, that would be a statement with no harm in it. But as for making it apply to matters that carry risk, such as real estate or large, important debts that require writing or witnesses, then saying that this verse is abrogating is something that troubles the mind. For this reason some scholars objected to the claim that it is abrogating and said: "How can it be abrogating within a single context, with the beginning of the verse followed by its end abrogating it?!" But this objection is itself open to objection. Consider fasting in two verses: the first of them gives a choice, and the second makes it obligatory. That is, there is no barrier to abrogation occurring between two adjacent verses, as in this verse.

But we say: when a matter is important and carries risk, writing may be obligatory, especially when a person is acting on behalf of someone else.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to discharge the trust on the part of the one who has been entrusted.

From this follows: the prohibition of betrayal, because of His words: ﴿let him who has been entrusted discharge his trust﴾. So when discharging a trust is obligatory, betrayal is forbidden. Is that clear?

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the item held in trust is lost in the hands of a trustworthy person, he bears no liability, so long as he has not transgressed or been negligent, because of His words: ﴿let him who has been entrusted discharge his trust﴾. Allah called it a trust, and the trustee's hand is not an aggressive hand, so he is not liable unless transgression or negligence has occurred.

Among transgression: if a person is given something to keep in trust and he deals with it, as some people do, by selling, buying or otherwise, and says: "When its owner comes, I am ready to give it to him." We say: this is forbidden and not permitted. It is not lawful for you to do this. If you wish to do it, seek the permission of its owner, and if he grants you permission, it becomes a loan in your hands.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one who has been entrusted must not be deceived by people's trust in him, because of His words: ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾. When a person is trusted, he may be deceived by people's confidence in him and not take matters seriously. He says: "People trust me," and he does not care. So Allah the Exalted commanded him to fear Allah, saying: ﴿and let him fear Allah﴾.

Taqwa (God-consciousness) has been explained to us many times: taking a shield against Allah's punishment by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

He said: ﴿and let him fear Allah﴾, and He followed it with: ﴿his Lord﴾. In this there is a benefit: in these situations a person looks to the station of lordship just as he looks to the station of divinity. By looking to the station of divinity, he does this in worship of Allah and seeking nearness to Him. By looking to the station of lordship, he guards against disobedience, because the Lord is the One who possesses creation, dominion and management. So a person must combine the station of divinity with the station of lordship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of what these two names indicate, namely "Allah" and "Lord." This is the tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) of worship and the tawhid of lordship. Both include the tawhid of the Names and Attributes, because the one worshipped must be worthy of worship, and the Lord must be worthy of lordship, and this is not realised except through the perfection of attributes. For this reason we say: the tawhid of lordship entails the tawhid of worship, and both of them include the tawhid of the Names and Attributes, since none is worshipped except one who is characterised by the attributes of perfection. For this reason Abraham said to his father: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor avails you anything?﴾ [Maryam 42].

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And do not conceal testimony; and whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful.﴾

From the noble verse it is derived: the prohibition of concealing testimony, that is, hiding it. Is the meaning testimony given for others, or for others and for oneself?

* Students: It includes both.

* Shaykh: It includes both meanings, because a person bears witness against himself, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿O you who believe, be persistent in standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [an-Nisa 135]. His testimony against himself is his acknowledgment and admission of the truth that is upon him. So the verse, as it appears, covers both: a person's testimony for another against another, and for another against himself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: concealing testimony is one of the major sins (kaba'ir), because of the specific punishment attached to it, which is His words: ﴿indeed his heart is sinful﴾.

* Among its benefits: the gravity of concealing testimony, because He attributed the sin of it to the heart. When the heart is sinful, the limbs are sinful too, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599) from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.] And because of his words: "Taqwa is here" [Muslim (2546) from Abu Hurayrah], pointing to his chest. Taqwa is in the heart. It is not taqwa of the tongue, nor of actions, nor of states. Taqwa is in the heart. A person may be God-conscious in his deeds and his speech while not being God-conscious in his heart.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And do not conceal testimony; and whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah 283].

* From the noble verse it is derived: the prohibition of concealing testimony, that is, hiding it.

Is the meaning testimony for others, or for others and for oneself? It includes both meanings, because a person bears witness against himself, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿O you who believe, be persistent in standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [an-Nisa 135]. His testimony against himself is his acknowledgment and admission of the truth that is upon him. So the verse, as it appears, covers both: a person's testimony for another against another, and his testimony against himself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: concealing testimony is one of the major sins, because of the specific punishment attached to it, which is His words: ﴿indeed his heart is sinful﴾.

* Among its benefits: the gravity of concealing testimony, because He attributed the sin of it to the heart. When the heart is sinful, the limbs are sinful, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) words: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107) from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir], and because of his words: "Taqwa is here" [Muslim (2564/32)]. Taqwa is in the heart, not in the tongue, nor in actions, nor in states. Taqwa is in the heart. A person may be God-conscious in his deeds and in his speech while not being God-conscious in his heart, do you see or not?

You find him, in his outward conduct, dressed in the attire of the sincere Muslim: he lets his beard grow, has dignity and tranquillity. Likewise he says the words of a sincere Muslim: "I seek Allah's forgiveness, O Allah forgive me," and he remembers Allah, says "There is no god but Allah," and says "Allahu akbar." These are undoubtedly taqwa outwardly. But is this evidence that there is taqwa inwardly?

* Student: Usually.

* Shaykh: Usually, yes. And for us this is the ruling. That is, as far as we are concerned, if we see his taqwa outwardly, we are obliged to judge him to have taqwa inwardly. We have nothing but the outward. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said to Usamah ibn Zayd, when he had killed a polytheist who had said "There is no god but Allah" while the sword's flash was over his head: "Did you kill him after he said: There is no god but Allah?" He said: "Yes." And he kept saying it until Usamah wished that he had not embraced Islam before that day [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4269) and Muslim (96/158) from Usamah ibn Zayd]. So we have nothing but the outward. But if indications and signs show that he is a hypocrite inwardly, his outward taqwa is of no benefit to him. It does not benefit him and is not considered. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We testify that you are the Messenger of Allah"﴾ [al-Munafiqun 1]. Look: they emphasised the sentence with three emphases: the verb "testify," then "inna" (indeed), then the lam. ﴿We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah﴾. This is what we judge by the outward: that they are fully believers. For this reason they emphasised it. But look at this emphasis, which is countered by: ﴿Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾. Testimony against testimony, emphasis against emphasis. ﴿Allah testifies that the hypocrites are indeed liars.﴾ Reflect on His saying ﴿Allah knows that you are His Messenger﴾ before He says ﴿Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars﴾, so that nothing improper comes to mind, and so it is known that the Messenger is true by Allah's knowledge, and that the testimony of these people is a false testimony. In sum, Allah said: ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, and I have told you that this includes the tawhid of worship, lordship, and the Names and Attributes.

* Student: A man lent another a thousand riyals, then the borrower denied it. Then later the borrower came and entrusted this same person with a thousand. Is his recompense to betray him?

* Shaykh: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you" [Abu Dawud (3535) from Abu Hurayrah].

* Student: What is the right (haqq) here?

* Shaykh: It is not a right. It is a hidden right. I say: this is a hidden right, and it is not permitted. This is unlike the person who does not spend on you while he is one whose maintenance is obligatory on you. In that case, if you are able to take something from his wealth, then take it.

* Student: Shaykh, is this not changing the evil (munkar)?

* Shaykh: No, brother. Changing the evil is that you come and advise him, saying: "Fear Allah, return the trust to me." But to betray him, no.

* Student: Shaykh, is it known that the sinners (fussaq) argue with this hadith?

* Shaykh: Yes, well said. He does not say, "I argue with this hadith," while striking the tips of his fingers on his chest, until he nearly collapses from the intensity of his verification: "Taqwa is here" [already cited]. We say to him: You are right. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Taqwa is here." But the one who said "Taqwa is here" is the one who said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt" [already cited]. So the corruption of your outward is evidence of the corruption of your inward, whether you like it or not.

* Student: Shaykh, what about those who say that a pledge (rahn) must be taken into possession (maqbudah)? Do they stipulate that the pledge must be in possession?

* Shaykh: For its validity, or for its binding effect?

* Student: For its validity. We replied to them (...) the journey. That is, Allah the Exalted stipulated the journey in the verse, and they reply to us that we have taken it as an exception, since the Prophet (ﷺ) did this while at home. How do we answer them?

* Shaykh: We replied to them by saying: this is evidence that these conditions are not a requirement for the validity of the ruling. They apply to a particular occurrence. Otherwise, if they were a condition, the beginning of the verse would be more strictly conditional than its end.

* Student: But if the condition came as an exception, namely the Prophet's (ﷺ) action?

* Shaykh: It indicates that it is not binding.

* Student: Why does it indicate only that this condition is absent, and not the rest (...)?

* Shaykh: It does not indicate that. Because, what excluded this?

* Student: The Sunnah.

* Shaykh: Good. And what excluded this restriction from the Qur'an by the Sunnah?

* Student: The Prophet's (ﷺ) action.

* Shaykh: Good. Then it means these conditions are only for added assurance. Just as the Sunnah came with His words: ﴿And bring to witness two witnesses from among your men; and if there are not two men, then a man and two women﴾ [al-Baqarah 282], the Sunnah came with the testimony of one man together with an oath.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not conceal testimony; and whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾ We have already discussed this, and we explained that Allah attributed the sin to the heart, because when the heart is sound, the body is sound.

The Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿and whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾. Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾

His words ﴿of what you do﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun conveys generality, so it includes everything we do of the deeds of the hearts and the deeds of the limbs. The deeds of the limbs are actions with the body parts and speech with the tongue. The deeds of the heart are the movements of the heart in love, hatred, fear, hope and the like. Likewise the sayings of the heart, which are affirmation, acknowledgment and certainty regarding a thing. So these are four categories: the sayings and deeds of the heart, and the sayings and deeds of the limbs. The sayings of the limbs are specifically by the tongue, which speaks and pronounces. The sayings of the heart, as we said, are acknowledgment and admission, that is, belief in a thing, affirmation and certainty about it. This is the saying of the heart. The deeds of the limbs are actions such as standing, sitting, bowing, prostrating and the like. The deeds of the heart are the movements of the heart in fear, hope, reliance, love, dislike and the like. All deeds revolve around these four categories: the deeds and sayings of the heart, and the deeds and sayings of the limbs. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah alluded to this in al-Wasitiyyah (the creed), where he said: "Among the principles of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah is that religion and faith are speech and action: the speech of the heart and tongue, and the action of the heart, tongue and limbs."

So His words ﴿of what you do﴾ include all of this. Whatever we do, Allah the Exalted knows it. Moreover, He knows what we have not done yet of what we will do, which we do not know, for Allah knows what will be in the manner in which it will be.

As for His words ﴿of what you do, is Knowing﴾: if someone asks: what is the purpose of placing the object first here?

If he says: for the sake of the rhyme endings (fawasil), we reply: the nun also appears often in the rhyme endings, as in ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾ [Yusuf 19]. If he says: for restriction (hasr), we reply: that is not valid, because Allah knows everything. His knowledge is not restricted to what we do alone, so there is no basis for restriction.

So what is the purpose? The purpose is intensifying the warning and alerting, as if He were saying: even if He knew nothing, which is far above Him, He would still know our deeds. So for the sake of the intensity of warning and admonition the expression is composed in a form of restriction, though it is certainly not meant as restriction, because if we took it as restriction it would imply that Allah knows only what we do, and the matter is not so.

As for His words ﴿of what you do, is Knowing﴾: if someone asks, do we derive from this that al-'Alim (the Knowing) is one of Allah's names? We say: we may say that, and we may not. We may say that when a name is qualified by an object of relation, it becomes an attribute. So "Knowing of such-and-such" is not like His words: ﴿And He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 137], because that is qualified by an object, "Knowing of it," so it is an attribute and not a name. But if He said "the Knowing, the Wise," that would undoubtedly be a name.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the warning that Allah the Exalted is Knowing of what we do. The aspect of warning is the fronting of the object, since, as we have indicated, it does not convey restriction.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a refutation of the extreme Qadariyyah (those who deny divine foreknowledge), who say that Allah does not know the actions of servants until they occur. His words ﴿is Knowing of what you do﴾ include what we have already done and what we will do.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning should be used in a context of warning, and encouragement in a context of encouragement. Since He said ﴿and whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾, is the appropriate tone here warning or encouragement?

* Student: Warning.

* Shaykh: The appropriate tone is warning, and this conforms to eloquence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 284:

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And whether you show what is within your souls or conceal it, Allah will hold you accountable for it.﴾

His statement: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a declarative sentence in which the predicate has been placed first. His statement: ﴿And whether you show what is within your souls or conceal it﴾ is a conditional sentence, whose response is: ﴿Allah will hold you accountable for it.﴾

His statement: ﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ means: He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, in matters other than disbelief, as will come later, God willing.

There are two readings of it: one reading is ﴿fa-yaghfir﴾ and ﴿wa-yu'adhdhib﴾ (in the jussive), and another reading is in the nominative (raf'). Their explanation: the meaning of the verse according to the jussive reading is very clear, because it is conjoined to ﴿yuhasibkum﴾, which is the response of the conditional, and what is conjoined to a jussive is jussive. The meaning of the nominative reading is that it is in the manner of a resumption (isti'naf), so the fa' is an resumptive fa', indicating that the sentence after it is cut off from what precedes it.

His statement: ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ means that He is capable of all things, so nothing can overpower Him.

We begin with the verse. His statement: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ means that everything in the heavens or on the earth belongs to Allah in ownership and in governance, and no one other than Him has any ownership in it. The evidence that His ownership is exclusive to Allah is the placing of the predicate first, because we have a rule: when something that ought to be postponed is placed first, that indicates restriction (hasr). Whenever something that ought to be postponed is placed first, the sentence conveys restriction.

His statement: ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ includes what is in the heavens of rational and non-rational beings, so it includes the children of Adam and the jinn, and it includes the other animals, and it includes trees, seas, rivers, and other things. Likewise, what is in the heavens includes the angels and the spirits of the children of Adam that are in the heavens, such as the spirits of the believers in Paradise. Indeed, it also includes what lies between the heaven and the earth of the spheres and stars and other things, since they are included within the heavens, being in their direction.

He said: ﴿And whether you show what is within your souls or conceal it, Allah will hold you accountable for it.﴾ ﴿Show﴾ means reveal, and ﴿what is within your souls﴾ means what is in your hearts. ﴿Or conceal it﴾ means you keep it secret so that no one knows of it. As for what a person shows of what is in his soul, it is like wanting to say a statement and saying it, or wanting to do an action and doing it while people witness it. Concealment is when a person wants to say a statement and keeps it secret within himself so that no one knows of it, or wants to do an action and does it while moving in ways that no one perceives, such as when he looks at something forbidden, and people do not know that he looked at something forbidden, because this is something only Allah knows. The point is that whether a person shows it or conceals it, ﴿Allah will hold you accountable for it.﴾ Accountability does not necessarily entail punishment, and for this reason He said: ﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.﴾ He holds the servant accountable for what is in his soul, whether he shows it or conceals it; He holds him accountable, saying: "You did such and such," meaning: "You said such and such in your soul, you harbored such and such in your soul." If he displays it, Allah holds him accountable for it.

Allah's accountability of a person for what he has shown is clear, because it is his deed and his action, and his statement if it was speech. But Allah's accountability for what is in his soul that he has not shown, we say: this divides into two categories. One: that he hides something and resolves upon it, but does not incline to it, does not feel at rest with it, and does not affirm it. This is like the whisperings that enter the human heart, such as doubts and other things, or the desire for evil, but which have no effect on the heart. Is he held accountable for it or not? We say: the apparent meaning of the noble verse is that he is held accountable for it if he conceals something, even if he does not incline to it and feel at rest with it; he is held accountable.

The third category: showing and concealing without inclining to it. The third category is that which he has not shown or made apparent, and has not inclined to, but which has come to his soul and which he harbored, yet did not incline to it, such as when his soul suggests committing an act of disobedience, a mere thought, but he does not incline to it, nor does he take the means that would lead him to it; or his soul suggests something related to the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and faith in Him, but he does not incline to this and does not feel at rest with it. No, my intention is that he inclined to it and felt at rest with it. In this case, there is no doubt that he is held accountable for this matter. For example: his soul suggested to him that Allah's istiwa' over the Throne is like a man's sitting on a couch, and he inclined to that and felt at rest with it, but he did not express it or make it apparent to people. The first category is that he made it apparent and began saying to people: "Allah's istiwa' over His Throne is like a man's istiwa' on a couch or a camel." The third category is that he spoke to himself about this but did not feel at rest with it, and his soul rejected it and did not accept it.

The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that all three categories are subject to accountability; this is the apparent meaning of the noble verse. For this reason, when this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Companions, and they said: "Then we are doomed." So Allah, Exalted, revealed the verse that follows: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It will have [the consequence of] what it has earned, and it will bear [the consequence of] what it has earned.﴾ A person is then not taken to account for what is in his soul except for what he has inclined to and felt at rest with. As for mere whispering of the soul without assurance and inclination, the Prophet ﷺ said: «Indeed, Allah has overlooked for my nation what their souls whisper, so long as they do not act upon it or speak of it»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6664) and Muslim (127 / 201) from Abu Hurayrah.]] Thus He lifted the hardship from the nation. Do we understand now? The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that a person is held accountable for three matters: what he showed, what he concealed and inclined to, and what he concealed without inclining to. But the last has been abrogated by the verse that follows it, and likewise by the hadiths indicating that a person is not held accountable for mere whispers of the soul.

He said: ﴿Allah will hold you accountable for it.﴾ Accountability (muhasabah) means that a person is scrutinized for what he did; it is said: "You did such and such on such and such a day, you left such and such on such and such a day," and he is scrutinized. This is the accountability of full scrutiny. As for the accountability in which there is no scrutiny but only the person being made aware of his deed, this is an easy accountability, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand, he will be judged with an easy judgment﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 7, 8].

He said: ﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.﴾ ﴿Yaghfir﴾: forgiveness (maghfirah) is derived from (al-maghfar), which is what a person puts on his head in battle to protect himself from arrows. This (al-maghfar) combines covering and protection. For this reason we say that Allah's forgiveness of a sin includes two things: one, covering, and the second, pardon and protection from the effect of the sin. As for covering, it means that Allah conceals this sinner's sin from the servants and does not make it known. As for pardon and overlooking, it means that Allah does not punish this sinner, does not punish him, because He has forgiven him. So forgiveness is covering the sin, and then overlooking it, pardoning it, and not punishing for it, and is not merely covering; for it is derived from (al-maghfar).

His statement: ﴿for whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾: ﴿whom He wills﴾ is a form of generality; meaning, whomever Allah wills to forgive, He forgives, and whomever He wills not to forgive, He does not forgive. But it has been mentioned to us repeatedly that every act of Allah's acts that is connected to His will follows from wisdom: if wisdom requires it, it occurs, and if wisdom does not require it, it does not occur, based on His statement, Exalted: ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30]. Accordingly, He forgives whomever He wills among those whose forgiveness His wisdom requires, and punishes whomever He wills among those whom His wisdom requires to punish.

His statement: ﴿punishes﴾: punishment (adhab) is suffering from a thing and being distressed by it, and it may be a punishment or it may not be a punishment. It may be a punishment by which a person is chastised, proportionate to his sin without addition, and it is subject to reduction; and it may not be a punishment but merely pain. From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: «Indeed, the dead person is punished for the wailing over him, or for the weeping of his family over him»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1287) and Muslim (927 / 16) from Umar ibn al-Khattab.]]. This punishment is not a punishment of retribution, because Allah says: ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am 164], but it is a punishment of suffering: suffering and distress. It is similar to his saying ﷺ: «Travel is a piece of punishment». And sometimes you say: "The smell of onion tortured me, the smell of smoke tortured me," although it is neither a punishment nor harmful, but it is hurtful.

As for what is meant by his statement here, ﴿punishes﴾, which of the two categories is it? It is the punishment that is a retribution, because it is for a sin: ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ means by retribution.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾: Allah is competent over everything that can possibly be. Everything possible is one over which Allah has power without exception; even over His own actions He is capable: He is capable of descending to the lowest heaven, of establishing Himself upon the Throne, of coming to judge between the servants, of laughing, of being pleased, of being angry, and of being content. Allah is capable of all of that without exception. As for matters unrelated to power, the impossibilities, that is not possible.

If someone said: Is Allah able to make Himself forget something of what He has known, when He knows everything? We say: That is impossible.

If someone said: Is Allah able to make Himself ill? We say: That is impossible.

If someone said: Is Allah able to make the heavens and the earth all within an egg while they remain as they are and the egg remains as it is? We say: That is impossible.

The point is that power relates to the possible; as for the impossible, it is impossible. The impossible is impossible. Whoever ties power to something impossible, this is a kind of mockery of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, just as if you said to a person: "Are you able to bring the moon down to the earth?" Is he able or not?

* The students: He is not able.

* The Shaykh: He is not able. I mock him; this would be mockery of the person. (...)

* * *
* A student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. All of them believe in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers, [saying], "We make no distinction between any of His messengers." And they say, "We hear and we obey. [We seek] Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the [final] destination." Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It will have [the consequence of] what it has earned, and it will bear [the consequence of] what it has earned. "Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we have forgotten or erred. Our Lord, and lay not upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear. And pardon us; and forgive us; and have mercy upon us. You are our protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people."﴾ [al-Baqarah 285, 286].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Before we begin today's lesson, let us take the benefits from what preceded in the remaining verse, which is His statement, Exalted: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾

In this noble verse there is a demonstration of the comprehensiveness of the ownership of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The basis of this is from His statement: ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, because (ma) is a relative pronoun, and a relative pronoun indicates generality.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 2, verse 285–286 (part 1 of 7):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. Each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers...﴾ to the end of the verse.

We explained His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers﴾, and we explained: ﴿Each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers﴾ to the end of the verse. Is that right or not?

He said: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾, meaning he believes in what was sent down to him of revelation in the Book of Allah and in what is revealed to him of the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ.

In His saying: ﴿what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾ there is a special lordship (rububiyyah), because it is attributed to the Messenger ﷺ. The lordship attributed to the messengers is the most specific type of lordship, followed by the lordship attributed to the believers, and then the most general, the lordship attributed to all people, such as: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah 2]. This special lordship undoubtedly entails a special nurturing that no other nurturing of the nurtured can match.

As for His saying: ﴿and the believers﴾, it is in the nominative, coordinated with His saying ﴿the Messenger﴾, meaning: and the believers likewise believe in what was sent down to the Prophet ﷺ from Allah. So they believe in the Messenger, they believe in the One who sent him, and they believe in what he was sent with: three things. The sender, who is Allah; the one sent, who is the Messenger ﷺ; and what he was sent with, which is the revelation: the Book and the Sunnah.

And as for His saying: ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ and ﴿and the believers﴾: if someone asks, "How does He say ﴿and the believers﴾ and describe them with belief, when they are believers?" We say: this is from the category of affirmation (tahqiq), meaning that the believers have realized (haqqaqu) faith, and their faith is not merely outward, as is the case with the hypocrite who displays faith while concealing disbelief.

﴿Each one⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾, meaning of the Messenger and the believers: ﴿Each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers﴾ to the end. ﴿Each one believes in Allah﴾: the word (āmana, believed) has come up for us many times, and what is meant by it is an acknowledgment that includes acceptance and submission, not merely belief in the existence of Allah. That is not faith in the full sense, which would entail accepting what He brought, accepting what He informed of and what He commanded, with submission and surrender.

And His saying: ﴿Each one believes in Allah﴾: belief in Allah includes four matters. The first: belief in His existence. The second: belief in His lordship. The third: belief in His divinity. The fourth: belief in His names and attributes. Faith must include these four things. Belief in the existence of Allah is to guard against those who deny the existence of Allah and say: this universe is nothing but things interacting, with one producing another, wombs expelling and earths swallowing, and there is nothing (we seek refuge in Allah). We must believe in the existence of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and we must believe in His lordship. When we say "we believe in His lordship," we mean His being singular in lordship, that He is the absolute Lord, and that the lordship of anything other than Him is restricted, not comprehensive, not general, and not complete, but deficient and restricted as well: deficient in its limits and deficient in its authority. As for the lordship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it is complete and vast; there is no one to repel His judgment, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.

The third: belief in His divinity, the true divinity, and there is no divinity for other than Him. Everything to which divinity is ascribed is false, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [al-Hajj 62].

The fourth: belief in His names and attributes: that He has names and attributes in which He is unique, and none resembles Him in them. So we affirm the names and attributes and negate partnership or likeness, for this is the reality of tawhid.

Thus, whoever does not believe in the existence of Allah is not a believer. Whoever believes in His existence but not His lordship, by saying that He has a partner or helper in creating the heavens and the earth, or that there is another god who alone created what was created, we say that this person has not believed in Allah. And whoever believes in the existence of Allah and His lordship, and that He alone possesses complete lordship, but denies His divinity, by saying as the disbelievers said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing﴾ [Sad 5], then he has not believed in Allah. And whoever believes in the existence of Allah, His lordship and His divinity, but does not believe in His names and attributes, has not believed in Allah either. His faith may be nonexistent or may be deficient, according to what has been established in his heart of faith and assent, or denial and rejection.

Thus, those who believe in some of the names and not others, we say: they have not realized belief in Allah. Those who believe in the names but not the attributes have not realized belief in Allah. Those who believe in some attributes and disbelieve in others have not realized belief in Allah. Then, if their denial of what they deny of that is rejection and repudiation, they are what?

* The students: Disbelievers.

* The Shaykh: Disbelievers (kufrah). If it is a ta'wil (interpretation), they are not disbelievers, but one looks at their interpretation: whether it has a basis, or whether it is an interpretation that amounts to denial, in which case they are judged according to what their condition requires.

If someone asks: how do we establish the proofs for the existence of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic? We say: we establish them in several ways: by the senses, by reason, by revelation, and by innate nature (fitrah). As for reason: we say, these existing beings, which change morning and evening through non-existence, existence, and changes of state, who changes them? Do we look to who? Does so-and-so change them, or so-and-so, or so-and-so?! Never. They cannot change them; rather they are themselves changed. So these beings necessarily require a Creator who brings into existence and changes, and we find none but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We find none but Allah. For this reason Allah pointed to it in His saying: ﴿Were they created from nothing, or are they the creators?﴾ [al-Tur 35]. We find the heavens and the earth: who created this earth? Were they workers who made it and put in it the sands, the mountains, the valleys, the rivers and the seas?

The answer: No. Even if the whole world gathered with all its workers, they could not do that. Therefore it must have a Creator. The heavens likewise, and greater: no one can create them except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason He said: ﴿Or did they create the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Tur 36]. The answer: No. ﴿Rather, they are not certain.﴾ This is a rational proof for the existence of Allah, and no one denies it.

If someone said to you: "This lamp was made by no one," what would you say? You would say: "Take this man quickly to the madhouse, because he is insane, isn't that so?"

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: And if he said: "This recorder was made by no one," we would say the same. It is related that a group of the Samaniyya, atheists among the Indians, came to Abu Hanifa in Baghdad and said to him: "How can we establish the existence of a Creator?" He lowered his head and was silent. They said: "Answer!" They thought he had been cut off and had become incapable. He said: "I am thinking about a ship that has anchored in the water of the Euphrates or the Tigris without having a sailor, and unloaded its cargo without workers, and departed without a captain. Look, is this possible or not?"

* The students: Not possible.
